42853452.title: Hemodynamic trajectory phenotypes may modify associations between corticosteroid timing and outcomes in septic shock.
42853452.journal: Journal of clinical monitoring and computing
42853452.abstract: Corticosteroid trials in septic shock show conflicting results, with patient heterogeneity and treatment timing as likely contributors. We evaluated whether associations between corticosteroid timing and clinical outcomes differed by hemodynamic trajectory phenotype defined by dynamic time warping clustering of Blood Pressure-Vasopressor Index (BPRI) trajectories across three ICU cohorts. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using MIMIC-IV as the derivation cohort and eICU-CRD and PINES as validation cohorts. Adult patients with septic shock receiving vasopressors were included. Hemodynamic phenotypes were identified from 168-h BPRI trajectories. Corticosteroid timing was classified as early (≤ 6 h) or late (> 6 h) after sepsis onset. In MIMIC-IV, inverse probability of treatment weighting with cause-specific Cox regression was used to estimate associations between timing and 28-day mortality, hospital length of stay, and ventilation duration within each phenotype. Validation cohorts were analyzed using multivariable Cox regression, and cohort-specific estimates were summarized using random-effects meta-analysis with I2. Two phenotypes were identified in MIMIC-IV: Deteriorated (N=2,082, 38%), with declining hemodynamics and higher mortality, and Improved (N=3,361, 62%), with stable or rising trajectories. Similar trajectory patterns were observed in eICU-CRD and PINES. In the Deteriorated phenotype, late corticosteroids were associated with lower 28-day mortality in MIMIC-IV (HR 0.88 [0.78-0.98]) and shorter ventilation duration (HR 0.65 [0.58-0.73]) compared with early administration. The mortality association was not consistently replicated in validation cohorts, whereas the ventilation association was observed in PINES Deteriorated patients. In the Improved phenotype, late steroids showed no consistent mortality or hospital length-of-stay association. Exploratory hemodynamic response analysis showed a more favorable BPRI slope for late versus early steroids in the Deteriorated phenotype. Hemodynamic trajectory phenotypes identified clinically meaningful variation in the relationship between corticosteroid timing and outcomes in septic shock. In the Deteriorated phenotype, delayed corticosteroid initiation was associated with lower 28-day mortality and shorter recovery, whereas the Improved phenotype showed no mortality advantage from delayed treatment. These findings support incorporating dynamic hemodynamic trajectories into future studies of corticosteroid timing in septic shock.

42840779.title: Point-of-care ultrasound in emergency department sepsis and septic shock: a pragmatic framework for source-oriented assessment and physiologic reassessment.
42840779.abstract: In emergency department (ED) sepsis and septic shock, early management is often dominated by two bedside uncertainties: identifying a clinically plausible infection source and determining whether additional fluid is likely to improve perfusion or worsen pulmonary or systemic congestion. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) may contribute to both questions when it is used as a trigger-based, time-boxed adjunct rather than as a comprehensive screening test or stand-alone diagnostic adjudicator. This article presents a pragmatic narrative review of multiorgan POCUS in adult ED sepsis and septic shock, based on a focused, non-systematic search of major databases and a synthesis of sepsis guidelines, landmark resuscitation trials, and clinically relevant reviews and representative studies addressing source-oriented assessment, shock phenotyping, fluid responsiveness, and congestion assessment. Particular attention was given to separating diagnostic capability and physiologic plausibility from demonstrated clinical utility and patient-centered outcome benefit. Priority was given to adult ED literature; intensive care unit (ICU), perioperative, and physiologic studies were used only when ED-specific evidence was limited and the underlying principles were clinically transferable. The proposed framework is organized around two linked arms. First, a source-oriented scan may support pneumonia or pleural complication as a working source and may identify biliary disease, obstructive urinary infection, urinary retention, or drainable soft-tissue infection when clinical features make these sources plausible. Its intended role is to trigger formal imaging, drainage planning, specialist consultation, or source-control pathways, not to prove the source at the bedside. Second, physiologic reassessment can use focused cardiac ultrasound (FoCUS), dynamic flow-based assessment such as passive leg raise with left ventricular outflow tract velocity-time integral (PLR-LVOT VTI), and serial lung ultrasound to provide context for fluid and vasopressor decisions after the initial resuscitation step. Venous Doppler and the venous excess ultrasound (VExUS) framework are discussed as optional advanced congestion assessments, not as routine ED requirements, because ED sepsis-specific evidence remains limited. Overall, current evidence supports POCUS mainly as an adjunct for bedside clarification, escalation support, and physiologic reassessment; direct evidence that POCUS-guided ED sepsis pathways improve patient-centered outcomes remains limited. POCUS should therefore be used as a decision-support tool, not a stand-alone adjudicator or a reason to delay antimicrobials, CT, formal imaging, or specialist involvement.

42953236.title: Incidence and risk factors of acute skin failure in patients with sepsis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42953236.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine the incidence and risk factors of acute skin failure (ASF) in patients with sepsis. Two reviewers independently searched PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Database, Embase, CNKI, Wanfang Database, and VIP Database from database inception to December 2025. Observational studies reporting ASF incidence and risk factors in sepsis patients were included. Random-effects meta-analysis was used to pool incidence and odds ratios (ORs); case-control studies were excluded from incidence pooling and analyzed only for associated factors. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots, Begg's and Egger's tests. Study quality was evaluated using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) and the AHRQ checklist. Eighteen observational studies comprising 3,295 adult participants were included. After exclusion of two case-control studies from incidence pooling, the pooled ASF incidence across the 16 cohort and cross-sectional studies (n = 2,697) was 45.2% (95% CI: 34.5-56.2%), with a 95% prediction interval of 12.2-83.0% and substantial heterogeneity (I 2 = 96.1%, p < 0.0001). Elevated arterial blood lactate [OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.15-1.25; p < 0.00001; I 2 = 50%], higher SOFA score [OR 1.23, 95% CI 1.16-1.31; p < 0.00001; I 2 = 20%], and higher APACHE II score [OR 1.16, 95% CI 1.10-1.21; p < 0.00001; I 2 = 34%] were significantly associated with increased ASF risk, whereas lower mean arterial pressure was associated with ASF [OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.93-0.96; p < 0.00001; I 2 = 47%]. Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the pooled estimates, and no significant publication bias was detected (Egger's p = 0.467; Begg's p = 0.239). ASF affects a substantial proportion of patients with sepsis. Lactate, SOFA score, APACHE II score and MAP are variables associated with ASF that may support early identification of patients at heightened risk; prospective studies are needed to validate predictive models.

42947065.title: Association of jugular venous oxygen saturation and mean arterial pressure variability with dynamic cerebral autoregulation and outcomes in sepsis-associated encephalopathy.
42947065.abstract: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) is a frequent and clinically important manifestation of sepsis-related acute brain dysfunction. Impaired cerebral autoregulation and altered cerebral oxygen supply-demand balance are considered relevant pathophysiological features, but the temporally aligned and statistically adjusted relationships among jugular venous oxygen saturation (SjvO2), mean arterial pressure (MAP) variability, and dynamic cerebral autoregulation (dCA) remain insufficiently defined. This retrospective study examined the associations between SjvO2, MAP variability, and dCA indices in neurocritical care patients with SAE and evaluated whether these monitoring variables were associated with impaired dCA and short-term outcomes. We retrospectively analyzed 200 adult neurocritical care and intensive care patients with SAE selected from an indication-based advanced neuromonitoring registry between January 2022 and December 2025. Jugular bulb catheterization was performed for clinical indications rather than as universal screening. SjvO2 monitoring, invasive arterial pressure monitoring, and transcranial Doppler-based dCA assessment were matched within the same early neuromonitoring window after SAE recognition. MAP variability was quantified using the coefficient of variation (MAP-CV) over the 24-hour period containing the first valid dCA session, and SjvO2 was derived from the matched 60-minute monitoring epoch rather than pooled ICU-stay data. Dynamic cerebral autoregulation was assessed by transfer function analysis and the mean flow index (Mx). Multivariable logistic and Cox regression models were adjusted for prespecified illness-severity and physiological covariates. The mean SjvO2 was 62.4 ± 11.8%, with 34.5% of patients demonstrating abnormal values (< 55% or > 75%). MAP-CV was 14.2 ± 5.6%, and impaired dCA (Mx > 0.3) was observed in 58.0% of patients. SjvO2 was negatively correlated with Mx (r=-0.487, p < 0.001) and positively correlated with phase difference (r = 0.412, p < 0.001). MAP-CV was positively correlated with Mx (r = 0.523, p < 0.001) and negatively correlated with phase difference (r=-0.394, p < 0.001). Multivariable analysis identified SjvO2 < 55% (OR = 3.24, 95%CI: 1.78-5.89, p < 0.001), MAP-CV > 15% (OR = 2.87, 95%CI: 1.56-5.28, p = 0.001), and SOFA score (OR = 1.18, 95%CI: 1.06-1.32, p = 0.003) as independent predictors of impaired dCA. Patients with both abnormal SjvO2 and high MAP-CV had higher 28-day mortality than those with normal SjvO2 and low/moderate MAP-CV (51.0% vs. 22.1%, p < 0.001). In a simultaneous Cox model including impaired dCA, the combined abnormal SjvO2/high MAP-CV phenotype remained associated with 28-day mortality (adjusted HR = 2.54, 95%CI: 1.42-4.55, p = 0.002). Lower SjvO2 and greater MAP variability were associated with impaired dCA in SAE patients. The combined assessment of cerebral oxygenation and MAP variability may help identify patients with higher neurological and mortality risk within an observational risk-stratification framework. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation before being used to define individualized hemodynamic targets or treatment effects.

42939964.title: Heart in Distress: How Different Shock States Converge on Cardiac Dysfunction.
42939964.abstract: Shock is traditionally classified according to its primary etiology-septic, hypovolemic, obstructive, or cardiogenic-yet these syndromes frequently converge on a common feature: disturbances of cardiac performance, ventricular loading, and tissue perfusion. Despite distinct initiating mechanisms, altered preload and afterload, ventricular interdependence, vascular dysfunction, maladaptive neurohormonal responses, and, in selected states, impaired myocardial contractility may ultimately reduce effective forward flow and tissue perfusion. Echocardiography provides a rapid, noninvasive bedside tool for characterizing these evolving cardiovascular effects. It enables assessment of left and right ventricular function, cardiac filling, preload responsiveness, pulmonary and systemic venous congestion, fluid tolerance, and broader hemodynamic profiles while facilitating recognition of reversible causes such as cardiac tamponade, acute pulmonary embolism, or severe hypovolemia. This allows clinicians to move beyond static etiologic classifications toward a physiology-based assessment of shock. Beyond diagnosis, echocardiography can inform fluid resuscitation and vasoactive or inotropic therapy. Serial assessment also permits evaluation of therapeutic response and evolving hemodynamic phenotypes. This review synthesizes the mechanisms of cardiac involvement across shock syndromes and highlights echocardiography as a unifying tool for their evaluation and management. By integrating pathophysiology, bedside imaging, and hemodynamic treatment, we propose a physiology-based framework that complements traditional shock classification and may improve diagnostic precision and individualized management in critically ill patients.

42933021.title: When Source Control Is Not Enough: Bilateral Adrenal Hemorrhage After Group A Streptococcal Necrotizing Soft Tissue Infection.
42933021.abstract: Refractory septic shock following adequate surgical source control presents a major clinical challenge. While persistent vasopressor dependence in necrotizing soft tissue infections (NSTI) is frequently attributed to ongoing tissue necrosis or overwhelming cytokine release, acute primary adrenal failure due to Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome (WFS) represents an underrecognized, reversible etiology. We report a 41-year-old male who developed fulminant right upper extremity Group A Streptococcus (GAS) necrotizing fasciitis requiring emergent forequarter amputation. Despite definitive source control, targeted antitoxin antimicrobial therapy, and guideline-directed resuscitation, he experienced persistent vasopressor-dependent shock. On postoperative day 5, CT imaging revealed new-onset bilateral adrenal hemorrhage. The initiation of stress-dose hydrocortisone led to rapid hemodynamic stabilization and successful recovery. Surgeons must maintain a high index of suspicion for acute adrenal crisis in postoperative ICU patients with refractory shock despite source control, rather than solely driven by ongoing sepsis.

42931723.title: Fournier's Gangrene-Associated ECG-Pickelhaube Sign: The Evanescent STEMI-Mimic.
42931723.abstract: The spiked helmet sign (SHS), or Pickelhaube sign, is a rare pseudo-ST-segment elevation pattern described in critically ill patients without acute myocardial infarction. A 30-year-old man with class III obesity and diabetes presented in septic shock from extensive Fournier's gangrene. After emergent debridement, telemetry showed anterior ST-segment elevation prompting ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) activation. Serial electrocardiograms demonstrated pre-QRS baseline elevation merging with the QRS and transient anterolateral ST-segment elevation consistent with the Pickelhaube sign. Troponins remained normal, and contrast echocardiography showed hyperdynamic systolic function without regional wall-motion abnormalities. ST elevation resolved spontaneously within 30 minutes, and angiography was deferred. He required vasopressors, continuous venovenous hemofiltration, repeated debridement, and wound vacuum-assisted closure before discharge to long-term acute care. This case demonstrates the Pickelhaube sign during Fournier's gangrene with septic shock. Recognizing its morphology and evolution, along with biomarkers, echocardiography, and clinical context, can distinguish pseudo-STEMI from acute coronary occlusion and avoid unnecessary angiography. The Pickelhaube sign can occur in severe necrotizing soft-tissue infection and septic shock and may closely mimic acute STEMI. Serial electrocardiograms, cardiac biomarkers, echocardiography, and hemodynamic context help distinguish this pseudo-STEMI pattern from acute coronary occlusion.

42918809.title: Discordance between actual care and recommendations by a reinforcement learning model for sepsis.
42918809.abstract: Fluid and vasopressor management of sepsis requires a complex set of sequential treatment decisions tailored to individual responses. We examined the frequency and implications of disagreement between reinforcement-learning (RL), using the AI Clinician as a test example, and actual clinical decisions. A novel discordance score was defined as the Euclidean distance between clinical team actions and RL-recommended treatments (range 0 to 5.66), across 25 treatment options of vasopressors and intravenous (IV) fluids. Among 30,678 ICU patients with sepsis cared for across 309,415 time-epochs, discordance was more common among epochs of patients with SOFA > 6 than those with SOFA < 6, and for intravenous fluid choices than for vasopressors. After multivariable adjustment, greater discordance was associated with 90-day mortality (adjusted odds ratio (OR) 1.11, 95%CI: 1.05,1.18) in the SOFA strata > =6 but not for SOFA < = 4 (adjusted odds ratio (OR): 1.02, 95%CI: 0.97,1.08).

42903731.title: Falciform Ligament Inflammation Complicated by Umbilical Vein Thrombophlebitis, Left Portal Vein Thrombosis, and Multiple Hepatic Abscesses: A Case Report.
42903731.abstract: Falciform ligament pathology is a rare cause of acute upper abdominal pain and may resemble more common pancreatic and hepatobiliary disorders. A woman in her 50s presented with sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to her back and marked hyperamylasaemia of 1,747 U/L. This combination fulfilled clinical and biochemical diagnostic criteria for acute pancreatitis, although computed tomography (CT) demonstrated no pancreatic inflammation and instead showed severe inflammatory change centred on the falciform ligament, with associated focal fat infarction, left portal vein thrombosis, and gas locules within segment IV of the liver. The patient subsequently developed fever, tachycardia, lactic acidosis, and profound hypotension requiring intensive care admission, intravenous antimicrobial treatment, fluid resuscitation, and vasopressor support. Serial CT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated progressive falciform ligament inflammation, thrombophlebitis of the recanalised umbilical vein, occlusive left portal vein thrombosis, and multiple left-lobe hepatic abscesses. Blood cultures obtained during the febrile deterioration subsequently showed no growth. She improved with prolonged broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy and therapeutic anticoagulation. Percutaneous drainage was deferred because she remained clinically stable, her inflammatory markers improved, and the hepatic abscesses remained small and stable on serial imaging. Follow-up CT demonstrated resolution of the hepatic abscesses, reduction in the falciform ligament collection, and recanalisation of the umbilical vein, although the left portal vein thrombosis persisted. Transabdominal ultrasonography during the index admission demonstrated small gallstones. She was subsequently readmitted with recurrent upper abdominal pain, marked hyperamylasaemia, and CT evidence of acute cholecystitis, with the overall clinical picture considered consistent with gallstone pancreatitis. An outpatient CT four weeks after the second discharge demonstrated resolution of the gallbladder inflammatory changes, while the falciform ligament thickening and fluid density remained stable. This case demonstrates a rare and potentially life-threatening falciform ligament inflammatory process associated with portovenous thrombosis and hepatic abscess formation in the context of sepsis. The index presentation also met accepted diagnostic criteria for acute pancreatitis, and a concomitant biliary contribution could not be excluded. The case highlights the value of serial cross-sectional imaging, multidisciplinary management, and cautious interpretation of overlapping pancreatic, biliary, and falciform ligament pathology.

42902161.title: Early hemodynamic changes after the use of push-dose noradrenaline in patients presenting to the emergency department with septic shock: a descriptive study.
42902161.abstract: Although continuous noradrenaline infusion (CNI) is standard vasopressor therapy during the initial resuscitation of patients with septic shock, hemodynamic stabilization may not be immediate. Push-dose noradrenaline (PDNA) has been proposed as a temporary measure while CNI is being established. However, its clinical use, dosing, early hemodynamic response, and short-term safety in the emergency department (ED) are not well described. To address this gap, we conducted a single-center retrospective descriptive study at a tertiary care hospital in Japan in 2019. Adults with Sepsis-3 septic shock who received PDNA in the ED and were admitted to the intensive care unit were included. We assessed the context and dosing of PDNA administration, CNI use, mean arterial pressure (MAP) within 15 min after PDNA administration, and adverse events. Of 91 patients with septic shock, 50 (55%) received PDNA. PDNA was administered at CNI initiation in 25 patients, during CNI dose escalation in 6, and as rescue administration before CNI initiation in 19. The median (interquartile range [IQR]) initial PDNA dose was 20 (20-30) µg. During the 15-minute observation window, 32 (64%) patients received one bolus, 14 (28%) received two, 3 (6%) received three, and 1 (2%) received four. The directly observed median (IQR) MAP was 52 (44-61) mmHg at initial PDNA administration (n = 30) and 62 (50-68) mmHg 1 min later (n = 25). One of 36 patients evaluable for prespecified physiological adverse events experienced an adverse event; however, no serious adverse events were documented. In this single-center retrospective descriptive study, PDNA was most commonly administered at CNI initiation, and administration was followed by an early increase in median MAP. However, the noncomparative design and concurrent resuscitative interventions preclude attribution of this change solely to PDNA administration. No serious adverse events were documented; however, safety assessment was limited owing to missing data and retrospective ascertainment. These findings do not establish the effectiveness or safety of PDNA. Prospective comparative studies with standardized monitoring are required.

42896710.title: Clinical characteristics of necrotizing soft tissue infection among patients with high LRINEC scores.
42896710.journal: Journal of infection and chemotherapy : official journal of the Japan Society of Chemotherapy
42896710.abstract: The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) score is a widely used adjunctive diagnostic tool for necrotizing soft tissue infection (NSTI). However, patients with high LRINEC scores do not uniformly have NSTI and often represent a diagnostic gray zone requiring urgent differentiation from other severe soft tissue infections. This study aimed to clarify the clinical characteristics of NSTI among patients with high LRINEC scores. We retrospectively reviewed patients hospitalized for severe soft tissue infections with sepsis between January 2014 and December 2023 with LRINEC scores ≥6, classified as NSTI (n = 11) or non-NSTI (n = 9). Non-NSTI cases were limited to severe cellulitis with bacteremia requiring intensive care. Clinical findings, laboratory parameters, imaging findings, and vasopressor use within 24 h after hospital arrival were compared. Patients with NSTI had significantly higher white blood cell counts and serum creatinine levels. Fluid collection along the fascia and gas formation on CT were more frequent in the NSTI group. Mean blood pressure at presentation did not differ between groups; however, vasopressor use within 24 h after hospital arrival was significantly more common in the NSTI group, suggesting early hemodynamic deterioration or greater disease severity. In patients with high LRINEC scores, NSTI was associated with marked inflammatory response, renal dysfunction, specific CT findings and early hemodynamic instability. Early vasopressor requirement should be interpreted primarily as a marker of early hemodynamic deterioration or disease severity, rather than a diagnostic characteristic specific to NSTI.

42895627.title: Vasopressors Combination Therapy (Norepinephrine Plus Vasopressin Receptor Agonists) Improve Septic Shock Outcome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
42895627.abstract: BackgroundStudies showed different results of vasopressors combination therapy in septic shock patients. This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the outcomes of combination of norepinephrine plus vasopressin receptor agonists in adult septic shock.MethodsCochrane Library, Embase, Web of Science, and PubMed databases were searched up to September 27, 2026, to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing the combination of norepinephrine plus vasopressin receptor agonists versus norepinephrine alone in septic shock patients. Two reviewers independently extracted data on mortality, ICU length of stay, renal replacement therapy (RRT) and adverse events. Trial sequential analysis (TSA) was applied to assess random error.ResultsTwenty-one RCTs involving 3873 septic shock patients were included. The results showed that the combination of norepinephrine plus vasopressin receptor agonists was associated with lower mortality at the longest complete follow-up compared with norepinephrine alone (RR = 0.90, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.99, P = .02), but with an increased risk of digital ischemia (RR = 2.21, 95% CI 1.15 to 4.27, P = .02). Subgroup analysis indicated that the combination of norepinephrine plus vasopressin receptor agonists may provide survival benefits for more severe septic shock patients (RR = 0.90, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.00, P = .04). Moreover, compared with norepinephrine alone, the combination of norepinephrine plus vasopressin showed a trend towards reducing the longest follow-up mortality (RR = 0.89, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.00, P = .05). TSA indicated lack of firm evidence for a beneficial effect.ConclusionsIn adults with septic shock, the combination of norepinephrine plus vasopressin receptor agonists may reduce mortality at the longest complete follow-up compared with norepinephrine alone (low quality of evidence), but may increase risk of digital ischemia (low quality of evidence). This benefit mainly appeared in more severe septic shock patients. Moreover, norepinephrine plus vasopressin may confer a survival advantage.

42892717.title: [A delayed threat: S. aureus sepsis 4 years post-IUD insertion in a healthy young woman].
42892717.abstract: Intrauterine devices (IUDs) are highly effective long-acting reversible contraceptives with an established safety profile. Infectious complications are rare and usually occur shortly after insertion, typically involving polymicrobial pathogens. Staphylococcus aureus is an uncommon pathogen in this context, but its biofilm-forming ability may contribute to delayed and severe presentations. A healthy 25-year-old primiparous woman developed septic shock four years after the insertion of a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (Mirena®). She was admitted to the intensive care unit with fever, abdominal pain, and hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressor support. The IUD was removed, and cultures grew methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), while blood cultures were negative. She subsequently improved following device removal, targeted intravenous antibiotics, and supportive intensive care. Notably, nasal carriage was negative in the patient but positive in her partner, suggesting a possible source of colonization. This case illustrates a rare but life-threatening complication of IUD use: septic shock secondary to S. aureus biofilm infection, manifesting years after device insertion. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for device-related infection in women with unexplained sepsis. Prompt device removal, targeted antimicrobial therapy, and multidisciplinary ICU care are critical for optimal outcomes. The possible contribution of partner colonization to the pathogenesis of such infections warrants further investigation.

42892565.title: The Association of the Systemic Oxygen Delivery to Oxygen Consumption Ratio With Mortality, Heart Transplantation, and Mechanical Circulatory Support.
42892565.journal: Journal of cardiothoracic and vascular anesthesia
42892565.abstract: To identify if the delivery of oxygen over consumption of oxygen (DO2/VO2) ratio is significantly associated with clinical outcomes such as mortality, need for heart transplantation, or need for a mechanical circulatory support device. Retrospective cohort study. Medical and surgical cardiac intensive care units of the Mayo Clinic. Adult patients (≥18 years old) admitted to the cardiothoracic surgical or cardiac intensive care units between January 2012 and December 2025 were included if they underwent invasive hemodynamic assessment with simultaneous arterial blood gas, mixed venous blood gas, hemoglobin, and mean arterial pressure. Patients were excluded if they had their venous oxygen saturations drawn from a central line or a peripherally inserted central catheter, as well as those admitted for sepsis/septic shock. No interventions were performed on patients. DO2/VO2 demonstrated a nonlinear association with mortality. Using the median value of 4.73 as a reference point, patients with a DO2/VO2 value of ∼2 had the highest likelihood of mortality. Kaplan-Meier analysis using a prespecified cut-point of 5 did not demonstrate any significant relationship with mortality, likely because of the underlying nonlinear relationship. There was no significant association between DO2/VO2 ratio and the need for mechanical circulatory support or heart transplantation. DO₂/VO₂ is a marker of systemic oxygen balance that complements conventional hemodynamic indices. A categorical threshold of 5 did not show an association with clinical outcomes, but continuous analyses did suggest that a low DO₂/VO₂ may identify a high-risk phenotype.

42882191.title: IgM- and IgA-Enriched Polyclonal Intravenous Immunoglobulin Therapy in Sepsis: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study.
42882191.abstract: Background/Objectives: Evidence for adjunctive intravenous immunoglobulin therapy in sepsis remains conflicting. This study evaluated the association of IgM- and IgA-enriched polyclonal intravenous immunoglobulin (IgGAM) therapy with clinical outcomes, including post hoc analyses according to initial empiric antibiotic therapy (IEAT) appropriateness. Methods: This single-center retrospective cohort study included 50 adults with sepsis or septic shock according to Sepsis-3 criteria, treated between November 2006 and March 2010. Twenty-five patients received adjunctive IgGAM plus standard sepsis management, and 25 received standard management alone. Primary outcomes were 28-day intensive care unit (ICU) mortality, overall ICU mortality, and in-hospital mortality. Results: Overall, 28-day ICU mortality was 28.0% with IgGAM and 32.0% with control (relative risk, 0.88; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.37-2.05; p = 0.758); other mortality outcomes did not differ significantly. Kaplan-Meier survival distributions also did not differ significantly (log-rank p = 0.208). During the ICU stay, vasopressor therapy was required in 68% of the IgGAM group and 92% of the control group (p = 0.034); corresponding study day 1 requirements were 60% and 76% (p = 0.225). In the complete-case longitudinal analysis (IgGAM group, n = 20; control group, n = 25), SOFA scores decreased significantly over time within the IgGAM group (p = 0.017), whereas no significant within-group change was observed in the control group (p = 0.616). In the post hoc appropriate-IEAT subgroup, 28-day ICU mortality was 0.0% versus 36.8% (p = 0.026), in-hospital mortality was 25.0% versus 63.2% (p = 0.038), and Kaplan-Meier survival distributions differed significantly (log-rank p = 0.004). The 60-day restricted mean survival time was 58.1 versus 38.4 days, with a difference of 19.8 days (95% CI, 11.1-28.4). Conclusions: Adjunctive IgGAM therapy was not associated with significant differences in mortality overall. Findings in the post hoc appropriate-IEAT subgroup were hypothesis-generating and should be interpreted cautiously given potential selection bias, residual confounding, and multiple comparisons. Prospective evaluation within optimized sepsis care is warranted.

42965188.title: Hyponatremia in septic shock: Pathophysiology, fluid resuscitation challenges, and neurological complications.
42965188.journal: Journal of family medicine and primary care
42965188.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening condition characterized by organ dysfunction due to a dysregulated host response to infection, with septic shock representing its most severe form and carrying high mortality in intensive care units (ICUs). Among critically ill patients, hyponatremia (serum sodium) <135 mmol/L is a common electrolyte disturbance associated with worse outcomes. While prior studies have explored hypernatremia in septic shock, the pathophysiology, clinical implications, and management of hyponatremia in this context remain underexplored, creating uncertainty for clinicians regarding fluid resuscitation strategies and neurological safety. This narrative review aimed to synthesize current evidence on hyponatremia in septic shock, focusing on underlying mechanisms, resuscitation challenges, and neurological complications. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, EMBASE, and Google Scholar for studies published between 2017 and 2025, including clinical cohorts, case reports, and systematic reviews. The findings indicate that hyponatremia in septic shock arises from non-osmotic vasopressin release, systemic inflammation, acute kidney injury, and fluid shifts during aggressive resuscitation. Large-volume crystalloid administration may exacerbate sodium derangements, while rapid correction poses a risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), even under guideline-adherent practices. Case reports suggest plasma exchange may provide the most consistent benefit in severe neurological complications. In conclusion, hyponatremia in septic shock reflects complex neuroendocrine, inflammatory, and renal interactions. Optimized management requires individualized fluid strategies, cautious sodium correction, and prolonged neurological monitoring to mitigate complications and improve outcomes in critically ill patients.

42933949.title: Rethinking Resuscitation: Integrating Dynamic Hemodynamic Monitoring at the Bedside.
42933949.journal: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
42933949.abstract: Hemodynamic monitoring is essential for guiding resuscitation in critically ill patients, yet reliance on static indicators such as central venous pressure persists despite evidence of their poor predictive value. This evidence-based clinical review challenges outdated practices and highlights dynamic parameters to include pulse pressure variation, stroke volume variation, pleth variability index, and passive leg raise, as superior tools for assessing fluid responsiveness. Practical strategies for integrating these measures with bedside perfusion assessments, such as capillary refill time and mottling, are presented to help nurses implement evidence-based, multimodal monitoring and reduce iatrogenic harm.

42876909.title: The red blood cell distribution width-to-albumin ratio and 28-day mortality in patients with severe cardiogenic shock: a retrospective cohort study based on MIMIC-IV with single-center external validation.
42876909.abstract: Cardiogenic shock (CS) is a critical syndrome with a very high fatality rate, and in-hospital mortality ranges from 27% to 51%. Among the various prognostic approaches, serum biomarkers have attracted considerable attention because they are easy to measure, inexpensive, and can be monitored dynamically. The red cell distribution width-to-albumin ratio (RAR) is a novel composite marker that integrates red blood cell heterogeneity (reflecting inflammation and oxidative stress) with albumin levels (indicating nutritional and anti-inflammatory capacity). It has shown initial promise for risk stratification in critically ill patients. However, the independent prognostic value of RAR specifically in CS remains unclear. Therefore, this study aims to systematically evaluate the ability of RAR to predict 28-day mortality in these patients. This study used a two-cohort retrospective design. The internal training cohort was derived from CS patients in the MIMIC-IV v2.2 database, and the external validation cohort came from the medical record system of the Affiliated Hospital of Guizhou Medical University. To explore the association between RAR and short-term poor outcomes in severe CS, we applied multivariable Cox regression, restricted cubic spline (RCS) regression, subgroup analysis, and Kaplan-Meier survival curves. To develop a simple prediction model, the internal cohort was randomly split into a training set and a test set in a 7:3 ratio. In the training set, we used five methods-Boruta algorithm, LASSO-Cox regression, random forest (RF), gradient boosting (GBDT), and support vector machine (SVM)-to select key features associated with poor CS prognosis, covering laboratory indicators, comorbidities, demographic characteristics, and vital signs. Based on the selected feature variables, we built prognostic prediction models using multivariable Cox regression in each of the three cohorts. The discriminative ability of the model was compared with that of traditional disease severity scores using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, with the area under the curve (AUC) as the measure of predictive performance. A total of 1,314 CS patients were included in this study. In the fully adjusted model (Model 3), both continuous RAR and RAR quartiles were independently associated with 28-day adverse outcomes. For 28-day ICU mortality, each unit increase in RAR was associated with a 13.4% higher risk (HR 1.134, 95% CI 1.076-1.197, p < 0.001); compared with the lowest quartile (Q1), the highest quartile (Q4) had a significantly increased risk of 51.7% (HR 1.517, 95% CI 1.123-2.049, p = 0.007). For 28-day in-hospital mortality, the HR for continuous RAR was 1.085 (95% CI 1.031-1.141, p = 0.002), and the HR for Q4 vs. Q1 was 1.576 (95% CI 1.196-2.076, p = 0.001). Restricted cubic spline analysis further confirmed a significant positive dose-response relationship between RAR and mortality (overall p < 0.05). In the external validation cohort, the predictive value of RAR for 28-day ICU mortality remained consistent and was even stronger (HR for continuous RAR: 1.359, 95% CI 1.177-1.568, p < 0.001). the RAR-based risk prediction model showed moderate but consistent discriminative performance, with areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.71, 0.70, and 0.75 in the training, test, and external validation sets, respectively, all of which were higher than those of traditional severity scores (all DeLong tests p < 0.05). This study demonstrated in both cohorts that RAR is an independent associated with 28-day mortality risk in CS patients. The prediction model built on RAR and five other clinical features exhibited good clinical performance. With further prospective validation, this model may become a valuable exploratory tool for risk stratification in CS patients.

42871062.title: Healthcare providers' confidence, satisfaction, and perceived preparedness following a multicomponent simulation-based cardiopulmonary resuscitation training program in Gaza.
42871062.abstract: High-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) requires not only technical competence but also confidence, effective teamwork, and psychological readiness among healthcare providers. Evidence regarding the impact of simulation-based CPR training on healthcare providers' confidence, satisfaction, and perceived preparedness remains limited in conflict-affected and resource-constrained settings. To assess healthcare providers' self-confidence, satisfaction, and perceived preparedness following an intensive, multicomponent simulation-based CPR training program implemented among physicians and nurses working in governmental critical care facilities in Gaza. This was a single-group evaluation of an intensive, 8-h multicomponent simulation-based CPR training program delivered to 100 healthcare providers (50 physicians, 50 nurses) working in emergency rooms, intensive care units, and coronary care units at Al-Shifa Medical Complex, Gaza, between August and December 2022, aligned with the 2020 American Heart Association Guidelines. Participants were recruited using purposive, non-probability sampling of all eligible clinical staff in these units. Self-reported confidence in CPR-related competencies was assessed before and after the intervention using identical questionnaire items; satisfaction and perceived preparedness were assessed only after the intervention. Outcomes were measured on a structured, five-point Likert-scale questionnaire (Cronbach's α = 0.87), content-validated by an expert panel and refined through a pilot study, analyzed descriptively using SPSS version 26. Participants reported very high satisfaction across all training domains, with instructor feedback usefulness rated highest (4.75 ± 0.39). Self-reported confidence increased markedly from pre- to post-training across all assessed domains: confidence in performing CPR rose from 2.91 ± 0.82 to 4.63 ± 0.51, airway management confidence from 2.85 ± 0.79 to 4.58 ± 0.54, and CPR team leadership confidence from 2.73 ± 0.88 to 4.49 ± 0.57. Most participants (92%) preferred simulation-based training over traditional lecture-based methods, and post-training perceived preparedness for real cardiac arrest situations was high (rapid response ability, 4.71 ± 0.40). Multicomponent simulation-based CPR training was associated with marked improvement in healthcare providers' self-reported confidence, and was accompanied by high levels of post-training satisfaction and perceived emergency preparedness in a conflict-affected healthcare environment. Integrating structured simulation-based education into continuing professional development programs may strengthen emergency response capacity and workforce readiness in resource-limited settings.

42870983.title: Case Report: Renal rupture and massive urine extravasation following flexible ureteroscopic lithotripsy: analysis of 4 cases and literature review.
42870983.abstract: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 4 patients who developed renal rupture and urinary extravasation after retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS) in our hospital. Their clinical data, intraoperative findings, rescue procedures, and outcomes were reviewed, alongside a narrative literature review of relevant studies. For the literature review, we searched PubMed and CNKI databases using the terms "RIRS," "renal rupture," "urinary extravasation," "intrarenal pressure," and "ureteroscopic complications," without applying strict systematic selection criteria. Because these cases were collected over an extended period without a dedicated procedural registry, we did not attempt to calculate the overall incidence of this complication at our institution; rather, this series focuses on the clinical presentation, risk factors, and management strategies. We acknowledge that the small sample size, retrospective single-center design, and absence of a control group are inherent limitations of this case series. All 4 cases were successfully managed without mortality. The primary contributing factors included pre-existing moderate-to-severe hydronephrosis with thinning of the renal parenchyma (n = 4), duplicated kidney (n = 1), prior renal surgery (n = 2), prolonged operative time (2.5 to 3.7 h), presumed elevated intrarenal pressure (inferred from poor outflow and prolonged operative time), and pre-existing urinary tract infection (n = 1). Emergency interventions comprised broad-spectrum antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, percutaneous drainage of ascites (1,000-1,200 mL drained within 30 min in relevant cases), and selective renal artery embolization for active bleeding (n = 1). All patients recovered and were discharged; follow-up imaging showed gradual resolution of perinephric hematoma and extravasation. Renal rupture with massive urinary extravasation is a rare but severe complication of RIRS. Key preventive measures, as suggested by the published literature, may include strict case selection, adequate preoperative infection control, preoperative ureteral stenting (generally for 7-14 days according to prior reports), efforts to keep intrarenal pressure below the commonly cited threshold of 30 mmHg, and limiting operative time to the generally recommended 60-90 min, alongside early intraoperative or postoperative detection via ultrasound or CT. This series underscores that early recognition, multidisciplinary collaboration, and timely intervention, including prompt drainage, intensive care support, and selective arterial embolization when indicated, are critical for successful management.

42870279.title: Temporal changes in clinical practices for patients considered clinically brain dead: a single-center cohort study.
42870279.abstract: Patients considered clinically brain dead undergo neurological assessment and critical care management, along with discussions with their families regarding goals of care and, when appropriate, organ donation. However, how these clinical and organ donation-related practices have evolved over time remains poorly characterized in Japan. We aimed to evaluate temporal changes in neurological assessment, critical care management, and organ donation-related processes among patients considered clinically brain dead. We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study including consecutive patients considered clinically brain dead in the Emergency ICU of Okayama University Hospital between January 2017 and December 2025. Patients were identified through routine auditory brainstem response testing during evaluation for a brain-death-compatible state. Temporal changes in the determination of a brain-death-compatible state, organ donation discussion, and critical care management were evaluated by calendar year, with three study phases (2017-2019, 2020-2022, and 2023-2025) used for descriptive presentation. Annual trends were assessed using logistic regression and nonparametric trend analyses. Among 128 eligible patients, organ donation was discussed with the families of 110 (85.9%), and 41 (37.3%) subsequently underwent organ donation after brain death. Calendar-year analyses showed increasing corticosteroid use (odds ratio [OR] per year, 1.64; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.34-2.01; p < 0.001) and earlier initiation of corticosteroids and vasopressin, whereas no significant trends were observed in vasopressin use or in the timing of determination of a brain-death-compatible state or the initial organ donation discussion. The likelihood of organ donation discussion increased significantly over time (OR per year, 1.44; 95% CI 1.17-1.79; p = 0.001) and remained significant in a sensitivity analysis restricted to patients in whom discussion was considered feasible (OR per year, 2.11; 95% CI 1.42-3.15; p < 0.001). The opportunity for organ donation discussion increased over time among patients considered clinically brain dead, while the proportion of families consenting to donation remained relatively stable. This increase occurred alongside the progressive development of structured multidisciplinary processes, although their contribution to the observed temporal trend cannot be determined from this descriptive study.

42868968.title: Enhanced Early Risk Stratification in Cardiogenic Shock Using Machine Learning: A Hierarchical Clustering Analysis.
42868968.abstract: Cardiogenic shock (CS) exhibits marked clinical heterogeneity, limiting the performance of conventional risk stratification tools like the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) staging system. Machine learning (ML) has identified reproducible CS phenotypes that improve risk prediction, but their temporal consistency across the progression of shock remains incompletely described. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the temporal evolution of ML-derived CS phenotypes across the first 3 intensive care unit (ICU) days and determine whether phenotype trajectories enhance mortality stratification beyond SCAI staging. In a multicenter retrospective registry of 2,906 adults with CS admitted to ICUs between 2016 and 2022, hierarchical agglomerative clustering was applied independently to clinical variables on ICU days 1, 2, and 3. On day 1, 3 phenotypes emerged: Cardiac (younger, acute myocardial infarction-predominant, preserved renal function; 15% mortality), Cardio-Renal (older, non-acute myocardial infarction-predominant, isolated renal extracardiac impairment, predominantly SCAI A and B on admission; 27% mortality), and Cardio-Metabolic (severe renal and tissue malperfusion, predominantly SCAI D and E on admission; 55% mortality). Similar phenotypes persisted on day 2 and day 3. These ML-derived phenotypes enhanced mortality stratification within each SCAI stage across days 1 to 3. Hierarchical clustering reproduced previously identified CS phenotypes that were consistent across the first 3 days of ICU stay, providing an enhanced framework for early risk stratification. Prospective validation is required for clinical implementation.

42868703.title: Early hemodynamic profiles in severely burned patients: A single center cohort study.
42868703.journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
42868703.abstract: Large burns are associated with a massive inflammatory response and catecholamine release leading to complex cardiovascular disorders. Our aim was to describe the early hemodynamic trajectories following severe burns and to identify distinct hemodynamic trajectory patterns. We retrospectively collected data from patients admitted to our burn center for severe burn injuries between January 2017 and April 2025. Hemodynamic data were obtained by transpulmonary thermodilution coupled with pulse wave analysis. Time series for cardiac index (CI), systemic vascular resistance index (SVRI) and heart rate (HR) were analyzed for the first 96 h. Hemodynamic profiles were compared using dynamic time warping (DTW). Clusters were identified through hierarchical clustering. A total of 107 patients were included (median age 52 years [IQR: 36-65], median total burn surface area burned 40% [IQR: 30-54]); 22 patients died during their ICU stay. In the entire cohort, the hemodynamic profile progressively shifted from a low-cardiac output, vasoconstrictive state to a hyperkinetic, vasoplegic state (CI 2.6 ± 0.8-4.8 ± 1.3 L/min/m2; SVRI 3362[2659-4489] to 1382[1118-1698] dyn.s.cm-5.m2, p < 0.05). Cluster analysis identified two hemodynamic trajectory patterns, one with CI stabilization after an initial rise and another with a continuous increase in CI. SVRI decreased similarly in both clusters. ICU mortality differed between clusters in univariate analysis. This study confirms a two-phase hemodynamic response to severe burns under active fluid resuscitation. It provides evidence for distinct hemodynamic trajectory patterns. These profiles could help optimize individual resuscitation strategies.

42866100.title: Cardiogenic Shock Systems of Care Best Practices. Part 2: The Shock Team and Inpatient Management.
42866100.abstract: This paper describes the contemporary inpatient management of cardiogenic shock, including critical care management and the use of mechanical circulatory support as part of a cardiogenic shock system of care. It highlights the importance of multidisciplinary shock teams for improving patient outcomes through advanced mechanical circulatory support systems and critical care management strategies. Drawing on successful models in trauma care, the paper discusses the evolution of specialized teams, the reduction of care variability, and the enhancement of survival rates through standardized best practices. A case study illustrates the effective implementation of these principles, resulting in improved short-term survival and long-term recovery for patients.

42863383.title: Long-term functional outcome after post-anoxic brain injury: model development and internal validation from a multicentre cohort.
42863383.journal: Clinical neurophysiology : official journal of the International Federation of Clinical Neurophysiology
42863383.abstract: To identify biomarkers of long-term functional recovery after cardiac arrest (CA). This is a prospective longitudinal cohort study based on the Veneto Registry of CA (July 2021- June 2023). We collected demographic, clinical, biochemical, and electroencephalography and short- and middle-latencysomatosensory-evoked-potentials (S-SSEP and ML-SSEP) within 72 hours. Functional scales were collected at discharge, 3, 6, and 12 months after the event. Multiple imputation was used to avoid statistical loss. Calibration was verified. A penalised logistic regression and a penalised continuation ratio were fitted to model the effect of covariates. The quality of prediction or fitting was verified computing the rank probability score for ordinal outcomes, the Brier score, and area under the ROC curve for binary outcomes. Decision curve analysis confirmed clinical utility. We included 160 persons (mean 62.80 ± SD 14.36 years; 123 males) out of 186. The interaction between continuous/nearly continuous EEG and N20/P25 predictor of survival (β = 0.840) and recovery (β = 1.160) of consciousness at 12 months after CA. ML-SSEP was a predictor of good outcome on all scales at 12 months after CA (0.739<β <1.708). ML-SSEPs associated with standard neurophysiological assessments are robust predictors of long-term functional outcomes after CA. ML-SSEPs associated with EEG and standard SSEP might be incorporated in routine clinical practice in ICU post-anoxic coma assessment.

42859740.title: Perioperative Anesthetic Considerations for Temporal Bone Tumor Resection in Fibroblast Growth Factor 23 (FGF23)-Related Tumor-Induced Osteomalacia: A Case Report.
42859740.abstract: Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors (PMTs) are uncommon, predominantly benign neoplasms frequently associated with dysregulated phosphate metabolism through the overproduction of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23). Elevated levels of FGF23 lead to phosphate depletion, which may impair tissue oxygen delivery, central respiratory drive, and respiratory muscle function. Systemic manifestations may include osteomalacia and neuromuscular dysfunction, with an increased risk of respiratory and cardiovascular complications. PMTs often present with nonspecific clinical findings and may remain unrecognized during the perioperative period, presenting significant challenges for anesthetic planning and management. We report the case of a 72-year-old male with tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO), a right temporal mass, and multiple comorbidities, including hypertension and obstructive sleep apnea. The patient reported progressive headaches and general weakness. After neurosurgical evaluation, he underwent elective surgical excision under general anesthesia. Intraoperatively, he developed hypotension following induction of anesthesia, requiring vasopressor support with ephedrine boluses and a continuous phenylephrine infusion. The remainder of the procedure was uneventful, and the patient was extubated and transferred to the intensive care unit in stable condition. This case highlights the importance of recognizing potential complications in patients with metabolic abnormalities presenting with PMTs, particularly disturbances in phosphate homeostasis that may have significant anesthetic implications. The use of video laryngoscopy, judicious administration of neuromuscular blocking agents, and an individualized anesthetic strategy facilitated secure airway management, minimized cervical manipulation, and supported an uneventful recovery. Moreover, integrating anesthetic selection with comprehensive perioperative planning is essential to address the metabolic, musculoskeletal, respiratory, and hemodynamic challenges associated with TIO, particularly in patients with significant comorbidities.

42857397.title: Early-Phase Computed Tomography Bowel Diameter and Neurological Outcomes Post-Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation.
42857397.abstract: We aimed to conduct an exploratory investigation on the association between bowel diameter on early-phase abdominal computed tomography (CT) and neurological outcomes in patients undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). This observational study included patients who underwent ECPR for OHCA and abdominal CT before intensive care unit admission between January 2015 and December 2021 at a tertiary emergency medical center. Maximum bowel diameter was measured with a picture archiving and communication system by an investigator blinded to outcomes. The primary endpoint was unfavorable neurological outcomes at 1 month, defined as Cerebral Performance Category 3-5. The discriminatory ability of bowel diameter was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Data from 181 patients were analyzed (median age, 57 years; 84.5% male). Bowel diameter demonstrated a weak ability to predict unfavorable neurological outcomes, with an AUC of 0.58 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.47-0.70). However, higher discriminatory performance was observed in subgroups of patients aged ≥ 65 years (AUC, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.69-0.96) and those with initial nonshockable rhythms (AUC, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.47-0.91). The results of this exploratory investigation suggest that bowel diameter may represent a potential adjunctive marker associated with functional outcomes post-ECPR for OHCA.

42853139.title: Pressure Points: A Scoping Review of Intracranial Pressure and Mean Arterial Pressure Measurement and Reporting Practices in Neurocritical Care.
42853139.abstract: Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is a cornerstone of neurocritical care, but the literature shows substantial heterogeneity in how its components-intracranial pressure (ICP) and mean arterial pressure (MAP)-are reported. We conducted a scoping review following the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR to map this variability. Structured searches in PubMed and Scopus (January 1997 to May 2026) identified 350 eligible original clinical studies. For each study, we extracted whether the ICP measurement method, ICP device, ICP zero reference, MAP measurement method, and arterial line zero reference were reported. Reporting completeness was analyzed overall and stratified by guideline era and primary diagnosis, using the χ2 tests, odds ratios with 95% CI, and the Cochran-Armitage test for trend. The ICP measurement method was reported in 84.0% of studies, and the ICP zero reference in 14.6%; the MAP method in 66.9%, and the arterial line zero reference in 28.6%. Only 6.6% of studies reported all 5 domains. After publication of the Brain Trauma Foundation fourth Edition, reporting improved across most domains-ICP method (79.0% vs. 96.1%, P<0.001) and arterial line zero reference (20.2% vs. 49.0%, P<0.001)-and the composite reporting score rose from 2.37 to 3.06 (P<0.001). ICP zero-reference reporting was similar between eras (16.5% vs. 9.8%, P=0.105) while showing a significant declining trend across the study period (Cochran-Armitage Z=-2.52, P=0.012). Traumatic brain injury and hemorrhagic conditions had the lowest ICP zero reference reporting (8.8% and 9.3%; OR=0.35 for TBI vs. non-TBI, 95% CI: 0.19-0.65). Improvements in reporting have not reached the level needed to determine whether CPP values are comparable across studies. We propose an 11-item Minimum Reporting Set for CPP-related studies.

42849795.title: CS-MORT-6: A mortality score that refines risk within EHR-derived SCAI stages in cardiogenic shock.
42849795.abstract: Cardiogenic shock carries high in-hospital mortality, and the ordinal SCAI classification does not rank risk within a stage. Existing scores generally require imaging, procedural, or support-dependent data. We identified 3103 adults with documented cardiogenic shock in MIMIC-IV. Six predictors (lactate, urine output, cardiac arrest, age, blood urea nitrogen, red cell distribution width) were selected by bootstrap LASSO screening and clinical review. CS-MORT-6 was derived as two continuous ridge logistic models (lactate or anion gap) fitted at a 24-h landmark and a 0-to-15-point integer score. The primary outcome was subsequent in-hospital death among patients alive in the ICU at the landmark (n = 2694; 892 deaths). The models were externally validated in 1047 patients from 117 eICU hospitals. The integer score's AUROC was 0.727 (95% CI, 0.706-0.747) on cross-validation and 0.759 (0.729-0.790) externally; corresponding values were 0.734 and 0.759 (lactate model) and 0.726 and 0.748 (anion-gap model). Externally, the integer score over-predicted on average (calibration-in-the-large -0.22, slope 1.15). Within EHR-derived SCAI stages, mortality differed by 20 to 47 percentage points between the lowest and highest score tertiles in MIMIC-IV, with a similar pattern in eICU. Adding the anion-gap model to stage increased apparent AUROC by 0.139 (0.116-0.162) in MIMIC-IV and 0.141 (0.101-0.178) in eICU. Compared with BOS,MA2 (654 eICU patients scorable by both), the anion-gap model's AUROC difference was 0.004 (-0.039 to 0.046). At 24 h, CS-MORT-6 distinguished mortality risk within EHR-derived SCAI stages and retained moderate discrimination externally. Repeated scoring and real-time performance require prospective evaluation.

42848727.title: Functional Recovery Patterns and Baseline Cardiac Power Output During Impella 5.5 Support in Heart Transplant Candidates: A Descriptive Study.
42848727.abstract: The Impella 5.5 microaxial pump facilitates ambulatory mechanical circulatory support via axillary implantation, providing a model for active prehabilitation in critically ill heart transplant candidates. Whether patients with severely reduced baseline cardiac power output (CPO) can achieve meaningful ambulation during Impella 5.5 support remains uncertain. This is a retrospective descriptive study of consecutive adults with cardiogenic shock (SCAI stages C-E) who received an Impella 5.5 as a bridge to heart transplantation between April 2022 and September 2024. Cardiac Power Output was calculated via pre-implantation right heart catheterization, defined as low (≤0.60 W) or higher (>0.60 W). Measures of functional recovery include maximum walking distance per day, cumulative walking distance during Impella 5.5 support, time to first walk, and percentage of patients who walked at least once. The LOWESS method is used to illustrate overall walking distance trajectories. The final analytic cohort included 80 patients: 37 (46.3%) with baseline CPO ≤0.60 W and 43 (53.8%) with baseline CPO >0.60 W. Overall, 75 of 80 patients (93.8%) ambulated at least once before transplantation, including 89.2% in the low-CPO group and 97.7% in the higher-CPO group (p = 0.176). The time to first walking day was 5 days (IQR 3-7) in the low-CPO group vs. 3 days (IQR 2-7) in the higher-CPO group (p = 0.27). Maximum daily walking distance was 5,200 ft (IQR 2,000-10,400 ft) vs. 4,000 ft (IQR 2,400-8,000 ft) (p = 0.26), while cumulative distance was 15,400 ft vs. 11,000 ft (p = 0.81). Prehabilitation is feasible in patients undergoing Impella 5.5 support across the spectrum of hemodynamic status. Patients with severely compromised baseline cardiac performance achieved early, substantial ambulation. Thus, Impella 5.5 appears feasible as a platform for both hemodynamic support and prehabilitation of patients awaiting heart transplantation, though larger, non-selected cohorts are needed to confirm these findings.

42847974.title: Age-Based Preoperative Transthoracic Echocardiography, Intraoperative Hypotension, and Postoperative Outcomes in Older Adults Undergoing Noncardiac Surgery: A Regression Discontinuity Analysis.
42847974.abstract: The clinical value of routine preoperative transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) in older adults remains controversial. Existing evidence is largely observational and vulnerable to confounding by indication, limiting causal interpretation of whether preoperative TTE improves intraoperative management and perioperative outcomes. We aimed to evaluate the local effect of routine age-based preoperative TTE using a quasi-experimental design. This single-center retrospective cohort study used a fuzzy regression discontinuity design based on an institutional policy of routine preoperative TTE in patients aged ≥75 years. Eligible patients were aged 60 to 89 years and underwent elective noncardiac surgery under general anesthesia from July 2017 to August 2024. To minimize confounding by indication, patients with guideline-based indications or other clinical conditions likely to prompt preoperative TTE independent of age were excluded. The primary outcome was intraoperative hypotension (IOH), defined as the duration of mean arterial pressure <65 mm Hg. Exploratory secondary outcomes included 30- and 90-day mortality, acute kidney injury (AKI), planned and unplanned intensive care unit (ICU) or cardiac care unit (CCU) admission, and postoperative length of hospital stay. Continuity of baseline characteristics and density of the running variable were assessed. Among 7270 patients, the probability of undergoing preoperative TTE increased by 43.1 percentage points (95% confidence interval [CI], 33.3-52.9) at the 75-year-old cutoff, confirming a strong first-stage discontinuity. The estimated local effect of preoperative TTE on IOH was a 24.8-minute reduction (95% CI, -71.1 to 21.5). Sensitivity analyses using alternative bandwidths and covariate adjustment yielded similar findings. Point estimates for 30-day mortality (-2.1%; 95% CI, -6.0 to 1.8), 90-day mortality (-3.2%; 95% CI, -10.4 to 3.9), and AKI (-3.6%; 95% CI, -15.9 to 8.6) were below zero but imprecise. Point estimates were also below zero for unplanned ICU or CCU admission (-6.0 percentage points; 95% CI, -12.2 to 0.2) and postoperative length of hospital stay (-7.0 days; 95% CI, -14.6 to 0.5). Baseline characteristics and the density of the running variable (age) showed no clear discontinuity at the cutoff. Using a quasi-experimental design that reduces susceptibility to confounding by indication, we found no clear evidence that routine age-based preoperative TTE reduced IOH or improved postoperative outcomes near the threshold. The estimates were imprecise, and clinically meaningful benefit or harm could not be excluded. These findings suggest that age alone may be insufficient to justify routine preoperative TTE and support further evaluation of selective risk-based strategies.

42846417.title: Early adjunctive vasopressin was not associated with a lower 7-day risk of renal replacement therapy in norepinephrine-treated patients with cirrhosis: a target-trial-informed study with external replication.
42846417.abstract: Early adjunctive vasopressin can reduce catecholamine exposure in vasodilatory shock, but whether it prevents severe kidney failure in norepinephrine-treated patients with cirrhosis is uncertain. We conducted a target-trial-informed landmark study using MIMIC-IV as the primary cohort and eICU-CRD as an external replication cohort. Adults with a first intensive care unit admission, cirrhosis or advanced chronic liver disease, and norepinephrine initiation within 24 h of admission were eligible. Treatment was classified at a 6-h landmark as vasopressin initiated within 6 h of norepinephrine or no vasopressin during that window; patients in the latter group could receive vasopressin later. The primary outcome was new renal replacement therapy (RRT) between the landmark and day 7. Propensity-score overlap weighting was prespecified as the primary analysis. The MIMIC-IV cohort included 1,086 patients (early vasopressin, n = 295; no early vasopressin, n = 791), and the eICU-CRD cohort included 356 patients (n = 91 and n = 265, respectively). Before weighting, vasopressin recipients had greater shock and liver-disease severity. Early vasopressin was not associated with lower odds of new RRT in MIMIC-IV (overlap-weighted odds ratio [OR] 1.37, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.83-2.26; P = 0.214), eICU-CRD (OR 1.10, 95% CI 0.45-2.69; P = 0.833), or the pooled analysis (OR 1.30, 95% CI 0.84-2.01; P = 0.235). Mortality was higher among early-vasopressin recipients, but this secondary association remained highly vulnerable to confounding by indication. Weighted absolute-risk estimates, cumulative RRT incidence, subgroup analyses, and sensitivity analyses provided no supporting renal-benefit signal; creatinine trajectories were evaluated descriptively because follow-up measurements were susceptible to survivor selection. Among norepinephrine-treated patients with cirrhosis or advanced chronic liver disease who were alive and RRT-free 6 h after norepinephrine initiation, early adjunctive vasopressin was not associated with less RRT by day 7. The findings do not challenge vasopressin use for hemodynamic support when clinically indicated, but do not support early initiation solely as a renal-protective strategy.

42845073.title: Airway Stenting for Benign and Malignant Central Airway Obstruction: A Case Series.
42845073.abstract: Central airway obstruction (CAO) is a life-threatening condition caused by malignant or benign processes involving the trachea and main bronchi. Bronchoscopic airway stenting is an established intervention to restore airway patency, relieve symptoms, and stabilize patients, particularly in urgent or critical settings. However, its clinical role varies according to underlying etiology and disease context. We report a single-center case series of seven adult patients with symptomatic CAO who underwent bronchoscopic airway stenting. Six cases were associated with malignant disease, and one involved benign obstruction due to endobronchial tuberculosis. Interventions included rigid and/or flexible bronchoscopy, with adjunctive techniques such as balloon dilatation, cryotherapy, and argon plasma coagulation. Stent selection was individualized based on anatomical and etiological considerations. Airway stenting led to immediate improvement in respiratory status in all cases. In benign obstruction, stenting achieved sustained airway patency without significant complications. In malignant CAO, stenting served primarily as a palliative or bridging intervention, providing temporary stabilization and enabling further oncologic or supportive therapy. In critically ill patients, including those with impending airway collapse or post-cardiac arrest, stenting functioned as a lifesaving or salvage procedure. Complications included tumor ingrowth, mucus retention, and infection; no fatal stent-related procedural events occurred. Airway stenting is a versatile and effective modality for managing CAO. Its role differs by etiology, offering durable benefit in benign disease, palliative or stabilizing effects in malignancy, and potential life-saving intervention in selected critically ill patients. Individualized decision-making and multidisciplinary management remain essential to optimize outcomes.

42841834.title: Predictors of High Self-Efficacy in Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Regression Model Analysis.
42841834.abstract: Cardiac arrest remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Effective cardiopulmonary resuscitation relies not only on technical proficiency but also on contextual and psychological factors. Identifying determinants of high cardiopulmonary resuscitation self-efficacy among emergency nurses and physicians is therefore crucial to improving cardiopulmonary resuscitation performance and patient outcomes. A cross-sectional descriptive-correlational study was conducted with emergency nurses and physicians (N = 399) from emergency and critical care units in Spain. Data were collected in February 2025 using validated Spanish instruments, including the Spanish versions of the Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Motivation Scale and the cardiopulmonary resuscitation subscale of the Basic Resuscitation Skills Self-Efficacy Scale. Predictors of cardiopulmonary resuscitation self-efficacy were examined using multiple linear regression analysis. A 95% confidence level was established, and P values < .05 were considered statistically significant. Motivation (β = 0.31, P < .001), recent institutional cardiopulmonary resuscitation training (β = -0.23, P < .001), clinical experience in emergency and critical care (β = 0.12, P = .03), advanced postgraduate education (β = 0.11, P = .02), and age (β = 0.11, P = .049) were identified as significant independent predictors of cardiopulmonary resuscitation self-efficacy. Greater motivation, recent institutional cardiopulmonary resuscitation training, greater clinical experience in emergency and critical care settings, advanced postgraduate education, and age were associated with higher cardiopulmonary resuscitation self-efficacy among emergency nurses and physicians. These findings support implementing regular training, advanced educational pathways, and workforce strategies within emergency and critical care settings to strengthen cardiopulmonary resuscitation preparedness and improve the quality of care for patients who experience cardiac arrest.

42840193.title: Serial plasma proenkephalin A 119-159 and dipeptidyl peptidase 3 after cardiac arrest: association with long-term neurological outcome.
42840193.abstract: To evaluate whether serial plasma proenkephalin A 119-159 (penKid) and circulating dipeptidyl peptidase 3 (cDPP3) after cardiac arrest are associated with long-term neurological outcome and mortality. We performed a retrospective multicentre cohort study of adults admitted to intensive care after cardiac arrest in southern Sweden. Biomarkers were measured on admission and at 12 and 48 h. The primary outcome was poor neurological outcome, defined as Cerebral Performance Category 3-5 at 2-6 months. The secondary outcome was 180-day mortality. Models were adjusted for established peri-arrest prognostic variables. Odds ratios and hazard ratios are reported per 1-SD increase in log10transformed biomarker concentration. Among 417 patients, 271 (65%) had poor neurological outcome and 266 (64%) died within 180 days. PenKid was independently associated with poor neurological outcome at admission (adjusted odds ratio 1.62, 95% confidence interval 1.15-2.28) and 12 h (1.50, 1.08-2.09), and with mortality at admission (adjusted hazard ratio 1.36, 1.20-1.54) and 12 h (1.33, 1.17-1.51). cDPP3 was independently associated with mortality at 12 h (1.26, 1.11-1.43), but not with poor neurological outcome after adjustment. Neither biomarker significantly improved discrimination beyond the clinical reference model. Early penKid was associated with poor neurological outcome and mortality after cardiac arrest, whereas cDPP3 was associated with mortality at 12 h. These biomarkers added limited discriminatory value beyond established clinical predictors.

42837646.title: Dual Antiglutamate Therapy in Super-Refractory Status Epilepticus After Cardiac Arrest (SUPER-CAT Study).
42837646.abstract: The SUPER-refractory status epilepticus (SE) after Cardiac Arrest Treatment (SUPER-CAT) study evaluated the efficacy and safety of dual antiglutamate therapy (combined AMPA and NMDA receptor blockade) in patients with super-refractory SE (SRSE) after cardiac arrest and without unfavorable prognostic indicators. Multicenter cohort study including patients with postanoxic SRSE meeting the following criteria: bilaterally preserved N20 cortical responses, intact pupillary reflexes, and absence of generalized periodic discharges. Patients treated with dual antiglutamate therapy (DUAL; ketamine 1.5-7.5 mg/kg/h for 3 days plus perampanel 6-12 mg/d for 5 days with tapering) were compared with patients receiving other combinations of antiseizure and anesthetic agents (OTHERS). The primary outcome was resolution of SE. Secondary outcomes included awakening to follow commands and good neurologic outcome at 6 months (modified Rankin Scale 0-3) in patients with fewer than 2 unfavorable multimodal prognostic indicators and 6-month mortality for the entire cohort. Safety analysis included in-hospital mortality and potentially treatment-related adverse events. Patients treated with single antiglutamate agents were described separately. Between May 2012 and May 2025, 95 of 1,352 consecutive post-cardiac arrest intensive care unit patients met inclusion criteria (mean age 66, interquartile range 55-73; 41% female; DUAL = 43; OTHERS = 41; single antiglutamate = 11). Compared with OTHERS, DUAL was associated with a higher rate of SE resolution (84% vs 49%; OR 5.4; 95% CI 1.9-14.9; p = 0.001), a greater likelihood of awakening before discharge (56% vs 32%; OR 2.7; 95% CI 1.0-7.3; p = 0.053) and lower 6-month mortality (52% vs 74%; OR 0.37; 95% CI 0.15-0.97; p = 0.043). A trend toward better 6-month neurologic outcome was observed in the DUAL group (39% vs 25%; OR 1.89; 95% CI 0.64-5.56; p = 0.245). Reversible cholestatic liver injury occurred more frequently in DUAL group, compared with OTHERS (77% vs 27%; OR 9.00; 95% CI 3.34-24.19; p < 0.001). In patients with postanoxic SRSE without unfavorable prognostic indicators, dual antiglutamate therapy was highly effective in resolving SE and was associated with improved short-term clinical outcomes. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05756621.

42836281.title: Incidence, Process of Care, and Outcomes of In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in China: A Multicenter Prospective Registry Study.
42836281.abstract: In-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) is an acute event associated with high mortality. Although survival has improved in high-income countries, contemporary multicenter data from low- and middle-income countries remain scarce, limiting global benchmarking and the identification of system-level opportunities for improvement. This cohort study used data from the BASIC-IHCA (Baseline Investigation of In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest) registry. Adult patients (≥18 years) who experienced IHCA and received cardiopulmonary resuscitation between July 1, 2019, and December 31, 2020, at 37 hospitals across 29 provinces in China were included. The primary outcome was survival to 30 days or hospital discharge. Secondary outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation, 6- and 12-month survival, and favorable neurological outcome (Cerebral Performance Category score 1-2). Process measures focused on the timeliness of resuscitation response and the implementation of postresuscitation interventions. Among 17 602 patients (median age, 66 years; 65.5% male), the annual incidence of adult IHCA was 4.1 per 1000 admissions. Cardiac etiology was identified in 6569 (37.3%) patients, and 2380 (13.5%) presented with initial shockable rhythm. Among all patients, 16 872 (95.9%) received cardiopulmonary resuscitation within 1 minute; timely defibrillation or epinephrine was achieved in 71.4% and 84.4% of patients with initial shockable and nonshockable rhythms, respectively.
