CT, MRI and electroencephalogram (EEG) ruled out a diagnosis of MSE, making LAS more likely. Ketamine was ultimately required to terminate the generalised myoclonic seizures after which antiepileptic drugs were optimised to reduce residual intention myoclonus.This report highlights key features prompting the clinical suspicion of LAS in a patient who has no significant evidence of brain injury, preserved consciousness with continued severe generalised myoclonus and outlines pharmacological and neurophysiological management.

42880622.title: Translating the R-EDByUS score into clinical decisions after cardiac arrest.

42879791.title: Microcirculatory Hemodynamic Changes on Full Support Microaxial Flow Pump in Cardiogenic Shock.
42879791.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
42879791.abstract: Impaired microcirculation predicts mortality in cardiogenic shock independent of systemic hemodynamics, yet current treatment strategies focus primarily on restoring macrocirculatory markers. We studied whether full-support microaxial flow pump (mAFP) therapy improves sublingual microcirculation in cardiogenic shock. A prospective, single-arm, observational study of serial sublingual microcirculation imaging via incident darkfield handheld videomicroscopy was performed in 18 cardiogenic shock patients undergoing Impella 5.5 (mAFP) placement. Microvascular flow index (MFI), microvascular heterogeneity index (MHI), proportion of perfused vessels (PPV), and perfused vessel density (PVD) were measured. Eighteen patients were enrolled. Microvascular flow index (p = 0.004), MHI (p = 0.055), PPV (p = 0.003), and PVD (p = 0.067) improved immediately on support, including when adjusted for vasoactive-inotropic score. Improvement in MFI, MHI, PPV, or PVD was most pronounced in those with impaired baseline microcirculatory hemodynamics (all p < 0.05), whereas those with preserved baseline values demonstrated no change. Improved agreement between systemic and microcirculatory hemodynamics was observed in association with mAFP support, and none experienced worsening microcirculatory function. These exploratory findings suggest full-support mAFPs may improve impaired microcirculation during cardiogenic shock, although device-specific effects cannot be isolated from overall clinical improvement; validation in larger studies is warranted. Although agreement between systemic and microcirculatory hemodynamic markers improved, no macrohemodynamic marker proved sufficient to ensure adequate microcirculatory perfusion.

42878771.title: Toward very early vasopressin use in septic shock: observational data accumulate but trial evidence still lacking.

42870300.title: Documenting graft outcome to substantiate the organ-donation rationale after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest due to aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage.

42870277.title: Early versus deferred intravenous calcium in patients with sepsis and ionized hypocalcemia: a target-trial emulation.
42870277.abstract: Intravenous calcium is frequently administered during sepsis, yet whether early treatment improves 24-h hemodynamic recovery remains uncertain. We compared 24-h hemodynamic recovery between calcium initiation within 2 h of a non-emergency low-ionized calcium (iCa) result and no calcium initiation during the first 6 h after the result. We conducted a retrospective target-trial emulation of 2016-2025 high-resolution electronic health records from Zigong Fourth People's Hospital. Adults with sepsis, final or corrected iCa of 0.90-1.10 mmol/L, and no emergency indication were eligible at result availability. Strategies were executed calcium within 2 h versus no calcium through 6 h; care after 6 h was unrestricted. Clone-censor weighting and overlap tilting addressed grace periods, measured time-varying confounding, and clinical equipoise. The primary outcome was being alive and vasopressor-free at 24 h. Estimates and two-sided 95% percentile intervals came from 2,000 patient-level bootstrap samples with model refitting. Of 5,993 patients, 1,538 initiated calcium within 2 h, 147 initiated at 2-6 h, and 4,308 received none through 6 h; none of the latter initiated calcium during 6-24 h. The standardized probability of 24-h hemodynamic recovery was 69.9% with early calcium and 61.1% with deferral, corresponding to a risk difference of + 8.69 percentage points (95% percentile interval, + 4.66 to + 12.84) and a risk ratio of 1.142 (1.074-1.214). The estimated association varied with baseline norepinephrine-equivalent dose (Holm-adjusted P = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶), whereas the iCa interaction did not remain statistically supported after adjustment (P = 0.097). Early calcium was associated with a 1.29-percentage-point higher observed risk of hypercalcemia (95% percentile interval, + 0.64 to + 2.05). Intervals for severe arrhythmia, new renal replacement therapy, and hospital mortality included the null. Early intravenous calcium was associated with a higher probability of 24-h hemodynamic recovery than the deferred strategy, whose observed pathway involved no calcium through 24 h. Estimated effects were larger at higher vasopressor doses. Early calcium was associated with a modestly higher observed risk of hypercalcemia. These findings support randomized evaluation in vasopressor-treated patients. Baseline iCa modification remains exploratory.

42864741.title: Forty-Eight Hour Lactate Normalization Predicts Favorable Neurologic Recovery and Survival in Venoarterial ECMO for Cardiogenic Shock.
42864741.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
42864741.abstract: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for cardiogenic shock (CS) is associated with high mortality and poor neurological outcomes. Dynamic assessment of metabolic recovery, reflected by lactate normalization, may offer additional prognostic value compared with static severity indices. We retrospectively analyzed 662 consecutive patients from the multicenter RESCUE II registry who remained on venoarterial ECMO for at least 48 hours. Patients were stratified by 48 hour lactate level: 48 hour lactate normalization group (< 2.0 mmol/L, n = 371) and persistent lactate elevation group (≥ 2.0 mmol/L, n = 291). The primary outcome was favorable neurologic discharge (FND), defined as discharge with a Cerebral Performance Category score of 1 or 2. The persistent lactate elevation group had a higher SOFA score (9.8 ± 3.2 vs. 8.5 ± 3.4, p < 0.001) and initial serum lactate (7.9 ± 4.8 mmol/L vs. 6.0 ± 4.3 mmol/L, p < 0.001). Lactate normalization was associated with a higher rate of FND (71.4% vs. 41.9%, p < 0.001), remained an independent predictor of FND (odds ratio [OR]: 3.12, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.21-4.41, p < 0.001), and was associated with lower risks of all-cause death (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.49, 95% CI: 0.38-0.64, p < 0.001) at 12 months. In conclusion, lactate normalization within 48 hours of ECMO initiation is associated with favorable neurologic status and 12 month survival.

42863592.title: Mechanical versus manual bag-valve ventilation during cardiopulmonary resuscitation in adults with cardiac arrest: a systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis.
42863592.abstract: Optimal ventilation delivery during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) remains uncertain. Current resuscitation guidelines do not recommend mechanical ventilation (MV) over manual bag-valve ventilation (BV). We evaluated the association between MV use during CPR and clinical outcomes in adults with cardiac arrest compared with manual BV. We searched 6 bibliographic databases from inception through May 31, 2026. Included studies compared MV and BV ventilation CPR in adult cardiac arrest patients. Patients receiving MV at any moment during CPR were classified as the MV group; those receiving only BV comprised the BV group. Primary outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to hospital admission, survival to hospital discharge, and good neurological outcome. Secondary outcomes included physiologic variables and pneumothorax. We calculated pooled risk ratios (RRs) and mean differences with 95% credible intervals (CrIs) using Bayesian random-effects meta-analyses. Eight studies involving 6847 patients were included. For the primary outcome, MV use during CPR was associated with a higher rate of ROSC than BV use (pooled RR, 1.20; 95% CrI, 1.04-1.42), with a 99% posterior probability of benefit. Posterior probabilities favoring MV for survival to admission, survival to discharge, and good neurological outcome were 92.3%, 93.6%, and 92.2%, respectively. Pneumothorax incidence was similar between groups. In adult cardiac arrest, MV use during CPR was associated with higher ROSC compared with manual BV. Evidence for improved survival and neurological outcomes remains imprecise and inconclusive.

42863115.title: Acute Effects of Impella 5.5 on Biventricular Filling and Pressure-Volume Area in Patients With Heart Failure Associated Cardiogenic Shock.
42863115.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
42863115.abstract: Use of Impella 5.5 in patients with decompensated heart failure-associated cardiogenic shock (ADHF-CS) is increasing as a bridge to advanced therapies. The effects of maximal trans-valvular unloading on biventricular filling and pressure-volume area (PVA) in ADHF-CS are poorly understood. Nine patients with medically refractory ADHF-CS underwent Impella 5.5 placement with simultaneous invasive arterial, venous, and biventricular pressure-volume loop analysis. Acutely after Impella 5.5 activation, cardiac output (3.4 ± 0.5 vs. 5.0 ± 0.7 L/min, p = 0.0011), diastolic (67.2 ± 8.0 vs. 80.7 ± 9.7 mm Hg, p = 0.0044) and mean arterial pressures (77.9 ± 7.1 vs. 86.9 ± 10.4 mm Hg, p = 0.029) increased, compared to baseline. Left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (24.1 ± 6.7 vs. 16.8 ± 5.4 mm Hg, p = 0.0027), volume (262.1 ± 103.9 vs. 231.5 ± 104.3 ml, p = 0.0036), and PVA (21,913 ± 7,055 vs. 18,357 ± 7,758 mmHg·ml, p = 0.013) decreased. Right ventricular end-diastolic (12.4 ± 4.6 vs. 9.1 ± 3.8 mm Hg, p = 3.8E-5) and end-systolic pressure (42.1 ± 11.9 vs. 34.4 ± 11.1 mm Hg, p = 0.030) and PVA (6,303 ± 3,851 vs. 4,437 ± 2,473 mm Hg·ml, p = 0.027) also decreased. These findings suggest that maximal left ventricular unloading can acutely reduce biventricular filling pressures and PVA in patients with ADHF-CS.

42859281.title: Effect of vasopressin and its analogues on microcirculatory perfusion: a systematic review.
42859281.abstract: Arginine vasopressin (AVP) is a non-adrenergic vasopressor increasingly used in the management of shock. While it restores arterial pressure, its effects on the microcirculation remain uncertain, with potential for reduced regional perfusion and tissue oxygenation. The aim of this systematic review is to evaluate the effects of intravenous AVP and its analogues on microcirculatory perfusion across different haemodynamic conditions and vascular beds. A systematic search of MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Web of Science was conducted. Animal and human publications evaluating the effects of intravenous AVP or analogues on microcirculatory perfusion assessed with in vivo microcirculatory imaging or flowmetry techniques were included. Publications were grouped by haemodynamic condition and vascular bed. Of 1693 records, 39 publications (31 animal, 7 human, 1 combined) were included, comprising 43 study-units and 152 individual measurements. Overall perfusion was decreased in 33%, unchanged in 48%, and increased in 19% of measurements, compared with baseline, saline, or other vasopressors. By haemodynamic condition, perfusion was decreased/unchanged/increased (n=study-units; % of measurements) in physiological conditions (n = 14: 57/38/4), vasodilatory or septic shock (n = 23: 24/55/21; versus baseline, fluid resuscitation or noradrenaline), haemorrhagic shock (n = 3: 17/17/67; versus baseline, saline or noradrenaline), cardiac dysfunction or arrest (n = 2: 0/67/33; versus adrenaline or noradrenaline) and cirrhosis-related portal hypertension (n = 1: 0/0/100). Across vascular beds: gastrointestinal tract (n = 18: 30/42/27), kidney (n = 9: medulla 77/23/0, cortex 27/64/9), sublingual bed (n = 7: 19/68/13), cerebral cortex (n = 2: 0/67/33), cutaneous bed (n = 6: 42/42/17), and conjunctiva (n = 1, 100/0/0). AVP and its analogues reduced microcirculatory perfusion most consistently under physiological conditions, whereas effects in vasodilatory or septic shock were more heterogeneous. Across vascular beds, the highest proportion of measurements showing reduced perfusion was in the renal medulla. These results highlight the divergent effects of vasopressin across vascular beds and clinical conditions.

42855036.title: Early post-ROSC laboratory phenotypes and clinical outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a 10-year national cohort study.
42855036.abstract: Prior phenotyping in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) relied predominantly on prehospital indicators, which neither describe nor grade the underlying ischemia-reperfusion injury. We aimed to derive laboratory-based phenotypes and describe their clinical characteristics and outcome associations. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adult resuscitated OHCA patients of presumed cardiac etiology between 01/02/2011 and 01/01/2022, linking Singapore's national OHCA and cardiovascular databases. Unsupervised latent class analysis (LCA) was applied to 14 laboratory variables within six hours post-return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Stability was confirmed through split-sample validation. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards model, adjusted for age, sex and initial cardiac rhythm, assessed poor neurological recovery at hospital discharge, 30-day and 3-year mortality. Among 1514 eligible patients (median age 65.0 years, 73.6% males), LCA identified three distinct phenotypes: multi-organ dysfunction (MOD, N = 286), homeostatic (HOM, N = 967), and immune-dysregulated (IMD, N = 261), independently reproduced in derivation (entropy = 0.817) and replication (entropy = 0.892) subsamples. The most discriminative variables were creatinine, eosinophil and lymphocyte. Compared to MOD, both HOM (aOR: 0.50, 95% CI 0.30-0.78, p = 0.004) and IMD (aOR: 0.46, 95% CI 0.26-0.78, p = 0.005) phenotypes had significantly lower odds of poor neurological recovery. This pattern was consistent for 30-day mortality (HOM aHR: 0.71, 95% CI 0.61-0.83; IMD aHR: 0.78, 95% CI 0.64-0.94) and 3-year mortality (HOM aHR: 0.70, 95% CI 0.60-0.82; IMD aHR: 0.74, 95% CI 0.62-0.90), all p ≤ 0.01. Early post-ROSC laboratory data identified three prognostically distinct phenotypes among resuscitated OHCA patients. These exploratory findings support external validation and investigation of phenotype-guided therapies.

42855034.title: Opioid-associated vs undifferentiated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: examining differences in outcomes and the relationship with Utstein variables.
42855034.abstract: The pathophysiology of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) due to opioid toxicity is different from other OHCAs. Our aims were to determine: (1) whether opioid-toxicity is associated with OHCA outcomes; and, (2) whether the relationship between Utstein variables and outcomes differ between those with opioid-associated (OA) and other OHCA. We analysed adult emergency medical services (EMS)-treated OHCAs from the British Columbia Cardiac Arrest Registry. Using post-mortem toxicological investigations, death certificates, and hospital-based diagnoses, we classified as OA-OHCA or "undifferentiated OHCA". We fit a multivariable logistic regression model to assess the association between OA-OHCA (versus undifferentiated OHCA) and favourable neurological outcome at hospital discharge. We then added pre-specified interaction terms to individual models for: sex, initial cardiac rhythm, bystander CPR, witnessed arrest, and location type. Of 10,786 OHCAs: 1349 (13%) were OA-OHCA, of whom 331 (25%) were female, and the median age was 40 years (IQR 31-50); 9437 (87%) were undifferentiated, of whom 2910 (31%) were female, and the median age was 70 years (IQR 58-81). We did not detect an association between OA-OHCA (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.77, 1.35) and survival with favourable neurological outcomes. Models adding interaction terms demonstrated statistically significant interactions for: sex (p = 0.032), initial cardiac rhythm (p = 0.024), and bystander-witnessed status (p ≤ 0.001). Overall, we did not detect an association between opioid toxicity and outcomes. In models with interaction terms, the relationship between Utstein and outcomes differed between opioid-associated and other OHCAs, highlighting the impact opioid-associated cases may have in observational OHCA analyses.

42849561.title: Outcomes following impedance threshold device use during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
42849561.abstract: Existing work is equivocal regarding the benefit of impedance threshold device (ITD) use among patients experiencing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). We examined the association of ITD use with prehospital outcomes and longer-term dispositions in a nationally representative sample of OHCA patients. We included adult, non-traumatic, OHCA scene runs from the 2024 ESO Data Collaborative. We compared patients treated with (a) ITD only; (b) ITD and active compression-decompression device (ITD + ACD); and (c) neither device (no ITD). Prehospital outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and survival to hospital arrival (SHA); disposition outcomes included survival to hospital discharge and favorable neurologic outcome (i.e., discharge to home). We used multivariate logistic regression to examine the association of treatment group with outcomes, adjusting for demographics and several potential confounders. We included 97,439 patient records (85.3% no ITD; 13.1% ITD only; 1.6% ITD + ACD). Disposition outcomes were available for 13,026 patients (13.4%). ROSC was higher for patients treated with ITD only (26.7%) than those treated with no ITD (23.8%; aOR = 1.09 [1.04, 1.14]); a similar pattern emerged for SHA. Conversely, survival to discharge was lower for patients treated with ITD only (23.9%) than those treated with no ITD (32.0%; aOR = 0.68, [0.61, 0.76]); a similar pattern emerged for favorable neurologic outcome. The ITD + ACD group showed more extreme versions of the trends observed for ITD only. ITD use was associated with improved prehospital outcomes but worsened dispositional outcomes among patients experiencing OHCA, suggesting this device may prove beneficial early in resuscitation of OHCA patients.

42843615.title: Spectral characteristics and parameters of pulse oximetry waveforms for assessing resuscitation status.
42843615.abstract: Real-time assessment of physiological resuscitation status is critical for guiding personalised cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and avoiding unnecessary harm from prolonged chest compressions. Non-invasive, objectively trackable tools for this purpose remain limited. This multicentre retrospective study (2013-2018) included 451 adult patients with cardiac arrest (497 CPR episodes) from 14 Chinese tertiary hospitals, comprising 158 Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (OHCA) episodes with prehospital SpO2/ECG monitoring continued upon ED arrival and full pulse oximetry plethysmography (POP)/ECG/end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2) monitoring established in the ED, and 339 In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (IHCA) episodes occurring in the ED. We analysed POP waveforms across four statuses: compression-only (CC), chest compression with return of spontaneous circulation (CC + ROSC, spontaneous circulation during ongoing compressions), non-compression without ROSC, and spontaneous circulation-only (SC). Time-domain (area under the POP curve [POPAUC]) and frequency-domain spectral features were evaluated against clinically documented ROSC. A frequency-domain "hybrid" pattern during the CC + ROSC identified ROSC with 100% specificity (PPV 1.000). In CC status, POPAUC was higher in stable-ROSC than unstable-ROSC (3232.2 ± 1008.2 vs. 2769.6 ± 1013.0 PVPG, P = 0.007). The POPAUC was lower in CC + ROSC status than in SC status for stable-ROSC (2768.2 ± 997.8 vs. 3335.8 ± 842.4 PVPG, P = 0.001), but the reverse was observed for unstable-ROSC (2697.5 ± 941.0 vs. 1338.1 ± 952.6 PVPG, P < 0.001). POP waveforms disappearance with concurrent ECG presence identified pulseless electrical activity with 100% specificity. Pulse oximetry plethysmography waveform analysis-using signals already available on standard monitors-may provide a non-invasive, real-time approach that may help identify ROSC during ongoing compressions and distinguish between stable and unstable circulation.

42839245.title: Clinical trials testing early multimodal vasopressor therapy require a dose ceiling, not a dose floor.

42838501.title: Amiodarone after conversion from a non-shockable to a shockable rhythm in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: A propensity score-matched analysis from the German resuscitation registry.
42838501.abstract: Amiodarone should be administered after three shocks according the current ERC ALS guidelines. However, its effect in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients with an initial non-shockable rhythm who subsequently convert to a shockable rhythm is not established. We performed a retrospective observational cohort study using data from the German Resuscitation Registry. Adult patients with non-traumatic OHCA, having an initial non-shockable rhythm and subsequently received at least two defibrillations were included. Propensity-score-matched patient pairs (1:1) were analysed to compare outcomes between patients who received amiodarone during resuscitation and those who did not. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge. Secondary outcomes included hospital admission with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), 24-h survival, survival to hospital discharge, and favourable neurological outcome at hospital discharge. Of 5535 patients included 3181 received amiodarone and 2354 did not. After propensity-score matching, 1843 patients remained in each group. Amiodarone administration was associated with higher rates of hospital admission with ROSC (26.7% vs. 23.0%; OR 1.22, 95% confidence interval 1.05-1.42), 24-h survival (21.4% vs. 14.7%; OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.33-1.87), and survival to hospital discharge (6.5% vs. 4.2%; OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.18-2.12). Favourable neurological outcome at hospital discharge was not statistically significant (3.7% vs. 2.9%; OR 1.31, 95% CI 0.91-1.89). In OHCA patients with an initial non-shockable rhythm who subsequently converted to a shockable rhythm, amiodarone administration was associated with improved short-term and long-term survival, but not with a statistically significant improved favourable neurological outcome. Future controlled studies might define the proper (earlier) time of amiodarone administration.

42838500.title: Impact of cardiac rhythm dynamics during cardiopulmonary resuscitation on clinical outcomes in patients treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR): a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42838500.abstract: Although the initial presenting cardiac rhythm is an established prognostic factor for extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation, heart rhythm dynamics during conventional cardiopulmonary resuscitation remain poorly studied. We evaluated how the evolution of rhythm affects neurological outcomes and survival among recipients of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation. We systematically searched PubMed and Embase for studies evaluating rhythm dynamics, focusing on Rhythm Improvement (from non-shockable to shockable) or Rhythm Decay (from shockable to non-shockable). The primary outcome was survival with a favorable neurological outcome at the longest follow-up; the secondary outcome was overall survival. A random-effects model analysis with the Hartung-Knapp adjustment was used. Ten observational studies evaluating 5183 subjects with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation were included. Rhythm improvement was associated with a higher probability of a favorable neurological outcome (RR 3.12, 95% CI 1.26-7.74; GRADE: Low) compared with refractory non-shockable rhythms. Conversely, rhythm decay reduced the likelihood of a favorable neurological outcome compared with a sustained shockable rhythm (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.21-0.80; GRADE: Moderate). Notably, decay toward asystole showed a robust negative association with good neurological recovery (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.09-0.45; GRADE: Moderate), whereas decay toward pulseless electrical activity did not reach statistical significance (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.31-1.25; GRADE: Low). Rhythm dynamics provide valuable prognostic insights for candidates for extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Rhythm decay toward asystole may predict resuscitation failure and poor neurological survival, suggesting that it should prompt a critical re-evaluation of the appropriateness of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

42838499.title: Non-enrolment and non-completion of cardiac rehabilitation among survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with ischaemic aetiology: a nationwide register-based cohort study.
42838499.abstract: Survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) of ischaemic aetiology is increasing, yet access to and completion of cardiac rehabilitation remain uncertain. To investigate non-enrolment in and non-completion of cardiac rehabilitation among OHCA survivors of ischaemic aetiology including temporal trends, and to examine sociodemographic characteristics associated with non-participation and non-completion. This nationwide Danish register-based cohort study included adults surviving ≥30 days after a first-time OHCA between 2019 and 2023. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to examine the association between non-enrolment and non-completion, respectively, and sociodemographic parameters of age, sex, cohabitation, comorbidity, education, and employment. A total of 1684 OHCA survivors were included. Overall, 55% did not enrol in CR, and among those who enrolled, 50% did not complete the programme. Non-enrolment was highest in 2020-2022 (60-62%) and declined to 43% in 2023. Survivors who were retired had higher odds of non-enrolment (OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.42-2.44), whereas higher education (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.55-0.98) and moderate/severe comorbidity (OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.43-0.65) were associated with lower odds of non-enrolment. No sociodemographic characteristics were significantly associated with non-completion. A large proportion of OHCA survivors of ischaemic aetiology either did not enrol in or did not complete cardiac rehabilitation. The findings underscore the need for systematic referral to cardiac rehabilitation after OHCA and more tailored rehabilitation approaches.

42838497.title: Time to return of spontaneous circulation and long-term outcomes in bystander-witnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survivors.
42838497.abstract: Immediate Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) survival is time-sensitive, however, evidence linking resuscitation time to recovery is limited. We examined time from emergency call to return of spontaneous circulation (time-to-ROSC) and survivor outcomes. From the Danish Cardiac Arrest Registry, we included adults with bystander-witnessed OHCA (2016-2023) surviving ≥30 days, without prior anoxic brain damage or nursing home admission. Time-to-event and multivariable regression analyses stratified by time-to-ROSC (A: 0-10, B: 11-18, C: >18 min) assessed 11-month anoxic brain damage and nursing home admission, plus long-term survival and return-to-work through December 2024. We included 2583 patients (n = 875, 869, 839; groups A-C, respectively), 78% male; median age 65; median time-to-ROSC 14 min. Anoxic brain damage increased with time-to-ROSC (A-C: 0.3%, 1.8%, 3.2%; p < 0.001). Adjusted analyses showed an overall association (p = 0.03); HRs: 5.58 (95% CI 1.58-19.64) for B and 9.98 (95% CI 2.93-33.96) for C versus A. Nursing home admission decreased with time-to-ROSC (A-C: 3.1%, 2.2%, 1.3%; p = 0.04), but adjustments attenuated the association (p = 0.3). Long-term survival was similar (5-year Kaplan-Meier estimate: 79%; 95% CI 77-81%; p = 0.80; adjusted p = 0.99). Among employed patients (n = 177, 168, 179), return-to-work was similar (5-year cumulative incidence: 60%; 95% CI 56-65%; p = 0.31; adjusted p = 0.29). In bystander-witnessed 30-day OHCA survivors, prolonged resuscitation does not preclude recovery, time-to-ROSC was associated with anoxic brain damage but not nursing home admission, return-to-work, or long-term survival.

42838496.title: Automated external defibrillators for in-hospital cardiac arrest: a systematic review.
42838496.abstract: Automated external defibrillators (AEDs) improve survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, but their role in in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) remains uncertain. This systematic review evaluates whether ward-accessible AED capability prior to code blue team arrival improves survival and neurologic outcomes compared with standard resuscitation systems. Six databases were searched. Eligible studies compared AED use to manual defibrillation in IHCA outside specialized areas. Primary outcome was survival with favorable neurological status (CPC 1-2, mRS 0-3, or no deterioration from baseline). Secondary outcomes included ROSC, survival at 24 h, survival to discharge, 30-day survival, CPR quality, and timing metrics. Three independent reviewers performed study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment. Due to substantial heterogeneity, results were synthesized descriptively. Six reports from five unique study cohorts met inclusion criteria (total screened = 5510). Neurologically favorable survival was inconsistent. One study reported improved outcomes following a combined AED-and-training intervention, whereas the largest multicentre cohort found no significant difference in neurological disability among survivors (adjusted relative risk 1.01, 95% CI 0.93-1.09). ROSC and survival to discharge were not consistently improved. Only one study directly quantified AED-associated compression pauses, and effects on time to defibrillation varied by setting. Available evidence is insufficient to determine whether routine ward-level AED deployment improves IHCA outcomes. Included studies were observational and heterogeneous and CPR quality and training were incompletely characterized. Potential benefit from earlier defibrillation in shockable rhythms must be weighed against possible compression interruptions. Contemporary comparative studies are needed.

42838495.title: Prehospital prognostication after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in tertiary care centers: the R-EDByUS score in the JAAM-OHCA registry.
42838495.abstract: The R-EDByUS score predicts unfavorable neurological outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) using prehospital variables alone, with separate models based on return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) status at hospital arrival. However, whether the score remains valid in patients transported to tertiary care centers is uncertain. We therefore aimed to validate it externally in this setting. Using the JAAM-OHCA Registry, we analyzed adult patients with presumed cardiogenic OHCA transported to tertiary care centers. The regression-based R-EDByUS score was applied to predict unfavorable neurological outcome (Cerebral Performance Category 3-5) at 1 month in the prehospital ROSC and ongoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) cohorts. Discrimination and calibration were assessed, and score performance was examined across in-hospital intervention subgroups (percutaneous coronary intervention, targeted temperature management, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation). We also assessed the proportion of patients with unfavorable outcomes among those with a predicted probability ≥99%. Of 29,345 patients, 3305 were classified into the prehospital ROSC cohort and 26,040 into the ongoing CPR cohort. The score showed good discrimination, with areas under the curve of 0.906 and 0.913, and good calibration in the prehospital ROSC cohort. Discrimination was lower among patients who received PCI, TTM, or ECMO in the ongoing CPR cohort. Among patients with a predicted probability ≥99%, 100% (112/112; prehospital ROSC) and 99.9% (20,560/20,588; ongoing CPR) had unfavorable outcomes. The R-EDByUS score showed good discrimination in the JAAM-OHCA Registry, supporting its use for early risk stratification in cardiogenic OHCA even in tertiary care centers.

42837137.title: Integrating Hemodynamic Indices Into the Definition of Refractory Septic Shock: Is There a Role for Catecholamine Refractoriness and Assistance Guide Based on Cardiogenic Shock Hemodynamics (CRASH) Index?

42831066.title: High blood pressure-targeted management associated with reduced benefits of higher body mass index in elderly patients with septic shock: a post hoc analysis of a multicenter randomized controlled trial.
42831066.abstract: Body mass index (BMI) is an important prognostic factor in sepsis, and an obesity paradox has been reported. A higher mean arterial pressure (MAP) target has been associated with worse outcomes in elderly patients with septic shock. However, whether MAP target strategy alters the association between BMI and outcomes in this population is unknown. We conducted a post hoc analysis of the OPTPRESS trial, a multicenter randomized controlled trial at 29 Japanese centers reporting worse outcomes with a high MAP target in elderly patients with septic shock. A total of 489 patients aged ≥65 years with septic shock were assigned to a control MAP target of 65-70 mmHg (n = 245) or high target of 80-85 mmHg (n = 244). Patients were categorized using Asian BMI cutoffs into underweight (<18.5 kg/m2), normal-weight (18.5-22.9 kg/m2), and higher-BMI (≥23 kg/m2) categories. The primary outcome was 90-day mortality. The primary analysis assessed the interaction between BMI category and MAP target strategy. In the control group, mortality decreased across increasing BMI categories (P = 0.03 for the trend), while no trend was observed in the high-target group (P = 0.26 for the trend). After adjustment for age, sex, APACHE II score, Clinical Frailty Scale, and site of infection, MAP target strategy significantly interacted with the higher-BMI category (P = 0.02), but not with underweight (P = 0.41). In the high-target group, both underweight and higher-BMI patients had higher mortality than those with normal BMI (underweight, adjusted HR 1.74 [95% CI 1.02-2.98], P = 0.04; higher BMI, adjusted HR 1.72 [95% CI 1.02-2.87], P = 0.04). Fluid volume per body weight decreased across increasing BMI categories in both groups. The proportion of patients receiving vasopressin increased across BMI categories only in the control group, whereas the body weight-adjusted vasopressin dose among recipients showed no significant trend in either group. In elderly patients with septic shock, mortality decreased across increasing BMI categories under a standard MAP target, whereas patients in the higher-BMI category had higher mortality under a high MAP target. High MAP targets may attenuate the survival benefit of higher BMI, possibly in association with BMI-related patterns in fluid and vasopressor management. Not registered. The original OPTPRESS trial was registered at UMIN Clinical Trials Registry (UMIN000041775) on 13 September 2020.

42956925.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted, Electrocardiogram-Derived, Sequential Rule-Based Decision Tree for Exclusion of Acute Coronary Syndrome as the Etiology of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study.
42956925.abstract: After out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), deciding which patients without ST-segment elevation warrant emergency coronary angiography is difficult, as standard electrocardiogram (ECG), troponin, and echocardiography are limited in the early post-arrest window. We aimed to develop a sequential rule-based decision tree to identify post-ROSC patients in whom acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is unlikely to be the arrest etiology. In this single-center retrospective study, adult patients with OHCA were divided into development (2020-2024; n=329) and temporal validation (2025; n=71) cohorts. Post-ROSC 12-lead ECGs were analyzed by a deep-learning platform generating ten digital biomarkers. Five candidate biomarkers were combined into a rhythm-stratified sequential decision tree under a zero false-negative constraint; its performance was compared with that of individual biomarkers and validated in the temporal cohort. The tree classified 171/329 (52.0%) and 32/71 (45.1%) patients in the development and validation cohorts, respectively, as "ACS not likely," with no adjudicated ACS case misclassified at any node. Yield concentrated in the non-shockable subgroup, in which the model excluded 169/261 (64.8%) non-ACS cases (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC], 0.824), outperforming each individual biomarker. In the shockable subgroup, which carries a high pretest probability of ACS, 38/40 patients (95.0%) were retained as "ACS not excluded." A rhythm-stratified, rule-based decision tree combining AI-assisted ECG-derived biomarkers classified approximately half of post-OHCA patients as "ACS not likely" with no adjudicated ACS case misclassified, principally in the non-shockable subgroup. This transparent, bedside-deployable framework warrants prospective multicenter evaluation.

42956924.title: Ventilation Monitoring in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Care.
42956924.abstract: Adherence to American Heart Association (AHA) ventilation guidelines during cardiac arrest is challenging. Prospective, Before/After quality assurance study determining adherence to AHA ventilation guidelines in adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated by Milwaukee County Emergency Medical Services and Kenosha Fire in Wisconsin using (Before) end tidal carbon dioxide [ETCO2] to monitor ventilations - Real BVM Help® applied but blinded versus (After) Real BVM Help®. mean per-person proportion (%) of ventilations in-target for rate, tidal volume, and both rate and tidal volume. AHA 2020 guidelines were followed. From 9/29/22-12/22/23, 278 patients were entered (148 Before/130 After). Average age: 62.3±16.7 years; 185 (67%) male. Mean per-person proportion (%) of ventilations in Before/After Groups in-target for rate (47.7±25.1% vs 74.4±24.1% respectively, p<0.0001), tidal volume (15.3±15.4% vs 45.4±23.8% respectively, p<0.0001), and rate and tidal volume (7.5±9.6% vs 39.0±23.3% respectively, p<0.0001) were significantly higher in the After Group. In the Before Group, using ETCO2 to monitor all ventilations (N=22,037 ventilations), only 43.8% were in-target for rate, 13.5% in-target for tidal volume, and 6.8% in-target for rate and tidal volume with a lower-than-target tidal volume delivered in 58.2% of all ventilations. Real BVM Help® was associated with statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in adherence to AHA ventilation guidelines. ETCO2 monitoring failed to approach both rate and tidal volume guideline adherence with a lower-than-target tidal volume being the most common parameter delivered out-of-target (58.2%). Ventilation rate and tidal volume monitoring with real-time feedback should be considered during treatment of cardiac arrest.

42956923.title: Early Identification of Recurrent Out-of-hospital Cardiac Arrest Using Clinical ECG Features.
42956923.abstract: Recurrent cardiac arrest (rearrest) after initial return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) is associated with relatively poor outcomes. Early identification of rearrest might allow for intervention to prevent rearrest. In this study, we sought to determine whether clinical ECG features can predict rearrest. We performed a retrospective cohort study of adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients who achieved ROSC between 2018-2024. We evaluated the association of ECG features (QRS width, standard deviation of NN intervals, root mean square of successive NN interval differences, and percentage of NN intervals that differ by more than 50 milliseconds) within individual 15-second segments throughout a 5-minute window prior to rearrest as well as their temporal trends over the 5-minute analytic window. Of the 1,489 OHCA patients achieving ROSC, 1,298 were analyzed; 528 (40.7%) experienced rearrest. Rearrest patients were older, less likely to receive bystander CPR (48.7% vs. 61.9%), and had lower survival (20.4% vs. 43.1%) and favorable neurologic outcomes (7.8% vs. 21.2%; all p<0.001). We found lower heart rate, wider QRS, and higher HR variability in those with rearrest. Identification was highest 1 minute prior to rearrest (AUROC 0.74), declining beyond 3 minutes. Models using temporal trends achieved AUROC 0.67; strongest predictors were heart rate variability measures and QRS width. Established ECG features achieved good prediction for rearrest with identification improving closer to time of rearrest. Future work leveraging novel features or more advanced artificial intelligence models may further improve prediction.

42956360.title: Dynamic Early Postreperfusion Physiology Is Associated With Organ Recovery After Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation.
42956360.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
42956360.abstract: Prognostication after extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) predominantly relies on characteristics available before or at initiation of extracorporeal support. We investigated whether the early metabolic response to extracorporeal reperfusion provides complementary information on subsequent recovery. We retrospectively analyzed 91 patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated with ECPR. Lactate was assessed before and 12 h after extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) initiation. Outcomes included in-hospital mortality, successful ECMO weaning, cerebral edema/hypoxic brain injury, and favorable neurological survival. Associations were adjusted for low-flow duration. Twelve hour lactate was lower in survivors than nonsurvivors (5.45 vs. 9.04 mmol/L; p = 0.002), whereas prereperfusion lactate did not differ. In paired measurements (n = 38), mortality discrimination increased from an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.47 before reperfusion to 0.80 at 12 h. Each 5 mmol/L higher 12 h lactate was associated with mortality (odds ratio [OR] = 2.73), lower odds of ECMO weaning (OR = 0.44), and cerebral edema/hypoxic injury (OR = 2.07) after low-flow adjustment. Early metabolic response after extracorporeal reperfusion was associated with survival and both circulatory and cerebral recovery. Dynamic post-reperfusion physiology may provide complementary information beyond static pre-reperfusion assessment.

42950975.title: Traumatic Emergency Thoracotomy for Resuscitation in Shock (TETRiS): a national service evaluation of resuscitative thoracotomy practice outside the operating theatre.
42950975.abstract: Resuscitative thoracotomy (RT) is performed in patients with traumatic cardiac arrest or peri-arrest to treat potentially reversible causes of circulatory collapse. Optimal patient selection and timing remain uncertain, and existing evidence is largely retrospective, often excluding prehospital deaths. This prospective service evaluation examined contemporary RT practice and outcomes across a national major trauma system, including prehospital and emergency department settings. Prospective 12-month observational study across 20 UK Helicopter Emergency Medical Services and 26 Major Trauma Centre Emergency Departments, using the PHOTON, TERN, and NaTRIC research networks. A total of 116 patients underwent RT, of which 82 (70.7%) were performed prehospital. Median age was 30 years, 97 patients (83.6%) were male, and 81 (69.8%) sustained penetrating injury. Suspected cardiac tamponade was the most common indication for RT (72/116 [62.1%]), although operative findings demonstrated exsanguinating haemorrhage in 82 patients (70.7%). Overall, 50 patients (43.1%) achieved return of spontaneous circulation and eight (6.9%) survived to hospital discharge. Survival was strongly associated with pathophysiological cause, duration of arrest, and physiological state at the time of intervention, with substantially better outcomes observed in patients with cardiac tamponade than exsanguination. Patients undergoing emergency department RT demonstrated shorter arrest durations, more favourable physiology, and higher survival than those undergoing prehospital RT. There were no survivors beyond 10 minutes of traumatic cardiac arrest. In this prospective national evaluation of RT practice, outcomes were strongly associated with the pathophysiological cause and duration of arrest, and the residual physiology present at the time of intervention. The most favourable outcomes were observed in patients with cardiac tamponade and those undergoing RT before irreversible physiological deterioration.

42946298.title: Closest to the patient, furthest from survival? Reframing the family witness for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in our aging world.

42934779.title: Heterogeneous cardiovascular responses to acute mean arterial pressure augmentation in septic shock: the role of ventriculo-arterial coupling and venous return.
42934779.abstract: In patients with septic shock, vasopressor-induced mean arterial pressure (MAP) augmentation is commonly used to restore tissue perfusion; however, patients may exhibit divergent cardiovascular responses despite achieving similar arterial pressure targets. We hypothesized that this heterogeneity reflects the differences in ventricular adaptation to increases in arterial load and venous return determinants. We conducted a prospective physiological observational study in mechanically ventilated adults with septic shock who underwent transient MAP augmentation from approximately 65 to 85 mmHg after the initial hemodynamic resuscitation. MAP was increased by norepinephrine dose escalation or by adding vasopressin according to clinical judgment. Comprehensive transthoracic echocardiography was performed immediately before and after MAP augmentation. Patients were classified a priori according to the relative changes in cardiac output (CO): flow recruitment (> 15% increase), stable flow (- 15% to + 15%), or flow deterioration (> 15% decrease). Changes in effective arterial elastance (Ea), end-systolic elastance (Ees), VA coupling (Ea/Ees), stroke volume, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), analogue mean systemic filling pressure (Pmsa), and derived venous return variables were analyzed. Thirty-two patients were included. Despite comparable increases in MAP, the cardiovascular responses were heterogeneous: 10 patients (31%) exhibited flow recruitment, 17 (53%) maintained a stable flow, and 5 (16%) developed flow deterioration. Patients with flow deterioration showed a greater increase in Ea without a proportional increase in Ees, resulting in worsening VA coupling (ΔEa/Ees + 0.22 IQR [0.01-0.81]), whereas VA coupling remained stable or improved in patients with preserved or increased flow (p = 0.035). Flow deterioration was also associated with reduced LVEF and changes in the derived venous return indices, which may have contributed to the observed reduction in forward flow. Changes in VA coupling correlated with changes in IVCT (ρ = 0.788, p < 0.0001), MPI (ρ = 0.599, p < 0.0003), stroke volume (ρ =-0.418, p = 0.017), and LVEF (ρ=-0.431, p = 0.0139). Acute MAP augmentation elicits heterogeneous cardiovascular responses in patients with septic shock despite similar increases in arterial pressure. Flow deterioration is characterized by worsening VA coupling, reduced stroke volume, and impaired systolic adaptation, potentially modulated by changes in the derived venous return indices.

42924421.title: GDF-15 as an early marker for prognosis in patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest - Experience from the HAnnover COoling REgistry.
42924421.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine

42920184.title: Laxative use after cardiac arrest: exposure timing, treatment selection, and outcome interpretation.
42920184.abstract: We commend Duan et al. for examining laxative use after cardiac arrest. However, because follow-up began at return of spontaneous circulation, whereas exposure timing was not reported, the observed association may reflect both immortal time and treatment selection: patients who survived and recovered sufficiently may have been more likely to receive laxatives. A time-varying exposure defined by first administration, with landmark analysis as a sensitivity analysis, would better align treatment and risk time. The reported time-varying-effect model does not estimate the effect of initiating treatment on a particular day and, therefore, cannot support a 15-day treatment window. The findings should be framed as observational associations rather than evidence that laxatives improve survival.

42901371.title: Fatigue, anxiety and depression 12 months after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a population based cohort study.
42901371.abstract: To determine the prevalence and factors associated with fatigue, anxiety, and depression 12 months after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA); examine their associations with health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and functional recovery; and compare symptom burden with population norms. This prospective, population-based cohort study included adults (≥18 years) who received EMS-attempted resuscitation and survived to hospital discharge following non-traumatic OHCA in Victoria, Australia, between July 2019 and June 2022. Survivors were identified from a statewide OHCA registry and completed a 12-month telephone interview. Primary outcomes were fatigue (Modified Fatigue Impact Scale), anxiety and depression (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale). Secondary outcomes included HRQoL (EQ-5D, SF-12), functional recovery (GOSE), living arrangement, and return to work. Of 1068 eligible 12-month survivors, 728 (68.2%) completed follow-up (median age 61 years; 555 [76.2%] male). Fatigue was reported by 35.8% (250/699), anxiety by 22.6% (162/716), and depression by 18.0% (129/716). Higher symptom burden was associated with lower EQ-5D and SF-12 scores, worse GOSE outcomes (all p < 0.001) and reduced return-to-work rates. Compared with population norms, survivors reported greater fatigue (SMD 0.64; 95%CI, 0.50-0.78; p < 0.001), and depression (SMD, 0.12; 95%CI, 0.02-0.21; p = 0.02) but lower anxiety (SMD, -0.27; 95%CI, -0.35 to -0.18; p < 0.001). In adjusted models, younger age, preexisting anxiety or depression, diabetes and initial non-shockable arrest were associated with higher symptom burden, whereas EMS-witnessed arrests were associated with lower symptom burden. Fatigue, anxiety, and depression were common at 12 months after OHCA and are associated with poorer recovery. Fatigue exceeded population norms and may be an under-recognised component of cardiac arrest survivorship.

42901370.title: Regional implementation of a prehospital advanced life support program with video-assisted physician direction and outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
42901370.abstract: The smart advanced life support (SALS) program was introduced to provide prehospital advanced life support under real-time video-assisted physician direction for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). This study evaluated the association between regional SALS implementation and OHCA outcomes. This retrospective cohort study used difference-in-differences and event-study analyses with data from the OHCA surveillance system in South Korea and included adult OHCA cases (aged ≥19 years) from 2 years before through 4 years after SALS implementation in August 2015. The exposure was region-level implementation of SALS. Outcomes were the prehospital time interval, prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to discharge, and favorable neurological outcome. Pre- to post-implementation changes were compared between regions with and without SALS. A total of 129,207 cases were included. SALS regions had greater increases in the prehospital time interval (4.12 min; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.91-5.33) and prehospital ROSC (1.35 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.56-2.15) than regions without SALS. No significant additional improvements were observed in survival to discharge (-0.35 percentage points; 95% CI, -1.31 to 0.62) or favorable neurological outcome (-0.35 percentage points; 95% CI, -1.08 to 0.37). Event-study analyses suggested differential pre-intervention trends for prehospital time, but not for the other outcomes. SALS regions showed greater increases in prehospital time and prehospital ROSC without significant improvements in survival to discharge or favorable neurological outcome, but the finding for prehospital time should be interpreted cautiously because differential pre-intervention trends were observed.

42901369.title: Association between capnographic changes during pulse checks of varying durations and clinical outcomes during cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a multicenter study from Türkiye (CaPTuRe).
42901369.abstract: To investigate the association between capnographic changes during pulse checks of different durations and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) outcomes. This multicenter, prospective, controlled, quasi-randomized study categorized patients according to pulse check duration: Group A (≤5 s) and Group B (>5-≤10 s). Five measurements were obtained during the first six CPR cycles. Four capnographic parameters were evaluated for each measurement: Post-CPR end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2), Pre-CPR ETCO2, loss rate (percentage decrease between Post- and Pre-CPR ETCO2), and recovery time (time required to regain the previous cycle's Post-CPR ETCO2). The study included 252 cardiac arrest patients (Group A, n = 124; Group B, n = 128). In Group A, patients with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) had markedly lower loss rates and shorter recovery times than non-survivors, together with higher pre- and post-CPR ETCO2 values (all p < 0.001). Group A also had a higher ROSC rate than Group B (36.3% vs. 19.5%; p = 0.005). Logistic regression identified pulse check duration as an independent predictor of ROSC, with Group A having 2.39-fold higher odds of ROSC than Group B (odds ratio [OR] = 2.39, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.347-4.242; p = 0.003). Pre-CPR ETCO2 was strongly negatively correlated with loss rate (ρ = -0.770), whereas Pre- and Post-CPR ETCO2 values (ρ = 0.96) and loss rate and recovery time (ρ = 0.89) were strongly positively correlated. Pulse checks completed within 5 s were associated with more favorable capnographic dynamics and higher ROSC rates than those lasting 6-10 s. These findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant prospective validation.

42901368.title: Identifying the operational bottleneck to shock delivery after automated external defibrillator activation.
42901368.abstract: Cardiac arrest registries record automated external defibrillator (AED) use and shock delivery but not post-activation operational timing. We aimed to identify the largest measurable bottleneck and an exploratory pad-application target for shock delivery within 60 s of AED power-on. We retrospectively analyzed timestamps from remotely monitored Nihon Kohden AEDs between January 2018 and February 2026. After excluding inspection records, we grouped records into activation events and quantified intervals. Shock-timing and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were restricted to initially shock-advised events with recorded shock delivery. We analyzed 8115 activation events. Median times were 42 s (interquartile range [IQR], 30-56) from power-on to completion of pad application, nine seconds (IQR, 9-11) from pad application to the first analysis, and 52 s (IQR, 40-66) from power-on to the first analysis endpoint. The power-on-to-pad-application interval accounted for a median of 81% (IQR, 75-85) of the total power-on-to-first-analysis interval, increasing to 87% (IQR, 85-90) when first analysis occurred more than 60 s after power-on. Among 900 initially shock-advised events with recorded shock delivery, the median pad-application-to-shock interval was 15 s (IQR 13-17). Exploratory ROC analysis yielded a power-on to pad-application threshold of ≥51 s in relation to first recorded shock delivery occurring more than 60 s after AED power-on. The interval from AED power-on to electronically detected completion of pad application, encompassing all intervening actions, was the largest measurable post-activation bottleneck. Completion within 50 s may serve as an exploratory process target for first recorded shock delivery within 60 s among initially shock-advised events.

42901367.title: Association between burst-suppression with identical bursts and multimodal measures of cerebral oxygenation after cardiac arrest.
authors: Pittsburgh Post Cardiac Arrest Service Investigators
42901367.abstract: Burst-suppression with identical bursts (BSIB) is an electroencephalographic (EEG) pattern associated with severe post-cardiac arrest brain injury (PCABI). Whether modifiable mechanisms of brain injury underlie BSIB is unknown. We hypothesized BSIB is associated with impaired cerebral oxygen metabolism, reflected as pathologically elevated jugular bulb venous oxygen saturation (SjvO2), higher brain tissue oxygen tension (PbtO2), normal jugular bulb venous-to-arterial carbon dioxide gradient (PbCO2 gap, and lower intracranial pressure (ICP) compared to other EEG patterns. This single-center retrospective study included patients resuscitated from cardiac arrest who underwent EEG and SjvO2 or PbtO2 monitoring. We categorized EEG patterns as BSIB, malignant without BSIB, and non-malignant. Using mixed effects linear regression, we examined associations between EEG and SjvO2, PbCO2 gap, PbtO2, and ICP. The SjvO2 and PbtO2 cohorts included 109 and 33 patients, respectively. SjvO2 did not differ between BSIB and malignant EEGs (β = 3; 95% CI, -0.6 to 7.0), but was higher with BSIB compared to non-malignant patterns (β = 12; 95% CI, 7.0 to 16.0). BSIB was associated with lower PbCO2 gap compared to malignant (β = -1.4; 95% CI, -2.6 to -0.3) and non-malignant (β = -2.6; 95% CI, -4.1 to -1.0) patterns. PbtO2 was highest with BSIB, but not significantly higher compared to malignant patterns in our adjusted model (β = 4.0; 95% CI, -4.7 to 13.0). ICP was lower in those with BSIB compared to malignant patterns (β = -19.0; 95% CI, -32.5 to -5.6). BSIB may represent a distinct subtype of PCABI characterized by impaired oxygen metabolism with preserved oxygen delivery and diffusion.

42901366.title: Real-time feedback during bag-valve-mask ventilation for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a before-and-after study (VEntilation during Cardiac Arrest Resuscitation Study, VECARS-2).
authors: Paris Fire Brigade Cardiac Arrest Task Force
42901366.abstract: This study compared bag-valve-mask ventilation quality and adherence to the guideline-recommended ventilation volume range during 30:2 cardiopulmonary resuscitation for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest before and after the implementation of real-time feedback. We conducted a before-and-after observational study of two sequential adult cohorts with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest managed by basic life support teams from the Paris Fire Brigade. A bidirectional sensor measured insufflated volume (Vi) and expiratory tidal volume (Vt). The display was masked during Period-1 and provided real-time feedback during Period-2. We assessed adherence to the guideline-recommended range using mixed-effects regression; we analyzed Vt and leak volume using gamma log-link generalized linear mixed models. We analyzed 4300 ventilations in 163 patients, 96 without feedback and 67 with feedback. Median Vi was lower with feedback (471 mL) than without (513 mL, p = 0.03 for the first ventilation of each cycle) but median Vt was unchanged (235 vs. 243 mL, p = 0.84). Vi dispersion was reduced by 35% (mean within-patient IQR ratio 0.65 [95%-CI, 0.53-0.77]). Vi was 400-600 mL in 68% of ventilations with feedback vs. 42% without feedback. In contrast, Vt was 400-600 mL in only 14% of ventilations with feedback vs. 15% without feedback. In multivariable analysis, leak volume was 12% lower with feedback (mean ratio, 0.88 [95%-CI, 0.77-0.99]). Real-time feedback was associated with improved adherence to the guideline-recommended range for Vi, less dispersed VI, and lower leak volume. Causal inference, clinical significance, and generalizability warrant further evaluation.

42892479.title: Making blood work: Toward precision care after cardiac arrest.

42881421.title: Hemoglobin trends and transfusion practices after cardiac arrest: a cohort study.
42881421.abstract: Hemoglobin targets are absent from post-cardiac arrest guidelines. New trials suggest that patients with brain and myocardial injury, injuries common post-arrest, may benefit from higher hemoglobin targets. Trends in post-arrest hemoglobin and real-world practices remain poorly characterized. We performed a retrospective cohort study of consecutive adult cardiac arrests at three academic hospitals. We screened in-hospital and out-of-hospital arrests with resuscitation efforts ongoing at hospital arrival for inclusion. Patients who survived the initial resuscitation and had a hemoglobin value measured were included. All post-arrest hemoglobin values and red blood cell transfusions were collected through 30 days; descriptive statistics and graphical visualization were used to present hemoglobin trends and transfusion practices. Exploratory analyses evaluated the association between hemoglobin and in-hospital mortality. Of 2,634 cardiac arrests, 958 met inclusion criteria, with 152 (15.9%) out-of-hospital arrests and 806 (84.1%) in-hospital. The mean initial post-arrest hemoglobin was 9.75 g/dL (SD 2.60), with hemoglobin levels declining progressively over the first 20 days post-arrest. Red cell transfusions were delivered for 369 (38.5%) patients in the 30 days post-arrest, with 1,238 total transfusions. The mean pre-transfusion hemoglobin value was 6.96 g/dL (SD 1.06). Pre-transfusion hemoglobin levels were < 7 g/dL for 762 (61.6%) of transfusions, and ≥ 7 g/dL for 476 (38.4%) of transfusions. Over 30 days, the highest proportion of patients transfused was in the first 48 h. Patients with initial post-arrest hemoglobin ≥ 9 g/dL had lower in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.46-0.84, p<0.01). In time-varying analysis, post-arrest hemoglobin through 30 days demonstrated an L-shaped association with mortality, with 95% of the total reduction in mortality hazard captured below 9.20 g/dL. Anemia is common after cardiac arrest, worsening in initial survivors. There is substantial variation in pre-transfusion hemoglobin levels, reflecting clinical equipoise. Clinical trials are needed to disentangle anemia as a driver versus a marker of outcomes, and test whether the risk is modifiable.

42962233.title: Outcomes and Complications of Axillary Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump Support: A Single-Center Experience.
42962233.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
42962233.abstract: Axillary intra-aortic balloon pump (axi-IABP) support has emerged as an alternative to femoral access for patients with advanced heart failure, offering improved mobility and potential benefits in pretransplant conditioning; however, data on associated complications remain limited. We conducted a retrospective study of 55 patients who underwent axi-IABP placement between January 2019 and July 2025 at our institution. The cohort had a median age of 59 (interquartile range [IQR], 52-65) years and presented with cardiogenic shock requiring mechanical circulatory support (MCS). Axi-IABP successfully bridged 87.3% of patients to advanced therapies. A total of 83 complications were identified in 60.0% of patients, most commonly malposition in 23.6% of patients, gas leak alarms in 16.4% of patients, and kinking in 16.4% of patients. Serious vascular complications were infrequent. The median time to first complication was 10.5 (IQR, 2.75-25.5) days. Female sex was associated with a higher hazard of first complication when controlled for height (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] = 2.75, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.04-7.27; p = 0.041). In conclusion, axi-IABP is an effective bridging strategy that enhances patient mobility but is associated with a high rate of device-related complications, predominantly mechanical in nature, underscoring the importance of careful patient selection and monitoring.

42819483.title: Derivation of a novel clinical phenotype of sepsis in critically ill patients: a secondary analysis of a multicentre, prospective, observational study.
42819483.abstract: Sepsis is a highly heterogeneous syndrome. Providing personalized treatment for the various clinical phenotypes of sepsis has been a major challenge for critical care physicians. This study was a secondary analysis of data derived from a multicenter, prospective, observational study of sepsis patients. Based on relevance to sepsis onset or outcome, 25 parameters were selected by the derived cohort to derive sepsis phenotypes. Clustered phenotypes were derived via k-means clustering and examined in a sensitivity analysis using divisive hierarchical clustering. Then, the relationship between fluid resuscitation therapy and survival outcomes was assessed for each clustered phenotype using generalized estimating equations. Patients with sepsis were categorized into Cluster A, B and C. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed Cluster A patients had the highest 28-day mortality (P = 0.029 by Log-rank test). In Cluster A, septic patients who received fluid resuscitation had a association than those who did not, with an adjusted RD for 28-day mortality of 16.2% (95% CI, 1.4 to 31.0%, P = 0.032). Sensitivity analyses adjusted for APACHE II and infection site confirmed these findings, with an adjusted RD for 28-day mortality of 6.3% (95% CI, 0.3 to 12.3%, P = 0.040). Hierarchical clustering methods yielded consistent conclusions. The association between fluid resuscitation and clinical outcomes varied across sepsis phenotypes, suggesting potential heterogeneity in treatment response that requires further prospective validation.Trial registration: The primary study was registered in the China Clinical Registry on February 1, 2022, with the registration number ChiCTR2200056179.

42940415.title: Multidimensional Factors and Predictors of Vulnerability and Frailty in Older Adults: A Systematic Review.
42940415.abstract: Population ageing is characterized by rising multimorbidity and multifaceted vulnerability. While vulnerability is inherently a biopsychosocial state, clinical research predominantly operationalizes risk through physical frailty phenotypes, constraining holistic geriatric care. Identifying the interplay across biological, functional, and psychosocial domains is essential for comprehensive risk evaluation. To synthesize multidimensional factors associated with vulnerability and frailty in adults aged ≥65, categorizing cross-sectional correlates and prospective longitudinal predictors to inform multidimensional assessment. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, systematic searches were conducted across PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar (2020-2025). Independent reviewers performed screening, selection, extraction, and Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal (PROSPERO: CRD420251039796). Forty studies (22 cross-sectional, 17 cohort, 1 quasi-experimental) comprising 77,229 cumulative participant observations across community, outpatient, inpatient, and residential care settings were synthesized. Thirty-seven candidate determinants were mapped across five domains: biological/clinical, psychological, socioeconomic/relational, lifestyle, and self-care profile. Advanced age, multimorbidity, and polypharmacy were the most frequent clinical factors; prospective cohorts specifically linked high anticholinergic burden and functional dependence in complex activities to incident frailty. Depressive symptoms, cognitive decline, low education, financial strain, and social isolation consistently delineated vulnerable states. Vulnerability in older adults is a multifaceted construct requiring assessment tools that extend beyond isolated physical markers. Rather than a definitive feature set, these identified factors provide an evidence-based pool of candidate variables that may inform future risk-stratification and predictive modeling initiatives, supporting integrated, person-centered care.

42919167.title: Prediction of death by neurologic criteria in patients with non-traumatic acute brain injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42919167.abstract: Robust predictors of death by neurologic criteria (DNC) after non-traumatic acute brain injury remain insufficiently defined. We therefore aimed to systematically synthesize the available evidence on prediction of DNC in non-traumatic brain injury. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, the Cochrane Library and Web of Science were searched to August 31, 2026. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials, observational studies, case series and registry data. Studies were included in the quantitative synthesis when sufficient comparable data for the same prognostic factor were available from at least two studies. Pooled effect estimates were calculated using random-effects models. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality in Prognosis Studies (QUIPS) tool. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The database search identified 2,091 records. Eighteen studies comprising reported study cohorts of 9,070 participants were included. Quantitative synthesis included four studies (n=1,738), comprising two post-cardiac arrest and two stroke cohorts. In stroke populations, CT markers of severe intracranial mass effect were associated with a more than threefold increased odds of DNC (pooled OR 3.14, 95%CI 1.98-4.96; p<0.0001; I2=0%), while in post-cardiac arrest cohorts lower gray-white matter ratio values were associated with progression to DNC (pooled mean difference -0.15, 95%CI -0.22 to -0.07; p<0.001; I2=72%). Evidence on predictors of DNC after non-traumatic acute brain injury remains limited and methodologically heterogeneous, with only a small number of studies providing robust analyses. Across these studies, CT-based markers - particularly indicators of diffuse cerebral edema or intracranial mass effect - show the most reproducible associations with progression to DNC.

42920117.title: Considerations for emergency airway management and resuscitation in cancer patients: a review.
42920117.abstract: Cancer patients frequently present to the emergency department (ED) with malignancy or treatment-related critical illness, requiring airway intervention or resuscitation. Multiple factors such as anatomical distortion, treatment sequelae, frailty, and complex goals-of-care considerations create unique challenges. This narrative review aims to provide practical, evidence-informed guidance in airway management and resuscitation of oncologic patients. We conducted a review of the literature addressing airway management, physiologic alterations associated with malignancy and cachexia, pharmacologic considerations for rapid sequence intubation, and resuscitation outcomes in cancer populations. We synthesized relevant clinical guidelines and studies to develop an overview of recommendations applicable to ED practice. Cancer patients present numerous airway management challenges due to tumor or surgical airway alternations, post-radiation fibrosis, edema, and bleeding. Physiologic factors-including reduced functional residual capacity, anemia, muscle wasting, and systemic inflammation-shorten safe apnea time, increase risk of peri-intubation hypoxia, and hemodynamic instability. Malnutrition, organ dysfunction, and chemotherapy toxicity alter pharmacokinetics, necessitating individualized selection and dosing of induction and paralytic agents. Early anticipation of difficulties in airway management, optimized preoxygenation, advanced airway techniques, and multidisciplinary involvement are essential. Resuscitation planning must incorporate realistic prognostication and clear discussions regarding code status. Late or absent documentation of goals-of-care remains common. Airway management and resuscitation in cancer patients require a specialized, patient-centered approach. Future research should address comparative outcomes in the cancer population and support development of ED-specific oncologic protocols. Integration of structured goals-of-care frameworks and early palliative care help ensure ethically aligned, high-quality emergency care.

42818838.title: Interpretable machine learning models using early dynamic clinical features to predict early hemodynamic stabilization after vasopressor initiation in patients with septic shock: development in MIMIC-IV and external validation in eICU.
42818838.abstract: Early hemodynamic stabilization after vasopressor initiation in septic shock is heterogeneous and difficult to predict. We aimed to develop and externally validate interpretable machine learning models for predicting early hemodynamic stabilization. This retrospective study used MIMIC-IV for model development and internal validation and eICU for external validation. Adult ICU patients with septic shock receiving vasopressors were included. Dynamic clinical features during the first 6 h after vasopressor initiation were used to predict stabilization during 6-24 h, defined by sustained mean arterial pressure (MAP) control without vasopressor escalation or increased norepinephrine-equivalent dose. Seven machine learning models were compared. Performance was assessed using discrimination, calibration, Brier score, decision curve analysis, external validation, and SHAP. The MIMIC-IV and eICU cohorts included 3,445 and 453 patients, with stabilization rates of 41.77% and 32.67%, respectively. Gradient boosting machine (GBM) showed the best overall performance, with an AUC of 0.720 and Brier score of 0.209 in internal validation and an AUC of 0.730 and Brier score of 0.192 in external validation. At the training-derived threshold, external sensitivity and specificity were 0.466 and 0.797. SHAP identified early MAP stability, lactate clearance, platelet count, renal function, inflammatory burden, and vasopressor intensity as major predictors. The stabilization endpoint was associated with ICU and hospital mortality and remained robust to alternative MAP definitions. However, predictive performance was substantially driven by proximal hemodynamic features, particularly MAP trajectories, and the full GBM did not consistently outperform simpler hemodynamic benchmarks externally. Early dynamic clinical features provided moderate discrimination for predicting hemodynamic stabilization after vasopressor initiation, with similar external performance. The model should be interpreted as a structured risk-stratification tool rather than a measure of pharmacological vasopressor responsiveness. Prospective validation is required before clinical implementation.

42967102.title: Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation With Ventricular Unloading in Fulminant Influenza A (H1N1) Perimyocarditis: A Case Report.
42967102.abstract: Fulminant perimyocarditis is an uncommon cause of cardiogenic shock and refractory cardiac arrest. We describe Influenza A (H1N1)-associated perimyocarditis managed with a stepwise extracorporeal resuscitation strategy. A 54-year-old woman presented with chest pain, hypoxemia, and cardiogenic shock. Electrocardiography (ECG) showed diffuse ST-segment elevation. Echocardiography revealed severe biventricular dysfunction and a fibrinous pericardial effusion and coronary angiography excluded obstructive disease. Despite vasoactive support and mechanical circulatory support with microaxial flow pump Impella CP (flow 2.7 L/min.), she deteriorated to Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) Stage E with pulseless electrical activity (PEA). During automated chest compressions, mechanical circulatory support with femoral Impella CP was rapidly escalated to venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO). Respiratory polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for Influenza A (H1N1) virus. Antiviral therapy, heparin anticoagulation, ventilation, and organ support were instituted. Hemodynamics stabilized, lactate cleared, and neurological examination after decannulation was intact. Progressive myocardial recovery permitted VA-ECMO explant on Day 3 and Impella CP removal 24 h thereafter. She was extubated on Day 6 and discharged from intensive care unit (ICU) on Day 10. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging confirmed myocarditis; echocardiography at follow-up showed preserved biventricular function. In fulminant perimyocarditis with refractory arrest, rapid activation of an extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) pathway with early VA-ECMO-combined with ventricular unloading-can bridge to myocardial recovery and favorable neurological outcome. Regional systems enabling safe transfer under continuous cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) are critical.

42970124.title: Sodium bicarbonate therapy for metabolic acidosis in critically ill patients: a Bayesian systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
42970124.abstract: To evaluate the effects of sodium bicarbonate therapy on mortality and renal outcomes in critically ill adults with metabolic acidosis. We performed a systematic review and Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing intravenous sodium bicarbonate with placebo or usual care in adult intensive care unit patients with metabolic acidosis. MEDLINE, Embase and CENTRAL were searched from inception to December 2025, with an updated search on 2 April 2026. The primary outcome was short-term all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included renal replacement therapy (RRT) initiation, 90-day mortality, RRT-free days, vasopressor-free days, intensive care unit and hospital length of stay and adverse events. Four RCTs including 1544 patients were analysed. Sodium bicarbonate did not show a clear short-term mortality benefit (RR 0.94, 95% CrI 0.73-1.22), with a posterior probability of benefit of 72.1%. For RRT initiation, sodium bicarbonate was associated with a lower risk (RR 0.74, 95% CrI 0.59-0.98), with a posterior probability of benefit of 97.2%. Effects on other outcomes were small or imprecise, and no consistent safety signal was identified. Current randomised evidence does not demonstrate a clear survival benefit from sodium bicarbonate therapy in critically ill adults with metabolic acidosis, but suggests a high probability of reducing RRT initiation. Further trials should define the patients most likely to benefit. PROSPERO registration: CRD420251246519.
