42968810.title: Comparison of Peripherally Inserted Central Catheters versus Central Venous Catheters in a Medical Intensive Care Unit: A Single-Center Retrospective Study.
42968810.abstract: Patients in medical intensive care units (MICUs) often require prolonged intravenous therapy, making optimal catheter selection critical. While central venous catheters (CVCs) remain common, peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs) are increasingly used. This single-centre retrospective study compared indwelling time, clinical utility, and complication profiles between PICCs and CVCs in MICU patients. We analyzed 276 MICU patients with either a PICC or CVC, comparing catheter selection, length of stay, dwell time, and complication rates. Complication rates were also standardized per 1000 catheter-days. PICCs were used more frequently in patients with malignancy (P < 0.001) or requiring chemotherapy (P < 0.001), whereas CVCs were preferred in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (P = 0.012), diabetes (P = 0.012), COVID-19 (P = 0.020), or vasopressor infusion (P = 0.001). PICCs were associated with longer indwelling times (≥12 days, P < 0.001). In the unstandardized analysis, PICCs had higher rates of catheter dislodgement (P < 0.001) and occlusion (P = 0.005), but lower rates of puncture-site complications (bleeding, hypersensitivity, fluid leakage; all P < 0.05) and deep vein thrombosis incidence (P = 0.038). After standardization per 1,000 catheter-days, dislodgement remained significantly more frequent with PICCs, whereas the difference in occlusion was no longer statistically significant. No bloodstream infections occurred with PICCs, versus 5.4% with CVCs (P = 0.169). Because groups differed substantially in patient selection, clinical indication, dwell time, insertion site, and securement method, these findings should be interpreted as associations rather than evidence of superiority. PICCs were associated with longer indwelling times and a higher rate of dislodgement, but lower rates of puncture-site complications and deep vein thrombosis; the difference in occlusion was no longer significant after standardization. Vascular access selection should be individualized according to patient characteristics, therapy requirements, anticipated duration, and device-related risks.

42962929.title: Acute-on-chronic liver failure: A global multisociety consensus on definitions.
authors: European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL)
American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)
Asia-Pacific Association for the Study of the Liver (APASL)
Latin American Association for the Study of the Liver (ALEH)
Society on Liver Disease in Africa (SOLDA). Electronic address: jasmohan.bajaj@vcuhealth.org
Society on Liver Disease in Africa (SOLDA)
42962929.abstract: The acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) multisociety harmonisation initiative represents a global collaborative effort to establish a unified, evidence-based framework for the definition, diagnosis, grading, and management of ACLF. Building on the strengths of existing regional definitions and integrating diverse international perspectives, this consensus provides a pragmatic, globally applicable foundation for clinical practice, research, and education. It also establishes a common framework for patient stratification, organ dysfunction and failure assessment, critical care management, liver transplantation, and the design of future phase II/III trials. Standardised, regulatory-aligned endpoints are expected to improve cross-study comparability, strengthen collaboration, and accelerate development of effective ACLF therapies.

42970821.title: A Retrospective Audit of Maternal Bacteraemia in a Tertiary Referral Maternity Hospital in Brisbane, Australia From 2015 to 2024.
42970821.journal: The Australian & New Zealand journal of obstetrics & gynaecology
42970821.abstract: Maternal infection is a major cause of pregnancy-related maternal morbidity and mortality in Australia. To determine the prevalence, microbiology, probable source, clinical characteristics, laboratory results, time to antibiotic therapy, reasons for intensive care admission, and maternal morbidity and mortality of maternal bacteraemia at a tertiary referral maternity hospital in Brisbane, Australia, over a ten-year period. A retrospective review of pregnant patients with positive blood cultures between January 2015 and December 2024 at a tertiary level obstetric hospital in Brisbane, Australia, was performed. There were 59 patients with pathogenic organisms grown on blood cultures (0.96 per 1000 deliveries) and 29 patients with presumed contaminants. Physical signs and laboratory investigations were not useful in differentiating between patients whose blood cultures grew pathogenic bacteraemia, those which grew presumed contaminants, and those whose blood cultures were negative. The predominant bacterial species were Streptococcus species and Escherichia coli (E. coli). Despite 57 of the 59 patients with pathogenic bacteraemia receiving antibiotics and fluid resuscitation within 60 min of presentation, 10 patients were admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU), principally because of hypotension developing 6-24 h after initial treatment. Seven of the 10 ICU admissions were due to E. coli bacteraemia, four secondary to urosepsis, and three secondary to chorioamnionitis. There were no maternal deaths. A continuing policy of early identification of possible maternal infection, and prompt antibiotic therapy and resuscitation are indicated. Despite expeditious management, a significant proportion of patients deteriorated and required admission to an intensive care unit, emphasising the importance of close observation following initial antibiotic therapy, particularly in patients with suspected urosepsis and/or E. coli bacteraemia.

42970461.title: Impact of Beta-Blocker Use on Mortality Across Traumatic Brain Injury Severity: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
42970461.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality. The initial insult can lead to tissue and cellular damage that results in an excessive catecholamine release, which may be mitigated with beta-blockers (BB). However, guidelines recommend their use only under specific conditions. This study compared the use of BB to no BB use in patients with TBI at an urban trauma center. This was a retrospective chart review of all adult patients with TBI admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). Patients who received at least 2 consecutive doses of any scheduled BB were compared with those who did not receive any BB. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes were the rate of 28-day mortality, in-hospital length of stay, ICU length of stay, and discharge disposition. Safety outcomes were bradycardia, hypotension, and use of vasopressors following BB administration. Subgroup analyses of propranolol, mild/moderate, and severe TBI populations were also evaluated. A total of 1197 patients were included in the study, of whom 375 received BB and 822 did not. The majority of patients were male (71.1%) and had a mean age of 53.5 years. Propranolol (42.1%) was the most commonly ordered initial BB. There was no difference in the rate of in-hospital mortality between the BB and no-BB groups (13.1% vs. 11.9%; P=0.570); however, in the adjusted analysis, BB use was associated with reduced in-hospital mortality (odds ratio: 0.589; 95% CI: 0.381-0.909; P=0.017). Regression analysis based on severity showed that the use of BB was associated with reduced mortality in severe TBI (odds ratio: 0.298; 95% CI: 0.173-0.513; P<0.001), but not mild or moderate TBI (odds ratio: 1.948; 95% CI: 0.970-3.914; P=0.061). The use of BB in patients with severe TBI was associated with lower in-hospital mortality.

42970082.title: Refining ECPR candidate selection: from fixed criteria to a dynamic probability-of-benefit framework.
42970082.abstract: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) has emerged as a rescue strategy for selected patients with refractory cardiac arrest. However, identifying patients most likely to achieve neurologically meaningful survival remains challenging. Conventional selection criteria, including age, initial rhythm, witnessed arrest, bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), and no-flow and low-flow duration, are clinically useful but may be insufficient when interpreted as isolated thresholds. We conducted a narrative review of contemporary evidence on ECPR patient selection, incorporating randomized trials, observational studies, registries, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and current guideline and consensus recommendations. Evidence was critically evaluated with particular attention to patient-level prognostic factors, arrest setting, dynamic physiological and metabolic variables, ECPR logistics, and system-level determinants of outcome. Current evidence supports a multidimensional rather than single-variable approach to ECPR candidacy. Favorable arrest characteristics, potentially reversible etiology, shorter low-flow duration, and preserved physiological reserve remain important; however, chronological low-flow time should be interpreted alongside the quality and effectiveness of ongoing CPR. Dynamic information-including transient return of spontaneous circulation, lactate kinetics, arterial pH, end-tidal carbon dioxide, and hemodynamic parameters-may further refine assessment of biological viability. Frailty, comorbidity burden, cerebral perfusion, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation-related contraindications should also be incorporated into decision-making. Importantly, selection cannot be separated from system performance: Cannulation strategy, transport logistics, institutional experience, and the ability to establish extracorporeal circulation rapidly may substantially modify the likelihood of benefit. Differences between out-of-hospital and in-hospital cardiac arrest further limit the universal application of rigid eligibility criteria. Candidacy for ECPR should be viewed as a dynamic, probability-based assessment rather than a checklist of fixed thresholds. Integrating arrest characteristics, reversibility, evolving physiology, patient reserve, and system capability may provide a more clinically meaningful framework for identifying patients most likely to achieve neurologically favorable survival after ECPR.

42971312.title: Wearable-based automated cardiac arrest detection and alerting: A systematic review.
42971312.abstract: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a leading cause of death worldwide, with survival strongly dependent on rapid recognition and timely emergency care. Wearables capable of automated cardiac arrest detection and alerting may reduce delays to treatment, particularly in unwitnessed arrests.Therefore, this review aims to systematically evaluate the existing evidence on the performance of wearable sensors and algorithms designed for OHCA detection. A systematic search was performed using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Libraries, forward citation and backward citation to identify all eligible studies up to 22 September 2026. Studies describing non-invasive, intended wearable systems designed to detect OHCA and reporting on their detection performance were included. The methodology and report of the present review are based on recommendations of the PRISMA statement and Cochrane Collaboration. Primary outcome is the sensitivity for cardiac arrest detection. Secondary outcomes include false positives cardiac arrest alerts and specificity. Studies were evaluated using the QUADAS-2 tool. From 6,344 records screened, 13 publications were included with the number of participants ranging from 18 to 1,423. Wristbands were the most prevalent device type (n=9). Nine studies used photoplethysmography as primary sensor type, with accelerometry as additive sensor modality (n=2). Other sensors used were mechanical plethysmography (n=1), electrocardiography (n=1), sound-based (n=1) and a nonlinear resonant circuit (n=1). Sensitivity ranged between 43.8 and 100%, with ten studies reporting a sensitivity of ≥ 90%. False positives ranged between multiple per day and one per twenty-one user-years. Wearable devices have demonstrated promising sensitivity for detecting cardiac arrest. However, (external) validation and real-life data are scarce, and the sensitivity-false alarm trade-off requires further investigation. OSF, doi: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/AEPF8.

42971311.title: Long-Term Survival Following Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Two-Center Five-Year Analysis.
42971311.abstract: Randomized trials have shown short-term benefit of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but the long-term durability of survival and neurological recovery after hospital discharge remains poorly defined. We performed a retrospective cohort study of consecutive patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory VT/VF OHCA from two academic centers (University of Minnesota, USA, and Charles University, Prague) from January 2013 through December 2022. The primary outcome was 5-year survival. Secondary outcomes included neurological status by Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) and associations of age and discharge disposition with long-term outcomes. Among 728 patients treated with ECPR, 211 (29.0%) survived to discharge; 138 from Minnesota and 73 from Prague. Median follow-up was 3.9 years; 68 patients (32%) completed 5 years. No patients were lost to follow-up. Among hospital survivors, 76.9% and 67.2% were alive at 1 and 5 years, respectively, with most deaths occurring within 90 days of discharge. CPC 1-2 was present in 78.7% at discharge and remained high among survivors beyond 1 year (93.4%-94.2%). Five-year survival declined by age from 91.6% for those between 18-39 years to 52.9% for >70 years. Discharge disposition also strongly stratified long-term prognosis. Among patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory OHCA, long-term survival was substantial, with approximately two-thirds alive at 5 years with favorable CPC in most. Younger age and discharge home or to acute rehabilitation identified subgroups with particularly favorable prognosis. These findings support the long-term durability of benefit among selected patients treated within established ECPR systems of care.

42971310.title: Post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation and coronary angiographic phenotypes in angiography-evaluable survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with presumed coronary lesion-related arrest.
42971310.abstract: The clinical meaning of post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients with suspected coronary etiology remains uncertain. We aimed to describe coronary angiographic phenotypes and clinical outcomes according to post-resuscitation ST-segment findings in an angiography-evaluable subset of OHCA survivors with presumed coronary lesion-related arrest. We retrospectively analyzed 149 successfully resuscitated OHCA patients admitted to our institution between January 2015 and December 2023, who underwent post-resuscitation coronary angiography and had presumed culprit lesions, defined by integrating angiographic findings with electrocardiographic, echocardiographic, and biomarker data in the clinical context. Patients were classified according to the presence or absence of post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation. ST-segment elevation was associated with a more acute occlusive coronary phenotype, with more impaired culprit-vessel flow and greater myocardial injury. In contrast, patients without ST-segment elevation more frequently had multivessel disease and chronic total occlusion, suggesting more complex coronary artery disease. Favorable neurological outcome was less frequent with ST-segment elevation in unadjusted analyses, but this association was not independent of pre-hospital factors. In this selected OHCA subset, post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation was associated with an acute occlusive coronary phenotype and greater myocardial injury, as in non-arrest acute coronary syndromes. However, the absence of ST-segment elevation did not exclude a coronary culprit lesion, so comprehensive coronary assessment is essential. ST-segment elevation was not independently associated with clinical outcomes after adjustment for pre-hospital factors. These findings should be interpreted considering substantial selection inherent to the study population.

42970130.title: Is a noradrenaline dose threshold already too late for adjunctive vasopressin initiation? Author's reply.

42970127.title: Is a norepinephrine dose threshold already too late for adjunctive vasopressin initiation?

42977378.title: Intensive Care Unit Management of the Hemodynamically Significant Pulmonary Embolism.
42977378.abstract: Acute pulmonary embolism remains a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, with prognosis determined by right ventricular (RV) adaptation to the abrupt rise in pulmonary vascular resistance. Although most cases can be managed outside the intensive care unit, patients with RV failure, hemodynamic instability, or cardiac arrest require advanced monitoring and intervention. Management in this setting emphasizes rapid diagnosis and risk stratification, timely initiation of reperfusion therapies, and carefully tailored hemodynamic and respiratory support. Optimal outcomes rely on multidisciplinary collaboration, early escalation of care, and individualized, evidence-based decision-making.

42975222.title: Clinical Predictors of Neurological Status and Hospital Length of Stay in Patients with Sepsis from Intensive Care Unit.
42975222.abstract: Sepsis frequently leads to muti-organ dysfunction and neurological impairment, contributing to increased morbidity and prolonged hospitalisation. The present study aimed to determine the clinical predictors of multi-organ failure, neurological status and hospital stay duration in patients with sepsis. Patient characteristics, clinical profiles and biochemical markers were recorded for 100 patients with sepsis from intensive care units (ICUs), including serum lactate, albumin, leucocyte count, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) score. Regression analyses were used to perform the associations. The SOFA score was 12 (interquartile range 8-15) and 75% required ICU admission. Mean lactate-albumin ratio (LAR) was 1.73 ± 1.31 and 47% of the study population fell into the high-LAR category. LAR was not independently associated with SOFA score (β =0.45, P = 0.132) or GCS (β =0.18, P = 0.284). GCS scores were significantly higher in males than in females (13.6 ± 1.86 vs. 12.75 ± 1.88). Gender (β =0.86, P = 0.026) and leucocyte count (β = -0.01, P = 0.048) emerged as independent predictors of GCS, with gender exhibiting the strongest effect (0.223). Leucocyte count was inversely correlated with GCS (effect size = -0.198) and served as an independent predictor of hospital stay duration (β =0.205, P = 0.040). LAR was not an independent predictor of level of consciousness/neurological status or organ dysfunction in sepsis. However, gender and leucocyte count independently influenced neurological status, with leucocyte count also predicted length of hospital stay. These findings suggested that inflammatory profiles play a critical role in the development of neurological dysfunction during sepsis.

42977593.title: Critical Care Management of Patients With Acute Fulminant Myocarditis.
42977593.journal: Journal of cardiothoracic and vascular anesthesia
42977593.abstract: Fulminant myocarditis is a life-threatening inflammatory cardiac syndrome characterized by severe myocardial injury and abrupt deterioration of cardiac function, leading to rapidly progressive cardiogenic shock. Patients often require intravenous vasoactive therapy and/or temporary mechanical circulatory support to maintain systemic perfusion and prevent multiorgan failure. Although frequently preceded by a viral prodrome and affecting young and healthy individuals, fulminant myocarditis encompasses diverse etiologies, including immune-mediated and toxin-related subtypes, with major implications for diagnosis and treatment. Optimal management relies on early recognition, prompt admission to specialized cardiac intensive care units, and rapid access to advanced diagnostics, including endomyocardial biopsy and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, to confirm myocardial inflammation, exclude ischemic disease, and guide etiology-directed therapy. Hemodynamic stabilization requires tailored use of vasopressors and inotropes while minimizing catecholamine-related arrhythmias and myocardial oxygen demand. For refractory shock, early escalation to temporary mechanical circulatory support, most commonly venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, is central to restore perfusion and provide a bridge to recovery or advanced therapy. Because fulminant myocarditis frequently involves malignant arrhythmias and multiorgan dysfunction, integrated critical care management is essential. This review summarizes a practical intensive care approach to fulminant myocarditis, emphasizing early diagnosis, individualized hemodynamic and device-based support, multiorgan management, and phenotype-driven immunomodulatory treatment strategies.

42974192.title: From cytokine storm to adaptive dysregulation: temporal evolution of the inflammatory network and phase-specific intervention strategies in fulminant viral myocarditis.
42974192.abstract: Fulminant viral myocarditis (FVM) is characterized by acute onset and rapid progression, often deteriorating into cardiogenic shock, malignant arrhythmias, and multi-organ failure within days. Its pathological essence does not lie in the "quantitative accumulation" of focal lymphocytic infiltration seen in ordinary myocarditis, but rather in a "qualitative shift" driven by diffuse myocardial edema compounded by a multi-cytokine cascade. Accumulating evidence indicates that the "inflection point" of myocardial injury is determined not by viral load per se, but by the dysregulated pattern recognition of viral antigens by the innate immune system and the resultant imbalance of the inflammatory network. The organising framework of this review is temporal (hyperacute to acute to reparative immune states). A spatial dimension, contrasting the circulating and the cardiac-resident immune compartments, is developed wherever direct or closely analogous data exist, but it carries far less evidence than the temporal dimension and is treated as secondary to it. Myocarditis that is immune-mediated without a replicating cardiotropic virus, including vaccine-associated and checkpoint-inhibitor disease, is used here as a labelled comparator and not as part of the entity under review. The virus invades cardiomyocytes and vascular endothelium via receptors with non-canonical distribution, subsequently triggering type I interferon responses and necroptosis through endosomal and cytosolic pattern-recognition receptors, and initiating a cascade effect via damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). The driver of cardiomyocyte death does not stay constant across this course: virus-intrinsic cytopathic and ferroptotic death predominates in the first days, myeloid-mediated killing takes over through the remainder of the first week, and cytotoxic lymphocytes become the principal effectors thereafter. The hyperacute phase is characterized by macrophage phenotypic drift, neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, and a "cytokine storm" whose earliest cellular sources in viral myocarditis are myeloid rather than T-cell derived. The acute phase features the "clearance-injury" paradox of cytotoxic T cells and the failure of immune checkpoint regulation, and a subset of patients may subsequently follow what the authors describe as a candidate immunoparalysis trajectory rather than an established third stage of disease - a state provisionally characterized by regulatory T cell (Treg) expansion, paradoxical elevation of interleukin-10 (IL-10), and downregulation of monocyte human leukocyte antigen-DR (HLA-DR). Its reported association with secondary infection and adverse outcome derives largely from sepsis and critical-care cohorts and has not been demonstrated in FVM. Building on this "inflammatory time window," the authors propose a phase-specific framework intended to generate hypotheses rather than to recommend treatment: in the hyperacute phase, "fire-extinguishing" approaches (complement blockade and cytokine adsorption) may represent a potential alternative to broad-spectrum immunosuppression; in the acute phase, selective blockade of individual pathways according to inflammatory subtype may be worth exploring; and in the reparative phase, measures aimed at restoring regulatory immune capacity may be considered for study. None of these pathways, and none of the biomarker values discussed in the main text, has been prospectively validated in FVM. Finally, this review envisions individualized decision-making guided by multi-omics and dynamic immune monitoring, emphasizing that the prognosis of FVM depends on the capacity for "dynamic phenotyping and real-time switching" of immune status, rather than reliance on any single therapeutic modality.

42972097.title: [New sepsis guidelines: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 and German Sepsis Society 2025 -Competing or complementary?].
42972097.abstract: Sepsis is one of the leading causes of death in intensive care units worldwide. In German-speaking countries, patient management is primarily guided by two sets of guidelines: the international Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) guidelines and the S3 guidelines of the German Sepsis Society (DSG). While the DSG guidelines were published in 2025 as an evidence-based adaptation of the SSC 2021 guidelines, the SSC has since released an updated international version in 2026. To provide a structured analysis of the key content areas, similarities and differences between the two guidelines, with a particular focus on the timing of treatment initiation, anti-infective treatment and hemodynamic management. Both guidelines reflect not so much a fundamental shift in strategy but more a consolidation of evidence and a refinement of concepts. Three overarching themes can be identified: a broadened perspective encompassing the entire continuum of care, from the prehospital setting to post-sepsis follow-up, the increasing integration of antibiotic stewardship principles and in SSC 2026, the introduction of a graded sepsis terminology (definite/probable/possible/unlikely). Areas of agreement include the importance of early anti-infective treatment, the preferential use of balanced crystalloids, norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor, the inclusion of capillary refill time as a perfusion parameter and a strong recommendation for prolonged or continuous beta-lactam infusion. Differences are evident in the specificity of antimicrobial recommendations, the definition of risk factors warranting empirical antifungal treatment and several new recommendations introduced in SSC 2026, such as a lower mean arterial pressure (MAP) target of 60-65 mm Hg for patients aged ≥ 65 years, initiation of treatment in the prehospital setting and source control within 6 h. The DSG 2025 and SSC 2026 guidelines should be regarded as complementary rather than competing frameworks. The DSG 2025 remains the practical, high-resolution handbook for care in the Central European context, while the SSC 2026 outlines the international direction: away from a purely acute care set of rules towards an individualized, continuum-based model of care.

42974747.title: Distinct Doppler echocardiographic patterns of elevated left ventricular filling pressure in acute decompensated heart failure and AMI-related cardiogenic shock: a simultaneous Doppler-hemodynamic study.
42974747.abstract: Doppler echocardiography supports noninvasive hemodynamic assessment, but its interpretation may vary across acute heart failure syndromes. We compared Doppler filling patterns and their relationship with pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) in acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) and acute myocardial infarction-related cardiogenic shock (AMI-CS). This single-center observational study included 61 patients with ADHF (n = 34) or AMI-CS (n = 27) who underwent contemporaneous echocardiographic and invasive hemodynamic assessment. Transmitral inflow, pulmonary venous flow, and tissue Doppler indices were compared between groups and analyzed in relation to PCWP. Exploratory ROC analyses assessed discrimination of PCWP ≥ 18 mmHg. Patients with ADHF had greater cardiac chamber enlargement and higher mean PCWP than those with AMI-CS (24.7 ± 8.4 vs. 18.0 ± 5.4 mmHg; p < 0.001). ADHF was characterized by higher E/A (2.8 ± 1.2 vs. 1.3 ± 1.2; p < 0.001), lower pulmonary venous S/D (0.7 ± 0.5 vs. 1.1 ± 0.5; p < 0.01), and higher average E/e' (21.0 ± 7.3 vs. 12.5 ± 4.7; p < 0.001). Deceleration time did not differ significantly. Average and septal E/e' correlated with PCWP in the pooled cohort but not within either group separately. Septal E/e' yielded AUCs of 0.868 (95% CI, 0.722-1.000) in ADHF and 0.762 (95% CI, 0.511-1.000) in AMI-CS. ADHF and AMI-CS exhibit distinct Doppler filling profiles alongside differences in invasive filling pressure and cardiac remodeling. These findings support contextual interpretation of Doppler indices during bedside hemodynamic assessment of critically ill patients. The diagnostic value of syndrome-specific interpretation requires independent validation.

42972234.title: Serial cardiac ultrasound in acutely ill adults: a systematic review.
42972234.abstract: Cardiopulmonary symptoms frequently prompt emergency department (ED) visits. Serial as-sessment of dynamic cardiac ultrasound parameters may support monitoring, but their asso-ciation with patient outcomes and role in guiding management is uncertain. This systematic review evaluated whether serial changes in ejection fraction (EF), tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), and the right ventricular-to-left ventricular (RV/LV) ratio are associated with mortality, readmissions, length of stay, or intensive care unit trans-fer in acutely ill patients. We searched MEDLINE (PubMed), Embase (Ovid), CENTRAL (Wiley), Scopus (Elsevier), Web of Science (Clarivate), Google Scholar, ProQuest, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the International Clini-cal Trials Registry Platform. The initial search was conducted on 16 April 2024 and updated on 31 October 2025. We included randomized and non-randomized trials and observational stud-ies of adults (≥18 years) undergoing at least two in-hospital cardiac ultrasound assessments and reported mortality, readmission, length of stay, and/or intensive care unit transfer. Risk of bias was assessed with study design-specific tools. Results were summarized using synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM). Of 15,174 screened records, 11 studies with a total of 941 patients were included. Study popu-lations were defined by presenting symptoms (dyspnea, hypotension) or by clinical conditions (toxicological, infectious, and cardiopulmonary diseases). Echocardiography was most used, and patients underwent 3-4 scans during admission. Overall risk of bias was moderate to high. Four studies compared serial changes in EF, TAPSE, and/or the RV/LV ratio with outcomes and found no consistent pattern. One randomized study evaluated ultrasound-guided treatment and found no difference compared with usual care. Across studies, EF, TAPSE, and RV/LV ratio were generally stable or improved over time. Available evidence is limited and does not demonstrate a consistent association between serial cardiac ultrasound parameters and outcomes in acutely ill adults. However, serial changes are frequently observed, highlighting the need for trials evaluating whether decision-linked, ultrasound-guided management strategies can improve outcomes. PROSPERO, CRD42024524740.

42975521.title: Documented Thermoregulation Strategies Alone Do Not Benefit Comatose In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Survivors.

42975405.title: Physiologic, Metabolic, and Protein Redox Effects of Methylene Blue in a Porcine Hemorrhage Model.
42975405.abstract: Methylene blue (MB) has established benefit in vasodilatory shock, and a potential role in hemorrhagic shock. Some evidence suggests that MB could lower anesthetic requirements. The aim of this study was to investigate the effect of MB on volatile anesthetic requirements (primary), metabolic markers (secondary), and protein redox modifications (tertiary) in a porcine hemorrhage model. This was a randomized 2 x 2 factorial animal study conducted at a tertiary medical center in 2019-2020. Forty swine were randomized to the following experimental interventions: hemorrhage (0 v. 30 mL/kg, at t = 0 min) and MB (0 v. 2 mg/kg, at t = 20 min). End-tidal isoflurane, blood pressure, and arterial blood gas parameters were recorded at prespecified intervals. Skeletal muscle was used for redox analyses. Group differences were investigated with mixed effects and one-way analyses of variance. There was no effect of MB on volatile requirements or metabolic markers (all P > 0.05). Hemorrhage was associated with 2.4 mg/dL higher lactate (95% CI, 1.4 to 3.4) and 23 mmHg lower mean arterial pressure (95% CI, 11 to 34). Hemorrhage was also associated with increased protein carbonyl levels (P < 0.001) that were non-significantly attenuated by MB (P = 0.130), and increased protein S-nitrosylation (P < 0.001) that was significantly attenuated by MB (P < 0.001). MB does not have a significant effect on volatile anesthetic requirements or systemic physiologic and metabolic responses during hemorrhagic shock. However, MB significantly attenuates protein S-nitrosylation and partially attenuates protein carbonyl accumulation.

42972430.title: Differentiated effect of hypothermia versus normothermia after cardiac arrest by neurological status and clinical correlates of ischemic burden.
42972430.abstract: The optimal temperature target after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains uncertain, as major randomized trials have not demonstrated a clear benefit of lower-target hypothermia compared with normothermia. Despite this, patients with differing degrees of ischemic burden or early neurological injury may hypothetically respond differently to temperature targets, raising the possibility of heterogeneous treatment effects. This study aimed to determine whether outcomes differ after OHCA with 33 °C versus controlled normothermia (36.0-37.7 °C) according to correlates of ischemic burden and neurological findings at hospital admission. This secondary analysis of the TTM and TTM2 trials employed effect-based machine learning to probe for heterogeneous treatment effects. Causal forests and Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) estimated individualized treatment effects (ITE) based on ischemia duration, prehospital factors, and neurological examination findings at hospital admission. Treatment effect modifier variable importance parameter (TEM-VIP) analysis ranked the baseline variables most likely to modify effect. The primary outcome was six-month all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was poor functional outcome (modified Rankin scale score 4-6). Primary analyses evaluated potential heterogeneity within each trial, while secondary analyses pooled all participants. All 2789 adult OHCA patients from the trials' primary analyses were included (median age 65 years (IQR 56-73), 79.9% male). Death occurred in 49.4% of patients in the 33 °C group, and in 47.9% in the controlled normothermia group. Variation in six-month mortality ITEs estimated from ischemic burden correlates and initial neurological findings was minimal, and no significant heterogeneity of treatment effect was identified across all methods and analysis populations. In the pooled analysis, estimated conditional mean mortality risk difference ranged from - 1.2% to 2.1% in causal forest (p = 0.99), and from - 0.5% to 1.5% in BART, with posterior probabilities for hypothermia benefit ranging from 42% to 53%. Absolute subgroup estimates in TEM-VIP analysis were small and non-significant. Results were consistent for the six-month functional outcome. Among TTM and TTM2 participants randomized to 33 °C versus controlled normothermia post-OHCA, no evidence of detectable heterogeneity of treatment effect based on available clinical correlates of ischemic burden or initial neurological findings was identified, with minimal estimated variation in treatment effect.

42972412.title: Deconstructing cardiovascular heterogeneity in septic shock: V0-LV invariance, vasopressin mismatch, and RVR circularity.

42978852.title: Hypotension prediction index to predict hemodynamic instability related to renal replacement therapy in critically ill patients: A prospective observational study.
42978852.abstract: Fluid removal during continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is a frequent cause of hemodynamic instability (HI) in critically ill patients, yet clinicians lack reliable tools to anticipate intolerance to ultrafiltration. We aimed to determine the performance and clinical utility of the hypotension prediction index (HPI) to predict HI in critically ill patients undergoing fluid removal with CRRT. We conducted a prospective observational study including consecutive patients receiving CRRT with fluid removal in a tertiary intensive care unit (ICU) of Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Vaudois, Lausanne, Switzerland, between March 2022 and August 2023. Arterial pressure waveforms were recorded using FloTrac and HemoSphere Advanced Monitor and HPI was computed every 20 s (offline, for blinding). An HPI alarm was defined as three consecutive HPI values ≥85; an HI event was defined as three consecutive mean arterial pressure readings <65 mmHg, initiation or escalation of vasopressor therapy, or clinical signs of hemodynamic intolerance. We evaluated the performance of HPI for predicting HI within the following 15-min window. To assess HPI clinical utility at bedside, we computed alarm-to-event delays, the proportion of HPI alarms followed by HI and the proportion of HI preceded by at least one HPI alarm. We repeated analyses considering only "new" alarms and "new" HI, defined respectively as alarms and HI events preceded by a 60-min event-free interval. We recorded 223,660 observations corresponding to 1243 h of monitoring. HPI was ≥85 in 33.4% of observations and MAP <65 mmHg in 11.0%. Overall, HPI demonstrated good discriminative performance for predicting HI (area under the curve of the receiver operating characteristic curve=0.89), with high sensitivity (99.7%) and specificity (81.6%). However, positive predictive value (PPV) was low, as only 54.7% of alarms were followed by HI, with a mean alarm-to-event delay of 103 s. Bootstrapped analyses performed to adjust for varying importance of individual patients confirmed these findings. When considering new alarms (n=147) and events (n=174), only 33 (22.4%) alarms were followed by an HI, and 34 (19.4%) HI were preceded by an alarm. Sensitivity analyses considering a lower cutoff for HPI and a shorter event-free period to define a new event confirmed these findings. Although HPI shows excellent statistical performance for predicting HI during CRRT with fluid removal, its clinical utility is limited by short time-to-event delay, frequent false-positive alarms, and prolonged time with high HPI values. These findings underscore the gap between predictive accuracy and bedside utility of monitoring tools in critical care.

42980468.title: Dynamic phenotyping and organ cross-talk in sepsis-associated organ injury: from physiological trajectories to precision critical care.
42980468.abstract: Sepsis-associated organ injury remains a major cause of mortality in critically ill patients. Conventional assessment relies largely on physiological indicators, including lactate, mean arterial pressure (MAP), PaO2/FiO2 ratio, creatinine, urine output, and organ dysfunction scores. However, these isolated values or single-variable trends may incompletely capture the temporal instability and biological heterogeneity that characterize sepsis. Increasing evidence indicates that dynamic trajectories, variability patterns, and evolving subphenotypes may better characterize disease progression, organ recovery, and treatment responsiveness. In parallel, critical care medicine is moving from syndrome-level classification toward treatable traits, individualized treatment effects, and precision critical care. Dynamic phenotyping focuses on physiological trajectories, including lactate clearance, oxygenation evolution, hemodynamic variability, glycemic variability, and renal recovery, but its major value may lie in interpreting relationships among trajectories across organ systems. Interpretation of dynamic phenotypes therefore requires attention to cross-system temporal relationships, including coordinated recovery, coupled deterioration, and discordant recovery. From this trajectory-based perspective, sepsis-associated organ injury can be viewed as an interconnected multiorgan network involving lung-kidney, gut-lung, gut-liver, gut-kidney, and endothelial-organ cross-talk. Organ cross-talk may help explain dynamic coupling among organ systems, whereas microcirculatory-mitochondrial dysfunction may contribute to trajectory mismatch through impaired tissue perfusion, oxygen delivery-utilization uncoupling, bioenergetic failure, maladaptive metabolic reprogramming, and defective mitochondrial quality control. This trajectory-based perspective may inform future precision critical care, while most trajectory-guided strategies remain investigational and require prospective validation before routine clinical adoption.

42981236.title: Safety of Dexmedetomidine Use in Adult ICU Patients With Right Ventricular Dysfunction.
42981236.abstract: BackgroundDexmedetomidine is commonly used in the intensive care unit (ICU) and is associated with hemodynamic adverse events, including hypotension and bradycardia. Use of dexmedetomidine has not been described in critically ill patients with right ventricular (RV) dysfunction and may be particularly relevant given the tenuous hemodynamics in this patient population.ObjectiveDetermine the prevalence of adverse events in adult ICU patients with RV dysfunction receiving dexmedetomidine.MethodsThis single-center, retrospective cohort study included adult ICU patients with RV dysfunction measured by echocardiogram who received dexmedetomidine between January 2017 and December 2022. The primary outcome was a composite of adverse events after dexmedetomidine initiation including bradycardia, hypotension, increasing vasopressor/inotrope requirements, and asystole. Secondary outcomes included individual components of the primary outcome and a comparison of adverse events based on RV dysfunction severity.ResultsA total of 245 patients met study inclusion criteria. A total of 178 adverse events occurred in 153 patients (62.4%). The most common adverse event was hypotension occurring in 129 patients (72.5%). Increased vasopressor requirements occurred in 35 patients (19.7%), and mean change in norepinephrine equivalents from baseline was 0.06 µg/kg/min. Adverse event rates did not differ among patients with mild, moderate, or severe RV dysfunction.ConclusionAdult ICU patients with RV dysfunction receiving dexmedetomidine experienced high rates of hypotension and increased vasopressor requirements. Findings from this study may assist in tailoring sedation regimens for critically ill patients with RV dysfunction. Future research is needed to explore optimal sedative agents in this patient population.

42979336.title: Intradermal thumbtack needling as an adjunctive therapy for sepsis-induced gastrointestinal dysfunction: A pilot randomized controlled trial.
42979336.journal: Journal of traditional and complementary medicine
42979336.abstract: Sepsis-induced gastrointestinal dysfunction (GID) is common in critically ill patients, leading to impaired motility, feeding intolerance, and poor outcomes. Evidence for acupuncture-related neuromodulation remains limited. Intradermal thumbtack needling (ITN), a minimally invasive technique that provides continuous low-intensity stimulation, may serve as an adjunct in Intensive Care Unit (ICU), but its clinical effects remain unexamined. This study aims to assess the efficacy and safety of ITN in patients with sepsis-induced GID. Sixty patients with sepsis-induced GID were randomly assigned to the conventional treatment (CT) group or ITN group. Both groups received standard therapies (ventilation, vasopressors, anti-infectives, fluid resuscitation, gastrointestinal mucosal protection, and prokinetics). The ITN group also received ITN at auricular and body acupoints for 7 days. Gastrointestinal function indicators (acute gastrointestinal injury [AGI] grade, gastric antrum motility index [MI], abdominal circumference, intra-abdominal pressure [IAP]), inflammatory markers, and severity scores were assessed before and after treatment. 28-day mortality, ICU length of stay and adverse events were assessed after treatment. The ITN group showed greater improvement in AGI grade, abdominal circumference, and IAP (all P < 0.05). No significant differences were observed for MI, inflammatory markers, or severity scores (all P > 0.05). 28-day mortality and ICU length of stay did not differ significantly between groups. No ITN-related adverse events occurred. ITN may improve gastrointestinal parameters in sepsis-induced GID patients, but it did not significantly affect gastric motility, systemic inflammation, or global severity scores. Larger, controlled trials are needed to confirm its potential role as adjunctive therapy.

42978144.title: EXPRESS: Comparing hypertonic saline and mannitol for management of elevated intracranial pressure in adults: A PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis.
42978144.journal: Journal of investigative medicine : the official publication of the American Federation for Clinical Research
42978144.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to compare the efficacy of mannitol and hypertonic saline (HTS) in reducing elevated intracranial pressure (ICP). We conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases to identify eligible trials comparing HTS and mannitol in adults with elevated ICP; only studies that used ICP monitoring to obtain objective measurements were included. The primary outcome was the change in ICP at different time points, and secondary outcomes included changes in other clinical indicators. A total of 16 studies (583 patients, 2,219 episodes) were included. The pooled results showed that HTS was significantly more effective than mannitol in reducing ICP at 30 min, 1 h, and 3 h post-intervention. However, the numerical differences were small. And there were no statistically significant differences between HTS and mannitol groups in ICU length of stay, mortality, or unfavorable Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) scores. In addition, the increases in cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), mean arterial pressure (MAP), and serum sodium were significantly greater in the HTS group than in the mannitol group at various time points. While HTS produced a larger ICP-lowering effect, the statistically significant difference was modest. Accordingly, existing synthesized evidence fails to clearly establish whether HTS is superior or inferior to mannitol for reducing intracranial pressure.

42978048.title: A retrospective cohort study of a midodrine protocol for the prevention of post-operative hypotension for lower limb arthroplasty and emergency hip fracture surgery.
42978048.abstract: Hypotension is a common post-operative complication that is associated with morbidity and mortality. There has been growing interest in the use of midodrine (oral alpha-1 adrenergic vasopressor agent) to increase systolic and mean arterial blood pressure in a variety of clinical applications. Our institution developed a 48-h midodrine protocol in 2020 for patients undergoing elective lower limb arthroplasty and emergency hip fracture fixation. The aim of this retrospective, single-centre metropolitan tertiary hospital cohort study was to evaluate the efficacy of the protocol in reducing the incidence and severity of perioperative hypotension (SBP <110 mmHg) within the first 24 h following surgery compared to the pre-protocol period (primary outcome). Secondary outcomes included frequency of hypotension 24-48 h post-operatively, bradycardia, incidence of MET calls and unplanned critical care admission. In total, 328 patients were identified for inclusion in the pre-protocol group and 298 in the protocol group. Introduction of the midodrine protocol was not associated with a significant difference in the incidence of the primary outcome. There was no statistically significant difference in the incidence of hypotension between groups post-operatively at 24 or 48 h. Of the secondary outcomes, patients receiving midodrine were more likely to be bradycardic in the post-anaesthesia care unit (43.8% vs 55.9%, p = 0.001) and at 24 h post-operatively (40.7% vs 53.8%, p = 0.003).

42987115.title: Medical nutrition therapy during the first 5 days of critical illness: a retrospective cohort study.
42987115.abstract: The aim of this study was to describe the prescription of medical nutrition therapy for critically ill patients who were admitted to an intensive care unit during the first 5 days. In an observational, longitudinal, retrospective study conducted at the intensive care unit of a tertiary hospital in Mexico City, adult patients admitted from January to December 2018 and from November 2024 to February 2025 were included. Indications for fasting, the route of medical nutrition therapy (enteral nutrition-parenteral nutrition), caloric and protein intakes, sequential organ failure assessment score and lactate levels, and vasopressor requirements during the 5 days were evaluated. Delay in initiating medical nutrition therapy was defined as initiated after 48 h of intensive care unit admission. 100 critically ill patients were included; aged 53±18.8, and with a median sequential organ failure assessment score of 10 (7-12). The most frequent diagnoses at admission were pulmonary disease and septic shock. On the first day, 98% of patients were fasting, and 25% received high-dose vasopressor therapy (if the norepinephrine equivalent dose >0.3 μg/kg/min). Over 5 days, medical nutrition therapy transitioned progressively, predominantly from fasting through enteral nutrition (45%) and parenteral nutrition (11%). medical nutrition therapy delay in 54 patients and in a multivariate analysis was associated with age (OR 1.04; 95%CI 1.01-1.07), sequential organ failure assessment score (OR 1.20; 95%CI 1.02-1.40), and lactate levels (OR 1.8; 95%CI 1.10-3.00). Prescription of medical nutrition therapy in critically ill patients admitted to a intensive care unit during 5 days is dynamic, and in all patients, it is not possible to initiate at 48 h, associated with higher age and illness severity.

42988176.title: Early Hypoxemia and Hypocapnia Burdens and 28-Day Mortality in ICU Patients With Cardiac Arrest: A Retrospective Cohort Study From the MIMIC-IV Database.
42988176.abstract: The association of cumulative oxygen and carbon dioxide deficits with mortality in patients with cardiac arrest remains uncertain. We examined hypoxemia and hypocapnia burdens during the first 24 hours of ICU care. This retrospective MIMIC-IV study included adult ICU patients with cardiac arrest identified using hospital diagnosis codes, eligible arterial blood gas measurements, and confirmed survival to 24 hours after ICU admission. Burdens were calculated as the integrated deficits below PaO2 75 mmHg or PaCO2 35 mmHg divided by 24 hours. Multivariable logistic regression assessed mortality within 28 days of ICU admission. Restricted cubic splines assessed nonlinear associations. The cohort included 1,028 ICU patients with cardiac arrest, of whom 487 (47.4%) died within 28 days; complete-case models included 972 patients. In the joint model, the adjusted odds ratio was 1.71 (95% CI 1.20-2.45) per 10 mmHg higher hypoxemia burden and 1.88 (1.42-2.47) per 5 mmHg higher hypocapnia burden. For hypoxemia, the high-exposure group had higher adjusted odds of death than the no-exposure group (1.95, 1.33-2.85), but the low-exposure group had lower odds (0.68, 0.47-0.98). Hypocapnia showed evidence of nonlinearity (P=0.014); its low-exposure group had lower odds than the no-exposure group, while the difference between the high-exposure and no-exposure groups was not statistically significant. Among ICU patients with cardiac arrest who survived the first 24 hours after ICU admission, greater hypoxemia burden was associated with higher 28-day mortality in continuous analyses. In categorical analyses, the high-exposure group had higher adjusted odds of death than the no-exposure group, whereas the low-exposure group had lower adjusted odds. Hypocapnia burden showed a nonlinear association with mortality. These findings warrant prospective validation.

42981693.title: Oxygen consumption as a measure of metabolic demand during early rehabilitation and bedside activity in critically ill adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
42981693.abstract: Early rehabilitation and bedside activity can increase oxygen demand during invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), but the magnitude and variability of this response remain uncertain. To quantify acute changes in oxygen consumption (VO₂) during rehabilitation and bedside activity in adults receiving IMV and compare intervention domains. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception through July 6, 2026. Activity-related percentage changes in VO₂ were pooled using random-effects models. Risk of bias was assessed using revised Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Twenty studies were included, and 11 contributed 14 estimates to the primary meta-analysis. VO₂ increased by 29.2% from baseline (95% CI, 16.2%-43.6%; I2 = 96.2%; 95% prediction interval, -9.7% to 84.7%). All 14 point estimates were above baseline (+3.1% to +66.3%), although not all were individually statistically significant. Pooled estimates were higher for respiratory physiotherapy (43.3%; 95% CI, 32.3%-55.2%) than for other rehabilitation and bedside interventions (18.4%; 95% CI, -0.2%-40.5%), although this domain comparison was exploratory and confounded by study era and case mix. Mean arterial pressure and cardiac output showed pooled increases; other secondary analyses included few comparable studies. Oxygen consumption was above baseline in all 14 point estimates, with a pooled increase of 29.2% and estimates ranging from 3.1% to 66.3%. Responses did not follow a simple passive-to-active pattern, showing that clinically indicated bedside care and rehabilitation can impose markedly different metabolic loads. When perceived exertion cannot be assessed, VO₂ offers an objective measure of session-specific metabolic demand that can be interpreted alongside the patient's cardiorespiratory reserve.

42986174.title: Creation and verification of an interpretable machine learning model for forecasting in-hospital results in Cardiorenal syndrome patients in critical condition.
42986174.abstract: Cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) encompasses a spectrum of disorders in which acute or chronic dysfunction of the heart or kidneys induces dysfunction of the other. The heart-kidney crosstalk underlying CRS has since been extended into the broader cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome by incorporating metabolic risk factors.CRS is associated with significantly increased mortality in intensive care unit (ICU) patients. However, dedicated tools for predicting short-term outcomes remain lacking, which limits timely risk stratification and treatment optimization. This multicenter cohort study enrolled 6,668 CRS patients from MIMIC-IV (v2.2) for model development and 3,602 from eICU-CRD (v2.0) for external validation. In patients remaining in the ICU for ≥24 hours, candidate predictors were ascertained within the first 24 hours, including early treatment exposures. Subsequent all-cause in-hospital mortality was predicted at this 24-hour landmark. Eleven machine learning algorithms were systematically compared after 1:1 random undersampling of the development cohort. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was applied to enhance interpretability and identify key prognostic features. The artificial neural network (ANN) model performed best. The final model incorporated six readily obtainable variables: AKI stage, age, mechanical ventilation, vasopressor use, β-blocker use, and ACEI/ARB use. It achieved an AUC of 0.810 (95% CI 0.757-0.860) in internal validation and 0.704 (95% CI 0.679-0.729) in external validation, indicating good internal but moderate external discrimination. We developed the first interpretable machine learning model specifically for predicting in-hospital mortality in critically ill CRS patients. SHAP provides transparent feature contribution analysis, and a web-based interface facilitates clinical implementation. When applied 24 hours after ICU admission, the model enables early identification of high-risk patients. It may also support risk stratification and resource allocation in the ICU.

42985722.title: A Case Report on a Life-Threatening Occult Supraglottic Granulating Mass Masquerading as Life-Threatening Asthma and Presenting as Cardiac Arrest.
42985722.abstract: Structural upper-airway lesions are uncommon but important mimics of asthma. A 74-year-old man with asthma and multiple recent admissions for presumed exacerbations presented with acute dyspnoea and subsequently sustained a pulseless electrical activity (PEA) cardiac arrest. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after five minutes, followed by emergency intubation and admission to intensive care. He was diagnosed and treated for presumed acute severe asthma and respiratory infection. By the following day, there was no significant wheeze or bronchospasm and extubation was attempted. He immediately developed severe stridor and profound hypoxaemia, with oxygen saturation falling to approximately 60%. Emergency video laryngoscopy revealed a large mobile supraglottic mass causing apparent "ball-valve" obstruction. Re-intubation restored oxygen saturation to 100%. The lesion was subsequently completely excised by the otorhinolaryngology team, with histopathology demonstrating granulation tissue. This case highlights the importance of considering structural upper-airway pathology when presumed asthma follows an atypical course, particularly when post-extubation stridor persists despite resolution of bronchospasm.

42988561.title: Descending Necrotizing Mediastinitis After Thyroidectomy.
42988561.abstract: Thyroidectomy is a commonly performed endocrine procedure with generally low complication rates. Descending necrotizing mediastinitis (DNM) is an exceptionally rare but life-threatening complication resulting from cervical infections that spread into the mediastinum. DNM following thyroid surgery has been reported only rarely. We analyzed retrospectively five patients who developed DNM following thyroid surgery between 2023 and 2025 at two tertiary centers. The patients' demographics, comorbidities, surgical procedures, clinical presentation, imaging, microbiology, treatment, complications, and outcomes were reviewed. The diagnosis was based on clinical and radiological evidence of cervicomediastinal infection, with operative confirmation in the four patients who underwent surgical drainage. A literature review was conducted using PubMed, MEDLINE, and Embase. The case series included four women and one man (age 35-68, mean 53.8 years). All patients had at least one comorbidity, including obesity, cardiovascular or respiratory disease, immune compromise, and chronic nicotine use. Surgical procedures included total thyroidectomy (n = 3) and hemithyroidectomy (n = 2). Symptoms developed 2-10 days postoperatively, including cervical pain, swelling, fever, dysphagia, dyspnea, tachycardia, and subcutaneous emphysema. Contrast-enhanced (CT) of the neck and chest demonstrated findings consistent with DNM in all patients, with operative confirmation in the four patients requiring surgical drainage. Microbiological analyses identified Streptococcus pyogenes in three patients and Streptococcus pneumoniae in one patient. Concomitant methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) was isolated in one of the patients with S. pyogenes, while an additional patient had a positive rapid Group A Streptococcus test without confirmatory culture. Treatment included cervical drainage (n = 4), thoracic intervention (n = 2), tracheal repair (n = 1), and ICU admission (n = 4). Complications included acute kidney failure, septic shock, pleural/pericardial effusions, pulmonary embolism, and cardiac arrest. All patients survived with hospital stays ranging 7 to 42 days (median 21). Although the acute infectious process resolved in all patients, some required rehabilitation and one experienced long-term disability affecting daily activities and work capacity. DNM after thyroidectomy is rare but potentially life-threatening. Early recognition, contrast-enhanced CT, prompt surgical drainage, and broad-spectrum antibiotics are essential. Awareness of predisposing factors and vigilant postoperative monitoring improves outcomes.

42986805.title: Compliance with the 2021 surviving sepsis campaign Hour-1 Bundle and impact on patient outcomes in a resource-limited setting: A quality improvement initiative in a referral hospital in Rwanda.
42986805.abstract: Sepsis and septic shock are common life-threatening conditions associated with high mortality globally. Compliance with the Society of Critical Care Medicine's Hour-1 Bundle for sepsis management has the potential to improve outcome, but the bundle is infrequently applied in resource-constrained settings. We assessed level of compliance with the Hour-1 bundle among patients diagnosed with sepsis and septic shock at the Accident and Emergency Department (AED) or Intensive Care Unit (ICU) of University Teaching Hospital of Butare, Rwanda. We conducted training for nurses and doctors in the AED and ICU, with the goal of improving compliance. We re-assessed bundle compliance one month after the training. We used univariate and multivariate analyses to evaluate the association of compliance and fluid resuscitation with hospital mortality while adjusting for severity of illness and other covariates. Our finding showed that seventy-eight patients were enrolled during the pre-intervention period, and 82 in post-intervention. The overall compliance with at least 4 elements of the Hour-1 bundle before the intervention was 14%, and 76% after the intervention (p < 0.001). Mortality was lower in the post-intervention period than in the pre-intervention period (51.2% vs 74.4%; p = 0.003). Non-survivors had a significantly lower bundle compliance than survivors (35% vs 80%; adjusted OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.05-0.57; p = 0.004). Administered 2 liters of IV fluids and beyond during the first hour was independently associated with higher mortality (adjusted OR 19.38, 95% CI 5.63-66.75; p < 0.001). Findings from this Quality Improvement project suggest that compliance with the Hour-1 sepsis bundle in a resource-constrained setting can be improved with training, can improve outcome.. Administration of ≥2 liters during the first hour in those was independently associated with a higher in-hospital mortality, although bundle-compliant resuscitation was not. More research is needed, both on the implementation of sepsis bundles in resource-constrained settings, to assess if all bundle elements are as effective in these settings as recommended in the international guidelines.

42981732.title: Early post-resuscitation profiles after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: A latent class analysis.
42981732.journal: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care
42981732.abstract: Early cardiopulmonary heterogeneity after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) may be associated with prognosis and treatment response. To identify early post-resuscitation profiles and explore their associations with outcomes and randomized treatment effects. In this post hoc analysis of the BOX pulmonary artery catheter substudy, latent class analysis (LCA) was applied to early clinical, echocardiographic, and invasive hemodynamic variables. The primary outcome was 365-day all-cause mortality. Exploratory cross-cohort replication used a separately fitted LCA in the Targeted Temperature Management (TTM) cohort, with 180-day mortality. Among 700 BOX patients, a two-class model was selected. Class 2 (n = 352) showed longer time to return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), higher lactate, greater cardiopulmonary dysfunction, higher filling pressures, and greater noradrenaline requirements. Mortality was 48% in Class 2 versus 21% in Class 1. No treatment interaction was detected for mean arterial pressure (MAP; P = 0.606), oxygenation (P = 0.483), or fever-control duration (P = 0.946). Mortality discrimination was not superior to time to ROSC alone. In 152 TTM patients, mortality was 38% versus 24% (P = 0.057), with less pronounced hemodynamic separation. Two early post-resuscitation profiles were identified after OHCA, with more pronounced separation in filling pressures than cardiac output in BOX. The profiles were associated with prognosis but did not identify differential responses to the randomized interventions. BOX trial, ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT03141099; TTM trial, ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT01020916.

42986437.title: Vasopressors as immunomodulators: a hidden axis in septic shock.

42994883.title: Association between early central venous pressure monitoring and 30-day mortality in critically ill patients with comorbid heart failure and sepsis: A retrospective cohort study.
42994883.abstract: Central venous pressure (CVP) is widely used in the intensive care unit (ICU), but the optimal timing to initiate CVP monitoring remains unclear for patients with comorbid heart failure and sepsis. We explored the association between time to initial CVP measurement and 30-day mortality in this high-risk population. This retrospective cohort study included 9246 critically ill patients with comorbid heart failure and sepsis from the MIMIC-IV database. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis examined the relationship between time to initial CVP measurement and 30-day mortality. Inverse probability of treatment weighting followed by weighted logistic regression was used to assess the association between early CVP monitoring (≤6 hours after ICU admission) and 30-day mortality. A nonlinear J-shaped association emerged, with the lowest risk at 2.89 hours post-admission. Early CVP monitoring was associated with lower 30-day mortality (OR = 0.816, 95% CI: 0.688-0.967, P = .019). A landmark sensitivity analysis comparing no monitoring, early (≤6 hours), intermediate (6-86 hours), and late (>86 hours) monitoring showed a time-dependent relationship: intermediate (OR = 1.396, 95% CI: 1.194-1.632, P < .001) and late monitoring (OR = 3.141, 95% CI: 2.263-4.359, P < .001) were associated with progressively higher mortality. In critically ill patients with comorbid heart failure and sepsis, early CVP monitoring within 6 hours of ICU admission was associated with lower 30-day mortality, while delayed monitoring carried an elevated risk. Early integration of CVP within a multimodal hemodynamic assessment framework may be a prudent approach in this high-risk population.

42989152.title: Prediction of 30-day mortality risk in patients with acute pancreatitis in ICU: a study based on the MIMIC-IV database.
42989152.abstract: Acute pancreatitis (AP) in the intensive care unit (ICU) exhibits rapid progression and high 30-day mortality, necessitating efficient early risk prediction methods. This study analyzed 724 ICU patients from the MIMIC-IV database. Key predictors were screened using LASSO regression, and a multivariate logistic regression model was constructed to evaluate 30-day mortality risk. Twelve key predictors-including blood urea nitrogen (BUN), red blood cell distribution width (RDW), pH, sepsis status, and vasopressor use-were identified. The model demonstrated strong discrimination, with area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.85 and 0.89 across sets, an overall accuracy of 77%, and significantly lower 30-day survival in high-risk groups (60% vs. 97%). The proposed model effectively stratifies 30-day mortality risk in ICU AP patients, offering valuable support for early clinical intervention and personalized management. Not applicable.

42991039.title: Update in short-term mechanical circulatory support: indications, devices and complications.
42991039.abstract: Despite advances in early recognition, aetiology-directed therapy, intensive cardiovascular care and short-term mechanical circulatory support (MCS), cardiogenic shock (CS) remains associated with high mortality and morbidity. MCS can restore systemic perfusion and stabilise patients as a bridge to recovery or advanced heart failure therapies, or as a bridge-to-decision when the final therapeutic destination remains uncertain. However, appropriate patient and device selection remains challenging. The optimal timing of support is uncertain, as both premature implantation and delayed use in advanced shock may limit benefit while increasing complications. Device selection should therefore be individualised according to the predominant patient phenotype, including left ventricular, right ventricular or biventricular failure, concomitant respiratory failure, vascular access and anatomical considerations. Randomised trials have focused predominantly on acute myocardial infarction-related CS, whereas data in heart failure-related and acute-on-chronic CS remain limited. Recent trials have also shown that greater haemodynamic support does not uniformly translate into improved survival, highlighting the importance of matching device physiology to shock phenotype and clinical trajectory. MCS is associated with clinically relevant complications, including major bleeding, haemolysis, limb ischaemia, stroke, thrombosis and vascular injury. Accordingly, its use should be considered within a strategy integrating reversibility, neurological prognosis, recovery potential, a realistic definitive therapeutic strategy, technical feasibility and anticipated complication risk. This Mini Review summarises contemporary indications, devices and complications of MCS in CS, with emphasis on phenotype-guided selection, timing, intensive care management and current evidence gaps.

42994604.title: Transfer of prehospital defibrillator recordings to receiving hospitals after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a 16-year retrospective study in Paris.

42994603.title: Metabolic Failure and EEG Abnormalities After Cardiac Arrest: Which Comes First, the Chicken or the Egg?

42995612.title: Fluid-intolerance signals as bedside safety limits during early septic shock resuscitation: a multicenter randomized trial.
42995612.abstract: Fluid resuscitation in early septic shock has a narrow therapeutic index. Signals of fluid intolerance are frequently present during early resuscitation, yet current resuscitation strategies do not incorporate them to guide when to limit fluid administration. We evaluated whether integrating fluid-intolerance signals as safety limits could reduce fluid-induced harm without compromising hypoperfusion resolution. In this multicenter, open-label randomized trial in three Chilean ICUs, mechanically ventilated adults with septic shock, persistent hypoperfusion, fluid responsiveness, and at least one high-risk criterion for fluid-induced harm were randomized 1:1 to a fluid-intolerance-limited resuscitation strategy or standard care during a 6-hour protocol window. In the intervention arm, before each bolus, fluid-intolerance signals (lung ultrasound score, VExUS, E/lateral e', and central venous pressure) were graded as traffic-light: green received a 500-mL bolus, yellow 250 mL, and red no further fluid. Standard care delivered 500-mL boluses while hypoperfusion and fluid responsiveness persisted. The primary outcome was the change in PaO2:FiO2 from baseline to 6 h (ΔPaO2:FiO2). Recruitment was discontinued before the planned sample size was reached because continued enrollment was no longer feasible. Among 113 screened patients, 36 of a planned 62 were randomized, and 35 were analyzed (18 standard care, 17 intervention). The intervention group received a lower protocol bolus volume during the 6-hour intervention window than the standard-care group (250 [125-500] vs. 650 [500-1500] mL; between-group difference, - 500 mL [95% CI, - 750 to - 250]). Cumulative fluid exposure from pre-randomization through the end of the protocol window was similar between groups (3375 [2375-3875] vs. 3750 [1875-4851] mL; between-group difference, - 150 mL [95% CI, - 1470 to 1250]). The primary outcome favored the intervention: median ΔPaO2:FiO2 was 40.5 [24.0-58.5] versus - 37.9 [-69.2 to -12.5]; p < 0.001 (between-group median difference + 78.3 points; 95% CI 50.5 to 110.0), and 0-6-hour changes in lactate and capillary refill time did not differ. Because the trial was stopped early, the effect of a fluid-intolerance-limited resuscitation strategy on oxygenation remains uncertain. A larger trial would be needed to determine whether this strategy improves oxygenation. Such a trial appears feasible. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier NCT06568744, registered August 21, 2024.

42996897.title: Beyond flow: a ventricular-load framework for VA-ECMO in cardiogenic shock.
42996897.abstract: Cardiogenic shock still carries a 30-day mortality of approximately 40%-50% despite reperfusion, vasoactive support and modern intensive care. Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) can rapidly restore systemic perfusion, but recent randomised evidence has reframed its role. In infarct-related shock, randomised trials have not shown a clear survival benefit from routine early VA-ECMO; ECLS-SHOCK and pooled analyses also found more bleeding and vascular complications. In the same period, DanGer Shock showed that a primary microaxial-pump (Impella CP) strategy improved survival in a carefully selected population with ST-elevation myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock, although it was tested against standard care rather than head-to-head against VA-ECMO and does not isolate unloading as the causal mechanism. Read together, these data motivate the central argument of this review: peripheral VA-ECMO is usefully managed not only as a problem of circulatory flow, but also as a dynamic problem of ventricular loading. We advance this as an organising framework rather than as a demonstrated mechanism, since differences in patient selection between these trials offer a competing and equally tenable explanation. Retrograde aortic return increases effective LV afterload, while venous drainage reduces preload; the clinical result depends on the interaction between circuit flow, native contractility and biventricular loading conditions. This narrative, non-systematic review synthesises contemporary trial evidence, the physiology and treatment of LV loading, and approaches to serial assessment of the supported heart, from haemodynamics and bedside echocardiography to emerging deformation and advanced imaging tools. VA-ECMO should therefore be viewed as a time-limited bridge whose net benefit depends on reversible disease, early recognition of clinically relevant ventricular overload and repeated assessment of recovery, escalation options and futility.

42995194.title: A Shock to the System: Vasopressors for Sepsis in Africa and Beyond.

42999955.title: [Post-resuscitation care 2025: neurological prognosis of post-cardiac arrest brain injury].
42999955.abstract: Post-cardiac arrest brain injury represents a central component of the post-resuscitation syndrome, driven not only by the initial hypoxic-ischemic insult but also by reperfusion injury after the return or start of mechanical circulation. Complex neuronal damage accounts for a substantial proportion of mortality among successfully resuscitated patients, making reliable neurological prognostication a key objective of post-resuscitation care and clinical decision-making. The 2025 European Resuscitation Council guidelines emphasize a structured, multimodal approach to neuroprognostication. Prognosis should not rely on a single parameter; instead, it requires the integrated interpretation of clinical findings, electrophysiological data, neuroimaging results, and circulating biomarkers. This strategy aims to reduce falsely pessimistic predictions, prevent premature withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy, and avoid the unnecessary prolongation of futile intensive care in cases of irreversible brain injury. In the early phase of return of spontaneous circulation, neurological assessment may be confounded by several factors, including residual sedation, neuromuscular blockade, metabolic disturbances, and cardiorespiratory instability. Therefore, accurate prognostication depends on the correction of reversible conditions and stabilization of physiological parameters before definitive conclusions are drawn. Importantly, neurological outcome assessment is inherently time-dependent, and appropriate timing is essential for safe and evidence-based decision-making. Overall, the 2025 recommendations advocate standardized, multidisciplinary, and stepwise neuroprognostication as a cornerstone of post-resuscitation management, prioritizing patient-centered care while minimizing uncertainty and supporting long-term neurological recovery whenever possible. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(45): 1799-1809.

43003534.title: Valvular Shock in the Cardiac Intensive Care Unit: Perioperative Care for Transcatheter Valve Interventions.
43003534.abstract: Valvular heart disease is an uncommon but high-risk cause of cardiogenic shock requiring rapid, multidisciplinary management aimed at bridging patients to definitive surgical or transcatheter valve intervention. Early comprehensive Doppler echocardiography is essential, as clinical signs may be subtle. Distinguishing decompensated chronic valvular disease from acute unstable lesions guides urgency and treatment strategy. Medical stabilization and mechanical circulatory support vary markedly between stenotic and regurgitant lesions, and standard shock therapies may be harmful in specific contexts. Transcatheter approaches are preferred when feasible, though their expanding use introduces added complexity in cardiac intensive care.

43003685.title: Cold septic shock: recognising the low-output phenotype.
43003685.abstract: Septic shock is commonly taught as a warm, vasodilated state, but the cold, low-output phenotype, in which the underlying process is still sepsis but cardiac output is low and vascular resistance high, is under-recognised. Escalating vasopressors alone in these patients support the blood pressure while leaving the low output untreated.
