TRIAL REGISTRATION: This study was prospectively registered Netherlands: Trial Register/International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, NL9812, October 21, 2021.

42658259.title: Balancing lung and brain: physiological strategies for ARDS management in acute brain injury.
42658259.abstract: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a common and clinically significant complication in patients with acute brain injury (ABI), affecting up to one-third of critically ill individuals and contributing to increased mortality, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and worse neurological outcomes. The coexistence of ARDS and ABI creates a fundamental therapeutic dilemma: strategies that protect the lung may adversely affect cerebral physiology, whilst neuroprotective targets may compromise respiratory management. This narrative review examined the pathophysiological interactions between the injured lung and brain, highlighting the competing effects of key ventilatory variables. Lung-protective ventilation, including low tidal volume and higher positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), reduces ventilator-induced lung injury but may increase arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO2), resulting in intracranial hypertension and impaired cerebral perfusion. Conversely, strict control of PaCO₂ and optimisation of cerebral perfusion may necessitate deviations from conventional ARDS strategies. Oxygenation targets further illustrate this tension, as both hypoxaemia and hyperoxaemia can exacerbate secondary brain injury. We synthesised current evidence on respiratory support, including non-invasive strategies, invasive mechanical ventilation, rescue therapies such as prone positioning and extracorporeal support, and pharmacological interventions, with emphasis on their differential effects on pulmonary and cerebral physiology. Attention was also given to the role of multimodal neuromonitoring, including intracranial pressure and brain tissue oxygenation, as tools to individualise ventilatory management and reconcile competing organ priorities. Overall, available data support a shift from protocolised approaches towards physiology-driven, patient-specific strategies that integrate lung mechanics, gas exchange and cerebral haemodynamics in patients with concomitant ARDS and ABI. Future studies should incorporate combined lung and brain endpoints to define strategies that simultaneously minimise ventilator-induced lung injury and secondary brain injury.

42765454.title: Semi-recumbent position for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia in adults requiring mechanical ventilation.
42765454.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
42765454.abstract: RATIONALE: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is associated with increased mortality, hospital stay, and healthcare costs in critically ill patients. Although guidelines recommend a semi-recumbent position for VAP prevention, the evidence remains uncertain due to limitations in prior reviews. This update revises the 2016 review. OBJECTIVES: To assess the effectiveness and safety of semi-recumbent versus supine or another positioning, and different degrees or types of semi-recumbent positioning in mechanically ventilated intensive care unit (ICU) patients. SEARCH METHODS: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, AMED, three Chinese databases, and two trial registries up to 3 October 2025, and screened reference lists. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing semi-recumbent versus supine or another positioning, or different degrees or types of semi-recumbent positioning in mechanically ventilated adult ICU patients. OUTCOMES: Outcomes include clinically suspected or microbiologically confirmed VAP, ICU or hospital mortality, length of ICU or hospital stay, duration of ventilation, and pressure ulcers. RISK OF BIAS: We assessed the risk of bias using Cochrane's RoB 1 tool. SYNTHESIS METHODS: Paired review authors independently screened studies, assessed risk of bias, and extracted data. We performed random-effects meta-analyses using mean difference (MD) for continuous and risk ratio (RR) for binary outcomes with 95% confidence intervals (CI). We evaluated evidence certainty using GRADE. INCLUDED STUDIES: This update includes 38 new RCTs, making a total of 48 included studies (7955 participants). SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: 1. Semi-recumbent position versus supine position: 17 studies, 2640 participants A semi-recumbent position, versus a supine position, reduces clinically suspected VAP (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.52; 14 studies, 2411 participants; high-certainty evidence), but may result in little to no difference in microbiologically confirmed VAP (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.25 to 1.27; 5 studies, 555 participants; low-certainty evidence), and probably results in little to no difference in ICU or hospital mortality (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.08; 3 studies, 430 participants; RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.12; 5 studies, 570 participants; both moderate-certainty evidence). Due to very low-certainty evidence, we do not know the effects on ICU or hospital length of stay (MD -3.25 days, 95% CI -7.14 to 0.63; 5 studies, 466 participants; MD -8.17 days, 95% CI -40.10 to 23.76; 3 studies, 320 participants). It may reduce the duration of ventilation (MD -3.26 days, 95% CI -6.02 to -0.51; 7 studies, 688 participants; low-certainty evidence). We do not know the effect on pressure ulcers (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.56; 4 studies, 840 participants; very low-certainty evidence). 2. Semi-recumbent position 30° to 45° versus < 30°: 11 studies, 1153 participants A semi-recumbent position at 30° to 45°, versus < 30°, reduces clinically suspected VAP (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.59; 8 studies, 810 participants; high-certainty evidence). It may result in little to no difference in microbiologically confirmed VAP (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.02; 5 studies, 451 participants), ICU or hospital mortality (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.20 to 2.29; 3 studies, 271 participants; RR 0.66, 0.37 to 1.17; 2 studies, 145 participants), or duration of ventilation (MD -0.62 days, 95% CI -4.17 to 2.93; 1 study, 87 participants) (all low-certainty evidence). There is no evidence for ICU or hospital stay. It probably increases pressure ulcers (RR 2.79, 95% CI 1.28 to 6.11; 6 studies, 712 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). 3. Semi-recumbent position 40° to 45° versus 30°: 14 studies, 1374 participants A semi-recumbent position at 40° to 45°, versus 30°, probably results in little to no difference in clinically suspected VAP (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.33; 10 studies, 1026 participants; moderate-certainty evidence), but may reduce microbiologically confirmed VAP (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.99; 4 studies, 218 participants; low-certainty evidence). There were no deaths in ICU (1 study, 46 participants; low-certainty evidence). Due to very low-certainty evidence, we do not know the effects on hospital mortality (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.27 to 5.50; 2 studies, 221 participants), length of ICU stay (MD -1.28 days, 95% CI -6.69 to 4.12; 2 studies, 221 participants), or duration of ventilation (MD -1.09 days, 95% CI -4.60 to 2.43; 2 studies, 206 participants). There is no evidence for hospital stay. It probably increases pressure ulcers (RR 2.42, 95% CI 1.16 to 5.06; 10 studies, 943 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). 4. Semi-recumbent position versus semi-recumbent lateral or lateral rotation position: 7 studies, 708 participants A semi-recumbent position, versus semi-recumbent lateral or lateral rotation, probably increases clinically suspected and microbiologically confirmed VAP (RR 1.99, 95% CI 1.48 to 2.70; 6 studies, 608 participants; RR 5.14, 95% CI 2.53 to 10.44; 1 study, 100 participants; both moderate-certainty evidence), but may result in little to no difference in hospital mortality (RR 2.50, 95% CI 0.53 to 11.89; 1 study, 60 participants; low-certainty evidence). There is no evidence on ICU mortality. It probably prolongs the length of ICU or hospital stay and the duration of ventilation (days: MD 5.69, 95% CI 5.44 to 5.94; 2 studies, 120 participants; MD 6.25, 95% CI 4.09 to 8.41; 2 studies, 240 participants; MD 5.99, 95% CI 1.60 to 10.38; 4 studies, 400 participants; all moderate-certainty evidence). There is no evidence for pressure ulcers. Evidence was limited on the semi-recumbent position at 60° versus 45°, or versus other positions (e.g. semi-recumbent rotation, lateral Trendelenburg, or prone position). AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Compared with supine positioning, semi-recumbent positioning reduces VAP, and may shorten the duration of ventilation. Higher head-of-bed angles (≥ 30° or 40° to 45°) probably reduce VAP, but increase pressure ulcers, with other comparisons remaining uncertain. Compared with fixed-angled semi-recumbent positioning, semi-recumbent lateral or lateral rotation positioning probably reduces VAP and shortens the duration of ventilation, and length of ICU and hospital stay. Evidence on adverse events and comparisons with alternative positions remains inconclusive. LIMITATIONS: evidence certainty was limited by risk of bias, imprecision due to small sample sizes, and inconsistency across studies. Inadequate reporting of actual head-of-bed angle for semi-recumbent positioning and variation in VAP definitions may influence our findings. FUNDING: No funding. REGISTRATION: Protocol (2012) DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD009946 Original review (2016) DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD009946.pub2.

42778957.title: The NLRP3 inflammasome in physiological and dysfunctional host response in human sepsis and critical illness: a narrative review.
42778957.abstract: BACKGROUND: The NLRP3 inflammasome is a cytosolic multiprotein complex that serves as a key regulator of innate immunity by reacting to pathogen- and damage-associated signals and orchestrating downstream inflammatory responses. Inflammasome activation induces caspase-1-dependent maturation of interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-18 and gasdermin D, which results in pyroptotic cell death. MAIN TEXT: While tightly controlled inflammasome activation is essential for effective host defence and pathogen clearance, accumulating evidence implicates its dysregulation as a central driver of host response imbalance in critical illness. In conditions such as sepsis and acute respiratory distress syndrome, excessive activation contributes to hyperinflammation, endothelial dysfunction, immunothrombosis, and multi-organ failure. Conversely, insufficient or exhausted inflammasome responses may impair microbial clearance and predispose to secondary infections. These observations underscore the context-dependent and temporally dynamic role of inflammasome signalling as being either protective or pathogenic. Emerging therapeutic strategies aim to restore immune homeostasis through targeted modulation of inflammasome pathways, including IL-1 blockade (e.g., anakinra) and inhibition of upstream signalling components. However, clinical translation remains challenging, requiring improved patient stratification, biomarker-guided approaches, and a deeper understanding of disease heterogeneity. CONCLUSIONS: Inflammasome signalling plays a highly dynamic role in critical illness, contributing to effective host defence, if functional, or to pathological inflammation, if dysregulated. Although targeted modulation of inflammasome pathways represents a promising therapeutic strategy, further research is needed to refine patient selection, identify reliable biomarkers, and better characterise disease heterogeneity to enable successful clinical translation.

42790625.title: Cough Function During Mechanical Ventilation.
42790625.abstract: TOPIC IMPORTANCE: Cough is a vital physiologic function that clears the tracheobronchial tree and facilitates effective gas exchange through secretion clearance. In patients in the ICU, ineffective cough is frequent, primarily because of respiratory muscle dysfunction and the presence of the endotracheal tube, which prevents glottic closure. Ineffective cough has been identified as an independent risk factor for extubation failure and prolonged mechanical ventilation. REVIEW FINDINGS: Current guidelines recognize ineffective cough as a key criterion for successful weaning from mechanical ventilation. Nevertheless, its clinical assessment remains challenging and lacks standardization. Accurate and objective evaluation of cough may improve the identification of patients at high risk of extubation failure. Beyond extubation failure, ineffective cough also has been associated with increased incidence of postextubation pneumonia, longer ICU stay, and impaired long-term respiratory function. Poor outcome highlights the broader clinical impact of ineffective cough and reinforces the need for standardized assessment during ventilator weaning. SUMMARY: This narrative review aimed to decipher the mechanisms underlying the cough reflex, to outline the pathophysiologic alterations observed in critically ill patients, particularly during the weaning process, and to examine the available methods for cough quantification.

42714473.title: Distinct weaning phenotypes in patients unsuccessful in weaning from invasive mechanical ventilation: a secondary analysis of the WEAN SAFE cohort.
42714473.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To characterise the trajectories and outcomes of patients who enter the weaning process but fail to wean from invasive mechanical ventilation (MV). METHODS: In this secondary analysis of the WorldwidE AssessmeNt of Separation of pAtients From ventilatory assistancE (WEAN SAFE) cohort, we examined weaning duration and intensity, decisions to withdraw or withhold life-sustaining therapy (WLST), and clinical outcomes in patients not weaning from invasive ventilation. The primary outcome was ICU mortality. RESULTS: Of the 5664 patients in the study population, 1270 (22.4%) never underwent a separation attempt (SA), while 4394 (77.6%) had at least one SA; of these, 664 (15.1%) eventually failed weaning from invasive MV at day 90, while 3730 (65.9%) successfully weaned. Failed-Wean patients had the longest duration of invasive ventilation and longest ICU stay of all groups. Compared with Successful-Wean, Failed-Wean patients underwent more separation attempts, but fewer attempted extubations and more reintubations and tracheostomies. ICU mortality was 78% in Failed-Wean compared with 2% in Successful-Wean. Three clinically distinct Failed-Wean phenotypes were identified, distinguished by separation attempt count and WLST timing: Phenotype A (single SA + WLST), Phenotype B (single SA, no WLST), and Phenotype C (> 1 SA). A failed-first SA was strongly associated with WLST decisions. In this cohort, a WLST decision was associated with a higher hazard of ICU mortality and shorter median time to ICU death. CONCLUSIONS: Three weaning failure phenotypes were identified with distinct clinical profiles, weaning trajectories, and outcomes. A strong relationship exists between failed first separation attempts, WLST decision, and the risk of death, which deserves further investigation. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03255109.

42618770.title: Respiratory mechanics modifies the impact of ventilator settings on clinical outcome in patients with acute brain injury.
42618770.abstract: PURPOSE: To investigate whether respiratory system elastance (ERS) modifies the associations of tidal volume (VT) and respiratory rate with clinical outcomes in mechanically ventilated patients with acute brain injury. METHODS: In this post hoc analysis of the VENTIBRAIN study, ERS was computed as the ratio of driving pressure (ΔP) to VT/PBW. Effect modification by ERS on outcome associations was assessed. RESULTS: In 1158 patients, VT was similar across ERS tertiles (median 7.9, 7.6 and 7.1 mL/kg), resulting in a marked ΔP gradient across tertiles (median 5, 9, and 12 cmH2O). Higher VT was associated with lower ICU mortality in patients with low ERS (OR 0.52, 95%CI 0.36-0.74) but not in those with high ERS (OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.89-1.51; Pint < 0.001). Higher respiratory rate was associated with worse outcomes, particularly at low ERS, with the association attenuating at higher ERS. The Bayesian optimal VT/PBW decreased continuously with ERS, from 11.4 mL/kg at ERS 0.5 cmH2O/(mL/kg) (≈ ΔP 6 cmH2O) to 4.4 mL/kg at ERS 2.5 cmH2O/(mL/kg) (≈ ΔP 11 cmH2O), while the optimal respiratory rate increased from 15 to 19 breaths/min. At constant alveolar ventilation, 1-cmH2O ΔP increase had comparable prognostic impact to ≈ 3 breaths/min respiratory rate increases. These results were consistent irrespective of ARDS diagnosis. CONCLUSIONS: The impact of ventilator settings is modulated by ERS. A physiological framework for VT adjustment could consider ΔP along with the respiratory rate required to maintain isocapnia, with outcome effects governed by a trade-off of ≈ 3 breaths/min per 1-cmH2O change in ΔP.

42593537.title: Decades of intensive care medicine trials: what randomised evidence has changed, corrected, and still questions to resolve.
42593537.abstract: BACKGROUND: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) have reshaped intensive care medicine (ICM), a discipline defined by acute, interacting organ failures, time-sensitive decisions, biological uncertainty, and heterogeneous recovery trajectories. Many interventions supported by strong physiological rationale failed to improve patient-centred outcomes, whereas durable advances often emerged from optimisation of supportive care, avoidance of iatrogenic harm, and reassessment of established practices. METHODS: We conducted an interpretive historical review of landmark multicentre RCTs in adult ICM from the early 1990s onwards. PubMed searches, reference lists from major trials and reviews, and international guidelines were used to identify trials with conceptual influence on practice, guidelines, physiological reasoning, therapeutic strategy, research priorities, de-implementation, or outcome framing. Evidence was organised into overlapping paradigms rather than rigid chronological periods. FINDINGS: Across haemodynamic support, mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, antimicrobial treatment, nutrition, glucose control, transfusion, and sedation, landmark RCTs describe more than therapeutic expansion. Early biological and haemodynamic trials exposed the limits of reductionist strategies in syndromic critical illness. Protocol-driven approaches improved timeliness and consistency, but later pragmatic trials showed that rigid targets and invasive algorithms often added little once high-quality usual care was established. More recent trials challenge the assumption that greater intervention intensity improves outcomes, emphasising timing, disease phase, baseline risk, heterogeneity, patient selection, and treatment-related harm. Modern ICM RCTs have clarified not only what works, but what can be reduced, delayed, avoided, or applied selectively. Future progress requires biologically informed, context-sensitive trials focussed on meaningful survival, recovery, and long-term function.

42823746.title: A specialist-led interprofessional weaning program to prevent weaning failure in high-risk patients: the PRiVENT study.
42823746.abstract: PURPOSE: Effective strategies to prevent weaning failure and prolonged invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in patients at high risk of weaning failure are limited. We evaluated a structured, specialist-led interprofessional weaning program. METHODS: In this prospective, multicenter, non-randomized interventional study, mechanically ventilated patients were screened 96 h to 11 days after intubation. Patients meeting predefined high-risk criteria received a specialist-led interprofessional weaning program, while a parallel control group was derived from health insurance claims data. The primary outcome was successful weaning at ICU discharge. RESULTS: The primary analysis included 349 intervention patients and 1,768 controls. Successful weaning occurred in 58.3% of intervention patients and 51.7% of controls. In the adjusted primary analysis, the odds ratio for successful weaning was 1.46 (95% CI, 0.99-2.17; P = 0.057), and the difference did not reach statistical significance. In prespecified propensity score-matched analysis, successful weaning occurred in 58.3% of intervention patients and 46.4% of matched controls (OR, 2.90; 95% CI, 1.61-5.24; P < 0.001). An exploratory analysis restricted to ICU survivors also showed higher odds of successful weaning in the intervention group (OR, 2.10; 95% CI, 1.09-4.04; P = 0.026). Overall, 16.3% of intervention patients were transferred to a specialized weaning center. These patients had longer ventilation durations, contributing to a longer overall duration of IMV in the intervention group. CONCLUSIONS: The PRiVENT intervention was feasible and successful weaning was numerically more frequent in the intervention group, although the prespecified adjusted primary analysis did not reach statistical significance. These findings suggest a potential benefit of structured, multidisciplinary weaning support. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05260853, registered on March 2, 2022.

42872606.title: Fluid Therapy in Mechanically Ventilated Critically Ill Adult Patients.
42872606.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Fluid therapy is ubiquitous in the intensive care unit (ICU) but carries risks, especially in mechanically ventilated patients. Contemporary global practice across dose, indication, and type is unknown. OBJECTIVE: To characterize ICU fluid practices in mechanically ventilated adults. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: International prospective observational cohort study between April 2024 and July 2025, across 206 ICUs in 41 countries on 6 continents. Consecutive adult patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation within 3 days of ICU admission and ventilated 24 hours or more. Exclusion criteria were age younger than 16 years and transfer under mechanical ventilation from another ICU. EXPOSURES: Fluid volume, indication, and type after intubation. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Key measures included (1) total infused volume and daily fluid balance over 7 days after intubation; (2) the indication for fluid therapy over the first 3 days after intubation; (3) the proportion of total administered fluid volume attributable to each fluid type over the first 3 days after intubation. RESULTS: Among 2454 patients analyzed (median age, 63 years [IQR, 49-73 years]; 63.6% [1560] male), median daily fluid input peaked on day 1 at 3.0 L (IQR, 2.2-4.0 L) and declined to 2.6 L (IQR, 1.8-3.5 L) through day 6. Daily fluid balance (median, 0.9 L; IQR, 0.1-1.9 L on day 1) decreased to less than 0.3 L (IQR, -0.5 to 1.2 L) by day 3 and remained near-neutral through day 6. Maintenance and replacement fluids (to meet daily requirements and to correct ongoing losses; 31.9%) and creep fluids (to deliver medications and maintain catheter patency; 30.9%) were the primary indications, whereas resuscitation (to restore circulating blood volume; 16.0%) accounted for a smaller proportion. Isotonic balanced crystalloids (48.9%) and isotonic saline (0.9% sodium chloride) (27.0%) were common; colloids were rare (1.3%). Substantial between-site variation persisted after adjustment for case-mix. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this prospective international cohort study, fluid therapy varied widely among mechanically ventilated critically ill patients, with maintenance and creep fluids-rather than resuscitation fluids-accounting for most total volume.

42878628.title: Weaning Strategies for High-Flow Nasal Cannula in Critically Ill Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
42878628.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study evaluated the efficacy of different high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) weaning protocols in critically ill adults. DESIGN: This multicenter, randomized controlled trial was conducted from December 1, 2022, to August 31, 2024, based on the suggested protocol (SLOWH trial). Experts reviewed the trial between October 2, 2024, and April 15, 2025. SETTING: Randomization was performed by a research coordinator using a sequence of random numbers generated by an independent statistician blinded to both researchers and participants. PATIENTS: Adults (≥ 18 yr old) in the ICU who met the weaning criteria after receiving HFNC were included. Among 102 patients from three tertiary care hospitals, 15 were excluded. INTERVENTIONS: The remaining patients were randomized into three intervention groups: flow reduction (FR) first, Fio2 reduction (OR) first, or simultaneous reduction (SR). The primary outcome was the HFNC weaning success rate, defined as successful transition to conventional oxygen therapy without the need for HFNC reapplication, noninvasive ventilation, or endotracheal intubation within 24 hours. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: A total of 87 adults completed the trial (FR, n = 31 [male, 52%]; OR, n = 26 [male, 77%]; SR, n = 30 [male, 53%]). The weaning success rates in the FR, OR, and SR groups were 94%, 81%, and 77%, respectively (p = 0.15). The median [interquartile range] weaning duration was 31.0 hours (29.0-45.8 hr), 29.5 hours (28.0-60.4 hr), and 29.5 hours (26.5-45.0 hr) in the FR, OR, and SR groups, respectively, with no statistically significant difference among groups (p = 0.87). CONCLUSIONS: In this randomized trial, no statistically significant differences were observed among the three HFNC weaning strategies in terms of weaning success or duration.

42878609.title: Ventilatory Management in Neurocritical Versus Non-Neurocritical Care Patients: A Pooled Analysis From the PRIME Database.
authors: PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients without ARDS (PRoVENT), PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients in Middle-income Countries (PRoVENT-iMiC), and Extubation strategies in Neuro-ICU patients and associations with Outcomes (ENIO) investigators
42878609.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To describe ventilatory management in neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients and determine whether specific ventilator settings are associated with development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and mortality in neurocritical care patients. The primary endpoint was a diagnosis of ARDS after initiation of invasive ventilation; one secondary endpoint was ICU mortality. DATA SOURCES: Post hoc pooled analysis of harmonized individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies combined into the PRIME database. STUDY SELECTION: PRIME is a harmonized pooled database comprising individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies on ventilatory management in critically ill patients: "PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients without ARDS" (PRoVENT), "PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients in Middle-income Countries" (PRoVENT-iMiC), and "Extubation strategies in Neuro-ICU patients and associations with Outcomes" (ENIO). We excluded patients with ARDS at the start of ventilation. DATA EXTRACTION: Demographic and clinical characteristics, ventilator settings, respiratory variables, arterial blood gas values, and clinical outcomes were extracted from the harmonized PRIME database. Derived ventilation parameters included tidal volume normalized to predicted body weight, driving pressure, respiratory system compliance, mechanical power, ventilatory ratio, and Pao2/Fio2 ratio. DATA SYNTHESIS: This analysis included 3848 patients, including 1702 neurocritical care and 1920 non-neurocritical care patients. Based on recorded ventilatory variables, neurocritical care patients received lower median tidal volumes (Vts), positive end-expiratory pressure, and Fio2. They had lower median driving pressure (ΔP), mechanical power (MP) of ventilation, and ventilatory ratio, as well as higher respiratory system compliance compared with non-neurocritical care patients. These differences were consistently observed at both assessed time points. ARDS was diagnosed more frequently in neurocritical care patients than in non-neurocritical care patients (8.7% vs. 3.9%; p < 0.001), while ICU mortality was lower (14.3% vs. 22.8%; p < 0.001). Among neurocritical care patients, those who developed ARDS were ventilated with lower median Vt and higher Fio2 and had higher median ΔP and MP. Vt normalized for predicted body weight in neurocritical care patients was independently associated with the development of ARDS. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, ventilatory management at the initial and 48-hour assessments differed between neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients, particularly with respect to key ventilator settings like Vt, positive end-expiratory pressure, and Fio2. In neurocritical care patients, ARDS was more often diagnosed than in non-neurocritical care patients.

42902295.title: Toward targeted assessment of inspiratory muscle weakness before extubation: a pooled individual patient data analysis from multiple observational cohorts in critically ill ventilated patients.
42902295.abstract: BACKGROUND: Bedside neuromuscular tests are commonly proposed to assess readiness for extubation in critically ill patients. However, when used in unselected populations, their ability to predict clinically relevant outcomes such as extubation failure has been inconsistent. A more targeted use of these tests, restricted to patients in whom neuromuscular weakness is more likely to contribute to weaning failure, may improve their clinical relevance. METHODS: We conducted a pooled individual patient data analysis of multiple observational cohorts including adult ICU patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation. The primary outcome was extubation failure, defined as reintubation or death within 48 h after extubation. Available neuromuscular assessments included maximal inspiratory pressure (MIP), maximal expiratory pressure (MEP), peak cough flow (PCF), and Medical Research Council (MRC) sum score. Prespecified thresholds were MIP ≤ 30 cmH₂O, MEP ≤ 50 cmH₂O, PCF ≤ 60 L/min, and MRC < 48/60. Associations with extubation failure were assessed in the overall population and according to prior mechanical ventilation duration. RESULTS: Among 494 included patients, 458 had an available extubation outcome and 72 (16%) experienced extubation failure. MIP was available in 230 patients, MEP in 124, PCF in 156, and MRC score in 252. In the overall population, MIP ≤ 30 cmH₂O showed only a borderline association with extubation failure (24% vs. 14%; OR 1.94, 95% CI 0.98 to 3.84; p = 0.06). In patients ventilated for more than 5 days, extubation failure occurred in 33% with MIP ≤ 30 cmH₂O versus 14% with MIP > 30 cmH₂O. After adjustment, MIP ≤ 30 cmH₂O remained associated with extubation failure (adjusted OR 3.52, 95% CI 1.37 to 9.03; p = 0.009). No significant adjusted association was observed for MEP, PCF, or MRC. CONCLUSIONS: Neuromuscular tests may have limited prognostic value when applied broadly before extubation. Low MIP appears more informative after prolonged mechanical ventilation, supporting a targeted rather than systematic use of respiratory neuromuscular assessment before extubation.

42904879.title: Music Therapy During Weaning From Invasive Mechanical Ventilation in the ICU: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
42904879.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The study examined the effect of daily music therapy on weaning from invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in the ICU, with a primary focus on weaning duration. Secondary agitation, sedation, and analgesia doses, pain, delirium, and perceived stress after 90 days were assessed. Additionally, total IMV and ICU stay durations and tracheostomy rates were studied. Physiologic parameters were assessed in the music therapy group (MG). The study also aimed to promote the humanization of critical care through a biopsychosocial and creative music therapy approach. DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups: control group receiving standard care during weaning and MG receiving music therapy additionally. SETTING AND PATIENTS: Adult critically ill patients (n = 100) admitted to a general ICU who received IMV for at least 48 hours. INTERVENTIONS: MG received daily, individualized music therapy sessions averaging 25 minutes, based on patient needs and musical preferences, which included music relaxation, music listening, and clinical improvisation. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: No significant difference in weaning duration was observed between groups (p = 0.97). Patients in the MG group showed significant improvements in agitation and sedation levels (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale) on days 1 and 3 (p = 0.048, 0.005, and 0.024) and a lower percentage required propofol (p = 0.028). No significant difference in perceived pain (Visual Analog Pain Scale). The MG obtained lower Perceived Stress Scale-14 scores (p = 0.24). Additionally, MG significantly reduced tracheostomy rates (14%; p = 0.025). Median total IMV and ICU stay duration were shorter in the MG group, but not significantly (p = 0.206 and 0.203). Heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygenation showed no significant difference before and after music therapy. CONCLUSIONS: Music therapy may serve as a nonpharmacological complementary adjunct during weaning by reducing agitation, sedation, and tracheostomy rate. It may potentially decrease perceived stress and IMV and ICU stay durations. Further research is warranted.

42958418.title: Chlorhexidine within a standardized oral-care bundle for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia: a pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover trial in six medical intensive care units.
42958418.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chlorhexidine (CHX) has been a long-standing component of oral-care bundles for preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), but recent evidence has questioned its benefit in non-cardiac-surgery ICU. We evaluated whether adding 0.12% CHX to standardized oral-care bundle provides incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU. METHODS: We conducted a prospective, pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover (AB/BA) trial in six adult medical ICUs of a single tertiary-care academic hospital in Bhubaneswar, India. ICUs were randomized as three ICUs of two Period of 9 months with the multicomponent oral-care bundle without chlorhexidine and three with the same bundle plus 0.12% chlorhexidine with a 1-month wash-in and re-training interval. Consecutive adults ventilated for ≥ 48 h were included. The primary outcome was VAP incidence density (Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score (CPIS) > 6) as per 1,000 ventilator-days. Secondary outcomes were 28-day all-cause mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, 28- day ventilator-free days, Beck Oral Assessment Scale (BOAS) and Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) scores. The primary model was a population-averaged Poisson generalized estimating equation (GEE) and adjustment for treatment, period, sequence, age, sex, APACHE II, and SOFA. RESULTS: A total of 1,035 patients (637 No CHX, 398 CHX) accrued 10,024 ventilator-days (5,918 vs. 4,106). Groups were well balanced at baseline (mean age ≈ 55 years; APACHE II ≈ 19.6; SOFA ≈ 13.4). VAP occurred in 100/5,918 ventilator-days (16.9 per 1,000) vs. 77/4,106 (18.8 per 1,000) (No CHX vs. CHX). The adjusted Poisson incidence rate ratio was 1.08 (95% CI 0.84-1.38; p = 0.56). 28-day mortality was 28.7% vs. 26.4% (no CHX vs. CHX) (adjusted OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.65-1.15; p = 0.33). ICU length of stay was longer in the CHX arm (adjusted mean difference + 0.89 days, 95% CI + 0.19 to + 1.58; p = 0.013). BOAS and CPOT scores did not differ. CONCLUSIONS: In this trial, adding 0.12% chlorhexidine to a standardized oral-care bundle did not reduce VAP incidence density or 28-day mortality and was associated with a modest increase in ICU length of stay. Routine CHX use provided no clear incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU population. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinical Trials Regisrty- India (CTRI) identifier [CTRI/2024/02/062201], registered [01 February 2024].

42880916.title: [Correlation between acute kidney injury diagnosed by serum creatinine and urine output criteria and short-term prognosis in critically ill patients following non-cardiac surgery].
42880916.journal: Beijing da xue xue bao. Yi xue ban = Journal of Peking University. Health sciences
42880916.abstract: To analyze the correlation between acute kidney injury (AKI) diagnosed by elevated serum creatinine (Scr) versus only meeting the urine output (UO) reduction criteria and short-term adverse outcomes in critically ill patients following non-cardiac surgery, and to evaluate the association between even mild elevations in Scr and clinical outcomes furthermore. This study was a secondary analysis of data from a prospective cohort study. A total of 1020 non-cardiac surgery adults admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) of Peking University First Hospital from May 20, 2019 to March 7, 2022 were included. According to Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guideline, AKI patients were classified into two groups: the AKI-Scr group (those meeting the Scr elevation criteria) and the AKI-UO group (those fulfilling only the UO reduction criteria). The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality in patients with AKI, and the secondary outcomes were major renal adverse events, post-operative renal replacement therapy (RRT), postoperative complications, postoperative mechanical ventilation time, ICU stay, postoperative hospital stay, total hospital stay, and total medical costs. Multivariate Logistic regression analysis was used to identify risk factors of hospitalized death in critically ill patients with AKI following non-cardiac surgery. A total of 1020 non-cardiac surgical patients admitted to the ICU were enrolled, among whom 429 were diagnosed with AKI. There were 91 cases in the AKI-Scr group and 338 cases in the AKI-UO group. The primary study endpoint: no statistically significant difference in in-hospital mortality was observed between the AKI-Scr and AKI-UO groups (5.5% vs. 2.1%, P>0.05). The secondary study endpoints: compared with the AKI-UO group, the patients in the AKI-Scr group had a higher incidence of major renal adverse events (9.8% vs. 4.4%), postoperative RRT (4.4% vs. 0.3%) and postoperative complications (50.5% vs. 24.0%, all P < 0.05), a significantly longer duration of postoperative mechanical ventilation (12.0 d vs. 7.5 d), ICU stay (2 d vs. 1 d), postoperative hospital stay (14 d vs. 9 d) and total hospital stay (21 d vs.17 d, all P < 0.05), and a significantly higher total medical expenditure (112000 yuan vs. 89000 yuan, P<0.001). Multivariate Logistic regression analysis showed that postoperative RRT (OR=33.164, 95%CI: 1.305-842.794, P=0.034) and sepsis during hospitalization (OR=23.096, 95%CI: 4.242-125.175, P < 0.001) were independent risk factors for hospitalized death in the critically ill patients with postoperative AKI. Compared with the ΔScr≤24% patients (Scr increased by less than 24% from baseline within 7 d), even in the patients with only a minor elevation in Scr (ΔScr increase of 25%-49% from baseline but < 26.5μmol/L), the incidence of postoperative complications was significantly higher (48.6% vs. 19.2%, P < 0.001), along with prolonged ICU stay [1(1, 3) d vs. 1(1, 2) d], postoperative hospital stay (13 d vs. 9 d), and total hospital stay (23 d vs. 16 d, all P < 0.05). Compared with the non-AKI group, the incidence of in-hospital mortality (2.1% vs. 0.3%, P < 0.05) and postoperative complications (24.0% vs. 18.3%, P < 0.05) was higher in the AKI-UO group, and the ICU stay [1(1, 3) d vs. 1(1, 2) d, P < 0.001] was longer. In critically ill patients with AKI following non-cardiac surgery, the short-term prognosis of patients with AKI whose diagnosis was mainly based on increased Scr was worse than patients who only met the diagnostic criteria of oliguria. Even a mild elevation in serum creatinine was associated with adverse patient outcomes.

42876844.title: Impact of early goal-directed mobilization on ICU-acquired weakness: a meta-analysis.
42876844.abstract: ICU-acquired weakness (ICU-AW) significantly impairs muscle strength and physical function in critically ill patients. Early mobilization interventions have been increasingly adopted, yet the specific effects of a structured EGDM program on ICU-AW and functional outcomes have not been systematically quantified. This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of EGDM on ICU-AW, muscle strength, and functional outcomes. PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Data, and Viper Information Products (VIP) databases were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) up to November 30, 2025. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using RoB 2.0. RevMan 5.4 was used for meta-analysis. Subgroup analysis was prespecified by allocation concealment. Nine RCTs (907 patients) were included. EGDM reduced ICU-AW [RR = 0.57, 95%CI (0.33 ~ 0.97), p = 0.04 for the overall effect; I2 = 77%, p = 0.002 for heterogeneity], but sensitivity analysis of high-quality trials showed no significant effect [RR = 0.84, 95%CI (0.48 ~ 1.46), p = 0.54 for the overall effect]. EGDM improved muscle strength [MD = 4.94, 95%CI (3.39 ~ 6.50), I2 = 59%, p = 0.02 for heterogeneity], shortened the duration of mechanical ventilation [MD = -81.95 h, 95%CI (-115.45 ~ -48.46), p < 0.00001 for the overall effect; I2 = 85%, p < 0.00001 for heterogeneity], and reduced ICU stay[MD = -4.55 days, 95%CI (-6.22 ~ -2.89), p < 0.00001 for the overall effect; I2 = 74%, p = 0.0004 for heterogeneity], both with substantial heterogeneity. Although the primary Barthel Index analysis was not statistically significant, sensitivity analysis suggested improvement in patients with moderate baseline function [MD = 8.27, 95%CI (5.66 ~ 10.87), p < 0.00001 for the overall effect]. EGDM may improve muscle strength and physical function in ICU patients. The available evidence does not confirm a reduction in ICU-AW. The effects on ventilation duration and ICU stay varied substantially across studies, likely influenced by sedation protocols, weaning practices, and other context-specific factors. Further rigorous trials with detailed reporting of interventions and contextual factors are needed to guide precise clinical implementation. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261280603, CRD420261280603.

42875243.title: [Clinical characteristics of critically ill patients based on early activity dose subtypes: a cluster analysis].
42875243.journal: Zhonghua wei zhong bing ji jiu yi xue
42875243.abstract: To identify potential subtypes of critically ill patients based on early activity-related indicators and compare the differences in activity characteristics and clinical characteristics among different subtypes. A prospective observational study was conducted using convenience sampling. Critically ill patients who received early mobilization in the intensive care units (ICUs) of Peking Union Medical College Hospital and Beijing Chaoyang Hospital from December 2021 to August 2023 were enrolled. General information, disease-related data, and laboratory indicators were obtained from electronic medical records. The first early mobilization session was defined as the starting point, and the last early mobilization session before ICU discharge was defined as the endpoint. Activity type, duration, and participation level were collected using the Early Mobilization Record Form for Critically Ill Patients to calculate activity dose indicators. Activity dose, activity duration, activity participation, and activity type were used as clustering variables. A two-step clustering method followed by K-means clustering analysis was performed. A total of 149 critically ill patients who received early activity were included, and were stably classified into three potential subtypes, namely the high activity dose group (Class I, 65 cases), the moderate activity dose group (Class II, 44 cases), and the low activity dose group (Class III, 40 cases). There were statistically significant differences in activity dose, activity duration, activity participation, and activity type among the three types of patients. Among them, the high activity dose group had higher activity dose, activity duration, activity participation, and activity type, showing more positive early activity behavior. The moderate activity dose group was at a moderate level in terms of activity dose and duration, but has lower activity participation. The low activity dose group showed lower levels of activity dose, activity duration, activity participation, and activity type, characterized by insufficient activity exposure and limited activity participation. Regarding clinical characteristics, significant differences were observed among the three classes in primary disease type, proportion of surgical treatment, duration of mechanical ventilation, pain score, and muscle strength score (all P<0.05). Specifically, respiratory diseases were the predominant primary disease type in Classes I and II [46% (30/65) and 52% (23/44), respectively], whereas other disease categories accounted for a higher proportion in Class III [42% (17/40)]. Class II patients had the highest proportion of surgical treatment [82% (36/44)] and the longest duration of mechanical ventilation [118.50 (49.00, 192.00) hours]. Class III patients had the highest pain scores [2.0 (1.0, 4.0) points], whereas Class I patients had the highest muscle strength scores [53.0 (48.0, 60.0) points] and Class III patients had the lowest muscle strength scores [42.0 (34.5, 48.0) points]. Critically ill patients undergoing early mobilization can be classified into three potential subtypes (high, moderate, and low activity dose groups) based on activity dose-related indicators. Different subtypes demonstrate heterogeneity in clinical characteristics, including disease type, surgical treatment status, duration of mechanical ventilation, pain level, and muscle strength status. Clinical attention should be paid to factors such as activity participation, activity type, pain, muscle strength, and duration of mechanical ventilation, and early activity management should be carried out in a stratified and individualized manner.

42875239.title: [Development and validation of a predictive model for high-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy failure in patients with type I respiratory failure].
42875239.journal: Zhonghua wei zhong bing ji jiu yi xue
42875239.abstract: To explore the independent risk factors for failure of high-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy (HFNC) in patients with type I respiratory failure, and to establish and validate an effective risk prediction model. A retrospective observational study was conducted, Patients with type I respiratory failure who received HFNC treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU) of the Affiliated Hospital of Xuzhou Medical University from January 2019 to December 2024 were selected as the research subjects. Clinical data within 24 hours after admission to the ICU were collected, including demographic information and general conditions, underlying diseases, early acute organ dysfunction, vital signs, laboratory examinations, disease severity scores, and treatment measures. Patients were divided into the HFNC success group and the HFNC failure group based on whether HFNC failure (endotracheal intubation and/or death during treatment) occurred. The overall cohort was randomly divided at a ratio of 7 : 3 into a training set and a validation set. Multivariate logistic regression analysis was used to screen independent predictors of HFNC failure, and a nomogram prediction model was constructed accordingly. The receiver operator characteristic curve (ROC curve), Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test, calibration curve, and decision curve analysis (DCA) were used to evaluate the model's discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility. A total of 700 patients with type I respiratory failure were included, of whom 601 experienced HFNC success and 99 experienced HFNC failure, with a failure rate of 14.1%. Compared with the HFNC success group, patients in the HFNC failure group had lower height, proportion of coronary heart disease, serum sodium, oxygenation index, Glasgow Coma Score (GCS), and proportion of patients receiving human albumin, while exhibiting significantly higher incidence of acute kidney injury (AKI), heart rate, respiratory rate, blood urea nitrogen level, serum creatinine level, blood lactate level, Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, and Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II(APACHE II) score, as well as longer prothrombin time (all P<0.05). Multivariate logistic regression analysis showed that the presence of AKI [odds ratio (OR)=2.113, 95% confidence interval (95%CI) was 1.159-3.854, P=0.015] and elevated blood lactate level (OR=1.148, 95%CI was 1.027-1.283, P=0.015) were independent risk factors for HFNC failure, while elevated oxygenation index (OR=0.973, 95%CI was 0.963-0.983, P<0.001) and higher GCS score (OR=0.815, 95%CI was 0.760-0.874, P<0.001) were independent protective factors. Based on these four independent predictors, a nomogram prediction model was established. The ROC curves showed that the area under the curve (AUC) of the training set and validation set were 0.844 (95%CI was 0.794-0.895) and 0.794 (95%CI was 0.706-0.881), respectively. At a cutoff value of 0.160, the sensitivities were 73.9% and 60.0%, the specificities were 81.0% and 82.8%, and the accuracies were 80.0% and 79.5% in the training set and validation set, respectively. The Hosmer-Lemeshow test showed good fit for the model in both the training set (χ 2=8.636, P=0.374) and validation set (χ 2=6.652, P=0.575). The calibration curves indicated good agreement between the model predicted probabilities and the actual observations. DCA demonstrated that the model exhibited good clinical net benefit over a wide range of threshold probabilities. The nomogram model constructed based on AKI, blood lactate level, oxygenation index, and GCS score has good predictive performance for the risk of HFNC failure in patients with type I respiratory failure, providing a reference for early identification of high-risk patients and optimization of clinical decision-making.

42875236.title: [Impact of active surveillance for carbapenem-resistant organisms on healthcare-associated infections and clinical prognosis of patients in intensive care unit: a propensity score-matching historical cohort study].
42875236.journal: Zhonghua wei zhong bing ji jiu yi xue
42875236.abstract: To evaluate the impact of active surveillance for carbapenem-resistant organisms (CRO) on healthcare-associated infections and clinical prognosis of patients in intensive care unit (ICU), and to provide real-world clinical evidence for developing scientific CRO active surveillance protocols in medical institutions. A prospective intervention study with a post-hoc retrospective historical control cohort design was conducted. ICU inpatients at the General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University from January 1, 2024 to December 31, 2025 were enrolled. The routine testing group comprised patients hospitalized from January 1 to December 31, 2024, who underwent routine microbiological testing with only retrospective chart review (690 cases). The CRO active surveillance group comprised patients hospitalized from January 1 to December 31, 2025, who received active CRO surveillance within 24 hours of ICU admission (608 cases). The active surveillance protocol involved collecting nasal swabs, rectal swabs, sputum specimens, and secretions or drainage fluids from existing wounds or drainage sites, which were inoculated onto chromogenic media. Patients with positive CRO results were considered colonized or infected with CRO and placed under contact precautions; those with negative results continued to receive standard precautions. Propensity score matching (PSM) at a 1 : 1 ratio was used to control for confounding factors including age, sex, acute physiology and chronic health evaluation II(APACHE II), severity of surgical insult (surgical grade×number of surgeries), and durations of mechanical ventilation, central venous catheterization, and urinary catheterization, with a caliper value of 0.02. After matching, the two groups were compared for CRO healthcare-associated infection incidence and clinical outcomes (in-ICU mortality, treatment abandonment rate, and improvement-to-discharge rate). A total of 634 patients in the CRO active surveillance group underwent active surveillance (608 of whom met inclusion criteria), with a CRO positivity rate of 22.4% (142/634). A total of 1 298 patients were enrolled, including 690 in the routine testing group and 608 in the CRO active surveillance group. After PSM, 477 pairs were successfully matched, with 477 cases in the routine testing group and 477 cases in the CRO active surveillance group. After matching, baseline characteristics were well balanced and comparable between the two groups [all standardized mean differences (SMD)<0.1, all P>0.05]. After PSM, there was no statistically significant difference in CRO nosocomial infection incidence between the CRO active surveillance group and the routine testing group [2.3% (11/477) vs. 2.5% (12/477), both P>0.05]. However, the CRO active surveillance group had significantly lower in-ICU mortality [2.1% (10/477) vs. 4.6% (22/477)] and treatment abandonment rate [8.6% (41/477) vs. 18.0% (86/477)] compared with the routine testing group (both P<0.05), and a significantly higher improvement-to-discharge rate [89.3% (426/477) vs. 77.4% (369/477), both P<0.05]. In ICUs with well-established basic infection prevention and control measures, implementation of CRO active surveillance combined with contact isolation did not further reduce the incidence of CRO healthcare-associated infections. However, it significantly improved patient outcomes by enabling early warning and guiding precise antimicrobial therapy.

42872906.title: Association of Iron Homeostasis With One-Year All-Cause Mortality Among Intensive Care Unit Patients with Atrial Fibrillation: A Retrospective Study.
42872906.abstract: Perturbations in iron homeostasis can substantially affect cardiovascular outcomes. This study aims to evaluate the prognostic value of various iron homeostasis indicators for all-cause mortality in critically ill AF patients. Data for this retrospective study were obtained from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database. Based on the iron homeostasis-related indicators (ferritin, serum iron, transferrin, and total iron-binding capacity [TIBC]), the risks of 1-year mortality among critically ill patients with atrial fibrillation were calculated using Cox proportional-hazards regression. Associations of iron homeostasis indicators with all-cause mortality in critically ill AF patients were assessed via Kaplan-Meier curves, restricted cubic splines, and subgroup analyses. After multivariable adjustment, patients in the highest ferritin quartile had a greater risk of 1-year mortality than those in the lowest quartile (Q4 HR 1.277, 95% CI 1.083-1.506, p < 0.01). In contrast, the highest quartiles of transferrin (Q4 HR 0.732, 95% CI 0.622-0.861, p < 0.01) and TIBC (Q4 HR 0.732, 95% CI 0.622-0.861, p < 0.01) were associated with lower mortality. No significant association was observed between serum iron quartiles and 1-year mortality (Q4 HR 1.067, 95% CI 0.914-1.245, p = 0.41). Restricted cubic spline analyses further characterized the exposure and outcome patterns for these iron-related parameters. Among critically ill patients with AF, ferritin, transferrin and TIBC levels were independently associated with 1-year all-cause mortality. No significant association was observed for serum iron.

42861657.title: Nurses' Experiences of Intrahospital Patient Transfer in a University Hospital.
42861657.abstract: Intrahospital transfer is a fundamental component of critical care. However, the clinical instability of critically ill patients, their need for continuous monitoring and their dependence on advanced life-support equipment may pose various patient-safety risks during intrahospital transfer. To explore the intrahospital patient transfer experiences of nurses working in a university hospital. A qualitative descriptive study design was used. The study was conducted with 22 nurses working in the adult intensive care units and inpatient wards of a university hospital. Data were collected through face-to-face, in-depth interviews using a semi-structured interview guide developed by the researchers. Content analysis was used to analyse the data. Content analysis identified three themes and seven subthemes describing nurses' experiences of intrahospital patient transfer. The themes were: (1) Gaps in Information Transfer and Collaboration, (2) Organisational and Procedural Barriers and (3) Conditions Supporting Safe Coordinated Patient Transfer. The findings showed that nurses experienced intrahospital patient transfer as a multidimensional process involving clinical information transfer, patient preparation, interprofessional and interunit coordination, workflow organisation, staffing adequacy, appropriate timing, standard procedures, teamwork and organisational support. The study concluded that safe intrahospital patient transfer is not limited to the physical movement of the patient; rather, it is a holistic process requiring effective information transfer, interprofessional and interunit coordination, appropriate timing, adequate staffing and organisational support. Healthcare organisations are advised to integrate standard procedures and structured communication tools into institutional practice. Safe intrahospital transfer requires effective coordination and communication between sending and receiving teams at all stages of the transfer process. Healthcare organisations should establish standardised protocols that clearly define pre-transfer patient preparation, transfer timing, requirements for clinical information transfer and the responsibilities of healthcare professionals. Structured communication tools should be used to support continuity of care and patient safety. These practices are particularly important for ensuring the safe transfer of critically ill patients.

42860727.title: Nurses' Experiences With Artificial Intelligence and the Association Between Clinical Decision-Making and Missed Nursing Care: A Convergent Mixed-Methods Study.
42860727.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being incorporated into clinical nursing practice, but evidence remains limited on how nurses experience AI-supported systems and how decision-making orientation relates to missed nursing care (MNC). To explore nurses' experiences with AI-supported clinical decision support (CDS) and examine associations among clinical decision-making orientation, professional characteristics, and MNC. A convergent parallel mixed-methods study. The study was conducted in six hospitals in Beni Suef Governorate, Egypt. The quantitative sample included 210 intensive care unit (ICU) nurses who completed the Nursing Decision-Making Instrument-Revised 2014 (NDMI-R) and the Missed Intensive Nursing Care Scale (MINCS). Fourteen nurses completed semistructured interviews, and all transcripts were included in the thematic analysis. NDMI-R scores showed a small negative bivariate correlation with MNC (r = -0.178, p < 0.01), but the adjusted association was not statistically significant (β = -0.124, p = 0.063). The regression model explained 16.9% of the variance in MNC (adjusted R2 = 14.5%). Years of experience (β = 0.198, p = 0.004) and bachelor's degree or above compared with a technical nursing diploma (β = -0.255, p < 0.001) were significant predictors. The other education contrast, AI training/support and MISSCARE Reasons were not statistically significant. In interviews, nurses described AI-related tools as potentially helpful for alerts, information review, workflow, and communication while also raising concerns about trust, overreliance, empathy, and training. Nurses perceived potential benefits from AI-supported tools, but the quantitative findings did not establish an independent effect of AI or a statistically significant adjusted association between decision-making orientation and MNC. These findings support cautious, nurse-centered implementation and further longitudinal evaluation. Managers should pair any AI-supported CDS implementation with role-specific training, clear accountability, usability monitoring, and safeguards that preserve clinical judgment and humanistic care.

42858349.title: Utility of nano-impregnated surface coating to achieve continuous active disinfection in ICU of a tertiary trauma center.
42858349.journal: Journal of infection in developing countries
42858349.abstract: Implementing continuous active disinfection presents challenges as conventional cleaning methods may not fully mitigate risks. Hence, evaluating innovative technologies becomes imperative. This study assessed a nanoparticle-based surface coating containing titanium dioxide engineered into nano-molecules that is activated by normal light and provides ongoing disinfection. The research took place in two intensive care units (ICUs): ICU A (coated) and ICU B (control). Data on healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and environmental factors were collected pre- and post-coating application to gauge its impact. The change in percentage of positive swabs/HAI cases in ICU A was compared to ICU B and statistically analyzed using a 2-sample test for equality of proportions. ICU A witnessed a 26.5% decrease in positive environment swabs post-coating, while ICU B saw a 160.9% increase. This disparity was statistically significant (p = 0.000). Both ICUs experienced decreased ventilator associated pneumonia (VAP) cases, though central line associated-blood steam infection (CLA-BSI) and catheter associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) cases increased in ICU A post application. Following coating, positive environmental swabs and VAP decreased by 71.8%, and 72.5%, while CLA-BSI and CAUTI increased by 198% and 43.5%. The evaluation showed that the coating may serve to supplement traditional cleaning and disinfection methods. Further research into the efficacy and cost-effectiveness of such antimicrobial coating is needed for overall improvement in patient care.

42855769.title: [Expert consensus on the clinical application of continuous glucose monitoring in critically ill patients (2026 edition)].
authors: Branch of Critical Care Medicine, China Association for Disaster & Emergency Rescue Medicine
42855769.abstract: Glycemic fluctuations are highly prevalent among critically ill patients. Glycemic abnormalities constitute an independent risk factor for adverse outcomes, and their effective identification and management are essential to improving clinical prognosis in this population. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) technology, which continuously and in real time captures interstitial fluid glucose concentrations, provides multidimensional glycemic metrics and offers a novel technical approach to overcoming the inherent limitations of conventional intermittent glucose monitoring, thereby enabling refined glycemic management in critically ill patients. However, systematic guidance for its standardized application in the intensive care units (ICU) setting remains lacking. To address this gap, the Branch of Critical Care Medicine, China Association for Disaster and Emergency Rescue Medicine, convened a multidisciplinary panel of experts in critical care medicine, endocrinology, and nursing. Drawing on international evidence-based literature and clinical practice issues specific to China, the panel jointly developed the present consensus, with the aim of providing guidance for the standardized and individualized application of CGM in adult ICU patients. This consensus puts forward 27 recommendations addressing 12 questions regarding the use of CGM in critically ill patients. The content covers the definition, classification and hazards of glycemic abnormalities in critically ill patients, common blood glucose monitoring methods and their clinical implications, eligible populations for CGM, data interpretation, quality control and routine care of CGM, as well as accessibility and economic costs.

42855690.title: Designing a hybrid surgical ICU to avoid intrahospital transport in selected critically Ill patients: the CUHK-SZ institutional concept.
42855690.journal: World journal of emergency surgery : WJES
42855690.abstract: Intrahospital transport for surgery exposes critically ill patients to equipment failure, displacement of tubes and lines, interrupted monitoring, and physiologic instability. Although transport protocols can reduce these hazards, they do not address the underlying physical decoupling of surgical infrastructure from the critical care environment. This institutional perspective describes the rationale and design of a hybrid surgical ICU planned for the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen (CUHK-SZ) Medical Center: a dedicated clinical space designed to function as both a critical care unit and a procedural suite, bringing surgery to the patient rather than transporting the patient to the operating room (OR). The model is presented as an illustrative, hypothesis-generating concept rather than a validated clinical pathway. The design concept, which is a patient-centered approach, should guide healthcare delivery in modern medicine by placing the patient at the forefront of all decisions and mobilizing all available resources to serve them. This approach addresses all three domains: personnel, environment, and equipment. Overlapping anesthesiology and critical care competencies support integrated staffing. Connectable ICU rooms, adequate space and electrical capacity, anterooms, and switchable HEPA-filtered positive-pressure ventilation meet environmental requirements. Total intravenous anesthesia, portable surgical platforms, and minimally invasive or robotic techniques reduce dependence on fixed OR infrastructure. At CUHK-SZ, the concept is planned as a prototype in the trauma building using two adjacent ICU rooms with an openable partition and switchable ventilation. Candidate patient groups, procedural levels, and implementation requirements are presented as provisional, expert-derived proposals, and engineering testing and simulated drills are planned before any clinical use. The hybrid surgical ICU is a technically plausible option for carefully selected patients at high risk from transport, but its clinical effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness remain unproven. The CUHK-SZ concept is intended to generate hypotheses for prospective evaluation, and its transferability to existing hospitals is likely to depend on incremental adaptation rather than direct replication.

42855084.title: Interpretable machine learning predicts successful weaning and ICU discharge alive following prone positioning ventilation in moderate-to-severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) secondary to pneumonia.
42855084.abstract: We developed and validated interpretable machine learning models predicting successful weaning and survival to ICU discharge in patients with moderate-to-severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) secondary to pneumonia receiving prone position ventilation (PPV). We included 131 patients with moderate-to-severe ARDS secondary to pneumonia undergoing PPV for internal, temporal, and external validation. Models were developed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC), calibration, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Model interpretability was assessed using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). The support vector machine (SVM) model had the highest internal AUC (0.715 weaning; 0.807 ICU discharge). The weaning model was stable in temporal (AUC 0.841) and external (AUC 0.707) validation. The ICU discharge model had limited temporal/external stability (AUCs 0.657, 0.665) and was preliminary. Calibration was good for weaning and acceptable for ICU discharge. DCA suggested potential utility across broad thresholds. SHAP identified key predictors for weaning (septic shock, platelet count, PaO2/FiO2 ratio at PPV, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), and peak airway pressure at PPV) and ICU discharge (APACHE II, peak airway pressure at PPV, multidrug-resistant organism infection, and NLR). The weaning SVM model showed promising but exploratory performance and may serve as an adjunct for individualized risk stratification during the conventional ventilation/PPV phase, complementing rather than replacing clinical judgement. The ICU discharge model was less stable and should be interpreted cautiously. SHAP improved transparency and generated hypotheses, not causal evidence. Further multi-center prospective validation is needed.

42855082.title: Barriers to early rehabilitation and mobilization in adult ICUs: A multicenter survey in the Eastern region of Saudi Arabia.
42855082.abstract: Prolonged Intensive Care Unit (ICU) immobilization leads to complications such as ICU Acquired Weakness (ICU-AW). While Early Rehabilitation and Mobilization (ERM) is proven to improve functional independence and reduce mechanical ventilation (MV) duration, its implementation remains inconsistent. This study aimed to identify barriers to ERM as perceived by adult ICU healthcare practitioners in the Eastern region of Saudi Arabia. A multicenter, cross-sectional survey using a 21-question adapted self-administered questionnaire was conducted between January and April 2023 through QuestionPro platform. The survey was distributed to critical care practitioners including physicians, nurses, respiratory therapists, physiotherapists, and other allied health staff. Respondents represented three hospital categories in the Eastern region: private, Eastern Health Cluster, and other governmental sector hospitals. Barriers were assessed a priori at three levels: patient, provider, and institutional. Internal consistency of the patient-level barrier scale was assessed using Cronbach's alpha. Chi-square and Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact tests compared ERM protocol availability between hospital sectors and knowledge, practice, and resource variables across professional groups. Of 137 practitioners who accessed the survey, 121of 137 who accessed the link completed the questionnaire (88%completion rate). Although 66 (55%) rated ERM as very important, only 48 (40%) reported always participating in or observing it in practice. The most frequently endorsed ideal initiation time was within 24 h of admission (38, 31%), whereas the most commonly reported actual initiation point was when patients were conscious and able to cooperate (28, 23%); only 10 (8%) reported initiation within 24 h. Patient-level barriers were mainly sedation and physiological instability. Provider-level barriers included safety concerns, limited staffing, and inadequate training. At the institutional level, only 57 (47%) respondents reported the presence of a formal ERM protocol, with a significant difference between private hospitals (36/54, 67%) and government hospitals (21/67, 31%) (χ2 = 13.59 df = 1, p < 0.001; OR 4.38, 95% CI 2.04-9.42). Protocol availability, ERM participation, and physiotherapy access also differed significantly across professional groups, with respiratory therapists consistently reporting the lowest access p = 0.013; p < 0.001; p = 0.038; p < 0.001. Despite high awareness of its benefits, ERM implementation across adult ICUs in the Eastern region remains suboptimal relative to the 72-h initiation window recommended by current consensus guidance and is delivered reactively rather than proactively. Barriers operate at patient, provider, and institutional levels, and both formal ERM protocol availability and profession-based access to ERM structures differ significantly, with respiratory therapists the most excluded despite managing the highest-risk patients. These findings identify protocol availability and interdisciplinary delivery structures as the principal targets for regional implementation efforts.

42853896.title: Post-Extubation Recall of Thirst During Mechanical Ventilation Among Intensive Care Unit Patients: A Conventional Content Analysis.
42853896.abstract: In ICU patients, particularly after extubation, thirst is a common and troubling symptom. Although earlier research has focused mainly on quantifying thirst severity and its clinical correlates, less is known about the subjective experiences of patients, including their emotional responses, sense of helplessness, help-seeking actions, and the challenges they face in obtaining relief within the ICU. Therefore, this study aimed to examine how post-extubation ICU patients experience thirst and the strategies they use to manage or alleviate it. Between January and August 2024, this qualitative research was carried out in Tehran, Iran, using conventional content analysis. Participants were recruited through purposive sampling, and data were collected via semi-structured interviews conducted in Persian with 20 patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) following extubation. Interviews proceeded until data saturation occurred, and even though they were held after extubation, the thirst experiences participants reported mostly pertained to the time of mechanical ventilation and intubation. The Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) guideline was followed in this study. Three main categories were identified in this study: 'Unrelieved Thirst' (Hope despite Disappointment and Cognitive and Emotional Burden of Thirst), 'Seeking Relief' (Spiritual Coping and Endurance and Non-Verbal Pleading for Water), and 'Emotional Collapse and Withdrawal' (Resigned Withdrawal and Emotional Isolation and Perceived Neglect). Participants experienced persistent thoughts about water, employed spiritual coping strategies, used gestures without words to express thirst, and eventually emotionally withdrew when their needs were persistently ignored. The study revealed that post-extubation thirst is experienced as a deeply upsetting phenomenon affecting physical, psychological, and existential levels, where patients face physical discomfort, emotional distress, challenges in communication, and a sense of being overlooked in the ICU. The findings highlight the urgent necessity for systematic thirst assessment, improved non-verbal communication techniques, and compassionate, patient-focused nursing care to reduce thirst-related distress. Healthcare providers must be trained to identify both verbal and non-verbal thirst signals and to incorporate patients' cultural and spiritual resources into supportive care. The research delivers a comprehensive understanding of the multifaceted nature of thirst in ICU patients, demonstrating that unresolved thirst may result in emotional collapse and withdrawal. It highlights the significance of managing thirst as an essential human requirement in critical care. The study followed the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) guideline. No patient or public contribution.

42853842.title: Development and internal validation of prediction models for ICU-level intervention and 14-day mortality at Medical Emergency Team activation: A retrospective cohort study.
42853842.abstract: Medical Emergency Team (MET) activation represents acute clinical deterioration requiring rapid decisions regarding escalation of care. Previous post-MET prediction studies have evaluated outcomes including unplanned intensive care unit (ICU) admission and mortality; however, ICU admission is a location-based outcome that may be influenced by institutional factors. Prediction based on treatment intensity rather than location of care has received less attention. We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study of adult patients undergoing MET activation on general wards at a tertiary-care hospital in Japan between May 2021 and December 2025. Two outcomes were evaluated: initiation of ICU-level interventions within 24 hours and all-cause 14-day mortality. ICU-level interventions were defined as the initiation of mechanical ventilation, vasopressor or inotropic infusion, renal replacement therapy, or polymyxin B hemoperfusion (PMX). Multivariable logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models were developed using variables available at the time of MET activation. Model performance was evaluated using discrimination (C-index), calibration, decision curve analysis, and bootstrap-based internal validation. Among 533 patients, 303 (56.8%) required ICU-level interventions and 147 (27.6%) died within 14 days. Lower albumin levels and higher blood urea nitrogen, potassium, and white blood cell count were associated with both outcomes, whereas higher heart rate was associated with 14-day mortality. The model demonstrated moderate discrimination for ICU-level intervention (C-index 0.721, 95% CI 0.660-0.745) and good discrimination for 14-day mortality (C-index 0.784, 95% CI 0.720-0.814). Calibration analyses indicated modest overfitting but generally good agreement between predicted and observed risks. Decision curve analysis demonstrated clinical net benefit across a range of threshold probabilities. In this single-center cohort, treatment escalation and short-term mortality represented related but distinct dimensions of clinical risk. Defining intensive care need based on treatment intensity rather than ICU admission may provide an operational framework for risk stratification at MET activation. External validation is required before clinical implementation.

42851912.title: Development and external validation of an interpretable machine learning model for early prediction of in-hospital mortality in neurocritical care.
42851912.abstract: Early risk assessment is a routine part of neurocritical care, yet mortality prediction remains difficult because neurological injury often coexists with respiratory, circulatory, renal, and inflammatory dysfunction. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an interpretable machine learning (ML) model for predicting in-hospital mortality in neurocritical-care patients using variables available within the first 24 h after intensive care unit (ICU) admission. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using two public critical-care databases. The Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) database was used for model development and internal testing, and the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD) was used for independent external validation. The report follows the Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) statement. Adult ICU patients with neurocritical-care diagnoses were identified by predefined International Classification of Diseases codes. Candidate predictors were restricted to information recorded during the first 24 h after ICU admission and included demographics, comorbidities, vital signs, laboratory results, neurological status, organ-support therapies, and severity scores. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used for feature selection. Logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, and multilayer perceptron models were trained.
