Discrimination was assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC). Calibration, decision curve analysis (DCA), and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used to evaluate probability reliability, potential clinical utility, and interpretability. The operating threshold used for classification metrics was fixed in the MIMIC-IV development data before internal and external evaluation. The MIMIC-IV cohort included 6,842 patients, of whom 1,014 died during hospitalization; the held-out internal test set contained 1,368 patients and 203 deaths. The external validation cohort included 5,236 eICU-CRD patients, of whom 686 died. LightGBM showed the best overall performance. In the internal test cohort, it achieved an AUROC of 0.841 (95% CI: 0.821-0.861) and an AUPRC of 0.518 (95% CI: 0.486-0.552). In external validation, the AUROC was 0.801 (95% CI: 0.779-0.824) and the AUPRC was 0.413 (95% CI: 0.380-0.449), with sensitivity of 72.8%, specificity of 73.9%, positive predictive value of 30.3%, negative predictive value of 94.7%, and F1 score of 0.428. Thus, approximately 70% of patients classified as high risk at this operating point survived to hospital discharge. Calibration was acceptable in the external cohort, with a Brier score of 0.101, calibration intercept of 0.050, and calibration slope of 0.84. SHAP analysis identified GCS total score, invasive mechanical ventilation, age, lactate, SOFA score, vasopressor use, and creatinine as leading contributors to predicted mortality risk. A model based on routinely collected first-day ICU data provided externally validated and interpretable risk stratification for in-hospital mortality in neurocritical care. Its low positive predictive value at the reported operating point precludes use as a stand-alone basis for prognostic pessimism, treatment limitation, or withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment. Prospective validation in diverse countries and health systems is required before clinical implementation.

42847956.title: Neutrophil-Lymphocyte-Platelet Ratio as a Prognostic Marker in Rural ICU Patients: a Two-Year Cross-Sectional Study.
42847956.abstract: Early risk identification can improve treatment outcomes for sepsis patients, leading to timely intervention and better quality of life. An identification of certain parameters in such patients is necessary to determine the risk in such patients. The present study evaluated the predictive efficiency of various critical care assessment scores (CAS), including SOFA, qSOFA, APACHE IV, and biomarkers such as NLR and NLPR, for in-hospital mortality, the need for mechanical ventilation (MV), and hospital length of stay (LOS), as a risk for sepsis patients. A total of 300 patients were included in the study; however, 70 mortalities were recorded. A significant difference was observed in the hematological and biochemical parameters between the survivors and non-survivors (p < 0.001). Associations between CAS, biomarkers, and clinical outcomes were assessed by binary logistic regression, while receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to determine optimal cutoffs for mortality and MV prediction. SOFA was the best predictor of mortality (OR: 2.98, p < 0.001) and MV requirement (OR: 2.90, p < 0.001), with a cutoff of ≥ 9 having 94% sensitivity and 86% specificity for mortality. APACHE IV with a cutoff > 71, AUC: 0.840, and NLPR with a cutoff > 3.1, AUC: 0.716, also significantly predicted mortality. PaO2/FiO2 had a negative correlation with both mortality (OR: 0.022, p < 0.001) and MV need (OR: 0.004, p < 0.001). An inverse prediction of LOS with SOFA scores was seen (β = -0.191, p = 0.003), whereas higher PaO2/FiO2 ratios indicated prolonged hospitalization (β = 0.193, p = 0.011). When predicting sepsis-related mortality and MV requirement, SOFA is a better option than other CAS and biomarkers. In setups with limited resources, NLPR is a helpful substitute. Important information about mortality risk and length of hospital stay is provided by PaO2/FiO2. However, to confirm these results in various contexts, more investigation is necessary.

42847304.title: Pressure ulcer prevention in mechanically ventilated patients in intensive care units: a quality improvement project.
42847304.abstract: Despite ongoing attempts to prevent hospital-acquired pressure ulcers (HAPUs), they remain a common occurrence in hospitalised patients. Improving policies and processes to provide a standardised approach to assessments, documentation and equipment is linked to decreasing HAPUs. Among hospitalised patients, those in intensive care units (ICUs) and who are mechanically ventilated are at the highest risk of developing a pressure ulcer (PU). A quality improvement (QI) project was created to provide a foundation of basic nursing care to be delivered to the patient for the prevention of HAPUs. The primary objective of the QI project was to decrease the incidence of HAPUs at the author's facility, Mercy Hospital, Arkansas, US. The year prior to the implementation of the QI project, the HAPU incidence was n=17 in the ICU at this facility. This article highlights the importance of education, training and the use of a preventive dressing upon admission to the ICU. It can be used as an approach to improve current policies. The overall length of the QI project including education, implementation and monitoring was 12 weeks. The framework used in the QI project was that of Failure Modes and Effects Analysis. The outcome of this QI project resulted in a reduction of HAPUs. Within the 12-week timeframe, one HAPU developed. An effective prevention tool was the use of a preventive dressing at pressure points (coccyx/sacral) upon arrival to the ICU before an injury occurred. Providing continuous structured education on interventions for the prevention of HAPUs was found to be a successful component of prevention during this QI project. Although many of the risk factors, such as poor perfusion and lack of mobility, for HAPUs are not able to be prevented, the incorporation of evidence-based research into practice in the clinical setting can facilitate a reduction in the prevalence of HAPUs.

42847302.title: Pressure injuries in an intensive care unit exclusively dedicated to treating patients with COVID-19: a prospective cohort study.
42847302.abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, and as growing numbers of critically ill patients were treated in prone position in COVID-19-dedicated intensive care units (ICUs), the incidence of pressure injuries (PIs) remained relevant. Limited data are available on this topic; this study is intended to add to the literature on these injuries in proned patients who are ventilated during intensive care to contribute to prevention of PIs and better management of these patients. All patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome treated via invasive mechanical ventilation (endotracheal tube or tracheostomy) in an ICU exclusively dedicated to patients with COVID-19 in Porto Alegre, Brazil from 15 March-10 September 2020 were recruited prospectively following admission to the ICU, including patients who received extracorporeal membrane oxygenation therapy. Patients treated with non-invasive ventilation were excluded. The following variables were analysed: body mass index, immobility time (assessed via duration of mechanical ventilation), nutritional status (assessed by albumin level), age, smoking status, and history of previous PI. During the study period, 267 patients were admitted to the ICU for COVID-19 support. The median patient age was 61 years, and most were male (58.8%). Most patients (235, 88.0%) had associated comorbidities-186 (69.7%) had multiple comorbidities, and hypertension and diabetes were most common. PIs were present in 150 (56.2%) patients. In 132 patients, the ulcers were examined and ranked according to the Shea classification-65.16% were classified as grade 2. Duration of mechanical ventilation and age were associated with higher ulcer grades. For each additional day on mechanical ventilation, the risk of PIs rose by approximately 7%. The incidence of PIs in patients on invasive mechanical ventilation in an ICU exclusively dedicated to treating patients with COVID-19 was high. The risk of developing a PI in these conditions rose significantly for each day on mechanical ventilation. Ventilation in the prone position was associated with development of PIs in less common areas.

42845054.title: Intensive Care Nurses' Experiences and Attitudes Towards Family Involvement in Delirium Care: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.
42845054.abstract: Delirium is a common neuropsychiatric complication among critically ill patients, particularly those who are mechanically ventilated. Evidence suggests family involvement may improve delirium-related outcomes in adult intensive care units (ICUs). However, limited evidence exists on intensive care nurses' (ICNs) experiences and attitudes towards family involvement in delirium care in South Africa. The study aimed to explore intensive care nurses' experiences and attitudes towards family involvement in the care of mechanically ventilated patients with delirium in adult ICUs. A descriptive qualitative study design was utilised. Four focus group discussions were conducted with 32 ICNs from two adult ICUs at a tertiary academic hospital in Johannesburg between April and August 2022. Participants who had at least 2 years of intensive care experience were purposively sampled. Data were analysed using inductive qualitative content analysis. The study adhered to Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Studies guidelines. Three categories were identified: emotional burden and psychological demands of delirium care, communication and psychosocial support for families in delirium care and barriers to effective family involvement in delirium care. While recognising the therapeutic value of family engagement, the nurses reported experiencing emotional stress related to family expectations and anxiety. They adopted strategies such as structured communication, empathetic listening and technology-assisted contact to support families. However, barriers such as time constraints, limited intensive care space, staffing shortages and restrictive policies limited sustained involvement. This study provides context-specific insight into how ICNs facilitate family involvement in the care of patients with delirium in a public tertiary ICU. ICNs recognise the therapeutic value of family involvement in the care of patients with delirium and are willing to facilitate engagement. However, systemic and environmental barriers limit consistent implementation. Therefore, strengthening institutional policies and supporting nurses through structured training and team-based approaches may enhance sustainable family-centred delirium care. This study's findings demonstrate the need for ICNs to adopt structured communication strategies, flexible visitation policies and empathy towards families and their patients in the ICU. Perhaps incorporating family-centred care into daily intensive care practices could strengthen family involvement in critical care, particularly for patients with delirium.

42844803.title: The First 48 Hours: Incidence, Timing and Predictors of Adverse Events After ICU-To-Ward Transfer: A Prospective Cohort Study.
42844803.abstract: The transition from the intensive care unit (ICU) to a general ward is a period of heightened vulnerability, yet the precise timing and modifiable predictors of adverse events remain poorly defined. To determine the incidence, timing and types of adverse events following ICU-to-ward transfer, evaluate the predictive accuracy of four early-warning scores and identify independent risk factors. A prospective cohort study of 207 adult patients transferred from ICUs to general wards at a tertiary university hospital over 20 months (March 2024-October 2025) was enrolled. Four early warning scores (PACS, MEWS, SWIFT, LACE) were calculated daily for 5 days post-transfer. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent risk factors. The total number Adverse events occurred in 52 patients (25.1%), most commonly ICU readmission (n = 46, 22.2%) and healthcare-associated infections (n = 29, 14.0%). Critically, 88% of events occurred within the first 48 h (day 1: 56.0%; day 2: 32.0%). SWIFT demonstrated the highest predictive accuracy at transfer (AUC 0.856). Mechanical ventilation was the strongest independent risk factor (OR 10.11), followed by prolonged ICU stay (OR 6.40), respiratory diagnosis (OR 4.99), > 3 invasive devices (OR 4.41) and comorbidities (OR 3.64). These five factors collectively explained 88.5% of adverse events. Adverse events affect one in four patients after ICU-to-ward transfer, with the vast majority occurring within the first 48 h. A simple set of readily identifiable risk factors can guide nursing surveillance and targeted interventions during this critical window. Bedside nurses should prioritize enhanced monitoring for patients with a history of mechanical ventilation, prolonged ICU stay, multiple invasive devices and significant comorbidities during the first 48 h post-transfer. Daily use of early-warning scores can inform monitoring frequency and rapid response activation.

42842833.title: Determinants of Adoption of a Mechanical Ventilation Dashboard in Intensive Care: Measurement Instrument for Determinants of Innovations-Based, Single-Center, Cross-Sectional Evaluation.
42842833.abstract: Lung-protective ventilation (LPV) reduces complications of mechanical ventilation, yet adherence in intensive care units (ICUs) remains inconsistent. Digital dashboards may support LPV by improving situational awareness and supporting protocol adherence. However, adoption of such tools in high-acuity clinical environments depends on a range of cognitive, professional, and contextual determinants. The Measurement Instrument for Determinants of Innovations (MIDI) provides a validated framework to systematically assess these factors. This study aims to identify determinants influencing the adoption of a newly piloted mechanical ventilation dashboard in the ICU using the MIDI framework. We conducted a single-center, cross-sectional evaluation among ICU health care professionals during a dedicated survey period within a pilot introduction of a mechanical ventilation dashboard at Amsterdam University Medical Center. Participants completed a structured questionnaire consisting of 24 MIDI items adapted to the ICU context rated on a 5-point Likert scale ("completely disagree" to "completely agree"), supplemented by open-ended questions on perceived barriers and facilitators to its use. Determinants were classified as facilitators when ≥80% of respondents selected "agree" or "completely agree" and as barriers when ≥20% selected "disagree" or "completely disagree." Open-ended responses were analyzed using a general inductive thematic approach. A total of 71 completed questionnaires were analyzed, including responses from nurses, physicians, intensivists, ventilation specialists, and researchers in mechanical ventilation. Six determinants met the criteria for facilitators: outcome expectations, self-efficacy, procedural clarity, low complexity, correctness, and observability. Two determinants met the criteria for barriers: relevance for client and professional obligation. Analysis of open-ended responses highlighted perceived barriers such as additional workload, the need for an extra device, overlap with existing systems, and limited role-specific relevance. Facilitators included improved situational overview, educational value, easier trend monitoring, and increased efficiency. This evaluation identified key determinants influencing the adoption of a mechanical ventilation dashboard in the ICU. While the dashboard was generally perceived as useful and easy to understand, adoption was shaped by determinants related to workflow integration, role-specific relevance, and professional responsibility. These findings suggest that successful introduction of digital clinical support tools in intensive care requires attention not only to technical design, but also to how such tools align with users' roles, daily work processes, and shared clinical responsibilities. Systematic assessment of determinants provides actionable insights into the adoption of digital decision-support tools in high-acuity care settings.

42842548.title: Association between red blood cell distribution width-to-albumin ratio and ICU/hospital mortality in patients receiving mechanical ventilation within 24 hours of ICU admission: A multicenter retrospective study.
42842548.abstract: ObjectiveTo assess the association of early red blood cell distribution width-to-albumin ratio (RAR) with mortality in mechanically ventilated ICU patients and its value alongside routine clinical assessment.MethodsThis retrospective cohort study used MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD data. Adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation within 24 hours of ICU admission who remained in the ICU at 24 hours were included. RAR was calculated from first-day laboratory measurements. Multivariable Cox regression assessed its association with subsequent in-hospital and ICU mortality. Additional analyses examined whether RAR improved prediction beyond its components and established severity scores.ResultsThe study included 3,534 MIMIC-IV patients and 1,929 eICU-CRD patients. Compared with the lowest RAR quartile, the highest quartile was associated with greater in-hospital mortality in both databases (adjusted HR 1.855, 95% CI 1.474-2.335, and HR 1.698, 95% CI 1.231-2.341, respectively). The corresponding ICU mortality association was significant in MIMIC-IV but not in eICU-CRD. Adding RAR to clinical models improved discrimination and reclassification for in-hospital mortality, with performance similar to including RDW and albumin separately. Improvements beyond severity scores varied by outcome and measure.ConclusionsHigher first-day RAR was associated with subsequent in-hospital mortality among mechanically ventilated adults in two ICU databases. RAR may provide supplementary prognostic information, although its role in clinical decisions requires prospective evaluation.

42842343.title: Perme Mobility Scale Is Associated With Morbidity and Mortality in Patients Undergoing Lung Transplant: 1-Year Follow-Up.
42842343.journal: Physiotherapy research international : the journal for researchers and clinicians in physical therapy
42842343.abstract: Lung transplantation (LTx) is an effective treatment for patients with advanced chronic lung disease who are unresponsive to other therapies. Functional capacity is increasingly recognized as an important prognostic indicator in transplant candidates and recipients. To assess functional status using the Perme Mobility Scale in patients undergoing LTx, and to examine its association with mechanical ventilation (MV) duration, ICU and hospital length of stay, and mortality over a 1-year follow-up. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of patients admitted to the ICU at Dom Vicente Scherer Hospital, Porto Alegre, following lung transplantation between January 2018 and December 2019. Perme Mobility Scale scores were recorded at ICU admission and hospital discharge. Data on MV duration, ICU and hospital length of stay, readmissions, and mortality were collected from medical records and follow-up calls. Sixty-seven patients were included (median age 57 years; 52.2% female). Higher Perme scores were significantly associated with shorter MV duration, shorter ICU and shorter hospital stay. Specifically, the total Perme score at hospital discharge was negatively correlated with mechanical ventilation duration (r = -0.408; p = 0.001) and ICU length of stay (r = -0.314; p = 0.01). Additionally, mechanical ventilation duration categories were significantly associated with 1-year mortality (p = 0.005), with the highest mortality observed in patients requiring mechanical ventilation for > 48 hours. Improved functional status as measured by the Perme Mobility Scale was associated with better clinical outcomes in lung transplant recipients. The Perme Mobility Scale represents a potentially useful prognostic marker that warrants further validation in prospective multicenter studies before being established as a tool for prognostic risk stratification.

42841720.title: Pulmonary Herpes Simplex Virus Reactivation in Invasively Mechanically Ventilated Patients With COVID-19 in Intensive Care Unit.
42841720.abstract: Patients in intensive care units (ICU) under mechanical ventilation, particularly those with SARS-CoV-2 infection, are highly susceptible to Herpes simplex virus (HSV) reactivation. Given the lack of data on the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron and Delta variants, this study aimed to assess the prevalence of pulmonary HSV reactivation in mechanically ventilated patients with SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia. The impact of HSV replication on SARS-CoV-2 replication, and conversely, was investigated, along with the susceptibility of HSV strains to antiviral therapies. This retrospective study included 381 mechanically ventilated ICU patients in Lyon. Overall, 103 patients (27.0%) experienced HSV reactivation, with a trend toward a higher prevalence among SARS-CoV-2-positive patients (32.8%) compared to SARS-CoV-2-negative (24.1%; p value = 0.058). HSV reactivation was significantly higher with the Delta variant (46.2%) compared to Omicron (27.1%; p value = 0.045); the Delta variant was associated with a 2.38-fold increased risk of HSV reactivation. HSV-positive patients exhibited a 1-log lower SARS-CoV-2 viral load compared to HSV-negative patients, a finding indicative of the natural course of SARS-CoV-2 infection followed by HSV reactivation, rather than viral interference. Unexpectedly, acyclovir resistance mutations appeared in the UL23 gene in at least 13.6% of HSV-1 strains in patients with an HSV load above 105 copies/mL. Complementary phenotypic and genotypic approaches allowed to identify three novel substitutions in UL30: Q217R, D741A, and E756K, classified as polymorphisms. Further optimization is needed in the management of mechanically ventilated ICU patients with pulmonary HSV reactivation, especially regarding antiviral resistance testing.

42839922.title: Interpretable machine learning for postoperative sepsis prediction in ICU patients following intracranial hematoma evacuation.
42839922.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
42839922.abstract: Sepsis is a prevalent and life-threatening complication in ICU patients after intracranial hematoma evacuation. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an interpretable machine learning model for predicting sepsis risk in this high-risk neurocritical care population. A multicenter retrospective study was designed. The MIMIC-IV was based on for model development and internal testing; MIMIC-III, eICU and an independent clinical cohort from Jiangsu Provincial Hospital of Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine for external validation. Sepsis during ICU stay was defined according to the operationalized Sepsis-3 criteria. Early ICU variables were selected using Boruta and LASSO, and six machine learning algorithms were developed and compared. Model performance was evaluated by discrimination, calibration, and decision curve analysis, and its interpretability was assessed using SHAP and LIME. A sensitivity analysis was conducted by retraining all six models after excluding baseline SOFA. A total of 1,729 patients were included, of whom 717 developed sepsis during ICU stay. The final model retained 13 predictors, including WBC, SOFA score, SpO2, glucose, chloride, pneumonia, aspirin use, mannitol use, vasopressor use, mechanical ventilation, RBC, sedative use, and GCS score. XGBoost showed the most balanced overall performance, with AUCs of 0.794 in the internal test set and 0.820, 0.837, and 0.796 in the MIMIC-III, eICU, and independent clinical validation cohorts, respectively. SHAP analysis identified SOFA score, vasopressor use, glucose, pneumonia, and sedative exposure as major contributors to model predictions, while LIME supported individual-level interpretability. A web-based calculator was implemented for individualized risk prediction. Sensitivity analysis showed that XGBoost retained discrimination after SOFA exclusion, with no significant AUC changes across the external cohorts. This study developed and externally validated an interpretable XGBoost-based model for predicting sepsis risk during ICU stay among patients after intracranial hematoma evacuation. The model showed generally consistent AUC-based discrimination across multiple validation cohorts and may support individualized risk stratification. Further prospective validation and clinical impact assessment are required before routine clinical implementation.

42839232.title: Impact of pre-tracheostomy continuous enteral feeding on aspiration pneumonia risk and clinical outcomes: a prospective observational study.
42839232.abstract: The optimal management of enteral nutrition before tracheostomy in mechanically ventilated patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) remains uncertain, and pre-procedural fasting is widely practiced in clinical settings to reduce the risk of aspiration. However, interruption of enteral nutrition (EN) may adversely affect metabolic stability and caloric intake in critically ill patients. This study aimed to prospectively evaluate whether continuation of EN before tracheostomy increases aspiration risk or influences clinical outcomes in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. This prospective observational study was conducted in the anesthesiology and resuscitation intensive care units of a tertiary care center. Adult mechanically ventilated patients scheduled for elective percutaneous tracheostomy were included. Patients were divided into two groups according to the enteral nutrition strategy applied before the procedure: the continuous feeding group and the fasting group. The primary endpoint was the incidence of aspiration pneumonia within 72 h after tracheostomy. Secondary endpoints included respiratory parameters, arterial blood gas measurements, delta (Δ) changes in physiological variables, procedure-related complications, and ICU and hospital outcomes. A total of 110 patients were assessed for eligibility, and 91 patients were included in the final analysis (continuous feeding group n = 45; fasting group n = 46). Baseline demographic characteristics, disease severity scores, and pre-tracheostomy respiratory parameters were comparable between groups. The incidence of aspiration pneumonia was 6.7% in the continuous feeding group and 4.4% in the fasting group, corresponding to an absolute risk difference of 2.3% (95% CI, - 6.6 to 11.2) and a crude odds ratio of 1.57 (95% CI, 0.25-9.88). Post-tracheostomy FiO2 requirements were higher in the fasting group (p = 0.005), while other respiratory and arterial blood gas parameters were similar. Delta analyses showed greater increases in PaO2 and more stable lactate levels in the continuous feeding group (p = 0.024 and p = 0.033). ICU and hospital length of stay, complication rates, and mortality were comparable. Continuation of EN before tracheostomy with passive nasogastric drainage was not associated with a statistically significant increase in aspiration pneumonia or adverse outcomes compared with conventional fasting. However, the small number of events and wide confidence intervals indicate that clinically relevant differences cannot be excluded. Larger, adequately powered studies are needed to confirm safety and clarify the clinical implications of pre-tracheostomy feeding strategies. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07508293. Registered on March 21, 2026, retrospectively registered.

42834802.title: Global Research Trends in Sleep Quality, Sleep Deprivation and Sleep Promotion Among ICU Patients: A Descriptive and Evaluative Bibliometric Analysis.
42834802.abstract: Sleep deprivation and poor sleep quality are critical problems among intensive care unit (ICU) patients, with significant implications for recovery, delirium onset and clinical outcomes. Despite growing scientific interest, no bibliometric study has systematically mapped the intellectual structure and thematic evolution of this field. To analyse the bibliometric characteristics and thematic structure of publications on sleep deprivation, sleep promotion and sleep quality in ICU patients indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database between 1983 and 2026. A descriptive and evaluative bibliometric analysis was conducted. Data were retrieved on April 26, 2026, from the WoS Core Collection using a comprehensive search strategy. Publications were filtered by document type, WoS categories (nursing, critical care medicine, anaesthesiology) and index (SCI-EXPANDED, SSCI, ESCI). Data were analysed using R software with the Biblioshiny interface, and annual publication trends were evaluated using Microsoft Excel. Of 11 418 publications retrieved, 379 met the inclusion criteria, spanning 37 years (1983-2026). Linear regression revealed a statistically significant positive trend in publication output (β = 0.643, R2 = 0.704, r = 0.839, p < 0.001), with mean annual publications of 10.24 ± 8.83 and notable acceleration from the 2000s onwards. Thematic mapping identified 'sleep', 'sleep deprivation' and 'delirium' as motor themes both highly central and well developed. Emerging concepts included circadian rhythm, actigraphy, fatigue, pain and anxiety. ICU sleep research has grown substantially over four decades, with sleep deprivation and delirium emerging as co-dominant research priorities. Thematic gaps and emerging clusters identified in this analysis highlight important directions for future nursing research and evidence-based practice development in critical care. This bibliometric analysis identified sleep deprivation and delirium as the co-dominant motor themes of ICU sleep research, and intervention-related concepts such as earplugs, eye masks and melatonin as emerging clusters. These evidence-based trends can guide ICU nurses in prioritizing targeted sleep promotion protocols and support policymakers in directing resources toward the most scientifically mature intervention areas in critical care.

42830462.title: Quality frameworks in intensive care units: a scoping review of accreditation, certification, and standards-based pathways to safer care.
42830462.journal: International journal for quality in health care : journal of the International Society for Quality in Health Care
42830462.abstract: Accreditation, certification, recognition, and standards-based quality frameworks are widely implemented across hospitals and intensive care units (ICUs) to promote safety, standardization, and professional excellence. However, the nature and extent of the empirical evidence evaluating these frameworks specifically in critical care settings remain unclear. This scoping review aimed to map and characterize empirical studies evaluating accreditation-, certification-, recognition-, and standards-based programmes relevant to ICU care. We conducted a scoping review informed by established methodological frameworks and reported according to PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews guidance. Structured searches of MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase, and the Cochrane Library were performed from database inception to 10 April 2026. Eligible studies evaluated organizational accreditation, certification of critical care services, professional recognition programmes, or formal standards-based organizational frameworks relevant to ICU care. Study designs were classified as quasi-experimental studies, observational analytical studies, or structured implementation evaluations. Data were charted descriptively and synthesized narratively. Fourteen empirical studies published between 2006 and 2025 met inclusion criteria. Studies evaluated hospital accreditation or organizational quality management, ICU or critical care service certification, professional recognition or professional certification, and standards-based unit-level frameworks. Outcomes most frequently addressed organizational processes, safety indicators, workforce-related measures, and implementation outcomes, whereas patient-level clinical outcomes such as mortality, length of stay, and ICU readmission were evaluated less consistently. The empirical evidence evaluating accreditation and related quality frameworks in ICU settings is limited and heterogeneous. These frameworks are predominantly assessed as organizational and cultural mechanisms influencing processes, safety, workforce dynamics, and unit-level implementation, with less consistent evaluation of clinical outcomes. A tiered perspective distinguishing hospital-wide accreditation, service-level certification, and professional recognition may better inform future research, policy, and implementation in critical care.

42830038.title: IMPACT OF THE COVID-19 PANDEMIC ON THE SEVERITY AND OUTCOMES OF GUNSHOT INJURIES.
42830038.abstract: To evaluate the impact of COVID-19 infection on injury severity, clinical course, complications, and hospital outcomes in patients with gunshot injuries. This retrospective descriptive-analytical study was conducted at the Central Clinical Military Hospital of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Armenia. The study included 80 male patients with gunshot injuries who were hospitalized during 2020. Of these, 55 (68.8%) patients were COVID-19-positive and 25 (31.2%) were COVID-19-negative. Injury severity was assessed using the Injury Severity Score (ISS) and the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). The rates of intensive care unit (ICU) admission, requirement for mechanical ventilation, length of hospital stay, complications, and in-hospital mortality were analyzed. The mean ISS was significantly higher in COVID-19-positive patients than in COVID-19-negative patients (22.8±7.4 vs. 15.2±5.8, p<0.01). Conversely, the mean GCS score was significantly lower in the COVID-19-positive group (12.9±2.5 vs. 14.6±1.8, p<0.05). ICU admission was required in 43.6% of COVID-19-positive patients compared with 16.0% of COVID-19-negative patients. Mechanical ventilation was required in 21.8% and 8.0% of patients, respectively. The incidence of complications was 29.1% in the COVID-19-positive group and 12.0% in the COVID-19-negative group. In-hospital mortality was 10.9% and 4.0%, respectively. Correlation analysis demonstrated a significant positive association between ISS and length of hospital stay (r=0.61, p<0.001), as well as between ISS and mortality (r=0.58, p<0.001). COVID-19 infection in patients with gunshot injuries is associated with greater injury severity, an increased need for intensive care, a higher incidence of complications and mortality, and prolonged hospitalization. The coexistence of COVID-19 infection and gunshot trauma may be regarded as a mutually aggravating clinical condition that requires early diagnosis, intensive monitoring, and a multidisciplinary treatment approach.

42829456.title: Community-acquired Escherichia coli pneumonia: clinical, radiological, laboratory, and prognostic characteristics in a retrospective single-center study.
42829456.abstract: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) caused by Escherichia coli (E. coli) is uncommon, and its clinical features and prognosis remain insufficiently characterized. To compare the clinical, laboratory, radiological, and prognostic characteristics of community-acquired E. coli pneumonia (CAECP) with CAP caused by other pathogens. Single-center retrospective observational cohort study. Department of Pulmonology, Kocaeli City Hospital, İzmit, Kocaeli, Türkiye from April 2023 to March 2025. Adult patients hospitalized with CAP and positive sputum cultures were reviewed. Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonias were excluded. Patients were classified as CAECP or Other-CAP. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, radiological, CURB-65, Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI), and outcome data were compared. A targeted multivariable logistic regression model adjusted for age and malignancy evaluated 90-day mortality. In-hospital mortality, 90-day mortality, intensive care unit admission, and hospital length of stay. Sixty-eight patients (37 CAECP, 31 Other-CAP). Median age (69 [interquartile range, IQR 50.7-71] vs 67 [56-70] years; P=.805), sex distribution (P=.452), comorbidity burden (P=.094), body temperature (P=.970), heart rate (P=.592), C-reactive protein (P=.731), procalcitonin (P=.749), multilobar involvement (P=.246), and air bronchogram (P=.938) were comparable between groups. Mean CURB-65 (1.73±0.90 vs 1.45±0.99; P=.253) and PSI (108.6±40.6 vs 95.4±27.6; P=.143) were also similar. Hospital stay was significantly longer in CAECP (15.7±15.5 vs 9.6±7.0) days; P=.047). In-hospital mortality was numerically higher (14% vs 0; P=.058), while 90-day mortality was significantly higher (49% vs 16%; P=.005). After adjustment for age and malignancy, CAECP remained independently associated with 90-day mortality (aOR, 7.41; 95% CI, 1.85-29.71; P=.005). CAECP resembles other CAP etiologies at presentation, but is associated with longer hospitalization and markedly higher 90-day mortality despite similar baseline severity scores. Single-center retrospective design, small sample size, and limited number of mortality events.

42825612.title: Characteristics and Outcomes of Patients Referred but Declined for ICU Admission in a Resource-Limited Setting in South Africa.
authors: of the South Africa ICU Capacity Strain (SA-ICU-Strain) Study Group
42825612.abstract: ICU beds are a limited resource and assessing net benefit from ICU admission remains incompletely understood. We sought to examine characteristics and outcomes of patients referred but declined for ICU admission, stratified by clinician-perceived likelihood of ICU benefit. Descriptive, retrospective cohort study. Two public hospitals in the KwaZulu-Natal Department of Health, South Africa, from January 2022 to June 2022. Adult ICU-referred patients classified into four triage cohorts by clinician-assessed acuity and ICU triage status: ICU admissions; high-acuity capacity-declined ICU referrals; high-acuity prognosis-declined ICU referrals; and low-acuity prognosis-declined ICU referrals. None. We report descriptive statistics of ICU-referred patient characteristics stratified by triage cohorts and mortal status. Among 866 ICU referrals, 469 patients (54.2%) were admitted, and 397 patients (45.8%) were declined for ICU admission. ICU admissions had an observed all-cause 30-day hospital mortality of 27.7%. Among declined ICU referrals with nonmissing triage priority scores (n = 327), 250 patients (76.5%) were declined ICU admission for prognosis reasons, and 77 patients (23.5%) were declined for capacity reasons. Seventy-seven (9.7% of ICU referrals) high-acuity capacity-declined ICU referrals ("appropriate patient; no bed capacity; not admitted") had a 26.0% mortality (74.0% survival), 111 (13.9%) high-acuity prognosis-declined ICU referrals ("too sick; not admitted") had a 53.2% mortality (46.8% survival), and 139 (17.5%) low-acuity prognosis-declined ICU referrals ("too well; not admitted") had a 7.2% mortality. Declined ICU referrals were less likely surgical/trauma patients and more likely medical patients coming from wards and emergency departments. In one sampling in the South African public healthcare system, many patients are referred but declined for ICU admission due to perceptions of being both "too well" or "too sick" to benefit and due to bed capacity, with a proportion of such patients experiencing potential clinical deviations from triage-expected trajectories.

42825231.title: Characteristics and Outcomes of Patients Referred but Declined for ICU Admission in a Resource-Limited Setting in South Africa.
42825231.abstract: ICU beds are a limited resource and assessing net benefit from ICU admission remains incompletely understood. We sought to examine characteristics and outcomes of patients referred but declined for ICU admission, stratified by clinician-perceived likelihood of ICU benefit. Descriptive, retrospective cohort study. Two public hospitals in the KwaZulu-Natal Department of Health, South Africa, from January 2022 to June 2022. Adult ICU-referred patients classified into four triage cohorts by clinician-assessed acuity and ICU triage status: ICU admissions; high-acuity capacity-declined ICU referrals; high-acuity prognosis-declined ICU referrals; and low-acuity prognosis-declined ICU referrals. 42824319.title: Participation in antimicrobial stewardship among intensive care unit nurses: a cross-sectional study based on the COM-B model.
42824319.abstract: This study aimed to investigate antimicrobial stewardship participation and its associated factors among intensive care unit (ICU) nurses based on the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation, and Behavior (COM-B) model. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among ICU nurses from 11 hospitals across China in March 2026. Data on demographic and occupational characteristics were collected using a general information questionnaire. Antimicrobial stewardship participation and its influencing factors were assessed using the ICU Nurses' Participation in Antimicrobial Stewardship Behavior and Influencing Factors (ASP-BF) Scale, and nursing professional self-efficacy was measured using the Nursing Professional Self-Efficacy (NPSE) Scale. A total of 497 ICU nurses were included. The mean scores were 48.80 ± 9.86 for capability (possible range: 13-65), 38.42 ± 10.60 for opportunity (possible range: 11-55), 82.55 ± 16.86 for motivation (possible range: 23-115), 59.94 ± 13.57 for behavior (possible range: 16-80), and 29.60 ± 4.45 for NPSE (possible range: 7-35). Structural equation modeling (SEM) showed that capability (β = 0.41), opportunity (β = 0.84), and NPSE (β = 0.77) were positively associated with motivation, and motivation was positively associated with behavior (β = 0.75; all p < 0.001). ICU nurses had generally favorable levels of capability, opportunity, motivation, behavior, and NPSE in relation to antimicrobial stewardship participation. Motivation was directly associated with participation behavior, while capability, opportunity, and NPSE were associated with behavior through motivation. In addition, antimicrobial stewardship training was associated with better participation behavior. Future interventions should focus on strengthening institutional support, improving multidisciplinary collaboration and workflow conditions, and providing structured training to enhance nurses' participation in antimicrobial stewardship.

42823658.title: Risk factors associated with carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacterial infections in intensive care units in Jordan.
42823658.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacteria (CR-GNB) pose major challenges in intensive care units (ICUs) due to limited treatment options and high mortality. Data describing their predictors in Jordan are scarce. This study aimed to identify risk factors associated with CR-GNB infections among ICU patients. A retrospective analysis was conducted using national surveillance data from 18 ICUs across 13 public hospitals in Jordan between September 2018 and September 2024. Patients with confirmed Gram-negative infections were included. Laboratory testing followed CLSI M100 standards. Logistic regression was performed to determine independent predictors of carbapenem resistance. Of 1,180 Gram-negative isolates tested, 451 (38%) were carbapenem-resistant. Acinetobacter baumannii and Klebsiella spp. were the predominant resistant pathogens, while E.coli was mainly carbapenem-susceptible. Independent predictors of carbapenem resistance identified by multivariate logistic regression were: ICU-acquired infection (OR: 2.44; 95% CI: 1.31-4.54; p = 0.004), pneumonia (OR: 2.77; 95% CI: 1.48-5.23; p = 0.001), invasive device use (OR: 3.37; 95% CI: 1.28-9.95; p = 0.019), and admission to high-risk ICU units (OR: 3.33; 95% CI: 2.06-5.48; p < 0.001). Mortality was significantly higher among CR-GNB patients (69.8%) compared to carbapenem-susceptible patients (42.0%), with a 3.15-fold increased risk of death (OR: 3.149; 95% CI: 2.392-4.145; p < 0.001). The findings of this study underscore the need for strategies to prevent and control carbapenem-resistant infections, particularly in high-risk populations such as patients with invasive devices and those diagnosed with pneumonia. Enhanced infection control measures, including strict hand hygiene practices, judicious antibiotic stewardship, and proper management of invasive devices, are essential to minimize the transmission of carbapenem-resistant bacteria in healthcare settings.

42952202.title: Sense of Coherence in Patients After Intensive Care Treatment: A 1-Year Follow-Up Cohort Study.
42952202.abstract: Patients endure physical, mental and cognitive symptoms after critical illness, and coping is vital to their healing process. Little research exists on associations between sense of coherence (SOC) and patients' health improvements after intensive care unit (ICU) discharge. To describe the trajectory of SOC and how demographic, clinical and psychosocial variables affect SOC in discharged ICU patients during 12 months of follow-up. A prospective cohort substudy of a neutral randomized controlled trial in Norway involving discharged ICU patients receiving nurse-led follow-up consultations or standard care. Data were collected in the ward (baseline) and after 3, 6 and 12 months. Univariate and multivariate linear mixed models for repeated measures were fitted with SOC-13 score as the dependent variable. We included 523 patients with a median of three ICU days, median age 57 years, 47% females, 54% receiving mechanical ventilation and stable SOC during follow-up. Higher SOC was associated with increased age (B = 0.12, 95% CI [0.05, 0.18]), no prior mental health problems (B = 6.69, 95% CI [4.19, 9.19]), no prior use of psychotropics (B = 2.37, 95% CI [0.16, 4.58]) and lower post-traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS) at baseline (B = 5.56, 95% CI [3.50, 7.61]). Low educational level (B = -2.25, 95% CI [-4.10, -0.40]), higher pain interference at baseline (B = -0.46, 95% CI [-0.84, -0.08]) and less social support 3 months later (B = -5.93, 95% CI [-7.87, -3.99]) were associated with lower SOC. During 12 months after ICU discharge, SOC remained stable. Higher age, no previous mental health problems or use of psychotropics, and lower PTSS were associated with higher SOC. Low education, more pain and low social support were associated with lower SOC. More vulnerable patients deserve greater attention during general rehabilitation after ICU treatment due to low SOC.

42952193.title: Nurse Competencies, Patient Characteristics, and Pain Management Protocol Adherence in Intensive Care Units: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study Accounting for ICU Clustering.
42952193.abstract: To examine the associations between nurse competencies (knowledge, self-efficacy, and attitude), patient characteristics, and pain management protocol adherence in adult intensive care units, while accounting for between-ICU clustering. Adherence to pain management protocols remains suboptimal despite available guidelines. Nurse competencies are essential for evidence-based practice, yet their translation into clinical performance may depend on contextual factors. ICU-level organizational context has been described in recent reviews, but empirical examination of these relationships remains limited. This multicenter cross-sectional study included 525 ICU nurses from seven hospitals in Tehran, Iran (July-October 2025). One index patient was assessed for each nurse. ICU-level organizational characteristics were assessed through unit observation and head nurse interviews. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for protocol adherence was computed from an empty mixed model. Multivariable linear regression with ICU entered as a fixed effect was used to identify individual-level factors associated with adherence. Organizational context was retained as a descriptive variable only. Protocol adherence was moderate (mean 8.5/12; 32.4% good adherence). The ICC for protocol adherence was 0.02 (95% CI: 0.001-0.15), indicating minimal clustering. In the multivariable model with ICU as a fixed effect (18 predictors), knowledge (β = 0.311), self-efficacy (β = 0.290), and attitude (β = 0.276) remained independently associated with adherence (all p < 0.001). Patient characteristics remained significantly associated: substance use history (β = -0.138, p = 0.016), inability to communicate (β = -0.148, p = 0.010), GCS < 9 (β = -0.160, p = 0.008), and mechanical ventilation (β = -0.121, p = 0.028). The full model explained 53.4% of the variance in adherence. Organizational support across the seven ICUs ranged from 1 to 5 (weighted mean 3.42 ± 1.15). Nurse competencies and patient characteristics are independently associated with pain management protocol adherence in this multicenter ICU sample. Between-ICU clustering was minimal (ICC = 0.02), suggesting that individual-level factors are the primary correlates of adherence in this sample. Given the small number of ICU clusters (n = 7), organizational findings are descriptive only and require confirmation in larger multilevel studies. Nurse managers may consider competency-based pain management education and regular audits with feedback. Given the small number of ICU clusters (n = 7), these recommendations are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multilevel studies.

42952060.title: The Relationship Between Caring Roles and Fatigue in Intensive Care Nurses: A Cross-Sectional Study.
42952060.abstract: Intensive care nurses experience significant levels of fatigue while providing care to their patients. High levels of fatigue may negatively impact nurses' orientation to their caring roles, and this orientation may also be a cause of fatigue. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between intensive care nurses' orientations towards their caregiving roles and their fatigue levels. The sample of this cross-sectional and correlational study was conducted with nurses working in the intensive care units of a hospital in northwestern Turkey. The 'Personal Information Form', 'Chalder Fatigue Scale' and 'Nursing Care Role Orientation Scale' were used for collecting research data. In this study, conducted with 110 nurses, the average fatigue score for intensive care nurses was 19.00 ± 7.60, with a physical fatigue score of 13.13 ± 5.20 and a mental fatigue score of 5.87 ± 2.81. The average score of nurses' orientation towards caregiving roles was 82.00 ± 7.68. Female nurses and those working in critical care for less than a year experienced greater fatigue levels (t = 2.131, p = 0.035 and F = 2.858, p = 0.041, respectively). Nurses' orientation towards caregiving roles differed based on their education level and professional experience (p < 0.05). There was a positive correlation between nurses' fatigue scores and orientation towards caregiving roles (p < 0.05). Intensive care nurses were able to effectively adapt to their nursing care roles despite high levels of fatigue and there was a positive relationship between nurses' physical and mental fatigue levels and their adaptation to their care roles. The results of this study, which cannot be generalised to all intensive care nurses because it was conducted in a single hospital, reveal that as nurses' orientation towards their caring roles increases, their fatigue levels also increase. For intensive care nurses to effectively care for their patients, they need to be well oriented in their caregiving roles. However, efforts to be well oriented in caregiving can increase nurses' fatigue levels. Considering that reducing physical and mental fatigue will increase the success of the care nurses provide, the importance of providing work environments that will facilitate intensive care nurses' orientation to their caregiving roles in reducing the fatigue levels they experience becomes evident.

42946514.title: Flight Physician Training and Workforce Sustainability Within an Integrated Emergency Department-Intensive Care Unit-Helicopter Emergency Medical Services Staffing Model: A Rural Helicopter Emergency Medical Services Experience in Japan.
42946514.abstract: Maintaining physician-staffed helicopter emergency medical services (HEMS) in rural regions is increasingly challenging because of physician shortages, workforce sustainability concerns, and limited opportunities for dedicated flight physician staffing. We developed an integrated staffing and training model in which emergency physicians collectively provide emergency department (ED), intensive care unit (ICU), pediatric emergency, and HEMS care while participating in a regional physician-sharing collaboration. This single-center retrospective study evaluated all consecutive HEMS missions conducted between April 2021 and March 2026 at a rural tertiary emergency and critical care center in Japan. Flight physician training was conducted through on-the-job training (OJT) embedded within routine ED, ICU, pediatric emergency, and HEMS practices. Missions performed during supervised OJT were compared with those performed after independent certification. Operational performance was assessed using on-scene time, scene intervention rates, intubation rates, cardiopulmonary resuscitation rates, and hospital mortality. Six physicians completed training; 4 achieved independent practice within 6 months and 2 within 12 months. The average annual flight volume was approximately 30 missions per physician. A total of 189 missions were analyzed. Patient characteristics were comparable between 98 OJT and 91 independent missions. No differences were observed across operational performance measures; no procedural, medication, or operational incidents occurred. Despite relatively limited individual flight exposure, most trainees achieved independent practice within 6 months, and operational performance following certification was not inferior to that of supervised training. Integrated acute care practice may support the development and maintenance of flight physician competency in resource-limited rural environments.

42944582.title: Discussing Future Treatment and Care in the ICU: Perspectives From Patients.
42944582.abstract: Treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU) is usually predicated on curative treatment, but continuing all available treatment options may not always be beneficial for the patient or in line with their wishes. However, patients admitted to the ICU are often assessed as incapable of making decisions regarding their care; hence conversations about wishes for treatment are postponed. This study aimed to investigate the experiences of patients who participated in a conversation concerning treatment and care following ICU discharge based on the Danish version of the Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment (ReSPECT) form. Semi-structured telephone interviews were conducted with patients who had a conversation about future treatment and care with an intensivist using the ReSPECT form during an ICU admission between November 2024 and July 2025. Relatives who participated in the conversation and were present during the interviews were asked to elaborate on their experiences of the conversation's timing and how they felt about participating in the conversation. Data was analysed using content analysis. Nineteen patients were included in the study, of whom 15 patients (83%) participated in a telephone interview. Two themes were identified: Timing of the conversation and Clarifying goals of care and options. Based on these, four sub-themes were identified, two for each theme: Too soon, but not much later; Wishes in accordance; Hard, but necessary and Communicating in an understandable manner. Most patients were satisfied with having had a conversation about future treatment and care. Patients found the conversation relevant and necessary. The intensivists were praised for their communication skills and their ability to know and explain recommendations for future treatment and care. However, most patients believed that the conversation was conducted too soon after recovering from intensive care. They would have preferred to have had the conversation later during their admission. Most participating ICU patients found a conversation about future treatment and care relevant but preferred it to be held after ICU discharge. Future research should investigate the benefits of incorporating intensivists in these conversations in general wards. In this prospective study, former ICU patients were interviewed and asked about their experiences and opinions regarding a structured ReSPECT discussion that had been conducted in the end of their ICU stay. The goal of that interview was advance care planning, involving the patients and their family members. This study reports a qualitative analysis of interviews conducted at least 4 weeks later. Two main themes and four subthemes were identified. Almost all patients remembered having had the discussion, but the content was less clearly remembered. ICU physicians' communication skills were appreciated. The study assesses a function of our daily work from patient and family perspective, and discusses important issues such as optimal timing of the advance care planning.

42942533.title: HDL-C Levels Are Associated with Clinical Outcomes and Hospital Mortality in Critically Ill Patients with Sepsis: A Prospective Cohort Study.
42942533.abstract: Background and Objectives: Metabolic perturbations frequently occur during the acute phase of critical illness and may disrupt lipid homeostasis. Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a severe condition and is associated with high mortality in critically ill patients with sepsis. This study aimed to evaluate the association between conventional plasma lipid parameters and clinical outcomes in critically ill sepsis patients. Materials and Methods: We conducted a prospective observational cohort study of critically ill sepsis patients in Taiwan between October 2020 and July 2025. Conventional plasma lipid parameters and clinical variables were measured at intensive care unit admission. Clinical outcomes were compared between patients stratified by plasma HDL-C levels. Results: A total of 285 critically ill patients with sepsis were included. Pneumonia was the presumed source of infection in 91% of patients, and 78% met the criteria for ARDS. The overall hospital mortality rate was 37.9%. Patients with ARDS had significantly higher C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels, higher risk of organ failure (i.e., APACHE II and SOFA scores), and lower plasma HDL-C levels (all p < 0.05). Non-survivors exhibited significantly greater organ failure severity and lower HDL-C levels compared with survivors (all p < 0.05). Patients with low HDL-C (≤17.5 mg/dL; n = 106, 37.2%) had significantly higher CRP and IL-6, greater organ failure severity, and increased 28-, 60-, 90-day, and hospital mortality, compared with those with high HDL-C (> 17.5 mg/dL; n = 179, 62.8%) (all p < 0.05). In multivariable analyses, lower HDL-C were independently associated with hospital mortality. Conclusions: Lower HDL-C levels were associated with hospital mortality in critically ill patients with sepsis, most of whom had pneumonia and concomitant ARDS. These findings suggest that HDL-C may have prognostic value in this selected critically ill population, although external validation in broader sepsis populations is warranted. An easily accessible and useful for early risk stratification.

42942515.title: High-Flow Nasal Cannula Outcomes in COVID-19-Associated Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: Illness Severity, Awake Prone Positioning, and Risk of Intubation in a Single-Center ICU Cohort.
42942515.abstract: Background and Objectives: High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) is widely used in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, yet predictors of successful noninvasive support and the role of awake prone positioning remain incompletely defined, and observational analyses are vulnerable to immortal-time bias. We evaluated factors associated with HFNC success and the association of awake prone positioning with HFNC outcomes in critically ill adults with COVID-19-associated acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, using analyses designed to reduce time-related and indication-related bias. Materials and Methods: In this retrospective, single-center intensive care unit (ICU) cohort study, adults with virologically confirmed COVID-19 who received HFNC, with awake prone positioning considered as part of the initial HFNC strategy, between April 2020 and December 2021 were followed from HFNC initiation until endotracheal intubation or ICU discharge. HFNC success was defined as avoidance of intubation during the index ICU stay. Multivariable logistic regression with multiple imputation of missing covariates, propensity score-based inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and landmark time-to-event analyses were used to assess the association between awake prone positioning and HFNC failure. Results: Among 222 patients, HFNC was successful in 72 (32.4%) and unsuccessful in 150 (67.6%). Failure was associated with lower PaO2/FiO2 ratios, higher FiO2 requirements, and higher APACHE II and SOFA scores at ICU admission (all p ≤ 0.011). In the imputed multivariable model, awake prone positioning was associated with lower HFNC failure (odds ratio [OR] 0.23; 95% CI 0.10-0.53; p < 0.001), whereas higher APACHE II score (OR 1.09 per point; 95% CI 1.02-1.17; p = 0.012), higher HFNC FiO2 (OR 1.41 per 10%; 95% CI 1.15-1.73; p < 0.001), and lower PaO2/FiO2 ratio (p = 0.037) were independently associated with failure. IPTW yielded a consistent estimate (OR 0.22; 95% CI 0.10-0.47). In time-to-event analyses, the unadjusted association was strong but likely influenced by early deterioration; after a day-1 landmark it attenuated yet remained significant (hazard ratio [HR] 0.52; 95% CI 0.34-0.79; p = 0.002), and at a day-2 landmark it was non-significant unadjusted (HR 0.66; 95% CI 0.39-1.11) but significant after adjustment for illness severity (HR 0.47; 95% CI 0.25-0.88; p = 0.019). Conclusions: Patients undergoing awake prone positioning during HFNC had a lower observed incidence of intubation, although the difference was more modest than crude analyses suggested and sensitive to landmark timing, whereas greater illness severity and more severe hypoxemia at ICU admission were independently associated with failure. These findings support severity-informed monitoring and timely escalation during HFNC. Causality cannot be inferred because of the retrospective design and residual confounding, particularly confounding related to the ability to tolerate prone positioning.

42942448.title: Association of Perioperative Colchicine Use with Morbidity and Inflammation in Heart Valve Surgery.
42942448.abstract: Background and Objectives: Valvular heart disease (VHD) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, and valve replacement surgery performed under cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) with full sternotomy remains an important treatment modality. Colchicine has well-established anti-inflammatory effects in ischemic heart disease and pericardial disease, but its association with postoperative morbidity in patients undergoing valvular heart surgery has not been well studied. This study aimed to investigate the association of perioperative colchicine use with clinical morbidity and inflammatory parameters in patients undergoing valvular heart surgery with CPB. Materials and Methods: In this retrospective study, 82 patients who underwent elective on-pump valvular heart surgery through full sternotomy were divided into a control group (n = 42) who did not receive colchicine and a colchicine group (n = 40) who received oral colchicine (0.5 mg once daily) for three days before and ten days after surgery. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data, including length of hospital and intensive care unit (ICU) stay, transfusion requirements, sternal wound complication, surgical re-exploration, and inflammatory parameters on postoperative day 5 (C-reactive protein [CRP], white blood cell count, albumin, platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio [PLR], and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio [NLR]), were compared between the groups. Results: Length of ICU stay was significantly shorter in the colchicine group than in the control group (4.1 ± 1.6 vs. 5.3 ± 2.4 days; p = 0.009), and fresh frozen plasma transfusion requirement was significantly lower in the colchicine group (4.2 ± 2.1 vs. 6.9 ± 3.3 units; p < 0.001). Total hospital stay, erythrocyte transfusion requirement, and inflammatory parameters (CRP, white blood cell count, NLR, PLR, and albumin) did not differ significantly between the two groups (all p > 0.05). Conclusions: Perioperative colchicine was associated with a shorter ICU stay and a reduced requirement for fresh frozen plasma transfusion in patients undergoing valvular heart surgery with CPB, suggesting that colchicine may have a potential role in this surgical population. After correction for multiple comparisons, the difference in ICU length of stay was no longer statistically significant. Larger prospective studies are warranted to confirm these findings.

42942153.title: Beyond Resistance: Carbapenemase Gene Profiles and Mortality in ICU Patients with Carbapenem-Resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae Infections.
42942153.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) causes serious infections in intensive care units (ICUs), but the relationship between carbapenemase gene profiles and mortality remains uncertain. This prospective two-center cohort included 94 adult ICU patients with clinical CRKP infection from April to September 2026. The first clinical isolate from each patient was included. blaKPC, blaNDM, blaVIM, blaIMP, blaOXA-48, and blaCTX-M genes were investigated by polymerase chain reaction. The primary outcome was 28-day ICU mortality; 14-day and final ICU mortality were secondary outcomes. blaOXA-48, blaNDM, blaKPC, and blaCTX-M were detected in 65 (69.1%), 49 (52.1%), 19 (20.2%), and 73 (77.7%) of isolates, respectively; blaNDM and blaOXA-48 co-occurred in 39 (41.5%). Fourteen-day, 28-day, and final ICU mortality rates occured in 38 (40.4%), 48 (51.1%), and 53 (56.4%), respectively. No statistically significant associations were observed between individual genes, the presence of two carbapenemase genes, or carbapenemase profiles and any mortality endpoint; adjusted analyses of 28-day ICU mortality yielded similar findings. In the exploratory Firth model, the profile effect was not significant (p = 0.198), whereas a higher age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index and bloodstream infection or ventilator-associated pneumonia, compared with urinary tract infection, were associated with higher odds of 28-day ICU mortality. Frequent gene co-occurrence was observed; however, clinically meaningful gene-mortality associations cannot be excluded because of imprecise estimates.

42935203.title: Predictive value of glucose metabolism indices for short-term outcomes in critically ill patients with congestive heart failure.
42935203.journal: Zhong nan da xue xue bao. Yi xue ban = Journal of Central South University. Medical sciences
42935203.abstract: Congestive heart failure (CHF) is a major global public health problem, affecting approximately 64 million people worldwide, with a 5-year survival rate of less than 50%. The short-term risk of death is particularly high among patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). Disturbances in glucose metabolism are an important pathophysiological feature of CHF, and effective glycemic monitoring is of considerable importance for prognostic assessment in critically ill patients with CHF. This study aims to evaluate the predictive value of 3 glucose metabolism-related indices, blood glucose level, stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR), and hemoglobin glycation index (HGI), for the risk of 7-day mortality in critically ill patients with CHF. This study was based on the MIMIC-IV database and included 851 critically ill patients with CHF who met the eligibility criteria between 2008 and 2019. The primary outcome was 7-day all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality. Kaplan-Meier (K-M) survival curves with log-rank tests were used to assess the associations between each index and survival outcomes. Univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to calculate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Three models were constructed to progressively evaluate the influence of potential confounders: an unadjusted model, Model 1 adjusted for demographic and clinical characteristics, and Model 2 further adjusted for laboratory parameters. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis was used to explore the dose-response relationships between the 3 indices and mortality risk. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and the area under the curve (AUC) were used to evaluate the discriminative ability of each index, and incremental ROC analysis was performed to determine whether adding each index improved the predictive performance of the baseline model. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used to select features from 15 candidate variables and to objectively assess the independent predictive contribution of each index in a multivariable setting. In addition, stratified analyses were conducted across multiple clinically relevant subgroups defined by sex, age, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) status, vasopressin use, acute myocardial infarction (AMI), acute kidney injury (AKI), and sepsis to evaluate the consistency and robustness of the prognostic value of SHR. A total of 851 critically ill patients with CHF were included, of whom 70 (8.226%) died from any cause within 7 days. Cox regression analysis showed that, when analyzed as a continuous variable, SHR was independently associated with 7-day all-cause mortality in the fully adjusted model (HR=1.760, 95% CI 1.193 to 2.595; P<0.05), whereas the association between blood glucose and 7-day all-cause mortality was no longer significant after full adjustment (HR=1.002, 95% CI 0.999 to 1.004; P>0.05). HGI, when analyzed as a continuous variable, was associated with 7-day all-cause mortality (HR=0.787, 95% CI 0.650 to 0.954; P<0.05); however, no significant association was observed after HGI was categorized into tertiles in the fully adjusted model (P>0.05). Tertile analysis of SHR showed that the highest tertile remained significantly associated with 7-day all-cause mortality in the fully adjusted model (P<0.05). K-M survival analysis further showed that patients with higher blood glucose levels or higher SHR had a greater risk of 7-day all-cause mortality, whereas patients with lower HGI also had a significantly increased risk of 7-day all-cause mortality (all P<0.05). ROC curve analysis showed that SHR tended to have better predictive performance for mortality risk than blood glucose and HGI, although the differences did not reach statistical significance (P>0.05). Notably, adding SHR to the baseline model significantly improved its predictive performance (P=0.048). LASSO regression analysis showed that among the 9 predictors ultimately selected, SHR was the only glucose-related variable retained, whereas blood glucose and HGI were excluded. SHR is an independent predictor of short-term mortality risk in critically ill patients with CHF and has considerable potential for clinical application in risk stratification and prognostic assessment.

42933952.title: Intensive Care Unit Liberation: Transforming Critical Care Through the ABCDEF Bundle.
42933952.journal: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
42933952.abstract: This article highlights the shift from traditional intensive care unit practices, including deep sedation, immobility, and restricted visitation, to evidence-based, patient-centered care. These outdated methods, once considered protective, are now known to increase delirium, muscle weakness, cognitive decline, and health care costs. Implementing the ABCDEF bundle (eg, pain management, awakening and breathing trials, sedation choice, delirium management, early mobility, and family engagement) is a proven evidence-based framework that improves patient outcomes. Critical care nurses play a central role in driving bundle adherence. Successful implementation requires interdisciplinary teamwork, leadership support, education, and integration into practice standards.

42933948.title: Reevaluating Chlorhexidine Gluconate Oral Care in Mechanically Ventilated Patients: Evidence for De-implementation.
42933948.journal: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
42933948.abstract: Chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) oral care was incorporated into ventilator bundles as a preventive strategy for ventilator-associated pneumonia. Recent evidence challenged the efficacy and safety of this long-standing practice. Systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials show minimal benefits (non-significant reduction in intensive care unit length of stay and ventilator days) and potential for harm (trend toward increased mortality). International and national consensus statements have withdrawn recommendations to use CHG for oral care. This article synthesizes the evidence supporting de-implementation of CHG oral care and outlines practical steps for adopting safer, evidence-aligned oral care protocols focused on toothbrushing for mechanically ventilated adults.

42931235.title: Characteristics and Resistance Patterns of Gram-Negative Bacterial Isolates to Third-Generation Cephalosporins in Oncology ICU Patients: A Ten-Year Retrospective Analysis.
42931235.abstract: Third-generation cephalosporin (3GC) resistance threatens empirical therapy in vulnerable critically ill patients. We conducted a decade-long single-center retrospective study of 3528 Gram-negative isolates from 1946 adult and pediatric oncology intensive care unit (ICU) patients between 2015 and 2024 at King Hussein Cancer Center. This study aims to characterize 3GS resistance in oncology ICU patients. The 3GC resistance was 59.2% among Enterobacterales and other fermenting organisms (evaluated against the full three-agent panel) and 67.2%among non-fermenters (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter spp., Stenotrophomonas maltophilia; evaluated against a narrower, organism-appropriate agent subset); these two estimates are not directly comparable given the differing susceptibility panels tested. Resistance was highest among the Acinetobacter calcoaceticus-baumannii complex (96.9%), followed by Escherichia coli (70.5%), Enterobacter cloacae (65.5%), and Klebsiella pneumoniae (59.6%). In unadjusted patient-level analyses, resistance was significantly higher among patients with hematological malignancy than solid tumors (73.1% vs. 57.8%; OR 1.98, 95% CI 1.59-2.48; p < 0.001) and among pediatric versus adult ICU isolates (70.8% vs. 60.9%; OR 1.55, 95% CI 1.11-2.18; p = 0.010). Seven-day mortality did not differ by resistance status (44.1% vs. 41.6%; unadjusted OR 1.11, 95% CI 0.92-1.33). The 3GC resistance varies by organism, malignancy type and ICU population in unadjusted analyses, supporting population-specific antibiograms and stronger stewardship.

42928669.title: Prevalence and Associated Factors of Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome in Adults Admitted to an Intensive Care Unit: A Retrospective Observational Descriptive Study.
42928669.abstract: Prolonged opioid administration for pain control and to facilitate tolerance of mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit (ICU) may lead to tolerance and physical dependence. Following opioid discontinuation, opioid withdrawal syndrome (OWS) may occur. Although this condition has been well described in pediatric populations, its incidence and associated factors in critically ill adults remain uncertain because of diagnostic heterogeneity and the frequent clinical overlap with delirium. The aim of this study was to assess the prevalence of OWS and to identify factors associated with its development in adult patients. We conducted a retrospective, descriptive, observational study including patients evaluated at the post-ICU follow-up clinic of Lozano Blesa University Clinical Hospital (Zaragoza, Spain) over a 12-month period. This study investigated the association between multiple opioid medications and adjunctive medications and the occurrence of OWS. Eligible patients had an ICU stay of >7 days, received mechanical ventilation for >48 hours, and had been exposed to opioids. Demographic, clinical, and pharmacological variables were collected, including types of opioids, weight-adjusted cumulative dose, and use of adjuvant medications. OWS was diagnosed during the first 48 hours after opioid discontinuation using a combination of the Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) and Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were performed to evaluate the impact of morphine exposure. A total of 66 patients were included (mean age 59.9 ± 13.6 years; predominantly male). The leading cause of ICU admission was respiratory disease (48.5%). Mean Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II) score at admission was 17.0 ± 6.1, and median ICU length of stay was 19 days. Twenty-two patients (33.3%) developed OWS, which was mild in 90.9% and moderate in 9.1% according to the COWS. No significant differences were observed between groups in baseline characteristics or delirium occurrence. Patients who developed OWS were more likely to have received morphine (100% vs. 75%; p = 0.010) and had a higher weight-adjusted cumulative morphine dose (3.15 ± 2.33 vs. 2.21 ± 2.50 mg/kg; p = 0.047), whereas no differences were found for fentanyl exposure. In addition, they more frequently required benzodiazepines (68.2% vs. 18.2%), neuroleptics (68.2% vs. 6.8%), and dexmedetomidine (31.8% vs. 4.5%) (p < 0.01 for all comparisons). Cumulative morphine dose showed modest discriminatory performance for OWS (area under the curve (AUC) 0.653; p = 0.048). OWS is a common complication among adult ICU survivors, although it is predominantly mild in severity. A higher cumulative dose of morphine was associated with its onset, although no association was found with the total duration of exposure. Clinical overlap with delirium and the reactive use of psychoactive medications may contribute to under-recognition of this condition, underscoring the need for structured OWS screening during ICU stay and in post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) follow-up.

42922243.title: Effectiveness of Quality Improvement Strategies in Preventing Healthcare-Associated Infections Among Neurosurgical Patients Admitted to Intensive Care Units: A Systematic Review.
42922243.abstract: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) remain a major and largely preventable cause of morbidity, excess mortality, prolonged hospitalization, and escalating healthcare costs in intensive care units (ICUs) worldwide.
