42874160.journal: Journal of clinical virology : the official publication of the Pan American Society for Clinical Virology
42874160.abstract: The diagnostic value of upper respiratory tract (URT) viral testing as a surrogate for lower respiratory tract (LRT) viral detection in mechanically ventilated patients remains uncertain. We evaluated URT/LRT concordance in intubated intensive care unit (ICU) patients and identified factors associated with non-concordance. We retrospectively studied adult and pediatric ICU patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation who underwent paired URT and LRT respiratory viral polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing between January 2014 and January 2025. Concordance was defined as detection of at least one identical virus in both specimens or negative results in both. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with concordance. A simplified bedside prediction score was developed to predict non-concordance. Among 112 patients, 70 (62.5%) had concordant results. Specific positive agreement varied by virus: human metapneumovirus (88.9%), respiratory syncytial virus (80.0%), rhinovirus/enterovirus (75.0%), influenza virus (68.4%), adenovirus (34.8%), and human bocavirus (0.0%). A longer symptom-to-URT testing interval (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.74 per day; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.62-0.87) and chronic lung disease (aOR, 0.22; 95% CI, 0.06-0.80) were associated with lower concordance, whereas positive end-expiratory pressure > 5 cmH₂O was associated with higher concordance (aOR, 2.85; 95% CI, 1.07-7.59). The bedside score showed good discrimination for non-concordance (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.818). URT/LRT concordance was moderate and varied by symptom timing, clinical factors, and viral pathogen. LRT testing may provide additional diagnostic value in patients at high risk of non-concordance. The bedside score may help identify these patients but requires further internal and external validation.

42873100.title: Clinical application of volatile sedation in adult intensive care units: pharmacological mechanisms, delivery systems, and safety.
42873100.abstract: Sedation is essential in critically ill mechanically ventilated patients, yet conventional intravenous agents carry risks of accumulation, organ-dependent clearance, and adverse effects. Volatile anesthetics offer several pharmacokinetic advantages, but their adoption in the intensive care unit has historically been limited by technical constraints. This review offers an updated, clinically focused overview of volatile- based sedation in adult intensive care units, covering pharmacological mechanisms, delivery systems, clinical outcomes, safety, and practical application. This review was conducted through systematic searching of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between January 2016 and December 2025. Sevoflurane and isoflurane achieve sedation primarily via γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptor modulation and offer organ-independent clearance, rapid onset/offset, and real-time end-tidal monitoring. Modern delivery systems, including reflection devices (Sedaconda-ACD) and automated platforms (MIRUS), have improved intensive care unit feasibility. Clinical evidence suggests volatile sedation may reduce awakening times and duration of mechanical ventilation compared with intravenous agents; however, results across randomized trials and meta-analyses are heterogeneous. Potential benefits have been reported in acute respiratory distress syndrome, post-cardiac arrest care, neurocritical illness, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and refractory agitation, but robust evidence is lacking across all settings. Limitations include hemodynamic effects, increased circuit dead space, renal safety concerns with sevoflurane, infrastructure requirements, occupational exposure, environmental impact, and cost. Volatile sedation is a feasible and pharmacologically rational option for selected mechanically ventilated intensive care unit patients, particularly those requiring prolonged sedation or with organ dysfunction limiting conventional agents. Current evidence does not support universal superiority over intravenous sedation. Inhaled anesthetics should be incorporated into individualized, multimodal sedation strategies within structured institutional frameworks. Large multicenter trials are needed to clarify effects on mortality, long-term neurological outcomes, and quality of life.

42872958.title: Isoflurane-Based Inhaled Sedation in Mechanically Ventilated Adults With Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: The SAVE-ICU Randomized Clinical Trial.
authors: SAVE-ICU Investigators and the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group
42872958.abstract: Rigorous evidence for inhaled sedation using isoflurane in mechanically ventilated patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) is limited. To evaluate whether an inhaled sedation strategy lowers hospital mortality compared with usual care intravenous sedation strategy in mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF. Pragmatic, effectiveness, open-label, superiority, randomized clinical trial in 14 intensive care units (ICUs) in Canada. Adults (≥18 years) receiving sedation for less than 72 hours and receiving mechanical ventilation for AHRF from non-COVID respiratory failure (ratio of partial pressure of arterial oxygen [Pao2] to fraction of inspired oxygen [Fio2] <300 mm Hg) or COVID-19 were enrolled between September 2020 and March 2025 with follow-up through June 2025. Patients were randomized to an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed or to a usual intravenous sedation care strategy. Sedatives were titrated to achieve the desired target sedation score guided by clinical teams and continued until extubation or death. Primary outcome was all-cause hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU- and ventilator-free days at day 30; hospital-free days at day 60; use of refractory hypoxemia adjunctive therapies; delirium- and coma-free days at day 14; and quality-of-life and disability scores at 3 months. Of 786 patients randomized, 780 were included in the primary analysis (mean age, 61.1 years; 34.0% female; 73.7% non-COVID AHRF, mean Pao2:Fio2 ratio, 152.6 mm Hg); 385 in the inhaled sedation and 395 in the intravenous sedation groups. In the inhaled sedation group, 49.9% to 55.4% of patients received concomitant intravenous sedation on any day during the first 14 days after randomization. At hospital discharge, 161 of 379 patients (42.5%) in the inhaled sedation group had died, compared with 171 of 390 patients (43.8%) in the intravenous sedation group (risk ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.84 to 1.14]; P = .85). There was no effect modification in prespecified subgroup analyses for age, sex, and COVID-19 status. ICU-, ventilator-, and hospital-free days were similar between groups. The inhaled sedation group received more adjunctive therapies for hypoxemia (239 [63.9%] vs 214 [55.0%]; between-group difference, 8.89% [95% CI, 1.95% to 15.83%]) and had fewer delirium- and coma-free days (between-group difference, -0.95 [95% CI, -1.69 to -0.22]). There was no difference in quality-of-life and disability scores between groups. In mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF, an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed did not reduce hospital mortality compared with an intravenous sedation strategy. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04415060.

42869181.title: Post-intensive care syndrome at 6 months and 1 year among survivors of severe COVID-19 requiring invasive mechanical ventilation: a single-center observational study.
42869181.journal: Journal of infection and chemotherapy : official journal of the Japan Society of Chemotherapy
42869181.abstract: Long-term multidomain impairment after critical coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) overlaps with post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) and post-COVID-19 condition. We assessed PICS at 6 months and 1 year after hospital discharge and explored associated clinical factors in Japanese patients with COVID-19 requiring invasive mechanical ventilation. This single-center observational study included adult patients with COVID-19 who required invasive mechanical ventilation and survived to discharge. PICS was assessed using the Barthel Index, Short-Memory Questionnaire, and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale. Exploratory multivariable logistic regression examined factors associated with 1-year PICS. Of 67 discharged survivors, 37 completed both 6-month and 1-year assessments; 17 (45.9%) received extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. PICS was present in 22 (59.5%) patients at 6 months and 21 (56.8%) at 1 year, and 15 (40.5%) had cognitive impairment at both assessments. Delirium was more frequent in patients with PICS than in those without at 6 months (63.6% vs 26.7%, p = 0.045) and 1 year (66.7% vs 25.0%, p = 0.020). In the exploratory multivariable analysis, delirium was associated with 1-year PICS after adjustment for age and mechanical ventilation duration (odds ratio, 7.09; 95% confidence interval, 1.54-32.7; p = 0.012). PICS was common 6 months and 1 year after hospital discharge among survivors of severe COVID-19. In an exploratory analysis, delirium was associated with 1-year PICS after adjustment for age and mechanical ventilation duration. This hypothesis-generating finding requires confirmation in larger prospective cohorts.

42868988.title: Central line-associated bloodstream infections outside the intensive care unit: Burden, pathogens, and antimicrobial susceptibility identified through a Victorian surveillance program.
42868988.abstract: Prevention of central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) is a priority in Australian intensive care units (ICUs). However, the epidemiology of CLABSI in non-ICU settings remains inadequately characterised, despite extensive use of central lines beyond the ICU. We aimed to determine CLABSI rates and microbiological aetiology in non-ICU wards and to compare these with corresponding ICU data from Victorian hospitals. CLABSI surveillance was undertaken voluntarily in non-ICU wards by Victorian health services between 2014 and 2025, utilising the Victorian Healthcare Associated Infection Surveillance System (VICNISS) CLABSI surveillance module, capturing CLABSI rates per 1000 central line days (CLD) as well as bloodstream infections related to mucosal barrier injury (MBI-BSI), in accordance with CDC/NHSN criteria. Retrospective analysis was performed to determine rates, pathogens, and antimicrobial susceptibility. Sixteen facilities participated in surveillance during the study period. 67 CLABSI events and 66,096 central line days were reported in non-ICU wards (predominantly haematology-oncology), corresponding to a CLABSI rate of 1.01 per 1000 CLD, which was significantly higher than the contemporaneous ICU CLABSI rate of 0.50 per 1000 CLD (IRR 3.13, 95% CI 1.88-5.22, p = 0.000). The most frequent pathogens responsible for non-ICU CLABSI were coagulase-negative Staphylococcus spp., Staphylococcus aureus, and Pseudomonas spp. A large burden of MBI-BSI events (n = 90) were also reported. CLABSI rates outside ICU are significantly higher than those reported in ICU settings. A substantial burden of CLABSI and MBI-BSI events were identified in haematology-oncology populations, supporting focused surveillance and infection prevention efforts in these high-risk cohorts.

42868959.title: Risk factors and preventive strategies for pressure injury and medical device-related pressure injury in ICU patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation: A scoping review.
42868959.abstract: Adult ICU patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) are at risk of pressure injury (PI) and medical device-related pressure injury (MDRPI) due to immobility, impaired perfusion, and device contact. This scoping review synthesized evidence on PI and MDRPI risk factors and preventive strategies. This scoping review followed the Arksey and O'Malley framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Five databases (PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, MEDLINE, ScienceDirect) were searched from inception to April 2026. Studies of adult ICU patients receiving IMV reporting PI, MDRPI, risk factors, or preventive strategies were eligible. Forty-two studies from 14 countries (2009-2026) were included. PI incidence ranged from 10.3 to 36.3% (up to 88.7% when prone-positioned); MDRPI (oral mucosal injury) ranged from 25.9 to 43.1% (80.1% with a broader erythema criterion). Cutaneous PI mainly affected the sacrum, heels, occiput, face, and thorax (generally Stage 1-2); oral mucosal MDRPI, assessed using heterogeneous severity criteria, was typically mild-to-moderate. Onset was commonly reported on days 3-9. PI risk factors included immobility, impaired perfusion, vasopressor therapy, and poor nutrition; MDRPI risk factors involved prolonged intubation and device exposure. Preventive strategies included device repositioning, securement adjustment, device-contact protection, and oral care. Prolonged mechanical loading and reduced tissue tolerance are intensified by immobility, sedation, hemodynamic instability, impaired perfusion, vasopressor use, and device exposure. Early-stage cutaneous PI and mild-to-moderate mucosal MDRPI were more commonly reported than severe cutaneous and mucosal injuries; given the descriptive, non-comparative evidence, this cannot be attributed to preventive effectiveness. Early monitoring may be important for detecting early-stage injury and identifying progression toward more severe injury. Prevention should combine pressure redistribution with tolerance-based repositioning, skin monitoring, device securement, device-contact protection, and oral mucosal care. An exploratory, hypothesis-generating observation is that the first 10 days of ICU stay may be a high-risk period, requiring prospective validation.

42867522.title: Dynamic course and outcomes of acute-on-chronic liver failure in the intensive care unit : Insights from a real-world cohort.
42867522.abstract: Acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) frequently requires intensive care unit (ICU) management, yet real-world data on dynamic disease course, organ support and mortality predictors in critically ill ACLF patients remain scarce. All ACLF patients admitted to a tertiary care hepatology ICU between 2013 and 2023 were analyzed in this retrospective single-center study for ACLF grade trajectories, organ support, and independent predictors of 90-day mortality. Among 209 patients (228 admissions), 54.4% had ACLF grade 3 at ICU admission (median CLIF‑C ACLF 56). Most patients required vasopressors (86.8%), invasive mechanical ventilation (59.6%), and renal replacement therapy (53.5%). The ICU and 90-day survival were 56.1% and 34.2%, respectively. One third of the patients (33.3%) showed improvement in ACLF grade during the ICU stay, including grade 3 patients, indicating meaningful reversibility under comprehensive organ support. The CLIF‑C ACLF score (OR: 1.07, 95% CI: 1.03-1.11, p < 0.001) and the peak noradrenaline dose (OR: 13.5, 95% CI: 3.18-69.7, p < 0.001) were identified as independent predictors of 90-day mortality. Critically ill ACLF patients retain potential for partial recovery under full organ support, justifying ICU escalation even in grade 3 disease. Peak noradrenaline dose, alongside the established prognostic scores, provides a readily available parameter to guide individualized decision-making regarding full organ support or timely de-escalation.

42866542.title: Patient-level critical care trajectories in adults with cystic fibrosis in Türkiye: A seven-year single-center case series.
42866542.abstract: Critical illness in adults with cystic fibrosis (CF) may involve recurrent intensive care unit (ICU) admissions that admission-level summaries can obscure. We characterized patient-level critical care trajectories among adults with CF in Türkiye. This retrospective longitudinal case series included 12 adults with CF who contributed 20 admissions to a tertiary ICU between January 1, 2019, and December 31, 2025. Patients were the primary unit of analysis; admissions were nested episodes. Analyses were descriptive, without hypothesis testing. Twelve adults (median age, 24.5 years; IQR, 21.8-29.5) accounted for 20 ICU admissions; five patients with recurrent stays accounted for 13 admissions. Acute respiratory failure was the principal indication in 17 admissions (85.0%). Noninvasive ventilation, high-flow nasal oxygen, and invasive mechanical ventilation were used in 14 (70.0%), 13 (65.0%), and 12 admissions (60.0%), respectively. One patient received extracorporeal carbon dioxide removal for 3 days followed by venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for 10 days. Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonization was documented in 11 patients (91.7%), and multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa was identified in 14 admissions (70.0%). Four patients (33.3%) died within 28 days of the index admission, and seven (58.3%) died during an ICU-associated hospitalization. Critical illness was predominantly respiratory and recurrent in a subset of patients. Five individuals accounted for 13 of 20 ICU admissions, demonstrating concentrated critical care burden that admission-level summaries may obscure. Multicenter longitudinal studies using standardized patient- and admission-level definitions are needed to assess these trajectories across healthcare systems.

42866168.title: Association of synergistic trajectories between early mobilization potential and actual implementation with clinical outcomes among ICU patients with pneumonia: a multivariate latent class mixed model analysis.
42866168.abstract: Although early mobilization is a key intervention in the management of patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU), its effects on patients remain controversial in previous studies. This study aimed to explore the synergistic trajectories of early mobilization potential and actual implementation in ICU patients with pneumonia and their impacts on clinical outcomes. Data were extracted from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC) database. Multivariate latent class mixed model (MLCMM) was adopted to identify mobilization trajectories within the first 72 hours of ICU admission among patients with pneumonia and perform subgroup stratification. Linear regression analysis was applied to investigate the association between early mobilization and length of stay (LOS) in the ICU across each subgroup. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore the heterogeneity of the above association in populations with different characteristics. Kaplan-Meier curves were used to depict survival disparities, and Sankey diagrams were applied to illustrate discharge destinations. A total of 3,226 patients with pneumonia were included. In the fully adjusted model, Class 2 showed no statistically significant difference in ICU LOS relative to Class 1 [β=-0.04, 95% confidence interval (CI): -0.11 to 0.04, P=0.35]. Class 3 (β=-0.43, 95% CI: -0.51 to -0.35, P<0.001) and Class 4 (β=-0.42, 95% CI: -0.50 to -0.33, P<0.001) were associated with shorter ICU LOS. Sensitivity analyses yielded results consistent with the primary analysis. Significant interaction effects were observed in the subgroups of age (P for interaction =0.01) and mechanical ventilation (P for interaction <0.001) on the above association. Compared with Class 1, the other three subgroups were associated with higher survival probabilities (log-rank P<0.001). The Sankey diagram revealed that Class 1 was characterized by adverse clinical prognoses. This study demonstrates that low-level stable early mobilization is associated with longer ICU LOS and lower survival rate in patients with pneumonia. These findings suggest that distinct mobilization trajectories may reflect patients' early recovery status.

42861224.title: Standardising Emollient Prescribing in Critically Ill Patients: A Quality Improvement Project.
42861224.abstract: Introduction Critically ill patients are vulnerable to skin dryness, irritation, and skin barrier impairment due to factors associated with critical illness and prolonged intensive care admission. Consistent skin care and the use of a standardised emollient may support a more uniform approach to skin barrier protection. However, variation in prescribing and product selection may result in inconsistent practice. This quality improvement project aimed primarily to increase prescribing of the locally recommended standard emollient, thereby reducing variation in product selection and standardising emollient therapy. Materials and methods This single-centre quality improvement project was conducted in a general intensive care unit (GICU) and was reported with reference to the Standards for Quality Improvement Reporting Excellence (SQUIRE) 2.0 framework. A baseline audit of 30 adult inpatients was conducted over two weeks in March 2026. Data were collected to assess documentation of skin assessment, emollient prescribing, documentation of moisturiser or emollient application, and prescription of the locally recommended standard emollient. An anonymous nursing staff survey was also undertaken; 42 responses were collected, representing all nurses invited to participate. The survey explored reported knowledge and practice, product selection, and perceived barriers to consistent moisturiser use. Findings informed an intervention of staff education and visual prescribing prompts promoting the locally recommended standard emollient. A repeat audit of a further 30 adult GICU inpatients was conducted over two weeks in August 2026 using the same outcome measures and data collection methods. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients prescribed the locally recommended standard emollient. Secondary outcomes included prescription of any emollient, documentation of moisturiser or emollient application, and documentation of skin assessment. Results At baseline, skin assessment was documented in 25 of 30 patients (83.3%), while documentation that a moisturising product had been applied was present in 21 patients (70.0%). An emollient was formally prescribed in two patients (6.7%), and the locally recommended standard emollient was prescribed in one patient (3.3%). Among 42 nursing staff surveyed, 39 (92.9%) reported applying moisturisers to their patients, while 28 (66.7%) reported using any moisturiser available in the ICU. The most frequently reported barrier was lack of product availability (81.0%). Following the intervention, prescribing of any emollient increased to 21 of 30 patients (70.0%), while prescribing of the locally recommended standard emollient increased to 19 patients (63.3%). Thus, although overall emollient prescribing increased substantially, not all emollient prescriptions were for the locally recommended standard product. Documentation of skin assessment increased to 26 patients (86.7%), whereas documentation of moisturiser or emollient application decreased slightly to 20 patients (66.7%). Conclusion Baseline assessment identified substantial variation in skin barrier protection practices within the general ICU, particularly a marked discrepancy between documented emollient application and formal prescribing. Standardised prescribing provides a practical approach to reducing variation in product selection and may support more consistent skin barrier protection in critically ill patients.

42861073.title: Multiple Neurological Complications and Multidrug-Resistant Bacterial Infections During Prolonged Intensive Care for Undocumented Meningoencephalitis in Côte d'Ivoire: A Case Report.
42861073.abstract: Acute meningoencephalitis requiring intensive care may be complicated by severe neurological injury and nosocomial infections. Hydrocephalus is well recognized, whereas spinal cord ischemia, central diabetes insipidus, and flaccid tetraparesis are rarely reported. Their coexistence, together with successive infections involving multidrug-resistant organisms, presents substantial diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. A previously healthy 32-year-old man presented with neck and back pain following a road traffic accident, subsequently developing cerebellar signs, acute confusion, and meningeal signs without fever. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed neutrophilic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and marked hypoglycorrhachia. Microbiological investigations were negative, and no causative pathogen was identified. Empirical antimicrobial therapy was followed by normalization of the CSF leukocyte count by hospital day 6. Despite this initial response, the patient required mechanical ventilation and developed shunt-dependent tetraventricular hydrocephalus, probable central diabetes insipidus, imaging findings suggestive of thoracic spinal cord ischemia, and areflexic flaccid tetraparesis with diffuse axonal sensorimotor neuropathy. His prolonged intensive care course was further complicated by successive nosocomial infections involving multidrug-resistant bacteria. He died on hospital day 70 from septic shock associated with Enterobacter cloacae bacteremia and multiorgan failure. Negative microbiological findings do not exclude meningoencephalitis when clinical and CSF abnormalities support the diagnosis, although alternative etiologies require consideration. Improvement in CSF findings does not preclude subsequent neurological deterioration or nosocomial infection. Continued neurological assessment, rigorous infection-prevention measures, and prompt investigation of suspected nosocomial infections remain essential throughout prolonged intensive care, particularly in resource-limited settings.

42861006.title: Process mapping of a collaborative quality improvement study to optimise the use of antibiotics in intensive care units in Argentina: a Pathfinder study.
42861006.abstract: To systematically document the operational components, barriers, facilitators, and solutions of a quality improvement collaborative for antibiotic stewardship in intensive care units (ICUs) in the public sector of Argentina, using the Pathfinder methodological framework. Retrospective, descriptive observational study using mixed methods. Data sources included a documentary review of protocols, standard operating procedures, monitoring reports, and host study publications; an online survey with closed and open-ended questions administered to research team members; interviews with team researchers to estimate effort and triangulation with findings from the host study's previously published process evaluation, structured according to Normalisation Process Theory. Integration was performed using the Pathfinder Tracker. Analysis combined descriptive statistics with content analysis of open-ended responses. Eleven stages of the research process were mapped, from question formulation to dissemination, with an estimated total effort of approximately 1,020 person-hours. The stages with the highest perceived difficulty (4/5) were ethical and institutional approvals, data collection, analysis, and dissemination, which together accounted for approximately 50% of the total estimated effort. Barriers were identified across three domains: institutional and regulatory (heterogeneity of ethical requirements, absence of stable local coordinators, publication costs); operational and technical (complex data collection forms, displacement of implementation focus due to the burden of data collection, variable connectivity); and human resources and capacity (clinical workload, staff turnover, insufficient training in implementation science). Solutions included a collaborative format with mentoring, agile communication via accessible digital tools (REDCap, WhatsApp, Zoom), and the use of theoretical frameworks for structuring (NPT, CFIR). The Pathfinder framework enabled a systematic reconstruction of the host study's processes, revealing barriers and solutions that conventional results reports do not capture. The findings are relevant for research teams in middle-income countries designing quality improvement collaboratives in complex hospital settings.

42859779.title: Clinical practice guideline for renal replacement therapy in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury (2026 edition).
authors: Guideline working group of Chinese Society of Critical Care
42859779.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and severe complication in critically ill patients, associated with high morbidity and mortality. Renal replacement therapy (RRT) is a vital life-support modality for critically ill patients with AKI. However, there remains a lack of unified clinical standards for core issues including the timing of RRT initiation, treatment modality, anticoagulation strategy, and weaning from RRT. In response, the Chinese Society of Critical Care Medicine organized a multidisciplinary expert panel to develop the "Clinical practice guideline for RRT in critically ill patients with AKI (2026 edition)" in accordance with the GRADE approach for grading evidence quality. This guideline was developed through systematic literature retrieval, meta-analysis, and evidence-based medical evidence synthesis, followed by multiple rounds of manuscript review and revision via online and offline meetings of the working group, and final approval by the Standing Committee of the Society. A total of 34 recommendations were finalized, covering key clinical topics including timing of RRT initiation, establishment and maintenance of vascular access, selection of treatment modalities, application of specialized membrane filters, anticoagulation regimens, replacement fluid formulations, prescribed treatment dose, and RRT weaning strategies. This guideline aims to provide scientific, standardized, and clinically actionable guidance for critical care practitioners in China, promoting standardized RRT management in adult critically ill patients with AKI.

42859645.title: Improving Antibiotic Stewardship Through a Retrospective Study of the Diagnostic Value of Nasal Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus Polymerase Chain Reaction for Pneumonia in Intensive Care Unit Settings.
42859645.abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a major cause of pneumonia in intensive care unit settings. Nasal swabs with subsequent polymerase chain reaction (PCR) are commonly performed in hospitals and intensive care units to screen for MRSA nasal colonization. A retrospective data analysis of patients presenting to the intensive care unit at the University of North Carolina Health Southeastern between January 1, 2024, and December 31, 2024, was performed. The goal was to evaluate the correlation between MRSA PCR results from nasal swabs and the presence of MRSA in lower respiratory cultures. The sensitivity of MRSA nasal swabs in the intensive care unit for the growth of MRSA in lower respiratory cultures was 90% (18/20). The positive predictive value of MRSA nasal swabs for the growth of MRSA in lower respiratory cultures was 60% (18/30). These retrospective study data indicate that an MRSA nasal swab may have good clinical utility. A negative MRSA nasal swab may substantially lower the likelihood of MRSA in a lower respiratory culture. These findings also indicate that a positive MRSA nasal swab alone may not mandate anti-MRSA therapy. However, large-scale studies across diverse intensive care settings are necessary to confirm these findings.

42859641.title: Clinical and Economic Outcomes Associated with Rapid Antimicrobial Susceptibility Reporting and Dual-Card Testing in ICU Bloodstream Infections.
42859641.abstract: To evaluate the clinical and economic outcomes associated with implementation of an optimized blood culture workflow in intensive care unit (ICU) patients with bloodstream infections. From March 2022 to June 2023, the laboratory implemented a multi-modal workflow optimization including satellite blood culture incubation in the emergency department, upgraded blood culture bottles, rapid MALDI-TOF MS identification, automated rapid antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) reporting, and dual AST cards for Gram-negative bacteria. The pre-optimization group included 107 adult ICU patients with positive blood cultures (March 2021 - February 2022). The post-optimization group included 153 patients (September 2023 - August 2024). Compared to the final AST report in the pre-optimization group, the rapid AST report in the post-optimization group was 19.6 hours faster (P < 0.001). Total antibiotic use duration was 1.5 days shorter (P = 0.055). Use of two broad-spectrum antibiotics, meropenem (P < 0.001) and tigecycline (P = 0.045), decreased significantly. Hospital length of stay was 5 days shorter (P = 0.006). In unadjusted comparisons, antibiotic and hospitalization costs were reduced by 4871 CNY ([US$ 684], P < 0.001) and 13,336 CNY ([US$ 1873], P = 0.073), respectively. This multimodal workflow optimization for ICU patients with BSIs, incorporating automated rapid AST reporting and dual-AST-card-enabled expanded antimicrobial panels, shortened laboratory turnaround time. It was associated with earlier opportunities for targeted antimicrobial therapy and suggests potential clinical-economic benefits, alongside possible mitigation of antimicrobial-resistance risk.

42858643.title: Nursing management of postoperative hemorrhagic shock: A case study in intensive care.
42858643.abstract: Postoperative hemorrhagic shock is a time-critical complication associated with high morbidity and mortality, particularly in older surgical patients, requiring rapid, coordinated management in the intensive care unit (ICU). This case report describes specialized nursing management guided by the International Classification for Nursing Practice (ICNP®/CIPE®) and Benner's Clinical Wisdom Theory. An 89-year-old woman underwent emergency gastrojejunostomy for intestinal obstruction and subsequently developed hemorrhagic shock with profound anemia (hemoglobin nadir 5.8 g/dL), severe hyperlactatemia (12 mmol/L), hypothermia (33.6 °C), peripheral hypoperfusion, and hypotension (mean arterial pressure <65 mmHg). She required orotracheal intubation, invasive mechanical ventilation, and deep sedation. Diagnostic reassessment included serial hemoglobin and arterial blood gas analyses, lactate trending, invasive hemodynamic monitoring, and surgical re-exploration with intraoperative upper endoscopy, which suggested an upper gastrointestinal source (suspected Mallory-Weiss type lesion) treated endoscopically. Nursing priorities, structured using ICNP®, focused on perfusion restoration and correction of the lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy), multimodal analgesia, continuous monitoring, prevention bundles (infection and pressure injury prevention), and structured family communication. The patient progressively stabilized, with hemoglobin increasing to 9.6 g/dL, lactate decreasing to <1 mmol/L, normothermia recovery, discontinuation of vasopressors, and no documented ICU-acquired complications during the ICU stay. This case highlights how standardized nursing language (ICNP®/CIPE®), combined with advanced clinical reasoning and evidence-based ICU bundles, can improve the structure, traceability, and continuity of nursing care in postoperative hemorrhagic shock.

42858067.title: Association of dexmedetomidine use with stroke-heart syndrome in critically ill patients with ischemic stroke: a MIMIC-IV study.
42858067.abstract: Stroke-heart syndrome (SHS) is associated with poor outcomes after ischemic stroke (IS), but the relationship between dexmedetomidine (DEX) use and SHS remains unclear. To evaluate the association between DEX use and SHS in critically ill patients with IS. This retrospective cohort study used MIMIC-IV v2.2. Patients with IS receiving mechanical ventilation were included. DEX exposure was defined as use within 72 hours after ICU admission. Multivariate logistic regression, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), restricted cubic splines, and subgroup analyses were performed. Among 953 patients, 146 (15.3%) received DEX. In the fully adjusted model, DEX use was associated with lower odds of SHS (OR = 0.611, 95% CI: 0.398-0.929, p = 0.023). The associations of cumulative DEX dose (p-nonlinearity = 0.018) and treatment duration (p-anonlinearity = 0.011) with SHS were nonlinear. Antiplatelet therapy significantly modified the DEX-SHS association (p-interaction = 0.042). DEX use was associated with lower odds of SHS in critically ill patients with IS. Antiplatelet therapy may modify this association. Prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings.

42857409.title: Retrospective Cohort Study on the Association Between a Laboratory Test-Derived Frailty Index and Mortality in Elderly Critically Ill Patients With Chronic Kidney Disease.
42857409.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a growing worldwide health concern. There is a need for easily obtainable markers that can improve risk evaluation in affected patients. Here, we investigated whether a laboratory-derived frailty index (FI-Lab) carries prognostic information for older CKD individuals admitted to intensive care. A retrospective cohort design was adopted, drawing on the MIMIC-IV repository. Records of elderly ICU patients with diagnosed CKD were retrieved. The endpoints of interest were all-cause death within 30 and 90 days. Cox proportional hazards regression with incremental covariate adjustment and propensity score matching were employed to quantify the independent contribution of FI-Lab to survival. The analytic sample consisted of 5013 hospitalized CKD patients (mean age 77.9 ± 7.6 years; 61.4% male). Following full adjustment, a 0.1-unit rise in FI-Lab corresponded to a 94% higher mortality risk at 30 days (HR 1.94; 95% CI 1.57-2.40) and a 65% higher risk at 90 days (HR 1.65; 95% CI 1.43-1.91; both p < 0.001). Propensity-matched analyses yielded comparable estimates. No meaningful association emerged between FI-Lab and ICU or hospital length of stay. Conversely, higher FI-Lab values were accompanied by greater odds of acute kidney injury and continuous renal replacement therapy utilization. An elevated FI-Lab score at ICU entry is independently tied to elevated short- and intermediate-term mortality in older critically ill patients with CKD. Confirmatory prospective work is needed to establish its clinical role in this population.

42857206.title: Low-intensity versus medium-intensity continuous renal replacement therapy for critically ill patients (LIMIT) trial: Protocol summary and statistical analysis plan of a randomised clinical trial.
42857206.journal: Critical care and resuscitation : journal of the Australasian Academy of Critical Care Medicine
42857206.abstract: Severe acute kidney injury in critically ill patients may require continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), yet mortality remains high. A standard CRRT intensity is 20-25 mL/kg/hr, because higher doses have not improved outcomes. Excessive treatment may cause harm by removing antibiotics and other essential substances and potentially impairing renal recovery. Observational data suggest that lower-intensity CRRT may be effective, warranting a clinical trial to compare low-versus standard-intensity therapy. The objective of this study was to describe the prespecified protocol and the statistical analysis plan of the low-intensity versus medium-intensity continuous renal replacement therapy for critically Ill patients (LIMIT) trial. The LIMIT trial is an investigator-initiated, multicentre, open-label, randomised clinical trial, with a target sample size of 400 participants. The trial compares low-intensity CRRT (12 mL/kg/hr) and medium-intensity CRRT (25 mL/kg/hr) in adult patients with acute kidney injury requiring CRRT in the participating intensive care units. The primary outcome is a hierarchical composite of survival and time to successful liberation from RRT through day 28 from randomisation, analysed using a win-ratio. Secondary outcomes include intensive care unit mortality, hospital mortality, dialysis dependence at hospital discharge among survivors, vasopressor-free days at day 28, and ventilator-free days at day 28. The LIMIT trial will evaluate the effect of low-intensity CRRT on mortality and time to successful liberation from RRT compared with medium-intensity CRRT in adults with acute kidney injury. Its findings may also inform future research on broader patient-centred and societal implications of CRRT intensity.

42857101.title: Effects of higher versus lower protein intake in critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42857101.abstract: The optimal protein dose for critically ill patients remains uncertain, and emerging evidence suggests that the effects of higher protein intake may differ across clinically relevant subgroups. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating protein delivery in critical illness adults (up to July 2026). Higher and lower protein groups were defined according to each trial's original allocation. Primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included mechanical ventilation (MV) duration, Intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay (LOS), muscle outcomes, health-related quality of life (HRQoL), biochemical outcomes, and adverse events. Results were reported as risk ratios (RRs) or mean difference (MD) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Trial Sequential Analysis (TSA) was performed to control for random error, and the certainty of evidence was rated using the GRADE framework. Thirty three RCTs involving 11,622 participants were included. No significant differences were observed between higher and lower protein groups for all-cause mortality (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.08), MV duration (MD -0.48, 95% CI -1.08 to 0.13), or ICU LOS (MD -0.18, 95% CI -0.86 to 0.51), with TSA confirming these null findings. Some muscle metrics favored the higher protein group; however, there was a trend towards poorer HRQoL (SMD -0.12, 95% CI -0.24 to 0.00). The higher protein group showed improved nitrogen balance (MD 5.58, 95% CI 2.89 to 8.27) and higher serum albumin levels (SMD 0.18, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.29), but increased urea (MD 2.06, 95% CI 1.49 to 2.64) and blood urea nitrogen concentrations (MD 2.94, 95% CI 1.32 to 4.56). Sensitivity analyses restricted to 27 isocaloric-design trials yielded consistent results. Subgroup analyses revealed that higher protein intake was linked to increased mortality in patients with acute kidney injury (RR 1.46, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.87); however, higher protein intake combined with rehabilitation interventions was associated with reduced mortality (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.93), shorter MV duration (MD -1.45, 95% CI -2.61 to -0.29), and beneficial muscle effects. Higher protein intake was not associated with better clinical outcomes. While it may increase mortality in patients with AKI, combining it with physical rehabilitation yields survival and clinical benefits, warranting confirmation in future factorial RCTs. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251109618, identifier [CRD420251109618].

42856966.title: Characterization of Delirium in an Intensive Care Unit: Real-World Data Based on the Application of the Confusion Assessment Method.
42856966.abstract: Introduction Delirium is a neuropsychiatric syndrome of acute onset characterized by disturbances in attention, awareness, and cognition. It is common in intensive care units (ICUs), and the Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU) is the most widely used bedside instrument for its detection. Methods We conducted a retrospective, observational, single-centre study of all patients admitted to the ICU of a Portuguese community hospital, Unidade Local de Saúde do Alto Minho (ULSAM), between January 1, 2021, and December 31, 2022. Delirium was defined as at least one positive CAM-ICU assessment during the ICU stay. Sociodemographic data, comorbidities, admission characteristics, severity scores (Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II), Simplified Acute Physiology Score (SAPS), Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score (SOFA)), and outcomes were compared between patients with and without delirium using chi-square, Mann-Whitney U, and multivariable logistic regression. Results Of 788 ICU admissions (742 patients), 66 (8.4%) had at least one positive CAM-ICU assessment. Patients with delirium were older (median 71 vs 68 years, p=0.021) and had higher APACHE II, SAPS, and SOFA scores, longer ICU stay (median 8 vs 3 days, p<0.001), and a higher rate of invasive mechanical ventilation among those with known ventilation status (n=40/64, 62.5% vs n=279/692, 40.3%, p=0.001) than patients without delirium. In multivariable logistic regression, older age (OR 1.03, p=0.017) and male sex (OR 3.09 relative to female, p=0.001) were independently associated with delirium. Conclusions Delirium affected a modest but clinically important proportion of ICU admissions in this cohort and was associated with older age, male sex, greater severity of illness, and longer, more complicated ICU stays. These findings support the need for continued systematic CAM-ICU screening and multidisciplinary delirium-prevention strategies.

42856792.title: "I got a bit of closure": A thematic analysis of experiences of attending a post intensive care multidisciplinary follow up clinic.
42856792.journal: Journal of the Intensive Care Society
42856792.abstract: The impact of critical illness is recognised; however, interventions to support optimal recovery post-ICU are less clear. There is no single accepted model of follow-up services and an uncertain evidence base. Thematic analysis was used to analyse semi-structured interviews with 27 ICU-survivors from an ICU in the southwest of Britain on their experience of attending a multi-disciplinary (MDT) follow up clinic. The participants' follow up clinic letters were reviewed to identify related actions by team members. Eight themes emerged from the data: gaining understanding, family involvement, addressing the future, safe space to explore experiences, clinic structure, virtual versus face-to-face appointments, and perception of staff. Clinic letters evidence a range of onwards referrals and provision of advice. Participants valued the MDT follow up clinic. The option to attend in person or virtually increased accessibility. The opportunity to enhance understanding of critical care related experiences and integrate this with self identity and ongoing recovery processes was meaningful for patients. Several participants were referred for further medical and psychological intervention. Patient experience and need should be at the heart of informing potential outcome measurement.

42854718.title: Predictors of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales enteric colonization among patients admitted to a companion animal intensive care unit.
42854718.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
42854718.abstract: To estimate prevalence and identify factors associated with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) enteric colonization in companion animals admitted to an ICU. The study population included canine and feline patients admitted to The Ohio State University Veterinary Medical Center ICU between January 2024 and June 2025. In total, 5,552 rectal swabs were collected from 3,834 patients during routine screening. A retrospective case-control study included all CRE-positive patients (n = 61) and randomly selected CRE-negative controls (137). Cases were defined as ICU patients with at least 1 positive CRE fecal culture during hospitalization, whereas controls had no positive CRE fecal cultures during their hospitalization. Prevalence of CRE colonization was 1.59% (61 of 3,834 patients; 95% CI, 1.24% to 2.04%). Escherichia coli carrying blaNDM was the most frequently identified isolate, accounting for 78.7% (48 of 61 patients; 95% CI, 66.9% to 87.1%). Predictors of CRE colonization included increased comorbidity burden (unit OR, 1.96; 95% CI, 1.43 to 2.75), intact reproductive status (OR, 4.39; CI, 1.47 to 11.03), longer hospitalization (unit OR, 1.31; CI, 1.14 to 1.53), recent surgery (OR, 2.72; CI, 1.29 to 5.87), and antimicrobial use within the previous 3 months (OR, 2.71; CI, 1.23 to 6.07). These predictors suggest targets for infection prevention and control measures to protect patients and staff. The association between recent antimicrobial exposure and CRE colonization reinforces the importance of antimicrobial stewardship in veterinary medicine. Although uncommon, CRE-colonized patients can serve as reservoirs for transmission and are at risk of subsequent infection.

42852905.title: Epidemiology of medication-related problems and antimicrobial utilisation among critically ill cancer patients: Determinants, pharmacist interventions and clinical outcomes-A prospective observational study.
42852905.journal: Journal of oncology pharmacy practice : official publication of the International Society of Oncology Pharmacy Practitioners
42852905.abstract: BackgroundCritically ill patients with cancer are highly vulnerable to medication-related problems (MRPs) because of complex treatment regimens, organ dysfunction, immunosuppression, and extensive antimicrobial exposure.ObjectivesTo determine the prevalence, patterns, and determinants of MRPs; describe antimicrobial utilisation; evaluate clinical pharmacist interventions; and assess clinical outcomes.MethodsA prospective observational study was conducted over 14 months in an oncology ICU of a tertiary cancer centre. Adults admitted for ≥48 h were enrolled. MRPs were identified using the Pharmaceutical Care Network Europe classification V9.1. Antimicrobial utilisation was measured as defined daily doses (DDD) per 100 bed-days and classified according to WHO AWaRe categories. Pharmacist interventions were documented. Multivariate logistic regression identified predictors of MRP occurrence.ResultsAmong 325 patients (mean age 54.6 ± 12.3 years; 58.5% male), 268 (82.5%) experienced at least one MRP, with 612 identified (mean 1.88/patient). Treatment-effectiveness (38.1%) and treatment-safety (28.9%) problems predominated. Antimicrobials were prescribed in 296 patients (91.1%), with consumption of 142.6 DDD/100 bed-days; Watch agents accounted for 54.2%. Pharmacists made 540 interventions, of which 466 (86.3%) were accepted. Polypharmacy, prolonged ICU stay, renal impairment, hematological malignancy, and use of ≥2 concurrent antimicrobials independently predicted MRP occurrence. Mortality was higher among patients with unresolved or severe MRPs than among those without MRPs (34.2% vs 18.6%, p = 0.002).ConclusionMRPs were highly prevalent and associated with medication burden, organ dysfunction, malignancy type, and antimicrobial exposure, while pharmacist interventions showed a high acceptance rate, supporting their potential role in medication safety and antimicrobial stewardship.

42851402.title: Incidence, burden, and associated factors of severe potential drug-drug interactions in intensive care unit patients: a real-world retrospective study.
42851402.abstract: Severe potential drug-drug interactions (pDDIs) in intensive care unit (ICU) patients remain insufficiently characterized. This study investigated the incidence, patterns, burden, and associated factors of severe pDDIs. This single-center retrospective cohort included ICU admissions from January 2023 through December 2024 for adults aged ≥18 years who received ≥2 eligible systemic medications administered orally or intravenously. Category D and X pDDIs were identified with Lexi-Interact (Lexidrug, UpToDate) using confirmed administration records. Logistic and ordinal logistic regression were performed to evaluate severe-pDDI occurrence (≥1) and admission-level burden (0, 1-2, or ≥3). A total of 1,170 ICU admissions were included, involving 26,627 medication administrations. 64.44% were male and 55.38% received mechanical ventilation support. The most common implicated pharmacological group was alimentary-tract and metabolism agents, while ambroxol and glutathione emerged as the top two individual drugs. Among 1,170 ICU admissions, 1,092 (93.33%) exhibited pDDIs, and 769 (65.73%) experienced at least one category D or X pDDI. The 2,704 severe pDDIs comprised 1,681 (62.17%) category D and 1,023 (37.83%) category X events, yielding 231.1 pDDIs per 100 admissions and 101.6 pDDIs per 1,000 medication administrations. Nervous-system agents predominated; butorphanol [948/5,408 ingredient involvements (17.53%)] and dexmedetomidine [824/5,408 (15.24%)] were most frequently implicated. Butorphanol-dexmedetomidine [335/2,704 events (12.39%)] and noscapine-chlorphenamine [176/2,704 (6.51%)] were the leading category D and X pairs, respectively. Additive pharmacodynamic central nervous system depression predominated. Mechanical ventilation and medication count were the strongest adjusted correlates of severe-pDDI occurrence and burden, while baseline variables (sex, APACHE II score) lost significance after adjusting for ICU process variables. These associations remained materially unchanged after excluding 29 readmission encounters. In an exploratory review of 50 severe-pDDI episodes, 32 (64.0%) had temporally associated clinical signs or events documented and 29 (58.0%) had a documented management action. Category D or X pDDI alerts were frequent, primarily driven by pharmacodynamic additive central nervous system depression from sedative-analgesic combinations. Treatment intensity rather than baseline characteristics was associated with severe-pDDI exposure. Regional ICU-tailored surveillance and pharmacist-integrated medication management may facilitate identification of high-risk combinations, although specific drug pairs require validation across different healthcare settings.

42849961.title: Association between invasive mechanical ventilation and acute kidney injury in critically ill patients: a protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
42849961.abstract: Invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) may contribute to the development and progression of acute kidney injury (AKI) in critically ill patients. Given the expanding evidence-base and the immense variation in the association described, particularly following the COVID-19 pandemic era, a rigorous synthesis is warranted. This systematic review and meta-analysis will evaluate this association and identify potential risk-mitigation strategies. We will conduct a comprehensive search of databases, including Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection and the Cochrane Library, using keywords to capture relevant literature on IMV and AKI. The search will include studies published from database inception through March 2026. Two reviewers will independently screen, select and extract studies using the web-based platform Covidence. Eligible studies will include randomised controlled trials reporting the occurrence of new-onset or worsening AKI following initiation of IMV in adult patients admitted to intensive care units. Studies in which IMV was initiated after the onset of AKI will be excluded. Study quality and risk of bias will be assessed using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias 2 Tool. The primary outcome will be the proportion of critically ill patients who develop new-onset or worsening AKI after initiation of IMV. Secondary outcomes will include AKI trajectory, use of organ support and length of stay. Ethics approval is not required, as this study will synthesise data from previously published studies and will not involve direct contact with human participants. The findings will be disseminated through presentations at academic conferences and publication in a peer-reviewed journal. CRD420261303862.

42849544.title: Diaphragm ultrasound beyond numbers: A call for Bayesian reasoning in critical care.
42849544.abstract: Diaphragm ultrasound (DUS) has become a widely available tool in critical care for assessing respiratory muscle function, monitoring ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction (VIDD), and supporting weaning prediction. However, its expanding use as a routine or screening examination, including in clinical scenarios where the pre-test probability of clinically relevant diaphragm dysfunction is low, raises concerns about diagnostic overuse. This narrative opinion article argues that DUS should be understood through the lens of Bayesian reasoning applied to clinical decision-making. The framework is intended to strengthen clinical reasoning rather than to assert superiority over alternative diagnostic strategies. Without explicit estimation of pre-test probability and prior definition of decision thresholds, the positive predictive value of DUS decreases, favoring false-positive findings, physiological overinterpretation, and potentially inappropriate clinical decisions. The available evidence indicates substantial heterogeneity in protocols, populations, and cut-off values, limiting the generalizability of findings and reinforcing the need for clinical contextualization. We propose a conceptual repositioning of DUS as a confirmatory and integrative tool, grounded in genuine clinical uncertainty, explicit Bayesian reasoning, and value-based care.

42849168.title: Measurement properties of instruments for post-extubation dysphagia in critically ill patients: A systematic review.
42849168.abstract: Post-extubation dysphagia (PED) is a common but often under-recognised complication in critically ill patients following invasive mechanical ventilation. Systematic assessment of PED in routine ICU practice is not common. This systematic review aimed to identify clinical instruments used to assess PED in critically ill adult patients and to evaluate their measurement properties. This review was conducted in accordance with the COSMIN methodology for systematic reviews of measurement instruments. A comprehensive evidence search was performed in multiple databases and other sources. Studies were included if they developed or applied standardised assessment instruments for the identification of PED in critically ill adults (≥18 years). Of 2769 abstracts reviewed, 22 studies met criteria for inclusion. Sixteen different instruments for the assessment of PED were identified. These were categorised into water swallow tests, multi-consistency tests, and assessments without a swallowing evaluation. For nine instruments, measurement properties were reported, focusing on content validity, criterion validity and reliability, and demonstrated mostly good measurement properties. The Post-Extubation Dysphagia Screening Tool was the only evaluated across all three properties and showed sufficient measurement properties. The overall quality of evidence was mostly low to very low. There are various clinical assessment instruments for PED in critically ill adults. Most instruments showed good criterion validity, indicating their potential for clinical use. However, other measurement properties are largely unknown, and the quality of evidence is generally low. Thus, it is currently unclear which tool is best suited for assessing PED. Further research investigating validity and reliability is needed to identify instruments suitable for routine ICU use. Systematic detection of PED is important. Assessment instruments with good diagnostic performance should be used to improve ICU care.

42849010.title: Clarifying the Concept of "Unanticipated Transfer to the ICU": A Scoping Review.
42849010.abstract: Unanticipated transfer to the intensive care unit (ICU), typically defined as an unscheduled escalation of care from inpatient general wards, is widely used in clinical research as a marker of adverse events, clinical deterioration, and system failure. However, its conceptual meaning, definition, and operationalization vary substantially across the literature, complicating interpretation and cross-study comparison. We conducted a scoping review following PRISMA-ScR guidelines to map how unanticipated ICU transfers are defined, framed, and used in empirical research. Searches of PubMed, CINAHL, and Web of Science identified 4,019 studies through August 7, 2025. After removing duplicates, 2,092 studies were screened for title and abstract, 565 underwent full-text review, and 219 studies met the inclusion criteria. Most studies were observational studies and terminology varied widely, with "unplanned admission to ICU" being the most common. Definitions were heterogeneous but generally focused on unscheduled ICU admission from inpatient wards, often excluding transfers from the emergency department or operating room and sometimes incorporating triggers such as rapid response activation or time-based thresholds. Unanticipated ICU transfer was predominantly used as a dependent variable and was overwhelmingly framed as a negative outcome or proxy for clinical deterioration. However, a smaller body of literature conceptualized these transfers as appropriate or beneficial escalations of care, particularly when occurring early in the course of deterioration. Our findings highlight definitional and conceptual inconsistency and suggest that unanticipated ICU transfer is a context-dependent process measure influenced by both patient condition and institutional factors. Greater standardization and a reframing toward appropriateness and timing of escalation may improve its utility in research and practice.

42844743.title: EXPRESS: Association of Systemic Immune-inflammation Index and Systemic Inflammation Response Index with All-cause Mortality in the Critically Ill Population with Coronary Heart Disease and Heart Failure - A Study Based on the MIMIC-IV Database.
42844743.journal: Journal of investigative medicine : the official publication of the American Federation for Clinical Research
42844743.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the associations of the systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) and systemic inflammation response index (SIRI) with all-cause mortality (ACM) in critically ill patients with coronary heart disease (CHD) and heart failure (HF). Data from critically ill patients with CHD and HF were extracted from the MIMIC-IV database. Cox proportional hazards models were used to examine the associations of SII and SIRI with ACM. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) models were applied to assess potential nonlinear relationships between SII, SIRI, and ACM. The area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC), integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), and net reclassification improvement (NRI) were calculated to evaluate the incremental predictive value of adding SII and SIRI to the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score. A total of 1,865 participants were included. Cox proportional hazards models showed that patients in the third quartile (Q3) and fourth quartile (Q4) of SII had significantly higher risks of 30-day ACM. RCS analyses demonstrated nonlinear associations between SII, SIRI, and ACM. The ROC analysis showed that the AUCs of SII and SIRI were 0.651 and 0.685, respectively, indicating moderate discriminatory ability for adverse outcomes. In addition, incorporating SII and SIRI into the SOFA score improved the predictive accuracy of the model. SII and SIRI were associated with adverse prognosis in critically ill patients with CHD complicated by HF and may have potential prognostic value.

42843783.title: Adverse events and associated factors during intra-hospital transport of mechanically ventilated intensive care patients.
42843783.abstract: Intra-hospital transport (IHT) of critically ill patients remains a high-risk procedure, particularly in intubated and mechanically ventilated intensive care unit (ICU) patients requiring multiple invasive devices. Data from prospective multicentre studies using standardized definitions of adverse events (AEs) remain limited. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of AEs during IHT and to identify factors associated with their occurrence. We conducted a prospective multicentre observational study in nine French ICUs. All consecutive IHTs involving intubated and mechanically ventilated adult patients were included. AEs were defined according to the 2011 SFAR recommendations and recorded across five predefined transport phases, from preparation to patient reinstallation. Logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with AE occurrence. Among 160 analysed transports, at least one AE occurred in 56.4% of IHTs (95% CI 48.6-64.2). Most events were clinical (47.5%); serious AEs were rare (0.6%). The procedural phase accounted for the highest proportion of events (66.7%). In multivariable analysis, AE occurrence was independently associated with neuromuscular blocking agent use (OR 4.0 [1.2-13.5]), ≥4 invasive devices (OR 2.6 [1.1-6.1]), and ≥3 accompanying staff members (OR 2.7 [1.4-5.5]). Emergency status and transport indication were not significantly associated with AE occurrence. IHT of mechanically ventilated ICU patients is associated with a high rate of AEs, driven primarily by patient severity and procedural complexity. These findings support the need for structured transport protocols and larger multicentre studies to evaluate targeted safety strategies.

42843214.title: Critical care escalation in the peripartum population; a single center retrospective study at an academic quaternary care center.
42843214.abstract: Identify the admission characteristics and interventions of patients transferred from a labor and delivery unit to an intensive care unit. Single-center, retrospective descriptive cohort study at an academic center. We identified 117 of 48,045 (0.2%) patients who required ICU transfer. Patients with multifetal gestation and cesarean delivery were more likely to be admitted to the ICU. Maternal early warning criteria were positive in 12% of patients in the ICU group compared to 4% of those not admitted to ICU (Odds Ratio [OR] 3.27, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 1.87 to 5.73; p < 0.001). A quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score of 1 and 2 was associated with an OR 6.45 (95% CI 4.28 to 9.72; p < 0.001) and 28.98 (95% CI 6.88 to 122.13; p < 0.001), respectively, for ICU admission compared to a score of 0. The most common indications for ICU admission were postpartum hemorrhage, sepsis, and respiratory failure. Vasoactive medications were required in 51% of patients admitted to the ICU. High flow nasal cannula, non-invasive ventilation, and intubation were described in 3%, 2%, and 40% of patients, respectively. 30% of patients did not require vasoactive infusions or respiratory support during ICU admission. The most common patient characteristics, medical comorbidities, and indications for ICU transfer were consistent with the published literature. Scoring systems performed reasonably well in differentiating patients who required escalation of care. A subset of patients may have benefitted from increased monitoring rather than ICU admission.

42843014.title: Chelsea critical care physical assessment tool (CPAx) for adult patients hospitalized in the ward: measurement properties.
42843014.abstract: To evaluate the measurement properties of the Brazilian version of the Chelsea Critical Care Physical Assessment Tool (CPAx-Br) and evaluate the evidence of validity in adult general ward patients, extending its application beyond the critical care setting for which it was originally developed. This longitudinal study included 100 adults (57.5 ± 16.7 years; 54% female) consecutively admitted to hospital wards. The CPAx-Br was applied at three time points: within 48 h of admission, alongside the De Morton Mobility Index (DEMMI) and the Global Rating Scale of Change (GRC); 24 h later to assess reliability; and at hospital discharge, again with the DEMMI and GRC. As part of construct validity, hypothesis testing was performed using Spearman's correlation with the DEMMI. Reliability was tested using the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC2,1) and Standard Error of Measurement (SEM). Responsiveness was evaluated using ROC curve analysis, effect size (ES), and correlation with external measures. Floor and ceiling effects were also examined. The CPAx-Br demonstrated adequate reliability (ICC2,1 = 0.99; 95%CI:0.99-1.00) and measurement error (SEM=0.985). Evidence supporting construct validity was obtained through hypothesis testing, demonstrating a positive correlation with the DEMMI (r = 0.895; p < 0.001). Internal responsiveness was low (ES=0.35), while external met the predefined criterion (r = 0.70; p < 0.001). The CPAx-Br showed acceptable discriminative ability (AUC=0.70; 95% CI 0.54 to 0.85), with no floor effect (0%), whereas the ceiling effect was 16%. The CPAx-Br demonstrated validity based on hypothesis testing, as well as good reliability and acceptable responsiveness for assessing physical function among adult ward patients.

42842203.title: Intensive care infection score outperforms inflammatory biomarkers in detecting infection in critically ill patients.
42842203.abstract: Identification of infection in critically ill patients remains challenging, as conventional biomarkers such as C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT) and white blood cell count (WBC) frequently lack diagnostic accuracy. The Intensive Care Infection Score (ICIS), a host-response biomarker derived from hematological parameters, reflects both innate and adaptive immune response. To compare diagnostic performance of ICIS, CRP, PCT, and WBC, expert adjudication was used to determine presence or absence of infection. Diagnostic accuracy parameters including receiver operating characteristic curve analysis were calculated. 770 samples from 382 critically ill patients were included. ICIS demonstrated the highest diagnostic accuracy with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.914 (95% CI 0.892-0.933), compared with CRP (AUC 0.889; 95% CI 0.865-0.910), PCT (AUC 0.847; 95% CI 0.819-0.871), and WBC (AUC 0.697; 95% CI 0.663-0.729). At the optimal cut-off value of > 3, ICIS achieved a sensitivity of 80.7% and specificity of 89.3%. ICIS showed the lowest false-positive rate (10.7%) and a negative predictive value of 88.7%. ICIS demonstrated good diagnostic performance in critically ill patients and can contribute to antimicrobial stewardship as a novel host-response diagnostic.

42841714.title: Race and Ethnicity Are Associated With Physical Impairment Among ICU Survivors.
42841714.abstract: To evaluate whether race and ethnicity are associated with increased odds of physical impairment among post-ICU survivors and to assess how impairment influences healthcare utilization after hospital discharge. This was a retrospective cohort study. The study was conducted at an academic medical center. We included 4370 adult ICU survivors who experienced shock, respiratory failure, or received extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. None. The primary exposure was self-reported race and ethnicity. The primary outcome was impairment at hospital discharge, defined using the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision codes and/or a Johns Hopkins Highest Level of Mobility score of less than or equal to 5. Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess associations with impairment, and Fine-Gray models evaluated post-discharge healthcare utilization. Impairment was identified in 31% of ICU survivors. Non-Hispanic Black race was associated with increased odds of any impairment (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.34; 95% CI, 1.04-1.72), and Hispanic ethnicity was associated with increased odds of new impairment (aOR, 1.42; 95% CI, 1.05-1.91), compared with non-Hispanic White-identifying survivors. Among those with impairment, both non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic individuals had increased risk of healthcare utilization within 1 year. Non-Hispanic Black race and Hispanic ethnicity are associated with increased odds of post-ICU physical impairment and subsequent healthcare utilization. These findings highlight the need to understand root causes better and explore targeted interventions to reduce disparities among ICU survivors.

42841108.title: Perspectives of intensive care professionals on extubation practices, causes of delays, and proposed solutions: A cross-sectional study.
42841108.journal: Canadian journal of respiratory therapy : CJRT = Revue canadienne de la therapie respiratoire : RCTR
42841108.abstract: Timely extubation is essential to ensure patient safety and efficient intensive care unit (ICU) management. Delays in extubation can lead to adverse outcomes and extended hospital stays. Although several factors affect timely extubation, those contributing to delays, especially in Saudi Arabian ICUs, have not been well described. This study aimed to identify factors contributing to delayed extubation in Saudi Arabian ICUs from the perspective of ICU healthcare professionals (HCPs), including physicians, nurses, and respiratory therapists (RTs). A cross-sectional survey was conducted in Saudi Arabia among physicians, respiratory therapists (RTs), and nurses with at least three months of ICU experience. The questionnaire assessed perceived extubation timing, comfort with extubation order placement, perceived barriers to delayed extubation, and suggested solutions. Likert-scale items were interpreted as perceived barrier scores, with higher scores indicating stronger perceived barriers to delay. Open-ended responses were analyzed using Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis framework. In total, 292 ICU professionals participated in the study (22% physicians, 31% nurses, and 45% RTs). Although most respondents (78%) reported that extubation usually occurred within 3 hours of a successful spontaneous breathing trial (SBT), their perceptions of the appropriateness of this timing differed. The most frequently reported barriers to timely extubation were staffing limitations (18%), communication and teamwork issues (16%), and procedural inefficiencies (14%). Physician comfort levels with placing extubation orders varied significantly by seniority (p < .001). Suggested solutions included standardized protocols (20%), adequate staffing (18%), and routine assessments (16%). ICU healthcare professionals perceived delayed extubation as mainly associated with modifiable organizational and workflow-related barriers. Addressing these barriers through interprofessional collaboration, protocol standardization, and targeted training may optimize the extubation process and ultimately may inform future quality improvement initiatives in Saudi ICUs.

42840398.title: Association Between Hour-by-Hour ICU Admission Timing and 24-h Mortality: A Single-Center Retrospective Observational Study.
42840398.abstract: Prior studies of ICU admission timing often use broad categories (day vs. night), potentially masking hour-level effects. We examined hour-by-hour ICU admission timing and mortality, with attention to nighttime periods and routine handovers. We conducted a single-center retrospective observational study in a closed ICU with 24/7 on-site intensivist coverage, using prospectively registered data from the Japanese Intensive Care Patient Database. Adults (≥ 18 years) admitted to the E-ICU between April 2017 and July 2025 were included. Admission hour (0-23) was modeled as a continuous exposure using restricted cubic splines (reference 14:00). The primary outcome was 24-h mortality and the secondary outcome was ICU mortality. Multivariable logistic regression was adjusted for demographics, APACHE II, invasive mechanical ventilation at admission, comorbidities, diagnostic categories, admission source, and post-cardiac arrest status. Bootstrap resampling was used to estimate 95% confidence intervals. Additional analyses examined handover, nighttime, and 24-h periodic patterns. Among 5724 patients, 24-h and ICU mortality were 3.4% and 10.6%, respectively. Compared with 14:00, adjusted odds of 24-h mortality were higher in the early morning. The early-evening estimate was imprecise, with the 95% CI including unity. In contrast, ICU mortality showed no clear temporal pattern. Handover comparisons showed no clear mortality association; nighttime admission was not associated with higher mortality, and cosinor analysis was nonsignificant. Hour-by-hour analysis showed higher adjusted odds of 24-h mortality in the early morning, whereas evidence of an increase in the early evening was inconclusive. Direct comparisons of handover periods showed no clear association with mortality.

42838510.title: Effect of intensive care unit sedation strategy on patient-reported experience: secondary mediation analysis of the A2B randomised controlled trial.
42838510.abstract: The optimal ICU sedation strategy to improve patient-reported experience is unknown. In a planned secondary analysis of the A2B randomised trial, we evaluated the effect of sedation strategy (dexmedetomidine, clonidine or propofol) on recalled patient experience at 90 days post-randomisation. Using mediation analyses, we explored plausible mediators of the relationship between sedation strategy and patient experience. We analysed data for all patients from A2B who completed the Intensive Care Experience Questionnaire (ICE-Q) at 90 days. The primary outcome was patient-recalled experience, measured by the four ICE-Q domain scores (awareness, frightening memories, recall, satisfaction). Sedation strategy effect was evaluated using linear regression, adjusting for potential confounders. Mediation analyses were conducted for duration of mechanical ventilation; ICU stay; and days with pain behaviour, agitation and coma/delirium. Of 1404 patients included in the primary trial analysis, 1009 (71.9%) were alive at 90 days post-randomisation with ICE-Qs completed by 289/1009 (28.6%). Compared with propofol, dexmedetomidine sedation was associated with higher awareness of surroundings (median score 32 vs. 28, adjusted mean difference 3.6, 95%CI 1.0-6.2, p = 0.01), but clonidine sedation had no association (difference 2.4, 95%CI -0.2-5.0, p = 0.07). No associations were found with other ICE-Q domains. The contribution of the five potential mediators on the dexmedetomidine-awareness relationship was small. Dexmedetomidine compared with propofol sedation strategy may be associated with increased recalled awareness of surroundings, which is considered a favourable indicator of ICU experience. Together with the primary A2B trial results, which showed no effect on ventilation duration, these hypothesis-generating findings in a subgroup of the A2B cohort do not support the use of dexmedetomidine over propofol based on patient-reported experience. Based on our findings, we advocate that a personalised approach to sedation strategies should continue to be used.

42836669.title: Educational Priorities in Oncologic Critical Care: A Modified Delphi Study.
42836669.abstract: Advances in cancer diagnosis and treatment have prolonged survival, expanded therapeutic options, and introduced novel treatment-related toxicities. Patients with cancer now account for more than 20% of ICU admissions, exposing intensivists to increasingly complex clinical scenarios. Despite this evolving landscape, oncologic critical care education within PCCM fellowship training remains unstructured, with no consensus on educational priorities or expectations for trainee practice.
