To define consensus-based educational priorities in oncologic critical care for PCCM fellowship training and clarify expectations regarding trainee management responsibility. We conducted a modified Delphi study between October and December 2025. Expert panelists were purposively recruited based on clinical or educational expertise in PCCM, hematology, oncology, and fellowship education. Using a REDCap-based survey, panelists rated 47 proposed topics across 11 oncologic critical care domains for importance to graduating PCCM fellows without additional sub-specialty training. Topics were rated using a four-point scale, with consensus defined a priori as ≥ 70% "Must Know" ratings. Open-ended feedback informed addition of a secondary rating scale in Round 2 assessing expected management responsibility (independent management vs. co-management with Hematology/Oncology). Responses were analyzed descriptively and in aggregate. Of 58 invited experts, 41 (70%) completed Round 1. All Round 1 respondents were invited to participate in Round 2, of whom 32 (78%) completed the survey. Panelists represented diverse disciplines, geographic regions, and levels of experience. Of the 47 topics presented in Round 1, 33 met consensus criteria. Three topics close to consensus were carried forward based on panelist feedback. Five new topics were introduced in Round 2, three of which achieved consensus. In total, 39 topics were retained across both Delphi rounds. Consensus items emphasized core principles of oncologic critical care including ICU triage, procedural safety, management of infectious, metabolic, neurologic and oncologic emergencies, respiratory failure and therapy-related complications. Management-responsibility ratings differentiated topics appropriate for independent PCCM management from those requiring co-management with hematology/oncology. This study defines consensus-based educational priorities in oncologic critical care and clarifies expectations for trainee management and interdisciplinary collaboration, providing a practical framework to align PCCM fellowship training with contemporary ICU practice.

42836021.title: Reintubation in the ICU: A Prospective Observational Study of Its Impact on Recovery Outcomes and Mortality.
42836021.abstract: Background Extubation is an important step in the recovery of critically ill patients, but some patients deteriorate after removal of the endotracheal tube and require reintubation. Extubation failure can prolong intensive care and is associated with poor outcomes. This study examined the factors associated with reintubation and the clinical outcomes of patients who failed planned extubation. Methods We prospectively followed adult patients undergoing planned extubation in the adult ICU of a tertiary care hospital between June 2025 and June 2026. Patients were observed for 72 hours after extubation, and those requiring reintubation during this period were considered to have experienced extubation failure. Demographic, clinical, physiological, and laboratory characteristics were compared between patients who remained successfully extubated and those who required reintubation. Factors associated with reintubation and in-hospital mortality were examined using multivariable logistic regression. Results A total of 180 patients were included, of whom 27 (15.0%) required reintubation within 72 hours. The patients who required reintubation were older and had higher Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II) and Rapid Shallow Breathing Index (RSBI) scores, while their Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores and serum albumin levels were lower. Positive fluid balance, emergency admission, congestive heart failure, chronic lung disease, and acute kidney injury requiring renal replacement therapy were also more frequent in this group. Reintubation was associated with a longer duration of mechanical ventilation, longer ICU and hospital stays, and higher rates of ventilator-associated pneumonia and tracheostomy. ICU and in-hospital mortality were also considerably higher among patients who required reintubation. After adjustment for other factors, APACHE II score >20, GCS <12, RSBI >105, serum albumin <3.5 g/dL, positive fluid balance >1 L, and mechanical ventilation >7 days were associated with reintubation. Reintubation was strongly associated with in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR, 5.84; 95% CI, 2.31-14.78; P < 0.001). Conclusions In this cohort, patients who required reintubation after planned extubation had a substantially more difficult clinical course and a higher risk of death. Greater illness severity, poor respiratory reserve, low serum albumin, positive fluid balance, and prolonged mechanical ventilation were associated with extubation failure. Identifying these features before extubation and maintaining close observation after extubation may help clinicians recognize patients at higher risk of deterioration.

42835295.title: Acute Pain Trajectory Phenotypes are Associated with Kinesiophobia and Functional Recovery in Surgical/Trauma ICU Patients: A 5-Year Retrospective Cohort Study Using a PERMA-Informed Framework.
42835295.abstract: Early mobilization (EM) mitigates Post-Intensive Care Syndrome (PICS). However, kinesiophobia (fear of movement) driven by severe acute pain is often overlooked. This study aimed to identify acute pain trajectory phenotypes, evaluate their association with kinesiophobia, and explore outcomes under a PERMA-informed exploratory framework. A single-center retrospective cohort study was conducted including surgical/trauma ICU patients (January 2021-December 2025). Group-based trajectory modeling (GBTM) identified latent classes of pain over the first 5 ICU days. Kinesiophobia and PERMA-related proxy variables (Relationships, Accomplishment) were extracted. Multivariable logistic regression, restricted cubic splines (RCS), and Cox proportional hazards models assessed outcomes. Among 586 eligible patients, four pain trajectories were identified: "Rapid Relief" (38.4%), "Persistent Moderate" (29.5%), "Delayed Onset/Flare-up" (21.3%), and "Persistent Severe" (10.8%). After adjusting for confounding factors, Delayed Onset (Adjusted OR 3.85, 95% CI 2.15-6.84) and Persistent Severe (Adjusted OR 6.12, 95% CI 3.25-11.56) trajectories were independently associated with kinesiophobia. RCS demonstrated a significant plateauing association between cumulative opioid doses and kinesiophobia. Patients with kinesiophobia exhibited significant delays in first out-of-bed mobilization, prolonged ICU lengths of stay, and a reduced likelihood of direct discharge to home. In adjusted outcome models, kinesiophobia was associated with delayed first target mobilization (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.33-0.54, P<0.001) and lower odds of direct-to-home discharge (OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.14-0.32, P<0.001). Acute pain in surgical/trauma ICU patients is highly heterogeneous. Higher-risk pain trajectory phenotypes were associated with kinesiophobia, which may represent a psychological barrier to functional recovery. Prospectively testing PERMA-informed strategies-particularly family support, meaning-oriented reframing, and goal-based achievement-may help clarify whether this approach can disrupt the pain-fear-immobility cycle.

42835169.title: Association of carvedilol with mortality in critically ill patients with sepsis: a retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study.
42835169.abstract: To evaluate the association between carvedilol use and mortality in patients with sepsis. All adult critically ill patients with sepsis were retrospectively identified from the MIMIC-IV database. Patients who received carvedilol between sepsis diagnosis and Intensive Care Unit(ICU) discharge were designated as the intervention group and were matched 1:1 with non-users using propensity score matching. The primary outcomes were 28-day and 365-day all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Kaplan-Meier survival curves and Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to examine the association between carvedilol and outcomes. Subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses including time-dependent Cox regression were conducted to test robustness. A total of 33,453 patients were included, of whom 1,084 received carvedilol. After propensity score matching, 1,082 pairs were successfully matched. Kaplan-Meier survival curves showed significant differences in survival probabilities between the two groups. After adjusting for confounders using multivariate Cox regression, the hazard ratios (95% confidence intervals) for carvedilol use on 28-day and 365-day all-cause mortality were 0.53 (0.43-0.66) and 0.66 (0.57-0.76), respectively. Furthermore, carvedilol use was associated with lower in-hospital mortality (OR = 0.49, 95% CI: 0.37-0.64; P < 0.001). Subgroup and sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of the findings. Carvedilol use during the period from sepsis diagnosis to ICU discharge was associated with reduced mortality in critically ill patients with sepsis. However, prospective studies are warranted to further guide the use of carvedilol in this population.

42834317.title: Oscillation and Lung Expansion Therapy as Rescue Airway Clearance in Critically Ill Adults: A Case Series.
42834317.abstract: Retained airway secretions and lobar collapse are common in hospitalized adults with advanced lung disease. Conventional airway clearance depends on respiratory effort, requiring both an adequate inspiratory volume and sufficient expiratory airflow, and on cough strength, and therefore fails most often in the patients who need it most. Oscillation and lung expansion (OLE) therapy delivers continuous positive expiratory pressure (CPEP), continuous high-frequency oscillation (CHFO), and aerosolized medication in a single 10-min treatment, but reported experience is largely confined to postoperative prophylaxis and the home setting. We describe six consecutive adults (aged 18-77 years) treated with OLE (Volara system) at a Canadian tertiary center between March 2023 and April 2026, after conventional airway clearance had failed or after escalation to near-maximal noninvasive respiratory support. Feasibility (delivery of OLE as prescribed at the prevailing level of respiratory support) and tolerability (absence of adverse events or discontinuation for intolerance) were assessed retrospectively. Diagnoses were cystic fibrosis exacerbation (n = 2), thoracic malignancy with lobar collapse from mucus plugging (n = 2), metapneumovirus pneumonia in VEXAS (vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory, somatic) syndrome (n = 1), and autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis with sepsis (n = 1). In each, the realistic alternatives were bronchoscopy, intubation, or palliation. All six demonstrated secretion clearance, radiographic re-expansion, or both. Supplemental oxygen requirements fell in five, two did not require the intensive care transfer or intubation that had been anticipated, and no adverse event was observed following OLE, including in one patient with a recently drained pneumothorax. One patient with metastatic malignancy died of her cancer during the same admission despite radiographic re-expansion. OLE was feasible and well tolerated when used as rescue airway clearance in high-acuity adults. These observations, while hypothesis-generating, require prospective, protocolized evaluation before OLE can be recommended for this indication.

42833119.title: Harnessing artificial intelligence to modulate mechanical power: Toward safer and outcome-oriented ventilation in critical care.

42831577.title: Effects of ketamine infusion rate and cumulative dosing on incidence of delirium in medical intensive care unit patients.
42831577.journal: American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists
42831577.abstract: Ketamine is increasingly used for analgosedation in mechanically ventilated intensive care unit (ICU) patients, but its association with delirium remains unclear. This study evaluated the relationship between maximum hourly ketamine rate and cumulative dose during hospitalization, with the incidence of delirium. This multicenter retrospective cohort study included mechanically ventilated adult medical ICU patients who received ketamine infusions for sedation (January 2013-June 2025) at two tertiary centers. Data collected included demographics, sedation requirements, and daily Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU). The primary outcome was delirium at any point during ICU stay. Primary and secondary exposure variables included maximum hourly ketamine rate and cumulative ketamine dose. A modified Poisson regression was used to evaluate associations between the exposure variables and incidence of delirium, adjusting for confounders. Of 837 screened patients, 114 met inclusion criteria and 42 (36.8%) developed delirium. Baseline characteristics were similar. Patients with delirium had longer duration of mechanical ventilation, (210.7 vs 140.9 hours, P <0.01), ICU length of stay (364.7 vs 268.6 hours, P =0.04), and higher morphine milligram equivalents (5,126.8 vs 2911.8, P = 0.04). No association was observed between delirium with maximum hourly ketamine rate (RR 1.15, P = 0.21) or cumulative dose (RR 1.0, p=0.97). Restricted cubic spline analysis showed a trend towards increased delirium risk with increasing maximum hourly ketamine rates (P = 0.06). Maximum hourly ketamine infusion rate and cumulative dose in mechanical ventilated patients in the medical ICU were not associated with ICU delirium.

42831012.title: ICU-Associated Exposure Keratopathy and Preventable Corneal Blindness: A Clinical Review.
42831012.abstract: Exposure keratopathy is an ocular surface injury caused by prolonged corneal exposure, most often from incomplete eyelid closure. Critical illness can intensify exposure through reduced blinking, chemosis, impaired corneal reflexes, sedation, mechanical ventilation, and tear film instability. This narrative clinical review synthesizes contemporary evidence on epidemiology, mechanisms, risk factors, bedside assessment, prevention, protocol implementation, and care in resource-constrained intensive care units (ICUs). PubMed/MEDLINE was searched for English language literature from January 2000 through 15 September 2026, supplemented by reference list and guideline searches. Systematic reviews, randomized trials, cohort studies, quality improvement reports, and relevant guidance were prioritized. Pooled evidence indicates that exposure keratopathy is common among critically ill patients, and recent trials support scheduled lubrication, eyelid closure support, and moisture chamber approaches, particularly when the cornea remains exposed. Fluorescein assessment and clear ophthalmology referral criteria improve detection of epithelial injury and complications that threaten vision. The review distinguishes evidence from randomized and observational studies and proposes a pragmatic bedside risk framework without presenting it as a validated score. Its principal contribution is the integration of prevention, nursing workflow, clinical escalation, and resource appropriate implementation into a single ophthalmic patient safety framework. The intended audience is ophthalmologists, intensivists, ICU nurses, optometrists, and quality improvement teams. Early structured eye care may reduce avoidable corneal morbidity while supporting consistent practice across settings with different resources.

42828295.title: Effects of substance use on sedation requirements in critically ill patients.
42828295.abstract: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effect of substance use on sedation requirements in critically ill patients to optimize dosing in this population. This was a multicenter, retrospective, observational, institutional review board-approved, cohort study. Included individuals were aged 18 years and older, required mechanical ventilation for more than 24 hours, and had a history of substance use in the intervention group, defined as documentation of using 1 or more substances within the past year. The primary outcome was the maximum number of concurrent continuous analgesic and sedative infusions required during intubation and mechanical ventilation. The primary outcome, maximum number of concurrent continuous analgesic and sedative infusions, was significantly higher when comparing subjects with substance use to those without substance use (3 vs 2 infusions; P < 0.001). Significantly higher doses of analgesia and sedation were also required in the substance use group, including fentanyl (150 vs 100 mcg/hr; P = 0.024), dexmedetomidine (1.2 vs 1.0 mcg/kg/hr; P = 0.040), and benzodiazepines measured in lorazepam equivalents (3 vs 1.5 mg/hr; P < 0.001). In mechanically ventilated subjects, a statistically significantly higher number of concurrent continuous analgesic and sedative infusions were used in the substance use group, with larger doses required to sedate subjects.

42826764.title: Effects of dexmedetomidine on postoperative outcomes in adult non-cardiac surgical patients admitted to the intensive care unit: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
42826764.abstract: The role of dexmedetomidine in patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) following non-cardiac surgery remains unclear. While dexmedetomidine is widely used for its sedative and potential delirium-sparing properties, its pooled effects on clinically relevant postoperative outcomes in this population are not well established. This systematic review and network meta-analysis evaluated the comparative effectiveness and safety of dexmedetomidine compared with other sedative strategies in postoperative non-cardiac surgical ICU patients. We systematically searched PubMed, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Embase from inception to 26 May 2026 for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing postoperative dexmedetomidine with normal saline or other sedatives in adults (≥18 years) admitted to the ICU after non-cardiac surgery. The primary outcome was incidence of delirium during the ICU stay. Secondary outcomes were time to extubation, ICU length of stay, duration of mechanical ventilation, and haemodynamic adverse events. Effect estimates were expressed as relative risks (RRs) or mean differences (MDs) using random-effects models. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework. Interventions were ranked using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) for each outcome. Twenty-four RCTs involving 2,777 patients were included in the systematic review, of which 22 RCTs involving 2,544 patients contributed to the network meta-analysis. Compared with midazolam (RR 0.11, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.80; very low certainty) and normal saline (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.59; low certainty), dexmedetomidine may reduce the risk of delirium. Evidence is insufficient to determine whether propofol differs from dexmedetomidine in its effect on delirium. There were no differences in time to extubation, duration of mechanical ventilation, or ICU length of stay across sedative strategies. Dexmedetomidine probably increases the risk of bradycardia compared with propofol (RR 3.03, 95% CI 1.39-6.25; low certainty), but the evidence is insufficient to determine whether the two agents differ in their effects on hypotension. In safety rankings, dexmedetomidine performed least favourably for bradycardia (SUCRA 0.03) and hypotension (SUCRA 0.13). Dexmedetomidine may reduce postoperative delirium in non-cardiac surgical ICU patients but does not appear to improve ventilatory recovery or ICU length of stay and is associated with higher bradycardia risk. Its principal benefit lies in delirium prevention, supporting an individualised approach to sedative selection.

42825927.title: [Documentation of changes in goals of care in intensive care units - retrospective medical record analysis of deceased patients].
42825927.abstract: End-of-life intensive care interventions correlate with a reduced quality of life of dying patients. Reassessment of clinical indication and patients' preferences, along with potential changes in goals of care, is needed. Changes in goals of care are not sufficiently documented in some instances. Analysis of terms used to document changes in goals of care in medical records and documented therapy adjustment. Retrospective analysis of n = 160 records of deceased patients from four intensive care units (n = 40 per unit) of one university hospital. Descriptive and qualitative content analysis were performed using Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington, USA) and MAXQDA 24 (VERBI Software GmbH, Berlin, Germany). Documentation of changes in goals of care were found in 78% (125/160) of the records. Terms describing changes could be categorized into eleven groups: 'Palliative' (n = 29), 'Treatment withdrawal' (n = 19), 'Best supportive care/symptom control' (n = 18), 'Do not escalate' (n = 13), 'Limitation of therapy' (n = 11), 'Changes in goals of care' (n = 10), 'Do not resuscitate/do not intubate' (n = 10), 'Freeze' (n = 7), 'Specific interventions' (n = 3), 'Mixed terms of changes in goals of care' (n = 3) and 'Others' (n = 2). In the sample, descriptive differences were observed in the frequency of terms depending on ward and patients' age. Therapy adjustments varied in some cases between the terms. For example, mechanical ventilation was discontinued most frequently in the group 'Palliative', at 71% (17/24). Recommended terms to describe goals of care were used inconsistently. Changes in measures and the terms showed only partially similar patterns. A uniformly defined understanding of the team and a structured application of the terms could support the interdisciplinary implementation of changes in goals of care.

42824054.title: Association between vitamin D supplementation and mortality in elderly critically ill patients: a retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study.
42824054.abstract: Vitamin D deficiency is highly prevalent among elderly critically ill patients and has been associated with adverse outcomes. However, evidence regarding the prognostic benefit of vitamin D supplementation in this population remains limited. This study aimed to investigate the association between vitamin D supplementation and 28-day mortality in elderly patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). This retrospective cohort study utilized data from the medical information mart for intensive care IV (MIMIC-IV) database, including patients aged ≥65 years. Propensity score matching (PSM) balanced baseline characteristics between patients who received vitamin D within 48 h of ICU admission and those who did not. Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and E-value analysis assessed unmeasured confounding. After PSM, 8,111 patients were included, with 1,338 (16.5%) deaths within 28 days. The 28-day mortality rate was significantly lower in the vitamin D supplementation group than in the non-supplemented group (14.5% vs. 17.0%, P = 0.017). Multivariable Cox regression demonstrated that vitamin D supplementation was independently associated with lower 28-day mortality (HR = 0.819, 95% CI: 0.710-0.946, P = 0.006). Subgroup analyses revealed more pronounced associations in females and patients without certain chronic comorbidities. Vitamin D supplementation within 48 h of ICU admission was significantly associated with reduced 28-day mortality in elderly critically ill patients. Further prospective interventional studies are required to verify causal relationships and optimize administration regimens.

42956910.title: Population pharmacokinetics of oseltamivir and oseltamivir carboxylate in critically ill adults receiving veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation without renal replacement therapy - an ASAP ECMO study.
42956910.abstract: To characterise the population pharmacokinetics of oseltamivir and oseltamivir carboxylate in critically ill adults receiving veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) without renal replacement therapy (RRT), and to compare oseltamivir carboxylate exposure with an exploratory exposure-response threshold and published pharmacokinetic data. This multinational ASAP ECMO analysis included 8 critically ill adults receiving oseltamivir 75 mg every 12 hours during VV-ECMO. Serial blood samples were collected over a dosing interval, and oseltamivir and oseltamivir carboxylate concentrations were measured using a validated assay. Population pharmacokinetic modelling was performed in Monolix using an integrated parent drug-metabolite model. Fifty-eight plasma concentration-time points were available for analysis. The cohort was relatively young and 63% had augmented renal clearance (ARC). A one-compartment model best described both oseltamivir and oseltamivir carboxylate, with a transit compartment required to account for delayed metabolite formation. Median oseltamivir carboxylate exposure was generally comparable to values reported in healthy adults and critically ill patients receiving standard dosing. Median oseltamivir carboxylate area under the concentration-time curve from 0-12 hours (AUC0-12) was lower in patients with ARC than in those without (1877.78 vs. 8253.39 ng·h/mL; p=0.07). Only 2 of 8 patients achieved the primary exploratory exposure-response threshold (AUC0-12 ≥7000 ng∙h/mL) and none of the 5 patients with ARC achieved this threshold. Marked variability and lower exposure were observed in adults receiving VV-ECMO without RRT, particularly ARC patients. Higher doses may be required in ARC patients, but the optimal dosing regimen remains undefined. Routine dose escalation is not supported by current evidence.

42955793.title: Pre-ICU medication vulnerability and healthcare-access barriers associated with unplanned intensive care admission among cancer patients: A case-control study.
42955793.journal: Journal of oncology pharmacy practice : official publication of the International Society of Oncology Pharmacy Practitioners
42955793.abstract: BackgroundUnplanned intensive care unit (ICU) admission is a critical event in the cancer trajectory and is associated with substantial mortality. Medication-related vulnerabilities and healthcare-access barriers may contribute to acute deterioration but remain insufficiently studied together.ObjectiveTo identify medication-related and healthcare-access factors independently associated with unplanned ICU admission among adults with cancer.MethodsThis hospital-based case-control study was conducted at a tertiary oncology centre. Cases were adults with cancer with unplanned ICU admission (n = 150), and controls were adults with cancer admitted to wards or day-care units without ICU requirement (n = 150), frequency-matched by age group, sex, and cancer type. Medication vulnerabilities and healthcare-access barriers were assessed using medical records and structured interviews. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to estimate adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).ResultsCases had higher prevalence of polypharmacy (64.0% vs 38.7%), clinically significant drug-drug interactions (42.0% vs 20.7%), and medication non-adherence (51.3% vs 29.3%). Financial barriers (58.7% vs 34.7%) and delayed care-seeking (46.0% vs 24.0%) were also more frequent. After adjustment, financial barriers (aOR 2.31, 95% CI 1.34-3.99), drug-drug interactions (2.14, 1.19-3.85), delayed care-seeking (2.08, 1.16-3.72), polypharmacy (2.05, 1.21-3.47), and non-adherence (1.94, 1.12-3.36) remained independently associated with unplanned ICU admission. ICU mortality was 32.0%.ConclusionMedication vulnerabilities and healthcare-access barriers were associated with unplanned ICU admission. These findings identify potentially modifiable areas for further evaluation, but the case-control design does not establish that interventions targeting these factors would directly reduce ICU admissions.

42955613.title: Portable ultra-low field MRI in neurocritical care and intensive care units: A systematic review of diagnostic performance and feasibility.
42955613.abstract: To synthesise evidence on the diagnostic performance, safety, feasibility and clinical impact of ultra-low-field portable magnetic resonance imaging (pMRI) in adult neurocritical care and intensive care unit (ICU) populations. PubMed, Scopus and Embase were searched from inception to 6 February 2026 and supplemented by grey literature and citation searching. We included original English-language studies of adult ICU, neurocritical care or emergency department patients undergoing pMRI at ≤ 0.1 T. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Risk of bias in diagnostic comparisons was assessed with an adapted QUADAS-2 framework, and feasibility and safety outcomes were appraised narratively. Because of heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively. The review was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261302014). Eleven studies published between 2020 and 2024 were included, comprising 694 patient participants and 715 patient examinations, plus 40 healthy controls. Cohorts overlapped substantially: six studies came wholly and one partly from a single institution, and one ECMO study was a subset of another. The number of unique patients is therefore estimated at 281 to 677. In the multicentre ECMO study, adverse events occurred in 3 of 50 patients (6%). One was serious: an intra-aortic balloon pump malfunction attributed to electrocardiographic artefact. No adverse events were reported in the other seven independent cohorts that reported safety outcomes, and two studies did not report safety outcomes. For ischaemic stroke, pMRI detected infarction in 45 of 50 patients (90%). By sequence, sensitivity was 100% for FLAIR, 98% for T2-weighted imaging and 86% for diffusion-weighted imaging. Visual DWI-FLAIR mismatch identified patients scanned within 4.5 h with 60% sensitivity, 82% specificity and a 93% negative predictive value. Sensitivity for intracerebral haemorrhage was 80.4% (specificity 96.6%) on initial blinded evaluation. It was 92.1% (specificity 99.3%) in a later cohort in which raters had clinical context and images used deep-learning reconstruction, with lower sensitivity for infratentorial haemorrhage (75.0%). Only one subdural haemorrhage and no extradural haemorrhages were reported. Midline-shift detection showed 93% sensitivity, 96% specificity and a kappa of 0.87. pMRI detected hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury in 12 of 12 affected post-cardiac-arrest patients. In ECMO patients, pMRI detected 8 of 8 ischaemic events, compared with 4 of 8 on head CT, but only 1 of 2 haemorrhages. Up to 28% of examinations were nondiagnostic, mainly because of motion. Ultra-low-field pMRI is a feasible bedside neuroimaging adjunct with a low but non-zero adverse-event rate. It is of particular value for ischaemic injury, midline shift and serial monitoring. Lower and variable sensitivity for haemorrhage, the nonspecificity of FLAIR hyperintensity, overlapping single-institution cohorts and small samples mean that larger multicentre validation studies are needed.

42953742.title: Best Evidence Summary for Peri-Extubation Management Among Difficult-to-Wean Patients in the Intensive Care Unit.
42953742.abstract: To systematically synthesize the best available domestic and international evidence regarding peri-extubation management among difficult-to-wean ICU patients, so as to offer evidence-based recommendations for routine clinical practice. A systematic search was conducted across various domestic and international databases and websites, including Up To Date, National Institute of Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE), National Guideline Clearinghouse (NGC), Guideline International Network (GIN), Chinese Medical Journal Full-text Database, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Yimaitong, Wanfang Database, and VIP Database, to obtain the best evidence on peri-extubation management for ICU patients with difficult extubation, including guidelines, expert consensus documents, clinical decision-making materials, systematic reviews or meta-analyses, and randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The search period covered from the establishment of each database until March 2026. Literature quality assessment was independently performed by two researchers who have published evidence-based research articles and received professional evidence-based training, with expert input solicited; eligible literature was selected for evidence extraction and summarization. This study ultimately included 23 publications, comprising 8 guidelines, 5 expert consensus documents, 8 systematic reviews, and 2 randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Through analysis, organization, and evidence synthesis of the included literature, evidence was summarized across seven key areas: multidisciplinary team (MDT) collaboration, pre-weaning preparation and assessment, comprehensive management strategies for difficult weaning, management of special patient populations, intubation removal strategies during weaning, post-intubation management strategies, and health education, encompassing 48 pieces of best available evidence. This study summarizes the optimal evidence for peri-extubation management in patients with difficult weaning from seven perspectives, providing guidance for ICU clinicians to develop and implement tailored weaning protocols aimed at improving clinical outcomes and quality of life for these patients.

42953638.title: Multidisciplinary Antimicrobial Stewardship Program in an Indian ICU: A Time-Series Analysis of Diagnostic Practices and Antibiotic Use.
42953638.abstract: Background ICUs are high-risk environments for antimicrobial resistance (AMR). We evaluated the impact of a multidisciplinary Antimicrobial Stewardship Program (AMSP) on diagnostic stewardship, prescribing patterns, and antimicrobial consumption in an Indian tertiary critical care setting. Methods  A 17-month retrospective observational study was conducted, comparing an eight-month pre-implementation phase (January-August 2024) with a nine-month post-implementation phase (September 2024-May 2025). The AMSP included staff training, structured prescription orders, prospective audits, and monthly feedback. Key metrics included pre-antibiotic culture collection, institutional guideline adherence, surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis (SAP) compliance, and standardized consumption densities (defined daily dose (DDD)/100 bed-days and days of therapy (DOT)/1,000 bed-days), evaluated using interrupted time-series (ITS) regression. Results  Across 7,682 ICU admissions (3,514 pre- vs. 4,168 post-implementation), pre-antibiotic culture collection increased significantly: blood cultures increased from 331 (20.2%) to 560 (45.8%; p < 0.001), and urine cultures increased from 1,365 (53.0%) to 1,583 (64.6%; p < 0.001). Empirical guideline adherence improved from 1,618 (46.0%) to 3,005 (72.1%; p < 0.001), and SAP compliance increased from 1,352 (35.5%) to 2,083 (63.2%; p < 0.001). Total antimicrobial consumption density decreased by 44.0% (120.04 to 67.17 DDD/100 bed-days; p < 0.001), and duration density declined by 39.6% (981.23 to 592.91 DOT/1,000 bed-days; p < 0.001; ITS regression step-reduction p < 0.001). Meropenem exposure remained strictly controlled and stable (165 (4.7%) vs. 208 (5.0%); p = 0.549). Conclusion  The multidisciplinary AMSP successfully contained overall antibiotic selection pressure while preserving carbapenems through optimized beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor utilization. Microbial ecology remained stable, with Klebsiella spp. and Escherichia coli predominating. Unadjusted case-mix differences represent a recognized study limitation. Implementing a multidisciplinary AMSP achieved sustained reductions in antimicrobial consumption and improved diagnostic practices, providing a feasible framework to combat resistance in resource-limited ICUs.

42952167.title: Family Engagement and Shared Decision-Making in Adult Intensive Care Nursing: A Bibliometric Review and Thematic Analysis.
42952167.abstract: Family members contribute information, emotional support, bedside care and surrogate decision-making in adult intensive care, yet the nursing literature on family engagement remains conceptually and geographically fragmented. To map the development, intellectual structure, collaboration patterns and thematic evolution of research on family engagement and shared decision-making in adult intensive care nursing. This study was a bibliometric review with complementary thematic content analysis. Following the framework of Donthu et al., Scopus was searched on 16 July 2026 from inception, with bibliometric coverage restricted to complete calendar years through 31 December 2025. Scopus was used because it provides the cited-reference data required for co-citation and bibliographic-coupling analyses. Eligible records were journal articles and reviews concerning adult intensive care that examined family engagement or shared decision-making and included an identifiable nursing component. Performance analysis, co-authorship analysis, reference co-citation, bibliographic coupling, and keyword co-occurrence analysis were conducted using Python and VOSviewer, while cluster content was interpreted using inductive qualitative content analysis. Reporting followed the BIBLIO guideline. The review included 278 publications (1993-2025) from 117 journals and 47 countries. Annual output increased from two publications in 1993 to 32 publications in 2025; 141 publications (50.7%) were published during 2020-2025. Nursing journals produced most publications, whereas two multidisciplinary critical care journals produced 23 publications (8.3%) but 3090 of 11 220 citations (27.5%). The United States led with 104 publications; 23.9% were internationally co-authored. Co-citation analysis identified four intellectual foundations and bibliographic coupling five research fronts, led by family participation and nurse-family engagement. Thirty-nine author keywords formed six themes spanning end-of-life communication and ethics, family-centred nursing engagement and surrogate participation, family support and visitation, family presence in high-acuity care, caregiver experience and bereavement. Keyword trends moved from family needs and withholding treatment towards active engagement, implementation barriers and family nursing. The field has progressed towards partnership but continues to under-specify nurses' roles, use inconsistent terminology and draw disproportionately on high-income Western settings. Critical care services should formalise nurses' responsibilities in family assessment, communication, advocacy and decision support while developing culturally responsive and implementable engagement models.

42951783.title: Association between stress hyperglycemia ratio and short-term all-cause mortality in non-diabetic critically ill patients: a multi-database cohort study.
42951783.journal: Nutrition, metabolism, and cardiovascular diseases : NMCD
42951783.abstract: Stress hyperglycemia is common in non-diabetic critically ill patients. However, the association between the stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR) and short-term mortality in this population remains incompletely characterized in large cohorts. This retrospective cohort study used data from MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-III. Non-diabetic adults with available admission glucose and HbA1c measurements were included. The primary outcomes were 28-day and 90-day all-cause mortality. Patients were grouped by SHR quartiles. Cox proportional hazards models with progressive adjustment were used to assess the associations between SHR and 28-day and 90-day all-cause mortality. Restricted cubic spline (RCS), subgroup, and sensitivity analyses were performed. A total of 6994 non-diabetic patients were included. In the MIMIC-IV cohort, 28-day and 90-day mortality rates were 9.30% and 13.22%, respectively; corresponding rates in MIMIC-III were 4.75% and 5.47%. In the primary adjusted models, the highest SHR quartile (Q4) was associated with higher 28-day and 90-day all-cause mortality compared with Q1 in both cohorts (MIMIC-IV: 28-day HR 3.07, 95% CI 2.56-3.68; 90-day HR 3.34, 95% CI 2.84-3.94; MIMIC-III: 28-day HR 4.26, 95% CI 2.95-6.14; 90-day HR 4.39, 95% CI 3.06-6.30). RCS analyses demonstrated significant nonlinear associations between SHR and both 28-day and 90-day all-cause mortality in both cohorts, with the increase in mortality hazard becoming more pronounced at higher SHR levels. Higher SHR was associated with increased short-term all-cause mortality in non-diabetic critically ill patients, with significant nonlinear associations observed in both cohorts.

42948314.title: Sulbactam/Durlobactam for CRAB Bacteremia and Pneumonia in a Critically Ill Patient in China: A Case Report.
42948314.abstract: Evidence supporting sulbactam/durlobactam (SUL-DUR) for carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) bloodstream infection remains limited, particularly in critically ill patients with multiorgan failure. A 25-year-old man underwent emergency splenectomy for a ruptured splenic artery aneurysm with 7500 mL estimated blood loss. On transfer to our ICU, PaO2/FiO2 was 68 mm Hg, consistent with severe ARDS. He subsequently developed a grade B postoperative pancreatic fistula. A quality-graded sputum specimen grew carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae and CRAB, and a peripheral blood culture drawn during cefoperazone-sulbactam therapy grew CRAB, indicating breakthrough bacteremia; the blood isolate was susceptible to SUL-DUR but resistant to both carbapenems. Ceftazidime-avibactam was replaced with imipenem-cilastatin plus SUL-DUR for eight days, with nebulized colistimethate sodium. Concurrent care included source control, prone ventilation, and pancreatic collection drainage. Procalcitonin had normalized before SUL-DUR began, whereas IL-6 and hs-CRP rose around the positive blood culture and fell during SUL-DUR; he was extubated on ICU day 27. A post-extubation withdrawal episode with convulsions, bronchospasm, and lactic acidosis resolved with rescue sedation. He was discharged from the ICU on June 17, 2026, with negative follow-up blood cultures, and remained well at outpatient review on July 30. This case adds real-world experience regarding the potential role of SUL-DUR in CRAB bacteremia with pneumonia. Because recovery occurred alongside source control, ventilatory support, and sequential antimicrobial therapy, the outcome cannot be attributed to SUL-DUR alone. Larger prospective studies are required to define its role in CRAB bloodstream infection.

42948266.title: Comparative Performance of Oxygenation Indices for Mortality Prediction in Patients With Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome at a Tertiary Care Intensive Care Unit in Bangladesh.
42948266.abstract: Background Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a syndrome of acute inflammatory lung injury and impaired gas exchange, not hypoxemia alone, and carries high mortality. This study compared the discrimination of the partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO₂)/fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO₂) (PF) ratio, oxygenation index (OI), and oxygen saturation index (OSI), measured on the day of ARDS diagnosis, for intensive care unit (ICU) mortality in a Bangladeshi tertiary ICU. Methods This single-center prospective observational study enrolled 80 consecutive adults meeting the 2012 Berlin definition of ARDS and requiring invasive mechanical ventilation at Bangladesh Medical University between June 2024 and May 2025. Time zero (day 1) was the day the Berlin criteria were first met. Indices were calculated on days 1, 3, and 7 from simultaneous blood gas, oximetry, and ventilator data. Groups were compared by independent t- and chi-square tests, serial change by paired t-tests in survivors only, and discrimination by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis with Youden cutoffs. Correlated areas under the curve (AUCs) were not formally compared, and no multivariable model was fitted. Results Forty-five of 80 patients (56.3%) died in the ICU, and 35 (43.8%) survived. Non-survivors had lower blood pressure, higher heart and respiratory rates, and greater ventilatory requirements (p<0.05). OI and OSI were higher and the PF ratio was lower among non-survivors (p<0.05). Discrimination was numerically highest for OSI (AUC=0.879; 95% CI: 0.786-0.977), followed by OI (AUC=0.867; 95% CI: 0.788-0.963) and the PF ratio (AUC=0.731; 95% CI: 0.612-0.881); as the intervals overlapped and no paired test was applied, this ordering is descriptive only. Specificity was 91.4% for both OSI and OI, and accuracy was 86.3% and 83.8% versus 70% for the PF ratio. Serial improvement among survivors was not statistically significant. Conclusions OI and OSI were higher among non-survivors and showed numerically higher discrimination for ICU mortality than the PF ratio, with OSI performing best. As the analysis was univariable and cutoffs were internally derived, these findings indicate discrimination and association rather than independent prognostic value, and the thresholds are exploratory. Larger multicenter studies with formal paired comparison of ROC curves, multivariable adjustment, and independent validation are warranted.

42948080.title: Editorial: Extracorporeal organ support: innovations and challenges in critical care.

42948071.title: Twenty-four-hour continuous attending coverage in a dedicated cardiovascular intensive care unit decreases mortality after cardiac surgery.
42948071.abstract: The effect of continuous in-house attending coverage in a dedicated cardiovascular intensive care unit (CVICU) on postoperative cardiac surgery outcomes remains incompletely defined. This study evaluated morbidity and mortality data immediately before and after implementation of a 24/7 in-house critical care attending coverage model, in a dedicated CVICU, using the Society of Thoracic Surgeons risk-adjusted data for coronary artery bypass grafting and valvular repair/replacement surgeries. Four hundred nineteen patients underwent coronary artery bypass grafting, and/or a mitral valve repair or replacement, and/or an aortic valve replacement at a single institution between April 2022 and 2024. From April 2022 to April 2023 patients recovered in a general surgical intensive care unit, with daytime attending critical care coverage and nighttime resident coverage with attending home call. From April 2023 to April 2024, patients recovered in a dedicated CVICU with continuous in-house, intensivist attending and resident coverage. Society of Thoracic Surgeons risk-adjusted outcomes were compared using exact Poisson and Fisher exact tests. Despite greater predicted mortality in the postintervention period, observed mortality was significantly reduced (0.46% vs 3.94%, P = .017), with a lower observed-to-expected ratio (P = .007). No significant differences were found in secondary outcomes: renal failure, prolonged ventilation, and long length of stay (P = .97, P = .47, and P = .94, respectively). A dedicated CVICU with 24/7 in-house critical care attending coverage significantly reduced mortality as compared with resident-driven, lower-intensity intensive care unit model. This coverage change did not appear to influence renal failure, prolonged mechanical ventilation, or length of hospital stay.

42947576.title: From Framework to Toolkit: Practical Guidance for Using the PrOcess Evaluation of Trials In Critical care (POETIC) Framework.
42947576.abstract: The PrOcess Evaluation of Trials In Critical care (POETIC) framework was developed to support systematic evaluation of Context, Fidelity, Dose, Reach, and an integrative assessment of Quality of Delivery (QoD). Its practical use, however, requires explicit guidance on selecting measures, constructing QoD, assessing changing context, and governing prospective use. We undertook a retrospective comparative synthesis of process evaluations embedded in four randomized U.K. critical care trials: Biomarker-guided antibiotic stewardship in suspected ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAPrapid-2), Provision of Psychological Support to People in Intensive Care (POPPI), Sedation AND Weaning In CHildren (SANDWICH), and Alpha-2 agonists for sedation to produce Better outcomes from critical illness (A2B). We selected them because they informed POETIC's development or application and provided sufficiently detailed quantitative and qualitative evidence. We mapped the reports, protocols, and process evaluation findings to the five dimensions; compared recurring and contradictory patterns, quantitative-qualitative agreement, measurement and interpretation problems, and mechanism-specific limitations; and translated our learning into guidance for applying the framework. The relevance and measurement of POETIC dimensions varied according to how each intervention was expected to work. Contextual influences changed over time and differed between sites. Combined assessments of QoD required explicit decisions about component selection, weighting, thresholds, aggregation, and missing data. VAPrapid-2 showed why a separate Dose measure and a QoD composite were not meaningful for a one-off diagnostic recommendation; POPPI used a weighted site composite; SANDWICH summarized delivery of four intervention components, staff training, and patient Reach; and A2B combined four equally weighted indicators in a 0-12 site score. This cross-trial learning informed practical guidance on selecting measures, assessing context over time, integrating quantitative and qualitative findings, constructing QoD, and governing prospective use. POETIC is best used as a mechanism-aligned, mixed-method scaffold rather than a requirement to measure every dimension or calculate a universal composite. Prospective use is feasible when outputs, recipients, review times, permitted actions, and safeguards are prespecified. The framework and accompanying toolkit support reproducible assessment while protecting trial integrity.

42943609.title: Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia in Critical Care: Evolving Host Populations, Diagnostic Uncertainty, and Management Controversies.
42943609.abstract: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) remains a major cause of acute respiratory failure in immunocompromised patients and is increasingly encountered in critical care outside the traditional human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) population. This narrative review examines the evolving epidemiology, diagnosis, management, prophylaxis, and prognosis of PCP in critically ill adults. The epidemiological landscape has shifted toward patients with haematological and solid malignancies, solid organ or haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, and exposure to corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive therapies. Emerging data also implicate states of immune dysregulation such as cirrhosis. Diagnosis remains challenging because Pneumocystis cannot be routinely cultured and molecular detection alone cannot reliably distinguish colonisation from active infection. Accordingly, respiratory polymerase chain reaction (PCR) results require interpretation alongside host factors, imaging, serum β-D-glucan, microscopy, and, increasingly, metagenomic sequencing. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole remains first-line therapy. Lower-dose regimens may reduce toxicity while maintaining efficacy, but current evidence is largely retrospective and prospective trials are needed. The benefit of adjunctive corticosteroids in non-HIV PCP remains uncertain, with conflicting observational data and no definitive mortality benefit demonstrated in the first randomised trial. Echinocandins remain investigational adjuncts, whereas venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation may provide rescue support in selected patients with refractory acute respiratory distress syndrome. Prophylaxis is effective but remains inconsistently applied in several at-risk groups. Mortality among intensive care unit (ICU) patients remains high, particularly in non-HIV PCP, and varies substantially according to underlying disease, immune phenotype, co-infection, and severity of respiratory failure. Improved risk stratification and adequately powered prospective studies are priorities.

42942399.title: Mechanical Power and Acute Kidney Injury in Mechanically Ventilated Critically Ill Patients: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study.
42942399.abstract: Background and Objectives: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is highly prevalent among critically ill patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) and is associated with adverse outcomes. Mechanical power (MP) reflects the total energy delivered to the respiratory system, but its association with AKI in mechanically ventilated critically ill patients remains incompletely understood. Few studies have examined the relationship between MP and AKI development. Materials and Methods: Adult patients with MP data available for each of the first five consecutive days of IMV constituted the study population. MP and ventilatory parameters were recorded during this period. Factors independently associated with AKI were identified using multivariable logistic regression. The discriminative performance of MP for AKI and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) use was evaluated. Results: Among 924 patients, 605 (65.5%) developed AKI. MP was consistently higher in patients who developed AKI during the first five days of IMV (11.45 ± 2.88 vs. 9.48 ± 2.50 J/min; p < 0.001). Although PEEP, peak inspiratory pressure, driving pressure, respiratory rate, and FiO2 were higher in the AKI group, tidal volume and respiratory system compliance did not differ significantly. In multivariable analysis, higher mean MP (OR = 1.330, 95% CI 1.235-1.432; p < 0.001), greater mean fluid balance (OR = 1.477, 95% CI 1.225-1.780; p < 0.001), older age, and trauma were independently associated with AKI. MP showed moderate discrimination for AKI (AUC = 0.681), with an optimal cutoff of 10.38 J/min. For CRRT use, MP showed significant but limited discrimination (AUC = 0.624; 95% CI, 0.584-0.664; p < 0.001). Conclusions: In critically ill patients receiving IMV, higher MP remained associated with AKI after adjustment for measured covariates. The 10.38 J/min threshold is hypothesis-generating and requires external validation.

42941684.title: Clinical Factors and Composite Biomarkers Associated with Intensive Care Unit-Acquired Weakness: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
42941684.abstract: Background/Objectives: Intensive care unit-acquired weakness is a common neuromuscular complication among critically ill patients, but associations of readily available composite biomarkers with this condition remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to investigate the clinical characteristics, risk factors, and composite biomarkers associated with intensive care unit-acquired weakness. Methods: This single-center retrospective cohort study included 135 critically ill patients admitted to intensive care units between December 2020 and December 2023. Patients were classified into an intensive care unit-acquired weakness group (n = 57) and a group without intensive care unit-acquired weakness (n = 78) according to Medical Research Council sum score criteria. Clinical characteristics, laboratory parameters, composite biomarkers, and hospitalization outcomes were compared. Multivariable logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic curve analyses were performed. Results: Older age, sepsis, hemodialysis, mechanical ventilation, and glucocorticoid use remained associated with intensive care unit-acquired weakness after adjustment for the other covariates in the model. Affected patients had lower albumin and hemoglobin levels and longer intensive care unit and hospital stays. The neutrophil-to-albumin ratio, inflammatory burden index, creatinine-to-albumin ratio, and serum urea-to-creatinine ratio were higher in affected patients. Receiver operating characteristic analysis showed modest discrimination, with areas under the curve ranging from 0.602 to 0.665. Conclusions: Intensive care unit-acquired weakness was associated with clinical and treatment-related factors, hypoalbuminemia, prolonged hospitalization, and elevated composite biomarkers. The composite biomarkers showed only modest discrimination, and their incremental values beyond clinical assessment and clinical utility remain unestablished. Residual confounding by illness severity and nutritional exposure cannot be excluded.

42941660.title: Initial Red Cell Infusion Rate and Escalation of Respiratory Support in Critically Ill Adults: A Target Trial Emulation.
42941660.abstract: Background/Objectives: Current transfusion guidelines address when red cells should be given, not how fast. We estimated the association between the initial infusion rate of a first red cell transfusion and escalation of respiratory support in critically ill adults. Methods: We emulated a target trial in MIMIC-IV v3.1. Of 2790 eligible adults, 1787 received a slower (50-175 mL/h) and 1003 a faster (>175-350 mL/h) initial rate; the primary outcome was escalation to advanced respiratory support or death within 12 h. Overlap weighting estimated marginal risk differences in the overlap population, with 2000 bootstrap resamples refitting the propensity-score model. Sensitivity and continuous dose-response analyses were pre-specified. Results: The primary outcome was classifiable in 2671 patients, with 143 events. Weighted 12 h risks were 4.95% and 6.60%: risk difference 1.65 percentage points (95% CI -0.41 to 3.74), risk ratio 1.33 (0.93 to 1.92). Invasive mechanical ventilation or death, a nested key secondary outcome unadjusted for multiplicity, gave 2.55 percentage points (0.71 to 4.59); 28-day mortality gave -1.45 (-4.10 to 1.30). In the pre-specified dose-response analysis, standardised 12 h risk was lowest near 140 mL/h (4.27%) and rose to 8.83% (6.56 to 11.28) at 350 mL/h. Conclusions: The primary analysis did not distinguish the two initial-rate strategies, although the interval remained compatible with a clinically important increase in risk. The secondary and dose-response findings are hypothesis-generating and do not support changing current infusion-rate practice. These estimates support the design and sample-size planning of a prospective trial assigning infusion rate.

42941595.title: Current Practices of Prone Positioning in ARDS Reported by European ICU Clinicians (CUPIDO)-A Cross-Sectional Questionnaire-Based Survey.
42941595.abstract: Background: Prone positioning improves survival in patients with moderate to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), yet its implementation in routine clinical practice remains poorly characterized. We conducted a survey to assess contemporary prone positioning practices and their heterogeneity in the management of ARDS across European intensive care units (ICUs). Methods: A cross-sectional, questionnaire-based survey was conducted among clinicians involved in ARDS management between March and August 2025. The survey was developed by a panel of experts in intensive care medicine and underwent testing for face and content validity prior to dissemination. The questionnaire was distributed through European networks, including the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM), the PROtective VEntilation Network (PROVE Network), the European Society of Anaesthesiology and Intensive Care (ESAIC), and national societies. Results: Out of 592 eligible responses, 451 responses were complete and from European clinicians (66.1% male), with the largest contributions being from Italy (28.6%), Germany (18.4%) and Austria (11.5%). Of these, 446 respondents (98.9%) reported performing prone positioning. Initiation thresholds for prone positioning varied, most commonly a ratio of arterial partial pressure of oxygen to fraction of inspired oxygen (PaO2/FiO2) ≤ 150 mmHg (55.4%), followed by ≤100 mmHg (26.9%), ≤200 mmHg (11.4%), and ≤300 mmHg (1.8%). Full prone positioning was reported as always or often used by 38.6% and 37.7% of participants, whereas semi-prone positioning (7.0% and 21.1%) or lateral positioning (2.5% and 14.8%) was used less often. The duration of prone positioning varied: 47.8% reported 16 h, 17.0% 12 h and 7.8% 8 h per session. Conclusions: Among self-selected clinicians working in European ICUs, prone positioning was commonly reported, though reported practice varied with respect to initiation thresholds, prone positioning strategy and duration. These findings identify specific areas where practice diverges and where current guidance and evidence remain incomplete.

42941586.title: Prognosis Prediction in Adult Intensive Care-A Critical Analysis.
42941586.abstract: Background: Prognosis prediction in adult intensive care units (ICUs) guides clinical decision-making, realistic goal-setting with families, and resource allocation, but is challenged by the marked heterogeneity of critically ill patients in multi-speciality wards. Methods: This narrative review critically analyses commonly used prognostic scoring systems by clinical application timeline. Results: Admission prognostic models, including the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE II/III/IV), Simplified Acute Physiology Score (SAPS II/SAPS 3) and Mortality Probability Model (MPM), estimate in-hospital mortality from acute physiological derangement and comorbidity; the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) adds prognostic value. During the ICU stay, organ dysfunction is tracked with the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA/SOFA-2), designed for repeated reassessment, and the Multiple Organ Dysfunction Score (MODS), while the Therapeutic Intervention Scoring System (TISS-28) quantifies nursing workload. At discharge, the Barthel Index, Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) and Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) measure functional independence and neurological outcome. Admission-based mortality models use an initial assessment window and may require local recalibration, and discrimination alone does not establish clinical utility. Conclusions: Future directions include trajectory-based models, phenotyping, biomarkers, time-limited trials and machine learning. Prognostic estimates should inform multidisciplinary evaluation and shared decision-making, rather than independently determine treatment intensity or withdrawal.

42941500.title: Clinical Reasoning, Pathophysiology, and Artificial Intelligence in Critical Care: A Conceptual Framework for Integrating Decision-Making.
42941500.abstract: Medical practice is an interpretive, decision-making activity conducted under uncertainty, and care quality depends on clinicians' ability to organize knowledge into hypotheses, understand mechanisms, estimate probabilities, and revise decisions as the clinical course evolves. In critical care, where physiology is unstable and trajectories are nonlinear, these demands are magnified. We propose a conceptual framework integrating three complementary dimensions: clinical reasoning, which provides the cognitive architecture of decision-making; pathophysiology, which supplies the causal structure to interpret biological phenomena; and artificial intelligence, which, when well designed and critically used, can organize data, generate hypotheses, and reduce cognitive load. Tracing the evolution of clinical reasoning from the anatomoclinical model to hypothetico-deductive, probabilistic, cognitive, and sociotechnical models, we examine how diagnostic and therapeutic errors arise from interacting cognitive biases, system factors, and case characteristics, and how better problem representation, differential diagnosis, and team culture may mitigate them. We also frame Bayesian reasoning and decision thresholds as the probabilistic grammar of bedside decisions, analyze the risks of artificial intelligence, including automation bias, opacity, and limited metacognition, and propose principles for its safe use. Rather than replacing physicians, artificial intelligence should strengthen clinical reasoning and reinforce calibrated, accountable bedside judgment. These principles are intended as a framework for future research and require empirical validation before clinical translation.

42941396.title: Diverging Trends in Treated In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in Intensive Care Units and General Wards Using Location-Specific Patient-Days.
42941396.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hospital-level incidence estimates may obscure differences between intensive care units (ICUs) and general wards. We compared temporal trends in treated adult in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) using location-specific patient-days. Methods: This retrospective study covered January 2016 to June 2026 at a South Korean teaching hospital. Monthly treated IHCA counts were modeled using negative binomial regression with patient-days as an offset, a setting × time interaction, and adjustment for the COVID-19 period and seasonality. Calendar-month score-based HAC analyses assessed robustness to serial correlation. January-March 2022 was excluded because arrest location was unavailable. Results: The incidence cohort comprised 1712 events: 1373 in ICUs and 339 in general wards. The combined rate was 1.06 per 1000 patient-days. The setting × time interaction was significant (monthly IRR 0.9843, model-based 95% CI 0.9768-0.9918), corresponding to a 17.3% annual decrease in the ICU-to-ward rate ratio. Calendar-month score-based HAC confidence intervals also excluded 1. ICU incidence declined (monthly IRR 0.9875, 95% CI 0.9825-0.9925), whereas the general-ward model showed no statistically significant temporal trend (IRR 1.0033, 95% CI 0.9975-1.0090; p = 0.263). Conclusions: Location-specific patient-day denominators identified different temporal trajectories in treated IHCA. These findings describe observed treated events and do not establish changes in underlying arrest risk or resuscitation performance.

42940427.title: Artificial Intelligence in Intensive Care: From Clinical Applications to Ethical and Medico-Legal Challenges.
42940427.abstract: From a medico-legal perspective, AI functions as a clinical decision support tool without legal autonomy. Responsibility for AI-assisted clinical decisions remains subject to the applicable legal and regulatory framework and depends on the degree of human oversight. The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming intensive care medicine, offering advanced tools for data processing, prediction, and clinical decision support. This narrative review explores current applications of AI in the intensive care unit (ICU), along with associated ethical, medico-legal, and regulatory challenges. AI systems, particularly those based on machine learning and deep learning, have demonstrated promising predictive performance across several intensive care applications. Systematic reviews of machine learning models for ICU prediction tasks have reported AUROC values generally ranging from approximately 0.80 to over 0.90 for early sepsis prediction and ARDS risk stratification, although performance decreases in external validation cohorts. AI has also shown encouraging performance in predicting weaning success and supporting mechanical ventilation management, while evidence of improved patient-centered clinical outcomes remains limited A narrative literature search was conducted in PubMed and Scopus for studies published between January 2015 and December 2025. Additionally, AI contributes to continuous patient monitoring, reduction in false alarms, and improved workflow efficiency. Despite these advances, most models are derived from retrospective and single-center datasets, limiting generalizability and real-world applicability. Moreover, only a limited number of AI systems have undergone prospective clinical evaluation or demonstrated improvements in patient-centered outcomes following real-world implementation. A key limitation of current AI systems is the "black box" nature of many algorithms, which reduces interpretability and may undermine clinician trust. Furthermore, algorithmic bias, data quality issues, and limited external validation raise concerns regarding safety, equity, and reliability. Importantly, improved predictive accuracy does not necessarily translate into better clinical outcomes, highlighting the need for prospective validation studies. From a medico-legal perspective, AI functions as a clinical decision support tool without legal autonomy. Responsibility for AI-assisted clinical decisions remains subject to the applicable legal and regulatory framework and depends on the degree of human oversight, the intended use of the AI system, and the relevant jurisdiction. The emergence of regulatory frameworks, such as the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), reflects the increasing regulation of healthcare AI according to the intended purpose, level of autonomy, and potential impact of each system, emphasizing requirements for transparency, human oversight, and data protection.

42938754.title: The Impact of an Intensive Care Unit Antimicrobial Stewardship Program on the Appropriateness of Meropenem Prescribing at a Tertiary Hospital: A Retrospective Quasi-Experimental Study.
42938754.abstract: Background: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) prevalence has been increasing in Saudi Arabia, posing a significant public health concern. Antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs) play an important role in reducing resistance by ensuring appropriate antibiotic use. Our study aimed to assess the appropriateness of meropenem prescriptions pre-ASP and post-ASP implementation in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) ward. Method: This is a retrospective quasi-experimental pre-post study conducted over 3 years, from 2020 to 2023 at King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz University Hospital (KAAUH). The study included adult ICU patients who received meropenem therapy. The primary objective was to evaluate the appropriateness of meropenem prescriptions in the ICU before and after ASP implementation. The secondary objectives were to identify reasons for inappropriate prescribing and evaluate the interventions implemented to address inappropriate meropenem use. Result: A total of 113 patients were included: 34 in 2020, 41 in 2022, and 38 in 2023. Appropriate meropenem prescribing increased significantly from 23.5% in 2020 to 26.8% in 2022 and 57.9% in 2023 (p = 0.003), while inappropriate prescribing decreased from 76.5% to 73.2% and 42.1%, respectively. Treatment duration also differed significantly across study periods (p = 0.002), with courses of 7-10 days increasing from 24.2% in 2020 to 53.7% in 2022 and 52.6% in 2023, while courses exceeding 10 days decreased from 51.5% to 12.2% and 18.4%, respectively. Among inappropriate prescriptions, an inappropriate antimicrobial spectrum was the predominant reason (81.9%), with no inappropriate dosing identified. Documented stewardship interventions differed significantly across periods (p < 0.001): de-escalation increased from 0% in 2020 to 43.3% in 2022 and 50.0% in 2023, while prescriptions completed without documented intervention decreased from 69.2% to 23.3% and 18.8%, respectively. Conclusion: ASP implementation was associated with a significant improvement in the appropriateness of meropenem prescribing and a shift toward shorter treatment durations among adult ICU patients. Nevertheless, inappropriate prescribing remained substantial in the second post-implementation year, emphasizing the need for continued antimicrobial stewardship interventions and ongoing monitoring of carbapenem use.

42938719.title: Integrating Plasma mNGS into ICU Antimicrobial Stewardship: A Four-Phase Framework.
42938719.abstract: Background: Plasma metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) may complement conventional microbiology in critically ill patients, yet its contribution to antimicrobial stewardship in the intensive care unit (ICU) remains unclear. Methods: In this retrospective, single-center observational study, we analyzed 243 paired mNGS-blood culture episodes from 180 ICU patients. We applied a four-phase stewardship framework that integrated clinical severity, biomarker kinetics, blood culture results, mNGS findings, and clinical assessment. Treatment adaptations were classified as escalation, de-escalation, discontinuation, or no change. Multivariable regression identified factors associated with stewardship modification and mortality. Results: Active treatment adaptation occurred in 121 of 243 episodes (49.8%), comprising 61 escalations, 39 de-escalations, and 21 discontinuations. mNGS positivity was independently associated with treatment modification (OR 2.66, 95% CI 1.23-5.75; p = 0.014), whereas blood culture positivity showed an inverse association (OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.20-1.04; p = 0.062). Mortality was primarily linked to physiologic severity and host-response markers, particularly SAPS II and procalcitonin. In-hospital survival did not differ between patients who received stewardship-guided adaptation and those in whom empirical antibiotic therapy was maintained (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.57-1.81; log-rank p = 0.951). Conclusions: Microbiological findings, particularly mNGS, were associated with antimicrobial treatment adaptation but not independently with mortality. Because mNGS was embedded within a multimodal diagnostic and clinical pathway, its independent contribution cannot be fully separated from concurrent microbiological, biomarker, and clinical information. These findings should be regarded as exploratory and require prospective multicenter validation.

42936739.title: Integrated Rehabilitation, Airway, and Nutritional Nursing is Associated with Short-Term Outcomes in Critically Ill Patients: A Historical Controlled Before-After Study.
42936739.abstract: This study evaluated the association between an integrated rehabilitation, airway-management, and nutritional nursing protocol and short-term outcomes in critically ill patients. This historical controlled before-after study included 101 adult ICU patients: 58 received conventional nursing and 43 received the integrated protocol. The primary outcome was pulmonary infection within 14 days or before ICU discharge, transfer, or death. Stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles, was used to balance baseline covariates. Weighted risk differences (RDs), risk ratios (RRs), and mean differences (MDs) were estimated with robust variance. After weighting, all baseline covariates had absolute standardized mean differences below 0.10. Pulmonary infection occurred in 14.1% of the intervention phase and 24.0% of the control phase after weighting (RD, -9.9 percentage points; 95% CI, -27.6 to 7.8; RR, 0.59; 95% CI, 0.21-1.66). The difference was not statistically significant. Exploratory analyses showed less gastrointestinal bleeding (RD, -16.0 percentage points; 95% CI, -25.1 to -6.9), higher SpO2 (MD, 2.09%; 95% CI, 0.99-3.19), shorter mechanical ventilation duration (MD, -4.57 days; 95% CI, -5.84 to -3.31), and shorter ICU stay (MD, -7.34 days; 95% CI, -9.11 to -5.57) during the intervention phase. The integrated protocol was associated with favorable secondary outcomes, but the reduction in the primary outcome was not statistically significant. Larger prospective studies are required.

42936253.title: Gastrointestinal point-of-care ultrasound for enteral nutrition management in critically ill adults: a scoping review.
42936253.abstract: Gastrointestinal point-of-care ultrasound has been investigated as a non-invasive, bedside adjunct for gastrointestinal assessment and enteral-feeding decision-making in critical care; however, existing protocols and their outcome reporting remain fragmented. This scoping review mapped the existing evidence landscape on the use of gastrointestinal point-of-care ultrasound in the management of enteral nutrition in critically ill adults. Comprehensive searches in 10 databases (PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, Cochrane, CINAHL, Scopus, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang, VIP, China Biological Medicine Literature Database) identified 5,123 records. Studies focusing on ultrasound-assessed gastrointestinal function to guide enteral nutrition, or to predict enteral nutrition intolerance and clinical prognosis, were screened, summarized, and descriptively analyzed. 49 unique studies were identified, including 36 interventional and 13 observational studies. Geographically, the synthesized evidence was heavily concentrated in China. Ultrasound indicators for gastrointestinal function included the gastric antrum (gastric residual volume, motility index, cross-sectional area), colon (colon diameter and peristaltic frequency), small intestine (small intestine diameter, wall thickness, peristalsis), and superior mesenteric artery hemodynamics. Observational studies showed Area Under the Curve point estimates frequently around or above 0.70, with substantial heterogeneity and no independent external validation reported for enteral nutrition intolerance and mortality. Among interventional studies, time to achieve feeding goals and intensive care unit length of stay were the most frequently evaluated outcomes (27/36), whereas in-hospital mortality was evaluated in only 8 of 36 studies; outcome reporting was heterogeneous and is presented descriptively. The synthesized literature suggests the potential utility of gastrointestinal point-of-care ultrasound as an objective, non-invasive bedside tool for gastrointestinal assessment and feeding protocol modulation. However, because no formal critical appraisal or pooled comparative or diagnostic analysis was performed, this review cannot establish clinical effectiveness, universal thresholds, or patient-important benefit. Future research priorities include consensus definitions and acquisition standards, effect estimates with confidence intervals and patient-important outcomes, inter-operator reliability and training evaluation, and external validation across diverse health systems.

42935102.title: Singapore Society of Anaesthesiologists Position Statement: sustainability in anaesthesiology and intensive care in Singapore.
42935102.abstract: Healthcare accounts for 7% of Singapore's carbon emissions. Given the role of planetary health in health outcomes, healthcare must be sustainable, evidence- and value-based. This consensus paper provides Singapore-specific recommendations to guide sustainable anaesthesia and intensive care practice while maintaining clinical care standards. It aims to support discussion, planning and implementation of initiatives without superseding clinical judgement or local policies. A workgroup from the Singapore Society of Anaesthesiologists conducted a review of international sustainability guidelines, peer-reviewed literature and evidence. Iterative consensus building was undertaken through discussion and consultation. Evidence was derived from life cycle analyses, laboratory or environmental studies, and quality improvement initiatives rather than conventional randomised controlled trials, but can nevertheless provide a robust scientific basis for recommendations underpinned by the triple bottom line framework.
