A Delphi study was conducted among pulmonologists from the Groupe d'Endoscopie Thoracique et Interventionnel Francophone (GETIF). The first-round questionnaire included 18 statements. Consensus was defined as ≥ 70% of experts expressing agreement or disagreement. Non-consensual statements were reformulated based on expert comments and resubmitted for a second round. Thirty experts participated in the first round, of whom 26 completed the second round. Thirteen of 18 statements reached consensus. FB was considered ethically acceptable after systematic verification of advance directives. It was indicated in cases of bronchial congestion with radiologic atelectasis, foreign body aspiration, food aspiration, or after failed tracheal suction following inhaled vomitus. FB was not recommended in COPD exacerbation, acute heart failure, non-obstructive tumoral lesions, or exacerbation of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Experts agreed that high-flow oxygen therapy and non-invasive ventilation could improve procedural tolerance. No consensus was reached for certain situations, particularly hemoptysis regardless of severity and tracheobronchial tumoral obstruction. This study provides the first expert opinion on the indications for FB in elderly patients (≥ 75 years) with HRF who are not eligible for intensive care. The heterogeneity of responses for certain situations reflects the complexity of medical decision-making and underscores the need for further studies.

42890400.title: A Behavior-Based Quality Improvement Initiative for Intensive Care Unit Calmness: A Single-Center Before-After Evaluation.
42890400.abstract: Introduction Intensive care units (ICUs) are acoustically and cognitively demanding environments in which modifiable behavioral factors, unnecessary verbal communication, non-actionable alarms, disorganized workflow, and unstructured handovers contribute substantially to noise burden and cognitive overload for nursing staff. Published Indian ICU literature on this problem remains predominantly measurement-focused. We developed the CALMER bundle, a six-component, no-capital-expenditure behavioral intervention (communication discipline, alarm discipline, leadership modeling, mindful workflow and equipment handling, emotional reset, and reinforcement). We evaluated its feasibility and perceived impact in an Indian tertiary ICU. Materials and methods This was a single-center, uncontrolled, before-after quality improvement study conducted in a 20-bed mixed medical-surgical ICU at GEM Hospital, Coimbatore, India, reported per the Standards for Quality Improvement Reporting Excellence (SQUIRE) 2.0 guidelines. The primary outcome, composite perceived ICU calmness, was assessed using a retrospective paired then-now 11-item questionnaire (five-point Likert scale; Cronbach's alpha 0.831), administered to all 40 nursing staff with complete-case analysis in 28 nurses (28/40, 70%). Secondary outcomes included a six-item work environment score (same 28 nurses) and a post-intervention adapted NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) workload assessment (n = 40). We assessed patient/surrogate perception cross-sectionally post-intervention (n = 100). We analyzed paired ordinal data using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with effect size r and 95% confidence intervals (Fisher's z-transformation). Results Composite ICU calmness improved from a pre-intervention median of 2.0 (IQR: 1.75-2.0) to 4.0 (IQR: 4.0-4.0) (p < 0.001; r = 0.910; 95% CI: 0.813-0.958). All four calmness domains improved significantly (r = 0.842-0.874). Twenty-six of 28 nurses (92.9%) met a prespecified ≥2-point responder threshold; none declined. The work environment score improved from 2.25 to 4.0 (p < 0.001; r = 0.874), with all six secondary items improving significantly (r = 0.751-0.872). Post-intervention workload was at the scale midpoint (NASA-TLX median: 3.0/5). Patient/surrogate perceptions were favorable across all five domains (median: 5.0/5); as a post-intervention-only assessment, these are reported descriptively without a baseline comparator. A later-phase implementation-fidelity audit (141 shift-level audits, May 7 to June 30, 2026) showed 82.9% overall compliance (highest: leadership modeling 91.8%; lowest: emotional reset 76.2%). No alarm-related sentinel events occurred. Conclusions A zero-capital-expenditure, behavior-based bundle was associated with large, statistically significant improvements in nurse-perceived ICU calmness and work environment in an Indian tertiary ICU, alongside a post-intervention workload rating at the scale midpoint. Unblinded, investigator-administered assessment and the absence of objective acoustic data are important limitations. Multicenter validation with objective noise measurement and independent data collection is needed before generalizing these findings.

42887892.title: Empirical Antifungal Treatment of Critically Ill Patients With Influenza-Associated Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Bayesian Perspective.
42887892.journal: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America
42887892.abstract: We reanalyzed 172 critically ill patients with influenza-associated ARDS in a Bayesian framework. Empirical mold-active antifungal treatment yielded a posterior median hazard ratio for influenza-associated pulmonary aspergillosis of 0.51 (95% credible interval 0.20-1.17; probability of benefit 94%), without mortality benefit. Findings remained consistent across skeptical, non-informative and externally informed priors.

42887421.title: Swanson's theory of caring applied to mechanical ventilation weaning in the ICU: Humanizing care.
42887421.abstract: To analyze the scientific evidence on the application of Swanson's Theory of Caring in the process of invasive mechanical ventilation weaning in Intensive Care Units (ICU), identifying nursing interventions that correspond to Swanson's five theoretical processes (knowing, being with, doing for, enabling, and maintaining belief) and assessing their implications for clinical practice. Scoping review conducted according to the methodological framework of Arksey and O'Malley (2005), enhanced by Levac et al. (2010), and the updated JBI guidance for scoping reviews (Peters et al., 2020). Reporting followed the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). A search of scientific literature published between January 2020 and January 2026 was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, SciELO, CUIDEN, Cochrane Library and CINAHL, complemented by backward citation tracking. Forty-five articles were included after applying rigorous selection criteria, through independent screening by two reviewers with discrepancies resolved by consensus. Data were analyzed through structured extraction and narrative synthesis, organizing interventions according to Swanson's five caring processes. The review identified multiple nursing interventions during ventilator weaning that showed conceptual correspondence with Swanson's theory. Only 8 of the 45 articles (18%) explicitly used Swanson's framework, and a single study directly linked it to ventilator weaning, identifying a significant knowledge gap. The "knowing" process includes individualized assessment using validated scales and continuous monitoring. "Being with" is manifested through therapeutic presence, effective communication, and facilitation of family contact. "Doing for" encompasses sedation titration, ventilation management, and respiratory physiotherapy techniques. "Enabling" comprises health education, use of augmentative communication systems, and support in decision-making. "Maintaining belief" is materialized through positive reinforcement, management of realistic expectations, and emotional accompaniment. Swanson's Theory of Caring provides a relevant and potentially operational theoretical framework to structure and humanize nursing care during ventilator weaning in the ICU. The conceptual correspondence identified suggests that its systematic application could contribute to improving patient experience, reducing psychological complications, and optimizing weaning outcomes. Implementation gaps are evident due to the absence of prospective studies, scarcity of data to quantify the impact of relational care on the weaning process, and the absence of specific protocols that merge the NANDA-NIC-NOC taxonomy and the Swanson theoretical framework. Prospective studies applying Swanson's framework from the design phase are required to evaluate the specific impact of interventions based on this theory through controlled clinical trials.

42882408.title: The Critical Clock: Time-Dependent Inflammation, Catabolism and Immunosuppression Syndrome Is Associated with ICU Mortality.
42882408.abstract: Background/Objectives: Chronic critical illness (CCI) is increasingly recognized as a major challenge in intensive care, yet its definition remains heterogeneous. The triad of inflammation, catabolism, and immunosuppression (ICS) is central to proposed CCI pathophysiology, but the association between its changing components and prognosis has not been systematically evaluated. We examined whether the current presence of the biomarker-defined ICS syndrome was associated with ICU mortality. Methods: In this retrospective single-center cohort study, we analyzed 820 ICU patients from the Russian Intensive Care Dataset (RICD v3.0) who had at least one episode of the biomarker-defined ICS syndrome, operationally defined by concurrent C-reactive protein > 20 mg/L, albumin < 30 g/L, and absolute lymphocyte count < 0.8 × 109/L within a 24 h period. After the index ICS syndrome event, each patient's ICU course was classified according to the current syndrome status: ICS syndrome present (all three criteria met) or ICS syndrome absent (at least one criterion not met). We compared organ dysfunction, laboratory parameters, life-support interventions, and mortality between periods with the syndrome present and absent using linear mixed-effects models, generalized estimating equations, and time-dependent Cox regression. Mortality density was calculated per 1000 patient-days. Results: Periods with the ICS syndrome present accounted for 5271 (22.2%) of 23,796 post-index patient-days and periods with the syndrome absent accounted for 18,525 (77.8%). Variables not used to define the syndrome showed greater contemporaneous severity while the ICS syndrome was present, including higher SOFA and SOFA-2 scores, worse neurological status, lower platelet and total protein levels, and more frequent mechanical ventilation initiation (32.8% vs. 23.6%; OR: 1.59, p < 0.001). The ICS syndrome was present at the time of 133 of 243 deaths (54.7%), with a mortality density of 25.23 versus 5.94 per 1000 patient-days (IRR: 4.25, 95% CI: 3.30-5.47). In time-dependent Cox regression, the current presence versus absence of the biomarker-defined ICS syndrome was associated with a higher hazard of ICU death (unadjusted HR: 4.02, 95% CI: 2.14-7.55; adjusted HR: 3.86, 95% CI: 1.86-8.02). Conclusions: In this cohort, the current presence of the biomarker-defined ICS syndrome was associated with substantially higher ICU mortality risk than its absence. These findings support dynamic risk assessment and closer clinical evaluation; however, the biomarker combination may partly reflect contemporaneous illness severity, and the present analysis does not establish a causal effect of syndrome presence or an independent effect of cumulative prior time with the syndrome present.

42881898.title: Implementation of a Multidisciplinary Rounding Tool in a Medical Intensive Care Unit and Its Association with Rounding Efficiency and Multidisciplinary Collaboration.
42881898.abstract: Background: Multidisciplinary rounds are essential for high-quality intensive care but are frequently hindered by inconsistent team participation and logistical inefficiencies. We evaluated the associated impact of implementing a standardized multidisciplinary rounding checklist and real-time paging system on multidisciplinary team attendance, rounding efficiency, and selected clinical outcomes in the ICU. Methods: A retrospective, observational pre- and post-intervention cohort study featuring a concurrent control group was conducted at a tertiary care hospital. The study included 331 adults admitted to the medical ICU (MICU) and neurovascular critical care unit (NCCU; control). The intervention combined a standardized rounding checklist incorporating the ICU Liberation (ABCDEF) bundle and FAST HUGS BID mnemonic with a real-time paging notification system to alert team members of round start times and locations. The primary outcome was change in multidisciplinary team participation at the start and end of rounds; secondary outcomes included rounding time per patient and exploratory care-process outcomes. Results: Multidisciplinary participation at the start and conclusion of rounds significantly improved for both the MICU advanced practice provider (APP) team (p = 0.003 and p = 0.002, respectively) and the resident team (p = 0.006 and p < 0.001, respectively), while attendance in the NCCU group remained unchanged. Median rounding time per patient decreased by 20.8% (13.0 to 10.3 min, p < 0.001). In a survivor-only sensitivity analysis, the streamlined workflow decreased the median time to physical and occupational therapy consultations from 4 to 2 days (p ≤ 0.002). Invasive device stewardship significantly improved; central venous catheter utilization decreased from 58.0% to 25.0% (p < 0.001), and arterial line utilization fell from 55.0% to 26.5% (p < 0.001), with median arterial catheter duration decreasing from 5 to 3 days (p = 0.001). Conclusions: Implementing low-cost, reliable workflow standardization tools was associated with significantly improved multidisciplinary participation and shorter rounding time per patient. Favorable changes in selected care-process measures were also observed, although patient-level clinical outcomes should be interpreted as exploratory and future studies are warranted.

42881850.title: Biofilm Formation on Invasive Medical Devices in Adult Intensive Care Units: A Scoping Review of Biomedical and Clinical Evidence.
42881850.abstract: Background/Objectives: Biofilm formation on invasive medical devices represents a major challenge in intensive care units (ICUs), contributing to device-associated infections, antimicrobial resistance, and adverse clinical outcomes. Despite its clinical relevance, the extent and characteristics of the available evidence on biofilm formation in invasive medical devices used in adult ICUs remain heterogeneous and incompletely mapped. The objective was to map and characterize the available evidence on biofilm formation in invasive medical devices used in adult ICUs. Methods: A scoping review was conducted following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. The review was structured using the Population-Concept-Context (PCC) framework. A comprehensive search was performed in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and ScienceDirect. Primary studies evaluating biofilm formation on invasive medical devices in adult ICUs were included. Data were extracted on study characteristics, device type, microorganisms, biofilm detection methods, and clinical outcomes. Results were synthesized descriptively and presented through tables and an evidence map. Results: Sixteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Evidence was primarily focused on endotracheal tubes, vascular catheters, and urinary catheters. Biofilm formation was consistently documented across these devices, involving Gram-negative bacteria, Gram-positive cocci, and fungal pathogens. Detection methods were heterogeneous, with early reliance on electron microscopy and increasing use of quantitative phenotypic assays, while molecular approaches remained limited. The evidence map revealed a concentration of studies in vascular devices and significant methodological variability across studies. Conclusions: Biofilm formation on invasive medical devices in adult ICUs is a clinically significant and microbiologically complex phenomenon. The available evidence highlights key device categories and pathogen profiles but is limited by methodological heterogeneity and gaps in molecular characterization and translational research. Future studies should prioritize standardized, multimodal approaches and clinically oriented designs to improve prevention and management of device-associated biofilm infections in critical care settings.

42881764.title: Prioritising Content for Continuing Education in Non-Invasive Ventilation Care: A Needs Assessment Survey of Intensive Care Unit Nurses.
42881764.abstract: The success of non-invasive ventilation (NIV) depends on bedside nursing judgement, yet nurses report insufficient preparation, and educational content is usually decided before the competencies nurses most need are identified. To prioritise NIV competencies, derived for this study from three clinical practice guidelines, by educational need, and, as secondary aims, describe intensive care unit nurses' perceived knowledge, self-efficacy and implementation climate for evidence-based practice and their correlates. A cross-sectional survey questionnaire was completed by 142 nurses in four intensive care units of a tertiary teaching hospital in the Republic of Korea in June and July 2026 (response rate 97.3%). Each of 35 competencies was rated for importance and present competency; priorities were derived by combining the Borich needs assessment with the Locus for Focus model, and their stability was examined by bootstrap resampling. Item means were 5.47 (SD 2.05) for perceived knowledge and 5.53 (SD 2.20) for self-efficacy on a 10-point scale and 1.81 (SD 0.78) for implementation climate on a 4-point scale. Perceived knowledge and self-efficacy were higher among nurses with experience of NIV care and previous NIV education, and these associations remained after adjustment. Length of intensive care experience was not independently associated with either variable, and neither was correlated with implementation climate. Importance exceeded present competency for all 35 items. Seven items were identified as priority candidates; ventilator waveform monitoring was the only item selected by both methods, but its classification was not stable across resamples. The self-perceived priorities concentrated on monitoring and recognising treatment failure, competencies that require interpretation of changing physiological data. Needs assessment before programme design can inform the selection of content, provided that its self-report basis and the instability of items near classification thresholds are recognised.

42881432.title: Delayed methotrexate toxicity after initial clearance in a critically ill patient with severe fluid overload.
42881432.abstract: Methotrexate (MTX) toxicity is a life-threatening complication in oncology patients. We report a 19-year-old male with newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma who received high-dose methotrexate as part of induction chemotherapy and initially met protocol-defined serum clearance criteria with suspected delayed MTX toxicity. This prolonged toxicity was due to possible redistribution from extravascular fluid compartments in the setting of severe fluid overload and renal dysfunction. Five weeks after methotrexate administration, a detectable serum methotrexate concentration (0.4 µmol/L) was identified despite no additional exposure. His course was complicated by tumor lysis syndrome, pleural effusions and anasarca, bowel perforations requiring multiple surgeries, acute respiratory distress syndrome, persistent pancytopenia, progressive renal and hepatic dysfunction, recurrent infections, and multiorgan failure. Despite treatment with leucovorin, urine alkalinization, continuous kidney replacement therapy, and high-flux hemodialysis, serum MTX concentrations demonstrated recurrent detectable elevations. This case highlights how altered pharmacokinetics in critical illness may render serum clearance thresholds unreliable and underscores the need for heightened clinical suspicion for delayed drug toxicity in critically ill patients with dynamic volume shifts or unexplained multiorgan dysfunction.

42966070.title: Retrospective review of a novel antithrombotic stewardship program in an Australian intensive care unit.
42966070.abstract: The risk of bleeding and thrombosis is high in critical care settings. Antithrombotic Stewardship (ATS) is an organisational-level intervention which can reduce bleeding and thrombosis in hospitalised patients. However, acceptance for ATS programs on antithrombotic-related care in the critically ill has not been explored. To explore the acceptance of an ATS program involving a recurring multidisciplinary team (MDT) round within an intensive care unit (ICU). Primary outcomes were rates of ATS recommendation and acceptance. Secondary outcomes were rates of clinically relevant bleeding (CRB) and thrombosis in cases where clinical management was suboptimal within 7 days post ATS review. A retrospective, cross-sectional audit was conducted at a 400-bed tertiary referral hospital in metropolitan Sydney, Australia between February 2024 and February 2025. Only inpatients within the 13-bed ICU during a round were included. Twenty-nine meetings were held, resulting in 299 patient reviews, with a mean meeting duration of 20 min (SD 6.4). MDTs occurred where possible, every 1-2 weeks. There was a 35% recommendation and 82% acceptance rate. Most recommendations were treatment changes (87/108 recommendations, 81%). These included VTE prophylaxis initiation (28%), changing VTE prophylaxis drug class (25%), anticoagulant dose change (14%), addition of anticoagulant reversal (9%), change in anticoagulant intensity (5%) and anticoagulant or antiplatelet omission (5%). There were 33 CRB and 15 thrombosis events, most occurred in the absence of detectable clinical error (96%). Implementing an ATS MDT round within the ICU can prompt changes in treatment. Future comparator studies are needed to explore the impact of ATS on patient health outcomes.

42965137.title: Comments on Kroken et al.'s "Long-term frailty trajectory in older ICU survivors requiring mechanical ventilation: a prospective cohort study in Norway"- Author's reply.

42964839.title: Patient-ventilator asynchrony during critical care transport: evidence and framework.
42964839.abstract: Transport of invasively ventilated patients is a necessary but vulnerable phase of critical care, yet patient-ventilator asynchrony (PVA) has rarely been measured directly during transport. This structured narrative review integrates transport studies, ventilator bench evaluations, ICU physiology, and monitoring research, with a targeted PubMed update on 1 October 2026. Transport-associated waveform reports, clinical labels, and treatment records provide different levels of diagnostic certainty. We identified no prospective cohort continuously comparing PVA before, during, and after transport using synchronized ventilator and patient-effort signals; incomplete historical search documentation limits this absence statement. Transport-specific incidence and clinical consequences remain uncertain. Bench performance is device- and condition-dependent, and ICU studies show heterogeneous outcome associations and intervention effects. We therefore propose an unvalidated framework spanning patient vulnerability, circuit integrity, transport ventilator performance, and environmental and operational disturbance. These domains may influence triggering, flow delivery, cycling, and respiratory rhythm through overlapping mechanisms. A proposed safety-first workflow prioritizes effective oxygenation and ventilation, airway-circuit-device assessment, and contextual interpretation of suspected phenotypes. Motion artifact, true triggering disturbances, and indeterminate patterns must be distinguished; advanced effort measurements primarily support research validation. Initial studies should establish synchronized-signal completeness, interpretable recording time, artifact burden, and inter-rater agreement before testing clinical benefit and balancing harms.

42964279.title: Feasibility and barriers to implementing a nurse-led hand hygiene intervention in intensive care units: a mixed-methods study.
42964279.journal: Journal of research in nursing : JRN
42964279.abstract: Hand hygiene (HH) is essential for infection prevention, but compliance in intensive care units (ICUs) often falls short of recommended standards. Leadership-driven audit and feedback could enhance compliance, though its practicality in resource-limited, high-acuity settings is still unclear. To evaluate the feasibility of a nurse-led, real-time HH audit and feedback intervention in ICUs and to explore contextual barriers influencing its implementation. A mixed-methods study was conducted over 6 weeks in two Jordanian ICUs. Fourteen supervisors were trained to deliver digital HH audits and real-time feedback. A total of 128 HH observations were recorded pre- and post-intervention, and qualitative data were obtained through post-intervention semi-structured interviews with 22 supervisors. HH compliance increased from 63.5% to 89.5% (p < 0.001; Cohen's d = 1.29). However, qualitative findings revealed that the intervention was not implemented as intended. Supervisors identified four major barriers: competing workload demands, technological challenges, role ambiguity and lack of managerial reinforcement. Compliance gains were instead attributed to contextual influences, including heightened awareness, peer accountability and observational effects. In resource-limited ICUs, HH improvement efforts should prioritise low-burden, context-sensitive strategies that leverage peer accountability, observational effects and organisational support mechanisms.

42964221.title: Oral colonization patterns according to ventilatory support modality in critically ill patients.
42964221.abstract: To evaluate oral colonization patterns according to ventilatory support modality in critically ill patients, with particular emphasis on colonization involving hospital-associated Gram-negative bacilli because of their relevance to healthcare-associated respiratory infections. A cross-sectional study included 120 adults admitted to two intensive care units in Brazil. Participants were equally allocated into three groups according to ventilatory support modality: no invasive ventilation, endotracheal tube, and tracheostomy. Oral samples collected from the dorsal surface of the tongue were analyzed using conventional culture methods. Oral colonization patterns differed significantly according to ventilatory support modality (p < 0.001). Colonization involving hospital-associated Gram-negative bacilli (isolated or mixed) increased progressively from 45.0% among patients without invasive ventilation to 62.5% among those with an endotracheal tube and 92.5% among tracheostomized patients. Conversely, conventional oral microbiota decreased from 40.0% to 25.0% and 5.0%, respectively. Salivary flow patterns also differed significantly among groups (p = 0.047). Increasing invasiveness of ventilatory support was associated with progressive oral colonization involving hospital-associated Gram-negative bacilli and a concomitant reduction in conventional oral microbiota. Although causality cannot be inferred because of the cross-sectional design, the findings support the concept that the oral cavity may serve as a reservoir of respiratory pathogens in critically ill patients. Characterizing oral colonization patterns according to ventilatory support modality may support infection prevention and control programmes by informing risk stratification and evidence-based oral care strategies in intensive care units.

42963532.title: Types of adult intensive care units and admissions in Türkiye between 2018 and 2023: a nationwide cohort study.
42963532.journal: Canadian journal of anaesthesia = Journal canadien d'anesthesie
42963532.abstract: Türkiye has one of the highest intensive care unit (ICU) bed capacities among middle-income countries but also globally. Nevertheless, little is known about the characteristics of ICUs in Türkiye, their temporal trends, and ICU admissions and readmissions. We sought to analyze the structural characteristics of all adult ICUs and the clinical profiles of ICU admissions across Türkiye. We conducted a retrospective nationwide cohort study using data from the Turkish Ministry of Health National Electronic Database. We analyzed adult ICU admissions across all levels and types over 6 years (2018-2023) and documented patient demographics, comorbidities, admission diagnoses, and ICU outcomes. We retrieved data on 3,362,539 ICU admissions. Among 22 ICU types, mixed ICUs accounted for the highest proportion of admissions (31.4%), followed by coronary (23.7%), anesthesiology (14.3%), medical (6.1%), and surgical (6.0%) ICUs. The proportion of mixed ICU beds decreased from 44.0% in 2018 to 25.1% in 2023. Most ICU beds were in state (public) hospitals (50.8%), followed by private hospitals (34.8%). The number of ICU beds increased from 2019, with a notable rise in state hospitals after 2020. The average number of ICU admissions was 659 per 100,000 population annually. The median patient age was 65 [interquartile range, 39-91] yr, and the ICU mortality was 15.5%. The leading admission diagnoses were respiratory failure (10.1%), cerebrovascular disease (7.1%), and acute kidney injury (5.2%). Hypertension (67.5%) and coronary artery disease (44.8%) were common comorbidities, particularly in nonsurvivors. The 7-day ICU readmission rate was 3.0%. The present comprehensive analysis of ICU admissions in Türkiye between 2018 and 2023 highlights a shift toward specialization with a decrease in mixed ICUs. The impact of ICU diversity on resource use and patient outcomes requires further evaluation.

42963486.title: Empirical linezolid target attainment in critically ill patients: integrating local susceptibility data and dosing strategies.
42963486.abstract: Linezolid is important for treating infections caused by Gram-positive bacteria resistant to first-line agents. Severe infections often require empirical therapy before pathogen identification and susceptibility testing. This evaluation aims to compare different empirical linezolid dosing strategies in intensive care unit (ICU) patients to improve pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic target attainment while minimising toxicities. Three dosing strategies were compared: (i) standard dosing, (ii) therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)-guided dosing, and (iii) a theoretical model-informed precision dosing (MIPD) strategy based on Bayesian forecasting with a population pharmacokinetic model. Each scenario was combined with an ICU-specific minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) distribution comprising more than 19,000 isolates collected over 10 years. Data from 117 critically ill patients with 2184 TDM samples were available. Linezolid resistance was highest in ICU isolates (9.6%) compared with isolates from the intermediate care unit (4.3%), general wards (3.6%), and emergency room (1.6%). Among ICU isolates, resistance increased significantly over the 10-year study period, from 6.3% in 2015 to 11.4% in 2024. Empirical target attainment was 36.6% with standard dosing and 48.5% with TDM-guided dose adaptation, in two different ICU cohorts that showed 35.9% and 59.4% baseline target attainment, respectively. Theoretical MIPD projected target attainment in 71.4-81.6% of patients. After excluding resistant isolates, the corresponding values were 40.5%, 53.7%, and 79.0-90.3%, respectively. Integrating a large contemporary ICU-specific MIC distribution with patient-level pharmacokinetic data, our results suggest MIPD may represent a promising strategy improving target attainment, in contrast to standard regimens and TDM-guided dosing which failed to achieve adequate target exposure in ICU patients.

42962764.title: Longitudinal evaluation of a multidisciplinary infection prevention and control bundle in a high AMR prevalence ICU.
42962764.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a major threat in intensive care units (ICUs). We evaluated changes associated with a multidisciplinary infection prevention and control (IPC) bundle in a high-AMR-prevalence setting. This longitudinal quasi-experimental ICU study (2022-2024) involved sequential, cumulative implementation of a bundle integrating infection prevention, rapid diagnostics and colonization screening, antimicrobial stewardship, and surveillance with data feedback. Hand hygiene compliance increased from 29.5% at baseline to 64.6% during sustainment, while PPE compliance increased from 67.1% to 73.3% after monitoring was introduced. Piperacillin/tazobactam consumption increased (+3.33 DDD/100 patient-days per phase; 95% CI, 1.92-4.73), whereas colistin (-5.85; 95% CI, -9.17 to -2.54) and tigecycline (-2.50; 95% CI, -4.25 to -0.75) decreased. Klebsiella pneumoniae meropenem resistance decreased (OR per phase, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.43-0.69), whereas colistin resistance showed a borderline increase in Acinetobacter baumannii (OR, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.00-1.65). ICU-acquired bloodstream infections decreased across implementation phases for CRE (IRR per phase, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.26-0.51) and CRAB (IRR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.46-0.68), as did CLABSI (IRR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.56-0.73) and ICU-acquired rectal colonization with CRE (IRR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.63-0.84) and CRAB (IRR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.70-0.87), whereas CRPA ICU-acquired colonization increased (IRR, 1.56; 95% CI, 1.32-1.85). IPC bundle implementation was followed by improved IPC practices and reductions in several ICU-acquired infections and colonization outcomes; continued surveillance and stewardship are essential.

42961348.title: An Approach to Navigating the Lorazepam Challenge Test for Catatonia in Critical Care Settings.
42961348.abstract: Catatonia often occurs in the setting of psychiatric illness; however, it is also found in other medical conditions, especially within critical care settings. The lorazepam challenge test (LCT) is a key diagnostic and therapeutic intervention for catatonia; however, no specific guidance exists for patients within the intensive care unit (ICU). This review synthesizes psychiatric and critical care literature to propose a structured LCT framework adapted to the ICU. Specific indications and contraindications across gradients of catatonia likelihood and medical complexity are reviewed, along with practical dosing and monitoring recommendations. An interdisciplinary collaborative workflow is also outlined along with post-LCT documentation standards. Our structured approach offers a practical foundation for future standardized protocols, education, and catatonia research in critical care.

42959610.title: Comprehensive Echocardiographic Assessment of Right Ventricular Afterload and Right Ventricular-Pulmonary Arterial Coupling in the Intensive Care Unit.
42959610.abstract: Right ventricular (RV) dysfunction is common in critical illness, yet RV afterload cannot be adequately characterized by pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) alone. Bedside echocardiography can estimate right atrial and pulmonary artery pressures, suggest increased pulmonary vascular resistance, and assess RV-pulmonary arterial coupling while simultaneously evaluating RV size, systolic function, septal interaction, and forward flow. Peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity combined with right atrial pressure estimates RV systolic pressure and, in the absence of outflow obstruction, approximates PASP. Pulmonary regurgitation velocities provide complementary estimates of mean and end-diastolic pulmonary artery pressure, whereas pulmonary artery acceleration time, RV outflow tract velocity-time integral, and systolic notching provide information regarding pulmonary vascular load and forward flow. A multiparametric assessment of RV systolic performance is essential because tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion, tissue Doppler systolic velocity, fractional area change, RV free-wall strain, and three-dimensional RV ejection fraction assess different aspects of contraction. The tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion/PASP ratio relates longitudinal systolic performance to pulmonary pressure but remains a surrogate of coupling, without a universal intensive care threshold. These measurements depend on image quality, loading conditions, and ventilatory support and may differ substantially from invasive hemodynamics in individual patients. Their greatest value lies in integrated physiologic assessment and serial reassessment after treatment. Echocardiography complements right heart catheterization, which remains necessary when precise hemodynamic classification or measurement of pulmonary artery wedge pressure, cardiac output, or pulmonary vascular resistance will change management.

42959017.title: Incidence and Outcomes of Acute Kidney Injury in Critically Ill Patients: A Retrospective Study at a Tertiary Care Hospital.
42959017.abstract: Acute kidney injury is common among critically ill patients and is associated with longer ICU stay, higher resource use and increased mortality. Evidence from low- and middle-income countries, including Nepal, remains limited. This study describes the incidence, severity distribution and clinical outcomes of AKI in a tertiary care ICU. We conducted a hospital based retrospective observational study at Dhulikhel Hospital, Nepal. All adults admitted to the ICU from 1 st may 2023 to 30 th April 2024 were screened using ICU registry. AKI was defined and staged using KDIGO serum criteria. Demographic data, comorbidities, ICU interventions and outcomes were extracted. Associations were examined using appropriate statistical tests. Among 1113 patients, 1064 were enrolled for analysis. The incidence of AKI was 29.6%. Patients with AKI were older (median age 60 vs 55 years, p < 0.001), had longer ICU stays (median 3 vs 2 days, p < 0.001), were more frequently on invasive mechanical ventilation (39.6%vs 26%, p < 0.001). Type 2 diabetes mellitus was significantly associated with AKI (39.0% vs 28.0%, p = 0.001). AKI severity correlated with worse outcomes including higher mortality and adverse outcomes increasing from 12.7% in patients without AKI to 38% in stage 3 AKI. Renal replacement therapy was required in 2.3% of patients, mainly in stage 2 and 3 AKI. Acute kidney injury is a common and a serious complication among critically ill patients, associated with increased mortality and prolonged ICU stay. Early recognition and targeted management strategies, particularly for high-risk groups, are needed in resource limited settings.

42957972.title: Impact of a Nurse-Led, Target-Directed Light Sedation Strategy on the Incidence of Delirium in Septic Patients in the Emergency Intensive Care Unit.
42957972.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the impact of a nurse-led, target-directed light sedation strategy on delirium incidence and short-term outcomes in septic patients undergoing invasive mechanical ventilation in the emergency intensive care unit (EICU).MethodsWe analyzed 221 consecutive septic patients requiring invasive mechanical ventilation for more than 24 h at a single center (January 2022-May 2024). Based on a sedation protocol change, patients were assigned to conventional sedation group (control, n = 123) or nurse-led, target-directed light sedation group (exposed, n = 98). The primary outcome was delirium incidence. Secondary outcomes included delirium-free days (DFD-28), ventilator-free days (VFD-28), mechanical ventilation duration, EICU length of stay, and 28-day mortality. Multivariable logistic regression examined the independent association between the nurse-led strategy and delirium risk.ResultsDelirium occurred less frequently in the nurse-led sedation group than in the control group (20.4% vs 37.4%, P = .007). The exposed group had shorter mechanical ventilation duration and EICU length of stay (both P < .05), whereas VFD-28 did not differ significantly between groups. The two groups did not differ significantly in 28-day mortality (28.6% vs 26.0%, P = .671) or in the rate of airway-related adverse events. On multivariable analysis, the nurse-led strategy was independently associated with a lower risk of delirium (OR = 0.428, 95% CI: 0.215-0.854, P = .016). Subgroup analyses showed that this protective benefit was consistent across age strata, disease severity levels, and comorbidity burden.ConclusionIn septic patients undergoing mechanical ventilation, a nurse-led, target-directed light sedation strategy was associated with reduced delirium incidence, shorter mechanical ventilation duration, and decreased EICU length of stay, without increasing adverse events. However, no improvement in 28-day mortality was observed. Further validation through multicenter prospective randomized controlled trials is warranted to assess long-term efficacy and safety.

42839267.title: VIDD or CIADD? The ventilator remains a bona fide culprit.
42839267.abstract: Rosà and colleagues recently proposed that mechanical ventilation (MV) may not be the primary driver of diaphragm dysfunction in critically ill patients, advocating the term "critical illness-associated diaphragm dysfunction" (CIADD) over "ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction" (VIDD). While we support distinguishing VIDD from CIADD, we contend that the review's central conclusion underestimates the causal role of MV itself.This commentary addresses three questions in turn. First, does MV injure the diaphragm under controlled conditions? Here the evidence is strong: brain-dead donor studies-dismissed by the authors as a "unique patient category"-are a uniquely informative, though not pure, human model of controlled MV exposure, and their dismissal creates an unfalsifiable position. Second, how much does MV contribute to diaphragm dysfunction in critically ill patients? This is considerably less certain: the molecular abnormalities observed in critically ill patients (ubiquitin-proteasome activation, RyR1 calcium leak, mitochondrial oxidative stress) coincide with pathways that MV reliably induces in controlled animal experiments, providing biological plausibility-though not proof-that MV contributes to the molecular phenotype of critical illness. Third, do MV and critical illness interact? We propose that CIADD should serve as an umbrella term encompassing VIDD as a distinct mechanistic subtype-rather than replacing it-analogous to how "pneumonia" subsumes VAP, HAP, and CAP, and we propose three differentiated model types for future research: pure VIDD models, pure CIADD models, and combined models with factorial design.VIDD and CIADD are mechanistically distinct but interacting entities. Future research should employ models that minimize confounding from critical illness to isolate ventilation-specific injury pathways. Importantly, establishing that VIDD exists is not equivalent to establishing that preventing VIDD is beneficial; clinical trials are needed to demonstrate the feasibility and benefit of diaphragm-protective strategies. Diminishing MV's role risks undermining the mechanistic foundation of diaphragm-protective ventilation strategies.

42881072.title: Haemodynamic effects of induction agents are context-dependent. Comment on Br J Anaesth Advance Access published on Apr 7, 2026, doi: 10.1016/j.bja.2026.02.023.

42881055.title: Comparing High-Flow Nasal Cannula Therapy and Conventional Oxygen Therapy in Adult Patients Post-Cardiac Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
42881055.journal: Journal of cardiothoracic and vascular anesthesia
42881055.abstract: Cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass structurally alters respiratory mechanics and carries a substantial risk of postoperative morbidity. Historically, patients have routinely received conventional oxygen therapy (COT) following extubation. High- flow nasal cannula (HCNC) therapy has emerged as an innovative respiratory support system. By synthesizing all currently available high-quality randomized controlled trials (RCTs), this study aimed to rigorously evaluate the efficacy and safety of HFNC compared to COT, focusing primarily on determining the need for escalation of respiratory support. A thorough electronic search was carried out in the PubMed, Embase, and Scopus databases from their inception to May 2026. Only RCTs were considered for analysis. A random-effects model was applied to compute pooled estimates and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). A total of 11 RCTs, comprising 2473 patients, were included in this systematic review and meta-analysis. HFNC had a statistically significant effect on reducing the requirement for escalation of respiratory support (risk ratio [RR] = 0.71; 95% CI, 0.55-0.93; p = 0.01). HFNC had a statistically significant effect on improving the arterial partial pressure of oxygen, as well as forced expiratory volume in 1 second, while also increasing delirium complications (RR = 3.63; 95% CI, 1.80-7.30; p = 0.0003). There were no statistically significant differences between the 2 approaches in the other secondary clinical and resource utilization outcomes, including intubation, overall mortality, hospital length of stay, intensive care unit length of stay, and postoperative atrial fibrillation. In adult patients recovering from cardiac surgery, HFNC therapy improves oxygenation and significantly curtails the need to escalate respiratory support compared to COT. However, these physiologic and intermediate clinical benefits do not translate into reductions in mortality, reintubation rate, or hospital length of stay and may come at the cost of increased postoperative delirium.

42879942.title: Emergency medicine pharmacotherapy literature of 2025.
42879942.journal: The American journal of emergency medicine
42879942.abstract: The purpose of this article is to summarize pharmacotherapy-related emergency medicine (EM) literature indexed in 2025. Articles were selected using a modified Delphi approach. The table of contents from predetermined journals were reviewed and independently evaluated via the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) system by paired authors. Pharmacotherapy-related publications deemed to be GRADE 1A and 1B were reviewed by the collective group for inclusion in the review. This article synthesizes and evaluates findings from 7 randomized controlled trials, 10 guidelines, clinical policies, position statements, or consensus recommendations, and 11 meta-analyses, providing critical insight into their potential clinical impact. Covered topics include guideline or policy updates on advanced cardiac life support, rapid sequence intubation, tranexamic acid in trauma, acute coronary syndromes, and hypertension. Randomized controlled trials covering sedative use in rapid sequence intubation, treatment of sexually transmitted infections and bacterial vaginosis, sodium bicarbonate for severe acidemia and acute kidney injury in the critically ill, and thrombolytic therapy beyond traditional time windows for ischemic stroke are also reviewed. Additional topics include nebulized and low-dose ketamine for analgesia, erector spinae plane block for renal colic, two-bag versus three-bag acetylcysteine regimens for acetaminophen overdose, QT prolongation in antipsychotic overdose, and naltrexone for opioid dependence.

42879641.title: Hematological indices as predictors of in-hospital adverse outcomes in patients with COVID-19.
42879641.journal: Brazilian journal of medical and biological research = Revista brasileira de pesquisas medicas e biologicas
42879641.abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic required medical teams to make rational decisions with limited resources, especially in Brazil. Various diagnostic tools, clinical guidelines, and existing indices were adopted to predict the risk of death and other adverse outcomes. The objective of this study was to validate three hematological indices [neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), and lymphocyte-monocyte ratio (LMR)] for predicting adverse hospital outcomes in patients with COVID-19 in an observational cohort at a hospital in northeastern Brazil between April 2020 and October 2021. Hematological indices were calculated based on admission blood counts and correlated with hospital outcomes: in-hospital death, invasive mechanical ventilation, and renal replacement therapy. The analysis determined the frequencies of outcomes, established index thresholds, and assessed their association and accuracy and factors associated with hospital survival. Intra-hospital outcomes reflected disease severity; 34.62% of patients required admission to the ICU, 26.21% invasive mechanical ventilation, 4.2% renal replacement therapy, and 21.04% died. Advanced age, ICU requirement, and higher NLR were associated with higher risk of death. Multivariate analysis identified NLR as the only index associated with worse prognosis, with a cutoff point of 5.24 at hospital admission, showing a sensitivity of 84.0% and accuracy of 86.9%. The negative predictive value of 95.52% was highly significant, assisting hospital management by focusing efforts on higher-risk patients. These findings highlight the predictive value of the NLR, PLR, and LMR indices as valuable markers for risk stratification in patients hospitalized with COVID-19, offering a broader view of prognosis and guiding more personalized management and care strategies.

42879513.title: Development and Validation of End-Of-Life Indicators for Dialysis Patients: A National Consensus Study in Taiwan.
42879513.journal: The American journal of hospice & palliative care
42879513.abstract: BackgroundIdentifying end-of-life (EOL) dialysis patients who may benefit from palliative care remains challenging in Asian healthcare settings where relational autonomy predominates over individual decision-making. We conducted a national consensus study in Taiwan during 2015-2016 to develop validated EOL indicators for dialysis patients, with findings subsequently validated through a decade of clinical experience including the COVID-19 pandemic.MethodsWe conducted a three-phase study: (1) systematic literature review; (2) two-round expert focus groups using the RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method with 15 multidisciplinary experts; and (3) national survey of nephrologists from 624 dialysis facilities. Nine indicators were evaluated using 9-point Likert scales. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses identified latent constructs.ResultsOf 624 facilities, 337 responded (54.0%), yielding 254 nephrologists with complete responses (22.6% of registered specialists). Two indicators achieved high consensus (≥90%) for both hospice/dying care and advance care planning: prolonged mechanical ventilation (PMV) with dialysis in unconscious state, and PMV with multi-organ failure. Factor analysis identified three EOL patient subgroups: ventilator-dependent, critically ill, and functionally dependent, with acceptable CFA model fit (χ2 = 27.6, df = 19, P = 0.091; RMSEA = 0.042; CFI = 0.99). ACP ratings yielded a two-factor structure with adequate fit (χ2 = 35.5, df = 20, P = 0.018; RMSEA = 0.055).ConclusionsDialysis patients with PMV combined with unconsciousness or multi-organ failure represent the highest-consensus EOL indicators in Taiwan. These validated findings offer actionable guidance for hospice and end-of-life care referral within healthcare systems characterized by relational autonomy and collective family-patient-clinician deliberation.

42878614.title: Open Visiting Policy and Delirium in Adult Patients in ICUs: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials.
authors: and the Padova Intensive Care Unit (PADUA-ICU) Group
42878614.abstract: To critically evaluate the comparative effects of open or flexible family presence policies vs. restricted or traditional family presence policies on the occurrence of delirium and other major outcomes among adult patients admitted to ICUs. We conducted a comprehensive electronic search of MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from inception to November 21, 2025. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing open or flexible vs. restricted ICU visiting policies in adult patients. The primary outcome extracted was delirium occurrence. Secondary outcomes included the duration of invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), ICU length of stay, hospital-acquired infections, and ICU mortality. Thirteen RCTs comprising 3861 patients were included. Random-effects models showed that compared with restricted policies, open/flexible family presence reduced delirium occurrence (risk ratio [RR], 0.48; 95% CI, 0.29-0.81; low certainty) and IMV duration (mean difference [MD], -0.36 d; 95% CI, -0.46 to -0.26 d; low certainty). The intervention did not affect the ICU length of stay (MD, 4.21 d; 95% CI, -4.65 to 13.07 d; very low certainty), the rates of hospital-acquired infections (RR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.81-1.23; low certainty), or ICU mortality (RR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.72-1.08; very low certainty). Open/flexible ICU family presence may reduce delirium and shorten the duration of IMV slightly, without increasing infections or ICU mortality, although the certainty of evidence is low and heterogeneity remains substantial.

42877799.title: Progressive Dysphagia Revealing Glioma: Diagnostic Overshadowing by Suspected Myasthenia Gravis.
42877799.journal: European journal of case reports in internal medicine
42877799.abstract: Progressive dysphagia in older adults presents a diagnostic challenge with a broad differential including neuromuscular, structural and malignant causes. Dysphagia associated with aspiration may lead to significant respiratory compromise requiring intensive care management. We report the case of a 78-year-old patient with rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate who presented with progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids, weight loss, and cough. She subsequently developed aspiration pneumonia complicated by repeated type 2 respiratory failure and required mechanical ventilation. Initial investigations focused on aspiration pneumonitis and possible neuromuscular disease, particularly myasthenia gravis, given the presence of bulbar symptoms and an insensate epiglottis on nasendoscopy. However, subsequent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated a glioma explaining the progressive bulbar dysfunction. This case demonstrates diagnostic overshadowing, as recurrent type 2 respiratory failure was repeatedly managed as aspiration pneumonia, delaying the diagnosis of glioma. Early neuroimaging should be considered in patients with progressive dysphagia when initial investigations fail to explain symptoms. Progressive dysphagia in an older adult warrants a broad differential - neuromuscular, structural and intracranial causes - not just aspiration-related respiratory disease.A bulbar syndrome (insensate epiglottis, dysphagia) can be produced by an intracranial lesion as well as by myasthenia gravis; negative acetylcholine receptor antibodies do not fully exclude either possibility and should not halt the diagnostic search.Recurrent type 2 respiratory failure that responds poorly to treatment for presumed aspiration pneumonia should prompt reconsideration of the working diagnosis, rather than repeated management of the same presumed cause - a pattern of diagnostic overshadowing and anchoring bias.Early neuroimaging should be considered when dysphagia and respiratory failure evolve atypically or fail to resolve despite appropriate treatment, as magnetic resonance imaging was ultimately pivotal in revealing the underlying glioma in this case.

42877130.title: Identification of Heterogenous Treatment Response to Corticosteroids Among Patients With Ventilator-Dependent Respiratory Failure: An Observational Cohort Study.
42877130.abstract: Corticosteroids increasingly are recommended as adjunctive treatments in critical illness syndromes; however, the existing literature supporting their benefit remains uncertain. Ventilator-dependent respiratory failure (VDRF) is a critical illness syndrome with low-acuity and high-acuity subphenotypes identifiable with electronic health record (EHR) data. Do conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) from corticosteroids with respect to hospital mortality differ by clinical subphenotypes in VDRF? In this multicenter, retrospective observational cohort, we measured CATE by clinical subphenotype among patients > 18 years of age receiving > 48 hours of mechanical ventilation with adjusted doubly robust estimator models using EHR data from the first 24 hours after initiation of mechanical ventilation. Low-acuity and high-acuity subphenotypes from the Medical University of South Carolina (MUSC) and Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care III (MIMIC-III) cohorts showed heterogeneous CATEs on mortality resulting from corticosteroid treatments (low-acuity MUSC, -4.1%; low-acuity MIMIC-III, -5.2%; high-acuity MUSC, 9.3%; and high-acuity MIMIC-III, 4.5%) with mean differences of 13.4% (95% CI, 11.8%-14.9%) and 9.7% (95% CI, 9.3%-10.1%), respectively. Protective effects in the low-acuity subphenotype were attenuated among patients with ARDS, pneumonia, or sepsis identified by administrative diagnosis codes; however, the risk of harm was consistent for the high-acuity subphenotype. Our results show that clinical subphenotypes in VDRF can identify heterogeneous treatment effects from corticosteroids. These findings support the usefulness of clinically derived subphenotypes and may inform enrichment strategies for future prospective clinical trials.

42876985.title: Development and validation of a prediction model for hypernatremia in patients with severe burns.
42876985.abstract: Hypernatremia is a prevalent and serious electrolyte disturbance in patients with severe burns, associated with significantly increased mortality and prolonged ICU stays. Early identification of high-risk patients could enable timely preventive interventions; however, practical tools for individualized risk stratification are currently lacking. This study aimed to develop and validate a nomogram and a web-based calculator for the early prediction of hypernatremia in patients with severe burns. A total of 592 patients with burns covering ≥30% total body surface area were retrospectively included and randomly assigned to a training cohort (n = 415) and an internal validation cohort (n = 177). Six independent predictors were identified: TBSA, mechanical ventilation, blood urea nitrogen ≥10 mmol/L, sepsis, glucose ≥9 mmol/L, and inhalation injury. The nomogram achieved an apparent C-index of 0.929 and a bootstrap-corrected C-index of 0.923 in the training cohort, and a C-index of 0.953 in the internal validation cohort. Using dual cutoffs of 90 and 135 points, the low cutoff yielded negative predictive values of 96.4% and 98.1%, and the high cutoff yielded positive predictive values of 75.4% and 65.3% in the training and internal validation cohorts, respectively. The nomogram and web-based calculator provide accurate, individualized risk prediction, facilitating early identification of high-risk individuals and supporting preventive strategies.

42876922.title: The Prognostic Value of PaCO(2) on the Response to Noninvasive Ventilation in Patients with AECOPD Complicated by Type II Respiratory Failure.
42876922.journal: International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
42876922.abstract: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) complicated by Type II respiratory failure frequently requires noninvasive ventilation (NIV). However, 10-25% of patients fail NIV and require intubation. The optimal timing and threshold of partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO2) for predicting NIV failure remain unclear. In this two-center retrospective cohort study of 676 patients with AECOPD and Type II respiratory failure treated with NIV between 2012 and 2025, we used multivariable logistic regression and restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis (4 knots at the 5th, 35th, 65th, and 95th percentiles) to assess the dose-response relationship between 24-hour post-treatment PaCO2 and NIV failure. NIV failure occurred in 73 patients (10.8%). After full adjustment for age, heart rate, white blood cell count, hemoglobin, albumin, blood urea nitrogen, D-dimer, and baseline HACOR score, each 1 mmHg increase in 24h PaCO2 was associated with 3% higher odds of NIV failure (OR 1.03, 95% CI 1.01-1.06). RCS analysis revealed a nonlinear L-shaped association (overall P < 0.001; nonlinear P < 0.01), with a threshold at 60.2 mmHg. Below this threshold, no significant association was observed; above it, odds increased markedly; this threshold requires further external validation in independent patient populations. After adjustment for confounding variables, the fully‑adjusted multivariable model yielded an AUC of 0.805 (95% CI 0.751-0.860). A 24-hour post-treatment PaCO2 exceeding 60.2 mmHg identifies patients at high risk for NIV failure. This readily available bedside measure may guide escalation decisions in AECOPD with Type II respiratory failure.

42875240.title: [Application of a spontaneous breathing trial based on high-flow oxygen therapy in weaning of mechanically ventilated patients].
42875240.journal: Zhonghua wei zhong bing ji jiu yi xue
42875240.abstract: To evaluate the application efficacy of a spontaneous breathing trial (SBT) based on high-flow oxygen therapy (HFOT) during the weaning process in mechanically ventilated patients. A randomized controlled trial was conducted. A total of 163 patients undergoing invasive mechanical ventilation admitted to the Department of Critical Care Medicine, Zhongda Hospital, Southeast University, from September 2024 to July 2025 were enrolled and randomly assigned to the HFOT group (80 cases) or the pressure support ventilation (PSV) group (83 cases). The HFOT group received SBT based on HFOT, while the PSV group received SBT based on PSV. Baseline data were collected and compared between the two groups, and adverse events during SBT were recorded. The primary outcome was the success rate of extubation within 48 hours. Secondary outcomes included vital signs, sputum grade, arterial blood gas parameters measured before SBT and 30 minutes after SBT initiation, SBT success rate, and prognostic outcomes [duration of mechanical ventilation, length of intensive care unit (ICU) stay, hospitalization costs, ICU mortality, in-hospital mortality, and 28-day mortality]. A total of 163 mechanically ventilated patients were included, with 80 in the HFOT group and 83 in the PSV group. There were no statistically significant differences in baseline data or prognostic outcomes between the two groups. The SBT success rates were 100% (80/80) in the HFOT group and 98.8% (82/83) in the PSV group, and the 48-hour extubation success rates were 87.5% (70/80) and 80.5% (66/82), respectively, with no statistically significant differences (both P>0.05). At 30 minutes after SBT initiation, the heart rate (HR0.5) and the decrease in HR (ΔHR0.5) in the HFOT group were significantly lower than those in the PSV group [HR0.5: 87.10±12.73 vs. 94.28±13.60; ΔHR0.5: 0.0 (-3.0, 2.0) vs. -1.0 (-5.0, 1.0); both P<0.05]. No significant differences were observed in other vital signs, sputum grade, or arterial blood gas parameters between the two groups. No safety events occurred in either group during the trial, indicating good safety. Subgroup analysis showed statistically significant interactions between intervention modality and both age and duration of mechanical ventilation (both P<0.05). In patients aged≥65 years, the ICU length of stay in the HFOT group was significantly shorter by a mean of 83.12 hours [95% confidence interval (95%CI) was -151.28 to -14.96] compared with the PSV group. In patients with mechanical ventilation duration≥24 hours, the ICU length of stay in the HFOT group was significantly shorter by a mean of 157.40 hours (95%CI was -254.60 to -60.20) compared with the PSV group. SBT based on HFOT is safe for weaning mechanically ventilated patients and offers certain physiological advantages in improving HR. In elderly patients (≥65 years) and those with prolonged mechanical ventilation (≥24 hours), HFOT-based SBT can significantly shorten ICU length of stay, but it does not show a clear advantage in improving the 48-hour extubation success rate.

42875150.title: Continuous wound infiltration with local anesthetics in adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery: A PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis.
42875150.journal: Chinese medical sciences journal = Chung-kuo i hsueh k'o hsueh tsa chih
42875150.abstract: Effective postoperative analgesia is critical to recovery after cardiac surgery. Continuous wound infiltration (CWI) with local anesthetics (LAs) has been proposed as an opioid-sparing adjunct, but its efficacy beyond pain control and its safety profile remain incompletely defined. We conducted a PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing CWI with control in adult cardiac surgery. PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from inception to August 30, 2025, and updated on April 2, 2026. Primary outcomes were postoperative Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) pain scores and cumulative morphine consumption. Secondary outcomes included mechanical ventilation duration, length of stay, mortality, complications, patient satisfaction, and adverse events. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE). Twelve RCTs involving 2,117 patients were included. CWI significantly reduced VAS during mobilization at 24 h (MD=-0.93, 95% confidence interval [CI]: -1.53--0.33, P = 0.002) and 48 h (MD=-0.80, 95% CI: -1.17--0.44, P < 0.001), and decreased 48-hour morphine consumption (MD=-8.10 mg, 95% CI: -13.41--2.79, P = 0.003). No significant effects were observed on VAS at rest, mechanical ventilation duration, ICU or hospital length of stay, mortality, or major cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal, gastrointestinal complications, or postoperative infections. Patient satisfaction was higher with CWI. Technical complications were uncommon, and no clinically significant LA toxicity was reported. In adult cardiac surgery, CWI with LAs modestly improves analgesia during mobilization and reduces opioid requirements without clear improvement in major clinical outcomes or length of stay. CWI appears safe and feasible and may serve as an adjunct in multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia strategies. Further adequately powered trials are warranted to define its comparative effectiveness within contemporary enhanced recovery after surgery pathways.

42874912.title: High-Frequency Chest Wall Oscillation in Acute Respiratory Failure With Bronchial Hypersecretion: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
42874912.abstract: Airway secretion retention is common in patients with acute respiratory failure (ARF), particularly in those requiring noninvasive respiratory support (NIRS). High-frequency chest wall oscillation (HFCWO) may improve airway clearance but critical care evidence remains limited. Does adding HFCWO to standard care improve clinical outcomes in patients with bronchial hypersecretion and ARF requiring NIRS? We conducted a single-center randomized controlled trial in a RICU. Patients with ARF requiring NIRS, including high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) and/or noninvasive ventilation (NIV), bronchial hypersecretion, and ineffective cough (peak cough expiratory flow <270 L/min) were randomized 1:1 to HFCWO plus standard care or standard care alone. The primary endpoint was therapeutic bronchoscopy. Secondary endpoints included hospital length of stay (LOS), RICU-LOS, NIRS duration, endotracheal intubation and mortality. Outcomes were analyzed using unadjusted and adjusted models accounting for age, sex, and main cause of hospitalization. Eighty-eight patients were enrolled (44 HFCWO, 44 control), with comparable baseline characteristics. Bronchoscopy was required in 6 patients (13.6%) versus 14 (31.8%) (unadjusted p=0.042); after adjustment the association did not retain statistical significance (adjusted OR 0.336, 95% CI 0.111-1.021; p=0.055). Secondary outcomes, analyzed without correction for multiple testing, are exploratory. Hospital stay (12 [10-15.5] vs 16.5 [13-21] days) and RICU stay (8 [7-10.5] vs 12 [9-17] days) were shorter, with adjusted reductions of 4.5 and 3.6 days. HFNC duration was shorter (6 [4-8] vs 9.5 [6-11.5] days) and remained significant after adjustment, whereas the reduction in NIV duration did not (adjusted p=0.166). No patient required intubation and mortality did not differ. In this exploratory trial, HFCWO did not significantly reduce the need for therapeutic bronchoscopy after adjustment. Associated reductions in LOS and HFNC duration are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in adequately powered multicenter trials. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05751707; Tuscany Ethics Committee (Protocol: 21987-10/17/2022).

42874749.title: COMPREHENSIVE ORAL CARE IS ASSOCIATED WITH A SIGNIFICANT DECREASE IN VENTILATOR-ASSOCIATED PNEUMONIA: A SINGLE CENTER PROSPECTIVE COHORT STUDY.
42874749.abstract: Mechanically ventilated patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) are at risk for developing ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), with a 13% mortality rate and cost of $50,000 per patient. Toothbrushing is associated with positive outcomes, including lower VAP rates. Electric toothbrushes (eTBs) have greater effectiveness in the general population compared with manual toothbrushes (mTBs), and eTBs may provide benefits to ventilated patients. The aim of the study was to evaluate VAP rates for patients receiving a comprehensive oral care protocol (COCP) including an eTB versus a standard oral care protocol (SOCP) including an mTB. We conducted a prospective cohort study in a tertiary hospital's ICUs. SOCP or COCP consisting of an electric toothbrush was followed. VAP rates and hospital costs were compared between groups. Our study included 72 ICU patients (63.9% male, mean age 53.5±16.6 years). Patients treated with COCP were less likely to develop VAP (2.6% vs 21.2%, P=0.020), had significantly fewer ventilation days (5.4±1.8 vs 6.2±1.3, P=0.031), and fewer ICU days (9.0±5.6 vs 13.8±9.1, P=0.012). The COCP group had significantly fewer VAPs per 1,000 patient ventilation days, 1 in 209 days, or 4.8 (0.1-26.7) events per 1,000 ventilation days versus standard oral care with 7 in 190 days or 36.8 (14.8-75.9), P=0.037. Cost savings if COCP would have been used in the SOCP group of 33 patients were estimated at $283,428. We compared standard versus comprehensive oral care protocols. Significantly fewer patients treated with the comprehensive protocol developed VAP and hospital savings were significant.

42874048.title: Case Report: Veno-Arteriovenous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Management of Pheochromocytoma-Induced Cardiac Arrest in a Post-Partum Patient.
42874048.abstract: A 34-year-old woman, 2 days post-partum, was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for management of hypertensive crisis and respiratory failure. An 18-cm left adrenal mass was found on computed tomography (CT), suspicious for a pheochromocytoma. After cardiac arrest, the patient was placed on veno-arteriovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (V-AV ECMO) given recurrent destabilizing arrhythmias. After successful ECMO decannulation, the patient underwent an uncomplicated resection of her adrenal mass. Although VA-ECMO has been used to support patients with pheochromocytoma, this appears to be the first published case describing the use of a V-AV configuration in the management of a complex cardiac arrest.

42873237.title: [Acute heart failure-management during the first 120 min : Approach for early stabilization and decongestion].
42873237.abstract: Acute heart failure (AHF) is among the most common causes of emergency department, intermediate care, and intensive care unit admission and remains associated with substantial early mortality despite advances in contemporary therapy. The first 120 min of management are particularly critical, as this period determines not only respiratory and hemodynamic stabilization, but also trigger identification, decongestion strategy, and the foundation for subsequent prognostic improvement. This CME article provides a practical, phenotype-based approach to the early management of AHF. The proposed strategy is centered on the rapid classification of patients according to congestion ("wet" vs. "dry") and perfusion ("warm" vs. "cold") status. Stabilization and diagnostic work-up must occur simultaneously. Early assessment should focus on identifying acute coronary syndrome, clinically relevant arrhythmias, hypertensive crisis, pulmonary embolism, structural heart disease, and infectious triggers. In addition to clinical examination, electrocardiography, blood gas analysis, and biomarkers, point-of-care ultrasound with lung ultrasound and focused echocardiography play a pivotal role in the first-line evaluation. From a therapeutic perspective, early noninvasive ventilation in cardiogenic pulmonary edema, prompt vasodilation in hypertensive presentations, and effective decongestion with intravenous loop diuretics constitute the core interventions. In cases of insufficient response, escalation strategies such as sequential nephron blockade or selective use of vasoactive agents should be considered. Structured reassessment at short intervals is essential to detect persistent congestion, evolving hypoperfusion, inadequate therapeutic response, or overlooked differential diagnoses. The article emphasizes that successful acute management must already establish the transition toward guideline-directed long-term therapy during the first hours of hospitalization, including early initiation of evidence-based heart failure medication once hemodynamic stabilization has been achieved.

42871886.title: Anesthetic Management of a Patient With Myasthenia Gravis Undergoing Thoracoscopic Thymectomy: A Case Report and Literature Review.
42871886.abstract: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder characterized by fluctuating skeletal muscle weakness and fatigability. Perioperative management is challenging because patients may have bulbar or respiratory muscle involvement and altered sensitivity to neuromuscular blocking agents, increasing the risk of postoperative respiratory failure and myasthenic crisis. Thymectomy is an established therapeutic option in selected patients with myasthenia gravis and may be performed using minimally invasive thoracoscopic techniques. We report the anesthetic management of a 48-year-old man with generalized acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody-positive myasthenia gravis (MGFA class IIb) scheduled for thoracoscopic thymectomy. The patient had a recent relapse with diplopia, dysphagia, and easy fatigability, which improved after medical therapy. Preoperative optimization included intravenous immunoglobulin therapy for four days. General anesthesia was induced with propofol and remifentanil without initial neuromuscular blockade. Tracheal intubation was facilitated using video laryngoscopy after topical lidocaine. Anesthesia was maintained with sevoflurane, and invasive monitoring was established. Because of the surgical requirement for improved thoracoscopic visualization, a reduced dose of rocuronium was administered intraoperatively under train-of-four monitoring. At the end of surgery, neuromuscular blockade was reversed with sugammadex, and the patient was successfully extubated and transferred to the intensive care unit in stable condition. This case highlights the importance of careful preoperative optimization, avoidance of neuromuscular blocking agents when possible, quantitative neuromuscular monitoring, and individualized use of low-dose rocuronium with sugammadex reversal when muscle relaxation is required during thoracoscopic thymectomy in patients with myasthenia gravis.

42871854.title: Mechanical ventilation in acute brain injury.
42871854.abstract: Acute brain injury (ABI) includes traumatic brain injury, subarachnoid and intracerebral haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke and global hypoxic-ischaemic injury, and patients often require admission to intensive care. Although pathologically heterogeneous, they share common mechanisms of primary injury followed by secondary brain injury. Systemic derangements such as hypoxaemia, dysregulated carbon dioxide tension and elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) may exacerbate secondary injury and should be avoided. Patients with ABI often require invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), and of these up to 19-22% may develop acute respiratory distress syndrome. Lung-protective ventilation (LPV) strategies using low tidal volumes and moderate positive end-expiratory pressure to minimise ventilator-induced lung injury are established practices in patients requiring IMV. However, strict application of LPV principles may conflict with neuro-protective goals, particularly carbon dioxide control to optimise cerebral blood flow and avoid rises in ICP. This review examines the physiological tension between lung and brain protection, focusing on neuro-respiratory interactions and brain-lung crosstalk. We synthesise the evidence on ventilatory strategies in the context of patients with ABI, discuss the implications for neurological and pulmonary outcomes, and highlight the need for an integrated, individualised approach to ventilation in these patients.

42871818.title: Outcomes of small-size graft in highly urgent living donor liver transplantation: Korean national data.
42871818.abstract: The major concern for living donor liver transplantation (LDLT) is the selection of donor graft size because small grafts are often unable to meet metabolic demands or fail to function after implantation in highly urgent LDLT (HU-LDLT). We aim to compare the outcomes between the small graft volume group (graft-to-recipient weight ratio, GRWR <0.8%) and the non-small graft volume group (GRWR ≥0.8%) in the national data of HU-LDLT cases in Korea. We conducted a retrospective analysis of Korean Network of Organ Sharing (KONOS) data involving consecutive HU-LDLT patients between 2017 and 2021. The proportion of the small graft group (GRWR <0.8%) was 7.6% (n=30). The overall survival and graft survival in the small-graft group were inferior to those in the non-small graft group (P=0.03 and P=0.004, respectively) despite there being no significant differences in intensive care unit (ICU) stay in the post-transplant period, postoperative complications, hospitalization, and in-hospital mortality between the groups. Long ICU stays in the post-transplant period and the small graft group were predisposed to mortality and graft failure in multivariate analysis. The present study suggested that the use of small-size grafts in HU-LDLT patients requires careful living liver donor selection regarding the interaction between GRWR and preoperative patient severity.

42870819.title: Transaxillary minimally invasive mitral valve surgery: early and mid-term outcomes in 763 patients.
42870819.abstract: The transaxillary (TAxA) approach has been developed as a simplified direct-vision minimally invasive access for heart valve surgery.
