Awareness, patient information, and rapid initiation of antibiotics are critical. Clinicians should counsel patients and relatives that meningitis may occur despite vaccination and promote early recognition strategies.

42845153.title: Bilateral vs unilateral pleural drains in tetralogy of Fallot repair.
42845153.abstract: To compare postoperative outcomes after tetralogy of Fallot repair in patients managed with unilateral versus bilateral pleural drains. In this single-centre retrospective cohort study, patients undergoing complete tetralogy of Fallot repair between 2020 and 2025 were included. Patients with previous complete repair, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, delayed sternal closure, or chylothorax were excluded. The primary outcome was undrained postoperative pleural effusion on routine chest radiographs. Secondary outcomes were postoperative pleural drain insertion, duration of invasive mechanical ventilation, diuretic score, ICU length of stay, and pleural drain-related complications. Multivariable regression adjusted for repair type, bypass duration, cross-clamp duration, and surgeon. Of 180 patients, 122 (68%) underwent unilateral pleural drain placement and 58 (32%) bilateral placement. Complex repairs were more common in the bilateral group. Undrained pleural effusion was more frequent after unilateral than bilateral pleural drain placement (42.6% vs 5.2%; p < 0.001). Postoperative pleural drain insertion was required in 9 patients (7.4%) in the unilateral group and in none in the bilateral group (p = 0.06). Pleural drain-related complications were more frequent with bilateral pleural drains, with 4 pneumothoraces requiring intervention versus 1 self-resolving subcutaneous emphysema in the unilateral group (p = 0.01). In multivariable analysis, bilateral pleural drain placement remained independently associated with lower odds of undrained pleural effusion, but not with duration of mechanical ventilation, diuretic score, or ICU length of stay. Bilateral pleural drains were associated with fewer radiographic pleural effusions but no measurable short-term clinical advantage. Placement should therefore be individualised according to intraoperative findings and local practice.

42844551.title: Prone Positioning in Neurocritical Care Patients with Invasive Intracranial Pressure Monitoring: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
42844551.abstract: Pulmonary complications are common after acute brain injury and may worsen neurologic outcomes. Although prone positioning (PP) is an established treatment strategy for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) with severe hypoxemia in general intensive care unit populations, it is often avoided in neurocritical care due to concerns that PP may increase intracranial pressure (ICP). However, evidence supporting these concerns remains limited. A systematic search of multiple databases and supplementary sources using keywords related to ICP and PP yielded 778 records. Ten studies with 177 patients met the inclusion criteria for the systematic review and eight (n = 120 patients) provided extractable data for meta-analysis of the primary outcome [change in ICP from baseline (supine) to PP]. Pooled means and mean differences were calculated using random-effects models. The pooled within-subject mean change in ICP from baseline to PP was + 5.06 mm Hg (95% CI 2.05-8.06; I2 = 76.7%). Accordingly, pooled mean ICP increased from 11.10 mm Hg (95% CI 8.43-13.76) at baseline to 16.13 mm Hg (95% CI 13.83-18.43) during PP, remaining below commonly used treatment thresholds for intracranial hypertension although clinically relevant ICP elevations occurred in a small subset of patients. By contrast, the pooled change in ICP between baseline and after returning to the supine position in five studies (n = 45) was - 0.41 mm Hg (95% CI - 2.34 to 1.51), indicating that the increase in ICP during PP was transient and reversible. Systemic oxygenation and brain tissue oxygenation improved in PP. In patients with acute brain injury, PP improves systemic and brain tissue oxygenation while causing a modest, transient increase in ICP that resolves after resupination. These findings support cautious use of PP in selected neurocritical care patients with respiratory failure when invasive ICP monitoring is available. Given the limited evidence base, larger prospective studies are needed.

42844031.title: Essential aspects of the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia: A State-of-the-Art Review.
42844031.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in the ICU and is associated with high antibiotic consumption and increased healthcare resource utilization. This review provides an updated overview of current strategies for VAP prevention. A narrative review of the literature was conducted, including randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and recent international guidelines and position papers on VAP prevention. Successful VAP prevention depends on both effective implementation strategies and evidence-based clinical interventions. Current preventive measures target the main mechanisms involved in VAP pathogenesis, including prolonged mechanical ventilation, microaspiration, endotracheal tube biofilm formation, and colonization of the aerodigestive tract. Routine preventive measures with the strongest supporting evidence include minimizing the duration of mechanical ventilation and sedation, avoiding unnecessary intubation and re-intubation, semi-recumbent positioning, oral care with toothbrushing rather than chlorhexidine, early enteral nutrition, and the use of structured prevention bundles. Additional interventions, such as subglottic secretion drainage, selective digestive or oropharyngeal decontamination, inhaled antibiotics, early tracheostomy, and post-pyloric feeding, may be beneficial in appropriately selected patients or specific clinical settings. In contrast, some interventions have inconsistent evidence of clinical benefit and are not recommended for routine use. Preventing VAP requires a multimodal approach that integrates organizational support with evidence-based preventive measures. As new evidence continues to emerge, prevention bundles should be regularly updated to optimize effectiveness while avoiding interventions that are ineffective or potentially harmful. Implementation of VAP prevention strategies should focus on interventions supported by the best available evidence, while tailoring selected strategies to local epidemiology, available resources, and individual patient characteristics. Consistent adherence to multidisciplinary prevention bundles remains fundamental for reducing the burden of VAP.

42843107.title: Impact of obstructive sleep apnea on outcomes of acute respiratory distress syndrome: propensity matched analysis of a national cohort.
42843107.journal: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care
42843107.abstract: The effects of co-existing OSA on the outcomes of ARDS are unclear. This retrospective study aimed to compare the outcomes and resource utilization rates of OSA patients who develop ARDS with a matched control group. Adult patients hospitalized between 2016 and 2019 with a diagnostic code for ARDS were identified within the Nationwide Inpatient Sample. Patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema were excluded. By utilizing propensity score calculations, patients with OSA were individually matched with and compared to patients without OSA. Primary outcomes were mortality, length of stay and total hospitalization charges. 9405 OSA patients were matched with 9206 controls. OSA was independently associated with 34% lower odds of in-hospital mortality (21.1%vs 24.9%; aOR 0.66, 95% CI 0.61-0.72; p < 0.001), shorter length of stay (B - 2.0 days; p < 0.001), and lower total hospitalization charges (B -$74,601; P < 0.001). OSA patients had lower rates of invasive mechanical ventilation (aOR 0.79; p < 0.001) and tracheostomy (aOR 0.66; p < 0.001) but higher noninvasive ventilation use (aOR 1.40; p < 0.001). In a subgroup analysis of OSA patients, NIV was associated with fewer tracheostomies (aOR 0.61; p < 0.001) and lower charges (B -$26,625; p < 0.001) but was not associated with mortality or length of stay. In this nationally representative cohort, preexisting OSA was paradoxically associated with lower mortality, shorter hospitalization, and reduced resource utilization in ARDS. These findings suggest possible protective mechanisms warranting further prospective investigation.

42840731.title: Acute Intrapartum Seizure in a Pregnant Woman with Epilepsy Receiving Divalproex: Maternal-Fetal Consequences and Emergency Obstetric Management-A Case Report.
42840731.abstract: Epilepsy, a prevalent neurological disorder affecting 70 million people globally, necessitates special care for women of reproductive age during pregnancy. Abnormal brain activity causes seizures, atypical behavior, and loss of consciousness. Early and consistent reproductive health guidance is crucial. This case investigates epileptic seizures during delivery in women with a history of epilepsy. A 30-year-old G2P1A0 woman at 31-32 weeks of gestation presented with preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) and a history of epilepsy treated with divalproex sodium since adolescence. The patient had remained seizure-free for 15 years prior to admission. Initial maternal examination and cardiotocography (CTG) findings were reassuring, with ultrasound confirming a live singleton fetus appropriate for gestational age. During labor observation, the patient experienced an intrapartum seizure characterized by confusion and repetitive licking movements, followed by fetal heart rate decelerations on CTG classified as category III, indicating fetal distress. Emergency cesarean section was subsequently performed after intrauterine resuscitation and maternal stabilization. A preterm male neonate weighing 1815 grams was delivered with low initial APGAR scores requiring immediate neonatal resuscitation and neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission for respiratory distress syndrome and respiratory failure. Postoperatively, the mother remained hemodynamically stable without recurrent seizures and was discharged in satisfactory condition with continued antiepileptic therapy. Careful multidisciplinary management of epilepsy during pregnancy is essential. Breakthrough seizures during labor may lead to acute fetal compromise and require emergency delivery. Close antenatal, intrapartum, and postpartum monitoring is crucial to optimize maternal and neonatal outcomes.

42840056.title: Detection of Aspergillus in the lower respiratory tract and its association with mortality in patients with different viral pneumonias: a retrospective multicenter cohort study from China.
42840056.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
42840056.abstract: The detection of Aspergillus in the lower respiratory tract complicates the clinical course of viral pneumonia and is linked to poor outcomes, but prior evidence is confined to the intensive care unit (ICU) or single-virus settings (e.g., influenza or SARS-CoV-2). Whether its frequency and prognostic significance differ across viral etiologies in hospitalized adults remains unknown. This multicenter retrospective cohort study included adults with community-acquired viral pneumonia at seven tertiary hospitals in China (2017-2025). Patients were categorized into SARS-CoV-2, influenza, or other viral groups. The exposure was lower respiratory tract Aspergillus detection (via using culture, real-time PCR, or metagenomic next-generation sequencing). The primary outcome was in-hospital all-cause mortality. Among 929 patients, Aspergillus was detected in 175 (18.8%). The detection rates differed significantly across viral etiologies (33.2% in patients with influenza, 14.6% in those with SARS-CoV-2, and 7.4% in those with other viruses; P < 0.001). In the fully adjusted model, Aspergillus detection was independently associated with increased overall mortality (aOR = 2.99; 95% CI 1.60-5.58; P < 0.001), but the association varied markedly by viral etiology. Virus-stratified analyses revealed that in influenza, Aspergillus detection remained independently associated with mortality after multivariable adjustment, and the association was consistently observed across prespecified subgroups, including non-ventilated patients, whereas in SARS-CoV-2, the association was largely confined to ventilated patients. Lower respiratory tract Aspergillus detection differed substantially by viral etiology and was most frequent in patients with influenza pneumonia. It was independently associated with increased mortality across all influenza subgroups, including non-ventilated patients, whereas in SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia this association was largely confined to mechanical ventilation patients. These findings support a virus-stratified approach to fungal surveillance and warrant prospective validation.

42839200.title: Physiological Effects of High-Flow Tracheal Oxygen vs. Pressure Support Ventilation in Neurosurgical Patients with Brain Tumors Facing Delayed Extubation: A Pilot Study.
42839200.abstract: Postoperative neurosurgical patients who successfully pass a spontaneous breathing trial (SBT) may still require delayed extubation due to impaired airway protection. Continued mechanical ventilation may contribute to diaphragm underuse. High-flow tracheal oxygen (HFTO) offers an alternative-discontinuing positive pressure while maintaining airway access-but its physiological effects in intubated neurosurgical patients remain poorly characterized. In this prospective, randomized physiological pilot study, postoperative neurosurgical patients who required delayed extubation were assigned (1:1) to HFTO or low-level pressure support ventilation (PSV). Esophageal pressure monitoring and diaphragmatic ultrasound were performed at baseline and at 2, 12, 24, and 48 h. The primary endpoint was inspiratory effort assessed by esophageal pressure-time product (PTPes) per min. Secondary outcomes included diaphragmatic function, respiratory parameters, safety, and clinical outcomes. A total of 24 patients were randomized; 1 patient was withdrawn due to intracranial rebleeding, leaving 23 patients for analysis (HFTO, n = 12; PSV, n = 11). HFTO exhibited a significantly different temporal trajectory in inspiratory effort (group-by-time interaction P = 0.019), characterized by an acute physiological step-up immediately after withdrawing positive pressure support, followed by a stable plateau from 2 to 48 h. Diaphragmatic indices remained unchanged in both groups over 48 h. Airway pressures were significantly lower in the HFTO group (all P < 0.001), accompanied by modest declines in partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO2)/fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) and slight partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO2) increases. Respiratory deterioration rate was similar between groups (25.0% vs. 18.2%, P = 1.000). Ventilator-free days at day 28 were univariately higher with HFTO (27.0 [23.0-27.0] vs. 21.0 [17.0-24.0] days, P = 0.022); artificial airway-free days and ICU length of stay were comparable between groups. HFTO was univariately associated with increased inspiratory effort compared with low-level PSV, without short-term diaphragmatic harm or increased clinical instability in postoperative neurosurgical patients requiring delayed extubation. These findings suggest HFTO as a feasible strategy for liberation from mechanical ventilation while maintaining airway safety. Larger multicenter studies are warranted.

42836598.title: Association of RSV Vaccination With Clinical Outcomes in Older Adults With Heart Failure: A Propensity-Matched Analysis.
42836598.abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is increasingly recognized as a trigger for adverse outcomes in older adults with heart failure (HF). Following FDA approval of RSV vaccines for adults ≥ 60 years in 2023, real-world evidence in HF populations remains limited. We conducted a multicenter retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network. Adults ≥ 60 years with HF were identified and stratified by RSV vaccination status from May 1, 2023, to January 01, 2026. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included respiratory failure, healthcare utilization, and cardiovascular events. After PSM, 777 vaccinated and 777 unvaccinated HF patients were analyzed. All-cause mortality (HR 0.51, 95% CI, 0.33-0.79) and ICU admissions were significantly lower in vaccinated patients (2.7% vs. 5.8%, HR 0.46, 95% CI 0.25-0.86), while healthcare utilization was significantly higher in the vaccinated cohort (HR 1.85, 95% CI 1.65-2.08). No significant differences were observed in respiratory failure (7.3% vs. 9.4%, HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.61-1.23), inpatient or emergency visits (29.9% vs. 35.1%, HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.81-1.16), HF exacerbations, myocardial infarction, or stroke. Age-stratified subgroup analyses (60-75 and 75-90 years) showed consistent findings, with no significant cardiovascular differences and significantly higher healthcare utilization in vaccinated patients across both age groups. In older adults with HF, RSV vaccination was associated with lower mortality and fewer ICU admissions, without a corresponding reduction in overall inpatient/emergency use or acute-care utilization. These findings are hypothesis-generating and may reflect prevention of severe respiratory illness.

42835989.title: Experiences of emergency care practitioners on pre-hospital rapid sequence intubation in South Africa.
42835989.abstract: Pre-hospital Rapid Sequence Intubation (RSI) is a complex, high-stakes and time-sensitive procedure performed in unpredictable resource-constrained environments. Successful execution of pre-hospital RSI demands coordinated teamwork, thorough preparation and clear communication. This qualitative study explored the experiences of Emergency Care Practitioners (ECPs) during pre-hospital RSI. The study was conducted across three South African provinces: Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape. The study adopted a descriptive qualitative design, using focus group discussions (FGDs) to understand ECPs' experiences during prehospital RSI. Six FGDs were conducted online via Microsoft Teams. All discussions were audio-recorded, transcribed and analysed using qualitative data analysis software, NVivo 13 (2020 R1). A total of 39 ECPs voluntarily participated in six FGDs, representing both public and private sectors. The following themes emerged; system-driven administrative demands and procedural complexity, resource and workforce constraints affecting RSI performance and communication-related challenges and information gaps affecting clinical decision-making. The ECPs voice concerns about challenges that require Emergency Medical Services (EMS) management to implement supportive measures, including improved access to resources and equipment during pre-hospital RSI. Additionally, they argue that practitioner proficiency promotes the effective execution of pre-hospital RSI. The findings of this study and the insights gained can guide EMS leadership and policymakers in formulating targeted strategies that will ensure the availability of essential resources and strengthen operational support to enhance the safety and quality of care delivered to critically ill or injured patients requiring RSI.

42835754.title: Inhaled Heparin to Shorten Antibiotic Duration in Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia: A Randomized Double-Blind Controlled Trial.
42835754.abstract: Prolonged antibiotic therapy in ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) contributes to antimicrobial resistance. Inhaled heparin has pleiotropic anti-inflammatory and mucolytic properties. This trial evaluated whether adjunctive nebulized heparin reduces antibiotic duration in VAP using a procalcitonin (PCT)-guided discontinuation algorithm. In this single-center, double-blind, randomized controlled trial, 82 mechanically ventilated adults with VAP (CPIS ≥ 6) were assigned to standard care plus nebulized heparin (10,000 IU every 6 h) or placebo (sterile distilled water). Both groups followed a PCT-guided antibiotic discontinuation algorithm (≤ 0.2 µg/L or ≥ 90% reduction from peak, plus clinical stability). Primary outcome: antibiotic duration (days). Secondary outcomes: duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU/hospital length of stay (LOS), serial CPIS, CRP, PCT, SOFA, APACHE II, adverse events, and 28-day mortality rate. Antibiotic duration was significantly shorter with heparin (mean difference -3.2 days; 95% CI: -4.8 to -1.6; p < 0.001). Baseline characteristics were similar except for higher mean APACHE II in the control group (18.8 vs. 15.2). After adjusting for baseline APACHE II imbalance, the treatment effect remained significant (adjusted mean difference -2.9 days; 95% CI: -4.5 to -1.3; p = 0.001). Heparin also reduced duration of mechanical ventilation (mean difference -1.47 days; p = 0.01), ICU LOS (- 3.5 days; p = 0.02), and hospital LOS (- 4.1 days; p = 0.01). CPIS and CRP improved more rapidly in the heparin group (group×time interaction p < 0.05). No major bleeding or heparin-related adverse events occurred. Adjunctive nebulized heparin (40,000 IU/day) significantly shortens antibiotic duration and improves clinical recovery in VAP without increasing adverse events. However, given the single-center design and modest sample size, our results require confirmation in future multicenter trials with optimum heparin doses and comprehensive biomarker panels to better elucidate the mechanisms of action and establish the definitive role of inhaled heparin in antimicrobial stewardship.

42835185.title: Efficacy and safety of early mobilization in patients with ARDS: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42835185.abstract: To evaluate the effect of early mobilization in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Computerized searches were conducted in PubMed, EMbase, The Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang Data, CBM, and VIP databases for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on early mobilization in ARDS patients. The retrieval period was from the establishment of each database to September 30, 2025. Two reviewers independently assessed the quality of included literature and extracted data in accordance with Cochrane systematic review methodology. Meta-analysis was performed using RevMan 5.4.1 software for eligible studies. A total of 7 RCTs were included, consisting of 4 English and 3 Chinese articles. Meta-analysis showed that compared with conventional treatment, early mobilization significantly reduced the incidence of intensive care unit-acquired weakness (ICU-AW) [OR = 0.35, 95% CI (0.19,0.64), P = 0.0006] and delirium [OR = 0.51, 95% CI (0.28,0.91), P = 0.02], shortened the duration of mechanical ventilation [MD = -2.40,95% CI (-2.96,-1.84), P < 0.00001], length of ICU stay [MD = -3.36, 95% CI (-4.21,-2.52), P < 0.00001] and total hospital stay [MD = -2.74,95% CI (-3.49,-1.98), P < 0.00001]. Meanwhile, it improved patients'functional independence score (Barthel Index) [MD = 17.27, 95% CI (11.18, 23.35), P < 0.00001] and decreased the incidence of complications [OR = 0.39, 95% CI (0.17, 0.86), P = 0.02]. All pooled effects were statistically significant. Early mobilization yields significant clinical benefits for ARDS patients, improving short-term clinical outcomes and functional recovery. It is worthy of clinical promotion and application. However, multicenter, large-sample, and methodologically standardized RCTs are still needed to further verify its long-term effects and optimal implementation protocols.

42833910.title: Twenty Years of Respiratory Intermediate Care: Clinical Outcomes, Safety Indicators, and Resource Utilization in a Respiratory Intermediate Care Unit.
42833910.abstract: Respiratory Intermediate Care Units (RICUs) are specialized units between conventional hospitalization and intensive care units (ICU), designed to manage patients with acute respiratory failure who require advanced respiratory support and monitoring, but do not necessarily require invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV). To describe the clinical outcomes, safety indicators, and estimated financial impact and resource utilization of a RICU over a 20-year period. Retrospective study (2003-2023) of all patients admitted to the RICU of a tertiary level hospital in Spain between January 2003 and December 2023. Analysed activities include: non-invasive mechanical ventilation (NIMV), high-flow oxygen therapy (HFOT), weaning from IMV, and interventional procedures. Primary outcomes included mortality, intubation rate, and length of stay (LOS). Financial impact was estimated by comparing the observed RICU costs with a theoretical ICU scenario. Seven thousand six hundred fifty-four patients were included (mean age 67±14 years, 62% male). The main diagnoses were: COVID-19 pneumonia (30.6%), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation (28.7%), and severe pneumonia (22.2%). Additionally, 18.3% were IMV weaning admissions. Overall mortality was 8.4%, and the intubation rate was 12.1%. Among the patients admitted for weaning, survival reached 91.8%. The mean LOS was 6.9 days. Financial impact assessment estimated an average daily cost of €587 for RICU care compared with €940 for the theoretical ICU scenario, corresponding to an estimated annual difference of €485,000. Over a 20-year period, this RICU provided specialized care for a large cohort of patients with acute respiratory failure, achieving favourable clinical outcomes with a lower estimated resource utilisation and costs.

42831107.title: When a Lung Collapses: A Case of Polymicrobial Empyema Presenting as Massive Hydropneumothorax.
42831107.abstract: Aspiration-related pneumonia can progress to empyema and massive hydropneumothorax, potentially fatal complications not frequently documented in the literature. Patients with structural lung disease and poor dentition can be particularly vulnerable to severe polymicrobial infections arising from seemingly minor aspiration events. We report the case of a man in his early 70s with chronic bronchiectasis, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, coronary artery disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, and poor dentition who presented with progressive dyspnea and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. Imaging demonstrated a massive right-sided hydropneumothorax with complete right lung collapse and mediastinal shift. Pleural fluid cultures grew Streptococcus anginosus and Prevotella nigrescens, consistent with aspiration-related polymicrobial empyema. His hospital course was complicated by septic shock requiring vasopressor support, atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response requiring synchronized cardioversion, and pulseless ventricular tachycardia with successful return of spontaneous circulation. Management included chest tube drainage, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics followed by de-escalation, invasive hemodynamic monitoring, and multidisciplinary critical care support. Despite severe multiorgan compromise, the patient ultimately improved and was discharged home on prolonged oral antibiotic therapy. This case illustrates how a seemingly simple aspiration event can progress into catastrophic pleuropulmonary disease with life-threatening cardiopulmonary collapse. Early recognition, prompt source control, and multidisciplinary management were critical to improving the outcome for this patient.

42830948.title: Timing of Endotracheal Intubation After High-Flow Nasal Cannula Initiation in Patients With Mild-to-Moderate Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Prospective Observational Cohort Study.
42830948.abstract: High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) is widely used in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, including mild-to-moderate acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Some patients deteriorate and require invasive mechanical ventilation, but the appropriate timing of intubation remains uncertain. This study examined the association between intubation within 24 hours of HFNC initiation and clinical outcomes among patients with mild-to-moderate ARDS in whom HFNC failed. This prospective observational cohort included 109 adults with mild-to-moderate ARDS treated at the General Hospital of Athens "G. Gennimatas," Greece, from August 2023 to August 2024. All initially received HFNC and were subsequently intubated. Mild and moderate ARDS were classified by Berlin oxygenation criteria (PaO₂/FiO₂ 201-300 and 101-200 mmHg, respectively). HFNC failure was defined as subsequent endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation. A predefined 24-hour cutoff, supported by previous studies, classified patients as early or delayed intubation. Intubation decisions were based on arterial blood gases and overall clinical condition. Outcomes included in-hospital mortality, successful ventilator weaning, hospital and intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay, and duration of the initial controlled mechanical ventilation phase. Multivariable models adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, comorbidity burden, admission blood pressure, and peripheral oxygen saturation. Twenty-two patients (20.2%) were intubated within 24 hours and 87 (79.8%) after 24 hours. In-hospital death occurred in 0 of 22 patients (0.0%) in the early group and 15 of 87 (17.2%) in the delayed group (p = 0.038). Successful ventilator weaning occurred in 17 of 22 patients (77.3%) and six of 87 (6.9%), respectively (p < 0.001). After adjustment, intubation within 24 hours was associated with lower odds of in-hospital death (OR = 0.03, 95% CI: 0.001-0.89; p = 0.043), although the wide confidence interval indicates substantial uncertainty. The early group had a longer hospital stay (adjusted β = 0.14, 95% CI: 0.03-0.25; p = 0.017), shorter ICU stay (adjusted β = -0.44, 95% CI: -0.72 to -0.17; p = 0.002), and shorter initial controlled mechanical ventilation phase (adjusted β = -0.30, 95% CI: -0.53 to -0.07; p = 0.015). Among patients with mild-to-moderate ARDS requiring invasive mechanical ventilation after HFNC failure, intubation within 24 hours was associated with lower observed in-hospital mortality, more frequent successful ventilator weaning, and shorter ICU and controlled ventilation durations. These findings support close monitoring and timely escalation when deterioration indicates insufficient non-invasive support. The observational design and limited outcome events preclude causal interpretation, and larger multicenter cohorts are needed to confirm these associations.

42829714.title: Prior Use of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists versus SGLT2 Inhibitors and Clinical Outcomes After Sepsis in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes: A Propensity Score-Matched Cohort Study.
42829714.abstract: Whether pre-existing glucose-lowering therapy influences outcomes after sepsis remains uncertain. We compared clinical outcomes among patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) who developed sepsis according to prior GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) or SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) use. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network. Adults with T2D who developed sepsis had received a GLP-1RA or an SGLT2i within 3 months before sepsis were identified. After 1:1 propensity score matching, 11,969 patients were included in each group. The primary outcome was 90-day all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE), major adverse kidney event (MAKE), intensive care unit (ICU) admission, major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular event (MACCE), septic shock, and acute respiratory failure. Compared with prior SGLT2i use, prior GLP-1RA use was associated with lower 90-day all-cause mortality (incidence rate, 48.6 vs 60.6 per 100 person-years; HR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.75-0.88; E-value: 1.6) and lower risks of MACE (HR, 0.77; 0.65-0.91; E-value, 1.7), myocardial infarction (HR, 0.82; 0.67-0.99; E-value, 1.7), ICU admission (HR, 0.89; 0.84-0.94; E-value, 1.4), and MACCE (HR, 0.86; 0.74-0.99; E-value, 1.5). No significant difference was observed for septic shock (HR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.74-1.02), acute respiratory failure (HR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.83-1.06), or MAKE (HR, 1.08; 95% CI, 0.92-1.27). The mortality benefit remained consistent through 365 days and across all prespecified subgroups. After Holm correction for multiple comparisons across the seven secondary outcomes, only the associations with MACE (adjusted P=0.012) and ICU admission (adjusted P<0.007) remained statistically significant, while those with MACCE, myocardial infarction, MAKE, septic shock, and acute respiratory failure did not. Among patients with T2D who developed sepsis, prior GLP-1RA use was associated with lower mortality and select cardiovascular/renal risks than prior SGLT2i use, though roughly half of secondary outcomes showed no significant difference. Exposure was defined at the drug-class rather than individual-agent level, and modest E-values alongside baseline imbalances before matching suggest residual confounding cannot be excluded. These hypothesis-generating findings warrant confirmation in prospective studies.

42829580.title: Cipepofol versus Conventional Sedation for Pneumonia Patients Receiving Mechanical Ventilation: A Real-World Retrospective Study of Effectiveness and Hemodynamic Safety.
42829580.abstract: Severe pneumonia often necessitates invasive mechanical ventilation (MV) and prolonged sedation in the ICU. This real-world retrospective cohort study aimed to compare cipepofol vs conventional sedation regimens in this vulnerable population, with MV duration as the primary endpoint and hemodynamic safety as a key safety outcome. This retrospective cohort study evaluated mechanically ventilated patients with severe pneumonia who received continuous sedation for more than 48 hours. Patients were classified into cipepofol or conventional sedation (propofol-, midazolam- or dexmedetomidine-based) groups. Propensity score matching (PSM) was performed at a 1:1 ratio based on age and APACHE II scores. After PSM, 198 patients (99 per group) were analyzed. The primary endpoint-MV duration did not differ significantly between the cipepofol and conventional groups (median 218.23 vs 227.25 hours, P = 0.740). Subgroup analysis further confirmed that there was no significant difference in MV duration between propofol- and midazolam-based regimens compared to the cipepofol-regimen. Notably, cipepofol demonstrated superior hemodynamic safety, showing significantly lower incidences of early hypotension within the first hour (11.1% vs 27.3%, P=0.007) and overall bradycardia (19.1% vs 36.1%, P=0.014). Post-hoc subgroups analysis revealed that cipepofol reduced the risks of early hypotension and overall bradycardia compared to propofol- or midazolam-based regimens in hospital-acquired pneumonia patients. Multivariate analysis confirmed cipepofol use as an independent protective factor against early hypotension (adjusted OR 0.300, 95% CI: 0.136-0.665, P=0.003) and bradycardia (adjusted OR 0.414, 95% CI: 0.212-0.808, P=0.010). No significant differences were found regarding sedation success, length of ICU stay, 28-day ventilator-free days, 28-day mortality, vasopressor requirements, or organ function parameters (all P>0.05). In mechanically ventilated patients with severe pneumonia requiring prolonged sedation, cipepofol did not shorten MV duration compared with propofol- or midazolam-based conventional regimens, but it significantly reduced risks for early hypotension and overall bradycardia events. ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06514781).

42829547.title: Acinetobacter baumannii Nosocomial Meningitis Secondary to Neurosurgical Intervention: A Case Report.
42829547.abstract: Nosocomial meningitis is a serious complication of neurosurgical procedures, associated with high morbidity and mortality, as well as significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Among the causative pathogens, Acinetobacter baumannii (A. baumannii) is particularly concerning due to its ability to survive for prolonged periods in the hospital environment, its opportunistic virulence, and, especially, its tendency to develop multidrug resistance to antimicrobial agents. Diagnosis is often difficult in the postoperative setting, particularly when the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is altered as a result of the surgical procedure. Rapid identification of the causative agent and early initiation of appropriate antibiotic therapy are essential to limit complications and improve patient prognosis. We report the case of a 27-year-old patient with a history of surgically treated craniopharyngioma complicated by anterior hypopituitarism. Three weeks after surgery, he was admitted to the ICU with suspected postoperative meningitis due to the onset of behavioral disturbances associated with nasal discharge, without a fever. Brain CT was normal. CSF analysis, obtained by lumbar puncture under strict aseptic conditions, revealed a turbid fluid with leukocytosis of 5,760 cells/mm³, predominantly composed of neutrophils, along with elevated protein levels (5.7 g/L) and low glucose levels (0.05 g/L). Direct examination after Gram staining showed Gram-negative coccobacilli with a marked inflammatory reaction. CSF culture grew a multidrug-resistant (MDR) strain of A. baumannii, which was sensitive only to colistin. The patient received antibiotic therapy with colistin, administered intravenously and intrathecally for 18 days, with initial neurological improvement and sterilization of the CSF by the 15th day of treatment. The subsequent course was unfavorable, marked by the development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) secondary to ventilator-associated pneumonia caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), complicated by refractory septic shock, which ultimately led to his death after one month of hospitalization in the ICU. This report highlights the severity of nosocomial meningitis caused by MDR A. baumannii and underscores the importance of implementing infection prevention measures in healthcare settings.

42828950.title: Protocolised analgosedation in mechanically ventilated adult patients: A scoping review.
42828950.abstract: Our objectives were to assess structure and content of analgosedation protocols used for mechanically ventilated adult patients, including those receiving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), against current international sedation guidelines, and to explore reported barriers and facilitators to their implementation. Scoping review searching five databases (December 1999 to September 2026). We included all study types reporting on analgosedation protocol structure and content, and/or implementation barriers/facilitators. Two authors independently screened citations, extracted data, and coded reported barriers and facilitators using the Theoretical Domains Framework. We screened 18,457 citations with 81 studies meeting inclusion criteria. Of these, 35 (43%) were observational studies, 27 (33%) non-randomised interventional studies, and 19 (23%) randomised controlled trials. Few studies published between 2019 and 2026 included propofol or dexmedetomidine, multi-modal analgesia and delirium assessment in analgosedation protocols, and no studies in ECMO patients. The most frequently reported structure and content of protocol was use of a sedation score (77%), recommending opioid and sedative drugs (74%), and setting a daily target sedation score (65%). Most reported barrier was a protocol insufficiently detailed to cover the breadth of patient needs, reported in 12 (63%) studies. The most frequently reported facilitator was availability of the analgosedation protocol in an easily accessible format, reported in four (31%) studies. Easy to follow protocols sufficiently detailed to cover patient need from a heterogenous ICU population are considerations to successful implementation. Healthcare staff fear of adverse effects is a potential barrier to adoption of protocolised analgosedation.

42828373.title: Mechanical Ventilation Practices in Traumatic Brain Injury: A Systematic Review of Contemporary Evidence.
42828373.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) frequently necessitates mechanical ventilation to maintain adequate gas exchange, protect the airway, and support cerebral physiology during the acute phase of critical illness. Although ventilatory management is an integral component of neurocritical care, the optimal approach remains uncertain because interventions aimed at pulmonary protection may influence intracranial dynamics and neurological outcomes. This systematic review aimed to critically evaluate contemporary evidence on mechanical ventilation practices in adults with TBI, with emphasis on ventilatory strategies, lung-protective ventilation, airway management, tracheostomy, weaning approaches, and clinically relevant outcomes. A systematic literature search was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), EBSCOhost, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Google Scholar, and selected grey-literature sources for studies published from January 2000 through June 2026. Eligible studies included adult patients with TBI who were receiving mechanical ventilation and reported ventilation-related interventions or outcomes. Methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklists, and the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, as appropriate for the study design. Owing to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. Eleven studies, comprising randomized controlled trials, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, and cross-sectional surveys, met the inclusion criteria. Considerable variation was observed in ventilatory management, particularly regarding tidal volume, positive end-expiratory pressure, carbon dioxide targets, airway management, and tracheostomy timing. The available evidence suggests that individualized ventilatory management may help balance pulmonary protection with preservation of cerebral physiology when guided by appropriate neurological and respiratory monitoring. Early tracheostomy may be associated with shorter durations of mechanical ventilation and intensive care unit stay in selected patients, although consistent benefits in mortality or long-term neurological recovery have not been established. Overall, the included studies demonstrated substantial variability in ventilatory practices and clinical outcomes across different settings and patient populations. Current evidence suggests that ventilation strategies in adults with TBI should be tailored to individual respiratory mechanics and cerebral physiological status rather than applied uniformly. However, substantial heterogeneity, limited TBI-specific comparative evidence, and variation in clinical practice limit the certainty of the available evidence. High-quality multicenter studies are needed to establish evidence-based ventilatory targets and determine their effects on patient-centered neurological and pulmonary outcomes.

42827705.title: Timing of nebulized colistimethate sodium following bronchodilator airway conditioning in hospital-acquired pneumonia: a target trial emulation study.
42827705.abstract: Evidence for nebulized colistimethate sodium (CMS) in hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) remains inconsistent, potentially due to heterogeneity in airway conditions and delivery timing. We evaluated whether timely initiation of nebulized CMS following bronchodilator airway pre-treatment was associated with microbiological outcomes in critically ill patients. We conducted a multicenter retrospective cohort study using target trial emulation among adult ICU patients with HAP who received nebulized CMS following bronchodilator nebulization. Two per-protocol strategies were compared: initiation within 90 min of bronchodilator nebulization (LE90) versus later initiation (GT90). Cloning, censoring, and inverse probability of censoring weighting were applied to address time-dependent confounding. The primary outcome was 14-day cumulative incidence of microbiological clearance, treating death as a competing event. Among 218 eligible patients, timely initiation was associated with a higher weighted cumulative incidence of microbiological clearance at day 14 (71.9% vs. 52.6%; absolute difference 19.3%, 95% CI 4.8-32.5; P = 0.012) and a shorter restricted mean time alive and not microbiologically cleared (6.85 vs. 10.08 days; difference -3.23 days, 95% CI -4.30 to -2.08; P < 0.001). Findings were consistent across subgroups and robust in sensitivity analyses. No significant differences were observed in clinical success, superinfection, mortality, ICU length of stay, or ventilator-free days. Bronchospasm incidence was similar between strategies. Timely initiation of nebulized CMS within a defined post-bronchodilator window was associated with higher microbiological clearance and reduced persistent infection, without increased airway adverse events. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation, particularly with respect to patient-centered outcomes.

42827170.title: Serum cholinesterase as a prognostic marker in respiratory critical illness: a narrative review.
42827170.abstract: Prognostication in respiratory critical care rests largely on composite severity scores derived from mixed medical, surgical or sepsis populations. Serum butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase) is a liver-synthesized plasma enzyme, a negative acute-phase reactant and an established index of hepatic synthesis and nutrition, and has re-emerged as a candidate prognostic biomarker in critical illness. A direct cytokine-driven mechanism is inferred, not demonstrated, and whether the circulating enzyme modulates the cholinergic anti-inflammatory axis is unproven. This narrative review synthesizes the evidence across community-acquired pneumonia, acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and acute respiratory failure including coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). A reproducible inverse association between enzyme activity and mortality or disease severity emerges, but it rests on small, mostly retrospective single-center studies with heterogeneous assays and data-derived thresholds. The review therefore asks one decisive question, almost never addressed in respiratory cohorts: whether the enzyme adds information beyond albumin and established severity scores, judged by incremental discrimination and reclassification. On that test it is a consistent signal in search of methodological rigour rather than an established independent marker. Prospective, setting-specific and adequately adjusted validation is required before clinical adoption, capturing the activity nadir and the slope of any recovery, whose prognostic role is untested. Mislabelling could influence decisions on escalation and limitation of treatment.

42826762.title: Impact of Nasal Staphylococcus aureus Carriage on Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia after Acute Brain Injury.
42826762.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is a frequent complication in brain-injured patients requiring mechanical ventilation. Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is a major causative pathogen, but the role of nasal carriage at Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admission in the development of S. aureus VAP in this specific population remains poorly defined. We conducted a single-center observational study including consecutive adults admitted to the ICU with acute brain injury requiring invasive mechanical ventilation for at least 48 hours. Nasal screening for S. aureus was performed within 24 hours of ICU admission. Patients were classified as carriers or non-carriers. The primary outcome was the occurrence of S. aureus VAP during ICU stay. Secondary outcomes included overall VAP incidence, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, neurological status at ICU discharge, catheter, vasoactive support, and antibiotic exposure, and ICU mortality. Ninety-six patients were included, of whom 37 (38.5%) were nasal carriers of S. aureus. Overall, 44 patients (45.8%) developed VAP. The incidence of S. aureus VAP was significantly higher among carriers than non-carriers (40.5% vs. 10.1%; RR 3.99, 95% CI 1.70-9.53; p = 0.001). Early VAP, regardless of pathogen, occurred more frequently in carriers than in non-carriers (45.9% vs. 18.6%; p = 0.02). The overall incidence of VAP and other secondary outcomes did not differ significantly between groups. Nasal carriage of S. aureus at ICU admission could be associated with the occurrence of S. aureus VAP and overall early VAP in brain-injured patients.

42826395.title: Antibiotic Stewardship in Nonoperative Facial Trauma: Necessary or Not?
42826395.abstract: Closed facial fractures are common and often treated nonoperatively. Routine systemic antibiotic prophylaxis is controversial because infection rates are low and antibiotics can cause harm. We assessed whether prophylactic antibiotics reduce infectious complications in closed, nonoperative facial fractures. A systematic review was conducted of adults with closed, nonoperative facial fractures (emergency department, inpatient, intensive care unit). PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched from inception through September 19, 2025. Studies compared systemic prophylaxis versus none and/or ≤24 hours versus >24 hours. Seven US studies comprising 3274 patients met the inclusion criteria. Across studies, fracture-related infection rates were low and were not reduced by prophylactic antibiotics. In the largest prospective multicenter cohort, Mian et al reported a 30-day facial fracture-associated infection rate of 1.0%, with no significant benefit for ≤24 hours or >24 hours of prophylaxis compared with none (adjusted odds ratio 1.24-1.32). Orbital and zygomatic cohorts reported no infectious complications regardless of prophylaxis strategy. In sinus-involving and intensive care unit cohorts, fracture-site infection and sinusitis were rare; most infectious events were pneumonia or ventilator-associated pneumonia rather than facial fracture-specific infections. Longer antibiotic exposure was associated with isolated cases of Clostridioides difficile colitis. Available evidence does not support routine systemic prophylaxis for uncomplicated closed, nonoperative facial fractures. The strongest inference applies to patients without another indication for antibiotics. Current data do not identify fracture-specific subgroups in whom prophylaxis improves outcomes; accordingly, management should emphasize local care, return precautions, and structured follow-up.

42825243.title: Prognostic value of the SPICE score for 1-year functional outcomes in patients with acute stroke requiring mechanical ventilation.
42825243.abstract: Approximately 15 million people suffer from strokes each year and accurate prognostication is crucial for care management. This study evaluated the performance of the Stroke Prognosis in Intensive CarE (SPICE) score to predict functional outcomes at 1 year in patients who underwent mechanical ventilation following a stroke. Ancillary analysis of the SPICE prospective multicentre cohort study conducted from 2017 to 2019 in 33 intensive care units (ICUs) of the Greater Paris area. All patients requiring mechanical ventilation on ICU admission and within 7 days of a non-traumatic stroke were included. The primary outcome was poor functional prognosis at 1 year (severe disability or death: modified Rankin Scale score of 4-6). Variables independently associated with the outcome were used to compute a prognostic score (SPICE score). Retained variables were stroke subtype, time between stroke diagnosis and initiation of mechanical ventilation, age, the Charlson Comorbidity Index and the Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) at ICU admission. The median SPICE score of the 364 patients of the cohort was 15 (IQR 11-19) and demonstrated acceptable predictive power (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.752) for poor outcome and outperformed GCS (AUROC 0.658) and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (AUROC 0.655) scores. A threshold of >18 points on the SPICE score had a sensitivity of 35.7% and a specificity of 95% for poor outcome prediction, yielding a positive predictive value of 93.5% (95% CI 86.5% to 97.6%) and a positive likelihood ratio of 7.16 (95% CI 3.22 to 15.9). For mechanically ventilated patients after a stroke, the SPICE score showed adequate predictive power for poor functional outcome at 1 year. Validation of the SPICE score in an external cohort is needed.

42824912.title: National Overview of Designated Infectious Disease Control Institutions and Medical Response Resources in the Republic of Korea, 2025.
42824912.abstract: This study assessed the regional distribution of infectious disease control institutions and medical response resources to support preparedness and resource management. We examined 223 institutions designated for infectious disease control or operating national infectious disease beds as of June 30, 2025. Institutional characteristics were obtained from Regional Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and local governments, while medical resource data were obtained from the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service. We assessed regional distribution, bed capacity, ownership, institution type, national infectious disease bed status, negative-pressure isolation beds, critical care equipment, and personnel. The largest numbers of institutions were in Jeonnam (44), Gyeongnam (40), and Busan (30). Of the 223 institutions, 123 (55.2%) had fewer than 300 beds and accounted for 239 negative-pressure isolation beds, compared with 1,571 negative-pressure isolation beds in institutions with ≥300 beds. Overall, the institutions had 5,823 ventilators, 314 extracorporeal membrane oxygenation devices, and 812 continuous renal replacement therapy devices. There were 174 infectious disease specialists, 318 pulmonologists, and 40 pediatric infectious disease specialists. Major equipment and specialist personnel were concentrated in regions with large hospitals, particularly Seoul, Gyeonggi, and Busan. Medical response resources varied by region and hospital size, with negative-pressure isolation beds, critical care equipment, and specialized personnel concentrated in larger hospitals and select regions. These findings reveal that infectious disease response capacity should be assessed not only by the number of designated institutions but also by the distribution and availability of medical resources.

42824807.title: Association Between Cardiopulmonary Bypass Time and Early Postoperative Acute Kidney Injury in Adults.
42824807.abstract: Introduction Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) has improved the safety and precision of complex cardiac surgery, but its inflammatory, embolic, and hemodynamic effects may contribute to postoperative acute kidney injury (AKI). This study explored whether longer CPB duration was associated with early postoperative AKI and related renal and clinical recovery outcomes in adult cardiac surgical patients. Methodology This prospective observational comparative study was conducted at the Department of Cardiac Surgery of the National Institute of Cardiovascular Diseases (NICVD) in Dhaka, Bangladesh, from July 1, 2022, to June 30, 2024. It included 100 adult cardiac patients aged 18-65 years who underwent cardiac surgery under CPB, selected by convenience sampling after ethical approval. Patients were divided into two equal groups after surgery according to recorded CPB duration: Group A included 50 patients with CPB time ≤120 minutes, while Group B included 50 patients with CPB time >120 minutes. Patients with pre-existing chronic kidney disease, kidney transplant history, emergency surgery, ejection fraction below 30%, previous cardiac surgery, or surgery without CPB were excluded. Results The two study groups were broadly comparable at baseline, with similar mean age (37.8±13.73 vs. 38.46±13.30 years; p=0.8), age distribution (p=0.93), gender distribution (male 58% vs. 52%; p=0.69), comorbidities, body mass index (BMI) profile, and underlying cardiac disease pattern. Smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and dyslipidemia were distributed without significant difference, while most patients in both groups had normal BMI, and isolated valvular heart disease was the commonest diagnosis. The intended difference between the groups was clearly established by CPB duration, with a mean CPB time of 93.00±11.42 minutes in Group A and 137.10±12.08 minutes in Group B (p<0.001). After surgery, patients with longer CPB time showed lower urine output at 24, 48, and 72 hours, with all differences reaching statistical significance (p<0.001). Although baseline serum creatinine was statistically insignificant (0.83±0.11 vs. 0.86±0.13 mg/dL; p=0.108), postoperative serum creatinine became significantly higher in Group B at 24, 48, and 72 hours (p<0.001). Postoperative AKI occurred in seven patients (14%) in Group A but in 23 patients (46%) in Group B, showing more than a threefold higher occurrence among patients with CPB time >120 minutes (p<0.001). Renal replacement therapy was required only in Group B in four patients (8%), and in-hospital mortality also occurred only in Group B in three patients (6%), though these differences were not statistically significant. Patients in the longer CPB group required longer mechanical ventilation (8.90±3.84 vs. 6.98±2.69 hours; p<0.001), longer ICU stay (10.15±4.68 vs. 4.87±1.58 days; p<0.001), and longer postoperative hospital stay (14.36±5.55 vs. 10.11±3.05 days; p<0.001). Conclusion Prolonged CPB time was significantly associated with greater early postoperative renal stress, higher AKI occurrence, and slower recovery, though the findings require cautious interpretation due to the single-center design, convenience sampling, short follow-up, and unadjusted perioperative factors.

42824758.title: Paradoxical Acute Hypoxemic Deterioration During Treatment of Bilateral Bronchopneumonia: A Case Report.
42824758.abstract: Community-acquired pneumonia may occasionally be associated with unexpected respiratory deterioration despite apparent clinical, laboratory, and radiological improvement. We report a case of a previously healthy adult male who presented with progressive dyspnea, persistent cough, generalized weakness, malaise, and low-grade fever. Initial chest radiography showed no significant abnormalities despite marked respiratory symptoms, whereas chest computed tomography revealed bilateral bronchopneumonia with multiple centrilobular nodules and patchy ground-glass opacities. The patient was treated with intravenous meropenem, systemic corticosteroids, inhaled therapy, supplemental oxygen, and supportive care, with gradual improvement in inflammatory markers. On hospital day three, however, he developed sudden severe hypoxemic respiratory failure shortly after antimicrobial administration, requiring intensive care unit admission and high-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy. Urgent CT pulmonary angiography excluded pulmonary embolism, follow-up imaging demonstrated partial regression of the pulmonary infiltrates, and cardiological evaluation showed no evidence of acute cardiac pathology. Meropenem was replaced with levofloxacin because a drug-related reaction could not be completely excluded. The patient's respiratory status subsequently improved rapidly with supportive treatment, and he was discharged without residual respiratory insufficiency. This case demonstrates that severe transient hypoxemic deterioration may occur during apparently successful treatment of bilateral bronchopneumonia and emphasizes the importance of promptly excluding pulmonary embolism, acute cardiac disease, drug-related reactions, and other potentially life-threatening causes of respiratory worsening.

42824716.title: Microbiological profiles of Gram-negative bacteria isolated from respiratory samples of mechanically ventilated patients at a tertiary Moroccan hospital.
42824716.abstract: To characterise the Gram-negative bacteria implicated in ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), focusing on their antimicrobial resistance profiles and phylogenetic relationships. Seventy-eight isolates were collected from protected distal samples over two years; patients were under mechanical ventilation in the three adult ICUs of a Moroccan tertiary hospital. Isolates were identified using VITEK2. PFGE and FTIR determined genetic relationships, whereas the detection of genetic resistance determinants was carried out using PCR. Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii harbouring the bla-OXA-23 was the predominant Gram-negative bacterium. Klebsiella pneumoniae was the most prevalent among the Enterobacterales, with a high resistance rate to almost all antibiotics, due to the coexistence of (bla) CTX-M-1, TEM, SHV, and OXA-48-like genes. Escherichia coli exhibited high resistance to ciprofloxacin (86%), ceftazidime (86%), and cotrimoxazole (71%). Proteus mirabilis was highly resistant to cotrimoxazole (60%) and ticarcillin (80%). Pseudomonas aeruginosa was resistant to carbapenems in 39% of cases, in which bla NDM and bla VIM were the only metallo-beta-lactamase genes detected. In phylogenetic analysis, both FTIR and PFGE techniques underscored no epidemiological relationship among strains. The prevalence of MDR and XDR bacteria among VAP cases in a tertiary hospital in Morocco is increasing, potentially due to the coexistence of antimicrobial resistance genes.

42824523.title: Life-Threatening Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis During Omalizumab Therapy for Chronic Urticaria: Missed Diagnosis, Induction, or Unmasking?
42824523.abstract: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a rare form of vasculitis characterized by late-onset asthma, eosinophilia, and systemic manifestations involving small- and medium-sized vessels. We report a severe case of EGPA occurring during treatment with omalizumab in a patient diagnosed with chronic urticaria. A 67-year-old woman presented with acute dyspnea, epistaxis, hemoptysis, and fatigue. Her medical history included late-onset asthma and chronic urticaria with persistent eosinophilia and elevated IgE levels, under treatment with omalizumab. Laboratory investigation revealed eosinophilia and elevated inflammatory markers, while chest computed tomography demonstrated bilateral ground-glass opacities. Bronchoalveolar lavage showed marked eosinophilia and progressively hemorrhagic sequential aliquots, confirming diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. Autoimmune panel was positive for MPO-p-ANCA, supporting the diagnosis of EGPA. The patient was initially treated with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, followed by rituximab. Despite treatment initiation, the patient rapidly deteriorated, requiring endotracheal intubation and admission to the intensive care unit. Treatment was escalated with therapeutic plasma exchange and intravenous cyclophosphamide. After a prolonged hospitalization, the patient gradually recovered and was transferred for rehabilitation. This case report highlights the diagnostic challenges of EGPA and the importance of early recognition. Whether omalizumab unmasked, coincided with, or induced EGPA remains uncertain. Clinicians should investigate unexplained, persistent eosinophilia as it could be an expression of a systemic disease.

42957499.title: Effect of remimazolam versus propofol anaesthesia on postoperative delirium in neurovascular surgery: a randomised noninferiority trial.
42957499.abstract: Propofol-based total intravenous anaesthesia (TIVA) is commonly used in neurovascular surgery, in which intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring limits inhalation anaesthetic use. However, propofol causes hypotension, and prolonged infusions can delay emergence. Remimazolam, a benzodiazepine whose effects are reversible with flumazenil, has been associated with less intraoperative hypotension than propofol, but its use raises concerns about postoperative delirium (POD). We tested whether remimazolam-based TIVA is noninferior to propofol-based TIVA for POD. In this single-centre, double-blind, randomised noninferiority trial, adults undergoing elective intracranial aneurysm clipping, arteriovenous malformation resection, microvascular decompression, or superficial temporal artery-middle cerebral artery bypass received remimazolam-based TIVA with flumazenil reversal at emergence, or propofol-based TIVA, both with remifentanil. The primary outcome was the cumulative incidence of POD within 5 days, assessed twice daily with the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) or the 3-Minute Diagnostic Interview for CAM-defined delirium (3D-CAM). The prespecified noninferiority margin was 10 percentage points. Among 686 patients in the modified intention-to-treat analysis, POD occurred in 44 of 344 (12.8%) with remimazolam and 37 of 342 (10.8%) with propofol (risk difference, 1.97 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.85 to 6.80; one-sided P<0.001 for noninferiority); per-protocol results were consistent. Hypotensive burden below a mean arterial pressure threshold of 65 mm Hg was lower in the remimazolam group (median, 0 vs 7.5 mm Hg min; P<0.001), and tracheal extubation in the operating room was more frequent (85.2% vs 67.3%). Remimazolam-based TIVA met the prespecified criterion for noninferiority to propofol-based TIVA with respect to postoperative delirium after elective neurovascular surgery. Interpretation should take into account that the observed incidence of postoperative delirium was lower than anticipated when the noninferiority margin was defined. NCT06115031 (ClinicalTrials.gov).

42955320.title: Ventilator-associated pneumonia after traumatic brain injury: a timing-sensitive ecological framework of neuroimmune-pulmonary vulnerability.
42955320.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is frequent after traumatic brain injury (TBI), but its biological meaning and outcome impact remain incompletely defined. Traditional models emphasise mechanical ventilation, aspiration, colonisation, endotracheal tube biofilm, and hospital pathogens. These mechanisms remain essential, but they do not fully explain the early clustering, heterogeneous susceptibility, changing bacteriology, and variable mortality effect observed after TBI. Severe brain injury creates an early vulnerable host state through impaired consciousness and airway protection, neuroimmune dysregulation, autonomic and endocrine activation, altered pulmonary immune surveillance, and, in many patients, extracranial trauma, shock, transfusion, or thoracic injury. These processes interact with ventilation, antibiotic pressure, and rapid respiratory microbiome disruption. Early VAP may reflect abrupt loss of control after injury and intubation, whereas late VAP may reflect persistent or secondary failure driven by biofilm maturation, antibiotic selection, multidrug-resistant pathogens, and intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired immune dysfunction. Clinically, VAP consistently prolongs ventilation, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and resource use, while its independent effect on mortality is phenotype- and context-dependent. This model proposes a timing-sensitive ecological framework in which established mechanisms may converge early and with particular clinical intensity after severe TBI, creating a vulnerable host-microbe state that may lower the threshold for clinically apparent infection. Future studies should distinguish isolated TBI from polytrauma, compare TBI with other acute brain injuries and non-neurological ventilated populations, and incorporate dynamic immune, microbial, and trajectory-based outcomes. VAP after TBI should be viewed as a timing-sensitive interaction between ventilator exposure and early host vulnerability, not as a distinct disease entity or as a pneumonia pathway unique to traumatic brain injury. The TBI-focused contribution lies in the early convergence of otherwise non-unique mechanisms: impaired airway control, aspiration risk, neuroimmune-endocrine activation, treatment exposure, dysbiosis, and extracranial injury burden, rather than in any single TBI-specific mechanism. Isolated TBI and TBI with polytrauma are biologically different phenotypes and should be separated in future studies. Early and late VAP may represent different phases of loss of pulmonary host-microbe containment; this distinction is probabilistic rather than TBI-specific in itself and requires validation in TBI-stratified cohorts. Mortality remains clinically relevant but context-dependent; VAP more consistently modifies recovery trajectory, ventilator dependence, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and possibly neurological recovery.

42955122.title: Electromagnetic stimulation of the phrenic nerve of intubated patients with obesity : A proof-of-concept study.
42955122.abstract: Noninvasive electromagnetic phrenic nerve stimulation generates diaphragmatic contractions, inducing tidal volumes above 3 ml/kg ideal body weight in both anesthetized, pulmonary healthy patients and critically ill patients. This intervention has the potential to mitigate critical illness-associated diaphragm weakness. In obese patients (15-20% of critically ill admissions) altered respiratory mechanics and anatomical changes could impair stimulation effectiveness. We aimed to assess the feasibility of noninvasive electromagnetic phrenic nerve stimulation to generate diaphragm contractions that produce tidal volumes above 3 ml/kg ideal body weight as a possible preventive or therapeutic option for critical illness-associated diaphragm weakness in obese anesthetized patients. This single-center proof-of-concept study included five obese patients scheduled for elective surgery under general anesthesia and endotracheal intubation. After induction of anesthesia, patients received anterior bilateral phrenic nerve noninvasive electromagnetic stimulation at 30%, 40% and 50% intensity. The primary endpoint was the tidal volume of 10 consecutive stimulations per patient. The median age of the five anesthetized patients was 36 (interquartile range, IQR 22-45) years and their mean body mass index was 41.2 (IQR 36.8-49.1) kg/m2. Median tidal volumes increased linearly (p < 0.001) from 0 to 1.61 (IQR 1.30-2.37) and 3.71 (IQR 3.38-4.15) ml/kg ideal body weight with 30%, 40%, and 50% stimulation intensity, respectively. At 50%, the stimulation generated tidal volumes above 3 ml/kg ideal body weight in 98% of breaths. Bilateral noninvasive phrenic nerve stimulation generates tidal volumes above 3 ml/kg ideal body weight in pulmonary healthy, non-critically ill anesthetized obese patients.

42954722.title: Consensus-derived clinical sepsis profiles and mortality across six international cohorts.
42954722.abstract: Clinical phenotyping may help characterize sepsis heterogeneity, but the applicability of derived profiles across healthcare settings remains uncertain. We evaluated consensus-derived clinical profiles and their associations with mortality across six international cohorts. We analyzed 62,458 adults from six critical care databases in four countries. In the MIMIC-IV discovery cohort (n = 28,733), six clustering algorithms were applied to 24 routinely available clinical variables to derive consensus profiles. The profiles were assigned in five external cohorts using fixed discovery-cohort templates. We examined clinical characteristics, mortality associations, and exploratory treatment-outcome associations. Three profiles were selected based on the Calinski-Harabasz peak and clinical interpretability. Profiles 1, 2, and 3 comprised 32.6%, 20.0%, and 47.4% of the discovery cohort, with in-hospital mortality of 30.3%, 13.8%, and 9.3%, respectively. Profile 1 showed greater multiorgan dysfunction, Profile 2 relatively preserved hemodynamics, and Profile 3 greater ventilatory support with less extrapulmonary dysfunction. Profile 1 had the highest mortality in all five external cohorts, with a decreasing mortality gradient across profiles in most cohorts. After adjustment for age and SOFA score, Profile 3 was associated with lower 1-year mortality than Profile 1 (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.57-0.67). Treatment-outcome associations were exploratory. Consensus-derived profiles characterized clinically interpretable patterns of sepsis heterogeneity with mortality differences across the evaluated cohorts. These findings support further evaluation of clinical profiling for risk stratification and phenotype-informed research.

42953943.title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Major Postoperative Complications After Noncardiac Surgery Under General Anesthesia Using Routinely Available Electronic Health Record Data: Retrospective Multicenter Development and Validation Study.
42953943.abstract: Postoperative complications after noncardiac surgery under general anesthesia remain a major cause of morbidity, mortality, and resource-intensive care. Conventional risk assessment tools rely mainly on preoperative information and may not capture perioperative physiological and procedural factors associated with postoperative risk. This retrospective multicenter observational study aimed to develop and validate electronic health record (EHR)-based machine learning (ML) models for predicting major postoperative complications and to evaluate their discrimination, overall probabilistic performance, calibration, and potential clinical utility. We analyzed 35,702 adults who underwent noncardiac surgery under general anesthesia at 3 tertiary hospitals between January 2021 and March 2025. Preoperative, intraoperative, and early postoperative variables were extracted from diagnosis procedure combination (DPC) claims, EHRs, and anesthesia information systems. The primary outcome was a 30-day composite of in-hospital death, unplanned reoperation, prolonged mechanical ventilation, new initiation of renal replacement therapy, and postoperative infection. Logistic regression (LR), extreme gradient boosting (XGB), and light gradient boosting machine (LGBM) models were developed using preoperative variables alone or with 7 additional intraoperative and early postoperative variables. Leave-one-facility-out internal-external cross-validation (IECV) was the primary validation framework, with a stratified random 80:20 hold-out analysis as secondary validation. Performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC), Brier score, scaled Brier score, calibration measures, and decision curve analysis. The primary composite outcome occurred in 3884 of 35,702 patients (10.9%). In pooled IECV, perioperative models consistently outperformed the corresponding preoperative models. AUROC increased from 0.784-0.791 to 0.810-0.817, PR-AUC increased from 0.356-0.361 to 0.405-0.413, Brier scores decreased from 0.082-0.083 to 0.078-0.080, and scaled Brier scores increased from 0.144-0.151 to 0.175-0.191. Calibration varied across facilities; pooled calibration slopes for the perioperative models ranged from 0.875 to 0.902, and calibration intercepts ranged from -0.367 to -0.222, indicating overly extreme predictions and overall risk overestimation. Exploratory decision curve analysis generally showed greater net benefit for perioperative models across threshold probabilities of 0.01-0.30, although the curves overlapped substantially. Secondary and sensitivity analyses were consistent with the primary findings. Adding routinely available intraoperative and early postoperative variables produced modest but consistent improvements in postoperative risk prediction compared with preoperative variables alone. However, facility-specific variation in calibration limits direct transportability of absolute risk estimates. The models may support prioritization for postoperative clinical reassessment, but exploratory decision curve analysis did not establish a specific intervention or triage threshold. Local recalibration and prospective workflow evaluation are required before clinical implementation.

42953825.title: Effectiveness of combined management of automated red cell exchange and therapeutic plasma exchange in a patient of sickle cell disease presenting with acute chest syndrome and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.
42953825.abstract: Acute chest syndrome (ACS) is a severe complication of sickle cell disease (SCD) that demands prompt medical attention. Approximately one-fifth of patients with a history of ACS progress rapidly to respiratory failure within 24 h, often leading to multiorgan failure. A 23-year-old male with a history of SCD and multiple vaso-occlusive crises presented to the emergency department with fever, chest pain, and breathlessness. Diagnosed with SCD 8 years prior, he had been on hydroxyurea 500 mg daily but had discontinued the medication 3 months back. He was admitted to the intensive care unit for urgent management and placed on noninvasive ventilation. The chest X-ray revealed new right lung consolidation. As the clinical condition deteriorated, he was intubated and placed on mechanical ventilation in the prone position. Routine management included intravenous (IV) morphine, antibiotics, and IV fluids. The patient urgently required a transfusion of two packed red blood cell units due to a critically low hemoglobin level of 4.1 g/dl, followed by automated red cell exchange (RCE). Automated RCE improved the PaO2/FiO2 ratio, and prone ventilation was no longer necessitated. He was suspected of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis due to fever, splenomegaly, hypertriglyceridemia, and hyperferritinemia. He was treated with therapeutic plasma exchange of 1.2 plasma volumes, followed by IV immunoglobulin. Hemodialysis was performed to treat acute kidney injury. His condition gradually improved, and he was extubated.

42953666.title: The Rising Burden of Atrial Fibrillation and Respiratory Failure Mortality in the United States: A 25-Year Nationwide Retrospective Analysis of Death Certificate Data.
42953666.abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) and respiratory failure (RF) frequently co-occur in critically ill patients, but long-term national trends in deaths recording both remain unknown. CDC WONDER multiple-cause-of-death data identified U.S. adults aged ≥ 55 years with both AF (including atrial flutter) and RF listed on death certificates from 1999 to 2024. Age-adjusted mortality rates (AAMRs) and annual percent changes (APCs) were estimated using joinpoint regression. Sensitivity analyses included adults aged ≥ 25 years, exclusion of COVID-19-related deaths, and stratification by co-listed heart failure (HF). A total of 462 284 deaths listed both AF and RF. The AAMR increased roughly five-fold (7.84 to 41.76 per 100 000), rising steadily through 2018 (APC 7.81), accelerating through 2021 (APC 18.78), and declining thereafter (APC -5.90). Excluding deaths listing COVID-19, the 2018-2021 acceleration was not detected, and AAMRs rose through 2024 (2017-2024 APC 5.25). AAMRs for deaths without HF recorded rose over fourfold.
