Further high-quality randomized controlled trials are required.

42985158.title: Severe pneumonia-associated lung injury: gut-lung-immune-metabolic connections in the critically ill host environment-microecology, barrier function, and mechanical ventilation.
42985158.abstract: Severe pneumonia-associated lung injury is a major cause of acute respiratory failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and death in critically ill patients. Its course is shaped within the critically ill host environment by pulmonary infection and tissue injury, systemic inflammation, circulatory and organ dysfunction, host reserve, and ICU treatment exposures, and may be accompanied by changes in gut microbiota, barrier integrity, and cellular immune metabolism. Thus, pulmonary, intestinal, circulatory, and metabolic changes should be viewed as interrelated processes occurring at different physiological levels rather than as a predefined linear pathway. Emerging studies suggest links among gut microbiota remodeling, barrier disruption, microbial or host-derived circulating signals, altered microbial metabolites, and immune-cell metabolic reprogramming. However, their biological significance varies. Some may represent parallel responses to severe infection and critical illness, whereas others may arise secondary to lung injury, hypoxia, hypoperfusion, or treatment exposure. Longitudinal human evidence remains insufficient to establish whether gut-derived signals achieve physiologically effective remote exposure and independently modify lung injury. Mechanical ventilation is essential for severe respiratory failure, and its direct mechanical contribution to ventilator-induced lung injury has a relatively clear physiological basis. In contrast, sedation, hemodynamic and splanchnic perfusion changes, oxygenation and ventilation status, antibiotics, and nutritional support are distinct concomitant exposures that may independently influence gastrointestinal function, microbiota, barrier integrity, and immune metabolism. Using the critically ill host response as the overarching framework, this review evaluates the temporality, directionality, and functional support of relationships among gut microbiota, barrier function, candidate remote signals, cellular immune metabolism, and ventilation-related exposures, and assesses whether current evidence supports biologically and clinically meaningful gut-lung-immune-metabolic interactions. It also discusses lung-protective ventilation, nutritional support, microbiota modulation, anti-inflammatory therapy, and barrier protection. Current evidence derives mainly from limited studies in severe pneumonia or pneumonia-associated ARDS, clinical evidence from other critically ill populations, and preclinical studies. Evidence that pulmonary and systemic critical illness responses affect the gut is stronger than evidence for an independent gut-to-lung effect. Future longitudinal multi-compartment studies, source tracing, multi-omics integration, and mechanism-oriented interventions are needed to clarify functional cross-compartment relationships and their incremental clinical value for risk stratification and targeted treatment.

42984973.title: Pre-extubation calculated serum osmolality and early invasive reintubation in critically ill adults: a dual-database study with multicenter external replication.
42984973.abstract: Extubation assessment focuses on respiratory, neurologic, and airway readiness, whereas osmotic-metabolic status has received less attention. We examined whether pre-extubation calculated hyperosmolarity was associated with early invasive reintubation and whether this association replicated across independent critical care databases. We analyzed the first eligible extubation in each hospital admission in MIMIC-IV and independently replicated the analysis in the multicenter eICU-CRD. Calculated serum osmolality was derived from sodium, glucose, and blood urea nitrogen measured within 24 h before extubation. Modified Poisson models estimated adjusted risk ratios (RRs) for 48-h invasive reintubation comparing calculated serum osmolality >300 with ≤300 mOsm/kg, using the same prespecified adjustment set in both databases. Secondary analyses evaluated 72-h reintubation and continuous associations, with additional sensitivity analyses addressing respiratory severity, fluid and renal status, threshold stability, and competing events. We included 2,639 eligible extubations in MIMIC-IV, with 317 reintubations, and 1,390 in eICU-CRD, with 93 reintubations. In MIMIC-IV, 48-h reintubation occurred in 13.6% of index extubations with calculated serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg and 10.8% with values ≤300 mOsm/kg (adjusted RR, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.05-1.62). The association replicated in eICU-CRD, where the corresponding risks were 10.5% and 4.6% (adjusted RR, 1.88; 95% CI, 1.27-2.77). The corresponding adjusted 72-h RRs were 1.25 (95% CI, 1.02-1.52) and 1.53 (95% CI, 1.19-1.97). Additional adjustment for respiratory severity produced little change within the corresponding measured subsets, whereas the continuous association was weaker in MIMIC-IV. Pre-extubation calculated hyperosmolarity was associated with a higher risk of early invasive reintubation in two independent critical care databases. It may serve as an adjunctive metabolic-renal marker that complements established extubation assessment.

42984951.title: JICS Education: Death in intensive care. Pathophysiology and diagnosis.
42984951.journal: Journal of the Intensive Care Society
42984951.abstract: Death is a daily reality of intensive care medicine and its safe and timely diagnosis is a core competency for the intensive care physician. This article addresses the philosophical and physiological basis of death as a neurological event and the history of its clinical recognition. The pathophysiology of coning, including the systemic consequences that follow neurological death are addressed in detail along with the maintenance of haemodynamic stability to allow brain stem testing. The clinical diagnosis of death using somatic, circulatory, and neurological criteria, including the updated 2025 Academy of the Medical Royal Colleges (AoMRC) Code of Practice and specific guidance for patients supported by extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), is explored to give FCICM exam candidates the knowledge necessary for the exam.

42984667.title: Ventilator brand, not ventilation mode, determines electricity consumption and estimated carbon emissions: a bench study of nine intensive care ventilators.
42984667.abstract: Health care generates 4%-5% of global greenhouse gas emissions, and the intensive care unit (ICU) is among its most energy-intensive environments, where energy rather than consumables dominates the carbon footprint. Ventilators run continuously, yet their electricity consumption has rarely been measured directly and never compared between brands. Active power was measured with a single plug-in digital meter on three devices from each of three brands, in every available ventilation mode plus standby (90 measurements). The device was the independent experimental unit, giving an effective sample of nine ventilators. All used integral internal gas delivery, with a shared circuit and test balloon under standardised settings. Power was read every 60 s over 10 min per mode and averaged, then modelled by linear mixed effects (brand and harmonised mode as fixed effects, random intercept for device within brand, brand-specific residual variance). The brand effect was corroborated by parametric bootstrap, the mode effect by equivalence testing; a brand-by-mode interaction was fitted. Emissions were projected across several utilisation and grid scenarios. Estimated marginal means were 64.9 W (Brand A), 95.4 W (Brand B) and 56.3 W (Brand C). Brand exerted a strong effect (bootstrap p = 0.003 ); mode showed no detectable effect under the tested conditions (bootstrap p = 0.51 ), every mode was equivalent to the reference at a pre-defined ± 10 W margin, and no brand-by-mode interaction was detected ( p = 0.27 , limited power). Brand B exceeded Brand C by 39.1 W (95% CI 17.0-61.2): a projected 161 kg  CO 2  -equivalent (95% CI 70-252) per ventilator annually at the Turkish grid factor under continuous operation, and 17 to 161 kg across scenarios. Standby reached 92.6% of active consumption in one brand; the active-minus-standby increment (4.8, 28.7 and 15.2 W) placed most of the between-brand difference in the idle baseline rather than in ventilation. Brand, not ventilation mode, dominated electricity consumption among the devices tested. The findings support requiring measured power to be declared and evaluated as a standardised criterion in ventilator tenders; because all devices were approximately ten years old, they do not identify which currently marketed platform is preferable.

42983576.title: Assessing vascular barrier permeability in critically ill patients: what are we really measuring?
42983576.abstract: Perturbation of vascular barrier permeability is a central mechanism in the pathophysiology of critical illness, contributing to tissue edema, impaired oxygen diffusion, and organ dysfunction. Despite advances in the field, direct bedside assessment of vascular permeability remains unavailable. Current approaches rely on indirect and compartment-specific surrogates, raising important questions about what is actually being measured. This narrative review summarizes the physiological principles underlying vascular barrier function and its disruption in conditions such as sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and major surgery. Currently available bedside tools used to assess vascular permeability or its consequences are critically appraised, including clinical examination, ultrasonography, transpulmonary thermodilution, bioelectrical impedance analysis, circulating biomarkers of endothelial injury (e.g., glycocalyx degradation products, angiopoietin-2), and albumin kinetics-based methods. While these techniques provide valuable insights, they predominantly reflect downstream consequences such as tissue edema, intravascular volume shifts, or endothelial activation rather than permeability itself. In addition, vascular permeability is a dynamic, context-dependent, and organ-specific process influenced by inflammatory, hemodynamic, and therapeutic factors, further complicating its interpretation. Each method therefore captures only a partial dimension of vascular barrier dysfunction, with important limitations related to specificity, feasibility, validation and standardization. No single bedside tool currently provides a comprehensive assessment of vascular permeability in critically ill patients. A multimodal approach integrating clinical evaluation, imaging, hemodynamic monitoring, and biomarkers is required to better characterize vascular barrier dysfunction. Future research should focus on validating composite indices and developing reliable, real-time bedside tools capable of directly assessing vascular permeability, with the ultimate goal of improving risk stratification and guiding personalized therapeutic strategies.

42982537.title: Rethinking Fluid Balance: The Shift Toward Deresuscitation in Critical Care.
42982537.journal: Advances in kidney disease and health
42982537.abstract: Intravenous fluid therapy is central to resuscitating critically ill patients, yet accumulating evidence shows that excessive fluid administration and positive fluid balance contribute directly to respiratory failure, acute kidney injury, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and mortality. Modern fluid stewardship reframes intravenous fluids as pharmacologic agents with dose-dependent toxicity and emphasizes the ROSE (Resuscitation, Optimization, Stabilization, and Evacuation) model. Observational studies consistently link fluid overload (often defined as fluid balance >5% baseline weight) to worse outcomes, and early or protocolized deresuscitation (removal of accumulated fluid once perfusion goals have been achieved) through diuretics or ultrafiltration can reliably achieve negative fluid balance and improve pulmonary parameters without increasing acute kidney injury. Randomized trials of restrictive strategies demonstrate improved ventilator-free days and shortened length of stay but no mortality benefit, underscoring the need for individualized, physiology-guided approaches. Evidence for active deresuscitation remains mixed. Diuretic-based protocols can lower mortality and reduce renal replacement therapy use in select populations, while ultrafiltration studies highlight the importance of avoiding both insufficient (<1 mL/kg/h) and excessive (>1.75 mL/hg/h) fluid removal rates. Knowledge gaps persist around optimal timing, patient selection, hemodynamic monitoring, and fluid removal targets. Ongoing trials aim to refine protocolized resuscitation and better define strategies to safely restore euvolemia, mitigate organ dysfunction, and improve outcomes in critical illness.

42981695.title: Remimazolam versus propofol for sedation in mechanically ventilated ICU patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
42981695.abstract: Propofol is widely used for sedation in the intensive care unit (ICU), but its use may be limited by cardiovascular depression, hypertriglyceridemia, and propofol infusion syndrome. Remimazolam has emerged as a potential alternative to propofol, with rapid metabolism, predictable recovery, and flumazenil reversibility. However, evidence regarding its use in mechanically ventilated ICU patients remains limited. PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, and ClinicalTrial.gov databases were reviewed for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing remimazolam with propofol in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. The primary outcome was percentage of time within the target sedation range. Secondary outcomes included sedation success rate, 28-day mortality, ICU mortality, length of ICU stay, and duration of mechanical ventilation. Safety outcomes including adverse events leading to dose reduction, hypotension, and delirium were evaluated. Continuous endpoints were reported using mean differences (MDs), and dichotomous outcomes were analyzed using risk ratios (RRs), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Six RCTs including 705 patients were analyzed. No statistically significant difference was detected in the percentage of time within the target sedation range (MD, -0.45%; 95% CI, -2.46 to 1.55; p = 0.56; I2 = 0%). No significant differences were detected in sedation success rate, 28-day mortality, ICU mortality, ICU length of stay, and duration of mechanical ventilation, or safety outcomes, although several estimates were imprecise. Remimazolam probably results in little to no difference in sedation efficacy compared with propofol in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. However, uncertainty remains regarding clinical and safety outcomes. Larger multinational RCTs are warranted to clarify these effects.

42981693.title: Oxygen consumption as a measure of metabolic demand during early rehabilitation and bedside activity in critically ill adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
42981693.abstract: Early rehabilitation and bedside activity can increase oxygen demand during invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), but the magnitude and variability of this response remain uncertain. To quantify acute changes in oxygen consumption (VO₂) during rehabilitation and bedside activity in adults receiving IMV and compare intervention domains. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception through July 6, 2026. Activity-related percentage changes in VO₂ were pooled using random-effects models. Risk of bias was assessed using revised Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Twenty studies were included, and 11 contributed 14 estimates to the primary meta-analysis. VO₂ increased by 29.2% from baseline (95% CI, 16.2%-43.6%; I2 = 96.2%; 95% prediction interval, -9.7% to 84.7%). All 14 point estimates were above baseline (+3.1% to +66.3%), although not all were individually statistically significant. Pooled estimates were higher for respiratory physiotherapy (43.3%; 95% CI, 32.3%-55.2%) than for other rehabilitation and bedside interventions (18.4%; 95% CI, -0.2%-40.5%), although this domain comparison was exploratory and confounded by study era and case mix. Mean arterial pressure and cardiac output showed pooled increases; other secondary analyses included few comparable studies. Oxygen consumption was above baseline in all 14 point estimates, with a pooled increase of 29.2% and estimates ranging from 3.1% to 66.3%. Responses did not follow a simple passive-to-active pattern, showing that clinically indicated bedside care and rehabilitation can impose markedly different metabolic loads. When perceived exertion cannot be assessed, VO₂ offers an objective measure of session-specific metabolic demand that can be interpreted alongside the patient's cardiorespiratory reserve.

42988712.title: Haemodynamic responses to tracheal intubation are context-dependent rather than patient-specific: risk is patient-derived but sympathetic tone-dependent. Comment on Br J Anaesth 2026; 137: 872-4.

42988639.title: Female Sex and Ventilatory Recovery After Isolated Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting in Heart Failure With Reduced Ejection Fraction: A Multicenter Cohort Study.
42988639.journal: Journal of cardiothoracic and vascular anesthesia
42988639.abstract: This study evaluated whether female sex is associated with postoperative mechanical ventilation duration and prolonged ventilation >24 hours after isolated coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Retrospective multicenter cohort study. Four German academic centers, 2017-2023. Five hundred seventy-four adults with left ventricular ejection fraction ≤40%; 70 (12.2%) were women. None. Primary outcomes were postoperative mechanical ventilation duration and intensive care unit length of stay. The primary models were adjusted for baseline/preoperative covariates without CPB. Female sex corresponded to +30.2% longer ventilation (95% CI -3.6% to +75.8%; p = 0.086), which did not reach conventional statistical significance, and higher odds of ventilation >24 hours (aOR 1.82, 95% CI 1.01-3.26; p = 0.045). Adding CPB strengthened the estimates, whereas extracorporeal life support exclusion and center fixed-effects adjustment attenuated them. In 69 matched pairs, women had longer ventilation (16.0 [8.0-33.2] v 11.0 [5.8-18.0] hours; p = 0.021) and more ventilation >24 hours (30.9% v 13.2%; p = 0.029). No clear association was observed with acute kidney injury or 30-day mortality. Female sex showed a model-dependent association with prolonged postoperative ventilation in this HFrEF CABG cohort. The findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation with standardized perioperative and extubation protocols.

42987229.title: Postoperative Neuromuscular Paresis and Overlap Syndrome Related to Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors: A Case Report.
42987229.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) can cause rare, severe immune-related adverse events. ICI-related overlap syndrome of myositis, myocarditis, and myasthenia gravis (3M) is uncommon yet carries high morbidity and mortality. We report a case with postoperative ICI-induced 3M syndrome that developed extremity paresis following proximal humerus resection and reconstruction. His clinical course was complicated by respiratory failure and septic shock, requiring intensive care. He was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin, corticosteroids, and plasmapheresis, leading to gradual recovery. This case highlights a rare postoperative presentation of 3M syndrome and underscores the importance of early recognition and prompt management.

42987193.title: Feasibility and Safety of Prone Positioning for Atelectasis in Neurocritical Patients: A Historically Controlled Study.
42987193.journal: The Journal of neuroscience nursing : journal of the American Association of Neuroscience Nurses
42987193.abstract: Prone positioning is effective for atelectasis but underutilized in neurocritical care due to concerns about neurological safety. This study examined the clinical outcomes and tolerability of prone positioning in a neurocritical care population predominantly comprising patients with encephalitis and status epilepticus. In this historically controlled study, neurocritical care patients with atelectasis received either 135-degree semiprone positioning plus standard physiotherapy (intervention) or standard physiotherapy alone (historical control). The cohort primarily included patients with encephalitis or status epilepticus (66%); those with intracerebral hemorrhage or traumatic brain injury were not represented. Outcomes included oxygenation (PaO2/FiO2 ratio), CT-based atelectasis score, and clinical endpoints. Forty-seven patients in the prone group and 50 controls were analyzed. The prone group demonstrated significantly improved PaO2/FiO2 ratios at days 3, 5, and 7 (all P<.05) and greater atelectasis resolution (P=.002). Mechanical ventilation duration was shorter in the prone group (14.11 vs. 16.82 d, P=.045). ICU stay, mortality, and neurological outcomes were comparable between groups. No serious adverse events attributable to prone positioning occurred. Prone positioning was feasible and well-tolerated in this selected neurocritical care cohort, with improved respiratory outcomes and no detectable safety signals. These findings support consideration of prone positioning in similar patient populations, though further research is needed in patients with elevated intracranial pressure risk. In clinical practice, prone positioning can be safely implemented by a trained nursing team using clinical observation in selected neurocritical care patients with stable intracranial pressure.

42986174.title: Creation and verification of an interpretable machine learning model for forecasting in-hospital results in Cardiorenal syndrome patients in critical condition.
42986174.abstract: Cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) encompasses a spectrum of disorders in which acute or chronic dysfunction of the heart or kidneys induces dysfunction of the other. The heart-kidney crosstalk underlying CRS has since been extended into the broader cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome by incorporating metabolic risk factors.CRS is associated with significantly increased mortality in intensive care unit (ICU) patients. However, dedicated tools for predicting short-term outcomes remain lacking, which limits timely risk stratification and treatment optimization. This multicenter cohort study enrolled 6,668 CRS patients from MIMIC-IV (v2.2) for model development and 3,602 from eICU-CRD (v2.0) for external validation. In patients remaining in the ICU for ≥24 hours, candidate predictors were ascertained within the first 24 hours, including early treatment exposures. Subsequent all-cause in-hospital mortality was predicted at this 24-hour landmark. Eleven machine learning algorithms were systematically compared after 1:1 random undersampling of the development cohort. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was applied to enhance interpretability and identify key prognostic features. The artificial neural network (ANN) model performed best. The final model incorporated six readily obtainable variables: AKI stage, age, mechanical ventilation, vasopressor use, β-blocker use, and ACEI/ARB use. It achieved an AUC of 0.810 (95% CI 0.757-0.860) in internal validation and 0.704 (95% CI 0.679-0.729) in external validation, indicating good internal but moderate external discrimination. We developed the first interpretable machine learning model specifically for predicting in-hospital mortality in critically ill CRS patients. SHAP provides transparent feature contribution analysis, and a web-based interface facilitates clinical implementation. When applied 24 hours after ICU admission, the model enables early identification of high-risk patients. It may also support risk stratification and resource allocation in the ICU.

42985722.title: A Case Report on a Life-Threatening Occult Supraglottic Granulating Mass Masquerading as Life-Threatening Asthma and Presenting as Cardiac Arrest.
42985722.abstract: Structural upper-airway lesions are uncommon but important mimics of asthma. A 74-year-old man with asthma and multiple recent admissions for presumed exacerbations presented with acute dyspnoea and subsequently sustained a pulseless electrical activity (PEA) cardiac arrest. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after five minutes, followed by emergency intubation and admission to intensive care. He was diagnosed and treated for presumed acute severe asthma and respiratory infection. By the following day, there was no significant wheeze or bronchospasm and extubation was attempted. He immediately developed severe stridor and profound hypoxaemia, with oxygen saturation falling to approximately 60%. Emergency video laryngoscopy revealed a large mobile supraglottic mass causing apparent "ball-valve" obstruction. Re-intubation restored oxygen saturation to 100%. The lesion was subsequently completely excised by the otorhinolaryngology team, with histopathology demonstrating granulation tissue. This case highlights the importance of considering structural upper-airway pathology when presumed asthma follows an atypical course, particularly when post-extubation stridor persists despite resolution of bronchospasm.

42985657.title: Hyperlactataemia and Hypocalcaemia as Predictors of Mortality in Adult Polytrauma Patients: A Prospective Observational Study.
42985657.abstract: Early identification of high-risk polytrauma patients remains a major challenge in critical care. This study aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of serum lactate and serum calcium in predicting in-hospital mortality among adult polytrauma patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). One hundred adult polytrauma patients aged 18-65 years with an Injury Severity Score (ISS) >16 and admitted within 48 hours of injury were enrolled. Baseline serum calcium and serial arterial lactate levels were measured during ICU stay. ISS, Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II), Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, days of mechanical ventilation, ICU stay, and mortality were noted. Overall in-hospital mortality was 62%. Non-survivors demonstrated significantly higher serial serum lactate concentrations throughout ICU admission than survivors (p < 0.001). Baseline serum lactate showed a significant negative correlation with survival (r = -0.379, p < 0.001), while peak lactate demonstrated an even stronger association (r = -0.498, p < 0.001). Baseline serum calcium was significantly associated with mortality and demonstrated inverse correlations with APACHE II, SOFA, and ISS, indicating that lower calcium levels were associated with greater injury severity and poorer clinical outcomes. Peak serum lactate also correlated positively with established severity scoring systems. Hyperlactataemia and hypocalcaemia are significant predictors of mortality in critically ill polytrauma patients. Both biomarkers correlate closely with validated trauma severity scores and provide valuable prognostic information early during ICU admission.

42985501.title: Clinical Factors Associated With Early Ketamine Initiation Among Mechanically Ventilated Adults: A Retrospective MIMIC-IV Cohort Study.
42985501.abstract: Ketamine is used for analgesia and sedation in mechanically ventilated ICU patients; however, the clinical factors associated with its early initiation remain poorly characterised. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV Version 3.1 among adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation and continuous first-line sedation with propofol, dexmedetomidine or midazolam. Early ketamine was defined as recorded administration by a continuous infusion or medication push within 48 h after qualifying first-line sedation began. Concurrent ventilation or continued first-line sedation was not required. Associations were assessed using multivariable logistic regression with patient-clustered robust standard errors. Among 24,363 qualifying ICU stays in 22,396 patients, 226 stays (0.9%) met the early-ketamine definition. The primary complete-case analysis included 21,342 stays and 196 early-ketamine events. Surgical/trauma intensive care unit admission (adjusted odds ratio 2.05, 95% confidence interval 1.39-3.04; p < 0.001), Black race (adjusted odds ratio 1.63, 95% confidence interval 1.05-2.53; p = 0.028) and Stage 3 acute kidney injury (adjusted odds ratio 1.67, 95% confidence interval 1.10-2.53; p = 0.016) were associated with higher odds of early ketamine initiation. Cardiac ICU admission and higher P/F ratio were associated with lower odds. Mean PEEP showed a nonlinear association (p = 0.005). Of 226 starts, 165 (73.0%) occurred during recorded invasive ventilation. Estimates were similar after bolus exclusion, whereas restricting initiation to recorded ventilation attenuated several associations, including surgical/trauma ICU admission (adjusted odds ratio 1.49; 95% CI, 0.97-2.31). Early ketamine administration was uncommon under the study definition and did not always begin during recorded invasive ventilation. Associations were similar after bolus exclusion, but some attenuated when initiation was restricted to recorded ventilation. These findings describe patterns of ketamine use and do not establish treatment indications or therapeutic benefits.

42984297.title: Beyond Early vs. Late: A Bayesian Evaluation of Tracheostomy Timing and Outcomes in Critical Illness.
42984297.abstract: The ideal timing of tracheostomy in critically ill patients remains controversial. Although early procedures may yield better outcomes, the specific contributions of each decision-making interval remain poorly defined. Here, we aimed to evaluate the associations of overall tracheostomy timing and component intervals with ventilator weaning, intensive care unit (ICU) discharge, mortality, and hospital costs. In this retrospective cohort study, we included 480 patients admitted to the ICU who underwent tracheostomy between 2021 and 2023 at a single center. Patients were classified by tracheostomy timing into early (< 7 days), standard (7-14 days), and late (> 14 days) groups. Timing was also evaluated as a continuous variable and divided into 3 clinical intervals: from intubation to suggestion, suggestion to consultation, and consultation to the procedure. Ventilator weaning and ICU discharge were modeled using a Bayesian competing-risk survival approach. Mortality and medical expenditures were assessed using Bayesian logistic regression and Bayesian Gaussian regression, respectively. Propensity score matching was applied in the sensitivity analyses. Late tracheostomy was associated with lower probabilities of ventilator weaning and ICU discharge and with higher medical costs. Early tracheostomy was associated with the most favorable outcomes. Delays in the interval between intubation and tracheostomy were consistently associated with poor weaning outcomes. Mortality associations were less certain but suggested a potentially unfavorable pattern with delayed procedures. These findings remained consistent after matching. Among patients who ultimately underwent tracheostomy, timing < 7 days was associated with the most favorable observed outcomes, whereas the 7-14-day group generally showed intermediate results. These associations should not be interpreted as evidence that an early-tracheostomy strategy is optimal for all patients.

42984162.title: Outcomes after lung transplantation for connective tissue disease-related interstitial lung disease: single center in South Korea.
42984162.abstract: Pulmonary involvement is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in connective tissue diseases (CTDs), particularly in the form of CTD-related interstitial lung disease (CTD-ILD), and patients with severe CTD-ILD may eventually require lung transplantation (LT). However, post-transplant outcomes specific to CTD-ILD remain poorly characterized. We performed a retrospective cohort study of adult patients who underwent LT for ILD between 2008 and 2025 at a single tertiary center. Patients were classified into CTD-ILD and non-CTD-ILD groups. Clinical and perioperative data were obtained through chart review. Overall survival was analyzed using Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox proportional hazards models. A total of 170 patients were included; 39 had CTD-ILD and 131 had non-CTD-ILD. CTD-ILD recipients were more often female (22/39, 56.4% vs. 32/131, 24.4%; P<0.001) and had a numerically higher prevalence of preoperative pulmonary hypertension (7/39, 17.9% vs. 12/131, 9.2%; P=0.094). Overall survival did not differ significantly between the CTD-ILD and non-CTD-ILD groups (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.923; 95% CI, 0.383-2.229; P=0.859; log-rank P=0.334). CTD-ILD recipients had a longer postoperative intensive care unit stay (median [interquartile range], 23.0 days [13.0-35.0] vs. 17.0 days [11.0-28.0]; P=0.026), a longer duration of mechanical ventilation (17.0 days [8.0-32.0] vs. 8.0 days [5.0-18.0]; P=0.009), fewer ventilator-free days (8.0 [0.0-19.0] vs. 11.0 [0.0-22.0]; P=0.002), and a higher incidence of postoperative thromboembolic events (10/39, 25.6% vs. 6/131, 4.6%; P<0.001). Although survival did not differ significantly in the present study, CTD-ILD recipients had a greater perioperative burden, including higher rates of thromboembolic events and greater use of intensive care resources.

42983673.title: Respiratory fungal colonization in hospitalized patients in western Iran: species distribution and antifungal susceptibility patterns.
42983673.abstract: Respiratory fungal colonization is frequently observed among hospitalized patients with underlying pulmonary disorders; however, its clinical significance, species distribution, and local antifungal susceptibility patterns remain incompletely characterized, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. This study aimed to determine the frequency of culture-confirmed fungal detection in respiratory specimens, describe the distribution of fungal species, assess antifungal susceptibility profiles of predominant isolates, and examine associations between culture positivity and selected demographic and clinical characteristics in western Iran. This prospective cross-sectional observational study was conducted over a 12-month period (July 2020-July 2021) at two tertiary-care hospitals in western Iran. A total of 127 consecutive respiratory specimens, including sputum (with quality assessment using Bartlett criteria), bronchoalveolar lavage, and tracheal aspirates, were examined by direct microscopy and fungal culture. Fungal isolates were identified using a combination of conventional phenotypic and molecular methods. CHROMagar, germ tube testing, and carbohydrate assimilation profiling were applied exclusively to yeast isolates, while filamentous fungi were identified using phenotypic methods and confirmed by ITS rDNA sequencing for representative isolates. Antifungal susceptibility testing of predominant isolates was conducted using CLSI broth microdilution methods (M27 A4 for yeasts, M38 A2 for filamentous fungi). MICs were interpreted using CLSI species-specific breakpoints or epidemiological cutoff values where available; for Candida glabrata, fluconazole MICs were categorized as Susceptible Dose-Dependent (SDD), and for Aspergillus species, isolates were categorized as wild-type (WT) or non-wild-type (NWT) based on ECVs. Demographic and clinical data were extracted from medical records. Fungal growth was detected in 62 of 127 respiratory specimens (48.8%). Yeasts constituted the majority of isolates (71.0%). Candida albicans was the most frequently identified species (37.1%), followed by C. glabrata (17.7%), C. tropicalis (9.7%), and C. parapsilosis (6.5%). Among filamentous fungi, Aspergillus flavus was the most commonly isolated mold (9.7%), followed by Rhizopus spp. (6.5%), A. fumigatus (4.8%), A. niger (4.8%), and Penicillium spp. (3.2%). Culture positivity was highest in sputum specimens (51.9%), followed by bronchoalveolar lavage (44.4%) and tracheal aspirates (33.3%); however, these differences were not statistically significant (p = 0.19). No significant associations were found between culture positivity and demographic or clinical variables, including age, sex, COPD, pneumonia, malignancy, diabetes mellitus, or COVID-19 status; however, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to the limited sample size. C. albicans isolates exhibited high susceptibility to the tested antifungal agents (with MIC₅₀ and MIC₉₀ values of 0.5 and 2 µg/mL for fluconazole), whereas elevated fluconazole MICs (with 36.4% of isolates categorized as SDD) were observed among C. glabrata isolates. All A. flavus isolates tested were categorized as wild-type for amphotericin B and voriconazole based on CLSI ECVs. Culture-confirmed fungal detection was common in respiratory specimens from hospitalized patients with suspected lower respiratory tract disorders. Yeasts, particularly Candida species, predominated, while A. flavus was the leading mold isolate, reflecting regional epidemiological patterns. The high proportion of Candida isolates should be interpreted with caution, as recovery of Candida from respiratory secretions almost always represents colonization rather than infection and should not routinely prompt antifungal therapy in non-neutropenic patients. No significant associations were observed between culture positivity and the evaluated clinical variables, although this may be attributable to the limited sample size and incomplete data on clinically relevant risk factors such as ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, and corticosteroid exposure. These findings emphasize the need for cautious interpretation of respiratory fungal culture results, species-level identification, and antifungal susceptibility testing as components of antifungal stewardship. Larger multicenter studies with comprehensive risk factor assessment, fungal biomarkers, and longitudinal follow-up are needed to clarify the clinical significance of respiratory fungal colonization and its potential progression to invasive disease.

42983326.title: Mucormycosis in adult hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients during the antifungal prophylaxis era: a single-center retrospective case series.
42983326.abstract: Mucormycosis is an uncommon but severe invasive fungal infection in hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients. Contemporary cases may occur outside the classic early neutropenic post-transplant window and during antifungal prophylaxis. We performed an International Classification of Diseases code-screened retrospective case series using the institutional denominator of adult hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients at Mayo Clinic from January 1, 2008, through December 1, 2025. Cases were adjudicated using 2020 European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer and Mycoses Study Group Education and Research Consortium criteria. We analyzed transplant characteristics, immune and pulmonary host factors, prophylaxis and therapeutic drug monitoring, diagnostic evidence, management, critical care use, and outcomes. Among 6,340 adult transplant recipients, 13 met criteria for invasive mucormycosis; eleven had allogeneic transplant and 2 had autologous transplant. Median age was 61 years, and median onset was 681 days after transplant. Underlying conditions included acute myeloid leukemia in 4 patients, chronic lymphocytic leukemia and chronic myeloid leukemia in 2 each, and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, T-cell lymphoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, multiple myeloma, and VEXAS syndrome in one each. All patients were receiving systemic antifungal prophylaxis; 11 were receiving mold-active azoles and 6 were receiving posaconazole. Five patients had pre-diagnosis azole levels available. Neutropenia was present in 4 patients, while lymphopenia, low helper T-cell counts when measured, graft-versus-host disease, targeted or immunomodulatory therapies, and pulmonary host-defense abnormalities were frequent. Pulmonary or mixed pulmonary involvement occurred in 8 patients, disseminated disease in 3, and 9 cases were proven. Liposomal amphotericin B was used in 12 patients, source-control surgery in 6, intensive care unit admission in 6, mechanical ventilation in 5, and all-cause mortality was 5 of 13 at 30, 42, and 90 days. This series describes mucormycosis in adult transplant recipients rather than establishing causal attribution to transplantation in every case. The findings support diagnostic vigilance for Mucorales infection in chronically immunocompromised transplant recipients, including those remote from transplant, receiving prophylaxis, and without neutropenia.

42983154.title: Bedside endoscopy for significant acute upper gastrointestinal bleed.
42983154.journal: Indian journal of gastroenterology : official journal of the Indian Society of Gastroenterology
42983154.abstract: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding (AUGIB) is a frequent life-threatening scenario in everyday clinical practice. We undertook a study to assess the etiology and important clinical outcomes in patients with significant AUGIB unstable for transfer to an endoscopy suite. This is a prospective observational study conducted between December 2019 and December 2022, including patients above the age of 16 years with a history of clinically significant AUGIB undergoing bedside endoscopy in an intensive care (ICU)/high dependency unit (HDU) setting. Seventy patients with a mean age (SD) of 51.27 (13.45) years were included. The initial mean (SD) hemoglobin, APACHE score, SOFA score and GCS of these patients were 6.71 (2.14) g%, 20.3 (8.3), 8.28 (4.64) and 10.9 (4.68), respectively. The major causes for AUGIB were portal hypertension in 28 (40%) and peptic ulcer disease in 24 (34.2%) patients. Eight patients (19.5%) experienced rebleed. Radiological intervention was needed for three patients (4.3%) and surgery for two (2.9%) patients. Overall, 30-day mortality was 54.2%. AUGIB, per se, was the cause for mortality in only 21% of those who died. Sepsis, respiratory failure and liver failure were the factors that independently predicted 30-day mortality. This is the first study specifically looking at the role of bedside endoscopy in AUGIB among South Asian patients. The most common etiologies of AUGIB in our cohort were portal hypertension and peptic ulcer disease. Rebleed, surgery and 30-day mortality rates were 19.5%, 2.9% and 54.2%, respectively. A majority of the deaths were due to underlying co-morbidities.

42982028.title: Cardiac Surgery Outcomes in Japanese Patients Receiving Peritoneal Dialysis Versus Hemodialysis.
42982028.journal: Therapeutic apheresis and dialysis : official peer-reviewed journal of the International Society for Apheresis, the Japanese Society for Apheresis, the Japanese Society for Dialysis Therapy
42982028.abstract: Comparative postoperative outcomes after cardiac surgery in Japanese patients receiving peritoneal dialysis (PD) and hemodialysis (HD) remain unclear. We retrospectively evaluated 26 dialysis patients who underwent cardiac surgery from 2016 to 2022. The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause death, ischemic stroke, bleeding complications, and infections during hospitalization. The secondary endpoints included intubation duration, intensive care unit (ICU) stay, and postoperative stay in the cardiovascular surgery department. Seven patients received PD and nineteen received HD. The composite outcome occurred in 14% in PD and 42% in HD patients (p = 0.36). Median intubation duration and ICU stay were 1 vs. 2 days (p = 0.18) and 4 vs. 4 days (p = 0.91), respectively. Median postoperative stay was shorter in PD than HD patients (14 vs. 17 days, p = 0.03). No statistically significant difference in the composite in-hospital outcome was observed between groups, although estimates were imprecise because of the small sample size.

42981727.title: The 'cost of complexity' of boarding mechanically ventilated patients in emergency department crowding: A retrospective NEDOCS analysis with deterministic scenario modelling in a Chilean university hospital.
42981727.abstract: Emergency department (ED) crowding and the boarding of critically ill patients compromise patient safety and emergency nursing care. We described crowding in the adult ED of a high-complexity university hospital using the National Emergency Department Overcrowding Scale (NEDOCS) and quantified the "cost of complexity": the additional crowding attributable to boarding mechanically ventilated patients. Retrospective observational study of 21,620 adult ED episodes (2023). NEDOCS was reconstructed from electronic timestamps (12 treatment spaces; 305 hospital beds) and classified using the original levels. Because ventilated patients were not recorded, the ventilator term was fixed at zero (reference, V = 0), one (V = 1) or two (V = 2) patients, keeping all other components at observed values. Admission was required in 23.5% of episodes; mean door-to-doctor time was 48.4 min (median 7.7), and occupancy exceeded the 12 treatment spaces during 40.1% of hours. The mean annual NEDOCS was 104.5 points ("overcrowded") in the reference scenario. Each ventilated boarder adds a constant 13.4 points: with V = 2, the annual mean rose to 131.3, days with a mean above 180 increased from 40 to 74, and months above 140 from none to four. On weekdays, NEDOCS was below 100 only from 03:00 to 10:00; an evening plateau (15:00-22:00; 164-177 points) exceeded 180 points from 14:00 to 23:00 under V = 2. Ventilated boarders add a fixed increment to NEDOCS that, in an already overcrowded ED, pushes peak days and hours into the dangerously overcrowded range. Earlier inpatient discharges, timely critical care bed allocation and NEDOCS-triggered full-capacity protocols warrant prospective evaluation to protect patient safety and nursing capacity.

42981604.title: A Volatilomics Approach for the Identification of Volatile Organic Compounds as Biomarkers of Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia Using GC-MS.
42981604.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is a common and serious complication of patients at intensive care units (ICUs), contributing to increased morbidity and mortality. Current diagnostic approaches for VAP rely on clinical, radiological, and invasive methods, which are time-consuming, carry risks, and may result in delayed or inconclusive findings. The need for rapid, reliable, and non-invasive diagnostic tools is critical. Biomarkers and specifically volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in exhaled breath have emerged as promising candidates for this purpose. In this study, we applied gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) with solid-phase microextraction (SPME) to analyze breath VOC profiles in critically ill children and explore their potential as early indicators of VAP. Results reveal significant challenges in breath volatilomics, including batch effects and variability in VOC detection. However, normalization strategies allowed for meaningful comparisons across multiple time points, revealing subtle trends in VOC profiles that could differentiate patients with high and low suspicion of VAP. Notably, VOCs such as octanol and benzyl alcohol showed reduced levels in patients with higher suspicion of VAP at Day 6, suggesting potential associations with respiratory infection severity. While preliminary, these findings support further investigation into breath-based VOC signatures as a non-invasive, early diagnostic tool for VAP in pediatric ICUs. This approach could enhance diagnostic accuracy and inform timely clinical decisions, improving patient outcomes.

42979555.title: Inflammatory cytokines and neurotrauma biomarkers are acutely elevated in military combat casualties and predict resource use.
42979555.journal: Frontiers in disaster and emergency medicine
42979555.abstract: Triage of and evacuation decisions for military service members deployed into combat zones experiencing traumatic injuries are serious challenges for military medical providers. We explored the utility of inflammatory biomarkers in determining injury severity and predicting hospital resource utilization to improve the effectiveness of casualty care. Serum levels of inflammatory cytokines (eNAMPT, IL-6, PSGL-1, ANG-2, IL-1β, IL-1RA, TNF-α, and S100A8) and neurotrauma biomarkers (GFAP, NfL, and tau) were analyzed in trauma-exposed warfighters (n = 39) evacuated to a medical treatment facility. Prior to analysis, outliers were removed via robust regression and outlier removal, with the results analyzed using the Mann-Whitney test, Kruskal-Wallis test w/ Dunn, or Spearman correlation. All the tested biomarkers were significantly elevated (p < 0.0001) in combat casualties vs. healthy controls (n = 46) and exhibited injury type-specific elevations. Serum eNAMPT (p = 0.033) and TNF-α (p = 0.047) were significantly higher in penetrating wounds vs. blunt trauma; IL-1β (p = 0.005) and S100A8 (p = 0.005) were significantly elevated in thermal injures vs. blunt trauma; and GFAP (p < 0.001) and NfL (p = 0.017) were significantly elevated in blunt trauma vs. thermal injury. Statistical correlations between biomarkers and clinical outcomes indicated the following: (i) duration of mechanical ventilatory support correlated with IL-1RA level (p = 0.021); (ii) duration of hospital stay correlated with IL-6 (p = 0.016) and eNAMPT levels (p = 0.046); and (iii) duration of ICU stay correlated with eNAMPT (p = 0.016) and S100A8 (p = 0.017) levels. Our results extend prior reports of innate immune activation following traumatic injury and suggest a diverse panel of inflammatory biomarkers may predict hospital resource utilization to inform prioritization of local resources and evacuation to higher levels of care.

42979219.title: Herpesvirus reactivation in COVID-19: clinical evidence, mechanistic insights, and research gaps.
42979219.abstract: Herpesviruses establish lifelong latency and can reactivate when antiviral immune surveillance is compromised. Since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic, reactivation of multiple human herpesviruses has increasingly been documented, particularly in patients with severe or critical illness. Herpesvirus reactivation has been associated with prolonged intensive care unit stays, secondary infections, greater ventilatory support requirements, and increased mortality. This review summarizes the latency and reactivation characteristics of the major human herpesviruses and evaluates the clinical evidence linking their reactivation to SARS-CoV-2 infection. We further propose a multifactorial mechanistic framework involving impaired T-cell and natural killer cell surveillance, defective interferon-mediated immunity, sustained inflammation and cytokine signaling, direct and indirect effects of SARS-CoV-2 proteins, and host transcriptional and epigenetic reprogramming. However, despite accumulating clinical and experimental evidence supporting a biologically plausible association between SARS-CoV-2 infection and herpesvirus reactivation, the precise mechanisms underlying this interplay remain incompletely understood. Longitudinal viral monitoring, physiologically relevant latency models, and mechanistic intervention studies are therefore needed to establish causality and identify patients who may benefit from targeted surveillance or antiviral treatment.

42978929.title: Perioperative Anaphylaxis and Respiratory Failure During AVF Surgery in an End-Stage Renal Disease Patient.
42978929.abstract: Perioperative anaphylaxis can cause sudden, catastrophic respiratory and cardiovascular collapse in high-risk ESRD patients, even during regional anesthesia. Early recognition, prompt epinephrine administration, serum tryptase measurement, vigilant respiratory monitoring, and multidisciplinary preparedness-including ECMO capability-are critical to improving survival and preventing recurrent perioperative events.

42980831.title: Systemic corticosteroids in critical illness: an evidence-based framework for clinical decision-making.
42980831.abstract: Systemic corticosteroids are pivotal in managing inflammation-driven critical illnesses, yet bedside translation remains inconsistent. This systematic review establishes an evidence-based framework for clinical decision-making by horizontally synthesizing contemporary evidence across severe community-acquired pneumonia (sCAP), acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and septic shock. A systematic electronic search was conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library up to early 2026. Peer-reviewed randomized controlled trials (RCTs), systematic reviews, and meta-analyses published in English were eligible. Data regarding population characteristics, dosing regimens, initiation timing, duration, and safety profiles were independently extracted and qualitatively synthesized. Landmark trials define context-dependent efficacy: early hydrocortisone continuous infusion significantly reduces 28-day mortality in sCAP (CAPE COD), while a 10-day dexamethasone regimen improves ventilator-free days and survival in moderate-to-severe ARDS (DEXA-ARDS). In septic shock, early hydrocortisone-fludrocortisone combination accelerates shock resolution and lowers 90-day mortality (APROCCHS). These outcomes align with distinct pharmacological profiles: hydrocortisone provides dual glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid activity to restore vascular tone, whereas dexamethasone exerts potent transrepression of proinflammatory transcription factors. To mitigate steroid-induced harm, protocolized safety targets are essential, including maintaining blood glucose at 140-180 mg/dL and actively monitoring for secondary infections. Corticosteroids do not exert a uniform class effect. Bedside success requires personalized, protocolized regimens optimized by scenario-specific timing, dosing, and proactive adverse-event monitoring.

42986025.title: Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia With Propofol Infusion Syndrome in Severe Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome.
42986025.abstract: Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS) is a rare, potentially fatal complication of prolonged or high-dose propofol exposure characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction, rhabdomyolysis, metabolic derangements, and cardiovascular collapse. The classically described mode of cardiac death is bradycardia progressing to asystole. A previously healthy 21-year-old woman presented 5 days after a vaginal delivery with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome requiring sedation with propofol escalated to 100 μg/kg/min. She developed rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, acidosis, and progressive ventricular ectopy that evolved into pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Propofol was stopped, and continuous renal replacement therapy was arranged, but the patient experienced cardiac arrest before initiation. No arrhythmias occurred after metabolic correction. This case highlights pulseless ventricular tachycardia as a rare cardiac manifestation of PRIS with evolving metabolic abnormalities before cardiovascular collapse occurs. Rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalemia during prolonged propofol therapy should prompt evaluation for PRIS. Early propofol discontinuation and aggressive metabolic correction may prevent fatal ventricular arrhythmias.

42983546.title: SERPINC1-mediated hereditary antithrombin deficiency with refractory pulmonary embolism: successful treatment with VA-ECMO and interventional thrombus aspiration.
42983546.abstract: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) carries substantial global morbidity and mortality, with 50%-60% of disease variability attributed to genetic factors. Hereditary antithrombin deficiency (HATD), caused by pathogenic variants in the SERPINC1 gene, is an autosomal dominant thrombophilia that confers a 20-40-fold higher risk of VTE, predominantly manifesting as recurrent pulmonary embolism (PE) and deep vein thrombosis (DVT). We report a 22-year-old male with recurrent PE secondary to type II HATD driven by a heterozygous SERPINC1 missense variant (c.1315 C > A, p.Pro439Thr). His second episode of PE progressed to obstructive cardiogenic shock refractory to systemic thrombolysis, accompanied by hemoptysis. Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) was initiated, yet recurrent oxygenator thrombosis occurred despite high-dose unfractionated heparin (UFH) infusion. Laboratory testing revealed an antithrombin III (AT-III) activity level of 39.5%, confirming the diagnosis. Pulmonary angiography followed by mechanical thrombus aspiration was performed, and long-term anticoagulation was switched to rivaroxaban. The patient was successfully weaned from VA-ECMO, with no PE recurrence or adverse cardiovascular events recorded during 5 years of follow-up. This case represents the first published report of a young patient with a SERPINC1 variant complicated by recurrent high-risk PE unresponsive to rt-PA thrombolysis who survived after VA-ECMO-supported pulmonary thrombus aspiration. Early etiological genetic screening for hereditary thrombophilia is essential for managing refractory PE induced by SERPINC1 variants. Individualized regimens combining VA-ECMO, interventional thrombectomy, and direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) yield favorable clinical outcomes and provide a reference for managing critically ill patients with hereditary thrombophilia.

42984267.title: Implementation of the seizure code in a tertiary hospital: Effects on emergency care times and clinical outcomes in severe seizures.
42984267.abstract: To assess the impact of implementing the Seizure Code (SC), a structured multidisciplinary emergency protocol for severe seizures, on care times and clinical outcomes at a tertiary hospital. Single-center, retrospective observational study including episodes of severe seizures in patients aged 18 years or older managed between January 2023 and December 2024, comparing pre-SC and post-SC periods. The primary outcome was time from seizure onset to administration of the first anti-seizure medication (ASM). Secondary outcomes included other care intervals, process indicators, and clinical outcomes. Care intervals were analyzed with accelerated failure time models (percentage change in median time), length of stay in a competing-risks framework, and binary outcomes with Firth-penalized logistic regression (odds ratios, OR), all adjusted for prespecified covariates and clustered by patient. Of 1959 episodes identified, 378 (175 pre-SC, 203 post-SC) met SC activation criteria. Time to the first ASM, the primary outcome, did not differ significantly (27% shorter, 95% CI -15% to 53% for benzodiazepines; 27%, -6% to 50% for others). Time to urgent video-EEG (VEEG) was 48% shorter (29%-61%) and the neurological assessment-VEEG interval 63% shorter (31%-80%). Pre-notification by Emergency Medical Services increased (22.9% vs. 37.8%; p = 0.003). Hospital stay (7.48 vs. 5.08 days; subdistribution hazard ratio for discharge alive 1.36, 1.02-1.89) and intensive care unit stay (3.20 vs. 1.48 days) were shorter. Thirty-day seizure recurrence was lower (8.0% vs. 3.0%; adjusted OR 0.33, 0.12-0.84). Mortality and functional status at discharge did not differ. The primary outcome, time to first anti-seizure medication, was not significantly shorter after implementation of the structured emergency protocol. The observed benefits were concentrated in secondary process and resource-utilization indicators: implementation of the Seizure Code was associated with faster access to urgent VEEG, shorter hospital and intensive care unit stays, and lower 30-day seizure recurrence, without a significant effect on mortality. These findings support protocolized emergency pathways in severe seizures. Severe seizures are emergencies in which fast, coordinated care matters. We compared how patients were treated at one hospital before and after a new protocol, the Seizure Code, was introduced. Afterwards, patients had urgent video-EEG (a recording of brain activity) sooner and spent fewer days in hospital and in the intensive care unit, and fewer had another seizure within 30 days. However, the time to the first anti-seizure medication did not change significantly, and deaths and disability at discharge were unchanged.

42985811.title: Antimicrobial-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the USA: implications of a national surveillance gap.
42985811.abstract: Surveillance data for Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the USA are distributed across systems designed for different purposes, potentially limiting standardized national surveillance of high-priority resistant phenotypes. We evaluated whether the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS) can support surveillance of multidrug-resistant (MDR) P. aeruginosa and synthesized available CDC surveillance data to characterize the residual surveillance gap. We reviewed the 2026 NNDSS list of nationally notifiable conditions for P. aeruginosa. Because neither P. aeruginosa infection nor a resistant phenotype was present, NNDSS case counts were unable to be analysed. We therefore conducted a descriptive secondary analysis of CDC National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) reports for 2018-21 and the 2022 NHSN Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Option report. In 2018-21 adult NHSN data, 11.9% of tested P. aeruginosa isolates from device-associated infections were MDR, compared with 3.9% from surgical-site infections. Among central-line-associated bloodstream infection isolates, MDR proportions were highest in long-term acute-care hospitals (LTACHs, 25.3%), followed by hospital intensive-care units (14.2%), hospital wards (11.9%) and oncology units (8.5%). Among catheter-associated urinary tract infection isolates, MDR phenotype was observed in 20.8% of LTACH isolates. In the 2022 AR Option report, carbapenem non-susceptibility exceeded 10% among community-onset isolates and approached 20% among hospital-onset isolates. NNDSS cannot currently quantify the burden of MDR P. aeruginosa, but substantial resistance surveillance is available through NHSN and the CDC AR Laboratory Network. The principal gap is not an absence of surveillance data but fragmentation across systems with different populations, denominators, objectives and reporting mechanisms.

42984548.title: Genomic surveillance uncovers high-risk resistance profiles in Escherichia coli and Klebsiella spp. from Central Mexico.
42984548.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
42984548.abstract: To generate actionable genomic evidence for antimicrobial-resistance (AMR) surveillance in Central Mexico by characterizing the diversity, resistome, and mobilome of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and K. michiganensis belonging to the K. oxytoca complex (KoxSC) circulating between 2021 and 2023, and by contextualizing these findings within national genomic data. We sequenced 65 MDR/XDR isolates referred to the State Public Health Laboratory of Aguascalientes (LESPA) and compared them with 268 publicly available Mexican genomes. Phenotypic susceptibility profiles (BD Phoenix M50) were integrated with genomic predictions to assess concordance. Phylogenomics, pangenomics, resistome and mobilome profiling, and virulence analyses were performed using standardized pipelines. Because LESPA receives referral cases from severe or treatment-refractory infections, this dataset represents a high-risk clinical subset rather than a population-level sample. The sequenced isolates displayed substantial lineage diversity (34 sequence types across E. coli and Klebsiella spp.) and more than 100 distinct antimicrobial-resistance gene combinations. Several determinants not previously reported in Mexican resistant microorganisms-such as TEM-116, aadA22, ermB, and uhpA-were identified. Carbapenemase NDM-1 and colistin-associated MCR-9.1 were widespread, and resistance genes frequently co-localized with mobile genetic elements, suggesting active horizontal gene-transfer dynamics. Post-2020 isolates exhibited increased resistome richness, higher XDR rates, and more frequent coinfections, particularly in critical-care settings. The K. michiganensis isolates represent the first MDR genomes of this species from Aguascalientes and contribute to the expanding genomic characterization of this underrepresented member of the K. michiganensis (KoxSC) in Mexico. This study provides the first genomic baseline for MDR E. coli and Klebsiella spp. in Central Mexico and documents an increasingly complex resistome likely shaped by clinical practices, referral patterns, and structural limitations in microbiological capacity. Embedding real-time whole-genome sequencing into routine diagnostics and public-health workflows is essential to strengthen stewardship, guide infection control, and support equitable AMR surveillance across Mexico.

42988569.title: Effectiveness and major bleeding complications with venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in category E pulmonary thromboembolism: a multicentre retrospective study.

42987328.title: Cardiac Output From Right Ventricular Pressure: Not the Solution for Venovenous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation.
42987328.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
42987328.abstract: Cardiac output (CO) monitoring is challenging during venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV ECMO), as thermodilution techniques are unreliable. Cardiac output from right ventricular pressure (RVP) waveforms has recently been considered. We evaluated whether RVP-derived CO (CORV) accurately reflects cardiac output measured by echocardiography (COUS) during VV ECMO. Ten anesthetized pigs underwent femoro-jugular VV ECMO implantation. A Swan-Ganz IQ catheter provided continuous CORV monitoring throughout the experiment. Cardiac output was modulated using either dobutamine (5-20 µg/kg/min) or landiolol (10-40 µg/kg/min) infusions. Agreement between CORV and COUS was assessed using Pearson correlation and Bland-Altman analysis. Overall, 596 paired CO measurements were performed in seven animals. Cardiac output ranged from 1.05 to 9.46 L/min. Correlation between CORV and COUS was poor (R = 0.24; R2 = 0.057; p < 0.05). Bland-Altman analysis showed a mean bias of +1.94 L/min with wide limits of agreement (-1.44 to +5.32 L/min). Correlations between individual right ventricular pressure waveform components and COUS were heterogeneous and weak to moderate (diastolic RVP, R = 0.36; right ventricle +dP/dt [delta pressure/delta time] R = 0.40; systolic RVP R = 0.60). CORV is not reliable during VV ECMO in our experiment. Further studies are needed to assess CORV performances.

42987192.title: Long-Term Mortality in Sepsis Survivors: A Population-Based Study During 15 Years.
42987192.abstract: To evaluate long-term mortality among sepsis survivors in Catalonia over a 15-year period and to identify factors associated with increased mortality within 2 years after hospital discharge. Retrospective population-based cohort study. Acute-care hospitals in Catalonia, Spain. Adult and pediatric patients hospitalized with sepsis between 2005 and 2019 identified using the International Classification of Diseases, 9th Revision, Clinical Modification and International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification codes for infection and acute organ dysfunction. Patients who died during hospitalization, were transferred to another facility, or represented readmission episodes were excluded. None. Data were obtained from the Catalan Minimum Basic Dataset of Acute-Care Hospitals, with longitudinal follow-up through the Central Registry of Insured Persons. Comorbidities were assessed using the Charlson comorbidity index. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models were used to identify predictors of long-term mortality. Among 296,554 hospital admissions for sepsis, 237,075 patients (79.9%) survived to hospital discharge. Of these, 42% died (99,571) within 2 years. Long-term mortality increased significantly with age, ranging from 5.8% in patients younger than 15 years to 62% in those older than 84 years (p < 0.0001), and with comorbidity burden (21%, 38%, 51%, and 67% for Charlson index 0, 1-2, 3-4, and ≥ 5, respectively; p < 0.0001). Neoplasia (hazard ratio [HR], 2.011), liver cirrhosis (HR, 1.562), and dementia (HR, 1.304) were the comorbidities most strongly associated with mortality. Longer hospital stays were also associated with increased mortality. A progressive decline in long-term mortality was observed during 2017-2019. Long-term mortality among sepsis survivors remains high, with more than 40% dying within 2 years after hospital discharge. These findings support the need for structured post-sepsis care strategies focused on high-risk patients, improved continuity of care, and prevention of long-term sepsis-related complications.

42980479.title: Network Trauma Research series: Modeling Trauma Complexity: Rodent Platforms for Studying Bone Healing and Hemorrhagic Shock.
42980479.abstract: Polytrauma, defined as severe injury to multiple body regions often accompanied by physiological instability, remains a major global health burden with high morbidity and mortality. Among the most clinically relevant two-injury combinations, long-bone fractures and hemorrhagic shock are particularly important, as both critically influence systemic inflammation, remote organ dysfunction such as lung or kidney damage, and tissue regeneration itself. To improve translational understanding of these complex interactions, robust small-animal models, particularly murine systems, have been developed to experimentally dissect the biological mechanisms underlying fracture healing, hypovolemic shock, and their combined effects. This review provides a comprehensive overview of current rodent models for isolated fracture, hemorrhagic shock, and combination trauma. Key methodological variables, such as fracture induction methods, fixation strategies, hemorrhage protocols, anesthesia and analgesia, and the influence of age, sex, and comorbidities are outlined to support informed model selection. Additionally, this manuscript highlights the challenges and opportunities in designing clinically relevant "double-hit" models that mimic real-world trauma patterns while maintaining high reproducibility and animal welfare standards. Collectively, the summarized evidence underscores the importance of standardized, physiologically meaningful preclinical trauma models to advance mechanistic insights and foster the development of effective therapeutic interventions.

42994848.title: Development and pilot feasibility testing of an evidence-based endotracheal tube maintenance protocol for critically ill patients: A delphi consensus study.
42994848.abstract: This study aimed to develop and preliminarily pilot-test an evidence-based endotracheal tube (ETT) maintenance protocol for adult critically ill patients in intensive care units. Based on the Population, Intervention, Professional, Outcome, Setting, Type of Evidence framework, an initial protocol draft was constructed via systematic literature synthesis. Two rounds of modified Delphi expert consultations were conducted among a multidisciplinary panel of 12 specialists across 8 tertiary hospitals. Subsequently, a 3-month feasibility pilot involving 10 frontline intensive care unit nurses was implemented to evaluate bedside usability and protocol adherence. Expert questionnaire recovery rates were 100% in both rounds, with an expert authority coefficient (Cr) of 0.896. In Round 2, all retained items achieved acceptable convergence (coefficients of variation ≤ 0.18, mean scores 4.42-5.00), while Kendall W was 0.329 (P < .001). The feasibility pilot demonstrated an overall nursing compliance rate of 88.5% and informed 7 targeted modifications to resolve bedside operational barriers. The finalized protocol comprises pre-procedure governance, intra-procedure interventions (ETT securement, cuff pressure maintenance at 25-30 cm H2O, subglottic drainage, indication-driven suctioning, oral care), and post-procedure emergency response and quality auditing. This study established a standardized, granular, and clinically operable ETT maintenance protocol with robust expert consensus and high bedside usability. It provides a practical framework for critical care nursing, laying the foundation for future multicenter clinical efficacy trials.

42993752.title: Assessment of the appropriateness of stress ulcer prophylaxis practice among hospitalized patients across Lebanese hospitals: A multicenter prospective study.
42993752.abstract: Stress ulcer prophylaxis (SUP) is recommended for critically ill patients at high risk of stress-related gastrointestinal bleeding. Despite established guideline recommendations, inappropriate use of acid suppressant medications (ASMs), particularly proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), remains common worldwide and may expose patients to unnecessary adverse effects and increased healthcare costs. This study aimed to assess the appropriateness of SUP prescribing practices among hospitalized patients across Lebanese hospitals, focusing on indication, choice of pharmacologic agent, dosing regimen, route of administration, duration of therapy, discharge prescribing, and factors associated with inappropriate SUP practice. A multicenter prospective study was conducted between April 20 and May 22, 2026, across ten tertiary-care hospitals in different regions of Lebanon. Adult patients (≥18 years) admitted to Internal Medicine Unit, Intensive Care Unit (ICU), or Coronary Care Unit wards were assessed for the appropriateness of SUP, regardless of whether ASMs were prescribed. The appropriateness of SUP practice was evaluated according to the Society of Critical Care Medicine and American Society of Health-System Pharmacists (SCCM/ASHP) 2024 and ASHP 1999 guidelines. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify factors associated with inappropriate SUP practice. A total of 552 patients were enrolled, with a mean age of 64.3 ± 18.5 years, and 58.7% were male. According to the SCCM/ASHP 2024 and ASHP 1999 guidelines, 90.8% and 77.2% of patients, respectively, were not eligible for SUP. Omeprazole was the most frequently prescribed agent (75.4%), and PPIs were used in all SUP prescriptions. Among patients admitted to ICU, 11.2% continued receiving ASMs after the SUP indication had resolved or following ICU transfer without a persisting indication. Overall, SUP practice was inappropriate in 77.9% of patients. Multivariable analysis demonstrated that anticoagulant therapy was associated with higher odds of inappropriate SUP practice (AOR = 2.78, 95% CI = 1.35-5.74, P = 0.006). Inappropriate SUP practice is highly prevalent among hospitalized patients in Lebanon, largely due to prescribing without guideline-based indications. Inappropriate continuation after resolution of the SUP indication or ICU transfer was also observed. Strengthening adherence to evidence-based recommendations through stewardship programs, prescribing audits, standardized protocols, and updated national guidance may help optimize SUP use and improve patient care.

42993042.title: Impact of frailty on acute kidney injury in patients followed-up in the intensive care unit.
42993042.journal: Ulusal travma ve acil cerrahi dergisi = Turkish journal of trauma & emergency surgery : TJTES
42993042.abstract: Frailty in elderly patients is an important determinant of clinical outcomes in intensive care units, particularly in relation to acute kidney injury (AKI). This study investigated the association between frailty and AKI in the geriatric population. This prospective observational study included 120 patients. Frailty was assessed via the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) and the Edmonton Frail Scale (EFS). Patients were categorized according to the presence or absence of AKI. Demographic data, frailty scores, laboratory parameters, and clinical outcomes, including mortality, mechanical ventilation, and vasopressor use, were compared. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were used to identify factors associated with the development of AKI. The mean age of the participants was 79.7±7.5 years. Comorbidities such as diabetes and hypertension were common, and AKI was observed in 29.1% of patients. The incidence of AKI was significantly higher among patients classified as frail according to the CFS (p=0.002). Patients with AKI presented increased mortality rates and an increased need for mechanical ventilation and vasopressors. The AKI group presented significantly lower hemoglobin, platelet, and albumin levels and higher baseline creatinine levels. Multivariate analysis revealed that elevated baseline creatinine was an important predictor of AKI. Frailty assessed by the CFS was associated with AKI development in unadjusted analyses; however, this association was not maintained after multivariable adjustment. No significant association was observed between AKI and frailty assessed by the EFS. Baseline serum creatinine was the only independent predictor of AKI. These findings suggest that frailty assessment, particularly using the CFS, may serve as a complementary clinical tool for early risk recognition and patient stratification rather than an independent predictor of AKI. AKI development in critically ill older adults appears to be multifactorial.

42991237.title: Association between short-term fine particulate matter exposure and hospital-acquired pneumonia risk in critically ill post-cardiac surgery patients: a 10-year cohort study using distributed lag non-linear models.
42991237.abstract: Ambient air pollution (AAP) exposure is a substantial health threat to humans globally. However, whether AAP could promote hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) onset in critically ill patients, a vulnerable population undergoing cardiac surgery in the intensive care unit (ICU), remains elusive. This study evaluated the correlation of HAP onset with fine particulate matter (PM2.5). In total, this study included 6,196 patients who underwent cardiovascular surgery at the ICU of a major hospital in Shandong province, China, over 10 years, from January 1, 2014, to December 31, 2023. The daily mean levels of sulfur dioxide (SO2), PM2.5, carbon monoxide (CO), PM10, and ozone (O3) were assessed from publicly available data. The outcome was HAP, defined according to CDC/NHSN pneumonia criteria as pneumonia developing >48 h after hospital admission and not present or incubating at admission; VAP was not analyzed as a separate endpoint. The association between PM2.5 and HAP was estimated via a distributed lag non-linear model, adjusted for pollutants, time trends, and weather conditions. This study analyzed 1938 (31.278%) HAP cases. The mean levels of PM10, O3, PM2.5, and SO2 were 120, 75, 59, and 25 μg/m3, respectively, and the mean CO level was 0.979 mg/m3. The association between PM2.5 and HAP was statistically significant at lag 1 day within the perioperative exposure window.
