42851912.abstract: Early risk assessment is a routine part of neurocritical care, yet mortality prediction remains difficult because neurological injury often coexists with respiratory, circulatory, renal, and inflammatory dysfunction. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an interpretable machine learning (ML) model for predicting in-hospital mortality in neurocritical-care patients using variables available within the first 24 h after intensive care unit (ICU) admission. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using two public critical-care databases. The Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) database was used for model development and internal testing, and the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD) was used for independent external validation. The report follows the Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) statement. Adult ICU patients with neurocritical-care diagnoses were identified by predefined International Classification of Diseases codes. Candidate predictors were restricted to information recorded during the first 24 h after ICU admission and included demographics, comorbidities, vital signs, laboratory results, neurological status, organ-support therapies, and severity scores. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used for feature selection. Logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, and multilayer perceptron models were trained. Discrimination was assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC). Calibration, decision curve analysis (DCA), and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used to evaluate probability reliability, potential clinical utility, and interpretability. The operating threshold used for classification metrics was fixed in the MIMIC-IV development data before internal and external evaluation. The MIMIC-IV cohort included 6,842 patients, of whom 1,014 died during hospitalization; the held-out internal test set contained 1,368 patients and 203 deaths. The external validation cohort included 5,236 eICU-CRD patients, of whom 686 died. LightGBM showed the best overall performance. In the internal test cohort, it achieved an AUROC of 0.841 (95% CI: 0.821-0.861) and an AUPRC of 0.518 (95% CI: 0.486-0.552). In external validation, the AUROC was 0.801 (95% CI: 0.779-0.824) and the AUPRC was 0.413 (95% CI: 0.380-0.449), with sensitivity of 72.8%, specificity of 73.9%, positive predictive value of 30.3%, negative predictive value of 94.7%, and F1 score of 0.428. Thus, approximately 70% of patients classified as high risk at this operating point survived to hospital discharge. Calibration was acceptable in the external cohort, with a Brier score of 0.101, calibration intercept of 0.050, and calibration slope of 0.84. SHAP analysis identified GCS total score, invasive mechanical ventilation, age, lactate, SOFA score, vasopressor use, and creatinine as leading contributors to predicted mortality risk. A model based on routinely collected first-day ICU data provided externally validated and interpretable risk stratification for in-hospital mortality in neurocritical care. Its low positive predictive value at the reported operating point precludes use as a stand-alone basis for prognostic pessimism, treatment limitation, or withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment. Prospective validation in diverse countries and health systems is required before clinical implementation.

42845054.title: Intensive Care Nurses' Experiences and Attitudes Towards Family Involvement in Delirium Care: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.
42845054.abstract: Delirium is a common neuropsychiatric complication among critically ill patients, particularly those who are mechanically ventilated. Evidence suggests family involvement may improve delirium-related outcomes in adult intensive care units (ICUs). However, limited evidence exists on intensive care nurses' (ICNs) experiences and attitudes towards family involvement in delirium care in South Africa. The study aimed to explore intensive care nurses' experiences and attitudes towards family involvement in the care of mechanically ventilated patients with delirium in adult ICUs. A descriptive qualitative study design was utilised. Four focus group discussions were conducted with 32 ICNs from two adult ICUs at a tertiary academic hospital in Johannesburg between April and August 2022. Participants who had at least 2 years of intensive care experience were purposively sampled. Data were analysed using inductive qualitative content analysis. The study adhered to Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Studies guidelines. Three categories were identified: emotional burden and psychological demands of delirium care, communication and psychosocial support for families in delirium care and barriers to effective family involvement in delirium care. While recognising the therapeutic value of family engagement, the nurses reported experiencing emotional stress related to family expectations and anxiety. They adopted strategies such as structured communication, empathetic listening and technology-assisted contact to support families. However, barriers such as time constraints, limited intensive care space, staffing shortages and restrictive policies limited sustained involvement. This study provides context-specific insight into how ICNs facilitate family involvement in the care of patients with delirium in a public tertiary ICU. ICNs recognise the therapeutic value of family involvement in the care of patients with delirium and are willing to facilitate engagement. However, systemic and environmental barriers limit consistent implementation. Therefore, strengthening institutional policies and supporting nurses through structured training and team-based approaches may enhance sustainable family-centred delirium care. This study's findings demonstrate the need for ICNs to adopt structured communication strategies, flexible visitation policies and empathy towards families and their patients in the ICU. Perhaps incorporating family-centred care into daily intensive care practices could strengthen family involvement in critical care, particularly for patients with delirium.

42844827.title: Olanzapine for the Prevention and Treatment of ICU Delirium: Protocol for a Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis.
42844827.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) delirium is a multifactorial acute brain dysfunction associated with prolonged hospitalization, increased morbidity and mortality, and higher healthcare costs. Despite these substantial negative impacts of delirium, the optimal prevention and treatment strategies are unclear. Olanzapine, an atypical antipsychotic drug, is commonly used for delirium management. We will perform an updated systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the benefits and harms of olanzapine for the prevention and treatment of ICU delirium. This protocol is developed in accordance with the recommendations of The Cochrane Collaboration and is reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) guidelines. We will include all randomized clinical trials (RCTs) evaluating prophylactic or therapeutic olanzapine versus any comparator, including pharmacological, non-pharmacological, placebo, or routine care/no specific delirium-directed intervention (treated as a single comparator) in ICU patients. Observational studies will be included solely to address potential harms. We will systematically search the following databases: Embase, MEDLINE, The Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CINAHL, Scopus, and PsycINFO, as well as clinical trial registries. We will perform meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis (TSA) to investigate the risk of both Type I and II errors. We will assess the risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB-2). The quality of trials will be evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations (GRADE) approach. The review is registered in the PROSPERO database (CRD420261474813). The primary outcome is days alive and out of the hospital. The secondary outcomes include all-cause mortality at 90 days, number of CAM-ICU (Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit) negative days at 30 days, number of days without pharmacological treatment for delirium other than study drug during the intervention period and serious intervention-related harms. This protocol outlines the methodology we will use in a systematic review with meta-analysis designed to evaluate the beneficial and harmful effects of olanzapine for prevention and treatment of delirium in ICU patients. The findings of the systematic review will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication. We hope this review will inform future RCTs and improve clinical practice.

42834811.title: Postoperative Delirium in Intensive Care Units: A Bibliometric Analysis of Nursing Studies.
42834811.abstract: Delirium is a common and serious postoperative complication in intensive care units, associated with increased morbidity, mortality and long-term cognitive impairment, and despite the pivotal role of nurses in its assessment and management, variations in prevalence and gaps in intervention-focused nursing research persist, underscoring the need for a bibliometric evaluation of the literature. The aim of the study was to quantitatively analyse and visually map trends, citations, key terms and country contributions in nursing research on postoperative delirium in intensive care as well as to characterize the overall structure of the literature. This study was conducted as a retrospective and descriptive research using the bibliometric analysis method on December 1, 2025. No time restrictions were imposed on the literature. Data analysis was performed using R Studio software. The earliest study on postoperative delirium in intensive care units within the field of nursing was published in 2001, and the analysed publications covered the period from 2001 to December 2025. In addition, 55.96% of all publications have been released in the past 7 years. The journal with the highest number of publications is Nursing in Critical Care, while the United States stands out as the country with the highest research output. It can be suggested that topics such as 'cardiac surgery', 'nursing care', 'postoperative delirium', 'postoperative care' and the 'Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit' represent areas that warrant further investigation and development in future research. The analysis showed a marked increase in publications on postoperative delirium in intensive care nursing in recent years. The United States and the Journal Nursing in Critical Care were identified as the leading contributors to the literature. Thematic mapping indicated that the literature primarily focused on delirium assessment and intensive care nursing, with several interconnected research areas. The findings emphasize the critical role of nurses in delirium screening and management in intensive care units. While assessment tools are well represented in the literature, further research is needed to develop and evaluate nurse-led interventions aimed at delirium prevention and care. Enhancing nursing education and institutional support may contribute to improved patient outcomes and quality of postoperative intensive care.

42834802.title: Global Research Trends in Sleep Quality, Sleep Deprivation and Sleep Promotion Among ICU Patients: A Descriptive and Evaluative Bibliometric Analysis.
42834802.abstract: Sleep deprivation and poor sleep quality are critical problems among intensive care unit (ICU) patients, with significant implications for recovery, delirium onset and clinical outcomes. Despite growing scientific interest, no bibliometric study has systematically mapped the intellectual structure and thematic evolution of this field. To analyse the bibliometric characteristics and thematic structure of publications on sleep deprivation, sleep promotion and sleep quality in ICU patients indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database between 1983 and 2026. A descriptive and evaluative bibliometric analysis was conducted. Data were retrieved on April 26, 2026, from the WoS Core Collection using a comprehensive search strategy. Publications were filtered by document type, WoS categories (nursing, critical care medicine, anaesthesiology) and index (SCI-EXPANDED, SSCI, ESCI). Data were analysed using R software with the Biblioshiny interface, and annual publication trends were evaluated using Microsoft Excel. Of 11 418 publications retrieved, 379 met the inclusion criteria, spanning 37 years (1983-2026). Linear regression revealed a statistically significant positive trend in publication output (β = 0.643, R2 = 0.704, r = 0.839, p < 0.001), with mean annual publications of 10.24 ± 8.83 and notable acceleration from the 2000s onwards. Thematic mapping identified 'sleep', 'sleep deprivation' and 'delirium' as motor themes both highly central and well developed. Emerging concepts included circadian rhythm, actigraphy, fatigue, pain and anxiety. ICU sleep research has grown substantially over four decades, with sleep deprivation and delirium emerging as co-dominant research priorities. Thematic gaps and emerging clusters identified in this analysis highlight important directions for future nursing research and evidence-based practice development in critical care. This bibliometric analysis identified sleep deprivation and delirium as the co-dominant motor themes of ICU sleep research, and intervention-related concepts such as earplugs, eye masks and melatonin as emerging clusters. These evidence-based trends can guide ICU nurses in prioritizing targeted sleep promotion protocols and support policymakers in directing resources toward the most scientifically mature intervention areas in critical care.

42831296.title: Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (EMDR) for ICU-related psychological distress among adult intensive care survivors: a scoping review.
42831296.abstract: Background: Psychological morbidity is common following admission to adult intensive care units (ICUs), with many patients experiencing post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety, and depression as part of post-intensive care syndrome. Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (EMDR) is an established trauma-focused psychological therapy; however, its evidence base within critical care populations remains emerging.Objectives: This scoping review aimed to map the extent, characteristics, and findings of the available literature on the use of EMDR for ICU-related psychological distress.Methods: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. The review aimed to systematically identify and synthesise evidence relating to the application and reported outcomes of EMDR in ICU survivors.Results: Seven publications representing six independent study populations were included. Participants included adult ICU patients experiencing PTSD symptoms, delirium-related psychological disturbances, and COVID-19-related distress. EMDR was delivered using either standard protocols or the Recent Traumatic Episode Protocol (R-TEP). Across the evidence base, EMDR was associated with reductions in trauma-related distress, although evidence for improvements in anxiety and depression was less consistent. Where qualitative data were available, participants additionally reported improved integration and processing of ICU experiences. Overall, methodological heterogeneity, overlapping samples, small sample sizes, and limited controlled evidence restrict the strength of conclusions that can be drawn.Conclusions: This review highlights growing but preliminary evidence supporting the feasibility and potential utility of EMDR, including R-TEP, for ICU-related psychological distress. While findings are promising, the current evidence base remains insufficient to determine effectiveness. Future research should prioritise adequately powered controlled studies, standardised outcome measures, longer-term follow-up, and more diverse ICU populations to strengthen the evidence base and inform clinical implementation.

42830659.title: Exploring the Cognitive Phenotypes of Implementation Barriers to Analgesia and Sedation Management Among ICU Nurses: A Q Methodology Study.
42830659.abstract: Despite the importance of "analgesia-first" guidelines in intensive care units (ICUs), clinical implementation remains suboptimal due to systemic pressures and subjective dilemmas. However, it remains unclear how ICU nurses comparatively prioritize competing implementation barriers and whether shared patterns of viewpoints exist. This study aimed to explore shared patterns of ICU nurses' subjective viewpoints regarding barriers to analgesia and sedation management using Q methodology. A Q methodology study was conducted from April 7 to May 7, 2026. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) informed development of the 50-statement Q-set and was subsequently used as an interpretive framework after factor extraction. Thirty purposively sampled ICU nurses completed the Q-sort and brief postsort interviews. By-person factor analysis was used to identify shared viewpoint patterns. Three factors were identified, explaining 52.46% of the cumulative variance. Factor 1, "Professionally Confident and Responsibility-Driven," emphasized professional responsibility, confidence in analgesia and sedation management, and standardized, guideline-informed practice. Factor 2, "Experience-Driven with Perceived Organizational Support Gaps," emphasized experiential clinical judgment alongside perceived limitations in previous formal preparation, departmental prioritization, and physician-nurse consensus. Factor 3, "Systemically Isolated and Communication-Restricted," highlighted communication-related and contextual barriers, including perceived discrepancies between nurse and physician observations, handover discontinuities, environmental constraints, and patient/family-related influences. As Factor 3 was defined by only two participants, this viewpoint should be considered preliminary. CFIR-informed interpretation indicated that the three viewpoints reflected different configurations of implementation influences at the individual, organizational, interprofessional, and contextual levels. The identified heterogeneity in viewpoints suggests that uniform implementation approaches may not fully address the different barriers perceived by ICU nurses. Nursing leaders could consider strategies that are responsive to the implementation influences emphasized across different viewpoints, while the preliminary Factor 3 findings require confirmation in larger and more diverse samples.

42952193.title: Nurse Competencies, Patient Characteristics, and Pain Management Protocol Adherence in Intensive Care Units: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study Accounting for ICU Clustering.
42952193.abstract: To examine the associations between nurse competencies (knowledge, self-efficacy, and attitude), patient characteristics, and pain management protocol adherence in adult intensive care units, while accounting for between-ICU clustering. Adherence to pain management protocols remains suboptimal despite available guidelines. Nurse competencies are essential for evidence-based practice, yet their translation into clinical performance may depend on contextual factors. ICU-level organizational context has been described in recent reviews, but empirical examination of these relationships remains limited. This multicenter cross-sectional study included 525 ICU nurses from seven hospitals in Tehran, Iran (July-October 2025). One index patient was assessed for each nurse. ICU-level organizational characteristics were assessed through unit observation and head nurse interviews. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for protocol adherence was computed from an empty mixed model. Multivariable linear regression with ICU entered as a fixed effect was used to identify individual-level factors associated with adherence. Organizational context was retained as a descriptive variable only. Protocol adherence was moderate (mean 8.5/12; 32.4% good adherence). The ICC for protocol adherence was 0.02 (95% CI: 0.001-0.15), indicating minimal clustering. In the multivariable model with ICU as a fixed effect (18 predictors), knowledge (β = 0.311), self-efficacy (β = 0.290), and attitude (β = 0.276) remained independently associated with adherence (all p < 0.001). Patient characteristics remained significantly associated: substance use history (β = -0.138, p = 0.016), inability to communicate (β = -0.148, p = 0.010), GCS < 9 (β = -0.160, p = 0.008), and mechanical ventilation (β = -0.121, p = 0.028). The full model explained 53.4% of the variance in adherence. Organizational support across the seven ICUs ranged from 1 to 5 (weighted mean 3.42 ± 1.15). Nurse competencies and patient characteristics are independently associated with pain management protocol adherence in this multicenter ICU sample. Between-ICU clustering was minimal (ICC = 0.02), suggesting that individual-level factors are the primary correlates of adherence in this sample. Given the small number of ICU clusters (n = 7), organizational findings are descriptive only and require confirmation in larger multilevel studies. Nurse managers may consider competency-based pain management education and regular audits with feedback. Given the small number of ICU clusters (n = 7), these recommendations are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multilevel studies.

42952074.title: Incidence of Intensive Care Unit Delirium After Heart Surgery: A Feasibility Study of a Forest Environment Intervention.
42952074.abstract: Postoperative delirium is a serious complication in intensive care units (ICUs), particularly following cardiac surgery. It is associated with circadian rhythm disruption, sleep disturbances and adverse outcomes. ICU environments often lack natural time cues, which may exacerbate circadian misalignment and increase delirium risk. The primary aim of the study was the evaluation of the implementation of two chronotherapeutic ICU interventions regarding recruitment, implementability and safety. Its secondary aim was to descriptively assess postoperative delirium across intervention groups. This randomized feasibility study was conducted in a tertiary cardiac surgery ICU in Austria. Adult patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery were allocated to one of three groups: (1) forest environment, (2) light exposure or (3) standard ICU care. Interventions were applied for 12 h daily. Delirium was assessed at three postoperative time points using the confusion assessment method for the ICU (CAM-ICU) and intensive care delirium screening checklist (ICDSC). This study was conducted between March 2020 and 2025. Seventy-seven patients were enrolled, and 64 remained in the final analytical cohort. Interventions were delivered within routine care. Patients and ICU staff did not report intervention-related concerns. Implementation challenges included ICU restructuring, patient transfers due to COVID-19 and deviations from randomized allocation because of operational constraints. No intervention-related adverse events occurred. Delirium assessments were limited at several time points because of sedation, early ICU discharge or transfer. Across all groups, postoperative delirium was detected in 5 of 130 CAM-ICU completed assessments (3.8%) and 8 of 115 ICDSC completed assessments (6.9%), precluding inferential group comparisons. Chronotherapeutic environmental interventions were feasible and safe in ICU care. Feasibility results highlighted challenges related to ICU logistics, sedation-related assessment limitations and pandemic-related disruptions. The unexpectedly low delirium incidence limited conclusions regarding intervention efficacy. Future trials should include larger high-risk populations and prospectively defined feasibility outcomes. Optimized ICU environments, including noise reduction and light management, may support delirium prevention. Chronotherapeutic environmental interventions are feasible additions to routine ICU care.

42937747.title: The overall effects of virtual reality interventions on ICU patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
42937747.abstract: Adult intensive care unit (ICU) patients frequently experience psychological distress, pain, sleep disruption, and motor impairments. Virtual reality (VR) has emerged as a promising nonpharmacological adjunct to improve these outcomes, yet existing evidence remains fragmented and inconsistent. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized recent clinical trials to evaluate the effectiveness of VR on mental health, pain, sleep, functional outcomes, and delirium in adult ICU patients. This review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (2020) guidance and was registered in International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD42023482529). Eight databases were searched for randomized controlled trials published between January 2000 and September 2025. Eligible studies included adult ICU patients receiving immersive or non-immersive VR interventions. Primary outcomes were anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD); secondary outcomes included pain, sleep quality, lower-limb function, and bedside balance. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB tool, and certainty of evidence was graded using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation. Twenty randomized controlled trials were identified, involving a total of 1551 patients. This meta-analysis showed that VR intervention helped improve anxiety (standardized mean difference [SMD] = -0.67, 95% confidence interval [CI: -1.00 to -0.35], P < .0001), depression (SMD = -0.46, 95% CI [-0.72 to -0.21], P = .0004), PTSD [mean difference = -5.48, 95% CI (-9.36 to -1.59), P = .006], lower-limb function score [mean difference = 2.83, 95% CI (1.99 to 3.67), P < .001] and sleep quality (SMD = 0.70, 95% CI [0.47 to 0.92], P < .0001), but had no significant effect on pain score (SMD = -0.57, 95% CI [-1.49 to 0.36], P = .23) and bedside balance score (SMD = 0.61, 95% CI [-0.44 to 1.66], P = .25). Most studies were assessed as having varying degrees of risk of bias. All evidence was rated from very low to moderate. VR interventions may confer meaningful benefits for anxiety, depression, PTSD, and sleep quality in adult ICU patients, and may improve lower-limb function in selected populations. However, evidence for analgesic effects and bedside balance remains inconclusive. Standardized VR protocols, objective outcome assessment, and adequately powered multicenter trials are needed to clarify the clinical value of VR in ICU care.

42933954.title: Revisiting Rest: Evidence-Based Shifts in Adult Intensive Care Unit Early Mobility.
42933954.journal: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
42933954.abstract: Improvements in intensive care unit (ICU) survival have highlighted the long-term burdens faced by survivors, including physical, cognitive, and psychological impairments. Immobility is a key contributor to these outcomes. Over the past 2 decades, ICU practices have shifted from deep sedation and bedrest toward early mobility and patient engagement. ICU early mobility (EM) is an evidence-based intervention that is safe and feasible. However, implementation remains inconsistent. This article explores the historical context of ICU bedrest, reviews current evidence supporting ICU EM, and offers strategies for its adoption.

42933953.title: Intensive Care Unit Delirium in Critically Ill Adults: Evidence-Based Approaches to Prevention and Management.
42933953.journal: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
42933953.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) delirium affects up to 80% of critically ill adults and is associated with increased mortality, prolonged hospitalization, and long-term cognitive decline. Despite strong evidence supporting strategies for delirium management, adherence to best practices is inconsistent, and traditional practices often override their implementation. This clinical review highlights opportunities for deimplementation of outdated practices and adoption of evidence-based strategies to detect, prevent, and manage ICU delirium. Emphasis is placed on validated screening tools, light sedation practices, sleep promotion, and multicomponent care bundles. Empowering nurses with knowledge, autonomy, and interdisciplinary collaboration is essential to improving delirium-related outcomes.

42933952.title: Intensive Care Unit Liberation: Transforming Critical Care Through the ABCDEF Bundle.
42933952.journal: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
42933952.abstract: This article highlights the shift from traditional intensive care unit practices, including deep sedation, immobility, and restricted visitation, to evidence-based, patient-centered care. These outdated methods, once considered protective, are now known to increase delirium, muscle weakness, cognitive decline, and health care costs. Implementing the ABCDEF bundle (eg, pain management, awakening and breathing trials, sedation choice, delirium management, early mobility, and family engagement) is a proven evidence-based framework that improves patient outcomes. Critical care nurses play a central role in driving bundle adherence. Successful implementation requires interdisciplinary teamwork, leadership support, education, and integration into practice standards.

42932567.title: Silent Validation of a Longitudinal Model for Predicting Delayed Cerebral Ischemia in Real Time after Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.
42932567.abstract: Longitudinal prediction of delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) following subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is crucial for timely interventions. Machine learning models for DCI risk prediction and stratification may support clinical decision-making, but safety concerns and regulatory constraints have precluded real-time bedside validation. We utilized the ICU (intensive care unit) Cockpit information technology infrastructure to establish a live data stream enabling real-time model predictions that were evaluated by independent research physicians in a silent validation framework, benchmarking algorithmic recommendations without influencing treatment decisions. We deployed a DCI algorithm validated on historical data in a live environment on running data streams of actual patients. Three independent physicians not involved in patient care reviewed real-time model outputs from day 2 through day 14 after SAH onset. With algorithm support, these physicians estimated DCI probability, decided on further diagnostic orders (computed tomography angiography with perfusion) and/or recommended the intervals for repetitive neurologic assessments (increased, 1-2 hourly; standard, ≥3 hourly). Researchers' decisions were compared with actual clinical decisions and the occurrence of DCI. Out of 63 aneurysmal SAH patients enrolled, 17 developed DCI (27%). A total of 794 assessments were made. The number of increased neurologic assessment orders was 466 with algorithm support and 629 without (a reduction of 163; 25.91%). Although the number of true positives and false negatives for DCI prediction was similar with and without the algorithm, false positives were reduced by 164 (P<0.01). Additional diagnostic orders were 128 with algorithm support and 153 without (reduction of 25; 16.34%). This study demonstrates that continuous, real-time risk estimates can be generated without disrupting standard care, and that clinicians - when supported by an algorithm - may safely reduce unnecessary investigations without compromising DCI event detection. In addition, silent validation showed potential to optimize monitoring strategies and reduce clinician workload without reducing diagnostic accuracy. (Funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation [project nos. 407540-167195 and 325230_200568].).

42928669.title: Prevalence and Associated Factors of Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome in Adults Admitted to an Intensive Care Unit: A Retrospective Observational Descriptive Study.
42928669.abstract: Prolonged opioid administration for pain control and to facilitate tolerance of mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit (ICU) may lead to tolerance and physical dependence. Following opioid discontinuation, opioid withdrawal syndrome (OWS) may occur. Although this condition has been well described in pediatric populations, its incidence and associated factors in critically ill adults remain uncertain because of diagnostic heterogeneity and the frequent clinical overlap with delirium. The aim of this study was to assess the prevalence of OWS and to identify factors associated with its development in adult patients. We conducted a retrospective, descriptive, observational study including patients evaluated at the post-ICU follow-up clinic of Lozano Blesa University Clinical Hospital (Zaragoza, Spain) over a 12-month period. This study investigated the association between multiple opioid medications and adjunctive medications and the occurrence of OWS. Eligible patients had an ICU stay of >7 days, received mechanical ventilation for >48 hours, and had been exposed to opioids. Demographic, clinical, and pharmacological variables were collected, including types of opioids, weight-adjusted cumulative dose, and use of adjuvant medications. OWS was diagnosed during the first 48 hours after opioid discontinuation using a combination of the Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) and Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were performed to evaluate the impact of morphine exposure. A total of 66 patients were included (mean age 59.9 ± 13.6 years; predominantly male). The leading cause of ICU admission was respiratory disease (48.5%). Mean Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II) score at admission was 17.0 ± 6.1, and median ICU length of stay was 19 days. Twenty-two patients (33.3%) developed OWS, which was mild in 90.9% and moderate in 9.1% according to the COWS. No significant differences were observed between groups in baseline characteristics or delirium occurrence. Patients who developed OWS were more likely to have received morphine (100% vs. 75%; p = 0.010) and had a higher weight-adjusted cumulative morphine dose (3.15 ± 2.33 vs. 2.21 ± 2.50 mg/kg; p = 0.047), whereas no differences were found for fentanyl exposure. In addition, they more frequently required benzodiazepines (68.2% vs. 18.2%), neuroleptics (68.2% vs. 6.8%), and dexmedetomidine (31.8% vs. 4.5%) (p < 0.01 for all comparisons). Cumulative morphine dose showed modest discriminatory performance for OWS (area under the curve (AUC) 0.653; p = 0.048). OWS is a common complication among adult ICU survivors, although it is predominantly mild in severity. A higher cumulative dose of morphine was associated with its onset, although no association was found with the total duration of exposure. Clinical overlap with delirium and the reactive use of psychoactive medications may contribute to under-recognition of this condition, underscoring the need for structured OWS screening during ICU stay and in post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) follow-up.

42922243.title: Effectiveness of Quality Improvement Strategies in Preventing Healthcare-Associated Infections Among Neurosurgical Patients Admitted to Intensive Care Units: A Systematic Review.
42922243.abstract: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) remain a major and largely preventable cause of morbidity, excess mortality, prolonged hospitalization, and escalating healthcare costs in intensive care units (ICUs) worldwide. Neurosurgical patients are particularly vulnerable because of frequent exposure to invasive devices such as external ventricular drains (EVDs), central venous catheters, urinary catheters, and mechanical ventilation, combined with impaired neurological status and prolonged ICU stays. Although quality improvement (QI) strategies have been widely implemented across critical care settings, evidence specific to neurosurgical and neurocritical care populations remains fragmented. To systematically evaluate the effectiveness of QI interventions in reducing HAI incidence among neurosurgical and neurological ICU patients and to assess their impact on secondary outcomes including ICU length of stay, device utilization, and bundle compliance. A comprehensive search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science from January 2010 to May 2026, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Eligible studies for the primary evidence synthesis included randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies, and observational cohort studies evaluating structured QI interventions for HAI prevention in neurosurgical or neurological ICU populations, or mixed ICU settings with extractable neurocritical care data. Systematic reviews identified during screening were retained for contextual interpretation and reference screening but were excluded from the primary evidence synthesis to avoid duplication of overlapping primary data. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I, Cochrane RoB 2, and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale according to study design. Seventeen primary studies from 14 countries met eligibility criteria and were included in the primary narrative synthesis. Three systematic reviews were retained for contextual interpretation. Structured QI interventions consistently reduced device-associated infection rates across studies. The strongest evidence was observed for EVD-specific care bundles, with EVD-related infection rates decreasing from 14.35 to 3.21 per 1,000 catheter-days following bundle implementation, and one study reporting 20 consecutive infection-free months after interprofessional bundle adoption. Device-associated infection prevention bundles also demonstrated clinically meaningful reductions, including VAP rates decreasing from 68.2 to 47.4 per 1,000 ventilator-days and CAUTI rates from 24.9 to 13.4 per 1,000 catheter-days following structured educational interventions. CLABSI rates declined substantially following standardized central venous catheter bundle implementation, reaching zero in one study with sustained monitoring. Risk of bias was predominantly low to moderate across included primary studies. Structured QI interventions, particularly EVD-specific care bundles, device-associated infection prevention protocols, and staff education programs with compliance monitoring, consistently reduce HAI incidence in neurosurgical and neurological ICU settings. Although the evidence base is predominantly non-randomized, findings are directionally consistent across diverse healthcare systems and institutional contexts. Universal adoption of evidence-based infection prevention frameworks in neurocritical care is strongly supported.

42912019.title: Statistical analysis plan for a stepped-wedge cluster randomized clinical trial for the evaluation of the clinical impact of different telemedicine practices in intensive care units - TELESCOPE 2 trial.
42912019.abstract: The optimal model for delivering Tele-ICU is still to be determined. In the TELE-critical Care verSus usual Care on ICU Performance (TELESCOPE) trial, implementing medical-led daily multidisciplinary rounds did not show evidence of improved clinical outcomes. The TELESCOPE 2 trial was therefore designed to evaluate whether expanding this model to include a structured multidisciplinary care bundle, along with a formalized quality and safety management framework, would translate process improvements into measurable patient-centered outcome benefits. To evaluate whether a structured Tele-ICU intervention, comprising intensivist-led daily multidisciplinary rounds, a multidisciplinary care bundle (nursing, physical therapy, pharmacy), and a quality and safety management package, can reduce intensive care unit length of stay in Brazilian public intensive care units. TELESCOPE 2 is a multicenter, open-label, stepped-wedge cluster randomized trial including 25 intensive care units in Brazil from January 2024 to January 2026. Intensive care units are randomized to five sequences, receiving the intervention at staggered times. All adult patients admitted to participating units are eligible, except those admitted for non-medical reasons or those previously included in the study. The multifaceted telemedicine intervention comprises: i) daily multidisciplinary rounds led by board-certified intensivists; ii) coordinated care by a multidisciplinary team; and iii) a management strategy focused on quality improvement and patient safety. The primary outcome is intensive care unit length of stay. Secondary outcomes include clinical endpoints (mortality, ventilator-free days at 28 days, and ventilator-associated events), process-of-care indicators (mobilization, head-of-bed elevation, and sedation management), and unit-level organizational outcomes. We describe the statistical analysis plan for the TELESCOPE 2 trial, finalized prior to database lock. This pre-specified approach mitigates analysis bias and ensures the transparency and robustness of the reported results.

42909682.title: Acute Pain Management in the Intensive Care Unit.
42909682.abstract: This review summarizes current approaches to pain assessment and pharmacologic therapy in the intensive care unit (ICU) and evaluates the expanding role of regional anesthesia (RA). Contemporary ICU analgesia emphasizes systematic pain assessment and multimodal therapy while avoiding unnecessary deep sedation. RA provides targeted, opioid-sparing analgesia for localized pain but is limited by coagulopathy, infection, altered anatomy, and practical considerations. Fascial-plane blocks may provide useful alternatives in selected patients. Thoracic epidural and paravertebral techniques remain options for selected patients but may cause hypotension and clinically significant bleeding. Ultrasound-guided techniques, including erector spinae, serratus anterior, parasternal, rectus sheath, and transversus abdominis plane blocks, expand analgesic options. Continuous catheter techniques may extend analgesia when prolonged pain is anticipated. However, evidence in heterogeneous ICU populations remains limited, and much of the current evidence is derived from perioperative or trauma populations rather than general medical ICU cohorts. Further ICU-specific comparative trials are needed to define patient selection and clinically meaningful outcomes.

42907844.title: Virtual reality-based therapeutic intervention to prevent delirium in the intensive care unit: a systematic review of participant experiences, acceptability, and implementation implications.
42907844.abstract: Delirium is common in intensive care units (ICUs) and is associated with adverse outcomes. Virtual reality (VR) is a non-pharmacological modality that may mitigate contributory factors such as sensory deprivation, anxiety, and immobility. This study aims to synthesise acceptability, feasibility, safety/tolerability, and implementation‑relevant outcomes of VR for ICU delirium prevention. Systematic review of 11 databases (PubMed, Web of Science, EMBASE, PsycINFO, AMED, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, CNKI, Wanfang, Weipu, CBM) from January 2012 to June 2026. Eligible studies evaluated VR-based interventions for delirium prevention in ICUs and reported outcomes on acceptability (e.g., satisfaction, feedback, immersion, comfort), feasibility (e.g. recruitment, completion), and safety/tolerability. Of 877 articles, seven met the criteria, including 190 patients and 21 healthcare professionals. Most interventions delivered nature-based audiovisual VR content via head-mounted displays, typically calm landscapes accompanied by ambient sounds. Patients consistently reported favourable acceptability, describing VR as enjoyable, immersive, and relaxing, while clinicians highlighted realism, engagement, and compatibility with existing ICU workflows. For feasibility, recruitment rates ranged from 12.6% to 67.6%, with a mean completion rate of 71%, despite substantial heterogeneity in intervention frequency and session duration (5-20 min per session). Safety profiles were favourable, with only mild, transient adverse effects such as dizziness or nausea, none leading to discontinuation. VR-based therapeutic interventions in ICU settings may be safe, feasible, and acceptable as adjuncts to multicomponent delirium-prevention strategies, but current estimates are preliminary and subject to substantial uncertainty. Fully powered clinical trials are needed to determine effectiveness and safety. Healthcare professionals might begin with calming, low-exertion, nature-based VR experiences; implement real-time and ongoing monitoring for cybersickness; and embed VR sessions within existing ICU delirium-prevention protocols. Structured staff training and standardised equipment-cleaning procedures will support safe, sustainable adoption while ensuring that technology enhances, rather than replaces, the therapeutic human interaction central to patient-centred ICU care. Clinical trial number PROSPERO REGISTRATION NUMBER: CRD420251086766.

42903095.title: Early hemoglobin trajectories and short-term mortality in ICU patients with traumatic brain injury: development in MIMIC-IV and external assessment in eICU-CRD.
42903095.abstract: Hemoglobin (Hb) changes dynamically after traumatic brain injury (TBI), but the prognostic relevance of distinct longitudinal patterns and their added value beyond early Hb remain uncertain. We characterized early Hb trajectories in ICU patients with TBI and examined associations with mortality after a 120-h landmark. MIMIC-IV was used for model development and multicenter eICU-CRD for external assessment. Daily median Hb values across five 24-h windows were modeled using a latent class linear mixed model. The three-class MIMIC-IV model was frozen before transport to eICU. Cox models evaluated mortality from 120 h through ICU day 28, with sensitivity analyses addressing selection, landmark attrition, simpler Hb summaries, classification uncertainty, PRBC exposure, missingness, and nonproportional hazards. In MIMIC-IV, 2,466 patients entered trajectory analysis and 2,409 entered post-landmark analysis. Three trajectories were identified: relatively high and stable, rapidly declining, and persistently low Hb. In fully adjusted models, rapidly declining (HR 1.74, 95% CI 1.18-2.57) and persistently low Hb (HR 1.57, 95% CI 1.19-2.08) were associated with higher mortality. In eICU, 2,097 patients were classified and 1,557 entered outcome analysis; persistently low Hb remained associated with mortality (HR 1.58, 95% CI 1.03-2.43), whereas the rapidly declining association was less precise (HR 1.24, 95% CI 0.80-1.92). Adding trajectory class to the MIMIC-IV clinical model increased the C-index from 0.786 to 0.792. After adjustment for first-day Hb, the rapidly declining trajectory remained associated with mortality (HR 1.77, 95% CI 1.20-2.62), whereas the persistently low association attenuated (HR 1.27, 95% CI 0.83-1.93). Independent three-class refitting in eICU did not recover the same latent-class structure (ARI 0.169). Early Hb trajectories after TBI showed distinct prognostic associations. Persistently low Hb had the most consistent transported association but was attenuated after first-day Hb adjustment; rapid decline retained an association in MIMIC-IV but had limited external support. Incremental discrimination was modest. These patterns should be interpreted as treatment-embedded clinical courses rather than fixed biological phenotypes or evidence for trajectory-specific transfusion thresholds.

42958096.title: Delirium in elderly critically ill patients: the value of cerebral regulation.
42958096.abstract: Delirium is a common neurological complication in elderly critically ill patients, and a uniform blood pressure target may not adequately address individual cerebral perfusion requirements. This study aimed to evaluate whether cerebral regulation-targeted optimal blood pressure management (OBPM) reduces the incidence of delirium and improve clinical outcomes in this population. This prospective, single-center, observational study was conducted at Xiangya Hospital, Central South University, from August 2023 to May 2025. A total of 119 elderly critically ill patients were enrolled, including 39 in the OBPM group and 80 in the standard of care (SOC) group. Using near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) and ICM+ software, the tissue oxygen reactivity index (TOx) was derived from the dynamic correlation between regional cerebral oxygen saturation (rSO2) and mean arterial pressure (MAP) across steady-state measurements obtained during stepwise norepinephrine titration, with the optimal MAP (MAPopt) defined as the MAP value at which TOx was minimized. In the OBPM group, blood pressure was targeted within MAPopt ± 5 mmHg, while the SOC group received standard care with blood pressure maintained within the normal range and no signs of inadequate tissue perfusion. The primary outcome, delirium, was screened twice daily throughout the ICU stay using the Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU) and the incidence of delirium was determined if the patients experienced it at least once. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality at hospital discharge, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, and hospital length of stay. The incidence of delirium was significantly lower in the OBPM group than in the SOC group (33.3% vs. 55.0%, p = 0.043), and ICU length of stay was significantly shorter [5.0 (3.0-9.0) d vs. 7.0 (4.0-11.0) d, p = 0.022]. Multivariable logistic regression showed that OBPM was independently associated with lower odds of delirium (OR = 0.409, 95% CI: 0.184-0.909, p = 0.028). Mechanical ventilation (OR = 3.500, P = 0.010), sepsis-related organ failure assessment (SOFA) score (OR = 1.139, p = 0.010), and ratio of arterial oxygen partial pressure to fraction of inspired oxygen (PaO2/FiO2) (OR = 0.995, p = 0.014) were also independently associated with delirium. No significant differences were observed between groups in hospital length of stay or mortality. Independent risk factors for mortality included sepsis, Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) II score, lactate level, and prothrombin time. Cerebral regulation-targeted optimal blood pressure management was associated with a reduced incidence of delirium and shorter ICU stay in elderly critically ill patients, without increasing mortality. Larger multicenter randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these findings and guide clinical implementation.

42880902.title: Failed quality improvement project to improve adherence to CAM-ICU and RASS documentation in a tertiary intensive care unit: a cautionary tale.
42880902.abstract: In a four-unit tertiary intensive care service in central London, baseline audit revealed poor compliance with documentation of the Richmond Agitation Sedation Scale (RASS) and the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU). To improve documentation compliance with RASS and CAM-ICU and to reflect on the determinants of success and failure of such interventions. A multifaceted intervention was designed comprising quarterly multidisciplinary education, an updated sedation and delirium guideline, proposed optimisation of the electronic health record (EHR) and a family information pack. Compliance was measured retrospectively from EHR data on day 2 of admission for patients staying ≥3 days. The audit ran from August to October 2023; the re-audit from January to March 2024. RASS documentation compliance fell from 17% to 5%, and CAM-ICU compliance fell from 42% to 36%. The intervention did not improve documentation and on the most stringent measure appeared to worsen it. Several planned components, including EHR optimisation and a delirium smartphrase, had not been implemented at the time of re-audit. A known EHR defect that auto-populated CAM-ICU as positive in deeply sedated patients also remained live throughout. This report sets out, honestly, why a multidisciplinary intervention did not work. We identified five interacting factors, namely incomplete bundle delivery; reliance on low-intensity didactic education without engaging content or visible bedside champions; a baseline unit culture in which the target assessments were de-prioritised; persistent EHR defects that disincentivised documentation; and a frequency-based outcome measure that did not capture clinical fidelity. These findings echo an implementation-science literature showing that passive education alone rarely changes clinician behaviour. ICU teams contemplating similar work should sequence system fixes before behavioural interventions, invest in local champions, and choose outcomes that reflect clinical care rather than the act of charting.

42879346.title: Dexmedetomidine Use and Short-Term All-Cause Mortality in Intensive Care Unit Patients with Ischemic Stroke and Atrial Fibrillation: A Propensity-Matched Analysis from MIMIC-IV.
42879346.abstract: Preclinical studies have demonstrated that dexmedetomidine (DEX), a sedative widely used in intensive care units (ICU), exerts neuroprotective effects. However, its potential protective role and underlying mechanisms in ischemic stroke patients with atrial fibrillation (IS-AF) remain unclear. The study's objective was to assess the connection between the early administration of DEX and short-term mortality from all causes in patients with IS-AF. From the MIMIC-IV database, patients with IS-AF were identified, including those who were administered DEX and those who were not. The primary endpoint was 7-day all-cause mortality, and the secondary endpoint was 90-day all-cause mortality. Propensity score matching (PSM) was utilized to ensure baseline covariates were balanced. Cox proportional hazards models and Kaplan-Meier survival curves and were utilized to evaluate the association between DEX use and mortality, with subgroup analyses conducted to ensure the findings' robustness. In total, 1,355 patients with IS-AF participated, with 253 (18.7%) receiving DEX. After PSM, 208 pairs were matched. In the fully adjusted model, DEX administration was significantly associated with lower all-cause mortality compared with the control group at both 7 days (before PSM, HR = 0.36, 95% CI: 0.19-0.68, p = 0.002; after PSM, HR = 0.26, 95% CI: 0.12-0.54, p < 0.001) and 90 days (before PSM, HR = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.66-1.07, p = 0.162; after PSM, HR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.53-0.97, p = 0.031). The subgroup analyses revealed that DEX's protective effect was stronger in patients aged 70 and above, females, those with hypertension, and those without heart failure or chronic kidney disease. Kaplan-Meier survival curves consistently illustrated that DEX users had greater survival probabilities both before and after matching. In patients with IS-AF, DEX administration is connected to decreased all-cause mortality mortality, underlining the possible importance of DEX in ICU settings.

42877019.title: Temporal patterns of respiratory rate exposure and mortality in critically ill patients: a retrospective multi-database cohort study.
42877019.abstract: To investigate the associations between respiratory rate (RR) exposure patterns-both intensity and duration-and mortality in critically ill patients. This retrospective cohort study analysed 160,075 adult ICU patients from three international databases (HiRID, MIMIC-IV, eICU). The primary analysis used a landmark design: RR exposure and all covariates were ascertained during the first 24 h after ICU admission, and outcome follow-up began at the 24-hour landmark. Heatmap visualisation examined RR intensity-duration patterns. Cox and logistic regression models related the proportion of monitoring time spent in each RR range to mortality, adjusted for demographics, disease severity, laboratory values, comorbidities, treatment limitations, ventilation and sedation. Restricted cubic splines assessed the dose-response relationship for time-weighted mean RR. Sensitivity analyses examined alternative exposure windows, competing risks, multiple imputation, hospital-level clustering and a harmonised in-hospital mortality outcome. A greater proportion of time in the 12-20 breaths/min range was associated with lower 28-day mortality in MIMIC-IV (HR 0.988, 95% CI 0.987-0.989 per 1 percentage point) and lower in-hospital mortality in eICU (OR 0.991, 95% CI 0.990-0.991). Risk rose progressively across the tachypnoeic ranges (>35 breaths/min: HR 1.026, 95% CI 1.023-1.028). Spline analysis identified a nadir of risk at a time-weighted mean RR of 16.3 breaths/min, with a markedly asymmetric relationship (P for non-linearity <0.001): the adjusted hazard ratio reached 1.38 at 20 and 2.19 at 24 breaths/min but rose only modestly below the nadir. The bradypnoea-mortality association seen with whole-stay exposure (HR 1.029) was absent under the landmark design (HR 0.990) in both databases. Tachypnoeic associations were robust to stratification by ventilation and sedation, clustering and multiple imputation. Respiratory rate showed an asymmetric, non-linear relationship with mortality, with lowest risk at approximately 16-17 breaths/min. The cumulative burden of tachypnoea during the first 24 h was consistently associated with higher mortality across three databases and robust to controls for reverse causation, ventilation and sedation; the apparent association for bradypnoea was not, and likely reflects terminal-phase respiratory depression. Respiratory rate should be regarded as a monitoring and early-warning signal that integrates both magnitude and duration, rather than as a therapeutic target.

42876490.title: Prognostic value of platelet-to-white blood cell ratio in critically ill patients with non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage: a machine learning-driven study of the public database and the hospital information system.
42876490.abstract: Assessment of prognosis is crucial for managing non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage (NSAH) patients. The study aimed to explore the association between platelet-to-white blood cell ratio (PWR) and all-cause mortality in this high-risk population and to develop machine learning models to improve prognostic accuracy. Using data from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-IV). The observational endpoints were 30-day and 365-day mortality. Patients were categorized into four groups based on the quartiles of PWR. Kaplan-Meier curves, multivariate Cox regression analyses, restricted cubic splines (RCS), and subgroup analyses were applied. We also developed machine learning models that include PWR and clinical features selected with the Boruta and LASSO algorithms to predict 30-day mortality. Model performance was evaluated by the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and the area under the curve (AUC). Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method was utilized to provide model interpretability. External validations in the eICU-Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD) and the Hospital Information System (HIS) of the First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University were used to assess generalizability. A total of 1,176 patients with critically ill NSAH were enrolled from MIMIC-IV, predominantly male (58.8%), with a median age of 62 years. In multivariable Cox models, higher PWR quartiles were independently associated with lower risk of 30-day (HR = 0.55, 95% CI 0.35, 0.86, p = 0.009) and 365-day (HR = 0.53, 95% CI 0.37, 0.77, p = 0.001) mortality after fully adjusting. RCS suggested a linear association. No significant interaction was observed by subgroup analysis across all subgroups. The top-performing machine learning model attained an AUC of 0.868 during internal validation (MIMIC-IV). External validations yielded AUC values of 0.874 (eICU-CRD) and 0.763 (HIS). SHAP analysis revealed a correlation between decreased PWR and an elevated predicted risk of mortality. PWR is an independent predictor of short- and long-term mortality in ICU patients with NSAH. Machine learning models incorporating PWR significantly improve risk stratification, thereby providing precious support for the early identification and personalized management of patients in the ICU.

42875877.title: Systematic CRS-R-based Evaluation of Disorders of Consciousness in the ICU: Development and Evolution of a Multidisciplinary Program.
42875877.journal: American journal of physical medicine & rehabilitation
42875877.abstract: Evaluation and prognostication following disorders of consciousness (DoC) is a complex task with significant implications. The Coma Recovery Scale, Revised (CRS-R) is a standardized neurobehavioral assessment that enables clinicians to accurately differentiate between coma, unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS), minimally conscious state (MCS), and emergence from MCS. Newly described paradigms present ambitious programs utilizing multidisciplinary clinical teams working in sync with new technologies to optimize and improve a systematic approach to prognostication following DoC. We developed a DoC program at a level 1 trauma and comprehensive stroke center to optimize diagnosis and management of DoC patients. Through an iterative approach our program developed a DoC team to standardize the use of the CRS-R for patients with DoC and formalize a training program for its use. In addition, a formal DoC consult group was created incorporating the neurocritical care faculty to provide expertise and to assist with collaborative decision making. We detail our program's development, barriers, outcomes, and future directions. The core features of this novel clinical paradigm-structured assessment, interdisciplinary collaboration, and iterative re-evaluation-can be adapted to more resource-limited settings to improve outcomes, communication, and the consistency and transparency of prognostication in disorders of consciousness.

42873100.title: Clinical application of volatile sedation in adult intensive care units: pharmacological mechanisms, delivery systems, and safety.
42873100.abstract: Sedation is essential in critically ill mechanically ventilated patients, yet conventional intravenous agents carry risks of accumulation, organ-dependent clearance, and adverse effects. Volatile anesthetics offer several pharmacokinetic advantages, but their adoption in the intensive care unit has historically been limited by technical constraints. This review offers an updated, clinically focused overview of volatile- based sedation in adult intensive care units, covering pharmacological mechanisms, delivery systems, clinical outcomes, safety, and practical application. This review was conducted through systematic searching of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between January 2016 and December 2025. Sevoflurane and isoflurane achieve sedation primarily via γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptor modulation and offer organ-independent clearance, rapid onset/offset, and real-time end-tidal monitoring. Modern delivery systems, including reflection devices (Sedaconda-ACD) and automated platforms (MIRUS), have improved intensive care unit feasibility. Clinical evidence suggests volatile sedation may reduce awakening times and duration of mechanical ventilation compared with intravenous agents; however, results across randomized trials and meta-analyses are heterogeneous. Potential benefits have been reported in acute respiratory distress syndrome, post-cardiac arrest care, neurocritical illness, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and refractory agitation, but robust evidence is lacking across all settings. Limitations include hemodynamic effects, increased circuit dead space, renal safety concerns with sevoflurane, infrastructure requirements, occupational exposure, environmental impact, and cost. Volatile sedation is a feasible and pharmacologically rational option for selected mechanically ventilated intensive care unit patients, particularly those requiring prolonged sedation or with organ dysfunction limiting conventional agents. Current evidence does not support universal superiority over intravenous sedation. Inhaled anesthetics should be incorporated into individualized, multimodal sedation strategies within structured institutional frameworks. Large multicenter trials are needed to clarify effects on mortality, long-term neurological outcomes, and quality of life.

42872958.title: Isoflurane-Based Inhaled Sedation in Mechanically Ventilated Adults With Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: The SAVE-ICU Randomized Clinical Trial.
authors: SAVE-ICU Investigators and the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group
42872958.abstract: Rigorous evidence for inhaled sedation using isoflurane in mechanically ventilated patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) is limited. To evaluate whether an inhaled sedation strategy lowers hospital mortality compared with usual care intravenous sedation strategy in mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF. Pragmatic, effectiveness, open-label, superiority, randomized clinical trial in 14 intensive care units (ICUs) in Canada. Adults (≥18 years) receiving sedation for less than 72 hours and receiving mechanical ventilation for AHRF from non-COVID respiratory failure (ratio of partial pressure of arterial oxygen [Pao2] to fraction of inspired oxygen [Fio2] <300 mm Hg) or COVID-19 were enrolled between September 2020 and March 2025 with follow-up through June 2025. Patients were randomized to an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed or to a usual intravenous sedation care strategy. Sedatives were titrated to achieve the desired target sedation score guided by clinical teams and continued until extubation or death. Primary outcome was all-cause hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU- and ventilator-free days at day 30; hospital-free days at day 60; use of refractory hypoxemia adjunctive therapies; delirium- and coma-free days at day 14; and quality-of-life and disability scores at 3 months. Of 786 patients randomized, 780 were included in the primary analysis (mean age, 61.1 years; 34.0% female; 73.7% non-COVID AHRF, mean Pao2:Fio2 ratio, 152.6 mm Hg); 385 in the inhaled sedation and 395 in the intravenous sedation groups. In the inhaled sedation group, 49.9% to 55.4% of patients received concomitant intravenous sedation on any day during the first 14 days after randomization. At hospital discharge, 161 of 379 patients (42.5%) in the inhaled sedation group had died, compared with 171 of 390 patients (43.8%) in the intravenous sedation group (risk ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.84 to 1.14]; P = .85). There was no effect modification in prespecified subgroup analyses for age, sex, and COVID-19 status. ICU-, ventilator-, and hospital-free days were similar between groups. The inhaled sedation group received more adjunctive therapies for hypoxemia (239 [63.9%] vs 214 [55.0%]; between-group difference, 8.89% [95% CI, 1.95% to 15.83%]) and had fewer delirium- and coma-free days (between-group difference, -0.95 [95% CI, -1.69 to -0.22]). There was no difference in quality-of-life and disability scores between groups. In mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF, an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed did not reduce hospital mortality compared with an intravenous sedation strategy. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04415060.

42869181.title: Post-intensive care syndrome at 6 months and 1 year among survivors of severe COVID-19 requiring invasive mechanical ventilation: a single-center observational study.
42869181.journal: Journal of infection and chemotherapy : official journal of the Japan Society of Chemotherapy
42869181.abstract: Long-term multidomain impairment after critical coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) overlaps with post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) and post-COVID-19 condition. We assessed PICS at 6 months and 1 year after hospital discharge and explored associated clinical factors in Japanese patients with COVID-19 requiring invasive mechanical ventilation. This single-center observational study included adult patients with COVID-19 who required invasive mechanical ventilation and survived to discharge. PICS was assessed using the Barthel Index, Short-Memory Questionnaire, and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale. Exploratory multivariable logistic regression examined factors associated with 1-year PICS. Of 67 discharged survivors, 37 completed both 6-month and 1-year assessments; 17 (45.9%) received extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. PICS was present in 22 (59.5%) patients at 6 months and 21 (56.8%) at 1 year, and 15 (40.5%) had cognitive impairment at both assessments. Delirium was more frequent in patients with PICS than in those without at 6 months (63.6% vs 26.7%, p = 0.045) and 1 year (66.7% vs 25.0%, p = 0.020). In the exploratory multivariable analysis, delirium was associated with 1-year PICS after adjustment for age and mechanical ventilation duration (odds ratio, 7.09; 95% confidence interval, 1.54-32.7; p = 0.012). PICS was common 6 months and 1 year after hospital discharge among survivors of severe COVID-19. In an exploratory analysis, delirium was associated with 1-year PICS after adjustment for age and mechanical ventilation duration. This hypothesis-generating finding requires confirmation in larger prospective cohorts.

42868959.title: Risk factors and preventive strategies for pressure injury and medical device-related pressure injury in ICU patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation: A scoping review.
42868959.abstract: Adult ICU patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) are at risk of pressure injury (PI) and medical device-related pressure injury (MDRPI) due to immobility, impaired perfusion, and device contact. This scoping review synthesized evidence on PI and MDRPI risk factors and preventive strategies. This scoping review followed the Arksey and O'Malley framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Five databases (PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, MEDLINE, ScienceDirect) were searched from inception to April 2026. Studies of adult ICU patients receiving IMV reporting PI, MDRPI, risk factors, or preventive strategies were eligible. Forty-two studies from 14 countries (2009-2026) were included. PI incidence ranged from 10.3 to 36.3% (up to 88.7% when prone-positioned); MDRPI (oral mucosal injury) ranged from 25.9 to 43.1% (80.1% with a broader erythema criterion). Cutaneous PI mainly affected the sacrum, heels, occiput, face, and thorax (generally Stage 1-2); oral mucosal MDRPI, assessed using heterogeneous severity criteria, was typically mild-to-moderate. Onset was commonly reported on days 3-9. PI risk factors included immobility, impaired perfusion, vasopressor therapy, and poor nutrition; MDRPI risk factors involved prolonged intubation and device exposure. Preventive strategies included device repositioning, securement adjustment, device-contact protection, and oral care. Prolonged mechanical loading and reduced tissue tolerance are intensified by immobility, sedation, hemodynamic instability, impaired perfusion, vasopressor use, and device exposure. Early-stage cutaneous PI and mild-to-moderate mucosal MDRPI were more commonly reported than severe cutaneous and mucosal injuries; given the descriptive, non-comparative evidence, this cannot be attributed to preventive effectiveness. Early monitoring may be important for detecting early-stage injury and identifying progression toward more severe injury. Prevention should combine pressure redistribution with tolerance-based repositioning, skin monitoring, device securement, device-contact protection, and oral mucosal care. An exploratory, hypothesis-generating observation is that the first 10 days of ICU stay may be a high-risk period, requiring prospective validation.

42868106.title: Changes in clinical management related to continuous versus routine EEG in critically ill adults: analysis of a randomized trial.
42868106.abstract: Continuous electroencephalogram (cEEG) is increasingly utilized in the intensive care unit for consciousness-impaired patients with various conditions. It is, however, costly in terms of technical and human resources, and its impact on prognosis compared with routine EEG (rEEG) remains debated. We aimed to characterize the effect of cEEG vs rEEG on clinical management modifications, and to determine if these correlated with a better outcome. This is an ancillary analysis using data of CERTA (NCT03129438), a randomized trial comparing cEEG versus repeated rEEG in critically ill adults with altered consciousness. Clinical management modifications due to the EEG intervention, pre-defined as performed within 60 hours of EEG start, were prospectively recorded (anti-seizure medication -ASM, sedation, new radiological examination, new surgical intervention, withdrawal of life sustaining therapy). Correlation with the EEG type were analyzed by 2x2 tables; Mantel-Haenszel tests explored the impact on mortality and functional outcome at 6 months. The trial included 364 patients completing follow-up (182 each in the cEEG and rEEG groups). While 58.2% of cEEG and 45.6% of rEEG patients had any management change (p= 0.018), ASM were modified in 22.0% (cEEG) and 12.1% (rEEG) (p = 0.012)); other clinical interventions were comparable across EEG groups. Adjusting for ASM modifications, mortality (p=0.845) and functional outcome (p=0.619) remained similar between the EEG groups. In critically ill adults, cEEG is associated with more clinical management modifications compared to repeated rEEG, particularly regarding ASM, but this does not seem to translate into improved patients' outcomes.

42867449.title: Development and external validation of a nomogram for predicting in-hospital mortality in status epilepticus patients in the intensive care unit: A MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD study.
42867449.journal: Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape
42867449.abstract: To develop and externally validate a nomogram for predicting in-hospital mortality in ICU patients with SE, using readily available clinical data collected within the first 24 h of ICU admission. We identified adult SE patients from MIMIC-IV (training cohort, 2008-2019) using ICD-9/ICD-10 codes. Twenty-seven candidate predictors were screened by LASSO logistic regression with 10-fold cross-validation. The final model was constructed with multivariable logistic regression and presented as a nomogram. Internal validation used 1000 bootstrap resamples with optimism correction. External validation was performed in an independent SE cohort from the eICU-CRD database (2014-2015). The training cohort comprised 299 patients (69 deaths, 23.1% mortality). LASSO selected nine predictors: age, first ICU care unit, Glasgow Coma Scale, temperature, SpO2, white blood cell count, glucose, bicarbonate, and the Elixhauser comorbidity index. The optimism-corrected AUC was .807 (95% CI, .754-.860) with a Brier score of .124. External validation in 597 eICU patients yielded an AUC of .750 (95% CI, .685-.815). In sensitivity analyses, a reduced model without the comorbidity score achieved an optimism-corrected AUC of .786 and an external AUC of .730, and a model without the ICU care-unit type achieved .817 and .764, respectively. This nine-variable nomogram provides a validated, bedside-applicable tool for mortality risk stratification in ICU SE patients, enabling manual risk calculation without electronic computation.

42867208.title: Impact of clinical frailty on mortality after elective surgery in patients aged ≥ 90 years admitted to critical care: a binational intensive care registry analysis.
42867208.abstract: Increasing numbers of patients aged ≥ 90 years require elective surgery. Frailty is increasingly recognised as a key determinant of peri-operative risk, but high-quality evidence to understand the impact on outcomes in this age group is limited. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Adult Patient Database. Patients aged ≥ 90 years admitted to ICU following elective surgery were included, encompassing planned and unplanned ICU admissions. Frailty was assessed at ICU admission using the Clinical Frailty Scale and patients categorised as non-frail or frail. Propensity score matching was performed to balance age; sex; acute illness severity; and comorbidities. Primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU mortality; in-hospital mortality; return to pre-admission residence; and ICU and duration of hospital stay. The matched cohort comprised 5398 patients (2699 without frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale 1-4) and 2699 living with frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale 5-8)), with good post-matching covariate balance. Mortality in ICU was low and not significantly different between patients who were frail and non-frail. Frailty was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality (matched hazard ratio (HR) 1.66, 95%CI 1.22-2.27, p = 0.001) and higher 1-year mortality (matched HR 1.66, 95%CI 1.47-1.87, p < 0.001). Patients without frailty had higher odds of returning to their pre-admission residence at hospital discharge than patients living with frailty (matched OR 1.45, 95%CI 1.29-1.62, p < 0.001). Patients who were frail experienced longer hospital stays and higher rates of postoperative complications, including delirium and acute renal failure. Among patients aged ≥ 90 years undergoing elective surgery with postoperative intensive care admission, frailty is strongly associated with prolonged recovery and worse short and long-term outcomes. Incorporation of frailty assessment into peri-operative pathways may improve risk stratification, shared decision-making and personalised care for patients aged ≥ 90 years.

42858067.title: Association of dexmedetomidine use with stroke-heart syndrome in critically ill patients with ischemic stroke: a MIMIC-IV study.
42858067.abstract: Stroke-heart syndrome (SHS) is associated with poor outcomes after ischemic stroke (IS), but the relationship between dexmedetomidine (DEX) use and SHS remains unclear. To evaluate the association between DEX use and SHS in critically ill patients with IS. This retrospective cohort study used MIMIC-IV v2.2. Patients with IS receiving mechanical ventilation were included. DEX exposure was defined as use within 72 hours after ICU admission. Multivariate logistic regression, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), restricted cubic splines, and subgroup analyses were performed. Among 953 patients, 146 (15.3%) received DEX. In the fully adjusted model, DEX use was associated with lower odds of SHS (OR = 0.611, 95% CI: 0.398-0.929, p = 0.023). The associations of cumulative DEX dose (p-nonlinearity = 0.018) and treatment duration (p-anonlinearity = 0.011) with SHS were nonlinear.
