Antiplatelet therapy significantly modified the DEX-SHS association (p-interaction = 0.042). DEX use was associated with lower odds of SHS in critically ill patients with IS. Antiplatelet therapy may modify this association. Prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings.

42856966.title: Characterization of Delirium in an Intensive Care Unit: Real-World Data Based on the Application of the Confusion Assessment Method.
42856966.abstract: Introduction Delirium is a neuropsychiatric syndrome of acute onset characterized by disturbances in attention, awareness, and cognition. It is common in intensive care units (ICUs), and the Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU) is the most widely used bedside instrument for its detection. Methods We conducted a retrospective, observational, single-centre study of all patients admitted to the ICU of a Portuguese community hospital, Unidade Local de Saúde do Alto Minho (ULSAM), between January 1, 2021, and December 31, 2022. Delirium was defined as at least one positive CAM-ICU assessment during the ICU stay. Sociodemographic data, comorbidities, admission characteristics, severity scores (Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II), Simplified Acute Physiology Score (SAPS), Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score (SOFA)), and outcomes were compared between patients with and without delirium using chi-square, Mann-Whitney U, and multivariable logistic regression. Results Of 788 ICU admissions (742 patients), 66 (8.4%) had at least one positive CAM-ICU assessment. Patients with delirium were older (median 71 vs 68 years, p=0.021) and had higher APACHE II, SAPS, and SOFA scores, longer ICU stay (median 8 vs 3 days, p<0.001), and a higher rate of invasive mechanical ventilation among those with known ventilation status (n=40/64, 62.5% vs n=279/692, 40.3%, p=0.001) than patients without delirium. In multivariable logistic regression, older age (OR 1.03, p=0.017) and male sex (OR 3.09 relative to female, p=0.001) were independently associated with delirium. Conclusions Delirium affected a modest but clinically important proportion of ICU admissions in this cohort and was associated with older age, male sex, greater severity of illness, and longer, more complicated ICU stays. These findings support the need for continued systematic CAM-ICU screening and multidisciplinary delirium-prevention strategies.

42852110.title: Multicomponent non-pharmacological interventions for preventing delirium in critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
42852110.abstract: It is necessary to evaluate the efficacy of multicomponent non-pharmacological interventions in preventing and managing intensive care unit (ICU) delirium and identify the most effective intervention combinations. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, and ProQuest Dissertations and Theses A&I databases from inception to July 3, 2026, supplemented by a hand search of prior meta-analyses. Only randomized trials were included. Meta-analysis was performed using risk ratios (RR) or mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation and modified Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals were used. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized controlled trials. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The search identified 13 randomized controlled trials encompassing 5,525 patients. Multicomponent interventions significantly reduced delirium incidence (RR 0.53, 95% CI [0.36, 0.76], I2 = 72.5%, low-certainty evidence). The effect remained significant after excluding the two cluster-randomized trials (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.30-0.67; I2 = 55.7%), the active-control trial (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.38-0.79; I2 = 73.0%), and all three trials simultaneously (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.31-0.70; I2 = 57.0%). In exploratory subgroup analysis, the within-subgroup pooled estimate for component pattern B, comprising cognitive assessment and stimulation, reorientation, sleep and environmental management, family or community support, and physical activity, showed a reduced incidence of delirium (RR 0.43, 95% CI [0.23, 0.82]); however, the formal test for subgroup differences was not significant (p = 0.604). No statistically significant effects were found for delirium duration, ICU or hospital length of stay, delirium-free days, or mortality. This study demonstrated that multi-component interventions effectively reduce delirium incidence in critically ill patients. The evidence did not establish that one component combination was superior to another. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42024592821.

42851402.title: Incidence, burden, and associated factors of severe potential drug-drug interactions in intensive care unit patients: a real-world retrospective study.
42851402.abstract: Severe potential drug-drug interactions (pDDIs) in intensive care unit (ICU) patients remain insufficiently characterized. This study investigated the incidence, patterns, burden, and associated factors of severe pDDIs. This single-center retrospective cohort included ICU admissions from January 2023 through December 2024 for adults aged ≥18 years who received ≥2 eligible systemic medications administered orally or intravenously. Category D and X pDDIs were identified with Lexi-Interact (Lexidrug, UpToDate) using confirmed administration records. Logistic and ordinal logistic regression were performed to evaluate severe-pDDI occurrence (≥1) and admission-level burden (0, 1-2, or ≥3). A total of 1,170 ICU admissions were included, involving 26,627 medication administrations. 64.44% were male and 55.38% received mechanical ventilation support. The most common implicated pharmacological group was alimentary-tract and metabolism agents, while ambroxol and glutathione emerged as the top two individual drugs. Among 1,170 ICU admissions, 1,092 (93.33%) exhibited pDDIs, and 769 (65.73%) experienced at least one category D or X pDDI. The 2,704 severe pDDIs comprised 1,681 (62.17%) category D and 1,023 (37.83%) category X events, yielding 231.1 pDDIs per 100 admissions and 101.6 pDDIs per 1,000 medication administrations. Nervous-system agents predominated; butorphanol [948/5,408 ingredient involvements (17.53%)] and dexmedetomidine [824/5,408 (15.24%)] were most frequently implicated. Butorphanol-dexmedetomidine [335/2,704 events (12.39%)] and noscapine-chlorphenamine [176/2,704 (6.51%)] were the leading category D and X pairs, respectively. Additive pharmacodynamic central nervous system depression predominated. Mechanical ventilation and medication count were the strongest adjusted correlates of severe-pDDI occurrence and burden, while baseline variables (sex, APACHE II score) lost significance after adjusting for ICU process variables. These associations remained materially unchanged after excluding 29 readmission encounters. In an exploratory review of 50 severe-pDDI episodes, 32 (64.0%) had temporally associated clinical signs or events documented and 29 (58.0%) had a documented management action. Category D or X pDDI alerts were frequent, primarily driven by pharmacodynamic additive central nervous system depression from sedative-analgesic combinations. Treatment intensity rather than baseline characteristics was associated with severe-pDDI exposure. Regional ICU-tailored surveillance and pharmacist-integrated medication management may facilitate identification of high-risk combinations, although specific drug pairs require validation across different healthcare settings.

42847592.title: Targeting delirium in gastric surgery: An interpretable predictive model and statistical analysis in critical care.
42847592.journal: Technology and health care : official journal of the European Society for Engineering and Medicine
42847592.abstract: BackgroundPostoperative delirium is a serious complication in elderly ICU patients after gastric surgery, increasing mortality and healthcare burden. Early identification of high-risk patients may support timely prevention and optimise perioperative care.ObjectiveTo develop and externally validate an interpretable machine learning model for predicting postoperative delirium in elderly ICU patients undergoing gastric surgery.MethodsThis retrospective multicohort study used three perioperative and critical care databases. MIMIC-IV supported model development and internal validation, while eICU and MOVER supported external validation. Feature selection used LASSO regression, followed by comparison of six machine learning algorithms. Logistic regression was selected using the MIMIC-IV internal validation cohort based on discrimination, recall, and clinical interpretability; the locked model was then evaluated in eICU and MOVER. SHAP analysis quantified predictor contributions and enhanced model transparency.ResultsThe final population included four cohorts: MIMIC-IV training (N = 4316), MIMIC-IV internal validation (N = 1851), eICU external testing (N = 1745), and MOVER external testing (N = 1152). The internally selected logistic regression model achieved AUCs of 0.819 in eICU and 0.827 in MOVER, with recalls of 0.827 and 0.936, respectively. SHAP analysis identified chloride, sodium, bicarbonate, and anion gap as dominant predictors across cohorts.ConclusionThis study presents an interpretable postoperative delirium risk-prediction model in elderly ICU patients following gastric surgery. Although the model achieved high recall, marked class imbalance and low outcome prevalence were associated with low precision and a substantial false-positive burden. Prospective validation, threshold optimisation, and assessment of clinical utility are required before implementation.

42840403.title: Progress of nursing management for delirium in critically ill geriatric patients: a narrative review.
42840403.abstract: Delirium is the most common and modifiable acute cognitive complication in elderly critically ill patients and is associated with prolonged hospital stays, increased mortality, persistent long-term cognitive decline, and a significant healthcare burden. A history of mild cognitive impairment or dementia further increases delirium risk, exacerbates symptom severity, and worsens clinical outcomes. Nonpharmacological nursing interventions form the cornerstone of delirium prevention and management. However, nurse-centered integrated comprehensive care pathways remain insufficiently integrated. This narrative review systematically synthesizes peer-reviewed evidence retrieved from the PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus databases up to July 2025, focusing on the nursing management of delirium in elderly critically ill patients. The content encompasses modifiable risk factors, validated bedside assessment scales (including CAM-ICU, ICDSC, 4AT, and home-based tools such as FAM-CAM and IQCODE), and evidence-based multicomponent nonpharmacological intervention strategies. The core intervention domains include the Hospital Elder Life Program (HELP), the eCASH care model, medication safety monitoring, early mobilization, sleep optimization, reduction in physical restraints, orientation training, behavioral symptom management, and postdischarge home safety guidance. Additionally, this review evaluates the current status, clinical value, and limitations of emerging digital technologies applied to delirium care, including wearable monitoring devices, virtual reality-assisted cognitive rehabilitation, and artificial intelligence-augmented clinical decision support systems. This review aims to provide a theoretical foundation and practical reference for frontline nurses implementing evidence-based delirium management in elderly critically ill patients.

42838510.title: Effect of intensive care unit sedation strategy on patient-reported experience: secondary mediation analysis of the A2B randomised controlled trial.
42838510.abstract: The optimal ICU sedation strategy to improve patient-reported experience is unknown. In a planned secondary analysis of the A2B randomised trial, we evaluated the effect of sedation strategy (dexmedetomidine, clonidine or propofol) on recalled patient experience at 90 days post-randomisation. Using mediation analyses, we explored plausible mediators of the relationship between sedation strategy and patient experience. We analysed data for all patients from A2B who completed the Intensive Care Experience Questionnaire (ICE-Q) at 90 days. The primary outcome was patient-recalled experience, measured by the four ICE-Q domain scores (awareness, frightening memories, recall, satisfaction). Sedation strategy effect was evaluated using linear regression, adjusting for potential confounders. Mediation analyses were conducted for duration of mechanical ventilation; ICU stay; and days with pain behaviour, agitation and coma/delirium. Of 1404 patients included in the primary trial analysis, 1009 (71.9%) were alive at 90 days post-randomisation with ICE-Qs completed by 289/1009 (28.6%). Compared with propofol, dexmedetomidine sedation was associated with higher awareness of surroundings (median score 32 vs. 28, adjusted mean difference 3.6, 95%CI 1.0-6.2, p = 0.01), but clonidine sedation had no association (difference 2.4, 95%CI -0.2-5.0, p = 0.07). No associations were found with other ICE-Q domains. The contribution of the five potential mediators on the dexmedetomidine-awareness relationship was small. Dexmedetomidine compared with propofol sedation strategy may be associated with increased recalled awareness of surroundings, which is considered a favourable indicator of ICU experience. Together with the primary A2B trial results, which showed no effect on ventilation duration, these hypothesis-generating findings in a subgroup of the A2B cohort do not support the use of dexmedetomidine over propofol based on patient-reported experience. Based on our findings, we advocate that a personalised approach to sedation strategies should continue to be used.

42838418.title: Neuro-oncological emergencies requiring critical care intervention.
42838418.abstract: Patients with primary or metastatic brain tumours can deteriorate abruptly, and the acute physician is often the first to respond. This review covers the recognition and initial management of the neurological emergencies most likely to need critical care: raised intracranial pressure from peritumoural oedema and herniation; seizures and status epilepticus, including non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE); intracranial haemorrhage; acute hydrocephalus; and venous thromboembolism. It also covers two treatment-related emergencies that the general physician must now recognise: immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome after chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitor encephalitis. Throughout, the text indicates whether recommendations rest on guidelines and where on observational data. The focus is on recognising time-critical treatment, timely escalation to neurosurgical and neurocritical care services, and the early, values-based discussion of goals of care.

42837971.title: Increasing the visibility of delirium as a hospital acquired complication: A consumer co-designed, nurse-led quality improvement program in a quaternary intensive care unit.
42837971.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
42837971.abstract: Delirium is common in critically ill patients but is frequently under-recognised, inconsistently documented, and poorly explained to families. In our 48-bed intensive care unit (ICU), baseline chart review identified probable delirium in 65% of sampled admissions, yet the term "delirium" was documented in only 23% of medical records. The objective of this study was to increase the visibility of delirium as a hospital-acquired complication through reliable screening, explicit interdisciplinary documentation, and consumer co-designed family engagement. We conducted a nurse-led quality improvement program in a quaternary adult ICU. The program was co-designed with a consumer representative with lived experience of ICU delirium and delivered through two linked workstreams: Humanising Delirium, focused on Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU screening documentation reliability, family engagement, and nonpharmacological care; and Communicating Delirium, focused on standardised terminology, medical documentation, and handover. Interventions included multidisciplinary education, delirium champions, bedside prompts, a co-designed ICU Admission Pack and "This is Me" bedside tool, and iterative audit and feedback. Outcomes were evaluated using run charts, statistical process control p-charts, and before-and-after comparisons. Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU screening documentation reliability improved significantly: shifts meeting all documentation requirements increased from 26.5% to 65.9% (p < 0.001), with special-cause variation confirming sustained change. Completion of the "This is Me" bedside tool increased from 18.8% to 54.5%, and documented ICU Admission Pack distribution rose to 34%. Explicit use of "delirium" in medical documentation increased from 23% to a sustained performance of 44-60%: documentation of an underlying cause improved from 36% to 79-95%, and medical management plan documentation from 50% to 80-89%. Nursing documentation of nonpharmacological strategies increased from 29.7% to 74%, and the nursing-medical recognition gap narrowed from 26% to 2.4%. A consumer co-designed, nurse-led quality improvement program improved process measures associated with delirium recognition and communication, including screening documentation reliability, delirium documentation, and caregiver engagement in a large adult ICU. Delirium improvement programs should treat recognition, explicit documentation, and caregiver communication as interdependent components of delirium care. Partnering with consumers helped shift project aims from clinician recognition to proactive family preparation and partnership.

42833556.title: Machine Learning for Predicting Long-Term Outcomes in Neurocritical Care: A Sub-Analysis from the SYNAPSE-ICU Study.
42833556.abstract: Neurocritical conditions present significant challenges in the intensive care unit (ICU), especially during the initial hours. Accurate early risk assessment is essential for guiding acute care and influencing long-term outcomes. This study aims to evaluate the potential of machine learning (ML) models for risk prediction in neurocritical patients. This retrospective sub-analysis of the SYNAPSE-ICU Study applied machine learning to predict the 6-month outcome for patients with 3 different neurocritical conditions: subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), traumatic brain injury (TBI), or intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). Models were trained at ICU admission, ICU day 3, ICU day 7, and Hospital discharge using the H2O framework, including GLM, DRF, GBM, XGBoost, and Stacked Ensembles. Predictive performance was evaluated using AUPRC and AUROC metrics. In all, 2202 patients were included with a complete data set to predict the 6-month outcome. At 6 months, 836 patients had a favorable outcome (Glasgow Outcome Scale Extended (GOSE) ≥5) and had a significantly higher GOSE at Hospital discharge (P < 0.001). Predictive performance (pooled across 5 multiply-imputed datasets) was highest at ICU admission (AUROC 0.841 [95% CI 0.804-0.878]) and Hospital discharge (AUROC 0.885 [0.845-0.925]), with a transient reduction during the ICU stay (Day 3: AUROC 0.830 [0.789-0.870]; Day 7: AUROC 0.821 [0.777-0.865]). Age was the most important parameter at the respective time points, except for Hospital discharge, where the GOSE at discharge had the highest impact on the 6-month outcome. This sub-analysis demonstrates that machine learning models can effectively predict long-term outcomes for neurocritical patients, with accuracy improving from ICU admission to Hospital discharge. GOSE at discharge and age are critical parameters. The findings underscore the potential of ML models to improve prognostic assessments in neurocritical care.

42832860.title: Longitudinal trajectories of health-related quality of life and cognitive function in ICU survivors with versus without delirium: A 6-month follow-up study.
42832860.abstract: To prospectively explore the 6-month longitudinal trajectories of health-related quality of life and cognitive function in intensive care unit survivors with and without delirium, and to compare inter-group recovery differences at key follow-up time points. Adult patients admitted to the intensive care unit were enrolled. Delirium status was assessed every 4 h using the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit. At 1, 3 and 6 months after discharge, the 12-Item Short Form Health Survey and the Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status were used to evaluate health-related quality of life and cognitive function, respectively. A total of 587 eligible patients were enrolled, with 508 completing follow-up. Among them, 232 patients (45.7%) developed delirium during their intensive care unit stay. At 1 month after discharge, patients with delirium exhibited significantly greater impairments in all quality-of-life domains (except general health and vitality) and cognitive function compared to patients without delirium. From 3 to 6 months post-discharge, while the overall Physical Component Summary and physical functioning of patients with delirium recovered to levels comparable to those of non-delirium patients (p > 0.05), persistent impairments were still observed in specific physical domains such as role-physical and bodily pain. Between-group differences in vitality were absent at 1 month (p = 0.346) but present at 3 months (p = 0.005) and 6 months (p = 0.002); the group-by-time interaction was significant (p < 0.001), indicating a slower rate of vitality recovery in patients with delirium. Furthermore, significant deficits in cognitive function and mental health domains persisted among delirious patients at all time points (all p < 0.01), demonstrating a slower recovery rate compared to their non-delirium counterparts. Intensive care unit acquired delirium is associated with sustained impairments in health-related quality of life and cognitive function, despite partial physical recovery by 3 to 6 months. These findings support the need for extended multidisciplinary care, including functional monitoring, cognitive rehabilitation, and psychosocial support, for delirium survivors after intensive care unit discharge.

42831577.title: Effects of ketamine infusion rate and cumulative dosing on incidence of delirium in medical intensive care unit patients.
42831577.journal: American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists
42831577.abstract: Ketamine is increasingly used for analgosedation in mechanically ventilated intensive care unit (ICU) patients, but its association with delirium remains unclear. This study evaluated the relationship between maximum hourly ketamine rate and cumulative dose during hospitalization, with the incidence of delirium. This multicenter retrospective cohort study included mechanically ventilated adult medical ICU patients who received ketamine infusions for sedation (January 2013-June 2025) at two tertiary centers. Data collected included demographics, sedation requirements, and daily Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU). The primary outcome was delirium at any point during ICU stay. Primary and secondary exposure variables included maximum hourly ketamine rate and cumulative ketamine dose. A modified Poisson regression was used to evaluate associations between the exposure variables and incidence of delirium, adjusting for confounders. Of 837 screened patients, 114 met inclusion criteria and 42 (36.8%) developed delirium. Baseline characteristics were similar. Patients with delirium had longer duration of mechanical ventilation, (210.7 vs 140.9 hours, P <0.01), ICU length of stay (364.7 vs 268.6 hours, P =0.04), and higher morphine milligram equivalents (5,126.8 vs 2911.8, P = 0.04). No association was observed between delirium with maximum hourly ketamine rate (RR 1.15, P = 0.21) or cumulative dose (RR 1.0, p=0.97). Restricted cubic spline analysis showed a trend towards increased delirium risk with increasing maximum hourly ketamine rates (P = 0.06). Maximum hourly ketamine infusion rate and cumulative dose in mechanical ventilated patients in the medical ICU were not associated with ICU delirium.

42831012.title: ICU-Associated Exposure Keratopathy and Preventable Corneal Blindness: A Clinical Review.
42831012.abstract: Exposure keratopathy is an ocular surface injury caused by prolonged corneal exposure, most often from incomplete eyelid closure. Critical illness can intensify exposure through reduced blinking, chemosis, impaired corneal reflexes, sedation, mechanical ventilation, and tear film instability. This narrative clinical review synthesizes contemporary evidence on epidemiology, mechanisms, risk factors, bedside assessment, prevention, protocol implementation, and care in resource-constrained intensive care units (ICUs). PubMed/MEDLINE was searched for English language literature from January 2000 through 15 September 2026, supplemented by reference list and guideline searches. Systematic reviews, randomized trials, cohort studies, quality improvement reports, and relevant guidance were prioritized. Pooled evidence indicates that exposure keratopathy is common among critically ill patients, and recent trials support scheduled lubrication, eyelid closure support, and moisture chamber approaches, particularly when the cornea remains exposed. Fluorescein assessment and clear ophthalmology referral criteria improve detection of epithelial injury and complications that threaten vision. The review distinguishes evidence from randomized and observational studies and proposes a pragmatic bedside risk framework without presenting it as a validated score. Its principal contribution is the integration of prevention, nursing workflow, clinical escalation, and resource appropriate implementation into a single ophthalmic patient safety framework. The intended audience is ophthalmologists, intensivists, ICU nurses, optometrists, and quality improvement teams. Early structured eye care may reduce avoidable corneal morbidity while supporting consistent practice across settings with different resources.

42830737.title: Variation in capability, organisational structure, and treatment processes for critically ill adults with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury in Australia and New Zealand.
42830737.journal: Critical care and resuscitation : journal of the Australasian Academy of Critical Care Medicine
42830737.abstract: To characterise between-centre variation in capability, organisational structure, and treatment processes for adults with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury (msTBI) admitted to intensive care (ICU) in Australia and New Zealand (ANZ). Cross-sectional questionnaire supplemented by linked Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society CORE Critical Care Resources Registry descriptors. ANZ ICUs treating adults with msTBI, October-December 2025. Variation in organisational structure and capability, ICU treatment processes, neuroprognostication, withholding or withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy, and fulfilment of selected Australian TBI Quality Indicator Set elements. Heterogeneity was assessed using the index of qualitative variation (IQV) for nominal items and Leik's dispersion for ordinal items; values <0.3 were considered low, 0.3-0.7 moderate, and >0.7 substantial. Moderate or substantial heterogeneity was observed in 39 of 74 measured items (53%). Substantial heterogeneity included neurocritical care subspecialty expertise (IQV 1.00), perceived devastating traumatic brain injury management (IQV 0.99), cerebrospinal fluid drainage timing (IQV 0.93), withholding or withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy decision-making processes (IQV 0.86), arterial transducer zero level for cerebral perfusion pressure calculation (IQV 0.82), haemoglobin targets (Leik's dispersion 0.81), and post-ICU follow-up interval (IQV 0.81). Low heterogeneity in several advanced neuromonitoring and neuroprognostication modalities reflected consistent non-use or unavailability. Fulfilment of the six measured Australian TBI Quality Indicator Set indicators ranged from 2/6 to 5/6 across centres. Among ANZ ICUs providing care for adults with msTBI, moderate or substantial variation was evident in over half of measured organisational and clinical aspects of care. These findings identify targets for research and quality improvement and highlight centre variation as a potential modifier of patient outcomes.

42828295.title: Effects of substance use on sedation requirements in critically ill patients.
42828295.abstract: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effect of substance use on sedation requirements in critically ill patients to optimize dosing in this population. This was a multicenter, retrospective, observational, institutional review board-approved, cohort study. Included individuals were aged 18 years and older, required mechanical ventilation for more than 24 hours, and had a history of substance use in the intervention group, defined as documentation of using 1 or more substances within the past year. The primary outcome was the maximum number of concurrent continuous analgesic and sedative infusions required during intubation and mechanical ventilation. The primary outcome, maximum number of concurrent continuous analgesic and sedative infusions, was significantly higher when comparing subjects with substance use to those without substance use (3 vs 2 infusions; P < 0.001). Significantly higher doses of analgesia and sedation were also required in the substance use group, including fentanyl (150 vs 100 mcg/hr; P = 0.024), dexmedetomidine (1.2 vs 1.0 mcg/kg/hr; P = 0.040), and benzodiazepines measured in lorazepam equivalents (3 vs 1.5 mg/hr; P < 0.001). In mechanically ventilated subjects, a statistically significantly higher number of concurrent continuous analgesic and sedative infusions were used in the substance use group, with larger doses required to sedate subjects.

42826764.title: Effects of dexmedetomidine on postoperative outcomes in adult non-cardiac surgical patients admitted to the intensive care unit: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
42826764.abstract: The role of dexmedetomidine in patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) following non-cardiac surgery remains unclear. While dexmedetomidine is widely used for its sedative and potential delirium-sparing properties, its pooled effects on clinically relevant postoperative outcomes in this population are not well established. This systematic review and network meta-analysis evaluated the comparative effectiveness and safety of dexmedetomidine compared with other sedative strategies in postoperative non-cardiac surgical ICU patients. We systematically searched PubMed, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Embase from inception to 26 May 2026 for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing postoperative dexmedetomidine with normal saline or other sedatives in adults (≥18 years) admitted to the ICU after non-cardiac surgery. The primary outcome was incidence of delirium during the ICU stay. Secondary outcomes were time to extubation, ICU length of stay, duration of mechanical ventilation, and haemodynamic adverse events. Effect estimates were expressed as relative risks (RRs) or mean differences (MDs) using random-effects models. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework. Interventions were ranked using the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) for each outcome. Twenty-four RCTs involving 2,777 patients were included in the systematic review, of which 22 RCTs involving 2,544 patients contributed to the network meta-analysis. Compared with midazolam (RR 0.11, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.80; very low certainty) and normal saline (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.59; low certainty), dexmedetomidine may reduce the risk of delirium. Evidence is insufficient to determine whether propofol differs from dexmedetomidine in its effect on delirium. There were no differences in time to extubation, duration of mechanical ventilation, or ICU length of stay across sedative strategies. Dexmedetomidine probably increases the risk of bradycardia compared with propofol (RR 3.03, 95% CI 1.39-6.25; low certainty), but the evidence is insufficient to determine whether the two agents differ in their effects on hypotension. In safety rankings, dexmedetomidine performed least favourably for bradycardia (SUCRA 0.03) and hypotension (SUCRA 0.13). Dexmedetomidine may reduce postoperative delirium in non-cardiac surgical ICU patients but does not appear to improve ventilatory recovery or ICU length of stay and is associated with higher bradycardia risk. Its principal benefit lies in delirium prevention, supporting an individualised approach to sedative selection.

42826125.title: Simulation-Based Neurodiagnostic Team Training for Critically Ill Patients with External Ventricular Drains: Design, Implementation, and Outcomes.
42826125.abstract: Simulation‑based training is increasingly used in healthcare; a review of the literature revealed no published studies describing structured simulation‑based training programs for neurodiagnostic technologists. This study introduces a high‑fidelity simulation curriculum designed to improve technical skills, clinical reasoning, and interdisciplinary communication during continuous EEG (cEEG) setup in critically ill adult and pediatric patients with external ventricular drains (EVDs). Using two standardized scenarios, learners practiced pre‑procedure coordination with nursing staff, safe electrode placement near neurosurgical sites, response to vital‑sign changes, and management of alarm events. Training followed best‑practice simulation frameworks, including structured pre‑briefing and PEARLS debriefing. Participants reported increased confidence, better workflow understanding, and improved communication with nursing teams. The curriculum addresses a critical gap in neurodiagnostic education by providing a realistic, safe environment to rehearse high‑risk neurocritical care procedures. Although single‑site and limited in scale, early results support simulation as an effective tool for enhancing safety, preparedness, and team performance in EVD‑dependent cEEG monitoring.

42824486.title: Nurse-led early mobilization and ICU-acquired weakness in mechanically ventilated adults: a retrospective before-after cohort study.
42824486.abstract: ICU-acquired weakness (ICU-AW) is a frequent complication of critical illness, and real-world evidence on nurse-led early mobilization (EM) in Asian ICUs remains limited. We conducted a single-center, retrospective before-after cohort study of invasively ventilated adults admitted during usual-care (n = 153) and nurse-led EM (n = 164) periods. ICU-AW, defined as a Medical Research Council (MRC) sum score <48, was assessed among evaluable ICU survivors (n = 266); ICU death made volitional strength testing non-evaluable and was addressed in a death-or-ICU-AW composite sensitivity analysis. The primary model estimated the association between protocol implementation and ICU-AW after adjustment for baseline confounders; post-exposure care processes were examined separately. ICU-AW occurred in 60/129 (46.5%) usual-care survivors and 40/137 (29.2%) nurse-led EM survivors (crude absolute risk difference 17.3 percentage points [95% CI 5.8-28.8] among evaluable survivors; crude OR 0.474, 95% CI 0.286-0.786). The baseline-adjusted OR was 0.436 (95% CI 0.248-0.766; P = 0.004). Morbidity-related secondary outcomes favored nurse-led EM, including lower delirium incidence (41.2% vs. 22.6%; OR 0.416), shorter ICU stay (median 11 vs. 8 days), and higher discharge Barthel Index (70 vs. 85). No statistically significant ICU mortality difference was detected (15.7% vs. 16.5%; OR 1.059, 95% CI 0.581-1.93), but the study was not powered to exclude clinically important mortality effects. Nurse-led EM implementation was associated with lower odds of ICU-AW and improved morbidity outcomes. Because exposure was assigned by historical period, residual and secular confounding remain important limitations, and confirmation in a randomized or stepped-wedge implementation study is warranted.

42955613.title: Portable ultra-low field MRI in neurocritical care and intensive care units: A systematic review of diagnostic performance and feasibility.
42955613.abstract: To synthesise evidence on the diagnostic performance, safety, feasibility and clinical impact of ultra-low-field portable magnetic resonance imaging (pMRI) in adult neurocritical care and intensive care unit (ICU) populations. PubMed, Scopus and Embase were searched from inception to 6 February 2026 and supplemented by grey literature and citation searching. We included original English-language studies of adult ICU, neurocritical care or emergency department patients undergoing pMRI at ≤ 0.1 T. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Risk of bias in diagnostic comparisons was assessed with an adapted QUADAS-2 framework, and feasibility and safety outcomes were appraised narratively. Because of heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively. The review was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261302014). Eleven studies published between 2020 and 2024 were included, comprising 694 patient participants and 715 patient examinations, plus 40 healthy controls. Cohorts overlapped substantially: six studies came wholly and one partly from a single institution, and one ECMO study was a subset of another. The number of unique patients is therefore estimated at 281 to 677. In the multicentre ECMO study, adverse events occurred in 3 of 50 patients (6%). One was serious: an intra-aortic balloon pump malfunction attributed to electrocardiographic artefact. No adverse events were reported in the other seven independent cohorts that reported safety outcomes, and two studies did not report safety outcomes. For ischaemic stroke, pMRI detected infarction in 45 of 50 patients (90%). By sequence, sensitivity was 100% for FLAIR, 98% for T2-weighted imaging and 86% for diffusion-weighted imaging. Visual DWI-FLAIR mismatch identified patients scanned within 4.5 h with 60% sensitivity, 82% specificity and a 93% negative predictive value. Sensitivity for intracerebral haemorrhage was 80.4% (specificity 96.6%) on initial blinded evaluation. It was 92.1% (specificity 99.3%) in a later cohort in which raters had clinical context and images used deep-learning reconstruction, with lower sensitivity for infratentorial haemorrhage (75.0%). Only one subdural haemorrhage and no extradural haemorrhages were reported. Midline-shift detection showed 93% sensitivity, 96% specificity and a kappa of 0.87. pMRI detected hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury in 12 of 12 affected post-cardiac-arrest patients. In ECMO patients, pMRI detected 8 of 8 ischaemic events, compared with 4 of 8 on head CT, but only 1 of 2 haemorrhages. Up to 28% of examinations were nondiagnostic, mainly because of motion. Ultra-low-field pMRI is a feasible bedside neuroimaging adjunct with a low but non-zero adverse-event rate. It is of particular value for ischaemic injury, midline shift and serial monitoring. Lower and variable sensitivity for haemorrhage, the nonspecificity of FLAIR hyperintensity, overlapping single-institution cohorts and small samples mean that larger multicentre validation studies are needed.

42955591.title: Impact of burst suppression duration on delirium and its diagnostic value in mechanically ventilated ICU patients.
42955591.journal: Journal of clinical monitoring and computing
42955591.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) delirium affects up to 50% of mechanically ventilated patients. This condition is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Although bispectral index (BIS) monitoring is widely used for sedation assessment, its predictive value for delirium remains limited. Burst suppression (BS) is an electroencephalographic pattern reflecting profound cerebral dysfunction. BS has been proposed as a predictor of delirium. However, the quantitative role of burst suppression duration (BSD) in delirium risk stratification has not been established. This prospective observational study enrolled 300 mechanically ventilated adult ICU patients between April 2021 and October 2024 at Harrison International Peace Hospital. Continuous video-electroencephalogram (vEEG) monitoring was performed. BSD was quantified from the vEEG recordings. Delirium was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU). Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify independent risk factors. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of BSD. Among 300 patients, 130 (43.3%) developed delirium. The delirium group had significantly longer BSD than the control group (median 81.1 s, IQR 41.5-148.5 vs. 17.2 s, IQR 5.8-32.9; P < 0.001). Multivariate analysis identified BSD (adjusted OR = 1.018, 95% CI 1.012-1.023; P < 0.001), BIS (adjusted OR = 0.964, 95% CI 0.946-0.982; P < 0.001), age (adjusted OR = 1.024, 95% CI 1.002-1.047; P = 0.031), and hypertension (adjusted OR = 1.748, 95% CI 1.002-3.051; P = 0.049) as independent risk factors. ROC analysis demonstrated that BSD achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.871 (95% CI 0.829-0.913). The optimal cutoff of 41.5 s yielded a sensitivity of 80.8% and a specificity of 78.2%. The combination of BSD and BIS improved the AUC to 0.914 (95% CI 0.882-0.946). BSD is an independent risk factor for delirium in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. It demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy as a quantitative biomarker. The combination of BSD and BIS provides superior predictive performance. This combined approach offers a practical quantitative tool for early delirium risk stratification.

42945737.title: Methodological caveats before adopting lower-intensity heparin nomograms in the neuro-ICU.

42939344.title: Intradialytic Hemodynamic Instability and Delirium in Critically Ill Patients Receiving Renal Replacement Therapy: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
42939344.abstract: Background: Acute kidney injury (AKI) requiring renal replacement therapy (RRT) is common in critically ill patients and is frequently accompanied by delirium. Intradialytic hemodynamic instability, particularly hypotension, may impair cerebral perfusion; however, its quantitative relationship with delirium remains unclear. This study investigated the association between intradialytic hemodynamic instability and Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU)-defined delirium in critically ill patients receiving RRT. Methods: This single-center retrospective study included 87 adult intensive care unit (ICU) patients undergoing RRT between September 2025 and May 2026. Delirium was assessed using the CAM-ICU. Intradialytic hemodynamic burden was quantified by the cumulative duration of mean arterial pressure (MAP) < 65 mmHg and the number of hypotensive episodes during RRT. Multivariable logistic regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, and admission SOFA score were performed to evaluate the associations between hemodynamic parameters and delirium, while receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were used to assess their discriminative ability. Results: Of 87 patients, 46 (52.9%) were classified as CAM-ICU-positive for delirium. Patients with delirium had a longer cumulative duration of MAP < 65 mmHg (median, 36.0 vs. 5.0 min; p = 0.048) and more hypotensive episodes (median, 3.0 vs. 1.0; p = 0.032). These differences were no longer significant after normalization to the number of RRT sessions (p = 0.153 and p = 0.249). In addition, neither parameter showed a statistically significant association with delirium after adjustment for age, sex, and admission SOFA score. ROC analysis demonstrated limited discriminative ability (AUC, 0.62 and 0.63, respectively). Mechanical ventilation duration, ICU length of stay or ICU mortality did not show a statistically significant association with CAM-ICU positivity in the adjusted models. Sensitivity analyses using alternative functional forms for cumulative MAP < 65 mmHg duration, including log-transformed, categorical, and natural cubic spline models, did not show statistically significant associations with CAM-ICU positivity. Conclusions: Critically ill patients with delirium had greater cumulative intradialytic hypotensive burden; however, these differences were attenuated after accounting for the number of RRT sessions, and the hemodynamic parameters did not show statistically significant associations with delirium in the adjusted regression models. These findings suggest a potential relationship between intradialytic hemodynamic burden and delirium but do not establish an independent or causal association.

42931902.title: European Society of Intensive Care Medicine consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the intensive care unit.
42931902.abstract: A human-centred partnership in the intensive care unit (ICU) aims to integrate person-centred care, communication, emotional support, equity, and collaboration into ICU environments. The European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) developed a consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the ICU following a systematic, multi-phase, evidence-informed methodology incorporating the views of ICU professionals, academics, and patient and family representatives. This international multidisciplinary panel of 46 members conducted rapid reviews addressing 20 Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes (PICO) questions across six domains: person-centred care; communication and transparency; emotional well-being; equity, diversity, and inclusion; ICU environment; technology and innovation. Based on the evidence synthesis, 53 draft statements were developed and evaluated through a two-round eDelphi study. The final set of statements was discussed and ratified at an expert consensus meeting with the initial panel of experts and with patients and family representatives. A total of 201 international stakeholders participated in round 1 and 149 in round 2. Members of the expert consensus meeting ultimately endorsed 43 consensus statements. Key recommendations supported flexible family visitation, structured interdisciplinary communication, empathy-based staff training, psychological support for patients and ICU professionals, culturally responsive care, environmental interventions to improve sleep and reduce delirium, and the integration of digital supported technologies. The consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the ICU provides a comprehensive framework for clinicians with evidence-informed directions to deliver high-quality practice across diverse ICU settings. By prioritising person-centred care, communication, inclusivity, and well-being alongside responsible technological innovation, the experiences and outcomes of patients, families, and ICU professionals may improve.

42930613.title: Physiology-Guided Management of Acute Right Ventricular Failure and Pulmonary Hypertension in Critically Ill Patients: Hemodynamic Phenotypes, Ventilator Interactions, and Rescue Strategies.
42930613.abstract: Patients with acute right heart failure or pulmonary hypertension require cautious resuscitation because the right ventricle is highly preload-sensitive and has a narrow therapeutic window; both hypovolemia and volume overload may worsen hemodynamics. Echocardiographic guidance can help optimize fluid administration. The management of right heart failure also includes increasing contractility and reducing systemic afterload with inodilators such as dobutamine and milrinone. In cases of high pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) contributing to right heart failure, the use of selective pulmonary dilators can decrease the right ventricular afterload, while largely avoiding the systemic hypotension associated with intravenous vasodilators. Hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis may increase PVR, while sedation, intubation, and positive-pressure ventilation (PPV) may reduce preload, precipitating hemodynamic collapse. When possible, noninvasive respiratory support may be cautiously used to optimize oxygenation and ventilation and avoid intubation. With either form of PPV, airway pressures should be minimized to reduce the risk of hemodynamic compromise. Additionally, preload should be carefully optimized; hypotension-inducing sedatives, such as propofol, should be minimized; vasopressors should be readily available. In ARDS complicated by acute cor pulmonale, a right ventricular-protective ventilation strategy should be considered alongside conventional lung-protective ventilation. This approach emphasizes limiting excessive plateau and driving pressures, avoiding severe hypercapnia and hypoxemia, and carefully titrating positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) to prevent excessive increases in PVR and right ventricular afterload. In patients with right-to-left intracardiac shunting, elevated right-sided pressures may worsen shunt flow and cause refractory hypoxemia that responds poorly to increasing FiO2 and ventilation pressures. Management should therefore focus on reducing PVR, optimizing right ventricular function, and limiting factors that increase right-sided pressures.

42929360.title: Safety and efficacy of volatile sedatives in critically ill patients receiving mechanical ventilation: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
42929360.abstract: Volatile sedatives are increasingly utilised for sedation in critically ill patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation. Despite numerous randomised controlled trials and observational studies comparing volatile sedation to intravenous sedation, questions regarding its safety and efficacy persist. A systematic search was performed in PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Web of Science databases for studies published up to July 2025. The analysis included randomised controlled trials and observational studies that compared the use of volatile sedation with intravenous sedation in patients admitted to the intensive care unit for mechanical ventilation. Eligible studies involved adults aged ⩾18 years, requiring mechanical ventilation, and utilising either volatile or intravenous sedatives. They also needed to report at least one outcome of interest: incidence of delirium, mortality, intensive care unit length of stay, or duration of mechanical ventilation. From 3182 identified publications, fifteen studies were included in the systematic review. Volatile sedation was not associated with a significant difference in the incidence of delirium compared to intravenous sedation (risk ratio 0.72; 95% confidence interval 0.38-1.34), mortality (risk ratio 0.97; 95% confidence interval 0.80-1.17), intensive care unit length of stay (mean difference 0.28 days; 95% confidence interval -1.74 to 2.30), or duration of mechanical ventilation (mean difference -37.20 h; 95% confidence interval -78.60 to 4.20). Volatile sedation was not associated with significant differences in mechanical ventilation duration, delirium incidence, intensive care unit length of stay, or mortality compared to intravenous sedation. Further large-scale, high-quality randomised trials are needed to clarify its clinical benefit in critical care settings.

42928657.title: Factors Associated With Behavioral Intentions Toward Pain Assessment and Management Among Critical Care Nurses: A Theory-Based Instrument Validation and Model Testing Study.
42928657.abstract: Optimal pain management remains elusive despite the implementation of standard practice guidelines. The theory of planned behavior (TPB) offers a framework for understanding nurses' clinical practices. Developing and validating theory-based instruments enables an in-depth exploration of the sociopsychological factors underlying nurses' behavioral intentions and practices in pain assessment and management. This study aimed to develop and validate the Intention to Perform Pain Assessment and Management Questionnaire (IPPAMQ) and a Behavioral Scale, identify factors associated with nurses' behavioral intentions, and evaluate the explanatory power of the TPB for nurses' clinical practices. A two-phase cross-sectional study was conducted across seven institutions (December 2023-April 2025). Phase I (n = 200) employed a methodological design to establish the psychometric properties of the developed instruments. Phase II (n = 308) utilized the validated instruments to identify factors associated with nurses' behavioral intentions and to evaluate the TPB's explanatory power for nurses' self-reported practices through path analysis. Both instruments demonstrated satisfactory psychometric properties. Nurses' attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control were significantly associated with their behavioral intentions, explaining 65% of the total variance, with perceived behavioral control being the strongest correlate. Nurses' behavioral intentions were significantly associated with self-reported practices, accounting for 47% of the variance and supporting the TPB's substantial explanatory power for nurses' practices. This study provides psychometrically robust instruments tailored to the TPB framework within the critical care context. The TPB framework effectively highlighted key sociopsychological correlates of nurses' behavioral intentions and adequately accounted for nurses' self-reported pain assessment and management practices. The IPPAMQ enables nurse managers and policymakers to conduct data-driven evaluations of the sociopsychological factors and identify areas for tailored interventions. The TPB framework's substantial explanatory power underscores the need for multilevel strategies to narrow the gap between nurses' behavioral intentions and clinical practices.

42926782.title: Dexmedetomidine Suspected Fever and Clinical Escalation: A Pilot Study Evaluating the Impact in the Intensive Care Unit.
42926782.journal: The Journal of pharmacy technology : jPT : official publication of the Association of Pharmacy Technicians
42926782.abstract: Dexmedetomidine, an alpha-2 agonist commonly used as a sedative agent in mechanically ventilated patients, has been associated with drug-induced fever. Concern for fever may prompt diagnostic evaluation and empiric antimicrobial therapy, potentially leading to unnecessary health care utilization. This pilot study aimed to evaluate if dexmedetomidine use in mechanically ventilated medical intensive care unit (ICU) patients was associated with increased escalation of care compared with alternate sedative agents. This single-center, retrospective, matched cohort study included patients 18 years or older who were admitted to the medical ICU and required a sedative agent to facilitate mechanical ventilation. Patients receiving dexmedetomidine were matched 1:1 with patients receiving alternate sedative agents. The primary outcome was the composite outcome of initiation of diagnostic evaluation and/or antimicrobial escalation (IDEA). A total of 150 patients were included (75 per group). Most patients were male (68%), and 45% had a primary diagnosis of respiratory failure. The primary outcome, IDEA, occurred in 53 patients (71%) receiving dexmedetomidine and 51 patients (68%) receiving alternate sedatives (P = .723). Fever occurred in 24 patients (32%) receiving dexmedetomidine compared with 17 patients (23%) receiving alternate sedatives. Median ICU length of stay was longer in the dexmedetomidine group (5 [interquartile range, IQR 1-8] vs 4 [IQR 1-5] days; [P = .002]). In-hospital mortality occurred in 14 patients (19%) receiving dexmedetomidine and 24 patients (32%) receiving alternate sedative (P = .060). There was no statistically significant difference between escalation of care in the use of dexmedetomidine versus other sedatives in ICU patients.

42925836.title: Effect of circadian-oriented goal-directed sedation on sleep quality and clinical outcomes in mechanically ventilated ICU patients.
42925836.journal: Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia
42925836.abstract: Sleep disruption and circadian rhythm disturbances are common in mechanically ventilated intensive care unit (ICU) patients and are associated with delirium, prolonged ventilation, and poor clinical outcomes. Conventional sedation strategies may further impair sleep architecture and circadian regulation. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the effects of circadian-oriented, goal-directed sedation on sleep quality and clinical outcomes in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. This study enrolled 65 mechanically ventilated patients admitted to ICU at Suzhou Ninth People's Hospital between March 2024 and December 2024. Using convenience sampling, 33 patients admitted between March and July 2024 were allocated to the control group and received routine sedation and nursing care, while 32 patients admitted between August and December 2024 were formed the intervention group and received sedation management individualized according to circadian sleep-wake patterns. Sleep quality was assessed on days 1, 3, 5, and 7 after intervention using the Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire (RCSQ) and a portable sleep monitor. Delirium was evaluated by Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU). Sedative dosage, duration of mechanical ventilation, length of ICU and hospital stay, , clinical improvement rate, complications, and hospitalization costs were compared between groups. Baseline characteristics were comparable between the two groups. Sleep quality improved over time in both groups; however, Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire scores were significantly higher in the intervention group at all assessment points (p < 0.05). Patients receiving circadian-oriented sedation experienced shorter durations of mechanical ventilation, reduced ICU and total hospital stays, higher rates of clinical improvement, and lower hospitalization costs compared with the control group (p < 0.05). The incidence of complications, including delirium, was also significantly lower in the intervention group. Sedation management aligned with circadian sleep-wake patterns significantly improves sleep quality, reduces sedative requirements, lowers delirium incidence, and shortens mechanical ventilation duration, demonstrating a favorable safety profile in mechanically ventilated patients.

42925835.title: Antidepressant use in invasively ventilated patients in intensive care: Frequency of withholding and association with delirium-An observational study.
42925835.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
42925835.abstract: The aim of this study was to explore antidepressant use in invasively ventilated patients in intensive care who were able to be given medicines enterally (i.e. via feeding tube). As a secondary observation, we examined whether withholding an antidepressant was associated with positive Confusion Assessment Method - Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) scores. A 12-month (1st Jan 2020 to 31st Dec 2020) retrospective cohort study was conducted in the ICU of a 484-bed tertiary referral hospital. Invasively ventilated patients capable of receiving enteral medicines were included. Of invasively ventilated ICU patients prescribed antidepressants prior to admission, 93% had their antidepressants withheld (for part, or all) of their ICU stay and antidepressant withholding was associated with higher odds of a positive CAM-ICU score. Invasively ventilated patients who had an antidepressant withheld were over five times more likely to have had a positive CAM-ICU score during their ICU stay. Availability of a buccal dosage form or a dosage form that could be given enterally did not impact prescribing or administration of pre-existing antidepressants or facilitate swapping to an alternative antidepressant. Antidepressant withholding is frequent in invasively ventilated patients in intensive care who were able to be given medicines enterally. An association was identified between antidepressant withholding and positive CAM-ICU scores, warranting further investigation. Given the observed association between antidepressant withholding and positive CAM-ICU scores, review of antidepressants management may be reasonable when managing invasively ventilated patients with positive CAM-ICU scores.

42919600.title: Inhaled sedation versus intravenous sedation in critically ill patients (IS-CRITIC): protocol for a multicentre, randomised, controlled clinical trial in Spain.
42919600.abstract: Intravenous sedatives are widely used in the intensive care unit (ICU) and are part of routine clinical practice. However, these agents and their active metabolites may be associated with adverse events. Volatile anaesthetics have recently emerged as an attractive alternative for ICU sedation, and isoflurane has been approved by regulatory agencies in several European countries for use in critically ill patients. Although isoflurane has been shown to be non-inferior to propofol-based sedation during short-term sedation periods, it remains unclear whether inhaled sedation with isoflurane offers advantages over intravenous sedation in patients requiring prolonged mechanical ventilation and, consequently, prolonged sedation. This is a phase IV, low-intervention, open-label, multicentre randomised clinical trial conducted on an intention-to-treat basis. A total of 620 patients will be randomised in a 1:1 ratio to receive either inhaled sedation with isoflurane administered using the Sedaconda ACD-S device or intravenous sedation with propofol. Adult patients expected to require more than 48 hours of mechanical ventilation will be included. The primary outcome is ventilator-free days through day 28 post-randomisation. The key secondary outcome is ICU-free days through day 28 post-randomisation. Patient recruitment began in December 2025 and is expected to conclude in December 2027. Final analysis is planned for 2028. The study protocol was approved by the ethics committee of Hospital Universitario La Paz, Madrid, Spain (#6844) and the European Medicines Agency on 13 March 2025. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations. NCT07000526. This clinical trial is registered in the European Union (EU) Clinical Trials Information System (CTIS), under the EU Clinical Trials Regulation (Regulation 536/2014). CTIS ID: (2024–5 18 521-14-00).

42913474.title: Virtual Reality for Delirium Prevention in Intensive Care Unit Nurses and Mechanically Ventilated Patients: Descriptive Qualitative Study.
42913474.abstract: Patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) who are on mechanical ventilation are at high risk of developing delirium. Virtual reality (VR) technology, as an emerging intervention method, shows promising application prospects in delirium prevention, but its specific experience in clinical practice still requires in-depth exploration. This study aims to explore the real experiences of ICU nurses and mechanically ventilated patients in participating in VR delirium prevention, with the aim of providing practical evidence for the optimization and application of this technology in clinical practice. A descriptive qualitative research design was adopted. From March to June 2025, using purposive sampling, participants were selected from the internal medicine, surgery, central, and respiratory ICU departments of a tertiary hospital in Zhengzhou. A total of 73 patients on mechanical ventilation were screened. Among them, 49 were excluded due to not meeting the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) or Barthel Index (BI) score criteria, 5 had delirium at the time of enrollment, 1 was excluded due to visual impairment, and 2 voluntarily withdrew during the study. Finally, 16 patients on mechanical ventilation and 16 nurses were included for semistructured interviews. Data analysis was conducted using the inductive content analysis method. Through the analysis of the interview data, a total of 3 main themes and 14 subthemes were extracted. In terms of perceived benefits, patients experienced an immersive environment and a sense of empowerment driven by tasks, while nurses felt the convenience of resource integration, the intimacy of the nurse-patient relationship, and a sense of professional significance. In terms of perceived challenges, patients faced difficulties with the interaction interface and physical and mental obstacles, while nurses encountered difficulties in communication assessment and responsibility definition. In terms of perceived needs, patients expected personalized content design and continuity of nursing services, while nurses suggested differentiated content adjustment, comprehensive functional integration, and standardized safety management. The participants expressed a positive attitude towards the prevention of delirium based on VR and reported various perceived benefits, challenges, and needs. Future research should prioritize content personalization, functional integration, and safety management. Meanwhile, it is necessary to recognize the limitations of this technology in specific target populations. For those who do not meet the inclusion criteria, adaptive alternative intervention measures should be developed to promote the precise and sustainable application of VR-based delirium prevention.

42912655.title: Differences in donation after circulatory determination of death (DCD) liver donor management. An international survey initiated by the international liver transplantation society (ILTS), society for the advancement of transplant anesthesia (SATA), and liver intensive care group of europe (LICAGE).
42912655.journal: Liver transplantation : official publication of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and the International Liver Transplantation Society
42912655.abstract: We conducted a survey to evaluate variability in determination of death and management of Donation after Circulatory Determination of Death (DCD) liver donors across different countries. 153 centers from 17 countries were included (48.4% US, 51.6% non-US). Most reported using onset of hemodynamic instability, rather than withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy (WLST), as the beginning of the waiting time for decision making related to organ acceptance (76.1% US vs. 47.1% non-US). Actual and maximum acceptable waiting times were comparable between groups (43.7 vs. 50.2 and 50.8 vs. 60.3 min, respectively), frequently exceeding limits defined by national policies. Onset of hemodynamic instability was most commonly defined using systolic blood pressure (SBP) alone (51.4% US vs. 31.6% non-US) or a combination of SBP and oxygen saturation (SpO2) (41.6% US vs. 56.6% non-US). Less commonly, centers used SpO2 (4.2% vs. 3.9%) or arrythmia alone (1.4% US vs. 0.0% non-US). Thresholds for SBP and SpO2 were similar between US and non-US centers (SBP 80 mmHg; and 80% for both). Sedation and analgesia for donor comfort was used less frequently in US centers compared to non-US centers (27.8% vs. 48.1%, p=0.02). Decision-making regarding waiting time was more commonly performed by a multidisciplinary team outside the US (26.1% vs. 52.0%). Over half of US and non-US centers reported using machine perfusion in over 50% of DCD grafts (64.9% vs. 51.9%). When used, normothermic regional perfusion cannulation was more commonly initiated after declaration of death (71.6% US vs. 62.0% non-US). These findings demonstrate substantial variability in DCD donor management. Standardization of definitions and practices, particularly with regard to exclusion of hemodynamic stability period from Warm Ischemic Time (WIT), may improve consistency in decision-making related to organ acceptance.

42903200.title: Early midazolam exposure and short-term risk of acute exacerbation of COPD in critically ill patients: a target trial emulation using the MIMIC-IV database.
42903200.abstract: Sedation is frequently required in the intensive care unit (ICU), but benzodiazepines may worsen respiratory outcomes in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). To evaluate whether early midazolam exposure after ICU admission is associated with the short-term risk of acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD) among critically ill COPD patients. Using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) database, we emulated a target trial and applied a clone-censor-weight (CCW) approach to address immortal time bias and informative censoring. Exposure was midazolam administration within a grace period after ICU admission (primary: 24 h; sensitivity: 12 and 36 h). The primary outcome was AECOPD, defined as initiation of systemic corticosteroids or antibiotics between 24 h and 7 days after ICU admission. Outcomes were compared using inverse probability of censoring weights (IPCW). Among 3,416 ICU stays, 233 (6.8%) received midazolam within 24 h. After IPCW weighting, AECOPD incidence was 29.8% in the midazolam group versus 23.5% in controls (risk difference +6.3%, 95% CI -2.7% to +15.8%; odds ratio 1.38, 95% CI 0.86-2.12; p = 0.158). Findings were directionally consistent across grace periods (12 h OR 1.64; 36 h OR 1.29), but none of the grace-period comparisons reached statistical significance. In the primary 24 h analysis, early midazolam exposure was associated with a numerically higher short-term AECOPD risk. These observational findings cannot establish causality, and the present study did not demonstrate a statistically significant causal effect; nevertheless, in view of existing ICU sedation evidence, continued caution in the use of midazolam in critically ill COPD patients appears prudent.

42901051.title: Determining ICU staff's conceptions, opinions, views, experiences and reflection (DISCOVER) of organ donation - Results from a Swiss multicenter survey.
42901051.abstract: We aimed to examine ICU professionals' perceptions, opinions, and understanding of post-mortem organ donation, and their associations with personal and professional experiences. Between October 2024 and April 2025, we conducted a cross-sectional survey in three Swiss ICUs, assessing perceptions, beliefs, and understanding of organ donation (primary endpoints), and their relationship with demographic characteristics and professional experiences (secondary endpoints). Emotional and ethical perspectives were rated using Likert scales. Among 338 professionals (median age 39 years; 75% women; 80% nurses; median ICU experience 15 years), most had cared for brain dead organ donors, and understanding/approval were high. While 75% would accept organs, 70% were open and 41% fully committed to donating; "helping others" motivated 30.7% of the open and 13.9% of the committed. Reluctance stemmed from dignity concerns, doubts on brain death, or fear to burden relatives. Lower willingness to donate correlated with higher age (ρ = -0.309), longer ICU experience (ρ = -0.335), and belief in life after death (ρ = -0.168), while approval of the brain death concept was positively correlated (ρ = 0.253; all p ≤ 0.002); physicians were more willing than nurses (10 vs. 9; p = 0.001), and willingness aligned with wishing to receive organs (10 vs. 2; p < 0.001). The latter was linked to lower age (36 vs. 50), fewer ICU years (13 vs. 28), stronger wish to donate (10 vs. 2), and better understanding of brain death (10 vs. 9; all p = 0.002). Swiss ICU professionals support organ donation, though strong commitment to donate their own organs is limited and helping others was not reported as a predominant motivation. NCT06640088, registered on October 10, 2024.

42900641.title: Ultrasound-guided glossopharyngeal nerve block for safe and effective anesthesia in a critically ill patient with acute myocardial infarction undergoing urgent endoscopy.
42900641.journal: Agri : Agri (Algoloji) Dernegi'nin Yayin organidir = The journal of the Turkish Society of Algology
42900641.abstract: Glossopharyngeal nerve block (GPNB) can provide effective anesthesia for procedures involving the oropharynx and upper airway. Ultrasound-guided GPNB (UGPNB) may be particularly useful when conventional sedation or topical anesthesia is undesirable because of the risk of respiratory or cardiovascular complications. In this article, we report the use of UGPNB as an alternative anesthetic technique for gastroduodenal endoscopy in a 57-year-old male patient with AMI and gastrointestinal bleeding. In this patient requiring emergency endoscopy, UGPNB was performed via the peristyloid approach to provide oropharyngeal anesthesia while minimizing the need for sedation. The block effectively suppressed the gag reflex and provided adequate procedural conditions while maintaining hemodynamic stability. No procedure-related complications or adverse effects were observed, and the patient reported no discomfort following the procedure. In conclusion, UGPNB may be a useful alternative to sedation for endoscopy in high-risk cardiac patients.

42899821.title: Screening and assessment of delirium in adult intensive care unit patients: a best practice implementation project.
42899821.abstract: Delirium affects up to 80% of adult intensive care unit (ICU) patients, resulting in a significant impact on clinical outcomes. This evidence implementation project evaluated and improved adherence to best practice guidelines for delirium screening and assessment in a specialized ICU setting. This project used the JBI Evidence Implementation Framework and was conducted in a 10-bed adult neurological ICU in São Paulo, Brazil. Compliance was assessed across seven best practice audit criteria measured at baseline (n = 27) and at follow-up (n = 27). Using JBI's Getting Research into Practice (GRiP) analysis, two primary barriers were identified: nurse knowledge deficits and operational time constraints due to documentation complexity. To address these barriers, micro-learning sessions were conducted using gamification, quick-access electronic health record templates, and visual huddle reminders. The follow-up audit demonstrated increased compliance across five criteria: daily observation, formal assessment (CAM-ICU), nurse training, clinical prioritization, and complete documentation. Compliance remained unchanged for two criteria: initial risk screening upon ICU admission and immediate observation following a positive screening. Strategic implementation using gamified education and streamlined workflows successfully bridged knowledge and operational gaps in a high-acuity neurological ICU. Combining active-learning strategies with workflow simplification proved essential for driving sustainable improvements in clinical delirium assessment. https://links.lww.com/IJEBH/A723.

42897610.title: Latent profiles and influencing factors of missed nursing care among ICU nurses.
42897610.abstract: Missed nursing care (MNC) is common in intensive care units (ICUs) and seriously threatens patient safety. Most existing studies treat ICU nurses as a homogeneous group, overlooking within-group heterogeneity. Based on the Job Demands-Resources model, this study aimed to identify latent profiles of missed nursing care among ICU nurses and examine their influencing factors. A cross-sectional study was conducted from November 30, 2025, to March 31, 2026. A convenience sample of 332 ICU nurses was recruited from five tertiary Grade A hospitals in Sichuan, China. Data were collected using the Missed Nursing Care Scale, Moral Sensitivity Questionnaire, and Perceived Organizational Support Questionnaire. Latent profile analysis, correlation analysis, hierarchical regression, and multinomial logistic regression were used for analysis. The overall score of missed nursing care was 67.54 ± 21.33. Three subgroups were identified: low (56.63%), moderate (28.31%), and high (15.06%) missed nursing care. The high group had the highest missed care scores and the lowest perceived organizational support, while the low group had the highest moral sensitivity and the highest proportion of ICU specialist nurses. The pattern of missed nursing care differed across profiles: the low group mainly reported omissions in supportive nursing activities, the moderate group showed additional deficits in care planning, and the high group demonstrated omissions in core clinical care activities, including sedation and analgesia management. The total moral sensitivity score was negatively associated with missed nursing care overall, and this association was significant only in the low MNC subgroup. Lower perceived organizational support was associated with membership in the high MNC group relative to the moderate group. Hierarchical regression identified monthly overtime, dissatisfaction with human resource allocation and communication climate, ICU specialist nurse qualification, moral sensitivity, and perceived organizational support as factors associated with missed nursing care. Missed nursing care among ICU nurses shows clear heterogeneity and can be divided into three subgroups. The associations of moral sensitivity and organizational support might be context-dependent. Stratified interventions tailored to subgroup characteristics may help address missed nursing care, though their effectiveness requires testing in future studies. Not applicable (this study is an observational study, not a randomized controlled trial). Not applicable.

42897407.title: Race, Gender, and Survival: a Scoping Review of Disparities in ICU Post-Resuscitation Care and Neurological Outcomes Following Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
42897407.journal: Journal of racial and ethnic health disparities
42897407.abstract: Racial and ethnic disparities in healthcare are well documented, yet limited attention has been given to the intersection of race/ethnicity and gender in high-acuity critical care. Black women experience compounded inequities affecting access to and quality of intensive care unit (ICU) treatment following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Because outcomes after OHCA are influenced by each link in the chain of survival, disparities in early intervention and subsequent clinical decision-making may contribute to differences in survival and neurological recovery. This study synthesizes evidence on disparities in ICU treatment and outcomes among Black women in the United States while examining how inequities across the chain of survival may influence post-resuscitation care, neurocritical care, and outcomes following OHCA. We conducted a scoping review, guided by the Arksey and O'Malley framework, to analyze peer-reviewed studies identified through electronic databases (e.g., PubMed, CINAHL, and ScienceDirect). Fifteen studies met inclusion criteria and were analyzed using thematic synthesis.
