Findings indicate persistent disparities, including lower bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) rates, delayed emergency response, reduced access to ICU interventions, and higher rates of early do-not-resuscitate (DNR) orders and withdrawal of life-sustaining therapies (WLST). These inequities may contribute to poorer outcomes and likely reflect a combination of systemic, institutional, and social factors, although relatively few studies directly examined Black women from an intersectional perspective. Addressing these disparities requires improved data disaggregation, culturally responsive care, and interdisciplinary interventions to promote equitable post-resuscitation care and outcomes.

42896654.title: Iatrogenic withdrawal syndrome in adult intensive care unit patients: An alternative perspective to design sedation protocols.
42896654.journal: Revista espanola de anestesiologia y reanimacion

42894669.title: Assessing the Influence of Propofol Sedation Versus Propofol-Free Sedation on Recovery From Sepsis and Septic Shock in Mechanically Ventilated ICU Patients: A Retrospective, Propensity-Score Matched, Cohort Study.
42894669.abstract: Propofol-mediated immunosuppression has been postulated in preclinical research, yet translational clinical evidence is lacking. We, therefore, retrospectively evaluated the influence, if any, of propofol versus non-propofol sedation on critical care requirements, prognosis, and risk of re-infection among mechanically ventilated patients with sepsis or septic shock. This single-center, retrospective cohort analysis included adult patients admitted to any ICU at our institution from July 2017 through December 2022 with a diagnosis of sepsis or septic shock who required mechanical ventilation with sedation. Patients who received propofol sedation with or without other means of non-propofol sedation were compared to patients who received non-propofol sedation only. Univariate analysis was used to compare the primary outcome, ICU-free days, and secondary outcomes including intubation and mechanical ventilation-free days, infusion vasopressor support, and antimicrobial medications. Incidence of combined or hospital 30-day mortality and sepsis recurrence within six months were also compared. Time to infection clearance from blood was reported, as available. Total duration and infusion rate of propofol sedation were compared between patients who expired versus survived and between patients with versus without six-month sepsis recurrence. One-to-one propensity-score matching (PSM) was applied using sepsis diagnostic status, age, sex, BMI, and chronic comorbidity burden as covariates to manage confounding effects and identify comparable subpopulations. A total of 615 patients were included, comprising 511 (83.1%) propofol-sedated patients and 104 (16.9%) non-propofol-sedated patients. Prior to PSM, propofol sedation was more common among younger patients (median (IQR) years, 62 (50-72) vs. 66 (58-75), p=0.021). Patients treated for septic shock comprised most of the dataset (n=498, 81.0%). The non-propofol group received fentanyl sedation more commonly (84 (80.8%) vs. 234 (45.8%), p<0.001), though the median duration of fentanyl sedation was longer in the propofol group (1.9 (0.9-4.2) vs. 1.5 (0.4-2.8) days, p=0.012). Median ICU-free days were similar between non-propofol and propofol-sedated groups (median (IQR) days, 6.3 (2.1-14.7) vs. 6.8 (3.3-13.3), p=0.303). The proportion of patients requiring three or four pressor infusions was significantly greater in the non-propofol group (32 (30.8%) vs. 110 (21.5%), p=0.041). The combined hospital or 30-day mortality rate was also higher in the non-propofol group (45 (43.3%) vs. 165 (32.3%), p=0.031). After PSM, fentanyl sedation remained more common in the non-propofol group. Median ICU-free days remained similar between groups, but there were no longer significant differences in extent of vasopressor support required or mortality rates. Propofol-containing sedation was not associated with fewer ICU-free days, poorer prognosis, or greater rate of re-infection among mechanically ventilated patients with sepsis and septic shock. Residual confounding and limited precision preclude exclusion of clinically important benefit or harm. Randomized controlled research is necessary to elucidate the clinical impacts of propofol sedation among mechanically ventilated patients with sepsis and septic shock.

42894097.title: Sedation strategy and the search for a better patient experience in ICU.

42887845.title: Early Nocturnal Care Disruption and the Hazard of Incident ICU Delirium in Critically Ill Adults: A Target-Trial Emulation in MIMIC-IV.
42887845.abstract: Nighttime care contacts fragment sleep and are often invoked as a contributor to intensive care delirium. Whether a higher intensity of those contacts early in the stay is associated with later incident delirium is unclear. Sicker, more sedated patients are monitored more often overnight and are also more likely to become delirious. We emulated a target trial in MIMIC-IV version 3.1. Adults were eligible if the first intensive care stay lasted at least 48 hours and the delirium screen was negative at that landmark. High exposure was a nocturnal contact rate above the cohort median, built from vital-sign charting, laboratory draws, and bedside medication administrations between 22:00 and 05:59 and divided by 16 nocturnal hours. Follow-up for incident delirium began at the landmark. We estimated the hazard ratio with stabilized inverse-probability weights and a pooled-logistic survival model. Of 12,922 eligible stays, 2,862 developed incident delirium. High nocturnal care-contact intensity was associated with a higher hazard (adjusted hazard ratio 1.43, 95% confidence interval 1.27 to 1.60). The hazard rose across tertiles of the contact rate and was higher for vital-sign charting and phlebotomy than for medication administration. A higher intensity of early nocturnal care contacts was associated with a moderately higher hazard of incident delirium. Residual confounding remains possible, including reverse causation if prodromal delirium itself increases overnight contacts before the first positive screen.

42887421.title: Swanson's theory of caring applied to mechanical ventilation weaning in the ICU: Humanizing care.
42887421.abstract: To analyze the scientific evidence on the application of Swanson's Theory of Caring in the process of invasive mechanical ventilation weaning in Intensive Care Units (ICU), identifying nursing interventions that correspond to Swanson's five theoretical processes (knowing, being with, doing for, enabling, and maintaining belief) and assessing their implications for clinical practice. Scoping review conducted according to the methodological framework of Arksey and O'Malley (2005), enhanced by Levac et al. (2010), and the updated JBI guidance for scoping reviews (Peters et al., 2020). Reporting followed the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). A search of scientific literature published between January 2020 and January 2026 was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, SciELO, CUIDEN, Cochrane Library and CINAHL, complemented by backward citation tracking. Forty-five articles were included after applying rigorous selection criteria, through independent screening by two reviewers with discrepancies resolved by consensus. Data were analyzed through structured extraction and narrative synthesis, organizing interventions according to Swanson's five caring processes. The review identified multiple nursing interventions during ventilator weaning that showed conceptual correspondence with Swanson's theory. Only 8 of the 45 articles (18%) explicitly used Swanson's framework, and a single study directly linked it to ventilator weaning, identifying a significant knowledge gap. The "knowing" process includes individualized assessment using validated scales and continuous monitoring. "Being with" is manifested through therapeutic presence, effective communication, and facilitation of family contact. "Doing for" encompasses sedation titration, ventilation management, and respiratory physiotherapy techniques. "Enabling" comprises health education, use of augmentative communication systems, and support in decision-making. "Maintaining belief" is materialized through positive reinforcement, management of realistic expectations, and emotional accompaniment. Swanson's Theory of Caring provides a relevant and potentially operational theoretical framework to structure and humanize nursing care during ventilator weaning in the ICU. The conceptual correspondence identified suggests that its systematic application could contribute to improving patient experience, reducing psychological complications, and optimizing weaning outcomes. Implementation gaps are evident due to the absence of prospective studies, scarcity of data to quantify the impact of relational care on the weaning process, and the absence of specific protocols that merge the NANDA-NIC-NOC taxonomy and the Swanson theoretical framework. Prospective studies applying Swanson's framework from the design phase are required to evaluate the specific impact of interventions based on this theory through controlled clinical trials.

42885179.title: Harm reduction opportunities following ICU admission for prescription opioid overdose: An 8-year comparative audit at the Royal Melbourne Hospital.
42885179.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) admission following prescription opioid overdose represents an important opportunity for multidisciplinary intervention and harm reduction, yet Australian data describing inpatient management are limited. A retrospective audit was conducted of 70 adults admitted to the ICU at the Royal Melbourne Hospital with prescription opioid overdose between 2021 and 2024. The primary outcome was provision of take-home naloxone (THN) before discharge among patients meeting institutional eligibility criteria. Secondary outcomes included opioid education, multidisciplinary involvement and discharge opioid management, with comparison with the previous institutional audit where comparable data were available. Only five patients (7.5%, 95% confidence interval 3.2-16.3) were supplied with THN despite all meeting institutional eligibility criteria. Polypharmacy overdose was common (77%). Most patients received at least one specialist referral (83%), although 15% received no inpatient specialist referral. Opioid education was documented in 58 patients (87%) compared with 17% previously (P <0.001), although content and documentation were inconsistent. These findings demonstrate persistent gaps in THN provision, structured opioid education and coordinated discharge planning, highlighting ICU admission as an important opportunity for prescription opioid harm reduction. Strengthening guideline-based multidisciplinary interventions during admission may improve patient outcomes and inform harm reduction strategies nationally.

42881887.title: Do Early Prognostic Measures Differentiate Mechanisms of ICU Death in Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage? An Analysis of Fatal Outcomes.
42881887.abstract: Background/Objectives: In aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH), intensive care unit (ICU) deaths may follow neurological or systemic pathways, but the relationship between early prognostic measures and the mechanism of death is unclear. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 261 consecutive adults with aSAH admitted to the ICU between January 2020 and June 2026. World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies (WFNS) grade, modified Fisher scale and Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Early Brain Edema Score (SEBES) were assessed at admission; the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and C-reactive protein (CRP)-to-albumin ratio (CAR) came from the first routine blood sample; and Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II) and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) came from the first 24 h. Brain death was assigned to the neurological category by a predefined rule; the remaining deaths were adjudicated independently by two intensivists. Results: Eighty-six patients (33.0%) died: 45 (52.3%) neurological, 37 (43.0%) systemic/medical and 4 (4.7%) mixed/undetermined; 94.6% of systemic/medical deaths were sepsis-related. Agreement among the 54 independently adjudicated deaths was high (κ = 0.829). CAR discriminated toward systemic/medical death (AUC 0.671; 95% CI 0.552-0.791), whereas APACHE II (0.702) and SOFA (0.682) discriminated toward neurological death; WFNS (0.643) and SEBES (0.638) showed the same direction. NLR did not discriminate mechanism of death in this cohort (0.449). CAR was very highly correlated with CRP (ρ = 0.994). Conclusions: Among aSAH decedents, early prognostic measures were associated with the mechanism of death in opposite directions; the systemic/medical association predominantly reflected sepsis-related deaths. Because the analysis was restricted to decedents and time to death differed by mechanism (7 versus 26 days), the findings are exploratory and do not establish cause-specific risk prediction in the overall aSAH population.

42966560.title: Postoperative Delirium in the ICU: Not One Syndrome, but Many?

42958234.title: A Delphi study to identify competencies of registered nurses in Kenyan intensive care units.
42958234.abstract: Nurses form the largest professional group in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) workforce. Their competency in care delivery contributes to improved patient outcomes, reduced morbidity and mortality, and overall reduced cost of care. Many countries have established frameworks to support a set of core competencies that all qualified ICU nurses are expected to possess. Kenya has yet to embark on a unifying competency framework, leading to ICU nurses' poor transfer of knowledge, skills, and attitudes because of differences in the scope and depth of competencies learned. Unification of competencies may best be achieved through stakeholders' agreement on the required set of competencies. The aim of this study was to establish consensus on the initial set of competencies required by registered nurses working in Kenyan ICUs. The study adopted a mixed-method design with a multistage approach. This involved two stages: an integrative review, and two rounds of e-Delphi. The integrative review of competencies and competency frameworks for ICU nurses informed the development of an initial set of 91 competencies. These competencies were subsequently subjected to expert evaluation by a heterogeneous panel of experts in a two-round e-Delphi process. However, All the competencies in the two rounds achieved consensus by attaining a priori mean of ≥ 4. This manuscript reports findings from the integrative review and the first round of the e-Delphi process. Findings from subsequent Delphi rounds are reported separately. Notably, despite ICU competencies being universal, some competencies are culturally specific and may require contextual tweaking for their acceptability. These include competencies touching on palliative and end-of-life care, involvement of patients and their families in pain management, and competencies that require autonomous practice of nurses, like performance of invasive procedures. This study identified and synthesised competencies for registered nurses in Kenyan ICUs through an integrative review and further evaluated their relevance through the first round of a Delphi process. The findings provide an initial, evidence-informed set of competencies that can inform curriculum development, clinical practice, and policy discussions. Further Delphi round will build on these findings to establish final consensus on the competency framework. Not applicable.

42957972.title: Impact of a Nurse-Led, Target-Directed Light Sedation Strategy on the Incidence of Delirium in Septic Patients in the Emergency Intensive Care Unit.
42957972.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the impact of a nurse-led, target-directed light sedation strategy on delirium incidence and short-term outcomes in septic patients undergoing invasive mechanical ventilation in the emergency intensive care unit (EICU).MethodsWe analyzed 221 consecutive septic patients requiring invasive mechanical ventilation for more than 24 h at a single center (January 2022-May 2024). Based on a sedation protocol change, patients were assigned to conventional sedation group (control, n = 123) or nurse-led, target-directed light sedation group (exposed, n = 98). The primary outcome was delirium incidence. Secondary outcomes included delirium-free days (DFD-28), ventilator-free days (VFD-28), mechanical ventilation duration, EICU length of stay, and 28-day mortality. Multivariable logistic regression examined the independent association between the nurse-led strategy and delirium risk.ResultsDelirium occurred less frequently in the nurse-led sedation group than in the control group (20.4% vs 37.4%, P = .007). The exposed group had shorter mechanical ventilation duration and EICU length of stay (both P < .05), whereas VFD-28 did not differ significantly between groups. The two groups did not differ significantly in 28-day mortality (28.6% vs 26.0%, P = .671) or in the rate of airway-related adverse events. On multivariable analysis, the nurse-led strategy was independently associated with a lower risk of delirium (OR = 0.428, 95% CI: 0.215-0.854, P = .016). Subgroup analyses showed that this protective benefit was consistent across age strata, disease severity levels, and comorbidity burden.ConclusionIn septic patients undergoing mechanical ventilation, a nurse-led, target-directed light sedation strategy was associated with reduced delirium incidence, shorter mechanical ventilation duration, and decreased EICU length of stay, without increasing adverse events. However, no improvement in 28-day mortality was observed. Further validation through multicenter prospective randomized controlled trials is warranted to assess long-term efficacy and safety.

42881055.title: Comparing High-Flow Nasal Cannula Therapy and Conventional Oxygen Therapy in Adult Patients Post-Cardiac Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
42881055.journal: Journal of cardiothoracic and vascular anesthesia
42881055.abstract: Cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass structurally alters respiratory mechanics and carries a substantial risk of postoperative morbidity. Historically, patients have routinely received conventional oxygen therapy (COT) following extubation. High- flow nasal cannula (HCNC) therapy has emerged as an innovative respiratory support system. By synthesizing all currently available high-quality randomized controlled trials (RCTs), this study aimed to rigorously evaluate the efficacy and safety of HFNC compared to COT, focusing primarily on determining the need for escalation of respiratory support. A thorough electronic search was carried out in the PubMed, Embase, and Scopus databases from their inception to May 2026. Only RCTs were considered for analysis. A random-effects model was applied to compute pooled estimates and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). A total of 11 RCTs, comprising 2473 patients, were included in this systematic review and meta-analysis. HFNC had a statistically significant effect on reducing the requirement for escalation of respiratory support (risk ratio [RR] = 0.71; 95% CI, 0.55-0.93; p = 0.01). HFNC had a statistically significant effect on improving the arterial partial pressure of oxygen, as well as forced expiratory volume in 1 second, while also increasing delirium complications (RR = 3.63; 95% CI, 1.80-7.30; p = 0.0003). There were no statistically significant differences between the 2 approaches in the other secondary clinical and resource utilization outcomes, including intubation, overall mortality, hospital length of stay, intensive care unit length of stay, and postoperative atrial fibrillation. In adult patients recovering from cardiac surgery, HFNC therapy improves oxygenation and significantly curtails the need to escalate respiratory support compared to COT. However, these physiologic and intermediate clinical benefits do not translate into reductions in mortality, reintubation rate, or hospital length of stay and may come at the cost of increased postoperative delirium.

42878614.title: Open Visiting Policy and Delirium in Adult Patients in ICUs: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials.
authors: and the Padova Intensive Care Unit (PADUA-ICU) Group
42878614.abstract: To critically evaluate the comparative effects of open or flexible family presence policies vs. restricted or traditional family presence policies on the occurrence of delirium and other major outcomes among adult patients admitted to ICUs. We conducted a comprehensive electronic search of MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from inception to November 21, 2025. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing open or flexible vs. restricted ICU visiting policies in adult patients. The primary outcome extracted was delirium occurrence. Secondary outcomes included the duration of invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), ICU length of stay, hospital-acquired infections, and ICU mortality. Thirteen RCTs comprising 3861 patients were included. Random-effects models showed that compared with restricted policies, open/flexible family presence reduced delirium occurrence (risk ratio [RR], 0.48; 95% CI, 0.29-0.81; low certainty) and IMV duration (mean difference [MD], -0.36 d; 95% CI, -0.46 to -0.26 d; low certainty). The intervention did not affect the ICU length of stay (MD, 4.21 d; 95% CI, -4.65 to 13.07 d; very low certainty), the rates of hospital-acquired infections (RR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.81-1.23; low certainty), or ICU mortality (RR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.72-1.08; very low certainty). Open/flexible ICU family presence may reduce delirium and shorten the duration of IMV slightly, without increasing infections or ICU mortality, although the certainty of evidence is low and heterogeneity remains substantial.

42878609.title: Ventilatory Management in Neurocritical Versus Non-Neurocritical Care Patients: A Pooled Analysis From the PRIME Database.
authors: PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients without ARDS (PRoVENT), PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients in Middle-income Countries (PRoVENT-iMiC), and Extubation strategies in Neuro-ICU patients and associations with Outcomes (ENIO) investigators
42878609.abstract: To describe ventilatory management in neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients and determine whether specific ventilator settings are associated with development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and mortality in neurocritical care patients. The primary endpoint was a diagnosis of ARDS after initiation of invasive ventilation; one secondary endpoint was ICU mortality. Post hoc pooled analysis of harmonized individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies combined into the PRIME database. PRIME is a harmonized pooled database comprising individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies on ventilatory management in critically ill patients: "PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients without ARDS" (PRoVENT), "PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients in Middle-income Countries" (PRoVENT-iMiC), and "Extubation strategies in Neuro-ICU patients and associations with Outcomes" (ENIO). We excluded patients with ARDS at the start of ventilation. Demographic and clinical characteristics, ventilator settings, respiratory variables, arterial blood gas values, and clinical outcomes were extracted from the harmonized PRIME database. Derived ventilation parameters included tidal volume normalized to predicted body weight, driving pressure, respiratory system compliance, mechanical power, ventilatory ratio, and Pao2/Fio2 ratio. This analysis included 3848 patients, including 1702 neurocritical care and 1920 non-neurocritical care patients. Based on recorded ventilatory variables, neurocritical care patients received lower median tidal volumes (Vts), positive end-expiratory pressure, and Fio2. They had lower median driving pressure (ΔP), mechanical power (MP) of ventilation, and ventilatory ratio, as well as higher respiratory system compliance compared with non-neurocritical care patients. These differences were consistently observed at both assessed time points. ARDS was diagnosed more frequently in neurocritical care patients than in non-neurocritical care patients (8.7% vs. 3.9%; p < 0.001), while ICU mortality was lower (14.3% vs. 22.8%; p < 0.001). Among neurocritical care patients, those who developed ARDS were ventilated with lower median Vt and higher Fio2 and had higher median ΔP and MP. Vt normalized for predicted body weight in neurocritical care patients was independently associated with the development of ARDS. In this cohort, ventilatory management at the initial and 48-hour assessments differed between neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients, particularly with respect to key ventilator settings like Vt, positive end-expiratory pressure, and Fio2. In neurocritical care patients, ARDS was more often diagnosed than in non-neurocritical care patients.

42875150.title: Continuous wound infiltration with local anesthetics in adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery: A PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis.
42875150.journal: Chinese medical sciences journal = Chung-kuo i hsueh k'o hsueh tsa chih
42875150.abstract: Effective postoperative analgesia is critical to recovery after cardiac surgery. Continuous wound infiltration (CWI) with local anesthetics (LAs) has been proposed as an opioid-sparing adjunct, but its efficacy beyond pain control and its safety profile remain incompletely defined. We conducted a PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing CWI with control in adult cardiac surgery. PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from inception to August 30, 2025, and updated on April 2, 2026. Primary outcomes were postoperative Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) pain scores and cumulative morphine consumption. Secondary outcomes included mechanical ventilation duration, length of stay, mortality, complications, patient satisfaction, and adverse events. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE). Twelve RCTs involving 2,117 patients were included. CWI significantly reduced VAS during mobilization at 24 h (MD=-0.93, 95% confidence interval [CI]: -1.53--0.33, P = 0.002) and 48 h (MD=-0.80, 95% CI: -1.17--0.44, P < 0.001), and decreased 48-hour morphine consumption (MD=-8.10 mg, 95% CI: -13.41--2.79, P = 0.003). No significant effects were observed on VAS at rest, mechanical ventilation duration, ICU or hospital length of stay, mortality, or major cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal, gastrointestinal complications, or postoperative infections. Patient satisfaction was higher with CWI. Technical complications were uncommon, and no clinically significant LA toxicity was reported. In adult cardiac surgery, CWI with LAs modestly improves analgesia during mobilization and reduces opioid requirements without clear improvement in major clinical outcomes or length of stay. CWI appears safe and feasible and may serve as an adjunct in multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia strategies. Further adequately powered trials are warranted to define its comparative effectiveness within contemporary enhanced recovery after surgery pathways.

42871886.title: Anesthetic Management of a Patient With Myasthenia Gravis Undergoing Thoracoscopic Thymectomy: A Case Report and Literature Review.
42871886.abstract: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder characterized by fluctuating skeletal muscle weakness and fatigability. Perioperative management is challenging because patients may have bulbar or respiratory muscle involvement and altered sensitivity to neuromuscular blocking agents, increasing the risk of postoperative respiratory failure and myasthenic crisis. Thymectomy is an established therapeutic option in selected patients with myasthenia gravis and may be performed using minimally invasive thoracoscopic techniques. We report the anesthetic management of a 48-year-old man with generalized acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody-positive myasthenia gravis (MGFA class IIb) scheduled for thoracoscopic thymectomy. The patient had a recent relapse with diplopia, dysphagia, and easy fatigability, which improved after medical therapy. Preoperative optimization included intravenous immunoglobulin therapy for four days. General anesthesia was induced with propofol and remifentanil without initial neuromuscular blockade. Tracheal intubation was facilitated using video laryngoscopy after topical lidocaine. Anesthesia was maintained with sevoflurane, and invasive monitoring was established. Because of the surgical requirement for improved thoracoscopic visualization, a reduced dose of rocuronium was administered intraoperatively under train-of-four monitoring. At the end of surgery, neuromuscular blockade was reversed with sugammadex, and the patient was successfully extubated and transferred to the intensive care unit in stable condition. This case highlights the importance of careful preoperative optimization, avoidance of neuromuscular blocking agents when possible, quantitative neuromuscular monitoring, and individualized use of low-dose rocuronium with sugammadex reversal when muscle relaxation is required during thoracoscopic thymectomy in patients with myasthenia gravis.

42871854.title: Mechanical ventilation in acute brain injury.
42871854.abstract: Acute brain injury (ABI) includes traumatic brain injury, subarachnoid and intracerebral haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke and global hypoxic-ischaemic injury, and patients often require admission to intensive care. Although pathologically heterogeneous, they share common mechanisms of primary injury followed by secondary brain injury. Systemic derangements such as hypoxaemia, dysregulated carbon dioxide tension and elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) may exacerbate secondary injury and should be avoided. Patients with ABI often require invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), and of these up to 19-22% may develop acute respiratory distress syndrome. Lung-protective ventilation (LPV) strategies using low tidal volumes and moderate positive end-expiratory pressure to minimise ventilator-induced lung injury are established practices in patients requiring IMV. However, strict application of LPV principles may conflict with neuro-protective goals, particularly carbon dioxide control to optimise cerebral blood flow and avoid rises in ICP. This review examines the physiological tension between lung and brain protection, focusing on neuro-respiratory interactions and brain-lung crosstalk. We synthesise the evidence on ventilatory strategies in the context of patients with ABI, discuss the implications for neurological and pulmonary outcomes, and highlight the need for an integrated, individualised approach to ventilation in these patients.

42862674.title: Comparative Efficacy of Pecto-Intercostal Facial Plane Block vs Transversus Thoracic Facial Plane Block Combined with Rectus Sheath Block for Post-Sternotomy Analgesia: A Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial.
42862674.abstract: Ultrasound-guided facial plane blocks are central to enhanced recovery after cardiac surgery (ERACS) protocols, yet evidence comparing pecto-intercostal facial plane block (PIFB) and transversus thoracic facial plane block (TTPB) with rectus sheath block (RSB) remains limited. This prospective, randomized, controlled trial enrolled 100 adult patients (ASA II-III) undergoing elective median sternotomy at a tertiary care hospital in South India. Patients received standardized general anesthesia and were randomized to bilateral PIFB or TTPB (20 mL 0.25% bupivacaine + 4 mg dexamethasone per side) with RSB after cardiopulmonary bypass. The primary outcome was 24-hour postoperative fentanyl consumption. Secondary outcomes included visual analog scale (VAS) pain scores at 0, 3-, 6-, 12-, and 24-hours post-extubation, rescue analgesia, extubation timing, ICU/hospital stay, and complications. A total of 96 patients completed analysis (PIFB: n = 47; TTPB: n = 49). Mean 24-hour fentanyl consumption was 267.23 ± 92.54 µg (PIFB) vs 297.18 ± 88.09 µg (TTPB), mean difference - 29.95 µg (95% confidence interval: -66.60 to 6.70; P = 0.108). VAS scores showed no significant between-group differences (P > 0.05). Rescue analgesia rates were similar, with 84% and 90% not requiring additional opioids. Four PIFB patients (8%) stayed intubated >24 hours due to cardiac issues, vs none in the TTPB group (P = 0.121). This trial found no significant difference in opioid consumption or pain scores between PIFB + RSB and TTPB + RSB for post-sternotomy analgesia. Both techniques were safe within ERACS protocols. Larger noninferiority trials are needed before establishing equivalence or recommending one technique over another.

42862662.title: Impact of Erector Spinae Block on Postoperative Analgesia and Hospital Recovery in Coronary Artery Bypass Surgery: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis, Meta-Regression, and Sequential Trial Analysis.
42862662.abstract: The erector spinae plane block (ESPB) is a promising regional technique for cardiac surgery. We evaluated the efficacy of ESPB regarding analgesia and in-hospital outcomes in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing ESPB versus control in adults undergoing CABG (CRD42025645045). Primary outcomes were opioid consumption (24 h/48 h) and pain intensity. Secondary outcomes included extubation time and intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay. Data were pooled using random-effects models. Meta-regression and trial sequential analysis (TSA) were used to assess sources of heterogeneity and robustness, respectively, while the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations framework provided the certainty of the evidence for each outcome. Twelve studies (704 patients) were analyzed. ESPB significantly reduced the morphine milligram equivalent consumption at 24 h (mean difference (MD) -19.05 mg; 95% confidence interval (CI) [-22.50 to -15.61]; P < 0.001; high certainty) and 48 h (MD -19.42 mg; 95% CI [-28.75 to -10.09]; P < 0.001; moderate certainty). Pain scores, by the Numerical Rating Scale, were lower within 12 h (MD -0.93; P < 0.001; moderate certainty) and at 24 h (MD -0.58; P = 0.016; low certainty). ESPB shortened extubation time (MD -2.50 h; high certainty) and ICU stay (MD -12.55 h; moderate certainty). TSA confirmed robust evidence for opioid reduction, early pain relief, and extubation benefits. ESPB provides effective early analgesia, reduces perioperative opioid requirements, and accelerates recovery in CABG, representing a fundamental complement to conventional isolated intravenous analgesia. Future research should investigate continuous techniques.

42860369.title: Managing the Hospital Capacity Challenges of Medetomidine Withdrawal: A Retrospective Report of Dexmedetomidine Use in Intermediate Care Units.
42860369.abstract: Medetomidine, a veterinary alpha-2-adrenergic agonist, has emerged as a dominant adulterant in the Philadelphia illicit opioid supply, producing a severe withdrawal syndrome requiring significant inpatient support. We developed an intravenous dexmedetomidine protocol for intermediate care units (IMCU) and describe the safety and feasibility of delivering this care outside the intensive care unit (ICU). A retrospective descriptive analysis of patients who received dexmedetomidine under an IMCU orderset for alpha-2 withdrawal was conducted at two urban medical centers in Philadelphia, PA, from April 2024 to February 2026. Encounters were classified as protocol-concordant or protocol-discordant by dosing and level of support; the concordant cohort was primary. Variables included demographics and addiction consult status. Outcomes included length of stay (hospital and IMCU), ICU admission, rapid response team activation, intubation, and discharge disposition. Of 487 encounters, 449 (92.2%) were protocol-concordant and 38 (7.8%) protocol-discordant. All subsequent results describe the protocol-concordant cohort (n=449) unless otherwise noted. The cohort was predominantly male (58.1%) with a mean age of 41.8 years. Median hospital stay was 6.0 days and median IMCU stay was 2.2 days. ICU admission was not required in 50.1% of encounters. Rapid response team activation occurred in 38 encounters (8.5%), the majority for escalating withdrawal management. Patient-directed discharge occurred in 41.4% of encounters. An IMCU dexmedetomidine protocol deployed across seven monitored units at 2 hospitals offers a replicable framework for managing medetomidine withdrawal while potentially mitigating critical care capacity challenges. Identified opportunities include modification of titration and dosing strategies and further investment in addiction consult infrastructure.

42844551.title: Prone Positioning in Neurocritical Care Patients with Invasive Intracranial Pressure Monitoring: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
42844551.abstract: Pulmonary complications are common after acute brain injury and may worsen neurologic outcomes. Although prone positioning (PP) is an established treatment strategy for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) with severe hypoxemia in general intensive care unit populations, it is often avoided in neurocritical care due to concerns that PP may increase intracranial pressure (ICP). However, evidence supporting these concerns remains limited. A systematic search of multiple databases and supplementary sources using keywords related to ICP and PP yielded 778 records. Ten studies with 177 patients met the inclusion criteria for the systematic review and eight (n = 120 patients) provided extractable data for meta-analysis of the primary outcome [change in ICP from baseline (supine) to PP]. Pooled means and mean differences were calculated using random-effects models. The pooled within-subject mean change in ICP from baseline to PP was + 5.06 mm Hg (95% CI 2.05-8.06; I2 = 76.7%). Accordingly, pooled mean ICP increased from 11.10 mm Hg (95% CI 8.43-13.76) at baseline to 16.13 mm Hg (95% CI 13.83-18.43) during PP, remaining below commonly used treatment thresholds for intracranial hypertension although clinically relevant ICP elevations occurred in a small subset of patients. By contrast, the pooled change in ICP between baseline and after returning to the supine position in five studies (n = 45) was - 0.41 mm Hg (95% CI - 2.34 to 1.51), indicating that the increase in ICP during PP was transient and reversible. Systemic oxygenation and brain tissue oxygenation improved in PP. In patients with acute brain injury, PP improves systemic and brain tissue oxygenation while causing a modest, transient increase in ICP that resolves after resupination. These findings support cautious use of PP in selected neurocritical care patients with respiratory failure when invasive ICP monitoring is available. Given the limited evidence base, larger prospective studies are needed.

42835185.title: Efficacy and safety of early mobilization in patients with ARDS: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42835185.abstract: To evaluate the effect of early mobilization in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Computerized searches were conducted in PubMed, EMbase, The Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang Data, CBM, and VIP databases for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on early mobilization in ARDS patients. The retrieval period was from the establishment of each database to September 30, 2025. Two reviewers independently assessed the quality of included literature and extracted data in accordance with Cochrane systematic review methodology. Meta-analysis was performed using RevMan 5.4.1 software for eligible studies. A total of 7 RCTs were included, consisting of 4 English and 3 Chinese articles. Meta-analysis showed that compared with conventional treatment, early mobilization significantly reduced the incidence of intensive care unit-acquired weakness (ICU-AW) [OR = 0.35, 95% CI (0.19,0.64), P = 0.0006] and delirium [OR = 0.51, 95% CI (0.28,0.91), P = 0.02], shortened the duration of mechanical ventilation [MD = -2.40,95% CI (-2.96,-1.84), P < 0.00001], length of ICU stay [MD = -3.36, 95% CI (-4.21,-2.52), P < 0.00001] and total hospital stay [MD = -2.74,95% CI (-3.49,-1.98), P < 0.00001]. Meanwhile, it improved patients'functional independence score (Barthel Index) [MD = 17.27, 95% CI (11.18, 23.35), P < 0.00001] and decreased the incidence of complications [OR = 0.39, 95% CI (0.17, 0.86), P = 0.02]. All pooled effects were statistically significant. Early mobilization yields significant clinical benefits for ARDS patients, improving short-term clinical outcomes and functional recovery. It is worthy of clinical promotion and application. However, multicenter, large-sample, and methodologically standardized RCTs are still needed to further verify its long-term effects and optimal implementation protocols.

42829580.title: Cipepofol versus Conventional Sedation for Pneumonia Patients Receiving Mechanical Ventilation: A Real-World Retrospective Study of Effectiveness and Hemodynamic Safety.
42829580.abstract: Severe pneumonia often necessitates invasive mechanical ventilation (MV) and prolonged sedation in the ICU. This real-world retrospective cohort study aimed to compare cipepofol vs conventional sedation regimens in this vulnerable population, with MV duration as the primary endpoint and hemodynamic safety as a key safety outcome. This retrospective cohort study evaluated mechanically ventilated patients with severe pneumonia who received continuous sedation for more than 48 hours. Patients were classified into cipepofol or conventional sedation (propofol-, midazolam- or dexmedetomidine-based) groups. Propensity score matching (PSM) was performed at a 1:1 ratio based on age and APACHE II scores. After PSM, 198 patients (99 per group) were analyzed. The primary endpoint-MV duration did not differ significantly between the cipepofol and conventional groups (median 218.23 vs 227.25 hours, P = 0.740). Subgroup analysis further confirmed that there was no significant difference in MV duration between propofol- and midazolam-based regimens compared to the cipepofol-regimen. Notably, cipepofol demonstrated superior hemodynamic safety, showing significantly lower incidences of early hypotension within the first hour (11.1% vs 27.3%, P=0.007) and overall bradycardia (19.1% vs 36.1%, P=0.014). Post-hoc subgroups analysis revealed that cipepofol reduced the risks of early hypotension and overall bradycardia compared to propofol- or midazolam-based regimens in hospital-acquired pneumonia patients. Multivariate analysis confirmed cipepofol use as an independent protective factor against early hypotension (adjusted OR 0.300, 95% CI: 0.136-0.665, P=0.003) and bradycardia (adjusted OR 0.414, 95% CI: 0.212-0.808, P=0.010). No significant differences were found regarding sedation success, length of ICU stay, 28-day ventilator-free days, 28-day mortality, vasopressor requirements, or organ function parameters (all P>0.05). In mechanically ventilated patients with severe pneumonia requiring prolonged sedation, cipepofol did not shorten MV duration compared with propofol- or midazolam-based conventional regimens, but it significantly reduced risks for early hypotension and overall bradycardia events. ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06514781).

42828950.title: Protocolised analgosedation in mechanically ventilated adult patients: A scoping review.
42828950.abstract: Our objectives were to assess structure and content of analgosedation protocols used for mechanically ventilated adult patients, including those receiving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), against current international sedation guidelines, and to explore reported barriers and facilitators to their implementation. Scoping review searching five databases (December 1999 to September 2026). We included all study types reporting on analgosedation protocol structure and content, and/or implementation barriers/facilitators. Two authors independently screened citations, extracted data, and coded reported barriers and facilitators using the Theoretical Domains Framework. We screened 18,457 citations with 81 studies meeting inclusion criteria. Of these, 35 (43%) were observational studies, 27 (33%) non-randomised interventional studies, and 19 (23%) randomised controlled trials. Few studies published between 2019 and 2026 included propofol or dexmedetomidine, multi-modal analgesia and delirium assessment in analgosedation protocols, and no studies in ECMO patients. The most frequently reported structure and content of protocol was use of a sedation score (77%), recommending opioid and sedative drugs (74%), and setting a daily target sedation score (65%). Most reported barrier was a protocol insufficiently detailed to cover the breadth of patient needs, reported in 12 (63%) studies. The most frequently reported facilitator was availability of the analgosedation protocol in an easily accessible format, reported in four (31%) studies. Easy to follow protocols sufficiently detailed to cover patient need from a heterogenous ICU population are considerations to successful implementation. Healthcare staff fear of adverse effects is a potential barrier to adoption of protocolised analgosedation.

42828373.title: Mechanical Ventilation Practices in Traumatic Brain Injury: A Systematic Review of Contemporary Evidence.
42828373.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) frequently necessitates mechanical ventilation to maintain adequate gas exchange, protect the airway, and support cerebral physiology during the acute phase of critical illness. Although ventilatory management is an integral component of neurocritical care, the optimal approach remains uncertain because interventions aimed at pulmonary protection may influence intracranial dynamics and neurological outcomes. This systematic review aimed to critically evaluate contemporary evidence on mechanical ventilation practices in adults with TBI, with emphasis on ventilatory strategies, lung-protective ventilation, airway management, tracheostomy, weaning approaches, and clinically relevant outcomes. A systematic literature search was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), EBSCOhost, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Google Scholar, and selected grey-literature sources for studies published from January 2000 through June 2026. Eligible studies included adult patients with TBI who were receiving mechanical ventilation and reported ventilation-related interventions or outcomes. Methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklists, and the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, as appropriate for the study design. Owing to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. Eleven studies, comprising randomized controlled trials, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, and cross-sectional surveys, met the inclusion criteria. Considerable variation was observed in ventilatory management, particularly regarding tidal volume, positive end-expiratory pressure, carbon dioxide targets, airway management, and tracheostomy timing. The available evidence suggests that individualized ventilatory management may help balance pulmonary protection with preservation of cerebral physiology when guided by appropriate neurological and respiratory monitoring. Early tracheostomy may be associated with shorter durations of mechanical ventilation and intensive care unit stay in selected patients, although consistent benefits in mortality or long-term neurological recovery have not been established. Overall, the included studies demonstrated substantial variability in ventilatory practices and clinical outcomes across different settings and patient populations. Current evidence suggests that ventilation strategies in adults with TBI should be tailored to individual respiratory mechanics and cerebral physiological status rather than applied uniformly. However, substantial heterogeneity, limited TBI-specific comparative evidence, and variation in clinical practice limit the certainty of the available evidence. High-quality multicenter studies are needed to establish evidence-based ventilatory targets and determine their effects on patient-centered neurological and pulmonary outcomes.

42824012.title: Case Report: Massive sustained-release valproate overdose with prolonged gastric tablet retention and partial pharmacobezoar formation managed by endoscopic removal and delayed extracorporeal therapy.
42824012.abstract: Valproate poisoning is a potentially life-threatening condition that may result in central nervous system depression, hyperammonemia, metabolic disturbances, and multiorgan dysfunction. Management of massive sustained-release valproate overdose remains challenging because delayed gastrointestinal absorption may lead to prolonged toxicity despite conventional decontamination measures. A 23-year-old woman with a history of previous suicide attempts was admitted approximately 6 hours after ingesting ninety 500-mg sustained-release valproate tablets (total dose 45 g) with alcohol. Upon arrival, she exhibited severe agitation and delirium. Endotracheal intubation was performed for airway protection because she was unable to cooperate with treatment and was at risk of aspiration. Gastric lavage and cathartic therapy were subsequently administered. The initial serum valproate concentration was 1,093.66 μg/mL. Because incomplete decontamination was suspected, bedside upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed approximately 11.5 h after ingestion. Fourteen intact and markedly swollen tablets were removed; some were separate, whereas others were adherent and partially aggregated, supporting partial pharmacobezoar formation and prolonged gastric drug retention. During intensive care unit management, the patient developed severe hyperammonemia (peak ammonia 205 μmol/L), hyperlactatemia with mixed metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis, acute kidney injury, marked creatine kinase elevation, hypernatremia, and suspected transient central diabetes insipidus. Meropenem was administered empirically from May 31 to June 3 because impaired airway defenses after intubation raised concern for aspiration-related infection, although no definite infectious focus or causative pathogen was identified. Because of substantial financial hardship, extracorporeal treatment was initially deferred. It was initiated at 20:00 on June 1, approximately 62 h after ingestion and 56 h after hospital admission. Two consecutive 2-h sessions of hemoperfusion combined with CVVH were followed by CVVH alone until 08:30 on June 2. The serum valproate concentration decreased from 397.05 μg/mL before extracorporeal treatment to 12.72 μg/mL during ongoing CVVH and was 8.61 μg/mL approximately 70 h after treatment cessation. The patient was discharged on June 15 without evident neurological, cognitive, or motor impairment. Massive sustained-release valproate overdose may cause prolonged gastric retention of intact and partially aggregated tablets, thereby sustaining systemic toxicity. In selected patients, endoscopic tablet removal may provide toxicological source control, while extracorporeal treatment may remain beneficial even when its initiation is delayed. The respective contributions of endoscopy, meropenem exposure, spontaneous elimination, and extracorporeal treatment cannot be separated in this single case.

42957499.title: Effect of remimazolam versus propofol anaesthesia on postoperative delirium in neurovascular surgery: a randomised noninferiority trial.
42957499.abstract: Propofol-based total intravenous anaesthesia (TIVA) is commonly used in neurovascular surgery, in which intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring limits inhalation anaesthetic use. However, propofol causes hypotension, and prolonged infusions can delay emergence. Remimazolam, a benzodiazepine whose effects are reversible with flumazenil, has been associated with less intraoperative hypotension than propofol, but its use raises concerns about postoperative delirium (POD). We tested whether remimazolam-based TIVA is noninferior to propofol-based TIVA for POD. In this single-centre, double-blind, randomised noninferiority trial, adults undergoing elective intracranial aneurysm clipping, arteriovenous malformation resection, microvascular decompression, or superficial temporal artery-middle cerebral artery bypass received remimazolam-based TIVA with flumazenil reversal at emergence, or propofol-based TIVA, both with remifentanil. The primary outcome was the cumulative incidence of POD within 5 days, assessed twice daily with the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) or the 3-Minute Diagnostic Interview for CAM-defined delirium (3D-CAM). The prespecified noninferiority margin was 10 percentage points. Among 686 patients in the modified intention-to-treat analysis, POD occurred in 44 of 344 (12.8%) with remimazolam and 37 of 342 (10.8%) with propofol (risk difference, 1.97 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.85 to 6.80; one-sided P<0.001 for noninferiority); per-protocol results were consistent. Hypotensive burden below a mean arterial pressure threshold of 65 mm Hg was lower in the remimazolam group (median, 0 vs 7.5 mm Hg min; P<0.001), and tracheal extubation in the operating room was more frequent (85.2% vs 67.3%). Remimazolam-based TIVA met the prespecified criterion for noninferiority to propofol-based TIVA with respect to postoperative delirium after elective neurovascular surgery. Interpretation should take into account that the observed incidence of postoperative delirium was lower than anticipated when the noninferiority margin was defined. NCT06115031 (ClinicalTrials.gov).

42955320.title: Ventilator-associated pneumonia after traumatic brain injury: a timing-sensitive ecological framework of neuroimmune-pulmonary vulnerability.
42955320.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is frequent after traumatic brain injury (TBI), but its biological meaning and outcome impact remain incompletely defined. Traditional models emphasise mechanical ventilation, aspiration, colonisation, endotracheal tube biofilm, and hospital pathogens. These mechanisms remain essential, but they do not fully explain the early clustering, heterogeneous susceptibility, changing bacteriology, and variable mortality effect observed after TBI. Severe brain injury creates an early vulnerable host state through impaired consciousness and airway protection, neuroimmune dysregulation, autonomic and endocrine activation, altered pulmonary immune surveillance, and, in many patients, extracranial trauma, shock, transfusion, or thoracic injury. These processes interact with ventilation, antibiotic pressure, and rapid respiratory microbiome disruption. Early VAP may reflect abrupt loss of control after injury and intubation, whereas late VAP may reflect persistent or secondary failure driven by biofilm maturation, antibiotic selection, multidrug-resistant pathogens, and intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired immune dysfunction. Clinically, VAP consistently prolongs ventilation, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and resource use, while its independent effect on mortality is phenotype- and context-dependent. This model proposes a timing-sensitive ecological framework in which established mechanisms may converge early and with particular clinical intensity after severe TBI, creating a vulnerable host-microbe state that may lower the threshold for clinically apparent infection. Future studies should distinguish isolated TBI from polytrauma, compare TBI with other acute brain injuries and non-neurological ventilated populations, and incorporate dynamic immune, microbial, and trajectory-based outcomes. VAP after TBI should be viewed as a timing-sensitive interaction between ventilator exposure and early host vulnerability, not as a distinct disease entity or as a pneumonia pathway unique to traumatic brain injury. The TBI-focused contribution lies in the early convergence of otherwise non-unique mechanisms: impaired airway control, aspiration risk, neuroimmune-endocrine activation, treatment exposure, dysbiosis, and extracranial injury burden, rather than in any single TBI-specific mechanism. Isolated TBI and TBI with polytrauma are biologically different phenotypes and should be separated in future studies. Early and late VAP may represent different phases of loss of pulmonary host-microbe containment; this distinction is probabilistic rather than TBI-specific in itself and requires validation in TBI-stratified cohorts. Mortality remains clinically relevant but context-dependent; VAP more consistently modifies recovery trajectory, ventilator dependence, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and possibly neurological recovery.

42942421.title: Efficacy of Ultrasound-Guided Pectointercostal Fascial Block Versus Control and Alternative Regional Techniques in Cardiac Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis with Dose-Response Analysis.
42942421.abstract: Background and Objectives: Ultrasound-guided pectointercostal fascial block (USG-PIFB) is increasingly used for post-sternotomy analgesia, but its efficacy remains uncertain. Prior meta-analyses pooled ultrasound-guided blocks with surgeon-performed infiltration, introducing heterogeneity. We aimed to determine the analgesic efficacy of USG-PIFB in adult cardiac surgery by restricting inclusion to ultrasound-guided techniques. Materials and Methods: Six databases were searched through December 2025, with an update search of open sources and trial registries in September 2026, for randomized controlled trials comparing USG-PIFB with control (Comparison 1) or with an alternative regional technique (Comparison 2) in adults undergoing sternotomy. The primary outcome was 24-h opioid consumption in intravenous morphine milligram equivalents. Random-effects meta-analysis (REML, Knapp-Hartung), subgroup, sensitivity and meta-regression analyses, an exploratory trial sequential analysis and GRADE assessment were performed. Results: Twenty-nine trials (2664 participants) were included: 24 in Comparison 1 and eight in Comparison 2. In 13 trials (902 participants), USG-PIFB reduced 24-h opioid consumption (mean difference -6.60 mg; 95% CI, -10.92 to -2.27; I2 = 97.7%), but the 95% prediction interval (-22.24 to 9.04 mg) included no effect and small-study effects could not be excluded. Pain scores were lower by 0.8 to 1.4 points at rest (extubation, 12 and 24 h) and during movement (12 h). Extubation was earlier and intensive care stay shorter, with extreme heterogeneity. No dose-response relationship was detected, and the difference from deep parasternal techniques was near zero. No local anesthetic systemic toxicity or block-attributable pneumothorax was reported; one block-site hematoma occurred in a USG-PIFB recipient. Certainty of evidence was low for rescue analgesic use and block-related complications and very low for all other outcomes. Conclusions: USG-PIFB may modestly reduce 24-h opioid consumption, but the magnitude and reproducibility of this effect across clinical settings remain uncertain. It is best regarded as one component of multimodal analgesia, and adequately powered multicentre trials are needed.

42937764.title: Retrospective evaluation of predictors and clinical impact of postoperative delirium in liver transplant recipients.
42937764.abstract: This study aimed to analyze the epidemiology, predictors, and clinical outcomes of postoperative delirium (POD) in liver transplant (LT) recipients. Clinical data from 427 LT recipients from the Third Xiangya Hospital were retrospectively reviewed. The epidemiology (incidence, onset, and duration), predictors, and associated clinical outcomes of POD were analyzed using standardized delirium assessment tools and multivariate regression. POD occurred in 19.0% of recipients, with a median onset at 26.0 hours posttransplant. Multivariate analysis identified 4 independent pre and postoperative predictors, including a higher model for end-stage liver disease score and hepatic encephalopathy within 24 hours before LT, infection within 2 months prior to LT, and abnormal sodium within 1 hour after LT (all P < .05). In a sensitivity analysis treating early death or persistent coma as a composite outcome with POD (n = 436), the same 4 independent predictors were identified, with consistent effect estimates. Regarding clinical outcomes, POD was significantly associated with prolonged intensive care unit stays, extended mechanical ventilation requirements, and increased use of renal replacement therapy (all P < .01). Although recipients with POD showed higher 1- and 6-month all-cause mortality in unadjusted analyses, POD was not an independent predictor of mortality after adjustment for confounding factors. POD occurs frequently and early after LT, with identifiable pre and postoperative risk factors. While POD markedly increases perioperative morbidity and resource utilization, it does not independently predict short-term all-cause mortality in this cohort.

42936306.title: Mild Hypothermia Versus Normothermia During Barbiturate Coma Therapy After Severe Traumatic Brain Injury: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial.
42936306.abstract: Severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of death and long-term disability worldwide. Therapeutic hypothermia may lower intracranial pressure (ICP) and reduce metabolic demand. This study aims to compare mild therapeutic hypothermia with controlled normothermia in adult TBI patients undergoing Barbiturate Coma Therapy (BCT), and to explore artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted prognostic models. This single-center, pilot, parallel-group randomized trial evaluates the feasibility and safety of adding mild hypothermia to BCT and explores early signals of benefit or harm. The primary outcome, six-month Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOSE), is reported descriptively with exact 95% confidence intervals. Secondary outcomes include Cerebral Performance Category, mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation and vasopressor use, intensive care unit (ICU)/hospital length of stay, complications, and physiological/laboratory trends. An exploratory AI-assisted substudy (using prospectively collected clinical, radiological, physiological, and laboratory data) applies LASSO regression to admission predictors of six-month unfavorable outcome and mortality.

42900938.title: Rural-Urban Parity and Socioeconomic Gaps in Traumatic Brain Injury Outcomes.
42900938.journal: The western journal of emergency medicine
42900938.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of death and disability in the United States. Rural residence and low community income are independently associated with poorer health outcomes, mediated by variations in injury mechanism and healthcare access. We evaluated the impact of geographic location on injury patterns and acute-care metrics in adults with TBI treated at Maryland's statewide Level I trauma center. Adults (≥18 years of age) with radiographically confirmed TBI admitted between 2017 and 2021 were identified retrospectively from the institutional trauma registry. Rural residence was defined using Rural-Urban Commuting Area codes. This single-center study included only patients surviving to hospital admission. Primary outcomes included hospital length of stay (LOS) and discharge to hospice or death. Secondary outcomes included intensive care unit (ICU) and ventilator days and discharge disposition. Of 2,812 patients diagnosed with TBI during the study period, 267 (9.5%) resided in rural areas. Compared with nonrural patients, rural patients were older (median age 67 vs 60 years, P < .001) and lived in lower income communities. However, after adjustment for demographic and clinical covariates, rural residence was not associated with higher hospital LOS quartile category (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.18; 95% CI, 0.91-1.53; P = .20), discharge to hospice or death (aOR 1.67; 95% CI, 0.95-2.94), or discharge to a nonhome setting (aOR 0.93; 95% CI, 0.66-1.31). Groups showed no significant differences in critical care use, including ICU and ventilator durations. Worse outcomes were associated primarily with injury severity, including lower Glasgow Coma Scale scores and higher Injury Severity Scores. In a well-established regional trauma network, we found that among patients admitted with traumatic brain injury, residing in a rural area was not independently associated with worse in-hospital outcomes compared to patients who resided in nonrural (urban and suburban) communities. These findings suggest that a coordinated statewide trauma triage and access to tertiary neurotrauma care may help other systems similarly reduce rural disparities after severe head injury.

42899468.title: Prospective, Population-Based Evaluation of Costs and Outcomes of Status Epilepticus According to the New Definition.
42899468.abstract: To address the paucity of data on outcomes and costs of status epilepticus (SE) following the updated 2015 International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) definition and changes in clinical practice guidelines in Germany. This prospective population-based study (October 2018-March 2020) included adult patients from postal code area prefix 35, representative of Germany, diagnosed with SE according to the 2015 ILAE definition. Costs were calculated using German Diagnosis-Related Groups (G-DRG). In total, 181 patients were included. Mean inpatient costs were €10,543 (median €6376; range €845-€133,267), corresponding to €939 per hospital day (median €580.8; range €76.8-€12,115). Mean length of stay (LOS) was 11 days (median 9; range 1-67). In univariable analyses, super-refractory SE was associated with higher costs and longer LOS (both p < 0.001), while acute symptomatic etiology was associated with longer LOS (p = 0.006). On multivariable analysis, mechanical ventilation was the strongest independent predictor of costs (Exp(B) = 2.918, 95% CI 1.753-4.857; p < 0.001), and etiology was overall significantly associated with cost variation (p = 0.022), with acute symptomatic SE showing the highest adjusted costs. Discharge destination correlated with SE severity, with most patients with non-refractory SE discharged home (p = 0.028). This study provides population-based data on costs and outcomes of SE in Germany, serving as a basis for future cost-effectiveness analyses. Compared with earlier studies, lower direct costs and shorter LOS were observed. Identification of high-risk constellations may support clinical decision-making and optimize monitoring, treatment escalation, and allocation of intensive care resources.

42895961.title: Weathering the storm: Predictors and resource burden of paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity after severe traumatic brain injury.
42895961.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
42895961.abstract: Reported incidence of paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity (PSH) after severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) approaches one-third, largely from cohorts that excluded early deaths. Predictors and resource consequences remain unclear. We identified predictors of PSH development and associations between diagnosis, PSH Assessment Measure (PSH-AM) subscores [clinical features scale (CFS) and diagnosis likelihood tool (DLT)], and resource utilization. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with severe TBI admitted to a tertiary care center intensive care unit (ICU) (October 2020-September 2025), stratified by PSH diagnosis. Two reviewers assigned PSH-AM scores. PSH cannot be diagnosed until the syndrome declares itself over days, so exposure is conditioned on survival; mortality is reported descriptively. Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of PSH diagnosis. Log-transformed linear regressions estimated associations of PSH diagnosis and subscores with hospital length of stay (LOS), ICU LOS, and ventilator days. Thirty-day composite outcomes, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and landmark analysis evaluated robustness. Of 509 patients with severe TBI, 86 (17%) developed PSH. Younger age [odds ratio (OR): 0.97 (95% CI: 0.96-0.98); P<0.001) and higher ISS [1.05 (1.02-1.07); P<0.001] independently predicted PSH. PSH was associated with longer hospital LOS (372.9%), ICU LOS (278.3%), and more ventilator days (266.4%; all P<0.001). Mortality was 11.6% (PSH) versus 35.9% (non-PSH). IPTW demonstrated PSH had fewer days alive and out of hospital (-46.8%; P<0.001) and landmark analysis highlighted fewer ventilator-free days (-40.2%; P=0.0097) and ICU-free days (-46.9%; P<0.001). Higher DLT subscores were associated with longer hospital (36.3%; P=0.001) and ICU (23.3%; P=0.005) stays, whereas the CFS subscore showed no associations. The PSH diagnosis is contingent on survival. Younger patients with severe TBI who survive their initial injuries are more likely to develop PSH and occupy hospital beds meaningfully longer. The diagnosis likelihood tool, not the clinical features scale, tracks with that burden. Level III, prognostic/epidemiological.

42894821.title: Beyond the Classic Triad: A Case of GQ1b Antibody-Positive Bickerstaff Brainstem Encephalitis Overlap Syndrome.
42894821.abstract: Anti-GQ1b antibody syndrome encompasses related postinfectious neurologic disorders, including Miller Fisher syndrome, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis. Recognizing overlap among these phenotypes can be difficult in the intensive care unit because profound unresponsiveness and loss of brainstem reflexes may be attributed to sedation or structural brain injury. A middle-aged man developed perioral numbness, blurred vision, ataxia, extremity paresthesias, and facial weakness after an upper respiratory infection. His condition progressed rapidly to respiratory failure, autonomic instability, generalized areflexia, and prolonged coma-like unresponsiveness. Brain imaging remained unrevealing. Cerebrospinal fluid showed albuminocytologic dissociation, and serum testing was positive for anti-GQ1b antibodies. He received intravenous immunoglobulin and intensive supportive care. Ocular and distal motor responses later returned, followed by resolution of the coma-like state, although ventilatory support was still required at transfer. This case demonstrates that severe anti-GQ1b overlap can produce profound but potentially reversible neurologic dysfunction and supports cautious neuroprognostication while the diagnostic evaluation is ongoing.

42894062.title: Immature neutrophil response is associated with cardiac complications after non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage.
42894062.abstract: Acute non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is complicated by systemic inflammation and cardiac dysfunction that contribute to the high rates of morbidity and mortality. To better define the mechanistic relationship between immune response and cardiac complications, we evaluated subpopulations of circulating immune cells and their associations with abnormalities of cardiac rhythm, injury biomarkers, and mechanical function after hemorrhage. In this single-site prospective observational study, we screened all adult patients presenting to our neurocritical care unit with non-traumatic SAH who required external ventricular drain (EVD) placement for treatment of hydrocephalus. Following informed consent, peripheral blood samples were obtained at post-bleed days (PBDs) 1, 3, 5, 7, and 10. Subjects were separated into groups based on evidence of cardiac abnormalities (cAbn(+))" versus "no cardiac abnormalities (cAbn(-))," and flow cytometric analysis was used to identify and quantify immune cell subpopulations. Circulating neutrophil-secreted factors, including myeloperoxidase (MPO), were measured in plasma using ELISA. We measured associations between these immune factors and cardiac abnormalities. Sixty patients were enrolled between January 2018 and August 2023. Our patient cohort was 65% female with a median age of 58 (IQR 51-68). Poor grade SAH (Hunt Hess = 4-5) occurred in 52% (n = 31) of patients. In the overall cohort 47 (78%) required prolonged mechanical ventilation (> 24-hours), and 52 (87%) underwent coil embolization/clipping of their aneurysm. The average ICU and hospital lengths of stay (LOS) were 18.5 (IQR 12.2-22) and 23 (IQR 18.2-33.8) days, respectively. In-hospital mortality for enrolled patients was 11.8% and overall mortality 6 months after discharge was 25% (n = 15). 40% (n = 24) of patients were discharged home, 37% (n = 22) to acute rehabilitation, 8% (n = 5) to SNF, and 3% (n = 2) to hospice. Cardiac abnormalities after SAH were associated with increased circulating neutrophil counts but not monocyte or lymphocyte levels. Circulating neutrophils in patients with cardiac abnormalities also had reduced cell-surface expression of maturation markers CD10, CD14, and CD16 in patients with cardiac abnormalities. Elevated levels of immature neutrophils and circulating levels of lipocalin-2, and myeloperoxidase (MPO) correlated with increased Hunt-Hess score, ICU, and hospital length of stay. Higher grade SAH was associated with increased immature neutrophil response, which was associated with cardiac abnormalities. These cardiac abnormalities tracked with increased levels of pro-inflammatory lipocalin-2 and MPO, and worse outcomes.

42889023.title: Association of delayed enteral nutrition with hospital-acquired pneumonia and 30-day mortality following craniotomy for severe traumatic brain injury: a retrospective cohort study.
42889023.abstract: Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) is a serious complication after craniotomy for severe traumatic brain injury (TBI), but evidence on modifiable factors, especially delayed enteral nutrition, remains limited. To evaluate factors associated with HAP after severe TBI surgery, focusing on enteral nutrition timing and the association between HAP and 30-day mortality. This retrospective cohort study included 600 adult patients undergoing craniotomy for severe TBI who survived >48 h. HAP was diagnosed according to CDC/NHSN criteria. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with HAP, and a fully adjusted model assessed the HAP-mortality association. Model performance was assessed by the AUC and Hosmer-Lemeshow test. Sensitivity analyses included forced inclusion of tracheostomy and comparison of the primary model (pre-HAP ventilation duration) with the total ventilation model. A 48-h landmark analysis was also performed. The primary outcome was postoperative HAP; secondary outcomes were ICU stay and 30-day mortality. Postoperative HAP incidence was 11.5%. After adjustment, delayed enteral nutrition (≥48 h) was independently associated with HAP (OR = 4.46, 95% CI: 2.52-8.19, p < 0.001). Other associated factors included age, admission GCS, mechanical ventilation duration, and serum albumin. The model showed good discrimination (AUC = 0.795) and calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow p = 0.829). In the time-dependent Cox model, HAP was associated with higher 30-day mortality (HR = 4.31, 95% CI: 1.52-12.25, p = 0.006). The primary model and total ventilation model yielded nearly identical results. In the landmark analysis, mechanical ventilation at 48 h was associated with subsequent HAP (OR = 2.19, 95% CI: 1.02-5.30, p = 0.06). Forced inclusion of tracheostomy did not materially alter core results. In severe TBI patients undergoing craniotomy, delayed enteral nutrition was independently associated with increased HAP risk, and HAP was associated with higher 30-day mortality. These findings highlight the potential importance of early enteral nutrition, but causal inference is limited by the observational design; prospective studies are needed.

42881739.title: Effects of a Standardized Music Intervention on Propofol Requirements and Serum Interleukin-6 and Prolactin in Deeply Sedated Mechanically Ventilated Adults: A Prespecified Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Clinical Trial.
42881739.abstract: Background/Objectives: Prolonged exposure to sedative agents in critically ill patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) is associated with adverse clinical outcomes. Music interventions have emerged as a promising non-pharmacological strategy to improve patient comfort and potentially reduce sedative requirements. This prespecified secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial originally powered to detect differences in cortisol concentrations evaluated the effects of a standardized music intervention on sedative requirements and selected inflammatory and neuroendocrine biomarkers in deeply sedated mechanically ventilated adults. Methods: An open-label randomized controlled trial involving 110 critically ill adults receiving IMV under deep sedation was conducted. Participants were randomly assigned to a 60-min standardized music intervention delivered through active noise-cancelling headphones or to standard care. Changes in sedative requirements, serum interleukin-6 (IL-6) and prolactin (PRL) concentrations, physiological parameters, and safety outcomes were assessed. Results: Among participants receiving propofol at the time of the intervention (n = 84), the music intervention group showed a significantly greater reduction in propofol requirements than those receiving standard care (between-group difference 0.079 mg/kg/h, 95% CI 0.008-0.149; p = 0.029). Any reduction in propofol requirements was observed in 46.7% of intervention participants compared with 7.7% of controls. BIS values remained within the target range for deep sedation throughout the intervention period, and no clinically relevant changes were observed in physiological or ventilatory parameters. No significant between-group differences were observed in IL-6 or PRL concentrations after adjustment for baseline values (IL-6: p = 0.606; PRL: p = 0.093). No intervention-related adverse events were reported. Conclusions: A standardized music intervention was associated with reduced propofol requirements without evidence of a between-group difference in BIS trajectory during the intervention period and without clinically relevant physiological instability in mechanically ventilated critically ill patients. No significant between-group effects were observed on IL-6 or PRL concentrations during the study period. As a prespecified secondary analysis of a trial originally powered for a different primary outcome, these findings should be interpreted in that context and warrant confirmation in future randomized trials specifically designed to evaluate music-related effects on sedative requirements.
