Future randomized trials incorporating appropriate attention-control conditions are warranted to further clarify the specific effects attributable to the musical stimulus.

42965346.title: Application of Electrical Impedance Tomography-Guided Pulmonary Rehabilitation Strategy in Patients with Respiratory Failure.
42965346.abstract: This study investigated pulmonary rehabilitation strategies guided by electrical impedance tomography (EIT) in patients with respiratory failure. A total of 92 patients with respiratory failure admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) of a tertiary Grade A hospital in Chongqing from July 2024 to January 2025 were selected and randomly divided into a control group and an experimental group, with 46 cases in each group, using a random number table. The control group received conventional pulmonary physical therapy nursing strategies. The experimental group additionally received EIT-guided positioning, vibratory sputum clearance, and early mobilization. Relative regional tidal-ventilation distribution, PaO₂/FiO₂, respiratory rate, and pulse oxygen saturation were assessed at baseline and on the following three days; ICU stay, and delirium incidence were also compared. Finally, 44 cases in the control group and 44 cases in the experimental group completed the study. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed significant time effects across the four ventral-to-dorsal layers and significant group and interaction effects for the dorsal layer. Dorsal ventilation share was higher in the experimental group on days 2 and 3, but not significantly different on day 1. No significant group, time, or interaction effects were found for the four lung quadrants. The experimental group had higher PaO₂/FiO₂, shorter ICU stay (6.55 vs. 7.75 days), and lower delirium incidence (25.0% vs. 45.5%). Respiratory rate decreased, and pulse oxygen saturation increased over time in both groups, without significant group or interaction effects. The EIT-guided strategy may improve regional ventilation distribution and oxygenation, shorten ICU stay, and reduce delirium in patients with respiratory failure.

42963310.title: Safety and Outcomes of Prone Positioning in the Early Postoperative Period following Cardiac Surgery.
42963310.journal: Journal of cardiothoracic and vascular anesthesia
42963310.abstract: To evaluate prone positioning (PP) safety and its respiratory and hemodynamic effects in patients with moderate-to-severe respiratory failure after cardiac surgery via median sternotomy. Retrospective, single-center, observational cohort study. Cardiovascular intensive care unit at a tertiary academic hospital. Thirty-eight consecutive adult patients undergoing PP for acute respiratory failure within 30 days of median sternotomy cardiac surgery between 2004 and 2024. Protocolized PP sessions under deep sedation, neuromuscular blockade, and advanced hemodynamic monitoring. Median PP duration was 24 hours (IQR 16-26); 47.4% underwent their first session within 5 postoperative days. The primary endpoint was PP-related complications (mediastinitis/sternal dehiscence). Secondary endpoints included gas exchange, vasoactive requirements, and in-hospital mortality. Mediastinitis occurred in one patient (2.6%), comparable to non-proned populations. PP significantly improved oxygenation, with the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio increasing from 82.8 ± 26.1 mmHg at baseline to 177.5 ± 68.9 mmHg at 4 hours into the maneuver and to 175.0 ± 70.8 mmHg at PP completion (both p < 0.001). No significant hemodynamic deterioration or increased vasoactive support occurred. Overall mortality was 44.7%. Advanced age (≥75 years) and baseline hypercapnia (PaCO₂ ≥50 mmHg) were independent predictors of mortality. PP was safe after recent median sternotomy and elicited a marked improvement in oxygenation without increasing sternal complications. These findings support considering PP for selected patients with moderate-to-severe postoperative adult respiratory distress syndrome following cardiac surgery.

42958471.title: What triggers intraoperative blood pressure/heart rate surges and postoperative hypertonia during unilateral biportal endoscopy?
42958471.abstract: Unilateral biportal endoscopy (UBE) is an increasingly utilized minimally invasive technique for lumbar degenerative disease. Dural tear is a recognized complication (incidence 1.9-5.8%), typically associated with cerebrospinal fluid leakage and intracranial hypotension. However, the unique irrigation dynamics of UBE - an open two-portal system permitting high-flow continuous irrigation - may produce a distinctly different pathophysiology when an occult dural defect is present. The anesthesiology literature contains few descriptions of the acute intraoperative hemodynamic manifestations of this phenomenon. A 49-year-old woman (ASA physical status I) underwent UBE for L4-L5 and L5-S1 disc herniation under total intravenous anesthesia. The procedure was complicated by intraoperative wrong-level surgery (L4-L5 misidentified as L5-S1), necessitating complete portal withdrawal, re-localization, and re-establishment of the surgical field, which prolonged the operation to 4 h 23 min with a cumulative irrigation volume of 51,000 mL. Approximately 2.5 h after incision, progressive, treatment-refractory tachycardia (70 → 117 beats/min) and hypertension (up to 183/102 mmHg) developed; esmolol and urapidil produced minimal antihypertensive effect despite concurrent augmentation of anesthetic depth. On postoperative review, the scrub nurse recalled observing a suspected dural tear approximately 10 min before the hemodynamic escalation, which had not been communicated intraoperatively. Following extubation, the patient exhibited impaired consciousness, persistent tachypnea (40-50 breaths/min), and generalized hypertonia with decerebrate posturing. Multidisciplinary evaluation excluded epileptic seizure, metabolic encephalopathy, malignant hyperthermia, and intraoperative awareness. Suspected acute intracranial hypertension secondary to massive irrigation fluid entry into the subarachnoid space via the unrecognized dural defect was considered the most likely diagnosis. The patient was reintubated and managed in the intensive care unit with osmotic diuresis (furosemide, mannitol), corticosteroids, and sedation. Consciousness recovered the following morning, limb hypertonia resolved by postoperative day 11, and the patient was discharged on day 14 without neurological deficit. This case suggests that an occult dural tear during UBE with large-volume irrigation may produce a paradoxical hemodynamic profile of progressive, therapy-resistant hypertension and tachycardia - contrasting with the bradycardia and hypotension classically associated with intracranial hypotension from cerebrospinal fluid leaks. The triad of (i) progressive, treatment-refractory hypertension and tachycardia, (ii) prolonged UBE duration (> 2 h), and (iii) large-volume irrigation (> 20 L) may represent a high-risk pattern warranting immediate intraoperative communication between anesthesia and surgical teams and consideration of intracranial pressure-directed interventions. This observation is hypothesis-generating and requires validation in larger studies.

42856548.title: Elevated blood urea nitrogen-to-albumin ratio is associated with incident sepsis-associated delirium: evidence from a weighted competing-risk analysis in a multicenter cohort study.
42856548.abstract: Sepsis-associated delirium (SAD) is a frequent manifestation of acute brain dysfunction in sepsis. Although the blood urea nitrogen-to-albumin ratio (BAR) has been associated with prognosis in critically ill patients, its relationship with incident SAD remains uncertain. We evaluated the association between early BAR and incident SAD. This multicenter retrospective cohort study included patients with sepsis from MIMIC-IV as the primary cohort and eICU-CRD as an independent replication cohort. BAR was calculated from eligible blood urea nitrogen and serum albumin measurements obtained within 24 h after the index time. The primary outcome was 7-day incident delirium; 3-day delirium was additionally evaluated in MIMIC-IV. Death before delirium was treated as a competing event. Covariates were selected using Boruta and LASSO regression. CBPS-based inverse probability weighting and Fine-Gray competing-risk regression were applied, with restricted cubic spline, subgroup, and exploratory XGBoost/SHAP analyses. A total of 10,565 patients were included (9,612 MIMIC-IV; 953 eICU-CRD). In MIMIC-IV, the highest BAR quartile was associated with a greater subdistribution hazard of 7-day delirium vs. the lowest quartile (fully adjusted sHR 1.36, 95% CI 1.13-1.64; P = 0.001; P for trend = 0.002). Continuous BAR was also associated with 7-day delirium (sHR per 1-unit increase 1.00, 95% CI 1.00-1.01; P = 0.013), with similar findings for 3-day delirium. In eICU-CRD, the highest BAR quartile was likewise associated with 7-day delirium (sHR 2.20, 95% CI 1.13-4.29; P = 0.020; P for trend = 0.012), whereas the continuous association was not statistically significant (sHR 1.01, 95% CI 1.00-1.02; P = 0.075). Restricted cubic spline analyses suggested potential nonlinearity, particularly in MIMIC-IV. Exploratory SHAP analyses ranked BAR among the most influential model-based predictors in both cohorts. Higher early BAR, particularly values in the highest quartile, was associated with a greater subdistribution hazard of incident SAD, and the highest-quartile association was independently reproduced in eICU-CRD. BAR may serve as a simple risk-associated marker for identifying patients with sepsis at higher risk of incident delirium.

42952567.title: Immune-programmed cell death crosstalk implicates plasma sTNFR1 as a candidate biomarker for sepsis-associated encephalopathy.
42952567.abstract: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) is a frequent neurological manifestation of sepsis characterized by acute and diffuse brain dysfunction. Despite increasing evidence of molecular alterations in the septic brain, clinically applicable circulating biomarkers for SAE remain limited. Immune dysregulation and programmed cell death (PCD) pathways have been implicated in SAE pathogenesis, but their translational relevance for peripheral biomarker development remains unclear. This study aimed to identify immune-PCD crosstalk-related biomarkers for SAE through an integrated transcriptomic and clinical evaluation strategy. Human brain transcriptomic data from GSE135838 were analyzed using differential expression analysis and gene set enrichment analysis. Immune-related pathways, PCD signatures, and extracellular protein annotations were integrated to prioritize candidate biomarkers with peripheral detection potential. An exploratory cross-species comparison was performed using mouse SAE microglial RNA-sequencing data (GSE198862). Plasma soluble TNFR1 (sTNFR1) was subsequently evaluated in a prospective cohort of 60 septic patients (26 SAE and 34 non-SAE). SAE was defined as acute diffuse cerebral dysfunction during sepsis, identified by reduced GCS and/or a positive CAM-ICU assessment after exclusion of alternative causes, including persistent deep sedation that precluded reliable neurological assessment. Plasma samples for sTNFR1 measurement were collected within 24 h after enrollment, while SAE status was determined during the baseline neurological assessment after ICU admission. Logistic regression, ROC analysis, and bootstrap validation assessed the incremental value of sTNFR1, with 28-day mortality examined exploratorily. Transcriptomic analysis revealed activation of immune inflammatory responses and multiple PCD-related pathways in SAE brain tissue. Integration of immune, PCD, and differential expression signatures identified 15 immune-PCD crosstalk genes. Extracellular prioritization further identified FAS, IL6, and TNFRSF1A as candidate biomarkers. The immune-PCD signature showed substantial directional concordance in mouse SAE microglial transcriptomes, including concordant increases in Fas and Tnfrsf1a. In the clinical cohort, plasma sTNFR1 levels were significantly elevated in SAE patients compared with non-SAE patients (p < 0.001). After adjustment for age and SOFA score, sTNFR1 remained independently associated with SAE. Adding sTNFR1 increased the observed AUC from 0.791 to 0.891; however, the difference did not reach statistical significance by the paired DeLong test (p = 0.086). Continuous NRI nevertheless indicated improved reclassification (NRI = 0.950, 95% CI 0.411-1.536; p = 0.001). Exploratory analyses also associated SAE and higher sTNFR1 levels with increased 28-day mortality. This study integrates sepsis-associated brain transcriptomic discovery with prospective peripheral clinical evaluation and identifies circulating sTNFR1 as a candidate biomarker associated with SAE. sTNFR1 may provide additional information beyond conventional severity assessment for SAE identification and merits further validation.

42941411.title: Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth in Severe Traumatic Brain Injury Is Associated with Late In-Hospital Mortality.
42941411.abstract: Background: Severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) is associated with high mortality. There is increasing evidence suggesting that intestinal dysbiosis may influence clinical outcomes; however, its prognostic significance in patients with severe TBI remains poorly defined. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 235 patients with severe TBI (Glasgow Coma Scale [GCS] score ≤ 8) admitted to the intensive care units of three participating hospitals between September 2023 and December 2024. Quantitative microbiological analysis of jejunal aspirates was performed at admission and repeated on days 12-14 of the ICU stay. Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) was defined as a bacterial load of ≥105 colony-forming units per milliliter (CFU/mL). Multivariable logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were performed. Results: At admission, SIBO was uncommon (3.8%) but increased to 27.9% among patients who underwent repeated assessment. Within the day-14 landmark cohort (n = 179), post-day-14 mortality was higher in patients with SIBO than in those without (34.0% vs. 23.3%). In multivariable logistic regression analysis, SIBO was independently associated with post-day-14 in-hospital mortality after adjustment for age, body mass index, GCS score, PaO2/FiO2 ratio, and blood glucose (OR 2.83, 95% CI 1.06-7.58; p = 0.039). The ROC model demonstrated good discriminative performance, with an apparent area under the curve (AUC) of 0.846 and an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.823 after bootstrap validation. Conclusions: In patients with severe TBI who survived and remained hospitalized through the day-14 landmark, SIBO detected at days 12-14 was independently associated with increased subsequent in-hospital mortality. However, its incremental contribution to discrimination beyond established clinical predictors was modest. Therefore, late SIBO should be interpreted primarily as a dynamic marker associated with prolonged critical illness and adverse outcome rather than as a demonstrated cause of mortality. Prospective validation is required.

42881967.title: Association of Postoperative Stress Hyperglycemia Ratio with Suspected Infection, Culture Positivity, Sepsis, and Septic Shock in 1408 Patients After Cranial Neurosurgery.
42881967.abstract: Background/Objectives: The early postoperative stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR) may capture acute glycemic stress relative to chronic glycemia, but its association with infection-related events after cranial neurosurgery remains uncertain. We evaluated these associations in critically ill patients after cranial neurosurgical procedures. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 1408 adults in MIMIC-IV after eligible cranial neurosurgical procedures. SHR was calculated from the first serum glucose measurement 6-24 h after surgery and estimated average glucose was derived from HbA1c. Primary outcomes were electronic health record (EHR)-defined suspected infection, culture-positive infection from any qualifying specimen, Sepsis-3-defined sepsis, and an EHR-based septic shock proxy. The secondary outcome was 90-day mortality. Results: In fully adjusted models, each 0.1-unit increase in SHR was associated with suspected infection (OR 1.08, 95% CI 1.04-1.12), culture-positive infection (OR 1.05, 95% CI 1.01-1.09), Sepsis-3-defined sepsis (OR 1.07, 95% CI 1.03-1.11), and septic shock (OR 1.10, 95% CI 1.05-1.15). In nested analyses, each 1-SD increase in SHR was associated with 90-day mortality (OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.29-1.96). Associations persisted in 24-h lag analyses. Adding SHR yielded small, non-significant AUC increases but improved reclassification for Sepsis-3-defined sepsis and septic shock. Conclusions: Higher early postoperative SHR was associated with EHR-derived, all-source infection-related and sepsis-related events and 90-day mortality in a heterogeneous postoperative neurocritical care cohort. These findings do not establish that SHR predicts postoperative neurosurgical infection; prospective external validation is required before clinical use.

42870279.title: Temporal changes in clinical practices for patients considered clinically brain dead: a single-center cohort study.
42870279.abstract: Patients considered clinically brain dead undergo neurological assessment and critical care management, along with discussions with their families regarding goals of care and, when appropriate, organ donation. However, how these clinical and organ donation-related practices have evolved over time remains poorly characterized in Japan. We aimed to evaluate temporal changes in neurological assessment, critical care management, and organ donation-related processes among patients considered clinically brain dead. We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study including consecutive patients considered clinically brain dead in the Emergency ICU of Okayama University Hospital between January 2017 and December 2025. Patients were identified through routine auditory brainstem response testing during evaluation for a brain-death-compatible state. Temporal changes in the determination of a brain-death-compatible state, organ donation discussion, and critical care management were evaluated by calendar year, with three study phases (2017-2019, 2020-2022, and 2023-2025) used for descriptive presentation. Annual trends were assessed using logistic regression and nonparametric trend analyses. Among 128 eligible patients, organ donation was discussed with the families of 110 (85.9%), and 41 (37.3%) subsequently underwent organ donation after brain death. Calendar-year analyses showed increasing corticosteroid use (odds ratio [OR] per year, 1.64; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.34-2.01; p < 0.001) and earlier initiation of corticosteroids and vasopressin, whereas no significant trends were observed in vasopressin use or in the timing of determination of a brain-death-compatible state or the initial organ donation discussion. The likelihood of organ donation discussion increased significantly over time (OR per year, 1.44; 95% CI 1.17-1.79; p = 0.001) and remained significant in a sensitivity analysis restricted to patients in whom discussion was considered feasible (OR per year, 2.11; 95% CI 1.42-3.15; p < 0.001). The opportunity for organ donation discussion increased over time among patients considered clinically brain dead, while the proportion of families consenting to donation remained relatively stable. This increase occurred alongside the progressive development of structured multidisciplinary processes, although their contribution to the observed temporal trend cannot be determined from this descriptive study.

42853139.title: Pressure Points: A Scoping Review of Intracranial Pressure and Mean Arterial Pressure Measurement and Reporting Practices in Neurocritical Care.
42853139.abstract: Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is a cornerstone of neurocritical care, but the literature shows substantial heterogeneity in how its components-intracranial pressure (ICP) and mean arterial pressure (MAP)-are reported. We conducted a scoping review following the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR to map this variability. Structured searches in PubMed and Scopus (January 1997 to May 2026) identified 350 eligible original clinical studies. For each study, we extracted whether the ICP measurement method, ICP device, ICP zero reference, MAP measurement method, and arterial line zero reference were reported. Reporting completeness was analyzed overall and stratified by guideline era and primary diagnosis, using the χ2 tests, odds ratios with 95% CI, and the Cochran-Armitage test for trend. The ICP measurement method was reported in 84.0% of studies, and the ICP zero reference in 14.6%; the MAP method in 66.9%, and the arterial line zero reference in 28.6%. Only 6.6% of studies reported all 5 domains. After publication of the Brain Trauma Foundation fourth Edition, reporting improved across most domains-ICP method (79.0% vs. 96.1%, P<0.001) and arterial line zero reference (20.2% vs. 49.0%, P<0.001)-and the composite reporting score rose from 2.37 to 3.06 (P<0.001). ICP zero-reference reporting was similar between eras (16.5% vs. 9.8%, P=0.105) while showing a significant declining trend across the study period (Cochran-Armitage Z=-2.52, P=0.012). Traumatic brain injury and hemorrhagic conditions had the lowest ICP zero reference reporting (8.8% and 9.3%; OR=0.35 for TBI vs. non-TBI, 95% CI: 0.19-0.65). Improvements in reporting have not reached the level needed to determine whether CPP values are comparable across studies. We propose an 11-item Minimum Reporting Set for CPP-related studies.

42837646.title: Dual Antiglutamate Therapy in Super-Refractory Status Epilepticus After Cardiac Arrest (SUPER-CAT Study).
42837646.abstract: The SUPER-refractory status epilepticus (SE) after Cardiac Arrest Treatment (SUPER-CAT) study evaluated the efficacy and safety of dual antiglutamate therapy (combined AMPA and NMDA receptor blockade) in patients with super-refractory SE (SRSE) after cardiac arrest and without unfavorable prognostic indicators. Multicenter cohort study including patients with postanoxic SRSE meeting the following criteria: bilaterally preserved N20 cortical responses, intact pupillary reflexes, and absence of generalized periodic discharges. Patients treated with dual antiglutamate therapy (DUAL; ketamine 1.5-7.5 mg/kg/h for 3 days plus perampanel 6-12 mg/d for 5 days with tapering) were compared with patients receiving other combinations of antiseizure and anesthetic agents (OTHERS). The primary outcome was resolution of SE. Secondary outcomes included awakening to follow commands and good neurologic outcome at 6 months (modified Rankin Scale 0-3) in patients with fewer than 2 unfavorable multimodal prognostic indicators and 6-month mortality for the entire cohort. Safety analysis included in-hospital mortality and potentially treatment-related adverse events. Patients treated with single antiglutamate agents were described separately. Between May 2012 and May 2025, 95 of 1,352 consecutive post-cardiac arrest intensive care unit patients met inclusion criteria (mean age 66, interquartile range 55-73; 41% female; DUAL = 43; OTHERS = 41; single antiglutamate = 11). Compared with OTHERS, DUAL was associated with a higher rate of SE resolution (84% vs 49%; OR 5.4; 95% CI 1.9-14.9; p = 0.001), a greater likelihood of awakening before discharge (56% vs 32%; OR 2.7; 95% CI 1.0-7.3; p = 0.053) and lower 6-month mortality (52% vs 74%; OR 0.37; 95% CI 0.15-0.97; p = 0.043). A trend toward better 6-month neurologic outcome was observed in the DUAL group (39% vs 25%; OR 1.89; 95% CI 0.64-5.56; p = 0.245). Reversible cholestatic liver injury occurred more frequently in DUAL group, compared with OTHERS (77% vs 27%; OR 9.00; 95% CI 3.34-24.19; p < 0.001). In patients with postanoxic SRSE without unfavorable prognostic indicators, dual antiglutamate therapy was highly effective in resolving SE and was associated with improved short-term clinical outcomes. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05756621.

42956386.title: Resting-State Functional MRI and Clinical Outcomes After Acute Disorders of Consciousness: A Systematic Review.
42956386.abstract: Accurate assessment and prognostication of patients with acute disorders of consciousness (DoC) after severe brain injury remain a substantial clinical challenge. Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) measures spontaneous, temporally correlated brain activity in the absence of external stimulation and provides objective insight into the integrity of large-scale neural networks that support brain function. Emerging evidence suggests that assessing neural integrity using rs-fMRI may improve outcome prediction in patients with acute DoC. This review summarizes the current evidence of rs-fMRI as an assessment tool during the acute phase of severe brain injury. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, we conducted a systematic literature search using MEDLINE and Embase databases from January 2006 to March 2026. Eligible studies included peer-reviewed empirical investigations of adult patients with acute DoC (<28 days postinjury) that examined associations between rs-fMRI measures and clinical outcomes. The systematic review protocol was registered in the PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420251085923). Of 396 studies screened, 30 met eligibility criteria. Across these studies, a total of 800 patients (mean age = 48, 69% male) were scanned at a weighted average of 9.31 days after intensive care unit admission. Ten studies included patients exclusively with traumatic brain injury, 8 with cardiac arrest, 2 with encephalopathy, and 10 included mixed etiologies. The most frequently assessed resting-state networks were the default mode (n = 20) and executive control networks (n = 11), followed by visual (n = 6), salience (n = 6), sensorimotor (n = 6), and auditory (n = 5) networks. Across studies, significant associations between rs-fMRI measures and outcome were consistently reported, despite heterogeneity in methodology. The most commonly reported patient outcomes were functional or neurologic status, assessed at hospital discharge or between 3 and 12 months postinjury. Current evidence consistently demonstrates that rs-fMRI acquired during the acute phase of brain injury is associated with neurologic and functional outcomes in patients with DoC. In addition, rs-fMRI may help identify patients more likely to recover consciousness and achieve favorable functional outcomes by characterizing the integrity of large-scale brain networks. However, substantial heterogeneity and small sample sizes limit comparability across studies. Standardized acquisition and analysis frameworks, along with larger prospective studies, are needed to validate the clinical utility of rs-fMRI and support translation into an assessment tool after brain injury.

42953261.title: Reverse Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy Complicated by Neurogenic Pulmonary Edema in Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Case Report.
42953261.abstract: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (TTC) is a recognized and potentially severe cardiac complication in patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH). Reverse TTC (rTTC), a rare variant characterized by basal hypokinesis with apical sparing, is infrequently reported in this setting. The coexistence of rTTC with neurogenic pulmonary edema has not been previously described and represents a complex neurocardiac interaction that can significantly worsen outcomes. We report the case of a previously healthy 30-year-old man who presented with high-grade aSAH secondary to rupture of an anterior communicating artery aneurysm. His course was complicated by neurogenic pulmonary edema, refractory hypoxemia, hemodynamic instability, and rTTC. Management required early airway protection, bronchoscopy, vasopressor support, and complex stent-assisted endovascular coiling. Echocardiography demonstrated reduced left ventricular ejection fraction with basal hypokinesis and apical sparing, consistent with rTTC. Careful hemodynamic management was essential to balance cerebral perfusion against myocardial dysfunction. With multidisciplinary critical care and structured rehabilitation, the patient achieved favorable neurological and functional recovery. This case highlights that rTTC in aSAH is not a benign condition and may be associated with increased morbidity when combined with neurogenic pulmonary edema due to massive catecholamine surge. Early recognition using bedside echocardiography, prompt aneurysm securing, and balanced hemodynamic support are critical for improving outcomes.

42900939.title: Hemodynamic Effects of Interfacility Dexmedetomidine Infusions During Transport of Patients with Alpha-2-adrenergic Agonist Withdrawal.
42900939.journal: The western journal of emergency medicine
42900939.abstract: In the Philadelphia region, there has been an increase in the potency of illicit opioids as well as the addition of nonopioid adulterants. Currently, medetomidine, a veterinary anesthetic that acts as an alpha-2-adrenergic agonist, is a common adulterant in the illicit opioid supply, causing both unique overdose and withdrawal syndromes. Although opioid withdrawal alone is not deadly, with added adulterants, especially medetomidine, this is no longer the case. Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2-adrenergic agonist frequently used for sedation in the emergency department and intensive care unit. Dexmedetomidine is also used off-label to treat the life-threatening withdrawal from alpha-2-agonists. This study describes the dosing and hemodynamic effects associated with the interfacility administration of dexmedetomidine in patients with alpha-2 adrenergic agonist withdrawal. Secondarily, we describe the safety of dexmedetomidine in this patient population. We conducted a retrospective case review of patients receiving dexmedetomidine infusions in the interfacility setting for presumed alpha-2-adrenergic agonist withdrawal. Demographic data, dosing, and vital signs were analyzed descriptively. Over a six-month period, of 217 cases identified, 182 contained complete hemodynamic data. The average age was 39.5 years, and 67% were male. The average transport time was 15.7 minutes (range, 5-40 minutes). The mean dexmedetomidine infusion rate was 1.32 (0.31) mcg/kg/hr. The average mean arterial pressure decreased from 122.1 mm Hg (21.7) at the time of initial patient contact to 118.3 mm Hg (21.7) (mean difference, 3.80; 95% CI, 1.96-5.64) at final patient interaction. Heart rate also showed a minimal change from 104.9 (23.7) to 103.6 (21.8) beats/min (mean 1.3; 95% CI, -0.48 to 3.08). No cases of severe hypotension or clinically significant bradycardia requiring intervention were documented (one-sided 95% CI, 0-1.7%). In this case series of patients, prehospital dexmedetomidine infusions to treat alpha-2-agonist withdrawal were associated with stable hemodynamics without significant bradycardia or hypotension. These findings support the safety of dexmedetomidine infusions for interfacility transport and provide a rationale for examining whether advanced life support clinicians can safely transport patients receiving dexmedetomidine infusions for this indication.

42932517.title: Physiological Signals Boosted by Artificial Intelligence Save Time and Brain Function.
42932517.abstract: AbstractPatients with acute neurologic injury in the neurologic intensive care unit are at high risk of secondary brain injury, yet timely detection and intervention remain limited by intermittent examination and delayed signal interpretation. This review explores emerging applications of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning in neurocritical care, highlighting how continuous physiological data streams - such as electroencephalography, intracranial pressure, and cerebral blood flow - can be used to detect subclinical deterioration and guide early treatment. Through three illustrative cases, we examine potential AI use cases for delayed cerebral ischemia, real-time seizure detection, and continuous physiological "nowcasting" that could improve prognostication and reduce preventable morbidity. Although current AI tools remain largely in developmental or validation stages, their clinical translation will require rigorous testing, thoughtful integration into workflows, and attention to ethical and regulatory considerations. The neurocritical care environment, characterized by rich data and narrow therapeutic windows, represents a uniquely fertile setting for developing clinically actionable AI systems.

42880808.title: Characteristics and outcomes of haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury and combined injuries from a South African Trauma Cohort Study.
42880808.abstract: To describe and compare injury severity, clinical management and mortality among haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury (TBI) and combined haemorrhage+TBI cohorts in a South African trauma population. Secondary analysis of data from the Epidemiology and Outcomes of Prolonged Trauma Care (EpiC) multicentre observational cohort study, April 2021 to December 2024. Six government health facilities and affiliated government ambulances across the Western Cape, South Africa. 18 840 adult patients with blunt and/or penetrating traumatic injuries enrolled in the EpiC registry were eligible for this secondary analysis. Patients <18 years of age and prisoners are excluded from EpiC. Burn injuries, non-haemorrhage and non-TBI injuries were excluded from this analysis. Patients were assigned to one of three mutually exclusive cohorts (haemorrhage, TBI or haemorrhage+TBI) using anatomic and physiologic criteria. The primary outcome was crude, all-cause prehospital or in-hospital mortality. Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios (RRs) for mortality were adjusted for injury severity, injury force type and mode of prehospital transportation. Secondary outcomes included critical interventions, hospital admission, length of stay and time from injury to death. A total of 7614 patients met inclusion: 5146 (67.6%) haemorrhage, 1556 (20.4%) TBI and 912 (12.0%) haemorrhage+TBI. The majority were male (85.1%) with a median age of 31 years. Patients with haemorrhage+TBI received more intensive care, including airway interventions (38%), transfusions (41%) and intensive care unit admissions (36%). Crude mortality was highest in haemorrhage+TBI (31.3%), followed by TBI (7.7%) and haemorrhage (5.4%). After injury-pattern specific severity adjustment, mortality risk remained significantly higher in haemorrhage+TBI than in TBI (RR 1.87, 95% CI 1.60 to 2.19) and haemorrhage (RR 3.38, 95% CI 2.96 to 3.85). Estimates were similar after additional adjustment for injury force and prehospital transportation (RR 1.84 and 2.98). In this South African population, haemorrhage+TBI was the least prevalent but most high-risk cohort with greater morbidity and mortality compared with haemorrhage or TBI alone, even after adjusting for injury severity. These findings may inform system level planning and resource allocation particularly in resource-limited settings.

42878137.title: Global Neurointensive Care: A Field Yet to Be Born.
42878137.abstract: Neurological conditions represent the leading cause of disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) and the second leading cause of death globally, with more than 11 million deaths annually, 87% of which occur in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). While global neurosurgery has emerged as a recognized field with dedicated frameworks for advocacy and action, the critical care continuum of neurological disease has been persistently overlooked. Global neurointensive care (GNIC) does not yet exist as a formally defined discipline, yet its need is urgent and measurable: ICU bed density in LMICs ranges from 0.1 to 2.5 per 100,000 inhabitants compared with 5 to 30 per 100,000 in high-income countries (HICs); a cross-sectional survey of 408 providers from 42 LMICs found that only 36.8% had access to a dedicated neurointensive care unit; and traumatic brain injury (TBI) mortality at 6 months exceeds 37% in Latin American LMICs. This viewpoint defines GNIC, characterizes the epidemiological and structural dimensions of the unmet need with granular supporting evidence, reviews existing initiatives and their limitations, and proposes a 6-domain strategic agenda for its development. GNIC must be established as a field parallel and complementary to global neurosurgery, ensuring the critical care continuum of neurological disease is not abandoned in the global effort towards universal health coverage.

42875815.title: Economic Evaluation of Prolonged Hypothermic Oxygenated Machine Perfusion Enabling Daytime Liver Transplantation.
42875815.abstract: Short-duration (1-2 h) dual hypothermic oxygenated machine perfusion (DHOPE) reduces ischemia-reperfusion injury-related complications. Prolonged DHOPE preservation (DHOPE-PRO) may facilitate logistics. We assessed the economic impact of DHOPE-PRO versus conventional short-duration DHOPE, hypothesizing that DHOPE-PRO would not be associated with increased one-year transplantation-related costs. This post hoc economic evaluation of the prospective DHOPE-PRO trial (NL8740) included adult recipients of livers donated after brain death. All transplantation-related medical expenses up to one year post-transplant were collected. The cost of resource use was calculated using 2022 full hospital prices indexed to 2024. Time-driven variable costing was applied to perfusion, surgery, and intensive care costs. The primary outcome was total one-year transplantation-related cost. Of 24 patients, 12 received a liver after DHOPE and 12 after DHOPE-PRO. Median one-year total costs were €83 583 [interquartile range (IQR) 78 400-104 158] for DHOPE and €78 582 [IQR 73123-92 855] for DHOPE-PRO (p = 0.347). Perfusion costs were higher with DHOPE-PRO (€23 926 [IQR 22711-24 697] versus €17 306 [IQR 16928-17 594]; p < 0.001), while surgery costs were lower (€18 560 [IQR 17806-20 747] versus €21 303 [IQR 19535-25 418]; p = 0.033). Costs related to other medical activities did not differ between groups. In this exploratory single-center economic evaluation, DHOPE-PRO enabled daytime liver transplantation without evidence of increased one-year transplantation-related costs compared with short-duration DHOPE. Higher perfusion-related costs were accompanied by lower surgery-related costs in this cohort. These findings warrant confirmation in larger studies. Netherlands Trial Registry number: NL8740.

42873412.title: Artificial Intelligence for Early Prediction of Intracranial Hypertension: From Single-Centre Development to Multicentre Validation.
authors: CENTER-TBI High-Resolution ICU (HR ICU) Sub-Study Participants and Investigators
42873412.abstract: Raised intracranial pressure is one of the most severe secondary insults after traumatic brain injury. Recognising physiological patterns before they progress to dangerous intracranial pressure elevations could enable preventive rather than reactive interventions. In our previous Uppsala single-centre study, an XGBoost machine learning model showed high discriminative performance for prediction of imminent intracranial pressure insults. The model identifies short-term physiological trajectories associated with imminent threshold crossing rather than predicting independent future clinical events. Whether these results are generalisable across centres is unknown. The aim was therefore to evaluate whether the XGBoost model trained on an Uppsala dataset maintains similar performance when applied to a multicentre TBI cohort - The CENTER-TBI High-Resolution ICU cohort. The XGBoost model trained on the Uppsala high frequency traumatic brain injury cohort was externally validated using data from the multicentre CENTER-TBI cohort. Minute-level averages of intracranial pressure and invasive arterial blood pressure were used to predict the onset of an intracranial pressure insult within 30 min on the basis of a 4h historical window. A bidirectional validation design was applied and performance was assessed using multiple metrics. The cohorts comprised 602 patients from Uppsala and 255 patients from the CENTER-TBI database. When trained on the Uppsala cohort and tested on CENTER-TBI, the model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 97.4%, sensitivity of 93.8%, and specificity of 98.6%. Training on CENTER-TBI and testing on the Uppsala dataset yielded an AUROC of 96.1%, sensitivity of 81.2%, and specificity of 98.7%. Balanced accuracy exceeded 88% in both validation directions. The XGBoost model retained high performance under external multicentre validation, indicating that pre-insult physiological patterns preceding increased intracranial pressure are shared across cohorts. Differences in sensitivity between validation directions were observed and may reflect cohort characteristics or dataset size. These findings support the need for local evaluation before clinical implementation.

42872033.title: Bedside Transcranial Doppler as a Dynamic Warning Tool for Rapidly Evolving Intracranial Hypertension in Pneumococcal Meningitis.
42872033.abstract: In severe bacterial meningitis, an initially non-critical or technically unreliable lumbar puncture opening pressure should not reassure when hydrocephalus and coma persist. Bedside transcranial Doppler cannot measure intracranial pressure, but bilateral near-absent diastolic flow may provide an urgent warning signal prompting repeat assessment and cerebrospinal fluid diversion.

42871870.title: Risk Factors for Poor Outcomes of Mild and Moderate Traumatic Brain Injury Patients in Tanzania: A Retrospective Cohort Study Using Latent Class Analysis.
42871870.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major global health concern, especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). LMICs have higher injury rates and limited quality of care. TBI patients can be stratified as mild, moderate, and severe risk based on the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). Although most poor outcomes are from severe TBIs, mild and moderate TBI patients significantly contribute to the overall morbidity and mortality, and may benefit from early monitoring to identify deterioration of status. Our goal was to identify unique subgroups within the mild and moderate TBI population at a high risk for poor outcomes. We selected mild (GCS 14-15) and moderate (GCS 9-13) TBI patients from a TBI registry collected at a small city, regional referral hospital in Moshi, Tanzania, from May 2014 to April 2017. With these subsets (mild: n = 1738, moderate: n = 346), we performed a latent class analysis (LCA) to define unique patient classes based on clinical course, vital signs, and demographics. We then performed a survival analysis using a Cox proportional hazard model to examine the association of the defined latent classes with clinical outcome. The predictor variables were demographic variables, hospital interventions, and vital signs. The outcome of interest was a dichotomized discharge Glasgow outcome scale extended score (good outcome 7-8 and poor outcome 1-6). The LCA identified five classes among mild TBI patients: Adolescent (18.8%), Assault (31.5%), Young Adult Polytrauma (32.7%), Adult Polytrauma (9.2%), and RTI with ICU (7.8%). Three classes were identified among moderate TBI patients: Assault (20.2%), RTI with ICU (26.3%), and RTI without ICU (53.5%). Road traffic injury was the predominant mechanism in both severity groups (67% and 68%, respectively), and poor outcomes occurred in 4% of mild and 16% of moderate TBI patients. Relative to the lowest-risk reference class, all other mild TBI classes had higher hazards of poor outcomes. Among moderate TBI classes, RTI with ICU had a higher hazard of poor outcome than RTI without ICU (HR 2.58, 95% CI 1.26-5.24). We identified clinically distinct latent classes within GCS-defined mild and moderate TBI groups, with differences in discharge outcomes across classes. These findings suggest that combining GCS category with demographic, physiological, injury, and care-process information may provide additional prognostic stratification. The results do not establish that GCS is inadequate; rather, they support further evaluation of complementary, context-appropriate risk-stratification approaches.

42871689.title: Early mobilization in neurocritical care as a threshold-regulated intervention: a narrative review of mechanistic integration and implications for neurological recovery and physiological stability.
42871689.abstract: The integration of early mobilization into neurocritical care remains constrained by uncertainty regarding how heterogeneous physiological systems respond to graded activity during neurological instability. Although early mobilization is increasingly used in intensive care, the relationships between intervention timing, intensity, neurological recovery, functional outcomes, and physiological tolerance remain incompletely defined in acute neurocritical populations. This narrative review integrates clinical and mechanistic evidence to examine how immobility and reactivation may influence interconnected neuromuscular, cerebrovascular, cardiopulmonary, metabolic, and inflammatory domains. Available evidence indicates that immobility is associated with progressive disruption of neural, vascular, and metabolic coordination, whereas early mobilization may provide structured physiological input that supports partial re-engagement of regulatory mechanisms when applied within individual tolerance limits. Low- to moderate-intensity activity has been proposed, based on clinical and mechanistic evidence, to involve pathways related to neurovascular coupling, mitochondrial bioenergetics, and activity-dependent neuroplasticity; however, direct patient-level evidence in acute neurocritical care remains limited. Physiological stability during mobilization should therefore be interpreted as a dynamic process rather than a binary condition, with transient hemodynamic, intracranial, and respiratory fluctuations requiring contextual assessment. Interpretation is further limited by methodological heterogeneity, variable outcome definitions, and differences in patient severity and monitoring approaches. Integrated monitoring and data-informed decision support may help identify patient-specific tolerance thresholds. Overall, early mobilization is best understood as a context-dependent, threshold-sensitive intervention requiring continuous system-level assessment.

42871403.title: Acute spinal cord injury.
42871403.journal: Journal of the Intensive Care Society
42871403.abstract: Spinal cord injury results in transient or permanent disruption to the central nervous system with far reaching multi-system consequences, alongside having profound and devastating effects on the individual, their family and wider society. This review provides an overview on the epidemiology, pathophysiology and clinical presentation of spinal cord injury. The clinical syndromes of spinal cord injury are also discussed in detail. The medical and surgical management strategies of spinal cord injury in the acute phase is considered, alongside highlighting the importance of early referral to dedicated spinal rehabilitation services. The natural history and prognosis of traumatic spinal cord injury are also discussed.

42864880.title: The Role of Decompressive Craniectomy for Severe Refractory Head Injury.
42864880.abstract: Decompressive craniectomy is a potential therapeutic option for patients with severe traumatic brain injury and refractory intracranial hypertension, although its indications and clinical benefits remain controversial. A total of 4060 articles were identified, with 94.6% published after 2010. Several major randomized clinical trials have shaped current understanding of decompressive craniectomy, including the RESCUE-ASDH for primary intracranial hypertension, and the DECRA and RESCUEicp for secondary intracranial hypertension. RESCUE-ASDH and DECRA showed no overall benefit and suggested potential harm associated with decompressive craniectomy. RESCUEicp trial showed reduced mortality and sustained long-term improvement in a subset of patients, although many survivors remained in a dependent state. Critical appraisal of the inclusion and exclusion criteria of these trials, together with supporting evidence from animal studies, suggest that decompressive craniectomy should not be treated as primary intervention for traumatic brain injury. Instead, it may be more appropriately used as an adjunct procedure to prevent worsening cerebral edema following other neurosurgical interventions - such as evaluation of contusions or hematomas - when the operative hemisphere is tight and swollen. Decompressive craniectomy performed solely to control refractory intracranial hypertension in traumatic brain injury is unlikely to provide meaningful patient-centered benefit. Its role as an adjunct procedure after evacuation of contusions or hematomas remains uncertain, particularly in patients with a low predicted risk of unfavorable outcome. Decision regarding decompressive craniectomy should incorporate shared decision making and reflect careful consideration of the functional outcomes acceptable to patients and their families.

42857555.title: Management of Bilateral Subacute Subdural Hematomas with Concomitant Subarachnoid Hemorrhage in a Diabetic Patient with HIV in Cameroon: A Case Report.
42857555.abstract: Bilateral subdural hematomas occurring simultaneously with subarachnoid hemorrhage in a traumatic context are rare and pose considerable diagnostic challenges. Comorbidities such as diabetes and HIV may further worsen prognosis and complicate management. This case underscores the vital importance of early diagnosis and multidisciplinary care in patients with subacute subdural hematomas and subarachnoid hemorrhage, particularly when compounded by comorbidities in resource‑limited settings. We report the case of a 44-year-old housewife who was diabetic and living with HIV. She presented with severe headaches followed by altered consciousness with severe coma, and Cushing's triad two weeks after a minor head trauma. Brain CT scan revealed a bilateral panhemispheric subacute subdural hematoma (SASDH) associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage. Management consisted of emergent bilateral burr hole craniotomy for drainage, combined with measures to reduce intracranial pressure and prevent secondary brain injury of systemic origin. Her course was complicated by infection and hypertensive crisis; both were successfully managed. Glycemic control was achieved and antiretroviral therapy optimized. Clinical and radiological outcomes were ultimately favorable. This case underscores the importance of early diagnosis and multidisciplinary management of subdural hematomas in patients with diabetes and HIV. Beyond timely surgical intervention with burr‑hole craniotomy, comprehensive intensive care - including vigilant monitoring, early detection, and prompt control of complications - can significantly improve survival and optimize neurological outcomes.

42857510.title: Novel Use of an Intravenous Flow Regulator for Controlled Cerebrospinal Fluid Drainage in External Ventricular Drains: A Prospective Single-Center Pilot Study of 300 Patients.
42857510.abstract: Accurate control of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) drainage through external ventricular drains (EVDs) is essential in neurosurgical intensive care. Conventional systems rely on hydrostatic level adjustment, which is operator-dependent and imprecise. This article evaluates the safety, feasibility, and performance of a simple intravenous flow regulator, commonly used in infusion sets, as a cost-effective means of controlling CSF drainage in EVDs across all clinical indications. A prospective observational study was conducted in 300 patients requiring EVD insertion. A standard intravenous flow regulator was attached inline between the EVD outlet tubing and the collection chamber, allowing graded mechanical control of CSF flow. Data regarding patient demographics, indication, drainage volumes, complications, and outcomes were collected. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS v25 and GraphPad Prism v9. Of 300 patients (mean age 46.3 ± 18.2 years; 186 males), indications included intraventricular hemorrhage (28%), subarachnoid hemorrhage (24%), traumatic brain injury (22%), hydrocephalus (14%), posterior fossa surgery (7%), and others (5%). Mean CSF output was 210 ± 50 mL/day. Overdrainage occurred in 3.7%, blockage in 2.3%, and infection in 4.3%. The mortality rate was 10%, unrelated to the device. Nursing satisfaction was high (92%), and cost reduction was approximately 40% compared with conventional adjustable systems. An intravenous flow regulator provides safe, precise, and low-cost mechanical control of CSF outflow in EVDs. This modification offers a viable alternative for resource-limited neurosurgical units.

42854416.title: The association between fluid management and hemodynamic parameters in patients with acute brain injury.
42854416.abstract: Higher fluid input (FI) resulting in more positive fluid balance (FB) is associated with worse outcome in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) and traumatic brain injury (TBI) patients. Although venous congestion could be a possible mechanism behind these associations, hemodynamic studies elucidating these associations are scarce. We aimed to explore the association of FI and FB with cardiac index (CI) and central venous pressure (CVP) in aSAH and TBI patients. We performed a prospective observational study, including aSAH and TBI patients aged ≥ 18 years admitted to the ICU and with an ICU stay of > 48 h. The association of daily FI and cumulative FB during the first week after admission with mean daily values of CI, CVP, intracranial pressure (ICP) and cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) were analyzed with linear mixed effects models and adjusted for time since ICU admission. We included 55 patients; mean age 51 years (SD 18), 58% female and median GCS 7 (IQR 3-12). CI change with 1 L higher cumulative FB was -0.060 L/min/m2 [95% CI -0.101 to -0.018]. CVP was 0.349 mmHg [95% CI 0.077-0.620] higher with 1 L higher cumulative FB, CPP 0.365 mmHg [95% CI -0.750-0.039] lower with 1 L higher cumulative FB, and ICP 0.499 mmHg [95% CI 0.166-0.866] higher with 1 L higher cumulative FB. Higher cumulative FB is associated with lower CI, higher CVP and ICP increase, which might indicate cerebral venous congestion and represent an important causal factor in the association of positive FB with poor outcome.

42851974.title: Refractory Status Epilepticus Following Erroneous Intrathecal Injection of Tranexamic Acid: A Case Report and Long-Term Follow-Up and Narrative Review.
42851974.abstract: Accidental intrathecal injection of tranexamic acid (TXA) is a rare but catastrophic preventable adverse event associated with high mortality and severe neurological consequences. It represents a major neurological emergency that requires immediate specialized management. A 32-year-old man erroneously received an intrathecal injection of 300 mg of TXA instead of bupivacaine during a saphenous vein stripping procedure. He rapidly developed refractory myoclonic status epilepticus, sympathetic hyperactivity, and rhabdomyolysis. Management included multiple antiseizure medications, continuous EEG-guided sedation, and targeted use of neuromuscular blockade. The patient recovered without immediate neurological deficit but developed persistent cognitive impairment and posttraumatic stress disorder at follow-up. This case highlights the severe neurotoxicity of intrathecal TXA and the importance of early and aggressive intensive care management. It also underscores the need for long-term multidisciplinary follow-up for the assessment of anesthetic procedure-related complications.

42851708.title: Functional recovery of patients with moderate and severe traumatic brain injury after extended and standard early rehabilitation.
42851708.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is one of the leading causes of morbidity, disability and mortality in all age groups. Treatment and early rehabilitation are crucial to the overall level of recovery. The objective is to compare the effects of standard and extended early rehabilitation on the functional recovery of patients with moderate and severe traumatic brain injury. A prospective experimental study comprised 114 patients with moderate and severe TBI, randomly divided into two groups. The patients of the experimental group had kinesitherapy 7 days a week, twice a day for 45 min, and the patients of the control group had kinesitherapy 7 days a week, twice a day for 30 min. The follow-up parameters were: age sex, clinical characteristics, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), Functional Independence Measure (FIM), Barthel Index (BI) on admission and discharge and Glasgow Outcome Score (GOS) at discharge. 114 patients were randomly divided into two groups of 57 patients each. Males dominate (75.4%), the average age of the sample was Me = 59.0. There was no statistically significant difference between the groups in gender, age and clinical characteristics, GCS on admission; 59(51.8%) patient had severe, 55 (48.2%) moderate TBI, at discharge: 12 (10.5%) had severe, 11(9.6%) moderate and 91(79.8%) mild TBI. FIM of the experimental group was 18 vs. 70 and of the control group was 18 vs. 50, BI of the experimental group was 0 vs. 61 and of the control group was 0 vs. 32. GOS at discharge: complete recovery in the experimental group 9, in the control group 7, mild deficit 22 vs. 15, severe deficit 22 vs. 28, vegetative state 4 vs. 7. Normalized improvement (ratio of achieved progress to maximum possible progress) was higher in the prolonged early rehabilitation group: for FIM (48% vs. 30%), BI (61% vs. 32%) and slightly less for GCS (100% vs. 92%). Although no statistically significant difference on functional recovery between the groups was found, however, a difference in percentage progress was found in favor of extended early rehabilitation, but for a final conclusion it is necessary to make a follow-up after inpatient rehabilitation.

42849085.title: Potential role of vitamin B12 supplementation in neurological recovery after severe traumatic brain injury.
42849085.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide, with limited disease-modifying therapeutic options. Preclinical studies suggest a neurotrophic role for vitamin B12 in neuronal repair and functional recovery. In this setting, the metabolic, neurotrophic and nutritional properties of vitamin B12 may play a crucial role. We report the case of a 47-year-old male presenting with severe TBI following a road traffic accident, presenting with a severe TBI at admission and leading to diffuse axonal injury. After initial stabilization and intensive care management, the patient showed persistent cognitive and motor deficits, including disorientation, agitation, and left upper limb weakness. Despite standard supportive care, neurological recovery remained limited. Based on emerging evidence, intramuscular vitamin B12 was initiated. A rapid and marked neurological improvement was already evident by the third day after initiation of intramuscular vitamin B12 supplementation. The patient achieved full cognitive recovery, restoration of motor strength, and resolution of behavioral disturbances, with minimal residual symptoms at discharge. This case highlights a possible adjunctive role of vitamin B12 in promoting neurological recovery after severe TBI. While causality cannot be established, the temporal association and biological plausibility support further investigation on vitamin B12 properties through controlled clinical studies.

42844081.title: Fat Embolism Syndrome as Cause of Death in a Multiorgan Donor With Successful Utilization of Thoracic and Abdominal Organs.
42844081.abstract: Fat embolism syndrome is an under-reported consideration in organ donation and is most often associated with long-bone trauma and intramedullary fixation. We describe a deceased donor who, after a traffic accident with bilateral femoral fractures treated by bilateral intramedullary nailing, developed hypoxemia, encephalopathy out of proportion to sedation, and a petechial rash consistent with fat embolism syndrome by clinical criteria. Despite intensive care, brain death was determined according to national standards and donation after brain death proceeded. Donor optimization followed lung-protective ventilation and standard hemodynamic targets. Predonation assessments met acceptance thresholds, and procurement showed no macroscopic intravascular fat in graft vessels with only scattered fat droplets in the abdominal cavity without luminal obstruction. The heart, bilateral lungs, liver, pancreas, and both kidneys were transplanted. Early courses were uncomplicated, with immediate heart and liver function, primary graft dysfunction grade 0 at 72 hours for the lungs, early insulin independence after pancreas transplantation, and primary kidney graft function. No embolic phenomena attributable to donor fat embolism syndrome were observed, and three-month follow-up was unremarkable. These findings support physiology-based evaluation rather than categorical exclusion of donors with suspected fat embolism syndrome.

42842056.title: Impact of initial disease severity and metabolic stress on mortality in patients with suspected external ventricular drain-associated infection.
42842056.abstract: External ventricular drainage (EVD) remains indispensable for managing intracranial pressure and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) disorders. Despite advances in neurosurgical care and infection prevention, EVD-related infections still contribute substantially to morbidity and mortality. This study aimed to identify predictors of mortality and evaluate the clinical relevance of infection-related and metabolic parameters in patients with suspected EVD-associated infection undergoing EVD placement. We retrospectively analyzed all adult patients who underwent EVD insertion and were clinically suspected of having an EVD-associated infection at a tertiary hospital over an 18-month period. Data from electronic medical records included demographics, neurological diagnosis, comorbidities, catheter characteristics, laboratory results, and antimicrobial therapy. EVD-associated infection was defined according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) criteria. Statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics 26. A total of 102 patients with clinically suspected EVD-associated infection were evaluated. CSF cultures were positive in 33 (32%) cases, most frequently yielding Staphylococcus epidermidis and Acinetobacter baumannii . Intensive care unit (ICU) admission was associated with higher crude mortality rates, likely reflecting greater baseline neurological severity. Initial Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score (aOR = 0.85, p = 0.005) was found to be an independent predictor of mortality. Neither sex nor comorbidities predicted death. Hyperglycemia (> 140 mg/dL) and elevated lactate (> 1.2 mmol/L) independently associated with 30-day mortality. Shorter catheterization duration (≤ 5 days) also predicted death, likely reflecting greater neurological compromise. In our selected cohort of patients with clinically suspected EVD-associated infection, CSF culture positivity was not independently associated with mortality, although patients with culture-confirmed infection exhibited higher CSF pleocytosis and Cell Index (CI) values. Among patients with clinically suspected EVD-associated infection, initial neurological severity, together with markers of systemic metabolic stress, were independently associated with 30-day mortality. Hyperglycemia and elevated lactate emerged as key prognostic markers. While elevated CI values may support the diagnosis of culture-confirmed infection, CI did not demonstrate independent prognostic value for mortality. These findings should be interpreted within the context of this selected cohort and should not be generalized to the overall EVD population. Larger prospective studies including a greater number of culture-confirmed infections are needed to confirm these results.

42838852.title: Response to: "Early benzodiazepine treatment and electrographic seizures after febrile status epilepticus".
42838852.abstract: We appreciate Inui et al.'s comments regarding the divergent prognostic outcomes of patients with electrographic seizures (ESz) between our studies. The poorer prognosis in their cohort compared to ours likely stems from three key differences. First, baseline disease severity significantly differed. Our cohort predominantly consisted of milder cases, such as febrile seizures, with only 17.2% requiring pediatric intensive care. Conversely, Inui et al. evaluated critically ill patients with acute encephalopathy, whose severe ESz EEG features-such as periodic discharges-inherently indicate a poorer prognosis. Second, the timing of EEG recordings varied. We evaluated EEGs during the hyperacute phase in the emergency department (median 77.5 min post-onset). In contrast, Inui et al. assessed patients 7-96 h post-onset, reflecting a substantially delayed timeframe. Third, diverging interpretations and treatments of evolving rhythmic delta activity (RDA) likely contributed to the prognostic gap. Our institution's protocol treats evolving RDA as a seizure equivalent, warranting immediate therapeutic intervention in the emergency setting. We have previously demonstrated that this early, RDA-targeted intervention yields better clinical outcomes. These discrepancies highlight the necessity for future studies incorporating comprehensive, early EEG evaluations. Further investigation is essential to clarify the precise prognostic implications of post-ictal evolving RDA and to establish a clinical consensus on the necessity of active therapeutic intervention.

42838703.title: Chronic posthypoxic myoclonus: Lance-Adams syndrome.
42838703.abstract: Lance-Adams syndrome (LAS) is a rare condition described as chronic intentional myoclonus following prolonged hypoxia. With limited cases of the condition, no standardised diagnostic criteria, and features overlapping acute myoclonus status epilepticus (MSE), diagnosis and management are challenging.Our case is a man in his 20s, who was admitted to the intensive care unit following two in-hospital cardiac arrests. He consequently developed persistent generalised myoclonic seizures despite multiple antiepileptics and sedation. CT, MRI and electroencephalogram (EEG) ruled out a diagnosis of MSE, making LAS more likely. Ketamine was ultimately required to terminate the generalised myoclonic seizures after which antiepileptic drugs were optimised to reduce residual intention myoclonus.This report highlights key features prompting the clinical suspicion of LAS in a patient who has no significant evidence of brain injury, preserved consciousness with continued severe generalised myoclonus and outlines pharmacological and neurophysiological management.

42835272.title: Ketamine use in the refractory and super refractory status epilepticus: a systematic review.
42835272.abstract: Refractory status epilepticus (RSE) and super-refractory status epilepticus (SRSE) are associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and intensive care requirements. Ketamine has emerged as a potential adjunct because of its N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonism and relatively favourable haemodynamic profile. To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of ketamine in RSE and SRSE resolution. This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020 and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024625516). PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Biblioteca Virtual en Salud were searched from inception to 20 November 2025. Two independent reviewers screened studies, extracted clinical, therapeutic, electroencephalographic, haemodynamic, and survival data, and assessed risk of bias using National Institutes of Health quality assessment tools. Meta-analysis was not performed because of substantial heterogeneity. Twelve studies comprising 491 patients were included. Ketamine was generally administered as part of multimodal therapy after failure of several antiseizure medications and intravenous anaesthetics. Infusion rates ranged from 0.05 mg/kg/h to 10.5 mg/kg/h, and treatment duration ranged from 6 h to 29 days. Study-defined response rates following ketamine initiation ranged from 43.3% for complete electrographic seizure cessation to 100% for overall RSE/SRSE resolution; however, the highest estimates often reflected combined treatment rather than ketamine alone. Short-term or hospital survival ranged from 45.8% to 81.8%. Immediate haemodynamic deterioration appeared uncommon, although attribution was limited by baseline instability and concomitant therapy. Ketamine-containing regimens were associated with clinically relevant seizure reduction or cessation in RSE/SRSE, without a consistent signal of acute haemodynamic harm. However, the independent effect of ketamine on sustained seizure control, survival, and functional recovery remains uncertain. Prospective comparative studies using standardised dosing, timing, and outcome definitions are required. PROSPERO identifier CRD42024625516.

42834321.title: Prognostic Significance of Early Fever in Convulsive Status Epilepticus: Insights from the ICTAL Registry.
42834321.abstract: Fever is one of the secondary brain insults that may alter outcome after acute brain injury. However, its deleterious role in convulsive status epilepticus (CSE) remains insufficiently established in humans. We aimed to determine whether early fever is associated with functional neurological outcome in patients with CSE. We conducted a prospective multicenter study using data from the ICTAL Registry, including adult patients with CSE admitted to 23 French intensive care units (ICUs). Fever, defined as a core temperature ≥ 38 °C, was assessed during the first 24 h following CSE onset. Multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to evaluate the independent association between early fever and 90-day favorable neurological outcome, defined as a Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) score of 4-5. Among 952 included patients, 382 (41.2%) developed fever within the first 24 h of ICU stay. The underlying causes of fever appeared to be multifactorial, including infectious etiologies related to CSE itself (either systemic or central nervous system infections), early aspiration pneumonia, and the intensity of convulsive activity. After matching, only the intensity of convulsive activity remained associated with the occurrence of fever. In multivariable analyses, independent predictors of favorable outcome were age < 60 years and a Charlson Comorbidity Index < 3, whereas cerebral insult as CSE etiology and refractory CSE were associated with unfavorable outcome. Early fever was not independently associated with 90-day functional outcome. Early fever is highly prevalent in convulsive status epilepticus and appears to reflect seizure intensity rather than overall disease severity. It was not independently associated with 90-day neurological outcome, suggesting no major prognostic impact, although a modest association cannot be excluded. These findings should therefore be interpreted with caution and do not allow conclusions regarding the impact of temperature-control strategies.

42829684.title: Reappraising the bifrontal decompressive craniectomy: A systematic literature review of indications, outcomes, and clinical applications.
42829684.abstract: Bifrontal decompressive craniectomy (BDC) is used to manage elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) from bilateral frontal swelling caused by severe traumatic brain injury (TBI), malignant cerebral edema, or other acute intracranial pathologies, but conflicting outcome data have been reported. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of BDC across various etiologies, identify gaps to guide research, and outline a framework for clinical decision-making. A systematic search of MEDLINE, PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Cochrane databases was conducted. In addition, 3 formalin-fixed, noninjected cadaveric head specimens were dissected to illustrate BDC and its anatomical correlates. Of 410 articles, 54 met inclusion criteria (742 patients). TBI was the leading etiology (656 of 742 patients; 88.4%), notably from motor vehicle collisions (58.4%) and falls (19.7%). On initial examination, 315 of 519 patients (60.7%) had a Glasgow Coma Scale score ≤8. Mean (standard deviation) time from injury to BDC was 2.5 (1.9) days, intensive care unit stay was 12.9 (5.0) days, hospital stay was 66.7 (38.9) days, and time to cranioplasty was 83.4 (40.7) days. Glasgow Outcome Scale values were reported for 494 patients: 205 patients, 5; 75 patients, 4; 71 patients, 3; 24 patients, 2; and 119 patients, 1. BDC may offer a survival benefit in patients with otherwise-fatal elevations in ICP, but cases require more detailed tracking. Functional outcomes vary, and the risks of developing severe disability are substantial. Implementing BDC in acute neurocritical care requires ethically grounded patient selection and family counseling, incorporating prognosis, patient values, and shared decision-making.

42826491.title: Impact of Ramadan on seizure-related emergency department visits in Qatar.
42826491.abstract: Whether Ramadan fasting influences seizure occurrence or severity is an important clinical question for Muslim patients with epilepsy. Prior studies are limited and show conflicting results. We conducted a retrospective observational study of all seizure-related emergency department (ED) visits in Hamad Medical Corporation hospitals (Qatar) during Ramadan and the adjacent month before and after, over 2021-2023. Patient data (demographics, seizure features, outcomes, and management) were collected. We compared Ramadan versus non-Ramadan periods, including subgroup analyses for first-time seizures and known epileptic patients. Additionally, an age- and sex-matched case-control analysis (n = 142) was performed, matching fasting Ramadan cases to non-Ramadan controls. Among 1492 seizure-related ED visits (470 during Ramadan; 1022 in combined non-Ramadan months), the proportion of total ED visits due to seizures was similar during and outside Ramadan (0.8%). No significant differences were found in clinical severity markers (rates of status epilepticus, seizure clustering, hospital admissions, ICU admissions, or 72-hour revisits) between Ramadan and non-Ramadan periods (all p > 0.05). In the matched case-control subset, fasting patients were more likely to receive intravenous antiseizure medication loading in the ED (40.0% vs 18.3%, p = 0.005). Fasting patients with history of epilepsy had a higher rate of prior good seizure control (69.8% vs 32.7%, p < 0.001) and were less likely to be started on new antiseizure medication (5.7% vs 20.4%, p = 0.026). Ramadan was not associated with increased seizure-related ED burden. Emergency physicians modified acute management for fasting subjects by favouring intravenous antiseizure medication loading and deferring new oral regimen initiation.

42826408.title: Diagnostic performance of bedside transcranial ultrasound after decompressive craniectomy: a comparative study with cranial computed tomography.
42826408.abstract: The aim of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic effectiveness and accuracy of bedside transcranial ultrasonography performed through the craniectomy in diagnosing typical post-decompressive craniectomy (DC) complications, using cranial CT as the reference standard. This retrospective study analyzed 88 consecutive patients who underwent DC between January 2023 and December 2024. In each case, bedside transcraniectomy ultrasonography (BTUS) was performed prior to CT imaging, and findings from both modalities were compared. Diagnostic agreement was evaluated using Cohen's kappa coefficient. The sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value were calculated for BTUS in identifying complications, including hematomas, hygroma, hydrocephalus, abscess, edema, and midline shift. BTUS has high diagnostic accuracy compared with CT, with overall sensitivities ranging from 59.4% (edema) to 100% (hematomas) and specificities between 94.2% and 100%. Strong or almost perfect agreement (κ > 0.8) was observed for most complications. The rate of false negatives was lowest for space-occupying lesions and highest for diffuse pathologies, such as edema. Negative predictive values remained above 80% for all major complication types. BTUS provides a rapid, noninvasive, and readily available tool for the initial detection and monitoring of postcraniectomy complications. While it does not entirely replace CT in complex cases, it holds significant potential as a first-line screening and monitoring modality in neurosurgical intensive care settings. Bedside ultrasonography can significantly reduce reliance on CT scans, particularly in unstable or radiation-sensitive patients. Incorporating routine BTUS into post-DC monitoring protocols could enhance patient safety, expedite diagnosis, and optimize resource utlization in neurocritical care.

42956907.title: Plasma and Pulmonary Exposure of Eravacycline in a 73-Year-Old Patient with Carbapenem-Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii Pneumonia.
42956907.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) is a major cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia, associated with high mortality and limited therapeutic options. While eravacycline, a novel fluorocycline antibiotic, demonstrates potent in vitro activity against CRAB, real-world pharmacokinetic data-particularly pulmonary exposure in critically ill patients-remain limited. We report a 73-year-old patient with severe traumatic brain injury who developed CRAB pneumonia during hospitalization. Eravacycline was administered intravenously at a weight-based dose of 69 mg every 12 h. Plasma concentrations were measured at steady state, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) samples were collected 13 h after the start of infusion for estimation of epithelial lining fluid (ELF) concentrations using the urea dilution method. The peak plasma concentration was 0.564 mg/L at approximately 1 h post-dose, with an AUC0-24,ss of 6.42 mg·h/L. At 13 h post-dose, eravacycline concentrations were 0.192 mg/L in plasma, 0.924 mg/L in left lung ELF, and 0.393 mg/L in right lung ELF. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of the isolate was 0.5 mg/L. No significant adverse events were observed. This case provides real-world evidence of systemic exposure and measurable pulmonary penetration of eravacycline in a critically ill patient with CRAB pneumonia.

42952828.title: Assessment of the duration of continuous EEG monitoring in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.
42952828.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) can detect seizures and delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) in patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH).
