Because a standard duration of continuous EEG monitoring to capture these complications has not been established in aSAH, we compared a standard 6- or 7-day cEEG monitoring protocol versus longer periods of monitoring. We performed a retrospective analysis of aSAH patients ≥18 years old grouped by standard monitoring protocol (6-7 days, group 1) and those with longer monitoring (>7 days, group 2). Clinical characteristics, EEG features, length of stay (LOS) and functional outcome were compared using univariate analyses. Multivariable analyses tested the association between the groups and vasospasm, DCI, LOS, and modified Rankin Scale (mRS). 19 patients met criteria for group 1 and 16 patients for group 2. We found no difference in EEG's detection of worsening abnormal EEG activity, vasospasm and DCI. ICU and hospital LOS in group 2 were nearly double that of group 1 (ICU: 25.5 (19.5-35) vs. 14 (11-21) days, p = 0.0003; hospital: 32.5 (29.5-48) vs. 18 (13-29) days, p = 0.003). Good outcome (mRS ≤2) at discharge and at 6 months was similar in both groups (21.1% vs. 0% and 56.3% vs. 46.2%). In multivariable analysis, EEG duration was independently associated with ICU and hospital LOS but not with vasospasm, DCI, and mRS at 6 months. Longer EEG monitoring correlated with significantly longer ICU and hospital LOS but not with vasospasm, DCI, and functional outcome at 6 months. Larger studies to confirm our findings are warranted.

42950555.title: Latent class phenotypes and emergency department disposition for patients with traumatic subdural hematoma and midline shift.
42950555.journal: The American journal of emergency medicine
authors: Johns Hopkins Neurotrauma Research Group (Tej D. Azad)
42950555.abstract: Guidelines recommend surgical evacuation for traumatic subdural hematoma (SDH) with >5 mm midline shift (MLS), but emergency department (ED) triage varies between the operating room (OR) and the intensive care unit (ICU). We investigated whether ED disposition to the OR versus ICU was associated with differences in outcomes and whether distinct patient phenotypes modified these associations. We retrospectively identified adult patients from the ACS TQIP dataset with traumatic SDH, MLS >5 mm, and ED disposition to either the ICU or OR. We defined patient phenotypes using latent class analysis (LCA) and investigated associations between ED disposition and outcomes (inpatient mortality, favorable discharge) using risk-adjusted hierarchical logistic regression. We tested for interaction between patient phenotype and ED disposition and repeated these analyses among patients undergoing an ICU stay ≥1 day and cranial surgery. Among 9582 patients, 29% (N = 2794) were triaged to the OR. Two LCA-informed phenotypes emerged: class 1 (older-mild injury) and class 2 (younger-severe injury). There was an interaction between ED disposition and patient phenotype, such that younger-severe patients had lower mortality with OR triage (P < 0.001). In the subgroup of 4573 patients (48%) with ≥1 day of ICU stay who underwent cranial surgery, there was a significant interaction between OR triage and the older-mild phenotype indicating increased mortality (P = 0.003). For traumatic SDH with MLS >5 mm, triage the OR was associated with improved outcomes only among younger, severely-injured patients, while older, mildly-injured patients may benefit from early ICU stabilization. These findings support phenotype-guided ED triage strategies to optimize outcomes.

42943029.title: How to Implement a Ketogenic Diet Therapy in Developing Countries: Colombian Consensus on Ketogenic Diet Therapy Use in the Management of Adults with Drug-Resistant Epilepsy.
42943029.abstract: Drug-resistant epilepsy affects up to one-third of patients with epilepsy and is associated with higher morbidity, mortality, trauma events, psychosocial challenges, and decline in quality of life. In Latin America, disease burden is high and access to advanced therapies remains limited. Ketogenic Diet Therapy (KDT) has been shown to be beneficial in adults, but its implementation requires standardized protocols and experienced multidisciplinary teams. This study aimed to develop practical, evidence-based recommendations to guide the indication, implementation, and follow-up of KDT in adults with drug-resistant epilepsy through expert consensus in Colombia. A modified version of the Nominal Group Technique was used to develop, discuss, and vote on management concepts. Clinical questions were structured using the PICO framework. Literature searches were conducted in PubMed and EMBASE for articles published since 2015, and the evidence was integrated with the experience of a multidisciplinary expert panel. Twelve recommendations were issued, covering commercial formulas, induction and follow-up protocols, individualized dietary interventions, safety, diagnostic support, nutritional supplementation, and drug-diet interactions. The consensus highlights the need for interdisciplinary teams, structured education, early adherence strategies, and close follow-up, and the role of enteral emergency formulas in intensive care settings. Evidence around KDT shows it can be implemented safely as an adjunctive treatment for adults with drug-resistant epilepsy and is reasonable to consider following the failure of two adequate antiseizure medications. Structured implementation may reduce seizure frequency, improve quality of life, and reduce the pharmacological burden. Multicenter prospective studies are needed to further assess efficacy, safety, and resource utilization. These recommendations contribute to closing the gap between evidence and clinical practice.

42940540.title: Knowledge, Confidence and Preparedness for Brain Death Determination Among Anaesthesiology and Reanimation Residents: A National Web-Based Survey with an Embedded Randomised Vignette.
42940540.abstract: Under Turkish law, brain death is determined by two physicians, one of whom is a specialist in anaesthesiology and reanimation or intensive care, a responsibility residents assume soon after qualifying. We assessed whether residents' confidence matches their accuracy, and whether the decision to initiate determination is influenced by the family's attitude toward organ donation. Cross-sectional web-based survey of a national convenience sample of anaesthesiology and reanimation residents in Türkiye. Ten knowledge statements and three clinical vignettes combined the answer and the respondent's confidence in one choice; the primary outcome was the high-confidence error rate. In an embedded participant-blinded randomised vignette, participants were allocated 1:1 to a medically identical scenario describing the family as favourable or opposed to donation. A total of 206 residents were analysed. They answered 80.9% of items correctly but endorsed only 64.2% with confidence; confident answers were correct in 90.8% of instances versus 63.3% of non-confident answers (p < 0.001). The mean high-confidence error rate was 5.9 ± 7.3%, yet 50.5% committed at least one such error, and these errors clustered in four domains. In this exploratory comparison, initiation of determination did not differ between arms (85.6% versus 87.4%; adjusted odds ratio 1.29, 95% CI 0.54-3.05). Only 18.0% felt prepared to serve on a determination board; in univariable and sensitivity analyses, preparedness was associated with case exposure and formal instruction but not with knowledge score. Residents answered most items correctly and were appropriately cautious, yet fewer than one in five felt prepared; self-reported preparedness is not a measure of clinical competence. Supervised clinical exposure, correction of specific misconceptions and communication training are priorities for future intervention studies.

42926880.title: Healthcare providers' perceptions of barriers and facilitators to implementation of an acute traumatic brain injury clinical practice guideline: a CFIR-informed qualitative study at a regional referral hospital in Northern Tanzania.
42926880.journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
42926880.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs), where the burden of injury is disproportionately high, and healthcare resources are often limited. Clinical Practice Guidelines (CPGs) improve the consistency and quality of TBI care by shifting medical decision-making from individual judgement to evidence-based recommendations. The strong link between improved TBI outcomes and CPG adoption has largely been established in high-income country (HIC) hospital settings; evidence on implementing TBI CPGs in LMIC hospital settings is limited. This study explored healthcare providers' experiences to identify barriers and facilitators to implementing a TBI CPG in the Emergency Department (EMD) at Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Center in Northern Tanzania, guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research 2.0 (CFIR). We conducted semi-structured in-depth interviews (IDIs) with doctors and nurses who regularly managed TBI patients at the EMD. We purposively sampled participants between June and August 2023. The research team analysed data using thematic content analysis guided by CFIR domains, developing codes and memos iteratively. 7 nurses and 8 doctors with an average of 5 years of experience caring for patients in the EMD completed in-person, in-depth interviews. Most providers reported frequent exposure to TBI cases and regular use of the CPG in routine clinical practice. However, not all participants reported consistent CPG use, highlighting variation in implementation among providers. Key facilitators included strong interprofessional teamwork, readily accessible guideline materials in clinical areas, availability of diagnostic imaging, and perceived improvements in patient outcomes. Barriers to consistent adherence included ICU bed shortages, limited operating theatre capacity, equipment and medication stock-outs, high patient volumes, staffing pressures, and a lack of structured refresher training or formal audit and feedback mechanisms. Variability in procedural confidence, particularly among less experienced providers, also affected implementation consistency. Our findings show that a TBI CPG is well accepted and largely integrated into routine care among experienced providers. However, sustainability depends on strengthening training, mentorship, audit, and feedback systems for CPG use and on addressing system-level resource constraints. Institutional investment in capacity building is essential to ensure consistent and sustained CPG uptake in our setting.

42925629.title: Monitoring the incidence of hypotension and hypoxemia as systemic secondary insults in patients with catastrophic brain injury evolving to brain death. A prospective observational pilot study.
42925629.abstract: Maintenance of systemic homeostasis and prevention of secondary injury are a cornerstone of treatment in neurocritical care to prevent organ dysfunction and adverse clinical outcome. This is a pilot descriptive and hypothesis generating study aiming to measure and characterize the incidence of systemic hypotension and hypoxemia occurring during the intensive care unit (ICU) stay in patients with catastrophic brain injury potentially evolving to brain death. Adult patients admitted to ICU with catastrophic brain injury and Glasgow coma scale ≤5 have been enrolled. Arterial blood pressure and SpO2 were collected minute by minute from a central station connected to patients' bedside monitors. We report on 24 patients recruited prospectively from the University Hospital of Messina, Italy as a part of a larger ongoing multi-centre study. Patient monitoring data ranged from 8-3000 hours (0.3-125 days). Admission diagnoses were intracerebral haemorrhage (N= 13), TBI (N=4), SAH (N=3), ischaemic stroke (N=3) and hypoxic encephalopathy (N=1). The proportion of valid monitoring time spent with secondary insults and the pressure time index (PTI) are presented and discussed. Day 3 and 4 demonstrated the largest number of secondary insults which were mainly hypotension. Patients who progressed to brain death (n = 9) or who died in ICU from cardiac complications (n = 7) exhibited a more severe and sustained hypotensive burden compared with patients alive at discharge (n = 8). This descriptive study proved useful for identifying an optimal window for tracking insults as well as piloting several key summary measures and visualisations which will be utilized in a larger multi-centre study. In patients with catastrophic brain injury, the incidence of hypotension remains the highest among systemic secondary insults in patients progressing to brain death and cardiac death.

42924157.title: Cenobamate in super-refractory status epilepticus: current evidence from a patient-level synthesis.
42924157.abstract: Super-refractory status epilepticus (SRSE) represents a challenging neurological emergency, with limited therapeutic options after conventional intravenous antiseizure medications (ASMs) and continuous anesthetic therapy have failed. Cenobamate has shown remarkable efficacy in drug-resistant focal epilepsy, but its role in SRSE is currently supported only by isolated case reports. We performed a patient-level synthesis of published cases of cenobamate-treated SRSE, focusing on treatment latency, titration strategy, electroclinical response, concomitant therapies, safety, and functional outcomes. Three publications reporting six patients were identified. Cenobamate was introduced between 13 and 103 days after SRSE onset, following failure of multiple intravenous and oral ASMs, anesthetic agents, and, in most cases, immunomodulatory therapies. Although the timing of treatment initiation varied substantially, electroencephalographic improvement generally occurred within two weeks after cenobamate initiation and was usually accompanied by clinical recovery, successful withdrawal of anesthetic therapy, and liberation from the intensive care unit. Most patients initiated cenobamate at the recommended dose of 12.5 mg/day but underwent individualized dose-escalation schedules compared with the approved outpatient regimen. No cases of drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, severe cardiac adverse events, or treatment discontinuation attributable to cenobamate were reported. Although the available evidence remains limited to a small number of observational reports, this patient-level synthesis identified consistent clinical patterns that support further investigation of cenobamate as an adjunctive therapy for SRSE. At present, no conclusions regarding treatment efficacy can be drawn. Prospective multicenter studies are needed to clarify cenobamate optimal timing, titration strategy, safety, and potential role within SRSE treatment algorithms.

42922046.title: Retrospective review of traumatic brain injury: is skull X-ray still clinically relevant?
42922046.abstract: Head computed tomography (CT) is the gold standard imaging modality for the evaluation of head injury. Skull radiography is no longer recommended in current guidelines due to its limited diagnostic value. Despite this, skull X-ray continues to be used in clinical practice. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of skull X-ray and its association with intracranial injury. We conducted a retrospective study of 12,392 patient encounters with head injury at a single centre between 2018 and 2023. We analysed imaging utilization and findings. Diagnostic performance of skull X-ray was assessed in 759 cases where both X-ray and CT were performed. CT served as the reference standard. Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and associations with intracranial haemorrhage were calculated. Most X-rays were without a fracture (97.0 %). Skull X-ray demonstrated low sensitivity (43.6 %) and high specificity (91.4 %) for detecting skull fractures. Intracranial haemorrhage was present in 13.3 % of cases and occurred in 11.2 % of patients without a fracture on X-ray. Notably, 14.2 % of all CT scans (441 of 3,103) showed haemorrhage without fracture. Fracture on X-ray was associated with increased risk of intracranial haemorrhage (Odds Ratio [OR] 2.85, 95 % Confidence Interval [CI] 1.74-4.68). Clinically significant traumatic brain injury (csTBI) occurred in 17 of 759 encounters (2.2 %), with 12 admissions to intensive care unit, 10 neurosurgical interventions and 8 deaths after head injury. However, the association was not statistically significant (OR 2.64, 95 % CI 0.91-7.67, p = 0.075). Skull radiography has limited diagnostic value, fails to detect intracranial injury and may provide false reassurance in a clinical setting. CT remains the preferred imaging modality, and routine use of skull X-ray should be reconsidered.

42911500.title: Intracranial EEG for Detecting Epileptic Activity in Acute Brain Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
42911500.abstract: Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) has been increasingly explored as part of multimodal neuromonitoring in acute brain injury, yet its diagnostic benefit compared with continuous surface EEG (suEEG) remains uncertain. We have performed a meta-analysis to quantify seizure and rhythmic and periodic pattern detection rates and concordance with suEEG. Secondary objectives were the assessment of correlations with brain injury, safety, and techniques. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, and Embase were searched for studies reporting iEEG monitoring in adults with acute brain injury. Epileptic patterns were harmonized to the American Clinical Neurophysiology Society Standardized EEG Nomenclature for Critically Ill Patients (ACNS) 2021 terminology, classifying events as seizures/status epilepticus (SZ/SE) or rhythmic and periodic/ictal-interictal continuum patterns (RPP/IIC). Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa scale and custom bias domains. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted for (i) pooled proportions and (ii) pooled paired within-patient comparisons. Twelve cohorts (n = 864 participants) with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (n = 343), traumatic brain injury (n = 351), and mixed etiologies (n = 170) were included. Six studies provided paired iEEG-suEEG data (n = 273). Techniques were based on a strip or depth electrode. No severe adverse events were reported. Pooled iEEG versus suEEG incidence rates were respectively: 26% vs. 15% for SZ/SE, 47% vs. 34% for RPP/IIC, and 57% vs. 37% for clinically relevant epileptic activity. Pooled paired analysis demonstrated that iEEG additionally detected SZ/SE in 16.5% of patients [pooled McNemar odds ratio (OR) 3.46 (0.51-23.6); I2 = 63%; p = 0.158] and RPP/IIC in 26% [pooled OR 4.25 (0.19-96.1); I2 = 73%; p = 0.236], while suEEG was negative. Sensitivity analyses for high-risk studies or cohort overlap did not alter the results. Invasive EEG monitoring substantially increased the detection of seizures and RPP/IIC patterns compared with suEEG alone in patients with acute brain injury, serving as a promising monitoring adjunct.

42908636.title: Cardiac troponin T and 28-day mortality in traumatic brain injury: a retrospective cohort study and machine learning prediction model.
42908636.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) frequently induces cardiac dysfunction via the brain-heart axis, yet the prognostic value of cardiac troponin T (cTnT) in TBI remains incompletely characterized. This study investigated thye association between cTnT levels and 28-day all-cause mortality in TBI patients and developed a machine learning-based prediction model. This retrospective cohort study included 837 adult TBI patients from the MIMIC-III/IV databases (development cohort) and 121 patients from a single Chinese center (external validation cohort). The first cTnT measurement within 24 h of ICU admission was analyzed. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) regression was used to explore nonlinear relationships. cTnT was categorized into quartiles (Q1 ≤ 0.03, Q2 0.03-0.06, Q3 0.06-0.17, Q4 > 0.17 ng/mL). A two-step Boruta plus LASSO feature selection identified 13 robust predictors. Five machine learning algorithms (Random Forest, BART, GBM, CTREE, SVM) were trained. The primary outcome was 28-day all-cause mortality. Among 837 patients, 217 (25.9%) died within 28 days. RCS revealed a significant nonlinear association (P for nonlinearity < 0.001). In multivariable Cox regression adjusted for the 12 LASSO-selected covariates (excluding cTnT quartile itself), patients in Q3 and Q4 had nearly twofold higher mortality risks compared with Q1 (HR = 2.01, 95% CI: 1.37-2.95, p < 0.001; and HR = 1.96, 95% CI: 1.31-2.93, p = 0.001, respectively). Random Forest achieved the best discriminative performance, with an internal AUC of 0.783 and an external validation AUC of 0.706 (95% CI: 0.584-0.828). The model also demonstrated good calibration (Brier score = 0.155) and favorable clinical utility across clinically relevant threshold probabilities as shown by decision curve analysis. Elevated cTnT is independently associated with 28-day mortality in TBI patients, with a potential risk threshold of ≥0.06 ng/mL. The Random Forest model integrating cTnT with clinical variables provides moderate mortality prediction. cTnT may serve as an integrative marker of systemic stress and multi-organ dysfunction in TBI.

42906612.title: Optimum timing of cerebral computed tomography angiography for determination of death using neurological criteria: a retrospective sensitivity cohort study.
42906612.abstract: Cerebral computed tomography angiography (CTA) is increasingly incorporated into national guidelines to confirm cerebral circulatory arrest during the determination of death using neurological criteria. However, implementation remains limited due to studies showing variable sensitivity. Clinical observations suggest the time elapsed from the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia, defined as the appearance of fixed and dilated pupils and loss of cough and gag reflexes, significantly influences CTA sensitivity. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of this time interval on test sensitivity. We retrospectively assessed 118 intensive care unit patients undergoing determination of death using neurological criteria. Cerebral CTA was used to confirm cerebral circulatory arrest based on a four-point scoring system. Patients were categorised according to the time elapsed from the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia to the investigation. Cerebral CTA did not confirm cerebral circulatory arrest in 15/118 (13%) patients, yielding an overall sensitivity of 87.3% (95%CI 79.6-92.5%). Notably, 93.3% (95%CI 66.0-99.7%) of false-negative results occurred within 12 h of the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia. Patients were secondarily stratified into early (≤ 12 h) and late (> 12 h) groups, revealing a significantly higher sensitivity in the late group (67.4%, 95%CI 51.3-80.5% vs. 98.7%, 95%CI 91.8-100%, p < 0.001). The sensitivity of cerebral CTA increases with the time elapsed after the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia. We recommend delaying cerebral CTA until at least 12 h after the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia, and, in case of inconclusive results, test repetition at least 12 h later. Further work is required to confirm our findings and increase diagnostic confidence.

42903085.title: Integrating 72-h BUN/Cr trajectories with interpretable machine learning for 28-day mortality after acute stroke: a dual-center landmark study.
42903085.abstract: The blood urea nitrogen-to-creatinine ratio (BUN/Cr) may reflect renal perfusion and systemic stress, but its early course after acute stroke is unclear. We identified 72-h BUN/Cr trajectories and assessed their role in interpretable machine-learning evaluation of 28-day mortality. This dual-center landmark study included 2,805 ICU patients with acute ischemic stroke, nontraumatic intracerebral hemorrhage, or nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) version 3.1. Before modeling, patients were split into a training set (n = 1,964) and an internal test set (n = 841). The trajectory and prediction models developed in the training set were applied without modification to the internal test set and the Qinghai external validation cohort (n = 387). Eight algorithms and prespecified nested models were evaluated using Cox regression, discrimination, calibration, paired comparisons, decision curves, and TreeSHAP. A quadratic three-class model identified low/stable, high U-shaped, and rising-to-plateau patterns, with mortality rates of 21.6, 35.9, and 39.7%. Adjusted hazard ratios versus Class 1 were 1.87 (95% CI 1.25-2.79) for Class 2 and 1.73 (1.31-2.29) for Class 3. The training-selected Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) achieved an AUROC of 0.734 (95% CI 0.695-0.773), a calibration slope of 0.894, and an O/E ratio of 1.015 in the internal test set. In the Qinghai external validation cohort, the AUROC was 0.624 (95% CI 0.559-0.689), the calibration slope was 0.459, and the O/E ratio was 1.920. Adding trajectory class to a model already containing routine clinical and static renal variables changed the AUROC by 0.003 in the internal test set (p = 0.515) and -0.014 in the Qinghai external validation cohort (p = 0.130), without a clear gain in discrimination. BUN/Cr trajectories were associated with post-landmark mortality and summarized the three-day renal course. Training-selected LightGBM showed moderate internal discrimination and underwent frozen external evaluation. Trajectory class added modest information beyond routine clinical and static renal variables, while the combined approach provides an interpretable framework for 72-h reassessment.

42899481.title: The CBI-M framework for characterization of traumatic brain injury: Evaluation of performance using data from the CENTER-TBI and TRACK-TBI prospective cohort studies.
42899481.abstract: The CBI-M Framework, incorporating Clinical, Biomarker, Imaging, and Modifier pillars, was recently proposed to provide a comprehensive characterization of patients with acute traumatic brain injury (TBI). Such detailed characterization reflects the clinical and biological heterogeneity of TBI, and is considered essential to inform appropriate clinical management. Still unclear is the extent to which CBI-M captures clinically relevant heterogeneity in relation to diagnosis, clinical care pathways, and longer-term outcome. Prior to broad implementation into clinical practice and research, its diagnostic and prognostic performance needs to be ascertained. In this study, we aim to explore how CBI-M and its constituent pillars relate to diagnosis, clinical care pathways, and outcome in two large contemporary TBI cohorts. We analyzed data of patients with acute TBI enrolled in the European-based CENTER-TBI (N = 4,509) and US-based TRACK-TBI (N = 2,552) prospective observational studies. We assessed associations of the CBI-M Framework, its pillars, and pillar components with key clinical endpoints: diagnosis (traumatic intracranial injury on computed tomography); care pathways (hospital admission, intensive care admission, intracranial pressure monitoring, and major cranial surgery); and outcomes at 6 months post-injury (mortality, Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOSE), and health-related quality of life (HRQoL)). Discriminatory performance was calculated using the AUC and explained variability expressed with Nagelkerke's pseudo-R2. Prognostic performance was compared to the established IMPACT-Lab and CRASH-CT prediction models in their respective target populations. For diagnostic and care path endpoints full CBI-M models achieved excellent discrimination (AUC CENTER-TBI: from 0.83 to 0.95; TRACK-TBI: from 0.88 to 0.98), and high proportions of explained variability (pseudo-R2 CENTER-TBI: from 0.41 to 0.72; TRACK-TBI: from 0.55 to 0.80). Contributions of individual pillars varied by endpoint, with the Biomarker pillar contributing most for CT-defined abnormalities and the Imaging pillar to major cranial surgery. For mortality and unfavorable outcome (GOSE ≤ 4) similarly strong performance was observed: CENTER-TBI: AUC 0.89 (95% Confidence intervals (CI) [0.88,0.90]) and 0.92 (95% CI [0.91,0.94]) respectively; pseudo-R2 0.53 (95% CI [0.50,0.57]) and 0.55 (95% CI [0.51,0.59]) respectively; TRACK-TBI: AUC 0.91 (95% CI [0.89,0.93]) and 0.95 (95% CI [0.93,0.97]) respectively; pseudo-R2 0.57 (95% CI [0.52,0.62] and 0.57 (95% CI [0.50, 0.64] respectively), whereas performance for HRQoL was modest. Compared to the IMPACT-Lab and CRASH-CT models in their respective target populations, pseudo-R2 values suggest that the full CBI-M model was more strongly associated with 6-month mortality and unfavorable outcomes. Methodological limitations include the restriction to analysis of data from high-income settings, limiting generalizability, the absence of three elements of the modifier pillar in the datasets accessed, and risk of possible reverse causality in some analyses. CBI-M provides a robust multimodal characterization of acute TBI that aligns closely with clinical decision-making and outcomes. Further prospective validation and optimization are justified and needed to inform implementation of the CBI-M Framework in clinical practice and research.

42895303.title: Assessing Medication Confounders Before Determination of Brain Death/Death by Neurologic Criteria: A Primer, with Opioids as a Worked Example.
42895303.journal: American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists
42895303.abstract: To provide a primer on how clinicians, particularly pharmacists, can systematically assess whether a medication may confound determination of brain death/death by neurologic criteria (BD/DNC), using pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic principles that can be applied to any agent with the aid of tertiary references, and using opioids as a worked example. All major guidelines require exclusion of central nervous system (CNS) depressant effect before BD/DNC determination, yet none provides a general method for deciding when a given medication has cleared. Rather than cataloging every agent, this primer sets out the parameters that govern how long any drug can suppress the neurologic examination: lipophilicity and volume of distribution, elimination pathway and the effect of hepatic or renal dysfunction, active metabolites, and the context-sensitive half-life, which lengthens with the duration of an infusion and is not predicted by the elimination half-life. Special states, including obesity, hypothermia, extracorporeal support, and overdose, further prolong effect; in overdose, delayed absorption and saturable elimination can invalidate the customary five-half-life rule. Routine toxicology screens miss many relevant substances, including synthetic opioids. Opioids illustrate the framework across three common scenarios: exposure before arrival, continuous infusion, and overdose. No validated serum concentration threshold defines clearance for most CNS depressants, and the safest determination rests on structured pharmacokinetic reasoning, toxicology consultation, and institutional protocols that specify how confounders are screened for and excluded, rather than on any single number or fixed waiting period.

42892218.title: Incidence of severe mountain bike-related injuries and mortality: A 15-year statewide analysis.
42892218.abstract: Mountain biking has grown in popularity and has seen widespread trail development but carries risk for severe trauma. No studies have analysed severe injuries in the context of contemporary mountain biking to understand trends and modifiable risk factors. To describe the incidence and longitudinal characteristics of severe injuries related to mountain biking in Tasmania, Australia. Retrospective analysis of all patients admitted to Tasmanian public hospitals with severe mountain bike (MTB)-related injuries from 1st January 2010-31 st December 2024. Incidence of severe MTB-related injuries (including mortality) as defined by hospital admission to an intensive care unit or neurosurgery high dependency unit; for emergency surgery (in <4 h); or transfer intra- or interstate for definitive treatment. Secondary outcomes were annual injury trends in mechanism of injury, body regions, injury profiles, and incident location. For the total period there were 85 severe injuries (including 4 mortalities) from 6643 MTB-related emergency department (ED) presentations. Annual severe MTB-related cases increased over the 15 years from 0.8 cases/year before 2015, to 8.1 cases/year in later years. Severe injury cases accounted for only 1.3% of all MTB-related ED presentations. Most severely injured riders were male (97%); the mean age was 36 years (SD 16.9) for the total period, but this increased from 18.5 years (SD 5.8) pre-2015-36.9 years (SD 16.8) post-2015. Executing a jump was the dominant mechanism of injury (44%), followed by fall over handlebars (14%), obstacle collision (11%) and adverse trail conditions (9%). The most injured body regions were abdomen (31%), neck (23%) and thorax/chest (20%). The most common types of injuries were fracture/dislocation (44%), abdominal organ injury (24%) and thoracic organ injury (15%). Spinal cord injury occurred in 6% of cases and traumatic brain injury in 7%. Over 50% of severe injury incidents occurred on purpose-built MTB trails. Severe MTB-related injuries increased proportionally to all MTB-related injuries suggesting the increase was largely driven by rider exposure. Targeted injury prevention strategies, safe trail design, and understanding risk factors are needed to ensure safe progression of this popular sport.

42885258.title: Key Predictors of Cerebral Vasospasm Following Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
42885258.abstract: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is a life-threatening condition often leading to complications such as cerebral vasospasm, which causes delayed cerebral ischemia and increases mortality. In intensive care, early identification of vasospasm risk factors by nurses is essential for timely intervention and improved outcomes. We sought to review and synthesize evidence on risk factors associated with cerebral vasospasm after SAH and inform early risk assessment and nursing care strategies in intensive care. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies. A comprehensive search was conducted on August 30 to 31, 2024, across 8 databases. Quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist and the Risk of Bias (RoB 2.0) tool. Thirty-eight studies were included in the systematic review, of which 27 were included in the meta-analysis, involving 19 033 patients. Clinical severity measures were most strongly associated with cerebral vasospasm, including Modified Fisher grade (odds ratio (OR) = 2.88; 95% confidence interval (CI), 2.04-4.07), Fisher grade (OR = 2.27; 95% CI, 1.91-2.69), and hemodynamic status (OR = 2.56; 95% CI, 1.17-5.59). Aneurysm-related factors and comorbid conditions were associated with increased risk of cerebral vasospasm, whereas clinical biomarkers and inflammatory markers showed relatively smaller effect sizes. Clinical severity scales and hemodynamic status are the strongest predictors of cerebral vasospasm following SAH. These findings support early risk stratification and the implementation of structured monitoring strategies to improve patient outcomes.PROSPERO trial registration number:CRD42024605605 (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42024605605).

42881356.title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Value of Sonographic Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter in Patients with Ischemic Stroke or Hypertensive Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
42881356.abstract: Elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) is a critical complication in nontraumatic brain injury, yet invasive monitoring carries significant risks, and noninvasive alternatives remain undervalidated. Optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) ultrasonography represents a promising bedside technique, but data in nontraumatic populations are limited. This study evaluated the diagnostic and prognostic value of ONSD in neurocritical patients with ischemic stroke or hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage. This prospective observational cohort study enrolled 100 neurocritical intensive care unit (ICU) patients with acute nontraumatic brain injury [ischemic stroke or hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage; Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) < 9] who underwent admission computed tomography (CT) and bedside ONSD ultrasonography. Sixty age- and sex-matched healthy volunteers were enrolled exclusively to provide descriptive reference values for physiological ONSD and were not included in the primary diagnostic or prognostic analyses. CT-based radiologic ICP surrogates were the reference standard. Exploratory analyses evaluated inter-eye variability, adjusted models, and in-hospital survival. ONSD increased stepwise across healthy controls, patients with negative CT, and patients with positive CT (4.62 ± 0.33, 5.52 ± 0.51, and 6.50 ± 0.51 mm, respectively). Among neurocritical patients, a cohort-derived cutoff of ≥ 6.00 mm yielded 86.7% sensitivity, 85.0% specificity, 89.7% positive predictive value, 81.0% negative predictive value, 86.0% accuracy, and 0.901 area under the curve (AUC). Above-threshold ONSD remained independently associated with CT-positive elevated ICP after adjustment for age, body mass index (BMI), GCS, and systolic blood pressure (SBP) in exploratory multivariable analysis. Exploratory survival analysis showed significantly higher in-hospital mortality in patients with ONSD above the cohort-derived threshold (log-rank p = 4.77 × 10-13). Bedside ultrasonographic ONSD measurement appears clinically useful for early triage and longitudinal bedside surveillance in neurocritical patients with ischemic stroke or hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage, particularly when invasive monitoring is unavailable or delayed.

42966638.title: Ultrasonographic Pupil Assessment in Patients With Severe Traumatic Brain Injury.
42966638.journal: American journal of critical care : an official publication, American Association of Critical-Care Nurses
42966638.abstract: In patients with severe traumatic brain injury, accurate pupillary assessment is critical for neurological monitoring but is often hindered by periorbital edema, trauma, or dressings that preclude direct visualization. To validate the feasibility and accuracy of ultrasonographic pupil assessment performed through the closed eyelid as an alternative to direct pupillometry in patients with traumatic brain injury. This prospective study enrolled 45 intensive care unit patients (36 male; mean [SD] age, 67.1 [12.9] years). Both direct pupillometry and ultrasonographic pupil assessment were sequentially completed within a 3-minute interval under standardized low-light conditions for both eyes. Direct pupillometry involved video recording of the exposed pupil with a calibrated reference scale. Ultrasonographic pupil assessment was performed by using a high-frequency linear probe placed on the closed eyelid. The primary outcome was the agreement between methods for calculating the percentage of pupillary constriction. Secondary outcomes included agreement on resting and minimum pupil diameters. Ultrasonographic pupil assessment showed excellent agreement with direct pupillometry for percent pupillary constriction (median [IQR] difference, 0.44% [-2.78% to 2.83%]; Wilcoxon P ≥ .48). Bland-Altman analysis showed narrow limits of agreement. Strong correlations were also noted for resting and minimum pupil diameters (0.6 ≤ r2 ≤ 0.873). Ultrasonographic pupil assessment is a reliable and accurate method for objective pupillary evaluation when direct visualization is obstructed. By enabling quantitative measurement of the pupillary light reflex through the closed eyelid, ultrasonographic pupil assessment addresses an important monitoring gap in the management of patients with severe traumatic brain injury and periorbital swelling.

42961386.title: NeuroPOCUS: what every intensivist should know.
42961386.abstract: Ultrasound has become a paramount tool in critical care. Nowadays, it is common for intensivists to use ultrasound to evaluate cardiac function, pulmonary alterations, guide vascular access, and monitor systemic venous congestion through ultrasound-based techniques. However, the brain remains often overlooked in the point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) practice. NeuroPOCUS encompasses cerebral hemodynamic assessment, mainly at the level of the middle cerebral artery, as well as evaluation of hydrocephalus, hematoma size, midline shift and intracranial pressure. Most of these are basic or basic-plus skills. In this manuscript, we present a concise guide on what every intensivist should know about NeuroPOCUS, including basic key concepts, technique and several real illustrative figures.

42960392.title: Mapping the Evolving Research Landscape of Frontobasal and Anterior Skull Base Trauma.
42960392.abstract: Frontobasal and anterior skull base fractures represent a subset of traumatic brain injury that is clinically complicated, with management spanning multiple fields such as neurosurgery, otorhinolaryngology, and critical care. A bibliometric analysis was conducted using the Web of Science Core Collection, with publication, citation, authorship, institutional, geographic, keyword, and network data analyzed using VOSviewer to map research trends, collaborative structures, and thematic evolution across the indexed literature. A total of 3415 publications were identified, demonstrating sustained growth peaking at 224 articles in 2025, with output concentrated in Clinical Neurology (47.2%) and Surgery (38.5%), led by US institutions and authors including Schievink WI (75 publications), and organized into 4 bibliographic coupling clusters spanning epidemiology, operative reconstruction, endoscopic approaches, and neuroendocrine complications. Publication and collaborative networks are concentrated among a small number of high-volume academic centers in North America and Europe. Emerging keyword trends include a focus on cerebrospinal fluid(CSF) leaks and spontaneous intracranial hypotension. This bibliometric analysis establishes a comprehensive map of the frontobasal skull base fracture literature and the need for multicenter collaboration and prospective outcomes-based research.

42859065.title: Acute Kidney Injury After Cardiac Surgery: A Systematic Review of Pharmacological and Non-Pharmacological Interventions.
42859065.journal: Journal of cardiothoracic and vascular anesthesia
42859065.abstract: To identify and synthesize all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions for the prevention of cardiac surgery‒associated acute kidney injury (CSA-AKI). We performed a systematic review of RCTs evaluating pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies. Interventions were qualitatively synthesized, and meta-analysis was performed when at least 4 RCTs were available. Hospitals. Adults undergoing cardiac surgery. Pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies to prevent CSA-AKI. A total of 207 RCTs, including 63,785 patients and evaluating 55 interventions, were identified. Most studies were small (median sample size 120) and single-center (76.7%) and reported neutral results (149/206), whereas 49 reported benefit and 8 reported harm. N-Acetylcysteine was the most frequently studied pharmacological intervention (19 RCTs), and remote ischemic preconditioning was the most frequently studied non-pharmacological intervention (34 RCTs). Among interventions evaluated in at least 4 RCTs were the use of dexmedetomidine (odds ratio [OR] 0.48, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.29-0.80), fenoldopam (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.33-0.98), nitric oxide (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.43-0.88), and remote ischemic preconditioning (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.67-0.90) were associated with lower odds of CSA-AKI. Among interventions evaluated in fewer than 4 RCTs were signals of benefit reported for amino acids, atrial natriuretic peptide, goal-directed perfusion, and KDIGO-based care bundles. Only a limited number of interventions were associated with lower odds of CSA-AKI; these findings require cautious interpretation and confirmation in adequately powered RCTs.

42857744.title: Successful conservative management of high-grade renal injury in a polytrauma patient: a rare case report.
42857744.journal: International journal of surgery case reports
42857744.abstract: Simultaneous high-grade renal and splenic trauma is rare and challenges the limits of non-operative management (NOM). High-grade renal injuries with collecting-system extravasation, especially when associated with severe splenic laceration, represent scenarios in which clinical decisions must rely primarily on physiologic stability rather than injury grade alone. An 18-year-old hemodynamically stable male presented 4 hours after a bicycle fall onto his left flank, with severe flank pain and gross hematuria. Computed tomography (CT) imaging revealed AAST Grade IV renal trauma with collecting-system involvement, together with concurrent Grade IV splenic laceration and associated nondisplaced rib fractures. The patient was managed with close ICU observation, multimodal analgesia, and serial monitoring. Diagnostic laparoscopy excluded ongoing intraperitoneal bleeding. A left double-J ureteric stent and intraperitoneal drain were placed for urinary diversion and controlled drainage. No nephrectomy, splenectomy, or splenic artery embolization was required. The patient improved steadily and was discharged in stable condition. Serial imaging demonstrated resolution of the perinephric hematoma and identified a nonenhancing, infarcted lower renal pole with preserved global renal function. Mild hydronephrosis, present while the stent was in place, resolved completely following elective removal. This case aligns with current NOM principles, showing that stability-guided conservative strategies with targeted minimally invasive interventions can safely preserve organs even in combined high-grade solid-organ injuries. Structured NOM involving ICU surveillance, temporary urinary diversion, selective minimally invasive procedures, and coordinated multidisciplinary care successfully preserved both renal and splenic function in this combined high-grade trauma case. The outcome supports stability-based decision-making over routine operative intervention and reinforces the safety and effectiveness of individualized conservative pathways in complex blunt abdominal trauma.

42843110.title: Effect of preoperative video-based digital educational program on incidence of delirium and length of hospital stay following coronary artery bypass grafting: A randomized controlled trial.
42843110.journal: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care
42843110.abstract: Postoperative delirium is common after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) and is associated with prolonged hospitalization and delayed recovery. Non-pharmacological educational interventions may improve outcomes, but evidence on structured video-based education for delirium prevention remains limited. To evaluate the effect of a preoperative video-based educational program on postoperative delirium incidence and hospital length of stay among patients undergoing CABG surgery. A parallel-group randomized controlled trial was conducted at Queen Alia Heart Institute, Jordan, between October 2025 and January 2026. Adult patients scheduled for elective first-time CABG surgery were randomized into intervention and control groups. Both groups received standardized multidisciplinary preoperative education through the institutional Preoperative Clinic, while the intervention group additionally received an 8-minute structured Arabic video-based educational program. Postoperative delirium was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU). Among 226 randomized participants, 213 were analyzed (105 intervention; 108 control). Delirium incidence was lower with intervention (7.6%vs 25.0%, p < .001) and remained significantly associated with study group after adjustment (OR = 3.14, 95% CI: 1.08-9.14, p = .036). Hospital stay was shorter in the intervention group unadjusted (8.38 vs 10.58 days, p < .001), but not after adjustment (B = -0.656, p = .182). Preoperative video-based education was associated with lower postoperative delirium incidence, while its association with shorter hospital stay was not maintained after adjustment. Larger multicenter trials are warranted.

42840768.title: Intraoperative Dexmedetomidine and Postoperative Delirium After Head and Neck Cancer Surgery with Free-Flap Reconstruction: A Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial.
42840768.abstract: Postoperative delirium is common after major head and neck cancer surgery. We investigated whether intraoperative dexmedetomidine infusion was associated with a lower incidence of postoperative delirium in patients undergoing head and neck cancer surgery requiring free-flap reconstruction. This was a delirium-focused secondary analysis of a single-centre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Adult patients with head and neck cancer scheduled for elective surgery requiring free-flap reconstruction under general anaesthesia were randomly assigned to receive intraoperative dexmedetomidine infusion at 0.3 μg kg-1h-1 until 1 h before the end of surgery; subjects in the placebo group were given comparable volumes of normal saline. The primary outcome was the incidence of delirium during the first 5 postoperative days, assessed once daily using the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) or the 3-Minute Diagnostic Confusion Assessment Method (3D-CAM). There was less delirium during the initial 5 postoperative days in patients assigned to dexmedetomidine (14.9%, 7 of 47 patients) than in those given placebo (34.7%, 17 of 49 patients). Dexmedetomidine was associated with lower odds of postoperative delirium after adjustment for age, preoperative Mini-Mental State Examination score, and operative time (adjusted odds ratio 0.31, 95% confidence interval 0.10-0.92; p = 0.036). Postoperative pain and early sleep outcomes were improved by dexmedetomidine. Haemodynamic adverse events and postoperative complications did not differ significantly between groups. In patients undergoing head and neck cancer surgery with free-flap reconstruction, intraoperative dexmedetomidine infusion was associated with a lower incidence of postoperative delirium during the first 5 postoperative days, without an apparent increase in perioperative adverse events. ChiCTR2300067376.

42901307.title: Veno-arterial ECMO for the management of propofol infusion syndrome following cardiac surgery.
42901307.journal: Revista espanola de anestesiologia y reanimacion
42901307.abstract: Propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS) has been described in patients requiring prolonged sedation with this drug, as may occur in some cases after cardiac surgery. Its treatment is based on discontinuation of the drug and supportive management of organ dysfunction until resolution. In the postoperative period of cardiac surgery, diagnosing PRIS poses a challenge, since it must be differentiated from other, more common complications such as postcardiotomy shock. In these patients, PRIS may fatally worsen the prognosis. Veno-arterial ECMO therapy may help maintain cardiac output. Both the diagnosis of PRIS after cardiac surgery and its treatment with ECMO have been scarcely reported. We present a case of PRIS after cardiac surgery successfully managed with ECMO.

42861658.title: Application of Combined Gastric Tube Tip Manometry and Auscultation for Nasogastric Tube Positioning in Neurocritical Care Patients With Artificial Airways: A Prospective Diagnostic Pilot Study.
42861658.abstract: Nasogastric tube placement is central to enteral nutrition support in neurocritical care patients. However, tube malposition, particularly accidental placement into the airway, can lead to fatal complications. To assess the accuracy of a combined gastric tube tip manometry and auscultation approach for confirming nasogastric tube placement in neurocritical care patients with artificial airways. This prospective study enrolled patients who underwent nasogastric tube insertion in the neurocritical care unit of a tertiary hospital in China between January 2025 and May 2025. Using chest X-ray as the reference standard, we compared the sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), positive likelihood ratio (PLR) and negative likelihood ratio (NLR) for gastric tube tip manometry alone, auscultation alone and their combination. In total, 120 patients participated. X-ray confirmed correct nasogastric tube positioning in 119 patients and malposition in 1 patient. For gastric tube tip manometry alone, the sensitivity was 97.48%, with a specificity of 0%, a positive predictive value (PPV) of 99.15% and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 0%. Auscultation alone yielded a sensitivity of 90.76%, a specificity of 100%, a PPV of 100% and an NPV of 8.33%. The combined manometry-plus-auscultation approach had a sensitivity of 88.24%, a specificity of 100%, a PPV of 100% and an NPV of 6.67%. The combined gastric tube tip manometry and auscultation method might serve as an adjunctive bedside strategy for confirming nasogastric tube placement in neurocritical care patients with artificial airways. However, only one malpositioned tube was observed in this study; the specificity and NPV should be interpreted with caution. When gastric aspirate cannot be obtained or immediate chest radiography is impractical, combined gastric tube tip manometry and auscultation provide a feasible, radiation-free bedside pathway for confirming nasogastric tube position; equivocal or negative bedside findings should still be verified radiographically before feeding. The study was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2300078001).

42849017.title: Managing the Sequelae of Delirium Associated With Critical Illness.
42849017.journal: The primary care companion for CNS disorders
42849017.abstract: The Psychiatric Consultation Service at Massachusetts General Hospital sees medical and surgical inpatients with comorbid psychiatric symptoms and conditions. During their twice-weekly rounds, Dr Stern and other members of the Consultation Service discuss diagnosis and management of hospitalized patients with complex medical or surgical problems who also demonstrate psychiatric symptoms or conditions. These discussions have given rise to rounds reports that will prove useful for clinicians practicing at the interface of medicine and psychiatry. Prim Care Companion CNS Disord 2026;28(5):26f04249. Author affiliations are listed at the end of this article.

42873156.title: Comparison of long-term outcomes between opioid-free and opioid-based anesthesia in head and neck cancer surgeries: A pilot study.
42873156.abstract: Background, aim, and objective: Literature is replete with studies evaluating opioid-sparing strategies in head and neck cancer (HNC) surgeries; however, no study has attempted opioid-free anesthesia (OFA). Various long-term outcomes have not been evaluated in any cancer surgeries. This study aimed to compare OFA with standard opioid-based anesthe-sia (OBA) in HNC surgeries. The primary objective was the incidence of chronic post-surgical pain (CPSP), and the sec-ondary objective included Numeric Rating Scale (NRS)-Pain scores, Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI), Douleur Neuropathique 4 (DN-4), Pain Detect Questionnaire (PDQ), and Short Form-12 (SF-12) scores. Following Instituitional Ethics Committee approval and prospective Clinical Trials Registry-India registration, the study included patients with American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status II or III, aged 20-65 years, who were undergoing HNC surgeries. Patients were excluded if they had a history of post-operative nausea, chronic pain, opioid use, local anesthetic allergies, coagulopathies, or cognitive dysfunction. Group OFA received oral pregabalin and dexmedetomidine and ketamine intravenous (IV) infusions perioperatively. Group OBA received standard OBA with IV morphine boluses. The various aforementioned secondary objectives were recorded at the fourth, sixth, eighth, and 12th weeks. Fifty patients, with 25 in each group, were included. The demographic profiles were comparable between the groups. NRS-Pain (Rest) was comparable; however, mean NRS (Cough) and NRS (Swallow) scores were lower in the OF group at the sixth week; however, this difference was not significant. No patients developed CPSP in any group. No sig-nificant differences were recorded in PDQ, NPSI, DN-4, Activity Assessment Scale, and SF-12 scores. Similarly, me-chanical ventilation duration, intensive care unit stay, total hospital stays, and mortality rates were comparable. We did not observe any association between CPSP and OFA in HNC surgeries. Additionally, pain intensity, neuropathic pain component, quality of recovery, and quality of life were comparable.

42872664.title: Human Brain Organoids for Studying General Anesthetic Mechanisms: Developmental Vulnerability, Cellular Stress, and Translational Perspectives.
42872664.abstract: General anesthetics are indispensable for surgical procedures, procedural sedation, and intensive care, but their mechanisms of action in the human brain are not fully understood. Classical biochemical approaches have delineated key targets of general anesthetics, such as GABAA and NMDA receptors, ion channels, mitochondria, neurotransmission, and inflammatory pathways. However, animal models and two-dimensional cultures do not represent human-specific neurodevelopment, regional cellular diversity, or three-dimensional brain architecture. Human brain organoids offer a complementary system to investigate anesthetic effects during human development. Recent reports on cerebral, forebrain, and midbrain organoids indicate that propofol and sevoflurane may affect neural progenitor cell proliferation, neuronal differentiation, apoptosis, autophagy, mitochondrial metabolism, long non-coding RNA networks, synaptic gene programs, and regionspecific maturation. These results do not preclude clinically required anesthesia, particularly as large-scale human studies have failed to demonstrate deficits in general intelligence following single short-term exposures. Rather, organoid models help establish which types of neural cells, developmental stages, and molecular mechanisms might be vulnerable to anesthesia. This review highlights recent advances in organoid-based research on the mechanisms of general anesthesia, particularly for propofol and volatile anesthetics. It also explores how region-specific organoids, assembloids, vascularized systems, microglia-enriched models, and multi-omics techniques may help resolve developmental vulnerability and aid more targeted translational studies of anesthesia.

42868093.title: Charting the future: A multi-setting medical chart study of advance care planning in Parkinson's disease and atypical Parkinsonism.
42868093.abstract: BackgroundAdvance Care Planning (ACP) enables people with progressive diseases to document and communicate future treatment preferences. For Parkinson's disease (PD) and atypical parkinsonism (AP), ACP is particularly important because of disease complexity, symptom burden, the progressive nature of the disease, and cognitive decline, yet its implementation across care settings remains unclear.MethodsWe conducted a medical chart review of 189 deceased patients with PD or AP who died in nursing homes (n = 91), hospitals (n = 58), or at home (n = 40) in the Netherlands. For patients who died at home, data were obtained from their general practice records. Data on treatment preferences, care discussions and palliative care goals were extracted at one year and six weeks before death.ResultsDocumentation of treatment preferences increased towards death but differed markedly between settings. Nursing homes recorded resuscitation and ICU limitations early and comprehensively, whereas hospitals made major updates only in the final weeks of life. In general practices, ACP documentation was limited. Nursing homes and hospitals more frequently addressed disease-specific scenarios, palliative sedation and end-of-life issues, while general practices more often reported preferred place of death and euthanasia. Palliative care goals in nursing homes covered all domains, while in hospitals and general practices they mainly related to physical aspects.ConclusionACP remains inconsistently documented and frequently delayed until the final weeks of life, when crises or cognitive decline may hinder meaningful participation. Earlier, iterative ACP-supported by clinician training, PD-specific guidance, and system-level measures such as ACP prompts in electronic medical records-could foster a more proactive and person-centered palliative approach aligned with patient values throughout the disease trajectory.

42864031.title: [ANAPHYLACTIC SHOCK DUE TO REMIFENTANIL DURING GENDER-AFFIRMING SURGERY: A CASE REPORT].
42864031.journal: Nihon Hinyokika Gakkai zasshi. The japanese journal of urology
42864031.abstract: A person in their twenties, assigned male at birth and diagnosed with gender incongruence, underwent gender-affirming surgery (GAS) after starting hormone therapy. Orchiectomy, penectomy, labiaplasty and vaginoplasty were planned. The preoperative evaluation revealed no contraindications to general anesthesia. Induction was performed with sevoflurane, propofol, fentanyl, remifentanil, and rocuronium. Cefazolin was administered as a prophylactic antibiotic. After bilateral orchiectomy, the patient developed rapidly worsening urticaria, wheezing, decreased oxygen saturation and hypotension. Anaphylaxis was diagnosed, and emergency treatment stabilized respiratory and circulatory function. Because the cause was unknown, the operation was paused. The patient was moved to the intensive care unit. Symptoms resolved within hours and the patient was discharged on the second postoperative day. Subsequent allergy testing, including prick and intradermal tests for anesthetics and antibiotics, revealed a positive intradermal response to remifentanil, which identified it as the cause. After detailed counseling, the patient and their family strongly wished to complete GAS, and reoperation was performed without remifentanil. The postoperative course was uneventful.

42855419.title: Impact of Cardiopulmonary Bypass Duration on the Development of Postoperative Delirium in Cardiac Surgery: A Secondary Subgroup Analysis of an Observational Study.
42855419.journal: Journal of cardiothoracic and vascular anesthesia
42855419.abstract: Postoperative delirium (POD) is an acute brain impairment linked to higher morbidity and mortality after surgery. This issue is especially prevalent in older cardiac surgery patients receiving cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), who face unique pathophysiological risks and heightened POD susceptibility. Identifying risk factors is crucial for targeted prevention and therapy. This investigation represents a subgroup analysis derived from a prospective observational study. In this subgroup analysis, 274 cardiac surgery patients from a prospective observational study were examined. Data collection was performed during the patients' postoperative hospital stay across 5 consecutive assessment days. A total of 274 adult patients were included in the analysis. POD was considered present if any of the following screening tools indicated delirium on at least 1 of the 5 evaluation days: Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU, Confusion Assessment Method, 4 'A's Test, or Delirium Observation Screening scale. No intervention was performed; the study was purely observational. The incidence of POD was 50.4% in a cohort with a mean age of 70.7 years (standard deviation, 6.4 years). The regression model showed a significant effect of CPB duration category (odds ratio [OR], 1.40; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.12-1.75; p = 0.003) and preoperative troponin T level (OR, 1.64; 95% CI, 1.07-2.51; p = 0.024) on POD. This subgroup analysis examined several risk factors for POD in a cardiac surgery cohort. The duration of CPB has been shown to be a risk factor for the development of POD. This information can help identify patients at increased risk of POD during the perioperative period.

42853304.title: Recent Evidence on Factors and Potential Interventions Affecting Patient Sleep in Inpatient and Hospital Settings.
42853304.abstract: Sleep is a critical but frequently disrupted part of hospital care, affecting patient recovery, length of stay, and physical and mental health. This review examines recent evidence (2022-2026) on why inpatient sleep is disrupted and how interventions can mitigate disturbance across different patient groups and hospital settings. Findings span five domains: environmental factors such as noise and light, hospital infrastructure and room configuration, patient-related factors including pain and anxiety, care routines, and interventions. Recent high-quality trials and meta-analyses increasingly support nonpharmacological strategies - including environmental modification, care-routine restructuring, and sensory therapies - while evidence for pharmacological agents such as melatonin remains weak outside specific contexts. This review highlights the multifactorial nature of sleep disruption in hospital settings. Prioritizing patient sleep through evidence-based, sustainable strategies can support faster recovery, reduce complications, and improve overall care quality, yet poor sleep remains pervasive. Current evidence supports system-level interventions (workflow restructuring, environmental redesign) and low-cost measures (earplugs, sleep masks, physical therapy) to improve sleep related outcomes including delirium, pain, and length of stay.

42849948.title: Effect of auricular acupressure as an adjunct to standard postoperative care on physical and psychological outcomes following coronary artery bypass graft surgery: protocol for a randomised, single-blind, sham-controlled trial.
42849948.abstract: Patients undergoing coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery frequently experience postoperative pain, anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance and physiological instability during recovery in the cardiac intensive care unit. Although auricular acupressure (AA) has been investigated as a non-pharmacological adjunct for symptom management, existing studies are limited by methodological shortcomings, including inadequate blinding, absence of appropriate sham controls and heterogeneous surgical populations. This study aims to evaluate whether AA, as an adjunct to standard postoperative care, improves physical and psychological outcomes following CABG surgery. This is a prospective, randomised, single-blind, sham-controlled, three-arm parallel-group superiority trial. Ninety-six adults undergoing elective on-pump CABG surgery will be randomly allocated (1:1:1) to active AA, sham AA or usual postoperative care. The intervention will be delivered two times per day on postoperative days 2 through 7 (six consecutive days). The primary outcomes are pain intensity assessed using the Visual Analogue Scale and anxiety and depression assessed using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale. Secondary outcomes include sleep quality, fatigue, delirium severity, physiological parameters, analgesic consumption and intensive care unit and hospital length of stay. Outcome assessments will be conducted at baseline, throughout the intervention period, at hospital discharge and 1 month after surgery. Analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle using linear mixed-effects models to evaluate between-group differences over time. Ethical approval has been obtained from the Ethics Committee of Tabriz University of Medical Sciences (IR.TBZMED.REC.1404.249). Written informed consent will be obtained from all participants before enrolment. Study findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, presentations at scientific conferences and updates to the trial registry. Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (IRCT20160110025937N9), registered on 4 September 2025 (https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/user/trial/84266/view).

42849346.title: Cognitive impairment after critical illness: A scoping review of recovery trajectories, assessment practices, and risk factors.
42849346.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
42849346.abstract: Persistent cognitive impairment is an important long-term sequela of critical illness, yet evidence regarding its post-intensive care unit (ICU) trajectories, determinants, and assessment practices remains fragmented. The aim of this study was to map the literature on persistent post-ICU cognitive impairment among adult survivors of critical illness, with particular attention to recovery trajectories, cognitive assessment practices, associated risk factors, and evidence gaps. A scoping review was conducted following the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. Cochrane, CINAHL, Embase, MEDLINE, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception to 20 November 2025. Studies involving adult ICU survivors (aged ≥18 years) reporting postdischarge cognitive outcomes, including persistent post-ICU cognitive impairment, were included. In contrast, studies assessing cognitive dysfunction exclusively during hospitalisation or delirium without postdischarge cognitive assessment were excluded. Data were synthesised using descriptive and evidence-mapping approaches. Forty-one studies were included, predominantly prospective cohort studies from Europe and North America. Cognitive impairment was most prevalent within the first month after ICU discharge, with substantial heterogeneity in recovery trajectories over time. While partial recovery occurred in some individuals, a considerable proportion experienced persistent impairment at mid- and long-term follow-up. Memory and executive functions were most frequently affected. Associated factors were clustered into six domains: patient vulnerability, ICU-related factors, sedation and treatment exposure, psychological factors, biomarkers/neurobiology, and protective or modifiable factors. Considerable variability existed in cognitive assessment tools and timing, with limited alignment across domains and follow-up phases. Evidence mapping revealed gaps in studies of older adults, low- and middle-income settings, and intervention-based research beyond early recovery. Persistent post-ICU cognitive impairment is common and heterogeneous among adult survivors of critical illness, with cognitive deficits often emerging early after ICU discharge and persisting in some survivors. These findings support the conceptualisation of cognitive recovery as a dynamic and multifactorial process influenced by patient vulnerability, critical illness, treatment exposures, and postdischarge factors. Evidence remains limited regarding predictors of prolonged or persistent impairment. Greater standardisation of cognitive assessment and longitudinal and interventional research is needed to characterise recovery trajectories, identify individuals at risk of persistent impairment, and evaluate potentially modifiable targets.

42846393.title: Corridor-based relative severity assessment of the canine anaesthetic course.
42846393.abstract: The Relative Severity Assessment (RELSA) score grades welfare severity based on the magnitude of multivariate deviations from a reference value. Many variables monitored during anaesthesia are homeostatic and become harmful when they leave the normal range in either direction. Building on the corridor concept of the PVS from human intensive care, we conducted a feasibility study to assess the application and behaviour of a corridor extension of RELSA in two canine anaesthesia datasets. Each homeostatic variable was given a normal band, and only its deviation was folded into the standard RELSA algorithm. Severity in this report denotes the number this algorithm returns, and that number has not been shown to represent clinical severity. We obtained two Beagle datasets, including one four-arm within-subject study, allowing a paired between-protocol comparison. This is an exploratory secondary analysis of existing data, with no a priori power calculation. Under the selected bands, the calculated score changed across the recorded anaesthetic course: low while awake, rising at the documented propofol induction, maintained, and resolving on recovery. The dominant departures were hypotension, hypothermia, and mild hypercapnia, sometimes coinciding with a single animal, though their magnitudes are band-dependent. Corridor RELSA produced a number that changed across the recorded anaesthetic course and represented bidirectional departures as a single continuous score. The between-protocol comparison is not interpreted as evidence about the protocols because the verdict it returns depends on the variable panel being scored. The approach is a domain extension and a small refinement of the human-ICU corridor concept.

42845729.title: Relationships of Preoperative and 24-Hour Postoperative Plasma and Cerebrospinal Fluid Cytokines with Postoperative Delirium.
42845729.journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
42845729.abstract: Postoperative delirium is a common syndrome of acute changes in attention, cognition, and consciousness that may result from inflammation and/or neuroinflammation, but few studies have distinguished the relationships of preoperative and 24-hour postoperative systemic inflammation (i.e. in blood) versus neuroinflammation (i.e. in cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF) in postoperative delirium. We measured CSF and plasma cytokine levels before and 24-hours after non-cardiac/non-neurologic surgery in 199 patients age ≥ 60 years who were enrolled in two prospective cohort studies. Delirium was assessed with the confusion assessment method (CAM), 3-minute diagnostic interview for CAM-defined delirium, or the CAM for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) in patients who remained intubated postoperatively and validated chart review. Cytokines were measured with immunoassays for IL-6, IL-7, IL-8, IL-10, IL-16, TARC, MCP-1, and IP-10. Associations of CSF and plasma cytokine levels with postoperative delirium were assessed with univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses with Holm correction for family-wise error. Surgery was associated with significant changes in nearly all measured CSF and plasma cytokines (p < 0.05) except plasma IL-16 and MCP-1. In multivariable analyses adjusted for preoperative Mini-Mental Status Exam (MMSE) score and surgery duration, higher preoperative CSF IL-6 (OR 1.80, 95% CI 1.18-2.75, Holm p=0.049) and CSF IL-8 (OR 1.94, 95% CI 1.22-3.06, Holm p = 0.040) levels were independently associated with postoperative delirium. Higher 24-hour postoperative CSF IL-10 was nominally associated with delirium (OR 1.57, 95% CI 1.06-2.33, p = 0.026) in a multivariable regression controlling for MMSE and surgery duration, but this association did not remain significant after multiple-comparison correction (Holm p = 0.21). No other preoperative or 24-hour postoperative CSF or plasma cytokine levels were associated with delirium (p > 0.05). Surgery elicited robust postoperative changes in CSF and plasma cytokines, but 24-hour postoperative cytokine elevations were not significantly associated with postoperative delirium after multiple-comparison correction. In contrast, elevated preoperative CSF IL-6 and IL-8 levels were associated with postoperative delirium independent of baseline cognitive status and surgery duration. Thus, our findings support an important role for preoperative neuroinflammation in postoperative delirium in older elective surgery patients.

42839262.title: Feasibility and candidate risk factors for postoperative delirium in older ward patients: a prospective pilot study.
42839262.abstract: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a frequent neuropsychiatric complication after surgery, characterized by acute disturbances in attention, awareness, and cognition. This pilot study assessed the feasibility of a multidimensional assessment protocol and investigated candidate risk factors for POD in older patients undergoing elective surgery. This prospective, observational, non-interventional, single-center pilot study enrolled 150 patients aged ≥ 65 years undergoing elective surgery lasting ≥ 60 min. Patients with dementia, neurological disorders (documented diagnoses), or emergency procedures were excluded. After enrollment, 10 patients were excluded due to surgery postponement or unplanned ICU admission, leaving 140 patients for analysis. Data were collected preoperatively, on postoperative days 1-3. Intraoperative and laboratory data were obtained from databases. Handgrip strength was measured by dynamometry. POD was assessed using the CAM-ICU once daily on postoperative days 1-3 by a single trained investigator. Cognitive function and reserve were evaluated using MMSE and MWT-B, frailty with the Clinical Frailty Scale, nutritional status with screening tools, and pain via the Numeric Rating Scale. Descriptive and inferential statistics were applied. POD incidence was 5.0% (n = 7/140; 95% CI: 2.0%-10.0%). Frailty (n = 4/7 [57%] vs. n = 26/133 [20%]) and malnutrition (n = 4/7 [57%] vs. n = 29/133 [22%]) were more common in the delirium group. In an exploratory, unpowered male subgroup analysis, patients with POD had lower preoperative handgrip strength; no statistically meaningful difference was testable in women (n = 3 with POD). During anesthesia induction, patients with POD experienced more hypotensive episodes (MAP<55 mmHg), (n = 3/7 [43%] vs. n = 11/133 [8.0%]). No comparison remained significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction. This pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of prospective POD assessment on a general surgical ward and provides an incidence estimate (5.0%) to inform sample-size calculation for confirmatory trials. Frailty, lower preoperative handgrip strength in men, and induction hypotension were more frequent among patients with POD. Given the low event rate and multiple comparisons, these associations are hypothesis-generating and require validation in adequately powered studies. German Clinical Trials Register DRKS00031157. Registered 20.03.2023.

42836182.title: Optimal Dosing Strategies for Remimazolam Across Diverse Patient Populations: A Clinical Narrative Review.
42836182.abstract: Remimazolam is an ultra-short-acting benzodiazepine that is hydrolyzed by carboxylesterase 1 (CES1) to the inactive metabolite CNS 7054.
