Since regulatory approval in 2020 it has been adopted globally for procedural sedation and general anesthesia, supported by an expanding evidence base of randomized trials, population pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) modeling studies, dose-finding sequential-allocation analyses, and meta-analyses. Synthesizing 92 studies published between January 2020 and April 2026, this narrative review defines dose optimization across diverse populations. For adult procedural sedation, a fixed 5 mg initial bolus followed by 2.5 mg maintenance titrations achieves moderate sedation with a hemodynamic and respiratory profile that compares favorably with propofol, whereas general anesthesia requires an induction rate of 6 to 12 mg kg-1 h-1 followed by maintenance at 1.0-2.0 mg kg-1 h-1. Dosing demands a 25-30% reduction in the elderly (≥ 65 years), higher weight-adjusted requirements in pediatric patients (1-18 years), and lean or corrected body weight scalars in obesity, while severe hepatic impairment reduces clearance by approximately 38% and opioid co-administration yields a 15-63% synergistic reduction in effective concentrations. Several quantitative estimates, however, derive from single-center trials with fewer than 30 participants per arm that have not been externally validated. To help clinicians weigh these recommendations, each population-level dosing estimate is graded by the strength and external validity of its supporting evidence (A, B, or C); most special-population point estimates rest on single-center studies (grade C) and are best regarded as starting points rather than established standards. Crucially, the halted Japanese Phase II intensive care unit trial (ONO-2745-04) serves as a key safety counter-narrative: continuous infusions exceeding 24 hours in critically ill patients may be associated with drug accumulation and delayed emergence, suggesting that organ-independent clearance may not be guaranteed when CES1 activity is compromised. Major evidence gaps persist for infants under one year of age, long-duration anesthesia, CES1 polymorphisms, and non-East-Asian populations.

42834424.title: Feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary estimates of a multimodal AKTIVER Heart Delirium Prevention Program in patients indicated for cardiac surgery: study protocol of a randomized controlled PREVENT POstoperative Delirium (PREVENT-POD) Pilot Study.
42834424.abstract: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a common complication in geriatric patients undergoing cardiac surgery. POD is associated with prolonged length of stay in the intensive care unit and hospital, increased mortality, institutionalization, distress, risk of cognitive impairment and dementia. The non-pharmacological, multimodal AKTIVER intervention from the multicenter PAWEL trial significantly reduced POD incidence and days with POD in older patients undergoing abdominal and orthopedic surgery. However, this positive effect on POD incidence has not yet been demonstrated in elderly patients undergoing cardiac surgery. Therefore, a specific AKTIVER Heart intervention with additional modules was developed. In the randomized controlled PREVENT-POD pilot study, 60 patients aged 65 years or older undergoing elective cardiac surgery will be recruited and 2:1 randomized in either into the AKTIVER Heart intervention group (AKTIVER Heart) or treatment-as-usual plus (TAU+) group. In total, 40 patients will receive the non-pharmacological and modified AKTIVER Heart intervention, while the other 20 will receive TAU+ with preoperative education. The primary outcome is the feasibility and acceptability of the AKTIVER Heart intervention. Secondary outcomes include the preliminary estimates of the AKTIVER Heart on POD incidence, duration and severity, cognition, quality of life, sleep, treatment- and disease expectations, distress, depression, and anxiety symptoms. This randomized controlled pilot study aims to evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of the non-pharmacological, multimodal AKTIVER Heart intervention in elderly patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery. This trial is designed to provide evidence on acceptability and feasibility of the AKTIVER Heart, and to perform a larger, well-powered multicenter POD prevention trial in cardiac surgery. German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS; http://www.drks.de ; DRKS00035091, Registered prospectively on November 4, 2024.

42832427.title: Impact of a Geriatric Co-management Service on Surgical Cancer Care for Older Adults.
42832427.abstract: In 2011, Brown University Health's Division of Geriatrics started its inaugural geriatric co-management service to improve older adult (OA) care for patients with hip fractures. Its success in care and cost reduction prompted the health system to expand geriatric co-management. Meanwhile, oncology surgeons treat increasingly older and frailer patients due to improved therapies and survival. The literature established what we saw here: increased mortality and complications in frail OA and failure of strategies like Enhanced Recovery After Surgery and Prehabilitation. In 2021, the division launched an oncologic surgery co-management program. Explicit to its launch, hospital sponsors required a 2-year study for benchmarks and quality metrics with a primary outcome of reducing mortality and delirium. QI metrics were developed through PowerBI dashboards using hospital and EMR data, analyzing 4,359 cases, which measured length of stay (LOS), readmissions, mortality, and disposition, from July 2018 to August 2024. We compared outcomes between the pilot (Geri) and those with no geriatric involvement (UC) using 1:1 propensity score matching. Bivariate analyses used chi-square and Student's t-tests for descriptive comparisons and multivariate linear or logistic regression analyses for outcome rates and adjusted when appropriate. The matched sample consisted of 309 cases in each group. 14% were underrepresented minorities. The Geri group had a lower odds ratio (OR) for hospice or in-hospital mortality (OR 0.27, 95% CI 0.12-0.61, p = 0.0016), as well as significantly lower odds of delirium, measured by a positive CAM (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.11-0.73, p = 0.0086). ICU admission was lower in the geri group, although not statistically significant (18 vs 25, p = 0.0690). Overall hospital length of stay was longer in the geri group (8.2 ± 15.4 vs. 6.2 ± 5.6 days, p = 0.0350). Geri patients were less likely to be discharged home (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.33-0.77) but were more likely to be discharged to a skilled nursing facility (OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.43-3.53) or inpatient rehabilitation facility (OR 8.52, 95% CI 1.04-69.6). Conclusion: Geriatric co-management in surgical oncology significantly reduced mortality and delirium as measured by CAM among OA, demonstrating meaningful improvements in patient outcomes. Although LOS increased and home discharges decreased, these results may indicate more appropriate discharge planning for this patient population. Geriatric co-management represents a critical, evidence-based component of surgical oncology care for OA. This study adds to the growing evidence supporting the role of Geriatric Medicine in improving the quality of care for OA.

42832002.title: Beyond processed depth targets: frontal EEG patterns, brain vulnerability, and postoperative delirium in older adults.
42832002.journal: Journal of clinical monitoring and computing
42832002.abstract: Limited-channel frontal electroencephalography is widely used during anesthesia through processed EEG platforms, but clinical interpretation often remains centered on numerical depth indices. This narrative review examines whether frontal EEG signals, including raw waveforms, suppression behavior, spectral features, and processed index behavior, may provide information beyond hypnotic depth in older adults at risk for postoperative delirium. A targeted literature search was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar for articles published from database inception through April 30, 2026. Priority was given to randomized trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, consensus statements, prospective observational studies, and mechanistic studies relevant to processed EEG monitoring, frontal EEG interpretation, postoperative delirium, aging, frailty, anesthesia, and critical care. Evidence from randomized trials and systematic reviews suggests that processed EEG-guided anesthetic titration and suppression minimization alone do not reliably prevent postoperative delirium. However, several clinically accessible frontal EEG patterns may provide contextual information about anesthetic sensitivity and reduced cerebral reserve. These include reduced frontal alpha power, early or disproportionate burst suppression, spectral slowing or low spectral edge frequency, and disorganized emergence. Their interpretation depends on anesthetic dose and agent, hemodynamics, signal quality, artifact burden, frailty, baseline cognition, and postoperative recovery context. Limited-channel frontal EEG should be interpreted as a contextual brain-monitoring signal rather than a single-number depth target. Future studies should test whether multimodal frameworks integrating frontal EEG patterns with physiologic and patient-level variables improve postoperative neurocognitive outcomes.

42831848.title: Beyond the Numerical Rating Scale: Comprehensive Pain Assessment in the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit.
42831848.journal: Journal of perianesthesia nursing : official journal of the American Society of PeriAnesthesia Nurses
42831848.abstract: Effective pain assessment during the perioperative period is a crucial responsibility for nurses. However, relying solely on numerical rating scales may not fully capture the complexity of postoperative pain experiences. This article offers perioperative nurses evidence-based guidance on comprehensive pain assessment strategies for the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU). We review validated subjective tools, such as the numerical rating scale, visual analog scale, verbal rating scale, and Wong-Baker FACES Pain Rating Scale, highlighting their psychometric properties and appropriate clinical applications. We also discuss behavioral assessment instruments validated for PACU use, including the Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability scale, the Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool, and the Acute Pain Assessment 5, noting their inter-rater reliability and diagnostic accuracy metrics. Additionally, we evaluate emerging objective monitoring technologies (the Surgical Pleth Index, Nociception Level Index, Analgesia Nociception Index, and pupillometry) for their predictive accuracy, potential confounds, and clinical impact. We present strategies for assessing movement-evoked pain and discuss multimodal integration approaches, while acknowledging existing evidence gaps requiring further research. By combining multiple assessment methods with multimodal pain management, we aim to optimize postoperative pain control.

42957094.title: Dexmedetomidine versus propofol for the prevention of postoperative delirium in older adults undergoing regional anaesthesia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42957094.journal: Revista espanola de anestesiologia y reanimacion
42957094.abstract: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a common complication in older adults undergoing surgery and is associated with adverse clinical outcomes. The choice of intraoperative sedative may influence its occurrence, particularly in the setting of regional anesthesia. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing dexmedetomidine versus propofol in patients aged ≥60 years was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines, with protocol registration in PROSPERO. The primary outcome was the incidence of POD assessed using validated instruments (CAM or CAM-ICU). Five randomized controlled trials involving a total of 1,613 patients were included. The incidence of POD was 7.7% in the dexmedetomidine groups and 16.7% in the propofol groups. The meta-analysis showed a significant reduction in POD with dexmedetomidine (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.36-0.64; p < 0.001), with low heterogeneity (I² = 13.4%). Egger's test did not show significant evidence of publication bias, and trial sequential analysis suggested that the available evidence is sufficient. The certainty of evidence was rated as moderate according to the GRADE approach. In older adults undergoing surgery under regional anesthesia, intraoperative sedation with dexmedetomidine is associated with a lower incidence of POD compared with propofol.

42954689.title: Hemodynamic Effects of Anesthetics, Sedatives, and Analgesics in the CICU: Clinical Decision Guidance.

42954268.title: The latest guidelines for the perioperative management of the thoracic noncardiac patient: a critical appraisal of the literature.
42954268.abstract: The management of patients before, during, and after surgical procedures on the thorax is influenced by a rapidly expanding set of guidelines that are only partially overlapping. The review is intended for clinicians who are interested in understanding how publication date influences their recommendations, and the points of agreement and divergence between sources. Across the preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative phases, the reviewed documents converge strongly on core process measures. These measures encompass multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, a single chest drain, early ambulation, and the avoidance of reflex ICU admission. However, there is less consistency in the numerical thresholds, including exercise-testing cut-offs, transfusion triggers, and drain-removal volumes. The most recent documents demonstrate a shift toward more permissive values and an increasing emphasis on frailty, sarcopenia, and patient-reported outcomes. The core enhanced recovery after surgery process measures have been demonstrated to be reliable. However, it is imperative for clinicians to ascertain the underlying guideline generation for any numerical threshold before its implementation. A significant number of intraoperative decisions are still made based on expert opinion rather than guideline-grade evidence, underscoring the necessity for future trials and consensus on patient-centered outcome measurement.

42951590.title: Association between Early Postoperative Sodium Change and Postoperative Delirium after General Anesthesia.
42951590.journal: Journal of Nippon Medical School = Nippon Ika Daigaku zasshi
42951590.abstract: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a frequent neuropsychiatric complication after surgery under general anesthesia and is associated with adverse outcomes. Although perioperative dysnatremia has been linked to POD, most studies relied on static sodium measurements and failed to capture early postoperative dynamics. We investigated whether early postoperative sodium change is associated with late-onset POD. This retrospective single-center cohort study included adults undergoing surgery under general anesthesia between July 2021 and December 2025. A Day-3 landmark design ensured temporal precedence between exposure and outcome. Perioperative sodium change (ΔNa) was defined as the difference between preoperative baseline sodium and the most recent sodium value within 48 hours after surgery and was categorized as decrease (≤-3 mmol/L), stable (-3 to +3 mmol/L), or increase (≥+3 mmol/L). Late-onset POD occurring on postoperative days 3 through 7 was identified using the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist and antipsychotic prescriptions. Multivariable logistic regression and restricted cubic spline models were applied. Among 18,424 patients, both perioperative sodium increase and decrease were independently associated with higher odds of late-onset POD, as compared with stable sodium levels. Baseline preoperative sodium was not associated with POD. Spline analyses showed a U-shaped association between ΔNa and POD, with the lowest risk was near ΔNa = 0 mmol/L. Findings were consistent across sensitivity and subgroup analyses. Early postoperative sodium fluctuations were associated with increased risk of late-onset POD. Monitoring of perioperative sodium trajectories may aid in stratifying early postoperative risk.

42944813.title: Knowledge of Childhood Autism and Care Experiences in Critical Settings: A Survey Among Italian Nurses.
42944813.journal: Journal of autism and developmental disorders
42944813.abstract: This study examined nurses' knowledge of childhood autism and their experiences caring for autistic patients in emergency and critical care. The Knowledge about Childhood Autism among Health Workers (KCAHW) questionnaire is child-focused, whereas the care-experience questions were age-neutral. From May to July 2025, 503 nurses and nurse coordinators recruited by non-probability convenience sampling completed an online survey with socio-demographic items, the 19-item KCAHW, and study-specific closed- and open-ended questions. Non-parametric group comparisons reported effect sizes with bootstrap confidence intervals. Open-text responses underwent content analysis. Using the original scoring key, the mean KCAHW score was 15.96/19 (SD = 2.54); at least 80% scored a point on 16 items, but only 39.8% recognized atypical eating patterns. Differences by sex, age, professional experience, educational level, geographic area, and clinical setting were mostly small, the largest being between clinical settings (ε² = 0.133-0.195). Care experiences told a different story: 74.0% reported difficulties in caring for autistic people, 90.9% felt not at all or not very prepared, and 91.1% had never attended ASD-specific training. The most frequent difficulty was communication and relational problems (58.6% of 266 answers). A crisis had been managed by 56.3%; of 133 accounts, 58.6% involved caregivers or the team and 15.8% medication, sedation, or restraint. Only 54.7%-55.7% routinely chose a quiet setting, avoided noise, or adapted lighting. Participants recognized much of the KCAHW's childhood-autism content, but this did not translate into perceived preparedness. Practice-oriented education is needed, together with tools that assess professional competence across the lifespan.

42940097.title: Statin Use and the Risks of Delirium and Short-Term Mortality in Hospitalized Adults: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
42940097.abstract: Background/Objectives: Delirium is a common and serious neuropsychiatric complication in hospitalized and critically ill patients and is associated with prolonged hospitalization and increased mortality. Previous meta-analyses found no clear association between statin use and delirium; however, newly published studies and emerging mortality data warrant re-evaluation. Methods: This updated systematic review and meta-analysis extended a previous meta-analysis and re-evaluated the association between statin use and delirium risk. PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched for eligible studies published from January 2022 through October 2025. Study-level estimates were synthesized using random-effects models. Because ORs, RRs, and HRs are not directly interchangeable, the combined synthesis was considered exploratory. Sensitivity analyses included an OR-only dataset, exclusion of the cross-sectional study, REML models with Hartung-Knapp adjustment, and restriction to observational studies reporting multivariable-adjusted ORs. Results: Nineteen studies (5 randomized controlled trials and 14 observational studies) involving 440,737 participants were included. The exploratory combined analysis yielded an OR of 0.79 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.66-0.95; p = 0.01; I2 = 90%). Results differed by study design: randomized trials yielded a lower pooled point estimate (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.20-0.82; I2 = 58%), whereas the pooled association among observational studies was not statistically significant (OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.71-1.03; I2 = 91%; p for subgroup difference = 0.04). However, in the three randomized trials contributing to incident delirium, REML with Hartung-Knapp adjustment substantially widened the confidence interval (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.09-1.86; p = 0.126). In the overall analysis, REML-Hartung-Knapp inference also increased uncertainty (OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.62-1.00; p = 0.047), as did restriction to multivariable-adjusted observational ORs (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.57-1.01; p = 0.062). In four studies comprising 21,687 participants, statin use was associated with lower 30-day all-cause mortality under the conventional random-effects model (OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.35-0.79; p = 0.002; I2 = 88%); this estimate remained similar under REML with Hartung-Knapp adjustment (OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.32-0.84; p = 0.022). No significant association was observed for delirium-free days. Conclusions: The available evidence suggests a possible association between statin exposure and lower delirium occurrence, but substantial heterogeneity, differences between randomized and observational evidence, and sensitivity to analytic assumptions limit causal interpretation. The findings do not establish statins as a preventive treatment for delirium or prove a mortality benefit. Further adequately powered randomized trials with clearly defined exposure timing and standardized delirium assessment are warranted.

42934939.title: Methadone to manage pain in pregnancy at Te Toka Tumai Auckland City Hospital: A retrospective observational analysis.
42934939.abstract: Pain during pregnancy is common, yet evidence-based management remains limited. While non-pharmacological treatments are first-line, severe pain may necessitate pharmacological intervention. Methadone is well studied for opioid use disorder, but its role in acute pain management during pregnancy is less defined. This retrospective observational study examined pregnant patients prescribed low-dose methadone for pain management between January 2022 and December 2023 at a tertiary multidisciplinary pain service. Patients receiving opioid substitution therapy were excluded. Data on methadone dosing, pain scores, maternal side effects, and neonatal outcomes were analysed. Twenty-three patients were identified, with 22 included in the analysis. The mean gestation at methadone initiation was 29.7 weeks (standard deviation 5.1), and the median starting dose was 5 mg per day (interquartile range 2.5 to 5). Pain severity decreased significantly: the proportion reporting severe pain at rest fell from 82% to 14% at 48 hours (absolute risk reduction (ARR) 68%, number needed to treat (NNT) 2), and the proportion reporting severe pain with movement fell from 95% to 32% (ARR 64%, NNT 2), with sustained improvement at 4 weeks. Side-effects included sedation (14%) and nausea (23%) and were generally well tolerated. Among 19 neonates, no cases of neonatal abstinence syndrome were observed. Six required neonatal intensive care unit admission, but none for opioid withdrawal. These findings suggest that low-dose methadone, when used within a closely monitored multidisciplinary setting, may provide effective pain relief in the pregnant patient without significant neonatal harm. However, this high level of oversight may limit generalisability to other care settings. Further research is warranted to guide safe implementation and optimise dosing.

42923991.title: Acute Encephalopathy during First Pembrolizumab Infusion Followed by Delayed Multisystem Immune Toxicity in Recurrent Vaginal Cancer: A Case Report.
42923991.abstract: Primary vaginal cancer is a rare malignancy, and treatment strategies are often extrapolated from cervical cancer due to limited prospective data. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), including pembrolizumab, have demonstrated efficacy in gynecologic cancers but are associated with immune-related adverse events (irAEs), which can involve multiple organ systems. Neurologic irAEs are uncommon but may be severe and diagnostically challenging. We present a 67-year-old woman with recurrent HPV-associated squamous cell carcinoma of the vagina who developed acute encephalopathy after receiving bevacizumab and paclitaxel and within minutes of initiating pembrolizumab during her first treatment cycle. Symptoms included confusion, hallucinations, and agitation. Extensive evaluation did not identify an infectious, metabolic, structural, epileptic, malignant, or antibody-mediated cause. She required intensive care support, and her mental status improved with supportive management. Although the temporal association raised concern for an immune-mediated neurologic event, the immediate onset, exposure to multiple agents, absence of objective inflammatory findings, and improvement without corticosteroids limited causal attribution. Four weeks later, she developed suspected multisystem irAEs characterized by myositis, transaminitis, and worsening thyroid dysfunction, necessitating high-dose corticosteroids and multidisciplinary management. Pembrolizumab was discontinued, and she was transitioned to single-agent chemotherapy. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of acute neurologic symptoms arising during ICI-containing combination therapy, followed by delayed multisystem immune-related toxicity. Clinicians should recognize that acute neurologic symptoms may arise during the first immunotherapy treatment and require prompt evaluation for immune-mediated toxicity as well as infusion-related, medication-associated, vascular, infectious, metabolic, and malignant causes. Early recognition and multidisciplinary collaboration are critical to reducing morbidity. Given the limited data on immunotherapy in vaginal cancer, continued reporting of such cases is essential to inform safety, guide management, and improve patient selection in this rare disease.

42919629.title: Comparison of oral and intravenous methadone for postoperative analgesia after cardiac surgery: a pilot randomized clinical trial.

42913494.title: Association of Altered Anteriorization of Electroencephalographic Alpha Oscillation During Transition to Unconsciousness With Postoperative Delirium: A Prospective Observational Study.
42913494.abstract: During sevoflurane-induced anesthesia, electroencephalography analysis demonstrates alpha oscillations shifting from the occipital to the frontal regions, with further characteristic changes during maintenance and emergence. We aimed to exploratorily investigate whether alterations in alpha anteriorization and functional network efficiency are associated with postoperative delirium. This prospective, exploratory observational study enrolled 100 patients from a single tertiary university hospital. Patients were classified into nondelirium (n = 81) and delirium (n = 19) groups based on delirium assessments. After excluding 17 patients due to artifacts on electroencephalography, 19-channel electroencephalography data were collected from 83 elderly patients under sevoflurane-induced anesthesia. Artifact-free epochs were extracted during the induction, maintenance, emergence, and postanesthesia care unit phases. Spectral, topographical, and network analyses were conducted. Postoperative delirium was assessed using confusion assessment method for intensive care unit and a chart review. Significant group differences emerged just before the loss of responsiveness, with the nondelirium group exhibiting robust alpha power amplification across all brain regions (median [interquartile range {IQR}] in dB; frontal: 4.24 [1.86-6.57] vs -0.88 [-1.59-3.38], P = .007; parietal: 3.71 [0.51-5.55] vs -0.95 [-2.33-1.11], P = .046; occipital: 2.81 [0.49-5.71] vs -0.04 [-2.06-1.27], P = .048), whereas the delirium group showed minimal changes. During the maintenance phase, spectral analysis revealed higher alpha power in the nondelirium group across all 19 channels (frontal: 5.42 [2.90-8.16] vs 2.89 [-0.03-5.09], P = .007; 18 of 19 channels significant by false-discovery-rate (FDR)-corrected permutation test). Network analysis demonstrated longer averaged characteristic path lengths in the delirium group (mean ± standard deviation [SD], 4.49 ± 0.62 vs 3.57 ± 0.16, P = .026, FDR-corrected), consistently in the frontal, parietal, and occipital regions, suggesting reduced network efficiency. Delirium was associated with early disruption of alpha anteriorization during induction and globally reduced functional network efficiency during maintenance. Perioperative electroencephalogram (EEG) transition features may serve as early markers of delirium susceptibility.

42911507.title: Pneumothorax rates following cardiac surgery with versus without continuous serratus anterior plane catheters: a secondary analysis of trial data with propensity score matching to a historic cohort.
42911507.journal: Canadian journal of anaesthesia = Journal canadien d'anesthesie
42911507.abstract: Moderate to severe pain is common after cardiac surgery, especially in the first two postoperative days. Inadequate pain control may prolong intensive care unit (ICU) stay, may increase cost, and contributes to chronic pain. Enhanced Recovery After Cardiac Surgery (ERACS) protocols prioritize multimodal analgesia, including regional anesthesia techniques. In a recent randomized trial with continuous serratus anterior plane (SAP) catheters, we found unexpectedly high pneumothorax rates. To address this, we aimed to design a propensity-score-matched comparison using patients from the same institution to control for institutional practice patterns, surgical techniques, and patient demographics that could confound comparisons with published literature rates from other centres. We conducted a secondary analysis of RCT data with propensity score matching to a historic cohort. We compared the pneumothorax rates in patients receiving continuous SAP catheters in our previous Cardiac-Serratus Anterior Plane (Cardiac-SAP) trial with those in a retrospective institutional database cohort of patients receiving standard care undergoing cardiac surgery via sternotomy. The two groups were propensity score matched in a 1:20 ratio based on age, sex, smoking status, surgery type, and pre-existing respiratory disease. We analyzed univariate comparisons using Fisher's exact test or the percentile bootstrapping method. We matched 50 patients from the Cardiac-SAP trial to 989 retrospective cohort patients. After matching, the SAP catheter group was associated with a significantly higher risk of pneumothorax (12% vs 3%; odds ratio, 5.3; 95% confidence interval, 2.1 to 13.6; P < 0.001). There were no significant differences for other outcomes, including ICU readmissions, length of ventilation, and length of ICU or hospital stay. Patients who developed a pneumothorax had longer ventilation time and longer hospital stays. Our data suggest that SAP catheter use as a part of a randomized trial for cardiac surgery was associated with a higher rate of pneumothorax in trial participants than in a historic cohort of a similar population, though causality is unclear. Differences in monitoring within the trial and the inherent risks in this population may have contributed.

42911252.title: Clinical safety, tolerability, and efficacy of fospropofol disodium for sedation: a systematic review.
42911252.abstract: Fospropofol disodium (fospropofol) is a water-soluble prodrug of propofol with a distinct pharmacological and tolerability profile. However, evidence regarding the safety, tolerability, and efficacy of fospropofol across broader sedation contexts and different comparators remains insufficiently synthesized. This systematic review summarized current research findings on fospropofol to clarify its clinical role and guide future research. This systematic review was registered prior to initiation (PROSPERO CRD42023477740). Comprehensive searches were performed in PubMed, Web of Science, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE via Ovid, Embase via Ovid, ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to 26 August 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating fospropofol for sedation and reporting extractable efficacy or safety outcomes were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated according to the GRADE approach. Meta-analysis was performed for clinically comparable evidence groups, with other findings synthesized according to SWiM principles. This systematic review included 10 original studies, comprising six procedural-sedation trials and four trials for ICU sedation. Quantitative synthesis was conducted for two comparable evidence groups, whereas the remaining outcomes were synthesized narratively. In three endoscopic procedural-sedation trials, fospropofol 6.5 mg/kg achieved a higher sedation success than 2 mg/kg (RR 3.27, 95% CI 2.62-4.08). In mechanically ventilated ICU patients, hypotension risk did not clearly differ between fospropofol and propofol (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.67-1.28). Procedural studies showed a dose-dependent pattern in sedation efficacy, whereas ICU studies generally reported comparable target-sedation attainment between fospropofol and comparator sedatives. Paresthesia/pruritus was commonly reported, while rates of cardiorespiratory adverse events varied across settings and doses and showed no consistent comparative advantage for fospropofol. Evidence for injection pain and satisfaction was limited. Certainty of evidence ranged from high to very low, mainly because of risk of bias and imprecision. Fospropofol can provide effective sedation across procedural and ICU settings, but its efficacy and safety profiles vary according to dose, comparator, and clinical setting. Higher doses may improve procedural-sedation efficacy but may also increase adverse effects in some settings. Current evidence does not establish a consistent cardiorespiratory safety advantage for fospropofol over other sedatives, and further adequately powered randomized trials are needed to clarify its comparative safety and optimal clinical role.

42898307.title: Preoperative nutritional status defined by GLIM criteria and postoperative delirium in older patients receiving general anesthesia.
42898307.abstract: Preoperative malnutrition may reflect reduced physiological reserve and increased vulnerability to postoperative delirium (POD) in older surgical patients. However, evidence based on standardized diagnostic criteria remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate the association between Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM)-defined malnutrition and POD among older patients undergoing surgery under general anesthesia. This retrospective observational cohort study included consecutive patients aged ≥65 years who underwent elective or emergency surgery under general anesthesia between January 2022 and December 2025. Preoperative malnutrition was retrospectively classified according to the GLIM framework using available phenotypic and etiologic criteria. Patients with and without GLIM-defined malnutrition were matched 1:2 using propensity score matching. POD documented during hospitalization was identified from Confusion Assessment Method assessments, Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit assessments, or explicit physician diagnoses. The association between GLIM-defined malnutrition and POD was examined using conditional logistic regression stratified by matched set. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses were also performed. The matched cohort comprised 495 patients, including 165 with GLIM-defined malnutrition and 330 without malnutrition. All propensity score covariates achieved acceptable post-matching balance, with absolute standardized mean differences <0.10. POD occurred in 42 patients with malnutrition (25.5%) and 37 patients without malnutrition (11.2%; p < 0.001). GLIM-defined malnutrition was associated with higher odds of POD after multivariable adjustment (adjusted odds ratio, 2.36; 95% confidence interval, 1.36-4.10; p = 0.002). No significant interactions were identified across age, surgical category, American Society of Anesthesiologists class, or immediate postoperative intensive care unit admission subgroups. Comparable associations were observed in the unmatched cohort, alternative matched analyses, fixed observation windows, restricted-length-of-stay cohorts, and analyses using alternative POD definitions. GLIM-defined malnutrition was associated with higher odds of POD during hospitalization in older patients undergoing surgery under general anesthesia. GLIM-based nutritional assessment may provide clinically useful information for perioperative delirium risk stratification.

42897881.title: Postoperative delirium and 1-year functional decline, institutionalization and mortality.
42897881.abstract: Postoperative delirium is a common and serious complication in older surgical patients and has been associated with increased morbidity, healthcare costs, long-term functional decline and mortality. To determine whether postoperative delirium is associated with functional status, quality of life, institutionalisation and mortality at 1 year after surgery in a large multicentre surgical cohort. Prospective multicentre observational study. Forty-three hospitals in Spain. Surgical patients were recruited in November 2023 and assessed for delirium 48 h after surgery, with follow-up at 1 year. A total of 2442 adult surgical patients undergoing elective or urgent procedures requiring hospital admission. Postoperative delirium was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM), CAM for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) or the telephone-administered 4AT according to clinical setting. None. Functional status and quality of life at 1 year assessed using the 12-item World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS 2.0). Secondary outcomes included institutionalisation and mortality. After excluding 81 deaths and 462 nonresponders, the 1-year telephone follow-up was completed for 1899 patients. Postoperative delirium within the first 48 h was independently associated with a 4.6-point higher WHODAS score at 1 year: adjusted mean difference = 4.60 [95% confidence interval (CI), 1.57 to 7.64, P = 0.003]. Delirium was also associated with increased institutionalisation and higher mortality: odds ratio (OR) 2.5 (95% CI, 1.07 to 5.84, P = 0.03), and (16.7 vs. 3.1%; P < 0.001), including 30-day, 60-day, and 365-day mortality (all P < 0.001), respectively. Postoperative delirium is independently associated with long-term functional decline, loss of independence, institutionalisation and increased 1-year mortality. These findings highlight delirium as a key perioperative complication and support prevention strategies and structured long-term follow-up after surgery. ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NC-T06127901).

42897595.title: Nursing students' first clinical encounters with delirium: a qualitative study of experiential learning and professional development.
42897595.abstract: Delirium is a complex neurocognitive condition that is often difficult to recognise and manage in clinical practice. Although nursing students receive theoretical education about delirium during undergraduate training, they may feel inadequately prepared when encountering patients with delirium in real clinical settings, reflecting a persistent theory-practice gap in nursing education. This study aimed to explore nursing students' experiences of their first clinical encounters with patients experiencing delirium. This qualitative descriptive study was conducted with 13 first-semester, fourth-year nursing students at a university in Türkiye who had recently completed delirium-related theoretical education and intensive care clinical placements. Participants were recruited using purposive sampling. Data were collected through face-to-face, semi-structured interviews and analysed using inductive reflexive thematic analysis. Five main themes were identified: (1) making sense of delirium through diagnostic uncertainty; (2) emotional burden, including fear, inadequacy, and empathy; (3) clinical and ethical challenges related to behavioural disturbances and restraint practices; (4) professional learning through role modelling, communication, and increasing self-efficacy; and (5) critical reflections on education, highlighting the limitations of theory-based preparation. Students described their first encounters with delirium as emotionally intense and clinically demanding experiences. Although students initially struggled with uncertainty, fear, and communication difficulties, repeated clinical exposure and supportive nurse role models contributed to the development of professional confidence, communication strategies, and more empathic approaches to delirium care. Students also reported that nurses' attitudes and approaches toward patients influenced their own professional perspectives on nursing care. Nursing students' first encounters with delirium were experienced as both emotionally challenging and professionally transformative. The findings suggest that theoretical education alone may be insufficient to prepare students for the complexity of delirium care. Integrating experiential and practice-oriented educational approaches, such as simulation, case-based learning, and communication-focused training, may help bridge the theory-practice gap and improve students' preparedness, confidence, and competence in delirium care.

42893497.title: [Thoracic trauma in Hungary today: heritage, current challenges and future directions].
42893497.abstract: Thoracic trauma is an important contributor to morbidity and mortality among severely injured patients. While the management of immediately life-threatening intrathoracic injuries is relatively well defined, the treatment of severe blunt chest wall injuries, particularly multiple rib fractures and flail chest, remains variable across institutions. This review aims to summarize the current situation of thoracic trauma care in Hungary, with special emphasis on chest wall injuries and the role of surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRF). SSRF should no longer be regarded as an isolated technical procedure, but as part of the complex, multidisciplinary management of patients with rib fractures. Therapeutic decision-making should be based not only on the number of fractured ribs, but also on fracture pattern, chest wall instability, pain, respiratory mechanics, pulmonary parenchymal injury, the patient's physiological reserve, overall injury severity and timing of surgery. The development of thoracic trauma care in Hungary requires a shared indication language, protocol-based imaging, early reassessment, multimodal analgesia, physiotherapy, transparent regional referral pathways and auditable outcome measurement. The existing Hungarian expertise in trauma surgery, thoracic surgery, emergency medicine and intensive care provides a realistic basis for establishing a structured, nationally applicable model of thoracic trauma care. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(42): 1686-1692.

42891598.title: Association of Admission Serum Homocysteine with Discharge Neurocognitive Dysfunction after Acute Cerebrovascular Disease in a High-Altitude Setting.
42891598.abstract: Discharge-phase neurocognitive abnormalities may affect rehabilitation participation, self-management, and discharge safety after acute cerebrovascular disease, but early clinically accessible correlates remain incompletely defined. We examined the association between admission serum homocysteine and clinically adjudicated discharge neurocognitive dysfunction in a high-altitude clinical setting. This single-center retrospective cohort included 227 adults admitted for acute ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, or transient ischemic attack. The first available serum homocysteine measurement within 24 h of hospital arrival was analyzed continuously and by cohort-derived tertiles. The primary outcome was neurocognitive dysfunction documented within 24-48 h before discharge and adjudicated independently by two reviewers blinded to homocysteine levels; standardized cognitive instruments were not systematically available. Logistic regression was sequentially adjusted for demographic, renal, neurological, neuroimaging, and cerebrovascular phenotype-related factors. Among 227 patients, 98 (43.2%) had discharge neurocognitive dysfunction. Admission homocysteine was higher in patients with dysfunction than in those without dysfunction (18.3 ± 6.2 vs. 12.4 ± 4.7 µmol/L, P < 0.001), and dysfunction prevalence increased from 22.4% in T1 to 38.5% in T2 and 69.9% in T3 (P for trend < 0.001). In the primary fully adjusted model, each 1 µmol/L increase in homocysteine was associated with higher odds of dysfunction (OR 1.14, 95% CI 1.07-1.21, P < 0.001), and T3 versus T1 remained associated with the outcome (OR 4.36, 95% CI 2.00-9.51, P < 0.001). Estimates were similar in prespecified sensitivity analyses, including exclusion of delirium or positive confusion assessment method for the intensive care unit (CAM-ICU) screening and restriction to acute ischemic stroke. Higher admission homocysteine was associated with discharge-phase neurocognitive dysfunction, supporting prospective evaluation of homocysteine as a potential marker of short-term neurocognitive vulnerability rather than a validated predictor of persistent post-stroke cognitive impairment.

42890932.title: Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting Using Two Different Anesthetic Techniques: Postoperative Outcome.
42890932.abstract: This study was performed to investigate the effect of prescribing remifentanil, along with paracetamol and gabapentin in comparison of fentanyl and morphine, on pain relief and faster recovery of patients undergoing coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). A double-blind controlled randomized clinical trial study was performed on 60 CABG candidates. In the control group, the patients underwent anesthesia drugs, analgesic drugs (fentanyl and morphine), and muscle relaxant drugs (without premedication with paracetamol, gabapentin, and remifentanil). In the intervention group, in addition to the control group medications, and bolus doses of remifentanil were used as an analgesic during the operation if analgesia was needed. Also, gabapentin 300 mg orally 1 h before surgery; gabapentin 300 mg every 8 h in the ICU; paracetamol 1 g as an intravenous infusion 30 min before the induction of anesthesia; Paracetamol 1 g every 6 h in the ICU for 3 days were prescribed. The pain scores mean in the intervention group on the first, second, and third days after CABG were significantly lower than the control group (P < 0.05). Also, the percentage of delirium in the control group was significantly higher than the intervention group in the first and second days after CABG (P < 0.05). According to the results, administration of remifentanil as a short-acting intraoperative opioid, and the gabapentin to treat nerve pain along with paracetamol before and after CABG surgery could effectively control pain and hemodynamic stability of patients with the least side effects besides reducing the need for additional opioids.

42889950.title: Relationship Between Blood Urea Nitrogen to Albumin Ratio and Risks of Mortality and Delirium in Pancreatitis Patients: A Retrospective Analysis of the MIMIC-IV Database.
42889950.abstract: This study is aimed at evaluating the predictive value of the blood urea nitrogen-to-albumin ratio (BAR) for both mortality and delirium risk in patients with pancreatitis. Pancreatitis carries a substantial mortality risk and significant long-term sequelae, with delirium being a severe neurological complication, underscoring the clinical need for effective prognostic markers. A retrospective cohort study was performed using the MIMIC-IV v3.0 database. A total of 1748 ICU patients meeting diagnostic criteria for pancreatitis (ICD-9/10 codes: 577.0, 577.1, K85) with documented baseline blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and albumin levels were included. BAR was calculated (BUN[mg/dL]/Albumin[g/dL]) and patients were stratified into quartiles (Q1: BAR < 3.0; Q2: BAR 3.0-5.0; Q3: BAR 5.0-9.2; Q4: BAR ≥ 9.2). The primary endpoints were all-cause mortality and delirium occurrence (identified using ICD-9 codes 293.0, 293.1, and ICD-10 codes F05, F05.9). Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression (mortality) and logistic regression (delirium) were employed, adjusting for demographics, illness severity scores (GCS, SAPS II, OASIS, and Charlson Comorbidity Index), and comorbidities. Restricted cubic splines (RCS) were used to explore nonlinear associations. Higher BAR levels significantly correlated with greater disease severity: compared with Q1, Q4 exhibited a higher Charlson Comorbidity Index and mortality rate. BAR was an independent predictor of delirium; each 1-unit increase in BAR was associated with a 2.7% increased risk of delirium (adjusted OR = 1.027, 95% CI: 1.009-1.044), and patients in Q4 had a significantly higher risk compared with those in Q1 (adjusted OR = 1.882, 95% CI: 1.157-3.108). After multivariable adjustment, BAR was not significantly independently associated with mortality (Q4 adjusted HR = 1.022, p = 0.8). RCS analysis revealed BAR > 9.0 as a high-risk threshold, characterized by delirium OR > 1.78 and mortality HR > 1.97. The BAR quartile model yielded AUCs of 0.635 and 0.599 for predicting mortality and delirium, respectively, indicating modest predictive ability. BAR independently predicts delirium risk and reflects disease severity in pancreatitis patients, but does not demonstrate significant independent predictive value for mortality after accounting for confounders. The identified threshold (BAR > 9.0) supports the utility of BAR as a supplementary biomarker for delirium risk stratification in this population.

42886821.title: Comparison of Shoulder Field Anesthesia (SFA) with Interscalene Block (ISB) for Analgesia After Arthroscopic Shoulder Surgery: A Randomized Noninferiority Trial.
42886821.journal: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
42886821.abstract: An interscalene brachial plexus block (ISB) is commonly used for analgesia after shoulder surgery but is associated with neurologic and respiratory complications, including hemidiaphragmatic paralysis. Surgeon-performed shoulder field anesthesia (SFA) is a landmark-guided, phrenic nerve-sparing technique that may provide effective analgesia with fewer complications. The purpose of this study was to compare SFA with ISB for pain control after arthroscopic shoulder surgery. We investigated whether SFA would provide noninferior analgesia as measured by cumulative 48-hour postoperative pain scores. In this randomized trial, patients undergoing arthroscopic shoulder surgery were assigned to SFA or ISB. Postoperative pain was assessed using the numeric rating scale (NRS) at 2, 4, 8, 24, and 48 hours. Patient satisfaction was assessed at 48 hours. Other secondary outcomes included opioid consumption, hospital stay, and block-related complications. Eighty patients (mean age, 47.7 ± 15.7 years; 53 men) completed the study. All patients were classified as White; 80% were of Middle Eastern ethnicity. Baseline characteristics were comparable between the SFA and ISB groups. The primary outcome analysis demonstrated a mean difference in the cumulative 48-hour NRS pain score of -0.824 (ISB - SFA), with a 95% confidence interval of -1.853 to 0.206. The upper limit of the confidence interval remained below the prespecified noninferiority margin of 1.5 NRS points, demonstrating noninferiority of SFA. ISB provided lower pain scores during the early postoperative period (4 to 8 hours), and pain scores converged thereafter. Hospital stay was shorter in the SFA group. Opioid consumption, patient satisfaction, and oxygen desaturation rates were similar between groups. Two cases of Horner syndrome and 1 respiratory event requiring intensive care occurred in the ISB group; none occurred in the SFA group. SFA was noninferior to ISB for the prespecified cumulative 48-hour pain end point. ISB provided superior pain relief during the first 4 to 8 hours, but SFA offered a lung-sparing alternative with similar cumulative opioid requirements and patient satisfaction, fewer clinically apparent block-related complications, and a shorter hospital stay. These findings support a risk-benefit framework to guide individualized analgesic selection. Therapeutic Level I. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

42881579.title: Research Trends in Frailty and Delirium in Older Adults: A Bibliometric Analysis.
42881579.abstract: Background/Objectives: Frailty and delirium represent critical geriatric syndromes with profound implications for older adults' health outcomes. This study aimed to quantitatively map global research trends and thematic developments in frailty and delirium among older adults through a bibliometric approach. Methods: A literature search was conducted in the Web of Science Core Collection up to 11 May 2026. Bibliometric analyses were performed using VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and the R package "bibliometrix". Results: The analysis included 911 publications published between January 2006 and May 2026, involving 6805 authors from 337 journals. The USA dominated research output with 185 articles (20.3%) and the highest total citations (8507). Harvard University led institutional contributions (139 articles), while Age and Ageing emerged as the most influential journal (h-index = 21). Bellelli Giuseppe was the most productive and impactful author. Keyword co-occurrence analysis identified six thematic clusters: adverse outcomes and comprehensive geriatric assessment, cognitive decline and neuropsychiatric disorders, perioperative and intensive care settings, postoperative delirium and geriatric complications, prediction and validation tools, and epidemiology and management-related themes. Temporal keyword bursts revealed recent emphases on "anesthesia" (2022-2026) and "cardiac surgery" (2023-2024). Conclusions: This bibliometric analysis demonstrated a sustained increase and diversification in research on frailty and delirium in older adults over the past two decades. The field has evolved from foundational clinical and epidemiological studies to multidisciplinary, outcome-oriented research, with growing attention to perioperative care and comprehensive assessment.

42966651.title: When In-Person Interpretation Matters: Perspectives From ICUs and Acute Inpatient Care Settings.
42966651.journal: American journal of critical care : an official publication, American Association of Critical-Care Nurses
42966651.abstract: Clinicians often care for multilingual patients and generally prefer in-person rather than remote interpretation. However, little is known about the reasons for selecting specific interpretation modalities in intensive care units (ICUs) and acute inpatient care settings. To examine the context and application of in-person interpretation in ICUs and acute care settings. Semistructured interviews of interprofessional stakeholders were conducted to understand the advantages and limitations of in-person and remote interpretation modalities in ICUs and acute care settings. Thematic analysis of the interviews was performed. Forty-one interviews were completed. Certain contexts motivated preferences for selecting in-person rather than remote interpretation in ICUs and acute care settings. Three overarching themes were identified: (1) specific types of conversations (eg, goals-of-care, end-of-life, and difficult conversations), (2) additional patient-related communication barriers (eg, hearing problems, delirium), and (3) other considerations related to in-person interpreter expertise (cultural contexts and prebriefing) and barriers to use (eg, delays, difficulty contacting interpreters). Acute care clinicians often prefer in-person interpretation owing to factors that are either specific to in-person interpretation or cannot be fully replicated via remote modalities. Acute care clinicians consider conversation complexity, patient factors, and unique benefits versus logistical barriers when considering in-person interpretation. Overall, in-person interpretation provides advantages over alternative modalities for several scenarios to improve the quality of care for patients with non-English language preference in ICUs and acute care settings.

42850547.title: Neurocritical Care Society Abstracts from the 24th Annual Meeting 2026.

42844637.title: Palliative and end-of-life care on the battlefield: a scoping review.
42844637.abstract: Modern conflicts have brought about a paradigm shift in military medicine. In Prolonged Field Care, recommendations have so far focused on damage control and care aimed at ensuring survival. But, particularly in large scale combat operation, not all patients will survive, and despite the development of palliative care in the civilian sector, no extension of this approach has yet been envisaged for military medicine. This review aims to identify knowledge gaps in palliative and supportive care in combat situations. We conducted a literature review in PubMed, CAIRN, Scopus and Embase, with the last search carried out on 31 December 2025, using triangulation at each stage of the screening process. Studies published since 1900 focusing on frontline palliative and end-of-life care for combatants were included. Of 3,629 unique records, 35 articles were included, ranging from World War II-era accounts to current prolonged field care guidelines. Pain management was the most extensively documented topic. Morphine, a historical mainstay, has been increasingly supplemented by oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate and ketamine. Ketamine was favored in austere settings for its hemodynamic stability and multi-route administration. Other analgesics, such as paracetamol and NSAIDs, were also briefly described. Regional anesthesia was recognized as an analgesic force multiplier, though never described in an explicitly palliative context. For expectant and dying casualties, a limited but consistent body of literature addressed opioid titration and palliative sedation, notably via continuous midazolam infusion. Diverse end-of-life-related symptoms were addressed, including nausea, dyspnea, secretions, and delirium. Non-pharmacological measures, such as thermal regulation, mouth care, disarming, and comfort items, were described as accessible across provider levels. Spiritual care and family communication, though addressed in few sources, emerged as important but under-formalized components. Overall, evidence specific to palliative and end-of-life battlefield care remains sparse and largely extrapolated from curative-care literature. Pain management in combat is a well-researched field, but one that is rarely examined in the specific context of end-of-life care. Similarly, there is a notable gap in the literature regarding palliative care in a combat context. Where such topics are addressed, they are often simply a transposition of civilian data. The lack of training and doctrinal guidance prevents the proper integration of this specialized care, which aims to ensure dignity for dying combatants and to reflect the values upon which military medicine is founded. The protocol was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) on 8 December 2025 (DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/U9RSG).

42842391.title: Individualized Treatment Effects of Cefepime vs Piperacillin-Tazobactam in Adults Hospitalized with Acute Infection.
42842391.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
authors: Evidence-based Individualized Treatment Effects (EvITE) Group and the Pragmatic Critical Care Research Group
42842391.abstract: Among adults hospitalized with acute infection, a recent randomized trial observed no significant average treatment effect of cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam on acute kidney injury or death, but fewer days-alive-and-free-of delirium and coma with cefepime. To determine whether patients' individual characteristics modify the effect of cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam on outcomes. In this secondary analysis of the Antibiotic Choice On Renal Outcomes (ACORN) trial, an effect model was derived and validated to predict the effect of cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam for adults hospitalized with acute infection. The primary outcome was survival without acute kidney injury; the secondary outcome was survival without delirium or coma. The individualized treatment effect predicted in the validation cohort significantly modified the effect of cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam on survival without acute kidney injury (Qini 1.68; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.25-3.18; p-value = 0.01). Among 626 patients predicted to experience ≥5% benefit from cefepime, 81.2% of patients randomized to cefepime survived without acute kidney injury, versus 74.2% randomized to piperacillin-tazobactam (difference, 7.1%; 95%CI, 0.25 to 13.9%). Among 203 patients predicted to experience ≥5% benefit from piperacillin-tazobactam, 56.6% of patients randomized to cefepime survived without acute kidney injury, versus 63.0% randomized to piperacillin-tazobactam (difference, -6.3%; 95%CI, -20.7 to 8.2%). The effect of trial group on survival without delirium or coma was not modified by individual characteristics. Patients' individual characteristics modified the effect of cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam on survival without acute kidney injury but not on survival without delirium or coma.

42841411.title: Comparison of cooling methods for drug-induced hyperthermia in a pre-hospital and emergency department setting: a systematic review.
42841411.abstract: Hyperthermia is a medical condition characterized by elevated body temperature above 39.0 °C due to imbalanced heat production and dissipation. Stimulant drugs such as cocaine and amfetamines, as well as intense physical exertion, commonly induce hyperthermia. In severe cases, hyperthermia presents life-threatening complications requiring immediate temperature reduction interventions. Management involves various cooling modalities that differ in efficacy and practicality within pre-hospital and emergency department settings. This systematic review evaluates and compares the efficacy of cooling modalities for managing drug-induced hyperthermia suitable for pre-hospital and emergency department settings. Due to the paucity of data on drug-induced hyperthermia, studies examining exercise-induced hyperthermia were also included to provide additional evidence on cooling efficacy. A comprehensive search for cooling efficiency studies across PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, CINAHL, APA PsycINFO, and SportDiscus from inception until October 2025, without language restrictions was conducted. Randomized controlled trials, observational studies, and case-based studies were included. Quality assessment utilized the GRADE approach for certainty of evidence, while the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and RoB 2.0 assessed risk of bias. Meta-analysis was performed when feasible. The search identified 6,920 citations, with 71 studies included in this systematic review comprising 1,932 patients treated with 12 different cooling modalities. Analysis demonstrated that an ice water immersion cooling rate of (0.169 ± 0.027 °C/min) and cold water immersion cooling rate of (0.162 ± 0.037 °C/min) achieved the highest cooling rates. Meta-analyses confirmed that cold water and ice water immersion were more effective than passive cooling. Ice water-soaked sheets or towels had a cooling rate of (0.121 ± 0.030 °C/min) and room temperature immersion a cooling rate of (0.089 ± 0.020 °C/min) produced adequate cooling rates, while all other cooling modalities proved inadequate as standalone treatments. Due to paucity of data on cooling methods specifically for drug-induced hyperthermia, this study incorporates data from exertional hyperthermia to inform treatment recommendations. Both populations share similar demographics and involve exertion as a primary or contributing factor, supporting the clinical relevance of this approach. However, important pathophysiological differences exist; in case of exertional heat stroke hyperthermia related to exertion improves as physical activity ceases, while stimulant-induced hyperthermia persists despite cessation of activity due to ongoing central drug effects. Although sedation can reduce physical activity in intoxicated patients, these patients often present with concurrent medical complications requiring simultaneous monitoring and treatment. When ice or cold water immersion is available, often at large events, and can be applied safely, this represents the preferred cooling method. For emergency and pre-hospital settings, ice water-soaked sheets or towels are a practical cooling method available to most emergency departments and pre-hospital settings to treat hyperthermic intoxicated patients that is less resource intensive than immersion techniques and maintains continuous patient monitoring capabilities. Given the limited data on drug-induced hyperthermia, further research should address these knowledge gaps and investigate combined cooling strategies and their practicality in pre-hospital and emergency department settings.

42839199.title: Rethinking Platelet Dysfunction in Traumatic Brain Injury: From Platelet Count to Hemostatic Phenotype.
42839199.abstract: Coagulopathy after traumatic brain injury (TBI) is multifactorial and dynamic, with major implications for hemorrhagic progression and outcome. Platelet dysfunction is an underrecognized component that may occur despite preserved platelet count. For the purpose of this point of view, platelet dysfunction refers to any measurable impairment in agonist-induced aggregation, receptor-pathway responsiveness [adenosine diphosphate (ADP)/P2Y12 and arachidonic acid (AA)/ cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) axes], or platelet contribution to whole-blood-clot strength, occurring disproportionate to or in the absence of thrombocytopenia. Functional impairment can appear early and has been associated with TBI severity, intracranial hemorrhage progression, transfusion requirements, and mortality. Conventional coagulation tests and platelet count are insufficient to identify this phenotype. Platelet function assays, including thromboelastography (TEG) with platelet mapping, may help characterize selected high-risk patients. However, the evidence remains largely observational, thresholds are heterogeneous, interassay concordance is poor, and platelet transfusion or desmopressin should not be regarded as routine interventions. This point of view reframes platelet dysfunction after TBI as a dynamic hemostatic phenotype and argues for prospective phenotype-guided trials.
