42955700.title: Penetrating Brain Injury: Neurocritical Care Perspectives on the Updated Brain Trauma Foundation Guidelines.

42953567.title: A Novel Resource-Adapted Neurocritical Care Education Program in Tanzania: Implementation, Outcomes, and a Framework for Sustainable Training.
42953567.abstract: Neurologic emergencies contribute disproportionately to morbidity and mortality in sub-Saharan Africa, yet structured neurocritical care training remains limited. Emergency Neurologic Life Support (ENLS) standardizes early management of neurologic emergencies, but implementation in resource-limited settings requires contextual adaptation. Limited access to neuroimaging and monitoring compounds diagnostic uncertainty. Portable neuroultrasound (NeuroUS) offers a feasible bedside adjunct. We developed, implemented, and evaluated Tanzania's first resource-adapted neurocritical care educational program, including hands-on NeuroUS training in a low- and middle-income country (LMIC) setting. We conducted a prospective observational study during a 2-day in-person training program (October 2025). Multidisciplinary healthcare professionals caring for neurocritical care patients completed pre- and postcourse assessments evaluating medical knowledge, self-reported knowledge, and confidence across ENLS and NeuroUS domains (5-point Likert scale). Ordinal Likert outcomes were summarized using median and interquartile range (IQR) and compared using two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests. Correct-response proportions were compared using Fisher exact tests. Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate adjustment was applied within each outcome family. Twenty-two participants completed precourse assessments; 17 completed postcourse assessments. Self-reported medical knowledge improved across 15 of 16 domains. The largest effects were observed for NeuroUS knowledge, which increased from a median of 1.5 (IQR, 1-2) to 4 (IQR, 4-5; rank-biserial, r = 0.85; 95% CI, 0.64-1.00; q < 0.001); Broad-Reaching Acute Interventions in Neurocritical Care, from 3 (IQR, 2-3) to 4 (IQR, 4-5; r = 0.73; 95% CI, 0.48-0.93; q < 0.001); and intracranial hypertension and herniation, from 3 (IQR, 3-4) to 5 (IQR, 4-5; r = 0.70; 95% CI, 0.45-0.89; q < 0.001). Confidence scores were higher in eight of 16 domains after adjustment. Both NeuroUS diagnostic-application items demonstrated large postcourse differences (q < 0.001). Correct-response proportions increased across all six exploratory knowledge items, but none remained statistically significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons. Ninety-four percent found the program relevant to their practice. Implementation of resource-limited ENLS integrated with structured neuroultrasound is feasible and significantly improved knowledge and confidence. This hybrid approach represents a scalable education model for LMICs.

42947240.title: Discordance between pupillometry indices: a matter of scale and sedation.

42946957.title: Management and Outcomes in Traumatic Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis.
42946957.abstract: Traumatic cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (tCVST) is a rare complication of head trauma associated with increased mortality. Unlike in non-traumatic CVST, there are no consensus guidelines to direct the management of tCVST. Anticoagulation is often used to prevent intracranial complications; however, concurrent traumatic brain injury (TBI) and other injuries complicate treatment decisions, and its clinical benefit remains uncertain. This study describes the epidemiology, management, and clinical and radiographic outcomes of tCVST. This is a retrospective single-center cohort study from a level 1 trauma center in Melbourne, Australia. Patients were identified from the Alfred Health Trauma Registry and hospital coding data between 1 January 2010 and 30 June 2024. Venous imaging was reviewed by two neuroradiologists to confirm tCVST diagnosis and thrombus characteristics. Primary outcomes were defined as discharge destination, with sinus recanalization on follow-up imaging as a secondary outcome. tCVST was confirmed in 138 patients with an incidence of 0.9% in the TBI population and an all-cause inpatient mortality of 10.9% (15 patients). Anticoagulation was used in 78 patients (56.5%) and commenced a median of 5 days after diagnosis [interquartile range (IQR) 2-9]. Patients with anticoagulation generally had less severe traumatic injury, as measured by Injury Severity Score (ISS) and admission Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), but were more likely to have occlusive thrombosis. Among 123 patients who survived to hospital discharge, 93 underwent follow-up venous imaging from day 14, with complete recanalization in 57% by final available imaging. Occlusive thrombosis and multiple sinus involvement were associated with poorer recanalization, while no association between anticoagulation and recanalization was identified. Traumatic CVST is a rare complication of head injury with multiple confounders influencing outcomes and uncertain optimal management. Clinical benefit of anticoagulation in this cohort requires further investigation.

42934458.title: Letter to Editor in Response to Medical Complications After Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: Analysis of Trends in US Admissions from 2006 to 2022.

42934457.title: Understanding Neurogenic Patient-Ventilator Discordance and its Management.
42934457.abstract: Patients with an acutely injured brain may resist the mechanical physics of the ventilator. Neurogenic respiratory breathing patterns generated by the patient may result in the ventilator failing to synchronize with this abnormal drive. This asynchrony may be perceived as distress and with a high respiratory drive could also lead to global lung stress and diaphragmatic myoinjury, and affect liberation from the mechanical ventilator at a later point. Patient-ventilator synchrony concerns have rarely been prioritized in neurocritical care guidelines and are often inappropriately treated with escalating sedation. Starting with the essentials of waveform interpretation and moving towards more complex interpretations of these asynchronies, this review provides insight into the common themes of neurogenic synchrony concerns in mechanically ventilated patients. High respiratory drive, double-triggering/ breath-stacking, and reverse triggering are the most prevalent observations. Adjusting the ventilator can improve patient-ventilator interaction and a number of options to remediate these synchrony concerns are provided.

42909576.title: Systems Before Sensors: PRx-Guided Care and the Neurocritical Care Gap.

42902103.title: Contrast-Enhanced NeuroPOCUS in Neurocritical Care: Overcoming Technical Barriers to Bedside Transcranial Ultrasound.
42902103.abstract: Neuro-point-of-care ultrasound (NeuroPOCUS) is an emerging bedside modality that extends the neurological examination through real-time assessment of cerebral structure and hemodynamics in neurocritical care. Despite increasing integration into clinical pathways and endorsement of transcranial ultrasound-based neuromonitoring by international guidelines, implementation is often hampered by inadequate acoustic windows and poor image and Doppler signal quality, frequently leading to nondiagnostic examinations. Ultrasound contrast agents (UCAs), traditionally used in specialist neurosonology, may overcome these barriers and recover diagnostic information in patients with limited acoustic windows. This clinically oriented narrative review synthesizes the available evidence on contrast-enhanced transcranial ultrasound and examines its potential translation into NeuroPOCUS as a bedside tool for frontline clinicians across vasospasm monitoring, intracranial pressure assessment, evaluation of steno-occlusive cerebrovascular disease, assessment of cerebral circulatory arrest, and other neurocritical care applications. A literature search of PubMed/Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE), Embase, and Scopus was conducted through June 2026, and relevant studies, reviews, and guideline documents were descriptively synthesized according to clinical application. Available evidence indicates that UCAs improve Doppler signal quality, enhance visualization of intracranial vessels, and increase the proportion of diagnostic examinations in patients with limited acoustic windows, thereby improving the interpretability of bedside hemodynamic assessments. However, implementation remains constrained by operator dependence, heterogeneous acquisition and interpretation protocols, limited standardization, and the need for structured training and validated, application-specific velocity cutoffs. Looking ahead, contrast enhancement may expand the scope of bedside neurovascular assessment, including in emergency and acute-care settings where dedicated probes and presets are not readily available. Its favorable safety profile and enhanced bedside feasibility may help bridge the gap between guideline recommendations and clinical practice, although further technical and clinical validation is needed to define its role in frontline NeuroPOCUS.

42901367.title: Association between burst-suppression with identical bursts and multimodal measures of cerebral oxygenation after cardiac arrest.
authors: Pittsburgh Post Cardiac Arrest Service Investigators
42901367.abstract: Burst-suppression with identical bursts (BSIB) is an electroencephalographic (EEG) pattern associated with severe post-cardiac arrest brain injury (PCABI). Whether modifiable mechanisms of brain injury underlie BSIB is unknown. We hypothesized BSIB is associated with impaired cerebral oxygen metabolism, reflected as pathologically elevated jugular bulb venous oxygen saturation (SjvO2), higher brain tissue oxygen tension (PbtO2), normal jugular bulb venous-to-arterial carbon dioxide gradient (PbCO2 gap, and lower intracranial pressure (ICP) compared to other EEG patterns. This single-center retrospective study included patients resuscitated from cardiac arrest who underwent EEG and SjvO2 or PbtO2 monitoring. We categorized EEG patterns as BSIB, malignant without BSIB, and non-malignant. Using mixed effects linear regression, we examined associations between EEG and SjvO2, PbCO2 gap, PbtO2, and ICP. The SjvO2 and PbtO2 cohorts included 109 and 33 patients, respectively. SjvO2 did not differ between BSIB and malignant EEGs (β = 3; 95% CI, -0.6 to 7.0), but was higher with BSIB compared to non-malignant patterns (β = 12; 95% CI, 7.0 to 16.0). BSIB was associated with lower PbCO2 gap compared to malignant (β = -1.4; 95% CI, -2.6 to -0.3) and non-malignant (β = -2.6; 95% CI, -4.1 to -1.0) patterns. PbtO2 was highest with BSIB, but not significantly higher compared to malignant patterns in our adjusted model (β = 4.0; 95% CI, -4.7 to 13.0). ICP was lower in those with BSIB compared to malignant patterns (β = -19.0; 95% CI, -32.5 to -5.6). BSIB may represent a distinct subtype of PCABI characterized by impaired oxygen metabolism with preserved oxygen delivery and diffusion.

42881358.title: Neurogenic Cerebral Edema: Proposed Mechanism for Vasogenic Cerebral Edema.
42881358.abstract: Global cerebral edema (GCE) is a frequent and devastating manifestation of early brain injury after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH), yet its exact inciting biology and sequence of events remain incompletely explained. In this viewpoint, we propose neurogenic cerebral edema (NCE) as a mechanistic hypothesis for vasogenic edema after aSAH, in which autonomic disequilibrium may amplify blood-brain barrier permeability within otherwise mixed cellular, ionic, and vasogenic edema. We integrate evidence that aSAH perturbs the central autonomic network, producing a sympathetic catecholamine surge that can coexist with parasympathetic system activation. This autonomic disequilibrium may indirectly amplify established neurovascular-unit injury pathways, including sulfonylurea receptor 1 (SUR1)-transient receptor potential melastatin 4 (TRPM4) upregulation and tight-junction dysfunction, thereby increasing the vasogenic component of early cerebral edema. We further highlight a pathophysiological parallel with neurogenic pulmonary edema, wherein neurally mediated hemodynamic and permeability forces culminate in protein-rich extravasation across an endothelial barrier. An analogous process in the brain provides a coherent framework for blood-brain barrier (BBB) breakdown and diffuse edema after aSAH. To illustrate the imaging pattern motivating prospective testing, we present a patient with poor-grade aSAH with malignant edema and diffusely elevated apparent diffusion coefficient values. Because autonomic measurements and direct BBB permeability assessment were not obtained, this case illustrates a vasogenic component but does not establish a neurogenic etiology. Our premise is that both arms of autonomic control must be considered. This hypothesis also emphasizes the need for prospective validation using BBB permeability imaging and translational autonomic biomarkers.

42963516.title: The Next Era in Cerebrovascular Autoregulation Assessment?
42963516.abstract: Management of the neurocritical patient has undergone an unprecedented conceptual and technological metamorphosis over the last seven decades. What was once understood as a simple, passive hydrostatic relationship between the heart and the brain has evolved into a discipline of precision, where individual dynamic physiology supersedes standardized protocols. For much of the 20th century, clinical practice was anchored in the dogma that cerebral blood flow (CBF) remained constant within broad and fixed blood pressure limits. Recent advances in bioengineering and signalprocessing technologies have demonstrated that the limits of cerebrovascular autoregulation (CA) are not fixed physiological constants, but dynamic boundaries that vary considerably between patients and over time. This recognition has prompted a paradigm shift away from standardized perfusion targets toward individualized cerebrovascular management. In this context, CA is no longer viewed solely as a physiological phenomenon; it has emerged as a measurable and actionable clinical variable. Continuous bedside assessment of autoregulatory function now offers the opportunity to tailor hemodynamic interventions to the individual patient, with the goal of preserving cerebral perfusion and minimizing secondary brain injury.

42823017.title: Management of the Critically Ill Patient with Opioid Use Disorder.
42823017.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
42823017.abstract: The management of critically ill patients with opioid use disorder presents a unique challenge, as overdose, withdrawal, or concomitant intoxication, due to an unregulated drug supply, leads to physiologic changes that potentially impact standard treatment. This review article outlines an emergency medicine-focused approach for early recognition and stabilization of opioid overdose or withdrawal. Topics include naloxone, use of medications for opioid use disorder, recognition of concurrent intoxication, treatment of α2-agonist withdrawal, multimodal analgesia, and sedation for opioid-tolerant patients. The acute management of opioid use disorder is an opportunity to prevent withdrawal-related decompensation, improve comfort, and support ongoing engagement in treatment.

42919167.title: Prediction of death by neurologic criteria in patients with non-traumatic acute brain injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42919167.abstract: Robust predictors of death by neurologic criteria (DNC) after non-traumatic acute brain injury remain insufficiently defined. We therefore aimed to systematically synthesize the available evidence on prediction of DNC in non-traumatic brain injury. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, the Cochrane Library and Web of Science were searched to August 31, 2026. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials, observational studies, case series and registry data. Studies were included in the quantitative synthesis when sufficient comparable data for the same prognostic factor were available from at least two studies. Pooled effect estimates were calculated using random-effects models. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality in Prognosis Studies (QUIPS) tool. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The database search identified 2,091 records. Eighteen studies comprising reported study cohorts of 9,070 participants were included. Quantitative synthesis included four studies (n=1,738), comprising two post-cardiac arrest and two stroke cohorts. In stroke populations, CT markers of severe intracranial mass effect were associated with a more than threefold increased odds of DNC (pooled OR 3.14, 95%CI 1.98-4.96; p<0.0001; I2=0%), while in post-cardiac arrest cohorts lower gray-white matter ratio values were associated with progression to DNC (pooled mean difference -0.15, 95%CI -0.22 to -0.07; p<0.001; I2=72%). Evidence on predictors of DNC after non-traumatic acute brain injury remains limited and methodologically heterogeneous, with only a small number of studies providing robust analyses. Across these studies, CT-based markers - particularly indicators of diffuse cerebral edema or intracranial mass effect - show the most reproducible associations with progression to DNC.

42822164.title: A scalable educational intervention to reduce airway-related harm in low-resource PICUs: A design-test-scale experience.
42822164.abstract: Across low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), an estimated 1.7 billion children lack access to safe surgical and perioperative care. In Latin America, pediatric postoperative mortality remains several-fold higher than in high-income countries, driven largely by preventable airway and critical-care complications. Following the death of an infant after an unplanned extubation in El Salvador, system-level gaps in airway safety, sedation, and communication were identified, motivating development of a scalable intervention to strengthen postoperative critical care for intubated children. This work was designed at Hospital Nacional de Niños Benjamín Bloom, in San Salvador and subsequently tested at Fundación Hospital Infantil Napoleón Franco Pareja in Cartagena, Colombia. Both institutions faced high unplanned extubation rates, variable airway-safety practices, and limited structured training. Using Ariadne Labs ARC (Design-Test-Scale) implementation pathway, we created a bilingual, online pediatric airway and critical-care curriculum alongside a telesimulation-based emergency team-training program. Forty-five short, multilingual video modules addressed airway management, sedation, respiratory therapy, nursing priorities, and teamwork. Remote, high-fidelity simulation reinforced crisis resource management and role clarity, with local champions trained to run courses independently. In El Salvador, early implementation was associated with reductions in unplanned extubations and PICU mortality. In Colombia, 101 clinicians completed the curriculum and 39 completed telesimulation training, with mortality declining from 22.4% to 9.5% post-intervention. A combined digital curriculum and telesimulation model can strengthen airway safety, communication, and crisis readiness in resource-constrained PICUs. Following successful design and testing, the model is positioned for scale across LMIC pediatric intensive care settings.

42820335.title: Atypical late neurosyphilis presenting as status epilepticus: diagnostic and screening implications.
42820335.abstract: Neurosyphilis is a serious complication of poorly treated syphilis due to Treponema pallidum invasion of the central nervous system. Symptoms vary from silent infection to severe neurological deficits. Despite progress in diagnostics and treatment, the diagnosis is frequently missed because it is not considered, particularly in atypical presentations and in patients with no evident risk factor. . A 45-year-old man presented with confusion, speech difficulties, and left-sided weakness following subtle behavioral changes. In the emergency department, he had a witnessed focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure starting with head deviation to the left and tonic posturing of the left arm. Brain CT was normal, while MRI revealed right thalamic and bilateral temporal FLAIR hyperintensities with diffusion restriction in the thalamus. CSF showed mild pleocytosis (17 WBC/µL) and raised protein (67.6 mg/dL). Serum treponemal screening was positive with an RPR titre > 1:32. Neurosyphilis was confirmed by a reactive CSF non-treponemal test (RPR 1:2) in a patient with compatible clinical and CSF findings; the CSF TPHA titre was >1:10,240, which is supportive but not in itself a diagnostic criterion.Levetiracetam was started on admission and intravenous penicillin G on day 2, after the diagnosis was confirmed. Because EEG and MRI suggested possible focal status epilepticus, valproate and phenytoin were added. The patient developed respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation and deep vein thrombosis. After extended ICU stay and rehabilitation, he recovered with mild residual critical illness myopathy and cognitive deficits. Neurosyphilis is not intrinsically difficult to diagnose, provided it is considered, including outside the classically recognised risk groups such as men who have sex with men.

42821848.title: Trends in Withdrawal of Life-Sustaining Treatment in Patients With Traumatic Brain Injury, 2013-2023.
42821848.abstract: Withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment (WOLST) is a common factor leading to death in traumatic brain injury (TBI). Recent guidelines have supported delaying WOLST given data suggesting that even patients with severe injuries may have meaningful recovery. However, temporal trends in WOLST are not well described. Here we investigate trends in WOLST among patients with TBI. We performed a retrospective cohort study using data from the American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Program (ACS-TQP) between 2013 and 2023. We included all adults aged 18+ years with TBI defined by ICD-9/ICD-10-CM codes who died before discharge from the index hospitalization. We captured demographic factors including age, race/ethnicity, and comorbidities, as well as hospital/outcome variables including interfacility transfer, hospital size and teaching status, and major hospital complications. WOLST is recorded by each participating trauma center and captured as a discrete variable in the ACS-TQP. For each year, we calculated proportions of death after WOLST as well as time to WOLST. We repeated the analyses, including only patients with isolated TBI and stratifying by TBI severity. We identified 3,864,837 patients with TBI from 2013 to 2023 of whom 164,860 (4.3%) died during index hospitalization and had documented WOLST status. Of these, 93,664 (56.8%) died after WOLST. In total, 31.7% of the WOLST group and 27.5% of the no WOLST group were female. Patients with WOLST were older with median age 68 (IQR 51-79) vs 53 (IQR 31-72) and were more likely to have preexisting comorbidities. The proportion of deaths with WOLST decreased from 60.7% (95% CI 59.4%-62.0%) in 2013 to 56.1% (95% CI 55.4%-56.8%) in 2023 (annual percent change = -0.8%; 95% CI -1.4% to -0.2%; p = 0.010). Time to WOLST increased from a mean of 5.7 days (SD 7.4) in 2013 to 7.1 days (SD 10.0) in 2023 (p < 0.001), while intensive care unit length of stay increased from a mean of 4.8 days (SD 6.5) in 2013 to 6.1 days (SD 7.1) in 2023 (p < 0.001). In sensitivity analyses of isolated TBI, the results were similar. The proportion of trauma patients with TBI who died after WOLST decreased modestly from 2013 to 2023 while time to WOLST increased. Although these may reflect shifting attitudes toward prognostication, WOLST nonetheless remains common and occurs early among patients with TBI.

42967138.title: Effect of Preoperative Intranasal Dexmedetomidine on Postoperative Myocardial Injury in Patients Undergoing Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting.
42967138.abstract: To evaluate the effects of preoperative intranasal dexmedetomidine on postoperative myocardial injury biomarkers in patients undergoing on-pump coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 70 patients undergoing on-pump CABG were assigned to receive intranasal dexmedetomidine (1 μg/kg) or saline 30 min before bedtime on the night before surgery and again 30 min before anesthesia induction. The primary outcome was serum high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-cTnT) at 24 h after surgery. Secondary outcomes included perioperative cardiac biomarkers, preoperative sleep quality, postoperative delirium, and adverse events. For the prespecified primary outcome, hs-cTnT concentrations at 24 h after surgery were significantly lower in the dexmedetomidine group than in the control group (estimated marginal means, 170.29 vs 357.29 ng/L; P < 0.001). Postoperative creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB) concentrations were also lower in the dexmedetomidine group (all P < 0.05). N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide showed a significant group-by-time interaction (P = 0.030), although between-group differences at individual postoperative time points were not significant. The dexmedetomidine group had higher Leeds Sleep Evaluation Questionnaire scores (62 [60-64] vs 44 [41-50]; P < 0.001) and a lower incidence of postoperative delirium (14.3% vs 37.1%; P = 0.029). Adverse events, mechanical ventilation duration, and intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay did not differ significantly between groups. In this single-center trial, two-dose preoperative intranasal dexmedetomidine was associated with lower postoperative hs-cTnT and CK-MB concentrations, better subjective preoperative sleep quality, and a lower observed incidence of postoperative delirium. These findings are preliminary and require confirmation in larger, adequately powered multicenter randomized trials to determine whether the biomarker reductions translate into clinically meaningful cardiovascular benefits. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2500111431.

42968011.title: Comparison of bedside clinical pupillary assessment with automated pupillometry in sedated ICU patients.
42968011.abstract: Pupillary assessment is central in neurocritical care and although inherently subjective, bedside penlight examination remains standard practice. While automated pupillometry provides objective, standardized measurements, the reliability of manual assessment across professional categories remains poorly characterized. Prospective observational study in a surgical and trauma intensive care unit (Reims, Feb-Dec 2025). Thirty sedated or comatose adults underwent repeated pupillary assessments by nurses, residents, and senior physicians, which were compared with automated pupillometry as the reference standard, yielding 1,692 paired bilateral measurements from 30 patients. Primary outcome was agreement for anisocoria detection (≥ 1 mm) and secondary outcomes were pupil size and reactivity, measured using Brennan-Prediger adjusted kappa and McNemar test. Agreement for anisocoria was substantial: nurses κ = 0.64 (95% CI 0.57-0.72), residents κ = 0.74 (0.68-0.81), physicians κ = 0.71 (0.64-0.78 ,p < 0.0001). False-positive rates were high (82-86%), while true anisocoria was detected in 55-73% of cases. For pupil size, agreement was substantial: nurses κ = 0.65 (0.60-0.70), residents κ = 0.64 (0.59-0.65), physicians κ = 0.66 (0.60-0.71), but mydriasis was largely missed (6-11% detection; p < 0.0001). Reactivity showed the weakest agreement: nurses κ = 0.40 (0.34-0.47), residents κ = 0.32 (0.26-0.39), physicians κ = 0.41 (0.34-0.47), with systemic underestimation in nurses (p ≤ 0.0001) and a bidirectional error pattern for residents (p = 0.81). In sedated ICU patients, bedside pupillary assessment showed substantial but systematically biased agreement with automated pupillometry, particularly for anisocoria, mydriasis, and pupillary reactivity. These findings highlight the limitations of subjective bedside assessment and support automated pupillometry as an objective complement to routine clinical examination. NCT06733207, registered 10 December 2024 - Retrospectively registered, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06733207.

42970126.title: Establishing curriculum priorities for intensive care recovery education: an international Delphi study.
42970126.abstract: To effectively support recovery, intensive care unit (ICU) clinicians require training to identify patients at risk of post-intensive care syndrome and implement interventions during and after ICU admission. This study aimed to identify and prioritise curriculum topics for educating interprofessional ICU clinicians on evidence-based ICU recovery care across the continuum of critical illness. A two-round e-Delphi study followed by a structured consensus meeting endorsed by the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) was conducted. A steering committee generated an initial list of curriculum topics. In round 1, participants rated topic importance (9-point Likert scale) and suggested additional topics. In round 2, they rated newly identified topics and ranked priorities. Topics reaching consensus (≥70% rating as critical [7-9]; ≤15% rating as not important [1-3]) were discussed during the final consensus meeting. Participants' mean age was 43.5 (±10.5) years and they were predominantly female (n = 90, 66.7%). Priority topics included early mobilisation during ICU admission, post-intensive care syndrome, delirium prevention and management, implementation of the ABCDEF bundle, and cognitive support and rehabilitation. The final set of learning modules for a future curriculum was established. Priority topics and learning modules for an expert-developed curriculum framework for ICU recovery were established with interprofessional ICU clinicians through a structured international consensus process with moderate levels of participant retention between the two Delphi rounds and full consensus agreement among experts. This framework may support in delivering recovery-focused care across the continuum of critical illness.

42968967.title: Severe Propofol Infusion Syndrome Managed With Multimodal Critical Care: A Case Report.
42968967.abstract: Rapid cardiovascular collapse with severe metabolic derangement during propofol sedation should raise concern for propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS). A 21-year-old man with previous traumatic brain injury presented with refractory status epilepticus requiring mechanical ventilation and prolonged propofol sedation. Following four days of infusion, he developed abrupt bradycardia, cardiogenic shock, severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, hypertriglyceridemia, and significant left ventricular dysfunction. The combination of prolonged propofol exposure and rapidly evolving multiorgan failure was considered consistent with PRIS. Propofol was discontinued immediately. Management included administration of multiple vasoactive infusions, sodium bicarbonate, calcium chloride, dual high-effluent continuous renal replacement therapy via two dialysis circuits, high-dose euglycemic insulin, and enteral L-carnitine. Hemodynamic improvement occurred within approximately six hours, followed by recovery of cardiac and renal function. He was discharged from the intensive care unit on day 30 and later returned home after rehabilitation without dialysis dependence. This case highlights the importance of early recognition of PRIS and rapid escalation of individualized organ support in severe presentations, while acknowledging that the contribution of individual adjunctive therapies cannot be determined from a single case.

42970461.title: Impact of Beta-Blocker Use on Mortality Across Traumatic Brain Injury Severity: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
42970461.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality. The initial insult can lead to tissue and cellular damage that results in an excessive catecholamine release, which may be mitigated with beta-blockers (BB). However, guidelines recommend their use only under specific conditions. This study compared the use of BB to no BB use in patients with TBI at an urban trauma center. This was a retrospective chart review of all adult patients with TBI admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). Patients who received at least 2 consecutive doses of any scheduled BB were compared with those who did not receive any BB. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes were the rate of 28-day mortality, in-hospital length of stay, ICU length of stay, and discharge disposition. Safety outcomes were bradycardia, hypotension, and use of vasopressors following BB administration. Subgroup analyses of propranolol, mild/moderate, and severe TBI populations were also evaluated. A total of 1197 patients were included in the study, of whom 375 received BB and 822 did not. The majority of patients were male (71.1%) and had a mean age of 53.5 years. Propranolol (42.1%) was the most commonly ordered initial BB. There was no difference in the rate of in-hospital mortality between the BB and no-BB groups (13.1% vs. 11.9%; P=0.570); however, in the adjusted analysis, BB use was associated with reduced in-hospital mortality (odds ratio: 0.589; 95% CI: 0.381-0.909; P=0.017). Regression analysis based on severity showed that the use of BB was associated with reduced mortality in severe TBI (odds ratio: 0.298; 95% CI: 0.173-0.513; P<0.001), but not mild or moderate TBI (odds ratio: 1.948; 95% CI: 0.970-3.914; P=0.061). The use of BB in patients with severe TBI was associated with lower in-hospital mortality.

42970330.title: From liberal to restrictive and beyond: a narrative review of red blood cell transfusion strategies in the modern era.
42970330.abstract: Red blood cell (RBC) transfusion remains a cornerstone of modern medicine, yet optimal transfusion thresholds continue to be debated. Historically, liberal strategies -maintaining hemoglobin (Hb) concentration above 10 g/dL- predominated, but evidence from the 1990s onward has favored restrictive approaches (Hb threshold 7-8 g/dL). This narrative review synthesizes contemporary evidence on restrictive versus liberal transfusion strategies published between 2021 and 2026, evaluates population-specific considerations, and explores emerging ultra-restrictive thresholds. A structured narrative literature search was conducted in PubMed and Google Scholar with particular emphasis on evidence published between 2021 and 2026. Evidence from randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and clinical practice guidelines is critically discussed. The 2025 Cochrane update (48 trials, >20,000 participants) provided high-certainty evidence that restrictive strategies induce a reduction in the risk or proportion of patients receiving at least one RBC transfusion by 41% without increasing 30-day mortality or major morbidity. Restrictive thresholds are safe in stable critically ill patients, in those undergoing non-cardiac surgery, and in patients with acute gastrointestinal bleeding. However, important exceptions include: acute myocardial infarction (in which liberal strategies may reduce cardiac events), neurocritical care (conflicting evidence on neurological outcomes), chronic transfusion-dependent conditions such as thalassemia (liberal strategies are disease-modifying), and hematologic malignancies (individualized approach required). Ultra-restrictive thresholds (Hb <6-7 g/dL) have emerged as a potential blood conservation tool during shortages but require further safety validation. Restrictive transfusion strategies are safe and effective for many stable adult hospitalized patients, reducing blood product utilization without compromising outcomes. However, individualized approaches remain essential for specific high-risk populations. Ultra-restrictive strategies are promising, but these approaches should currently be considered only in selected contexts pending further safety validation.

42969408.journal: Turkish journal of anaesthesiology and reanimation

42972259.title: Stress hyperglycemia ratio is associated with delirium in elderly cardiac surgery patients in the postoperative intensive care unit: a multicenter retrospective cohort study.
42972259.abstract: Postoperative delirium(POD) is severe in elderly cardiac surgery patients.Elevated glucose levels trigger oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and cerebral metabolic disturbances, which are key mechanisms linking dysglycemia to delirium. Current models lack predictors, and dysglycemia interpretation is confounded by diabetes. The stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR) integrates acute glucose and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) to quantify acute metabolic stress, but its predictive value for POD needs validation. This was a multicenter retrospective cohort study involving elderly patients (≥ 65 years) admitted to the ICU following cardiac surgery. The discovery cohort was derived from the MIMIC-IV database (n = 1,087), while the external validation cohort consisted of patients from six Chinese hospitals (n = 982). The primary outcome was POD. The optimal threshold for the SHR was identified using restricted cubic splines (RCS). Subsequently, the independent association between SHR and POD was evaluated via multivariable logistic regression with sequential covariate adjustment. The performance of the prediction model based on this threshold was assessed using the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC), calibration plots, and decision curve analysis. To further ensure the robustness of the findings, we performed propensity score matching (PSM) and comprehensive subgroup analyses. RCS analysis revealed a nonlinear relationship between the SHR and the risk of POD, with an inflection point at 1.09. After extensive covariate adjustment, an SHR ≥ 1.09 was strongly and independently associated with a significantly increased risk of POD (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 4.152; 95% CI, 3.054-5.676, P < 0.001). This robust association was consistently validated in the external cohort (aOR, 3.856; 95% CI, 2.687-5.593, P < 0.001) and persisted in the PSM analysis. Notably, the univariate model based solely on continuous SHR exhibited good discriminative performance (area under the curve [AUC] 0.734), along with favorable calibration and clinical utility, compared with conventional severity scores, indicating SHR's potential value for risk stratification. An elevated SHR (≥ 1.09) was independently associated with a higher odds of POD in elderly cardiac surgery patients. This readily calculable metric may help identify patients at increased risk and guide enhanced monitoring or future intervention trials.

42976438.title: Real-world outcomes of continuous infusion of sedative agents in critically ill patients with invasive mechanical ventilation.
42976438.abstract: Current guidelines recommend non-benzodiazepine (non-BZD) sedatives -dexmedetomidine (DEX) and propofol (PPF) - over benzodiazepines (BZD) in mechanically ventilated critically ill patients, but real-world evidence from Asian patients remains limited. We evaluated the clinical outcomes of different continuous-infusion sedatives in this population in Taiwan. This retrospective cohort study used electronic health records from a tertiary medical center in Taiwan. Adults receiving continuous intravenous sedation within 48 h of intubation were included. Patients with preexisting ventilator dependence, status epilepticus, or prior tracheostomy were excluded. Groups were 1:1 propensity score matched. Outcomes included intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay (LOS), time to extubation, mortality, and total hospitalization cost. Prespecified pairwise comparisons evaluated DEX vs. BZD, PPF vs. BZD, and DEX vs. PPF. Of 2065 eligible patients, 605 matched pairs were analyzed. Compared with BZD, non-BZD sedation was associated with shorter ICU LOS (9.4 vs. 11.9 days, P = 0.032), earlier extubation (4.1 vs. 6.5 days, P = 0.015), and lower hospitalization cost (US$21,559 vs. US$26,258, P < 0.001), without a significant difference in 90-day mortality (36.7% vs. 38.7%, P = 0.489). In pairwise comparisons with BZD, DEX was associated with significantly shorter ICU LOS and time to extubation, whereas the benefit of PPF was primarily a reduction in hospitalization cost. Non-BZD sedatives were associated with shorter ICU LOS, earlier extubation, and lower hospitalization costs without a detectable mortality difference. These findings are consistent with guideline recommendations favoring non-BZD sedation, although residual confounding remains possible.

42975538.title: Methodological Considerations Regarding Family Confusion Assessment Method Scoring in Delirium Screening for Spanish-Speaking ICU Patients.

42974604.title: Unexplained neurological deterioration after acute brain injury: A structured intensive care framework for targeted continuous electroencephalogram.
42974604.abstract: Neurological deterioration after acute brain injury is common in the intensive care unit, yet its cause may remain uncertain when repeat imaging is stable or does not fully explain the examination. Delayed recognition of occult structural, vascular, systemic, metabolic, medication-related, or electrographic mechanisms may postpone time-sensitive treatment. We aimed to provide a structured bedside framework and define the role of targeted continuous electroencephalography (cEEG). We performed a narrative synthesis of evidence and consensus recommendations across aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, intracerebral hemorrhage, ischemic stroke, traumatic brain injury, and acute subdural hematoma, emphasizing bedside examination, repeat neuroimaging, vascular reassessment, systemic physiology, medication effects, and critical care electroencephalogram (EEG). Deterioration should first be confirmed as a true change and classified as explained, unexplained, disproportionate, or fluctuating/episodic. Evaluation should proceed in parallel: Correct reversible systemic and metabolic derangements, review sedative and analgesic exposure, and reassess structural or vascular complications. cEEG is most informative when deterioration remains unexplained after stabilization, exceeds the apparent imaging burden, fluctuates, follows a clinical seizure, or presents as delayed awakening. It can identify electrographic seizures, status epilepticus, and rhythmic or periodic patterns; however, a nonexplanatory recording neither establishes neurological stability nor excludes nonelectrographic secondary injury. A structured intensive care framework may reduce premature diagnostic closure and support timely, selective cEEG. Continuous EEG should complement, not replace, repeated clinical examination, neuroimaging, vascular evaluation, and correction of systemic physiology.

42972481.title: Can full-stay lactate burden predict ICU mortality? The importance of a defined prediction time.
42972481.abstract: Deininger and colleagues reported that time-weighted average lactate calculated over the entire intensive care stay was strongly associated with mortality after traumatic brain injury. This finding supports full-stay TWAL as a summary of sustained lactate exposure; however, because the measure cannot be finalized before death or discharge, it does not establish prospective prognostic performance from a predefined, clinically actionable time. The 72-h analysis also represents conditional prognosis among patients remaining under intensive care at that landmark. The incremental value of time weighting over mean lactate remains uncertain, and performance estimated in an outcome-matched subset may not generalize to a consecutive population. A prespecified landmark framework would better define the clinical prognostic value of longitudinal lactate indices.

42972451.title: Reply to the comment by Kuzukıran Kocataş on "Can full-stay lactate burden predict ICU mortality? The importance of a defined prediction time".
42972451.abstract: We respond to the comment on lo​ngitudinal lactate indices after traumatic brain injury. Full-stay time-weighted average lactate characterizes longitudinal lactate exposure over the intensive care unit stay but is unavailable at an earlier prediction time. Additional post hoc 72 h landmark analyses showed modest discrimination of subsequent 14-day intensive care mortality among eligible patients. Paired comparisons demonstrated similar full-stay discrimination for time-weighted and arithmetic mean lactate. Both analyses yielded similar estimates in matched and full eligible cohorts. These findings support the prognostic relevance of longitudinal lactate measurements; however, prospective validation at prespecified landmarks is necessary before clinical implementation.

42975860.title: Contemporary management of severe generalized tetanus: an evidence-based review.
42975860.abstract: Severe generalized tetanus remains associated with substantial mortality despite being vaccine preventable. Management is complicated by limited high-quality evidence, conflicting trial results, and the need to balance effective control of spasms and autonomic dysfunction against the risks of prolonged mechanical ventilation. We describe the management of a 57-year-old man with Ablett grade III generalized tetanus and use this case as a clinical framework for an expert narrative review. The review synthesizes randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, prospective studies, and relevant observational literature addressing neuromodulatory therapy, airway management, autonomic dysfunction, intrathecal antitoxin, and supportive critical care. The patient was managed using a multimodal strategy comprising continuous midazolam infusion, magnesium sulphate, oral baclofen, dexmedetomidine, intramuscular and intrathecal human tetanus immunoglobulin, and meticulous low-stimulation supportive care. Therapy was titrated using serial bedside assessment of neuromuscular burden. He recovered without endotracheal intubation, neuromuscular blockade, or tracheostomy and was discharged on day 21. We argue that discordant findings in tetanus trials are substantially attributable to heterogeneity in disease severity, clinical practice, airway management thresholds, and resource availability, rather than to true therapeutic inconsistency. Available evidence supports a physiology-directed multimodal approach using agents with complementary mechanisms to suppress spasms and autonomic dysfunction while preserving spontaneous ventilation whenever safely feasible. Management of severe tetanus should focus on achieving physiological targets rather than escalating individual drugs. A structured, individualized, multimodal neuromodulatory strategy delivered within an experienced, low-stimulation critical care environment may allow selected patients to be managed without mechanical ventilation; safety cannot be established from a single case and requires prospective evaluation. Greater emphasis should also be placed on preventive adult immunization, as vaccination remains the intervention most likely to reduce the burden of severe tetanus.

42975624.title: Triphasic waves in leptomeningeal metastases and cycling alternating pattern of encephalopathy during sleep.
42975624.journal: Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape
42975624.abstract: Triphasic waves (TWs), now termed generalized periodic discharges with triphasic morphology, may be mistaken for nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE), particularly in critically ill patients. Changes in vigilance over time can help distinguish encephalopathic patterns from ictal activity. A 69-year-old woman with breast cancer and leptomeningeal metastases developed progressive mutism and impaired consciousness. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed atypical cells and markedly elevated protein, while brain MRI demonstrated bilateral sulcal hyperintensities, most prominent in the posterior regions. An EEG performed 1 week after bevacizumab and paclitaxel were discontinued showed only mild background slowing without epileptiform discharges. A repeat EEG 1 week later showed nearly continuous TWs. The discharges disappeared during spontaneous sleep and recurred periodically, consistent with a cyclic alternating pattern of encephalopathy during sleep (CAPE). In the absence of significant metabolic and toxic derangements, these features favored an encephalopathic rather than ictal pattern. Given the advanced disease and poor prognosis, care remained supportive and palliative. This case highlights the importance of interpreting TWs within their clinical context and in relation to the state of vigilance. Their disappearance at sleep onset, with periodic recurrence during sleep producing a CAPE, supports an encephalopathic rather than ictal interpretation, helping to avoid misdiagnosis of NCSE and unnecessary administration of antiseizure medications.

42980976.title: Brain Tissue Oxygenation in the Contralateral Hemisphere of Critically Ill Patients with Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage: A Prospective Observational Study.
42980976.abstract: Brain tissue oxygen pressure (PbtO2) monitoring is increasingly used in neurocritical care, but whether PbtO2 provides complementary information beyond conventional parameters such as intracranial pressure (ICP) and cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) in spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is unclear. We conducted a prospective, single-center observational cohort study in a dedicated neurocritical care unit between January 2021 and March 2023. Adult patients with spontaneous ICH requiring invasive multimodal brain monitoring were consecutively enrolled. Continuous monitoring included ICP, CPP, pressure reactivity index (PRx), bedside optimal CPP (CPPopt), and PbtO2 in the contralateral hemisphere. Neuromonitoring data were analyzed during the first 48 h and between days 3 and 7. Paired comparisons were used to assess temporal changes. Linear regression models were used to explore the relationship between PbtO2, CPP, and PRx. A total of 31 patients were included, of whom 18 underwent PbtO2 monitoring. ICP remained within normal ranges, while CPP increased significantly from the first 48 h to days 3-7. PRx improved over time, suggesting better cerebrovascular autoregulation. In contrast, PbtO2 values remained close to hypoxic thresholds and did not significantly differ between periods. During the first 48 h, median PbtO2 was 21.72 mm Hg [interquartile range (IQR) 18.67-27.04] despite preserved systemic oxygenation. No significant correlation was found between PbtO2 and partial pressure of oxygen (paO2)/fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) ratio. In linear regression models the association between PbtO2 and cerebral perfusion was more evident during the first 48 h although visual inspection suggested a nonlinear relationship, with higher PbtO2 values clustering around a relatively narrow CPP range. In critically ill patients with spontaneous ICH, local brain tissue oxygenation, evaluated with PbtO2 in the contralateral hemisphere, remained suboptimal despite controlled ICP, elevated CPP, and preserved pulmonary gas exchange (paO2/FiO2 ratio). PbtO2 may be closely related to cerebral perfusion dynamics with a potential role as a complementary tool for individualized neurocritical care management. However, no inferences regarding perihematomal oxygenation can be made from these data.

42981236.title: Safety of Dexmedetomidine Use in Adult ICU Patients With Right Ventricular Dysfunction.
42981236.abstract: BackgroundDexmedetomidine is commonly used in the intensive care unit (ICU) and is associated with hemodynamic adverse events, including hypotension and bradycardia. Use of dexmedetomidine has not been described in critically ill patients with right ventricular (RV) dysfunction and may be particularly relevant given the tenuous hemodynamics in this patient population.ObjectiveDetermine the prevalence of adverse events in adult ICU patients with RV dysfunction receiving dexmedetomidine.MethodsThis single-center, retrospective cohort study included adult ICU patients with RV dysfunction measured by echocardiogram who received dexmedetomidine between January 2017 and December 2022. The primary outcome was a composite of adverse events after dexmedetomidine initiation including bradycardia, hypotension, increasing vasopressor/inotrope requirements, and asystole. Secondary outcomes included individual components of the primary outcome and a comparison of adverse events based on RV dysfunction severity.ResultsA total of 245 patients met study inclusion criteria. A total of 178 adverse events occurred in 153 patients (62.4%). The most common adverse event was hypotension occurring in 129 patients (72.5%). Increased vasopressor requirements occurred in 35 patients (19.7%), and mean change in norepinephrine equivalents from baseline was 0.06 µg/kg/min. Adverse event rates did not differ among patients with mild, moderate, or severe RV dysfunction.ConclusionAdult ICU patients with RV dysfunction receiving dexmedetomidine experienced high rates of hypotension and increased vasopressor requirements. Findings from this study may assist in tailoring sedation regimens for critically ill patients with RV dysfunction. Future research is needed to explore optimal sedative agents in this patient population.

42978870.title: Respiratory medicine in the ICU 2026: From physiology to precision care.
42978870.abstract: This annual review summarizes major advances in respiratory medicine in the intensive care unit (ICU) published in 2025, focusing on high-impact clinical and translational studies most likely to influence current practice and future research. Across the field, 2025 strengthened the evidence base for key physiological concepts while more clearly defining where physiological strategies translate into clinical benefit and where broadly applied interventions remain insufficient, reflecting an increasing shift toward precision-based respiratory care. Precision medicine advanced through open-source inflammatory acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) subphenotype classifiers and trajectory-based physiological phenotypes that outperform static definitions and support time-dependent treatment strategies. Evidence for non-invasive respiratory support expanded in obesity, immunocompromised patients, and procedure-related hypoxemia, emphasizing that implementation factors such as duration, staffing, and positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) strategy strongly influence success. Prospective multicenter cohorts reinforced the prognostic relevance of driving pressure (DP) and mechanical power, whereas randomized trials indicated that DP-guided PEEP titration and advanced ventilator modes do not reliably improve patient-centered outcomes when broadly applied under lung-protective targets. A major 2025 development was the operationalization of spontaneous breathing risk, and bedside indices of inspiratory efforts (Pocc and P0.1) were linked to pendelluft and outcomes, with oxygenation severity modifying harm versus benefit, supporting an effort-guided framework for preventing patient self-inflicted lung injury. In ARDS, prolonged inhaled volatile sedation failed to improve outcomes and was associated with possible harm compared with intravenous sedation. The largest 2025 oxygen trial showed no mortality benefit for broadly conservative targets, while subgroup analyses suggested heterogeneity of treatment effect. Electrical impedance tomography advanced toward bedside stratification and individualized titration, including emerging three-dimensional approaches. Finally, 2025 strengthened long-term outcome data for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) and ICU survivorship, reinforcing recovery as a core component of respiratory critical care.

42979476.title: Remimazolam for Precision Sedation and Anaesthesia in Vulnerable Populations: A Narrative Review of Pharmacological Mechanisms, Stratified Clinical Evidence, and Individualised Perioperative Strategies.
42979476.abstract: Sedation and anaesthesia in vulnerable populations are complicated by altered pharmacokinetics, variable pharmacodynamic sensitivity, and limited physiological reserve. The extent of these differences depends on the underlying condition, disease severity, comorbidity, and treatment setting. These issues are common in older adults, patients with obesity or obstructive sleep apnoea, organ dysfunction, cardiovascular vulnerability, critical illness, and neurological or psychiatric comorbidity. Conventional sedatives may be poorly tolerated in these settings. Propofol can cause hypotension and respiratory depression. Midazolam may lead to delayed recovery and accumulation. Dexmedetomidine may be limited by bradycardia and slow onset. Remimazolam is an ultra-short-acting benzodiazepine that undergoes rapid carboxylesterase-mediated hydrolysis and can be antagonised with flumazenil. This narrative review examines its pharmacology, clinical evidence, and practical use across nine vulnerable populations. The synthesis prioritised population-specific clinical studies, pharmacokinetic studies, comparative trials, systematic reviews, and major guidelines. For short procedures, the most consistent evidence concerns older adults and haemodynamically vulnerable patients, in whom remimazolam has often been associated with less hypotension than propofol and faster recovery than midazolam. These findings are based mainly on short-term physiological and recovery outcomes. Evidence in mild to moderate hepatic or renal dysfunction is supportive but remains sparse in severe disease. Data for obesity or obstructive sleep apnoea, prolonged ICU sedation, paediatric care, obstetrics, and neurological or psychiatric vulnerability are limited or indirect. Remimazolam should therefore be considered according to the clinical objective, the expected duration and depth of sedation, opioid exposure, airway risk, and organ reserve. Its pharmacological advantages have not yet been shown to improve delirium, cognition, mechanical ventilation, functional recovery, or long-term safety. Further studies should focus on population-specific dosing models and patient-centred outcomes.

42978144.title: EXPRESS: Comparing hypertonic saline and mannitol for management of elevated intracranial pressure in adults: A PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis.
42978144.journal: Journal of investigative medicine : the official publication of the American Federation for Clinical Research
42978144.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to compare the efficacy of mannitol and hypertonic saline (HTS) in reducing elevated intracranial pressure (ICP). We conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases to identify eligible trials comparing HTS and mannitol in adults with elevated ICP; only studies that used ICP monitoring to obtain objective measurements were included. The primary outcome was the change in ICP at different time points, and secondary outcomes included changes in other clinical indicators. A total of 16 studies (583 patients, 2,219 episodes) were included. The pooled results showed that HTS was significantly more effective than mannitol in reducing ICP at 30 min, 1 h, and 3 h post-intervention. However, the numerical differences were small. And there were no statistically significant differences between HTS and mannitol groups in ICU length of stay, mortality, or unfavorable Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) scores. In addition, the increases in cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), mean arterial pressure (MAP), and serum sodium were significantly greater in the HTS group than in the mannitol group at various time points. While HTS produced a larger ICP-lowering effect, the statistically significant difference was modest. Accordingly, existing synthesized evidence fails to clearly establish whether HTS is superior or inferior to mannitol for reducing intracranial pressure.

42981091.title: External Validation of a Machine Learning Model for Delirium Risk.
42981091.abstract: Although external validation of machine learning (ML)-based delirium risk models is a key stage in the model development pipeline, few published reports exist. Moreover, ML-based delirium risk models commonly degrade in performance during external validation. To examine the performance of a fusion multimodal with natural language processing (NLP) delirium risk stratification model in live clinical practice with cross-hospital external validation. This quality improvement study evaluated live clinical deployment of the model among patients 60 years or older who were admitted to non-intensive care units at Mount Sinai Hospital (MSH), with external validation performed at Mount Sinai Morningside Hospital (MSM), from December 1, 2024, to December 31, 2025. Primary outcomes were performance of the risk stratification model, assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and monthly delirium detection rates. A 2 × 2 confusion matrix was created, and the 4 cells were used to calculate model performance metrics and compare associated diagnostic yield between premodel deployment and active model deployment periods. The overall sample included 33 095 admissions to non-intensive care units at MSM and MSH (mean [SD] age, 74.86 (9.22) years; 15 601 women [47.1%], 17 271 men [52.2%]). A total of 9020 MSM inpatient admissions were assigned a delirium risk score by the risk stratification model during live clinical operations and were compared to 21 186 MSH inpatient admissions that were assigned a risk score by the same model. Age at admission significantly differed between patients at MSM and MSH (MSM: median [IQR] age, 75.79 [68.25-83.88] years vs MSH: 72.62 [66.64-79.65] years; P < .001). Patients from MSM and MSH also significantly differed by sex, race and ethnicity, surgical vs medical primary diagnosis, length of stay, and dementia prevalence rate. Among 11 909 MSM patients, patients in the pre-ML cohort (median [IQR] age, 78.00 [71.00-85.00] years) were significantly older than those in the post-ML cohort (median [IQR] age, 75.79 [68.25-83.88] years) (P < .001). The AUROC of the model was 0.91 (95% CI, 0.90-0.92) for MSM and 0.94 (95% CI, 0.93-0.94) for MSH. The positive predictive value of the model was 25.9% for MSM and 19.4% for MSH. For MSM, the mean monthly delirium detection rate significantly increased from 9.23% (95% CI, 8.07%-10.38%) to 19.59% (95% CI, 17.32%-21.85%) after model deployment (P < .001). In this quality improvement study, an ML-based delirium risk stratification model maintained acceptable discriminative performance during external deployment without retraining and was similar to its performance at the development site without retraining. Model deployment was also associated with increased diagnostic yield but a high false positive rate. These findings provide further evidence of the potential generalizability of the model.

42988727.title: Light sedation and benzodiazepine minimization in mechanically ventilated ICU patients: Evidence, uncertainties, and research priorities.

42987438.title: Sleep and circadian research across critical care settings and populations, 2000-2025: a layered bibliometric and science-mapping analysis.
42987438.abstract: We characterised the growth, composition and intellectual structure of sleep and circadian research across critical care settings and populations from 2000 to 2025, with particular attention to the representation and citation visibility of Nursing-category journals. Web of Science Core Collection Article and Review records retrieved on 1 August 2026 yielded 4760 after deduplication. A deterministic title/author-keyword rule gave a field-central corpus of 1047 nested in an abstract-inclusive corpus of 3588. Two authors independently assessed a 200-record stratified sample. Growth, annual Nursing-category share and citations were modelled using log-linear, binomial logistic and negative binomial regression, respectively. Reporting followed the preliminary guideline for reporting bibliometric reviews of the biomedical literature (BIBLIO). The corpus held 859 Articles and 188 Reviews from 370 sources (29,660 citations; h-index 79), growing 15.30%/year (95% confidence interval [CI] 13.73-16.89). Nursing-category journals produced 21.2% of 2000-2024 records, with increasing annual odds (odds ratio [OR] 1.041, 95% CI 1.009-1.075; p = 0.013), but accounted for 13.3% of citations and 1 of the 46 most-cited records (2.2%). Median analysis did not detect a difference. Coupling of 84 highly cited documents yielded five multi-publication clusters with mean years from 2006.6 to 2016.6. Layer choice materially changed influential-publication rankings. Human validation yielded a positive predictive value (PPV) of 92.0% (95% CI 84.8-96.5%). The field expanded substantially. Among highly cited publications, older clusters concerned sleep physiology and later clusters included interventions and guidance. Nursing-category journals were under-represented in the upper citation tail. The map can help critical care teams locate literature on sleep assessment, environmental modification and care clustering across patient, survivor and staff populations. Searches for sleep-related guidance should include Nursing-category and multidisciplinary critical-care journals.

42986439.title: Consensus on a core outcome set for ventilation trials in critically ill patients with acute brain injury: results of an international Delphi consensus study.
42986439.abstract: Clinical research evaluating mechanical ventilation liberation in patients with acute brain injury (ABI) shows substantial outcome heterogeneity, limiting evidence synthesis. We aimed to develop an internationally endorsed core outcome set (COS) and a hierarchical composite endpoint for ventilation trials in neurocritical care. Following COS-STAD/COS-STAP standards, we conducted a 4-round international Delphi study. Candidate outcomes were identified via a scoping review. A multidisciplinary panel from 31 countries scored outcomes using a 9-point GRADE scale. Inclusion required >70% rating as "critical" (score 7-9) and ≤15% as "not important" (1-3). Two consensus meetings were held to categorize outcomes, select representative measures, and ratify a hierarchical composite endpoint. 78 stakeholders participated in Round 1; 60 completed all rounds (23.1% attrition). Fifty-four outcomes achieved Delphi consensus. At Consensus Meeting 1, these were organized into 16 categories; the highest-scoring outcome per category was selected. Three outcomes were not ratified due to disease-specificity (NIH Stroke Scale) or lack of universal applicability (brain death, coma-free days). The final COS comprised 13 outcomes across 5 domains: respiratory function, survival, complications, functional status, and quality of life. A 3-level hierarchical composite endpoint was ratified at Consensus Meeting 2: (1) intensive care unit survival, (2) no reintubation within 72 hours, and (3) days alive without mechanical ventilation. This study establishes the first COS for ventilation weaning trials in ABI patients. Widespread adoption of these 13 outcomes and the hierarchical composite endpoint will standardize reporting, enable meaningful evidence synthesis, and facilitate clinical translation in neurocritical care. Core Outcome Measures in Effectiveness Trials (COMET) Initiative, registration number 2320.

42986438.title: Vibroacoustic music therapy for postoperative delirium in the ICU: the VIMUD-ICU single-center exploratory randomized controlled trial.

42985158.title: Severe pneumonia-associated lung injury: gut-lung-immune-metabolic connections in the critically ill host environment-microecology, barrier function, and mechanical ventilation.
42985158.abstract: Severe pneumonia-associated lung injury is a major cause of acute respiratory failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and death in critically ill patients. Its course is shaped within the critically ill host environment by pulmonary infection and tissue injury, systemic inflammation, circulatory and organ dysfunction, host reserve, and ICU treatment exposures, and may be accompanied by changes in gut microbiota, barrier integrity, and cellular immune metabolism. Thus, pulmonary, intestinal, circulatory, and metabolic changes should be viewed as interrelated processes occurring at different physiological levels rather than as a predefined linear pathway. Emerging studies suggest links among gut microbiota remodeling, barrier disruption, microbial or host-derived circulating signals, altered microbial metabolites, and immune-cell metabolic reprogramming. However, their biological significance varies. Some may represent parallel responses to severe infection and critical illness, whereas others may arise secondary to lung injury, hypoxia, hypoperfusion, or treatment exposure. Longitudinal human evidence remains insufficient to establish whether gut-derived signals achieve physiologically effective remote exposure and independently modify lung injury. Mechanical ventilation is essential for severe respiratory failure, and its direct mechanical contribution to ventilator-induced lung injury has a relatively clear physiological basis. In contrast, sedation, hemodynamic and splanchnic perfusion changes, oxygenation and ventilation status, antibiotics, and nutritional support are distinct concomitant exposures that may independently influence gastrointestinal function, microbiota, barrier integrity, and immune metabolism. Using the critically ill host response as the overarching framework, this review evaluates the temporality, directionality, and functional support of relationships among gut microbiota, barrier function, candidate remote signals, cellular immune metabolism, and ventilation-related exposures, and assesses whether current evidence supports biologically and clinically meaningful gut-lung-immune-metabolic interactions. It also discusses lung-protective ventilation, nutritional support, microbiota modulation, anti-inflammatory therapy, and barrier protection. Current evidence derives mainly from limited studies in severe pneumonia or pneumonia-associated ARDS, clinical evidence from other critically ill populations, and preclinical studies. Evidence that pulmonary and systemic critical illness responses affect the gut is stronger than evidence for an independent gut-to-lung effect. Future longitudinal multi-compartment studies, source tracing, multi-omics integration, and mechanism-oriented interventions are needed to clarify functional cross-compartment relationships and their incremental clinical value for risk stratification and targeted treatment.

42981799.title: Objectively measured nursing time for structured CAM-ICU delirium screening: A single-Centre observational study.
42981799.abstract: To describe, using objectively captured system timestamps, the time nurses require to perform structured Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) delirium assessments, and to examine whether duration varies by unit, shift, or delirium status. Planned secondary analysis of a prospective, controlled pilot cohort study conducted across three perioperative/anaesthesiology-led intensive care units (ICUs) within a single university medical centre. During predefined "structured assessment weeks," CAM-ICU was performed twice daily; nurses manually pressed start/stop buttons within the clinical documentation system. Assessment duration was analysed descriptively and compared across ICU, shift, and CAM-ICU result using the Mann-Whitney U test; a mixed-effects linear model accounted for repeated measurements within patients. 1433 structured CAM-ICU assessments were analysed in 317 patients (median 2 assessments per patient, interquartile range [IQR] 1-5). Median assessment duration was 1 min (IQR 1-2, mean 1.6 ± 1.4, range 0-10). Duration did not differ significantly by ICU (p = 0.057), shift (p = 0.073), or CAM-ICU result (p = 0.192), and no covariate remained associated with duration after accounting for within-patient clustering. When embedded in routine workflow and supported by an integrated documentation system, structured CAM-ICU screening was consistently brief across units, shifts, and patient acuity, objectively confirming the lower end of previously reported estimates; confidence intervals around subgroup differences were narrow enough to exclude clinically relevant differences on the order of one minute or more. Perceived time burden may be a less decisive, stand-alone barrier to structured delirium screening than previously assumed. Units considering reduced screening frequency on time-burden grounds should first collect local, objective time data, and should prioritise streamlined documentation and sustained training over shortening the assessment itself. In this cohort, structured CAM-ICU screening took a median of only one minute per assessment.

42981695.title: Remimazolam versus propofol for sedation in mechanically ventilated ICU patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
42981695.abstract: Propofol is widely used for sedation in the intensive care unit (ICU), but its use may be limited by cardiovascular depression, hypertriglyceridemia, and propofol infusion syndrome. Remimazolam has emerged as a potential alternative to propofol, with rapid metabolism, predictable recovery, and flumazenil reversibility. However, evidence regarding its use in mechanically ventilated ICU patients remains limited. PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, and ClinicalTrial.gov databases were reviewed for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing remimazolam with propofol in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. The primary outcome was percentage of time within the target sedation range. Secondary outcomes included sedation success rate, 28-day mortality, ICU mortality, length of ICU stay, and duration of mechanical ventilation. Safety outcomes including adverse events leading to dose reduction, hypotension, and delirium were evaluated. Continuous endpoints were reported using mean differences (MDs), and dichotomous outcomes were analyzed using risk ratios (RRs), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Six RCTs including 705 patients were analyzed. No statistically significant difference was detected in the percentage of time within the target sedation range (MD, -0.45%; 95% CI, -2.46 to 1.55; p = 0.56; I2 = 0%). No significant differences were detected in sedation success rate, 28-day mortality, ICU mortality, ICU length of stay, and duration of mechanical ventilation, or safety outcomes, although several estimates were imprecise. Remimazolam probably results in little to no difference in sedation efficacy compared with propofol in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. However, uncertainty remains regarding clinical and safety outcomes. Larger multinational RCTs are warranted to clarify these effects.

42987193.title: Feasibility and Safety of Prone Positioning for Atelectasis in Neurocritical Patients: A Historically Controlled Study.
42987193.journal: The Journal of neuroscience nursing : journal of the American Association of Neuroscience Nurses
42987193.abstract: Prone positioning is effective for atelectasis but underutilized in neurocritical care due to concerns about neurological safety. This study examined the clinical outcomes and tolerability of prone positioning in a neurocritical care population predominantly comprising patients with encephalitis and status epilepticus. In this historically controlled study, neurocritical care patients with atelectasis received either 135-degree semiprone positioning plus standard physiotherapy (intervention) or standard physiotherapy alone (historical control). The cohort primarily included patients with encephalitis or status epilepticus (66%); those with intracerebral hemorrhage or traumatic brain injury were not represented. Outcomes included oxygenation (PaO2/FiO2 ratio), CT-based atelectasis score, and clinical endpoints. Forty-seven patients in the prone group and 50 controls were analyzed. The prone group demonstrated significantly improved PaO2/FiO2 ratios at days 3, 5, and 7 (all P<.05) and greater atelectasis resolution (P=.002). Mechanical ventilation duration was shorter in the prone group (14.11 vs. 16.82 d, P=.045). ICU stay, mortality, and neurological outcomes were comparable between groups. No serious adverse events attributable to prone positioning occurred. Prone positioning was feasible and well-tolerated in this selected neurocritical care cohort, with improved respiratory outcomes and no detectable safety signals. These findings support consideration of prone positioning in similar patient populations, though further research is needed in patients with elevated intracranial pressure risk. In clinical practice, prone positioning can be safely implemented by a trained nursing team using clinical observation in selected neurocritical care patients with stable intracranial pressure.

42985501.title: Clinical Factors Associated With Early Ketamine Initiation Among Mechanically Ventilated Adults: A Retrospective MIMIC-IV Cohort Study.
42985501.abstract: Ketamine is used for analgesia and sedation in mechanically ventilated ICU patients; however, the clinical factors associated with its early initiation remain poorly characterised. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV Version 3.1 among adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation and continuous first-line sedation with propofol, dexmedetomidine or midazolam. Early ketamine was defined as recorded administration by a continuous infusion or medication push within 48 h after qualifying first-line sedation began. Concurrent ventilation or continued first-line sedation was not required. Associations were assessed using multivariable logistic regression with patient-clustered robust standard errors. Among 24,363 qualifying ICU stays in 22,396 patients, 226 stays (0.9%) met the early-ketamine definition. The primary complete-case analysis included 21,342 stays and 196 early-ketamine events. Surgical/trauma intensive care unit admission (adjusted odds ratio 2.05, 95% confidence interval 1.39-3.04; p < 0.001), Black race (adjusted odds ratio 1.63, 95% confidence interval 1.05-2.53; p = 0.028) and Stage 3 acute kidney injury (adjusted odds ratio 1.67, 95% confidence interval 1.10-2.53; p = 0.016) were associated with higher odds of early ketamine initiation. Cardiac ICU admission and higher P/F ratio were associated with lower odds. Mean PEEP showed a nonlinear association (p = 0.005). Of 226 starts, 165 (73.0%) occurred during recorded invasive ventilation. Estimates were similar after bolus exclusion, whereas restricting initiation to recorded ventilation attenuated several associations, including surgical/trauma ICU admission (adjusted odds ratio 1.49; 95% CI, 0.97-2.31). Early ketamine administration was uncommon under the study definition and did not always begin during recorded invasive ventilation. Associations were similar after bolus exclusion, but some attenuated when initiation was restricted to recorded ventilation. These findings describe patterns of ketamine use and do not establish treatment indications or therapeutic benefits.
