42986025.title: Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia With Propofol Infusion Syndrome in Severe Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome.
42986025.abstract: Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS) is a rare, potentially fatal complication of prolonged or high-dose propofol exposure characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction, rhabdomyolysis, metabolic derangements, and cardiovascular collapse. The classically described mode of cardiac death is bradycardia progressing to asystole. A previously healthy 21-year-old woman presented 5 days after a vaginal delivery with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome requiring sedation with propofol escalated to 100 μg/kg/min. She developed rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, acidosis, and progressive ventricular ectopy that evolved into pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Propofol was stopped, and continuous renal replacement therapy was arranged, but the patient experienced cardiac arrest before initiation. No arrhythmias occurred after metabolic correction. This case highlights pulseless ventricular tachycardia as a rare cardiac manifestation of PRIS with evolving metabolic abnormalities before cardiovascular collapse occurs. Rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalemia during prolonged propofol therapy should prompt evaluation for PRIS. Early propofol discontinuation and aggressive metabolic correction may prevent fatal ventricular arrhythmias.

42987173.title: Blood-Based Biomarkers and Traumatic Intracranial Hypertension: A Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury Study.
42987173.abstract: The role of blood-based biomarkers in guiding the acute management of patients with established traumatic brain injury is unclear. We sought to determine whether concentrations of glial fibrillary acid protein (GFAP) or ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1) on hospital day 1 are associated with intracranial pressure (ICP) and therapeutic intensity level (TIL). We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury data set, including patients age 17 years and older with traumatic brain injury and invasive ICP monitoring, excluding those undergoing decompressive craniectomy on admission. Patients were stratified into biomarker quartiles, and the relationships with ICP and TIL were analyzed descriptively. Multivariable linear regressions were performed to test the hypothesis that GFAP and UCH-L1 concentrations were independently associated with ICP and TIL after adjusting for a priori defined covariates. Two hundred twenty-nine patients with a median age of 39 years (IQR 26-56) were included. Geometric mean concentrations for GFAP and UCH-L1 were 4423 and 989 pg/mL, respectively. Patients in the lowest GFAP quartile had a median of 7.3% of ICP readings >22 mm Hg vs 23.2% in the highest quartile (P < .001); secondary decompressive craniectomy was performed in 16% of the lowest quartile, compared with 39% of the highest quartile (P = .008). After adjusting for covariates, GFAP was significantly associated with ICP burden (B = 8.05, P = .014) and median TIL over 5 days (B = 1.65, P = .009). No significant relationship was seen for UCH-L1. Day 1 blood concentration of GFAP is associated with elevated ICP and may be a useful adjunct when risk-stratifying patients for intracranial hypertension.

42985557.title: Stellate Ganglion Block Combined With Subanesthetic Ketamine Versus Dexmedetomidine for the Management of Paroxysmal Sympathetic Hyperactivity (PSH) After Traumatic Brain Injury: A Randomized Trial.
42985557.abstract: With appropriate treatment of paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity (PSH) following a traumatic brain injury, there is hope for individuals to overcome storming, regain consciousness, and progress toward successful recovery from the brain injury. The primary goal was to monitor changes in mean arterial blood pressure (MABP) in TBI patients with PSH treated with stellate ganglion block combined with subanesthetic dose ketamine versus dexmedetomidine infusion. The secondary outcomes included monitoring changes in heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature decline, duration of the resolution of paroxysmal hypermyotonia, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) grading, intensive care unit (ICU) stay, and the number of patients who did not show improvement. This randomized, double-blind controlled study was conducted on 102 patients with traumatic brain injury experiencing PSH. They were randomly allocated into two groups: the SK group (n = 51), where patients received a unilateral stellate ganglion block with 5 mL of bupivacaine 0.5% combined with 0.5 mg/kg/h intravenous subanesthetic ketamine infusion, and the D group (n = 51), where patients received a loading dose of 1 μg/kg dexmedetomidine for 10 min and then starting an intravenous infusion at a rate of 1 μg/kg/h. The D group exhibited a significant earlier decrease in MABP compared to the SK group at 30 min, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24, and 48 h (p value = 0.0001). Both groups experienced similar reductions in RR at the same time points (p values ≥ 0.5). The temperature decreased after approximately 10 h from initiating treatment with no significant difference between the two groups. Four patients in the D group and three patients in the SK group did not show significant improvement. In terms of GCS, patients in both groups demonstrated significant improvement in GCS grading (18 [35.3%] Grade I, 29 [56.9%] Grade II, and only 1 [2.0%] and 3 [5.9%] Grades III and IV, respectively, in the D group, and 20 [39.2%] Grade I, 28 [54.9%] Grade II, and only 2 [3.9%] Grade III and 1 [2.0%] Grade IV in the SK group) (p = 0.0001). Both groups had similar durations of ICU stay (p = 0.222). A unilateral stellate ganglion block combined with subanesthetic ketamine improves overall neurological recovery and ICU length of stay in post-TBI PSH compared to continuous dexmedetomidine. However, dexmedetomidine provides a faster reduction in MABP and offers high practical value due to its noninvasive, intravenous delivery. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06354673.

42984267.title: Implementation of the seizure code in a tertiary hospital: Effects on emergency care times and clinical outcomes in severe seizures.
42984267.abstract: To assess the impact of implementing the Seizure Code (SC), a structured multidisciplinary emergency protocol for severe seizures, on care times and clinical outcomes at a tertiary hospital. Single-center, retrospective observational study including episodes of severe seizures in patients aged 18 years or older managed between January 2023 and December 2024, comparing pre-SC and post-SC periods. The primary outcome was time from seizure onset to administration of the first anti-seizure medication (ASM). Secondary outcomes included other care intervals, process indicators, and clinical outcomes. Care intervals were analyzed with accelerated failure time models (percentage change in median time), length of stay in a competing-risks framework, and binary outcomes with Firth-penalized logistic regression (odds ratios, OR), all adjusted for prespecified covariates and clustered by patient. Of 1959 episodes identified, 378 (175 pre-SC, 203 post-SC) met SC activation criteria. Time to the first ASM, the primary outcome, did not differ significantly (27% shorter, 95% CI -15% to 53% for benzodiazepines; 27%, -6% to 50% for others). Time to urgent video-EEG (VEEG) was 48% shorter (29%-61%) and the neurological assessment-VEEG interval 63% shorter (31%-80%). Pre-notification by Emergency Medical Services increased (22.9% vs. 37.8%; p = 0.003). Hospital stay (7.48 vs. 5.08 days; subdistribution hazard ratio for discharge alive 1.36, 1.02-1.89) and intensive care unit stay (3.20 vs. 1.48 days) were shorter. Thirty-day seizure recurrence was lower (8.0% vs. 3.0%; adjusted OR 0.33, 0.12-0.84). Mortality and functional status at discharge did not differ. The primary outcome, time to first anti-seizure medication, was not significantly shorter after implementation of the structured emergency protocol. The observed benefits were concentrated in secondary process and resource-utilization indicators: implementation of the Seizure Code was associated with faster access to urgent VEEG, shorter hospital and intensive care unit stays, and lower 30-day seizure recurrence, without a significant effect on mortality. These findings support protocolized emergency pathways in severe seizures. Severe seizures are emergencies in which fast, coordinated care matters. We compared how patients were treated at one hospital before and after a new protocol, the Seizure Code, was introduced. Afterwards, patients had urgent video-EEG (a recording of brain activity) sooner and spent fewer days in hospital and in the intensive care unit, and fewer had another seizure within 30 days. However, the time to the first anti-seizure medication did not change significantly, and deaths and disability at discharge were unchanged.

42983654.title: Traumatic brain injury in African urban centers: The role of road traffic accidents, outcomes, and health-system factors: a systematic review.
42983654.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of death and disability in low- and middle-income countries, particularly in rapidly urbanizing regions of Sub-Saharan Africa. Road traffic accidents (RTAs), especially motorcycle-related crashes, represent a leading mechanism of injury in many African urban settings. Limited access to neurosurgical care, neuroimaging, critical care services, and organized trauma systems may adversely affect patient outcomes. This systematic review synthesized evidence on outcomes and health-system factors among TBI cohorts in African urban centres where RTAs constitute a major mechanism of injury. PubMed and Google Scholar were systematically searched for studies published between January 2010 and May 2025. Eligible studies included observational studies, clinical audits, and hospital-based registries reporting outcomes among TBI patients treated in African urban centres. Primary outcomes were mortality and functional outcomes, including Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) or Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOSE) measures. Secondary outcomes included morbidity, length of hospital stay, and factors influencing access to neurosurgical care. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale tool. Owing to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively without meta-analysis. Thirteen studies from eight Sub-Saharan African countries were included. Study populations were predominantly composed of young adult males (mean or median age 28-34.5 years; 67-90% male), and RTAs were reported as the leading mechanism of injury in most settings. Severe TBI (Glasgow Coma Scale ≤ 8) was consistently associated with poor outcomes, with reported mortality ranging from approximately 25.8% to 47% among severe-injury cohorts. Predictors of adverse outcomes included low admission Glasgow Coma Scale score, hypotension, hypoxia, polytrauma, and delayed presentation to definitive care. Access to computed tomography (CT), intensive care unit (ICU) services, and neurosurgical intervention varied substantially across centres. Financial barriers frequently contributed to discharge against medical advice (DAMA), potentially compromising outcomes. Long-term functional and neuropsychological outcomes were infrequently reported. Most studies were judged to be at moderate risk of bias, with common limitations including retrospective study designs, single-centre recruitment, limited adjustment for confounding, and incomplete long-term follow-up. TBI remains a major cause of mortality and disability in African urban centres, with RTAs representing a dominant mechanism of injury in most included cohorts. Poor outcomes were associated with severe injury, delayed access to care, limited neuroimaging and critical care capacity, and financial barriers to treatment. The available evidence is constrained by heterogeneous outcome reporting and predominantly observational study designs. Future multicentre prospective studies with standardized outcome measures and longer-term follow-up are needed to better characterize outcomes and guide improvements in trauma and neurocritical care systems across Sub-Saharan Africa.

42981665.title: Severe and Unexpected Events After Acute Withdrawal of Tiapride Contaminating Vigabatrin: A Case Series.
42981665.abstract: In September 2023, the Polish Ministry of Health warned that two lots of Sabril (vigabatrin) powder for oral solution and tablets, released in 2021, contained trace amounts of tiapride. We identified three children with tuberous sclerosis complex who presented in the Department of Neurology and Epileptology, Children's Memorial Health Institute with sudden clinical worsening and unexplained symptoms after withdrawal of contaminated vigabatrin lots. The reported adverse effects included increased frequency and severity of seizures, significant behavioral problems, insomnia, weight loss, and secondary amenorrhea. One patient required admission to the intensive care unit due to drug-resistant status epilepticus. Our observations suggest that rapid withdrawal of tiapride, even administered in low doses, may result in significant and life-threatening deterioration in patients with epilepsy.

42987224.title: Propofol Infusion in a Mixed PICU: Prevalence of Propofol-Related Infusion Syndrome in a Retrospective Cohort, 2019-2022.
42987224.journal: Pediatric critical care medicine : a journal of the Society of Critical Care Medicine and the World Federation of Pediatric Intensive and Critical Care Societies
42987224.abstract: To describe usage and complications of propofol as a sedative agent in patients younger than 16 years old admitted to a PICU and to identify evidence of propofol-related infusion syndrome (PRIS). Retrospective analysis of routinely collected data with comparison between patients receiving propofol for less than 48 hours compared with greater than or equal to 48 hours. Single-center mixed PICU in London, United Kingdom. All patients admitted to the PICU, from November 2019 to November 2022, younger than 16 years old, in whom an infusion of propofol was administered. None. Propofol infusion was used in 1595 patients, 337 of whom had infusions of greater than or equal to 48 hours with a maximum dose of 5 mg/kg/hr and for a maximum duration of 45 days. The cohort age ranged from 1 day to 16 years and included patients with cardiac diagnoses. Patients were administered propofol for a median 76% of their ventilation time, and 26% of patients who were treated with propofol were also treated with noradrenaline. Physiologic variables, blood gases, laboratory values, and discharge summaries were reviewed, and no patients were clinically suspected of having PRIS. Variables previously reported in PRIS were analyzed across each patient's admission, and we failed to identify an association between abnormal physiologic values and receipt of a propofol infusion or whether duration of propofol infusion was greater than or equal to 48 hours. Hence, the upper limit of the 95% CI for 0 of 1595 gives a PRIS prevalence in our population up to 0.19%. In our single-center, mixed PICU experience during 2019-2022, we have used propofol infusion in children younger than 16 years old. This practice included neonates and children with cardiac pathology. We failed to identify any episodes of clinically suspected PRIS in 1595 patients, including in the group treated for greater than or equal to 48 hours, which gives an upper limit for PRIS prevalence of ~0.19%.

42989779.title: Immersive Virtual Reality Cognitive Stimulation for Delirium Prevention in Older Surgical Intensive Care Unit Patients With Cognitive Impairment: Protocol for a 3-Arm Randomized Pilot Trial.
42989779.abstract: Postoperative delirium is common among older adults after major surgery, especially those with cognitive impairment, and is associated with prolonged hospitalization, functional decline, mortality, and subsequent cognitive deterioration. Nonpharmacologic delirium-prevention strategies are recommended but are difficult to deliver reliably in high-acuity environments because they require repeated staff-intensive interactions, consistent patient engagement, and integration into complex intensive care unit (ICU) workflows. This study aims to evaluate the feasibility, usability, safety, acceptance, and adherence of ReCognitionVR 2.0, an immersive virtual reality (VR)-based cognitive stimulation intervention designed for older surgical ICU patients with mild-to-moderate cognitive impairment. This is a single-center, 3-arm, parallel-group randomized pilot trial. Ninety adults aged 65 years or older undergoing major surgery with expected postoperative ICU admission and Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores of 15 to 24 will be randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio to ReCognitionVR 2.0 cognitive stimulation, passive VR control exposure, or standard-of-care nurse-led reality orientation. VR sessions will be delivered once daily for up to 20 minutes on postoperative days 1 through 3 when participants are calm and alert. The primary outcomes are feasibility metrics, including recruitment, outcome completion, safety and tolerability, usability, acceptance, and adherence. Secondary outcomes estimate preliminary changes in attention and executive function using the Months Backward Test and NIH Toolbox Flanker Inhibitory Control and Attention Test. Postoperative delirium incidence is an exploratory clinical outcome. This study was funded in September 2025. Participant recruitment and data collection are currently ongoing. Preliminary data quality assessments and exploratory reviews of the collected data are underway. Formal statistical analyses of the trial outcomes will be conducted after participant enrollment is completed and the study database has been finalized and locked. As of July 29, 2026, we had enrolled 18 participants. Early operational experience informed the refinement of exploratory VR performance metrics and the documentation of protocol deviations. Following an oxygen-connection near miss, we added a preintervention oxygen/readiness checklist as an operational safety safeguard. Enrollment of 90 participants is projected to be completed in 2027 if the current recruitment pace is sustained. Results are expected to be published in winter 2027. This protocol will generate data on feasibility, safety, usability, adherence, digital performance, cognitive assessment, and delirium measurement, all needed to optimize ReCognitionVR 2.0 and to design a future multicenter efficacy trial of VR-enabled delirium prevention in critical care.

42990941.title: Evaluation of Phenobarbital and Benzodiazepine Use for Alcohol Withdrawal Treatment in the Medical Intensive Care Unit.
42990941.abstract: There is a high prevalence of alcohol use disorder (AUD) leading to a significant risk of alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS) in critically ill patients. However, despite existing guidelines, there is limited evidence on the use of phenobarbital for AWS as part of a standardized protocol for medical intensive care unit (ICU) patients. This study aims to compare ICU length of stay for patients receiving phenobarbital and benzodiazepines versus benzodiazepines alone when treating AWS. This study was a single-center, retrospective, pre-post analysis that compared pre-pathway patients admitted between January 2017 and January 2020 who received benzodiazepines alone to post-pathway patients admitted between August 2022 and September 2024 who received phenobarbital in addition to benzodiazepines for AWS. Patients were included if they were hospitalized with an ICD-10 code for alcohol withdrawal, admitted to the ICU with medical critical care as the primary team, and, for the post-pathway group, must have received phenobarbital from the pathway. The primary outcome was ICU length of stay, while secondary outcomes included hospital length of stay, incidence and length of mechanical ventilation, cumulative benzodiazepines dose, incidence of delirium, and use of adjunctive medications for AWS. A total of 132 patients were included in the analysis (n = 92 pre-pathway and n = 40 post-pathway). The median ICU length of stay for the pre-pathway group was 2.95 (interquartile range [IQR] 1.80-5.05) days compared to 2.60 (IQR 1.95-6.75) days for post-pathway group (P = .86). The median hospital length of stay was statistically significant at 8.9 (IQR 5.0-15.5) days for the pre-pathway group compared to 6 (IQR 3.3-12.05) days for the post-pathway group (P = .02). There was no significant difference in mechanical ventilation, use of anti-psychotics, or use of adjunctive agents for AWS (P > .05). There was no significant difference found in the ICU length of stay between the pre-pathway group and the post-pathway group. However, the hospital length of stay for the post-pathway group was statistically shorter than that of the pre-pathway group. These findings suggest that phenobarbital seems to be safe and effective alternative for AWS, and benzodiazepine-sparing regimens should be considered.

42992094.title: Reversal of severe diuretic resistance by dexmedetomidine-associated polyuria in type 1 cardiorenal syndrome: a case report.
42992094.abstract: Dexmedetomidine is a selective α2-adrenergic agonist widely used for sedation in intensive care settings. Although hypotension and bradycardia are well-recognized adverse effects, dexmedetomidine-associated polyuria is a rare and unpredictable adverse effect. An 84-year-old man with ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy, permanent atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic kidney disease was admitted to the Cardiac Intensive Care Unit with type 1 cardiorenal syndrome, severe systemic and pulmonary congestion, oliguria, and acute kidney injury. Despite continuous intravenous furosemide infusion, sequential nephron blockade, and dual vasoactive support with norepinephrine and dobutamine, the patient developed persistent oligo-anuria and worsening congestion. Dexmedetomidine infusion was initiated for psychomotor agitation and disorientation. Shortly thereafter, urine output abruptly increased to approximately 250 mL/h, accompanied by rapid decongestion and improvement in renal function. Following dexmedetomidine withdrawal, oliguria, congestion and renal dysfunction recurred. Rechallenge with dexmedetomidine again induced profound polyuria, with urine output peaking at 650 mL/h and a 10-kg weight loss over 48 h, allowing de-escalation of diuretic therapy and withdrawal of vasoactive support. The Naranjo score was 6, supporting a probable causal relationship. This case demonstrates a reproducible temporal association between dexmedetomidine administration and profound polyuria, confirmed by positive rechallenge. To our knowledge, this is the first report in which dexmedetomidine-associated polyuria was temporally associated with reversal of severe diuretic resistance and clinically meaningful decongestion in type 1 cardiorenal syndrome. Recognition of this rare adverse effect may be relevant in critically ill cardiac patients.

42993613.title: Donation After Circulatory Versus Brain Death Among Adult Trauma Donors: A Retrospective Multicenter Study.
42993613.abstract: Donation after circulatory death (DCD) is an increasingly important source of organs and tissues, yet differences between DCD and donation after brain death (DBD) among trauma donors remain incompletely characterized. We compared DCD and DBD donors among trauma patients who proceeded to donation. Adult trauma patients who died during hospitalization across four trauma centers from January 1, 2016, through July 15, 2022, were retrospectively screened; the analytic cohort comprised patients who proceeded to donation. Multivariable logistic regression examined factors associated with DCD versus DBD among donors. Among 173 donors, 90 (52%) were DCD and 83 (48%) were DBD. Compared with DBD donors, DCD donors were older (median 52 vs. 31 years, p = 0.006), more often White (78% vs. 47%, p < 0.001), had fewer severe head/neck injuries (AIS ≥ 3: 61% vs. 87%, p < 0.001), higher admission GCS (13-15: 24% vs. 8%, p = 0.003), and were less often admitted to the ICU (79% vs. 98%, p = 0.002). DCD donors had a lower median number of organs and tissues recovered (2 [IQR 1-3] vs. 3 [2-4], p < 0.001). After adjustment, GCS 9-15 vs. 3-8 (AOR 3.62, 95% CI (1.22-10.77)), White race (5.41, (2.24-13.06)), head/neck AIS ≤2 vs. ≥ 3 (5.15, (1.99-13.34)), and trauma center were independently associated with DCD. Among trauma donors, DCD and DBD donors differed in neurologic injury severity, hospital course, and organ and tissue recovery patterns. Studies that include all potential trauma donors are needed to identify factors that may influence referral, authorization, and conversion.

42992820.title: Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome: what the intensivist needs to know.
42992820.abstract: Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) is a significant complication of chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy, a revolutionary treatment for hematologic malignancies. This syndrome, which might affect approximately 30% of CAR-T therapy recipients, presents a wide spectrum of neurological symptoms, ranging from mild confusion to life-threatening cerebral edema. In the intensive care unit (ICU), managing ICANS is critical due to its potential severity. Pathophysiology of ICANS is driven by immune-mediated inflammation disrupting the blood-brain barrier, resulting in cerebral cytokine infiltration and glial cell activation. Its severity is associated with elevated cytokine levels in cerebrospinal fluid and serum, which points to the need for specific biomarkers and predictive tools. Standardized assessments, including the Immune Effector Cell-Associated Encephalopathy (ICE) Score, together with brain imaging and adjunctive diagnostic tests, provide clinicians with essential baseline information for the assessment and monitoring of neurological complications. ICU management focuses on supportive care and pharmacologic strategies. Corticosteroids represent the cornerstone of treatment, effectively targeting neuroinflammation while preserving the antitumor efficacy of CAR-T cell therapy. Anticonvulsants, hyperosmolar agents and advanced neurocritical care measures are also pivotal. Recent advances suggest potential benefits of alternative therapies, such as anti-cytokine agents and innovative immune cell products with reduced neurotoxic risks. Despite advancements, challenges persist, including diagnostic ambiguities, resource allocation, and variability in care protocols. This review highlighted challenges in ICANS management for ICU physicians, intending to underline the importance of early detection, rigorous monitoring, and tailored interventions to improve patient outcomes.

42989545.title: [Research advances on the application of artificial intelligence in the warning and management of burn-related delirium].
42989545.journal: Zhonghua shao shang yu chuang mian xiu fu za zhi
42989545.abstract: Delirium in burn patients presented a prominent challenge in intensive care, characterized by high incidence, difficult identification, and a narrow intervention window. Artificial intelligence (AI) technology, with its unique advantages of being adept at processing complex high-dimensional data, mining hidden patterns, and real-time continuous monitoring, provided new directions for the warning and management of burn-related delirium. Based on the main driving mechanisms and clinical heterogeneity of burn-related delirium, this article systematically reviewed the research advances of AI in establishment of predictive models for burn-related delirium, multimodal data fusion and interpretable outputs, multi-source data acquisition, intelligent processing and decision support, as well as clinical applications and closed-loop feedback. It analyzed current challenges such as data governance and algorithmic fairness, integration and collaboration in clinical scenarios, and liability attribution and ethical supervision, and prospected future research directions, aiming to provide references and insights for the application of AI in the field of burns.

42990117.title: Boerhaave's syndrome complicated by pneumorrhachis and chemical meningitis.
42990117.abstract: Boerhaave's syndrome is a life-threatening condition characterised by oesophageal perforation. This report presents a case of Boerhaave's syndrome complicated by pneumorrhachis (air in the spinal canal) and chemical meningitis. A 26-year-old male developed meningism and an agitated delirium following oesophageal rupture, with imaging confirming pneumorrhachis and cerebrospinal fluid analysis consistent with chemical meningitis. Despite a prolonged Intensive Care Unit stay complicated by encephalopathy and severe agitation, the patient made a full neurological recovery with supportive care. This case illustrates a unique pathophysiological progression and underscores the importance of early recognition, exclusion of bacterial meningitis, appropriate prognostication and multidisciplinary management of pneumorrhachis complicating Boerhaave's syndrome.

42997295.title: Association of composite liver function indices with trauma-induced coagulopathy in adult trauma patients.
42997295.abstract: Trauma-induced coagulopathy (TIC) is a life-threatening complication associated with uncontrolled hemorrhage and high mortality in critically ill trauma patients. This study aimed to evaluate the associations and discriminative performance of four composite liver-function indices-ALBI, TBil/ALB, DBil/TBil, and GGT/ALP-with TIC-related outcomes in adult trauma patients. This single-center retrospective cohort study included 634 adult trauma patients. Laboratory data were collected at baseline, 24 h after admission, and 48 h after admission. The primary outcome was the continuous ISTH DIC score assessed 48 h after admission. Overt DIC, non-overt DIC, and ATC were analyzed as secondary or exploratory TIC-related outcomes. Multivariable models adjusted for age, sex, admission lactate, admission pH, admission temperature, traumatic brain injury, hepatic injury, and surgery. Associations between each index and TIC-related outcomes were examined using multivariable linear and logistic regression analyses. ALBI showed the most consistent associations with TIC-related outcomes and the strongest index-alone discrimination for non-overt DIC among the evaluated indices. The TBil/ALB ratio retained independent predictive value, though with somewhat lower overall consistency. The DBil/TBil and GGT/ALP ratios, by contrast, exhibited weaker associations that varied across time points and outcome definitions. Serial measurements over the first 24 h contributed incremental prognostic information; however, no dynamic index outperformed the baseline ALBI score in predictive strength. ALBI was consistently associated with TIC-related outcomes assessed 48 h after admission, and this association remained stable across the examined clinical subgroups. ALBI may serve as a readily available adjunctive risk marker for early coagulopathy risk stratification. Prospective validation is warranted before clinical implementation.

42997588.title: In vitro Evaluation of the Physicochemical Stability of Multi-Drug Y-Site Admixtures Using Dynamic Monitoring and Chemometrics.
42997588.abstract: Concurrent continuous infusions of propofol, midazolam, insulin, dexmedetomidine, and morphine are commonly used in ICU for sedation, analgesia, and glycemic control. However, physicochemical compatibility data for Y-site administration are lacking, leading to risky empirical practice. This study evaluated their physicochemical stability to guide safe infusion. Twenty-six admixtures were prepared at clinical concentrations and stored at room temperature. Samples were analyzed at 0, 2, 4, 8, 12, and 24 h for appearance, pH, osmolality, subvisible particles, mean droplet diameter (MDD), polydispersity index (PDI), zeta potential, microscopic aggregation, and drug content by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Principal component analysis (PCA), hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA), Spearman correlation, and orthogonal partial least squares-discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) were performed to explore stability patterns and key discriminating variables. No obvious alterations in appearance, pH, or osmolality were observed over 24 h. In propofol-free admixtures, subvisible particles met pharmacopeial limits. In propofol-containing admixtures, MDD (95.6-124.3 nm) and PDI (0.338-0.469) remained acceptable, whereas zeta potential ranged from -12.50 to 6.14 mV. Microscopic aggregation was observed in seven propofol-containing admixtures. HPLC showed that all drugs retained >90% of their initial concentrations. OPLS-DA identified four independent variables with VIP values greater than 1 (R2 Y=0.71, Q2=0.689), and permutation tests confirmed no overfitting. Under the conditions studied, seven propofol-containing admixtures showed aggregation, while the other 19 remained stable for 24 h. Chemometric analysis supported the stability classification and indicated that drug composition, pH and zeta potential were key contributors to emulsion aggregation.

42996070.title: Functional and Structural Neuroanatomic Correlates of Intraoperative Anesthetic Dose-Adjusted EEG Alpha Power Among Older Surgical Patients.
42996070.journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
42996070.abstract: Alterations in intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) alpha power and anesthetic dose-adjusted EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) have been associated with both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium (POD) among older surgical patients, yet the neurologic underpinnings of alterations in these anesthetic brain response patterns are unknown. We conducted a single center prospective observational cohort study (ALADDIN), of older adults undergoing non-cardiac/non-cranial surgery, which included preoperative structural and resting state functional MRI, lumbar punctures to obtain CSF, 32 channel intraoperative EEG recordings, and repeated POD assessments. To account for anesthetic dose, frontoparietal EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) was adjusted using our established formula: [intraoperative alpha power]/(2.5 - end-tidal MAC fraction). Multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) with follow-up seed-to-voxel analyses identified functional connectivity patterns associated with intraoperative ADA-FP alpha power. Voxel-wise regression analysis with threshold free cluster estimation (TFCE) correction was used to evaluate associations between cortical thickness and ADA-FP alpha power. CSF biomarker values were obtained from NULISA proximity extension assays. Delirium incidence and severity was assessed with the 3-Minute Diagnostic Confusion Assessment Method (3D-CAM). Delirium severity area under the curve (AUC) during hospitalization was defined as the sum of all 3D-CAM delirium severity scores within the postoperative hospitalization period (for up to 7 days after surgery). The Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) was used in cases of non-verbal/intubated patients. ALADDIN enrolled 215 patients, of whom 168 underwent surgery and had high-quality intraoperative EEG data (44.6% female; mean age 70.9 years). MVPA showed that ADA-FP alpha power was associated with altered functional connectivity within the bilateral frontal poles, left superior frontal gyrus and the right superior parietal lobule (p-FWE < 0.05). Seed-to-voxel analyses revealed that higher ADA-FP alpha power was associated with increased connectivity between DMN MVPA regions and DMN, DAN and salience/ventral attention and decreased connectivity with visual regions. Conversely, right superior parietal lobule connectivity shifted towards greater DMN segregation and increased somatosensory/motor coupling (p-FWE < 0.05). Lower ADA-FP alpha power was also associated with lower cortical thickness in left occipitotemporal and superior parietal cortices (TFCE-corrected p < 0.05). ADA-FP alpha power was also lower among participants with (vs those without) postoperative ward/floor delirium (mean difference, 1.33; 95% CI, 0.22 to 2.44; p=0.019), and ADA-FP alpha power was inversely associated with peak delirium severity (spearman's rho = -0.26; 95% CI, -0.40 to -0.11; p <0.001) and delirium severity AUC (spearman's rho = -0.28; 95% CI, -0.42 to -0.13; p < 0.001). These findings suggest a functional and structural neuroanatomic basis for the decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power values seen among some older surgical patients, which may explain the association between decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and increased rates of both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium. More specifically, these findings suggest that altered default mode and dorsal attention network connectivity is linked to decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and raise the possibility that preoperative/baseline functional connectivity alterations within these networks may play a role in delirium risk.

43000177.title: Association Between Medication-Related Skin Punctures and Delirium in the ICU: An Exploratory Cohort Study.
43000177.journal: Journal of the American College of Clinical Pharmacy : JACCP
43000177.abstract: Delirium is among the most common neurological complications in intensive care unit (ICU) patients, yet many medication-related contributors remain poorly understood. As medication experts, pharmacists are uniquely positioned to lead efforts in identifying, mitigating, and preventing drug-related risk factors for delirium. One underexplored risk factor is the frequency of medication-related skin punctures. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the association between ICU delirium and the number of medication-related skin punctures, with the goal of identifying potential pharmacist-driven interventions to reduce delirium as well as improve patient experience and outcomes. This was a retrospective, observational, exploratory cohort study conducted in the ICU of a 384-bed community hospital. Patients were divided into two groups, low-punctures and high-punctures, using the median number of skin punctures per day as the threshold for defining groups. The primary outcome was the incidence of delirium. Secondary outcomes were delirium-free days, all-cause mortality, hospital length of stay (LOS), and ICU LOS. A total of 404 patients were included in this study. The median number of medication-related skin punctures was 3.79 per day. There were 205 patients in the low-punctures group (0 to less than 4 punctures per day) and 199 patients in the high-punctures group (at least 4 punctures per day). The high-punctures group was associated with increased odds of delirium (odds ratio [OR] 2.09, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.22-3.58, p = 0.007). There was no significant difference in delirium-free days, hospital LOS, and all-cause mortality between groups; however, ICU LOS was significantly longer in the high-punctures group (7 vs. 5 days, p < 0.001). The frequency of medication-related skin punctures ICU patients received may be associated with an increased risk of delirium. These exploratory findings support future research evaluating the impact of pharmacist-driven "skin puncture stewardship" on ICU delirium prevention, patient experience, and overall clinical outcomes.

42999828.title: Clinical Characteristics, Etiologies, and Outcomes of Adults Presenting With Altered Mental Status to the Emergency Department: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
42999828.abstract: Background Altered mental status (AMS) is a common emergency presentation with diverse neurological, infectious, metabolic, toxicological, and systemic causes. Objective The objective of this study was to describe the clinical characteristics, underlying etiologies, management patterns, and clinical outcomes of adults presenting to the emergency department with AMS, and to identify independent clinical factors associated with in-hospital mortality. Methods This retrospective cohort study was conducted at Allama Iqbal Teaching Hospital, Dera Ghazi Khan, Pakistan, from April 2024 to April 2026 and included 210 adult patients presenting with AMS. Demographic and baseline clinical characteristics, including age, gender, body mass index, smoking status, presenting symptoms, duration of AMS, known comorbidities, medication history, substance use, and relevant previous neurological or systemic illnesses, were recorded. Results Of 210 patients, 174 (82.9%) survived, and 36 (17.1%) died. The mean age was 61.74±16.64 years, and 118 (56.2%) were male. Neurological causes were most common (29.0%), followed by infectious (21.4%), metabolic/endocrine (16.2%), and toxicological causes (11.9%). Non-survivors were older than survivors (72.10±13.80 vs. 59.60±16.40 years, p<0.001) and had lower Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores (6.90±3.20 vs. 11.60±3.10, p<0.001), lower oxygen saturation (89.10±8.00% vs. 94.60±4.40%, p<0.001), and higher serum lactate levels (4.80±2.70 vs. 2.30±1.60 mmol/L, p<0.001). Intensive care unit (ICU) admission was required in 61 (29.0%) patients, while 42 (20.0%) required mechanical ventilation. Conclusion Altered mental status was associated with considerable ICU utilization and in-hospital mortality. Neurological and infectious causes predominated, while severe impairment of consciousness, elevated lactate, hypoxemia, hypotension, infectious etiology, and advanced age were independently associated with increased odds of mortality.

42999672.title: Cerebral Air Embolism Following Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography Stent Removal: A Rare and Fatal Complication.
42999672.abstract: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is a generally performed procedure for biliary pathology. Although usually safe, air embolism is an exceptionally rare but potentially fatal complication. We report the case of a 79-year-old female (ASA II) with a history of dyslipidemia and obesity, who presented for elective ERCP and biliary stent removal. She had previously undergone ERCP and open cholecystectomy for choledocholithiasis. During this time, sedation was administered by using fentanyl, midazolam, and propofol via target-controlled infusion. The procedure was initially uneventful; however, at its conclusion, the patient developed sudden desaturation, bradycardia, and a reduced level of consciousness. Computed tomography (CT) imaging revealed multiple cerebral air emboli. Despite intensive care management and ventilatory support, the patient deteriorated and died 2 days later. This case highlights the importance of maintaining vigilance for air embolism, even in seemingly straightforward ERCP procedures, especially in elderly patients. Early recognition and immediate management are vital to improving outcomes.

42999903.title: Recurrent Unexplained Fever and Suspected Promazine Toxicity: Why Probable Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome Was Left Undiagnosed in a Healthcare Worker.
42999903.abstract: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a potentially fatal adverse reaction to dopamine-antagonist medication that can resemble sepsis. A 51-year-old woman working in healthcare experienced recurrent episodes of fever, confusion and muscle rigidity, with six hospital presentations over approximately 10 months. Her prescribed medicines included promazine and amitriptyline. During an earlier severe admission, she developed hyperthermia, agitation, shock, and a creatine kinase concentration of 7272 U/L, requiring intensive care. Investigations did not identify a unifying diagnosis. During the most recent admission, review of previous records and a non-judgemental discussion elicited possible use of additional medication for sleep and neuropathic pain, although the preparation and quantity remained unclear. Six months' supply of promazine had been approved and dispensed within the preceding three months, supporting increased access without establishing the amount ingested. The clinical pattern supported a working diagnosis of probable promazine-associated NMS, with possible concomitant amitriptyline toxicity. Promazine was discontinued three days after admission. At follow-up approximately six months later, the patient remained off promazine and reported sustained symptom resolution and no further hospital attendances. This case highlights the importance of considering NMS in unexplained fever during antipsychotic treatment, conducting repeated medication reviews, and asking sensitive questions, regardless of a patient's professional healthcare background.

42999955.title: [Post-resuscitation care 2025: neurological prognosis of post-cardiac arrest brain injury].
42999955.abstract: Post-cardiac arrest brain injury represents a central component of the post-resuscitation syndrome, driven not only by the initial hypoxic-ischemic insult but also by reperfusion injury after the return or start of mechanical circulation. Complex neuronal damage accounts for a substantial proportion of mortality among successfully resuscitated patients, making reliable neurological prognostication a key objective of post-resuscitation care and clinical decision-making. The 2025 European Resuscitation Council guidelines emphasize a structured, multimodal approach to neuroprognostication. Prognosis should not rely on a single parameter; instead, it requires the integrated interpretation of clinical findings, electrophysiological data, neuroimaging results, and circulating biomarkers. This strategy aims to reduce falsely pessimistic predictions, prevent premature withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy, and avoid the unnecessary prolongation of futile intensive care in cases of irreversible brain injury. In the early phase of return of spontaneous circulation, neurological assessment may be confounded by several factors, including residual sedation, neuromuscular blockade, metabolic disturbances, and cardiorespiratory instability. Therefore, accurate prognostication depends on the correction of reversible conditions and stabilization of physiological parameters before definitive conclusions are drawn. Importantly, neurological outcome assessment is inherently time-dependent, and appropriate timing is essential for safe and evidence-based decision-making. Overall, the 2025 recommendations advocate standardized, multidisciplinary, and stepwise neuroprognostication as a cornerstone of post-resuscitation management, prioritizing patient-centered care while minimizing uncertainty and supporting long-term neurological recovery whenever possible. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(45): 1799-1809.

43000116.title: Biomarkers in Patients With Acute Ischaemic Stroke Undergoing Thrombectomy Compared With Controls: A Pilot Study.
43000116.abstract: Detection of cerebral ischaemia is challenging in patients who are anaesthetised, sedated or have reduced levels of consciousness, as neurological examination is difficult or even impossible to assess. Furthermore, as some patients cannot be transported for radiology, for example during surgery, a reliable blood biomarker for detecting acute cerebral events would be of considerable clinical value. We aimed to compare levels of brain injury biomarkers glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neurofilament light chain (NfL), and total tau (tau) in patients with acute ischaemic stroke (AIS) undergoing endovascular thrombectomy under general anaesthesia or sedation to controls undergoing non-cerebral surgery under general anaesthesia. These biomarkers were chosen because previous studies have demonstrated their potential as blood biomarkers of acute cerebral injury and ischaemic stroke. In this prospective, observational pilot study, conducted at the Sahlgrenska University Hospital, Gothenburg, Sweden, between 2021 and 2024, GFAP, NfL, and tau were analysed using the Simoa Neurology 4-plex assay, before thrombectomy or surgery and at 2- and 24 h thereafter. Blood samples from 21 patients with AIS and 19 controls were analysed. GFAP concentrations in patients with AIS increased significantly from baseline to 24 h (median 301.0 → 1443.0 pg/mL; p = 0.001) and were higher than in controls at all time points (p < 0.01). In the controls there was no significant increase in GFAP from baseline to 24 h (p = 0.449). NfL and tau increased significantly in patients with AIS (p = 0.001 and 0.002) but also in the controls (p = 0.001 and 0.047). GFAP and NfL concentrations were higher in patients with acute ischaemic stroke than in surgical controls at all sampling time points, whereas tau differed only after 24 h. Unlike NfL and tau, GFAP did not increase significantly in controls, suggesting that it may be less influenced by anaesthesia and surgery. These findings support further evaluation of GFAP as a potential biomarker of acute cerebral injury in perioperative and critical care settings. A biomarker of ischaemic cerebral injury could be attractive to support treatments to protect brain health during anaesthesia and surgery. In a pilot study, glial fibrillary acidic protein emerged as a potential candidate as it was increased in patients undergoing endovascular thrombectomy for large-vessel ischaemic stroke compared to anaesthetised patients undergoing non-cerebral surgery. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03919370.

43003547.title: Culture and the Intensive Care Unit Team: Factors Driving Teamwork, Safety, Quality, and Well-Being.
43003547.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) culture and teamwork strongly influence health care quality, patient safety, clinical outcomes, and clinician well-being. Culture shapes how multidisciplinary clinicians communicate, coordinate care, and adopt new practices. Persistent variability in ICU practices, including end-of-life care, sedation management, and mobility, often reflect differences in local culture and team dynamics. Emerging perspectives from complexity science, network science, and behavioral economics conceptualize the ICU as a complex adaptive human network in which collective behavior patterns emerge through repeated clinician interactions. Understanding ICUs through this lens may provide tools, processes, and strategies to improve health care delivery.

43001431.title: The Practice Gap in Managing Cognitive Impairment in Post-Intensive Care Syndrome: A Qualitative Study of Nurses' Perspectives.
43001431.abstract: Cognitive impairment that develops or worsens after critical illness is an important component of post-intensive care syndrome (PICS). It can persist beyond hospital discharge and affect everyday function, independence and quality of life. Nurses are well placed to recognise cognitive change across the intensive care trajectory, yet little is known about how they understand this problem or approach it in practice. To explore nurses' understanding of, experiences with and perspectives on cognitive impairment following intensive care. A qualitative descriptive study was conducted with 13 nurses recruited between August and December 2024. Data were generated through individual, semi-structured, face-to-face interviews and examined using collaborative inductive thematic analysis informed by Braun and Clarke's six-phase process. Three interrelated themes were developed. Conceptual ambiguity described fragmented knowledge, difficulty distinguishing persistent cognitive impairment from delirium and uncertainty about professional responsibility. The practice dilemma reflected an acute-care culture, workload pressures and the absence of feasible assessment and referral pathways. A call to action captured nurses' proposals for education, defined responsibilities, routine screening, multidisciplinary referral and follow-up across care settings. Nurses recognised cognitive problems after intensive care but lacked the conceptual clarity and organisational support needed to address them consistently. Education alone is unlikely to close this gap. Clinical pathways must also define when cognitive concerns should be assessed, documented, referred and followed after transfer or discharge. The findings identify practical targets for nursing education and service development. A shared clinical vocabulary, feasible screening triggers, clear referral responsibilities and continuity between the ICU, ward and community may help nurses identify cognitive concerns earlier and respond more consistently.

43001426.title: Complications of Midazolam-Containing Versus Midazolam-Free Analgosedation in Mechanically Ventilated Adult ICU Patients: A Systematic Review.
43001426.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) patients requiring mechanical ventilation (MV) frequently need analgosedation strategies that combine analgesia and sedation. Analgosedation, often administered with midazolam, is widely employed in middle and low-income countries, but it carries a substantial risk of complications, particularly in older or comorbid patients. Acknowledging these complications is critical for patient safety and quality of care. To examine complications associated with midazolam-containing versus midazolam-free analgosedation in mechanically ventilated adult intensive care unit patients. This systematic review was conducted according to the PRISMA guidelines. A comprehensive search of Scopus, MEDLINE (PubMed), and Web of Science identified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published between 2015 and 2025. Studies meeting predefined eligibility criteria underwent risk-of-bias assessment using the Cochrane RoB2 tool. Nine RCTs were included. Midazolam-containing analgosedation regimens were generally associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation, increased respiratory depression and higher incidence of neurological complications, particularly delirium. In contrast, midazolam-free analgosedation regimens, especially those using short-acting opioids, were associated with shorter mechanical ventilation duration and fewer haemodynamic incidents. ICU length of stay and healthcare costs favoured opioid-only analgosedation protocols, although mortality findings were inconsistent across studies. Compared with midazolam-free analgosedation, midazolam-containing analgosedation regimens in mechanically ventilated adult ICU patients are associated with a higher incidence of respiratory and neurological complications. Opioid-only protocols appear to offer a more favourable complication profile and may facilitate earlier weaning and shorter ICU stays. These findings support cautious use of midazolam and emphasize the importance of individualized, goal-directed analgosedation strategies. Enhancing critical care nursing staff's awareness of complications associated with different analgosedation regimens is essential to promote vigilant clinical monitoring, thereby reducing adverse events and supporting safer patient management.

43001416.title: Knowledge, Attitudes and Self-Reported Practices of Emergency and Intensive Care Nurses in Managing Traumatic Brain Injury.
43001416.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of mortality and disability worldwide, with a growing burden in low- and middle-income countries. Nurses in emergency and intensive care units (ICUs) play a critical role in TBI management, yet little is known about their competencies in Palestine. This study aimed to assess the knowledge, attitudes and self-reported practices of emergency and intensive care unit nurses regarding traumatic brain injury management and to identify factors associated with these outcomes. A descriptive cross-sectional survey using stratified random sampling was conducted in governmental and private hospitals in the northern West Bank, Palestine. Data were collected in January 2025 using a validated Arabic questionnaire. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation coefficients and multiple linear regression analyses were performed, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. A total of 151 nurses participated, yielding a response rate of 61.4% (151/246). Nurses demonstrated generally good foundational knowledge, particularly in Glasgow Coma Scale interpretation and recognition of neurological responses, although gaps remained in advanced monitoring. Attitudes were predominantly positive, with strong support for specialised training. Self-reported practices included maintaining adequate blood pressure and initiating deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prophylaxis. Knowledge correlated significantly with attitude and self-reported practice, and attitude correlated strongly with self-reported practice. Previous TBI training, higher educational level and longer clinical experience were associated with better outcomes. Emergency and intensive care unit nurses demonstrated adequate foundational knowledge and positive attitudes towards traumatic brain injury management, although gaps remained in advanced monitoring and selected self-reported practices. Structured continuing professional development, standardised protocols and organisational support are needed to strengthen neurotrauma nursing care. The findings support context-sensitive continuing education, simulation, standardised protocols and organisational measures that enable nurses to translate knowledge into consistent neurotrauma care in resource-constrained settings.

43002637.title: Effects of advanced practice nurse-driven sedation weaning and early extubation after cardiac surgery amid health care disruption in South Korea.
43002637.journal: Journal of the American Association of Nurse Practitioners
43002637.abstract: Cardiovascular disease has reached unprecedented levels, leading to a substantial increases in the number of cardiac surgeries. Despite the life-saving efforts of surgery, complications remain, including pulmonary complications, which can lead to death. To mitigate these complications, early extubation has emerged as an evidence-based practice for patients undergoing cardiac surgery. The physician shortages that occurred after the mass resignation of physician trainees in South Korea disrupted postoperative care provided in intensive care units (ICU) and impeded early extubation. Our institution accordingly expanded the advanced practice nurses' (APNs) scope of practice to include performing extubation when deemed clinically appropriate after cardiac surgery. This practice change led APNs to develop and implement a sedation weaning and early extubation protocol. To evaluate the effects of an APN-driven protocol implemented in the cardiac ICU. This retrospective study compared two group outcomes: preimplementation and postimplementation groups. This study revealed differences in health outcomes between the two groups of patients. Beneficial health outcomes were achieved due to this protocol in the opioid use and ventilator time of patients with low grade of heart failure in the postprotocol group, which were 16.7% lesser and 17.0% shorter than those in the preprotocol group. This APN-driven protocol proves its effectiveness without causing compromised health outcomes during a health care crisis in South Korea. This protocol incorporating nursing staff autonomy for both sedation and extubation can be implemented and tested for its usefulness for instances where gaps of care occur such as during physician shortages.

43001418.title: Tracheostomy and Home Invasive Ventilation in Severe Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia: A Scoping Review of Indications, Timing, Outcomes and Transitional Care.
43001418.journal: Journal of paediatrics and child health
43001418.abstract: To map the literature on tracheostomy and home invasive ventilation in infants and children with severe bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), including indications, timing, respiratory outcomes, comorbidities, complications, growth, neurodevelopment, social determinants and transitional care. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science and CINAHL/EBSCO from inception to 30 June 2026. Search terms combined BPD or chronic lung disease of prematurity with tracheostomy or tracheotomy. Eligible studies included infants or children with BPD who underwent tracheostomy, received chronic invasive ventilation or were discharged on home mechanical ventilation. Conference abstracts without full-text articles, duplicate precursor abstracts, reviews and editorials were excluded from primary synthesis. Forty-one studies were included. Evidence was mainly retrospective, including cohorts, administrative database studies, multicentre registries and single-centre observational studies. Tracheostomy was generally considered for persistent invasive ventilation, failed extubation, high respiratory support needs, pulmonary hypertension, airway malacia, growth failure, sedation burden or limited developmental progress. Timing varied widely across centres. Pulmonary hypertension was associated with illness severity and mortality risk, although many children receiving home ventilation improved over time. Among survivors, ventilator liberation and decannulation were common but often occurred over several years. Airway complications, readmissions and operative airway interventions were frequent. Evidence also highlighted centre-level variation, racial and social disparities and limited caregiver-centred data. Tracheostomy and home invasive ventilation in severe BPD represent a prolonged care trajectory. Future work should define consensus indications, optimise timing, standardise transitional care and prioritise family-centred and equity-focused outcomes.

43000275.title: Acute motor-sensory axonal neuropathy with brain death-like manifestations: two case reports and literature review.
43000275.abstract: Acute motor-sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN) presenting with brain death-like features is rare, rapidly progressive, and easily mistaken early in the course for brain death of unclear cause or for locked-in syndrome. Misdiagnosis may delay timely immunotherapy and supportive care. We describe two such patients from a single center and summarize the published adult literature to improve recognition of this fulminant presentation. We retrospectively reviewed two patients treated at Yichang Central People's Hospital between 2016 and 2024 who developed brain death-like manifestations in the setting of AMSAN. We also searched CNKI, Wanfang Data, and PubMed for relevant reports published up to June 2025. Both patients developed rapidly progressive generalized paralysis, external and internal ophthalmoplegia, respiratory failure, and disappearance of brainstem reflexes, thereby simulating brain death. Electrophysiological studies showed severe motor-sensory axonal neuropathy and cerebrospinal fluid findings supported the diagnosis. One patient improved after intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), whereas the second showed no early response to IVIG but improved after subsequent plasma exchange. Our literature review identified 28 adult patients with fulminant Guillain-Barré syndrome presenting with brain death-like manifestations, most of whom required prolonged mechanical ventilation and experienced slow, incomplete motor recovery. AMSAN presenting with brain death-like features is characterized by acute onset and complete systemic paralysis, typically initially manifesting as limb weakness and paralysis of both extraocular and intraocular muscles, followed by respiratory muscle paralysis. All patients require prolonged mechanical ventilation and intensive care treatment, rapidly presenting with clinical manifestations resembling "brain death." At this stage, electrophysiological studies and lumbar puncture are particularly crucial for definitive diagnosis. Early initiation of immunotherapy, such as IVIG infusion or plasma exchange, is critical. Patients often show gradual recovery of extraocular and intraocular muscles first; however, most experience poor recovery of respiratory muscle paralysis and limb weakness, significantly prolonging hospitalization and severely impacting patients' work and daily life, highlighting the need for prospective studies to evaluate therapeutic strategies beyond standard IVIG and plasma exchange. While emerging agents such as efgartigimod show preliminary promise in refractory GBS, current evidence is limited to small case reports, and prospective studies are critically needed.

43002802.title: External hydrocephalus in adult neurocritical patients.
43002802.journal: Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia
43002802.abstract: External hydrocephalus (EH) in adults is an underrecognized clinical entity characterized by CSF circulatory failure and progressive subarachnoid space (SAS) dilation under high intracranial pressure (ICP). Data regarding its incidence, pathophysiology, and management in adult neurocritical care are sparse. To describe the incidence, risk factors and outcome of EH in adult neurocritical patients. Prospective study of patients with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury (msTBI) or spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) admitted to intensive care unit (ICU). Three subgroups ere defined: 1) radiological EH: dilated SAS between two successive CT scans; 2) radiological EH in the context of intracranial hypertension (IH): suspected o confirmed elevated ICP; and 3) radiological EH and invasively documented elevated ICP. A total of 128 patients were included (78 msTBI, 50 SAH). The incidence of radiological EH was 20.3 % (26.9 % in msTBI and 10 % in SAH), while the incidence of radiological EH in the context of IH was 7.8 % (10.3 % in msTBI vs. 4 % in SAH). The median time to EH onset was 4.5. Radiological EH in the context of IH was significantly associated with younger age, refractory intracranial hypertension, surgical intervention, decompressive craniectomy, and prolonged ICU stay. Intracranial hypertension due to EH required external lumbar drainage in 70 %. The first prospective study on EH adult neurocritical patients is presented. EH presents as a not uncommon and complex driver of secondary neurological deterioration and prolonged hospital resource utilization in adult neurocritical care. Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion based on clinical and radiological findings. It is associated with refractory intracranial hypertension, generally requiring an external lumbar drainage.

43002171.title: Association Between Postoperative Pneumonia and Prognosis in Patients With Non-Traumatic Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: An Analysis of the MIMIC-IV Database.
43002171.abstract: To investigate the association between postoperative pneumonia (POP) and prognosis in patients with nontraumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). This retrospective cohort study used the MIMIC-IV database. Adult SAH patients who underwent surgical treatment with postoperative sedation were included, excluding traumatic SAH, nonsurgical cases, ICU stay ≤ 1 day, and those without sedative use. Patients were divided into the POP and non-POP groups. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent risk factors for POP, validated by LASSO regression and random forest analysis. A progressive adjustment strategy evaluated POP's association with in-hospital, 30-day, 90-day, and 1-year mortality, and length of stay (LOS). Sensitivity analyses included inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW)/doubly robust analysis, short-stay exclusion, survivor-restricted analysis, and Fine-Gray competing risk models. Mortality at 30 days, 90 days, and 1 year was ascertained only among patients who survived to hospital discharge and is therefore reported as post-discharge mortality. Among 505 included patients, 189 (37.4%) developed POP. Factors independently associated with higher POP odds included WFNS Grades IV-V (OR = 2.373, p < 0.001), dexmedetomidine use (OR = 2.026, p = 0.001), and COPD (OR = 1.817, p = 0.039). Higher admission potassium (OR = 0.526, p = 0.010) and acetaminophen use (OR = 0.597, p = 0.012) were independently associated with lower POP odds. POP was not independently associated with in-hospital mortality (OR = 1.030, p = 0.908) but significantly prolonged ICU LOS (ratio = 1.651, p < 0.001) and total hospital LOS (ratio = 1.765, p < 0.001). LOS findings were consistent across all sensitivity analyses, while in-hospital mortality results were less stable across analytical frameworks and should be interpreted cautiously. Post-discharge mortality among patients who survived to hospital discharge was 7.5% versus 3.7% at 30 days, 11.6% versus 8.2% at 90 days, and 18.5% versus 11.0% at 1 year. In surgical nontraumatic SAH patients, POP correlated with prolonged ICU and hospital LOS. High WFNS grade, dexmedetomidine use, and COPD were independently associated with increased POP odds. These findings highlight the potential value of POP prevention strategies to reduce LOS and healthcare resource consumption.

42995676.title: Pan-Adrenergic Inhibition Alleviates Post-Hemorrhagic Hydrocephalus by Attenuating Neutrophil Extracellular Traps-Mediated Glymphatic Dysfunction.
42995676.abstract: Post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus (PHH) is a devastating complication. This study aims to elucidate how the acute post-hemorrhagic adrenergic storm drives neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) formation, blocks the glymphatic system (GS), and causes an imbalance in intracranial fluid homeostasis, leading to PHH. It is necessary to explore whether pan-adrenergic inhibition as non-surgical intervention strategies can rescue this neuro-immune dysregulation. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was used to draw the immune infiltration map. Utilizing a rat PHH model, ventricular volumes and glymphatic fluid dynamics were assessed via MRI and fluorescent tracer tracking. Multiple behavioral analyses were used to observe the neurological dysfunction. The structural integrity of the GS was assessed using IF staining and TEM. The formation of NETs was detected using ELISA, WB, and IF. In vitro, flow cytometry and molecular assays were used to explore the changes in molecular pathways in epinephrine-stimulated primary neutrophils, and NETs were used to treat astrocytes to study the interaction between them. A pharmacological intervention using pan-adrenergic inhibitor cocktail PPA (prazosin, propranolol, atipamezole), NETs agonist, NETs inhibitor, and AKT activator was conducted to explore the mechanism. scRNA-seq identified a pathogenic neutrophil subset presented as a transcriptional phenotype consistent with NETs, which dominated hemorrhagic stroke. Structurally, adrenergic storm-driven NETs extrusion occluded perivascular spaces and stripped aquaporin-4 (AQP4) polarization at astrocytic endfeet, precipitating glymphatic stasis and severe ventricular dilation. Molecular analysis revealed that epinephrine might promote the formation of NETs by activating the PI3K/AKT/mTOR cascade. PPA blocked this pathological axis, inhibited NETs, polarized AQP4 distribution, restored the fluid dynamics of the GS, and relieved cognitive deficits after intraventricular hemorrhage and alleviated hydrocephalus. After PHH, targeted pan-adrenergic inhibition can block the adrenergic storm and inhibit NET formation, protect the clearance function and structural integrity of the GS, stabilize the intracranial fluid homeostasis, and alleviate hydrocephalus in the acute phase. The molecular mechanism may involve the PI3K/AKT/mTOR cascade. This mechanism provides a potential therapeutic strategy for neuro-immune-based drug protection.

43007421.title: Efficacy and safety of oliceridine versus remifentanil for analgesia in mechanically ventilated critically ill adults (CO-ROAM): a multicenter, assessor-blinded, non-inferiority randomized controlled trial.
43007421.abstract: Remifentanil provides effective analgesia during invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), but its utility is limited by opioid-related adverse events. Oliceridine, a G protein-biased μ-opioid receptor agonist, may decouple analgesia from these effects, but lacks evidence in critically ill patients. This multicentre, assessor- and patient-blinded, non-inferiority randomised controlled trial was conducted across 19 intensive care units (ICUs) in China. Adults receiving IMV were randomised 1:1 to oliceridine or remifentanil, titrated to a Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool score below 3. The primary endpoint was time in target analgesic range (TTR; non-inferiority margin -10%). Of 307 randomised patients, 304 comprised the modified intention-to-treat population (151 oliceridine, 153 remifentanil). Median TTR was 96.0% versus 92.3% (absolute difference 3.7%, 95% CI -0.3-5.7%). Oliceridine was associated with fewer mild-to-moderate adverse drug reactions (ADRs), occurring at 15.9 versus 22.2 events per 100 patient-days (IRR 0.72, 95% CI 0.52-1.00, P = 0.049), and a lower rate of respiratory depression during the study period (0% vs. 4.6%, P = 0.015). Post-extubation respiratory depression (0% vs. 7.9%, P = 0.005) and analgesic-sedation costs were both lower with oliceridine. IMV duration, ICU stay, and 28-day mortality did not differ. Subgroup analyses identified a nominal ADR benefit in patients with Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II > 17 and a larger nominal TTR difference in those without acute respiratory distress syndrome. Oliceridine provides non-inferior analgesia to remifentanil with a more favourable respiratory safety profile and lower costs in critically ill adults. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06454292 (registered June 11, 2024).

43004400.title: Multidisciplinary management of disseminated tuberculosis with tuberculous meningitis and active hepatitis B in a critically ill pregnant woman in the third trimester: a case report.
43004400.abstract: Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) in pregnancy is rare but life-threatening, with substantial maternal and fetal risks. Third-trimester disseminated tuberculosis involving the central nervous system with concurrent active hepatitis B infection has scarcely been reported, particularly among remote pastoral populations with limited healthcare access. This report highlights the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges of this triple comorbidity and underscores the value of multidisciplinary team (MDT) management in such complex scenarios. A 24-year-old pastoralist at 30 weeks of gestation presented with headache, vomiting, fever, and nuchal rigidity. Cerebrospinal fluidanalysis confirmed TBM, and chest computed tomography revealed diffuse miliary nodules suggestive of hematogenous disseminated tuberculosis. Serology was positive for hepatitis B surface antigen, e-antigen, and core antibody, indicating active viral replication. Given life-threatening intracranial hypertension [intracranial pressure (ICP) > 330 mmH2O] in late pregnancy, osmotic agents were withheld for fetal safety, and lumbar cisternal drainage was performed. An MDT comprising respiratory medicine, obstetrics, hepatology, pharmacy, and critical care nursing specialties was assembled. Anti-tuberculosis therapy was intensified to isoniazid, rifampicin, linezolid, and moxifloxacin; ethambutol was discontinued due to fetal optic neuritis, and tenofovir was added for hepatitis B management. Following stabilization, the patient was transferred to a higher-level facility at 35 weeks of gestation and underwent cesarean section at 36 weeks, delivering a live preterm female infant (2320 g, 1-min Apgar score of 8). Both mother and neonate were discharged without complications on December 1, 2025. This case demonstrates that early recognition, individualized anti-tuberculosis regimens, and coordinated multidisciplinary collaboration are critical for achieving favorable outcomes in pregnant patients with disseminated tuberculosis complicated by TBM and concurrent hepatitis B infection. The successful management relied on integrated critical care and a multidisciplinary approach, which proved effective even in resource-limited pastoral settings.

43004379.title: Association between glycemic variability and delirium in critically ill older adults patients: a retrospective cohort study.
43004379.abstract: Delirium affects 30-70% of critically ill older adults patients and is associated with poor outcomes. While glycemic control is essential in intensive care, the impact of glycemic variability (GV) on delirium remains understudied, particularly in older adults patients. This study investigated the association between GV and delirium in critically ill older adults patients. We analyzed 16,335 patients aged ≥ 65 years from the MIMIC-IV database. GV was calculated as the coefficient of variation of blood glucose measurements and categorized into quartiles. Delirium was assessed using Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU). Multivariate logistic regression evaluated the association between GV and delirium, adjusting for demographics, clinical parameters, and comorbidities. We assessed the added predictive value of GV using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), net reclassification improvement (NRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI). Random forest and Boruta algorithm determined variable importance. Delirium incidence increased across GV quartiles (28.7% in Q1 vs. 41.8% in Q4, p < 0.001). After full adjustment, the highest GV quartile showed 42% higher delirium risk compared to the lowest (OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.18-1.71, p = 0.003), with a significant dose-response relationship. Random forest and Boruta algorithm identified GV as the most important predictor of delirium. Adding GV to prediction models significantly improved risk reclassification, with significant NRI in the fully adjusted model (p = 0.01) and significant IDIs across all models (all p < 0.05). The association remained consistent across all subgroups regardless of diabetes status. Higher GV independently predicts increased delirium risk in critically ill older adults patients. Monitoring and managing GV may represent a modifiable target for delirium prevention in this vulnerable population.

43004116.title: Metabolic response during neuromuscular electrical stimulation in critically ill patients with deep sedation: a prospective observational study.
43004116.abstract: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) is a potential strategy to counteract skeletal muscle atrophy in critically ill patients unable to engage in early mobilization. However, it is difficult to confirm whether the exercise load applied by NMES is sufficient to elicit a physiological effect in patients under sedation or with impaired consciousness, as the appropriate stimulus intensity and exercise load of NMES are generally assessed using subjective responses. This study aimed to evaluate changes in energy expenditure during NMES in sedated, mechanically ventilated patients using indirect calorimetry. This single-center observational study included 22 mechanically ventilated patients under deep sedation in the intensive care unit (ICU). Energy expenditure was measured using indirect calorimetry during NMES sessions. The primary outcome was the difference in energy expenditure before and during NMES. Multivariable linear regression analysis was performed to calculate the adjusted mean difference in energy expenditure. A clinically meaningful increase in energy expenditure attributable to NMES was predefined as 150 kcal/day, which was assumed based on an increase in energy expenditure when sitting on the edge of the bed.
