Among 533 patients, 303 (56.8%) required ICU-level interventions and 147 (27.6%) died within 14 days. Lower albumin levels and higher blood urea nitrogen, potassium, and white blood cell count were associated with both outcomes, whereas higher heart rate was associated with 14-day mortality. The model demonstrated moderate discrimination for ICU-level intervention (C-index 0.721, 95% CI 0.660-0.745) and good discrimination for 14-day mortality (C-index 0.784, 95% CI 0.720-0.814). Calibration analyses indicated modest overfitting but generally good agreement between predicted and observed risks. Decision curve analysis demonstrated clinical net benefit across a range of threshold probabilities. In this single-center cohort, treatment escalation and short-term mortality represented related but distinct dimensions of clinical risk. Defining intensive care need based on treatment intensity rather than ICU admission may provide an operational framework for risk stratification at MET activation. External validation is required before clinical implementation.

42852716.title: Associations between advanced lung cancer inflammation index score and kidney outcomes in intensive care unit patients with diabetes: A retrospective cohort study.
42852716.journal: The Journal of international medical research
42852716.abstract: ObjectiveAcute kidney injury is commonly observed in critically ill patients with diabetes and is associated with adverse outcomes. The advanced lung cancer inflammation index score, which reflects nutritional and inflammatory status, has not been well studied in relation to acute kidney injury and subsequent kidney events in this population.MethodsWe conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database. Adult intensive care unit patients with diabetes were included. Associations of log-transformed advanced lung cancer inflammation index scores with acute kidney injury and major adverse kidney events within 30 days were assessed using logistic regression and Cox models, respectively. Restricted cubic spline analyses, eXtreme gradient boosting with SHapley Additive exPlanations interpretation, subgroup analyses, and sensitivity analyses were performed to evaluate model-based contribution, effect modification, and robustness.ResultsIn total, 2337 critically ill patients with diabetes were included in the acute kidney injury occurrence analysis, of whom 1624 developed acute kidney injury. Each 1-SD increase in log-transformed advanced lung cancer inflammation scores was associated with lower odds of acute kidney injury (odds ratio, 0.90; 95% confidence interval, 0.81-0.99). Among the 1624 patients with acute kidney injury, 750 developed major adverse kidney events within 30 days. Higher log-transformed advanced lung cancer inflammation index scores were associated with a lower hazard of major adverse kidney events within 30 days (hazard ratio, 0.89; 95% confidence interval, 0.82-0.96). Dose-response analyses revealed a consistent inverse association between the advanced lung cancer inflammation index score and adverse kidney outcomes, particularly major adverse kidney events within 30 days. Machine-learning interpretation supported the contribution of the advanced lung cancer inflammation index score to model output for kidney outcomes, and sensitivity analyses yielded similar results.ConclusionsAmong intensive care unit patients with diabetes, higher advanced lung cancer inflammation index scores were associated with lower odds of acute kidney injury and a lower hazard of major adverse kidney events within 30 days after acute kidney injury. The advanced lung cancer inflammation index score may serve as a simple marker for inflammation and nutritional status associated with short-term kidney outcomes; however, its clinical utility requires validation in independent cohorts.

42841896.title: Management of renal failure in earthquake-related crush syndrome: Multicenter intensive care outcomes.
42841896.journal: Ulusal travma ve acil cerrahi dergisi = Turkish journal of trauma & emergency surgery : TJTES
42841896.abstract: Crush syndrome (CS) is a clinical condition associated with multisystem organ dysfunction that develops after traumatic rhabdomyolysis and primarily affects the kidneys. The aim of this study was to characterize the incidence, risk factors, and treatment patterns of acute kidney injury (AKI) in earthquake victims with CS, with a particular focus on renal replacement therapy (RRT) use and clinical outcomes. In this retrospective multicenter study, 247 adult patients with earthquake-related CS who were admitted to intensive care units (ICUs) in 22 hospitals after the Kahramanmaraş 2023 earthquakes were analyzed. Demographic data, injury patterns, laboratory parameters, treatment protocols, and outcomes were evaluated during the first 15 days following ICU admission. AKI developed in 78.5% (n=194) of patients, and RRT was required in 62.4% (n=121) of those with AKI. Multiple logistic regression analysis demonstrated that myoglobin and creatinine levels were associated with an elevated risk of developing AKI (odds ratio [OR]: 1.001; 95% confidence interval CI: 1.000-1.001 and OR: 1.735; 95% CI: 1.151-2.615, respectively). Similarly, creatinine level and reasons for ICU admission were identified as factors influencing RRT administration. (OR: 1.7; 95% CI: 1.28-2.15 and OR: 2.9; 95% CI: 1.26-6.90, respectively). The 30-day mortality rate was higher in patients with AKI than in those without AKI. Mortality rates were similar between patients with AKI who received RRT and those who did not. This study demonstrates the high incidence of AKI in earthquake-related CS, underscores the need for improved disaster preparedness with adequate dialysis capacity and early risk stratification using serum myoglobin and creatinine levels for optimal management.

42935203.title: Predictive value of glucose metabolism indices for short-term outcomes in critically ill patients with congestive heart failure.
42935203.journal: Zhong nan da xue xue bao. Yi xue ban = Journal of Central South University. Medical sciences
42935203.abstract: Congestive heart failure (CHF) is a major global public health problem, affecting approximately 64 million people worldwide, with a 5-year survival rate of less than 50%. The short-term risk of death is particularly high among patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). Disturbances in glucose metabolism are an important pathophysiological feature of CHF, and effective glycemic monitoring is of considerable importance for prognostic assessment in critically ill patients with CHF. This study aims to evaluate the predictive value of 3 glucose metabolism-related indices, blood glucose level, stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR), and hemoglobin glycation index (HGI), for the risk of 7-day mortality in critically ill patients with CHF. This study was based on the MIMIC-IV database and included 851 critically ill patients with CHF who met the eligibility criteria between 2008 and 2019. The primary outcome was 7-day all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality. Kaplan-Meier (K-M) survival curves with log-rank tests were used to assess the associations between each index and survival outcomes. Univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to calculate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Three models were constructed to progressively evaluate the influence of potential confounders: an unadjusted model, Model 1 adjusted for demographic and clinical characteristics, and Model 2 further adjusted for laboratory parameters. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis was used to explore the dose-response relationships between the 3 indices and mortality risk. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and the area under the curve (AUC) were used to evaluate the discriminative ability of each index, and incremental ROC analysis was performed to determine whether adding each index improved the predictive performance of the baseline model. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used to select features from 15 candidate variables and to objectively assess the independent predictive contribution of each index in a multivariable setting. In addition, stratified analyses were conducted across multiple clinically relevant subgroups defined by sex, age, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) status, vasopressin use, acute myocardial infarction (AMI), acute kidney injury (AKI), and sepsis to evaluate the consistency and robustness of the prognostic value of SHR. A total of 851 critically ill patients with CHF were included, of whom 70 (8.226%) died from any cause within 7 days. Cox regression analysis showed that, when analyzed as a continuous variable, SHR was independently associated with 7-day all-cause mortality in the fully adjusted model (HR=1.760, 95% CI 1.193 to 2.595; P<0.05), whereas the association between blood glucose and 7-day all-cause mortality was no longer significant after full adjustment (HR=1.002, 95% CI 0.999 to 1.004; P>0.05). HGI, when analyzed as a continuous variable, was associated with 7-day all-cause mortality (HR=0.787, 95% CI 0.650 to 0.954; P<0.05); however, no significant association was observed after HGI was categorized into tertiles in the fully adjusted model (P>0.05). Tertile analysis of SHR showed that the highest tertile remained significantly associated with 7-day all-cause mortality in the fully adjusted model (P<0.05). K-M survival analysis further showed that patients with higher blood glucose levels or higher SHR had a greater risk of 7-day all-cause mortality, whereas patients with lower HGI also had a significantly increased risk of 7-day all-cause mortality (all P<0.05). ROC curve analysis showed that SHR tended to have better predictive performance for mortality risk than blood glucose and HGI, although the differences did not reach statistical significance (P>0.05). Notably, adding SHR to the baseline model significantly improved its predictive performance (P=0.048). LASSO regression analysis showed that among the 9 predictors ultimately selected, SHR was the only glucose-related variable retained, whereas blood glucose and HGI were excluded. SHR is an independent predictor of short-term mortality risk in critically ill patients with CHF and has considerable potential for clinical application in risk stratification and prognostic assessment.

42908551.title: Development and validation of an interpretable machine learning model for predicting early acute kidney injury and altered consciousness in cardiac surgery patients admitted to the intensive care unit: a retrospective study.
42908551.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) and altered consciousness are common and serious complications following cardiac surgery, both associated with increased morbidity and mortality in the intensive care unit (ICU). Early prediction of these complications is essential for timely intervention. We aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine learning model for predicting early AKI and altered consciousness risk in this population. We retrospectively extracted data from the MIMIC-IV database. Adult patients who underwent cardiac surgery within 24 h before ICU admission were included. The primary outcome was early AKI defined by KDIGO criteria within 48 h after ICU admission. The secondary outcome was altered consciousness within 24 h after ICU admission, defined as a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score ≤12. A comprehensive set of candidate variables was screened using four feature selection methods (LassoCV, mRMR, mutual information, and F-test) with a voting strategy. Eight machine learning models were developed and compared. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values were used to interpret the best-performing model. External validation was performed using data from cardiac surgery patients at Wuxi No.2 People's Hospital between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2025. A total of 5,288 patients were included, with an AKI incidence of 76.2% (4,031/5,288) and an altered consciousness incidence of 22.8% (1,206/5,288). For the primary outcome of AKI, the XGBoost model achieved a training AUC of 0.787 (95% CI: 0.770-0.804) and an internal test AUC of 0.659 (95% CI: 0.629-0.688). For the secondary outcome of altered consciousness, the XGBoost model achieved an internal test AUC of 0.951 (95% CI: 0.936-0.963). Calibration curve and decision curve analysis confirmed good calibration and clinical utility for both models. SHAP analysis identified SpO2, age, APSIII score, creatinine, and white blood cell count as the top 5 most important predictors for AKI. External validation was performed in an independent cohort of 395 cardiac surgery ICU patients from Wuxi No.2 People's Hospital, in whom the incidence of AKI and altered consciousness was 28.1% and 67.3%, respectively. The models retained acceptable discrimination in this external cohort (AKI: AUC 0.764, 95% CI: 0.711-0.818; altered consciousness: AUC 0.679, 95% CI: 0.615-0.737). We developed interpretable XGBoost-based prediction models for both early AKI and altered consciousness risk in cardiac surgery patients admitted to the ICU. The models exhibited excellent discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility, which may facilitate early identification of high-risk patients and guide personalized interventions.

42961212.title: Acute kidney injury in critically ill older adults: clinical severity and nursing workload.
42961212.abstract: To determine the incidence and association of acute kidney injury, clinical severity, and nursing workload with prognostic outcomes in older patients admitted to an Intensive Care Unit. A retrospective cohort study conducted between January and December 2023 in an Intensive Care Unit. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire applied to medical records. Two-sided p-values <0.05 were considered statistically significant. Among the 81 older patients analyzed, 32% developed acute kidney injury. Of these, 22.2% had moderate to severe impairment of renal function. The use of norepinephrine (p=0.019) and the need for mechanical ventilation (p<0.001) were significantly associated with the occurrence of acute kidney injury. In addition, nursing workload was significantly higher in the group with renal impairment (p=0.006). A relevant incidence of acute kidney injury of moderate to high severity was observed among older patients admitted to the Intensive Care Unit. Patients with acute kidney injury had a higher nursing workload, as evidenced by higher Nursing Activities Score values. In addition, acute kidney injury was associated with unfavorable prognostic outcomes, including prolonged length of stay and a greater need for advanced support.

42880435.title: Electrolyte disturbance phenotypes and adverse outcomes in the intensive care unit: The role of magnesium and potassium abnormalities.
42880435.journal: Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry
42880435.abstract: Magnesium and potassium disturbances are common in critically ill patients, but the prognostic value of their co-occurrence is poorly defined. To evaluate the association of combined magnesium-potassium phenotypes at intensive care unit (ICU) admission with 30-day in-hospital mortality, acute kidney injury (AKI), and invasive mechanical ventilation. This retrospective cohort included 9462 adults admitted to the ICU of a tertiary hospital in Jordan (2012-2022) with admission magnesium and potassium, classified into nine phenotypes. Mortality was analyzed by Cox regression, censoring patients discharged alive at discharge, and AKI and ventilation by logistic regression, adjusted for age, sex, and modified APACHE II score. Thirty-day mortality was 30.6%, ranging from 25.0% with normal magnesium and potassium to 63.6% with combined hypermagnesemia-hyperkalemia. The combined phenotype had the highest adjusted hazard of death (HR 3.01, 95% CI 2.60-3.49), with positive additive interaction (relative excess risk due to interaction 0.76, 95% CI 0.29-1.23). Isolated hyperkalemia (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.46-1.82) and isolated hypermagnesemia (HR 1.62, 95% CI 1.42-1.86) were also associated with mortality. The combined phenotype was associated with AKI (aOR 2.66, 95% CI 2.09-3.38) and ventilation (aOR 1.51, 95% CI 1.17-1.94). Modeled continuously, potassium showed a U-shaped and magnesium a J-shaped association with mortality. Co-occurring hypermagnesemia and hyperkalemia at ICU admission identify a high-risk phenotype. Because both are measured routinely, this combination may serve as a simple marker for early risk stratification.

42879328.title: Utilities of Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter-2 Inhibitor in the Intensive Care Units.
42879328.abstract: Background Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) have become foundational therapies for heart failure and chronic kidney disease and are increasingly used in critically ill patients. Their established benefits for kidney and heart health, along with emerging evidence from acute-care settings, indicate growing interest in their potential role in intensive care medicine. However, whether these benefits can be translated to critically ill populations remains uncertain, and concerns regarding safety continue to influence clinical practice. Summary Clinical evidence supporting the use of SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) during acute illness is expanding. Benefits have been most consistently observed in acute heart failure, perioperative care, and renal outcomes, where randomized and observational studies suggest improved decongestion, reduced acute kidney injury, and favorable cardiorenal outcomes. These observations are supported by several biological effects of SGLT2i that extend beyond glucose lowering, including modulation of fluid balance, renal hemodynamics, metabolic adaptation, inflammation, and endothelial function-pathways that are central to the development of organ dysfunction during critical illness. However, important uncertainties remain regarding which critically ill patients are most likely to benefit, whether chronic therapy should be continued during acute illness, and how potential benefits should be balanced against safety concerns in the ICU. This review integrates current mechanistic and clinical evidence, examines the balance between potential benefits and risks, discusses practical management considerations, and highlights key research priorities to better define the role of SGLT2i in critical care medicine.   Key Messages - SGLT2 inhibitors show promise in critical care but are not established therapies. - Cardiorenal benefits must be balanced against metabolic and hemodynamic risks. - Future research should define the right patient, the right timing, and the right treatment strategy.

42876873.title: Evaluation of Chromium Picolinate Supplementation and Insulin Requirements in Critically Ill Adults With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
42876873.journal: The Journal of pharmacy technology : jPT : official publication of the Association of Pharmacy Technicians
42876873.abstract: Chromium picolinate has been studied as an adjunct to improve glycemic indices in ambulatory type 2 diabetes mellitus, but its role in critically ill patients is unknown. To evaluate whether chromium picolinate supplementation was associated with reduced insulin requirements without worsening glycemic control in critically ill adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. We conducted a single-center retrospective pre-post cohort study of adult intensive care unit patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus or hemoglobin A1c ≥6.5% who received insulin and at least 4 consecutive chromium picolinate doses between July 2022 and January 2023. Patients served as their own controls during 24-hour pre- and post-chromium periods. The primary outcome was change in total daily insulin dose. Secondary outcomes included proportion of measured glucose values within 140 to 180 mg/dL, acute kidney injury, hypoglycemia, and exploratory Sequential Organ Failure Assessment-2 change. Among 91 screened patients, 45 met the inclusion criteria. Median total daily insulin dose decreased from 76.3 U/d (interquartile range [IQR], 40.1-96.9) before chromium to 40.0 U/d (IQR, 20.5-65.6) after chromium; the Hodges-Lehmann paired difference was -23.0 U/d (95% CI, -33.25 to -14.25; P < .0001). Proportion of measured glucose values within target did not differ significantly. No post-intervention hypoglycemia was observed, and 2 patients met the study-defined acute kidney injury criterion. Interpretation is limited by the retrospective design and absence of a concurrent control group. Chromium picolinate supplementation was associated with lower insulin requirements without worsening glycemic control. These hypothesis-generating findings require confirmation in prospective controlled studies.

42867522.title: Dynamic course and outcomes of acute-on-chronic liver failure in the intensive care unit : Insights from a real-world cohort.
42867522.abstract: Acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) frequently requires intensive care unit (ICU) management, yet real-world data on dynamic disease course, organ support and mortality predictors in critically ill ACLF patients remain scarce. All ACLF patients admitted to a tertiary care hepatology ICU between 2013 and 2023 were analyzed in this retrospective single-center study for ACLF grade trajectories, organ support, and independent predictors of 90-day mortality. Among 209 patients (228 admissions), 54.4% had ACLF grade 3 at ICU admission (median CLIF‑C ACLF 56). Most patients required vasopressors (86.8%), invasive mechanical ventilation (59.6%), and renal replacement therapy (53.5%). The ICU and 90-day survival were 56.1% and 34.2%, respectively. One third of the patients (33.3%) showed improvement in ACLF grade during the ICU stay, including grade 3 patients, indicating meaningful reversibility under comprehensive organ support. The CLIF‑C ACLF score (OR: 1.07, 95% CI: 1.03-1.11, p < 0.001) and the peak noradrenaline dose (OR: 13.5, 95% CI: 3.18-69.7, p < 0.001) were identified as independent predictors of 90-day mortality. Critically ill ACLF patients retain potential for partial recovery under full organ support, justifying ICU escalation even in grade 3 disease. Peak noradrenaline dose, alongside the established prognostic scores, provides a readily available parameter to guide individualized decision-making regarding full organ support or timely de-escalation.

42859779.title: Clinical practice guideline for renal replacement therapy in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury (2026 edition).
authors: Guideline working group of Chinese Society of Critical Care
42859779.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and severe complication in critically ill patients, associated with high morbidity and mortality. Renal replacement therapy (RRT) is a vital life-support modality for critically ill patients with AKI. However, there remains a lack of unified clinical standards for core issues including the timing of RRT initiation, treatment modality, anticoagulation strategy, and weaning from RRT. In response, the Chinese Society of Critical Care Medicine organized a multidisciplinary expert panel to develop the "Clinical practice guideline for RRT in critically ill patients with AKI (2026 edition)" in accordance with the GRADE approach for grading evidence quality. This guideline was developed through systematic literature retrieval, meta-analysis, and evidence-based medical evidence synthesis, followed by multiple rounds of manuscript review and revision via online and offline meetings of the working group, and final approval by the Standing Committee of the Society. A total of 34 recommendations were finalized, covering key clinical topics including timing of RRT initiation, establishment and maintenance of vascular access, selection of treatment modalities, application of specialized membrane filters, anticoagulation regimens, replacement fluid formulations, prescribed treatment dose, and RRT weaning strategies. This guideline aims to provide scientific, standardized, and clinically actionable guidance for critical care practitioners in China, promoting standardized RRT management in adult critically ill patients with AKI.

42857409.title: Retrospective Cohort Study on the Association Between a Laboratory Test-Derived Frailty Index and Mortality in Elderly Critically Ill Patients With Chronic Kidney Disease.
42857409.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a growing worldwide health concern. There is a need for easily obtainable markers that can improve risk evaluation in affected patients. Here, we investigated whether a laboratory-derived frailty index (FI-Lab) carries prognostic information for older CKD individuals admitted to intensive care. A retrospective cohort design was adopted, drawing on the MIMIC-IV repository. Records of elderly ICU patients with diagnosed CKD were retrieved. The endpoints of interest were all-cause death within 30 and 90 days. Cox proportional hazards regression with incremental covariate adjustment and propensity score matching were employed to quantify the independent contribution of FI-Lab to survival. The analytic sample consisted of 5013 hospitalized CKD patients (mean age 77.9 ± 7.6 years; 61.4% male). Following full adjustment, a 0.1-unit rise in FI-Lab corresponded to a 94% higher mortality risk at 30 days (HR 1.94; 95% CI 1.57-2.40) and a 65% higher risk at 90 days (HR 1.65; 95% CI 1.43-1.91; both p < 0.001). Propensity-matched analyses yielded comparable estimates. No meaningful association emerged between FI-Lab and ICU or hospital length of stay. Conversely, higher FI-Lab values were accompanied by greater odds of acute kidney injury and continuous renal replacement therapy utilization. An elevated FI-Lab score at ICU entry is independently tied to elevated short- and intermediate-term mortality in older critically ill patients with CKD. Confirmatory prospective work is needed to establish its clinical role in this population.

42857206.title: Low-intensity versus medium-intensity continuous renal replacement therapy for critically ill patients (LIMIT) trial: Protocol summary and statistical analysis plan of a randomised clinical trial.
42857206.journal: Critical care and resuscitation : journal of the Australasian Academy of Critical Care Medicine
42857206.abstract: Severe acute kidney injury in critically ill patients may require continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), yet mortality remains high. A standard CRRT intensity is 20-25 mL/kg/hr, because higher doses have not improved outcomes. Excessive treatment may cause harm by removing antibiotics and other essential substances and potentially impairing renal recovery. Observational data suggest that lower-intensity CRRT may be effective, warranting a clinical trial to compare low-versus standard-intensity therapy. The objective of this study was to describe the prespecified protocol and the statistical analysis plan of the low-intensity versus medium-intensity continuous renal replacement therapy for critically Ill patients (LIMIT) trial. The LIMIT trial is an investigator-initiated, multicentre, open-label, randomised clinical trial, with a target sample size of 400 participants. The trial compares low-intensity CRRT (12 mL/kg/hr) and medium-intensity CRRT (25 mL/kg/hr) in adult patients with acute kidney injury requiring CRRT in the participating intensive care units. The primary outcome is a hierarchical composite of survival and time to successful liberation from RRT through day 28 from randomisation, analysed using a win-ratio. Secondary outcomes include intensive care unit mortality, hospital mortality, dialysis dependence at hospital discharge among survivors, vasopressor-free days at day 28, and ventilator-free days at day 28. The LIMIT trial will evaluate the effect of low-intensity CRRT on mortality and time to successful liberation from RRT compared with medium-intensity CRRT in adults with acute kidney injury. Its findings may also inform future research on broader patient-centred and societal implications of CRRT intensity.

42857101.title: Effects of higher versus lower protein intake in critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42857101.abstract: The optimal protein dose for critically ill patients remains uncertain, and emerging evidence suggests that the effects of higher protein intake may differ across clinically relevant subgroups. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating protein delivery in critical illness adults (up to July 2026). Higher and lower protein groups were defined according to each trial's original allocation. Primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included mechanical ventilation (MV) duration, Intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay (LOS), muscle outcomes, health-related quality of life (HRQoL), biochemical outcomes, and adverse events. Results were reported as risk ratios (RRs) or mean difference (MD) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Trial Sequential Analysis (TSA) was performed to control for random error, and the certainty of evidence was rated using the GRADE framework. Thirty three RCTs involving 11,622 participants were included. No significant differences were observed between higher and lower protein groups for all-cause mortality (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.08), MV duration (MD -0.48, 95% CI -1.08 to 0.13), or ICU LOS (MD -0.18, 95% CI -0.86 to 0.51), with TSA confirming these null findings. Some muscle metrics favored the higher protein group; however, there was a trend towards poorer HRQoL (SMD -0.12, 95% CI -0.24 to 0.00). The higher protein group showed improved nitrogen balance (MD 5.58, 95% CI 2.89 to 8.27) and higher serum albumin levels (SMD 0.18, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.29), but increased urea (MD 2.06, 95% CI 1.49 to 2.64) and blood urea nitrogen concentrations (MD 2.94, 95% CI 1.32 to 4.56). Sensitivity analyses restricted to 27 isocaloric-design trials yielded consistent results. Subgroup analyses revealed that higher protein intake was linked to increased mortality in patients with acute kidney injury (RR 1.46, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.87); however, higher protein intake combined with rehabilitation interventions was associated with reduced mortality (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.93), shorter MV duration (MD -1.45, 95% CI -2.61 to -0.29), and beneficial muscle effects. Higher protein intake was not associated with better clinical outcomes. While it may increase mortality in patients with AKI, combining it with physical rehabilitation yields survival and clinical benefits, warranting confirmation in future factorial RCTs. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251109618, identifier [CRD420251109618].

42850609.title: From manual to digital: prospective ICU evaluation of the FIZE kUO(®) for continuous urine output measurement.
42850609.abstract: ICU nurses manage complex, time-sensitive care while also performing frequent manual tasks. Manual urine output (UO) measurement is one such task that remains labor-intensive, interruptive to workflow, and prone to delays - despite the need for timely and accurate recording. Automation may reduce this burden and improve consistency of monitoring. The FIZE kUO® is an electronic urinometer designed to provide continuous, real-time UO data without requiring manual handling. We conducted a prospective, single-center pilot study to evaluate the usability, workflow impact, and safety of the FIZE kUO® device in 10 critically ill patients. Nurses completed staged questionnaires before, during, and after use to assess perceptions of manual monitoring versus automated monitoring. Device performance and adverse events were documented throughout monitoring. Nursing staff reported positive perceptions regarding ease of setup (84-87%), time saving (74%), and improved recognition of changes in UO (87%). At treatment completion, 88.9% of nurses indicated the system prevented missing data, and 78% reported it facilitated earlier identification of situations requiring intervention. The device provided continuous monitoring for a total of 1,263 patient-hours, with no device-related adverse events or serious adverse events observed. Automating urine output monitoring was perceived by nurses as beneficial for workflow efficiency, data reliability, and clinical awareness. Nurses perceived the FIZE kUO® to reduce repetitive manual tasks and support timely decision-making. These findings support the potential of automated UO monitoring to alleviate components of ICU nursing workload.

42849961.title: Association between invasive mechanical ventilation and acute kidney injury in critically ill patients: a protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
42849961.abstract: Invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) may contribute to the development and progression of acute kidney injury (AKI) in critically ill patients. Given the expanding evidence-base and the immense variation in the association described, particularly following the COVID-19 pandemic era, a rigorous synthesis is warranted. This systematic review and meta-analysis will evaluate this association and identify potential risk-mitigation strategies. We will conduct a comprehensive search of databases, including Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection and the Cochrane Library, using keywords to capture relevant literature on IMV and AKI. The search will include studies published from database inception through March 2026. Two reviewers will independently screen, select and extract studies using the web-based platform Covidence. Eligible studies will include randomised controlled trials reporting the occurrence of new-onset or worsening AKI following initiation of IMV in adult patients admitted to intensive care units. Studies in which IMV was initiated after the onset of AKI will be excluded. Study quality and risk of bias will be assessed using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias 2 Tool. The primary outcome will be the proportion of critically ill patients who develop new-onset or worsening AKI after initiation of IMV. Secondary outcomes will include AKI trajectory, use of organ support and length of stay. Ethics approval is not required, as this study will synthesise data from previously published studies and will not involve direct contact with human participants. The findings will be disseminated through presentations at academic conferences and publication in a peer-reviewed journal. CRD420261303862.

42846739.title: Ethylene Glycol Poisoning Without Fomepizole in a Regional Australian Intensive Care Unit: The Lactate Gap as the Diagnostic Key and the Consequences of Nasogastric Ethanol Therapy.
42846739.abstract: A 62-year-old man presented comatose with pH 6.88 and no ingestion history. A point-of-care lactate above 31 mmol/L with a laboratory lactate of 0.8 mmol/L revealed a lactate gap, diagnosing ethylene glycol poisoning despite a near-normal osmolar gap. High-dose continuous renal replacement therapy corrected the acidosis; he survived.

42837307.title: Cerebral microembolic load during continuous versus intermittent renal replacement therapy in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury (COMET-AKI).
42837307.abstract: Microemboli generated during kidney replacement therapy (KRT) may contribute to cerebro-vascular injury in patients with acute kidney injury. Whether different KRT modalities influence cerebral microembolic burden remains uncertain. In this single-center, prospective, randomized controlled trial, intensive care unit patients with dialysis-dependent acute kidney injury receiving continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) were randomized to continue CRRT or convert to intermittent therapy (IRRT). Doppler assessments were performed during baseline CRRT and after randomization during CRRT or during the first IRRT session after a KRT-free interval. The primary outcome was the between-group difference in total cerebral microemboli count between baseline and the post-randomization assessment. Secondary outcomes included cerebral microemboli type and rates, extracorporeal venous microbubble counts and rates, 30-day mortality, and intensive care unit length of stay. The study was terminated early for technical reasons. Thirty-eight patients were analyzed (CRRT, n = 24; IRRT, n = 14). The median between-group difference in total cerebral microemboli count from baseline to post-randomization assessment was -216 events over 30 minutes (95% Confidence Interval (CI) -919 to 246; P = .79). Venous microbubble counts increased during CRRT but decreased during IRRT, with a between-group difference of -36 975 events (95% CI -63 621 to -15 899; P < .001). No significant differences were detected in 30-day mortality or intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay. This exploratory study did not detect a statistically significant difference in cerebral microembolic burden between modalities. Larger studies are needed to clarify the clinical and neurological relevance of microembolization during kidney replacement therapy.

42836021.title: Reintubation in the ICU: A Prospective Observational Study of Its Impact on Recovery Outcomes and Mortality.
42836021.abstract: Background Extubation is an important step in the recovery of critically ill patients, but some patients deteriorate after removal of the endotracheal tube and require reintubation. Extubation failure can prolong intensive care and is associated with poor outcomes. This study examined the factors associated with reintubation and the clinical outcomes of patients who failed planned extubation. Methods We prospectively followed adult patients undergoing planned extubation in the adult ICU of a tertiary care hospital between June 2025 and June 2026. Patients were observed for 72 hours after extubation, and those requiring reintubation during this period were considered to have experienced extubation failure. Demographic, clinical, physiological, and laboratory characteristics were compared between patients who remained successfully extubated and those who required reintubation. Factors associated with reintubation and in-hospital mortality were examined using multivariable logistic regression. Results A total of 180 patients were included, of whom 27 (15.0%) required reintubation within 72 hours. The patients who required reintubation were older and had higher Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II) and Rapid Shallow Breathing Index (RSBI) scores, while their Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores and serum albumin levels were lower. Positive fluid balance, emergency admission, congestive heart failure, chronic lung disease, and acute kidney injury requiring renal replacement therapy were also more frequent in this group. Reintubation was associated with a longer duration of mechanical ventilation, longer ICU and hospital stays, and higher rates of ventilator-associated pneumonia and tracheostomy. ICU and in-hospital mortality were also considerably higher among patients who required reintubation. After adjustment for other factors, APACHE II score >20, GCS <12, RSBI >105, serum albumin <3.5 g/dL, positive fluid balance >1 L, and mechanical ventilation >7 days were associated with reintubation. Reintubation was strongly associated with in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR, 5.84; 95% CI, 2.31-14.78; P < 0.001). Conclusions In this cohort, patients who required reintubation after planned extubation had a substantially more difficult clinical course and a higher risk of death. Greater illness severity, poor respiratory reserve, low serum albumin, positive fluid balance, and prolonged mechanical ventilation were associated with extubation failure. Identifying these features before extubation and maintaining close observation after extubation may help clinicians recognize patients at higher risk of deterioration.

42956910.title: Population pharmacokinetics of oseltamivir and oseltamivir carboxylate in critically ill adults receiving veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation without renal replacement therapy - an ASAP ECMO study.
42956910.abstract: To characterise the population pharmacokinetics of oseltamivir and oseltamivir carboxylate in critically ill adults receiving veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) without renal replacement therapy (RRT), and to compare oseltamivir carboxylate exposure with an exploratory exposure-response threshold and published pharmacokinetic data. This multinational ASAP ECMO analysis included 8 critically ill adults receiving oseltamivir 75 mg every 12 hours during VV-ECMO. Serial blood samples were collected over a dosing interval, and oseltamivir and oseltamivir carboxylate concentrations were measured using a validated assay. Population pharmacokinetic modelling was performed in Monolix using an integrated parent drug-metabolite model. Fifty-eight plasma concentration-time points were available for analysis. The cohort was relatively young and 63% had augmented renal clearance (ARC). A one-compartment model best described both oseltamivir and oseltamivir carboxylate, with a transit compartment required to account for delayed metabolite formation. Median oseltamivir carboxylate exposure was generally comparable to values reported in healthy adults and critically ill patients receiving standard dosing. Median oseltamivir carboxylate area under the concentration-time curve from 0-12 hours (AUC0-12) was lower in patients with ARC than in those without (1877.78 vs. 8253.39 ng·h/mL; p=0.07). Only 2 of 8 patients achieved the primary exploratory exposure-response threshold (AUC0-12 ≥7000 ng∙h/mL) and none of the 5 patients with ARC achieved this threshold. Marked variability and lower exposure were observed in adults receiving VV-ECMO without RRT, particularly ARC patients. Higher doses may be required in ARC patients, but the optimal dosing regimen remains undefined. Routine dose escalation is not supported by current evidence.

42956896.title: Dysnatremia in critically ill burn patients: incidence, timing and association with kidney outcomes.
42956896.abstract: Dysnatremia is common in critically ill patients and has been linked to poor outcomes and renal prognosis. Burn patients are particularly vulnerable, but the prognostic significance of dysnatremia in this population remains unclear. We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of 1,758 burn patients admitted to a French burn center between 2011 and 2023. Dysnatremia was defined as at least one episode of hyponatremia (<135 mmol/L) or hypernatremia (>145 mmol/L) during intensive care unit (ICU) stay. The primary endpoint was the incidence of dysnatremia; secondary endpoints included major adverse kidney events (MAKE) at ICU discharge and acute kidney injury (AKI) occurrence and severity. Dysnatremia occurred in 56.3% of patients (n = 990), with hyponatremia in 50.5% (n = 888) and hypernatremia in 23.8% (n = 418). MAKE at ICU discharge did not differ between hyponatremic and normonatremic patients (12.6% vs. 10.9%, p = 0.304) but was sixfold higher with hypernatremia (32.3% vs. 5.4%, p < 0.001). After adjustment for age and burned total body surface area, hypernatremia was independently associated with MAKE at ICU discharge (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 4.03; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.92-5.56; p < 0.001), whereas hyponatremia was not (aHR 1.15; 95% CI: 0.85-1.55; p = 0.377). Clustering analysis identified three phenotypes: Cluster B (severe burns, worst outcomes), Cluster A (older patients, mostly hyponatremic, intermediate outcomes), and Cluster C (younger patients, mild burns, best outcomes). Dysnatremia affects over half of burn patients. Sodium disturbances should be viewed as markers of systemic severity, warranting close monitoring and preventive strategies.

42952783.title: Development and multi-database validation of machine learning models for 28-day mortality prediction in ICU patients with COPD and pulmonary hypertension.
42952783.abstract: Early mortality prediction in critically ill patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) coexisting pulmonary hypertension (PH) remains challenging, particularly because prediction models developed in intensive care unit (ICU) database may not perform consistently across other healthcare systems. This retrospective multicenter study employed two large-scale databases to establish and validate ML models for predicting early mortality in ICU patients with COPD and PH. The MIMIC-IV database served as the model-development cohort (2555 patients), with external validation conducted on eICU CRD (292 patients) database. Six ML algorithms were adopted: Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Logistic Regression (LR), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Artificial Neural Network (ANN).The baseline variables were screened to identify potential predictors via least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (Lasso) regression. Model interpretability was evaluated via SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis. The overall cohort consisted of 2,847 ICU patients with COPD and PH. Twelve consistently crucial clinical features were identified, including acute kidney injury, pneumonia, age, weight, heart rate, red blood cell distribution width (RDW), white blood cell (WBC), anion gap, chloride, creatinine, base excess, potential of hydrogen (pH). The Random Forest algorithm achieved the optimal performance, with a training Area Under Curve (AUC) of 0.938, internal validation AUC of 0.748, and eICU CRD external validation AUC of 0.800. SHAP analysis indicated that acute kidney injury was the most influential predictor, followed by base excess and RDW. Additionally, a web tool was developed in this study to facilitate the application of early death risk prediction in clinical practice. This study is the multi-database validation of ML models for early mortality prediction in ICU patients with COPD and PH. The Random Forest model integrated with SHAP interpretability offers a reliable tool for clinical decision-making support, with consistent validity verified across two databases, including our internal validation cohort. This work provides a decision support tool to assist in identifying high-risk individuals within this complex comorbid population, and establishes a foundation for future studies with a more dynamic and personalized prognostic approach.

42952723.title: Association of red cell distribution width-to-albumin ratio with ICU outcomes in patients with aortic dissection.
42952723.abstract: Critically ill patients with aortic dissection remain at high risk of adverse ICU outcomes, including ICU mortality. The red cell distribution width-to-albumin ratio (RAR) has been investigated as a prognostic marker in various clinical settings. This study aimed to evaluate the association of RAR with ICU outcomes in patients with aortic dissection. Data were extracted from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) database. ICU mortality was defined as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included sepsis during hospitalization/ICU stay, acute kidney injury (AKI), and renal replacement therapy (RRT) use. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to assess the discriminative performance of RAR for ICU mortality. The optimal RAR cutoff was determined using Youden's index and was considered exploratory. Calibration plots and decision curve analysis were used to evaluate model performance. RAR showed modest discrimination for ICU mortality (AUC: 0.66; 95% CI: 0.552-0.765). The exploratory cutoff value of RAR was 5.182. Compared with the low-RAR group, the high-RAR group had higher ICU mortality (21.8% vs. 6.7%; P < 0.001), a higher prevalence of sepsis during hospitalization/ICU stay (82.8% vs. 61.1%; P < 0.001), and more frequent RRT use (33.3% vs. 9.4%; P < 0.001). The AUC increased from 0.706 for SOFA alone to 0.731 for SOFA plus RAR, indicating only limited incremental discrimination. Higher early-ICU RAR was associated with ICU mortality and other adverse ICU outcomes in patients with aortic dissection, but its discrimination was modest, its incremental value beyond SOFA was limited, and external validation is required.

42949725.title: Prognostic Value of the Delta Neutrophil Index for Predicting 28-Day Mortality in Intensive Care Unit Patients with Candidemia.
42949725.abstract: Candidemia is associated with substantial mortality in critically ill patients, and early identification of patients at increased risk of death remains challenging. The delta neutrophil index (DNI), an automated hematological parameter reflecting circulating immature granulocytes, has been proposed as a prognostic marker in sepsis, but its role in candidemia remains unclear. This retrospective study included adults who developed candidemia during intensive care unit hospitalization between January 1, 2020, and December 31, 2023; patients with neutropenia, haematological malignancy receiving ongoing chemotherapy, or granulocyte colony-stimulating factor therapy were excluded. Patients were classified as survivors or non-survivors according to 28-day all-cause mortality after blood culture collection. DNI, leukocyte count, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin were evaluated 24 hours before, at the time of, and 24 hours after blood culture collection. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors independently associated with mortality, and receiver operating characteristic analysis assessed the prognostic performance of DNI. Among 246 patients, 132 survived and 114 died. Non-survivors had higher APACHE II scores and more frequent acute kidney injury. DNI and procalcitonin levels were significantly higher in non-survivors at all three time points. In the primary multivariable model, acute kidney injury, DNI at blood culture collection, and procalcitonin at blood culture collection were independently associated with mortality; the association of DNI was attenuated and no longer statistically significant after further adjustment for Candida species and antifungal therapy. DNI showed limited discrimination, with area under the curve values ranging from 0.608 to 0.625; the highest value was observed at blood culture collection (0.625), with a cutoff of 2.4, 43.0% sensitivity, and 82.6% specificity. DNI may aid mortality risk stratification in candidemia but should not be used as a standalone prognostic marker.

42948545.title: Rapid Progression of Acute Acalculous Cholecystitis to Gangrenous Cholecystitis in an Initially Non-Critically Ill Patient: A Case Report.
42948545.abstract: Acute acalculous cholecystitis (AAC) is not confined to the critically ill and may behave like calculous disease. A 65-year-old hypertensive man with localized, stone-free cholecystitis deteriorated on hospital Day 4 with peritonism, acidosis, and acute kidney injury. Emergency open cholecystectomy confirmed gangrene; deterioration warrants urgent source control.

42948080.title: Editorial: Extracorporeal organ support: innovations and challenges in critical care.

42947795.title: Machine learning-based prediction model for hypoalbuminemia in ICU patients with venous thromboembolism and acute kidney injury.
42947795.abstract: Hypoalbuminemia is a prevalent and critical complication among intensive care unit (ICU) patients with venous thromboembolism (VTE) and acute kidney injury (AKI), significantly associated with increased mortality and prolonged hospitalization. However, reliable tools for early prediction of hypoalbuminemia in this high-risk population remain limited. This study aimed to develop and validate a machine learning-based prediction model for hypoalbuminemia in ICU patients with coexisting VTE and AKI. In this retrospective study, data from 585 ICU patients with VTE and AKI were analyzed. Patients were divided into a training cohort (n = 409) and a validation cohort (n = 176). Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression with standardization was applied for feature selection. Five machine learning models-logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM), and support vector machine (SVM)-were developed and evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation. Model performance was assessed by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Decision curve analysis (DCA), SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), and feature importance were performed for the optimal model. The performance of the best machine learning model was compared with conventional ICU severity scores (APSIII, LODs, and OASIS). The standardized LASSO regression identified ten optimal predictors: creatinine (cr), age, tumor/cancer, body mass index (BMI), low-density lipoprotein (LDL), urine output, D-dimer (D_D), Charlson comorbidity index, anticoagulant use, and alanine aminotransferase (ALT). Among the five models, XGBoost achieved the best predictive performance with a validation AUC of 0.882 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.832-0.924], followed by RF (AUC = 0.878), LightGBM (AUC = 0.870), LR (AUC = 0.838), and SVM (AUC = 0.662). The 5-fold cross-validation AUC for XGBoost was 0.901 ± 0.042, with minimal overfitting (CV-test difference = -0.019). Decision curve analysis demonstrated favorable clinical net benefit of the XGBoost model across a wide range of threshold probabilities. SHAP analysis and feature importance consistently identified urine output, age, LDL, BMI, and D-dimer as the top contributors. Compared with conventional ICU severity scores, the XGBoost model significantly outperformed APSIII (AUC = 0.661), LODs (AUC = 0.652), and OASIS (AUC = 0.647). The logistic regression-based nomogram achieved a C-index of 0.838, providing a user-friendly bedside tool for clinicians. The machine learning-based XGBoost model, incorporating ten readily available clinical variables, demonstrated excellent predictive performance for hypoalbuminemia in ICU patients with VTE and AKI. This model offers a practical and interpretable tool for early risk stratification and may guide proactive nutritional and therapeutic interventions in this vulnerable population.

42942850.title: Drug Dosing During Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy in Critically Ill Patients: A Practical Narrative Review.
42942850.abstract: Drug dosing during continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is difficult in critically ill patients because drug exposure is influenced by both the patient and the extracorporeal treatment. This narrative review provides a practical overview of drug dosing during CRRT, while intermittent hemodialysis and sustained low-efficiency dialysis are discussed only where they provide relevant contextual or comparative information. It summarizes the main drug-related, patient-related, and treatment-related factors that influence extracorporeal drug clearance and discusses their clinical implications for commonly used drug classes. Loading and maintenance doses should be considered separately: loading doses depend mainly on volume of distribution and the need for early therapeutic exposure, whereas maintenance dosing depends on total clearance, including residual renal, extracorporeal, and non-renal clearance. Therapeutic drug monitoring can help guide dose adjustment when validated targets are available, while model-informed precision dosing may provide additional support in selected patients. The review also proposes an eight-step practical framework based on residual kidney function, the actual delivered CRRT prescription, drug pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, therapeutic monitoring, and repeated reassessment. Future approaches may combine real-time CRRT data with pharmacokinetic models to support more individualized dosing.

42942835.title: Population Pharmacokinetics of Amikacin and Monte Carlo Simulation Study in Critically Ill Septic Patients Undergoing Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy with CytoSorb(®) or oXiris(®).
42942835.abstract: Background: Adsorptive devices, including CytoSorb® and oXiris®, are increasingly added to continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) in septic patients, but their effect on amikacin clearance and exposure is unknown. We characterized amikacin pharmacokinetics (PK) during adsorptive CRRT and derived dosing implications. Methods: A population PK model was developed in 24 critically ill septic patients (using NONMEM ver. 7.5.0), separating intrinsic clearance (CL_int) from filter-specific extracorporeal clearance (CL_CRRT). Sparse pre-filter sampling was handled using informative priors for distribution parameters. Robustness was assessed by sampling-importance-resampling (SIR) and prediction-corrected visual predictive checks (pcVPC). Monte Carlo simulations (9000 subjects) evaluated probability of target attainment (PTA; Cmax/MIC ≥ 8, AUC24/MIC ≥ 75) and cumulative fraction of response (CFR) against four Gram-negative pathogens across three regimens (500 mg q8h, 500 mg q24h, 1500 mg q24h), two filters, and three connection times. Results: While connected, the CytoSorb® and oXiris® CRRT configurations increased amikacin clearance by 61% and 93%, respectively, accounting for 38-48% of total clearance (CL_TOT). Because these devices were only applied for 10-14 h per 24 h interval in simulated scenarios, there were only minor differences in target attainment. Hence, dosing regimen, not device type or connection timing, dominated. Only amikacin at 1500 mg once daily achieved CFR ≥ 90%, and only for susceptible Enterobacterales. Conclusions: Adsorptive CRRT configurations substantially increase extracorporeal amikacin clearance. These exploratory findings support high-dose, once-daily, concentration-guided amikacin dosing during adsorptive CRRT, although this dose may be insufficient against pathogens with elevated MICs.

42942399.title: Mechanical Power and Acute Kidney Injury in Mechanically Ventilated Critically Ill Patients: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study.
42942399.abstract: Background and Objectives: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is highly prevalent among critically ill patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) and is associated with adverse outcomes. Mechanical power (MP) reflects the total energy delivered to the respiratory system, but its association with AKI in mechanically ventilated critically ill patients remains incompletely understood. Few studies have examined the relationship between MP and AKI development. Materials and Methods: Adult patients with MP data available for each of the first five consecutive days of IMV constituted the study population. MP and ventilatory parameters were recorded during this period. Factors independently associated with AKI were identified using multivariable logistic regression. The discriminative performance of MP for AKI and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) use was evaluated. Results: Among 924 patients, 605 (65.5%) developed AKI. MP was consistently higher in patients who developed AKI during the first five days of IMV (11.45 ± 2.88 vs. 9.48 ± 2.50 J/min; p < 0.001). Although PEEP, peak inspiratory pressure, driving pressure, respiratory rate, and FiO2 were higher in the AKI group, tidal volume and respiratory system compliance did not differ significantly. In multivariable analysis, higher mean MP (OR = 1.330, 95% CI 1.235-1.432; p < 0.001), greater mean fluid balance (OR = 1.477, 95% CI 1.225-1.780; p < 0.001), older age, and trauma were independently associated with AKI. MP showed moderate discrimination for AKI (AUC = 0.681), with an optimal cutoff of 10.38 J/min. For CRRT use, MP showed significant but limited discrimination (AUC = 0.624; 95% CI, 0.584-0.664; p < 0.001). Conclusions: In critically ill patients receiving IMV, higher MP remained associated with AKI after adjustment for measured covariates. The 10.38 J/min threshold is hypothesis-generating and requires external validation.

42939344.title: Intradialytic Hemodynamic Instability and Delirium in Critically Ill Patients Receiving Renal Replacement Therapy: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
42939344.abstract: Background: Acute kidney injury (AKI) requiring renal replacement therapy (RRT) is common in critically ill patients and is frequently accompanied by delirium. Intradialytic hemodynamic instability, particularly hypotension, may impair cerebral perfusion; however, its quantitative relationship with delirium remains unclear. This study investigated the association between intradialytic hemodynamic instability and Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU)-defined delirium in critically ill patients receiving RRT. Methods: This single-center retrospective study included 87 adult intensive care unit (ICU) patients undergoing RRT between September 2025 and May 2026. Delirium was assessed using the CAM-ICU. Intradialytic hemodynamic burden was quantified by the cumulative duration of mean arterial pressure (MAP) < 65 mmHg and the number of hypotensive episodes during RRT. Multivariable logistic regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, and admission SOFA score were performed to evaluate the associations between hemodynamic parameters and delirium, while receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were used to assess their discriminative ability. Results: Of 87 patients, 46 (52.9%) were classified as CAM-ICU-positive for delirium. Patients with delirium had a longer cumulative duration of MAP < 65 mmHg (median, 36.0 vs. 5.0 min; p = 0.048) and more hypotensive episodes (median, 3.0 vs. 1.0; p = 0.032). These differences were no longer significant after normalization to the number of RRT sessions (p = 0.153 and p = 0.249). In addition, neither parameter showed a statistically significant association with delirium after adjustment for age, sex, and admission SOFA score. ROC analysis demonstrated limited discriminative ability (AUC, 0.62 and 0.63, respectively). Mechanical ventilation duration, ICU length of stay or ICU mortality did not show a statistically significant association with CAM-ICU positivity in the adjusted models. Sensitivity analyses using alternative functional forms for cumulative MAP < 65 mmHg duration, including log-transformed, categorical, and natural cubic spline models, did not show statistically significant associations with CAM-ICU positivity. Conclusions: Critically ill patients with delirium had greater cumulative intradialytic hypotensive burden; however, these differences were attenuated after accounting for the number of RRT sessions, and the hemodynamic parameters did not show statistically significant associations with delirium in the adjusted regression models. These findings suggest a potential relationship between intradialytic hemodynamic burden and delirium but do not establish an independent or causal association.

42938689.title: Systematic Review of Vancomycin Population Pharmacokinetic Models in Critically Ill Patients: A Focus on Model Characteristics and External Predictive Performance.
42938689.abstract: Objective: Several population pharmacokinetic (PopPK) studies of vancomycin in intensive care unit (ICU) patients have been reported. However, substantial heterogeneity exists across these studies, and their predictive performance remains uncertain owing to a lack of external validation. This study systematically reviews published PopPK models of vancomycin in critically ill patients and externally validated selected models using real-world data, with the aim of clarifying factors contributing to variability in vancomycin pharmacokinetic parameters and identifying knowledge gaps that require further investigation. Methods: Databases such as PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library were searched for studies on vancomycin PopPK models in critically ill patients constructed using nonlinear mixed-effects methods. External validation of selected models was performed using the NONMEM software with external datasets. Results: A total of 16 PopPK studies of vancomycin in ICU patients were included. Factors such as renal function indicators, concomitant renal replacement therapy (RRT), and demographic characteristics significantly influenced vancomycin PopPK parameters in ICU patients. Serum creatinine levels and concomitant RRT significantly affected vancomycin clearance, with clearance increasing with higher creatinine clearance or the presence of RRT, whereas body weight significantly influenced the apparent volume of distribution, which increased with increasing body weight. External validation was performed for three of these models, but all models showed unsatisfactory external validation results, with poor predictive capability for the external validation datasets. Conclusions: The reported studies show variations in vancomycin PopPK parameters among ICU patients, with significant inter-individual variability. Clinical dosing should be adjusted based on patients' concomitant therapies, renal function, and body weight. Existing published models lack external validation, and the results of external validation have not been satisfactory. It is recommended that PopPK models undergo external validation to assess their predictive performance before application. Additionally, future research should place greater emphasis on external validation to thoroughly evaluate model performance.

42938231.title: Association Between the Modified Renal Angina Index and Major Adverse Kidney Events at 90 Days in Critically Ill Adults: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
42938231.abstract: Background/Objectives: Adult modified Renal Angina Index (mRAI) formulations predict acute kidney injury, but their association with major adverse kidney events at 90 days (MAKE90) remains unclear. We examined the association in critically ill adults without established chronic kidney disease (CKD). Methods: This retrospective cohort included 250 adults admitted to a tertiary intensive care unit (ICU) between December 2023 and April 2025. mRAI was calculated from data available at ICU admission. MAKE90 was defined as death, renal replacement therapy, or persistent renal dysfunction within 90 days. We used logistic regression, receiver operating characteristic analysis, and nested-model comparisons. Results: Admission mRAI was higher in patients with MAKE90 than in those without MAKE90 (median 10 [IQR 5-20] vs. 3 [IQR 1-6]; p < 0.001). After adjustment for SOFA score and sepsis, mRAI remained associated with MAKE90 (adjusted OR per point from the linear model, 1.073; 95% CI, 1.032-1.116). Spline analysis demonstrated a significant nonlinear association (p = 0.004), indicating that the per-point OR should be interpreted as a summary estimate rather than a constant effect across the score range. The AUC of mRAI was 0.752 (95% CI, 0.691-0.814), higher than that of admission AKI stage (0.653) and not significantly different from APACHE II (0.702) or SOFA (0.718). Adding mRAI to SOFA and sepsis raised the AUC from 0.735 to 0.782. Conclusions: In critically ill adults without established CKD, higher admission mRAI remained associated with MAKE90 after adjustment for SOFA score and sepsis and showed moderate discrimination. External validation in larger, independent cohorts is needed to confirm these findings.

42933821.title: Construction and External Validation of a Predictive Nomogram for Premature Unplanned Discontinuation in Elderly Patients Undergoing Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy in the ICU.
42933821.journal: Therapeutic apheresis and dialysis : official peer-reviewed journal of the International Society for Apheresis, the Japanese Society for Apheresis, the Japanese Society for Dialysis Therapy
42933821.abstract: To develop and validate a 2-h early-warning nomogram for the risk of unplanned discontinuation of continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) in elderly intensive care unit (ICU) patients. This study retrospectively enrolled elderly CRRT patients from two tertiary hospitals (2022-2024) via convenience sampling for model development. Predictive performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration plots, and internal validation using 1000 bootstrap resamples, with goodness of fit assessed by the Hosmer-Lemeshow test; an external cohort (Jan-Aug 2025) was used for clinical applicability. The unplanned CRRT discontinuation rate reached 27.4% in the modeling cohort and 32.8% in an external temporal validation cohort (n = 247 sessions). Independent predictors included hypotension, therapeutic intervention scoring system (TISS) score, transmembrane pressure (TMP) at 2 h > 86 mmHg, and diagnosis. The model demonstrated robust predictive performance, with an AUC of 0.860 (training) and 0.865 (validation), good calibration (Brier scores: 0.107 internal, 0.127 external), and clinical net benefit across thresholds per decision curve analysis. The model demonstrates robust discrimination, calibration, and clinical net benefit, with readily available variables indicating substantial potential for valuable clinical applications.

42933151.title: The secret life of dialysis catheters: A qualitative study of intensive care nurses' experiences of managing dialysis catheters.
42933151.abstract: In Australian intensive care units (ICUs), approximately 9000 patients require renal replacement therapy annually for acute kidney injury. This requires a large-bore dialysis catheter to facilitate effective extracorporeal blood flow. However, these catheters have the highest failure rate of all central venous catheters used in ICU at 7-20%. While catheter insertion and renal replacement therapy guidance is evidence-based, there is limited guidance for post-insertion catheter care and troubleshooting. To explore ICU nurses' experiences managing dialysis catheters, and how existing policies and bedside practices influence nurses' decision-making. Qualitative, descriptive design. Registered nurses with experience caring for patients undergoing dialysis were recruited between November 2024 and January 2025. Data were collected through small group, semi-structured interviews and analysed using inductive content analysis. Eighteen clinicians participated across three focus groups, with a mean of 10.6 years' experience in dialysis catheter care. Two themes were identified: (1) Troubleshooting is complex, characterised by reliance on experiential knowledge, time sensitive decision-making, and balancing risk against benefit; and (2) The hidden cost, reflecting the stress, unrecognised labour and financial burden associated with troubleshooting catheter dysfunction. The absence of evidence-based guidance to manage troubleshooting and catheter dysfunction places substantial burden on ICU nurses. Evidence-based troubleshooting decision tools may have the potential to improve dialysis efficiency, reduce healthcare-associated risks and workforce stress. Effective post-insertion management of dialysis catheters requires clear, evidence-informed policy, particularly regarding safe, appropriate troubleshooting techniques. A structured hierarchy of interventions may enable efficient clinician response to catheter dysfunction and improve post-insertion care and reduce complications. Targeted education and skills training are essential to strengthen clinical judgement in time-critical situations. Improved interdisciplinary communication is also needed to ensure medical teams better understand the workload and clinical risks associated with managing dialysis catheters.

42932975.title: Improving delivery and quality of renal replacement therapy in the ICU.
42932975.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) affects more than half of critically ill patients, and 10-15% require acute renal replacement therapy (RRT). Despite comparable outcomes among appropriately delivered RRT modalities, substantial practice variation persists due to differences in organizational structures, resources availability, and implementation of evidence-bases care. This review summarizes recent advances in quality improvement for acute RRT, including quality frameworks, key performance indicators (KPIs), and implementation science. The Acute Disease Quality Initiative (ADQI) established a framework for evaluating acute RRT quality across structure, process, and outcome domains and developed consensus-based KPIs for continuous RRT (CRRT). Key CRRT quality measures include program leadership, education and training, filter life, treatment downtime, access alarms, dose-intensity, ultrafiltration, adverse events, RRT discontinuation, and ICU mortality. Institutional QI initiatives demonstrate that multidisciplinary collaboration, standardized protocols, electronic medical record integration, and continuous audit and feedback can improve treatment delivery, adherence to evidence-based practices, and resource utilization. Contemporary registries are generating data to validate KPIs, characterize practice variation, and establish performance benchmarks. Quality improvement is essential for optimizing acute RRT delivery. Integrating standardized quality measurement with implementation science provides a practical framework to reduce practice variation, improve RRT delivery, and enhance patient outcomes.

42912115.title: Nursing Activities Score in critically ill patients on invasive mechanical ventilation.
42912115.abstract: to assess the association between invasive mechanical ventilation duration, classified as prolonged and non-prolonged, and nursing workload in critically ill patients. a prospective cohort study with adult patients on mechanical ventilation for up to 21 days or more. Nursing workload was measured using the Nursing Activities Score (NAS). Clinical data were collected using a structured questionnaire. A significance level of 5% was adopted. considering 61 patients, there was no significant difference in nursing workload between prolonged and non-prolonged mechanical ventilation according to NAS [111.2 (105.118) vs. 111.8 (107.119); p=0.880], nor was there an association between mechanical ventilation time and this score (AUC=0.512). Prolonged mechanical ventilation was associated with vasoactive drugs (96%; p=0.007) and greater severity of acute kidney injury (KDIGO=3.78%; p=0.009). mechanical ventilation duration was not associated with changes in nursing workload, which remained high regardless of the ventilatory support duration.

42904903.title: Rethinking Oliguria in the ICU: From Threshold to Trajectory.

42903729.title: Renal Dose-Adjustment Concordance in Critically Ill Patients with AKI and CKD: A Cross-sectional Study.
42903729.journal: Iranian journal of pharmaceutical research : IJPR
42903729.abstract: Kidney dysfunction complicates drug dosing in the intensive care unit (ICU). Guidance is well established for stable chronic kidney disease (CKD) but is less certain in acute kidney injury (AKI), in which renal function can change rapidly. To assess concordance between prescribed maintenance regimens and reference-based renal dose-adjustment recommendations for adults with AKI, CKD, or AKI superimposed on CKD. This cross-sectional study included 80 adults admitted to four ICUs in 2024. Acute kidney injury was classified according to the Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss, and end-stage renal disease (RIFLE) criteria using serial creatinine measurements and/or urine output, whereas CKD required documented chronicity. Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance (CrCl) was used to match patients to dosing-reference categories. Each patient-medication pair was classified once according to maintenance-dose amount and dosing interval, using UpToDate as the primary reference and the Sanford Guide as a supplementary source. Among 414 patient-medication pairs, 211 (51.0%; patient-level cluster-bootstrap 95% CI, 46.2%-55.8%) were discordant: 125 were lower and 86 were higher than recommended. Vancomycin (41.4%), ciprofloxacin (40.0%), and levofloxacin (40.0%) had the highest drug-specific discordance proportions. Nephrology and pulmonology had the highest patient-level service proportions (62.5% and 61.5%, respectively). Reference discordance was frequent, particularly for antimicrobials. Because measured exposure and clinical outcomes were unavailable, these findings identify regimens requiring review rather than confirming prescribing errors.

42897879.title: Meropenem Exposure, Target Attainment, and Therapeutic Drug Monitoring Practices in Critically Ill Adults Receiving Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy: A Systematic Review.
42897879.abstract: To critically evaluate meropenem pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) target attainment, therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM), infusion strategies, and clinical outcomes during continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). Ovid MEDLINE, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to August 15, 2026, using meropenem, TDM, β-lactam, and CRRT terms, with adult, human, and English-language limits. Thirteen reports representing 12 unique studies (2 randomized, 10 non-randomized) reporting meropenem concentration data during CRRT were included. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using RoB 2 or ROBINS-I. Total clearance ranged from 3.60 to 6.6 L/h. Lower or primary PK/PD target non-attainment ranged from 0% to 26.7%, while aggressive-target non-attainment ranged from 0% to 53.3% in most analyses and reached 93% in 1 study when a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 8 mg/L was assumed. Continuous or prolonged infusion may facilitate sustained exposure, but comparative evidence was limited. Four used routine TDM; only 2 implemented protocolized TDM-guided dose adjustment. Low exposure was associated with higher mortality in 1 adjusted observational analysis, but evidence for clinical outcomes was of very low certainty. Standardized meropenem regimens cannot be assumed to provide consistent exposure during CRRT. Optimized infusion and timely, protocolized TDM may support individualized dosing when multidisciplinary expertise is available. Available evidence supports a shift from standardized empirical dosing toward individualized, measurement-guided meropenem therapy in patients receiving CRRT.

42891121.title: National variation in acute kidney injury diagnosis and monitoring across adult intensive care units in china: a nationwide cross-sectional survey.
42891121.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is common in critically ill patients and strongly associated with adverse outcomes, yet national ICU-level evidence on AKI diagnosis and monitoring in China remains limited. We conducted a nationwide anonymous cross-sectional web survey of adult ICUs in China from June 25 to September 26, 2025. The survey assessed AKI diagnosis and staging, UO and SCr monitoring across clinical scenarios, biomarker use, early warning systems, and changes in UO monitoring after AKI. We used multivariable logistic regression to identify factors associated with UO-monitoring practices, with FDR correction for multiple comparisons. An exploratory 0-100-point AKI-MIS summarised ICU-level monitoring implementation, with higher scores indicating broader implementation.
