The primary comparison was the between-group difference in pre-to-post change in muscle protein synthesis. RESULTS: Twenty ICU survivors (60 ± 12 years, 30% female, BMI 26.9 (IQR 22.9-28.7), SAPS 3 62.3 ± 15.8) and 20 age- and sex-matched controls were included. ICU survivors had significantly lower quadriceps muscle thickness (p = 0.02) and handgrip strength (p = 0.04) than controls. In ICU survivors, muscle protein synthesis from plasma precursor amino acids was higher at baseline than in controls (0.041%/hour vs. 0.030%/hour, p = 0.009), but increased less (Δ 0.031 vs. Δ 0.040%/hour, p = 0.04). Post-intervention muscle protein synthesis was similar between groups (0.071%/hour vs. 0.070%/hour, p = 0.70). At baseline, ICU survivors showed lower activation of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway. In both groups, the intervention increased anabolic signalling, decreased initiation of autophagy and increased parts of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. CONCLUSIONS: In ICU survivors with persistent muscle loss and weakness, the increase in muscle protein synthesis after combined resistance exercise and protein intake was smaller than in controls, in the context of a higher baseline fractional synthetic rate. Post-intervention muscle protein synthesis rates were similar between groups. These findings provide the first mechanistic support for structured exercise-nutrition rehabilitation to promote muscle recovery after critical illness. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This study was prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05261984), 2022-02-20.

42873070.title: Intermittent or Continuous Renal-Replacement Therapy in Acute Kidney Injury.
42873070.journal: The New England journal of medicine
42873070.abstract: BACKGROUND: The preferred method of renal-replacement therapy for acute kidney injury in critically ill patients remains uncertain. METHODS: In this multicenter, open-label, noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned critically ill adults with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy to undergo intermittent hemodialysis or continuous renal-replacement therapy as the initial treatment. The primary outcome was a major adverse kidney event - defined as death, dependence on renal-replacement therapy, or a serum creatinine concentration more than 25% above the baseline value - by day 90. RESULTS: The trial was stopped early after sequential interim analyses showed a sustained signal of higher mortality with intermittent hemodialysis than with continuous renal-replacement therapy. A total of 554 patients underwent randomization, with 272 patients assigned to undergo intermittent hemodialysis and 282 to undergo continuous renal-replacement therapy; 535 patients (260 in the intermittent group and 275 in the continuous group) were included in the intention-to-treat population. A major adverse kidney event occurred by day 90 in 203 patients (78.1%) in the intermittent group and in 197 patients (71.6%) in the continuous group (adjusted absolute risk difference, 6.28 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.22 to 13.79). Death by day 90 occurred in 164 patients (63.1%) and in 147 patients (53.5%), respectively. Kaplan-Meier mortality estimates at day 90 were 63.3% and 53.6% (hazard ratio, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.63). The most common complication potentially related to acute kidney injury or renal-replacement therapy was hypotension, which occurred in 179 patients (68.8%) in the intermittent group and in 183 patients (66.5%) in the continuous group. CONCLUSIONS: Among critically ill patients with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy, intermittent hemodialysis as the initial treatment approach was not shown to be noninferior to continuous renal-replacement therapy with respect to major adverse kidney events by day 90 and was associated with higher mortality. (Funded by the French Ministry of Health; ICRAKI ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06032884.).

42839232.title: Impact of pre-tracheostomy continuous enteral feeding on aspiration pneumonia risk and clinical outcomes: a prospective observational study.
42839232.abstract: The optimal management of enteral nutrition before tracheostomy in mechanically ventilated patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) remains uncertain, and pre-procedural fasting is widely practiced in clinical settings to reduce the risk of aspiration. However, interruption of enteral nutrition (EN) may adversely affect metabolic stability and caloric intake in critically ill patients. This study aimed to prospectively evaluate whether continuation of EN before tracheostomy increases aspiration risk or influences clinical outcomes in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. This prospective observational study was conducted in the anesthesiology and resuscitation intensive care units of a tertiary care center. Adult mechanically ventilated patients scheduled for elective percutaneous tracheostomy were included. Patients were divided into two groups according to the enteral nutrition strategy applied before the procedure: the continuous feeding group and the fasting group. The primary endpoint was the incidence of aspiration pneumonia within 72 h after tracheostomy. Secondary endpoints included respiratory parameters, arterial blood gas measurements, delta (Δ) changes in physiological variables, procedure-related complications, and ICU and hospital outcomes. A total of 110 patients were assessed for eligibility, and 91 patients were included in the final analysis (continuous feeding group n = 45; fasting group n = 46). Baseline demographic characteristics, disease severity scores, and pre-tracheostomy respiratory parameters were comparable between groups. The incidence of aspiration pneumonia was 6.7% in the continuous feeding group and 4.4% in the fasting group, corresponding to an absolute risk difference of 2.3% (95% CI, - 6.6 to 11.2) and a crude odds ratio of 1.57 (95% CI, 0.25-9.88). Post-tracheostomy FiO2 requirements were higher in the fasting group (p = 0.005), while other respiratory and arterial blood gas parameters were similar. Delta analyses showed greater increases in PaO2 and more stable lactate levels in the continuous feeding group (p = 0.024 and p = 0.033). ICU and hospital length of stay, complication rates, and mortality were comparable. Continuation of EN before tracheostomy with passive nasogastric drainage was not associated with a statistically significant increase in aspiration pneumonia or adverse outcomes compared with conventional fasting. However, the small number of events and wide confidence intervals indicate that clinically relevant differences cannot be excluded. Larger, adequately powered studies are needed to confirm safety and clarify the clinical implications of pre-tracheostomy feeding strategies. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07508293. Registered on March 21, 2026, retrospectively registered.

42829458.title: Association between route of nutrition and serum I-FABP and MMP-9 levels in critically ill patients with acute ischemic stroke: a prospective cohort study.
42829458.abstract: Gut barrier dysfunction and neuroinflammation are increasingly recognised as linked pathophysiological processes in acute ischaemic stroke (AIS). However, the influence of nutritional routes on these processes remains poorly characterised. To compare the longitudinal effects of enteral nutrition (EN) versus parenteral nutrition (PN) on serum intestinal fatty acid-binding protein (I-FABP), a marker of intestinal epithelial integrity, and matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9), a marker of neuroinflammatory activity, in critically ill AIS patients. Prospective observational cohort study. A tertiary neurology intensive care unit (ICU) in Türkiye. Consecutive adults (≥18 years) admitted to the neurology ICU within 24 hours of a confirmed AIS diagnosis were enrolled between October 2024 and January 2026. Nutritional route was assigned by the treating clinician according to ESPEN guidelines. Serum I-FABP and MMP-9 concentrations were measured using commercial enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits at baseline and on day 7. Longitudinal changes in serum I-FABP and MMP-9 concentrations between baseline and day 7, and their correlations with neurological severity (NIHSS). 73 patients (40 EN, 33 PN). Median age was 73 years (interquartile range, 64-80) and 37 (51%) were female. At baseline, I-FABP and MMP-9 levels were comparable between groups (all P>.05). Over the 7-day observation period, I-FABP trajectories diverged between groups (EN: 7.22 (2.68) to 6.69 (2.78) ng/mL; PN: 6.74 (3.09) to 7.82 (2.97) ng/mL), as did MMP-9 trajectories (EN: 11.5 (1.45) to 10.9 (2.31) ng/mL; PN: 11.3 (2.41) to 11.8 (1.87) ng/mL). At day 7, both biomarkers correlated significantly with NIHSS score (ρ=0.385 and ρ=0.440, respectively; both P<.001). Repeated measures analysis of covariance, adjusted for baseline NIHSS score, confirmed significant time × nutritional route interactions for both biomarkers (I-FABP: F[1,70]=4.22, P=0.044, P_FDR=.044, η2p=.057; MMP-9: F[1,70]= 4.76, P=.033, P_FDR=.044, η2p=0.064). In critically ill AIS patients, EN was associated with more favourable 7-day trajectories of gut barrier integrity and neuroinflammatory activity compared with PN, after adjustment for baseline stroke severity. Single-center design, biomarker sampling restricted to two time points, reliance on delivered rather than utilised nutritional measures, and non-randomised nutritional route assignment with residual potential for confounding by indication.

42826338.title: Effect of enteral nutrition nursing combined with gastrointestinal function monitoring on gastric retention and abdominal distension in neurosurgical patients.
42826338.abstract: This study evaluated the clinical effects of enteral nutrition nursing combined with gastrointestinal function monitoring in neurosurgical patients receiving enteral nutrition. This single-center retrospective cohort study included 120 neurosurgical patients who received enteral nutritional support from June 2023 to June 2025. Sixty patients received routine enteral nutrition nursing (control group), and 60 received routine care plus dynamic gastrointestinal function monitoring (combined nursing group). Outcomes included gastric retention, abdominal distension, nausea and vomiting, overall gastrointestinal intolerance, enteral nutrition interruption, aspiration/reflux, nutritional delivery, gastrointestinal recovery, hospital and intensive care unit (ICU) stay, nutritional tolerance, and nursing satisfaction. Logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with gastric retention. Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups (all P > .05). Gastric retention occurred less frequently in the combined nursing group than in the control group (15.0% vs 30.0%), although the difference did not reach statistical significance (P = .053). The combined nursing group had lower incidences of abdominal distension (16.7% vs 36.7%, P = .011), nausea and vomiting (11.7% vs 26.7%, P = .038), and overall gastrointestinal intolerance (20.0% vs 43.3%, P = .006). Time to achievement of enteral nutrition targets, gastric residual volume, time to recovery of bowel sounds, and time to first defecation were also more favorable (all P < .001). Enteral nutrition interruption was less frequent (8.3% vs 23.3%, P = .022), and hospital and ICU stays were shorter (both P < .01). Good nutritional tolerance and nursing satisfaction were more frequent in the combined nursing group (both P < .05). Multivariable analysis showed that the combined nursing model was associated with lower odds of gastric retention. Enteral nutrition nursing combined with gastrointestinal function monitoring was associated with improved gastrointestinal tolerance, more efficient nutritional delivery, earlier gastrointestinal recovery, and shorter hospital and ICU stays. A lower observed incidence of gastric retention was also noted, and adjusted analysis suggested an association with reduced odds of gastric retention.

42952327.title: Clinical Phenotypes, Machine-Learning Risk Stratification and Treatment Outcomes of Constipation in Stroke Patients Receiving Enteral Nutrition: A Retrospective Study.
42952327.abstract: Stroke-related complications and frequent feeding interruptions often compromise nutritional intake, making enteral nutrition (EN) a cornerstone therapy to improve nutritional status and support recovery. Nevertheless, constipation is highly prevalent and clinically consequential among stroke patients receiving EN, particularly in critically ill populations, where enteral nutrition-associated constipation can impede rehabilitation, increase complications and prolong intensive care unit (ICU) stay. This study aimed to explore potentially important determinants of enteral nutrition-associated constipation (ENAC) in patients with stroke using artificial intelligence approaches, characterise relevant clinical subgroups, compare internally validated machine-learning models and examine how the temporal availability of candidate predictors may influence model performance. Clinical data from patients admitted to a neurological intensive care unit between December 2019 and December 2023 were retrospectively analysed. K-means clustering was used to identify clinical subgroups. Six algorithms-logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting tree, XGBoost, LightGBM and Table PFN-3-were compared under temporally restricted and expanded retrospective feature frameworks using five repeats of nested five-fold cross-validation. Performance was assessed using ROC-AUC, average precision, Brier score, calibration and decision-curve analysis. Treatment outcomes were summarised descriptively. Among 362 patients, 233 (64.4%) had documented constipation. Table PFN-3 achieved the highest discrimination in both frameworks. The temporally restricted model yielded a ROC-AUC of 0.629 (95% CI 0.567-0.689), whereas the expanded retrospective model achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.771 (95% CI 0.715-0.820), average precision of 0.857, Brier score of 0.177 and calibration slope of 0.965. The ROC-AUC increased by 0.142 (95% CI 0.090-0.201) after full-hospitalisation information was included. K-means clustering retained three subgroups (K = 3; silhouette coefficient = 0.108), with constipation frequencies of 67.35%, 56.98% and 88.89% in Clusters 0, 1 and 2, respectively. Among evaluable patients, observed relief was 80.3% with glycerin enema, 60.0% with lactulose, 72.7% with combination treatment and 65.7% with neither treatment; these treatment comparisons were descriptive. Table PFN-3 achieved the strongest internally validated performance, with the expanded retrospective framework combining good discrimination, strong precision-recall performance and close calibration. The 0.142 increase in ROC-AUC after completed hospital-course variables were incorporated quantifies the substantial discriminative information that emerges as hospitalisation evolves. Together with the distinct clinical phenotypes and descriptive treatment findings, these results establish a clinically relevant framework for trajectory-aware bowel monitoring and provide a clear rationale for developing dynamic, time-updated prediction models. By integrating machine-learning benchmarking, clinical phenotyping and observed treatment outcomes, this study identifies prolonged, treatment-intensive hospital trajectories as a particularly high-burden constipation phenotype and demonstrates that classification performance changes materially as hospital-course information accumulates. These findings support structured reassessment of bowel risk during neurological intensive care rather than reliance on a single static evaluation and provide a practical rationale for future dynamic monitoring tools.

42905668.title: Mathematical analysis of the relationship between glucose and sodium in a large Swedish cohort of critically ill patients.
42905668.abstract: Hyperglycemia causes compensatory decrease of plasma sodium concentration by an influx of water from the cellular compartment. When the glucose level is corrected, the sodium concentration will follow and increase to its original level. A complex MATLAB script incorporating the Katz and Hillier correction formulas was developed to evaluate the impact of hyperglycemia on sodium levels and to analyze sodium shifts in 9,863 patients across 297,714 paired sodium-glucose measurements. Intensive care unit (ICU) mortality and morbidity data were extracted for the full cohort to assess outcomes. 95.3% of the glucose values (283,686) implied a correction factor for the measured sodium levels in the cohort. Correction of all sodium values for hyperglycemia did not change the adjusted ICU mortalities. Increased maximum sodium shift/24 h starting from 4.00-5.99 mmol/L was related to increased independent ICU mortality. Correction of sodium levels by using Katz and Hillier formulas for hyperglycemia did not change the adjusted ICU mortalities. 602/9,863 (6.1%) patients showed a sodium shift more than 8 mmol/L/24 h. 31 patients (5.1%) were missed without correction for hyperglycemia by the Katz formula and 54 patients (9.0%) were missed without correction by the Hillier formula. Failure to correct sodium for hyperglycemia misses 5-9% of patients with large sodium shifts (>8 mmol/L per 24 hours). Additionally, a sodium shift as low as 4.00-5.99 mmol/L per 24 hours is an independent risk factor for increased ICU mortality.

42884667.title: Sarcopenia in Hospitalized Patients: A Critical Narrative Review of Diagnostic and Nutritional Management Approaches.
42884667.abstract: Sarcopenia is an independent predictor of adverse outcomes in hospitalized patients, associated with increased mortality, prolonged length of stay, and functional decline, yet it remains underdiagnosed owing to inconsistent diagnostic criteria and the practical challenges of assessing acutely ill patients. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on sarcopenia in hospitalized patients, with emphasis on diagnostic approaches, nutritional requirements, and optimal nutritional support strategies. Sarcopenia is particularly prevalent among critically ill patients and is driven by the convergence of systemic inflammation, immobility, and anabolic resistance. Diagnosis remains challenging: no ICU-specific framework exists, and the recent Global Leadership Initiative of Sarcopenia consensus established a unified, setting-independent conceptual definition as a foundation for future operational criteria, with ICU-specific frameworks yet to be developed. Bedside tools, including handgrip strength, bioelectrical impedance analysis, and ultrasound, retain strong prognostic value despite imperfect agreement with reference imaging. Nutritional intervention is a key component of management; however, large-scale trials have demonstrated that higher energy or protein delivery does not universally improve outcomes and may be harmful in selected critically ill patients. A gradual increase in energy and protein delivery according to the phase of illness, with protein targets of ≥1.2-1.5 g/kg/day, is recommended; leucine-enriched supplementation may help counteract anabolic resistance, although direct evidence in non-ICU hospitalized patients remains limited. Early mobilization is an essential complement, as nutrient provision without a mechanical stimulus cannot reverse immobility-induced muscle loss. A practical clinical algorithm integrating screening, nutritional target-setting, route selection, and reassessment is proposed to guide decision-making in this population. Future research should focus on improving the accuracy and feasibility of muscle assessment tools in critically ill patients to enable the timely diagnosis of sarcopenia and nutritional intervention, alongside the development of validated multi-marker panels and adequately powered trials examining the combined effect of nutrition and exercise in this population.

42879340.title: Clinical Course and Prognosis of the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition-Defined Malnutrition in Critically Ill Patients with Sepsis: A Multicenter Prospective Observational Study.
42879340.abstract: Sepsis is a critical condition with a high nutritional risk and mortality. Although the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM) criteria have been proposed for diagnosing malnutrition, their clinical relevance in sepsis remains unclear. Therefore, we conducted a descriptive study on GLIM-defined malnutrition in intensive care unit (ICU) patients with sepsis to investigate its clinical course and prognosis. This was a multicenter prospective study conducted at 15 centers. Malnutrition was identified at ICU admission when both phenotypic and etiologic criteria were present. The primary outcome was a composite of in-hospital mortality or a decline in activities of daily living (Barthel Index <90) at discharge. Secondary outcomes included ICU length of stay, use of parenteral nutrition, and days to achievement of each ICU Mobility Scale level. Among 254 patients, 106 (41.7%) had malnutrition. The malnutrition group showed a significantly higher occurrence of the composite of in-hospital mortality and Barthel index <90 (76.4% vs. 64.2%, p = 0.04) and had significantly longer ICU stays (7 vs. 5, p = 0.001). Total nutrition delivery did not significantly differ between groups, while a higher percentage of patients in the malnutrition group received parenteral nutrition (57.6% vs. 43.2%, p = 0.02). Significant delays in achieving higher mobility levels were observed in the malnutrition group. GLIM-defined malnutrition in patients with sepsis was significantly associated with the composite outcome of in-hospital mortality or Barthel index <90 at discharge. These results suggest the clinical importance of an early GLIM assessment after ICU admission.

42876873.title: Evaluation of Chromium Picolinate Supplementation and Insulin Requirements in Critically Ill Adults With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
42876873.journal: The Journal of pharmacy technology : jPT : official publication of the Association of Pharmacy Technicians
42876873.abstract: Chromium picolinate has been studied as an adjunct to improve glycemic indices in ambulatory type 2 diabetes mellitus, but its role in critically ill patients is unknown. To evaluate whether chromium picolinate supplementation was associated with reduced insulin requirements without worsening glycemic control in critically ill adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. We conducted a single-center retrospective pre-post cohort study of adult intensive care unit patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus or hemoglobin A1c ≥6.5% who received insulin and at least 4 consecutive chromium picolinate doses between July 2022 and January 2023. Patients served as their own controls during 24-hour pre- and post-chromium periods. The primary outcome was change in total daily insulin dose. Secondary outcomes included proportion of measured glucose values within 140 to 180 mg/dL, acute kidney injury, hypoglycemia, and exploratory Sequential Organ Failure Assessment-2 change. Among 91 screened patients, 45 met the inclusion criteria. Median total daily insulin dose decreased from 76.3 U/d (interquartile range [IQR], 40.1-96.9) before chromium to 40.0 U/d (IQR, 20.5-65.6) after chromium; the Hodges-Lehmann paired difference was -23.0 U/d (95% CI, -33.25 to -14.25; P < .0001). Proportion of measured glucose values within target did not differ significantly. No post-intervention hypoglycemia was observed, and 2 patients met the study-defined acute kidney injury criterion. Interpretation is limited by the retrospective design and absence of a concurrent control group. Chromium picolinate supplementation was associated with lower insulin requirements without worsening glycemic control. These hypothesis-generating findings require confirmation in prospective controlled studies.

42875940.title: The effects of intravenous glutamine supplementation in critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42875940.abstract: Studies evaluating intravenous (IV) glutamine supplementation in critically ill patients have shown inconsistent results. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of IV glutamine on mortality, infectious complications, length of stay, and duration of mechanical ventilation. A systematic search of Ovid Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and KoreaMed was conducted from inception through October 2023 and updated in April 2025. Randomized controlled trials comparing IV glutamine supplementation with standard care in critically ill adults were included. Pooled estimates were calculated using random-effects models. A total of 10 randomized trials involving 1,593 critically ill patients were included in the analysis. IV glutamine supplementation was not associated with reduced overall mortality (risk ratio [RR], 0.93; 95% CI, 0.77-1.13) or overall infection rates (RR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.63-1.18). No mortality benefit was observed in either non-surgical or surgical/trauma subgroups. Glutamine supplementation was associated with reduced pneumonia incidence (RR, 0.65; 95% CI, 0.49-0.87) and shorter mechanical ventilation duration (mean difference, -0.97 days; 95% CI, -1.62 to -0.32); however, these findings were based on a limited number of small studies. Intensive care unit and hospital length of stay were longer in the glutamine group. IV glutamine supplementation was not associated with improved survival or overall infection rates in critically ill adults. Current evidence does not support routine IV glutamine supplementation in unselected critically ill patients.

42857550.title: Construction and validation of a 28-day mortality prediction model for refeeding syndrome in critically ill patients.
42857550.abstract: Refeeding syndrome (RFS) is a common and serious metabolic reaction during nutritional support in critically ill patients, associated with substantially increased mortality risk and poor prognosis. Existing studies mainly focus on predicting its occurrence, while predictive models for 28-day mortality risk remain lacking. This study aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine learning model to support short-term prognostic assessment in clinical practice. Data for critically ill patients with RFS were extracted from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV, 2008-2019) as the internal cohort. A total of 8,705 patients were randomly assigned to training and test sets at a 7:3 ratio. Thirty-eight candidate variables were initially included, and feature selection was performed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) logistic regression. Three machine learning models were subsequently constructed, and the optimal model was validated using two independent datasets. Model interpretability was enhanced using Shapley additive explanations (SHAP). Kaplan-Meier curves were used to compare survival between the high- and low-risk, and nomograms were constructed to facilitate clinical application. Nine variables were ultimately selected to construct the logistic regression model. The model demonstrated excellent discriminative performance and generalizability, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.821, 0.809, and 0.731 in the internal test set, external validation set I (MIMIC-III), and external validation set II (the Affiliated Hospital of Yangzhou University), respectively. SHAP analysis identified partial pressure of oxygen, mean blood glucose level, and age as the key prognostic factors and further revealed nonlinear effects among the variables. Kaplan-Meier survival curves confirmed that the model significantly distinguished between the high- and low-risk groups across all cohorts (all p < 0.05). Decision curve analysis showed that the model provided favorable clinical net benefit in both external validation cohorts. The interpretable machine learning model developed in this study effectively predicts the 28-day mortality risk of RFS in critically ill patients, provides an objective reference for individualized clinical decision-making, and may help improve patient prognosis.

42851275.title: Enteral nutrition interruption in critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prevalence, causes, and clinical outcomes.
42851275.abstract: Enteral nutrition interruption (ENI) is common in critically ill patients and may compromise nutritional delivery, but its prevalence, causes, and clinical consequences remain uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized evidence on ENI prevalence, contributing factors, clinical outcomes, and potential interventions. PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CNKI, and WanFang Data were searched from inception through December 2025. Studies of critically ill adults receiving enteral nutrition were eligible. The review followed PRISMA guidance and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251266654). Random-effects models, subgroup analyses, sensitivity analyses, and GRADE assessments were performed. Forty-one studies involving 8,260 critically ill patients were included. Crude ENI prevalence ranged from 11.2% to 100%, with a median of 68.5% (IQR, 57.1%-96.6%). The estimated pooled prevalence was 79.2%, although heterogeneity was extreme (I 2 = 99%) and publication bias was evident (Egger's test, p < 0.001). Common causes included airway management, radiological or imaging procedures, gastrointestinal intolerance, and surgical procedures or preparation. ENI was associated with reduced energy adequacy (mean difference, -4.21 percentage points; 95% CI, -7.71 to -0.71; p = 0.02). No statistically significant association was observed with ICU length of stay (mean difference, -0.41 days; 95% CI, -2.05 to 1.23; p = 0.62). Short-term mortality was not statistically significantly associated with ENI (risk ratio, 1.86; 95% CI, 0.67-5.11), but the estimate was imprecise and heterogeneous (I 2 = 88%). ENI appears common and is predominantly procedure-related. It is associated with reduced energy adequacy, whereas its effects on ICU length of stay and short-term mortality remain uncertain because of inconsistent ENI definitions, substantial heterogeneity, publication bias, and limited outcome data. Standardized definitions, shorter peri-procedural fasting, improved gastrointestinal management, and multidisciplinary nutrition protocols may reduce avoidable interruptions. High-quality prospective studies and randomized trials are needed. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251266654.

42850757.title: Association of enteral nutrition reduction or discontinuation with diarrhea volume and caloric delivery in critically ill adults with diarrhea: A retrospective cohort study.
42850757.journal: Nutrition in clinical practice : official publication of the American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition
42850757.abstract: When critically ill patients receiving enteral nutrition (EN) develop diarrhea, clinicians often reduce or discontinue EN, although evidence supporting this practice is limited. We examined the association between EN management after diarrhea and diarrhea volume in critical care patients. This single-center retrospective cohort study included adult intensive care unit patients who developed new-onset diarrhea (Bristol Stool Form Scale ≥6 on 2 consecutive days) during EN. Based on Day 1 EN management, patients were classified as continuation (infusion rate decrease <10 mL/h) or reduction/discontinuation (decrease ≥10 mL/h or complete discontinuation). The primary outcome was cumulative diarrhea volume (grams) on Days 1-2. Cumulative EN calories (kcal) on Days 1-2 was a key secondary outcome. Inverse probability of treatment weighting with regression adjustment accounted for 8 pre-specified confounders. Sensitivity analyses included alternative exposure thresholds and propensity score models. Of 135 patients analyzed (median age, 74 years; 32% female), 96 (71.1%) continued EN and 39 (28.9%) underwent EN reduction/discontinuation. After adjustment, the reduction/discontinuation group had lower cumulative diarrhea volume on Days 1-2 (adjusted mean difference, -183.4 g; 95% confidence interval [CI], -350.1 to -16.7; p = 0.033) but received substantially fewer calories (-1260.1 kcal; 95% CI, -1464.4 to -1055.9; p < 0.001). The direction of the reduction in diarrhea volume was consistent across sensitivity analyses. Reducing or discontinuing EN after diarrhea was associated with a modest reduction in diarrhea volume but a substantial caloric deficit. This trade-off should be considered when reducing EN for diarrhea.

42837970.title: Evaluation of a device for insertion of a small intestinal feeding tube in the critically ill: A prospective multicentre international cohort study.
42837970.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
42837970.abstract: Critically ill patients sometimes require insertion of a feeding tube into the small intestine. This study evaluated the ease of placement of a proprietary small intestinal feeding tube incorporating a distal tip camera. investigator-initiated, industry-funded, prospective cohort study was conducted at four intensive care units across two countries. Patients were eligible if the treating clinician requested small intestinal feeding tube insertion. Operators were physicians or senior dietitians, and attempts were categorised as "inexperienced" (≤4 attempts) or "experienced" (≥5 attempts). The primary outcome was the overall probability of successful small intestinal placement. Secondary outcomes included procedural time and the posterior probabilities of success according to operator classification and experience, estimated using Bayesian hierarchical regression models incorporating minimally informative priors and random intercepts for clustering within operators. The device was used by 11 operators in 68 patients. Prior 24-h cumulative gastric residual volumes were 454 (standard deviation: 453) millilitres. The overall probability of success was 75% (95% credible interval: 61-86%). Experienced users and inexperienced users were successful in 30 of 38 (79%) and 21 of 30 (70%) attempts, respectively. Overall median (interquartile range) procedural times for successful versus unsuccessful placement were 23 (10-35) and 30 (20-42) minutes, respectively. In a multivariable analysis, the posterior probabilities of improved success (odds ratio >1) were 83% (gastrokinetic drug prescription), 82% (operative versus nonoperative admission), and 65% (device experience). The probability of successful small intestinal placement of feeding tubes by motivated clinicians in a critical care environment approximated the prespecified threshold of 80%, without the need for extensive specific device experience.

42832132.title: Clinical applications of gastric point-of-care ultrasound in adult emergency and critical care: a scoping review.
42832132.abstract: Point-of-care ultrasound (PoCUS) is a cornerstone of bedside assessment in emergency and critical care, providing rapid, radiation-free visualization of anatomy and pathology. Gastric PoCUS offers a non-invasive method to assess gastric content, volume, and motility, informing management of aspiration risk, airway interventions, and enteral feeding. Despite supporting evidence, its use remains limited and poorly standardized. The objective of this scoping review is to map the clinical applications of gastric PoCUS in adult emergency department (ED) and intensive care unit (ICU) patients. A scoping review was conducted according to PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Medline, Embase, Scopus, Cochrane, CINAHL, were searched from 1950 to May 2025 for studies evaluating gastric ultrasound in adult ED or ICU populations. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted, and charted data. Thirty-five studies met inclusion criteria. Clinical applications of gastric PoCUS among ED and ICU were clustered under three domains: aspiration risk assessment and airway management (n = 5); enteral nutrition and gastric residual volume monitoring (n = 12); and diagnostic evaluation or therapeutic monitoring (n = 18). Across studies, gastric PoCUS reliably differentiated gastric content types, estimated gastric volume, and informed airway and feeding decisions. In diagnostic contexts, gastric PoCUS enabled rapid bedside identification of gastric outlet obstruction, volvulus, intramural hematoma, and perforated viscus. No studies reported complications or harm caused by performing gastric PoCUS. Gastric PoCUS is a versatile bedside tool bridging diagnostic and therapeutic domains in emergency and critical care. It enhances patient safety, optimizes nutritional management, and reduces radiographic dependence. Standardization of scanning protocols, structured training, and multicenter outcome-based validation studies are needed to support routine integration in acute care.

42823888.title: Prevalence of Chronic Complications After Inaugural Admission in Intensive Care Unit for Type 1 Diabetes in the SFDT1 Cohort: The INAUGURAL Study.
42823888.abstract: Inaugural presentation at type 1 diabetes onset, as ketoacidosis, has been associated with poorer glycaemic control, but its relationship to diabetes-related complications remains unclear. We assessed the association between inaugural intensive care unit (ICU) admission and long-term diabetes-related outcomes in adults. This cross-sectional analysis used data from the Société Francophone du Diabète-Cohorte Diabète de Type 1 (SFDT1) cohort. We compared participants with and without an inaugural ICU admission regarding chronic complications, recent acute events, and cardiometabolic risk factors. Models were adjusted for age, sex, diabetes duration, smoking status, socioeconomic vulnerability, education, insulin therapy, HbA1c, and centre; interaction terms were tested. Among 3548 adults with type 1 diabetes (median duration 20 years [IQR 10-30]), 377 (10.6%) reported inaugural ICU admission. Retinopathy was more prevalent in the ICU group (36.6 vs. 31.4%; p < 0.05), including proliferative forms (11.1 vs. 7.7%; p < 0.05). These differences remained significant after adjustment (p < 0.05). An association with retinopathy was observed among individuals diagnosed before the age of 17 (OR = 1.5; 95% CI, 1.1-2.1; p = 0.015). Severe hypoglycaemia in the previous year was more frequent in the ICU group (15.4% vs. 10.5%; p < 0.01) and remained significant after adjustment (p < 0.05). No significant differences were observed for the other variables. In this multicentre cohort of adults with long-standing type 1 diabetes, inaugural ICU was associated with at least a 50% higher odds of severe hypoglycaemia and retinopathy, including proliferative forms. The association with retinopathy was mainly observed among individuals diagnosed at a young age. ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04657783).

42952864.title: A nurse-led standardized bedside gastric ultrasound monitoring protocol for abdominal distension management in critically ill patients receiving enteral nutrition: a pragmatic, exploratory randomized controlled trial.
42952864.abstract: To evaluate the feasibility and exploratory clinical effects of a standardized, nurse-led bedside gastric ultrasound-guided monitoring protocol for abdominal distension management in critically ill patients receiving enteral nutrition. In this single-center, pragmatic, exploratory randomized controlled trial, critically ill adults receiving enteral nutrition in the intensive care unit of Henan Provincial People's Hospital were assigned 1:1 to ultrasound-guided gastric residual volume (GRV) monitoring or syringe-aspiration monitoring. The primary outcome was abdominal circumference on day 7. Secondary outcomes included intra-abdominal pressure (IAP), exploratory biomarkers, gastric retention, feeding intolerance, and implementation measures. Of 112 patients assessed, 100 were randomized and 91 completed the 7-day protocol, giving an overall retention rate of 91%. In the intervention group, the median number of ultrasound assessments was 14 per patient (IQR, 10-19), and protocol adherence was 82/89 (92.1%). Day-7 abdominal circumference was lower in the intervention group after baseline adjustment (adjusted mean difference, -2.35 cm; 95% CI, -3.28 to -1.43; P < 0.001). Baseline-adjusted IAP was also lower (-1.68 mmHg; 95% CI, -2.51 to -0.86; P < 0.001). Feeding intolerance did not differ significantly between groups (31.9% vs. 47.7%; RR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.40-1.12; Fisher exact P = 0.139). Albumin was higher after baseline adjustment, whereas prealbumin did not differ significantly. The nurse-led protocol was feasible in this single-center population of non-intubated, relatively hemodynamically stable ICU patients and provided preliminary estimates for abdominal distension-related outcomes. The albumin result was exploratory and should not be taken as evidence of improved nutritional delivery. Secondary analyses were not adjusted for multiplicity and require cautious interpretation. The lack of prospective registration is a major limitation, and the findings do not apply to mechanically ventilated or hemodynamically unstable patients. The randomized design, outcomes, and analysis plan were specified in the ethics-approved protocol before enrollment. However, the separate requirement for registration in a public trial registry was overlooked, and the study was not prospectively registered [Ethics Committee of Henan Provincial People's Hospital, approval No. 2023(Ethics)127].

42936253.title: Gastrointestinal point-of-care ultrasound for enteral nutrition management in critically ill adults: a scoping review.
42936253.abstract: Gastrointestinal point-of-care ultrasound has been investigated as a non-invasive, bedside adjunct for gastrointestinal assessment and enteral-feeding decision-making in critical care; however, existing protocols and their outcome reporting remain fragmented. This scoping review mapped the existing evidence landscape on the use of gastrointestinal point-of-care ultrasound in the management of enteral nutrition in critically ill adults. Comprehensive searches in 10 databases (PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, Cochrane, CINAHL, Scopus, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang, VIP, China Biological Medicine Literature Database) identified 5,123 records. Studies focusing on ultrasound-assessed gastrointestinal function to guide enteral nutrition, or to predict enteral nutrition intolerance and clinical prognosis, were screened, summarized, and descriptively analyzed. 49 unique studies were identified, including 36 interventional and 13 observational studies. Geographically, the synthesized evidence was heavily concentrated in China. Ultrasound indicators for gastrointestinal function included the gastric antrum (gastric residual volume, motility index, cross-sectional area), colon (colon diameter and peristaltic frequency), small intestine (small intestine diameter, wall thickness, peristalsis), and superior mesenteric artery hemodynamics. Observational studies showed Area Under the Curve point estimates frequently around or above 0.70, with substantial heterogeneity and no independent external validation reported for enteral nutrition intolerance and mortality. Among interventional studies, time to achieve feeding goals and intensive care unit length of stay were the most frequently evaluated outcomes (27/36), whereas in-hospital mortality was evaluated in only 8 of 36 studies; outcome reporting was heterogeneous and is presented descriptively. The synthesized literature suggests the potential utility of gastrointestinal point-of-care ultrasound as an objective, non-invasive bedside tool for gastrointestinal assessment and feeding protocol modulation. However, because no formal critical appraisal or pooled comparative or diagnostic analysis was performed, this review cannot establish clinical effectiveness, universal thresholds, or patient-important benefit. Future research priorities include consensus definitions and acquisition standards, effect estimates with confidence intervals and patient-important outcomes, inter-operator reliability and training evaluation, and external validation across diverse health systems.

42934932.title: Current nutrition practices and additional reimbursement of intensive care units in Japan: A cross-sectional survey study.
42934932.journal: JPEN. Journal of parenteral and enteral nutrition
42934932.abstract: A unique reimbursement for early nutrition intervention was introduced in Japan to promote guideline-adherent nutrition practices in intensive care units. However, the current status of nutrition therapy implementation across Japanese intensive care units remains unclear. This cross-sectional survey study investigated intensive care units nationwide, led by the Japanese Society of Intensive Care Medicine. Facility characteristics, nutrition management structure, nutrition practices (nutritional assessment, nutrition planning, therapy implementation, and monitoring), and dietitian involvement were assessed. We examined relationships between reimbursement claim status and nutrition practices. Among 337 intensive care units, most performed nutritional assessment using at least one standardized tool and planned nutrition targeting 25-30 kcal/kg/day for energy and 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day for protein. Enteral nutrition-related practices were widely implemented. Of these, 255 intensive care units (75.7%) claimed the reimbursement; incentivized units more frequently implemented written enteral nutrition protocols, dietitian-conducted nutritional assessments, dietitian-led enteral nutrition design, and enteral nutrition initiation within 48 h. However, Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition assessment, indirect calorimetry, written protocols for parenteral nutrition/diarrhea/constipation, dietitian-led parenteral nutrition design, and post-intensive care unit nutritional follow-up remained limited even in incentivized units. In Japan, reimbursement incentives were positively associated with higher implementation of nutritional assessment, enteral nutrition-related practices, and dietitian involvement. To further advance specialized nutritional care, simultaneous system development may be warranted.

42933867.title: Management of dysglycemia in critically ill adults: current evidence, clinical practice and future directions.
42933867.abstract: Hyperglycemia is among the most common metabolic disturbances in critically ill patients, affecting up to 50% of adults admitted to intensive care units (ICUs), regardless of pre-existing diabetes. Both diabetes and stress-induced hyperglycemia are associated with increased risk of organ dysfunction, healthcare-associated infections, prolonged mechanical ventilation, longer ICU and hospital length of stay, and mortality. Clinical guidelines recommend initiating intravenous insulin therapy when blood glucose remains ≥180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L) and targeting 140–180 mg/dL (7.8–10.0 mmol/L) for most critically ill adults. Recent advances in continuous glucose monitoring, computerized insulin dosing algorithms, automated insulin delivery systems and artificial intelligence-enabled clinical decision support are transforming glucose management in the ICU and have the potential to improve safety and efficiency. This review summarizes current understanding of the pathophysiology of stress hyperglycemia, the clinical consequences of dysglycemia, contemporary glucose targets, insulin therapy and glucose monitoring strategies. We also highlight emerging technologies, special patient populations and future directions expected to shape precision glycemic management for critically ill adults.

42933108.title: Plasma amino acid profiles reveal metabolic signatures of mortality and infection in critically ill surgical patients requiring parenteral nutrition: A longitudinal analysis.
42933108.abstract: Surgical intensive care unit (SICU) patients experience high rates of adverse outcomes, underscoring the need for insights into pathophysiology. We aimed to evaluate associations between plasma amino acids (AAs), post-surgical mortality, and hospital-acquired infections in SICU patients requiring parenteral nutrition (PN). Secondary analysis of a multicenter trial including 148 adults receiving glutamine-supplemented or standard PN after major surgery. Levels of plasma AAs were quantified at baseline, Day 3, and Day 7. Mortality and infections were monitored through day 28. Associations between AAs and outcomes were assessed via generalized linear models adjusted for clinical covariates. Machine learning models evaluated the classification performance of AAs. At baseline, a four AA signature (plasma aspartate, histidine, leucine, and methionine concentrations) showed similar discrimination of 28-day mortality as the APACHE II score (AUC 0.88 vs. 0.78, DeLong test P = 0.28). Increased concentrations of these AA suggest impaired uptake and utilization. At baseline, BSI was best classified by a model that included decreased concentrations of alanine, cystine, glutamate, glutamine, and lysine (AUC 0.79), with glutamate elevated in cases. The best classification model for pneumonia at Day 7 included decreased cystine, lysine, ornithine, threonine, tyrosine, and valine concentrations (AUC 0.86). At baseline and Day 7, for any infections, the classification model included decreased glutamine, glycine, lysine, ornithine, proline, serine, threonine, and valine concentrations (AUC >0.79). Elevated essential AA concentrations were associated with SICU mortality, while lower levels of both essential and non-essential AAs were linked to hospital-acquired infections.

42908224.title: Association between augmented enteral protein and muscle mass attenuation in critically ill patients: A sub-study of a cluster randomized crossover trial.
42908224.journal: JPEN. Journal of parenteral and enteral nutrition
42908224.abstract: Critically ill patients experience muscle wasting, impacting recovery. The associations between augmented enteral protein and muscle mass, strength, physical function, and quality of life are uncertain. We performed a sub-study in adult TARGET Protein participants from two sites between 23/11/2022-23/05/2023. Our exposure of interest was enteral formula with augmented protein (100 g protein/L) and comparator usual protein formula (63 g protein/L), which were isocaloric. Our primary outcome was the change in quadriceps muscle layer thickness from Days 1 to 7, determined by ultrasonography and compared between groups. Our secondary outcomes were group differences in handgrip strength, change in physical function, and quality of life. Data are numbers (%), mean (standard deviation), and differences with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Seventy-two patients were included (augmented protein n = 46, 61 (16)y, 65% male; usual protein n = 26, 56 (16)y, 46% male), 56 had primary outcome data (augmented protein n = 35; usual protein n = 21). Delivered protein was higher with augmented protein (1.2 (0.4) vs 0.8 (0.3) g/kg/day). Quadriceps muscle layer thickness decreased in both groups, with change from Days 1 to 7 similar (0.01 cm; 95% CI, -0.27, 0.28; P = 0.970). Left handgrip strength at ICU discharge and quality of life at Day 90 were similar. Augmented protein was associated with greater right handgrip strength at ICU discharge (6.23; 95% CI, 0.67, 11.79) and was associated with greater decline in physical function at ICU discharge (-15.00; 95% CI, -19.75, -10.25), but not at Day 90. No clear difference was detected in quadriceps muscle layer attenuation over 7 days between augmented enteral protein and usual protein. Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry identifier: ACTRN12622001465741.

42906879.title: Clinical nutrition for critically ill patients: A practical appraisal of guideline gaps and perspectives for future research.
42906879.abstract: Malnutrition and accelerated muscle wasting are frequent during critical illness and make nutritional support a central component of ICU care. Nutritional support is therefore central to ICU care, but its optimal timing, route, dose, and composition remain debated. Recent randomized trials have challenged the traditional objective of early full feeding and shifted practice toward progressive, phase-adapted, and tolerance-based nutrition. This narrative review compares current international guidelines for nutritional support in critically ill adults. Guidelines broadly agree that nutrition should be initiated early after clinical stabilization, acute-phase overfeeding should be avoided, energy and protein delivery should be increased progressively, and refeeding syndrome should be anticipated. However, important differences remain regarding acute-phase energy targets, protein dosing, enteral versus parenteral nutrition, supplemental parenteral nutrition, indirect calorimetry, and enriched enteral formulas. These discrepancies reflect differences in methodology, healthcare context, and interpretation of evidence largely derived from mechanically ventilated patients during the first ICU week. Several clinically important situations remain insufficiently addressed, including prolonged critical illness, obesity, sarcopenia, post-extubation nutrition, post-ICU rehabilitation, and nutrition after major surgery. Future research should move toward individualized strategies based on illness phase, metabolic trajectory, nutritional phenotype, tolerance, and recovery-oriented outcomes.

42903103.title: Clinical evaluation of AI Chatbots' performance and safety for total parenteral nutrition planning in critically ill patients: a simulation-based benchmarking study.
42903103.abstract: Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) is essential for critically ill adults unable to meet their nutritional needs via the gastrointestinal tract. Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have sparked interest in their potential to support healthcare providers in complex clinical decisions. Nonetheless, no prior research has systematically compared publicly accessible chatbots to pharmacist-developed reference TPN plans across a diverse patient cohort, using a predefined, guideline-based rubric assessing accuracy, completeness, safety, error types, and numerical precision. This study presents a simulation-based benchmarking to evaluate (i) the accuracy and comprehensiveness of chatbot-generated TPN plans, (ii) their safety, acceptability, and error profiles, and (iii) the numerical agreement and concordance with expert pharmacist references. This benchmarking study, based on simulations and cross-sectional analysis, evaluated the performance of four publicly accessible AI chatbots-ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, and Perplexity-in formulating TPN plans for critically ill adults. Copilot declined to generate patient-specific TPN plans; this refusal was retained as a performance outcome, while Copilot was excluded from analyses requiring an analyzable TPN prescription. Each chatbot produced one plan for each of 10 standardized clinical cases, resulting in a total of 30 TPN plans. Friedman tests, Kendall's W, and Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used for comparative analyses. ChatGPT produced comprehensive plans for all 10 cases, compared to 6 plans from Gemini and 4 from Perplexity. The median accuracy was 57.7% for ChatGPT, 43.9% for Gemini, and 38.5% for Perplexity, with no statistically significant overall difference (p = 0.124). However, ChatGPT performed better than Perplexity in pairwise comparison (adjusted p = 0.035). There was a significant difference in completeness among the chatbots (p = 0.003; Kendall's W = 0.57), with median scores of 64.6, 41.9, and 32.3%, respectively. All 30 plans had at least one major or critical safety issue, 7 (23.3%) contained a critical concern, and 19 (63.3%) were rejected. The most common errors were related to electrolytes (90.0%), micronutrients (70.0%), and monitoring (66.7%). Recommendations from chatbots often exceeded pharmacist-derived values, with median relative differences of +47% for energy, +120% for lipids, and +100% for potassium. Bland-Altman analysis revealed considerable variability in the agreement. ChatGPT produced the most comprehensive TPN plans among chatbots. However, none showed enough accuracy, safety, or concordance for independent use. All plans had critical issues, especially with electrolytes, micronutrients, monitoring, and refeeding precautions. AI chatbots can support education or planning but require review by a well-trained clinician before clinical use.

42893059.title: Incidence and mortality of invasive fungal infections among patients admitted in intensive care units in India: findings from a multicentric registry-based study (2023-25).
42893059.journal: The Lancet regional health. Southeast Asia
42893059.abstract: Invasive fungal infections (IFIs) are challenging to treat in critical care, particularly among patients treated in Intensive care units (ICUs). The existing evidence on IFIs from India remains fragmented. This study characterises IFI incidence, risk factors, resistance pattern, treatment and outcome among patients admitted to ICUs. This multicentre observational study leveraged registry data on IFIs among patients admitted to 63 ICUs in eight Advanced Mycology Diagnostic and Research centres in India between January 2023 and November 2025. Patients with proven and probable IFI according to European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer/Mycoses Study Group Education and Research Consortium (EORTC/MSGERC) 2020 and the modified Aspergillus intensive care unit (AspICU) 2020 criteria were included. IFI incidence to hospital admission, all-cause in-hospital mortality, pathogen distribution and antifungal susceptibility were recorded. Mortality-associated factors were estimated using multivariable logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards analysis. Among 178,417 ICU admissions, 2500 IFI patients were identified with an incidence of 14/1000 admissions (95% CI 13.5-14.6) and all-cause mortality of 53.6% (95% CI 51.7-55.6%). Invasive candidiasis was the most frequently reported (57.1%), followed by invasive aspergillosis (37%), mucormycosis (3.4%), trichosporonosis (1.8%), pneumocystis pneumonia (1.1%), and cryptococcosis (1.2%). Median age of the patients was 45 years (IQR: 26-60), with 61.9% males and 38.1% females. Among candidiasis, Candida tropicalis predominated (35.6%), while Candida auris exhibited high fluconazole resistance (61.7%) and elevated amphotericin B minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) (40.7%). Aspergillus fumigatus (50.8%) and Aspergillus flavus (38.7%) predominated among culture-positive aspergillosis, with generally low MICs. Exploratory multivariable analyses showed that sepsis, chronic liver disease, immunosuppression, corticosteroid exposure, and total parenteral nutrition were associated with higher mortality in invasive candidiasis, whereas mechanical ventilation, corticosteroid exposure, and immunosuppression were associated with higher mortality in invasive aspergillosis. The study findings highlight a high IFI burden and mortality among patients admitted in ICUs of India, with mortality exceeding 50%, underscoring the need for continuous surveillance, rapid diagnostics, infection control and antifungal stewardship. This study was funded by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Delhi (Grant ID: 157401).

42890601.title: Knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding enteral nutrition interruption management in intensive care units: a multicenter cross-sectional study predominantly among nurses.
42890601.abstract: Enteral nutrition (EN) is essential for critically ill patients, yet enteral nutrition interruption (ENI) is common in intensive care unit (ICU) and compromises nutrient delivery. ENI reflects clinical conditions, workflows, team collaboration, and bedside implementation, but how knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) interact remains unclear. To assess ENI-related knowledge, attitudes, and practices among ICU healthcare professionals, predominantly nurses, and examine their interrelationships and associations with training, demographic, and organizational factors. This multicenter cross-sectional survey included 478 ICU healthcare professionals from 14 hospitals in Shandong and Henan, China, between December 2025 and February 2026; 93.5% were nurses. Self-reported KAP were assessed using a validated questionnaire. Descriptive statistics, Spearman correlation, multiple linear regression, and observed-variable path analysis were conducted. Self-assessed knowledge scores were lower than attitude and practice scores, particularly for items related to the operational definitions of ENI. The three KAP domains were positively correlated, with the strongest correlation between knowledge and practice (ρ = 0.738, p < 0.001). Path analysis suggested that knowledge was associated with both attitudes and practices and that attitudes were also associated with practices. Bootstrap analysis further indicated a possible indirect association between knowledge and practice through attitudes (indirect effect = 0.339, 95% CI 0.246-0.438). EN-related training was associated with higher scores across all three domains, whereas EN team membership was associated with higher knowledge and practice scores. Several demographic and hospital characteristics showed domain-specific associations. The regression models explained a modest proportion of the observed variance (adjusted R 2 = 0.054-0.141). Among ICU healthcare professionals, predominantly nurses, self-reported ENI management practices were associated with knowledge and attitudes, with attitudes potentially playing an intermediary role. EN-related training was also associated with more favorable KAP scores, while organizational and workflow factors may contribute to the observed variation. These findings may help identify potential targets for future intervention development and evaluation but do not establish causal relationships or improvements in actual ENI management, nutrient delivery, or patient outcomes.

42947684.title: Body mass index, diabetes, inflammation and survival in COVID-19: a retrospective study evaluating the obesity paradox in an urban hospital center.
42947684.journal: Frontiers in clinical diabetes and healthcare
42947684.abstract: Severe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is associated with increased morbidity and mortality, particularly among patients with comorbidities such as diabetes and obesity. The combined influence of glycemic control, hyperglycemia, and body mass index (BMI) on disease severity remains incompletely understood, particularly in underserved urban populations. This retrospective study evaluated 478 adults hospitalized with confirmed COVID-19 between March and May 2020 at an urban academic medical center to examine the impact of diabetes, glycemic control, and body mass index (BMI) on clinical outcomes. Data collected included demographics, comorbidities, BMI, diabetes type, baseline hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), inflammatory markers, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, mechanical ventilation, hyperglycemia, and glucocorticoid use. Among patients with available HbA1c measurements, those with diabetes who developed cytokine storm had significantly higher mean HbA1c than those without cytokine storm. Obesity and overweight were highly prevalent, with 45% of patients classified as obese (BMI ≥30 kg/m²) and 29% classified as overweight (BMI 25-29 kg/m²). Diabetes was associated with increased ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, and steroid-induced hyperglycemia. Mortality was higher among older patients, Black patients, and those with diabetes, hypertension, hyperglycemia, greater glucocorticoid use, or ICU admission. Notably, patients with overweight or obesity demonstrated improved survival compared with those of normal weight, consistent with an obesity paradox in this urban cohort. Multivariable analysis identified steroid-induced hyperglycemia, obstructive sleep apnea, and higher methylprednisolone use as independent predictors of ICU admission, whereas higher BMI was associated with a lower risk of adverse outcomes. Diabetes and hyperglycemia were associated with greater COVID-19 severity, increased ICU utilization, and higher mortality, while higher BMI offered potential survival benefits. These findings highlight the complex interplay between metabolic dysfunction, obesity, and COVID-19 outcomes, suggesting the presence of an obesity paradox in hospitalized patients, and emphasize the importance of early recognition and management of diabetes and hyperglycemia to improve clinical outcomes.

42928725.title: Euglycemic SGLT2 Inhibitor-Associated Ketoacidosis in a Nondiabetic Patient: A Case Report.
42928725.abstract: We present the case of a 62-year-old nondiabetic woman receiving dapagliflozin for dilated cardiomyopathy presenting to the emergency department with severe hypoxemic respiratory failure because of suspected cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Despite treatment, she remained symptomatic and required intubation and intensive care admission. After intubation, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis was unmasked. After exclusion of other common causes, SGLT2 inhibitor-associated ketoacidosis due to dapagliflozin was suspected. Marked ketonuria confirmed the diagnosis despite the absence of hyperglycemia. Dapagliflozin was discontinued, and intravenous insulin, glucose infusion, and early enteral nutrition were initiated. Metabolic acidosis resolved completely within 24 h. The patient was successfully extubated and discharged from the intensive care unit 48 h later. SGLT2 inhibitor-associated ketoacidosis should be considered in patients receiving sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors who develop otherwise unexplained high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, irrespective of diabetic status or blood glucose concentration. Fasting and acute illness are relevant precipitating factors; prompt drug withdrawal, carbohydrate administration, insulin therapy, and nutritional support can lead to rapid resolution.

42903563.title: Feeding practices during high-flow nasal cannula: current evidence and clinical implications for respiratory care.
42903563.abstract: High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy is increasingly used as a noninvasive respiratory support modality across acute and critical care settings. Although nutritional management is integral to the care of patients with respiratory failure, established guidelines for feeding patients receiving HFNC are lacking, and clinical decisions vary widely, reflecting persistent uncertainty about HFNC's effects on swallowing function, airway protection, and aspiration risk. This narrative review found that HFNC may alter swallowing biomechanics, particularly at flow rates >40 L/min, potentially increasing the risk of choking and aspiration. Evidence on aspiration risk is heterogeneous, deriving largely from healthy volunteers and pediatric bronchiolitis cohorts. Adult evidence is limited to retrospective studies; the largest found no increase in respiratory deterioration with enteral feeding. Most institutions lack formal feeding protocols, and practice is driven by individual clinician judgment. Areas of consensus include the safety of early enteral feeding in hemodynamically stable patients and the avoidance of routine prolonged withholding of nutrition based solely on HFNC use. Disagreement persists regarding routine swallowing assessment, optimal flow thresholds during feeding, and the prioritization of oral versus tube feeding. Safe feeding in patients receiving HFNC requires a multidisciplinary, individualized approach that balances respiratory support against nutritional adequacy. Prospective multicenter studies are needed to define safe flow thresholds, validate bedside assessment tools, and establish standardized feeding guidelines, particularly in adult and critically ill populations.

42890776.title: Protective Effect of Xuebijing Injection on Gastrointestinal Function in Septic Patients of Non-Gastrointestinal Origin.
42890776.abstract: The purpose of this study was to assess the 28-day prognosis and gastrointestinal protection of early Xuebijing in non-gastrointestinal sepsis. Septic patients with infection origins outside the gastrointestinal system and no history of acute gastrointestinal injury (AGI) were included in this single-center retrospective analysis. The two groups' baseline characteristics were balanced by propensity score matching (PSM). Secondary objectives were organ function, enteral nutrition tolerance, inflammatory markers, AGI onset time, and clinical outcomes. The primary endpoint was the incidence of 28-day AGI. After matching, each group had 87 patients, and the baseline variables were evenly distributed among them (P > 0.05). The 28-day cumulative AGI rate for the Xuebijing group was 44.8%, which was considerably lower than the control group's rate of 69.0% (P = 0.002). Additionally, there was a significant delay in the beginning of AGI in the treated group (log-rank P < 0.001). Furthermore, Xuebijing treatment resulted in shorter hospital and ICU stays as well as larger drops in CRP, PCT, and SOFA ratings (all between-group P < 0.05). Patients receiving Xuebijing achieved earlier enteral nutrition initiation (P = 0.0016) and a higher rate of day‑7 caloric targets (66.7% vs 49.4%, P = 0.031). Feeding intolerance showed a trend toward being lower in the Xuebijing group (24.14% vs 39.08%), but this difference did not reach statistical significance (P = 0.050); 28‑day mortality and adverse events also did not differ significantly between groups. Xuebijing use initiated within 24 hours of sepsis diagnosis in septic patients without pre-existing AGI was associated with protection of gastrointestinal function and improvement in several secondary outcomes, including lower AGI incidence, shorter hospital stays, reduced inflammation and organ dysfunction, and better enteral nutrition outcomes, without additional safety concerns. However, no significant difference in 28-day mortality was observed.

42965242.title: Manganese Deposition Encephalopathy Associated With Prolonged Total Parenteral Nutrition: A Case Report.
authors: Beluzzo da Mota de Lima Sinke G
42965242.abstract: Manganese encephalopathy is a rare neurological disorder most commonly associated with chronic occupational exposure or impaired hepatobiliary elimination. We report a case of suspected manganese deposition encephalopathy associated with prolonged total parenteral nutrition in a critically ill patient with severe abdominal disease and cholestatic dysfunction. A 50-year-old man was admitted with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, tachycardia, and jaundice. Computed tomography demonstrated acute pancreatitis with pancreatic necrosis, choledocholithiasis, cholelithiasis, and superior mesenteric artery thrombosis. His clinical course was complicated by abdominal sepsis, anasarca, anemia, spontaneous hematomas, and the need for prolonged intensive care and total parenteral nutrition. On hospital day 41, he developed rigidity and involuntary movements involving the tongue and upper limbs, prompting neurological assessment. Serum manganese was 3.1 µg/L (reference value: 2 µg/L), and brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated T1 hyperintensity in the globus pallidus, findings compatible with manganese encephalopathy. Treatment with levodopa/benserazide produced a limited response, with persistent severe parkinsonism and inability to ambulate despite gradual improvement in tetraparesis associated with concurrent critical illness neuropathy. The patient was discharged on hospital day 129. This case highlights the importance of considering manganese toxicity in critically ill patients receiving prolonged parenteral nutrition, particularly in the setting of impaired biliary elimination, and supports early neurological surveillance and monitoring of trace elements.

42962568.title: Metabolic phenotypes in sepsis: A conceptual framework for phenotype-informed nutrition.
42962568.abstract: Sepsis is a biologically heterogeneous syndrome characterized by profound alterations in immune function and intermediary metabolism that challenge standardized nutritional management. Current clinical nutrition guidelines recommend early enteral nutrition after hemodynamic stabilization, progressive caloric advancement, and avoidance of early full feeding, but they do not incorporate metabolic phenotyping. Emerging evidence from immunometabolism, metabolomics, and systems biology shows recurring, partially overlapping metabolic patterns in sepsis, including hyperglycolytic-hyperlactatemic, mitochondrial-bioenergetic dysfunction, hyperinflammatory Warburg-like, immunoparalytic-tolerant, lipidomic-acylcarnitine, gut-microbiota, and hypercatabolic-muscle wasting domains. These patterns share mechanisms and may coexist or evolve over time; their biological basis should be distinguished from their still unvalidated use as mutually exclusive bedside diagnostic classes. This narrative review examines these biological domains and their nutritional relevance while explicitly separating established, phase-based critical-care nutrition from phenotype-informed treatment hypotheses. In particular, sepsis-associated mitochondrial abnormalities may be tissue- and cell-specific and do not imply generalized suppression of whole-body oxygen consumption. Likewise, hyperglycemia, hyperlactatemia, or increased carbon dioxide production are not validated markers of overfeeding. Residual endogenous substrate production persists during acute critical illness but cannot currently be quantified as total energy flux at the bedside, limiting precise assessment of the combined endogenous and exogenous substrate load. No prospective randomized trial has yet tested nutrition prescribed according to the metabolic domains proposed here. The seven-domain framework therefore organizes recurrent components of sepsis biology; what remains to be validated is its operational use for patient classification and for predicting differential response to nutritional interventions.

42952486.title: Interprofessional collaboration in emergency department nursing care for patients with diabetic ketoacidosis: a narrative review.
42952486.abstract: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is an acute metabolic emergency requiring timely risk recognition, fluid resuscitation, insulin therapy, electrolyte correction, dynamic monitoring, and coordinated care transitions. These interdependent tasks pose substantial challenges to emergency nursing. This narrative review aimed to synthesise current evidence on interprofessional collaboration in emergency DKA nursing and propose a conceptual framework to support coordinated care. A structured narrative review was conducted using literature retrieved from PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and the Web of Science Core Collection from database inception to July 10, 2026. DKA-specific clinical and implementation evidence was integrated with broader literature on interprofessional collaboration, communication, and healthcare implementation. The evidence was synthesised using Donabedian's structure-process-outcome framework. Current collaborative approaches include nurse-led standardised pathways, risk-stratified subcutaneous insulin and non-intensive care unit management, collaborative medication management, laboratory and point-of-care monitoring, structured communication, digital decision support, and multidisciplinary discharge planning. Available evidence suggests that standardised collaborative pathways may improve the timeliness and consistency of care, shorten emergency department length of stay, and reduce intensive care resource use. However, evidence evaluating complete interprofessional nursing teams and nursing-sensitive outcomes remains limited. Based on the synthesis, a conceptual closed-loop collaboration framework comprising six interconnected stages was proposed: recognition and activation, shared risk stratification, coordinated monitoring and execution, escalation, care transition, and recurrence prevention. Effective interprofessional DKA nursing requires shared clinical information, explicit responsibility, timely feedback, and predefined escalation procedures, with emergency nurses serving as continuous information integrators and process coordinators. The proposed framework provides an evidence-informed approach to organising collaborative emergency care. However, it has not been prospectively validated, and further implementation research is required to evaluate its feasibility, safety, and effects on nursing-sensitive and patient outcomes.

42857555.title: Management of Bilateral Subacute Subdural Hematomas with Concomitant Subarachnoid Hemorrhage in a Diabetic Patient with HIV in Cameroon: A Case Report.
42857555.abstract: Bilateral subdural hematomas occurring simultaneously with subarachnoid hemorrhage in a traumatic context are rare and pose considerable diagnostic challenges. Comorbidities such as diabetes and HIV may further worsen prognosis and complicate management. This case underscores the vital importance of early diagnosis and multidisciplinary care in patients with subacute subdural hematomas and subarachnoid hemorrhage, particularly when compounded by comorbidities in resource‑limited settings. We report the case of a 44-year-old housewife who was diabetic and living with HIV. She presented with severe headaches followed by altered consciousness with severe coma, and Cushing's triad two weeks after a minor head trauma. Brain CT scan revealed a bilateral panhemispheric subacute subdural hematoma (SASDH) associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage. Management consisted of emergent bilateral burr hole craniotomy for drainage, combined with measures to reduce intracranial pressure and prevent secondary brain injury of systemic origin. Her course was complicated by infection and hypertensive crisis; both were successfully managed. Glycemic control was achieved and antiretroviral therapy optimized. Clinical and radiological outcomes were ultimately favorable. This case underscores the importance of early diagnosis and multidisciplinary management of subdural hematomas in patients with diabetes and HIV. Beyond timely surgical intervention with burr‑hole craniotomy, comprehensive intensive care - including vigilant monitoring, early detection, and prompt control of complications - can significantly improve survival and optimize neurological outcomes.

42950910.title: Resting Energy Expenditure in Mechanically Ventilated Surgical-Trauma Patients With and Without Acute Kidney Injury: a single-center retrospective study.
42950910.journal: Journal of renal nutrition : the official journal of the Council on Renal Nutrition of the National Kidney Foundation
42950910.abstract: To compare resting energy expenditure (REE) measured by indirect calorimetry (IC) in mechanically ventilated surgical-trauma critically ill patients with and without acute kidney injury (AKI); to evaluate differences in REE by sex, age, and body mass index (BMI); and to assess associations between REE, psoas muscle index (PMI) measured using computed tomography scans, and lean body mass (LBM) estimated by predictive equations.
