This single-center retrospective cohort study conducted at a tertiary academic medical center included mechanically ventilated critically ill adults admitted between 01/01/2012 and 12/31/2023. Exclusion criteria were pediatric, pregnant, or incarcerated patients; quadriplegia, paraplegia, cystic fibrosis; abnormal respiratory quotients; Medical ICU admission; major burns (≥20% TBSA); parenteral nutrition initiated on or after IC; tracheostomy on admission; discharge or death while ventilated; or absence of a nutrition prescription. Of 794 patients screened, 180 met inclusion criteria (AKI n=84; no AKI n=96). At baseline, patients with and without AKI differed significantly in age (59.9 vs 55 years; P = 0.046), BMI (32.2 vs 28.8 kg/m2; P = 0.046), CKD (23.8% vs 3.13%; P < 0.001), and serum creatinine (1.49 vs 0.84 mg/dL; P < 0.001). Of patients with AKI, 71.4% had stage I AKI and 20.2% required renal replacement therapy (RRT). No significant difference in mean REE was observed between patients with and without AKI (1,642 vs 1,665 kcal/day; P = 0.380) . REE was significantly higher in males compared with females (1,806 vs 1,425 kcal/day; P < 0.001), in patients aged 18-65 versus >65 years (1,768 vs 1,428 kcal/day; P = 0.002), and in obese versus non-obese patients (1,841 vs 1,500 kcal/day; P < 0.001). In multivariable linear regression, higher BMI (P = 0.003) and male sex (P = 0.028) were independently associated with higher REE, while AKI was not. LBM estimated by predictive equations was more strongly correlated with REE than PMI (P < 0.001), and correlation strength did not differ by AKI status. Measured REE did not differ between ventilated surgical-trauma patients with and without AKI. REE differed by sex, age, and obesity status, and AKI was not associated with within-group differences. BMI and sex were identified as independent predictors of REE. Estimated LBM was strongly correlated with REE independent of AKI status. Given possible residual confounding, further investigation is needed.

42868685.title: Clinical value of enteral nutrition combined with supplemental parenteral nutrition in patients with major burns: A retrospective cohort study.
42868685.journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
42868685.abstract: The hypermetabolic state following major burns frequently leads to severe negative energy balance, posing significant challenges to clinical nutritional management. This study aimed to retrospectively evaluate clinical outcomes associated with enteral nutrition (EN) combined with supplemental parenteral nutrition (SPN) compared with an EN strategy in real-world clinical settings. A retrospective cohort study was conducted using data from patients with major burns admitted to the burn unit of a tertiary hospital between January 2018 and December 2023. Group allocation was performed retrospectively according to actual parenteral nutrition (PN) contribution to total delivered calories during Days 1-14: patients with < 10% PN contribution were classified into the EN group and those with ≥ 10% were classified into the EN + SPN group. The primary outcome was time to complete wound healing (defined as ≥95% re-epithelialization). Key secondary outcomes included caloric achievement, prealbumin, nitrogen balance, ICU length of stay, catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBSI), hyperglycemia, and 28-day and 60-day mortality. A total of 186 patients were included (EN+SPN, n = 94; EN, n = 92). The primary outcome, time to complete wound healing, was significantly shorter in the EN + SPN group (32.4 ± 8.7 vs. 41.2 ± 11.3 days, P < 0.001). The EN + SPN group achieved a higher proportion of target calories (87.3% vs. 62.8%, P < 0.001) and showed higher day-14 prealbumin concentrations (196.8 ± 38.4 vs. 158.2 ± 34.1 mg/L, P < 0.001) and improved day-7 nitrogen balance (-1.2 ± 2.8 vs. -6.8 ± 3.4 g/day, P < 0.001). ICU length of stay was shorter (21.4 ± 8.6 vs. 28.2 ± 10.4 days, P < 0.001). Rates of CRBSI (6.4% vs. 4.3%, P = 0.529) and hyperglycemia (33.0% vs. 28.3%, P = 0.485) did not differ significantly. Neither 28-day nor 60-day mortality differed significantly between groups. In patients with major burns, when EN failed to meet target caloric requirements, EN combined with SPN was associated with improved energy delivery, favorable biochemical trajectories, and shorter wound healing time, without an increased association with infection risk. An EN-first burn care pathway with SPN added when EN remains inadequate warrants prospective evaluation.

42861658.title: Application of Combined Gastric Tube Tip Manometry and Auscultation for Nasogastric Tube Positioning in Neurocritical Care Patients With Artificial Airways: A Prospective Diagnostic Pilot Study.
42861658.abstract: Nasogastric tube placement is central to enteral nutrition support in neurocritical care patients. However, tube malposition, particularly accidental placement into the airway, can lead to fatal complications. To assess the accuracy of a combined gastric tube tip manometry and auscultation approach for confirming nasogastric tube placement in neurocritical care patients with artificial airways. This prospective study enrolled patients who underwent nasogastric tube insertion in the neurocritical care unit of a tertiary hospital in China between January 2025 and May 2025. Using chest X-ray as the reference standard, we compared the sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), positive likelihood ratio (PLR) and negative likelihood ratio (NLR) for gastric tube tip manometry alone, auscultation alone and their combination. In total, 120 patients participated. X-ray confirmed correct nasogastric tube positioning in 119 patients and malposition in 1 patient. For gastric tube tip manometry alone, the sensitivity was 97.48%, with a specificity of 0%, a positive predictive value (PPV) of 99.15% and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 0%. Auscultation alone yielded a sensitivity of 90.76%, a specificity of 100%, a PPV of 100% and an NPV of 8.33%. The combined manometry-plus-auscultation approach had a sensitivity of 88.24%, a specificity of 100%, a PPV of 100% and an NPV of 6.67%. The combined gastric tube tip manometry and auscultation method might serve as an adjunctive bedside strategy for confirming nasogastric tube placement in neurocritical care patients with artificial airways. However, only one malpositioned tube was observed in this study; the specificity and NPV should be interpreted with caution. When gastric aspirate cannot be obtained or immediate chest radiography is impractical, combined gastric tube tip manometry and auscultation provide a feasible, radiation-free bedside pathway for confirming nasogastric tube position; equivocal or negative bedside findings should still be verified radiographically before feeding. The study was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2300078001).

42820798.title: From Formula Composition to Precision Nutrition: Who Benefits, From What, and When?
42820798.abstract: Morowitz et al argue that the composition of enteral nutrition formulas deserves to be studied as an intervention in its own right. Building on this perspective, we consider how critical care nutrition research has progressively refined its questions from whether to feed to when and how much. We argue that enteral formula composition represents the next logical frontier in critical care nutrition research, while emphasizing the need for biologically informed, clinically meaningful, and practical interventions. We also highlight the importance of learning from previous translational challenges to ensure that future research identifies formulations that improve patient outcomes while remaining feasible for routine critical care practice.

42933947.title: Deimplementation of Tradition-Based Enteral Feeding Practices to Improve Clinical Outcomes.
42933947.journal: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
42933947.abstract: Enteral feeding is common in acute and critical care but there are many elements to this practice that are steeped in confusion and lack evidence. This article will focus on verification of feeding tube (FT) placement methods and timing, medication administration by FTs, unnecessary holding or stopping of enteral formula, gastric residual volumes, and volume-based feeding. Supporting evidence for these practices will be reviewed and recommendations made for evidence-based alternatives and possible deimplementation.

42879805.title: Optimizing Enteral Nutrition During and After Therapeutic Hypothermia: An Evidence-Based Practice Initiative.
42879805.journal: Advances in neonatal care : official journal of the National Association of Neonatal Nurses
42879805.abstract: Feeding practices during therapeutic hypothermia (TH) vary widely across neonatal intensive care units, and many centers delay enteral nutrition because of concerns about gastrointestinal intolerance and necrotizing enterocolitis. Current evidence suggests that early, clinically guided enteral feeding may be safe and beneficial for neonates with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. An evidence-based feeding guideline was implemented to promote enteral nutrition during and after TH. To evaluate whether initiating minimal enteral feeding in clinically stable neonates undergoing TH reduced time to full enteral feeds and parenteral nutrition days compared with delayed feeding practices. A preintervention and postintervention design was used to evaluate the impact of a standardized, stability-based feeding guideline. Retrospective data from neonates treated with TH between January 2023 and May 2025 established baseline outcomes (n = 26). The evidence-based practice change was implemented from June to December 2025, during which 8 neonates met inclusion criteria. Neonates who died were excluded. The median time to full enteral feeds decreased by 18% (from 8.5 to 7 days). Parenteral nutrition days remained unchanged (median 6 days), potentially reflecting the conservative feeding advancement incorporated into the guideline. No feeding-related complications occurred among neonates who received enteral feeds during TH. Our findings provide evidence for the feasibility and safety of minimal enteral feeding in clinically stable neonates undergoing TH. Earlier feeding may shorten time to full enteral nutrition and reduce reliance on parenteral nutrition without increasing feeding-related complications. Larger studies are needed to further evaluate optimal feeding strategies during TH.

42866789.title: Extravasation of TPN into the pleural space, a rare complication of central venous catheter placement: a case report.
42866789.abstract: Complications associated with central venous catheters are well documented in the literature, most of which relate to catheter placement or infections. Nonetheless, on rare occasions, the catheter can erode the arterial wall, allowing medication, fluids, or even total parenteral nutrition to pass into the pleural space. We present the case of a 68-year-old male who was critically ill in the intensive care unit and required total parenteral nutrition. A central venous catheter was placed, and the patient's condition improved. While in the intensive care unit, it became necessary to change the central line, and a new catheter was placed. Subsequently, he experienced respiratory distress and impaired oxygenation, with a significant pleural effusion. When the chest tube was placed, a milky-white fluid was detected, and subsequent tests revealed it to be an effusion of total parenteral nutrition. Following this event, the catheter was immediately changed, and with subsequent treatment, the patient recovered completely. Identification and management of central line complications are essential in patients with vascular access. These rare complications must always be considered in the differential diagnosis and recognized early to avoid potentially dangerous outcomes.

42953097.title: Glycemic control and COVID-19 outcomes across the continuum of glucose regulation: a retrospective cohort study.
42953097.journal: Frontiers in clinical diabetes and healthcare
42953097.abstract: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) has disproportionately affected individuals with underlying metabolic dysfunction. This study investigates the association between varying levels of pre-infection glycemic control and COVID-19-related health outcomes. A retrospective chart review was conducted on Kaiser Permanente Georgia patients with confirmed COVID-19. Participants (N = 2071) were categorized into five groups based on their HbA1c levels: patients without diabetes, those with prediabetes, and those with diabetes with varying degrees of glycemic control. We adjusted for demographics, social determinants of health, comorbidities, medications, and lifestyle factors. Among 2071 patients, 986 (47.6%) were without diabetes, 658 (31.8%) had prediabetes, 183 (8.8%) had diabetes with HbA1c<7%, 162 (7.8%) had diabetes with HbA1c ≥ 7% ≤ 9% and 82 (4%) had diabetes with HbA1c>9%. Patients with HbA1c>9% had the highest proportion hospitalized (38.3%, p<0.001), and admitted to ICU (14.8%, p<0.001). In multivariable logistic regression models, prediabetes and insulin use were associated with greater odds of hospitalization; odds ratio 1.43 [95% CI 1.09-1.87] and 3.02 [95% CI 1.95-4.68], respectively. There is a gradient of increasing COVID-19 severity with worsening glycemic control. The study shows the importance of recognizing prediabetes as a significant risk factor for severe COVID-19, comparable to poorly controlled diabetes.

42935932.title: Transforming Inpatient Glycemic Management: A System-Wide Approach to Reducing Hyperglycemia and Hypoglycemia.
42935932.abstract: Diabetes affects >37 million U.S. adults and poses major inpatient challenges. Up to 25% of noncritically ill hospitalized patients have diabetes, and many develop stress hyperglycemia. Hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia lead to complications, extended hospital stays, readmissions, and mortality. Our Northern California academic medical center launched a system-wide quality improvement initiative to optimize inpatient glycemic management. Key interventions included establishing an inpatient glycemic team consisting of endocrinologists and advanced practice nurses, implementing standardized insulin order sets with decision support tools, developing glycemic dashboards, and introducing an intensive care unit pharmacist-comanaged insulin protocol. Education emphasized the importance of evidence-based insulin use and workflow efficiency, including the synchronization of point-of-care (POC) glucose testing, meal delivery, and insulin administration. POC glucose data from acute care inpatients were analyzed over 7 years grouped into early (2017-2019), transition (2020-2021), and mature (2022-2024) phases of the quality improvement program. Glucometrics included percent patient-days with day-weighted mean (DWM) glucose >180 mg/dL, percent days with glucose ≥300 mg/dL, and percent days with hypoglycemia <70 mg/dL and severe hypoglycemia <54 mg/dL, assessed biannually. Logistic regression analysis was used to assess differences between phases. Hyperglycemia declined significantly: percent patient-days with DWM glucose >180 mg/dL fell from 35.2% to 31.0% (P < 0.001). Percent days with glucose ≥300 mg/dL decreased from 11.3% to 8.4%, hypoglycemia <70 mg/dL dropped from 3.5% to 2.9%, and severe hypoglycemia <54 mg/dL dropped from 1.1% to 0.8%. A quality improvement strategy incorporating standardized protocols and education sustainably improved glycemic control and safety across a large academic medical center.

42935208.title: [Electromagnetic navigation-guided nasojejunal tube placement in a patient with cerebral palsy and severe scoliosis causing difficult tube placement: A case report].
42935208.journal: Zhong nan da xue xue bao. Yi xue ban = Journal of Central South University. Medical sciences
42935208.abstract: Establishing a safe enteral nutrition route is highly challenging in critically ill patients with complex anatomical abnormalities. Conventional tube-placement techniques are often difficult to perform in such patients, necessitating exploration of more suitable alternatives. We report the case of a 20-year-old woman who was admitted to The Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University, on November 26, 2025, because of "coughing and choking during eating." She had a history of cerebral palsy, severe scoliosis, and cachexia [body mass index (BMI), 7.14 kg/m2], accompanied by marked displacement of the abdominal viscera. After multiple failed attempts at blind tube placement, and because both endoscopy-guided tube placement and gastrostomy were not feasible, bedside nasojejunal tube placement was successfully performed using the CORTRAK 2 electromagnetic navigation system. The procedure was uneventful and took approximately 5 minutes. The tube was inserted to a depth of 72 cm, with the tip accurately positioned in the jejunum. After the procedure, a peptide-based enteral nutrition formula was administered at an initial infusion rate of 20 mL/h and was well tolerated. The patient was discharged on post-procedure day 2 after her condition had stabilized, and home tube feeding was subsequently provided by family members with caregiving experience. No tube placement-related or nutrition-related adverse events occurred during the procedure or throughout the 4-week follow-up period, and enteral nutritional support proceeded successfully. This case suggests that, for critically ill patients with complex anatomical abnormalities in whom conventional tube-placement methods have failed, bedside electromagnetic navigation-guided nasojejunal tube placement may provide a safe, accurate, efficient, and minimally invasive alternative.

42913437.title: The Impact of Telemedicine Interventions on Maternal and Fetal Outcomes in Women With Gestational Diabetes: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
42913437.abstract: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) has a rising global prevalence and brings short-term and long-term adverse risks for mothers and fetuses. Conventional in-person GDM care is limited by time and geographic barriers, often resulting in suboptimal compliance and delayed individualized interventions. Telemedicine is increasingly applied in GDM management; however, randomized controlled trial (RCT) evidence remains inconsistent. The study aims to pool data from RCTs to quantify the effects of telemedicine on glycemic control and pregnancy-related outcomes in women with GDM and to inform optimized clinical management. We searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Scopus up to August 16, 2026. Two reviewers independently performed study screening and data extraction. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2. Meta-analyses were conducted in Stata 18.0. For heterogeneous outcomes, 95% prediction intervals (PIs) were calculated to estimate effect ranges for future studies. Heterogeneity was explored via leave-one-out sensitivity, meta-regression, and subgroup analyses. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) framework rated evidence certainty. Publication bias was evaluated for outcomes reported in ≥10 studies. Twenty-three RCTs (3055 women with GDM) were included. Pooled estimates suggested that telemedicine may reduce fasting glucose (mean difference [MD] -0.26, 95% CI -0.42 to -0.09, 95% PI -0.93 to 0.42; P=.002), 2-hour postprandial glucose (MD -0.50, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.14, 95% PI -1.84 to 0.84; P=.007), and gestational weight gain (MD -0.78, 95% CI -1.40 to -0.17, 95% PI -2.83 to 1.26; P=.01). Telemedicine was also associated with lower risks of cesarean section, emergency cesarean section, macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia, and neonatal respiratory distress. No significant differences were found for hemoglobin A1c, preterm birth, or neonatal intensive care unit admission. Notably, fasting glucose, 2-hour postprandial glucose, and gestational weight gain exhibited very high unexplained heterogeneity (I²>90%), with their 95% PIs crossing the null value despite statistically significant pooled effects. The GRADE certainty of evidence was very low to low across all assessed outcomes. Telemedicine may improve selected glycemic and perinatal outcomes for women with GDM and may serve as a promising supplementary option for prenatal care, particularly in resource-limited settings where routine in-person follow-up is difficult to implement. Nevertheless, the apparent benefits for glycemic control and gestational weight gain remain tentative due to extreme, unexplained between-study heterogeneity and 95% PIs crossing the null. Based on current evidence, telemedicine should not completely replace standard antenatal care. Future well-designed, large-sample RCTs are warranted; such trials should adopt standardized definitions for telemedicine interventions, fully report intervention components, and conduct long-term follow-up to verify sustained maternal and neonatal clinical benefits.

42898492.title: Incidence and risk factors for enteral nutrition intolerance in psychiatric patients with comorbid medical conditions: a retrospective cohort study.
42898492.abstract: Critically ill psychiatric patients frequently present with multiple physical comorbidities and poor nutritional status. Enteral nutrition plays a key role in comprehensive critical care, but enteral nutrition intolerance (ENI) is highly prevalent. To investigate the incidence, independent risk factors, and clinical outcomes of ENI in critically ill psychiatric patients with comorbid physical diseases. This is a single-center retrospective study. We enrolled 150 consecutive patients admitted between January 2024 and December 2025 who received enteral nutrition for at least 3 days. Data for analysis were sourced from the institutional electronic medical record database. Baseline characteristics, nutritional indicators, psychiatric parameters, comorbidity scores, and treatment-related variables were collected. To detect independent risk factors for ENI, univariate screening was performed first, followed by multivariate logistic regression. The overall incidence of ENI was 54.0% in critically ill psychiatric patients with physical comorbidities. Multivariate logistic regression showed the odds ratio (OR) of serum albumin <25 g/L (OR = 3.26, 95%CI: 2.11-5.04, P<0.001), APACHE II score ≥15 (OR = 2.89, 95%CI: 1.87-4.47, P<0.001), combined use of ≥3 antipsychotic agents (OR = 2.71, 95%CI: 1.75-4.19, P<0.001), schizophrenia (OR = 2.12, 95%CI: 1.43-3.21, P = 0.008), and duration of antibiotic use ≥7 days (OR = 2.18, 95%CI: 1.40-3.38, P = 0.001). ENI was significantly associated with longer hospital stay, lower nutritional goal attainment, more frequent EN interruption, and higher pulmonary infection rates. These findings indicate a high burden of ENI in this vulnerable population. The risk factors include hypoalbuminemia, high APACHE IIscore, combined use of three or more antipsychotic agents, schizophrenia, and prolonged antibiotic therapy.

42887928.title: Comparative analysis of pregnancy outcomes in women with type 1 vs type 2 diabetes mellitus: A 10-year retrospective study.
42887928.abstract: With the global rise in diabetes mellitus (DM), pregnancies in women with preexisting DM are becoming increasingly common and are associated with a higher risk of adverse outcomes. However, the relative impact of type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) vs type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) remains unclear. This retrospective cohort study included pregnant women with preexisting DM followed between 2014 and 2024. Demographic, clinical, biochemical, and obstetric data were compared according to DM type. Primary outcomes included maternal complications, fetal growth, and neonatal morbidity. Among 169 pregnancies, 114 (67.5%) involved T1DM and 55 (32.5%), T2DM. Compared with women with T2DM, those with T1DM were younger, had lower body mass index, longer diabetes duration, and a higher prevalence of diabetic retinopathy. They also had higher preconception HbA1c levels and greater gestational weight gain. T1DM was associated with higher odds of retinopathy progression, large-for-gestational-age neonates, and neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission, but lower odds of labor dystocia. Rates of miscarriage, preterm birth, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and cesarean delivery were similar between groups. Among women with T1DM, excessive gestational weight gain and higher late-pregnancy HbA1c levels were strongly associated with adverse neonatal outcomes. Pregnancies complicated by T1DM showed a higher burden of adverse outcomes than those complicated by T2DM. Glycemic control and gestational weight gain emerged as key modifiable risk factors, underscoring the need for tailored management strategies.

42882273.title: Explainable Machine Learning for Prediction of Future High-Severity States Using Longitudinal APACHE-II Trajectories: Internal Validation and Cross-Cohort Portability Assessment.
42882273.abstract: Background: Longitudinal severity assessment may provide more informative risk stratification than reliance on a single admission score in intensive care. This study developed and internally validated an explainable machine learning framework for predicting a subsequent APACHE-II-defined high-severity state using repeated APACHE-II assessments in intensive care unit (ICU) patients receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN). The endpoint was defined as an APACHE-II score of ≥ 20 at the final assessment (T10), while predictor information was restricted to measurements obtained at T0-T9. Methods: A retrospective institutional cohort of 844 adult ICU patients was analyzed, of whom 214 (25.4%) met the predefined high-severity endpoint. Four principal feature representations were evaluated: admission APACHE-II, longitudinal APACHE-II information combining the raw T0-T9 sequence with derived trajectory descriptors, longitudinal laboratory information, and multimodal combinations including baseline characteristics. Six machine learning algorithms were compared using stratified five-fold cross-validation and independent hold-out testing. Additional analyses included simpler APACHE-II comparators, sequential observation truncation, nested cross-validation, calibration assessment, threshold sensitivity analysis, and SHAP-based model interpretation. Because equivalent longitudinal APACHE-II measurements and an equivalent endpoint were unavailable in eICU, a separate harmonized XGBoost model was used only for exploratory cross-cohort portability assessment. Results: The longitudinal APACHE-II CatBoost model achieved the highest performance, with a cross-validated ROC-AUC of 0.924 and an independent hold-out ROC-AUC of 0.921 (95% CI: 0.878-0.960). Hold-out calibration was good (Brier score = 0.095, calibration intercept = - 0.03, slope = 0.98), and nested cross-validation yielded a pooled out-of-fold ROC-AUC of 0.908 and a mean outer-fold ROC-AUC of 0.920 ± 0.038. The latest APACHE-II assessment alone (T9; ROC-AUC = 0.553), change from baseline (0.576), ordinal slope (0.539), and logistic regression using engineered APACHE-II descriptors (0.633) performed substantially below the full longitudinal CatBoost model. Sequential truncation showed that discrimination was retained after removing later observations, although performance varied non-monotonically across truncated sequences. SHAP analysis showed that multiple APACHE-II observations contributed prominently to model predictions, with trajectory-derived descriptors providing complementary contributions. Adding laboratory trajectories or baseline characteristics did not improve discrimination over the longitudinal APACHE-II representation. Conclusions: Nonlinear modeling of repeated APACHE-II assessments provided strong internal discrimination of a subsequent APACHE-II-defined high-severity state in this TPN-treated ICU cohort and substantially outperformed single-score and simpler longitudinal comparators. However, the predictors and endpoint share the APACHE-II construct, observation indices were sequential rather than standardized clock-time intervals, and the primary model could not undergo conventional external validation in eICU. These findings therefore support the internal predictive value of longitudinal APACHE-II modeling for this specific severity-state task and warrant prospective multicenter evaluation using standardized timing and independent clinical outcomes.

42964729.title: Computed tomography-derived nasojejunal tube tip-to-gastric antrum path length and short-term outcomes in severe acute pancreatitis.
42964729.abstract: Nasojejunal (NJ) feeding is commonly used in severe acute pancreatitis (SAP), but whether deeper tube advancement improves clinical outcomes is uncertain. Computed tomography (CT)-based three-dimensional reconstruction can quantify the in-situ tube trajectory. To determine whether CT-derived NJ tube path length is associated with short-term outcomes in patients with confirmed SAP. This prospective single-center observational cohort included 63 patients with confirmed SAP. CT-based three-dimensional reconstruction measured the curved path length from the gastric antrum-pylorus junction to the tube tip. The primary outcome was intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay. Associations were assessed using Spearman correlation and Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II-adjusted median regression. Firth penalized logistic regression evaluated the exploratory composite outcome. Anatomical tube-tip position was independently classified on multiplanar CT. Median path length was 17.55 cm (interquartile range, 14.35-22.27 cm). Path length was not associated with ICU stay by Spearman analysis (rho = 0.055, P = 0.671) or adjusted median regression (difference per 5-cm increase = 0.192-day, 95% confidence interval: -0.922 to 1.305, P = 0.732). Post-CT ICU stay showed a similar null association. Anatomical position was duodenal in 28 patients, at the duodenojejunal flexure in 18, and jejunal in 17; path length correlated strongly with independently measured flexure-relative distance (rho = 0.997, P < 0.001). The exploratory composite outcome occurred in 17 patients, and path length remained non-significant in Firth regression. CT-derived NJ tube path length was not associated with ICU outcomes but closely reflected distal anatomical tube position. These findings do not establish an optimal advancement target.

42964628.title: Stepwise administration of de novo ketogenic parenteral nutrition for refractory epilepsy during prolonged bowel rest following duodenal perforation.
42964628.abstract: Ketogenic diet is an established therapy for pediatric patients with intractable epilepsy. By shifting energy metabolism from glucose to fat, the diet increases the production of ketone bodies, which alters neuronal excitability and modulates neurotransmitter signaling, thereby raising the seizure threshold. In critically ill children who are unable to tolerate enteral feeds, ketogenic parenteral nutrition (kPN) offers a valuable alternative to the standard ketogenic diet. However, its use has been underutilized and challenged by a lack of standardized protocols. In this report, we present a stepwise approach for initiating kPN in a ketogenic diet-naive toddler with refractory epilepsy and bowel dysfunction.

42820893.title: Perioperative Nursing Management of Patients Undergoing Nonsupercharged Cervical Roux-en-Y Esophagojejunostomy: A Single-Center Retrospective Descriptive Case Series.
42820893.journal: Journal of perianesthesia nursing : official journal of the American Society of PeriAnesthesia Nurses
42820893.abstract: Perioperative nursing after esophageal reconstruction is demanding, and nonsupercharged cervical Roux-en-Y esophagojejunostomy shifts nursing surveillance away from microvascular patency toward the more gradual signs of marginal conduit hypoperfusion. Nursing-focused reports describing phase-specific surveillance, documentation, and escalation for this reconstruction are lacking. This study aimed to describe an institutional perioperative nursing pathway together with the clinical outcomes and nursing process indicators observed in patients undergoing this procedure. This study adopted a single-center, retrospective descriptive case-series design. In this study, we reviewed 22 consecutive patients with esophageal cancer who underwent nonsupercharged cervical Roux-en-Y esophagojejunostomy between January 2021 and April 2025. Data were retrospectively abstracted from routinely maintained clinical and nursing records. An institutional perioperative nursing pathway combining routine esophageal perioperative care with procedure-specific surveillance of the cervical jejunal conduit was in use throughout the study period. No formal sample-size calculation was performed and no comparator group was available; therefore, clinical outcomes and nursing process indicators were summarized descriptively. The median operation time was 274.0 minutes (IQR 255.8-288.5), median mechanical ventilation time 18.0 hours (IQR 14.0-19.8), median intensive care unit stay 4.0 days (IQR 3.0-5.2), and median total hospital stay 12.0 days (IQR 8.8-14.0). Enteral nutrition was initiated at a median of postoperative day 5.0. The early mobilization target was documented in 86.4% (19/22) of patients by postoperative day 2, all patients ambulated by postoperative day 4, and respiratory exercises were recorded at a median of 4 sessions per day (IQR 3-5). Clavien-Dindo grade II or higher complications were recorded in 22.7% (5/22) of patients, anastomotic leakage in 18.2% (4/22, all endoscopically confirmed), and pulmonary complications in 4.5% (1/22). Perfusion warning events were documented in 31.8% (7/22) of patients; all were managed according to the predefined nursing escalation process and resolved or did not progress. No graft necrosis, re-exploration, or 30-day death occurred. This case series describes the implementation of a structured perioperative nursing pathway for nonsupercharged cervical Roux-en-Y esophagojejunostomy and the outcomes observed under it. Perfusion warning events and anastomotic complications were documented without graft necrosis or reoperation. These preliminary observational findings offer practical clinical insight but do not establish pathway effectiveness. Prospective multicenter studies are required to evaluate implementation fidelity, measurement reliability, clinical effectiveness, and generalizability.

42819038.title: Streamlining intrapartum glycemic control: Subcutaneous insulin for intrapartum diabetes management.
42819038.abstract: Optimal strategies for intrapartum glycemic control among patients with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) remain uncertain. In 2024, our labor and delivery unit implemented a subcutaneous (SC) insulin protocol to replace routine intravenous (IV) insulin initiation when glucose exceeded a treatment threshold. We hypothesized that this change would not worsen neonatal outcomes and would improve nursing (RN) satisfaction. We conducted a retrospective cohort quality improvement study of patients with GDM or T2DM who delivered at ≥36 weeks between March 2021 and December 2025. July 2024, when the protocol was introduced, was excluded as a washout period. The intervention included both a shift to SC insulin-first management and standardization of intrapartum glycemic treatment to a target of ≤ 120 mg/dL. The primary outcome was a composite of neonatal hypoglycemia or neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission for hypoglycemia within 24 h of life. Secondary outcomes included IV insulin duration and RN satisfaction. Outcomes were compared before and after implementation. Poisson regression with an interrupted time series framework assessed pre-implementation trends, immediate level changes, and post-implementation trends in the primary composite outcome. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated associations between insulin modality and the primary outcome. Surveys were analyzed by Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. Of 1140 deliveries in the analytic cohort, the primary outcome occurred in 269 (23.6%). Rates were similar before and after protocol implementation (23.4% vs. 23.9%, p = 0.837). Interrupted time series analysis showed no significant pre-implementation trend, but did demonstrate a significant immediate reduction in monthly event rates at implementation (incidence rate ratio [IRR], 0.20; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.04-0.90), with no significant post-implementation trend change (IRR, 1.03; 95% CI, 0.99-1.06). In adjusted analyses, insulin modality was not significantly associated with the primary outcome. RN satisfaction improved after implementation, with agreement or strong agreement increasing from 29.2% to 51.8% (p = 0.032). Implementation of an SC insulin-first intrapartum diabetes management protocol for patients with GDM and T2DM was not associated with increased neonatal hypoglycemia nor NICU admission for hypoglycemia. The protocol was associated with improved RN satisfaction. This approach may offer a pragmatic alternative to routine IV insulin initiation during labor.

42970009.title: [What is established in the interdisciplinary treatment of anorexia nervosa?].
42970009.abstract: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a serious mental illness that, due to chronic malnutrition and prolonged starvation, can affect multiple organ systems and become an internal medicine emergency. The goal of this article is to provide a structured presentation of acute internal medicine care for severe AN, with particular emphasis on somatic risk stratification, refeeding prevention, nutritional therapy, and multidisciplinary treatment structures. The recommendations are based on national and international guidelines, as well as additional scientific evidence and clinical experience. Inpatient care is indicated in cases of medical instability, severe physical complications, rapid weight loss, or inadequate food intake. The decision regarding internal medicine, psychosomatic, or intensive care treatment depends on the level of monitoring required. According to the Association of the Scientific Medical Societies in Germany (Arbeitsgemeinschaft der Wissenschaftlichen Medizinischen Fachgesellschaften, AWMF) S3 guideline, in a controlled inpatient setting, an initial daily intake of 2000 kcal is recommended, averaging 40-50 kcal/kg, with a rapid increase of 200 kcal/day and a target of 500-1500 g of weight gain per week. Oral nutrition is preferred, possibly with additional nutritionally complete liquid nutrition, before enteral tube feeding. Parenteral nutrition is reserved for life-threatening situations where gastrointestinal feeding is not possible. Treating severe AN requires a consistently multidisciplinary approach aimed at achieving internal medical stabilization. Nutritional medical expertise, psychosomatic-psychotherapeutic co-treatment, and good communication among all involved professional groups are crucial for the safe care of this high-risk group.

42972975.title: Pancreas-Intestine Composite Transplantation for Simultaneous Loss of Pancreatic and Intestinal Function (With Video).
42972975.abstract: Pancreas-intestine composite transplantation (PITx) is a therapeutic option for patients with irreversible loss of both pancreatic and intestinal function. We report a case of PITx in a 16-year-old male who developed fulminant Type 1 diabetes mellitus complicated by non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia, resulting in extensive intestinal necrosis. Despite intensive surgical and critical care management, the patient ultimately required total small intestinal resection and total pancreatectomy. After recovery from sepsis and multiorgan dysfunction, the patient's general condition stabilized, and PITx was considered an appropriate therapeutic option. The composite graft consisted of the pancreas, duodenum, small intestine, and right colon. Arterial inflow was reconstructed using a single Carrel patch incorporating the celiac axis and superior mesenteric artery, and venous outflow was established by portal vein anastomosis. Postoperatively, pancreatic endocrine function was restored, allowing stable glycemic control without exogenous insulin, and intestinal graft function enabled the gradual advancement of enteral and oral nutrition. This report highlights the key technical considerations and anatomical principles of PITx and demonstrates that tailored composite graft transplantation can restore both pancreatic and intestinal function while preserving unaffected abdominal organs in highly selected patients with combined pancreatic and intestinal failure.

42974750.title: Nutrition clinicians connecting with patients and family members to reduce the risk of ethical dilemmas.
42974750.journal: Nutrition in clinical practice : official publication of the American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition
42974750.abstract: Nutrition clinicians need to recognize the importance of establishing meaningful connections with their patients and family members. In this manuscript, we discuss skills for making these connections and possibly reducing the risk of nutrition-related ethical dilemmas. American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition leaders have stressed the importance of clinician-patient connections. Insights from Jonathan Rhoads, who was a developer of parenteral nutrition, indicated that availability and affability are important traits for nutrition clinicians, not just ability. These qualities reflect a patient-centered approach grounded in compassion, empathy, and effective communication. We present two examples of teaching tools designed to develop these skills in nutrition clinicians. (1) A nutrition clinician play performed at the ASPEN Clinical Nutrition Week 2015 that used spoken words and nonverbal communication to demonstrate approaches to connecting with a patient's family members. (2) A module developed for graduate nutrition students in 2025 that uses an artificial intelligence-generated role-play simulation to provide practice engaging in conversations with patients and caregivers involving crucial issues about the use of artificially administered nutrition and hydration.

42981093.title: Overall Survival in Adults With Acute Myeloid Leukemia Initiating Quizartinib vs Midostaurin With Chemotherapy.
42981093.abstract: Midostaurin and quizartinib are approved with intensive chemotherapy (IC) in patients with newly diagnosed FLT3 internal tandem duplication (ITD)-positive acute myeloid leukemia (AML), but no randomized clinical trials have directly compared them. To compare 1-year overall survival (OS) among patients with FLT3-ITD variant AML initiating IC with midostaurin or quizartinib. This multicenter, retrospective cohort study included patients with newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD variant AML treated at 12 US referral centers between January 1, 2018, and May 31, 2025. Data analysis was performed from January 2026 to August 2026. Induction therapy with IC plus midostaurin or quizartinib. The primary outcome was 1-year overall survival (OS). Secondary outcomes included 1-year event-free survival (EFS), induction response, and hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT) rates at first remission; FLT3 clearance after induction was exploratory. Safety outcomes included rates of febrile neutropenia, infections, intensive care unit use, total parenteral nutrition and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor use, discharge to a rehabilitation facility after index hospitalization, and early mortality. Cox proportional hazards regression models were adjusted for baseline covariates and HCT as time dependent. Among 215 patients (median [IQR] age, 56.0 [45.0-65.0] years; 119 [55.3%] female), 127 (59.1%) received midostaurin and 88 (40.9%) received quizartinib. Median (IQR) follow-up was 667.0 (289.0-1368.0) days for midostaurin and 324.0 (168.0-546.5) days for quizartinib, reflecting the latter's more recent approval. One-year OS was 78.0% for midostaurin and 93.0% for quizartinib (hazard ratio [HR], 0.22; 95% CI, 0.08-0.58; P = .002). The 1-year EFS was 56.0% for midostaurin and 77.0% for quizartinib (HR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.25-0.74; P = .003). Patients receiving quizartinib had higher rates of composite complete remission (75 [85.2%] vs 93 [73.2%]; P = .03), whereas rates of FLT3 clearance after induction (20 [38.5%] for quizartinib vs 27 [40.3%] for midostaurin; P = .84) and HCT in first remission (47 [53.4%] for quizartinib vs 83 [65.4%] for midostaurin; P = .08) were comparable. Midostaurin was associated with higher intensive care unit use (19 [15.0%] vs 4 [4.5%]; P = .02), discharge to a rehabilitation facility (9 [7.1%] vs 1 [1.1%]; P = .04), and treatment interruptions (32 [25.2%] vs 10 [11.4%]; P = .01). A sensitivity analysis limited to patients treated in 2023 or later (more balanced follow-up) showed directionally consistent but nonsignificant OS and EFS differences. In this cohort study of adults with FLT3-ITD variant AML, IC plus quizartinib was associated with improved 1-year survival, induction response, and safety compared with IC plus midostaurin.

42979027.title: Alogliptin-Pioglitazone and Insulin Regimen for Inpatient Glycemic Control: A Randomized Continuous Glucose Monitoring Pilot Trial.
42979027.abstract: Hospitalized patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) frequently develop hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia, and glycemic variability, which are associated with adverse outcomes outside the intensive care unit. This pilot randomized controlled trial evaluated whether adding a fixed-dose combination (FDC) of alogliptin/pioglitazone to standard basal-bolus insulin improved time in range (TIR), reduced hypoglycemia and/or bolus insulin requirements versus placebo, while generating effect size estimates for a future multicenter trial. In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study, the placebo group (n = 12) received basal-bolus insulin (neutral protamine Hagedorn plus regular insulin) with placebo, whereas the intervention group (IG) (n = 18) received the same insulin regimen plus daily alogliptin/pioglitazone FDC (25/15 mg). Continuous glucose monitoring (FreeStyle Libre 2) assessed TIR (70-180 mg/dL) as the primary endpoint, together with time above range and time below range, during a prespecified 4-d postrandomisation analysis period. The IG achieved significantly higher TIR than placebo (72.44% vs 38.58%; P < 0.001) and lower time above range >250 mg/dL (2.94% vs 28.16%; P < 0.001). Sensor-detected glucose exposure between 54 and 69 mg/dL was numerically higher with the FDC (4.16% vs 0.91%), although not statistically significant (P > 0.05). By day 4, the IG required significantly lower daily bolus insulin doses (P = 0.0003). In this highly selected inpatient population, adjunctive alogliptin/pioglitazone added to basal-bolus insulin improved continuous glucose monitoring-derived glycaemic stability. Larger adequately powered multicentre trials are needed to confirm safety and efficacy.

42987115.title: Medical nutrition therapy during the first 5 days of critical illness: a retrospective cohort study.
42987115.abstract: The aim of this study was to describe the prescription of medical nutrition therapy for critically ill patients who were admitted to an intensive care unit during the first 5 days. In an observational, longitudinal, retrospective study conducted at the intensive care unit of a tertiary hospital in Mexico City, adult patients admitted from January to December 2018 and from November 2024 to February 2025 were included. Indications for fasting, the route of medical nutrition therapy (enteral nutrition-parenteral nutrition), caloric and protein intakes, sequential organ failure assessment score and lactate levels, and vasopressor requirements during the 5 days were evaluated. Delay in initiating medical nutrition therapy was defined as initiated after 48 h of intensive care unit admission. 100 critically ill patients were included; aged 53±18.8, and with a median sequential organ failure assessment score of 10 (7-12). The most frequent diagnoses at admission were pulmonary disease and septic shock. On the first day, 98% of patients were fasting, and 25% received high-dose vasopressor therapy (if the norepinephrine equivalent dose >0.3 μg/kg/min). Over 5 days, medical nutrition therapy transitioned progressively, predominantly from fasting through enteral nutrition (45%) and parenteral nutrition (11%). medical nutrition therapy delay in 54 patients and in a multivariate analysis was associated with age (OR 1.04; 95%CI 1.01-1.07), sequential organ failure assessment score (OR 1.20; 95%CI 1.02-1.40), and lactate levels (OR 1.8; 95%CI 1.10-3.00). Prescription of medical nutrition therapy in critically ill patients admitted to a intensive care unit during 5 days is dynamic, and in all patients, it is not possible to initiate at 48 h, associated with higher age and illness severity.

42985864.title: Challenges in determining calorie and protein dosing in critically ill patients with obesity.
42985864.journal: American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists
42985864.abstract: To describe challenges in and provide current practical guidance for devising calorie and protein regimens for critically ill patients with obesity with a focus on clinicians who do not specialize in nutrition support. It has been over a decade since the American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition published a clinical practice guideline focusing on nutrition support in adult hospitalized patients with obesity. A literature review of recent studies and guidelines revealed no substantial evidence that predictive equations for estimating energy expenditure are more valid or reliable than weight-based dosing regimens of kcal/kg/day using some form of adjusted body weight for patients with obesity. Similarly, weight-based dosing regimens of g/kg/day of protein using some form of adjusted body weight for patients with obesity are a practical initial approach for many patients. During the early acute phase, lower initial calorie and protein delivery may be appropriate for many critically ill patients with obesity; however, this approach should not be applied uniformly to profoundly hypermetabolic or highly catabolic populations. Nutrition should be initiated without unnecessary delay when clinically appropriate and progressively advanced toward individualized goals as the patient stabilizes and enters recovery. Weight-based calorie and protein dosing provides a practical starting method for many critically ill patients with obesity when indirect calorimetry is unavailable or not technically valid. Initial prescriptions should be individualized according to nutrition status, metabolic phenotype, severity and type of illness, and phase of recovery. Hypermetabolic populations may require a different approach and the early involvement of nutrition support specialists.

42986663.title: Beyond blood: a narrative review of advancements in saliva-based diagnostics.
42986663.abstract: Human whole saliva is an accessible, noninvasive biofluid reflecting systemic and oral physiology, offering a viable alternative to invasive venipuncture and its associated pre-analytical vulnerabilities (e.g. ex vivo glycolysis). This narrative review synthesizes salivary biomarkers across major clinical domains, focusing on glycemic control (glucose, 1,5-anhydroglucitol, α2-macroglobulin), cardiovascular risk indices (cTnI, hs-CRP, sAA), critical care and sepsis surveillance (IL-10, acute-phase proteins), endocrinology (free steroid hormones), infectious diseases (HIV, HCV, SARS-CoV-2), oncological liquid biopsy (exosomal miRNAs, ctDNA), and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (Aβ42, p-tau181, lactoferrin). Analytical modalities - ranging from high-sensitivity immunoassays to wearable electrochemical biosensors and mass spectrometry - are critically evaluated. Furthermore, this review delineates regulatory-cleared diagnostic platforms (FDA PMA/510(k), EUA, CE-IVD, and SAMHSA-certified panels for viral antibodies, late-night salivary cortisol, and toxicology) from emerging discovery-phase panels. Widespread clinical translation remains constrained by unstandardized collection protocols, oral matrix interference, and a lack of normative reference intervals. Transitioning salivary testing into mainstream diagnostics requires three priorities: (1) universal sampling standardization incorporating flow-rate normalization, (2) engineering matrix-matched biosensors tailored for sub-picomolar detection, and (3) rigorous multicenter prospective trials to validate definitive clinical cutoffs, dynamic blood-saliva correlation kinetics, and digital point-of-care integration.

42979465.title: Pathophysiology-guided nutritional strategies for persistent inflammation, immunosuppression, and catabolism syndrome: an immunometabolic perspective.
42979465.abstract: Persistent inflammation, immunosuppression, and catabolism syndrome (PICS) is a phenotype of chronic critical illness characterized by unresolved inflammation, impaired immune competence, sustained catabolism, skeletal muscle loss, recurrent infections, and poor functional recovery. Although guideline-based nutritional support remains fundamental, persistent immunometabolic abnormalities may limit responsiveness to nutrient delivery and contribute to anabolic resistance, impaired substrate utilization, and defective tissue repair. This mini-review examines biological mechanisms limiting nutritional responsiveness in PICS and evaluates evidence for pathophysiology-guided nutritional strategies. A structured literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science was conducted from database inception through September 6, 2026, prioritizing English-language clinical guidelines, clinical studies, and mechanistic or translational evidence relevant to PICS, critical illness, nutritional responsiveness, and immunometabolic nutrition. We propose a framework addressing major barriers to recovery through strategies to restore anabolic responsiveness with protein, leucine, and rehabilitation; modulate inflammatory resolution and immune dysfunction with omega-3 fatty acids and arginine; optimize nutrient timing and circadian-metabolic regulation; and maintain a metabolic milieu conducive to nutrient utilization. Because direct interventional evidence in well-defined PICS populations remains limited, these strategies should complement rather than replace guideline-based nutritional support. The framework is conceptual and hypothesis-generating, and prospective PICS-specific studies incorporating biological stratification and clinically meaningful recovery outcomes are needed to determine its translational value.

42982464.title: NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT IN SURGICAL PATIENTS. PROTEIN-ENERGY METABOLISM DISORDERS.
42982464.abstract: Nutritional support plays a key role in the treatment of surgical patients. This review presents current information on the impact of protein-energy malnutrition on surgical outcomes and analyzes modern approaches to nutritional support across the preoperative and postoperative periods. Nutritional therapy methods are considered, including enteral and parenteral nutrition, as well as special immunomodulating formulas, along with their indications and contraindications. It has been shown that proactive nutritional support (especially in patients with malnutrition) helps reduce the incidence of postoperative complications, infections, shortens hospital stays, and improves long-term outcomes. The literature on the significance of nutritional support in enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) programs is discussed separately, including in oncological and geriatric patients and in intensive care units. Based on an analysis of 65 sources, it is concluded that early identification of nutritional deficiencies and the timely initiation of enteral or parenteral nutrition are integral components of comprehensive management for surgical patients, contributing to reduced mortality and improved treatment outcomes.

42992818.title: Nutritional support in immunosuppressed critically ill patients.
42992818.abstract: Immunosuppressed patients now make up a growing share of intensive care unit (ICU) admissions, largely as a result of advances in cancer treatment, organ transplantation, and immunomodulatory therapies. While their short-term ICU mortality may be similar to that of immunocompetent patients when illness severity is taken into account, these individuals often face longer ICU stays, more complications, and poorer long-term outcomes. In this context, artificial nutrition plays a central role in ICU management and represents a potentially modifiable intervention. Beyond meeting energy requirements, nutritional support may help sustain immune function, preserve gut integrity, and reduce the risk of infectious complications. Whenever possible, enteral nutrition should be favored, as it supports the intestinal barrier and gut-associated lymphoid tissue, even when delivered at low, trophic doses. Parenteral nutrition remains indispensable in the presence of intestinal failure but should be used cautiously, given its association with complications such as catheter-related bloodstream infections. Critical illness profoundly alters gut-immune interactions, promoting dysbiosis, increased intestinal permeability, and immune dysfunction - processes that may be further amplified by immunosuppressive therapies. This has fueled interest in immunonutrition strategies, including arginine, ω-3 fatty acids, glutamine, and nucleotides. However, evidence in immunosuppressed critically ill patients remains limited and inconsistent, preventing firm recommendations. Looking ahead, the integration of body composition assessment, immune-metabolic phenotyping, multi-omics technologies, and artificial intelligence may enable more personalized nutritional strategies. Future studies should focus on phenotype-specific randomized trials to better define the optimal route, composition, timing, and dosing of nutritional support in this complex population.

42989940.title: Outcomes of SGLT2-inhibitor-induced euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis in a North Queensland intensive care unit: A retrospective cohort study.
42989940.abstract: Evidence on sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i)-associated euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis (EuDKA) in the intensive care unit (ICU) and its comparison with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is limited. This study aims to describe ICU characteristics, management and outcomes of SGLT2i-associated EuDKA, identify predictors of poorer outcomes and compare findings with T1DM-DKA. Single-centre retrospective cohort (2017-2023) of adults admitted to a Northern Queensland ICU. EuDKA was defined by plasma glucose <13.9 mmol/L plus ⩾1 of acidaemia, low bicarbonate, raised anion gap or ketonaemia, in patients with T2DM on SGLT2i. A comparator cohort comprised ICU admissions with T1DM-DKA. Demographics, precipitants, biochemistry, insulin therapy, and outcomes were extracted and analysed with non-parametric tests. Fourteen EuDKA and 31 T1DM-DKA admissions were included. EuDKA patients were older with more frequent comorbidities; First Nations Australians were over-represented. Presenting features were heterogeneous, with overlapping precipitants (commonly caloric restriction/fasting or intercurrent illness). Compared with T1DM-DKA, EuDKA had milder biochemical derangement and lower 24-h insulin dose but required longer insulin therapy and longer ICU length of stay; time to acidosis resolution was similar. In exploratory analyses, end-organ complications in type 2 diabetes were associated with longer ICU stay, while obesity and pre-admission insulin therapy were associated with prolonged acidosis duration. ICU-admitted SGLT2i-associated EuDKA differs clinically and in management from classical T1DM-DKA. Findings highlight diagnostic challenges, potential high-risk subgroups, and the need for prospective, multicentre studies to inform risk-based management in critical care.

42995736.title: Clinical impact of early enteral nutrition support combined with comfort nursing on prognosis of critically ill ICU patients undergoing ventilator assisted ventilation.
42995736.journal: Malawi medical journal : the journal of Medical Association of Malawi
42995736.abstract: We aimed to clarify the impact of early enteral nutrition support combined with comfort nursing on the prognosis of critically ill patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) who received ventilator-assisted ventilation. 100 critically ill patients admitted to our ICU were selected and randomly divided into the control group (CG) and the observation group (OG). The OG initiated early enteral nutrition support within 24 h after admission to ICU and received comfort nursing. The CG initiated enteral nutrition support after admission to the ICU based on monitoring biochemical indicators and received routine ICU nursing. The nutritional status, immune function, total malnutrition rate, incidence of pulmonary infection, ventilator weaning time and ICU hospitalization time of the two groups were measured and compared. The levels of albumin (ALB), total protein (TP), and globulin (GLB) in both groups were higher than those at admission to the ICU, while OG group were higher than CG group (P < 0.05). The PCT levels of both groups decreased compared to the levels during the period from admission to the ICU, while OG group was greater decrease than CG group (P < 0.05). The overall malnutrition rate in OG group was lower than that in CG group (P < 0.05). The incidence of pulmonary infection in OG group was lower than that in CG group (P < 0.05). The time to weaning from the ventilator and the ICU stay time in OG group were shorter than those in CG group (P < 0.05). For critically ill ICU patients undergoing ventilator assisted ventilation, early enteral nutrition support combined with comfort nursing can effectively reduce risk of malnutrition and pulmonary infection, enhance immune function, create convenient conditions for early weaning and early conversion to general wards, with broad clinical application prospects.

42998837.title: The efficacy and safety of micronutrient complementation in adults during the acute phase of critical illness: A retrospective cohort study.
42998837.journal: The American journal of the medical sciences
42998837.abstract: Critically ill patients often experience metabolic imbalances and potentially low micronutrient blood levels that worsen oxidative stress and impair immune function. Despite guideline recommendations, micronutrient complementation is inconsistently applied due to accessibility issues and the lack of validated assessment tools during acute critical illness. This retrospective cohort study evaluated the impact of early intravenous micronutrient complementation on clinical outcomes in ICU patients using real-world electronic medical record data. Adult ICU patients at National Taiwan University Hsinchu Branch from July 2024 to November 2025 who received parenteral nutrition (PN) for at least 24 hours were included. Patients were divided into a treatment group receiving micronutrients within 72 hours of ICU admission and a control group without complementation. Primary outcomes included in-hospital mortality and infectious complications after day 6 of PN; secondary outcomes included ICU/hospital length of stay, inflammatory and metabolic biomarkers, organ support needs, and refeeding syndrome incidence. Among 462 patients analyzed, 213 received early micronutrient therapy. Baseline characteristics such as age (control 65.3±16.6 vs treatment 67.7±13.8 years), BMI (control 28.70±8.95 vs treatment 23.74±4.91 kg/m2), admission categories (control MICU 10.2%, SICU 43.7% vs treatment MICU 9.3%, SICU 36.8%), APACHE II score (control 16.8±8.5 vs treatment 17.3±8.1), and TISS score (control 20.5±7.5 vs treatment 19.6±6.2) were largely comparable. Thetreatment group significantly reduced infectious complications, with logistic regression confirming protective effects (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.20-0.49, p<0.001). Secondary outcomes showed no differences in LOS, vasopressor use, oxygen therapy, continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) requirement, PN duration, or refeeding syndrome. The treatment group exhibited delayed enteral nutrition (EN) initiation (control 8.9 ± 8.9 days vs treatment 11.0 ± 10.7 days; p=0.02) but demonstrated significant improvements in inflammatory and metabolic parameters. The linear regression model were performed and demonstrated significantly reductions in C-reactive protein (CRP)(B = -10.91 mg/dL, 95% CI -13.16 to -8.65, p<0.001), serum lactate levels (B = -1.49 mmol/L, 95% CI -2.58 to -0.40, p=0.007), and time to lactate normalization (B = -0.90 days, 95% CI -1.64 to -0.16, p=0.017). In subgroup analysis, a total of 213 patients were included, of whom 138 received standard micronutrient complementation, and 75 received micronutrients with additional zinc complementation, which demonstrated further benefits. For instance, the group receiving additional Zn reduced infectious complications (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.21-0.85, p=0.02), shorter ICU LOD (B = -3.97 days, 95% CI-7.64 to -0.30, p=0.03), and faster lactate clearance (B = -1.17 days, 95% CI -1.87 to -0.47, p=0.09). These results support early comprehensive micronutrient complementation to enhance immune and metabolic recovery in critically ill patients and highlight the need for prospective biomarker-guided studies.

42997588.title: In vitro Evaluation of the Physicochemical Stability of Multi-Drug Y-Site Admixtures Using Dynamic Monitoring and Chemometrics.
42997588.abstract: Concurrent continuous infusions of propofol, midazolam, insulin, dexmedetomidine, and morphine are commonly used in ICU for sedation, analgesia, and glycemic control. However, physicochemical compatibility data for Y-site administration are lacking, leading to risky empirical practice. This study evaluated their physicochemical stability to guide safe infusion. Twenty-six admixtures were prepared at clinical concentrations and stored at room temperature. Samples were analyzed at 0, 2, 4, 8, 12, and 24 h for appearance, pH, osmolality, subvisible particles, mean droplet diameter (MDD), polydispersity index (PDI), zeta potential, microscopic aggregation, and drug content by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Principal component analysis (PCA), hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA), Spearman correlation, and orthogonal partial least squares-discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) were performed to explore stability patterns and key discriminating variables. No obvious alterations in appearance, pH, or osmolality were observed over 24 h. In propofol-free admixtures, subvisible particles met pharmacopeial limits. In propofol-containing admixtures, MDD (95.6-124.3 nm) and PDI (0.338-0.469) remained acceptable, whereas zeta potential ranged from -12.50 to 6.14 mV. Microscopic aggregation was observed in seven propofol-containing admixtures. HPLC showed that all drugs retained >90% of their initial concentrations. OPLS-DA identified four independent variables with VIP values greater than 1 (R2 Y=0.71, Q2=0.689), and permutation tests confirmed no overfitting. Under the conditions studied, seven propofol-containing admixtures showed aggregation, while the other 19 remained stable for 24 h. Chemometric analysis supported the stability classification and indicated that drug composition, pH and zeta potential were key contributors to emulsion aggregation.

43000034.title: Efficacy Heterogeneity of Hemoperfusion Plus Continuous Venovenous Hemofiltration for Hypertriglyceridemia-Induced Acute Pancreatitis Stratified by Severity of Inflammatory Response.
43000034.journal: Therapeutic apheresis and dialysis : official peer-reviewed journal of the International Society for Apheresis, the Japanese Society for Apheresis, the Japanese Society for Dialysis Therapy
43000034.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the heterogeneity in the efficacy of hemoperfusion (HP) plus continuous venovenous hemofiltration (CVVH) versus CVVH alone in reducing the incidence of severe acute pancreatitis (SAP) among patients with hypertriglyceridemia-induced acute pancreatitis (HTG-AP), stratified by the inflammatory marker C-reactive protein (CRP). In addition, we assessed secondary outcomes encompassing laboratory response, disease severity and organ function, healthcare resource utilization, and treatment-related indicators, so as to delineate the broader efficacy profile of the combination therapy and its relationship with the primary endpoint. Furthermore, we sought to identify a CRP-based therapeutic window for the combination therapy. This single-center retrospective study included 204 patients who were assigned to the HP + CVVH group (n = 103) or the CVVH group (n = 101). Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess the overall difference in efficacy between the two groups. Restricted cubic splines (RCS) were employed to analyze the nonlinear relationship between treatment efficacy and CRP levels and to identify a CRP-based therapeutic window. Secondary outcomes were analyzed using multivariable logistic regression for categorical variables and generalized linear models for quantitative variables. After multivariable adjustment, the incidence of SAP did not differ significantly between the HP + CVVH and CVVH groups (p > 0.05). RCS analysis revealed a significant interaction between treatment group and CRP levels. The conditional odds ratio for SAP (HP + CVVH vs. CVVH) was significantly below 1 only within a specific CRP range: 194.96-296.91 mg/L in the primary analysis and 200.77-285.81 mg/L after propensity score adjustment (p < 0.05). Regarding secondary outcomes, HP + CVVH was associated with significantly lower CRP, procalcitonin, and triglyceride levels on day 3, more SIRS-free days within 14 days, lower peak intra-abdominal pressure, shorter ICU length of stay, fewer CVVH sessions, earlier initiation of enteral nutrition, and higher blood purification-related costs (all p < 0.05). No significant differences were observed in organ failure-free days, incidence of pancreatic necrosis, hospital length of stay, total hospitalization cost, total morphine equivalent dose, carbapenem use, or duration of mechanical ventilation (all p > 0.05). HP + CVVH showed no overall superiority to CVVH alone in preventing SAP. Nevertheless, secondary outcome analyses demonstrated improved inflammatory control, faster resolution of systemic inflammatory response, reduced intra-abdominal pressure, and better recovery in several resource-related and treatment-related indicators, indicating measurable biological and clinical process benefits. These benefits, however, did not translate into a uniform reduction in SAP. The effect of HP + CVVH on the hard endpoint was conditional, nonlinear, and dependent on baseline inflammatory burden, with significant benefit confined to a specific CRP therapeutic window. Therefore, improvements in secondary endpoints should not be equated with hard-endpoint benefit, and the decision to initiate HP + CVVH should be individualized according to the intensity of the inflammatory response.

43004379.title: Association between glycemic variability and delirium in critically ill older adults patients: a retrospective cohort study.
43004379.abstract: Delirium affects 30-70% of critically ill older adults patients and is associated with poor outcomes. While glycemic control is essential in intensive care, the impact of glycemic variability (GV) on delirium remains understudied, particularly in older adults patients. This study investigated the association between GV and delirium in critically ill older adults patients. We analyzed 16,335 patients aged ≥ 65 years from the MIMIC-IV database. GV was calculated as the coefficient of variation of blood glucose measurements and categorized into quartiles. Delirium was assessed using Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU). Multivariate logistic regression evaluated the association between GV and delirium, adjusting for demographics, clinical parameters, and comorbidities. We assessed the added predictive value of GV using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), net reclassification improvement (NRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI). Random forest and Boruta algorithm determined variable importance. Delirium incidence increased across GV quartiles (28.7% in Q1 vs. 41.8% in Q4, p < 0.001). After full adjustment, the highest GV quartile showed 42% higher delirium risk compared to the lowest (OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.18-1.71, p = 0.003), with a significant dose-response relationship. Random forest and Boruta algorithm identified GV as the most important predictor of delirium. Adding GV to prediction models significantly improved risk reclassification, with significant NRI in the fully adjusted model (p = 0.01) and significant IDIs across all models (all p < 0.05). The association remained consistent across all subgroups regardless of diabetes status. Higher GV independently predicts increased delirium risk in critically ill older adults patients. Monitoring and managing GV may represent a modifiable target for delirium prevention in this vulnerable population.

42500117.title: Predictors and Mortality Determinants of Non-Thyroidal Illness Syndrome Among Patients in the Medical Intensive Care Unit in Northeastern Tanzania.
42500117.journal: Clinical medicine insights. Endocrinology and diabetes
42500117.abstract: BACKGROUND: Non-thyroidal illness syndrome (NTIS) frequently occurs in critically ill patients and reflects alterations in thyroid hormone metabolism without intrinsic thyroid disease. It has been increasingly recognized as a potential marker of disease severity and poor outcomes in intensive care settings, yet data from Sub-Saharan Africa remain limited. To determine the prevalence of NTIS and identify determinants of mortality among patients admitted to a medical intensive care unit (ICU) in northern Tanzania. METHODS: We conducted a prospective cohort study among 120 adult patients admitted to the medical ICU at a tertiary referral hospital between October 2024 and March 2025. Thyroid function tests (T3, T4, and TSH) were measured within 24 hours of admission. NTIS was defined based on characteristic biochemical patterns in the absence of known thyroid disease. Clinical, laboratory, and outcome data were collected prospectively. Associations were assessed using Chi-square tests and modified Poisson regression to estimate adjusted risk ratios (aRR) with 95% confidence intervals. RESULTS: The prevalence of NTIS was 23.3%. Overall mortality was 42.5%, with significantly higher mortality among patients with NTIS (67.9%) compared with those without NTIS (34.8%). NTIS remained independently associated with mortality after adjustment (aRR 8.05; 95% CI: 2.27-28.56; p=0.001). Patients with NTIS were also more likely to experience prolonged hospital stays. Although several clinical variables showed associations in bivariate analysis, most did not remain significant after adjustment. Illness severity, as reflected by clinical scoring systems, remained an important contributor to outcomes. CONCLUSION: NTIS is common among critically ill patients and is strongly associated with increased mortality. It may serve as a practical prognostic marker in ICU settings, particularly in resource-limited environments. Further multicenter studies are needed to validate its prognostic utility and integration into routine clinical practice.

42496059.title: Glycemic Ratio Is a Superior Predictor of Mortality Compared With Stress Hyperglycemia Ratio in Critically Ill Patients.
42496059.journal: Journal of diabetes science and technology
42496059.abstract: BACKGROUND: The glycemic ratio (GR), defined as the ratio of mean intensive care unit (ICU) blood glucose (BG) to estimated preadmission BG (EPBG), may provide superior prognostic insight compared with the single admission snapshot represented by the stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR, the ratio of ICU admission BG to EPAG). METHODS: This retrospective study included 4148 patients treated in a university-affiliated medical-surgical ICU from 2019 to 2023 who had >4 ICU BG measurements and a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) measured at admission. We compared SHR and GR prognostic ability for mortality, analyzed across prespecified GR and SHR bands, and calculated observed:expected mortality ratios (OEMRs). RESULTS: We observed a more sharply defined J-shaped relationship between GR and mortality compared with that generated by SHR. Mortality in the reference band of 0.8 to <1.0 for GR and SHR mortality was 7.5% vs 10.9%, respectively (P = .0087), and for the strata ≥1.4, mortality was 25.6% vs 20.5% (P = .0376). Compared with the reference band, GR < 0.8 and GR > 1.0 had higher OEMR (P < .0001 for each), but the OEMR for SHR <0.8 and >1.0 compared with the reference band was not significantly different. CONCLUSIONS: Glycemic ratio was superior to SHR as a predictor of mortality. This study demonstrates that a mean ICU BG level representing 80% to 100% of the patient's EPBG was associated with the lowest mortality rate in a heterogeneous cohort of critically ill patients. These results may inform current BG management strategies and should be considered when designing future interventional trials in the critically ill.

42487967.title: Combined impact of glucose variability and mineral disorders on mortality and severe cardiorenal events in critically ill CKD patients: a multicenter cohort study.
42487967.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Elderly critically ill ICU patients with CKD face high mortality. The independent and combined prognostic roles of glycemic variability (Glucose CV) and calcium-phosphate metabolic disorders in this population remain unconfirmed. METHODS: This retrospective study contained three cohorts: MIMIC-IV (n = 1,319, development), multicenter eICU (n = 996, validation), and Chinese hospital cohort (n = 1,069, clinical validation). Multivariable Cox regression and meta-analysis were applied. RESULTS: Elevated Glucose CV independently predicted 28- and 90-day mortality with predominant early risk. Concurrent hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia indicated the poorest prognosis, and high GV produced synergistic harmful effects in this subgroup. All results were verified by external cohorts. DISCUSSION: Targeted glycemic variability management and calcium-phosphate homeostasis correction may effectively improve survival of elderly critically ill CKD patients.

42487955.title: Hemoglobin glycation index and short-term mortality in sepsis: a retrospective cohort study with external validation.
42487955.abstract: BACKGROUND: The hemoglobin glycation index (HGI) reflects interindividual variability in hemoglobin glycation beyond average glycemic exposure. Although stress-related dysglycemia is common in sepsis, the prognostic relevance of HGI in critically ill patients with sepsis remains unclear. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the MIMIC-IV database (n = 2,073) as the primary cohort.
