No statistically significant associations were observed between individual genes, the presence of two carbapenemase genes, or carbapenemase profiles and any mortality endpoint; adjusted analyses of 28-day ICU mortality yielded similar findings. In the exploratory Firth model, the profile effect was not significant (p = 0.198), whereas a higher age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index and bloodstream infection or ventilator-associated pneumonia, compared with urinary tract infection, were associated with higher odds of 28-day ICU mortality. Frequent gene co-occurrence was observed; however, clinically meaningful gene-mortality associations cannot be excluded because of imprecise estimates.

42933948.title: Reevaluating Chlorhexidine Gluconate Oral Care in Mechanically Ventilated Patients: Evidence for De-implementation.
42933948.journal: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
42933948.abstract: Chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) oral care was incorporated into ventilator bundles as a preventive strategy for ventilator-associated pneumonia. Recent evidence challenged the efficacy and safety of this long-standing practice. Systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials show minimal benefits (non-significant reduction in intensive care unit length of stay and ventilator days) and potential for harm (trend toward increased mortality). International and national consensus statements have withdrawn recommendations to use CHG for oral care. This article synthesizes the evidence supporting de-implementation of CHG oral care and outlines practical steps for adopting safer, evidence-aligned oral care protocols focused on toothbrushing for mechanically ventilated adults.

42931235.title: Characteristics and Resistance Patterns of Gram-Negative Bacterial Isolates to Third-Generation Cephalosporins in Oncology ICU Patients: A Ten-Year Retrospective Analysis.
42931235.abstract: Third-generation cephalosporin (3GC) resistance threatens empirical therapy in vulnerable critically ill patients. We conducted a decade-long single-center retrospective study of 3528 Gram-negative isolates from 1946 adult and pediatric oncology intensive care unit (ICU) patients between 2015 and 2024 at King Hussein Cancer Center. This study aims to characterize 3GS resistance in oncology ICU patients. The 3GC resistance was 59.2% among Enterobacterales and other fermenting organisms (evaluated against the full three-agent panel) and 67.2%among non-fermenters (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter spp., Stenotrophomonas maltophilia; evaluated against a narrower, organism-appropriate agent subset); these two estimates are not directly comparable given the differing susceptibility panels tested. Resistance was highest among the Acinetobacter calcoaceticus-baumannii complex (96.9%), followed by Escherichia coli (70.5%), Enterobacter cloacae (65.5%), and Klebsiella pneumoniae (59.6%). In unadjusted patient-level analyses, resistance was significantly higher among patients with hematological malignancy than solid tumors (73.1% vs. 57.8%; OR 1.98, 95% CI 1.59-2.48; p < 0.001) and among pediatric versus adult ICU isolates (70.8% vs. 60.9%; OR 1.55, 95% CI 1.11-2.18; p = 0.010). Seven-day mortality did not differ by resistance status (44.1% vs. 41.6%; unadjusted OR 1.11, 95% CI 0.92-1.33). The 3GC resistance varies by organism, malignancy type and ICU population in unadjusted analyses, supporting population-specific antibiograms and stronger stewardship.

42919194.title: Antibiotic de-escalation in severe intra-abdominal infections: a single-center retrospective cohort study on safety and prognostic factors.
42919194.abstract: Antibiotic de-escalation is a key antimicrobial stewardship strategy aimed at reducing the ecological and adverse effects of broad-spectrum therapy without compromising efficacy. However, its real-world safety and impact on clinical outcomes in patients with severe intra-abdominal infections (IAIs) remain underexplored. A single-center, retrospective cohort study was conducted from June 2022 to June 2025. Adults with severe IAIs who received initial broad-spectrum antibiotics and achieved source control within 48 h were included. Patients were stratified into de-escalation and non-de-escalation groups on the basis of the antibiotic management strategy. Propensity score matching (1:1) was used to balance baseline characteristics. The primary outcome was clinical cure at 30 days. Secondary outcomes included 28-day mortality, lengths of ICU and hospital stay, antibiotic duration, and the incidence of secondary infections and Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI). Among 405 eligible patients, 212 were matched (106 per group). The de-escalation group had a significantly higher clinical cure rate (79.8% vs. 63.5%; OR 2.24, 95% CI 1.29-3.89; P = 0.004) and lower 28-day mortality (9.6% vs. 21.2%; OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.18-0.88; P = 0.02). De-escalation was also associated with shorter ICU and hospital stays, reduced antibiotic duration, and fewer secondary infections. Multivariable analysis confirmed de-escalation (aOR 2.71, 95% CI 1.48-4.97) and adequate source control (aOR 3.52, 95% CI 1.81-6.85) as independent predictors of clinical cure. Antibiotic de-escalation following adequate source control is associated with improved clinical outcomes and reduced mortality in severe IAIs without increasing the risk of complications. These findings support its integration into antimicrobial stewardship programs for this high-risk population. Not applicable.

42913935.title: A nomogram for predicting in-hospital mortality in patients with coagulase-negative staphylococcus bloodstream infections.
42913935.journal: Journal of infection and chemotherapy : official journal of the Japan Society of Chemotherapy
42913935.abstract: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS) have emerged as significant pathogens in bloodstream infections (BSIs). Currently, no validated models exist for specifically predicting in-hospital mortality in patients with CoNS-BSIs. A retrospective study was conducted on adult patients with CoNS-BSIs using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-III) database. Participants were randomly allocated into a training set (n = 366) and a validation set (n = 157). Demographic characteristics, severity scores, comorbidities and laboratory examinations from the first 24 h of ICU admission were analyzed. The optimal predictive variables for establishing a nomogram were screened through univariate, multivariate logistic regression and stepwise regression analyses. Model performance was evaluated by receiver operator characteristic (ROC) curve, calibration curve, decision curve analysis (DCA) and clinical impact curve (CIC). Among 523 patients enrolled, the overall in-hospital mortality was 22.9%. Four independent predictors were incorporated into the nomogram: age (OR = 1.04), anion gap (AG: OR = 1.11), total bilirubin (TBil: OR = 1.26) and respiratory failure (OR = 1.97). The area under the curve (AUC) values in the training set and validation set were 0.758 and 0.823, respectively. The P-values of the calibration curve in two sets were 0.258 and 0.432. The DCA curves were above the two extreme curves. The CIC analysis revealed a high concordance between predicted high-risk cases and observed clinical events when the risk threshold exceeded 60%. Age, AG, TBil and respiratory failure were independent risk factors for in-hospital mortality among patients with CoNS-BSIs. The nomogram based on these four parameters demonstrated good performance and clinical utility for risk assessment.

42913228.title: Clinical factors associated with noninvasive ventilation-associated pneumonia in acute respiratory failure: a prospective cohort study.
42913228.journal: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care
42913228.abstract: Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) is preferred to invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) as treatment for acute respiratory failure due to its lower complication rate, but NIV may still be associated with serious complications such as nosocomial pneumonia. However, risk factors associated with NIV-associated pneumonia remain insufficiently characterized. To investigate factors associated with NIV-associated pneumonia in patients treated with NIV for acute respiratory failure in a respiratory intensive care unit. In this prospective cohort study, we followed adult patients who were admitted to a respiratory intensive care unit in a tertiary hospital for acute respiratory failure. None of the patients had pneumonia on admission. All patients were treated with NIV and monitored daily for the development of nosocomial pneumonia, which was defined using standardized criteria. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors independently associated with NIV-associated pneumonia. Among 191 eligible patients admitted between March 2023 and May 2024, 84 developed NIV-associated pneumonia. Age was not independently associated with pneumonia development. In multivariable analysis, poor oral hygiene, poor secretion control, and longer NIV duration were independently associated with NIV-associated pneumonia. Patients who developed pneumonia also had longer ICU stay and higher rates of antibiotic modification. In patients receiving NIV for acute respiratory failure, poor oral hygiene, poor secretion control, and prolonged NIV exposure were independently associated with NIV-associated pneumonia, whereas chronological age, sepsis, and frailty were not. These findings suggest that clinical factors related to bedside care and NIV exposure may be more relevant to pneumonia development than age alone.

42912053.title: Prognostic value of the blood urea nitrogen-to-albumin ratio for 28-day mortality in septic intensive care unit patients: a large-scale retrospective cohort study using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database.
42912053.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening condition characterized by dysregulated host responses to infection and high mortality in intensive care units. Existing prognostic models are often complex or resource-intensive. The blood urea nitrogen-to-albumin ratio, reflecting renal function, metabolic stress, and nutritional status, has emerged as a potential prognostic biomarker. The aim of this study was to evaluate the predictive value of blood urea nitrogen-to-albumin ratio for 28-day mortality in septic intensive care unit patients. This retrospective cohort study utilized data from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (version 2.0) database. Adult patients meeting Sepsis-3 criteria were included. Suspected infection was defined by antibiotic administration and microbiological culture within 24 h. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data were collected, and blood urea nitrogen-to-albumin ratio was calculated using values obtained within the first 24 h of intensive care unit admission. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, and multivariate Cox regression were performed. A total of 6,940 patients were included, with a 28-day mortality rate of 21.6%. Blood urea nitrogen-to-albumin ratio demonstrated superior predictive performance (area under the curve (AUC)=0.647, 95%CI 0.631-0.664) compared with serum urea (AUC=0.634) and albumin (AUC=0.428), and also outperformed the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score (AUC=0.613). The optimal cutoff value was 7.6. Patients with blood urea nitrogen-to-albumin ratio ≥7.6 had significantly higher mortality than those with lower values (p<0.001). Elevated blood urea nitrogen-to-albumin ratio remained an independent predictor of mortality after adjustment. Blood urea nitrogen-to-albumin ratio is a simple, objective, and readily available biomarker associated with 28-day mortality in septic intensive care unit patients and may contribute to risk stratification when used alongside other clinical parameters.

42907988.title: Therapeutic consequences of a diagnostic broncho-alveolar lavage in patients in the Intensive Care Unit due to COVID-19: a retrospective cohort study.
42907988.abstract: When patients with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) on the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) were not improving or clinically deteriorated, bronchoscopy with broncho-alveolar lavage (BAL) was performed to rule out potentially treatable bacterial, viral and fungal superinfections. The purpose of this study was to investigate the therapeutic consequences of a diagnostic BAL in ICU patients with COVID-19. We performed a retrospective analysis in a cohort of patients with COVID-19 on the ICU of the St. Antonius Hospital Nieuwegein in the Netherlands. We compared the administration of antibiotics, antifungal therapy and prednisolone on the day of the BAL and three days later. We hypothesized that a diagnostic BAL did not result in significant changes in therapeutic management. In 73 ICU-patients with COVID-19 who underwent a BAL, the results led to changes in medication prescription in 62% (p < 0.01) of patients. In these patients, the antibiotic management changed in 36% (p < 0.01), the antifungal management in 21% (p < 0.01) and the prednisolone management in 34% (p < 0.01) of the patients. In ICU-patients who did not improve and therefore underwent a BAL, there was a significant change in antibiotics, antifungal or prednisolone prescriptions in 62% of the patients.

42907983.title: Application of machine learning prediction models for in-hospital mortality in diabetic sepsis patients: a study based on the MIMIC IV database.
42907983.journal: BMC medical informatics and decision making
42907983.abstract: Sepsis complicated by diabetes mellitus represents a significant clinical challenge in intensive care units (ICUs), associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Accurate prognostication of in-hospital mortality in this complex patient population is crucial for optimizing clinical decision making, resource allocation, and patient management strategies. We conducted a retrospective cohort study utilizing data from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-IV) database. The study focused on adult ICU patients with concurrent diagnoses of sepsis and diabetes mellitus. Six machine learning algorithms were evaluated for their predictive performance: Logistic Regression (LR), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT), XGBoost and LightGBM. Additionally, we assessed the prognostic capability of the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score. Model discrimination was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). To enhance model interpretability, we employed SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values to elucidate the relative importance of predictor variables. The study cohort comprised 7716 patients, with 1357 (17.6%) experiencing in-hospital mortality. Among the machine learning models evaluated, GBDT exhibited superior predictive performance achieving an AUC of 0.792 (95% CI: 0.769-0.814). This performance surpassed that of other machine learning algorithms and the conventional SOFA score. SHAP analysis provided valuable insights into the hierarchical importance of various clinical and demographic features contributing to the GBDT model's predictions. Our findings demonstrate the potential of machine learning approaches in accurately predicting in-hospital mortality among ICU patients with sepsis and diabetes mellitus. These advanced analytical techniques outperform traditional scoring systems such as SOFA. The integration of SHAP values enhances model interpretability, potentially facilitating the adoption of these predictive tools in clinical practice. Further multi-center validation studies and prospective trials are warranted to confirm the generalizability of these results and to explore the clinical impact of implementing such models in diverse healthcare settings.

42902669.title: Candidemia in ICU and Non-ICU Settings: Species Distribution and Antifungal Resistance Patterns from a Tertiary Care Center in India with Reference to ICMR AMR 2024.
42902669.journal: The Journal of the Association of Physicians of India
42902669.abstract: Candidemia is a major cause of invasive fungal bloodstream infections associated with significant morbidity and mortality. An increase in bloodstream infections caused by nonalbicans Candida species is concerning because it has different epidemiological characteristics and antifungal susceptibility compared to C. albicans. Resistance to antifungal agents, particularly azoles, complicates treatment. This retrospective hospital-based observational study was carried out in the Department of Microbiology, Saveetha Medical College, Chennai, from January 2025 to December 2025. Blood samples were collected and loaded into the BACT/ALERT automated system for microbial detection. Identification and antifungal susceptibility testing (AFST) were performed using the VITEK 2 automated system. CLSI M60 guidelines were used for interpreting the results. Candida species were isolated in 68/1207 (5.6%) positive blood cultures; 38/68 (55.9%) from ICU and 30/68 (44.1%) from non-ICU settings. Males (27/38, 71.1%) predominated in ICU, whereas females (18/30, 60%) predominated in non-ICU. The most commonly isolated species in the non-ICU setting was C. auris (11/30, 36.7%), whereas in the ICU setting it was C. tropicalis (13/38, 34.2%). C. albicans and C. glabrata showed 100% susceptibility, whereas C. auris demonstrated high resistance to azoles with variable resistance to echinocandins. Diabetes mellitus was the most common risk factor in both settings. Mortality was higher in ICU patients (9/38, 23.7%) than non-ICU patients (5/30, 16.7%); however, this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.47). Candidemia remains a significant source of bloodstream infections with a notable trend toward nonalbicans species and emerging antifungal resistance. Continuous surveillance and appropriate infection control practices are essential.

42902572.title: Proenkephalin A and Heterogeneity of Hydrocortisone Treatment Effect in Septic Shock: A Post Hoc Analysis of the VANISH Trial.
42902572.abstract: Heterogeneity of treatment effect is thought to drive conflicting results for the benefits of corticosteroids in sepsis. Proenkephalin A (PENK) is a biomarker of renal function. Given the kidney's role in sepsis pathophysiology and corticosteroid metabolism, we hypothesized that baseline renal function, assessed using PENK, would be associated with hydrocortisone efficacy. A post hoc analysis of a double-blind, randomized clinical trial in septic shock (Effect of Early Vasopressin vs. Norepinephrine on Kidney Failure in Patients with Septic Shock [VANISH]). ICUs across the United Kingdom. One hundred seventy-three patients admitted to ICU with septic shock. Norepinephrine vs. vasopressin and hydrocortisone vs. placebo. PENK was measured in plasma, and patients were dichotomized using a PENK concentration above 89 pmol/L. PENK greater than or equal to 89 pmol/L was associated with 28-day mortality (odds ratio, 3.24; 95% CI, 1.62-6.74). We found no interaction between PENK and randomization to vasopressin or norepinephrine on outcome. However, there was a significant interaction between the PENK groups and hydrocortisone or placebo use in those patients who reached the maximum vasopressor threshold (n = 111) for kidney failure-free days (high PENK [≥ 89 pmol/L] placebo 26 [13-28], hydrocortisone 11 [0-26] and low PENK placebo 28 [15-28], hydrocortisone 28 [28-28]; p = 0.01). Patients with high PENK receiving hydrocortisone had the fewest kidney failure-free days. Although we found no significant interaction for 28-day mortality (p = 0.14), the patients with high PENK who received hydrocortisone had the highest mortality (high PENK hydrocortisone 50%, placebo 32% and low PENK hydrocortisone 14%, placebo 24%). This exploratory analysis identified a possible interaction between baseline PENK and hydrocortisone treatment on kidney failure-free days. These findings require validation in independent and prospective studies.

42902233.title: Changes in the microbial spectrum and antimicrobial resistance of bloodstream infections in intensive care units before and during the COVID-19 pandemic.
42902233.abstract: Bloodstream infections (BSIs) are major infectious conditions associated with high morbidity and mortality, particularly in intensive care units (ICUs). In critically ill patients, early and appropriate empirical antimicrobial therapy plays an important role in preventing adverse clinical outcomes. However, the increasing burden of antimicrobial resistance necessitates that empirical treatment strategies be continuously reassessed based on up-to-date local resistance data. This study aimed to compare the distribution of bacterial pathogens and antimicrobial resistance profiles of BSIs identified in ICUs before and during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. A total of 388 patients diagnosed with BSIs while hospitalized in the ICUs of Health Sciences University Prof. Dr. Cemil Taşçıoğlu City Hospital between March 2019 and April 2021 were retrospectively evaluated. During the pandemic period, patients with and without COVID-19 were analyzed together without stratification. Bacterial isolates recovered from blood cultures and their antimicrobial susceptibility results were compared between the pre-pandemic and pandemic periods. Multivariable analysis identified independent risk factors for multidrug resistance (MDR) in Klebsiella pneumoniae, adjusting for clinical confounders. Pre-pandemic, the predominant pathogens were K. pneumoniae (30.1%), A. baumannii complex (21.9%), and S. aureus (9.7%); during the pandemic, K. pneumoniae (34.4%), A. baumannii complex (21.2%), and E. faecium (10.4%) led the distribution. During the pandemic, non-fermentative Gram-negative bacilli showed a significant increase in ceftazidime resistance, while resistance to amikacin, gentamicin, and meropenem declined. In Enterobacterales, extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) production and carbapenem resistance increased during the pandemic. In K. pneumoniae, while carbapenem resistance remained statistically stable, colistin resistance increased significantly, raising a new concern. Prior antimicrobial therapy was the sole independent predictor of MDR in K. pneumoniae (adjusted Odds Ratio [aOR] = 8.296, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] = 1.471-46.794, p = 0.017). During the COVID-19 pandemic, Gram-negative pathogens continued to predominate among BSIs identified in ICUs, with an observed trend toward increased antimicrobial resistance, particularly among Enterobacterales species. Notably, prior antibiotic exposure was identified as the key independent determinant of MDR status in K. pneumoniae. Given the dynamic nature of pathogen distribution and resistance profiles in BSIs, consideration of local and period-specific resistance patterns in ICU settings may help inform empirical antimicrobial treatment strategies. Not applicable.

42897507.title: Clinical characteristics and outcomes of Candida auris in a tertiary intensive care unit: a four-year retrospective case series.
42897507.abstract: Candida auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant yeast associated with healthcare-associated transmission and severe outcomes in intensive care settings. Clinical ICU-based cohort data from Türkiye remain limited. We conducted a single-center retrospective case series in a tertiary adult intensive care unit in Türkiye, including patients with C. auris isolated from blood and/or urine cultures between January 1, 2021, and January 1, 2025. Species identification was performed by matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS). Antifungal susceptibility testing (AST) for selected isolates was conducted using the Sensititre™ YeastOne™ colorimetric microdilution system. Continuous variables were presented as mean ± standard deviation or median (minimum-maximum) according to distribution, whereas categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. Comparative statistical analyses were not performed because of the descriptive case-series design and limited sample size. Among 5,778 ICU patients evaluated during the study period, C. auris was identified in 36 patients. No cases were detected in 2021-2022; all cases occurred between September 18, 2023, and December 23, 2024, representing 2.37% of 1,517 ICU admissions during that interval. Isolation was most frequent in urine cultures (77.8%), followed by blood cultures (33.3%), with simultaneous urine and blood positivity in 11.1% of patients. The mean length of hospitalization before the first C. auris-positive culture was 44.9 days. All patients had urinary and central venous catheters and had received broad-spectrum antibiotics before C. auris detection. In the preceding month, MDR bacterial bloodstream infections were identified in 16 patients. AST data were available for four blood culture isolates from three patients; fluconazole MIC values were > 256 µg/mL in all tested isolates, whereas micafungin showed the lowest arithmetic mean MIC value (0.188 µg/mL). C. auris emerged in our ICU after 2023 and was mainly detected in patients with prolonged hospitalization, invasive devices, broad-spectrum antimicrobial exposure, and frequent MDR bacterial co-occurrence. These single-center data from Türkiye highlight the importance of reliable species-level identification, infection control awareness, and antimicrobial stewardship. Larger multicenter prospective studies using standardized surveillance and reference-method-based AST protocols are needed to better define transmission dynamics, resistance patterns, and clinical outcomes.

42890140.title: Prediction of vancomycin-resistant phenotype in ICU-onset sterile-site Enterococcus-positive cultures: development and pseudo-temporal validation of a clinical prediction model using MIMIC-IV.
42890140.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
42890140.abstract: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci challenge intensive care. During the interval between organism identification and final phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing, clinicians must balance delayed effective anti-VRE therapy against unnecessary anti-VRE exposure. We aimed to develop and pseudo-temporally validate a model for the vancomycin-resistance phenotype of the index isolate; the model does not determine whether the isolate represents clinically significant infection. In this retrospective MIMIC-IV cohort, adult ICU admissions with a sterile-site Enterococcus-positive culture obtained more than 48 hours after ICU admission were assigned by de-identified anchor-year group to development (groups labelled 2008-2016; n = 552) or pseudo-temporal validation (2017-2022; n = 259). Predictors were restricted to information available by specimen collection. Elastic Net with bootstrap stability screening retained 19 of 141 candidates; four tree-based models were comparators. Among 811 admissions (507 resistant isolates; prevalence, 62.5%), Elastic Net achieved a validation AUROC of 0.835 (95% CI, 0.778-0.889) and calibration slope of 0.91 (0.71-1.18). Tree-model AUROCs were 0.842-0.855; non-significant pairwise DeLong tests were evidence insufficient to detect differences, not evidence of equivalence. Removing both species indicators reduced AUROC to 0.657 (DeLong P < 0.001). Development-OOF-fitted Platt scaling improved validation slopes for Random Forest, XGBoost, and CatBoost from 1.41, 2.41, and 1.46 to 0.94, 1.02, and 1.01. At the Youden index threshold, Elastic Net sensitivity was 0.884 and specificity was 0.690. In exploratory decision-curve analysis, its net benefit did not exceed treat-all at thresholds 0.10 or 0.20; the paired difference was 0.044 (95% CI, 0.014-0.071) at 0.30. The model predicts isolate resistance phenotype, not adjudicated infection, and is not a stand-alone treatment rule. These estimates are specific to a single-center cohort with high VRE prevalence. Independent external validation, local recalibration, clinical adjudication, and periodic updating are prerequisites for use.

42888540.title: Impact of a zero-visitation policy on healthcare-associated infections in a non-COVID intensive care unit: A retrospective cohort study.
42888540.abstract: The impact of visitor restrictions in intensive care units (ICUs) during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic on healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) remains unclear. This study aimed to compare HAI rates between the pre-pandemic restricted-visitation period and the pandemic zero-visitation period in a non-COVID tertiary ICU. This single-center retrospective cohort study included patients admitted to the Anesthesiology and Reanimation ICU of the Duzce University Health Practice and Research Center between March 14, 2019, and March 13, 2021. Patients admitted during the pre-pandemic restricted-visitation period were assigned to Group 19 -20, whereas those admitted during the pandemic zero-visitation period were assigned to Group 20-21. Patients with an ICU stay of < 48 hours, infection at admission, or infection developing within the first 48 hours were excluded. The primary outcome was HAI incidence. Secondary outcomes included the standardized infection ratio, cumulative attributable difference, inflammatory markers, and microbiological findings. A total of 933 patients were screened, and 206 patients met the inclusion criteria (Group 20-21, n = 115; Group 19-20, n = 91). In the patient-based analysis, the HAI rate was significantly lower in Group 20-21 than in Group 19-20 (6.1% vs 22.0%, P < .001). Similar findings were observed in the episode-based analysis (10.4% vs 33.0%, P < .001). The time to infection onset was significantly longer in Group 20-21 (P = .003). Procalcitonin, C-reactive protein, white blood cell count, and lactate levels were significantly lower during the zero-visitation period. The standardized infection ratio for ventilator-associated pneumonia was significantly lower in Group 20-21 (P = .02). A marked reduction in the number of Acinetobacter spp. isolates was also observed during the pandemic. A zero-visitation policy in a non-COVID tertiary ICU was associated with lower HAI rates. The consistency of the surveillance indicators, inflammatory markers, and microbiological findings supports the observed association. However, these findings should not be attributed solely to visitor restrictions and should be interpreted in the context of multiple infection control measures implemented during the pandemic.

42888246.title: ICU-acquired pneumonia beyond pathogen detection.
42888246.abstract: Intensive care unit-acquired pneumonia is often treated as a binary diagnosis, although clinical deterioration, imaging and microbial detection describe different aspects of disease. This Perspective proposes an explicit, graded and revisable assessment of whether a detected organism plausibly causes the current lung injury. The framework encompasses pneumonia arising during ventilation, pneumonia that precedes intubation and pneumonia in non-ventilated ICU patients. It places molecular results within clinical, anatomical, microbiological and host context and uses formal reassessment at 48-72 hours to guide treatment continuation, narrowing or discontinuation.

42887216.title: Post-norepinephrine fluid volume and clinical outcomes in septic shock: a landmark retrospective cohort analysis of MIMIC-IV.
42887216.journal: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care
42887216.abstract: Fluid administered after norepinephrine initiation may reflect both resuscitation decisions and evolving illness severity, making observational comparisons susceptible to confounding and reverse causation. To evaluate associations between fluid volume during the first 6 h after norepinephrine initiation and mortality and incident invasive ventilation. We reconstructed an adult MIMIC-IV cohort with coded sepsis and norepinephrine initiated during ICU hours 0-24. Eligibility required complete pre-norepinephrine physiology and initial norepinephrine rate, survival, and ICU observation through a 6-hour landmark. Fluid exposure was ≤1,000 versus >1000 mL. Stabilized inverse-probability weights were truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles. Doubly adjusted logistic models used patient-clustered robust standard errors. The cohort included 2696 ICU stays from 2493 patients; 1572 received ≤1,000 mL. Maximum weighted standardized mean difference was 0.033. Twenty-eight-day mortality occurred in 1117 stays. Lower-volume exposure was not associated with mortality (odds ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.89-1.31; adjusted risks 42.6% versus 41.1%). Results were similar for other mortality analyses and thresholds. Among 1356 stays not ventilated at baseline, incident ventilation was not clearly associated with exposure (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.53-1.13). The spline showed no dose-response association (p = 0.983). After source-level cohort construction and expanded adjustment, post-norepinephrine fluid volume was not associated with mortality or incident invasive ventilation.

42886955.title: [Predictors of mortality and post-discharge quality of life in critically ill cancer patients].
42886955.abstract: The number of patients with cancer requiring intensive care is increasing. Critical illness and post-intensive care unit (ICU) syndrome may impair post-discharge recovery and quality of life. This study aimed to analyze ICU mortality, identify associated prognostic factors, and evaluate health-related quality of life after discharge in critically ill cancer patients. A prospective, observational, single-center cohort study was conducted including adults with oncologic disease admitted to a mixed ICU of a public hospital between 2021 and 2022. Clinical characteristics, illness severity, organ support, complications, and therapeutic adequacy were recorded. Quality of life was assessed at hospital discharge and at three months using the EQ-5D-3L instrument. Bivariate analyses and multivariable logistic regression were performed. A total of 204 patients with cancer were included. ICU mortality was 41.7%, and in-hospital mortality reached 53.4%. Independent predictors of ICU mortality were hospital length of stay before ICU admission, invasive mechanical ventilation, septic shock, higher SAPS II scores, and COVID-19 at admission. All EQ-5D-3L dimensions were impaired at discharge; at three months, only mobility and self-care improved. A substantial proportion of survivors did not resume oncologic therapy. Mortality was primarily driven by critical illness severity and the impact of COVID-19. Partial recovery of quality of life and difficulties in resuming cancer-directed treatment highlight the need to reinforce post-ICU follow-up and targeted rehabilitation in this vulnerable population.

42881501.title: Outcomes of Healthcare-Associated Infections in Respiratory Intensive Care Unit.
42881501.journal: Journal of Nepal Health Research Council
42881501.abstract: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are the major cause of morbidity and mortality. This study aimed to investigate the prevalence, microbiological profile, resistance patterns, risk factors, and outcomes of HAIs in a respiratory ICU (RICU) of a tertiary care hospital in Nepal. A prospective observational study was conducted in RICU. HAIs were diagnosed according to the CDC criteria. Descriptive statistics were reported as mean (SD) and frequencies. Unpaired t-tests, chi-square tests were used for comparisons, and multivariable logistic regression was used to assess the risk factors. Among 121 ICU admissions, 42 patients developed 50 episodes of HAI, yielding a prevalence of 34.7%. Ventilator-associated pneumonia was the most common HAIs. The most frequently isolated organisms were Acinetobacter baumannii in 42.0% and Klebsiella pneumonia in 18.0%. Both were resistance to Ceftriaxone. Resistance to Piperacillin-tazobactam were 85.8% and 77.8% and to carbapenems were 92% and 90% respectively. Tigecycline resistance was seen in 20% of Acinetobacter isolates and none of the Klebsiella isolates. Sensitivity to Polymyxin B was 100%. Mechanical ventilation, urinary catheters and history of prior hospitalization were the strongest predictors of HAI. Patients who developed HAI had a longer ICU stay (9.5 vs. 5.2 days, p=0.001) and higher mortality (28.6% vs. 13.9%, p=0.04). HAIs, particularly VAP caused by MDR organisms, were common in our ICU and there was a high resistance to beta lactams and carbapenem antibiotics. Low resistance to tigecycline and polymyxin B warrants careful stewardship.

42960561.title: Endpoint-specific mortality associated with malignancy among adults with sepsis or septic shock: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42960561.abstract: Sepsis is a major global health challenge and increasingly affects patients with complex conditions such as malignancy. Prior studies suggest higher mortality in this population, but interpretation is limited by aggregation of heterogeneous endpoints. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to clarify endpoint-specific prognostic associations between malignancy and mortality in adults with sepsis or septic shock. This study was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251141216). PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library and Epistemonikos were searched through 16 September 2025, for studies comparing all-cause mortality between sepsis patients with and without malignancy. Mortality endpoints were grouped as ICU, in-hospital, early, intermediate and extended follow-up mortality. Crude odds ratios (ORs) were estimated using random-effects meta-analysis. Subgroup, meta-regression and sensitivity analyses were performed to explore heterogeneity and assess consistency. Among 105 eligible studies comprising 20,089,138 participants, 85 studies contributing 101 endpoint estimates were included in the primary synthesis. Pooled estimates were elevated across endpoints: ICU (OR 1.21, 95% CI 0.94-1.56), in-hospital (OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.69-2.13), early (OR 1.81, 95% CI 1.59-2.06), intermediate (OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.72-3.03) and extended follow-up mortality (OR 2.41, 95% CI 1.70-3.42). Associations were sustained for haematologic malignancy, concentrated in in-hospital and early mortality for metastatic disease and more modest for solid tumours. Sensitivity analyses were directionally consistent, although risk ratio estimates were generally smaller than ORs. Exploratory meta-regression suggested that severity-related covariates may contribute to heterogeneity. Malignancy was associated with higher mortality among adults with sepsis or septic shock, with variation across mortality endpoints and clinical contexts. These findings support endpoint-specific prognostic assessment and highlight the need for future studies to incorporate more granular cancer characteristics. Because the primary estimates were unadjusted, results represent overall prognostic associations rather than independent causal effects.

42879340.title: Clinical Course and Prognosis of the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition-Defined Malnutrition in Critically Ill Patients with Sepsis: A Multicenter Prospective Observational Study.
42879340.abstract: Sepsis is a critical condition with a high nutritional risk and mortality. Although the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM) criteria have been proposed for diagnosing malnutrition, their clinical relevance in sepsis remains unclear. Therefore, we conducted a descriptive study on GLIM-defined malnutrition in intensive care unit (ICU) patients with sepsis to investigate its clinical course and prognosis. This was a multicenter prospective study conducted at 15 centers. Malnutrition was identified at ICU admission when both phenotypic and etiologic criteria were present. The primary outcome was a composite of in-hospital mortality or a decline in activities of daily living (Barthel Index <90) at discharge. Secondary outcomes included ICU length of stay, use of parenteral nutrition, and days to achievement of each ICU Mobility Scale level. Among 254 patients, 106 (41.7%) had malnutrition. The malnutrition group showed a significantly higher occurrence of the composite of in-hospital mortality and Barthel index <90 (76.4% vs. 64.2%, p = 0.04) and had significantly longer ICU stays (7 vs. 5, p = 0.001). Total nutrition delivery did not significantly differ between groups, while a higher percentage of patients in the malnutrition group received parenteral nutrition (57.6% vs. 43.2%, p = 0.02). Significant delays in achieving higher mobility levels were observed in the malnutrition group. GLIM-defined malnutrition in patients with sepsis was significantly associated with the composite outcome of in-hospital mortality or Barthel index <90 at discharge. These results suggest the clinical importance of an early GLIM assessment after ICU admission.

42876967.title: Antibiotic prescribing appropriateness among critically ill patients at a single tertiary care center in the United Arab Emirates: a retrospective cohort study.
42876967.abstract: Despite expanding antimicrobial stewardship initiatives, evidence evaluating the appropriateness of antibiotic prescribing and its clinical implications in intensive care settings in the United Arab Emirates remains limited. This study aimed to assess the appropriateness of antibiotic prescribing among intensive care unit patients, identify factors associated with appropriate antibiotic therapy, and examine its association with clinical outcomes. A retrospective cohort study was conducted in the intensive care unit of a tertiary care hospital in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi. Adult patients aged 18 years or older who were admitted between January 2023 and December 2024, had a length of stay exceeding 24 h but less than 30 days, received at least one systemic antibiotic, and had complete medical records were included. Data were extracted from electronic medical records and a regional health information exchange platform. Antibiotic appropriateness was evaluated against institutional or Infectious Diseases Society of America guidelines. Overall, 36% of patients received inappropriate antibiotic therapy. The most common reason for inappropriateness was the absence of a clear indication, particularly for postoperative prophylaxis (44.4%). At the individual agent level, cefepime (48.2%), metronidazole (36.2%), and cefazolin (33.9%) exhibited the highest rates of inappropriate use. Multivariable logistic regression identified positive microbiological culture results (AOR = 3.34, p < 0.001) and sepsis (AOR = 2.12, p = 0.002) as factors independently associated with higher odds of appropriate antibiotic use. Conversely, the presence of a central venous catheter (AOR = 0.30, p = 0.003) was associated with lower odds of appropriate antibiotic use. Appropriate antibiotic therapy was associated with higher odds of organ dysfunction (AOR = 1.69, p = 0.032), nosocomial infection (AOR = 2.28, p = 0.005), and persistent infection despite therapy (AOR = 2.13, p = 0.005). Approximately one-third of patients received inappropriate antibiotic therapy, representing a substantial antimicrobial stewardship concern despite the observed strengths in culture-guided therapy and infection-focused management.

42876204.title: Letter to the Editor: Association Between Fluid Overload and Pressure Injuries in ICU Patients With Sepsis: A Retrospective Cohort Study.

42872928.title: Population pharmacokinetics of piperacillin based on multicenter data to support model-informed precision dosing in critically ill women.
42872928.abstract: Sex-specific differences in pharmacokinetics are increasingly recognized as clinically relevant, yet most population pharmacokinetic models for antibiotics have been developed in predominantly male populations with limited transferability to female patients. This study aimed to develop and externally evaluate a population pharmacokinetic model of piperacillin specifically for critically ill women to support model-informed precision dosing (MIPD). A total of 923 samples from 165 critically ill women (from four previously published studies) receiving piperacillin/tazobactam were analyzed. The data set was randomly split into a training set (80%) and an independent external evaluation set (20%). Non-linear mixed-effects modeling was employed based on the training data using NONMEM, and covariates were identified using stepwise covariate modeling with cross-validation. Prediction accuracy and bias were quantified using the median prediction error (MDPE) and the median absolute prediction error (MDAPE) in an MIPD scenario. Model predictions for future concentrations were generated both a priori and through Bayesian forecasting based on one prior sample. A two-compartment model provided the best fit for the data. Clearance was significantly affected by renal function estimated by the Cockcroft-Gault equation, along with procalcitonin and serum albumin. The external evaluation demonstrated strong predictive performance with very low systematic bias. In the MIPD scenario, a priori predictions exhibited good predictive performance (MDPE < |5.2|%, MDAPE < 33.4%), which substantially improved with Bayesian forecasting (MDPE < |3.2|%, MDAPE < 19.1%). A female-specific population pharmacokinetic model of piperacillin was developed and externally validated, demonstrating robust predictive performance and clear benefits for Bayesian forecasting.

42872916.title: Long-Lasting Mental Disorders in Caregivers of ICU Sepsis Survivors and Their Association With Patients' Post-Intensive Care Syndrome: A Prospective Multicenter Cohort Study.
authors: Investigating Long-term Outcomes of ICU patients with Sepsis or Septic shock (ILOSS) Study Group
42872916.abstract: To investigate the prevalence of long-term mental disorders in caregivers of ICU sepsis survivors and examine associations with post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) in patients. Prospective observational study. Twenty-one mixed ICUs. Caregivers (the next of kin) of the patients diagnosed with sepsis between November 2020 and April 2022. None. Caregivers and patients were assessed at 3, 6, and 12 months after hospital discharge by telephone and mail. The primary outcome was caregiver mental disorders (mental post-intensive care syndrome-family [PICS-F]). Mixed-effects logistic regression analyses were performed to evaluate the association between caregiver PICS-F and patient PICS. Ninety-four caregiver-patient dyads were analyzed. Caregivers were a median of 67 years old (55-79 yr old), 31 (33.0%) were male, and 41 (43.6%) were spouses. Patients were a median of 74 years old (69-82 yr old), and 54 (57.4%) were male. The prevalence of mental PICS-F did not decrease from 3 to 12 months (43% vs. 42%, respectively), whereas the presence of PICS symptoms in patients decreased from 82% to 62%. In mixed-effects logistic regression, the presence of PICS symptoms in patients was significantly associated with PICS-F (adjusted odds ratio, 3.00; 95% CI, 1.54-5.88; p < 0.01). Among the individual patient PICS domains, only mental PICS was significantly associated with PICS-F (3.71; 2.03-6.77; p < 0.01), whereas physical and cognitive impairments in patients were not. The prevalence of mental PICS-F in caregivers of ICU sepsis survivors was frequent and long-lasting over the first year after hospital discharge. Since it was most strongly associated with patients' mental disorders rather than physical or cognitive impairments, the mental PICS domain in patients may be an important indicator of PICS-F and should be considered in future studies.

42871375.title: Nonlinear association of early serum albumin with 28-day ICU mortality in adults with an admission diagnosis of sepsis: a multicenter eICU cohort study.
42871375.abstract: Serum albumin is frequently measured early in intensive care, but its relation to short-term outcome in adults admitted with sepsis has varied across observational studies. We examined the shape and consistency of the association between early serum albumin and 28-day ICU mortality in a multicenter cohort. We conducted a retrospective multicenter cohort study using original eICU Collaborative Research Database version 2.0 tables. Adults with admission-diagnosis text containing sepsis were eligible. The exposure was the first valid albumin measurement obtained within 24 h of ICU admission and before ICU discharge; the endpoint was ICU death within 28 days. Hospital-clustered logistic regression and restricted cubic splines were used. Prespecified analyses addressed measurement timing, missing data, selective albumin testing, short stays, repeated admissions, and discharge alive as a competing event. Among 23,124 adults with an admission diagnosis containing sepsis, 13,634 (59.0%) had an eligible early albumin measurement. The primary cohort included 11,424 ICU stays and 1,161 deaths. In the primary complete-case model (n = 10,795; 1,105 deaths), each 1 g/dL higher albumin concentration was associated with lower odds of 28-day ICU mortality (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.48-0.62). Restricted cubic spline analysis in the same complete-case population showed an overall association and nonlinearity (both P < 0.001), with the steepest risk gradient at lower albumin concentrations. Estimates remained directionally consistent in severity-expanded, multiple-imputation, inverse-probability-weighted, short-stay, Cox, and competing-risk analyses. Early serum albumin was nonlinearly associated with 28-day ICU mortality and may provide complementary information for early risk assessment, particularly at lower concentrations. The clinical utility of particular concentration ranges and the effects of albumin administration require prospective evaluation.

42869163.title: Association between iron metabolism biomarkers and all-cause mortality in critically ill patients with sepsis: a retrospective cohort study.
42869163.journal: Clinica chimica acta; international journal of clinical chemistry
42869163.abstract: Iron metabolism disorders were frequently observed in sepsis, yet their association with outcomes remained incompletely understood. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of iron-related biomarkers and to develop models for predicting 30-day mortality in septic patients. This retrospective cohort study analyzed 2729 sepsis patients from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database to evaluate the prognostic value of iron metabolism biomarkers and to develop machine learning-based prediction models for 30-day mortality. We assessed associations using Kaplan-Meier analysis, multivariable Cox regression, and restricted cubic spline regression. Six machine learning models were developed and internally validated using 100 bootstrap resamples. The 30-day mortality rate was 19.57%. Ferritin levels above 680 ng/mL were associated with the strongest mortality risk increase, while transferrin above 160 mg/dL demonstrated a protective effect. Restricted cubic spline analysis revealed nonlinear relationships, with serum iron exhibiting an inverted U-shaped association between 35 and 328 μg/dL. The Light Gradient Boosting Machine model incorporating iron biomarkers achieved a validation area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.782 (0.743-0.819), with significant reclassification improvement (Net Reclassification Improvement: 0.076, p = 0.006). Iron metabolism biomarkers provide significant incremental prognostic value for 30-day mortality in sepsis patients. Integrating them into machine learning models enhances risk stratification beyond traditional clinical scores, offering a clinically actionable tool for early identification of high-risk patients.

42868988.title: Central line-associated bloodstream infections outside the intensive care unit: Burden, pathogens, and antimicrobial susceptibility identified through a Victorian surveillance program.
42868988.abstract: Prevention of central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) is a priority in Australian intensive care units (ICUs). However, the epidemiology of CLABSI in non-ICU settings remains inadequately characterised, despite extensive use of central lines beyond the ICU. We aimed to determine CLABSI rates and microbiological aetiology in non-ICU wards and to compare these with corresponding ICU data from Victorian hospitals. CLABSI surveillance was undertaken voluntarily in non-ICU wards by Victorian health services between 2014 and 2025, utilising the Victorian Healthcare Associated Infection Surveillance System (VICNISS) CLABSI surveillance module, capturing CLABSI rates per 1000 central line days (CLD) as well as bloodstream infections related to mucosal barrier injury (MBI-BSI), in accordance with CDC/NHSN criteria. Retrospective analysis was performed to determine rates, pathogens, and antimicrobial susceptibility. Sixteen facilities participated in surveillance during the study period. 67 CLABSI events and 66,096 central line days were reported in non-ICU wards (predominantly haematology-oncology), corresponding to a CLABSI rate of 1.01 per 1000 CLD, which was significantly higher than the contemporaneous ICU CLABSI rate of 0.50 per 1000 CLD (IRR 3.13, 95% CI 1.88-5.22, p = 0.000). The most frequent pathogens responsible for non-ICU CLABSI were coagulase-negative Staphylococcus spp., Staphylococcus aureus, and Pseudomonas spp. A large burden of MBI-BSI events (n = 90) were also reported. CLABSI rates outside ICU are significantly higher than those reported in ICU settings. A substantial burden of CLABSI and MBI-BSI events were identified in haematology-oncology populations, supporting focused surveillance and infection prevention efforts in these high-risk cohorts.

42867743.title: The use of capillary refill time In adult critically ill patients: a narrative review on potentials, pitfalls, and perspectives.
42867743.journal: Journal of clinical monitoring and computing
42867743.abstract: The evolution of Capillary refill time (CRT) use in clinical medicine is interesting, transforming a simple bedside observation into a reliable tool for assessing tissue perfusion in critically ill patients. When Henry Beecher and colleagues first systematized CRT measurement in 1947, they recognized its potential as a rapid method to evaluate circulatory status in trauma casualties, establishing a foundational framework that would influence intensive care practice for decades to come. However, clinicians soon discovered that relying on visual inspection alone introduced troubling variability between observers and even within the same observer's assessments, with expertise and training significantly influencing measurement accuracy. This recognition of CRT's limitations sparked a concerted effort to transform the measurement from a purely subjective exercise into a standardized, objective clinical tool. Researchers systematically refined protocols by establishing consistent pressure application techniques, standardized measurement sites, and defined normal thresholds (approximately 3 s for healthy adults). These methodological advances set the stage for rigorous clinical validation. Subsequent research revealed that CRT correlated powerfully with microvascular blood flow and independently predicted mortality and organ dysfunction in septic patients. Meta-analyses encompassing over 60,000 patients confirmed that abnormal CRT carried substantially elevated mortality risk, particularly when measured using standardized techniques. More recently, the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK trials demonstrated that CRT could serve not merely as a prognostic marker but as an actionable resuscitation target. CRT is nowadays considered an adjunct bedside marker to guide fluid and vasopressor resuscitation in adults with sepsis and septic shock, supporting individualized hemodynamic strategies while reducing over-resuscitation risks.

42861073.title: Multiple Neurological Complications and Multidrug-Resistant Bacterial Infections During Prolonged Intensive Care for Undocumented Meningoencephalitis in Côte d'Ivoire: A Case Report.
42861073.abstract: Acute meningoencephalitis requiring intensive care may be complicated by severe neurological injury and nosocomial infections. Hydrocephalus is well recognized, whereas spinal cord ischemia, central diabetes insipidus, and flaccid tetraparesis are rarely reported. Their coexistence, together with successive infections involving multidrug-resistant organisms, presents substantial diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. A previously healthy 32-year-old man presented with neck and back pain following a road traffic accident, subsequently developing cerebellar signs, acute confusion, and meningeal signs without fever. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed neutrophilic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and marked hypoglycorrhachia. Microbiological investigations were negative, and no causative pathogen was identified. Empirical antimicrobial therapy was followed by normalization of the CSF leukocyte count by hospital day 6. Despite this initial response, the patient required mechanical ventilation and developed shunt-dependent tetraventricular hydrocephalus, probable central diabetes insipidus, imaging findings suggestive of thoracic spinal cord ischemia, and areflexic flaccid tetraparesis with diffuse axonal sensorimotor neuropathy. His prolonged intensive care course was further complicated by successive nosocomial infections involving multidrug-resistant bacteria. He died on hospital day 70 from septic shock associated with Enterobacter cloacae bacteremia and multiorgan failure. Negative microbiological findings do not exclude meningoencephalitis when clinical and CSF abnormalities support the diagnosis, although alternative etiologies require consideration. Improvement in CSF findings does not preclude subsequent neurological deterioration or nosocomial infection. Continued neurological assessment, rigorous infection-prevention measures, and prompt investigation of suspected nosocomial infections remain essential throughout prolonged intensive care, particularly in resource-limited settings.

42861006.title: Process mapping of a collaborative quality improvement study to optimise the use of antibiotics in intensive care units in Argentina: a Pathfinder study.
42861006.abstract: To systematically document the operational components, barriers, facilitators, and solutions of a quality improvement collaborative for antibiotic stewardship in intensive care units (ICUs) in the public sector of Argentina, using the Pathfinder methodological framework. Retrospective, descriptive observational study using mixed methods. Data sources included a documentary review of protocols, standard operating procedures, monitoring reports, and host study publications; an online survey with closed and open-ended questions administered to research team members; interviews with team researchers to estimate effort and triangulation with findings from the host study's previously published process evaluation, structured according to Normalisation Process Theory. Integration was performed using the Pathfinder Tracker. Analysis combined descriptive statistics with content analysis of open-ended responses. Eleven stages of the research process were mapped, from question formulation to dissemination, with an estimated total effort of approximately 1,020 person-hours. The stages with the highest perceived difficulty (4/5) were ethical and institutional approvals, data collection, analysis, and dissemination, which together accounted for approximately 50% of the total estimated effort. Barriers were identified across three domains: institutional and regulatory (heterogeneity of ethical requirements, absence of stable local coordinators, publication costs); operational and technical (complex data collection forms, displacement of implementation focus due to the burden of data collection, variable connectivity); and human resources and capacity (clinical workload, staff turnover, insufficient training in implementation science). Solutions included a collaborative format with mentoring, agile communication via accessible digital tools (REDCap, WhatsApp, Zoom), and the use of theoretical frameworks for structuring (NPT, CFIR). The Pathfinder framework enabled a systematic reconstruction of the host study's processes, revealing barriers and solutions that conventional results reports do not capture. The findings are relevant for research teams in middle-income countries designing quality improvement collaboratives in complex hospital settings.

42859645.title: Improving Antibiotic Stewardship Through a Retrospective Study of the Diagnostic Value of Nasal Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus Polymerase Chain Reaction for Pneumonia in Intensive Care Unit Settings.
42859645.abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a major cause of pneumonia in intensive care unit settings. Nasal swabs with subsequent polymerase chain reaction (PCR) are commonly performed in hospitals and intensive care units to screen for MRSA nasal colonization. A retrospective data analysis of patients presenting to the intensive care unit at the University of North Carolina Health Southeastern between January 1, 2024, and December 31, 2024, was performed. The goal was to evaluate the correlation between MRSA PCR results from nasal swabs and the presence of MRSA in lower respiratory cultures. The sensitivity of MRSA nasal swabs in the intensive care unit for the growth of MRSA in lower respiratory cultures was 90% (18/20). The positive predictive value of MRSA nasal swabs for the growth of MRSA in lower respiratory cultures was 60% (18/30). These retrospective study data indicate that an MRSA nasal swab may have good clinical utility. A negative MRSA nasal swab may substantially lower the likelihood of MRSA in a lower respiratory culture. These findings also indicate that a positive MRSA nasal swab alone may not mandate anti-MRSA therapy. However, large-scale studies across diverse intensive care settings are necessary to confirm these findings.

42859641.title: Clinical and Economic Outcomes Associated with Rapid Antimicrobial Susceptibility Reporting and Dual-Card Testing in ICU Bloodstream Infections.
42859641.abstract: To evaluate the clinical and economic outcomes associated with implementation of an optimized blood culture workflow in intensive care unit (ICU) patients with bloodstream infections. From March 2022 to June 2023, the laboratory implemented a multi-modal workflow optimization including satellite blood culture incubation in the emergency department, upgraded blood culture bottles, rapid MALDI-TOF MS identification, automated rapid antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) reporting, and dual AST cards for Gram-negative bacteria. The pre-optimization group included 107 adult ICU patients with positive blood cultures (March 2021 - February 2022). The post-optimization group included 153 patients (September 2023 - August 2024). Compared to the final AST report in the pre-optimization group, the rapid AST report in the post-optimization group was 19.6 hours faster (P < 0.001). Total antibiotic use duration was 1.5 days shorter (P = 0.055). Use of two broad-spectrum antibiotics, meropenem (P < 0.001) and tigecycline (P = 0.045), decreased significantly. Hospital length of stay was 5 days shorter (P = 0.006). In unadjusted comparisons, antibiotic and hospitalization costs were reduced by 4871 CNY ([US$ 684], P < 0.001) and 13,336 CNY ([US$ 1873], P = 0.073), respectively. This multimodal workflow optimization for ICU patients with BSIs, incorporating automated rapid AST reporting and dual-AST-card-enabled expanded antimicrobial panels, shortened laboratory turnaround time. It was associated with earlier opportunities for targeted antimicrobial therapy and suggests potential clinical-economic benefits, alongside possible mitigation of antimicrobial-resistance risk.

42856644.title: Prognostic Impact of In-Hospital Emergency in Patients Admitted for Non-Surgical Intensive Care.
42856644.abstract: We aimed to elucidate the prognostic impact of in-hospital emergencies among patients who require non-surgical intensive care. In total, 4,483 patients requiring non-surgical intensive care from 2011 to 2021 were included. Patient backgrounds, in-hospital management, and prognoses were compared among 4 groups according to the hospitalization route: walk-ins (group A; n=636); ambulance (group B; n=2,748); helicopter/car-based emergency medical service (group C; n=565); and in-hospital emergencies (group D; n=534). The proportion of patients admitted to the intensive care unit after in-hospital emergencies was 38.0% among those with sepsis and 29.7% among those with other non-cardiovascular diseases. Furthermore, acute heart failure (AHF), sepsis and other non-cardiovascular disease were the most common diseases in patients with in-hospital emergencies (24.3%, 23.2% and 21.5%, respectively). Kaplan-Meier curve analysis revealed that the prognosis (365-day all-cause mortality) was significantly poorer in group D than in the other groups. A multivariable Cox regression model identified group D as an independent predictor of 365-day all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.227; 95% confidence interval 1.027-1.467) relative to out-of-hospital admissions, especially in AHF and non-cardiovascular disease. Patients who required non-surgical intensive care after in-hospital emergencies mainly have AHF and non-cardiovascular etiologies such as sepsis. In-hospital emergency was identified as a significant factor associated with a higher 365-day mortality rate. A clinical approach to reduce their mortality is urgently needed.

42854718.title: Predictors of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales enteric colonization among patients admitted to a companion animal intensive care unit.
42854718.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
42854718.abstract: To estimate prevalence and identify factors associated with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) enteric colonization in companion animals admitted to an ICU. The study population included canine and feline patients admitted to The Ohio State University Veterinary Medical Center ICU between January 2024 and June 2025. In total, 5,552 rectal swabs were collected from 3,834 patients during routine screening. A retrospective case-control study included all CRE-positive patients (n = 61) and randomly selected CRE-negative controls (137). Cases were defined as ICU patients with at least 1 positive CRE fecal culture during hospitalization, whereas controls had no positive CRE fecal cultures during their hospitalization. Prevalence of CRE colonization was 1.59% (61 of 3,834 patients; 95% CI, 1.24% to 2.04%). Escherichia coli carrying blaNDM was the most frequently identified isolate, accounting for 78.7% (48 of 61 patients; 95% CI, 66.9% to 87.1%). Predictors of CRE colonization included increased comorbidity burden (unit OR, 1.96; 95% CI, 1.43 to 2.75), intact reproductive status (OR, 4.39; CI, 1.47 to 11.03), longer hospitalization (unit OR, 1.31; CI, 1.14 to 1.53), recent surgery (OR, 2.72; CI, 1.29 to 5.87), and antimicrobial use within the previous 3 months (OR, 2.71; CI, 1.23 to 6.07). These predictors suggest targets for infection prevention and control measures to protect patients and staff. The association between recent antimicrobial exposure and CRE colonization reinforces the importance of antimicrobial stewardship in veterinary medicine. Although uncommon, CRE-colonized patients can serve as reservoirs for transmission and are at risk of subsequent infection.

42852905.title: Epidemiology of medication-related problems and antimicrobial utilisation among critically ill cancer patients: Determinants, pharmacist interventions and clinical outcomes-A prospective observational study.
42852905.journal: Journal of oncology pharmacy practice : official publication of the International Society of Oncology Pharmacy Practitioners
42852905.abstract: BackgroundCritically ill patients with cancer are highly vulnerable to medication-related problems (MRPs) because of complex treatment regimens, organ dysfunction, immunosuppression, and extensive antimicrobial exposure.ObjectivesTo determine the prevalence, patterns, and determinants of MRPs; describe antimicrobial utilisation; evaluate clinical pharmacist interventions; and assess clinical outcomes.MethodsA prospective observational study was conducted over 14 months in an oncology ICU of a tertiary cancer centre. Adults admitted for ≥48 h were enrolled. MRPs were identified using the Pharmaceutical Care Network Europe classification V9.1. Antimicrobial utilisation was measured as defined daily doses (DDD) per 100 bed-days and classified according to WHO AWaRe categories. Pharmacist interventions were documented. Multivariate logistic regression identified predictors of MRP occurrence.ResultsAmong 325 patients (mean age 54.6 ± 12.3 years; 58.5% male), 268 (82.5%) experienced at least one MRP, with 612 identified (mean 1.88/patient). Treatment-effectiveness (38.1%) and treatment-safety (28.9%) problems predominated. Antimicrobials were prescribed in 296 patients (91.1%), with consumption of 142.6 DDD/100 bed-days; Watch agents accounted for 54.2%. Pharmacists made 540 interventions, of which 466 (86.3%) were accepted. Polypharmacy, prolonged ICU stay, renal impairment, hematological malignancy, and use of ≥2 concurrent antimicrobials independently predicted MRP occurrence. Mortality was higher among patients with unresolved or severe MRPs than among those without MRPs (34.2% vs 18.6%, p = 0.002).ConclusionMRPs were highly prevalent and associated with medication burden, organ dysfunction, malignancy type, and antimicrobial exposure, while pharmacist interventions showed a high acceptance rate, supporting their potential role in medication safety and antimicrobial stewardship.

42846593.title: Prognostic value of 48-h reassessment of a laboratory-derived frailty index in ICU patients with sepsis: model development in MIMIC-IV and external transport evaluation.
42846593.abstract: Static laboratory-derived frailty index (FI-lab) measures have been associated with adverse outcomes in sepsis, but the value of reassessing acute multisystem laboratory abnormality burden after initial resuscitation and transporting a prespecified model to a new clinical setting remains uncertain. We conducted a retrospective 48-h landmark study using MIMIC-IV for model development and an independent single-center ICU sepsis cohort from January 2020 to December 2025 for supportive single-center transport evaluation. FI-lab-23 was calculated from 23 routine laboratory variables using prespecified thresholds, with at least 17 components required, and was interpreted as an acute laboratory deficit-accumulation index rather than chronic frailty. The primary extended model added FI-lab-23 measured at 24-48 h to clinical variables; the strict secondary model additionally included lactate clearance. Fixed-horizon logistic regression predicted 28-day mortality among patients alive and remaining in the ICU at 48 h. MIMIC-IV coefficients were frozen and applied without refitting to the local cohort. Performance was assessed by discrimination, Brier score, calibration, and exploratory decision-curve analysis. Baseline/change parameterizations were treated as secondary specification analyses; sensitivity analyses addressed testing intensity, component completeness, and a fixed 10-component common-core FI. The primary MIMIC-IV development cohort included 6,153 patients with 1,594 deaths. Each 0.05 increase in 24-48 h FI-lab-23 was associated with higher 28-day mortality (OR: 1.178, 95% CI: 1.149-1.207). Optimism-corrected AUC was 0.710. Of 722 local landmark-eligible patients, 328 met the primary complete-case requirements (85 deaths). In this selected cohort, the frozen model achieved an AUC of 0.774, Brier score of 0.160, calibration intercept of 0.109, calibration slope of 1.273, and observed-to-expected ratio of 1.074. Baseline FI-lab did not improve fit after the 48-h level was known, and baseline-by-change interactions were not significant. The direction of association was preserved across sensitivity analyses, although effect magnitude varied with component-completeness criteria. FI-lab-23 reassessed at 24-48 h provided updated prognostic information for 28-day mortality in ICU patients with sepsis. The frozen MIMIC-IV model showed encouraging but imprecise performance in a selected single-center complete-case cohort. These findings constitute supportive transport evidence rather than definitive external validation, and larger multicenter studies are required before clinical implementation.

42846293.title: Gut microbiome diversity, genus-level variation, and associations with clinical features in critically ill patients.
42846293.abstract: Gut microbiota alterations are common in critical illness, but differences between critically ill patients with and without sepsis and their clinical relevance remain incompletely understood. We investigated gut microbial diversity, genus-level differences and their associations with inflammatory profiles and clinical outcomes in critically ill patients. This single-centre case-control study enrolled adult critically ill patients grouped by Sepsis-3 criteria. Gut microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing. The primary M2 model, adjusted for age, intra-abdominal infection, pre-sampling anti-anaerobic antibiotic exposure, APACHE II score, and chronic kidney disease, was used for all adjusted analyses. Alpha diversity was analyzed with HC3-robust linear regression; beta diversity with PERMANOVA, PERMDISP, and dbRDA. Genus-level primary discovery used Wilcoxon rank-sum with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR and |log2 fold change| threshold. Complementary sensitivity analyses used fully adjusted MaAsLin2 and ANCOM-BC2 with pseudo-count sensitivity. Associations of the four Wilcoxon-identified genera with clinical variables were assessed via partial Spearman correlations, logistic regression, and longitudinal mixed-effects models. Of 103 participants, 68 had sepsis and 35 did not. After M2 adjustment, Shannon, Simpson, and Pielou evenness were lower in sepsis (β = -0.60, -0.54, -0.60; all q = 0.025), whereas Chao1 richness and observed species did not differ. Bray-Curtis and Jaccard group effects did not meet FDR threshold. Wilcoxon identified higher Lactococcus_A and lower Ezakiella, Fenollaria, Peptoniphilus_B in sepsis. ANCOM-BC2 signals were not robust to pseudo-count sensitivity, and MaAsLin2 identified no significant genus (min q = 0.333), indicating genus-level findings inconsistent across methods. No cross-sectional clinical association met significance after FDR correction. Longitudinal analyses found time-by-genus interactions: Fenollaria with CRP (q = 0.010), Peptoniphilus_B with PCT (q = 0.042) and CRP (q = 0.010). Sepsis was associated with lower values for selected alpha-diversity measures, whereas differences in overall community composition were modest. Four genera met the primary FDR- and effect-size-adjusted Wilcoxon criteria, but genus-level differences were not consistently supported across Wilcoxon, ANCOM-BC2 and MaAsLin2, indicating these are exploratory signals rather than confirmed candidates. Associations with clinical features and inflammatory markers were limited; therefore, these findings should be considered exploratory and validated using multiple analytical approaches in independent cohorts.

42845719.title: Factors Associated with ICU Admission and In-Hospital Mortality in a Decade of HIV/AIDS Admissions to a Tertiary Hospital at the Epicenter of the Brazilian Epidemic (2015-2024).
42845719.abstract: South Brazil experiences disproportionately high HIV/AIDS morbidity and mortality. To characterize the regional epidemic profile, we evaluated HIV hospitalizations over time. In a retrospective cohort of adults hospitalized with HIV between 2015-2024 to a tertiary institution in Porto Alegre, data extracted from institutional records was analyzed for hospitalization outcomes. Severe outcomes (SO) were defined as critical care admission or in-hospital mortality. Among 5218 infectious disease hospitalizations, 3596 were due to HIV (69%), encompassing 2376 participants; 1555 (65%) met WHO stage III/IV criteria for advanced HIV disease (AHD). Most patients were white (65%), male (53%), urban (65%). Among AHD participants, 77% had not completed high school. From 2015 to 2024, median age of patients increased from 41 to 44 years (p < 0.001). Declines in new HIV diagnoses following admission (p = 0.017) and AHD admissions (p = 0.015) occurred over time; new HIV diagnoses in AHD patients remained unchanged (p = 0.107). AHD case fatality rate of 11% remained stable (p = 0.287). Tuberculosis was the most prevalent reason for admission (21%, n = 488) followed by bacterial pneumonia (14%, n = 312) in AHD patients. Bacterial pneumonia was leading cause of admission in non-AHD patients (12%, n = 151). OIs and nosocomial infections were implicated in over half of in-hospital mortalities. Factors associated with SO were sepsis, pneumocystis pneumonia, nosocomial infections, non-opportunistic malignancy, tuberculosis, new HIV diagnoses and/or CD4 < 50 cells/mm3. In south Brazil, late HIV diagnoses and barriers to care appear to drive mortality. Targeted efforts to diagnose and engage patients in care earlier are warranted to prevent severe outcomes.

42843214.title: Critical care escalation in the peripartum population; a single center retrospective study at an academic quaternary care center.
42843214.abstract: Identify the admission characteristics and interventions of patients transferred from a labor and delivery unit to an intensive care unit. Single-center, retrospective descriptive cohort study at an academic center. We identified 117 of 48,045 (0.2%) patients who required ICU transfer. Patients with multifetal gestation and cesarean delivery were more likely to be admitted to the ICU. Maternal early warning criteria were positive in 12% of patients in the ICU group compared to 4% of those not admitted to ICU (Odds Ratio [OR] 3.27, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 1.87 to 5.73; p < 0.001). A quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score of 1 and 2 was associated with an OR 6.45 (95% CI 4.28 to 9.72; p < 0.001) and 28.98 (95% CI 6.88 to 122.13; p < 0.001), respectively, for ICU admission compared to a score of 0. The most common indications for ICU admission were postpartum hemorrhage, sepsis, and respiratory failure. Vasoactive medications were required in 51% of patients admitted to the ICU. High flow nasal cannula, non-invasive ventilation, and intubation were described in 3%, 2%, and 40% of patients, respectively. 30% of patients did not require vasoactive infusions or respiratory support during ICU admission. The most common patient characteristics, medical comorbidities, and indications for ICU transfer were consistent with the published literature. Scoring systems performed reasonably well in differentiating patients who required escalation of care. A subset of patients may have benefitted from increased monitoring rather than ICU admission.

42842203.title: Intensive care infection score outperforms inflammatory biomarkers in detecting infection in critically ill patients.
