PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched from inception through September 19, 2025. Studies compared systemic prophylaxis versus none and/or ≤24 hours versus >24 hours. Seven US studies comprising 3274 patients met the inclusion criteria. Across studies, fracture-related infection rates were low and were not reduced by prophylactic antibiotics. In the largest prospective multicenter cohort, Mian et al reported a 30-day facial fracture-associated infection rate of 1.0%, with no significant benefit for ≤24 hours or >24 hours of prophylaxis compared with none (adjusted odds ratio 1.24-1.32). Orbital and zygomatic cohorts reported no infectious complications regardless of prophylaxis strategy. In sinus-involving and intensive care unit cohorts, fracture-site infection and sinusitis were rare; most infectious events were pneumonia or ventilator-associated pneumonia rather than facial fracture-specific infections. Longer antibiotic exposure was associated with isolated cases of Clostridioides difficile colitis. Available evidence does not support routine systemic prophylaxis for uncomplicated closed, nonoperative facial fractures. The strongest inference applies to patients without another indication for antibiotics. Current data do not identify fracture-specific subgroups in whom prophylaxis improves outcomes; accordingly, management should emphasize local care, return precautions, and structured follow-up.

42824758.title: Paradoxical Acute Hypoxemic Deterioration During Treatment of Bilateral Bronchopneumonia: A Case Report.
42824758.abstract: Community-acquired pneumonia may occasionally be associated with unexpected respiratory deterioration despite apparent clinical, laboratory, and radiological improvement. We report a case of a previously healthy adult male who presented with progressive dyspnea, persistent cough, generalized weakness, malaise, and low-grade fever. Initial chest radiography showed no significant abnormalities despite marked respiratory symptoms, whereas chest computed tomography revealed bilateral bronchopneumonia with multiple centrilobular nodules and patchy ground-glass opacities. The patient was treated with intravenous meropenem, systemic corticosteroids, inhaled therapy, supplemental oxygen, and supportive care, with gradual improvement in inflammatory markers. On hospital day three, however, he developed sudden severe hypoxemic respiratory failure shortly after antimicrobial administration, requiring intensive care unit admission and high-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy. Urgent CT pulmonary angiography excluded pulmonary embolism, follow-up imaging demonstrated partial regression of the pulmonary infiltrates, and cardiological evaluation showed no evidence of acute cardiac pathology. Meropenem was replaced with levofloxacin because a drug-related reaction could not be completely excluded. The patient's respiratory status subsequently improved rapidly with supportive treatment, and he was discharged without residual respiratory insufficiency. This case demonstrates that severe transient hypoxemic deterioration may occur during apparently successful treatment of bilateral bronchopneumonia and emphasizes the importance of promptly excluding pulmonary embolism, acute cardiac disease, drug-related reactions, and other potentially life-threatening causes of respiratory worsening.

42824716.title: Microbiological profiles of Gram-negative bacteria isolated from respiratory samples of mechanically ventilated patients at a tertiary Moroccan hospital.
42824716.abstract: To characterise the Gram-negative bacteria implicated in ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), focusing on their antimicrobial resistance profiles and phylogenetic relationships. Seventy-eight isolates were collected from protected distal samples over two years; patients were under mechanical ventilation in the three adult ICUs of a Moroccan tertiary hospital. Isolates were identified using VITEK2. PFGE and FTIR determined genetic relationships, whereas the detection of genetic resistance determinants was carried out using PCR. Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii harbouring the bla-OXA-23 was the predominant Gram-negative bacterium. Klebsiella pneumoniae was the most prevalent among the Enterobacterales, with a high resistance rate to almost all antibiotics, due to the coexistence of (bla) CTX-M-1, TEM, SHV, and OXA-48-like genes. Escherichia coli exhibited high resistance to ciprofloxacin (86%), ceftazidime (86%), and cotrimoxazole (71%). Proteus mirabilis was highly resistant to cotrimoxazole (60%) and ticarcillin (80%). Pseudomonas aeruginosa was resistant to carbapenems in 39% of cases, in which bla NDM and bla VIM were the only metallo-beta-lactamase genes detected. In phylogenetic analysis, both FTIR and PFGE techniques underscored no epidemiological relationship among strains. The prevalence of MDR and XDR bacteria among VAP cases in a tertiary hospital in Morocco is increasing, potentially due to the coexistence of antimicrobial resistance genes.

42954722.title: Consensus-derived clinical sepsis profiles and mortality across six international cohorts.
42954722.abstract: Clinical phenotyping may help characterize sepsis heterogeneity, but the applicability of derived profiles across healthcare settings remains uncertain. We evaluated consensus-derived clinical profiles and their associations with mortality across six international cohorts. We analyzed 62,458 adults from six critical care databases in four countries. In the MIMIC-IV discovery cohort (n = 28,733), six clustering algorithms were applied to 24 routinely available clinical variables to derive consensus profiles. The profiles were assigned in five external cohorts using fixed discovery-cohort templates. We examined clinical characteristics, mortality associations, and exploratory treatment-outcome associations. Three profiles were selected based on the Calinski-Harabasz peak and clinical interpretability. Profiles 1, 2, and 3 comprised 32.6%, 20.0%, and 47.4% of the discovery cohort, with in-hospital mortality of 30.3%, 13.8%, and 9.3%, respectively. Profile 1 showed greater multiorgan dysfunction, Profile 2 relatively preserved hemodynamics, and Profile 3 greater ventilatory support with less extrapulmonary dysfunction. Profile 1 had the highest mortality in all five external cohorts, with a decreasing mortality gradient across profiles in most cohorts. After adjustment for age and SOFA score, Profile 3 was associated with lower 1-year mortality than Profile 1 (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.57-0.67). Treatment-outcome associations were exploratory. Consensus-derived profiles characterized clinically interpretable patterns of sepsis heterogeneity with mortality differences across the evaluated cohorts. These findings support further evaluation of clinical profiling for risk stratification and phenotype-informed research.

42946130.title: Which spontaneous breathing trial should be used to reproduce post-extubation respiratory effort in COVID-19-related ARDS? A multicenter randomized crossover study.
42946130.abstract: Spontaneous breathing trials (SBT) guide extubation decisions in intensive care unit (ICU), predicting the respiratory effort required by the patient after extubation. Different SBTs exist and should be adapted to critical illness. Viral pneumonias such as COVID-19 combine lung injury, sepsis-induced systemic inflammation, and encephalopathy, making classification challenging. The objective was to assess which SBT could be used to reproduce postextubation respiratory effort in COVID-19-related acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) patients. In this multicenter randomized crossover study, COVID-19-related ARDS patients mechanically ventilated at least 24 hours and ready for extubation underwent 3 different 15-minute SBT at random order: pressure support ventilation of 7-cmH2O with positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 0-cmH2O (PSV7PEEP0), PSV 0-cmH2O with PEEP 0-cmH2O (PSV0PEEP0) and T-piece trial. At baseline, end of each SBT, and 20 minutes after extubation, surrogates of respiratory effort were measured: esophageal pressure-time-product (PTPes), PTPes per minute (PTPes.min), swing esophageal pressure (SwingPes), and SwingPes per minute (SwingPes.min). Sixty measurements of respiratory effort from 12 patients were analyzed. Median PTPes.min increased from 193.8 [170.8-227.2] cmH2O.s/min at baseline to 236.6 [192.1-313.6] after extubation, with no significant differences between SBTs and postextubation. SwingPes and SwingPes.min were lower during PSV7-PEEP0 than after extubation, with median paired differences of 4.7 (95% CI 0.6-9.8) and 115.3 (95% CI 4.8-297.8), but these differences did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons. No SBT modality differed significantly from post-extubation respiratory effort, suggesting that none could be excluded in COVID-19-related ARDS patients.

42944623.title: Low-Use vs. High-Use Physical Restraint in Older Adults With Sepsis Receiving Mechanical Ventilation: A Multicenter Randomized Clinical Trial.
42944623.journal: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
42944623.abstract: Physical restraints are commonly used in patients receiving mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit (ICU), yet evidence regarding their effectiveness in older patients with sepsis is limited. This study evaluated whether a low-use physical restraint strategy improves outcomes in older patients with sepsis requiring invasive mechanical ventilation. This multicenter, open-label, randomized controlled trial was conducted in five ICUs in China from August 2023 to March 2026. Patients aged ≥ 65 years with invasive mechanical ventilation were randomly assigned (1:1) to a low-use restraint strategy (restraints applied only for severe agitation) or a high-use restraint strategy (routine restraint use until recovery of consciousness and liberation from mechanical ventilation). The primary outcome was days alive without delirium or coma within 7 days after randomization. Secondary outcomes included delirium incidence, ventilator-free days, coma-free days, sedative exposure, 28-day mortality, and safety events. Analyses were performed using intention-to-treat, per-protocol, and inverse probability weighting approaches. Among 485 randomized patients (median age, 74 years; 60.4% male), 244 received low-use and 241 high-use restraint. Delirium- and coma-free days did not differ between groups (adjusted mean difference, 0.17 days; 95% CI, -0.20 to 0.54; p = 0.37). Low-use restraint was associated with more ventilator-free days (0.69 days; 95% CI, 0.48-0.91; p < 0.001) and coma-free days (0.46 days; 95% CI, 0.19-0.74; p = 0.001). No significant between-group differences were observed in delirium incidence, sedative exposure, 28-day mortality, or safety outcomes. Among older mechanically ventilated patients with sepsis, a low-use physical restraint strategy did not improve days alive without delirium or coma but was associated with more ventilator-free and coma-free days. These findings suggest that reducing restraint use may facilitate short-term recovery, although the safety of restraint minimization requires further evaluation. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: ChiCTR1900025850.

42943553.title: Predictive Performance of Inflammatory Markers for Severe Disease Progression in Measles: A Retrospective Cohort Analysis.
42943553.abstract: The recent European measles resurgence has driven record-high hospitalization, yet objective tools for early risk stratification remain scarce. This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of routine admission inflammatory biomarkers for predicting severe disease and prolonged hospitalization. We retrospectively analyzed 509 patients with laboratory-confirmed measles hospitalized during a Romanian outbreak (November 2023-August 2025). Severe disease was defined via a clinical composite endpoint (intensive-care admission, mechanical ventilation, supplemental oxygen, acute respiratory failure, or sepsis). Biomarker discriminative performance was assessed using receiver-operating-characteristic (ROC) curves, Youden-optimal cut-offs, and DeLong tests. Multivariable logistic and Cox proportional-hazards regression evaluated independent predictors of severity and time to discharge. The cohort exhibited a pediatric predominance (median age: 3.0 years; 20% infants) with an 82% unvaccinated rate; 33% developed severe disease. Interleukin-6 (IL-6) demonstrated superior diagnostic accuracy (AUC 0.863, 95% CI 0.820-0.898; cut-off ≥ 7 pg/mL, sensitivity 73%, specificity 93%), significantly outperforming ferritin (AUC 0.800) and conventional markers (all p < 0.001). Multivariable modeling established IL-6 and ferritin as the sole independent predictors of severity. All intensive-care admissions occurred exclusively for unvaccinated patients (5.0% vs. 0%). Severe disease, pneumonia, male sex, unvaccinated status and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) independently predicted prolonged hospitalization. Admission IL-6 and ferritin serve as robust, independent prognostic biomarkers that accurately identify high-risk measles patients, providing objective criteria with which to optimize clinical triage and inpatient management during outbreaks.

42943441.title: A Comprehensive Review of the Underlying Mechanisms of Resistance and Therapeutic Options for DTR-PA in Bloodstream Infection and Pneumonia: A Clinical Vignette-Based Approach.
42943441.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a ubiquitous opportunistic pathogen and a leading cause of severe healthcare-associated infections, particularly ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) and bloodstream infections (BSIs) in critically ill patients. Its remarkable capacity for both intrinsic and acquired resistance leads to complex phenotypic profiles, culminating in difficult-to-treat resistant P. aeruginosa (DTR-PA). Managing DTR-PA presents a daunting clinical challenge characterised by a narrow therapeutic armamentarium, treatment delays, and high attributable mortality. To bridge the gap between complex molecular microbiology and bedside decision-making, this narrative review employs a pragmatic, clinical vignette-based approach. Through six representative fictional scenarios of pneumonia and BSI, we systematically dissect the underlying mechanisms of resistance and their direct therapeutic implications. The vignettes explore combinations of intrinsic adaptations-such as Pseudomonas-derived cephalosporinase (PDC/AmpC) hyperexpression, OprD porin loss, and efflux pump upregulation-as well as the acquisition of serine- (e.g., GES) and metallo-β-lactamases (e.g., VIM, NDM, IMP). Grounded in the updated 2026 Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guidelines, we evaluate the optimal deployment of newer β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations. We highlight the specific preference for ceftolozane-tazobactam in pneumonia, the roles of ceftazidime-avibactam and imipenem-relebactam, and the critical use of cefiderocol for metallo-β-lactamase producers and highly resistant phenotypes. Furthermore, the review addresses pressing clinical controversies: the superiority of targeted monotherapy over historical, toxic combination regimens; the risks of unconditionally applying "shorter-is-better" duration paradigms to DTR-PA; and the alarming frequency of treatment-emergent cross-resistance among novel agents. We also clarify common clinical misconceptions, such as the limited utility of meropenem-vaborbactam and aztreonam-avibactam against specific pseudomonal mechanisms. Ultimately, effective DTR-PA management precludes class-based empirical assumptions. By providing a phenotype-driven bedside aide-mémoire, this review reinforces that rapid recognition, direct agent-specific antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD)-optimised dosing, and prompt source control remain the absolute cornerstones of survival for patients afflicted by these formidable infections.

42941358.title: A Simplified Physiology-Laboratory Score (PLS4) for Early Risk Stratification in Acute Cholangitis.
42941358.abstract: Objectives: Acute cholangitis is a common biliary infection in the emergency department (ED) that can progress rapidly to septic shock and multiorgan dysfunction. The Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG2018) is the current reference standard for severity assessment but may be cumbersome during the initial ED encounter. We aimed to develop a simplified physiology-laboratory score (PLS4) computable from four routine bedside variables and to compare its early risk-stratification performance with TG2018. Materials and Methods: This single-center retrospective observational cohort study included 482 adult patients with acute cholangitis (International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision code K83.0) presenting to a tertiary university hospital ED between January 2016 and December 2021. Primary outcomes were ICU admission, vasopressor use, and prolonged hospital stay (length of stay ≥ 14 days); intubation was analyzed as an exploratory outcome. PLS4 assigned 1 point each for albumin < 3.5 g/dL, systolic blood pressure ≤ 100 mmHg, heart rate ≥ 100/min, and prothrombin time-international normalized ratio ≥ 1.2 (range 0-4). Discrimination was assessed by receiver operating characteristic curves, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals and bootstrap optimism-corrected internal validation. Results: ICU admission occurred in 81 patients (16.8%), vasopressor use in 53 (11.0%), and prolonged stay in 111 (23.0%). The areas under the curve (AUCs) for ICU admission were 0.850 for TG2018 and 0.800 for PLS4 (p = 0.116), and the optimism-corrected AUC of PLS4 was 0.779. For vasopressor use, which is part of the TG2018 grade III definition, the AUCs were 0.936 and 0.843. When PLS4 was added to TG2018, the AUC for ICU admission increased to 0.886. At PLS4 ≥ 3, specificity reached 0.978 for ICU admission and 0.970 for vasopressor use, with event rates rising stepwise from 5.96% to 100% and 2.55% to 90.0%, respectively. Conclusions: In this single-center derivation study, PLS4 showed high specificity and added prognostic information to TG2018. It should be validated in other centers before clinical use.

42936115.title: Case Report: Sepsis With Multisystemic Amyloid Light-Chain Amyloidosis.
42936115.abstract: Systemic light-chain (AL) amyloidosis is a complex disorder characterized by extracellular fibril deposition, leading to severe multisystem dysfunction. When sepsis superimposes on preexisting organ impairment, early clinical recognition becomes particularly challenging yet critical. We present a case of a 60-year-old female who presented with generalized edema, dyspnea, and cardiac/renal involvement, subsequently diagnosed with AL amyloidosis based on laboratory, imaging, bone marrow biopsy, and Congo red staining findings. Following chemotherapy with bortezomib and cyclophosphamide, the patient experienced transient cardiac arrest, received an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, and subsequently developed massive ascites. Upon developing Pseudomonas guariconensis bacteremia, she progressed to septic shock requiring intensive care unit admission, mechanical ventilation, vasopressor support, and targeted antimicrobial therapy. Through aggressive supportive care and source control, hemodynamic stabilization was achieved, allowing successful extubation and transfer to the general ward. Superimposed sepsis on severe, multi-organ amyloidosis significantly complicates diagnosis and management. High clinical vigilance, early infection recognition, and prompt targeted therapy are essential to prevent fatal outcomes in patients with preexisting chronic organ dysfunctions.

42934935.title: Prognostic significance of nucleated red blood cells in trauma patients.
42934935.abstract: Nucleated red blood cells are early erythroid precursors typically confined to the bone marrow. Their appearance in peripheral blood reflects stress erythropoiesis and has been linked to hypoxia and systemic inflammation. While nucleated red blood cells have prognostic value in sepsis and critical illness, their significance in trauma remains poorly understood. This study aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of nucleated red blood cells during the first 10 days in the intensive care unit following severe trauma, and their association with 30-day mortality. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study including 1636 adult trauma patients admitted to the Reims Level-1 Trauma Center between January 2019 and March 2025, recorded in the TraumaBase© registry. Nucleated red blood cell counts were measured daily for the first 10 intensive care unit days. K-means clustering identified four nucleated red blood cell phenotypes based on temporal patterns. Outcomes included 10- and 30-day mortality, incidence of acute respiratory distress syndrome, septic shock, mechanical ventilation, and length of stay. Survival analyses used Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, Injury Severity Score, Simplified Acute Physiology Score II, and the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment, and propensity-weighted regression assessed dichotomised nucleated red blood cell status. Nucleated red blood cells were detected in 221 patients (13.5%). Phenotype classification revealed: transient early nucleated red blood cells (phenotype 1), single peak (phenotype 2), multiple intermittent peaks (phenotype 3), and persistent elevation (phenotype 4). Phenotype 2 was associated with reduced 10-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 0.06, 95% confidence intervals 0.01-0.46), while phenotype 4 exhibited markedly increased mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 9.6, 95% confidence intervals 2.23-41.4, P < 0.001). Nucleated red blood cell+ patients had higher risks of acute respiratory distress syndrome, septic shock, mechanical ventilation, and 30-day mortality. Kaplan-Meier curves confirmed significant differences in survival across phenotypes (log-rank P < 0.001). Nucleated red blood cell presence, particularly persistent elevation, identifies trauma patients at higher risk of adverse outcomes. Routine, daily nucleated red blood cell monitoring may serve as a simple, low-cost prognostic tool in intensive care unit trauma care. Prospective studies are needed to validate these findings and integrate nucleated red blood cell dynamics into risk stratification.

42933694.title: Comparison of meropenem-based triple therapy vs minocycline-based triple therapy for carbapenem resistant Acinetobacter baumannii ventilator associated pneumonia - a prospective observational study.
42933694.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) resulted from Carbapenem-Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) poses serious treatment challenges. Our objective was to assess two triple medication combinations for VAP caused by CRAB. This prospective observational research was performed in the critical care unit of an academic medical center from January 2024 to March 2025. Two hundred adult patients with culture-proven CRAB-VAP were enrolled and treated with either minocycline-polymyxin-sulbactam or meropenem-polymyxin-sulbactam. Various outcomes assessed were clinical recovery, 7 and 28-day mortality, microbiological eradication, duration of ICU and hospital stay. The clinical recovery rates were comparable in both groups (54% minocycline vs. 47% meropenem, p = 0.322). The microbiological eradication rate was similar (39%) at day 28 in both groups. Patients treated with the minocycline regimen had significantly shorter ICU stay (16 vs. 18 days, p = 0.003) and hospital stays (24 vs. 28 days, p < 0.001) than the meropenem group. There was no significant difference between 7-day mortality (21% vs. 32%, p = 0.078) or 28-day mortality (46% vs. 53%, p = 0.322). Minocycline-based triple therapy was comparable to meropenem-based therapy in treating CRAB-VAP, with potential advantages in reducing duration of ICU and hospital stay. Minocycline may be a suitable alternative for CRAB-VAP in resource-limited settings.

42933334.title: Doxycycline versus azithromycin in combination with beta-lactams for hospitalized community-acquired pneumonia: A propensity score-matched cohort study.
42933334.abstract: Azithromycin plus a beta-lactam is a commonly used empiric regimen for hospitalized community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). Concerns about azithromycin resistance and patient-specific safety considerations have increased interest in doxycycline as an alternative; however, comparative effectiveness data for these two regimens remain scarce. Using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network (240 healthcare organizations; data accessed June 14, 2026), we conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults hospitalized with CAP between January 2016 and December 2023. Doxycycline plus beta-lactam recipients were compared with azithromycin plus beta-lactam recipients following 1:1 nearest-neighbor propensity score matching (11,906 patients per group). Thirty-day and 90-day all-cause mortality did not differ significantly between groups (HR: 1.03, 95% CI: 0.95-1.12; and HR: 1.06, 95% CI: 0.98-1.14, respectively), whereas 180-day mortality was modestly but significantly higher in the doxycycline cohort (HR: 1.08, 95% CI: 1.02-1.16; p = 0.014). Doxycycline-based therapy was associated with a consistently lower risk of antibiotic escalation at all time points assessed (RR: 0.59-0.65; p < 0.001). The 30-day risk of incident sepsis was significantly higher with doxycycline (RR: 1.29, 95% CI: 1.03-1.61; p = 0.024). ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, vasopressor use, and Clostridioides difficile infection did not differ significantly between the two groups. No statistically significant difference in 30-day mortality was detected between doxycycline plus beta-lactams and azithromycin plus beta-lactams. This finding does not establish equivalence or noninferiority. Secondary findings, including 30-day sepsis and 180-day mortality, were exploratory and require confirmation in prospective randomized studies.

42930678.title: Epidemiological Characteristics, Species Distribution, and Antifungal Resistance Profiles of Candidemia Cases.
42930678.abstract: Local species distribution and antifungal susceptibility are important for empirical candidemia management. We retrospectively evaluated patients with Candida-positive blood cultures from August 2019 to May 2024. Episodes were defined using a 30-day window; species distribution and susceptibility were analysed at the episode-species level and outcomes at the patient level. Among 566 patients, 605 episodes and 637 episode-species isolates were identified. Non-albicans Candida accounted for 59.7%; C. albicans (40.3%) and C. parapsilosis (34.2%) predominated. Of 217 C. parapsilosis isolates tested, 66 (30.4%) were fluconazole-susceptible, 58 (26.7%) were susceptible dose-dependent, and 93 (42.9%) were resistant. Recurrent candidemia occurred in 37 patients and documented microbiological persistence in 128 (22.6%); persistence was more frequent when the index culture included C. parapsilosis (27.6% vs. 20.1%; OR 1.52, 95% CI 1.01-2.28). Among 32 patients with a shared species in the initial and first recurrent episodes, newly detected resistance occurred in three, all involving fluconazole-resistant C. parapsilosis. Thirty-day all-cause mortality was 57.4%; older age, ICU care, mechanical ventilation, and solid malignancy were independently associated with higher mortality. These findings suggest that empirical reliance on fluconazole may be inappropriate in settings with similar resistance patterns and support species-level identification, repeat blood cultures, and episode-specific susceptibility testing.

42921992.title: Streptococcus constellatus-Associated Lemierre Syndrome Presenting With Cavitating Septic Pulmonary Emboli Managed by Video-Assisted Thoracoscopy.
42921992.journal: The American journal of case reports
42921992.abstract: BACKGROUND Lemierre syndrome is a rare septic thromboembolic disorder. Although historically associated with Fusobacterium necrophorum, non-fusobacterial cases caused by Streptococcus constellatus can present with dominant thoracic sepsis and delayed recognition. CASE REPORT A 25-year-old previously healthy man from northern Ecuador presented with 7 days of dyspnea, productive cough, fever, and hemoptysis, with profound hypoxemia and respiratory distress. Chest computed tomography showed bilateral cavitating septic pulmonary emboli and necrotizing pulmonary infection, and cervical vascular imaging confirmed left internal jugular vein thrombosis. One blood culture set grew Streptococcus constellatus susceptible to penicillin and ceftriaxone; sputum and pleural fluid cultures were sterile. He required intensive care, endotracheal intubation, empiric piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin, escalation to meropenem plus vancomycin during clinical deterioration while resistant or polymicrobial infection was considered, therapeutic anticoagulation, and 2 video-assisted thoracoscopic procedures for empyema and a subsequent pulmonary abscess. After 4 weeks of intravenous antibiotics, he improved and was discharged on a direct oral anticoagulant for 1 additional month, remaining asymptomatic at short-term follow-up. CONCLUSIONS Lemierre syndrome should be considered in young adults with severe sepsis and multifocal cavitating lung lesions, even without pharyngeal symptoms. Empiric therapy should initially cover oral aerobes and anaerobes; once penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus constellatus is confirmed and no co-pathogen is recovered, de-escalation to targeted beta-lactam therapy, such as penicillin G or ceftriaxone, should be considered together with drainage of empyema or abscess when present.

42919446.title: Metabolic Syndrome Is Associated With Worsened Clinical Outcomes in Individuals With Necrotizing Pancreatitis.
42919446.abstract: Evaluate the relationship between metabolic syndrome (MetS) and clinical outcomes in individuals with necrotizing pancreatitis (NP) and infected pancreatic necrosis (IPN). MetS affects a significant proportion of the global population and is associated with low-grade systemic inflammation and immune dysregulation. This has implications for several disease processes, but the impact of MetS on patients with NP is not well characterized. A retrospective cohort study of patients admitted with NP at a single tertiary center was performed. MetS was defined as meeting any 3 of the following criteria: BMI ≥30 kg/m2, triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL, fasting glucose ≥110 mg/dL, blood pressure ≥130/85 mm Hg, and low HDL (<40 mg/dL men, <50 mg/dL women). The need for intensive care, hospital length of stay, development of organ failure, and mortality were compared in patients with NP with or without MetS. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of IPN. A total of 276 (154 MetS, 55.8%) patients were identified. Individuals with MetS more frequently required ICU-level care (38.3% vs. 17.2%; P<0.001) and longer length of stay (9.0 vs. 5.0 d; P=0.029). There was a higher risk of sepsis in those with MetS (27.5% vs. 15.6%; P=0.019), as well as respiratory failure (31.2% vs. 18%; P=0.013), renal failure (35.7% vs. 21.3%; P=0.009), and in-hospital mortality (17.5% vs. 8.2%; P=0.024). The incidence of IPN was higher in patients with MetS (39.6% vs. 23.0%; P=0.003). The presence of MetS in individuals with NP was associated with worsened outcomes, including increased incidence of IPN, sepsis, organ failure, ICU admission, and mortality during index hospitalization.

42903899.title: Limiting collateral damage: Nosocomial infections in patients with temporary mechanical circulatory support.
42903899.abstract: The use of temporary mechanical circulatory support (tMCS) and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for patients with cardiopulmonary compromise is on the rise. While these tMCS systems provide life-saving interventions, they also pose a significant risk of nosocomial infections, which are associated with higher mortality rates. Patients receiving tMCS are critically ill and require intensive care, increasing their vulnerability to infections. Common nosocomial infections include bloodstream infections (BSI) and ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) in patients with ECMO and wound-related complications in patients with microaxial temporary ventricular assist devices (tVADs). Key preventative measures include the incorporation of sound ICU practices such as chlorhexidine washes, minimizing disconnections, instituting VAP bundles, and promoting enteral nutrition. The practice of continuing prophylactic antibiotics while patients are on ECMO is not routinely recommended. While treatment strategies hinge primarily on antibiotics, ensuring adequate therapeutic levels of antibiotics is challenging and may contribute to suboptimal response to systemic antibiotics in these patients. A strategy of early liberation of patients from ECMO and conversion to temporary ventricular support (temporary LVAD, RVAD, or both) may promote early extubation and patient mobilization. Whether this strategy independently reduces infectious complications remains unknown. This review examines the epidemiology and etiology of nosocomial infections in patients receiving tMCS, summarizes current prevention and treatment strategies, and discusses the impact of infection on clinical outcomes.

42891931.title: Diagnostic yield of endotracheal aspirate and bronchoalveolar lavage in ventilator-associated pneumonia: A single-centre study.
42891931.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in critically ill patients. This study aimed to compare the diagnostic accuracy of endotracheal aspirate (ETA) with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) culture, considered the reference standard, in identifying the causative pathogens of VAP. This study was conducted as a cross-sectional study at Haji Adam Malik General Hospital, Medan, Indonesia. A total of 95 samples from mechanically ventilated patients were analysed using both ETA and BAL in similar institutions. The results demonstrated that 49 samples were positive by both ETA and BAL, while 11 were BAL-positive but ETA-negative, and 31 were ETApositive but BAL-negative. The sensitivity of ETA culture was 81.67%, whereas specificity was 11.43%. The positive predictive value (PPV) was 61.25%, and the negative predictive value (NPV) was 26.67%, yielding an overall diagnostic accuracy of 55.79%. These findings highlight the moderate reliability of ETA in detecting VAP pathogens, with limitations in ruling out infection due to its low NPV. To conclude, the relatively high sensitivity and ease of use suggest that ETA remains a useful initial diagnostic tool, particularly in resource-limited settings, though confirmation with more definitive methods, such as BAL, is recommended to guide appropriate antimicrobial therapy.

42891078.title: Efficacy of combination therapy with minocycline for treating Stenotrophomonas maltophilia infections.
42891078.abstract: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is a multidrug-resistant opportunistic pathogen associated with substantial in-hospital mortality. However, data supporting the efficacy of treating S. maltophilia infections using a combination of antimicrobials remain inconclusive. To assess whether adjunctive minocycline improves clinical outcomes of S. maltophilia infections compared with standard monotherapy. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial was conducted at Siriraj Hospital, Thailand. Adults with confirmed S. maltophilia infections were randomized to receive minocycline or a matching placebo in addition to monotherapy with either levofloxacin or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. This trial enrolled 112 patients (71.4% [n = 80/112] of patients requiring an intensive care unit [ICU] and 66.1% [n = 74/112] of patients were diagnosed with ventilator-associated pneumonia [VAP]). Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were balanced between intervention and control groups. Adjunctive minocycline did not significantly reduce 28-day-mortality (n = 24/55[43.6%] vs n = 22/57[38.6%], P = 0.590) but did achieve significantly higher microbiological response rates at early assessment (n = 25/55[45.5%] vs n = 8/57[14.0%], P < 0.001) and the end of treatment (n = 44/55[80.0%] vs n = 32/57[56.1%], P = 0.023). In contrast, clinical response rates did not differ between groups at either 72 h after the start of study treatment or the end of study treatment. In multivariable analysis, two factors were independently associated with 28-day mortality: history of antibiotic use before admission (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]: 7.65, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.04-28.76; P = 0.030) and septic shock (aOR: 7.24, 95% CI: 2.75-19.23; P < 0.001). Although adding minocycline to either levofloxacin or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole therapy enhanced microbiological eradication, it did not confer a measurable survival or clinical advantage. Combination therapy was well tolerated. This study is potentially of interest to those treating ICU patients, as the majority of infections were VAP.

42889781.title: Phenotypic Characterization of Multidrug-Resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa Isolated From Patients With Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia: Insights Into Resistance Mechanisms and Biofilm Formation.
42889781.abstract: Background In patients receiving mechanical ventilation in intensive care units (ICUs), ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is a serious illness connected with healthcare. Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa)is among the most often used pathogens linked to VAP and is increasingly characterized by multidrug resistance, β-lactamase production, and biofilm-forming ability. This study focused on assessing the antimicrobial susceptibility pattern, prevalence of multidrug resistance, extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) production, metallo-β-lactamase (MBL) production, and biofilm-forming ability among isolates of P. aeruginosa collected from endotracheal tube (ETT) aspirates of individuals with VAP. Methods A descriptive cross-sectional research study was carried out in the Microbiology Department at Krishna Charitable Hospital and Medical Research Center, Karad, India. A total of 104 non-repetitive P. aeruginosa isolates acquired from ETT aspirates of patients clinically suspected of VAP were included. Identification was carried out utilising conventional microbiological and biochemical methods. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using the Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion method. ESBL and the production of MBLs were detected phenotypically by combined disk diffusion methods. The Congo red agar (CRA) method and the Christensen's tube method were used to evaluate biofilm development. Results Among the 104 VAP patients, 72 (69.23%) were male, and 32 (30.77%) were female. The highest proportion of cases was observed in the 21-40-year age group (45.65%). Most (49.04%) of VAP cases occurred in the medical intensive care unit (MICU), and 54.81% of cases appeared five days after starting mechanical ventilation. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing revealed complete resistance to piperacillin and imipenem (100% each), followed by piperacillin-tazobactam and meropenem (98.08% each), ciprofloxacin (97.12%), ceftazidime (95.19%), levofloxacin (94.23%), and cefepime (87.50%). Aztreonam demonstrated the highest susceptibility (83.65%). ESBL production was detected in 7 (6.73%) isolates, whereas MBL production was identified in 80 (76.92%) isolates. Biofilm formation was observed in 54 (51.92%) isolates by the Christensen's tube method and in 23 (22.12%) isolates by the CRA method. Conclusions A significant occurrence of multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa was found among those who had VAP. Extensive antimicrobial resistance, high MBL production, and frequent biofilm formation highlight the therapeutic obstacles linked to these infections. Continuous surveillance of antimicrobial resistance, strict infection-control measures, and judicious antibiotic use are essential to reduce the transmission of resistant strains and improve patient outcomes.

42889023.title: Association of delayed enteral nutrition with hospital-acquired pneumonia and 30-day mortality following craniotomy for severe traumatic brain injury: a retrospective cohort study.
42889023.abstract: Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) is a serious complication after craniotomy for severe traumatic brain injury (TBI), but evidence on modifiable factors, especially delayed enteral nutrition, remains limited. To evaluate factors associated with HAP after severe TBI surgery, focusing on enteral nutrition timing and the association between HAP and 30-day mortality. This retrospective cohort study included 600 adult patients undergoing craniotomy for severe TBI who survived >48 h. HAP was diagnosed according to CDC/NHSN criteria. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with HAP, and a fully adjusted model assessed the HAP-mortality association. Model performance was assessed by the AUC and Hosmer-Lemeshow test. Sensitivity analyses included forced inclusion of tracheostomy and comparison of the primary model (pre-HAP ventilation duration) with the total ventilation model. A 48-h landmark analysis was also performed. The primary outcome was postoperative HAP; secondary outcomes were ICU stay and 30-day mortality. Postoperative HAP incidence was 11.5%. After adjustment, delayed enteral nutrition (≥48 h) was independently associated with HAP (OR = 4.46, 95% CI: 2.52-8.19, p < 0.001). Other associated factors included age, admission GCS, mechanical ventilation duration, and serum albumin. The model showed good discrimination (AUC = 0.795) and calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow p = 0.829). In the time-dependent Cox model, HAP was associated with higher 30-day mortality (HR = 4.31, 95% CI: 1.52-12.25, p = 0.006). The primary model and total ventilation model yielded nearly identical results. In the landmark analysis, mechanical ventilation at 48 h was associated with subsequent HAP (OR = 2.19, 95% CI: 1.02-5.30, p = 0.06). Forced inclusion of tracheostomy did not materially alter core results. In severe TBI patients undergoing craniotomy, delayed enteral nutrition was independently associated with increased HAP risk, and HAP was associated with higher 30-day mortality. These findings highlight the potential importance of early enteral nutrition, but causal inference is limited by the observational design; prospective studies are needed.

42886404.title: Device-Associated Sepsis and Brain Injury: Transitioning From Early Infection Control to Late Neuroprotection.
42886404.abstract: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) is a complex neuroinflammatory condition characterized by diffuse brain dysfunction arising from systemic infection without direct central nervous system invasion. In modern critical care, device-associated infections (DAIs) caused by invasive medical devices, such as central line-associated bloodstream infections, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and catheter-associated urinary tract infections, have become critical drivers of intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired sepsis. Biofilm formation on these devices establishes persistent inflammatory reservoirs that continuously shed microorganisms, pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) into the circulation, sustaining systemic immune activation. This review outlines an integrated mechanistic framework linking DAIs to acute brain dysfunction. Systemic inflammation and endothelial activation trigger microvascular dysfunction, impaired cerebral autoregulation, and blood-brain barrier disruption. These peripheral vascular alterations allow inflammatory mediators to access the central nervous system, where they induce microglial and astrocytic reactivity. Persistent neuroimmune activation compromises neurotransmitter homeostasis-causing glutamate excitotoxicity and cholinergic deficits-while impairing neuronal mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. The resulting oxidative stress, energy failure, and self-amplifying neuroinflammatory feedback loops culminate in synaptic damage and neuronal injury. Clinically, this manifests as altered consciousness, delirium, seizures, and long-term neurocognitive impairment. By framing SAE as a concurrent, multidimensional continuum rather than a linear sequence, this review highlights the critical role of early infection prevention, timely device removal, and targeted neuroprotective strategies aimed at stabilizing vascular integrity and mitigating neuroinflammation.

42961991.title: Associated factors for stress ulcers and gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with sepsis or septic shock: A systematic review.
42961991.abstract: Sepsis continues to be a major contributor to death among critically ill individuals and places a heavy strain on healthcare resources. In addition to causing systemic inflammation and affecting hemodynamics, sepsis has a significant effect on the gastrointestinal system, leading to complications like stress ulcers and notable gastrointestinal bleeding (GIB), which worsen patient outcomes. While stress ulcer prophylaxis (SUP) has traditionally been included in sepsis treatment protocols, the concept of applying it universally is being increasingly scrutinized due to the absence of definitive mortality advantages and the risk of adverse effects, such as hospital-acquired pneumonia. Nevertheless, there is a notable gap in synthesized research that specifically addresses the independent risk factors for stress ulcers in sepsis patients. We carried out a systematic review in accordance with PRISMA standards, exploring eight databases (CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, Sinomed, PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library) from their inception until September 1, 2026. We included observational analytical studies (either cohort or case-control) that examined factors linked to stress ulcers or significant gastrointestinal bleeding in adult patients with sepsis. Two researchers independently handled the selection of studies, extraction of data, and evaluation of quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Due to the limited number of studies for each association between associated factors and outcomes, a narrative synthesis was utilized. A total of six studies encompassing 131,568 individuals suffering from sepsis or septic shock were analyzed. The incidence rates of stress ulcers or gastrointestinal bleeding (GIB) varied between 2.0% and 32.3%. The identified associated factors were divided into three categories: patient-related (older age, history of GIB, cirrhosis, HIV, cancer/immunosuppression), disease-related (coagulopathy, kidney impairment, high BUN levels, severity of illness scores, source of infection), and treatment-related (mechanical ventilation, use of anticoagulants, corticosteroid therapy, duration of ICU stay). Specifically for stress ulcer, factors such as respiratory failure, high BUN levels, shock, and increased HMGB1/TLR2/TLR4 levels were found to be independently linked to a higher odds. In summary, the likelihood of developing stress ulcers and gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with sepsis is shaped by a variety of factors related to the patient, their illness, and the treatments they receive. Key indicators that consistently emerge include issues with blood coagulation, the presence of shock, the need for mechanical ventilation, liver and kidney dysfunction, the severity of the disease, and any previous occurrences of gastrointestinal bleeding. These results advocate for tailored strategies for stress ulcer prophylaxis based on individual risk rather than a one-size-fits-all approach, offering crucial insights for precise clinical decision-making. Additional high-quality research is essential to confirm and enhance the understanding of these associated factors. PROSPERO (CRD420251242849).

42960060.title: Continuous versus intermittent endotracheal tube cuff pressure control for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia: A focused systematic review and exploratory meta-analysis.
42960060.abstract: Continuous endotracheal tube cuff pressure control is intended to maintain cuff pressure within the recommended range, reduce microaspiration, and prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP). However, randomized trials have produced apparently inconsistent findings. The clinical question is therefore not only whether continuous control lowers VAP overall, but also why physiologic benefits have not translated consistently into patient-important infection outcomes. We performed a focused systematic review and evidence synthesis of randomized studies comparing continuous versus intermittent endotracheal tube cuff pressure control in critically ill adults. Trial characteristics, comparator intensity, endpoint definitions, risk-of-bias considerations, and directly extractable outcome data were reviewed from the original reports. Because the included studies used non-identical primary outcomes, the primary synthesis was qualitative. Exploratory random-effects meta-analyses were restricted to outcomes with directly extractable binary event counts. Five randomized studies involving 1,355 analyzed patients were included. Early single-center studies suggested that continuous cuff pressure control improved cuff pressure stability, reduced microaspiration-related markers, and in some settings lowered infection-related endpoints. In contrast, the two largest later multicenter trials did not demonstrate a consistent reduction in VAP or ventilator-associated respiratory infection (VARI). An exploratory pooled analysis of four studies with directly extractable VAP-like binary outcomes showed no statistically significant reduction with continuous control (risk ratio 0.89, 95% confidence interval 0.63-1.24; I2 = 55.8%). A sensitivity analysis using the Vietnam trial's primary VARI endpoint rather than VAP yielded a similar result (risk ratio 0.92, 95% confidence interval 0.67-1.28; I2 = 57.7%). Exploratory pooled intensive care unit (ICU) mortality across all five studies was also not significantly different (risk ratio 0.91, 95% confidence interval 0.77-1.07; I2 = 0%). Continuous cuff pressure control improves cuff pressure stability and may reduce microaspiration-related markers, but current randomized evidence does not demonstrate a consistent overall reduction in clinically important infection outcomes across diverse ICU settings. The apparent inconsistency in the literature is best explained by differences in endpoint choice, comparator intensity, timing of intervention, baseline preventive practices, and patient population. Continuous control should therefore be regarded as a context-dependent adjunct rather than a universally proven stand-alone VAP-prevention strategy.

42957982.title: Bacterial epidemiology and attributable mortality of Ventilator-associated pneumonia before and after COVID-19 pandemic (2018-2021).
42957982.abstract: BackgroundVentilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in mechanically ventilated patients. The COVID-19 pandemic has profoundly modified VAP epidemiology and microbial ecology.MethodsWe conducted a prospective multicenter cohort study within the REA-REZO network (≈20% of French ICU beds), 1 January 2018-31 December 2021. All adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation were included. VAP was defined according to ECDC criteria. Primary endpoints were VAP incidence density (per 1000 ventilation-days) and 30-day attributable mortality. Secondary endpoints included resistance patterns and pre-pandemic versus pandemic trends.ResultsAmong 98,047 patients, 12,251 patients developed VAP, with an incidence of 18.9/1000 ventilation-days. Peak incidence occurred at day 10 (29/1000 ventilation-days). Thirty-day attributable mortality was 4.9% [95% CI 3.7;6.2], rising to 7.2% [6.0;8.5] at 60 days. Gram-negative bacteria accounted for 78.0% of isolates, predominantly Enterobacterales (46%) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (20%). Third-generation cephalosporin resistance reached 27% in Enterobacterales and 25% in P. aeruginosa. The COVID-19 patients had a higher VAP rate (19.5% vs 9.7%, p<0.001) and mortality (36.9% vs 31.0%, p<0.001).ConclusionsVAP remains highly prevalent in French ICUs with substantial attributable mortality. The COVID-19 pandemic nearly doubled VAP incidence and worsened resistance profiles. Intensified prevention bundles during the first 10 days of ventilation and reinforced antimicrobial stewardship are critical.

42857167.title: Relative suppression of pyroptosis- and necroptosis-related transcriptional programs and enrichment of ferroptosis-related signatures are associated with fatal sepsis: multi-cohort bulk and single-cell transcriptomic evidence.
42857167.journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology
42857167.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome caused by a dysregulated host response to infection and remains a major cause of mortality in critically ill patients. Multiple forms of programmed cell death (PCD) may contribute to immune dysregulation and organ injury, but their transcriptional patterns across disease severity and outcome remain incompletely defined. We performed an integrative transcriptomic analysis of five public sepsis cohorts, including single-cell RNA sequencing datasets GSE167363 and GSE151263 and three bulk transcriptomic cohorts. Primary outcome analyses focused on cohort-defined fatal sepsis (28-day non-survivors in GSE65682 and the deposited sepsis-death group in GSE63042), whereas pneumonia/ARDS comparisons were treated as secondary exploratory analyses. PCD-related transcriptional programs were evaluated across clinical groups and immune-cell populations. Six candidate genes were further assessed by RT-qPCR in LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 and THP-1 cells as targeted in vitro transcriptional validation. In GSE65682, 28-day non-survivors showed lower pyroptosis, necroptosis and apoptosis program scores but higher ferroptosis scores than survivors, and higher pyroptosis scores were associated with better 28-day survival. GSE154918 instead showed broader increases in PCD-related program scores from healthy controls to infection/sepsis groups, reflecting a disease-versus-control contrast rather than an outcome contrast. In the LPS model, CASP1, RIPK3 and NLRP3 were upregulated, whereas SIRT1, BCL2 and HIF1A were downregulated. These cell experiments assessed acute inflammatory transcriptional responsiveness and were not intended to reproduce the mortality-associated direction observed in patient cohorts. Multi-cohort analyses identified outcome-associated PCD transcriptional patterns in sepsis, including relative suppression of pyroptosis- and necroptosis-related programs and enrichment of ferroptosis-related signatures in non-survivors. The LPS experiments provide complementary mRNA-level evidence that selected PCD genes are transcriptionally responsive to inflammatory stimulation, but they do not constitute directional or functional validation of the fatal-sepsis signature. Functional and prospective clinical validation remains required.

42844585.title: Pre-ECMO characteristics, organ dysfunction and exploratory mortality prediction in COVID-19 versus non-COVID-19 ARDS treated with veno-venous ECMO: a retrospective cohort study.
42844585.abstract: The transferability of pre-ECMO characteristics and established mortality prediction tools across COVID-19 (C-19) and non-COVID-19 (nC-19) acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) remains uncertain. We compared clinical characteristics, organ dysfunction, respiratory support and outcome in a large cohort of patients treated with veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (vvECMO), and explored mortality prediction in C-19 ARDS. This retrospective single-center cohort study included n = 600 vvECMO patients (C-19: n = 245, nC-19: n = 355) hospitalized at the Charité ARDS ECMO Center from 01/2007 to 12/2018 (nC-19) and 03/2020-01/2022 (C-19). Pre-ECMO clinical and laboratory variables were compared between cohorts and by ICU survival. RESP score performance was assessed, and an exploratory C-19 ECMO mortality prediction (CEMP) score was derived from pre-ECMO variables using an explainable machine-learning workflow with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). C-19 patients were older (median 57.0 vs. 51.0 years, p < 0.0001), more often male (74.7% vs. 66.8%, p = 0.0337), and had a higher BMI (29.3 vs. 26.0 kg/m², p < 0.0001). nC-19 patients had a higher CCI (3 vs. 2, p = 0.0137) and SOFA score (12 vs. 11, p = 0.0004). Septic shock before vvECMO initiation was more prevalent in nC-19 patients (65.4% vs. 13.9%, p < 0.0001), and nC-19 patients had higher median baseline bilirubin, creatinine, and lactate levels (all p < 0.0001). nC-19 patients had higher median PEEP, pPeak, and plateau pressure than C-19 patients, whereas their PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio was lower (p < 0.0001). Duration of vvECMO support was longer in C-19 patients (26.0 vs. 12.6 days, p < 0.0001); ICU mortality did not differ significantly (55.1% vs. 47.9%, p = 0.0966). RESP showed limited discrimination in C-19 patients, and the CEMP derivation analysis yielded an apparent AUC of 0.757 (95% CI 0.69-0.82). This large single-center comparative vvECMO cohort highlights differences between C-19 and nC-19 ARDS in organ dysfunction burden, respiratory characteristics, and treatment duration. ICU mortality did not differ significantly between groups. RESP showed limited discrimination in C-19; CEMP remains exploratory and requires calibration and independent external validation before clinical application.

42948347.title: Intelligent nano delivery systems: Classification, stimuli-responsive mechanisms, and therapeutic applications in critical illnesses.
42948347.abstract: Critical illnesses such as sepsis and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) evolve rapidly and are dominated by systemic inflammatory dysregulation, oxidative stress, and abrupt microenvironmental remodeling, which collectively narrow the therapeutic window and amplify treatment-related toxicity. Conventional pharmacotherapy is often limited by non-selective biodistribution, insufficient lesion exposure, and dose-limiting adverse effects. Intelligent nano-delivery systems (INDS) address these barriers by coupling pathological cues (e.g., pH gradients, redox/ROS imbalance, and disease-associated enzymes) to defined carrier-state transitions, thereby enabling lesion-confined activation, controlled bioavailability, and, in selected designs, real-time readouts. In this review, we summarize the design logic of stimulus-responsive and targeting modules, and critically discuss how they translate endogenous signals into payload release or functional actuation in representative critical-illness settings. We further highlight emerging directions, including self-adaptive multi-input gating and biomimetic interfaces, and discuss key translational constraints (manufacturability, safety, and reproducibility) that must be addressed to advance INDS toward critical-care practice.

42945998.title: Molecular Subtypes in Acute Respiratory Illness and Sepsis.
42945998.journal: Seminars in respiratory and critical care medicine
42945998.abstract: Sepsis and acute respiratory illness are clinical syndromes that encompass profound biological heterogeneity. The resulting heterogeneity of treatment effect is now widely understood as the explanation to why immunomodulatory trials in critical care have not me their study endpoints, thereby misclassifying effective therapies as futile while concealing harm in biologically ineligible subgroups. High-dimensional molecular profiling offers a route to resolve this heterogeneity into tractable subgroups or subtypes. Here we review molecular subtypes across adult and paediatric sepsis, pneumonia, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), spanning transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic platforms. Blood transcriptomic frameworks derived independently in multiple countries, and subsequently harmonized by international consensus efforts, converge on recurring immune archetypes: a myeloid inflammatory state dominated by neutrophil activation; a mixed myeloid and lymphoid dysregulated state carrying the highest mortality; and a relatively immunocompetent state with preserved lymphocyte function and the most favourable clinical trajectory. Plasma proteomic and metabolomic profiling recapitulate this architecture at orthogonal molecular layers, arguing that these archetypes are platform-independent rather than artefacts of any single technology. Cross-syndrome convergence is asymmetric, which plausibly reflects the methodological differences between top-down latent class analysis in ARDS and bottom-up unsupervised clustering in sepsis. Secondary analyses of randomized controlled trials consistently show subtype-dependent responses to treatment strategies, with a coherent directionality with potential benefit in hyperinflammatory states, and harm in immunosuppressed or adaptive immune-prevalent states. Subtype membership is not static; trajectory, not baseline assignment, most strongly encodes prognosis. Realising precision critical care now requires prospective, subtype-stratified trials of which none has yet been completed.

42927821.title: Sepsis-associated efferocytosis deficiency: Molecular mechanisms and novel therapeutic targets.
42927821.abstract: Despite advances in critical care, sepsis remains a leading cause of mortality driven by a profoundly dysregulated host immune response. Increasingly, defective efferocytosis-the fundamental physiological process for clearing dead cells-has been identified as a critical catalyst in sepsis pathophysiology. Under normal conditions, efferocytosis resolves inflammation and maintains tissue homeostasis. However, during sepsis, the efferocytotic capacity of phagocytes is severely paralyzed. This clearance failure results in a massive accumulation of apoptotic and necrotic cellular debris within the tissue microenvironment, triggering an unabated release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). Consequently, this substrate overload sustains a self-amplifying inflammatory storm that accelerates tissue injury and precipitates multiple organ failure. In this review, we dissect the diverse modalities of programmed cell death in sepsis and map the subsequent breakdown of the core, multi-step efferocytotic machinery. We systematically explore the molecular basis of efferocytosis failure across distinct organ-specific complications, including acute lung injury, sepsis-associated encephalopathy, acute kidney injury, and septic cardiomyopathy. Finally, we evaluate emerging targeted therapies aimed at restoring efferocytotic efficiency, highlighting a crucial conceptual shift from primarily suppressing inflammation to actively promoting its resolution and repairing host immunity.

42910759.title: Development and Internal Validation of a 24-Hour Landmark Model for 28-Day Mortality in Sepsis-Associated Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome.
42910759.abstract: Sepsis-associated acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) carries substantial short-term mortality. Differences in predictor timing, validation design, and comparators complicate evaluation of published prediction models. This single-center retrospective cohort study included 955 adults with sepsis-associated ARDS who reached a 24-h landmark after intensive care unit (ICU) admission. All-cause mortality was assessed by day 28 from ICU admission. Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)-only logistic regression, conventional multivariable logistic regression, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) logistic regression, random forest, and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) were compared. The multivariable models used 26 candidate predictors (30 encoded parameters). Five repetitions of five-fold outer cross-validation with three-fold inner tuning provided held-out predictions. Evaluation included the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration, classification metrics, and decision-curve net benefit. Held-out tree-based Shapley additive explanations described XGBoost predictions. Among 955 patients, 474 (49.6%) died. AUCs based on averaged held-out probabilities were 0.732 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.698-0.761) for LASSO, 0.729 (0.696-0.761) for conventional regression, 0.709 (0.674-0.740) for XGBoost, 0.707 (0.673-0.739) for random forest, and 0.581 (0.545-0.617) for SOFA alone. The LASSO-minus-conventional-regression AUC difference was 0.003 (95% CI, -0.003 to 0.010). Intervals resampled fixed predictions without refitting. LASSO had a Brier score of 0.209, calibration intercept of -0.001, and slope of 1.065. The final equation retained age, Charlson Comorbidity Index, arterial oxygen partial pressure/fraction of inspired oxygen ratio, SOFA, lactate, bilirubin, other infection site, and vasopressor use. LASSO provided moderate discrimination without a clear advantage over conventional regression. The separately tuned final equation requires source-data verification, external validation, and prospective clinical-utility assessment before clinical use.

42844256.title: Plasma proteomics defines two reproducible subphenotypes of sepsis-associated acute kidney injury with distinct outcomes.
42844256.abstract: Sepsis is the leading cause of acute kidney injury in critically ill patients, and this complication carries a high risk of death. The biology underlying it varies between patients, which may explain why treatments have not succeeded. Here we show, using an ensemble method that groups patients by patterns across hundreds of blood proteins in three independent groups of patients, that sepsis-associated acute kidney injury comprises two reproducible subphenotypes. One subphenotype shows widespread activation of inflammation, metabolism, and oxidative stress; the other shows a quieter profile. Patients in the inflammatory subtype have higher mortality, more complications, and fewer days alive and out of the intensive care unit. A simple seven-protein test reproduces these groupings and identifies them accurately in separate cohorts. In a randomized trial, the drug ilofotase alfa appears to benefit the inflammatory subtype but not the other, suggesting that this classification could guide future treatment.

42942373.title: Lower Plasma Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor Levels During Critical Illness Are Associated with Subsequent Dialysis Requirement.
42942373.abstract: Background and Objectives: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), best known for its role in cognitive function, is an anti-inflammatory protein proposed as a potential therapeutic target and diagnostic biomarker in sepsis. However, studies investigating circulating BDNF levels in patients with sepsis have yielded conflicting results, reporting both increased and decreased concentrations. Comorbid conditions, particularly liver cirrhosis, pancreatitis, and kidney failure, may contribute to these discrepancies. Therefore, the primary aim of this study was to investigate the association between plasma BDNF levels and these comorbidities in patients with sepsis. Materials and Methods: Plasma BDNF concentrations were measured in 250 critically ill patients with systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), sepsis, or septic shock and 40 healthy controls. Among these patients, 56 had liver cirrhosis, 44 had pancreatitis, and 94 required dialysis. Results: Patients with SIRS/sepsis/septic shock exhibited significantly lower plasma BDNF levels than healthy controls. Plasma BDNF concentrations were unchanged in patients with concomitant liver cirrhosis, increased in the 44 patients with pancreatitis, and significantly decreased in those with acute kidney injury requiring dialysis (AKI-D), compared with patients without pancreatitis and those without AKI-D, respectively. When patients were stratified by dialysis status, plasma BDNF levels were similar among patients with SIRS, sepsis, and septic shock. Plasma BDNF levels did not change in ventilated patients or in those who did not survive. Furthermore, patients with COVID-19-related sepsis and those with non-COVID-19 etiologies showed comparable plasma BDNF concentrations. However, plasma BDNF levels in non-dialysis and dialysis patients were not, or were only weakly, associated with routine measures of renal function. Plasma BDNF levels positively correlated with platelet count, which predicted BDNF levels in patients with SIRS/sepsis/septic shock. Conclusions: Plasma BDNF levels are similarly reduced in patients with SIRS/sepsis/septic shock and are further decreased in AKI-D, whereas patients with pancreatitis exhibit higher BDNF levels. Platelet count, which decreased in AKI-D and was higher in pancreatitis, predicted plasma BDNF levels, suggesting platelet count as an important factor affecting plasma BDNF levels.

42902191.title: Controlling nutritional status score as a novel prognostic tool for hospital mortality risk stratification in sepsis: a large-scale retrospective cohort analysis.
42902191.abstract: Malnutrition is associated with poor outcomes in critically ill patients. However, the prognostic value of the Controlling Nutritional Status (CONUT) score in sepsis remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the association between CONUT score and hospital death in sepsis patients. In this retrospective cohort study, 2,143 sepsis patients from the eICU Collaborative Research Database were categorized into Mild (2-4 points), Moderate (5-8 points), and Severe (9-12 points) malnutrition groups based on the CONUT score. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was used to evaluate the relationship between CONUT score groups and hospital death. Subgroup analyses were performed to assess the stability of the association across different populations. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis was conducted to examine the potential non-linear relationship between CONUT score and hospital death. Hospital death rates increased progressively across malnutrition groups: 8.13% in Mild, 16.14% in Moderate, and 23.27% in Severe groups (P < 0.001). After fully adjusting for confounding factors, compared with the Mild group, the risk of hospital mortality was significantly higher in the Moderate group (adjusted OR: 1.60, 95% CI: 1.07-2.38, P = 0.021) and Severe group (adjusted OR: 2.66, 95% CI: 1.73-4.07, P < 0.001). Subgroup analyses demonstrated consistent associations across different demographic and clinical characteristics (all P for interaction > 0.05). RCS analysis revealed a significant linear dose-response relationship between CONUT score and risk of hospital mortality (P for overall < 0.001, P for nonlinearity = 0.685). Each one-point increase in CONUT score was associated with a 15% higher adjusted odds of hospital mortality (adjusted OR 1.15, 95% CI 1.09-1.21). The fully adjusted model showed good discrimination (AUC 0.773, 95% CI 0.747-0.799) and excellent calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow P = 0.390). Higher CONUT scores were independently associated with increased risk of hospital mortality in sepsis patients. The CONUT score might serve as a valuable prognostic indicator for risk stratification in sepsis.

42885414.title: [Persistent inflammation, immunosuppression, and catabolism syndrome].
42885414.abstract: Reduced early mortality in sepsis and severe injuries led to the formation of a cohort of patients with chronic critical conditions (diseases). One of the mechanisms of chronization of acute critical conditions is the development of persistent inflammation, immunosuppression and catabolism syndrome (PICS). Diagnosis of PICS is currently based on clinical and laboratory markers, whereas morphological changes insufficiently studied. Lack of pathogenesis and morphogenesis understanding makes it difficult to stratify patients with prolonged critical conditions and develop new treatment approaches, and also leads to the absence of PICS in clinical and anatomical diagnoses. The article systematized current understanding of PICS mechanisms of development and morphological manifestations. Examples of clinical cases are presented.

42880129.title: Association of early CD4⁺ T-lymphocyte depletion with 28 day mortality in sepsis: a retrospective single-center cohort study.
42880129.abstract: Sepsis-induced immune dysregulation, characterized by T-cell loss, is associated with poor outcomes. This study investigated the association between early peripheral T-lymphocyte subset profiles and 28 day mortality in patients with sepsis. In this single-center retrospective cohort study, 60 critically ill patients with sepsis and 30 healthy controls were included. Patients with sepsis were classified as 28 day survivors (n = 30) or non-survivors (n = 30). Peripheral T-lymphocyte subset percentages (CD3⁺, CD4⁺, and CD8⁺) were measured by flow cytometry within 24 h of ICU admission. Compared with healthy controls, patients with sepsis had lower CD3⁺ (55.23±9.15%vs. 68.12±8.04%) and CD4⁺ T-cell percentages (30.88±10.52%vs. 40.15±7.21%) and a lower CD4⁺/CD8⁺ ratio (all p < 0.001). Non-survivors had lower CD3⁺ and CD4⁺ T-cell percentages than survivors (both p < 0.001). In multivariable logistic regression, lower CD4⁺ T-cell percentage (OR = 0.85, 95% CI 0.77-0.94; p = 0.002) and higher APACHE II score (OR = 1.42, 95% CI 1.18-1.71; p < 0.001) were independently associated with 28-day mortality. Adding CD4⁺ T-cell percentage to APACHE II increased the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.86 to 0.91 (p = 0.03). Early reduction in peripheral CD4⁺ T-cell percentage was independently associated with 28 day mortality in this selected cohort. CD4⁺ T-cell assessment may provide incremental prognostic information beyond APACHE II, but external validation in larger prospective cohorts is required.

42879813.title: Factors associated with persistent methicillin-resistant staphylococcal bacteremia after initiation of anti-MRSA therapy in the NICU: A retrospective observational study.
42879813.abstract: BackgroundMethicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative staphylococci (MRCoNS) are important causes of bacteremia in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). However, clinical factors associated with persistent bacteremia after initiation of anti-MRSA therapy in NICU patients remain poorly defined.MethodsWe conducted a retrospective observational study of infants with MRSA or MRCoNS bacteremia admitted to a tertiary NICU between 2016 and 2025. Persistent bacteremia was defined as a positive follow-up blood culture on or after day 2 of initial anti-MRSA therapy. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify factors independently associated with persistent bacteremia.Results49 episodes of bacteremia were included, of which 16 (33%) met the criteria for persistent bacteremia. Younger postnatal age at bacteremia onset (adjusted odds ratio per 7-day decrease, 1.32; 95% confidence interval, 1.08-1.85; p = 0.001) and absence of central venous catheter removal or replacement within 2 days of starting initial anti-MRSA therapy (adjusted odds ratio, 11.20; 95% confidence interval, 2.16-86.60; p = 0.003) were independently associated with persistent bacteremia after initiation of anti-MRSA therapy.ConclusionsYounger postnatal age and the absence of central venous catheter removal or replacement were independently associated with persistent bacteremia after initiation of anti-MRSA therapy in NICU patients with MRSA or MRCoNS bacteremia. These findings may facilitate early identification of NICU patients at increased risk of persistent bacteremia and support closer monitoring and timely reassessment of treatment response. Prospective multicenter studies are warranted to validate these findings and establish optimal treatment strategies.

42879511.title: Clinical features and outcomes of neuroleptospirosis in French Guiana: Insights from a retrospective study (2015-2021).
42879511.abstract: Leptospirosis is a re-emerging public health threat in French Guiana with a broad clinical spectrum. Neurological involvement (neuroleptospirosis) lacks a consensus definition and may be underrecognized. This study aimed to characterize its epidemiology, clinical features, outcomes, and associated factors. A multicenter retrospective study was conducted across healthcare facilities in French Guiana from 2015 to 2021. Consecutive hospital-managed patients with laboratory-confirmed or probable leptospirosis were included. Neuroleptospirosis was defined by neurological symptoms combined with objective cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and/or neuro-imaging abnormalities. Patients with and without neurological involvement were compared. Among 146 patients, 18 (12%) met the criteria for neuroleptospirosis, corresponding to a mean annual incidence of 0.88 cases/100,000 inhabitants (95% conference interval [CI], 0.52-1.39). Presentations were meningeal (78% [14/18]), encephalitic (17% [3/18]) or meningoencephalitic (6% [1/18]). Lumbar puncture was performed in 28/146 (19%) patients; pleocytosis was observed in 18/28 (64%). The median CSF leukocyte count was 42 cells/mm3 (interquartile range [IQR], 13-240 cells/mm3), with lymphocytic predominance in 8/13 differential counts (62%). CSF protein was mildly elevated (median, 0.51 g/L; IQR, 0.32-0.88), without hypoglycorrhachia. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed abnormalities in 2/8 patients with neuroleptospirosis: one cerebral infarction and one case of pachymeningitis. Age under 30 years (odds ratio [OR], 5.56; 95% CI, 1.72-18), absence of leukocytosis during hospitalization (OR, 3.29; 95% CI, 1.04-10.39), and absence of thrombocytopenia (OR, 4.46; 95% CI, 1.39-14.32) were associated with neuroleptospirosis. Under our diagnostic criteria, neuroleptospirosis cases were associated with favorable outcomes, with lower odds of sepsis (OR, 0.28; 95% CI, 0.10-0.79), no intensive care unit admissions or deaths. This study clarifies the clinical spectrum and outcomes of neuroleptospirosis in French Guiana, highlighting the importance of clinical awareness in tropical endemic settings. Prospective studies incorporating systematic CSF analysis and microbiological testing are needed to improve understanding of its pathophysiology and standardize diagnostic pathways.

42877122.title: Machine learning prediction of early hypothermia in sepsis patients.
42877122.abstract: Sepsis is a systemic inflammatory response syndrome caused by infection and remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Abnormal body temperature, especially hypothermia (body temperature < 36°C), is a key clinical feature in sepsis patients and is closely associated with disease severity, impaired immune function, and poor prognosis. Early prediction of hypothermia is crucial for timely intervention and improving prognosis. This study used machine learning algorithms to train and validate a prediction model for early temperature changes in critically ill sepsis patients. Data were extracted from the MIMIC-IV database and five models were established: XGBoost, LR, SVM, KNN, and ANN. The XGBoost model demonstrated the best predictive performance with AUC values of 0.92 in the training cohort and 0.98 in the validation cohort.
