The expert panel evaluated seven phenotypes that were identified as the most clinically relevant and extensively addressed in the available literature. IVIg use was judged appropriate without formal disagreement in severe community-acquired pneumonia with hyperinflammation plus shock (median 8), low IgM < 60 mg/dL (median 8), or prior immunosuppression (median 8), whereas hyperinflammation without shock was uncertain (median 6). Appropriateness was also supported for abdominal infection with endotoxaemic shock, immune suppression/paralysis, or low IgM (all median 8); sepsis in solid-organ transplant recipients (median 7), particularly with low IgM (median 8), while prophylaxis in high-risk transplant recipients was uncertain (median 5). IVIg was rated appropriate for overwhelming septic shock with severe hyperinflammation (median 8), especially with low IgM (median 8) and toxin-mediated syndromes (median 9); for post-cardiac surgery sepsis with immune suppression (median 7) but not clearly for hyperinflammation (uncertain, median 6); for multidrug-resistant pathogen sepsis with immune suppression (median 7-8); and in haematologic malignancies, as prophylaxis or treatment primarily when immunoglobulins are low (medians 7-8), with prophylaxis otherwise uncertain. Across all phenotypes, IgM-enriched preparations were consistently preferred (median 8-9). Available evidence suggests no major safety signals, although adverse events are likely to be underreported. Overall, the consensus supports personalised, phenotype-oriented consideration of IgM-enriched IVIg as an adjunctive strategy to optimise standard care, while underscoring persistent evidence gaps and the need for adequately powered trials to define timing, dosing, and responsive subgroups.

42848609.title: Complex abdomen: proposal of a preliminary conceptual framework, clinical implications, and contemporary perspectives.
42848609.journal: Revista do Colegio Brasileiro de Cirurgioes
42848609.abstract: The open abdomen has become a cornerstone in the care of critically ill patients undergoing damage control surgery, with severe abdominal sepsis, or at risk of abdominal compartment syndrome. These patients frequently develop a multidimensional clinical course - persistent infection, organ failure, loss of abdominal wall integrity, nutritional depletion, and entero-atmospheric fistulas - whose severity appears to emerge from the dynamic interaction among these factors rather than from visceral exposure alone. Current classifications, notably Björck's amended classification, describe the anatomical progression of the open abdomen but do not integrate the physiological, infectious, nutritional, and organizational dimensions of care. The aim is to propose the term "complex abdomen" as a preliminary conceptual framework complementary to - and not a replacement for - existing classifications. Conceptual scientific communication grounded in a narrative review of the literature (MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, SciELO, and LILACS; 2000 to 2025; Portuguese, English, and Spanish), reported according to the SANRA scale. The synthesis followed best-fit framework synthesis, with the Cumulative Complexity Model as the a priori framework. Five constitutive domains are proposed - physiological instability; uncontrolled intra-abdominal infection; loss of abdominal wall domain; entero-atmospheric or complex enteric fistula; nutritional and intestinal failure - together with their associated cut-offs, a contextual organizational modifier recorded separately, and the criterion of simultaneous involvement of two or more domains. The domains, the cut-offs, and the criterion were proposed by the authors on the basis of the literature and clinical experience, without formal consensus and without empirical validation. The construct is presented as a dynamic clinical phenotype assessed at defined time points, not as an obligatory evolutionary stage or a prognostic score. This is a preliminary framework rather than a validated definition. Formalizing this phenotype may improve clinical reasoning, multidisciplinary communication, and the selection of more homogeneous study populations. A three-step validation agenda - modified Delphi consensus, reliability and content validity assessment, and prospective prognostic testing within a multicenter registry - is proposed, together with explicit refutation criteria.

42844600.title: Acute kidney injury at a tertiary nephrology referral center: predictors of renal recovery and in-hospital mortality.
42844600.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a global health problem associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. Despite advances in prevention and management, in-hospital mortality remains high, particularly among critically ill patients. To determine incidence, risk factors of AKI among patients admitted to Mansoura Nephrology and Dialysis Unit (MNDU), a tertiary nephrology referral center in Dakahlia governorate, Egypt, over one year, and to identify predictors of renal recovery at discharge and in-hospital mortality. This prospective observational study was conducted from June 2022 to May 2023 and included adult patients admitted with various kidney disorders. Patients were classified into AKI and non-AKI groups according to KDIGO 2012 criteria. Clinical, laboratory, and outcome data were analyzed, and multivariable regression analyses were used to identify independent predictors of in-hospital mortality and renal recovery after AKI. A total of 839 patients were enrolled, including 330 (39.3%) with AKI and 509 (60.7%) without AKI. The most common pathophysiological causes of AKI were pre-renal (54.2%) followed by intrinsic renal (38.5%) one. In-hospital mortality was significantly higher in AKI than non-AKI group (17.3% vs. 3.8%), with septic shock being the leading cause of death (84.2%). Among patients with AKI, 45.2% achieved complete renal recovery, 21.8% had partial recovery, and 33.0% had no recovery at discharge. On multivariable logistic regression analyses, KDIGO Stage 3 AKI (adjusted OR 0.277, P = 0.046), kidney replacement therapy (adjusted OR 0.409, P = 0.004), and requirement of vasopressor therapy (adjusted OR 0.041, P < 0.001) were independently associated with lower odds of renal recovery, whereas necessity of vasopressor therapy emerged as the only independent predictor of in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR 420.511, 95% CI 97.451-1814.543; P < 0.001). AKI was common among hospitalized patients and was associated with substantially increased in-hospital mortality. Vasopressor requirement was the strongest independent predictor of mortality, emphasizing the prognostic impact of hemodynamic instability and critical illness severity. Severe AKI (KDIGO Stage 3), kidney replacement therapy, and vasopressor necessity were independently associated with reduced renal recovery at discharge. These readily available clinical indicators may support early risk stratification and guide closer monitoring of high-risk patients.

42840966.title: Contemporary Economic, Hospitalization, and Mortality Burden Among Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension Patients: A Real-World US Claims Data Analysis.
42840966.abstract: This study quantified the recent real-world burden of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) using US real-world data. Adults (18+) with treated PAH were identified from the MarketScan Commercial/Medicare Databases using a claims-based algorithm requiring pulmonary hypertension diagnosis, PAH-specific treatment, and right heart catheterization from January 1, 2017 to August 31, 2024 (earliest treatment claim = index). Patients were followed for ≥ 30 days post-index, overall and stratified by payer and by treatment categories. Subsets of PAH-hospitalized and newly treated patients were also analyzed. Measures included demographics, clinical characteristics, all-cause healthcare utilization/costs, PAH-related hospitalization costs/characteristics, and all-cause mortality. Overall, 2712 treated PAH patients were included (mean age 61.8 years, 68.9% female, 57.9% commercial insurance). During mean 2.2 years of follow-up, mean (median) per-patient-per-year all-cause healthcare costs were $302,014 ($210,888) for commercially-insured patients and $200,581 ($147,706) for Medicare patients. Over half (56.2%) of patients had ≥ 1 all-cause hospitalization, 44.9% had ≥ 1 PAH-related hospitalization, and 31.0% were hospitalized for ≥ 1 complication (thrombosis [14.1%], hemorrhage [12.5%], sepsis [14.9%]). Among the PAH-hospitalized subset (N = 1079), median time to re-hospitalization was 1.2 years. The mean (median) cost per PAH-related hospitalization was $89,799 ($30,224) for commercially-insured and $37,288 ($15,733) for Medicare patients, and 57.2% of hospitalizations required an ICU stay. Among the newly treated subset (N = 2072), 9.7%, 18.6%, and 25.2% of patients died within 1, 2, and 3 years after treatment initiation. Despite recent therapeutic advancements, PAH patients continue to have a substantial clinical and economic burden. These findings highlight ongoing unmet need and underscore the importance of continued monitoring of disease burden as PAH therapies evolve.

42840779.title: Point-of-care ultrasound in emergency department sepsis and septic shock: a pragmatic framework for source-oriented assessment and physiologic reassessment.
42840779.abstract: In emergency department (ED) sepsis and septic shock, early management is often dominated by two bedside uncertainties: identifying a clinically plausible infection source and determining whether additional fluid is likely to improve perfusion or worsen pulmonary or systemic congestion. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) may contribute to both questions when it is used as a trigger-based, time-boxed adjunct rather than as a comprehensive screening test or stand-alone diagnostic adjudicator. This article presents a pragmatic narrative review of multiorgan POCUS in adult ED sepsis and septic shock, based on a focused, non-systematic search of major databases and a synthesis of sepsis guidelines, landmark resuscitation trials, and clinically relevant reviews and representative studies addressing source-oriented assessment, shock phenotyping, fluid responsiveness, and congestion assessment. Particular attention was given to separating diagnostic capability and physiologic plausibility from demonstrated clinical utility and patient-centered outcome benefit. Priority was given to adult ED literature; intensive care unit (ICU), perioperative, and physiologic studies were used only when ED-specific evidence was limited and the underlying principles were clinically transferable. The proposed framework is organized around two linked arms. First, a source-oriented scan may support pneumonia or pleural complication as a working source and may identify biliary disease, obstructive urinary infection, urinary retention, or drainable soft-tissue infection when clinical features make these sources plausible. Its intended role is to trigger formal imaging, drainage planning, specialist consultation, or source-control pathways, not to prove the source at the bedside. Second, physiologic reassessment can use focused cardiac ultrasound (FoCUS), dynamic flow-based assessment such as passive leg raise with left ventricular outflow tract velocity-time integral (PLR-LVOT VTI), and serial lung ultrasound to provide context for fluid and vasopressor decisions after the initial resuscitation step. Venous Doppler and the venous excess ultrasound (VExUS) framework are discussed as optional advanced congestion assessments, not as routine ED requirements, because ED sepsis-specific evidence remains limited. Overall, current evidence supports POCUS mainly as an adjunct for bedside clarification, escalation support, and physiologic reassessment; direct evidence that POCUS-guided ED sepsis pathways improve patient-centered outcomes remains limited. POCUS should therefore be used as a decision-support tool, not a stand-alone adjudicator or a reason to delay antimicrobials, CT, formal imaging, or specialist involvement.

42835426.title: Prognostic significance of the blood urea nitrogen-to-serum albumin ratio in patients with septic shock.
42835426.abstract: The blood urea nitrogen-to-serum albumin ratio (BAR) has been linked to clinical outcomes in multiple critical illnesses; however, its prognostic value in patients with septic shock remains inconclusive. The present retrospective observational study involved 120 patients with septic shock, who were classified into a survivor group (n=97) and a non-survivor group (n=23) based on discharge outcomes. Within 24 h of ICU admission, important clinical and laboratory data were collected and compared between the two groups. Multivariate logistic regression analysis identified BAR [odds ratio (OR)=1.052; 95% confidence interval (CI):1.014-1.117; P=0.012] and the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II; OR=1.096; 95% CI:1.014-1.185; P=0.030) as independent risk factors for in-hospital mortality in these patients. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis showed that the area under the curve (AUC) of BAR for predicting in-hospital mortality was 0.707. At the optimal cutoff value of 13.62, BAR had a sensitivity of 73.9% and a specificity of 63.9%. Further, the AUC of the multivariable model [including BAR, diastolic blood pressure (DBP), APACHE II, and partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO2)] was 0.859 (95% CI:0.778-0.939; P<0.001); the optimal cutoff value was 0.154; the sensitivity was 87% and the specificity was 74.2%, which was markedly improved over single BAR or APACHE II. Therefore, BAR emerged as a valid independent predictor of in-hospital mortality in patients with septic shock and may serve as a simple, readily accessible biomarker for the early risk stratification in this patient population. The BAR model incorporating DBP, APACHE II and PCO2 demonstrated high discrimination and stratification efficiency for patient mortality risk.

42835425.title: Early systemic heparin exposure is associated with lower mortality, reduced disseminated intravascular coagulation, and fewer thrombotic complications in septic shock.
42835425.abstract: Septic shock is characterized by thrombo-inflammatory dysregulation and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), contributing to organ failure and mortality. The clinical impact of heparin in septic shock remains uncertain. This study evaluated the association between early systemic heparin exposure and clinical outcomes. A retrospective multicenter cohort study was conducted using the TriNetX federated electronic health record network. Adult patients with septic shock receiving early systemic heparin exposure were compared with patients without heparin exposure. Propensity score matching balanced demographics, comorbidities, infection characteristics, organ dysfunction markers, and severity-related variables. Outcomes included mortality, DIC, thrombotic complications, renal outcomes, hematologic complications, and bleeding-related events. Clinical outcomes were assessed over a predefined 30-day follow-up period using risk-based and time-to-event analyses. A total of 105,472 patients per cohort were included. Early systemic heparin exposure was associated with lower mortality (15.3% vs. 20.8%; p < 0.001) and lower rates of DIC (p < 0.001). Thrombotic complications, including ischemic stroke, acute myocardial infarction, overall thrombotic events, and arterial or venous thrombosis, occurred less frequently among heparin-exposed patients (all p < 0.001). In contrast, heparin exposure was associated with higher rates of acute kidney injury, renal replacement therapy, thrombocytopenia, major bleeding, and transfusion requirement (all p < 0.01). Kaplan-Meier analyses were consistent with risk-based analyses. Early systemic heparin exposure was associated with lower mortality, reduced DIC, and fewer thrombotic complications, but increased rates of renal dysfunction and bleeding-related adverse events. These findings highlight a clinically relevant trade-off between potential benefit and harm. Prospective randomized studies are needed to define optimal patient selection and treatment timing.

42835371.title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of 28-Day Mortality in Patients with Sepsis-Induced Cardiomyopathy: An Integrated Analysis of Inflammatory Biomarkers.
42835371.abstract: Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy (SICM) is a common complication of sepsis and is associated with poor short-term outcomes. However, effective tools for early risk stratification remain limited. This study aimed to develop a machine learning (ML)-based model to predict 28-day mortality in patients with SICM. A single-center retrospective cohort study was conducted, including 762 patients with SICM admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). Clinical variables, including inflammatory biomarkers, were collected. The dataset was divided into training and validation sets at a ratio of 7:3. Feature selection was performed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Multiple ML algorithms, including Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Logistic Regression (LR), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), were used to develop prediction models. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration curves, and Brier score. Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) were applied to interpret the model. A total of 762 patients were included, with a 28-day mortality rate of 31.5%. Among all models, RF achieved the best performance (AUC = 0.88) with good calibration (Brier score = 0.149). SHAP analysis identified albumin (ALB), N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), age, pH (PH), systolic blood pressure (SBP), and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) as key predictors of mortality. A web-based interactive nomogram was constructed to generate individualized risk estimates tailored to each patient's clinical profile. The ML-based model demonstrated good predictive performance and interpretability for 28-day mortality in SICM patients. This model may serve as a useful tool for risk stratification and clinical decision-making. Further external validation in multicenter prospective cohorts is required before broader clinical implementation.

42832808.title: In methicillin-susceptible S aureus bacteremia, cefazolin was noninferior to flucloxacillin or cloxacillin for 90-d mortality.

42832503.title: Assessing community-acquired acute infection in an irish emergency department: A retrospective observational study protocol.
42832503.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening condition associated with substantial morbidity and mortality worldwide. In Ireland, the majority of sepsis cases are community-acquired; however, patients presenting to emergency departments (EDs) with suspected severe infection remain poorly characterised, particularly those not captured in administrative datasets. This retrospective cross-sectional observational study will be conducted in the ED of Mater Misericordiae University Hospital, Dublin. Adult (non-maternity) ED presentations across eight predefined 24-hour sampling periods will be reviewed. Community-acquired acute infection will be identified through manual review of ED clinical documentation, and possible sepsis will be identified using the ED triage sepsis discriminator supported by clinical documentation. Data collected will include demographic characteristics, referral pathways, clinical presentation, and patient outcomes. Multivariable logistic regression will be used to identify factors associated with adverse outcomes, defined as intensive care unit admission or in-hospital mortality. This study will provide a detailed evaluation of ED presentations with suspected severe infection in Ireland, including patients not captured in existing national datasets. Findings will contribute to improved understanding of early sepsis recognition, referral pathways, and resource planning in emergency care.

42829695.title: Ferritin-Based Biomarkers for Prediction of 28-Day Mortality in Septic Shock: A Prospective, Single-Centre, Observational Study From South India.
42829695.abstract: Introduction Septic shock is a life-threatening condition with high mortality despite advances in critical care. Ferritin, an acute-phase reactant involved in iron metabolism and inflammation, along with its derived biomarkers, has emerged as a potential biomarker of disease severity in sepsis. Methods This prospective observational study was conducted in an Intensive Care Unit in a Tertiary Care Hospital from December 2024 to October 2025. Adult patients meeting Sepsis-3 criteria for septic shock were included. Serum ferritin was measured on Day 1 and Day 3. Ferritin index, Delta ferritin and Ferritin-albumin ratio were calculated. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the discriminatory performance of serum ferritin, Ferritin Index (FI), delta ferritin (ΔFerritin), and ferritin-albumin ratio (FAR). Optimal cutoffs were determined using the ROC curves, and pairwise comparisons of the areas under the curves (AUCs) were performed using DeLong's test. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify predictors of 28-day mortality. Results A total of 79 patients were included, with a 28-day mortality rate of 64.6%. All ferritin-based biomarkers were significantly associated with 28-day mortality. Among these, the ferritin-albumin ratio demonstrated the best predictive performance (AUC: 0.849), with a sensitivity of 82.5% and specificity of 81.8% at a cutoff value of ≥239. Day 1 ferritin also showed excellent predictive ability (AUC: 0.840), with 94.1% sensitivity and 60.7% specificity at a cutoff of ≥574 µg/L. The ferritin index showed good discrimination (AUC: 0.795; sensitivity: 72.6%; specificity: 78.6% at ≥5.45), while delta ferritin demonstrated acceptable predictive performance (AUC: 0.737; sensitivity: 96.0%; specificity: 67.5% at ≥305 µg/L). DeLong pairwise comparison demonstrated that FAR was significantly superior to Ferritin Index, but its performance did not differ significantly from Day 1 serum ferritin or delta ferritin. On univariate analysis, Day 1 ferritin, Ferritin Index, FAR, SOFA, qSOFA, and lactate were associated with mortality; however, SOFA remained the only independent predictor in multivariable analysis. Conclusion Ferritin-derived biomarkers serve as valuable prognostic tools for risk stratification in septic shock. While the ferritin-albumin ratio demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy, the ferritin index and delta ferritin also show clinical utility. These inexpensive and widely available markers may aid early risk stratification in critically ill patients, though their prognostic value is closely aligned with baseline clinical severity scores.

42829404.title: miR-454-3p alleviates LPS-induced cardiomyocyte damage by negatively regulating STAT3 in sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy.
42829404.abstract: Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy (SICM) contributes greatly to high mortality in critically ill patients. Accumulating evidence indicates that miRNAs play key roles in sepsis-related organ injury. This work investigated the function and molecular mechanism of miR-454-3p in SICM, along with its potential clinical utility. A total of 100 healthy controls and 210 sepsis patients were enrolled. Sepsis patients were categorized into non-cardiomyopathy group (non-CM, n=105) and SICM group (n=105). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, multivariate logistic regression, and Cox regression were performed to assess the clinical value of miR-454-3p. In vitro functional experiments were conducted using LPS-stimulated AC16 cardiomyocytes. The dual-luciferase reporter assay verified the targeting relationship between miR-454-3p and STAT3. miR-454-3p expression decreased progressively from healthy controls to non-CM patients and further to SICM patients. miR-454-3p demonstrated good diagnostic performance for SICM. Multivariate analysis identified miR-454-3p as both an independent protective factor against SICM and an independent predictor of favorable prognosis. Cellular experiments revealed that miR-454-3p directly binds to the 3'UTR of STAT3 and suppresses STAT3 expression. Functional assays indicated that miR-454-3p attenuates LPS-induced cardiomyocyte apoptosis, inflammation, and oxidative stress, whereas STAT3 overexpression reverses these protective phenotypes. Furthermore, western blot analysis showed that miR-454-3p inhibits activation of the JAK2/STAT3/NF-κB inflammatory cascade. In vitro assays suggest that miR-454-3p alleviates LPS-triggered cardiomyocyte damage by negatively regulating STAT3 and suppressing the JAK2/STAT3/NF-κB inflammatory cascade. Our single-center observational data indicate that circulating miR-454-3p correlates independently with SICM incidence and 28-day all-cause mortality, implying its potential value as a candidate diagnostic and prognostic biomarker for SICM. Nevertheless, correlational findings from this cross-sectional cohort cannot confirm causal relationships, and large-scale multicenter prospective cohorts are needed for external validation to verify its clinical utility.

42829110.title: The regulatory landscape for clinical metagenomics-based diagnostics in Europe: a critical review.
42829110.abstract: Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) enables broad, untargeted pathogen detection and is increasingly used in the diagnosis of central nervous system infections, infections in immunocompromised or post-transplant patients, ICU patients, and sepsis. This growing clinical role makes the regulatory landscape surrounding mNGS an urgent subject for evaluation, particularly given the phased implementation of the European In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR). The transition from the In Vitro Diagnostic Directive (IVDD) to the IVDR marks a shift toward a harmonized, risk-based framework for in vitro diagnostics in the European Economic Area (EEA), but several aspects remain unclear for complex laboratory-developed tests (LDTs) such as clinical mNGS - including the practical implementation of the health institution exemption under Article 5(5), the classification of broad mNGS assays within the current risk tiers, and the scope of required analytical and clinical validation. Notably, validation strategies for mNGS may need to focus on the overall analytical method and intended use rather than on individual target pathogens. Further priorities include harmonized quality requirements, broader availability of external quality assessment (EQA), and clearer frameworks for transferring validated protocols between institutions. This review critically evaluates the current European regulatory framework for clinical mNGS-based LDTs and identifies areas requiring further clarification. Continued collaboration between healthcare institutions, regulators, scientific societies, and industry will be essential to keep requirements proportionate while supporting safe, reliable, and clinically useful implementation of mNGS in routine diagnostics.

42826382.title: Neutrophil CD64, Monocyte HLA-DR, and Immune Dysregulation Index as Biomarkers for Severe Coronavirus Disease of 2019 Infection, Bacterial Sepsis, and Other Systemic Inflammatory States.
42826382.abstract: Differentiating bacterial sepsis (BS), severe coronavirus disease of 2019 (SCOV-19), and noninfectious systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) remains challenging due to overlapping clinical features. We evaluated the diagnostic and prognostic utility of neutrophil CD64 (nCD64), Monocyte human leukocyte antigen-DR (mHLA-DR), and the immune dysregulation index (IDI) across these conditions. In this prospective observational study, 150 intensive care unit (ICU) patients were enrolled: BS (n = 44), SCOV-19 (n = 46), SIRS (n = 30), and healthy controls (n = 30). Flow cytometric quantification of nCD64 and mHLA-DR was performed, and IDI was calculated as (nCD64/mHLA-DR) ×100. Clinical, laboratory, and outcome data were analyzed to assess group differences and diagnostic performance. nCD64 expression was significantly elevated in sepsis (median 2310 antibody bound per cell) compared with SCOV-19 (931), SIRS (1034), and controls (348; P = 0.001). mHLA-DR was suppressed in sepsis and SCOV-19 (2711 and 2522) relative to SIRS (10,113) and controls (14,950; P = 0.031). IDI was highest in sepsis (84.16), intermediate in SCOV-19 (38.4), lower in SIRS (9.8), and minimal in controls (2.1; P < 0.0001). IDI demonstrated excellent discrimination between disease and controls (area under the curve [AUC] = 1.0), sepsis and SIRS (AUC = 0.96), and moderate discrimination between sepsis and SCOV-19 (AUC = 0.75). Higher IDI values were associated with mortality in both sepsis (107.80 vs. 35.00; P = 0.032) and SCOV-19 (73.02 vs. 19.80; P < 0.0001). Immune phenotyping using nCD64, mHLA-DR, and IDI effectively differentiates infectious from sterile inflammation and predicts mortality, supporting its integration into ICU risk stratification.

42825806.title: Clinical pathways of hospitalized extremity soft-tissue infections: a retrospective study.
42825806.abstract: Bacterial infections of the skin and soft tissues (SSTIs) are common and should be considered a key differential diagnosis in patients presenting with redness and swelling in these areas. They range from mild superficial cases to severe, complicated forms requiring prompt antimicrobial therapy and, often, surgical intervention. We aimed to describe clinical pathways, diagnostic evolution, treatment strategies, and outcomes in a hospitalized orthopedic/trauma surgery cohort. We performed a retrospective single-center analysis of all inpatients treated for extremity SSTIs between January 2020 and December 2023. Extracted variables included demographics, admission and discharge diagnoses, inflammatory markers, imaging, microbiology, surgical procedures, antibiotic regimens and duration, intensive care unit (ICU) utilization, and in-hospital outcomes. A total of 242 patients were included (mean age 55.7 ± 20.3 years; 40.1% female), with a median length of stay of 7.5 days. ICU care was required in 25/242 10.3%; in-hospital mortality was 7/242 2.9%. Surgical management was required in 134/242 patients (55.4%). Comorbidity burden was substantial (ASA III-IV: 41.3%), and sepsis was documented in 32/242 (13.2%). Diagnostic classification changed between admission and discharge in 80/242 cases (33.1%) of cases. Inflammatory markers declined markedly from admission to discharge (CRP 43.0 [Range: 0.6-640.2, IQR: 13.2-107.5] to CRP: 13.1 [Range: 0.4-541.0, IQR: 4.6-35.2]; leukocytes 11.9 ± 6.09 10/L to 7.68 ± 4.25 109/L). The hand, lower leg and foot were the most frequent sites. CT was performed in 111/242 (45.9%) and ultrasound in 65/242 (26.9%), with heterogeneous imaging strategies (CT only 87/242 (36.0%), US only 41/242 (16.9%), both 24/242 (9.9%), none 90/242 (37.2%)). CT use clustered with higher admission CRP and higher operative burden, including more re-interventions among operated patients. Cultures were frequently negative; when positive, staphylococci and streptococci predominated. Ampicillin/sulbactam and amoxicillin/clavulanate were the most common antibiotics, with frequent IV combination therapy. Hospitalized extremity SSTIs were characterized by frequent diagnostic reclassification, heterogeneous documentation and imaging pathways, and a high rate of operative management despite overall favorable outcomes. CT was more frequently used in patients with higher inflammatory activity and greater procedural burden. This descriptive association may, at least in part, reflect differences in clinical severity and selection for imaging. The findings support structured reassessment and targeted imaging when anatomical clarification is likely to alter management.

42825252.title: Comparative Effectiveness of Empiric Antibiotics for Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infection in Postmenopausal Women.
42825252.abstract: To compare the effectiveness of antibiotic regimens for acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection (UTI) in postmenopausal women using real-world clinical data. We conducted a retrospective cohort study in the TriNetX database of women aged 40 years or older with menopausal or postmenopausal status who developed acute uncomplicated cystitis or UTI between March 2006 and March 2026. Patients were stratified by initial antibiotic therapy of nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), or fosfomycin. The primary outcome was a composite measure of treatment failure within 7 days of treatment initiation, including antibiotic escalation, pyelonephritis, bacteremia, sepsis, hospitalization, critical care services, and mortality. Propensity score matching was used to balance demographics, laboratory values, comorbidities, and prior gynecological procedures. Outcomes were compared between matched groups with a two-sided z test for proportions. A total of 236,927 postmenopausal women initiating antibiotics to treat uncomplicated UTI were identified (nitrofurantoin n=152,793; TMP-SMX n=80,815; and fosfomycin n=3,319). After matching, TMP-SMX was associated with a higher risk of composite treatment failure compared with nitrofurantoin (10.2% vs 8.0%, relative risk ratio [RR] 1.28, 95% CI, 1.23-1.32). In addition, TMP-SMX was associated with higher rates of antibiotic escalation, pyelonephritis, bacteremia, sepsis, hospitalization, critical care services, and mortality. Compared with fosfomycin, TMP-SMX was associated with a higher risk of composite treatment failure (13.3% vs 9.6%, RR 1.39, 95% CI, 1.21-1.59), as well as higher rates of sepsis, hospitalization, and critical care services. Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin had similar rates of composite treatment failure (9.0% vs 9.6%, RR 0.93, 95% CI, 0.80-1.09), although hospitalization was less frequent with nitrofurantoin (1.8% vs 3.0%, RR 0.60, 95% CI, 0.44-0.82). Among postmenopausal women with acute uncomplicated UTI, treatment with TMP-SMX was associated with higher rates of adverse outcomes and serious infectious complications compared with nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin. Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin demonstrated similar short-term outcomes. These findings support the need for postmenopausal-specific evidence to inform empiric UTI treatment selection.

42824039.title: Bridging sepsis physiology and biosensor engineering: a clinical perspective on electrochemical cytokine sensor design.
42824039.abstract: Sepsis remains one of the most critical challenges in contemporary intensive care medicine, characterized by profound immunological and physiological heterogeneity. Cytokines have gained increasing attention as dynamic biomarkers that can complement conventional markers and bedside clinical assessment, enabling more refined diagnosis, risk stratification, and monitoring of treatment response. Most current work on cytokine biosensing is organized around a technological ambition: continuous, minimally invasive, wearable measurement. In this Perspective, we invert that starting point and derive sensor specifications from the pathophysiology and workflow of the septic patient in intensive care. Doing so yields a different set of priorities. Because septic concentrations of the principal mediators span three to four orders of magnitude, a wide linear range matters more than the lowest attainable limit of detection. Because resuscitation and antimicrobial decisions are made within the first hours, response times must be measured in minutes rather than tens of minutes. Because reference ranges, kinetics and outcome associations have been established only in blood, and because vascular access is already present in these patients, whole blood remains the medium of choice, and a discrete, single-use format is preferable to continuous operation in a fouling-prone matrix. Several of these conclusions run counter to the direction the field is currently taking. We argue that aligning sensor architecture with the pathophysiological context of sepsis is a precondition for cytokine-targeted biosensing to support decision-making at the bedside.

42957093.title: Predictors of severe measles outcomes in hospitalized patients in Jerusalem, 2025.
42957093.journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
42957093.abstract: Measles is a vaccine-preventable disease. Defining risk factors for poor outcomes in hospitalized patients can improve future measles outbreak preparedness. Data were collected on all confirmed measles cases that were evaluated at one of the emergency departments (ED) in the three main hospitals in Jerusalem from the first reported case of the current outbreak on April 10th to December 31st, 2025. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data were analyzed using robust Poisson multivariable models to calculate incidence rate ratios (IRR) for hospitalization, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) and death. Among 786 individuals who visited the ED with confirmed measles, the rates of hospital admission (≥1 day), ICU, ECMO and death were 83.4%, 6.4%, 0.8%, and 1.4%, respectively. Complete data were available for 567 patients, of whom 303 (53.4%) were males. Median age was 2.1 years (IQR 1.2-3.8), and 474 (83.6%) were younger than 5 years. Most patients were unvaccinated (91.0%). Secondary infections were frequent, including lobar pneumonia (28.7%) and community-acquired bacteremia (3.5%). Respiratory support and severe dehydration were associated with hospital admission (IRR 1.4, 95% CI 1.3-1.5; p<0.001 and 9.5, 4.8-18.4; p<0.001, respectively) and ICU admission (IRR 1.3, 1.2-1.4; p<0.001 and 5.2, 2.1-12.4; p<0.001, respectively). Community-acquired bacteremia was associated with death or ECMO (IRR 44.5, 12.5-158.6; p<0.001). Despite high access to medical care in this urban setting, measles caused substantial morbidity and mortality. Respiratory compromise, severe dehydration, and bacteremia identified patients at increased risk of severe outcomes.

42956713.title: Rural Pathologies: A Late Presentation Special.
42956713.abstract: Patients in rural and remote Australia often present later and with more advanced disease compared to major and regional cities. Drawing on experience as a junior doctor in the Cape and in rural emergency departments, this article explores how geographic isolation, limited resources, health literacy challenges and inequities in access shape these presentations. Cases include a critically unwell patient managed overnight in a makeshift intensive care bay when weather delayed retrieval, a family of young children with Norwegian Scabies, and a partial finger amputation complicated by weekend staffing shortages. The article reviews Australian evidence on sepsis, scabies and its link to rheumatic heart disease and trauma outcomes, all of which tend to be more challenging to manage. Timely care in rural and remote communities depends on early recognition, clear communication and close collaboration between rural generalists, FACEMs, retrieval services and specialist teams.

42955323.title: Immunological signatures of sepsis in abdominal solid organ transplant recipients: A multilayer and multicentric prospective cohort study.
42955323.abstract: Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction resulting from a dysregulated host response to infection. Patients with prior abdominal solid organ transplantation (SOT) are highly susceptible to infection due to chronic immunosuppression, yet exhibit improved survival once sepsis occurs. The underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. We conducted a post hoc analysis within a prospective multicenter cohort of septic patients (SepsisDataNet.NRW; n = 538). Clinical outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression. Immune profiling included serum cytokines, flow cytometric immunophenotyping, plasma proteomics, and intracellular signaling using proximity ligation assays (PLA) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). To reduce clinical confounding, complementary exploratory analyses were performed in a non-septic kidney transplant cohort (e:KID). SOT patients demonstrated improved 30-day survival compared with non-SOT patients (84% vs. 66%; adjusted HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.26-0.95). Cytokine analysis revealed lower IL-6 and TNF-α levels alongside higher IL-18 concentrations, indicating an altered inflammatory profile. Flow cytometry showed reductions in adaptive immune cells but relatively preserved innate immune function, reflected by higher monocytic HLA-DR expression. Proteomics identified enrichment of innate immune, complement, and lipid metabolic response networks. PLA-based cellular analyses revealed increased GLUT1 expression and enhanced TFAM/TFB2M interaction in SOT patients, indicating a distinct immunometabolic marker profile. In e:KID patients paired serum metabolomics demonstrated higher glucose and lower lactate concentrations 12 months after transplantation, accompanied by broader alterations in lipid and branched-chain amino acid profiles. In patients with sepsis, abdominal SOT is associated with significant better survival than in non-SOT patients. Septic abdominal SOT patients display a distinct immune phenotype characterized by attenuated systemic inflammation, relative preservation of selected innate immune readouts, and alterations in immunometabolic markers.

42954754.title: SEPSIS-INDUCED COAGULOPATHY ATTENUATES THE PROGNOSTIC VALUE OF THE HEMOGLOBIN-ALBUMIN-LYMPHOCYTE-PLATELET (HALP) SCORE IN SEPSIS.
42954754.abstract: The hemoglobin-albumin-lymphocyte-platelet (HALP) score predicts outcomes in sepsis, but its platelet denominator is also a core component of sepsis-induced coagulopathy (SIC), and may distort its prognostic meaning. We examined whether SIC modifies HALP's association with 28-day mortality. We analyzed 6,218 adults meeting Sepsis-3 criteria in MIMIC-IV. HALP was calculated from first ICU measurements; SIC was defined by the 2017 ISTH criteria (score ≥4). Analyses included multivariable regression, interaction testing, propensity-score methods, and platelet-independent coagulopathy definitions, and evaluation of modified HALP (m-HALP; platelets in the numerator). Twenty-eight-day mortality was 25.6%; SIC incidence was 26.1%. HALP showed a J-shaped association with mortality (P for nonlinearity <0.001). The lowest quartile independently predicted death (adjusted OR 1.43, 95% CI 1.20-1.70; HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.10-1.39). This association persisted in non-SIC patients (OR 1.51, 95% CI 1.28-1.79) but was attenuated and non-significant in SIC patients (OR 1.14, 95% CI 0.82-1.60; interaction P=0.006). Albumin carried HALP's discrimination in non-SIC patients, whereas platelets dominated in SIC (OR 0.51 per SD, P=0.001). When coagulopathy was redefined without platelets, the modification was no longer significant (P=0.295), indicating it partly reflects the shared platelet component. m-HALP was inversely associated with mortality in both strata (interaction P=0.691). Results were robust to weighting, 90-day mortality, and alternative Cox models. HALP is an independent prognostic marker mainly in septic patients without coagulopathy; once SIC develops, thrombocytopenia both raises mortality risk and arithmetically inflates HALP. Coagulation status should be assessed before HALP-based risk stratification; m-HALP may offer a platelet-consistent alternative.

42953236.title: Incidence and risk factors of acute skin failure in patients with sepsis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42953236.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine the incidence and risk factors of acute skin failure (ASF) in patients with sepsis. Two reviewers independently searched PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Database, Embase, CNKI, Wanfang Database, and VIP Database from database inception to December 2025. Observational studies reporting ASF incidence and risk factors in sepsis patients were included. Random-effects meta-analysis was used to pool incidence and odds ratios (ORs); case-control studies were excluded from incidence pooling and analyzed only for associated factors. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots, Begg's and Egger's tests. Study quality was evaluated using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) and the AHRQ checklist. Eighteen observational studies comprising 3,295 adult participants were included. After exclusion of two case-control studies from incidence pooling, the pooled ASF incidence across the 16 cohort and cross-sectional studies (n = 2,697) was 45.2% (95% CI: 34.5-56.2%), with a 95% prediction interval of 12.2-83.0% and substantial heterogeneity (I 2 = 96.1%, p < 0.0001). Elevated arterial blood lactate [OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.15-1.25; p < 0.00001; I 2 = 50%], higher SOFA score [OR 1.23, 95% CI 1.16-1.31; p < 0.00001; I 2 = 20%], and higher APACHE II score [OR 1.16, 95% CI 1.10-1.21; p < 0.00001; I 2 = 34%] were significantly associated with increased ASF risk, whereas lower mean arterial pressure was associated with ASF [OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.93-0.96; p < 0.00001; I 2 = 47%]. Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the pooled estimates, and no significant publication bias was detected (Egger's p = 0.467; Begg's p = 0.239). ASF affects a substantial proportion of patients with sepsis. Lactate, SOFA score, APACHE II score and MAP are variables associated with ASF that may support early identification of patients at heightened risk; prospective studies are needed to validate predictive models.

42952930.title: Circulating calprotectin and S100A8/A9-related biomarkers for diagnosis and prognostic stratification in adult acute infection and sepsis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42952930.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
42952930.abstract: Circulating calprotectin is a proposed marker of acute innate immune activation, but reported diagnostic and prognostic performance is inconsistent. We assessed circulating calprotectin and S100A8/A9-related biomarkers for diagnosing acute infection and sepsis and stratifying prognosis in adults. We searched biomedical databases and trial registries through July 4, 2026, for adult studies of circulating calprotectin/S100A8/A9 in acute infection or sepsis. Random-effects models pooled diagnostic and reported prognostic areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Threshold-based sensitivity and specificity were analyzed separately using bivariate random-effects models. We used the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2) and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) to assess diagnostic risk of bias and evidence certainty. Exploratory subgroup, sensitivity, biomarker-comparison, and combined-model analyses were also performed. Twenty-two reports representing 21 independent cohorts were included. The primary diagnostic meta-analysis yielded a pooled AUC of 0.741 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.657-0.810). The pooled AUC was 0.703 (95% CI, 0.600-0.789) for sepsis and 0.758 (95% CI, 0.636-0.849) for acute infection or infection-source-related outcomes. In separate threshold-based analyses, pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.70 (95% CI, 0.46-0.86) and 0.57 (95% CI, 0.55-0.59) for sepsis, and 0.46 (95% CI, 0.09-0.88) and 0.86 (95% CI, 0.60-0.96) for acute infection or infection-source-related outcomes, respectively. For mortality/survival outcomes, pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.72 (95% CI, 0.65-0.77) and 0.66 (95% CI, 0.53-0.77), respectively, while the pooled reported prognostic AUC was 0.737 (95% CI, 0.688-0.786). Exploratory analyses were directionally stable, but paired biomarker comparisons did not provide definitive evidence of superiority. Certainty was very low for all major outcomes. Circulating calprotectin and S100A8/A9-related biomarkers provide moderate, context-dependent information in adult acute infection and sepsis. They may serve as adjunctive host-response markers, particularly for selected infection/source contrasts, but current evidence does not support stand-alone diagnosis, universal thresholds, or replacement of established biomarkers and clinical assessment. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261441569, identifier CRD420261441569.

42952822.title: Landmark-specific phenotypic heterogeneity in CRRT discontinuation timing: a multi-landmark target trial emulation using MIMIC-IV.
42952822.abstract: The optimal timing for discontinuing continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) in critically ill patients remains uncertain. Observational studies commonly simplify discontinuation timing into "early" vs. "delayed" categories, yet the same label may correspond to different clinical states at different stages of illness. We evaluated whether the clinical meaning of the early-discontinuation label and its association with 30-day mortality varied across landmarks and analytic frameworks. Using MIMIC-IV (2008-2019), we emulated a target trial among adults who were alive and still receiving CRRT 48 h after initiation. Early discontinuation was defined as stopping CRRT within 24 h after the 48-hour landmark, whereas delayed discontinuation was defined as continuing CRRT beyond 24 h. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality. Analyses included crude Cox regression, baseline IPTW-Cox, multi-landmark analyses at 48, 72, 96, and 120 h, a marginal structural model (MSM) using time-varying IPTW, and clone-censor-weighting (CCW) with stabilized censoring weights under a 24-hour grace period. Phenotype decomposition was also performed to assess the clinical composition of patients classified as having early discontinuation at different landmarks. A total of 1,432 patients were included, of whom 369 (25.8%) met the definition of early discontinuation. Baseline IPTW-Cox suggested that early discontinuation was associated with higher 30-day mortality (HR 1.36, 95% CI 1.13-1.64; P = 0.001). Multi-landmark HRs ranged from 1.13 to 1.35 without a monotonic pattern; precision decreased at later landmarks, and the landmark-by-exposure interaction was not statistically significant. The MSM estimate was OR 1.16 (95% CI 0.82-1.63; P = 0.40), and the revised CCW estimate was HR 1.08 (95% CI 0.91-1.28; P = 0.38). Phenotype decomposition showed that sepsis prevalence increased from 55.6% at 48 h to 69.1% at 120 h, baseline vasopressor exposure increased from 55.8% to 71.9%, and urine output decreased from 818 mL to 524 mL. Baseline IPTW generated a significant signal suggesting harm from early CRRT discontinuation, but this was not reproduced in multi-landmark, MSM, or CCW analyses. Phenotype decomposition indicated that "early weaning" captures different clinical profiles at different time points rather than a stable, homogeneous exposure. Observational CRRT weaning studies should consider dynamic treatment strategies, time-varying causal methods, and clinically grounded outcome definitions.

42952644.title: Plasma metabolomic profiling identifies candidate biomarkers associated with sepsis diagnosis and mortality prediction.
42952644.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection; its early diagnosis and mortality prediction remain challenging, and conventional markers (CRP, PCT) have limited sensitivity and specificity. We aimed to characterize the plasma metabolome of sepsis and identify candidate metabolic biomarkers for diagnosis and 30-day mortality prediction. In this retrospective, single-center study, plasma from 30 healthy volunteers, 107 sepsis/septic shock patients and 19 non-septic ICU patients was analyzed by non-targeted LC-MS/MS and stratified into discovery (n=86) and replication (n=70) cohorts. Differential metabolites were defined by VIP > 1 and p < 0.05, with Benjamini-Hochberg q-values reported. Diagnostic and prognostic performance was assessed by ROC analysis and compared with CRP, PCT and the SOFA score; survival was analyzed by Kaplan-Meier with the log-rank test. A longitudinal subset was sampled on days 1, 3 and 5. Multivariate analyses identified nine significantly dysregulated metabolites in sepsis patients versus both controls and non-septic ICU patients. Three-3-methoxyanthranilate, docosahexaenoic acid and N-acetyl-beta-alanine-showed particular significance, with alterations in amino-acid, carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, and were elevated in non-survivors. Longitudinal analysis revealed distinctive temporal patterns for 3-methoxyanthranilate and N-acetyl-beta-alanine. The combined panel showed diagnostic and prognostic performance that compared favorably with CRP, PCT and the SOFA score for sepsis differentiation and 30-day mortality. 3-methoxyanthranilate, docosahexaenoic acid and N-acetyl-beta-alanine are candidate metabolic biomarkers for sepsis diagnosis and prognosis. Given the modest, single-center sample, these exploratory, hypothesis-generating findings require confirmation in larger, multi-center cohorts and targeted metabolomic studies.

42952602.title: Integrated transcriptomic and functional analyses identify LAIR1 as a key immunoregulatory molecule in postoperative sepsis.
42952602.abstract: Postoperative sepsis arises from a dysregulated host response to infection following surgical stress. Current non-specific biomarkers offer insufficient predictive value, highlighting the need to identify molecular signatures that may facilitate earlier recognition of postoperative sepsis while providing insight into the underlying immune regulatory mechanisms. Transcriptomic datasets comprising postoperative septic and non-septic surgical cohorts, together with independent cohorts of sepsis and non-infectious systemic inflammation, were analyzed using Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis and machine-learning approaches to identify hub genes. A diagnostic nomogram was constructed and validated across independent cohorts. A murine postoperative endotoxemia model (tibial fracture surgery followed by LPS challenge) was used for in vivo validation. Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis and LAIR1 antibody blockade were performed to assess cellular and functional relevance. A four-gene signature comprising LAIR1, PLAC8, ACSS2, and PCOLCE2 was identified. The resulting model achieved AUCs of 0.865 in GSE131761, 0.965 in GSE74224, 0.827 in E-MTAB-1548, 0.929 in GSE65682, and 0.997 in GSE77167. Among the four genes, LAIR1 showed the most sustained upregulation in peripheral blood and multiple organs during postoperative endotoxemia. Single-cell analysis identified monocytes as the predominant circulating source of LAIR1. LAIR1 blockade increased systemic cytokine release, aggravated multiorgan injury, and reduced survival. The four-gene signature reproducibly distinguished sepsis from infection-negative systemic inflammation across surgical and broader ICU cohorts. LAIR1 exhibited monocyte-enriched expression and a protective immunoregulatory role in postoperative endotoxemia, supporting its relevance to immune dysregulation of sepsis.

42952567.title: Immune-programmed cell death crosstalk implicates plasma sTNFR1 as a candidate biomarker for sepsis-associated encephalopathy.
42952567.abstract: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) is a frequent neurological manifestation of sepsis characterized by acute and diffuse brain dysfunction. Despite increasing evidence of molecular alterations in the septic brain, clinically applicable circulating biomarkers for SAE remain limited. Immune dysregulation and programmed cell death (PCD) pathways have been implicated in SAE pathogenesis, but their translational relevance for peripheral biomarker development remains unclear. This study aimed to identify immune-PCD crosstalk-related biomarkers for SAE through an integrated transcriptomic and clinical evaluation strategy. Human brain transcriptomic data from GSE135838 were analyzed using differential expression analysis and gene set enrichment analysis. Immune-related pathways, PCD signatures, and extracellular protein annotations were integrated to prioritize candidate biomarkers with peripheral detection potential. An exploratory cross-species comparison was performed using mouse SAE microglial RNA-sequencing data (GSE198862). Plasma soluble TNFR1 (sTNFR1) was subsequently evaluated in a prospective cohort of 60 septic patients (26 SAE and 34 non-SAE). SAE was defined as acute diffuse cerebral dysfunction during sepsis, identified by reduced GCS and/or a positive CAM-ICU assessment after exclusion of alternative causes, including persistent deep sedation that precluded reliable neurological assessment. Plasma samples for sTNFR1 measurement were collected within 24 h after enrollment, while SAE status was determined during the baseline neurological assessment after ICU admission. Logistic regression, ROC analysis, and bootstrap validation assessed the incremental value of sTNFR1, with 28-day mortality examined exploratorily. Transcriptomic analysis revealed activation of immune inflammatory responses and multiple PCD-related pathways in SAE brain tissue. Integration of immune, PCD, and differential expression signatures identified 15 immune-PCD crosstalk genes. Extracellular prioritization further identified FAS, IL6, and TNFRSF1A as candidate biomarkers. The immune-PCD signature showed substantial directional concordance in mouse SAE microglial transcriptomes, including concordant increases in Fas and Tnfrsf1a. In the clinical cohort, plasma sTNFR1 levels were significantly elevated in SAE patients compared with non-SAE patients (p < 0.001). After adjustment for age and SOFA score, sTNFR1 remained independently associated with SAE. Adding sTNFR1 increased the observed AUC from 0.791 to 0.891; however, the difference did not reach statistical significance by the paired DeLong test (p = 0.086). Continuous NRI nevertheless indicated improved reclassification (NRI = 0.950, 95% CI 0.411-1.536; p = 0.001). Exploratory analyses also associated SAE and higher sTNFR1 levels with increased 28-day mortality. This study integrates sepsis-associated brain transcriptomic discovery with prospective peripheral clinical evaluation and identifies circulating sTNFR1 as a candidate biomarker associated with SAE. sTNFR1 may provide additional information beyond conventional severity assessment for SAE identification and merits further validation.

42952521.title: IL-10 diplotype and septic shock: Genotype-Phenotype associations with hemodynamic dysfunction and IL-10 expression.
42952521.abstract: Early identification of patients with sepsis who are at increased risk of developing septic shock remains a major clinical challenge. Although genetic variation within the IL-10 locus has been associated with immune regulation, the relationship between the rs1518111-rs1554286 haplotype architecture, inflammatory phenotype, and hemodynamic status has not been fully characterized. This study investigated whether IL-10 haplotypes are associated with progression to septic shock and their relationship with blood pressure and systemic and urinary IL-10 concentrations. In this prospective observational study, 492 adult patients with sepsis admitted to the intensive care unit were enrolled according to the Sepsis-3 criteria. Genotyping of IL-10 rs1518111 and rs1554286 was performed using TaqMan allelic discrimination assays. Linkage disequilibrium, haplotypes, and diplotypes were reconstructed using Haploview and PHASE software. Serum and urinary IL-10 concentrations were quantified by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Associations between genetic variants, clinical phenotypes, and septic shock were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, admission white blood cell count, and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. The two loci demonstrated strong linkage disequilibrium (D' = 1.00, r 2 = 0.903). Compared with the reference heterozygous diplotype (C-G/T-A), the homozygous variant diplotype (T-A/T-A) was independently associated with septic shock (adjusted OR, 6.30; 95% CI, 3.68-10.78; P < 0.001), whereas the homozygous wild-type diplotype (C-G/C-G) was associated with lower odds (adjusted OR, 0.28; 95% CI, 0.14-0.61; P < 0.001). Variant homozygotes exhibited higher serum and urinary IL-10 concentrations and lower blood pressure than wild-type carriers. Serum IL-10 yielded an AUC of 0.851, while a combined clinical-genetic model achieved an AUC of 0.889 (95% CI, 0.820-0.958). Variation within the IL-10 rs1518111-rs1554286 Diplotype block was associated with susceptibility to septic shock, higher IL-10 concentrations, and lower arterial blood pressure in patients with sepsis. Integration of IL-10 diplotype information with routinely available clinical and laboratory variables modestly improved discrimination for septic shock. These findings support further evaluation of IL-10 genetic variation as a complementary biomarker for risk stratification in larger, multicenter cohorts.

42952460.title: Platelet transfusion biology: from hemostatic support to inflammatory and immune signaling.
42952460.abstract: Platelet transfusion remains indispensable for the prevention and treatment of bleeding in hematology, oncology, transplantation, critical care, surgery and trauma. Yet the biological impact of a platelet concentrate extends well beyond numerical correction of thrombocytopenia. Platelets are anucleate but metabolically active immune cells that express pattern-recognition receptors, release cytokines, chemokines, lipid mediators, extracellular vesicles, mitochondria-derived material and damage-associated molecular patterns; and interact with leukocytes, endothelial cells and complement. During collection, processing and storage, platelet concentrates acquire a distinct productspecific phenotype shaped by donor biology, residual plasma, additive solutions, leukoreduction, pathogen reduction, temperature and storage time. These variables affect not only post-transfusion recovery and hemostatic function, but also inflammatory signaling and immune related complications. The recipient is equally important: sepsis, chemotherapy, malignancy, neonatal immune development, endothelial activation and prior alloimmunization can determine whether transfused platelets restore hemostasis, amplify inflammation, or trigger refractoriness. This review explores platelet transfusion through the lens of a biological triad formed by the donor, the platelet product, and the recipient. We focus on how platelet immune receptors, storage-induced inflammatory remodeling, soluble biological response modifiers, extracellular vesicles and complement shape the interactions of transfused platelets with recipient leukocytes and endothelium. Alloimmunization and refractoriness are considered more briefly as recipient-dependent modifiers of platelet recovery and transfusion efficacy. The central challenge is no longer to define a single optimal platelet product, but to engineer and select the right platelet product for the right patient, at the right moment.

42948689.title: Discovery of a potent covalent inhibitor for the treatment of sepsis targeting DNAJC9: Identification of a druggable target for inflammation.
42948689.abstract: Sepsis is a leading cause of mortality among patients in intensive care units (ICUs), with no specific treatments for sepsis available in clinical practice. In this study, we report the discovery of compound A12, a tanshinone derivative featuring a covalent warhead, which demonstrates potent anti-inflammatory effects both in vitro and in vivo. In a lipopolysaccharide-induced mouse model of endotoxemia and acute systemic inflammation, A12 significantly reduces levels of TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-12. Distinct from current anti-inflammatory small molecules, A12 presents a unique mechanism, covalently binding to DNAJC9, thereby modulating the HSP complex and inhibiting the downstream inflammatory response. This work represents the first application of covalent drug design principles to the structural modification of the natural product tanshinone, and reveals the previously unrecognized role of DNAJC9 in inflammatory diseases, offering a novel therapeutic target for management of sepsis-associated acute systemic inflammation.

42947065.title: Association of jugular venous oxygen saturation and mean arterial pressure variability with dynamic cerebral autoregulation and outcomes in sepsis-associated encephalopathy.
42947065.abstract: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) is a frequent and clinically important manifestation of sepsis-related acute brain dysfunction. Impaired cerebral autoregulation and altered cerebral oxygen supply-demand balance are considered relevant pathophysiological features, but the temporally aligned and statistically adjusted relationships among jugular venous oxygen saturation (SjvO2), mean arterial pressure (MAP) variability, and dynamic cerebral autoregulation (dCA) remain insufficiently defined. This retrospective study examined the associations between SjvO2, MAP variability, and dCA indices in neurocritical care patients with SAE and evaluated whether these monitoring variables were associated with impaired dCA and short-term outcomes. We retrospectively analyzed 200 adult neurocritical care and intensive care patients with SAE selected from an indication-based advanced neuromonitoring registry between January 2022 and December 2025. Jugular bulb catheterization was performed for clinical indications rather than as universal screening. SjvO2 monitoring, invasive arterial pressure monitoring, and transcranial Doppler-based dCA assessment were matched within the same early neuromonitoring window after SAE recognition. MAP variability was quantified using the coefficient of variation (MAP-CV) over the 24-hour period containing the first valid dCA session, and SjvO2 was derived from the matched 60-minute monitoring epoch rather than pooled ICU-stay data. Dynamic cerebral autoregulation was assessed by transfer function analysis and the mean flow index (Mx). Multivariable logistic and Cox regression models were adjusted for prespecified illness-severity and physiological covariates. The mean SjvO2 was 62.4 ± 11.8%, with 34.5% of patients demonstrating abnormal values (< 55% or > 75%). MAP-CV was 14.2 ± 5.6%, and impaired dCA (Mx > 0.3) was observed in 58.0% of patients. SjvO2 was negatively correlated with Mx (r=-0.487, p < 0.001) and positively correlated with phase difference (r = 0.412, p < 0.001). MAP-CV was positively correlated with Mx (r = 0.523, p < 0.001) and negatively correlated with phase difference (r=-0.394, p < 0.001). Multivariable analysis identified SjvO2 < 55% (OR = 3.24, 95%CI: 1.78-5.89, p < 0.001), MAP-CV > 15% (OR = 2.87, 95%CI: 1.56-5.28, p = 0.001), and SOFA score (OR = 1.18, 95%CI: 1.06-1.32, p = 0.003) as independent predictors of impaired dCA. Patients with both abnormal SjvO2 and high MAP-CV had higher 28-day mortality than those with normal SjvO2 and low/moderate MAP-CV (51.0% vs. 22.1%, p < 0.001). In a simultaneous Cox model including impaired dCA, the combined abnormal SjvO2/high MAP-CV phenotype remained associated with 28-day mortality (adjusted HR = 2.54, 95%CI: 1.42-4.55, p = 0.002). Lower SjvO2 and greater MAP variability were associated with impaired dCA in SAE patients. The combined assessment of cerebral oxygenation and MAP variability may help identify patients with higher neurological and mortality risk within an observational risk-stratification framework. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation before being used to define individualized hemodynamic targets or treatment effects.

42947029.title: Esophagopericardial fistula secondary to battery acid ingestion in a 3-year-old boy: a case report.
42947029.abstract: Esophagopericardial fistula (EPF) is an extremely rare and life-threatening condition associated with a high mortality rate, particularly when diagnosis and intervention are delayed. Here we present the case of a 3-year-old boy who developed EPF secondary to accidental battery acid ingestion. A 3-year-old Yemeni boy presented with persistent epigastric pain, fever, and progressive dyspnea three weeks after accidental ingestion of battery acid, having initially received conservative supportive management at a regional hospital before delayed referral. Clinical examination revealed tachycardia, tachypnea, and a pericardial friction rub. Laboratory investigations demonstrated leukocytosis, severe thrombocytopenia, anemia, hypoalbuminemia, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers, consistent with sepsis. Imaging studies, including an iso-osmolar contrast swallow and CT, identified a 12-mm esophagopericardial fistula located in the distal esophagus, 2.5 cm above the gastroesophageal junction, accompanied by pyopneumopericardium. Following initial stabilization, the patient underwent a right posterolateral thoracotomy. Intraoperatively, gross inspection revealed extensive full-thickness ischemic necrosis and friability of the distal esophagus with inflammation extending to the pericardium, necessitating radical esophagectomy. The pericardium was opened, thoroughly irrigated with warm sterile saline, and a wide pericardial window was created for continuous drainage. An esophagectomy with gastric pull-up reconstruction was performed to achieve source control. Despite aggressive postoperative critical care, the patient developed refractory sepsis with multiorgan failure and died on the sixth postoperative day. This case highlights the poor prognosis of esophagopericardial fistula following corrosive ingestion in children, especially with delayed presentation and subacute progression. Early recognition and immediate referral to specialized tertiary pediatric surgery centers are paramount.

42946159.title: EZH2 lactylation: a key epigenetic regulator and potential therapeutic target for sepsis-associated lung injury.
42946159.abstract: Sepsis-associated lung injury (SALI) is a lethal infection-induced complication with high mortality and limited targeted therapies. Dysregulated lactate metabolism is closely linked to SALI, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study aims to investigate the role and molecular mechanism of EZH2 (Enhancer of zeste homolog 2) lactylation in SALI development, thereby uncovering a novel exploitable therapeutic target. A total of 209 ICU patients were enrolled and divided into the SALI group (n = 104) and non-SALI group (n = 105) to detect serum lactate levels. Cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) mouse models and endothelial cell-specific Ezh2 knockout (Ezh2ECKO) mouse models were established. Combined with lactate and lactate dehydrogenase inhibitor intervention, multi-omics analysis, ChIP, qPCR, immunofluorescence and other techniques were used in the study. Serum lactate levels were significantly elevated in patients with SALI and model mice, and lung tissue lactate levels were elevated in model mice. Lactate levels were positively associated with inflammatory markers and lung injury severity. EZH2 underwent site-specific lactylation at lysine 30 and 406 (EZH2 K30/K406la) in SALI, which was enhanced with disease progression. Inhibiting lactate production or EZH2 lactylation improved pulmonary function, reduced inflammatory infiltration and pathological lung tissue damage. EZH2 K30/K406la downregulated CITED2 (CBP-p300 interacting transactivator with Glu/Asp-rich carboxy-terminal domain 2) expression by reducing its occupancy at the CITED2 promoter and altering CITED2 promoter activity, relieving the inhibition of the NF-κB (Nuclear Factor-kappa B) pathway and exacerbating inflammatory responses and endothelial dysfunction. EZH2 lactylation aggravates SALI via the CITED2/NF-κB axis, highlighting this epigenetic modification as a promising therapeutic target that opens a new pharmacological avenue for developing site-specific inhibitors to combat SALI.

42945221.title: SIRT5 deficiency exacerbates sepsis acute renal injury by activating ACSL4/FTH1 axis dependent ferroptosis.
42945221.abstract: Sepsis‑associated acute kidney injury (S‑AKI) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in critically ill patients, yet effective targeted therapies remain lacking due to an incomplete understanding of its pathogenesis. Ferroptosis, an iron‑dependent form of regulated cell death driven by lipid peroxidation, has recently been implicated in AKI, but the upstream regulators of this process in sepsis remain undefined. Here, we identify SIRT5, a mitochondrial NAD ⁺ ‑dependent desuccinylase, as a critical endogenous suppressor of ferroptosis in S‑AKI. Using a cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) murine model and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)‑stimulated HK‑2 proximal tubular cells, we show that SIRT5 expression is significantly downregulated in septic kidney injury. Renal tubular‑specific ablation of Sirt5 exacerbated CLP‑induced renal dysfunction, structural damage, and tubular cell death, whereas AAV9‑mediated SIRT5 overexpression attenuated these pathological changes. Mechanistically, SIRT5 deficiency tipped the balance of the ACSL4/FTH1 axis toward ferroptosis: it increased ACSL4‑dependent membrane lipid remodeling and reduced FTH1‑mediated iron sequestration, accompanied by suppression of the antioxidant enzyme GPX4. Consequently, lipid peroxidation, iron overload, and mitochondrial damage were markedly amplified. Notably, knockdown of ACSL4 in SIRT5‑deficient HK‑2 cells effectively reversed lipid peroxidation, iron accumulation, and cell death, establishing ACSL4 as a key downstream effector of SIRT5‑mediated ferroptosis suppression. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized SIRT5-ACSL4/FTH1 regulatory axis that governs ferroptotic susceptibility in renal tubular cells during sepsis, and suggest that pharmacological restoration of SIRT5 activity or blockade of ACSL4‑driven ferroptosis may offer novel therapeutic avenues for S‑AKI.

42942043.title: What a Near-Perfect AUROC Does Not Show: Random-Panel and Label-Permutation Controls for a Sepsis Blood-Transcriptome Signature.
42942043.abstract: Sepsis blood-transcriptome signatures are usually judged against healthy controls. Two questions are rarely separated: whether the classifier exceeds chance, and whether its genes outperform an arbitrary list of equal size. We tested both on public microarray data (discovery GSE65682, n = 359; validation GSE57065, n = 53), using the 9983 of 11,222 genes measurable on both platforms. A 10-gene signature was selected by nested cross-validation and applied to validation without refitting. It separated sepsis from health perfectly (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUROC, 1.000). The pipeline exceeded chance: no label permutation in 1000 matched it (p = 0.001). The genes did not outperform random lists: 12.5% of 2000 random 10-gene panels matched or exceeded the signature, as did 67.6% of panels drawn from the same 300 preselected candidates. Against non-infected intensive care patients, cross-fitted AUROC fell to 0.730 (95% confidence interval 0.642-0.818), unchanged after age and sex matching. At a threshold of 0.5, the cross-fitted model called 70 of these 75 patients septic. Selection was unstable: 200 bootstrap resamples gave a median of 6 genes, from 109 distinct genes. A near-perfect AUROC against healthy controls reflects an easy benchmark, not a specific gene list.

42941668.title: Diagnostic Errors in Sepsis: A Systematic Review of the Literature.
42941668.abstract: Background/Objectives: Sepsis is a major cause of hospitalization and mortality which may be prevented with early diagnosis. This systematic review aims to evaluate the literature on diagnostic errors in sepsis. Methods: We conducted a systematic review to evaluate the rate and outcomes of diagnostic errors in sepsis. We searched MEDLINE and EMBASE in September 2026 for studies that evaluated diagnostic errors in sepsis. Data were extracted into tables and narratively synthesized. Results: Twenty-six studies involving 868,057 patients diagnosed with sepsis were included. Definitions of diagnostic error varied and included misdiagnosis, missed diagnosis, delayed diagnosis, failure of recognition systems, and overdiagnosis. Among adults, reported rates of diagnostic error ranged from 0.6% to 86.2%, depending on the definition used. Misdiagnosis of infection source occurred in 11.6% of patients, sepsis misdiagnosis rates ranged from 8.3% to 25.3% in most cohorts, and delayed recognition ranged from 20.0% to 72.9%. In pediatric studies, missed or delayed sepsis occurred in 2.9% to 16.9% of patients. Diagnostic error was associated with delayed antibiotic administration, increased illness severity, longer hospitalization, and higher intensive care utilization. However, findings regarding mortality were inconsistent, with several studies reporting no significant association after adjustment. In children, missed sepsis was associated with increased risk of intensive care admission, but no difference in mortality. Conclusions: Diagnostic error in sepsis is common and variably defined across studies. Evidence linking diagnostic error to mortality and intensive care admission is inconsistent; however, diagnostic error is frequently associated with delayed treatment.

42941541.title: oXiris-Based Blood Purification Efficacy in Adults with Septic Shock and Acute Kidney Injury: The PURE Multicenter Pilot Randomized Clinical Trial.
42941541.abstract: Background/Objectives: Randomized evidence for the oXiris adsorptive membrane in septic shock remains limited. We estimated its effect on 28-day mortality and explored short-term physiologic outcomes in adults with septic shock and acute kidney injury requiring continuous renal replacement therapy. Methods: PURE was a multicenter, single-blind, parallel-group pilot randomized trial in Saudi Arabia. Participants were randomized 1:1 to oXiris-based or conventional continuous venovenous hemodialysis. The primary comparison used unadjusted mortality risk estimates. Secondary observations were summarized descriptively; adjusted and post-hoc Bayesian sensitivity analyses are reported in the main text and supplement. Results: Of 204 randomized participants, 202 were analyzed (oXiris, 100; control, 102). Twenty-eight-day mortality was 39.0% (39/100) versus 47.1% (48/102), respectively (risk ratio, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.60-1.14; risk difference, -8.1 percentage points; 95% CI, -21.7 to 5.6; p = 0.247). Reported 72 h norepinephrine dose, lactate, C-reactive protein, and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score were lower with oXiris; reported intensive care unit (ICU) stay was also shorter. Secondary descriptive observations are limited by unverifiable time-specific denominators and handling of intercurrent events. Premature filter clotting was reported in 8/100 versus 7/102 participants; no device-related adverse events were reported, but safety ascertainment was limited.
