Conclusions: This pilot trial did not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in 28-day mortality, although mortality was numerically lower in the oXiris group. Consistent protocol implementation and encouraging, hypothesis-generating physiologic observations provide a foundation for a definitive trial with complete longitudinal ascertainment.

42941411.title: Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth in Severe Traumatic Brain Injury Is Associated with Late In-Hospital Mortality.
42941411.abstract: Background: Severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) is associated with high mortality. There is increasing evidence suggesting that intestinal dysbiosis may influence clinical outcomes; however, its prognostic significance in patients with severe TBI remains poorly defined. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 235 patients with severe TBI (Glasgow Coma Scale [GCS] score ≤ 8) admitted to the intensive care units of three participating hospitals between September 2023 and December 2024. Quantitative microbiological analysis of jejunal aspirates was performed at admission and repeated on days 12-14 of the ICU stay. Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) was defined as a bacterial load of ≥105 colony-forming units per milliliter (CFU/mL). Multivariable logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were performed. Results: At admission, SIBO was uncommon (3.8%) but increased to 27.9% among patients who underwent repeated assessment. Within the day-14 landmark cohort (n = 179), post-day-14 mortality was higher in patients with SIBO than in those without (34.0% vs. 23.3%). In multivariable logistic regression analysis, SIBO was independently associated with post-day-14 in-hospital mortality after adjustment for age, body mass index, GCS score, PaO2/FiO2 ratio, and blood glucose (OR 2.83, 95% CI 1.06-7.58; p = 0.039). The ROC model demonstrated good discriminative performance, with an apparent area under the curve (AUC) of 0.846 and an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.823 after bootstrap validation. Conclusions: In patients with severe TBI who survived and remained hospitalized through the day-14 landmark, SIBO detected at days 12-14 was independently associated with increased subsequent in-hospital mortality. However, its incremental contribution to discrimination beyond established clinical predictors was modest. Therefore, late SIBO should be interpreted primarily as a dynamic marker associated with prolonged critical illness and adverse outcome rather than as a demonstrated cause of mortality. Prospective validation is required.

42941294.title: Routinely Available Prognostic Factors for Adverse Outcomes in Adults with Complicated Parapneumonic Effusion and Empyema: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
42941294.abstract: Background: Pleural infection remains associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and frequent treatment escalation. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated routinely available prognostic factors associated with adverse clinical outcomes in adults with pleural infection, including complicated parapneumonic effusion and pleural empyema. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to 6 July 2026. Studies evaluating routinely available clinical, biochemical, microbiological, pleural fluid, radiological, or composite prognostic factors were included. Methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Comparable data were synthesized using random-effects meta-analysis. Results: Thirty studies involving 8443 participants were included. The evaluated outcomes comprised treatment failure, short-term mortality, need for surgery, intensive care unit admission, recurrence, readmission, and length of hospital stay. Five studies (877 participants) contributed to the RAPID score meta-analysis. High-risk RAPID classification was associated with greater short-term mortality than combined low- and intermediate-risk classification (RR 4.52, 95% CI 2.71-7.55; primary OR 6.09, 95% CI 3.25-11.38; I2 = 0% for the OR analysis). In a limited meta-analysis of three studies (1239 participants), each 10-year increase in age was associated with higher odds of short-term mortality (OR 1.54, 95% CI 1.02-2.30; I2 = 30.4%); however, mortality was assessed in hospital in two studies and at 90 days in one study. Additional prognostic factors associated with adverse outcomes included comorbidity burden, renal dysfunction, hypoalbuminemia, serial C-reactive protein trajectories, bacteremia, pleural fluid biochemical markers, pleural thickening, loculation, and delayed or ineffective drainage, although heterogeneous reporting precluded further quantitative synthesis. Conclusions: The RAPID score is the most consistently supported routinely available predictor of short-term mortality in adults with pleural infection. Increasing age may also be prognostic, but its pooled estimate is based on only three studies with different mortality windows and should be interpreted cautiously. Future prospective multicenter studies using standardized outcome definitions are needed to validate additional prognostic markers and improve risk-guided clinical decision-making.

42939964.title: Heart in Distress: How Different Shock States Converge on Cardiac Dysfunction.
42939964.abstract: Shock is traditionally classified according to its primary etiology-septic, hypovolemic, obstructive, or cardiogenic-yet these syndromes frequently converge on a common feature: disturbances of cardiac performance, ventricular loading, and tissue perfusion. Despite distinct initiating mechanisms, altered preload and afterload, ventricular interdependence, vascular dysfunction, maladaptive neurohormonal responses, and, in selected states, impaired myocardial contractility may ultimately reduce effective forward flow and tissue perfusion. Echocardiography provides a rapid, noninvasive bedside tool for characterizing these evolving cardiovascular effects. It enables assessment of left and right ventricular function, cardiac filling, preload responsiveness, pulmonary and systemic venous congestion, fluid tolerance, and broader hemodynamic profiles while facilitating recognition of reversible causes such as cardiac tamponade, acute pulmonary embolism, or severe hypovolemia. This allows clinicians to move beyond static etiologic classifications toward a physiology-based assessment of shock. Beyond diagnosis, echocardiography can inform fluid resuscitation and vasoactive or inotropic therapy. Serial assessment also permits evaluation of therapeutic response and evolving hemodynamic phenotypes. This review synthesizes the mechanisms of cardiac involvement across shock syndromes and highlights echocardiography as a unifying tool for their evaluation and management. By integrating pathophysiology, bedside imaging, and hemodynamic treatment, we propose a physiology-based framework that complements traditional shock classification and may improve diagnostic precision and individualized management in critically ill patients.

42939715.title: Secretory Phospholipase A(2)-Albumin-Membrane Interactions: A Proposed Mechanism of Internal Cell and Tissue Injury in Systemic Inflammation.
42939715.abstract: Systemic inflammation in sepsis causes internal cell and tissue injury through mechanisms that remain incompletely understood. Secretory phospholipase A2 (sPLA2-IIA; hereafter, sPLA2), a potent inflammatory mediator whose circulating levels rise dramatically during sepsis, hydrolyzes membrane phospholipids in injured and dying cells, thereby releasing fatty acids and lysophospholipids that further amplify inflammation. Serum albumin-particularly a specific membrane-binding fraction (SFA)-normally acts as a cytoprotective scavenger of these lipid products, thereby maintaining membrane phospholipid homeostasis in concert with sPLA2. This perspective synthesizes nearly two decades of work demonstrating that the sPLA2-albumin interaction is a critical, underappreciated determinant of internal cell and tissue injury during systemic inflammation. As sPLA2 activity rises during sepsis, fatty acids generated from injured membranes progressively saturate albumin's binding sites, inducing structural misfolding that abolishes its cytoprotective capacity and paradoxically enhances further sPLA2-mediated membrane degradation. Serial serum samples from ICU patients with sepsis revealed a statistically significant positive correlation between sPLA2 activity and albumin membrane-binding-site saturation, modifiable by nutritional intervention. Age-related albumin misfolding and oxidative stress are identified as important amplifying factors. The sPLA2-albumin axis represents a promising target for biomarker development and therapeutic intervention in critically ill patients.

42938154.title: Bloodstream Infections in Patients with Malignancy: Microbiological Epidemiology, Antimicrobial Resistance, and Factors Associated with Mortality in a Nine-Year Single-Center Retrospective Cohort.
42938154.abstract: Background/Objectives: Bloodstream infections (BSIs) are a major cause of morbidity and mortality among patients with malignancy because of disease-related immune dysfunction, intensive chemotherapy, neutropenia, and frequent exposure to invasive procedures. This study aimed to characterize the microbiological profile and antimicrobial resistance patterns of BSIs in patients with malignancy and to identify clinical and laboratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality, explicitly treating ICU admission as an associated marker of critical illness rather than a predictor. Methods: This retrospective study included 191 clinically significant BSI episodes recorded between 2016 and 2025; record review confirmed that each included episode represented a different patient. Demographic characteristics, underlying diagnoses, comorbidities, chemotherapy history, catheter status, infection source, hematological and biochemical parameters, bloodstream pathogen category, antimicrobial susceptibility patterns, ward and intensive care unit (ICU) lengths of stay, and in-hospital mortality were evaluated. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square or Fisher's exact test, while continuous variables were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors independently associated with in-hospital mortality. Results: Of the 191 episodes, 96 (50.3%) occurred in female patients and 95 (49.7%) in male patients. Acute leukemia was the most common underlying diagnosis (n = 70, 36.6%). Blood cultures yielded Gram-negative organisms in 110 episodes (57.6%), Gram-positive organisms in 58 (30.4%), fungi in 19 (9.9%), and polymicrobial growth in 4 (2.1%). Among 168 episodes with interpretable bacterial antimicrobial susceptibility results, 99 (58.9%) met the study-defined composite resistance category was not equivalent to multidrug resistance. An indwelling catheter was present in 27 episodes (14.1%), ICU admission occurred in 25 (13.1%), and severe neutropenia (<500 cells/µL) was documented in 72 (37.7%). The median ward length of stay was 8.0 days (interquartile range, 5.0-14.0 days). In-hospital mortality occurred in 39 episodes (20.4%). Patients who died had significantly lower neutrophil, platelet, lymphocyte, and albumin levels and significantly higher urea and C-reactive protein levels than survivors (p < 0.01). In multivariable analysis, ICU admission (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 18.94; 95% confidence interval [CI], 3.49-102.82; p < 0.001) and severe neutropenia (aOR, 6.06; 95% CI, 2.13-17.23; p < 0.001) were associated with in-hospital mortality. However, the wide confidence intervals, particularly for ICU admission, indicate substantial uncertainty in the magnitude of these associations. Conclusions: These estimates should therefore be interpreted cautiously, especially because the timing of ICU admission relative to BSI onset could not be established. Gram-negative organisms predominated among BSI episodes in patients with malignancy, and study-defined resistance phenotypes were frequent but heterogeneous. Severe neutropenia and ICU admission-analyzed specifically as a concurrent marker of critical illness rather than a predictor due to unestablished temporal sequence relative to BSI onset-were associated with in-hospital mortality. These estimates should be interpreted cautiously. Continuous surveillance of local pathogen distributions and resistance phenotypes, early identification of high risk patients, and institution-specific selection of empirical antimicrobial therapy may contribute to improved clinical outcomes.

42936862.title: Obstetric Shock Beyond Hemorrhage: Microcirculatory Shunting, Endothelial Glycocalyx Injury, and Mitochondrial Failure in Pregnancy-A Narrative Review.
42936862.abstract: Obstetric shock has traditionally been conceptualized within the framework of hemorrhage and macrocirculatory collapse. However, clinical deterioration may occur despite preserved blood pressure and cardiac output, indicating that disturbances in tissue perfusion and cellular metabolism can precede overt hemodynamic instability. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence examining the contributions of microcirculatory dysfunction, endothelial glycocalyx injury, mitochondrial impairment, immune-metabolic dysregulation, and placental signaling to the development and progression of obstetric shock beyond conventional hemodynamic paradigms. A literature review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE and PubMed Central, focusing on studies in obstetrics, critical care, endothelial biology, microcirculatory physiology, and mitochondrial function, with articles selected for their mechanistic, translational, and clinical relevance. Available evidence suggests that disruption of the microcirculation, endothelial injury, and impaired cellular energy metabolism may interact to produce tissue hypoperfusion despite preserved systemic hemodynamics, a phenomenon described as hemodynamic incoherence. These mechanisms may contribute to diverse clinical phenotypes, including normotensive hypoperfusion, endothelial dysfunction-associated shock, microthrombotic states, and impaired cellular oxygen utilization. Although much of the supporting evidence derives from studies of preeclampsia, sepsis, and non-obstetric critical illness rather than obstetric shock itself, these findings provide biologically plausible mechanistic insights that may improve understanding of unexplained maternal deterioration. Emerging physiologic monitoring techniques may facilitate earlier recognition of occult tissue hypoperfusion, although their validation and routine clinical application in obstetric practice remain limited. Overall, obstetric shock should be considered a heterogeneous syndrome that extends beyond hemorrhage alone, and an integrated framework incorporating microvascular, endothelial, metabolic, and placental processes may improve understanding of its pathophysiology while informing future diagnostic and therapeutic research. Further obstetric-specific studies are required to validate these concepts and define their clinical implications.

42935912.title: Incremental prognostic value of the T-helper 1/T-helper 2 immune phenotype and 72-h change in sequential organ failure assessment for in-hospital mortality in sepsis with and without type 2 diabetes: a retrospective two-cohort study.
42935912.abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is accompanied by chronic immunometabolic dysregulation and may alter the host response to sepsis. We compared immunometabolic profiles and early organ dysfunction trajectories in patients with sepsis with and without T2DM and evaluated 72-h mortality risk reassessment models. Of 1,200 consecutive adult intensive care unit (ICU) patients screened between January 2020 and December 2025, 1,023 met Sepsis-3 criteria and constituted the 72-h landmark cohort, defined by an ICU stay of at least 72 h and paired day-1/day-3 Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) measurements; all model comparisons were therefore conditional on survival and evaluability at 72 h. Patients were classified into a T2DM-sepsis cohort (n = 513) or non-T2DM-sepsis cohort (n = 510). Model 1 included day-1 SOFA; Model 2 added the T-helper 1/T-helper 2 (Th1/Th2) ratio and interleukin-6 (IL-6); and Model 3 further added the 72-h change in SOFA (ΔSOFA; day-3 minus day-1 SOFA). Post hoc secondary analyses evaluated age-only and age-adjusted benchmarks and a pooled model containing diabetes status, age, and interaction terms. Internal validation was performed using 1,000 bootstrap resamples. Compared with patients without T2DM, those with T2DM had higher glycemic, inflammatory, renal, and physiological severity measures. In the T2DM cohort, the apparent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.781 for Model 1, 0.838 for Model 2, and 0.861 for Model 3; the optimism-corrected Model 3 AUC was 0.858. Age alone had an AUC of 0.634, whereas adding age to Model 3 yielded an AUC of 0.870 (DeLong P = 0.099 vs. Model 3). The age-adjusted pooled model had an apparent AUC of 0.862, and the global predictor-by-diabetes interaction test was not statistically significant (P = 0.191). A 72-h reassessment model combining baseline organ dysfunction, early SOFA trajectory, the Th1/Th2 ratio, and IL-6 may improve mortality risk stratification beyond SOFA alone. The model is intended to prioritize structured clinical reassessment, not replace SOFA or prescribe treatment. Temporal and multicenter, external validation is required before clinical translation.

42935182.title: Artificial intelligence early-warning systems for sepsis: From risk scores to bedside action.
42935182.journal: Technology and health care : official journal of the European Society for Engineering and Medicine
42935182.abstract: BackgroundSepsis remains a leading cause of preventable mortality in critical care. Timely recognition is essential for effective bundle-based management, and artificial intelligence-enabled early-warning systems (AI-EWS) may facilitate earlier detection by converting electronic health record and bedside monitoring data into actionable risk estimates.ObjectiveThis review aimed to synthesize recent advances in the development, validation, and real-world deployment of AI-EWS for sepsis and to identify the factors that determine their clinical benefit at the unit level.MethodsWe conducted a structured narrative review based on a targeted search of PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar from database inception to December 2025. Search terms combined artificial intelligence, machine learning, or deep learning with sepsis and early-warning score or prediction. Priority was given to studies addressing prospective performance, clinical implementation, alert fatigue, workflow integration, governance, and regulation.ResultsAI-EWS may identify sepsis risk earlier than traditional scoring systems; however, retrospective discrimination alone does not ensure clinical benefit. Effective deployment depends on prospective calibration, site-specific threshold setting, precision-recall trade-offs, manageable alert budgets, and integration with nurse-centered workflows, standardized order sets, escalation pathways, and feedback loops. Major implementation risks include alert fatigue, data drift, and limited transportability. Silent-mode trials, group-aware recalibration, regular calibration and drift audits, throttle and rollback rules, and auditable change logs can help mitigate these risks.ConclusionAI-EWS should be evaluated as clinical interventions rather than solely as predictive models. Calibrated risk communication, unit-specific operating points, human-centered workflow integration, and accountable governance are essential for achieving safe, equitable, and measurable improvements in sepsis care.

42934949.title: Isolated Disturbance of Consciousness as Initial Presentation of Staphylococcus aureus Endocarditis: A Case Report With Brief Literature Review.
42934949.journal: The American journal of case reports
42934949.abstract: BACKGROUND Infective endocarditis (IE) typically presents with fever, a heart murmur, or constitutional symptoms, making diagnosis challenging when neurological manifestations predominate. We report an atypical case of IE in which disturbance of consciousness was the initial manifestation. CASE REPORT A man in his 50s was admitted to our hospital with isolated disturbance of consciousness and no history of fever; a temperature of 38°C was recorded on admission. Investigations confirmed an extensive acute right hemispheric watershed (border-zone) infarction involving the right temporoparietal lobe, without evidence of hemorrhagic transformation or intracranial hemorrhage. Subsequent workup identified Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia, mitral valve vegetation, and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome. The absence of classic IE risk factors contributed to a delayed diagnosis. Guideline-concordant clinical management was implemented. Long-term outcome data were unavailable because of patient transfer; only in-hospital mortality (after transfer) was confirmed. We discuss the application of the 2023 Duke criteria to this case and examine factors contributing to the delayed diagnosis of IE. Disturbance of consciousness as the predominant initial manifestation of S. aureus IE is rare and frequently results in diagnostic delay. This case underscores the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for IE in patients with sepsis complicated by acute cerebral infarction, particularly among critical care and neurology clinicians. CONCLUSIONS This case highlights isolated disturbance of consciousness as an atypical initial presentation of IE. Although IE is frequently complicated by acute cerebral infarction, clinicians may not routinely consider IE in the differential diagnosis of patients presenting with disturbed consciousness.

42934835.title: Circulating NLRP3 Inflammasome Activation Is Associated With Sepsis-Associated Acute Kidney Injury and Disease Severity: A Prospective Pilot Study.
42934835.abstract: Sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI) is a severe and prevalent complication in critically ill patients, characterized by high mortality and a lack of reliable biomarkers that reflect inflammatory pathway activation and disease severity. Although the NLRP3 inflammasome is known to mediate inflammatory responses, pyroptosis, and renal injury, its clinical relevance in human SA-AKI remains poorly defined. This study aimed to characterize the expression profiles, dynamic trajectories, and clinical associations of circulating NLRP3 inflammasome components in patients with SA-AKI. Thirty adult patients with sepsis (13 with SA-AKI and 17 without AKI) were prospectively and consecutively enrolled. Sepsis was defined according to the Sepsis-3 consensus criteria, whereas AKI was diagnosed and staged exclusively using the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. Serum protein levels of NLRP3, ASC, caspase-1, cleaved caspase-1, IL-1β, and IL-18, and transcript levels of NLRP3, ASC, and caspase-1, were determined on days 1, 3, 5, and 7 after enrollment using ELISA and quantitative real-time PCR. Statistical analyses included group comparisons, Spearman rank correlations, linear mixed-effects models, and exploratory receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses to assess concurrent group discrimination. Because samples were collected post-classification, these analyses describe post-diagnostic expression kinetics rather than prediction of future AKI onset. The expression of NLRP3 inflammasome-related molecules was significantly upregulated in the SA-AKI group and correlated with renal dysfunction and elevated illness-severity scores (SOFA and APACHE II). Exploratory ROC analyses suggested strong discrimination of concurrent AKI status for ASC, caspase-1, and NLRP3 transcript levels, with the strongest overall performance observed on day 3. These estimates are hypothesis-generating because of the small sample size and post-classification sampling. The NLRP3 inflammasome pathway is prominently activated in patients with SA-AKI and is closely associated with renal dysfunction and systemic illness severity. Circulating components of this pathway are candidate biomarkers of concurrent SA-AKI, but their ability to predict AKI onset or prognosis requires validation in larger prospective cohorts sampled before AKI develops.

42933245.title: Mitral annular plane systolic excursion as a prognostic marker in critical illness: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
42933245.abstract: Cardiac dysfunction is common in critical illness, yet conventional indices such as left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) may fail to detect early impairment. Mitral annular plane systolic excursion (MAPSE), a marker of longitudinal function, may provide prognostic information, but its role in critical illness remains uncertain. PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library were searched for studies evaluating MAPSE in critically ill adults. Studies were included if MAPSE could be dichotomized using prespecified cutoffs (10 or 12 mm). The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality; secondary outcomes included 28-30-day mortality and exploratory measures of cardiac function and organ support. Risk ratios (RRs) and mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled. Risk of bias was assessed with QUIPS and certainty of evidence with GRADE. Ten observational studies including 1313 patients were analyzed; 414 (31.5%) had reduced MAPSE. Most patients had sepsis or septic shock. Reduced MAPSE was associated with higher in-hospital mortality (37.7% vs 11.7%; RR 4.81; 95% CI 1.28-18.04; p = 0.02; I2 = 70.6%), with consistent effects across both cutoffs (p = 0.111) and adequate information size on trial sequential analysis. Reduced MAPSE was also associated with lower LVEF (MD -13.0%; 95% CI -20.6 to -5.4; p < 0.01; I2 = 94.6%), but not with 28-30-day mortality or exploratory outcomes. Certainty of evidence was low for in-hospital mortality and very low for secondary and exploratory outcomes. Reduced MAPSE was associated with higher in-hospital mortality and may be a bedside marker of myocardial dysfunction. Given the limitations of the available evidence, MAPSE remains a hypothesis-generating marker requiring prospective validation.

42933021.title: When Source Control Is Not Enough: Bilateral Adrenal Hemorrhage After Group A Streptococcal Necrotizing Soft Tissue Infection.
42933021.abstract: Refractory septic shock following adequate surgical source control presents a major clinical challenge. While persistent vasopressor dependence in necrotizing soft tissue infections (NSTI) is frequently attributed to ongoing tissue necrosis or overwhelming cytokine release, acute primary adrenal failure due to Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome (WFS) represents an underrecognized, reversible etiology. We report a 41-year-old male who developed fulminant right upper extremity Group A Streptococcus (GAS) necrotizing fasciitis requiring emergent forequarter amputation. Despite definitive source control, targeted antitoxin antimicrobial therapy, and guideline-directed resuscitation, he experienced persistent vasopressor-dependent shock. On postoperative day 5, CT imaging revealed new-onset bilateral adrenal hemorrhage. The initiation of stress-dose hydrocortisone led to rapid hemodynamic stabilization and successful recovery. Surgeons must maintain a high index of suspicion for acute adrenal crisis in postoperative ICU patients with refractory shock despite source control, rather than solely driven by ongoing sepsis.

42931723.title: Fournier's Gangrene-Associated ECG-Pickelhaube Sign: The Evanescent STEMI-Mimic.
42931723.abstract: The spiked helmet sign (SHS), or Pickelhaube sign, is a rare pseudo-ST-segment elevation pattern described in critically ill patients without acute myocardial infarction. A 30-year-old man with class III obesity and diabetes presented in septic shock from extensive Fournier's gangrene. After emergent debridement, telemetry showed anterior ST-segment elevation prompting ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) activation. Serial electrocardiograms demonstrated pre-QRS baseline elevation merging with the QRS and transient anterolateral ST-segment elevation consistent with the Pickelhaube sign. Troponins remained normal, and contrast echocardiography showed hyperdynamic systolic function without regional wall-motion abnormalities. ST elevation resolved spontaneously within 30 minutes, and angiography was deferred. He required vasopressors, continuous venovenous hemofiltration, repeated debridement, and wound vacuum-assisted closure before discharge to long-term acute care. This case demonstrates the Pickelhaube sign during Fournier's gangrene with septic shock. Recognizing its morphology and evolution, along with biomarkers, echocardiography, and clinical context, can distinguish pseudo-STEMI from acute coronary occlusion and avoid unnecessary angiography. The Pickelhaube sign can occur in severe necrotizing soft-tissue infection and septic shock and may closely mimic acute STEMI. Serial electrocardiograms, cardiac biomarkers, echocardiography, and hemodynamic context help distinguish this pseudo-STEMI pattern from acute coronary occlusion.

42928790.title: Factors Associated with Early Sepsis-Associated Liver Injury and Predictors of 30-Day Mortality: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
42928790.abstract: Sepsis-associated liver injury (SALI) is associated with higher mortality, but the factors associated with early SALI and the determinants of mortality in patients with SALI remain incompletely understood. This retrospective cohort study included 524 consecutive patients with sepsis (Sepsis-3) in a tertiary intensive care unit (ICU). SALI was defined as total bilirubin ≥2 mg/dL with international normalized ratio ≥1.5, or alanine aminotransferase ≥68 U/L (twice the local upper limit of normal), within 24 hours of ICU admission. Factors independently associated with SALI and with 30-day mortality in SALI were identified by logistic regression after multiple imputation and elastic-net selection, with bootstrap internal validation. Of 523 evaluable patients, 135 (25.8%) met the SALI definition, and their 30-day mortality was higher (63.4% vs 50.0%, p=0.010). Factors independently associated with SALI were macrophage activation-like syndrome (MALS) (aOR: 5.33), an abdominal focus (aOR: 4.03), disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) score ≥5 (aOR: 3.07), acute kidney injury on admission (aOR: 2.29) and log-ferritin (aOR: 1.31; 1.48 without MALS and DIC) (all p<0.05; optimism-corrected area under the curve [AUC]: 0.770). Among patients with SALI, immunosuppressive therapy (OR: 8.13), a thoracic focus (OR: 8.62), log-ferritin (OR: 2.04) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) (OR: 1.08 per second) were independently associated with 30-day mortality (all p<0.05); appropriate antibiotic therapy showed a non-significant protective trend (p=0.076). The mortality model showed good discrimination (optimism-corrected AUC: 0.857) but limited calibration (slope: 0.562). SALI was associated with higher 30-day mortality in sepsis. Because the factors associated with SALI were assessed concurrently with liver injury, they describe its clinical profile rather than predict its development. Immunosuppressive therapy, a thoracic focus, higher ferritin levels and prolonged aPTT were associated with 30-day mortality in SALI. These findings should be interpreted with caution and require external validation.

42928302.title: Consensus recommendations for patient selection and clinical implementation of polymyxin B hemoadsorption in endotoxic septic shock.
42928302.abstract: Despite long-standing clinical use and emerging evidence, no structured framework exists guiding clinicians in identifying septic shock patients for endotoxemia assessment, interpretation of the Endotoxin Activity Assay (EAA), or practical implementation of polymyxin B hemoadsorption (PMX-HA) therapy. A modified Delphi consensus process was conducted with ten critical care and nephrology experts, compromising a pre-meeting survey, a one-day in-person consensus conference, and iterative voting on draft statements. Consensus was predefined as ≥ 80% agreement. Consensus was achieved on 20 statements across three domains: (1) operational criteria to prompt endotoxemia assessment in suspected or presumed septic shock, (2) role and interpretation of the EAA, and (3) logistics and clinical implementation of PMX-HA. Key recommendations included standardized criteria to identify eligible patients, EAA thresholds of ≥ 0.60 and < 0.90 to support PMX‑HA consideration, initiation of therapy as early as possible once eligibility is confirmed, with ≤ 36 h from septic shock onset proposed as a pragmatic implementation benchmark, and standardized treatment protocols consisting of two sessions, 24 h apart, targeting 120 min each. A multidisciplinary team model was endorsed for implementation. Identified research priorities were in treatment effect heterogeneity, EAA kinetics, clinical implementation, and healthcare system integration. These consensus recommendations provide a structured, implementation-focused framework for PMX-HA use in suspected endotoxic shock. The framework emphasizes stepwise operational criteria, biomarker-guided decision-making, multidisciplinary team-based implementation, and standardized protocols. It is intended to support institutions currently using PMX-HA and to assist U.S. clinicians and health systems in preparing for potential adoption pending regulatory approval.

42928247.title: High-dose regular insulin as a potential rescue therapy in severe aluminum phosphide poisoning: a case report.
42928247.abstract: Aluminum phosphide (rice tablet) can cause cardiocirculatory collapse and has negative cardiac inotropic effect. Positive inotropic effect of insulin on the cardiac myocytes is through calcium flux. Insulin increases the intramyocytes calcium concentration by increasing conductance of calcium through the L-type calcium channels and by increasing intramyocytes concentration of cyclic adenosine monophosphate. In addition to increasing the intramyocytes calcium level, insulin also enhances the responsiveness of the cardiac cells to calcium. High-dose insulin is a potential therapy for hypodynamic and hypotensive septic shock due to its positive inotropic qualities. In this paper, a critical aluminum phosphide poisoning patient (a 25-year-old Iranian young woman), presented with mixed severe metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis, tachypnea, tachycardia, and hypotension. In contrast to our previous experiences that ingestion of aluminum phosphide tablets associated with multiple organ failure and severe shock in approximately all critical poisoning patients, early initiation of high-dose intravenous regular insulin for this patient prevented multiorgan dysfunction and death. Treatment with high-dose intravenous insulin associated with IV fluids, sodium bicarbonate, hydrocortisone, potassium, dextrose therapy and supportive care resolved completely signs and symptoms of patient after 3 days in ICU. High-dose intravenous regular insulin may be act as a rescue therapy for aluminum phosphide poisoning patients. While this single case suggests a potential benefit, further studies are required to confirm these findings.

42927469.title: Persistent Endothelial Glycocalyx Disruption in Sepsis: Translational Evidence for Melatonin-Mediated Vascular Protection.
42927469.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome driven by a dysregulated host response to infection, with endothelial dysfunction and glycocalyx disruption playing central roles in vascular failure. Despite growing recognition of the glycocalyx as a therapeutic target, its temporal dynamics and potential pharmacological modulation remain poorly understood. We performed a translational study combining longitudinal clinical observations in septic patients with mechanistic investigations in a murine cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) model. Plasma from patients was collected at intensive care unit admission and after clinical recovery to assess inflammatory mediators, coagulation parameters, and glycocalyx-related biomarkers. In parallel, the CLP model evaluated systemic and tissue-specific glycocalyx alterations and the effects of injectable melatonin. Acute sepsis induced marked alterations in multiple glycocalyx-related biomarkers in patients, with several changes persisting despite normalization of organ dysfunction and standard inflammatory indices, indicating ongoing endothelial injury and repair. In the CLP model, sepsis reproduced these alterations, while melatonin treatment significantly attenuated systemic cytokine responses and partially restored circulating and tissue glycocalyx components in an organ- and gene-specific manner. These results highlight persistent, dynamic glycocalyx disruption as a key driver of sepsis pathology and support pharmacological stabilization of the glycocalyx as a promising therapeutic strategy. Melatonin emerges as a potential endothelial-protective agent capable of promoting vascular recovery and homeostasis, providing translational insight for interventions targeting microvascular integrity in sepsis.

42926651.title: Clinically Contextualized State Spaces Provide Continuous Representations of Sepsis.
42926651.abstract: Precision medicine increasingly leverages molecular and clinical similarity to identify patient subgroups and guide individualized care. However, conventional cross-sectional approaches often characterize biological states independently of the clinical context in which they arise. Similar laboratory profiles may have different clinical implications depending on subsequent trajectory, while biologically distinct states may share similar clinical outcomes. Consequently, clustering based solely on clinical trajectory-agnostic clustering may incompletely capture clinically relevant heterogeneity. To address these limitations, we introduce CERL (Contextual Endotype and State Representation Learning), a clinical trajectory-informed representation learning framework that integrates clinical contexts to construct patient-state representations from clinical data. Rather than defining patients solely through discrete clusters, CERL learns a continuous clinical state space that preserves biological heterogeneity while organizing states according to clinically relevant trajectories. Across both simulated and real datasets, CERL robustly identified latent patient groups and reliably reproduced the learned patient groups in validation. In a proof-of-concept application across multi-institutional critical care cohorts, CERL identified three reproducible clinical state groups embedded within a state representation. The representation captured systematic variation in routine laboratory phenotypes and demonstrated clinical trajectory-specific redistribution dynamics within the continuous state space. These findings establish CERL as a framework for generating clinically contextualized state representations that integrate biological characteristics with clinical trajectories, providing a foundation for longitudinal pathological progression modeling and future digital twin approaches in critical care.

42925383.title: Incidence, clinical presentation, and outcomes of Pasteurella infections: a population-based study in the North Denmark Region (2009-2023).
42925383.journal: European journal of clinical microbiology & infectious diseases : official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology
42925383.abstract: Pasteurella is associated with human infections following animal bites, though non-bite infections have been reported. Few population-based studies have examined the incidence, clinical presentation, and outcomes of Pasteurella infections. We identified patients with Pasteurella-positive clinical samples in the North Denmark Region (2009-2023). Medical records of hospitalized patients were reviewed for comorbidities, clinical presentation, surgical and antibiotic treatment, and 30-day mortality. We identified 676 patients, of whom 375 were managed in general practice and 301 had a hospital contact. The annual incidence rate increased from 4.1 to 10.3 cases per 100,000 individuals (2009-2023). Pasteurella multocida (61%) predominated, followed by Pasteurella canis (26%), and 41% of samples were polymicrobial. Median age was 60 (IQR 47-70) years among patients with a hospital contact and 59 (IQR 42-70) years among those seen in general practice; 50% and 42% were male, respectively. Among patients with hospital contacts, 57% had underlying comorbidities. Clinical presentations included bite wound infections (59%), chronic wound infections (15%), lower respiratory tract infections (13%), concurrent or isolated bacteremia (6%), and other uncommon presentations (7%). Among patients with a hospital contact, 98% received antibiotic treatment, 65% surgical treatment, and 6% intensive care. The 30-day mortality was 2.7%. The annual incidence of Pasteurella-positive samples increased over time. Almost half of the patients had a hospital contact, and two-thirds of these underwent surgical intervention. While animal bite was the most common exposure, Pasteurella was also detected in chronic ulcers and respiratory tract infections. The incidence of bacteremia and 30-day mortality were low.

42924429.title: Hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenocortical responses to critical illness: new insights with clinical implications.
42924429.abstract: Critical illness profoundly affects the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenocortical (HPA) axis. In the acute phase of sepsis and other critical conditions, systemic cortisol levels rise markedly, yet circulating ACTH is low. Peripheral adaptations - reduced cortisol metabolism, decreased cortisol-binding proteins, and tissue-specific modulation of glucocorticoid receptor signaling - rather than sustained central HPA axis activation generate compartmentalized increased cortisol actions. As illness persists beyond one week, patients transition into prolonged critical illness characterized by a central HPA suppression, impaired adrenocortical structure and function, together increasing the risk for ICU-acquired adrenal insufficiency beyond 4 weeks. Although glucocorticoids, in stress doses, remain widely used for shock reversal, they exacerbate this HPA suppression and aggravate acute and long-term complications of critical illness. A better mechanistic understanding is essential to guide targeted and adequately dosed therapies.

42922205.title: Retroperitoneal Hematoma in Essential Thrombocythaemia: A Diagnostic Challenge.
42922205.abstract: Essential thrombocythaemia (ET) is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by sustained thrombocytosis and an increased risk of both thrombotic and haemorrhagic events. While thrombotic complications are more frequent, major bleeding remains a rare but potentially fatal occurrence, particularly when anticoagulant therapy is required. Retroperitoneal haematoma represents one of the most severe bleeding manifestations, often linked to anticoagulation or vascular fragility. We report the case of an 85-year-old woman with ET, obesity, and hypertension who underwent elective total right hip replacement. Postoperatively, she developed pulmonary micro-embolism and was treated with high-dose enoxaparin. Four days later, she suffered sudden haemodynamic collapse due to a massive retroperitoneal haematoma. Enoxaparin was discontinued and replaced with tranexamic acid infusion. Despite urgent surgical evacuation, multiple transfusions, and intensive care, her condition worsened with the development of femoral vein thrombosis, multidrug-resistant sepsis, worsening pulmonary embolism, and severe thrombocytopenia. She died 34 days after surgery. Autopsy confirmed a large organized haematoma compressing the right renal lodge and inferior vena cava, associated with femoral vein thrombosis. This case highlights the therapeutic and diagnostic challenges of ET, in which thrombotic and haemorrhagic risks may coexist and be further complicated by antithrombotic therapy. Despite individualized enoxaparin dosing based on body weight, the patient developed a major retroperitoneal haemorrhage followed by femoral vein thrombosis. Although disseminated intravascular coagulation and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia were both considered in the differential diagnosis, insufficient clinical and laboratory evidence prevented definitive diagnostic confirmation of either condition. Early and accurate diagnostic assessment is crucial in ET patients, where thrombotic and haemorrhagic risks coexist. In the absence of clear guidelines, clinical judgment prevails, underscoring the need to reassess physicians' criminal liability.

42921198.title: Association of SOFA-2 with in-Hospital Mortality in Refractory Septic Shock: A Multicohort Retrospective Study with a 12-Hour Landmark.
42921198.abstract: SOFA-2 is an updated organ dysfunction score designed to reflect contemporary intensive care practice. Its clinical relevance in refractory septic shock (RSS) remains unclear. We primarily evaluated the association between SOFA-2 and subsequent in-hospital mortality among patients who were alive and hospitalized at a 12-hour landmark after RSS identification. Comparison with conventional SOFA was secondary and exploratory. This retrospective cohort study used MIMIC-IV as the primary cohort, with external consistency analyses in eICU-CRD and a local institutional cohort. RSS was operationalized using available electronic health record variables based on the SCCM/ESICM consensus framework, although some consensus elements were incompletely captured. Patients who died or were discharged before the 12-hour landmark were excluded from the primary analysis. SOFA-2 and conventional SOFA were assessed during the first 12 hours after RSS identification, with follow-up beginning at the landmark. Cause-specific Cox models were used for the primary analysis. Proportional-hazards diagnostics, time-varying coefficient models, time-dependent AUC, restricted cubic spline, subgroup, and sensitivity analyses were also performed. The primary cohort included 1276 patients, of whom 719 died during hospitalization. In the fully adjusted model, each 1-point increase in SOFA-2 was associated with higher subsequent in-hospital mortality (HR 1.12, 95% CI 1.10-1.14), and the HR per 1-SD increase was 1.54 (95% CI 1.43-1.67). The association attenuated over follow-up but remained positive at 7, 14, and 28 days. Conventional SOFA showed similar per-point associations. Exploratory time-dependent AUC analyses showed only small numerical differences between the two scores. The association was generally consistent across subgroup and sensitivity analyses and directionally consistent in the external cohorts. Among patients meeting database-operationalized RSS criteria who were alive and hospitalized at the 12-hour landmark, higher SOFA-2 scores were associated with higher subsequent in-hospital mortality.

42920434.title: Identification and validation of early vital sign trajectory subphenotypes for risk stratification in sepsis-associated liver injury: a multicenter retrospective cohort study.
42920434.abstract: Sepsis-associated liver injury (SALI) is a serious clinical syndrome with heterogeneity in outcome among affected individuals. Physiological changes that are critical to outcome prediction are not considered in the existing system of stratification based on single-point observations. This could compromise the effectiveness of individualized treatment. To develop and validate dynamic clinical subphenotypes of SALI using early vital sign trajectories. This retrospective cohort study included 1,159 patients from MIMIC-IV as the derivation cohort and 168 patients from the Second Xiangya Hospital as the external validation cohort. Early vital sign trajectories within 12 h of ICU admission were summarized as trajectory-derived features and clustered using K-means. Candidate solutions (k = 2-6) were assessed using internal clustering metrics and bootstrap stability. A four-cluster solution was retained as an exploratory partition, considering trajectory interpretability and subgroup sizes. Clinical characteristics, organ support, and mortality outcomes were compared across the identified subphenotypes. Four exploratory SALI subphenotypes with distinct early vital sign trajectories were identified, ranging from relatively stable profiles to marked hemodynamic and physiological stress. Subphenotype 3 exhibited the most stable vital signs and was associated with lower adjusted 28-day (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.56-0.97) and 90-day mortality (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.59-0.97) compared with the highest-risk Subphenotype 4. These prognostic differences were consistently replicated in the external cohort, supporting short- to intermediate-term prognostic generalizability. Early vital sign trajectories identified exploratory SALI groups associated with differences in 28-day and 90-day mortality. Their reproducibility, incremental prognostic value, and clinical utility require further evaluation.

42919828.title: A longitudinal plasma metabolomics dataset of sepsis-associated liver injury across multiple clinical time points.
42919828.abstract: Sepsis-associated liver injury is a severe complication of sepsis characterized by substantial metabolic alterations, yet longitudinal metabolomics resources for this condition remain limited. Here, we present an LC-MS-based longitudinal metabolomics dataset comprising 88 blood samples collected from healthy controls and sepsis patients with or without liver injury across multiple ICU-associated clinical time points. Comprehensive metabolomic profiling generated 18,247 high-quality metabolic features and 2,894 annotated metabolites, providing a resource for investigating temporal metabolite patterns with annotations related to nucleotide, lipid, and bile acid metabolism across clinical groups and sampling time points. Exploratory analytical approaches, including temporal clustering, weighted correlation network analysis, and regularized regression-based feature selection, were applied to facilitate characterization of longitudinal metabolic patterns within the dataset. This dataset provides a reusable resource for future studies on longitudinal metabolic dynamics, biomarker validation, integrative multi-omics analyses, and methodological development in sepsis and critical care research.

42919591.title: Efficacy and safety of double plasma cytokine adsorption system with sequential low-volume plasma exchange in treating acute-on-chronic liver failure complicated by sepsis: protocol for a multicentre randomised controlled clinical trial.
42919591.abstract: Acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) and sepsis are both life-threatening clinical syndromes that frequently coexist. Patients with ACLF complicated by sepsis experience significantly higher mortality rates, yet therapeutic options remain limited. This randomised controlled trial aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the double plasma cytokine adsorption system with sequential low-volume plasma exchange (DPCAS+LPE) in patients with ACLF complicated by sepsis. This is a multicentre, prospective, open-label, parallel-group, randomised clinical trial. A total of 192 patients with ACLF complicated by sepsis will be recruited from five hospitals in China. Participants will be randomly assigned (1:1) to either the intervention group or the control group. Both groups will receive standard medical treatment and three sessions of artificial liver support system (ALSS) therapy administered every other day. The intervention group will receive two sessions of DPCAS+LPE followed by one session of plasma exchange (PE), while the control group will receive three sessions of PE. The primary outcome is the 4-week mortality rate. Secondary outcomes include the 12-week mortality rate; longitudinal changes in Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II, Sequential Organ Failure Assessment, Model for End-Stage Liver Disease and Chinese Group on the Study of Severe Hepatitis B-associated ACLF II scores; and the Vasoactive-Inotropic Score at weeks 1, 2, 3 and 4 post baseline. Furthermore, the clearance rates of various cytokines and lactate will be measured after the first ALSS session. Safety will be assessed by documenting and managing all adverse events throughout the study. This study has been approved by the medical ethics committee of the Third Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University (approval no: II2024-204-06). The trial will be conducted in strict accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the Good Clinical Practice guidelines. The results of this study will be disseminated through presentations at national and international hepatology or critical care conferences and through publication in peer-reviewed journals. The findings will also be shared with relevant clinical stakeholders to inform future treatment guidelines for ACLF and sepsis. NCT06562803.

42918809.title: Discordance between actual care and recommendations by a reinforcement learning model for sepsis.
42918809.abstract: Fluid and vasopressor management of sepsis requires a complex set of sequential treatment decisions tailored to individual responses. We examined the frequency and implications of disagreement between reinforcement-learning (RL), using the AI Clinician as a test example, and actual clinical decisions. A novel discordance score was defined as the Euclidean distance between clinical team actions and RL-recommended treatments (range 0 to 5.66), across 25 treatment options of vasopressors and intravenous (IV) fluids. Among 30,678 ICU patients with sepsis cared for across 309,415 time-epochs, discordance was more common among epochs of patients with SOFA > 6 than those with SOFA < 6, and for intravenous fluid choices than for vasopressors. After multivariable adjustment, greater discordance was associated with 90-day mortality (adjusted odds ratio (OR) 1.11, 95%CI: 1.05,1.18) in the SOFA strata > =6 but not for SOFA < = 4 (adjusted odds ratio (OR): 1.02, 95%CI: 0.97,1.08).

42911180.title: Clinical impact of a rapid urine diagnostic algorithm combined with antimicrobial stewardship in patients with suspected urinary sepsis.
42911180.journal: Revista espanola de quimioterapia : publicacion oficial de la Sociedad Espanola de Quimioterapia
42911180.abstract: Early appropriate antimicrobial therapy is a key determinant of outcome in sepsis, yet conventional urine culture takes 24-48 hours. We evaluated the clinical impact of a rapid microbiological algorithm applied directly to urine, combined with antimicrobial stewardship, in patients with suspected urinary sepsis. Prospective quasi-experimental two-phase cohort study at a tertiary hospital. In adults with simultaneous urine and blood cultures, an initial observational phase formed the comparison cohort (conventional culture), and a second phase the intervention cohort, in which urine underwent Gram stain, laser-nephelometry growth detection (Alfred 60/AST), MALDI-TOF-MS identification, rapid susceptibility testing, and immunochromatographic ESBL and carbapenemase detection, with immediate reporting and recommendations by an infectious diseases specialist. Multivariable models (logistic and negative binomial) were adjusted for age, sex, Charlson index, department and qSOFA. We included 594 patients (297 per cohort). The algorithm achieved organism identification in 92.6% of cases, with a median turnaround time of 7.25 versus 75.0 hours (p<0.001), and 98.6% agreement with culture. Overall mortality was 6.1% versus 11.1% (p=0.039). After adjustment, the intervention was associated with significant reductions in hospital stay (IRR 0.82; p=0.012), days of therapy (IRR 0.79; p<0.001), intravenous antibiotics (IRR 0.83; p=0.001), need for ICU admission (OR 0.42; p=0.003) and overall mortality (OR 0.44; p=0.011). A rapid urine diagnostic algorithm, integrated with an expert stewardship intervention, was associated with lower antibiotic consumption and improved outcomes in suspected urinary sepsis. Combining rapid diagnostics with expert advice appears key to translating microbiological information into effective therapeutic decisions.

42909947.title: Baseline and 7-Day Dynamic Changes of T Helper 17/Regulatory T Cells Ratio and Their Association with Renal Recovery and Prognosis in Sepsis-Induced Acute Kidney Injury: An Exploratory Analysis.
42909947.abstract: Sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SAKI) is a serious complication with high mortality. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between T helper 17 (Th17)/regulatory T cells (Treg) immune imbalance and renal function recovery in patients with SAKI, with a novel focus on evaluating both baseline and early dynamic changes as exploratory biomarkers for renal recovery and overall prognosis. Sixty adult patients with SAKI admitted to the intensive care unit were enrolled and followed for 28 days. Based on renal recovery, patients were stratified into recovery and non-recovery groups, with further subgroup analysis. Clinical data and blood samples were collected serially. Renal recovery occurred in 42 patients (70%). Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) stage 3, a higher baseline Th17/Treg ratio (time zero [D0]) and a greater decrease in this ratio over 7 days (Δ7) demonstrated potential statistical correlations with non-recovery. The D0 ratio differentiated non-recovery with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.804 (cut-off >0.31128), and the Δ7 ratio (reflecting early immune trajectories during the first week) with an AUC of 0.762 (cut-off <-0.2055). A low baseline ratio with a high Δ7 was associated with early, complete recovery. A D0 ratio >0.31128 or a Δ7 ratio <-0.2055 was retrospectively observed to correlate with significantly higher 28-day mortality (60.0% vs 40.0%, p<0.05). The discriminative efficacy of D0 and Δ7 Th17/Treg ratios was comparable to KDIGO staging for renal non-recovery in patients with SAKI. Baseline and early dynamic Th17/Treg measures showed an observational trend with renal non-recovery in this single-centre prospective cohort of patients with SAKI. However, this study is limited by its small sample size and observational design. These exploratory findings, including the data-derived thresholds, require validation in larger cohorts with prespecified temporal analysis before clinical application.

42908823.title: Case Report: Delayed complete transection of the sigmoid colon after severe pelvic fracture leading to septic shock.
42908823.abstract: Severe pelvic fractures caused by high-energy trauma may be complicated by bowel injuries. These injuries may be evident at initial presentation or remain occult, resulting in delayed diagnosis. Delayed complete transection of the sigmoid colon associated with pelvic fractures is extremely rare. We describe a 57-year-old woman who was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) following a traffic accident that resulted in a Young-Burgess lateral compression type III pelvic ring injury, hemorrhagic shock, impaired consciousness, and multiple associated injuries. Abdominal CT on post-injury days 1, 2, and 3, emergency focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST), and repeated bedside ultrasonography showed no definite bowel injury. Bowel sounds were normal on admission, reduced on day 2, and absent from day 3, but abdominal symptoms could not be assessed reliably. Some inflammatory and organ-function indices partially declined after antimicrobial and supportive treatment. On day 6, abrupt biomarker re-elevation, high fever, progressive abdominal distension, and hemodynamic deterioration prompted repeat CT, which demonstrated extraluminal gas adjacent to the sigmoid colon. Emergency laparotomy confirmed complete sigmoid transection with partial stump necrosis and extensive fecal contamination. The patient survived after colectomy, colostomy, prolonged intensive care, and staged pelvic fixation. This case shows that bowel injury may continue to progress despite repeated negative CT and ultrasonographic examinations and transient improvement in inflammatory markers. When a high-risk mechanism and the clinical trajectory remain discordant, renewed surgical assessment and escalation beyond repeated noninvasive observation should be considered.

42905264.title: [Sepsis-induced coagulopathy].
42905264.abstract: Sepsis-induced coagulopathy (SIC) represents a frequent and prognostically highly relevant complication of sepsis, characterized by a dysregulated interaction between inflammation, endothelial activation and coagulation. Pathophysiologically, the excessive host immune response to pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMP) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMP), activation of the complement cascade, formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NET) and disruption of the endothelial glycocalyx collectively promote a prothrombotic and antifibrinolytic microenvironment, resulting in microvascular thrombosis, organ dysfunction and increased mortality. Approximately 20-25% of critically ill patients with sepsis fulfil the diagnostic criteria for SIC. Current diagnostic approaches rely on scoring systems such as the International Society on Thrombosis and Hemostasis (ISTH)-SIC, ISTH overt-disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and Japanese Society on Thrombosis and Hemostasis (JSTH)-DIC scores; however, their clinical utility remains limited as they predominantly collate hemorrhagic parameters even though sepsis is typically characterized by a thrombotically dominated phenotype. Viscoelastic point-of-care assays enable dynamic bedside assessment of coagulation and fibrinolysis, including the frequently occurring hypofibrinolysis or fibrinolytic shutdown, which is associated with an unfavorable outcome; however, for this specific purpose, these methods have not yet been sufficiently validated or established as a diagnostic standard. Data and recommendations on specific therapeutic options are limited. A consistent pharmacological thromboprophylaxis remains the cornerstone in patients with sepsis, with low-molecular weight heparins demonstrating advantages over unfractionated heparin regarding venous thromboembolic complications. Coagulation modulating treatment, such as antithrombin, recombinant thrombomodulin or activated protein C, have thus far failed to demonstrate consistent survival benefits in large randomized clinical trials. Experimental approaches targeting NET formation, complement activation or fibrinolytic modulation appear mechanistically promising but require further clinical validation. Overall, SIC necessitates an individualized, pathophysiology-driven diagnostic and therapeutic approach integrating inflammatory, endothelial, thrombotic and fibrinolytic alterations.

42904954.title: Scientific Output in Septic Shock According to Country Income and Gender: A Meta-Epidemiological Study.
42904954.abstract: We aimed to assess trends in septic shock publications by country income and author gender. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science for articles indexed with "septic shock" between January 2014 and December 2024. All peer-reviewed publication types were eligible. Conference abstracts and non-peer-reviewed material were excluded. Bibliographic data, first and last author affiliations, country income level (World Bank classification: low- and middle-income countries [LMICs] and high-income countries [HICs]), and journal prestige (SCImago Journal Rank [SJR]) were extracted. Author gender was inferred using the NamSor application programming interface (API). Of 10,352 eligible publications, LMIC-affiliated first authors increased over time (+2.13% per year; 95% CI, +1.66 to +2.61; p < 0.001) from 18% in 2014 to 37% in 2024. Women represented 35.6% of first authors and 25.0% of last authors (with around 20% of authors not classifiable by the NamSor API), with higher proportions in LMICs than HICs (p < 0.001) for both first authors (44.5% vs. 32.5%) and last authors (35.2% vs. 21.5%). Gender concordance was more frequent, with female first authors more often paired with female last authors than male first authors (31.7% vs. 21.1%). Cross-income collaborations, especially involving LMIC last authors, remained rare. Articles led by men in HICs were more often published in higher-SJR journals compared with those led by women (p < 0.001), whereas no gender differences were observed among LMIC-affiliated authors. Despite encouraging growth in LMIC contributions and female representation, major inequities persist. Strengthening equitable collaborations and supporting underrepresented groups would broaden participation and enhance the global applicability in critical care research.

42904495.title: Clinical guideline highlights for the hospitalist: Surviving Sepsis Campaign Update (Adults) 2026.
42904495.abstract: Guideline title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock (2026). Release date: 2026. Prior version(s): Initial guidelines released in 2004 with major updates in 2008, 2012, 2016, and 2021; the 2026 report is the latest update. Developer: Surviving Sepsis Campaign (Society of Critical Care Medicine [SCCM] and European Society of Intensive Care Medicine [ESICM]). Funding source: SCCM and ESICM; no industry funding. Target population: Adults with suspected or confirmed sepsis or septic shock in hospital and acute care settings.

42903731.title: Falciform Ligament Inflammation Complicated by Umbilical Vein Thrombophlebitis, Left Portal Vein Thrombosis, and Multiple Hepatic Abscesses: A Case Report.
42903731.abstract: Falciform ligament pathology is a rare cause of acute upper abdominal pain and may resemble more common pancreatic and hepatobiliary disorders. A woman in her 50s presented with sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to her back and marked hyperamylasaemia of 1,747 U/L. This combination fulfilled clinical and biochemical diagnostic criteria for acute pancreatitis, although computed tomography (CT) demonstrated no pancreatic inflammation and instead showed severe inflammatory change centred on the falciform ligament, with associated focal fat infarction, left portal vein thrombosis, and gas locules within segment IV of the liver. The patient subsequently developed fever, tachycardia, lactic acidosis, and profound hypotension requiring intensive care admission, intravenous antimicrobial treatment, fluid resuscitation, and vasopressor support. Serial CT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated progressive falciform ligament inflammation, thrombophlebitis of the recanalised umbilical vein, occlusive left portal vein thrombosis, and multiple left-lobe hepatic abscesses. Blood cultures obtained during the febrile deterioration subsequently showed no growth. She improved with prolonged broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy and therapeutic anticoagulation. Percutaneous drainage was deferred because she remained clinically stable, her inflammatory markers improved, and the hepatic abscesses remained small and stable on serial imaging. Follow-up CT demonstrated resolution of the hepatic abscesses, reduction in the falciform ligament collection, and recanalisation of the umbilical vein, although the left portal vein thrombosis persisted. Transabdominal ultrasonography during the index admission demonstrated small gallstones. She was subsequently readmitted with recurrent upper abdominal pain, marked hyperamylasaemia, and CT evidence of acute cholecystitis, with the overall clinical picture considered consistent with gallstone pancreatitis. An outpatient CT four weeks after the second discharge demonstrated resolution of the gallbladder inflammatory changes, while the falciform ligament thickening and fluid density remained stable. This case demonstrates a rare and potentially life-threatening falciform ligament inflammatory process associated with portovenous thrombosis and hepatic abscess formation in the context of sepsis. The index presentation also met accepted diagnostic criteria for acute pancreatitis, and a concomitant biliary contribution could not be excluded. The case highlights the value of serial cross-sectional imaging, multidisciplinary management, and cautious interpretation of overlapping pancreatic, biliary, and falciform ligament pathology.

42903397.title: Anticoagulants beyond coagulation: repurposing heparin to mitigate immunothrombosis and inflammatory cascades in sepsis.
42903397.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, in which inflammation, coagulation, endothelial injury, and immune dysfunction interact to drive organ failure and death. Accumulating evidence identifies immunothrombosis as a central mechanism in this process, linking neutrophil extracellular traps, platelet activation, tissue factor expression, circulating histones, and glycocalyx degradation to microvascular collapse and multiple organ dysfunction. Although heparin has traditionally been used as an anticoagulant, its highly sulfated structure also permits interactions that are independent of antithrombin. In addition to inhibiting thrombin generation, heparin can neutralize extracellular histones, interfere with HMGB1- and lipopolysaccharide-related inflammatory signaling, inhibit heparanase, preserve endothelial glycocalyx integrity, and modulate leukocyte trafficking through selectin-related pathways. Most of these non-anticoagulant actions have been demonstrated in cell systems, animal models, human endotoxemia, or diseases other than sepsis, and should therefore be read as biological plausibility rather than as an established clinical effect. The clinical literature addresses three questions that should not be conflated: routine venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in critically ill patients, anticoagulation directed at sepsis-induced coagulopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation, and experimental immunomodulatory repurposing. The most recent meta-analysis restricted to randomized trials found no significant mortality reduction with heparin across three trials and 426 patients (risk ratio 0.86, 95% confidence interval 0.60-1.24), and the disseminated intravascular coagulation subgroup was also inconclusive. Favorable associations reported in retrospective sepsis-induced coagulopathy cohorts justify prospective phenotype-enriched trials but do not identify established responders. This review summarizes the pathophysiological rationale, mechanistic basis, current clinical evidence, and major safety considerations of heparin use in sepsis, and highlights future directions including precision phenotyping, biomarker-guided therapy, and non-anticoagulant heparin derivatives. At present no heparin preparation, salt, dose, or biomarker threshold is validated for sepsis-specific immunomodulation.

42902161.title: Early hemodynamic changes after the use of push-dose noradrenaline in patients presenting to the emergency department with septic shock: a descriptive study.
42902161.abstract: Although continuous noradrenaline infusion (CNI) is standard vasopressor therapy during the initial resuscitation of patients with septic shock, hemodynamic stabilization may not be immediate. Push-dose noradrenaline (PDNA) has been proposed as a temporary measure while CNI is being established. However, its clinical use, dosing, early hemodynamic response, and short-term safety in the emergency department (ED) are not well described. To address this gap, we conducted a single-center retrospective descriptive study at a tertiary care hospital in Japan in 2019. Adults with Sepsis-3 septic shock who received PDNA in the ED and were admitted to the intensive care unit were included. We assessed the context and dosing of PDNA administration, CNI use, mean arterial pressure (MAP) within 15 min after PDNA administration, and adverse events. Of 91 patients with septic shock, 50 (55%) received PDNA. PDNA was administered at CNI initiation in 25 patients, during CNI dose escalation in 6, and as rescue administration before CNI initiation in 19. The median (interquartile range [IQR]) initial PDNA dose was 20 (20-30) µg. During the 15-minute observation window, 32 (64%) patients received one bolus, 14 (28%) received two, 3 (6%) received three, and 1 (2%) received four. The directly observed median (IQR) MAP was 52 (44-61) mmHg at initial PDNA administration (n = 30) and 62 (50-68) mmHg 1 min later (n = 25). One of 36 patients evaluable for prespecified physiological adverse events experienced an adverse event; however, no serious adverse events were documented. In this single-center retrospective descriptive study, PDNA was most commonly administered at CNI initiation, and administration was followed by an early increase in median MAP. However, the noncomparative design and concurrent resuscitative interventions preclude attribution of this change solely to PDNA administration. No serious adverse events were documented; however, safety assessment was limited owing to missing data and retrospective ascertainment. These findings do not establish the effectiveness or safety of PDNA. Prospective comparative studies with standardized monitoring are required.

42901564.title: Evaluating Multiple Treatments and Strategies for Sepsis in Adaptive Platform (EURASSIA) trial in Japan: a core protocol.
42901564.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening infectious disease with increasing prevalence. Although several studies have reported high-quality evidence, therapeutic strategies still require further development to reduce the high mortality associated with sepsis. However, small effects of newly proposed treatments due to heterogeneity in sepsis hinder the feasibility of randomised controlled trials, a standard resource-demanding approach to validate benefits of therapy. This trial aims to rapidly evaluate various treatments and strategies for sepsis through an adaptive platform trial (APT) established as a semipermanent study platform. The Evaluating Multiple Treatments and Strategies for Sepsis in Adaptive Platform (EURASSIA) trial is an APT, incorporating 11 tertiary care centres in Japan. This trial was initiated in 2024 with two domains, where two different interventions will be separately and simultaneously investigated in a randomised controlled design. Domains will be added and removed during the conduct of this semipermanent trial. The EURASSIA trial will include adult patients with sepsis who require intensive care whereas those with withheld/withdrawn care at sepsis diagnosis will be excluded. Subsequently, eligibility will be assessed for each domain, and participants will be randomly assigned to either intervention in each domain (eg, intravenous low-dose landiolol or no medication for mild tachycardia in the haemodynamic management domain and chlorhexidine-containing or usual dressing for a catheter insertion site in the infection control domain). The primary outcome is 90-day survival after intensive care initiation for sepsis; however, additional outcomes will be defined at the domain admission. The outcome will be analysed following a statistical analysis plan that will be predefined in each domain. Although reweighted response-adaptive randomisation will not be adopted, intervention-by-subtype interactions will be assessed across the domains at interim and final analyses to modify the sample size and add a stratification factor for random allocation as needed. The Certified Review Board of Keio at the principal institution approved this study (approval number: N20240002). Written informed consent will be obtained from all participants or their legal representatives. The results will be disseminated via publications and presentations. jRCT1031240424.

42901145.title: Delivery and adherence of biomarker-guided antibiotic treatment protocols in the ADAPT-Sepsis clinical trial: an in-trial descriptive process evaluation of daily procalcitonin- and C-reactive protein-guided protocols.
42901145.abstract: Biomarker-guided antibiotic protocols using daily procalcitonin or C-reactive protein have been proposed to optimise antibiotic duration in sepsis. This pre-planned process evaluation of the ADAPT-Sepsis trial examined delivery and clinician adherence to procalcitonin- and C-reactive protein-guided protocols. An embedded descriptive process evaluation was conducted within the multicentre ADAPT-Sepsis trial including 2760 adults across 41 UK critical care units. Patients were assigned to procalcitonin-guided, C-reactive protein-guided or standard care. Algorithm-generated recommendations (strong stop, suggest stop or standard care) were relayed to research staff and clinicians who remained blinded to group allocation. Adherence was defined as stopping biomarker sampling after advice. Advice timings, frequencies, adherence rates and reasons for non-adherence were recorded and analysed. Among 2760 patients, strong stop advice occurred earlier in those allocated to the procalcitonin-guided group compared with the C-reactive protein-guided group (mean difference -1.7 days, 95%CI -2.5 to -0.9, p < 0.001). C-reactive protein guidance generated a higher proportion of standard care advice (mean difference -9.1%, 95%CI -10.9% to -7.3%, p < 0.001). Overall advice adherence was greater in patients allocated to the C-reactive protein group than those allocated to the procalcitonin group (mean difference -6.8%, 95%CI -9.0 to -4.5, p < 0.001), driven by the higher proportion of standard care advice and later stronger stop advice with higher adherence (mean difference -14.3%, 95%CI -21.8 to -6.8, p < 0.001). Reasons for advice non-adherence included fixed-duration microbiology guidance, illness severity, continuing fever and elevation of routine inflammatory markers, which did not differ between groups. A C-reactive protein-guided discontinuation protocol achieved higher clinician adherence, probably because its recommendations aligned more closely with established prescribing norms. In contrast, procalcitonin guidance produced earlier and more frequent stop signals, offering greater potential to reduce antibiotic exposure but requiring clinicians to accept earlier discontinuation than usual practice.

42900932.title: Efficiency of Early Warning Scores in Adult Emergency Department and Inpatient Populations: Overview of Reviews.
42900932.journal: The western journal of emergency medicine
42900932.abstract: Early Warning Scores (EWS) are used to support decisions regarding triage and early intervention of patient deterioration in emergency departments (ED) and other clinical environments. We synthesized evidence from systematic reviews on the predictive performance and clinical impact of EWS and their modifications in adult in-hospital populations. We conducted and reported an overview of reviews following the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology, PRIOR statement, and our predefined protocol. A systematic search of MEDLINE (Ovid) and Epistemonikos was performed in May 2025. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and critically appraised systematic reviews.
