Klebsiella pneumoniae was the predominant species (47.4%), followed by Enterobacter cloacae complex (20.8%). The neonatal intensive care unit was the main reservoir of cases (22.0%). Blood and purulent specimens were the most frequent sources of isolation (62.8% combined). Among the 322 non-duplicate isolates tested, 252 (78.3%) were carbapenemase producers. Antibiotic susceptibility profile displayed high rates of resistance to ciprofloxacin (91.0%), gentamicin (85.1%), and cotrimoxazole (86.6%). NDM (34.8%) and OXA-48-like (30.1%) were the predominant enzymes. NDM and OXA-48-like co-production was observed in 12.1% of isolates. A novel VIM + OXA-48-like combination was detected in an Enterobacter cloacae complex isolate. This study demonstrates an alarming increase in the proportion of Enterobacterales exhibiting decreased susceptibility to carbapenems, highlighting a need for robust infection prevention measures, rapid diagnostics, and continuous epidemiological surveillance in high-dependency units.

42860503.title: Molecular detection of biofilm-related genes and antimicrobial resistance patterns in Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates from Northern Iran.
42860503.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is widely recognized as one of the primary opportunistic pathogens responsible for a wide range of nosocomial infections, notably in immunocompromised patients. Antibiotic resistance and biofilm formation, as two major virulence factors of P. aeruginosa, are related to the persistence of prolonged infections. This study was designed to (1) evaluate the frequency of multidrug-resistant (MDR) P. aeruginosa in northern Iran and (2) analyze the frequency of biofilm-associated genes and their correlation with antimicrobial patterns. Clinical samples (n = 80) were collected from ICUs and other wards and processed for the isolation and identification of P. aeruginosa. Antimicrobial susceptibility was assessed using disk diffusion. PCR was performed to target the biofilm-associated genes. Out of 80 P. aeruginosa isolates, the prevalence of isolates was highest in the ICU (57.5%), and sputum was the most common specimen type (37%). Piperacillin/tazobactam demonstrated the highest activity (76.2% susceptible), followed by amikacin (52.5% susceptible). Notably, 45% of the isolates were MDR, 52.5% were XDR, while 2.5% were neither MDR nor XDR. The biofilm-associated genes ppyR and pslA were detected in 92.5% and 87.5% of the isolates, respectively, whereas pelA was found in 85% of the isolates. Among the 59 pelA, ppyR, and pslA-positive isolates, 47.45% were MDR, 42.37% were XDR, and 10.18% were non-MDR/XDR. Based on these outcomes, we strongly recommend strict infection prevention and control strategies to limit the transmission of MDR-PA, particularly in hospital settings. Piperacillin/tazobactam remains relatively effective; however, its administration should be guided by antimicrobial stewardship guidelines.

42859695.title: Postoperative Candida auris Bloodstream Infection Following Cardiac Surgery: Diagnostic Delay and Serial Changes in Azole MIC Values: A Case Report.
42859695.abstract: Candida auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant fungal pathogen associated with healthcare-associated outbreaks and invasive infections, particularly in critically ill patients. Early recognition remains challenging due to nonspecific clinical presentations and overlap with bacterial infections. Postoperative bloodstream infection due to C. auris, especially following cardiac surgery, is still relatively uncommon and may be underrecognized in clinical practice. A 69-year-old man developed persistent fever, dyspnea, and bilateral postoperative pulmonary infiltrates after modified Morrow surgery and bioprosthetic mitral valve replacement. The pulmonary findings were clinically diagnosed as severe pneumonia, although imaging was nonspecific and also raised the possibility of pulmonary edema or heart failure. Despite broad-spectrum anti-infective therapy, his condition did not improve. Three separate catheter-drawn blood cultures collected on 21, 24, and 28 July 2025 subsequently yielded Candida auris, confirming candidemia. No respiratory specimen yielded C. auris; therefore, the pulmonary abnormalities were considered concurrent with, rather than microbiologically attributable to, the bloodstream infection. Antifungal susceptibility testing showed persistently high fluconazole MICs, while itraconazole and voriconazole MICs increased in the third isolate. Because validated C. auris-specific clinical breakpoints were unavailable for these agents, the MIC findings were interpreted descriptively. Following adjustment of antifungal therapy and continued supportive care, the patient became afebrile, achieved clinical stabilization, and had a negative follow-up blood culture before discharge. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of Candida auris bloodstream infection in postoperative patients, where clinical features may mimic bacterial pneumonia. Persistent fever unresponsive to empirical antimicrobial therapy should prompt early consideration of invasive fungal infection. Timely microbiological diagnosis and appropriate antifungal treatment are essential for improving outcomes. Increased awareness of C. auris infection in surgical and hospitalized patients is critical for early recognition and effective management.

42859691.title: Characterization and Antimicrobial Susceptibility Patterns of Clinically Significant Non-fermenting Gram-Negative Bacilli Isolated From Clinical Specimens.
42859691.abstract: Background Non-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli (NFGNB) have emerged as significant opportunistic pathogens associated with infections in healthcare settings and multidrug resistance. Their ability to persist in hospital settings and develop resistance to multiple antimicrobial agents poses a serious challenge to patient management. The current study aimed to determine the distribution of NFGNB isolates across different clinical samples and to evaluate their antimicrobial susceptibility and multidrug resistance patterns. Materials and methods A cross-sectional investigation was carried out on 127 NFGNB that were isolated from clinical samples received in the Department of Microbiology Laboratory of a tertiary care hospital. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed in accordance with the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines, and the isolates were identified using conventional microbiological techniques. Demographic characteristics, specimen distribution, bacterial profile and multidrug resistance patterns were studied. Results A total of 127 NFGNB isolates were recovered, of which 86 (67.72%) were from male patients and 41 (32.28%) were from female patients. The highest prevalence of NFGNB was observed in the 61-70-year age group, with 26 (20.47%) isolates, followed by the 51-60-year age group, with 23 (18.11%) isolates. Endotracheal (ET) aspirates were the most common specimen source, accounting for 34 (26.77%) isolates, followed by pus/discharge/wound swabs with 27 (21.26%) and urine with 26 (20.47%) isolates. 88 (69.29%) of the NFGNB isolates were obtained from patients admitted to the intensive care unit, whereas 39 (30.71%) were isolated from patients admitted to the wards. Pseudomonas aeruginosa was the most common isolate, accounting for 61 (48.03%) isolates, followed by Acinetobacter baumannii with 53 (41.73%) and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia with 13 (10.24%) isolates. A. baumannii and P. aeruginosa were highly carbapenem-resistant and fluoroquinolones and β-lactam antibiotics. Conclusion A. baumannii and P. aeruginosa were the predominant NFGNB isolates and exhibited a high rate of multidrug resistance, whereas Stenotrophomonas maltophilia remained susceptible to the antibiotics tested. Continuous surveillance of antibiotic resistance patterns, implementation of prevention and management of infections, and policies for antimicrobial stewardship are crucial to curb the dissemination of multidrug-resistant NFGNB and optimize patient outcomes.

42859667.title: Biliary Microbiology and Antimicrobial Treatment Modification in Patients Undergoing Percutaneous Cholecystostomy for Acute Cholecystitis: A Single-Centre Retrospective Cohort Study.
42859667.abstract: To describe bile culture yield, organism distribution and antimicrobial treatment modification in patients undergoing percutaneous cholecystostomy (PC) for acute cholecystitis who were unsuitable for early cholecystectomy. We retrospectively reviewed 84 consecutive patients who underwent PC between December 2021 and December 2025. Index bile cultures were classified as positive, no growth, or not obtained. We analysed organisms, polymicrobial growth, empirical antimicrobial therapy, treatment modification and clinical outcomes by culture status and disease severity. Bile was cultured in 71 patients (84.5%), and 33 cultures were positive (46.5% of sampled patients; 39.3% of the cohort). Seven positive cultures (21.2%) were polymicrobial. The leading isolates were Escherichia coli (n=13), Enterococcus faecium (n=9) and Klebsiella pneumoniae (n=8). Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole was the most common empirical regimen (52/84, 61.9%). Treatment was modified in 20 patients (23.8%); half of the modified regimens contained a carbapenem. Modification was more frequent among patients requiring intensive care (46.2% versus 13.8%; crude odds ratio [OR] 5.36, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.83-15.67) and those with Tokyo grade III disease (41.9% versus 13.2%; crude OR 4.75, 95% CI 1.63-13.81). No statistically significant difference was detected between the positive-culture and no-growth groups in treatment modification (24.2% versus 23.7%), in-hospital adverse events (24.2% versus 31.6%), 30-day mortality (12.1% versus 13.2%) or 90-day mortality among evaluable patients (6/32 [18.8%] versus 10/37 [27.0%]). Bile obtained during PC had a substantial microbiological yield and grew predominantly enteric organisms. Treatment modification was more frequent in clinically severe disease, but no statistically significant difference was detected between positive-culture and no-growth groups. Bile culture should inform a structured reassessment of antimicrobials after source control, rather than automatic treatment escalation.

42859404.title: Screening for multidrug-resistant organism: clinical benefit or unquestioned routine.
42859404.abstract: Current strategies for multidrug-resistant organism (MDRO) screening are primarily intended to support infection prevention programs. However, accumulating evidence indicates that intestinal colonization also provides clinically relevant information for antimicrobial stewardship. This review examines the biological basis and clinical utility of mucosal screening for optimizing empirical antibiotic therapy and proposes a new conceptual framework linking intestinal pathobiont burden with endogenous bloodstream infection. Recent studies consistently show that the absence of MDRO carriage is associated with a very low risk of subsequent infection, supporting well tolerated antimicrobial de-escalation in patients with negative clinical cultures. Emerging evidence further indicates that prolonged exposure to antianaerobic antibiotics promotes expansion of intestinal pathobionts, whereas preservation or restoration of the gut microbiota limits this process. Experimental and clinical observations suggest that the abundance of pathobionts, rather than simple carriage status, determines the probability of bacterial translocation and invasive infection. We propose that physiological bacterial translocation from the intestinal microbiota is a common phenomenon and may represent one of the mechanisms of bloodstream infection in critically ill and immunocompromised patients. In this model, progression to invasive infection depends on intestinal pathobiont burden exceeding the capacity of host immune clearance. If validated, this concept would support a transition from qualitative MDRO screening to quantitative assessment of intestinal pathobiont burden to guide antimicrobial stewardship and targeted preventive strategies.

42858345.title: Impact of COVID-19 Pandemic on carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae bloodstream infection: a single-center study in China.
42858345.journal: Journal of infection in developing countries
42858345.abstract: The problem of carbapenem resistance in Enterobacteriaceae is becoming increasingly serious, and Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) has become a major problem in clinical infection, especially in intensive care units (ICU). The purpose of the study is to explore the impact of the occurrence of COVID-19 on the bloodstream infection of CRE (CRE-BSI) and carbapenem resistance. In this study, adult patients with CRE-BSI from January 2019 to January 2023 were collected to perform a single-center cross-sectional study, who were divided into pre-COVID-19, COVID-19 until "New Ten" (only accept non-COVID-19 patients), and post-"New Ten" group (accept COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 patients), according to the epidemic prevention and control policy. Among 184 CRE-BSI cases confirmed during pre-COVID-19, COVID-19 until "New Ten" and post-"New Ten" periods, the CRE-BSI rates were 7.81, 8.13, and 9.63 cases per 100,000 hospitalization days. Correspondingly, the carbapenem resistance rates in Enterobacteriaceae were 18.6%,16.4%, and 19.0%, respectively, although no significant statistical differences were noted between the examined periods. The intensity of antimicrobial use increased significantly (p < 0.001) after the outbreak of the epidemic, and even increased to 1.5 times after the implementation of the "New Ten" compared to the pre-COVID-19 period. Notably, the utilization of third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins experienced a significant increase in CRE-BSI patients during the COVID-19 epidemic (p = 0.013). During the epidemic, an increased broad-spectrum antimicrobial use happened in CRE-BSI patients.

42852395.title: Clinical, Bacterial, and Antibiogram Profiles of Infections Among Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Patients in a Tertiary Care Center.
42852395.abstract: Background Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) have an increased susceptibility to infection because of hyperglycemia-related immune dysfunction, vascular impairment, and associated comorbidities. Characterization of bacterial isolates and their antimicrobial susceptibility patterns is essential for selecting appropriate empirical therapy and limiting antimicrobial resistance. Methodology This hospital-based, cross-sectional study included 150 adults with T2DM and culture-positive infections admitted to a tertiary care hospital in Bengaluru, India, between April 2023 and November 2024. Clinical and microbiological characteristics, HbA1c levels, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, and in-hospital mortality were assessed. Bacterial identification, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) assessment were performed by the hospital microbiology laboratory as part of routine clinical care, with susceptibility results reported according to the applicable Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute criteria. Results Urinary tract infection was the most frequent infection, affecting 55/150 patients (36.67%). Escherichia coli was the predominant isolate (54/150 (36.00%)), followed by Klebsiella spp. (26/150 (17.33%)) and Pseudomonas spp. (24/150 (16.00%)). Multidrug-resistant (MDR) organisms were identified in 53/150 patients (35.33%), while ESBL production was recorded in 50/118 isolates with an evaluable ESBL result (42.37%); 32 isolates were classified as not applicable. Resistance was highest to meropenem (64/150 (42.67%)), followed by amoxicillin (60/150 (40.00%)) and ciprofloxacin (58/150 (38.67%)). Although glycemic control status differed between the MDR and non-MDR groups (p = 0.033), uncontrolled glycemia was less frequent in the MDR group; therefore, this finding does not establish poor glycemic control as a predictor of MDR infection. MDR infections were associated with higher ICU admission rates (26/53 (49.06%) versus 13/97 (13.40%); p < 0.001) and in-hospital mortality (9/53 (16.98%) versus 5/97 (5.15%); p = 0.017). Conclusions MDR bacterial infections were common among hospitalized patients with T2DM and were associated with higher rates of ICU admission and in-hospital mortality. Institution-specific antibiograms, prompt culture-guided therapy, and strengthened antimicrobial stewardship are needed given the observed resistance, including resistance to meropenem.

42852378.title: Clinical Distribution Characteristics and Antimicrobial Resistance Trends of Klebsiella pneumoniae in a Chinese Tertiary Hospital (2021-2025).
42852378.abstract: To investigate the distribution and antimicrobial susceptibility of Klebsiella pneumoniae from Anqing First People's Hospital of Anhui Medical University from 2021 to 2025 and to provide rational regimens for clinical anti-infection. The non-repetitive bacterial strains were detected and collected in this hospital, Pathogen identification was performed using a mass spectrometer. Susceptibility testing was performed using an automated system or disk diffusion. The 2025 CLSI clinical standards were applied to determine susceptibility. Experimental susceptibility data were statistically analyzed using WHONET 5.6 software and SPSS26.0. Chi-square tests and trend tests were used for the statistical analyses. 8992 pathogenic strains were isolated during 2021-2025, including 1135 KPN, and the total detection rate was 12.6%. The annual detection rates from 2021 to 2025 were 12.8% (225/1,756), 11.7% (203/1,733), 14.5% (261/1,804), 12.6% (234/1,863), and 11.5% (212/1,836), respectively. The overall detection rate of Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) was 13.8% (157/1135). Over the five-year period, the predominant specimen sources of the isolates were sputum (35.5%), midstream urine (27.8%), and secretions (17.3%). The top three departments by isolation rate were ICU, Neurosurgery, and Urology. The drug sensitivity results showed that the resistance of K. pneumoniae to most common antibiotics were different during 2021 to 2025 (P < 0.05), and it had certain resistance to common antibiotics. The resistance rate of K. pneumoniae to imipenem detected in the ICU was significantly higher than that in the neurosurgery and urology departments. During the five-year period from 2021 to 2025, the isolated K. pneumoniae showed varying levels of resistance to common antibacterial drugs in our hospital. The resistance rates varied among different departments. The situation of drug resistance remains severe. Therefore, The hospital must strengthen daily infection control measures and drug resistance monitoring to reduce the spread of drug-resistant bacteria.

42845807.title: Time to Effective Antibiotic Therapy and Clinical Outcomes in Bloodstream Infections With ESBL-Producing Enterobacterales: A Retrospective Multicenter Cohort Study.
42845807.abstract: Patients with bloodstream infections (BSIs) with antimicrobial resistant bacteria often receive ineffective empirical therapy (IET). The implications are still uncertain. We performed a retrospective, multicenter, study of patients with BSIs caused by extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing gram-negative bacteria in southern Sweden from 2013 to 2022. Patients were categorized based on time to effective therapy: ≤24 hours (EET) and >24 hours (IET). Therapy was considered effective if the agent was active in susceptibility testing and administered intravenously at an appropriate dose. The primary outcome was 30-day mortality. Secondary outcomes were ICU admission and hospital length of stay. A total of 289/644 (44.9%) patients received IET within the first 24 hours after the index blood culture collection. No significant impact of IET on 30-day mortality was found in univariable (Hazard ratio 0.66; P = .15) or multivariable Cox regression analysis (Hazard ratio 0.64; P = .13). Patients receiving EET were more likely to receive intensive care (Odds ratio 0.38; P = .008), but the association was nonsignificant after adjusting for severity of illness and comorbidities. IET was not associated with a longer hospital stay in Fine-Gray competing risks regression analysis (univariable: sHR 1.15; P = .082; multivariable: sHR 1.11; P = .20). IET was not associated with 30-day mortality, in patients with BSIs with ESBL-producing Enterobacterales. If confirmed in prospective studies, our findings could support antimicrobial stewardship efforts by reducing unnecessary empirical carbapenem use without compromising short-term clinical outcomes, particularly in low-prevalence settings.

42843784.title: Five common antibiotic stewardship mistakes every intensivist should avoid.

42840071.title: Antimicrobial susceptibility patterns in Jalisco, Mexico: a snapshot of regional resistance (2021-2023).
42840071.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
42840071.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global public health threat, responsible for an estimated 4.9 million deaths worldwide and associated with increased morbi-mortality, and healthcare costs. The burden is particularly high in hospital settings, where multidrug-resistant pathogens, including ESKAPE group, are prevalent. However, in Mexico, epidemiological data remain limited. This study aimed to determine the prevalence and distribution of AMR among clinically relevant bacterial pathogens isolated in three hospitals in Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico, and to compare resistance patterns across hospital wards and clinical specimen types. A retrospective multicenter study was conducted from January 2021 to December 2023. Bacterial identification and susceptibility tests were performed using VITEK 2 and MicroScan WalkAway systems. Results were analyzed using WHONET and interpreted according to CLSI criteria. Clinical specimens included urine, blood, biopsies, abscesses, lower respiratory tract (LRT) specimens, and sterile fluids. Species analyzed included, Enterococcus spp., Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter baumannii and Escherichia coli. Statistical comparisons were performed using R Statistical Software Studio. A total of 13,336 clinical isolates were analyzed, with E. coli (n= 5,737) and K. pneumoniae (n= 1,738) as the most predominant pathogens. Urine samples were the most frequently collected (n= 4,247). Bloodstream isolates exhibited the highest resistance levels for E. coli and K. pneumoniae. Non-fermenting pathogens showed high resistance in LRT isolates, especially for P. aeruginosa and A. baumannii, with elevated carbapenem resistance. Resistance levels were higher the ICU, particularly for K. pneumoniae, E. cloacae, P. aeruginosa, and A. baumannii. In contrast, the non-ICU settings showed a greater prevalence of ESBL-producing E. coli. This study reveals substantial AMR burden in Guadalajara, with particularly high levels among bloodstream pathogens, non-fermenters in LRT specimens, and carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae and A. baumannii. Resistance patterns varied across hospital wards and specimen types, with higher resistance in ICU. These findings contribute valuable regional data to national AMR monitoring efforts.

42839120.title: Outbreak of Multidrug-Resistant (MDR) Acinetobacter baumannii ST-15 Strains Co-producing OXA-23 and OXA-58 in South America.
42839120.abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a high-priority pathogen due to its global dissemination and antimicrobial resistance. This work describes the first report of A. baumannii ST-15 isolates belonging to the International Clone 4 group, that exhibited an MDR profile with the co-production of OXA-23 and OXA-58 enzymes. Strains were isolated from an intensive care unit in a hospital of the Brazilian Amazon. Eight strains were recovered from an intensive care unit, showing high clonal stability across diverse clinical sources, including tracheal aspirates, urine, and blood, which underscores the high versatility and systemic dissemination potential of this lineage.The blaOXA-23 and blaOXA-58 genes were detected in all strains. A. baumannii isolates AB_OXA58_IEC07 and AB_OXA58_IEC02 were selected for hybrid genome sequencing and plasmid reconstruction, respectively, as representative samples of the outbreak. The reconstructed mobilome revealed a genome size of 4,110,050 bp, a GC content of 39.2%, and 3846 coding sequences for the reference strain, while four distinct plasmids were fully resolved.The blaOXA-58 gene was detected flanked by ISAba3 and IS6-like elements.pdif modules were identified in another plasmid, together with mobilization and replication genes. The tet39 gene was also identified in a novel plasmid that is likewise mobilizable. VFDB found several genes related to biofilm formation and virulence. The identification of these high-risk genetic determinants within a monoclonal outbreak, involving diverse clinical sites, emphasizes the successful persistence of the ST-15 lineage in the hospital environment. This study describes a rare co-production of oxacillinases, highlighting the importance of constant genomic surveillance in monitoring the emergence of antibiotic-resistant pathogens that could pose a threat on a regional or global scale.

42838023.title: Clindamycin under pressure: resistance in hospitalized patients with odontogenic infections and a penicillin allergy label - a multicenter retrospective study.
42838023.journal: Journal of cranio-maxillo-facial surgery : official publication of the European Association for Cranio-Maxillo-Facial Surgery
42838023.abstract: Odontogenic infections may progress to deep space infection with systemic complications and require prompt surgical drainage and, when indicated, systemic antibiotics. In patients with a documented penicillin allergy label, empiric therapy is often shifted toward clindamycin, although resistance is increasingly reported. This multicenter retrospective cohort study included 88 hospitalized patients with surgically treated odontogenic infections and a documented penicillin allergy label at two German tertiary oral and maxillofacial surgery centers (Center A, n = 59; Center B, n = 29). Empiric antibiotic therapy was predominantly clindamycin-based (90.9%). Microbiological diagnostics were performed in 58.0% of patients and infections were mostly polymicrobial. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was available in 43.2%; among cases with clindamycin testing, resistance was 76.7%. Antibiotic regimen changes occurred in 25.0%, most frequently to ampicillin/sulbactam. Median length of stay was 5 days; ICU-level care was required in 5.7%, revision surgery in 15.9%, one intracranial complication and one in-hospital death occurred. These findings suggest a clinically relevant mismatch between label-driven empiric clindamycin use and observed susceptibility patterns. Early structured allergy assessment and delabeling strategies may strengthen antibiotic stewardship and support safe first-line β-lactam use.

42831538.title: Procalcitonin Reduces Overuse of Antibiotics in Nursing Facility Residents: A Quality Improvement Initiative.
42831538.journal: American journal of medical quality : the official journal of the American College of Medical Quality
42831538.abstract: Procalcitonin (PCT), a biomarker for bacterial infections, has been studied in different clinical settings, including primary care, emergency departments, and intensive care units. Much less in nursing facilities (NFs), where antibiotic use is usually excessive. The aim of this quality assurance performance improvement initiative was to determine the effectiveness and sustainability of PCT in reducing unnecessary antibiotics in a 304-bed skilled NF. The initiative consisted of: (1) a 9-month baseline as a reference point; (2) a 9-month intervention where eligible residents were tested for PCT to help guide and monitor their antibiotic treatments. During the intervention, the plan-do-study-act cycle was applied to gauge the initiative, and control charts were used to determine the intervention success; and (3) a 9-month follow-up to validate the PCT effectiveness. The control chart rule of ≥8 consecutive months below the chart centerline indicated that the PCT intervention was successful. Monthly number of residents on antibiotics decreased from 34 at baseline down to 24 at follow-up, an overall 29% reduction. Days of therapy and antibiotic starts decreased from 33.0 and 5.4 at baseline down to 21.6 and 4.2 at follow-up, an overall reduction of 35% and 22%, respectively. Thus, utilization of PCT as a tool of antibiotic stewardship was associated with a reduction in antibiotic overuse among residents in this skilled NF.

42830302.title: Optimising antibiotic switching via forecasting of patient physiology.
42830302.abstract: Timely transition from intravenous to oral antibiotic therapy shortens hospital stays, reduces catheter-related infections, and lowers healthcare costs, yet one in five patients in England remain on intravenous antibiotics despite meeting switching criteria. Clinical decision support systems can improve switching rates, but approaches that learn from historical decisions reproduce the delays and inconsistencies of routine practice. We propose using neural processes to model vital sign trajectories probabilistically, predicting switch-readiness by comparing forecasts against clinical guidelines rather than learning from past actions, and ranking patients to prioritise clinical review. The design yields interpretable outputs, adapts to updated guidelines without retraining, and preserves clinical judgement. Validated on datasets from US intensive care (6333 encounters) and a UK academic hospital group (10,584 encounters), the system selects 2.2-3.2 × more relevant patients than random. We show that forecasting patient physiology offers a principled foundation for decision support in antibiotic stewardship.

42829531.title: Prevalence and Molecular Characterization of Carbapenemase and Hypervirulence Genes in Klebsiella pneumoniae Isolates in Hospitals of Benghazi, Libya.
42829531.abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a leading cause of hospital-acquired infections, particularly in intensive care units (ICUs), where multidrug-resistant (MDR) and hypervirulent strains represent major therapeutic challenges. This study investigated the phenotypic and molecular features of isolates recovered from ICU patients and the hospital environment in Benghazi, Libya. Antimicrobial susceptibility was determined using disk diffusion and the colistin broth disk elution method. Extended-spectrum-β-lactamase (ESBL) and carbapenemase production were assessed phenotypically and confirmed by PCR and sequencing, whereas clonal relatedness was analyzed through OmpK36 typing. Hypervirulence was evaluated using the string test, PCR detection of virulence genes, and biofilm formation assays. A total of 56 isolates (46 clinical and 10 environmental) were included. All isolates were resistant to ceftriaxone, with high resistance rates to ceftazidime, cefotaxime, carbapenems, ciprofloxacin, and gentamicin. ESBL production was observed in 76% of clinical and 80% of environmental isolates, and 95% of all isolates were classified as MDR. A significant proportion of K. pneumoniae isolates (n = 15) exhibited resistance to colistin in the absence of detectable mcr genes. Strong and moderate biofilm production was detected in 30.4% and 17.9% of isolates, respectively. The bla NDM-5 was prevalent among clinical (45/46; 97.8%) and environmental (9/10; 90%) isolates. Similarly, bla CTX-M-15 was detected in 35/46 (76%) clinical isolates and 8/10 (80%) environmental isolates, whereas bla OXA-48 was detected in 26/46 (56.5%) clinical and 10/10 (100%) environmental isolates. A potentially hypervirulent phenotype was observed in 17.8% of the isolates, associated with the virulence genes iucA, iutA, and peg-344. OmpK36 Groups C and D predominated. These results highlight the alarming spread of MDR and hypervirulent strains in ICUs and underscore the need for reinforced infection control strategies.

42828630.title: Bacteriophage therapy for multidrug- and extensively drug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii: isolation, characterization, and therapeutic applications.
42828630.abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a WHO critical-priority pathogen that causes life-threatening healthcare-associated infections, particularly in intensive care units (ICUs). In South Asia and the Middle East, multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains are common and resistance to cephalosporins is 87-100% and to carbapenems 78-90%, leaving only a few remaining therapeutic options like colistin, tigecycline, and polymyxin B. This review aimed to provide an overview of the current knowledge regarding the epidemiology, virulence factors, and resistance mechanisms of MDR/XDR A. baumannii globally and within Pakistan, with particular emphasis on therapeutic approach using bacteriophages as potential alternative to conventional antimicrobial therapy. This review is distinguished from prior publications on A. baumannii phage therapy by its integration of Pakistan-specific epidemiological and phage-isolation data with a critical, comparative synthesis of phage-antibiotic synergy evidence and emerging (2024-2026) clinical and preclinical literature. This review synthesizes current isolation, purification, and genomic/proteomic characterization methods for A. baumannii-targeting bacteriophages, and critically evaluates phage-antibiotic synergy (PAS), in vivo and compassionate-use clinical evidence, and translational and regulatory barriers, alongside emerging alternative antimicrobial strategies and surveillance gaps in resource-limited settings such as Pakistan. In conclusion, combination therapy of phage and antibiotics, especially sequential phage-colistin therapy, is a promising strategy against MDR/XDR A. baumannii infections. There are several key priorities for the future to consider, such as the establishment of national phage banks, development of standardized phage susceptibility testing (phagograms), and the integration of phage therapy into antimicrobial stewardship and surveillance frameworks, especially in high-burden, resource-limited settings such as Pakistan.

42825262.title: In-hospital antimicrobial use and multidrug-resistant infections among COVID-19 patients in Northern Malaysia (COVAM): a multicentre study.
42825262.journal: Journal of pharmaceutical policy and practice
42825262.abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, empirical antimicrobials were frequently prescribed despite low documented rates of bacterial and fungal co-infections. While early pandemic data exist, evidence evaluating antimicrobial consumption and multidrug-resistant organism (MDRO) dynamics during subsequent pandemic surges remains limited. This study evaluated antimicrobial receipt, associated factors, and the prevalence of MDROs among hospitalised COVID-19 patients in Northern Malaysia. This multicentre retrospective observational cohort study included adults (≥18 years) with confirmed COVID-19 admitted to ten government hospitals in Northern Malaysia between February 2020 and December 2021. Among 19,116 admissions, 480 cases were sampled, yielding 476 eligible patients. Study outcomes included antimicrobial receipt and MDRO prevalence. Monthly antimicrobial days of therapy (DOT) per 1,000 patient-days were compared with state-level COVID-19 hospital admissions. Predictors were analysed using a Poisson Generalized Linear Mixed Model. Antibiotics were prescribed to 167 patients (35.1%), accounting for 381 prescriptions, predominantly β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitors (54.1%). Most were empirical (92.9%), largely among non-ICU patients (72.2%) with pneumonia (82.9%). Antifungals were used in 13 patients (2.7%; 15 prescriptions), mainly empirical echinocandins (60.0%), and predominantly in ICU settings (66.7%). MDROs were detected in 8.4% (10/119) of patients with cultured specimens, representing patient-level MDRO prevalence. A significant positive correlation was observed between DOT and admissions (r = 0.701, p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.37-0.87]). Severe/critical COVID-19 stage, diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and chronic kidney disease were consistently associated with antimicrobial prescription. Longer hospital stays, elevated neutrophil and C-reactive protein levels, smoking, and pre-hospital steroid/immunosuppressant use were additional predictors. Antimicrobial use was predominantly empirical and influenced by disease severity and admission surges. Although MDRO detection remained low, severity-driven prescribing highlights the risk of unnecessary antimicrobial exposure during pandemic waves. These findings inform outbreak-responsive antimicrobial stewardship strategies and support antimicrobial utilisation surveillance to guide resource planning during future public health emergencies.

42952654.title: Epidemiological characteristics and antimicrobial resistance profiles of clinical bacterial isolates in a tertiary hospital in Zigong, southwestern China, 2023-2025.
42952654.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
42952654.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) varies across hospitals, patient populations, and care settings, limiting the clinical utility of aggregate surveillance data. We characterized bacterial distribution and antimicrobial resistance at a tertiary hospital in Zigong, southwestern China, during 2023-2025, with explicit stratification by age and care setting. This retrospective laboratory surveillance study retained the first isolate of each bacterial species per patient per calendar year. We reinterpreted available minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) and inhibition-zone diameters using Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) M100 (35th edition, 2025). Resistance proportions used antimicrobial-specific tested denominators. We estimated temporal associations with logistic regression, modeling calendar year ordinally, using patient-clustered robust standard errors, and adjusting for age, sex, and care setting; we controlled exploratory comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate. From 18,581 laboratory records, 1,615 repeat records were excluded, leaving 16,966 isolates. Isolates were predominantly from general wards (15,478/16,966, 91.2%); 1,330 (7.8%) were ICU/critical-care isolates, and 158 (0.9%) were outpatient isolates. Carbapenem resistance occurred in 70/4,848 Escherichia coli (1.4%) and 63/1,769 Klebsiella pneumoniae (3.6%). Carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (CRPA) occurred in 190/1,659 isolates (11.5%), and carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) in 128/380 isolates (33.7%); ICU/critical-care status was associated with both phenotypes (adjusted OR 2.80 and 4.29, respectively). Phenotypic linezolid non-susceptibility was observed in 60/325 Enterococcus faecalis isolates (18.5%; annual range 17.3%-19.0%) without a temporal trend. Among adult Haemophilus influenzae, ampicillin resistance increased from 35/50 (70.0%) to 214/243 (88.1%; adjusted OR/year 1.73, 95% CI 1.19-2.50), and amoxicillin/clavulanate resistance increased from 8/50 (16.0%) to 145/243 (59.7%; adjusted OR/year 3.06, 95% CI 2.18-4.30). AMR differed by care setting and age. Carbapenem resistance in E. coli and K. pneumoniae remained uncommon, whereas CRAB and CRPA were concentrated in ICU/critical-care isolates. The substantial proportion of phenotypic linezolid non-susceptibility in E. faecalis warrants confirmation by reference susceptibility testing, and increasing β-lactam resistance among adult H. influenzae warrants continued surveillance. These findings support regularly updated institution- and care-setting-specific cumulative antibiograms, with age stratification where isolate numbers are adequate; causal inferences regarding stewardship effects or patient outcomes require linked clinical datasets.

42950986.title: In vitro activity of imipenem/relebactam against Enterobacterales isolates from China: results from the Study of Monitoring Antimicrobial Resistance Trends (SMART), 2020-2022.
42950986.abstract: Imipenem/relebactam (IMR) is a β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combination that enhances the activity of imipenem against carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative pathogens by inhibiting class A and class C β-lactamases, particularly KPC. With the increasing prevalence of carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) in China, evaluation of the in vitro activity of IMR is warranted. As part of the SMART surveillance program, Enterobacterales isolates were collected from 18 tertiary hospitals in China (2020-2022), including specimens from bloodstream, intra-abdominal, respiratory, and urinary tract infections (UTIs) in intensive care units (ICUs) and general wards. Species were identified by MALDI-TOF MS, and susceptibility was determined by broth microdilution. A total of 6182 Enterobacterales isolates were included, of which 19.1% were carbapenem-resistant. Higher rates of carbapenem resistance were observed among isolates from ICU patients and those causing urinary tract infections. IMR demonstrated substantially greater in vitro activity against CRKP than imipenem alone, resulting in a marked shift toward lower MIC distributions and an approximately fivefold reduction in the proportion of resistant isolates across both ICU and non-ICU settings. Compared with other β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations, IMR showed a higher proportion of isolates with MICs ≤1 mg/L and fewer isolates with elevated MICs than ceftazidime/avibactam or meropenem/vaborbactam, particularly among CRKP isolates. IMR exhibits in vitro activity against CRKP, particularly among isolates from ICU patients and those causing bloodstream infections. Our study suggests that IMR represents an important therapeutic option for infections caused by resistant Gram-negative pathogens, particularly carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales; however, further clinical data are needed to confirm efficacy.

42946128.title: Genomic Investigation of a Carbapenem-Resistant Chromobacterium haemolyticum Cluster Reveals Environmental Introduction and Nosocomial Transmission.
42946128.abstract: To investigate the source and transmission dynamics of a cluster of four Chromobacterium haemolyticum infections in an intensive care unit (ICU) and to characterize their antimicrobial resistance profiles. An epidemiological investigation was conducted involving four ICU patients identified between July 2024 and August 2025. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was performed on eight isolates, and core-genome single-nucleotide polymorphism (cgSNP) analysis was used to assess their genetic relatedness. Antimicrobial resistance genes were identified using the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD), while resistance-associated point mutations were detected using AMRFinderPlus. A maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree was constructed based on 26 genomes to investigate the genomic relationships among the isolates. Two distinct epidemiological events were identified. Three patients harbored closely related isolates forming a clonal cluster with 0-10 SNP differences, linked to an index case with a history of near-drowning. In contrast, an isolate recovered from a patient with independent environmental exposure was genetically unrelated to the cluster, differing by >38,000 SNPs. All cluster isolates carried the chromosomal blaCRH-2 gene, encoding a class A carbapenemase related to Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC), and displayed carbapenem resistance, unlike previously reported carbapenem-susceptible C. haemolyticum strains. Transmission ceased during the winter, with Patient 2 serving as a potential long-term reservoir. This study provides the first genomic evidence supporting nosocomial transmission of C. haemolyticum. The concordant resistance profiles observed in the outbreak and unrelated isolates suggest that blaCRH-2 may be a key determinant of carbapenem resistance in C. haemolyticum, challenging the assumption that empirical carbapenem therapy is reliably effective against this pathogen.

42945854.title: Candidozyma auris in hospital setting: Molecular characterization of clinical and environmental strains.
42945854.journal: Journal of infection and public health
42945854.abstract: Candidozyma auris is a yeast that has a strong ability to adapt, can cause serious invasive infections and contaminate various surfaces. After cases of C. auris have occurred in patients hospitalized in a healthcare facility of Apulia region, Italy, clinical and environmental surveillance was implemented. The aim of this study is to perform genotypic and phenotypic characterization between clinical and environmental isolations. In August and September 2024, in three hospital wards, axillary-inguinal swabs were performed on hospitalized patients; environmental monitoring was carried out simultaneously to detect C. auris in air and surfaces. C. auris strain was isolated from the blood culture and peritoneal fluid of a patient, and identified using mass spectrometry. Swabs were performed on surfaces in the patient's room using sterile swabs, analyzed by molecular method. Active and passive sampling of air was conducted. Out of the 194 surface swabs, C. auris DNA was detected in 50 samples. Passive air sampling identified C. auris in 33.3% of plates in Intensive Care patient areas. In the Infectious Diseases Unit, a sample tested positive. Active air sampling didn't detect C. auris. 66 patients were screened, all of which resulted negative for C. auris. Swabs collected from two patients were positive. All isolates were susceptible to amphotericin B, anidulafungin and resistant to fluconazole. Amino acid substitutions were identified in the ERG11 and TAC1B genes. Viable C. auris was detected in a small number of environmental samples and was genetically closely related to isolates from the corresponding patients.

42943415.title: Eleven-Year Trends in Antimicrobial Resistance and Outcomes Among Hospitalized Adults with Positive Enterococcus Cultures.
42943415.abstract: Enterococcal infections are major healthcare-associated infections associated with increasing antimicrobial resistance and substantial mortality. However, long-term epidemiological data integrating antimicrobial resistance trends with clinical outcomes remain limited in Saudi Arabia. This study evaluated antimicrobial resistance trends, clinical characteristics, and mortality among patients with enterococcal positive cultures over an 11-year period. We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of 2272 hospitalized adults with culture-positive Enterococcus spp. between March 2015 and November 2025. Demographic, clinical, microbiological, and outcome data were extracted from electronic medical records. Temporal resistance trends and independent predictors of in-hospital mortality were evaluated using logistic regression. Enterococcus faecalis accounted for 74.1% of isolates. Vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) prevalence showed no significant temporal trend during the study period, with an overall prevalence of 11.3%, whereas high-level gentamicin resistance declined significantly (OR per year 0.933, 95% CI 0.903-0.964; p < 0.001). Multidrug resistance showed no significant temporal change. Compared with E. faecalis, E. faecium exhibited substantially higher resistance to vancomycin, ampicillin, and ciprofloxacin, while susceptibility to linezolid, daptomycin, and tigecycline remained above 95%. Overall, in-hospital mortality was 15.6% and was independently associated with age ≥60 years, intensive care unit admission, bloodstream infection, coinfection, and E. faecium positive culture. This study provides one of the largest long-term evaluations of enterococcal positive culture in Saudi Arabia, demonstrating stable VRE prevalence, declining high-level aminoglycoside resistance, and persistent species-specific differences in antimicrobial resistance and mortality. These findings support local antimicrobial resistance surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship efforts by providing updated epidemiological data on enterococcal positive cultures.

42942550.title: Healthcare-Associated Infections with Pseudomonas spp. in a Neurosurgical Hospital: Epidemiological and Clinical Insights.
42942550.abstract: Background and Objectives: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa represent a challenge for healthcare systems worldwide, with significant incidence, high mortality, and increasing antibiotic resistance. This paper aims to describe and analyze the epidemiology of HAI cases with Pseudomonas aeruginosa in a tertiary neurosurgical hospital in the northeastern region of Romania during 2020-2024. Materials and Methods: Study inclusion criteria were patients of any age (as the hospital also admits pediatric patients from the region) and a diagnosis of P. aeruginosa HAI, with a signed informed consent form by the adult patient or relatives for pediatric patients. Results: During 2020-2024, 163 cases of P. aeruginosa HAIs were identified. The annual incidence decreased from 4.41‱ in 2020 to 2.37‱ in 2024 (p = 0.0038). Most cases occurred in the intensive care unit (ICU) (119/163; 73.0%), followed by neurosurgery wards (37/163; 22.7%). Overall, 110 cases (67.5%) occurred in men and 53 (32.5%) in women. The analysis also showed a predominance of late-onset cases and the presence of antimicrobial-resistant phenotypes among the identified P. aeruginosa isolates. Conclusions: This study provides an integrated epidemiological characterization of P. aeruginosa HAIs in a regional neurosurgical hospital, highlighting the predominance of ICU-associated cases, late-onset infections, and antimicrobial-resistant phenotypes. These findings support the need for continued epidemiological surveillance and antimicrobial resistance monitoring in high-risk neurosurgical settings.

42942544.title: Pleural Aerobic Culture Status, Clinical Phenotypes, and In-Hospital Outcomes in Adult Pleural Infection: A Retro-Spective Cohort Study.
42942544.abstract: Background and Objectives: Pleural infection is heterogeneous, and the clinical meaning of a positive pleural culture remains uncertain. We compared adults with positive and negative aerobic pleural-fluid cultures and examined associations with major in-hospital events. Materials and Methods: This retrospective, single-center, case-ascertained cohort included adults hospitalized with bacterial pleural infection in Western Romania during 2017-2025. The primary analytic cohort was restricted to patients whose first clinically relevant pleural specimen had an interpretable aerobic culture. Pleural fluid (PF)-positive and PF-negative status was defined exclusively by that result; unperformed tests and operative specimens were not used for classification. The composite outcome comprised in-hospital death, intensive-care unit (ICU) admission/transfer, or thoracic surgery/surgical transfer. Prespecified covariates were entered simultaneously in logistic regression. Results: Of 317 included patients, 276 had an interpretable aerobic pleural culture: 127 (46.0%) were PF-positive and 149 (54.0%) were PF-negative. PF-positive patients were more often institutionalized, had chronic kidney disease, nosocomial infection, frank empyema, and lower pleural-fluid pH and glucose. Streptococci predominated in community-acquired infection, whereas Gram-negative organisms and multidrug-resistant phenotypes were more frequent in healthcare-associated/nosocomial episodes. The composite occurred in 60/127 (47.2%) PF-positive and 51/149 (34.2%) PF-negative patients (OR 1.72, 95% CI 1.06-2.80). The adjusted PF-positive estimate remained imprecise (aOR 1.60, 95% CI 0.94-2.74; p = 0.084), whereas healthcare-associated/nosocomial acquisition was associated with the composite (aOR 1.76, 95% CI 1.03-3.00; p = 0.038). In a sensitivity analysis restricted to 249 patients whose pleural sampling preceded all recorded outcome components, the adjusted association remained imprecise (aOR 1.54, 95% CI 0.86-2.76). Conclusions: A positive aerobic pleural culture identified a distinct high-risk phenotype and influenced antimicrobial management, but its independent association with the heterogeneous in-hospital composite remained uncertain. Acquisition setting and local resistance ecology should guide empirical therapy, and outcome timing should be reported explicitly in future studies.

42942400.title: Carbapenem and Multidrug Resistance Among Gram-Negative Bacilli in a County Emergency Clinical Hospital from Western Romania: A Retrospective Study, 2024-2025.
42942400.abstract: Background and Objectives: Antimicrobial resistance among Gram-negative bacilli is a major clinical challenge, particularly in hospitals where carbapenem-resistant and multidrug-resistant organisms limit therapeutic options. This study aimed to characterize the distribution and resistance profiles of Gram-negative bacilli isolated in a university-affiliated hospital in western Romania during 2024-2025, focusing on temporal variation, intensive care unit (ICU) origin, carbapenem resistance, and multidrug resistance (MDR). Materials and Methods: This retrospective, single-center study included 8931 Gram-negative isolates recovered from clinical specimens between January 2024 and December 2025. Bacterial identification was performed using the VITEK 2 Compact system and/or MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, whereas antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using the VITEK 2 system and interpreted according to EUCAST criteria. Carbapenem resistance was defined as resistance to meropenem, imipenem, or ertapenem for Enterobacterales and to meropenem or imipenem for Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii. MDR was defined as resistance to at least one agent in at least three antimicrobial classes. Factors associated with MDR were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression. Results: Escherichia coli was the most frequent isolate (36.0%), followed by Klebsiella pneumoniae (22.8%), P. aeruginosa (9.6%), A. baumannii (9.4%), and Proteus mirabilis (8.0%). Among 8708 isolates evaluable for both outcomes, carbapenem resistance was 30.8% and MDR was 44.5%; both were significantly more frequent in 2025 than in 2024. ICU isolates showed higher carbapenem resistance (56.1% vs. 18.0%) and MDR (65.3% vs. 33.9%) than non-ICU isolates. A. baumannii had the highest burden, with 87.4% carbapenem resistance and 87.5% MDR. MDR was independently associated with study year, ICU origin, age group, sex, specimen type, and bacterial species; the strongest association was observed for A. baumannii versus E. coli (adjusted OR 23.45, 95% CI 18.38-29.91). Conclusions: Carbapenem resistance and MDR were frequent, particularly among ICU isolates and high-risk pathogens. The findings support intensified local surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, and targeted infection prevention and control measures.

42938744.title: Carbapenem-Resistant and Extensively Drug-Resistant Gram-Negative Healthcare-Associated Infections in a Romanian Tertiary Infectious Diseases Hospital: Phenotypic Landscape, Stewardship Gaps and Outcomes (2024-2025).
42938744.abstract: Romania reports among the highest rates of carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacteria in the European Union, but patient-level data on healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are scarce. We characterised carbapenem resistance, in-hospital outcomes, and carbapenem prescribing in a 24-month HAI cohort. This was a retrospective study of 315 patients with microbiologically confirmed HAI (2024-2025) at a tertiary infectious diseases hospital, contributing 243 Gram-negative isolates. Carbapenem resistance was determined by the hospital laboratory; extensively drug-resistant (XDR) status, defined as susceptibility to no more than two of the antimicrobial classes tested, was assigned under the hospital surveillance protocol. Risk-factor analysis was exploratory. Of 243 Gram-negative isolates, 162 (66.7%) were carbapenem-resistant and 150 of these (92.6%) were designated XDR. Resistance reached 90.6% in Klebsiella pneumoniae and 83.0% in Acinetobacter baumannii, against 33.3% in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and 0% in Escherichia coli, and occurred at every infection site. No routinely recorded characteristic distinguished resistant from susceptible infection after adjustment (area under the curve 0.62). In-hospital death was associated with intensive care transfer (adjusted odds ratio 6.92, 95% confidence interval 3.33-14.38) but not with carbapenem resistance (1.14, 0.52-2.50). Of 92 carbapenem recipients, 54 (58.7%) had a carbapenem-resistant isolate, against which carbapenems are inactive, and 12 (13.0%) had a Gram-negative isolate that was neither carbapenem-resistant nor extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing. At this centre, carbapenem resistance in Gram-negative HAI is endemic, could not be predicted from the routinely recorded characteristics examined, and exceeds European surveillance figures only among the Enterobacterales. No independent association with mortality was detected, although the susceptible comparison group was small. The XDR proportion was assigned under the hospital surveillance protocol and is not directly comparable with category-based estimates. Because antibiotic exposure was recorded without timing relative to culture sampling, these data support prospective audit of carbapenem prescribing rather than demonstrating missed de-escalation.

42938739.title: Phenotypic and Molecular Characterization of ESBL-Producing Enterobacterales from Intestinal Colonization in Loja, Ecuador.
42938739.abstract: Background/Objectives: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacterales pose a significant threat to public health due to increasing antimicrobial resistance. In Ecuador, molecular characterization of these microorganisms remains limited. The objective of this study was to phenotypically and molecularly characterize ESBL-producing Enterobacterales in patients treated at a referral hospital in Loja, Ecuador. Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted between November 2022-October 2023. 862 intestinal samples (stool samples and rectal swabs) were analyzed: 799 obtained from outpatient clinics, 34 from medical/surgical hospitalization wards, and 29 from the intensive care unit (ICU). Bacterial identification was performed using MALDI-TOF MS. Detection of ESBL and carbapenemase genes was performed using multiplex PCR. Phenotypic clustering was assessed by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR). Results: A total of 195 (22.6%) ESBL-producing Enterobacterales were identified, of which 89 were molecularly characterized. Escherichia coli was the predominant species (79.8%), followed by Klebsiella pneumoniae (15.7%). High resistance rates to ciprofloxacin (57.1-100%) were observed being lower resistance to aminoglycosides (amikacin 1.5-57.1%; gentamicin 10.3-100%). The gene blaCTX-M was the most frequent, detected in 79.8% of isolates, mainly in combination with blaTEM-1 (59.6%). Among the CTX-M family, the blaCTX-M-1 group was predominant (87.3%). Two isolates carried blaKPC. FT-IR analysis revealed species-dependent phenotypic clusters, particularly in K. pneumoniae, whereas E. coli showed greater spectral heterogeneity. Conclusions: ESBL-producing Enterobacterales were frequently identified among analyzed samples and exhibited a marked pattern of multidrug resistance, with a predominance of blaCTX-M genes. These findings support the strengthening of molecular surveillance that might impact antimicrobial use.

42936549.title: Predominance of NDM and OXA-48 Carbapenemase Coharboring Among Carbapenem Nonsusceptible Enterobacterales Isolates From Clinical Specimens at a Tertiary Hospital in Vietnam.
42936549.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance has emerged as a growing global public health threat. The increasing of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales limits treatment options. A better understanding of the phenotype and genotype distribution of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales is essential to prevent, reduce and control infection. This study is aimed at characterizing the phenotypic and genotypic carbapenemase profiles of carbapenem nonsusceptible Enterobacterales isolates collected from the diverse clinical specimens at a tertiary hospital in Ho Chi Minh City. A total of 619 carbapenem nonsusceptible Enterobacterales strains were isolated from 548 clinical specimens. Species identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing were performed using the BD Phoenix M50 system. Carbapenemase production was assessed using the modified Carbapenem Inactivation Method (mCIM). Carbapenemase-encoding genes, including bla KPC, bla NDM, bla IMP, bla OXA-23, and bla OXA-48, in isolates with positive or inconclusive mCIM results (559 of 619) were detected by multiplex RT-PCR. The results showed that median patient age was 71 years (IQR 60-81), with 55.7% of patient being male and 28.3% admitted to the intensive care unit. Klebsiella pneumoniae predominated (56.5%), followed by Klebsiella aerogenes (14.7%) and E. coli (14.4%). Resistance rates were 87.7% for ertapenem and 78.7% for meropenem. mCIM positivity was high in K. pneumoniae (92.9%), K. aerogenes (93.4%), and Serratia marcescens (92.7%), but lower in E. coli (59.6%) and E. cloacae (40.0%). All 9 carbapenemase-gene-positive isolates with inconclusive mCIM carried bla OXA-48 alone. In K. pneumoniae, bla NDM-bla OXA-48 co-carriage was most common (39.3%), followed by bla OXA-48 alone (26.2%), bla KPC alone (11.9%), and bla NDM alone (8.3%). E. coli and K. aerogenes predominantly harbored bla OXA-48 alone (66.7% and 58.1%). The findings show a high burden of carbapenem nonsusceptible Enterobacterales in a Vietnamese tertiary hospital, largely driven by K. pneumoniae coharboring bla NDM and bla OXA-48. Continuous molecular surveillance and strengthened antimicrobial stewardship are urgently needed to limit their dissemination in Vietnam.

42935035.title: Thirteen years of environmental surveillance of ESKAPE organisms and Escherichia coli in an equine hospital: Informing infection control.
42935035.abstract: Bacteria from the ESKAPE group (i.e., Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterobacter species) and Escherichia coli are frequently multidrug-resistant and can be associated with healthcare-associated infections, an increasing concern for veterinary settings. To determine the environmental prevalence of ESKAPE and E. coli on surfaces which can act as reservoirs of infection in clinical areas in equine hospitals. Observational study. Routine environmental sampling was performed in one busy equine hospital with Swiffer® wipes to screen surfaces from high-risk areas (e.g., surgical theatres, intensive care unit [ICU], isolation unit), equipment (e.g., endotracheal tubes) and high-touch areas (e.g., keyboards) following selective species-specific protocols for each target organism. Monitoring hand-hygiene of hospital staff and students was by hand-plate sampling. After a pilot phase E. faecium was excluded from routine screening. Nine hundred and ninety-five environmental and hand-plate samples were collected from April 2010 to February 2023. The overall E. coli-SKAPE (E. coli, methicillin-resistant S. aureus [MRSA], K. pneumoniae, A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa and Enterobacter spp.) prevalence was 37.9%, where E. coli was the most (and K. pneumoniae the least) common target organism identified (18.0% and 1.7% respectively). E. coli was most prevalent in general stables and yards (37.7%) and offices (25.7%). Enterobacter spp. was the main organism in the environmental samples from ICU (24.2%) and isolation unit (22.9%, along with E. coli). Concerningly, hand-plate sampling showed that MRSA was the most common organism detected on hands (8.4%), followed by A. baumannii (5.2%) and E. cloacae (3.9%); however, E. coli, P. aeruginosa and K. pneumoniae were not found in these samples. Inconsistent sampling limited longitudinal analysis. We generated baseline environmental contamination data and demonstrated high E. coli-SKAPE hospital surface and hand contamination, informing infection control to prevent environment-to-patient cross-transmission.

42934942.title: Next-Generation Immunotherapies for Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Monoclonal Antibodies and Immune Checkpoint Modulation.
42934942.journal: APMIS : acta pathologica, microbiologica, et immunologica Scandinavica
42934942.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa represents a critical healthcare challenge, accounting for 7%-10% of hospital-acquired infections globally, with particularly high prevalence in intensive care, burn, and respiratory units, alongside escalating rates of multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant strains. The bacterium evades host immunity through multiple mechanisms, including Type III Secretion System effector translocation and biofilm formation via polysaccharide matrices (alginate, Psl, Pel). Antibiotic-based therapies are increasingly ineffective, necessitating host-directed immunotherapeutic strategies. This review synthesizes emerging evidence on monoclonal antibody therapy and immune checkpoint modulation for P. aeruginosa infections. Bispecific antibodies targeting PcrV and Psl enhance opsonophagocytic killing and biofilm disruption through Fc-mediated mechanisms. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1) reverse T-cell exhaustion from chronic antigen exposure and LPS-driven upregulation of inhibitory receptors, restoring antimicrobial function. Combination approaches integrating mAbs with antibiotics and checkpoint blockade show potential for synergistic bacterial clearance in preclinical pneumonia and burn wound models. Clinical translation remains limited by antigen variability (Psl and PcrV epitope polymorphisms), biofilm heterogeneity, and host immunogenetic diversity (Fc receptor polymorphisms, HLA variants, cytokine profiles). Multi-omics profiling may enable personalized treatment selection. Safety concerns regarding immune hyperactivation require carefully dosed, biomarker-guided strategies. Future development demands genomic stratification of responders and optimized therapeutic windows for maximal clinical benefit.

42934711.title: Cost-effectiveness of empirical ceftazidime-avibactam for hospital-acquired urinary tract infections: a modeling study identifying key beneficiary subgroups.
42934711.journal: Cost effectiveness and resource allocation : C/E
42934711.abstract: Hospital-acquired urinary tract infections (HAUTIs) caused by Gram-negative bacilli are increasingly difficult to manage owing to rising carbapenem resistance. The novel antibiotic ceftazidime-avibactam (CAZ-AVI) is a potential alternative, but its cost-effectiveness in this setting is unknown. This study evaluated the cost-effectiveness of empirical CAZ-AVI versus a meropenem-first strategy for treating HAUTIs. Using a patient-level decision-tree model, we simulated adult patients with HAUTIs in general ward and intensive care unit (ICU) settings in Taiwan, drawing on local pathogen distribution and antimicrobial susceptibility data. The model compared total costs and quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs); in the meropenem arm, pathogen-susceptible cases underwent antibiotic de-escalation once culture-guided susceptibility results were available. Clinical outcomes, utility weights, and costs were obtained from secondary sources of published studies, with all costs expressed in 2024 U.S. Dollars (USD) and future QALYs discounted at 3% annually. The primary outcome was the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) per QALY gained, evaluated against a willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold equal to Taiwan's 2024 GDP per capita ($33,983/QALY). Uncertainty was assessed with one-way, probabilistic, and scenario sensitivity analyses. In the base case, CAZ-AVI was cost-effective in both settings. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) were $12,049/QALY (Ward) and $21,396/QALY (ICU), both below the WTP threshold. At Taiwan's WTP threshold, the probability that CAZ-AVI was cost-effective was 93.8% (Ward) and 76.9% (ICU). The 50% cost-effectiveness threshold was approximately $12,500/QALY (Ward) and $22,500/QALY (ICU). In scenario analysis, CAZ-AVI was dominant (more effective and cost-saving) for patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Empirical CAZ-AVI is cost-effective compared with meropenem for HAUTIs in both ward and ICU settings in Taiwan, with benefits most pronounced in critically ill patients and those with severe renal impairment. These findings support CAZ-AVI as a first-line empirical option in select patient populations, particularly in institutions with elevated rates of meropenem-resistant pathogens and may inform local antimicrobial stewardship policy.

42931241.title: Co-Circulation of ST11-KL30 and ST11-KL64 Carbapenem-Resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae in Urumqi, Xinjiang, China: Molecular Epidemiology, Antimicrobial Resistance, and Virulence.
42931241.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) and hypervirulent CRKP (hv-CRKP) are growing global threats with regional heterogeneity. We collected 93 non-duplicate CRKP isolates from a hospital in Urumqi, China, from January to December 2024. Antimicrobial susceptibility was tested using the VITEK 2 system, hypermucoviscosity was assessed by the string test, resistance and virulence genes were detected by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and clonal lineages were determined by multilocus sequence typing (MLST) and capsular typing. Isolates were mainly from the intensive care unit (ICU) (36.56%) and respiratory department (31.18%), with sputum (51.62%) the predominant specimen type. Resistance rates to most β-lactams exceeded 97%. blaKPC was the predominant carbapenemase gene (94.62%), and hv-CRKP accounted for 54.84% of isolates. Sequence type 11 (ST11) was the dominant clone (89.25%), with K-locus types (KL30) (44 isolates) and KL64 (31 isolates) most common. ST11-KL30 exhibited significantly lower resistance rates to amikacin, gentamicin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and tigecycline, and lower blaTEM carriage compared with ST11-KL64 (p < 0.05); it also showed a lower proportion of hv-CRKP and string test positivity. This study is the first to show that ST11-KL30 and ST11-KL64 co-circulate as dominant hv-CRKP-carrying clones in Urumqi, clarifying their resistance and phenotypic differences and providing key data for regional surveillance.

42930504.title: Perioperative Intravenous Antibiotic Regimens and Surgical Site Infection After Colorectal Surgery: Clinical Associations and External Evaluation of Risk Prediction Models.
42930504.abstract: Surgical site infection (SSI) remains a major complication after colorectal surgery. Comparative evidence for commonly used perioperative intravenous antibiotic regimens is limited, and risk prediction models require external evaluation before clinical use. We examined regimen-SSI associations and secondarily evaluated models using routine perioperative variables to distinguish patients with and without electronically recorded postoperative SSI. We analysed 732 adults from MIMIC-IV for regimen association and model development and 133 adults from ICU-based eICU-CRD for external model evaluation. SSI was identified using an electronic phenotype. Four intravenous antibiotic exposure groups were compared using multivariable logistic regression and exploratory interaction analyses. Predictors selected using LASSO screening followed by clinical refinement informed six models, which were assessed using discrimination, calibration, and classification metrics. SSI was recorded in 146/732 patients (19.9%), with no evidence of an unadjusted association across observed exposure categories (p = 0.947). Logistic regression achieved an external ROC-AUC of 0.858 (95% CI 0.764-0.934; PR-AUC 0.560) and detected 17/21 SSI cases, but generated 27 false positives. Positive predictive value was 38.6%, with limited calibration (expected calibration error 0.236) and a Brier score of 0.197. These data provide no evidence of an overall association, nor evidence of equivalent prophylactic efficacy. Heterogeneous exposures and residual confounding preclude regimen-level causal conclusions. The small ICU-based external evaluation informs higher-acuity populations, not routine elective surgery. Uncertain SSI onset, limited calibration, and false-positive burden preclude clinical implementation. Prospective multicentre studies should evaluate risk-adapted surveillance, not model-directed antibiotic selection.

42929453.title: Pregnancy in females with cystic fibrosis and chronic Burkholderia cepacia complex or non-tuberculous mycobacteria infection: A single centre case series.
42929453.abstract: Widespread availability of cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator modulator therapy (CFTRm) has resulted in improved health and quality of life for many people with cystic fibrosis (CF) and a subsequent rise in pregnancies among females with CF (FwCF). An increasing number of pregnancies are now occurring in women who are chronically infected with clinically significant respiratory pathogens, in particular the Burkholderia cepacia complex (BCC) and non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), including Mycobacterium abscessus complex (MABC). These pathogens are associated with accelerated pulmonary decline, multi-drug antimicrobial resistance patterns and complex, prolonged treatment regimens making them important considerations in pregnancy management. Historically, chronic BCC infection has been linked to poorer obstetric and perinatal outcomes in FwCF, although much of the available evidence predates the CFTRm era and may not reflect the current clinical landscape. Similarly, while NTM infection, most significantly MABC, remains a major clinical challenge and contraindication for lung transplantation in people with cystic fibrosis (PwCF), there is a paucity of published data describing pregnancy outcomes in FwCF living with chronic NTM infection. As CFTRm has shifted disease trajectories and expanded reproductive possibilities, updated evidence describing risks and outcomes is urgently needed. This case series addresses this gap by examining CF-specific, obstetric, and neonatal outcomes in ten pregnancies: four in FwCF chronically infected with BCC and six with NTM infection. All pregnancies ended in live births: nine infants born at term, and one at 32+5 weeks from spontaneous premature labour, requiring the only admission to neonatal intensive care. CFTRm were used in nine pregnancies, and admission to hospital was required in two pregnancies for infective exacerbations of CF. There were no maternal deaths and no maternal intensive care admissions. These findings contribute essential new insights to guide counselling, risk assessment, and multidisciplinary management for pregnant FwCF with chronic infection by these high-risk pathogens.

42926754.title: Molecular evidence of a dominant multidrug resistant Acinetobacter baumannii lineage in a tertiary hospital in northern Peru.
42926754.abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a major nosocomial pathogen because of its genomic plasticity and capacity to acquire multidrug resistance (MDR), particularly resistance to carbapenems. The World Health Organization classifies carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii as a critical-priority pathogen. Molecular epidemiological data from Latin America remain limited, especially for northern Peru. Drug-resistant A. baumannii isolates collected between 2015 and 2021 at a tertiary referral hospital in northern Peru were characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing, BOX-PCR, ERIC-PCR, REP-PCR, and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS). All seven isolates met the criteria for MDR, and Ac-4268 showed an extensively drug-resistant phenotype. Repetitive-element PCR identified a group of six isolates with similar banding profiles and a divergent isolate, Ac-4268. Several isolates in the six-isolate group retained susceptibility to one or more aminoglycosides, whereas Ac-4268 was resistant to all antimicrobials tested. The combined molecular and phenotypic findings are consistent with the possible persistence of a dominant related lineage, but they do not establish transmission without whole-genome sequencing and epidemiological linkage data. This study provides additional molecular epidemiological evidence on MDR A. baumannii in northern Peru. The findings suggest that a dominant related lineage may have persisted in the hospital alongside a genetically divergent isolate with an extensively drug-resistant phenotype. Confirmation of clonal transmission requires higher-resolution genomic and epidemiological analyses.

42923582.title: Resistance profile and clinical outcomes of Xuebijing injection combined with antibiotics for carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection: a single-center retrospective cohort study.
42923582.abstract: To examine the resistance profile of carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (CRPA) and to evaluate the clinical efficacy of Xuebijing injection (XBJ) combined with antibiotics versus antibiotics alone. This single-center retrospective cohort study included 295 hospitalized patients with microbiologically confirmed CRPA infection between January 2019 and June 2024. Patients received either antibiotics alone (control group, n=141) or XBJ plus antibiotics (combination group, n=154). The primary outcome was 28-day all-cause mortality. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied to balance baseline covariates. Logistic and Cox regression models were performed to evaluate the association between combination therapy and 28-day mortality. After IPTW adjustment, all covariates achieved satisfactory balance (standardized mean differences <0.10). Compared with control group, the combination group showed significantly higher clinical response rate (OR=1.705, 95% CI: 1.039-2.798, P=0.035) and bacterial eradication rate (OR=1.758, 95% CI: 1.097-2.817, P=0.019), as well as a lower risk of escalation of anti-infective therapy (OR=0.529, 95% CI: 0.302-0.925, P=0.026). The duration of hospital stay and ICU stay were numerically shorter in the combination group, though differences were not significant (both P>0.05). After IPTW adjustment, no significant difference was observed in 28-day mortality between the two groups (16.85% vs 22.72%, P=0.207); however, multivariable Logistic regression identified combination therapy as an independent protective factor for 28-day mortality (OR=0.250, 95% CI: 0.071-0.873, P=0.030). Older age, higher APACHE II scores, bloodstream infection, and absence of targeted antimicrobial therapy were independently associated with increased mortality risk. Sensitivity analyses confirmed model robustness. Subgroup analysis suggested greater benefit in patients with APACHE II score <20. XBJ combined with antibiotics improved infection control outcomes in patients with CRPA infections, with more evident benefits observed among patients with lower disease severity.
