42819483.abstract: Sepsis is a highly heterogeneous syndrome. Providing personalized treatment for the various clinical phenotypes of sepsis has been a major challenge for critical care physicians. This study was a secondary analysis of data derived from a multicenter, prospective, observational study of sepsis patients. Based on relevance to sepsis onset or outcome, 25 parameters were selected by the derived cohort to derive sepsis phenotypes. Clustered phenotypes were derived via k-means clustering and examined in a sensitivity analysis using divisive hierarchical clustering. Then, the relationship between fluid resuscitation therapy and survival outcomes was assessed for each clustered phenotype using generalized estimating equations. Patients with sepsis were categorized into Cluster A, B and C. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed Cluster A patients had the highest 28-day mortality (P = 0.029 by Log-rank test). In Cluster A, septic patients who received fluid resuscitation had a association than those who did not, with an adjusted RD for 28-day mortality of 16.2% (95% CI, 1.4 to 31.0%, P = 0.032). Sensitivity analyses adjusted for APACHE II and infection site confirmed these findings, with an adjusted RD for 28-day mortality of 6.3% (95% CI, 0.3 to 12.3%, P = 0.040). Hierarchical clustering methods yielded consistent conclusions. The association between fluid resuscitation and clinical outcomes varied across sepsis phenotypes, suggesting potential heterogeneity in treatment response that requires further prospective validation.Trial registration: The primary study was registered in the China Clinical Registry on February 1, 2022, with the registration number ChiCTR2200056179.

42819091.title: Association between lactate dehydrogenase-to-albumin ratio and short-term mortality in critically ill patients with urosepsis: evidence from dual retrospective cohorts.
42819091.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
42819091.abstract: The lactate dehydrogenase-to-albumin ratio (LDAR) reflects tissue damage, inflammation, and nutritional status. Its prognostic value in urosepsis remains unexplored. We evaluated LDAR's association with short-term mortality and developed an LDAR-based prediction model. This retrospective dual-cohort study used MIMIC-IV (n=3,060) and an external cohort (n=370). Exposure was log2-transformed LDAR (logLDAR); outcomes were 28-day intensive care unit (ICU) and in-hospital mortality. Cox regression with three adjustment models, restricted cubic splines (RCS), and Kaplan-Meier curves assessed associations; Fine-Gray models addressed competing risks. DeLong tests compared area under the curve (AUC) of six conventional scores with and without logLDAR. Net reclassification improvement (NRI) and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI) quantified incremental value of adding logLDAR; Machine learning selected predictors for a parsimonious model validated internally and externally. decision curve analysis (DCA) evaluated the 7-variable model's utility. Among 3,060 patients, higher logLDAR was associated with significantly elevated 28-day ICU (23.4% vs. 9.02%) and in-hospital (22.1% vs. 8.24%) mortality (both P<0.001). In the primary multivariable-adjusted model, per-unit increases in logLDAR yielded hazard ratios (HRs) of 1.26 (95% CI: 1.17-1.36) for ICU mortality and 1.35 (95% CI: 1.25-1.45) for in-hospital mortality. Compared with the lowest tertile, the highest tertile showed HRs of 1.79 (1.40-2.30) and 2.29 (1.77-2.96), respectively. RCS analysis revealed linear dose-response relationships (P<0.001), and the Fine-Gray model confirmed robust associations (subdistribution hazard ratio (sHR)=1.36, 1.27-1.46). Adding logLDAR significantly improved the AUCs of all six conventional scores (DeLong P<0.01), with NRI/IDI showing substantial reclassification improvement (P<0.001). A parsimonious 7-variable model achieved AUCs of 0.674, 0.677, and 0.783 in the internal training, internal validation, and external cohorts, respectively, with adequate calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow P > 0.05) and DCA demonstrating net clinical benefit. These findings were fully validated in an external real-world cohort. LDAR independently predicts short-term mortality in critically ill patients with urosepsis, supplementing conventional severity scores. The parsimonious risk model showed moderate performance with acceptable cross-cohort generalizability.

42822778.title: Intensive care unit-acquired infection is the main driver of resource utilization, independent of antimicrobial resistance.
42822778.abstract: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are frequent in intensive care units (ICUs) and are associated with substantial clinical and economic burden. However, the independent contribution of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) beyond the occurrence of infection remains uncertain. We conducted a retrospective cohort study including 802 adult ICU admissions in a tertiary university hospital. Patients were classified into three groups: no ICU-acquired HAI (N = 666), HAI without AMR (N = 105), and HAI with AMR (N = 31). Primary outcomes were ICU length of stay (LOS) and hospital costs; hospital mortality was analysed as a secondary outcome. Generalized linear models adjusted for age, sex, Simplified Acute Physiology Score II (SAPS II), and comorbidities were used. A restricted analysis among infected patients evaluated the independent association of AMR. ICU-acquired HAI occurred in 17% of patients, with AMR identified in 3.9%. ICU LOS increased across groups (6 vs 19 vs 21 days; P < 0.001). In adjusted analyses, ICU LOS was 7.6 days in patients without HAI, 21.7 days in patients with HAI without AMR, and 30.3 days in those with AMR. Adjusted hospital costs were €29,105, €60,065, and €70,164, respectively. In analyses restricted to infected patients, AMR was not independently associated with ICU LOS or hospital costs. ICU-acquired infection was the primary driver of increased ICU LOS and hospital costs. After adjustment for severity and comorbidity burden, AMR was not independently associated with additional resource utilization among infected patients. These findings highlight infection prevention as a priority for reducing ICU burden, alongside antimicrobial stewardship strategies.

42822676.title: Impact of antimicrobial stewardship implementation in an intensive care unit in Central India - A microbiologist-intensivist driven initiative.
42822676.abstract: This study evaluates a microbiologist-intensivist-driven prospective audit-feedback model in a 13-bedded tertiary-care critical care unit in Central India, using interrupted time-series analysis (ITS) to assess its impact on antimicrobial consumption (AMC), alongside diagnostic stewardship and patient outcomes. This quasi-experimental study included both retrospective and prospective data collected over 20 months, divided into a 3-month pre-intervention phase (PIP), 12-month intervention phase (IP), and 5-month follow-up phase (FUP). Patients receiving targeted antimicrobials for more than 48 h were included. Baseline AMC was recorded during PIP. During the IP, bi-weekly AMSP rounds with real-time recommendations on antimicrobial therapy, sample collection, and infection control practices were conducted. Culture reports, relevant laboratory parameters (leucocyte count, procalcitonin, invasive fungal markers), and clinical status (fever, vasopressor requirement, SOFA score) were reviewed to assess the appropriateness of therapy. AMC was measured as days of therapy/1000 patient-days and ITS analysis was done. A total of 398 patients were enrolled (PIP: 83; IP: 315). Cumulative average AMC significantly decreased from 2019.1 (PIP) to 1659.5 (IP) and was sustained during FUP (1635.2) even though ITS analysis revealed non-significant improvement. Use of reserve antimicrobials, including colistin/polymyxin, linezolid, and ceftazidime-avibactam-aztreonam, declined during IP. The mean number of antibiotics per patient decreased from 4.0 to 3.3, while ICU stay showed a numerical reduction from 13.5 to 10.7 days, although this difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.09). Mean SOFA across PIP (5.8) and IP (5.9) was similar. Urine, endotracheal and blood culture sampling declined significantly, reflecting more judicious, clinically guided testing. A microbiologist-intensivist-driven AMSP is feasible and may reduce AMC in Indian ICU where infectious disease specialists are scarce. Integrating microbiology expertise with bedside decision-making offers a practical and scalable stewardship model for high-burden Lower Middle-Income Countries, and a scalable template for programme expansion.

42818818.title: Association of early chloride-bicarbonate joint phenotypes with in-hospital mortality among intensive care unit patients with sepsis: a dual-database study.
42818818.abstract: Associations of chloride and bicarbonate abnormalities with sepsis outcomes have been studied separately, but whether a prespecified paired classification provides reproducible and interpretable risk characterization remains uncertain. We included adults with sepsis in MIMIC-IV v3.1 and eICU v2.0. Chloride (<98, 98-107, >107 mmol/L) and bicarbonate (<22, 22-26, >26 mmol/L) defined a 3 × 3 phenotype. In-hospital mortality was analyzed using multivariable logistic regression and predictive mean matching multiple imputation. Robustness was assessed through analyses of temporal ordering, threshold selection, cross-database heterogeneity, external transportability, and first-day changes in chloride and bicarbonate. The cohorts included 25,842 MIMIC-IV stays and 37,045 eICU stays, with mortality rates of 16.31% and 15.50%, respectively. In complete-case Model 3b, the phenotype was globally associated with mortality in both cohorts; the low-low contrast was individually significant in eICU but not MIMIC-IV. The low-low association was supported in multiple-imputation analyses (MIMIC-IV OR 1.276, 95% CI 1.066-1.527; eICU OR 1.507, 95% CI 1.277-1.779) and in strict pre-exposure analyses (OR 1.700 and 1.787, respectively). Formal 4-df categorical interaction tests were not significant (P = 0.095 and P = 0.109). MIMIC-IV-derived data-driven cut points did not significantly outperform the clinical 3 × 3 phenotype in eICU (CART vs. clinical ΔAUROC 0.0009, 95% CI -0.0010 to 0.0029). In the main MIMIC-IV-to-eICU validation, adding the clinical phenotype left discrimination essentially unchanged (ΔAUROC 0.0010, 95% CI -0.0013 to 0.0031), although the Brier score improved modestly (ΔBrier -0.0011, 95% CI -0.0016 to -0.0006); NRI and IDI did not support improved discrimination or reclassification. Incident and persistent low-low states were both associated with higher subsequent mortality in 24 h landmark analyses in both cohorts. Prespecified chloride-bicarbonate phenotypes were associated with mortality in both databases, and persistence or incident development of the low-low state during the first ICU day was associated with higher subsequent mortality. The 3 × 3 framework should therefore be interpreted primarily as a transparent, direction-preserving approach to descriptive risk characterization within a broader clinical assessment, rather than as a stand-alone prediction instrument, therapeutic threshold, or treatment guide.

42821858.title: From Knowledge to Outcomes: The Effect of Nursing Care Bundle Training on Knowledge, Compliance, and Ventilator-associated Pneumonia Rates in Intensive Care Units (A Quasi-intervention Study, 2025).
42821858.journal: Dimensions of critical care nursing : DCCN
42821858.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is a serious infection in ICUs, contributing to prolonged mechanical ventilation and higher mortality. This study aimed to enhance ICU nurses' knowledge and compliance with ventilator care bundle practices to reduce the incidence and mortality of VAP among mechanically ventilated patients at Benha University Hospitals. This quasi-experimental study included all nurses working in the central and intermediate ICUs (N = 262). The intervention comprised 12 structured educational sessions and bedside demonstrations. Data collection included pre-questionnaires and post-questionnaires to assess nurses' knowledge, observation checklists to measure compliance with the VAP care bundle, and patient surveillance records to track VAP incidence and mortality rates. Postintervention analysis revealed a significant improvement in nurses' knowledge scores on general infection control and VAP prevention guidelines, as well as a significant increase in compliance with the VAP care bundle (P < .001). General infection control knowledge score was a significant predictor of VAP prevention knowledge (B = 0.632, P < .01). Clinically, the program resulted in a nearly one-third reduction in VAP incidence (central ICU: -29.1%; intermediate ICU: -28.5%), preventing ∼1 infection for every 10 ventilated patients. Mortality among ventilated cases was cut by almost half in the intermediate ICU (-53.8%) and by one-third in the central ICU (-30.9%). The care bundle training program significantly improved ICU nurses' knowledge, boosted adherence to evidence-based ventilator care practices, and contributed to lowering the VAP incidence rate and related mortality. These results represent not only statistical significance but also a substantial, life-saving impact.

42820488.title: Association between age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index and risk of nonhome discharge in sepsis survivors: A retrospective analysis based on the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database.
42820488.journal: Journal of the American Association of Nurse Practitioners
42820488.abstract: Sepsis is a common complication in intensive care units, and the discharge disposition of survivors has clinical significance. The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) predicts long-term outcomes based on comorbidity burden. To investigate the association between age-adjusted CCI (ACCI) and nonhome discharge among sepsis survivors. A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database. Adult sepsis survivors (Sepsis-3.0 criteria) were included. Patients who died during hospitalization or had missing data were excluded. The primary outcome was nonhome discharge (i.e., discharge to skilled nursing facilities, long-term care, or rehabilitation). Multivariable logistic regression, subgroup, and sensitivity analyses were performed. Among 23,683 sepsis survivors, 44.9% were discharged home, and 55.1% had nonhome discharge. In the nonhome discharge group, 65% had a CCI score ≥5, compared with 40.4% in the home discharge group. Multivariable logistic regression showed that each 1-point increase in ACCI was associated with higher odds of nonhome discharge (odds ratio = 1.15, 95% confidence interval: 1.14-1.16, p < .001). This association remained robust across sensitivity analyses. An ACCI means people with sepsis are more likely to be discharged to a location other than home. The ACCI can help nurses figure out which patients with sepsis are at risk. This can help plan for their care after they leave the hospital, and it can also help make sure that the right resources are used for the patients.

42818587.title: Clinical significance of controlling nutritional status score in predicting ICU admission, prolonged hospitalization, and in-hospital mortality in emergency sepsis: a single-center retrospective study.
42818587.abstract: Sepsis is associated with high mortality in critically ill patients. Existing prognostic tools are often complex or require specialized testing. This study aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of the Controlling Nutritional Status (CONUT) score in patients with sepsis in the emergency department. A retrospective analysis of 1,200 sepsis patients admitted to the emergency department of the Affiliated Changsha Central Hospital, Hengyang Medical School, University of South China from January 2020 to June 2025 was conducted. Kaplan-Meier analysis, multivariable Cox regression, restricted cubic splines (RCS), receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA) were employed to evaluate the associations between the CONUT score and ICU admission, prolonged hospitalization, and in-hospital all-cause mortality. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses were performed. Time-dependent Cox regression revealed that each one-point increase in the CONUT score was associated with an 11% increase in the risk of in-hospital mortality (HR = 1.11, 95% CI:1.02-1.21). After adjusting for potential confounders, logistic regression analysis further demonstrated that, the CONUT score was significantly associated with ICU admission (OR = 1.16, 95% CI: 1.09-1.23) and prolonged hospitalization (OR = 1.11, 95% CI: 1.05-1.17). RCS revealed linear positive correlations. ROC analysis showed that CONUT was superior to SOFA for predicting prolonged hospitalization, and combining CONUT with SOFA enhanced predictive performance. DCA indicated the combined model provided the highest clinical net benefit. Advanced age, diabetes, and mechanical ventilation modified the associations between CONUT and certain outcomes. Elevated CONUT scores are independently associated with adverse outcomes in emergency department sepsis patients, serving as a simple prognostic indicator for early risk stratification.

42819557.title: Prospective Molecular and Phenotypic Characterization of blaCTX-M and blaTEM ESBL Genes in Uropathogenic Escherichia coli from ICU Patients at Three Tertiary-Care Hospitals in Tabriz, Iran.
42819557.abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) caused by extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli have become a major therapeutic challenge worldwide, especially in intensive care units. In northwestern Iran, the molecular epidemiology of the key resistance genes blaCTX-M and blaTEM, along with their potential co-carriage on plasmids, remains poorly understood. This gap limits the development of effective local empirical treatment guidelines and infection control strategies. A cross-sectional study was conducted at three tertiary-care hospitals in Tabriz, Iran (2025). We identified 100 non-duplicate Escherichia coli isolates recovered from ICU patients with UTIs using standard microbiological methods. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed by the disk diffusion method according to CLSI 2024 guidelines. ESBL phenotype was confirmed using the combined disk test with Ceftazidime and Clavulanic acid. Genotypic detection of blaTEM and blaCTX-M was performed by conventional PCR. Chi-square and Fisher's exact tests were used to assess statistical associations. Among 135 culture-positive urine specimens, E. coli was the predominant pathogen (74.07%), followed by Klebsiella pneumoniae (11.85%). Universal resistance to Cefotaxime (100%) and high resistance to Ceftazidime (95%) were observed. Imipenem retained the highest in vitro activity (82% susceptibility). Phenotypic ESBL production was detected in 48/100 (48%) isolates. Among ESBL producers, blaTEM was present in 28 (58.3%), blaCTX-M in 20 (41.7%), and both genes co-occurred in 18 isolates (37.5%). The observed co-occurrence significantly exceeded expected values under independence (observed: 18 vs. expected: 11.7; Chi-square p = 0.0005; Fisher's exact p = 0.00025), demonstrating non-random co-occurrence consistent with, but not proof of, plasmid-mediated co-carriage. ESBL-producing E. coli carrying both blaTEM and blaCTX-M are highly prevalent among ICU-associated UTI in Tabriz. The statistically significant non-random co-occurrence of these genes has direct implications for surveillance strategies, necessitating simultaneous genotyping of both genes. Carbapenems remain effective, underscoring the urgency of their stewardship to prevent the emergence of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) in this setting.

42869442.title: Association of Early Primary Care Follow-Up With Acute Care Use After ICU Discharge.
42869442.abstract: To determine if early primary care follow-up after pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) hospitalization is associated with reduced acute care use. Using claims data from publicly and privately insured children, we identified a cohort of PICU hospitalizations from January 2016 to December 2019. We matched children with and without early primary care follow-up (within 7 days of hospital discharge) 1 to 1 on demographic and clinical characteristics. We compared the number of days of acute care use (emergency department or rehospitalization) during days 8 to 90 postdischarge using negative binomial regression and reported incidence rate ratios (IRR). The sample included 180 516 PICU hospitalizations, including 158 544 for publicly insured children and 21 972 for privately insured children. Among PICU hospitalizations for publicly and privately insured children, 56 247 (35.4%) and 5156 (23.5%) were associated with acute care use with 8 to 90 days postdischarge. Hospitalizations of children with early primary care follow-up were less likely to be associated with acute care use than those without follow-up (public insurance: IRR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.90-0.96; P < .001; and private insurance: IRR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.63-0.77; P < .001). Subgroup analyses suggested early primary care follow-up was associated with larger decreases in acute care after hospitalizations of older children and children with sepsis. The association between early primary care follow-up and acute care use persisted in a secondary analysis using data from 2022 to 2023. Early primary care follow-up was associated with lower acute care use after discharge from PICU hospitalization. Promotion of early primary care follow-up may be warranted after pediatric critical illness.

42824567.title: Pancreatic microbiota composition and diversity in pancreatitis-associated infection: a systematic review with focus on infected pancreatic necrosis.
42824567.abstract: Pancreatitis-associated intra-abdominal infection (PA-IAI), particularly infected pancreatic necrosis (IPN), is a serious complication of severe acute pancreatitis and contributes substantially to late morbidity and mortality. Sequencing-based technologies have expanded the detection of microorganisms in pancreatic infection; however, the characteristics of pancreatic microbiota and their clinical relevance have not been systematically summarized. A systematic literature search was conducted in seven electronic databases to identify studies evaluating pancreatic microbiota in patients with pancreatitis-associated infection. Studies reporting microbial composition or diversity using sequencing-based approaches were included. Study characteristics, microbial findings, diversity patterns, clinical outcomes, and methodological details were systematically extracted and synthesized. Six studies involving 235 participants were included; 188 participants contributed pancreatic or peripancreatic microbiota data. Most available evidence was derived from patients with IPN. Sequencing-based approaches generally detected a broader range of microbial taxa than conventional culture, with enteric-associated microorganisms frequently detected, while phylum-level dominance varied among studies. Reported diversity patterns varied between studies and could not be directly compared because of methodological heterogeneity. Although IPN was associated with worse clinical outcomes, current evidence did not demonstrate that specific microbial taxa or microbiota characteristics independently predicted mortality, organ failure, or treatment response. Current evidence indicates that pancreatic microbiota in pancreatitis-associated infection, particularly IPN, are characterized by frequent detection of enteric-associated microorganisms and substantial methodological heterogeneity. Sequencing-based approaches may provide additional microbiological information beyond conventional culture and may influence clinical management; however, whether sequencing-guided management changes improve antimicrobial stewardship or patient-centered outcomes remains uncertain. Future prospective studies using standardized microbiome workflows are required to determine the clinical significance of pancreatic microbial characteristics. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261295285, identifier: CRD420261295285.

42819128.title: In-hospital outcomes and documented 90-day readmission to the index hospital in older patients with Parkinson's disease hospitalised for lower respiratory tract infection: a single-centre retrospective cohort study.
42819128.abstract: Lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) is a major cause of hospitalisation in older adults with Parkinson's disease (PD), but it remains uncertain whether PD-related measures provide clinically relevant information beyond general vulnerability and acute infection severity. We conducted a single-centre retrospective cohort study of patients aged ≥65 years with neurologist-diagnosed PD who were hospitalised for LRTI between 2018 and 2025. The primary outcome was a composite of intensive care unit admission, invasive mechanical ventilation, or in-hospital death. Documented readmission to the index hospital within 90 days among survivors was analysed as a secondary exploratory outcome. Multivariable logistic and Cox regression models evaluated clinical factors associated with these outcomes. A hierarchical extension added Hoehn-Yahr stage and pre-admission wheelchair- or bed-bound status to the base clinical model. Calendar-period analyses and bootstrap internal validation were performed. Among 246 patients, 62 (25.2%) experienced the composite in-hospital outcome. In the PD-specific extended model, higher Charlson Comorbidity Index (adjusted odds ratio [OR] per 1-point increase 1.19, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.00-1.42), hypoxaemia (OR 2.00, 95% CI 1.01-3.96), serum albumin <35 g/L (OR 3.18, 95% CI 1.65-6.14), sepsis or septic shock (OR 2.41, 95% CI 1.17-4.98), and pre-admission wheelchair- or bed-bound status (OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.08-4.01) were associated with the outcome. Hoehn-Yahr stage, PD duration, tube feeding, and antiparkinsonian medication burden were not independently associated. Among 228 patients discharged alive, 74 (32.5%) had a documented readmission to the index hospital. Hypoalbuminaemia (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 1.82, 95% CI 1.12-2.95) and non-home discharge (HR 1.96, 95% CI 1.19-3.24) were among the factors associated with documented same-hospital return. Bootstrap-corrected discrimination was 0.81 for the extended logistic model and 0.70 for the Cox model. Severe in-hospital deterioration was associated mainly with general physiological vulnerability, acute infection severity, and pre-admission mobility dependence, whereas most other available PD-specific measures showed no clear independent association. These findings support integrated clinical assessment but not a validated PD-specific prediction strategy; the post-discharge analysis reflects documented return to the index hospital rather than complete population-level readmission.

42819172.title: An explainable machine learning approach to predicting carbapenem resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae with imbalanced data and resistance-ratio validation.
42819172.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
42819172.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) is a major global health threat. Predicting resistance from electronic medical records (EMRs) may support infection control and antimicrobial stewardship, but class imbalance can impair detection of resistant isolates. This study developed an interpretable machine-learning framework for predicting carbapenem-resistant versus carbapenem-susceptible K. pneumoniae. We retrospectively analyzed 5,794 records collected from 2014 to 2024, including 999 carbapenem-resistant and 4,795 carbapenem-susceptible isolates. The prediction anchor was culture-specimen collection (T0), and all predictors were restricted to information available at or before T0. Seven algorithms and 18 sampling strategies were evaluated using patient-grouped five-fold cross-validation with fold-specific preprocessing. The selected resampling pipeline was compared with Platt-calibrated XGBoost using sensitivity-targeted, F2-maximizing, and cost-sensitive thresholds. Feature-restriction analyses, multiplicity-adjusted comparisons, ICU subgroup analysis, reconstructed prevalence scenarios, calibration assessment, and same-center temporal validation were also performed. XGBoost and LightGBM showed comparable discrimination after multiplicity adjustment. ENN-BLSMOTE-XGBoost increased sensitivity and reduced the very-major-error rate (VME) at the default threshold, but slightly reduced ranking discrimination and increased false-positive alerts. Sensitivity-targeted threshold optimization of calibrated XGBoost produced an operating point close to that of the resampled model, indicating that much of the sensitivity gain could be achieved without changing the training distribution. After all duration-based predictors were excluded, ENN-BLSMOTE-XGBoost retained an ROC AUC of 0.940 and a PR AUC of 0.833. In the 2025 temporal cohort, the calibrated ENN-BLSMOTE-XGBoost model achieved an ROC AUC of 0.889, a PR AUC of 0.684, a sensitivity of 0.749, and a VME of 0.251; Platt scaling reduced its Brier score from 0.121 to 0.108. SHAP analysis identified ICU admission, vascular system disease, days of indwelling urinary catheterization, days of carbapenem use, and days of endotracheal intubation as the five highest-attribution predictors. A web calculator was developed to provide calibrated probability estimates referenced to the 17.24% resistance prevalence of the development cohort. The proposed model effectively addresses class imbalance in predicting carbapenem resistance in K. pneumoniae and may support early identification of patients at risk of harboring carbapenem-resistant isolates, thereby informing infection control and antimicrobial stewardship.

42890624.title: Characteristics of Bacterial Isolates from Patients with Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia and the Hospital Environment in Urmia, Iran.
42890624.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia is a nosocomial infection involving hospitalized patients using mechanical ventilation. The endotracheal tube is a place for colonizing microbial populations and subsequent biofilm formation, leading to relative drug resistance. Also, the hospital environment may worsen the infection. This study aims to identify the microbial cause of the infection and evaluate its characteristics. Sampling was done using endotracheal tube suction among hospitalized patients and from different places in intensive care units in selected hospitals in Urmia, Iran. All specimens were identified by microbial and biochemical tests. Then, the antibiotic susceptibility tests were performed using disk diffusion and minimum inhibitory and bacteriocidal concentrations for selected antibiotics. Finally, the biofilm formation rates of all isolates were evaluated. The majority of clinical bacterial isolates were Gram-negative bacilli, including A. baumannii. Bacillus spp. and Staphylococcus aureus were the most isolated bacteria from environmental samples. The antibiotic susceptibility testing results showed that most Gram-negative bacilli were resistant to common antibiotics and were extensively-drug resistant. The intermediate rate was higher than resistance to colistin, but evidence showed the efficiency of colistin against Gram-negative bacilli. Most of the isolates were strong biofilm producers, and this was correlated with the extensively drug-resistant pattern of bacteria. The evidence shows that Ventilator-associated pneumonia is a critical infection. According to the findings, there is a high rate of biofilm formation and consequent drug resistance among bacterial causes of Ventilator-associated pneumonia, which needs new insights for preventing and controlling this healthcare problem.

42932768.title: FDA-Authorized AI/ML Tool for Sepsis Prediction: Development and Validation.
42932768.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening condition that demands prompt treatment for improved patient outcomes. Its heterogenous presentation makes early detection challenging, highlighting the need for effective risk assessment tools. Artificial intelligence (AI) models could potentially identify patients with sepsis, but none have previously been authorized by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for commercial use. This study outlines the development and validation of the Sepsis ImmunoScore, the first FDA-authorized AI-based software designed to identify patients at risk of sepsis. In this prospective study, we enrolled adult patients (18+ years of age) suspected of infection, as indicated by a blood culture order, from five U.S. institutions between April 2017 and July 2022. The participants were divided into an algorithm development cohort (n=2366), an internal validation cohort (n=393), and an external validation cohort (n=698). The primary end point was sepsis presence (as defined by Sepsis-3) within 24 hours of test initiation. Secondary end points included length of hospital stay, intensive care unit (ICU) admission within 24 hours, mechanical ventilation use within 24 hours, vasopressor use within 24 hours, and in-hospital mortality. The Sepsis ImmunoScore demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy, with an area under the curve of 0.85 (0.83 to 0.87) in the derivation cohort, 0.80 (0.74 to 0.86) in internal validation, and 0.81 (0.77 to 0.86) in external validation. The scores were categorized into four sepsis risk levels with corresponding likelihood ratios: low (0.1), medium (0.5), high (2.1), and very high (8.3). These risk categories also predicted in-hospital mortality: low (0.0%), medium (1.9%), high (8.7%), and very high (18.2%) in the external validation cohort. Similar trends were observed for other metrics, such as length of hospital stay, ICU utilization, mechanical ventilation, and vasopressor use. The Sepsis ImmunoScore demonstrated high accuracy for the identification and prediction of sepsis and critical illness metrics that could enable prompt identification of patients at high risk of sepsis and adverse outcomes, potentially improving clinical decision-making and patient outcomes. (Funded by the Defense Threat Reduction Agency and others.).

42818838.title: Interpretable machine learning models using early dynamic clinical features to predict early hemodynamic stabilization after vasopressor initiation in patients with septic shock: development in MIMIC-IV and external validation in eICU.
42818838.abstract: Early hemodynamic stabilization after vasopressor initiation in septic shock is heterogeneous and difficult to predict. We aimed to develop and externally validate interpretable machine learning models for predicting early hemodynamic stabilization. This retrospective study used MIMIC-IV for model development and internal validation and eICU for external validation. Adult ICU patients with septic shock receiving vasopressors were included. Dynamic clinical features during the first 6 h after vasopressor initiation were used to predict stabilization during 6-24 h, defined by sustained mean arterial pressure (MAP) control without vasopressor escalation or increased norepinephrine-equivalent dose. Seven machine learning models were compared. Performance was assessed using discrimination, calibration, Brier score, decision curve analysis, external validation, and SHAP. The MIMIC-IV and eICU cohorts included 3,445 and 453 patients, with stabilization rates of 41.77% and 32.67%, respectively. Gradient boosting machine (GBM) showed the best overall performance, with an AUC of 0.720 and Brier score of 0.209 in internal validation and an AUC of 0.730 and Brier score of 0.192 in external validation. At the training-derived threshold, external sensitivity and specificity were 0.466 and 0.797. SHAP identified early MAP stability, lactate clearance, platelet count, renal function, inflammatory burden, and vasopressor intensity as major predictors. The stabilization endpoint was associated with ICU and hospital mortality and remained robust to alternative MAP definitions. However, predictive performance was substantially driven by proximal hemodynamic features, particularly MAP trajectories, and the full GBM did not consistently outperform simpler hemodynamic benchmarks externally. Early dynamic clinical features provided moderate discrimination for predicting hemodynamic stabilization after vasopressor initiation, with similar external performance. The model should be interpreted as a structured risk-stratification tool rather than a measure of pharmacological vasopressor responsiveness. Prospective validation is required before clinical implementation.

42820465.title: Investigation of Wnt2's Role in Macrophage Polarization and Its Effects on Sepsis.
42820465.abstract: Sepsis, characterized by organ dysfunction from an uncontrolled immune response to infection, remains a leading cause of mortality in critical care settings. A key underlying mechanism involves the imbalance between pro-inflammatory M1-type macrophages and anti-inflammatory M2-type macrophages in the biphasic pathological process of 'cytokine storm-immunosuppression' in sepsis. These macrophages, as crucial effector cells of innate immunity, contribute to multi-organ injury. This article presents a comprehensive review of a large body of relevant literature. Wnt2, a secreted glycoprotein from the Wnt signaling family, performs distinct immunomodulatory roles. The classic Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway interacts with key regulatory nodes like NF-κB and metabolic reprogramming to regulate macrophage phenotype switching, balance inflammatory cytokine release, and protect organs including the lungs, intestines, heart, and liver during sepsis. This article provides a comprehensive overview of the molecular characteristics of Wnt2, the pathological significance of macrophage polarization in sepsis, the molecular network underlying Wnt2-mediated macrophage polarization and inflammatory regulation, and the prospects for clinical translation. The study establishes an integrative framework linking 'Wnt/β-catenin-macrophage polarization-sepsis,' providing a theoretical basis for the development of targeted immunotherapeutic strategies for sepsis.

42819071.title: Complex venous access in superior vena cava syndrome secondary to gray zone lymphoma, case report.
42819071.abstract: Mediastinal gray zone lymphoma (MGZL) is a rare and biologically complex lymphoma with overlapping features of primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma and classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Bulky mediastinal disease frequently complicates central venous access, particularly in the presence of superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome. Reports addressing optimal vascular access strategies in this setting remain limited. A 41-year-old man presented with newly diagnosed MGZL and a large mediastinal mass causing clinically significant SVC obstruction. The patient required urgent initiation of intensive systemic treatment; however, standard central venous access was contraindicated due to altered thoracic venous anatomy. A tunneled femoral catheter was therefore inserted to allow treatment initiation with rituximab plus dose-adjusted etoposide, doxorubicin, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and prednisone (R-DA-EPOCH). The clinical course was complicated by catheter-related bloodstream infections caused by multidrug-resistant pathogens, septic shock, and pulmonary embolism, necessitating intensive care management. Following partial tumor response and anatomical decompression, duplex ultrasound-guided evaluation enabled successful implantation of a chest port via the left internal jugular vein, during which a duplicated superior vena cava was identified. Subsequent catheter-tip thrombosis was managed with low-molecular-weight heparin. Through coordinated multidisciplinary care, full-intensity R-DA-EPOCH was completed up to dose level 4, resulting in complete metabolic remission. This case highlights the critical importance of individualized venous access strategies in patients with mediastinal lymphoma complicated by SVC syndrome. Imaging-guided vascular assessment, multidisciplinary coordination, and adherence to international and national guidelines can enable safe delivery of curative-intent intensive chemotherapy, even in the setting of severe anatomical distortion and life-threatening complications. The case offers a visually documented, practical framework for managing venous access in complex anatomical conditions associated with superior vena cava syndrome.

42922485.title: The electronic health record as a teaching and learning tool in residency training: A scoping review.
42922485.abstract: While electronic health records (EHRs) are a critical tool for clinical care in academic medical centers, there is a gap in the literature regarding utilization of EHRs for teaching and learning, outside of descriptions on EHR training or use for quality improvement projects. The research question for this scoping review is: How is the EHR purposefully used in educational interventions for teaching and learning in graduate medical education? We searched all publications in PubMed, SCOPUS, CINAHL, ERIC, Cochrane and MedEdPORTAL databases from 2010 to 2022 that met our search criteria and MeSH terms. Using Arksey and O'Malley's framework, the abstracts were reviewed by three team members, and the full text was reviewed by all authors using a standardized data extraction sheet. Of the 2431 records, 19 met inclusion criteria and were reviewed in full. All studies were set in North America, 79% at teaching hospitals, and 42% in Internal Medicine programs. The EHR was used purposefully to improve learning in sepsis, diabetes, asthma, critical care, post- and peri-operative care, and it was used to provide feedback about clinical performance, test utilization, costs of care, and errors. The educational interventions included simulation, direct feedback using EHR data, and workshops with pre-post knowledge and skills testing. This scoping review identifies how the EHR is being used as a teaching and learning tool for trainees. There is a need for more purposeful use of the EHR in designing educational interventions for residents.

42967515.title: Multidrug-Resistant Stenotrophomonas maltophilia Infections in Critically Ill and Immunocompromised Patients: Clinical Characteristics and Therapeutic Outcomes.
42967515.journal: International journal of infectious diseases : IJID : official publication of the International Society for Infectious Diseases
42967515.abstract: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is an emerging multidrug-resistant opportunistic pathogen associated with high morbidity and mortality, particularly among critically ill and immunocompromised patients. Data on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)-resistant isolates remain limited globally and in Saudi Arabia. We conducted a retrospective cohort study at a tertiary care center including adult patients with TMP-SMX-resistant S. maltophilia isolated from blood or respiratory specimens between May 2016 and April 2025. Demographic, microbiological, treatment, and outcome data were analyzed. Among 949 blood or respiratory S. maltophilia isolates screened, 79 TMP-SMX-resistant cases were identified (8.3%). Respiratory specimens accounted for 89.9% of resistant isolates, while blood culture isolates represented 10.1%. True infections accounted for 36 cases (45.6%), while the remaining 43 cases (54.4%) were classified as colonization. TMP-SMX resistance increased from 3.4% of isolates in 2017 to approximately 10% in 2024, with a marked rise after 2020. Patients were predominantly older adults (median age 66 years), with frequent ICU exposure (84.8%) and significant comorbidities. Overall 30-day and 180-day mortality rates were 34.2% and 49.4%, respectively. Minocycline demonstrated the highest susceptibility (75%), whereas levofloxacin susceptibility was limited (33.3%). Combination therapy was associated with numerically higher survival compared with monotherapy at both 30 and 180 days, although these differences were not statistically significant. TMP-SMX-resistant S. maltophilia isolates are increasingly identified during the study periord, particularly among critically ill patients, and are associated with substantial mortality. Combination therapy was associated with numerically higher survival, but differences were not statistically significant. Larger comparative studies are needed to determine whether combination therapy improves clinical outcomes.

42967154.title: Responsible use of new antibiotics for critically ill patients suffering from infections due to carbapenem-resistant organisms-a narrative review for an enablement strategy.
42967154.abstract: Infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative (MDR-GN) bacteria, particularly carbapenem-resistant organisms (CROs), constitute a significant burden in critically ill patients (CIPs). A multidisciplinary, collaborative approach is essential for responsible antibiotic use in CIPs, balancing the necessity for effective treatment with mitigation of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). While the efficacy of existing antibiotics against CROs is increasingly limited due to resistance development and suboptimal pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic properties, several barriers impede the widespread adoption of new agents, including selective susceptibility testing, limited availability, high costs, and concerns regarding the fostering of resistance. Antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) strategies aim to optimize antibiotic use; however, there is an ongoing debate between restrictive and enabling approaches for new antibiotics in CIPs with CRO infections. While restrictive strategies focus on limiting antibiotic use to mitigate resistance, they may delay necessary treatment and negatively impact professional culture. Enablement strategies promote informed decision-making and accessibility when needed but require substantial workforce and expertise. In this narrative review and expert opinion, we propose an algorithm supporting a coordinated AMS approach in CIPs, emphasizing the importance of early diagnosis and appropriate therapy. We advocate for an enablement strategy for new antibiotics in CIPs with MDR-GN infections, aiming to reduce mortality and toxicity associated with older agents. This strategy should be integrated into local AMS programmes under the guidance of experienced clinicians.

42967112.title: Absolute Eosinophil Count as a Corroborative Marker for Sepsis at ICU Admission: An Observational Study.
42967112.abstract: Background Among critically ill patients, sepsis continues to be a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Timely action requires an early diagnosis, but current screening methods have limitations. One commonly available hematological metric that has gained attention as a possible indicator of systemic illness is the absolute eosinophil count (AEC). The usefulness of AEC as a corroborative marker for sepsis diagnosis at intensive care unit (ICU) admission was studied in this study, along with its correlation with scores on the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) and quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA). Methods This observational study included 76 adult patients admitted to the ICU with suspected infection between February 7, 2025, and March 31, 2026. Sepsis was classified according to the Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3) criteria. SOFA and qSOFA scores were calculated, and AEC was assessed at ICU admission. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to derive an optimal AEC cutoff for identifying sepsis. Eosinopenia at the study-derived cutoff was incorporated as one additional point into qSOFA to construct an exploratory modified score, qSOFA-E. Correlations between AEC and SOFA/qSOFA scores were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. Results Among the 76 patients, 38 (50%) fulfilled the Sepsis-3 criteria, 18 (23.7%) developed septic shock, and 7 (9.2%) died during hospitalization. The optimal AEC cutoff for identifying sepsis was ≤152.5 cells/µL, with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.904 (95% CI: 0.828-0.979; p<0.001). At this cutoff, AEC demonstrated 92.11% sensitivity, 84.21% specificity, and 88.16% diagnostic accuracy. AEC showed significant inverse correlations with day-1 SOFA (r=-0.585, p<0.001), day-3 SOFA (r=-0.443, p=0.005), day-1 qSOFA (r=-0.664, p<0.001), and day-3 qSOFA (r=-0.534, p=0.001). In this study cohort, qSOFA-E demonstrated higher sensitivity and diagnostic accuracy than qSOFA alone (92.11% vs. 65.79% sensitivity; 96.05% vs. 82.89% accuracy). Conclusions AEC was associated with the presence of sepsis and with higher SOFA and qSOFA scores in this ICU cohort. Incorporation of study-derived eosinopenia into qSOFA was associated with higher diagnostic sensitivity and accuracy within the study population. These findings support further investigation of AEC as an adjunctive marker and qSOFA-E as a proposed exploratory modification. Larger multicenter studies with independent validation are required before these findings can be generalized to broader clinical practice.

42967146.title: Listeria monocytogenes Sepsis With Meningitis Complicating Biologic Immunosuppression in a Patient With Haemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis Secondary to Adult-Onset Still's Disease: A Case Report.
42967146.abstract: Adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) are treated with potent immunosuppression, including high-dose corticosteroids and biologic agents such as anakinra, which can result in an increased risk of opportunistic infections such as listeriosis (infection with Listeria monocytogenes (L. monocytogenes)). This case report describes a 34-year-old man on a background of AOSD receiving escalated doses of steroids and anakinra for a probable flare-up of HLH. Whilst inpatient, he developed high-grade pyrexia (39.3°C), acute confusion, and neurological deterioration, requiring admission to the ICU for intubation and ventilatory support. Investigations revealed blood cultures positive for L. monocytogenes, and lumbar puncture findings were consistent with acute bacterial meningitis. The patient clinically improved with targeted antimicrobial therapy and was successfully extubated, with subsequent normalisation of his inflammatory markers. He was discharged with a planned taper of his immunosuppressive therapy. This case emphasises the synergistic risk of infection associated with biologic therapy and high-dose corticosteroid use and the importance of maintaining a low threshold for considering listeriosis in immunocompromised patients, particularly in the presence of neurological deterioration.

42967404.title: Impact of early microbiology laboratory activation on rapid diagnosis and antimicrobial optimization in a sepsis alert pathway.
42967404.abstract: Rapid microbiological diagnosis is important in sepsis, but the contribution of early microbiology laboratory activation (EMLA) within sepsis alert pathways is unclear. We prospectively included consecutive adults with sepsis alert activation at a tertiary-care hospital between November 2022 and June 2023. EMLA was defined as direct telephone notification of the on-call microbiologist after sepsis alert activation. The primary outcome was etiological microbiological diagnosis within 24 hours. Secondary outcomes included rapid diagnostic techniques, antimicrobial de-escalation and time to de-escalation. Multivariable logistic regression assessed the association between EMLA and early diagnosis, adjusting for Charlson Comorbidity Index, septic shock, clinical service, and infection focus. Among 327 patients, an etiological diagnosis was established in 209 (63.9%); EMLA was documented in 213 (65.1%). Diagnosis within 24 hours was achieved in 127/213 (59.6%) patients with EMLA versus 40/114 (35.1%) without EMLA (p < 0.001). EMLA remained independently associated with early diagnosis (adjusted OR 2.99, 95% CI 1.80-4.98; p < 0.001). Rapid diagnostic techniques were used more frequently with EMLA (54.5% vs 43.0%, p = 0.045). De-escalation occurred in 171 patients (52.3%) and was performed earlier with EMLA (median 3 [IQR 2-4]. vs 4 [IQR 3-5]. days, p = 0.030). DOT, mortality, ICU admission, and hospital length of stay did not differ significantly. EMLA was independently associated with earlier microbiological diagnosis and antimicrobial de-escalation. These findings suggest that direct clinician-microbiologist communication may therefore be an important organizational component of diagnostic stewardship in sepsis.

42967233.title: Differences in circulating levels of non-classical monocytes and associated caspase 1 activation during Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli bacteremia.
42967233.abstract: Bloodstream infections (BSI) caused by Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus are frequent and are associated with substantial mortality rate. The host immune response major determinant of the clinical outcomes during BSI. Here, we investigated the innate immune response, by characterizing peripheral blood myeloid cell subsets and caspase-1 activation as a surrogate marker of inflammasome activation in patients with E. coli or S. aureus bacteremia. We prospectively enrolled patients with monomicrobial bacteremia and analyzed peripheral blood samples by flow cytometry. We observed distinct alterations in myeloid cell composition and caspase-1 activation associated with E. coli bacteremia, including an expansion in intermediate and non-classical monocytes, and increased caspase-1 activation in non-classical monocytes. In contrast, these changes were not observed in patients with S. aureus bacteremia. Additionally, we found differences in myeloid cell subset frequencies and caspase-1 activation between patients with and without sepsis, revealing distinct profiles associated with disease severity. Importantly, the differences in myeloid cell subsets and caspase-1 activation between E. coli and S. aureus bacteremia were primarily attributable to the infecting bacteria rather than disease severity. Furthermore, our findings suggest that eosinophil counts, and caspase-1 activation may serve as potential markers to distinguish between bacterial BSI and viral infections. Overall, our study highlights the importance of considering both the infecting pathogen and disease severity when studying the host immune response during bacteremia and suggests that potential innate immune biomarkers may improve the diagnosis and clinical management of BSI.

42971738.title: Validation of the SPiRO Score for the Prediction of ICU Admission in Patients Presenting With Leptospirosis in Tropical Australia.
42971738.journal: Tropical medicine & international health : TM & IH
42971738.abstract: In some resource-limited settings the case-fatality rate of severe leptospirosis can exceed 50%. Early recognition of severe disease can expedite transfer to referral centres for advanced supportive care. The entirely clinical, 3-point SPiRO score can be calculated rapidly at presentation to predict a patient's subsequent clinical course. In its derivation study, a SPiRO score of 0 had a negative predictive value (NPV) for intensive care unit (ICU) admission of 98% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 96-99). In this validation cohort we sought to confirm the SPiRO score's prognostic utility and to compare its performance to other leptospirosis-specific and general disease severity scores. We examined consecutive adults presenting to four high-caseload hospitals in tropical Australia with laboratory-confirmed leptospirosis between June 2016 and April 2026. The SPiRO score's ability to predict ICU admission before hospital discharge was compared with that of the leptospirosis-specific QuickLepto score and commonly used disease severity scores, namely the SOFA, qSOFA, qSOFA-lactate, NEWS-2, qNEWS, UVA and the SIRS scores. There were no deaths in 309 episodes of leptospirosis, but in 62 (20%) there was an ICU admission. The SPiRO score performed as well as, or better than, all the other scores in predicting ICU admission. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for the SPiRO score was 0.83 (95% CI: 0.77-0.89); only the SOFA score had a higher value: 0.84 (0.79-0.90), although the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.08). The SPiRO score had the highest NPV for ICU admission of any of the scores: 95 (95% CI: 91-97)%. The SPiRO score can be calculated easily at the bedside at presentation to expedite the recognition of patients with leptospirosis who are most likely to deteriorate. In resource-limited settings this entirely clinical score can also help reduce unnecessary escalation of care, optimising the use of finite health resources.

42971635.title: Randomised controlled trial of SHORT duration antibiotic thERapy for critically ill patients with sepsis (SHORTER trial): protocol for a mixed-methods process evaluation.

42969318.title: Clinico-epidemiological Spectrum of Candidemia in the Intensive Care Unit: A Prospective Observational Study from a Tertiary Care Center of Central India.
42969318.abstract: Candidemia represents the most common healthcare-associated bloodstream infection globally, with significant morbidity and mortality in intensive care units (ICUs). This study aimed to evaluate the clinico-epidemiological characteristics, species distribution, antifungal susceptibility patterns, and mortality predictors of ICU-acquired candidemia from a tertiary care hospital in Central India. The prospective observational study enrolled adult patients (≥18 years) admitted to the ICU with clinical sepsis. ICU-acquired candidemia was defined as a positive blood culture for Candida species developing ≥48 h after ICU admission. Demographic data, risk factors, antibiotic susceptibility, and clinical outcomes were systematically recorded. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 25.0. Among 1128 ICU patients with clinical sepsis admitted during the study period, 55 developed candidemia (55/1128, 4.88%). Nonalbicans Candida (NAC) species predominated (81.8%), with Candida parapsilosis being the most common (30.9%), followed by Candida tropicalis (27.3%), and Candida albicans (18.2%). The major risk factors included Foley catheterization (100%), recent antibiotic exposure (67.3%), diabetes (56.4%), chronic kidney disease (CKD)/dialysis, and central venous catheterization (38.2% each). Significant antifungal resistance was observed in NAC species, particularly Candida auris and Candida guilliermondii, showing complete resistance to fluconazole and voriconazole. Overall mortality was 23.6%, with Candida glabrata showing 100% mortality. Factors significantly associated with mortality on univariate analysis included diabetes (P = 0.003), CKD requiring dialysis (P = 0.001), mechanical ventilation (P < 0.001), and central venous catheterization (P < 0.001). This study demonstrates a significant epidemiological shift toward NAC species in ICU-acquired candidemia, with emerging multidrug-resistant pathogens posing therapeutic challenges. Enhanced infection control measures, routine susceptibility testing, and species-specific treatment strategies are essential for improving patient outcomes.

42968548.title: Use of a molecular syndromic panel for the etiological diagnosis of bloodstream infections in critically ill patients: impact on clinical outcomes and antimicrobial use from a multicenter, prospective study.
42968548.abstract: Bloodstream infections (BSI) frequently occur in critically ill patients and remain associated with high mortality rates. A prospective, observational, multicenter investigation was carried out through the MULTI-SITA platform to evaluate how the addition of a molecular syndromic panel, the BIOFIRE® Blood Culture Identification 2 (BCID2) Panel (BCID2 panel), to conventional blood culture diagnostics influenced key clinical endpoints and antimicrobial use. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality within 30 days following the onset of BSI. Among the 126 included critically ill patients with BSI, multivariable analysis identified SOFA score (hazard ratio [HR] 1.21, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.09-1.34, p < 0.001), other concomitant infections requiring antibiotic therapy (HR 2.61, 95% CI 1.18-5.79, p = 0.018), and BSI caused by Acinetobacter spp. (HR 4.35, 95% CI 1.10-17.18, p = 0.036), Staphylococcus aureus (HR 3.38, 95% CI 1.26-9.08, p = 0.016), or Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (HR 15.97, 95% CI 2.43-104.54, p = 0.004) as associated with increased mortality, while no association was observed between use of the BCID2 panel and mortality (HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.42-2.25, p = 0.941). In secondary analyses, the use of the BCID2 panel resulted in more events of either early antimicrobial de-escalation or initiation of appropriate therapy at day one from BSI onset compared with a standard blood culture workflow (55.6% vs. 31.7%, p = 0.015). In critically ill patients with BSI, implementation of a molecular syndromic panel influenced antimicrobial management decisions without affecting mortality. Additional investigations are warranted to clarify the long-term antimicrobial stewardship implications of treatment strategies guided by molecular syndromic panels-based diagnostic workflows.

42971690.title: Machine learning prediction of 30-day mortality in adults with a positive blood culture.
42971690.journal: Enfermedades infecciosas y microbiologia clinica (English ed.)
42971690.abstract: A positive blood culture is a clinically heterogeneous finding that may represent true bloodstream infection, transient bacteremia or contamination-diagnostic uncertainty that complicates early clinical decision-making. We aimed to develop and evaluate machine learning models to predict 30-day all-cause mortality in adults with a positive blood culture. Retrospective cohort study using MIMIC-IV. Adult hospitalizations with at least one positive blood culture were included (first positive culture per admission); potential contaminants were retained to reflect real-world uncertainty. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, organ support and microbiological variables were used as predictors. Nine supervised machine learning algorithms were trained with repeated 10-fold cross-validation, evaluated in an independent test cohort and calibrated; thresholds were optimized with the Youden index. Of 5731 episodes, 742 patients (12.9%) died within 30 days. Test-set ROC AUC ranged from 0.759 to 0.801. After threshold optimization, the random forest model showed the best overall performance (sensitivity 0.788, specificity 0.707, balanced accuracy 0.748; Brier score 0.0999, calibration slope 1.03). ICU admission at onset, mechanical ventilation, bilirubin, urea and the Charlson comorbidity index were the main predictors. Machine learning models can provide clinically meaningful early prediction of 30-day mortality in patients with a positive blood culture using routinely available data. Focusing on the moment of blood culture positivity rather than established sepsis syndromes, this approach supports early risk stratification in a diagnostically heterogeneous population.

42970120.title: Severe ARDS and secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis complicating a flare of adult-onset Still's disease: a case-based review.
42970120.abstract: Adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) is a rare systemic inflammatory disorder in which parenchymal lung disease is an increasingly recognised complication, and macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) - that is, haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) secondary to an autoinflammatory or autoimmune condition (MAS-HLH) is a well-established one. Both carry disproportionately high morbidity and mortality. Although AOSD-associated lung disease and MAS-HLH are increasingly recognised as co-occurring manifestations of the same hyperinflammatory process, their combination, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) as the most severe form of lung involvement, remain under-reported. We report a 42-year-old woman with a background of AOSD who developed severe ARDS in the context of a five-week interruption of conventional synthetic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (csDMARDs) around incision and drainage of a perianal abscess with complicating fistulous disease and a flare during that period. She developed severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure requiring intubation on the day of admission and later prone positioning, subsequently complicated by development of MAS-HLH, evidenced by hyperferritinaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia, fever and bone marrow-confirmed haemophagocytosis. Her disease trajectory was further complicated by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation. Management required sequential multi-target immunomodulation with corticosteroids, anakinra, ruxolitinib, tocilizumab and rituximab. She was mechanically ventilated for 19 days in intensive care and discharged from ICU on day 34 and from hospital following clinical stabilisation on day 73. This case illustrates that AOSD-related pulmonary disease can present as fulminant ARDS rather than the more indolent infiltrative patterns typically described and may be associated with other manifestations of AOSD including MAS-HLH. Because of concomitant infection and viral reactivation, the illness could not be attributed to AOSD alone. The case also describes survival following early multidisciplinary, multi-target immunomodulation delivered alongside antimicrobial cover, although the overlapping use of several agents precludes any conclusion about their individual or combined efficacy.

42969594.title: Seven versus 14 days of polymyxin-based therapy for ventilator-associated pneumonia due to carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii : A randomised feasibility trial.
42969594.journal: Lung India : official organ of Indian Chest Society
42969594.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) due to carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii ( CRAB ) is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality in intensive care units (ICUs), yet the optimal antibiotic duration of therapy remains uncertain. We compared outcomes of 7-day versus 14-day polymyxin-based therapy for CRAB-VAP. We conducted a single-centre, open-label, randomised feasibility trial in a tertiary-care respiratory ICU from March 2017 to October 2024. Patients with microbiologically confirmed CRAB-VAP who met predefined clinical stability criteria on day 7 were randomised 1:1 to either discontinue antibiotics on day 7 or continue treatment for 14 days. Treatment comprised intravenous colistin or polymyxin B with adjunctive nebulised colistin. The primary outcome was relapse of CRAB-VAP. Secondary outcomes included antibiotic-free days through day 28, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU and hospital length of stay, and 28-day all-cause mortality. We randomised 41 patients (7-day n = 22; 14-day n = 19). Relapse occurred in 1 (4.5%) versus 2 (10.5%) patients (risk ratio [RR] 0.43; 95% CI: 0.04, 4.31) in the 7-day versus 14-day groups, respectively. The 7-day group had more antibiotic-free days (mean difference: 6.9 days; 95% CI: 5.1, 8.7 days). Acute kidney injury occurred in 0% versus 31.6% (RR 0.07; 95% CI: 0.004, 1.15). Other outcomes, including 28-day mortality (45.5 vs 63.2%; RR 0.72; 95% CI: 0.40, 1.30), were similar. In clinically improving CRAB-VAP, a 7-day discontinuation strategy was feasible. Clinical outcome estimates, including relapse and mortality, were imprecise and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating. These findings support evaluation in larger, adequately powered multicentre trials.

42970339.title: Cefepime Dose Individualization in Early Sepsis: A Pragmatic Feasibility Trial Protocol.
authors: Beta-Lactam Optimization and Outcomes Management (BLOOM) Study Group
42970339.abstract: Cefepime is a core antibiotic in sepsis treatment, yet standard dosing yields 10- to 30-fold exposure variability in critical illness. In the early "golden hours" of sepsis, low cefepime levels (affecting up to 70% of cases) may lead to organ dysfunction progression, treatment failure, and antimicrobial resistance. Empiric dose escalation to overcome low levels can increase the risk of dose-dependent neurotoxicity. We developed and qualified a population pharmacokinetic model using patient weight and estimated glomerular filtration rate from creatinine and cystatin C that, in simulation, improved attainment of effective and safe drug levels. To describe the Beta-Lactam Optimization and Outcomes Management (BLOOM) 1 pragmatic feasibility trial. This single-center, cluster-randomized, pragmatic feasibility trial (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT07287332) was approved with a waiver of informed consent. Participants are critically ill adults (age ≥ 18 yr), hospitalized at Mayo Clinic (Rochester, MN), who are receiving cefepime for suspected or documented sepsis. A screening tool embedded in the electronic health record (EHR) identifies eligible patients newly initiated on cefepime (≤ 1 previous dose in 48 hr) who are then randomized to care groups (clusters) that use an individualized dosing algorithm (intervention) or usual-care dosing (control). Exclusions are cephalosporin allergy, acute kidney injury, kidney replacement therapy, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and missing inputs required for the algorithm (weight, creatinine, cystatin C). Recruitment began on January 15, 2026, and is expected to conclude by January 2027 (target enrollment, ≥ 300 patients). For eligible patients, EHR-embedded clinical decision support prompts the cluster-assigned dosing approach, with final dose decisions made by the clinical team. Feasibility, fidelity, and exploratory pharmacokinetic and clinical outcomes will be assessed using mixed methods. This workflow-integrated pragmatic feasibility trial will determine whether personalized cefepime dosing can be implemented in routine practice to optimize timely sepsis therapy while maintaining safety.

42971544.title: Characteristics, Implementation and Effects of Nurse-Driven Sepsis Protocols in Hospital Settings: A Systematic Review.
42971544.abstract: To synthesize evidence on the characteristics, implementation and effects of nurse-driven sepsis protocols on process-of-care indicators and clinical outcomes. Systematic review without meta-analysis. Studies were included if they described and evaluated nurse-driven sepsis protocols in hospitals. Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts and full texts for eligibility. The Johns Hopkins Nursing Evidence-Based Practice model was used to appraise included studies. Data were extracted and narratively synthesized. Eight databases were searched from database inception to 30 June 2025. Fifteen studies were included, most using before-and-after designs and conducted in the emergency departments (n = 7) and hospital-wide settings (n = 4). Protocols commonly used systemic inflammatory response syndrome criteria for screening (n = 12) and incorporated key Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommendations (n = 14). Most studies reported improved or comparable outcomes to baseline in overall sepsis bundle compliance and key process-of-care indicators, including timely antibiotic administration, blood culture collection, lactate measurement and fluid administration. All 11 studies evaluating mortality reported reductions, although only four were statistically significant. Findings for hospital length of stay were inconsistent. Common implementation strategies included nurse education and training, coupled with audit and feedback. Nurse-driven sepsis protocols may improve adherence to and timeliness of key sepsis care processes. Effects on clinical outcomes are less certain, given the predominance of before-and-after designs and inconsistent findings for hospital length of stay. The review identifies implementation strategies that can guide future sepsis quality improvement initiatives. Nurse-driven protocols may support nurses in initiating timely sepsis care and strengthening adherence to recommended care processes. Further high-quality studies are needed to establish effects on clinical outcomes and broader impacts, including healthcare costs, intensive care resource utilization, patient and nurse satisfaction, and safety outcomes. No patient or public contribution.

42971250.title: Trajectories of Coagulation-Fibrinolysis Balance Reveal Hemostatic Heterogeneity in Sepsis: Derivation and Multicenter Validation.
42971250.abstract: The imbalance between coagulation activation and fibrinolysis drives sepsis-induced coagulopathy and organ dysfunction. However, this dynamic process is highly heterogeneous. We aimed to identify longitudinal coagulation-fibrinolysis trajectory phenotypes and to develop a novel prothrombin time (PT)-D-dimer Z-balance score to quantify this evolving hemostatic imbalance. This study included a single-center training cohort (n=1672) and a prospective multicenter external validation cohort (n=1393) of adult septic ICU patients. Joint group-based trajectory modeling (GBTM) was applied to daily PT and D-dimer measurements over the first 7 days. Hemostatic, inflammatory and prognostic profiles were compared across phenotypes. Additionally, a daily Z-balance score [Z(PT) - Z(D-dimer)] was constructed to quantify the evolving hemostatic imbalance. Joint modeling reveals three phenotypes: Compensate (Class 1, 51.9%; preserved balance), Coupled (Class 2, 35.5%; intensive but balanced coagulation-fibrinolysis activation), and Consumptive (Class 3, 12.6%; profound coagulation factor consumption with blunted fibrinolysis). The Consumptive phenotype exhibited the most severe systemic inflammation, organ failure, and the highest 28-day mortality (52.1%). Multivariable analysis confirmed Class 3 as an independent predictor of 28-day mortality in both the training (adjusted HR 2.69) and validation cohorts (adjusted HR 3.78). The novel Z-balance score revealed distinct dynamic patterns: Class 3 was characterized by persistently positive yet declining Z-balance (a delayed, partial fibrinolytic response relative to coagulation). Joint longitudinal modeling of PT and D-dimer reveals three distinct coagulation‑fibrinolysis phenotypes in sepsis. The Consumptive phenotype, characterized by profound coagulation and inflammation activation alongside a positive PT-D-dimer Z-balance, identifies a high-risk subpopulation with markedly increased mortality.

42971065.title: Surgeons' Immediate Postoperative Prediction After Major Emergency Abdominal Surgery.
42971065.abstract: Major emergency abdominal surgery carries high morbidity and mortality, making accurate risk stratification important. Whether surgeons' immediate postoperative clinical judgment predicts outcomes and how it compares with established surgical risk models remains poorly characterized. Prospective single-center cohort of 411 patients undergoing major emergency abdominal surgery (February 2024-June 2025). Immediately after surgery, the operating surgeon estimated 30-d mortality (ordinal 10% intervals) and the risk of complications (0-10 scale). Discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC]) and calibration (observed-to-expected ratio, calibration slope and intercept, Brier score) were assessed. Mortality discrimination was compared with National Emergency Laparotomy Audit and Portsmouth Physiological and Operative Severity Score for the enUmeration of Mortality and Morbidity using the DeLong test. Thirty-day mortality was 11% (47/411). Surgeon-estimated risk showed good discrimination for mortality (AUC: 0.89; 95% confidence interval: 0.85-0.94), comparable to National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (0.90) and Portsmouth Physiological and Operative Severity Score for the enUmeration of Mortality and Morbidity (0.86; P = 0.83 and P = 0.30). Surgeons systematically overestimated absolute mortality (mean predicted: 23% versus observed: 11%; observed-to-expected: 0.48; intercept: -1.17; slope: 1.20). For complications, discrimination was good for sepsis/multi-organ failure (AUC 0.81) and acceptable for intensive care unit admission (0.78) and cardiac complications (0.78), but poor for reoperation (0.62) and mechanical bowel obstruction (0.62), and absent for prolonged paralytic bowel dysfunction (0.51). Higher estimated risk was associated with increased odds of complications. Predicted discharge destination agreed moderately with observed (accuracy 74%; weighted κ 0.61). Surgeons' immediate postoperative assessment showed discriminatory performance of a similar magnitude to established models but systematically overestimated absolute risk and performed better for systemic than procedure-specific complications. This bedside estimate may aid early risk stratification but requires external validation before clinical use.

42970821.title: A Retrospective Audit of Maternal Bacteraemia in a Tertiary Referral Maternity Hospital in Brisbane, Australia From 2015 to 2024.
42970821.journal: The Australian & New Zealand journal of obstetrics & gynaecology
42970821.abstract: Maternal infection is a major cause of pregnancy-related maternal morbidity and mortality in Australia. To determine the prevalence, microbiology, probable source, clinical characteristics, laboratory results, time to antibiotic therapy, reasons for intensive care admission, and maternal morbidity and mortality of maternal bacteraemia at a tertiary referral maternity hospital in Brisbane, Australia, over a ten-year period. A retrospective review of pregnant patients with positive blood cultures between January 2015 and December 2024 at a tertiary level obstetric hospital in Brisbane, Australia, was performed. There were 59 patients with pathogenic organisms grown on blood cultures (0.96 per 1000 deliveries) and 29 patients with presumed contaminants. Physical signs and laboratory investigations were not useful in differentiating between patients whose blood cultures grew pathogenic bacteraemia, those which grew presumed contaminants, and those whose blood cultures were negative. The predominant bacterial species were Streptococcus species and Escherichia coli (E. coli). Despite 57 of the 59 patients with pathogenic bacteraemia receiving antibiotics and fluid resuscitation within 60 min of presentation, 10 patients were admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU), principally because of hypotension developing 6-24 h after initial treatment. Seven of the 10 ICU admissions were due to E. coli bacteraemia, four secondary to urosepsis, and three secondary to chorioamnionitis. There were no maternal deaths. A continuing policy of early identification of possible maternal infection, and prompt antibiotic therapy and resuscitation are indicated. Despite expeditious management, a significant proportion of patients deteriorated and required admission to an intensive care unit, emphasising the importance of close observation following initial antibiotic therapy, particularly in patients with suspected urosepsis and/or E. coli bacteraemia.

42970569.title: Machine learning for predicting mortality in patients with sepsis and its associated complications: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
