The included studies were published between 2011 and 2025 and involved heterogeneous clinical settings, including intensive care, emergency department, postoperative, sepsis, COVID-19, and liver transplantation populations. The estimated sensitivity of uKIM-1 was 0.67 (95% CrI, 0.59-0.75), and the specificity was 0.73 (95% CrI, 0.61-0.84). The pooled DOR was 5.91 (95% CrI, 2.91-11.20), and the AUC was 0.75 (95% CrI, 0.62-0.84). Sensitivity analyses using alternative cutoff selections and prior specifications showed generally stable estimates. This Bayesian meta-analysis indicates that uKIM-1 has moderate diagnostic value for persistent severe AKI in adults. Current evidence does not support its use as a standalone biomarker, and future studies should evaluate its incremental value in combination with other biomarkers and clinical variables.

42983629.title: Fatal methanol poisoning with paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity, and putaminal hemorrhage: a case report and brief literature review.
42983629.abstract: Methanol poisoning is a widespread issue worldwide. In this case report, we describe a patient with methanol poisoning who experienced tonic spasms, cerebellar and putaminal hemorrhages, and severe neurological complications. Additionally, this report emphasizes the potential link between methanol poisoning and paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity (PSH). A 31-year-old male was referred to the emergency department with blurred vision, epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, restlessness, and severe respiratory distress. Two days ago, he drank a locally prepared alcoholic beverage while having dinner. The initial laboratory data showed metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) with a GCS of 4/15. General supportive treatment (normal saline, DVT prophylaxis, stress ulcer prophylaxis, etc.), sodium bicarbonate, ethanol, dialysis, methylprednisolone, and folic acid were initiated for poisoning management. In the brain CT scan, cerebellar and putamen hemorrhage, and brain edema were reported. We stopped heparin due to the brain hemorrhage, but after a few days, DVT occurred. During hospitalization, the patient experienced several brief and spontaneous tonic spasms with diaphoresis, tachycardia, and tachypnea, so paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity (PSH) was suspected. He was treated with midazolam and metoprolol for PSH treatment. Unfortunately, the patient developed sepsis and died after 53 days of stay in the ICU. This study highlights that exposure to methanol can result in a range of neurological complications. The administration of heparin in cases of methanol poisoning remains controversial and requires careful evaluation. Furthermore, paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity is an uncommon complication that can result from cerebral injury attributed to methanol poisoning.

42983577.title: Physiological determinants of piperacillin and cefazolin clearance in septic and trauma patients.
42983577.abstract: Physiological alterations in patients with sepsis and trauma can influence antibiotic clearance, yet reliable predictors remain poorly defined. We aimed to investigate the determinants of piperacillin and cefazolin clearance in these populations to identify bedside indicators of subtherapeutic exposure. Prospective physiological and pharmacokinetic study in patients receiving piperacillin/tazobactam for sepsis or prophylactic cefazolin post-trauma. Patients also received intravenous sinistrin. Intensive pharmacokinetic sampling, cardiac output (CO) monitoring and four urinary creatinine clearance (uCLCR) measurements were performed. Data were analysed with non-compartmental pharmacokinetic methods, and linear and logistic regression. We enrolled 49 septic and 28 trauma patients. Trauma patients were younger (33.5 vs. 46.5 years) and had higher uCLCR (155.5 vs. 107.5 mL/min). Linear regression identified that lower Sequential Organ Failure Assessment scores and an hyperdynamic state with higher CO and 2 and 8-h uCLCR were the strongest predictors of increased piperacillin total clearance; higher 2-h uCLCR and hypoalbuminemia were the main predictors for cefazolin total clearance. Sinistrin CL was a weak predictor. Logistic regression identified augmented renal clearance (8-h uCLCR > 130 mL/min) as the main risk factor for piperacillin subtherapeutic exposure (OR 10.9, p < 0.05), also when defined using the Cockcroft-Gault cut-off of 114.5 mL/min from ROC analysis. In sepsis, low sickness severity and a hyperdynamic state with high cardiac output lead to increased uCLCR and high piperacillin clearance. In trauma, high cefazolin clearance occurs in the presence of an elevated uCLCR and hypoalbuminemia. These bedside physiological indicators, along with Cockcroft-Gault CLCR, may serve as early indicators of risk for subtherapeutic exposure.

42981773.title: Immune function in burn patients: Pathophysiology, monitoring, and emerging therapeutic strategies.
42981773.journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
42981773.abstract: Severe burn injury causes extensive local tissue damage and systemic immune alterations that affect infection risk, wound healing, organ function, and survival. The immune response is characterized by rapid activation of innate immune cells, including neutrophils and monocytes, with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL‑6, TNF‑α, IL‑1β) and complement activity. Simultaneously, adaptive immunity is often impaired, with reduced T and B lymphocyte function, while diminished dendritic cell activity may further compromise antigen presentation and adaptive immune responses. This combined hyperinflammatory and immunosuppressive state, known as burn-induced immune dysfunction, contributes to delayed wound healing, increased susceptibility to secondary infections, sepsis, and multiple organ dysfunction. Monitoring immune function is essential but challenging. Routine markers, including white blood cell count (WBC) and C-reactive protein (CRP), provide limited insight, whereas procalcitonin (PCT), pancreatic stone protein (PSP), and cytokine panels (IL‑6, IL‑8, IL‑10) improve early detection of infection and immune classification. Flow cytometry allows characterization of immune cell populations and functional markers such as monocyte HLA‑DR and T cell PD‑1, while functional assays assess neutrophil, monocyte, and lymphocyte responsiveness. High-resolution molecular approaches, including transcriptomics, proteomics, and single-cell profiling, reveal persistent alterations not captured by conventional assays. Therapeutic strategies to restore immune balance include targeted cytokine modulation, immune checkpoint inhibition, hemoadsorption, metabolic and nutritional interventions, and novel approaches such as nanotechnology or microbiome modulation. Early surgical excision and topical treatments, including cerium-nitrate with silver sulfadiazine, may also attenuate systemic inflammation. However, robust clinical evaluation of these interventions is limited, and their timing, dosing, and patient selection remain under investigation. This review integrates mechanistic, translational, and clinical evidence to provide a framework for understanding burn-induced immune dysfunction. Future research should aim for standardized immune phenotyping, longitudinal multi-omics integration, AI-assisted monitoring, and evaluation of mechanism-based immunomodulatory strategies to improve patient outcomes.

42985811.title: Antimicrobial-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the USA: implications of a national surveillance gap.
42985811.abstract: Surveillance data for Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the USA are distributed across systems designed for different purposes, potentially limiting standardized national surveillance of high-priority resistant phenotypes. We evaluated whether the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS) can support surveillance of multidrug-resistant (MDR) P. aeruginosa and synthesized available CDC surveillance data to characterize the residual surveillance gap. We reviewed the 2026 NNDSS list of nationally notifiable conditions for P. aeruginosa. Because neither P. aeruginosa infection nor a resistant phenotype was present, NNDSS case counts were unable to be analysed. We therefore conducted a descriptive secondary analysis of CDC National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) reports for 2018-21 and the 2022 NHSN Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Option report. In 2018-21 adult NHSN data, 11.9% of tested P. aeruginosa isolates from device-associated infections were MDR, compared with 3.9% from surgical-site infections. Among central-line-associated bloodstream infection isolates, MDR proportions were highest in long-term acute-care hospitals (LTACHs, 25.3%), followed by hospital intensive-care units (14.2%), hospital wards (11.9%) and oncology units (8.5%). Among catheter-associated urinary tract infection isolates, MDR phenotype was observed in 20.8% of LTACH isolates. In the 2022 AR Option report, carbapenem non-susceptibility exceeded 10% among community-onset isolates and approached 20% among hospital-onset isolates. NNDSS cannot currently quantify the burden of MDR P. aeruginosa, but substantial resistance surveillance is available through NHSN and the CDC AR Laboratory Network. The principal gap is not an absence of surveillance data but fragmentation across systems with different populations, denominators, objectives and reporting mechanisms.

42984560.title: Clinical and microbiological characteristics of abscesses in patients with malignancy and factors associated with 90-day mortality.
42984560.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
42984560.abstract: Cancer-specific evidence on the outcomes and microbiology of abscesses is limited. We aimed to characterize these infections and evaluate factors associated with 90-day all-cause mortality. We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of adults with histologically confirmed malignancy and a first imaging-confirmed abscess; culture positivity was not required. All isolates came from percutaneous aspirates, were tested by an automated system, and were classified for extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) production and multidrug resistance; culture reports were adjudicated for contamination by two clinicians. Survival was measured from the index date (aspiration in 177 and first documentation in seven), with first imaging and admission as alternative origins, and follow-up extended to 1 year. Among 184 patients (median age, 62 years; 58.2% men; 53.8% stage IV), an organism was recorded in 124 (67.4%) and a probable pathogen in 108 (58.7%), of which 85 (78.7%) were gram-negative, mainly Escherichia coli (43) and Klebsiella pneumoniae (27). Phenotypic ESBL was recorded in 38 of 80 (47.5%) Enterobacterales isolates, 69 of 85 (81.2%) gram-negative isolates were multidrug- or extensively drug-resistant, and resistance to third-generation cephalosporins exceeded 80%, to piperacillin-tazobactam 65.7%, and to ertapenem 37.3%. A total of 42 patients died within 90 days; the 90-day survival was 76.6% (95% CI 69.7%-82.2%) from the index date and 77.7% from first imaging, both among patients who survived to the index date. In a Cox model stratified by abscess multiplicity and adjusted for age and stage, higher albumin at the index date was associated with a lower 90-day mortality (HR 0.37 per 0.5 g/dL, 95% CI 0.26-0.53; model-based risk 39.4% at 2.5 g/dL versus 6.8% at 3.5 g/dL). The association persisted after adjustment for intensive-care admission, organ support, corticosteroids, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin but weakened after day 90 (HR 0.48 per 1 g/dL), whereas stage IV disease, unrelated to 90-day mortality, was associated with mortality thereafter (HR 2.65, 95% CI 1.45-4.84). Ninety-day mortality was substantial, gram-negative organisms predominated, and resistance to these agents was frequent. Low albumin at the index date is a marker of early mortality that most likely reflects acute illness severity as well as nutritional and tumor-related factors, whereas cancer stage is associated with later mortality.

42984548.title: Genomic surveillance uncovers high-risk resistance profiles in Escherichia coli and Klebsiella spp. from Central Mexico.
42984548.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
42984548.abstract: To generate actionable genomic evidence for antimicrobial-resistance (AMR) surveillance in Central Mexico by characterizing the diversity, resistome, and mobilome of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and K. michiganensis belonging to the K. oxytoca complex (KoxSC) circulating between 2021 and 2023, and by contextualizing these findings within national genomic data. We sequenced 65 MDR/XDR isolates referred to the State Public Health Laboratory of Aguascalientes (LESPA) and compared them with 268 publicly available Mexican genomes. Phenotypic susceptibility profiles (BD Phoenix M50) were integrated with genomic predictions to assess concordance. Phylogenomics, pangenomics, resistome and mobilome profiling, and virulence analyses were performed using standardized pipelines. Because LESPA receives referral cases from severe or treatment-refractory infections, this dataset represents a high-risk clinical subset rather than a population-level sample. The sequenced isolates displayed substantial lineage diversity (34 sequence types across E. coli and Klebsiella spp.) and more than 100 distinct antimicrobial-resistance gene combinations. Several determinants not previously reported in Mexican resistant microorganisms-such as TEM-116, aadA22, ermB, and uhpA-were identified. Carbapenemase NDM-1 and colistin-associated MCR-9.1 were widespread, and resistance genes frequently co-localized with mobile genetic elements, suggesting active horizontal gene-transfer dynamics. Post-2020 isolates exhibited increased resistome richness, higher XDR rates, and more frequent coinfections, particularly in critical-care settings. The K. michiganensis isolates represent the first MDR genomes of this species from Aguascalientes and contribute to the expanding genomic characterization of this underrepresented member of the K. michiganensis (KoxSC) in Mexico. This study provides the first genomic baseline for MDR E. coli and Klebsiella spp. in Central Mexico and documents an increasingly complex resistome likely shaped by clinical practices, referral patterns, and structural limitations in microbiological capacity. Embedding real-time whole-genome sequencing into routine diagnostics and public-health workflows is essential to strengthen stewardship, guide infection control, and support equitable AMR surveillance across Mexico.

42987192.title: Long-Term Mortality in Sepsis Survivors: A Population-Based Study During 15 Years.
42987192.abstract: To evaluate long-term mortality among sepsis survivors in Catalonia over a 15-year period and to identify factors associated with increased mortality within 2 years after hospital discharge. Retrospective population-based cohort study. Acute-care hospitals in Catalonia, Spain. Adult and pediatric patients hospitalized with sepsis between 2005 and 2019 identified using the International Classification of Diseases, 9th Revision, Clinical Modification and International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification codes for infection and acute organ dysfunction. Patients who died during hospitalization, were transferred to another facility, or represented readmission episodes were excluded. None. Data were obtained from the Catalan Minimum Basic Dataset of Acute-Care Hospitals, with longitudinal follow-up through the Central Registry of Insured Persons. Comorbidities were assessed using the Charlson comorbidity index. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models were used to identify predictors of long-term mortality. Among 296,554 hospital admissions for sepsis, 237,075 patients (79.9%) survived to hospital discharge. Of these, 42% died (99,571) within 2 years. Long-term mortality increased significantly with age, ranging from 5.8% in patients younger than 15 years to 62% in those older than 84 years (p < 0.0001), and with comorbidity burden (21%, 38%, 51%, and 67% for Charlson index 0, 1-2, 3-4, and ≥ 5, respectively; p < 0.0001). Neoplasia (hazard ratio [HR], 2.011), liver cirrhosis (HR, 1.562), and dementia (HR, 1.304) were the comorbidities most strongly associated with mortality. Longer hospital stays were also associated with increased mortality. A progressive decline in long-term mortality was observed during 2017-2019. Long-term mortality among sepsis survivors remains high, with more than 40% dying within 2 years after hospital discharge. These findings support the need for structured post-sepsis care strategies focused on high-risk patients, improved continuity of care, and prevention of long-term sepsis-related complications.

42986437.title: Vasopressors as immunomodulators: a hidden axis in septic shock.

42981694.title: Impact of the updated SOFA-2 score on organ dysfunction assessment and trial outcomes in Sepsis: A reanalysis of two randomized trials.
42981694.abstract: The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score is the standard tool for quantifying organ dysfunction in sepsis. The updated SOFA-2 score may alter interpretation of prior trials. We reanalyzed two adult sepsis randomized trials, Ascorbic Acid, Corticosteroids, and Thiamine in Sepsis (ACTS) and Thiamine for Renal Protection in Septic Shock (TRPSS), to evaluate the impact of SOFA-2 on organ-specific scoring and trial interpretation. Patient data were rescored using a best available SOFA-2 reconstruction. Subscores were compared between SOFA-1 and SOFA-2 at baseline, 24, 48, and 72 h using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Gwet's AC2. Trial outcomes were reanalyzed using linear mixed-effects models with SOFA-2. A post hoc, exploratory sensitivity analysis incorporated approximated urine output into the renal subscore. SOFA-2 produced lower total scores than SOFA-1 in both cohorts (ACTS 9 vs. 7; TRPSS 11 vs. 10; both p < 0.001), with lower respiratory and cardiovascular and higher coagulation subscores. For the ACTS primary outcome, SOFA-2 (mean difference [MD] -0.8, 95% CI -1.6 to 0.0, p = 0.06) was similar to SOFA-1 (MD -0.8, 95% CI -1.7 to 0.2, p = 0.12) but became significant in the post hoc, exploratory urine-output analysis (MD -0.84, 95% CI -1.64 to -0.05, p = 0.04). In TRPSS, SOFA-2 did not change overall interpretation but attenuated the treatment effect at all timepoints. SOFA-2 changes how organ dysfunction is defined and may influence interpretation of prior trials, particularly when urine output is included. These findings support SOFA-version transparency and prospective SOFA-2 validation. ACTS: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03389555), registered December 28, 2017; TRPSS: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03550794), registered May 25, 2018.

42980977.title: Looking Beyond a Normal Cerebrospinal Fluid Profile: Lessons Learned About Sepsis-Associated Encephalopathy in Meningococcal Septic Shock.

42980939.title: Treating sepsis by targeting neutrophil extracellular traps: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42980939.abstract: Sepsis, a leading cause of death worldwide, is characterized by dysregulated host immune responses and multi-organ dysfunction. Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are extracellular fibers from activated neutrophils that contribute to the immune response. However, excessive NETs formation during sepsis may exacerbate inflammation, thrombosis, and tissue injury, potentially affecting sepsis prognosis. We examined whether NETs-modulating interventions are beneficial in experimental sepsis models. Following PRISMA guidelines, this review analyzed studies from PubMed and Scopus that reported NETs-targeting therapies and included outcome measures. A meta-analysis of random-effects models using a restricted maximum likelihood estimation was performed with a priori moderators including NETs quantification tier, intervention timing relative to insult, and intervention class. In 33 included studies, the therapies significantly reduced NETs levels, while three studies increased NETs following treatment. The a priori moderators, NETs tier and treatment timing, were not significant, whereas intervention class significantly modified treatment effects. The treated groups had a lower risk of death and reduced IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-ɑ levels when compared to the control group. The treatments reduced tissue injury with considerable heterogeneity (I2=68.4%) and should be cautiously interpreted due to small study numbers. NETs modulation was significantly associated with a decrease in cytokine concentration and tissue injury. The heterogeneity of protocols, diverse outcome measures, publication bias, and overall poor reporting quality of the studies warranted conservative effect estimates and cautious interpretation of findings. Our meta-analysis suggests NETs modulation is associated with reduced mortality risk, attenuated organ injury, and decreased inflammation, based primarily on LPS endotoxemia rodent models. Notably, experimental protocols and model limitations impede the translatability of these therapies for clinical care at this stage of research. In accordance with the guidelines, our systematic review protocol is registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) registration number CRD420251124339 and was published with INPLASY on 20 August 2025.

42994883.title: Association between early central venous pressure monitoring and 30-day mortality in critically ill patients with comorbid heart failure and sepsis: A retrospective cohort study.
42994883.abstract: Central venous pressure (CVP) is widely used in the intensive care unit (ICU), but the optimal timing to initiate CVP monitoring remains unclear for patients with comorbid heart failure and sepsis. We explored the association between time to initial CVP measurement and 30-day mortality in this high-risk population. This retrospective cohort study included 9246 critically ill patients with comorbid heart failure and sepsis from the MIMIC-IV database. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis examined the relationship between time to initial CVP measurement and 30-day mortality. Inverse probability of treatment weighting followed by weighted logistic regression was used to assess the association between early CVP monitoring (≤6 hours after ICU admission) and 30-day mortality. A nonlinear J-shaped association emerged, with the lowest risk at 2.89 hours post-admission. Early CVP monitoring was associated with lower 30-day mortality (OR = 0.816, 95% CI: 0.688-0.967, P = .019). A landmark sensitivity analysis comparing no monitoring, early (≤6 hours), intermediate (6-86 hours), and late (>86 hours) monitoring showed a time-dependent relationship: intermediate (OR = 1.396, 95% CI: 1.194-1.632, P < .001) and late monitoring (OR = 3.141, 95% CI: 2.263-4.359, P < .001) were associated with progressively higher mortality. In critically ill patients with comorbid heart failure and sepsis, early CVP monitoring within 6 hours of ICU admission was associated with lower 30-day mortality, while delayed monitoring carried an elevated risk. Early integration of CVP within a multimodal hemodynamic assessment framework may be a prudent approach in this high-risk population.

42994879.title: Association between inpatient aspirin exposure and 28-day mortality in critically ill patients with sepsis-induced coagulopathy: A cohort study.
42994879.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the association between inpatient aspirin exposure and 28-day mortality in critically ill patients with sepsis-induced coagulopathy (SIC). We conducted a retrospective cohort study extracting data from the MIMIC-IV v3.1 database (2008-2022). Adult critically ill patients with SIC in the intensive care unit (ICU) were included. The primary outcome was 28-day mortality. Secondary outcomes encompassed mortality (e.g., in-hospital, ICU, 60-day, 90-day, and 1-year) and duration of ICU-free, ventilation-free, or vasopressor-free days within 28 days of admission to the ICU. Multivariable Cox regression, propensity score matching (PSM), inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), overlap weighting (OW), pairwise algorithmic weighting (PA), and doubly robust estimation were employed to control confounders. Robustness of findings was assessed through subgroup and sensitivity analyses. Among 9095 critically ill patients with SIC, 3207 (35.3%) received aspirin during ICU hospitalization. After 1:1 propensity score matching (2069 pairs), inpatient aspirin exposure was independently associated with significantly lower 28-day mortality (hazard ratio [HR] 0.74; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.65-0.85; P < .001). This association remained consistent across multiple analytical methods including IPTW (HR 0.76; 95% CI: 0.70-0.84; P < .001), OW (HR 0.72; 95% CI: 0.61-0.84; P < .001), PA (HR 0.73; 95% CI: 0.61-0.84; P < .001), and doubly robust estimation (HR 0.76; 95% CI: 0.61-0.94; P < .001). Inpatient aspirin exposure was also associated with more favorable secondary clinical outcomes (all P < .001). In critically ill patients with SIC, inpatient aspirin exposure was independently associated with lower 28-day mortality and more favorable clinical outcomes. These findings should be interpreted as an association rather than evidence of a causal therapeutic effect. Prospective randomized studies are warranted to validate these findings.

42991237.title: Association between short-term fine particulate matter exposure and hospital-acquired pneumonia risk in critically ill post-cardiac surgery patients: a 10-year cohort study using distributed lag non-linear models.
42991237.abstract: Ambient air pollution (AAP) exposure is a substantial health threat to humans globally. However, whether AAP could promote hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) onset in critically ill patients, a vulnerable population undergoing cardiac surgery in the intensive care unit (ICU), remains elusive. This study evaluated the correlation of HAP onset with fine particulate matter (PM2.5). In total, this study included 6,196 patients who underwent cardiovascular surgery at the ICU of a major hospital in Shandong province, China, over 10 years, from January 1, 2014, to December 31, 2023. The daily mean levels of sulfur dioxide (SO2), PM2.5, carbon monoxide (CO), PM10, and ozone (O3) were assessed from publicly available data. The outcome was HAP, defined according to CDC/NHSN pneumonia criteria as pneumonia developing >48 h after hospital admission and not present or incubating at admission; VAP was not analyzed as a separate endpoint. The association between PM2.5 and HAP was estimated via a distributed lag non-linear model, adjusted for pollutants, time trends, and weather conditions. This study analyzed 1938 (31.278%) HAP cases. The mean levels of PM10, O3, PM2.5, and SO2 were 120, 75, 59, and 25 μg/m3, respectively, and the mean CO level was 0.979 mg/m3. The association between PM2.5 and HAP was statistically significant at lag 1 day within the perioperative exposure window. At a PM2.5 concentration of 30 μg/m3 compared with the reference concentration of 10 μg/m3, 14.2% higher odds of HAP were observed (95% CI: 2.6-27%). The stratified analyses indicated stronger associations among elders aged ≥ 60 years, patients with body mass index (BMI) > 23.9 kg/m2 and patients with diabetes. Additional adjustment for clinical covariates, including duration of mechanical ventilation, confirmed the robustness of the observed exposure-response association. These findings revealed a substantial and robust link between short-term PM2.5 exposure and elevated HAP incidence in the vulnerable population undergoing cardiovascular surgeries.

42989315.title: Early adequate empiric antifungal therapy and 28-day mortality in ICU patients with candidemia: a pooled patient-level analysis of EUROBACT-1 and EUROBACT-2 cohorts.
42989315.abstract: The optimal timing of empiric antifungal therapy in patients with suspected candidemia remains uncertain. In practice, many antifungal treatments initiated empirically are eventually found to be unnecessary, exposing patients to potential toxicity, selection of non-albicans Candida species, emergence of resistance, and additional costs. The objective of the study was to evaluate whether adequate empiric antifungal therapy initiated within 2 days after blood culture draw was associated with 28-day mortality. We performed a pooled secondary analysis of two prospective worldwide observational cohorts (EUROBACT-1 and EUROBACT-2) including adult patients with Candida bloodstream infection. The exposure was defined as receipt of adequate antifungal therapy within 2 days after blood culture draw. Propensity scores for receiving early adequate antifungal therapy were estimated using prespecified covariates, and inverse probability of treatment weights were applied in a weighted Cox proportional hazards model to assess the association with 28-day mortality. Prespecified subgroup analyses were conducted according to study cohort, Candida species, and presence of hypotension at the time of bloodstream infection. As a sensitivity analysis, a frailty Cox proportional hazards model including a random center effect was performed. The final study population included 272 patients with candidemia from 158 centers, including 81 from EUROBACT-1 and 191 from EUROBACT-2. One hundred and ten patients received early adequate antifungal therapy and 162 did not. Overall, 38.6% of patients (105/272) died within 28 days, including 40.9% (45/110) in the early adequate therapy group and 37.0% (60/162) in the non-early adequate therapy group. In the weighted Cox model, early adequate antifungal therapy was not significantly associated with 28-day mortality (HR 1.23, 95% CI 0.82-1.83, p = 0.314). Results were consistent across subgroup analyses according to study cohort, Candida species, the presence of hypotension at the time of bloodstream infection, as well as in the frailty Cox sensitivity analysis. Early adequate antifungal therapy was not independently associated with improved 28-day survival in ICU patients with candidemia. These findings support a more targeted approach to early empirical antifungal treatment and underscore the need to identify patient subgroups most likely to benefit from immediate therapy.

42989152.title: Prediction of 30-day mortality risk in patients with acute pancreatitis in ICU: a study based on the MIMIC-IV database.
42989152.abstract: Acute pancreatitis (AP) in the intensive care unit (ICU) exhibits rapid progression and high 30-day mortality, necessitating efficient early risk prediction methods. This study analyzed 724 ICU patients from the MIMIC-IV database. Key predictors were screened using LASSO regression, and a multivariate logistic regression model was constructed to evaluate 30-day mortality risk. Twelve key predictors-including blood urea nitrogen (BUN), red blood cell distribution width (RDW), pH, sepsis status, and vasopressor use-were identified. The model demonstrated strong discrimination, with area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.85 and 0.89 across sets, an overall accuracy of 77%, and significantly lower 30-day survival in high-risk groups (60% vs. 97%). The proposed model effectively stratifies 30-day mortality risk in ICU AP patients, offering valuable support for early clinical intervention and personalized management. Not applicable.

42993191.title: Independent predictors of 28-day mortality in ICU patients with Acinetobacter baumannii versus Non-Acinetobacter baumannii gram-negative tracheal aspirate isolates.
42993191.abstract: This study evaluated independent risk factors affecting 28-day mortality in intensive care unit (ICU) patients with Acinetobacter baumannii versus non-A. baumannii Gram-negative bacilli isolated from tracheal aspirate cultures. Overall, 120 ICU patients (66 males, 54 females; age: 36-94) enrolled between January 2024 and December 2025 were divided into two equal groups: the A. baumannii (n = 60) and the non-A. baumannii (n = 60). Age, sex, Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) score, APACHE II score, septic shock rates, and CRP levels were similar between groups (P > 0.05). However, carbapenem resistance (98.3% vs. 56.7%; P < 0.001), mechanical ventilation (MV) requirement (75.0% vs. 53.3%; P = 0.022), and 28-day mortality (63.3% vs. 40.0%; P = 0.018) were significantly higher in the A. baumannii group. ICU length of stay was significantly shorter in the A. baumannii group (16.5 vs. 26.5 days; P = 0.008), due to early-period mortality. Predominant non-A. baumannii pathogens were Klebsiella pneumoniae (51.7%) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (35%). Multivariate logistic regression identified MV requirement (aOR: 4.706, 95% CI: 1.792-12.359, P = 0.002), A. baumannii infection (aOR: 2.512, 95% CI: 1.055-5.983, P = 0.037), and higher CCI score (aOR: 1.523, 95% CI: 1.155-2.007, P = 0.003) as independent predictors of 28-day mortality. A. baumannii isolation from tracheal aspirates and MV requirement are strong independent risk factors for 28-day mortality in ICU patients. High carbapenem resistance restricts therapeutic options and drives early mortality. Early diagnosis, rapid microbiological identification, targeted antimicrobial therapy, and strict infection control practices are paramount to improving survival outcomes in critically ill patients.

42993165.title: Prolonged Versus Intermittent Piperacillin-Tazobactam Infusion in Critically Ill Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials.
42993165.abstract: Prolonged infusion of β-lactam antibiotics is recommended for adults with sepsis, but whether this benefit applies specifically to piperacillin-tazobactam remains uncertain. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing prolonged with intermittent infusion of piperacillin-tazobactam in critically ill adults. We searched PubMed, Scopus, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from inception to March 10, 2026. Eligible randomized controlled trials compared prolonged (continuous or extended) with intermittent infusion of piperacillin-tazobactam in critically ill adults. Primary outcomes were clinical cure and all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included intensive care unit length of stay and duration of antibiotic therapy. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to calculate pooled risk ratios for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences for continuous outcomes. Seven studies comprising 6,080 patients were included. For clinical cure, the pooled estimate favored prolonged infusion (risk ratio 1.23, 95% confidence interval 1.07-1.42, 6 trials, 585 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The effect on 28-day mortality was uncertain (risk ratio 0.47, 95% confidence interval 0.16-1.41, 2 trials, 104 participants; low-certainty evidence). There was no clear difference in 90-day mortality (risk ratio 0.92, 95% confidence interval 0.84-1.01, 2 trials, 5,532 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). BLING III contributed 99.3% of the weight in the analysis. The pooled mean difference in antibiotic treatment duration was -2.47 days (95% confidence interval -3.92 to -1.02, 2 trials, 120 participants; very low-certainty evidence), but the evidence was very uncertain. In this meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, prolonged infusion of piperacillin-tazobactam may improve clinical cure in critically ill adults, but the evidence is very uncertain. The estimate for 90-day mortality was consistent with the direction of benefit reported for β-lactams overall, but the confidence interval included no effect. These findings are consistent with the class-level evidence but do not independently confirm a mortality benefit specific to piperacillin-tazobactam. The effects on 28-day mortality and antibiotic treatment duration remain uncertain.

42991817.title: Characteristics and Hospital Outcomes of Patients Admitted to the Intensive Care Unit Because of Haematological Malignancy-A Service Evaluation.
42991817.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) admission due to haematological malignancy (HM) has previously been questioned due to high mortality. While mortality-associated factors have been studied in HM patients to guide decision making and clinical practice, UK-based research remains limited. This single-centre retrospective service evaluation (SE) aimed to review characteristics and hospital outcomes of patients admitted to our ICU because of HM. Consecutive adults with HM-related admissions to a multi-specialty ICU between January 2022 and October 2024 were retrospectively identified. Data were extracted for patient characteristics, ICU interventions and hospital outcomes. Associations with ICU mortality rates were also assessed. During the SE, there were 227 ICU admissions of HM patients, of which 168 were HM-related and, hence, included in subsequent analysis. The most common reasons for admission were respiratory failure (36.3%) and sepsis (26.2%). ICU and in-hospital mortality rates were 44.0% and 53.0%, respectively. ICU mortality rates increased significantly with APACHE II and SOFA scores (both p < 0.001), and in patients with leukaemia (p = 0.021), graft versus host disease (p = 0.001), treatment limitations (p < 0.001) or that were chemotherapy naïve (p = 0.044). In patients surviving to ICU discharge, 31.9% were unable to mobilise out of bed at this point. By hospital discharge, 94.9% of surviving patients were mobile; however, 25.3% required ongoing rehabilitation. This SE describes the characteristics, outcomes and mortality-associated factors in patients with HM-related admissions to our ICU, which may be useful in aiding clinician understanding and guiding future practice. Prospective, robust studies are needed to validate findings and explore future opportunities to enhance patient outcomes in this cohort. The authors have confirmed clinical trial registration is not needed for this submission.

42991563.title: Risk Factors for Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia in Patients Ventilated for Non-Pulmonary Conditions: A Prospective Multicenter Cohort Study (PULMIVAP).
42991563.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is a frequent complication of invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), yet its determinants in patients ventilated for non-pulmonary indications remain poorly characterized. Data were derived from the PULMIVAP multicenter prospective cohort (ClinicalTrial: NCT04849039), conducted in 8 Northern Italian intensive care units (January 2021-April 2024). All adults receiving IMV for non-pulmonary indications were enrolled if expected to require IMV >48 hours and antibiotic-free for ≥3 days preceding intubation. Clinical and therapeutic data were collected for up to 15 days of IMV; microbiological sampling was performed according to clinical indication. The primary outcome was time to first VAP within 15 days of IMV (VAP15). Associations between baseline characteristics, time-varying exposures, and VAP15 were evaluated. Thirty-day mortality from IMV initiation was a secondary outcome. Among 406 patients, 148 (36%) developed VAP15, at a median of 6 days (IQR 4.0-7.5) with an incidence rate of 43.2 per 1000 ventilator-days at risk (95% confidence intervals [95% CI], 36.4-49.9). Non-neurologic diagnosis (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 0.51; 95% CI, 0.31-0.86), female sex (aHR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.36-0.75), and early antibiotic initiation (days 1-2 of IMV, aHR, 0.65; 95% CI, 0.45-0.93) were independently associated with lower risk of VAP15. Predominant pathogens were Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella spp., and Haemophilus influenzae; multidrug-resistant organisms were uncommon. VAP15 showed no competing relationship or significant association with mortality (overall, 20.4%). In patients receiving IMV for non-pulmonary indications, non-neurologic diagnosis, female sex, and early antibiotic exposure were associated with lower observed VAP incidence, though causality cannot be inferred. Risk-stratified prevention strategies warrant further investigation into this population.

42989095.title: Risk factors and molecular epidemiology of ST2-type carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii carrying bla(OXA-23-like) and bla(OXA-51-like) genes.
42989095.abstract: The emergence and spread of carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB, A. baumannii) has raised significant concerns and challenges globally. This study analyzes the risk factors, distribution of antibiotic resistance genes, and virulence genes associated with CRAB infections, and explores the molecular epidemiological characteristics of CRAB. The findings provide scientific evidence for the development of prevention and treatment strategies for CRAB. A total of 100 patients diagnosed with A. baumannii(AB) infection through culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing were included in the study. These patients were classified into the CRAB group and the carbapenem-sensitive A. baumannii (CSAB) group based on their susceptibility to carbapenem antibiotics. Univariate analysis was used to screen for factors associated with CRAB infection, and significant variables were included in a multivariate logistic regression analysis. Additionally, five CRAB strains carrying both blaOXA-51-like and blaOXA-23-like genes were randomly selected for multilocus sequence typing (MLST) and whole-genome sequencing. The analysis included the identification of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), virulence factor genes, pathogen-host interaction annotations from the Pathogen Host Interactions Database, and functional annotations through Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG). Significant differences were observed between the CRAB group and the CSAB group in terms of length of hospital stay (P = 0.022, OR = 1.068), ICU admission rate (P = 0.019, OR = 8.032), prior carbapenem use (P = 0.028, OR = 4.445), and mechanical ventilation use (P = 0.044, OR = 7.226). In vitro antimicrobial susceptibility testing showed that all CRAB strains were resistant to ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, and ciprofloxacin, with some strains showing resistance to levofloxacin (87.5%) and doxycycline (93.8%), but remaining sensitive to tigecycline and polymyxin B. Through multiplex PCR analysis, we tested 48CRAB strains (carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii). The results revealed that 41 of these strains carried both the blaOXA-51-like and blaOXA-23-like genes. The presence rate of OXA-type β-lactamase genes and efflux pump genes in randomly selected positive strains is 100%. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) annotation results indicated that the genes of these randomly selected positive strains were primarily involved in cellular processes, metabolic pathways, and environmental information processing, and exhibited strong enzymatic activity and binding functions. Length of hospital stay, ICU admission, prior carbapenem use, and mechanical ventilation are susceptibility factors for carbapenem resistance in A. baumannii infections at this hospital. MLST typing and multiplex PCR analysis indicate the spread of ST2-type blaOXA-51-like and blaOXA-23-like positive CRAB infections in the hospital, with ST2-type CRAB potentially being the dominant clone in circulation. Whole-genome sequencing revealed the resistance and virulence characteristics of CRAB strains isolated from clinical samples at this hospital, and showed that these CRAB strains from the hospital are distinct from those found in different provinces and cities in China.

42994766.title: Early platelet count trajectories and short- and long-term mortality in patients with sepsis: a group-based trajectory modeling study based on the MIMIC-IV database.
42994766.abstract: Platelet abnormalities are common in sepsis; most studies evaluate single measurements. We characterized early platelet count trajectories during the first 48 h after intensive care unit (ICU) admission and evaluated associations with short- and long-term mortality. Adult Sepsis-3 patients were identified from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) database. Group-based trajectory modeling was applied to platelet counts at 12-48 h after ICU admission. Associations with mortality were examined using Kaplan-Meier, multivariable Cox and logistic models, with propensity-matched, multiple-imputation and reclassification analyses and the 48-h landmark analysis as primary; sepsis-induced coagulopathy was scored using International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis (ISTH) criteria. Among 5,046 ICU stays (4,775 patients), four trajectories were identified: persistently low (n = 1,153; 22.8%), moderate with mild decline (n = 1,847; 36.6%), high with moderate decline (n = 1,516; 30.0%) and very high with marked decline (n = 530; 10.5%). In the primary landmark analysis (n=4,930), adjusted 28-day mortality hazard ratios versus the moderate-with-mild-decline group were 1.66 (95% CI 1.40-1.97), 1.33 (1.12-1.57) and 1.34 (1.07-1.69), consistent at 90 days, 1 year and in whole-cohort and matched analyses. Sepsis-induced coagulopathy affected 82.6% of persistently low patients; trajectory and coagulopathy remained jointly associated with mortality. Trajectory membership improved reclassification over clinical variables (continuous NRI 0.193, 95% CI 0.160-0.281). Early platelet trajectories identify four sepsis patient groups with distinct mortality risk. The persistently low association was most robust; the high-but-declining association was attenuated in five-group analyses. Trajectories add information beyond single measurements.

42994751.title: Efficacy and Safety of Ulinastatin in the Treatment of Patients with Sepsis: The ADJUST Trial.
42994751.abstract: Urinary trypsin inhibitor (ulinastatin, UTI) has shown potential survival benefits in sepsis; however, conclusive clinical evidence is lacking. In patients with sepsis, does adjunctive ulinastatin, compared with placebo, reduce 28-day all-cause mortality? In this multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adult ICU patients with sepsis meeting Sepsis-3 criteria within 48 hours of admission were randomized (1:1) to receive intravenous UTI (400,000 IU every 8 hours) or placebo, for up to 10 days in addition to standard care. Randomization was stratified by site and septic shock. The primary endpoint was 28-day all-cause mortality. Secondary endpoints included ICU, hospital, and 90-day mortality, and ICU/hospital length of stay. Of 347 patients randomized, 340 (169 UTI, 171 placebo) received intervention and were included in the safety analysis; after 5 post-intervention withdrawals, 335 (165 UTI, 170 placebo) were included in the intention-to-treat analysis. At 28 days, death had occurred in 39 of 165 patients (23.6%) in the UTI group and in 39 of 170 patients (22.9%) in the placebo group (absolute difference, 0.7% [95% CI -8.4% to 9.7%]; P = .98; hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.61, P = .90). Secondary outcomes were similar in the two groups. Adverse events occurred in 56.8% (96/169) of UTI and 42.7% (73/171) of placebo patients (absolute difference 14.1%, 95% CI 3.6%-24.6%; P = 0.009). In patients with sepsis, adjunctive UTI did not reduce mortality compared with placebo. Routine use of UTI for sepsis is not supported by these findings. ClinicalTrials.gov; https://clinicaltrials.gov; NCT02647554.

42992862.title: Proteomics Reveals Novel Biomarkers in the Blood for Sepsis Diagnosis.
42992862.abstract: Early sepsis diagnosis in critically ill patients remains a major unmet need. We employed a multiphase proteomic strategy integrating discovery by data-independent acquisition, targeted verification by parallel reaction monitoring, clinical confirmation with ELISA, and machine learning to identify robust blood biomarkers. In discovery and verification cohorts, three consistently downregulated proteins, α-2-HS-glycoprotein (AHSG), clusterin (CLU), and kallistatin (SERPINA4), were prioritized. A random forest model combining these markers yielded an apparent area under the curve (AUC) of 0.94 in the training cohort. Crucially, in a prospective evaluation of 143 patients with suspected sepsis, representing the true test of generalizability, the model achieved an AUC of 0.87, significantly outperforming PCT and CRP, and correctly classified 73.0% of confirmed sepsis cases as high-risk. This triple-biomarker panel enables rapid, accurate early detection of sepsis and offers a readily translatable diagnostic tool for clinical practice.

42990986.title: Intraoperative hypotension and postoperative neurocognitive impairment in surgical patients with sepsis: A retrospective observational study.
42990986.journal: Journal of anesthesia and translational medicine
42990986.abstract: Postoperative neurocognitive impairment is frequently observed in critically ill surgical patients with sepsis, but its perioperative contributors remain insufficiently defined. This study evaluated the associations of intraoperative hypotension and disease severity-assessed using the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) and Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II) scores-with postoperative neurocognitive impairment and 28-day all-cause mortality in this population. This single-center retrospective observational study included 285 adult patients with sepsis who were admitted to the intensive care unit after surgery. Postoperative neurocognitive impairment was operationally defined as new-onset disturbance of consciousness, attention, orientation, or mental status during the first postoperative intensive care unit stay, after excluding primary central nervous system disease, overt metabolic encephalopathy, and direct sedative or analgesic effects. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with postoperative neurocognitive impairment. A secondary analysis was conducted among patients who developed postoperative neurocognitive impairment to explore factors associated with 28-day all-cause mortality. Postoperative neurocognitive impairment occurred in 140 of 285 patients (49.1%). In multivariable analysis, older age, longer duration of intraoperative hypotension, greater intraoperative hypotension burden, higher SOFA score, and higher APACHE II score were independently associated with postoperative neurocognitive impairment. Among patients with postoperative neurocognitive impairment, intraoperative hypotension exposure and higher SOFA and APACHE II scores were independently associated with 28-day all-cause mortality. Operationally defined postoperative neurocognitive impairment was common in surgical patients with sepsis admitted to the intensive care unit after surgery. Intraoperative hypotension exposure and higher SOFA and APACHE II scores were associated with postoperative neurocognitive impairment and 28-day all-cause mortality, suggesting that perioperative hemodynamic instability may have prognostic relevance in this high-risk population.

42989793.title: Nurse-Led Sepsis Scoring System for Adult Febrile Neutropenia: Protocol for a Two-Phase Clinical Prediction Model Study With Remote Patient Monitoring.
42989793.abstract: Adults with hematological malignancies who develop febrile neutropenia (FN) face elevated risks of sepsis, intensive care admission, and treatment interruptions. Early sepsis detection is challenging, as classical clinical signs are often attenuated or delayed in this population. Current risk stratification tools demonstrate limitations when applied to adults with FN. A tailored, nurse-led scoring system integrating clinical, laboratory, and physiological predictors may enhance early sepsis identification. This 2-phase study aims to develop and internally validate a nurse-led sepsis risk score for adults with FN in phase I and to temporally validate its performance in phase II. The new score will be compared to the MASCC risk index, CISNE, NEWS2_ and qSOFA at FN onset . The secondary objectives include evaluating associations between risk groups and remote patient monitoring alerts within 24 hours of FN onset, interrater agreement, and bedside feasibility. The study is being conducted in the hematology and bone marrow transplantation department of a tertiary care hospital in Bengaluru, India. Phase I uses a nested matched case-control design within a retrospective cohort of approximately 140 patients with FN. We will analyze clinical, laboratory, and physiological predictors measured at FN onset using multivariable conditional logistic regression, with internal validation via bootstrapping. In Phase II, which utilizes a prospective temporal validation cohort, bedside nurses will calculate the proposed score at FN onset alongside the MASCC, CISNE, NEWS2, and qSOFA scores A substudy will include additional nurses scoring independently to assess interrater agreement and feasibility. Two blinded reviewers will adjudicate phase I outcomes within 14 days of FN onset, while assessors blinded to all scores will adjudicate phase II outcomes within the same time frame. The primary outcome is sepsis within 14 days of FN onset. Phase II evaluates discrimination, calibration, and comparative diagnostic performance. We obtained ethics approval in April 2025, and the study was registered in June 2025 (CTRI/2025/06/088290). The initial phase I derivation was completed in November 2025, using sepsis within 14 days of FN onset as the primary outcome. A protocol amendment in September 2026 harmonized the outcome window to 14 days, prompting rederivation of the model and superseding the initial analysis. Phase II commenced in December 2025. As of September 2026, enrollment and data collection were ongoing, with study completion anticipated in December 2026. Main results are expected in 2027. This protocol evaluates an FN-specific, nurse-led sepsis score integrating clinical and laboratory predictors with contactless physiological measurements. We will examine remote patient monitoring alerts as secondary markers of clinical instability. Validation findings will establish the score's predictive performance and inform future implementation studies.

42992167.title: Bloodstream Infections After Cardiac Surgery: Pathogen Distribution, Antimicrobial Resistance, and a Nomogram Prediction Model.
42992167.abstract: Postoperative bloodstream infection (BSI) is a severe complication following cardiac surgery, associated with significant mortality. This study aims to characterize pathogen profiles, antimicrobial resistance and independent risk factors for BSI in a Chinese cardiac surgery cohort. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of postoperative BSI in patients who underwent cardiac surgery at the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University from January 2019 to December 2024. Patients who developed postoperative BSI were identified and a 1:1 propensity score matched analysis were performed to adjust for baseline characteristics of patients. Univariate and multivariate analysis were applied to identify independent risk factors for postoperative BSI. R software was used to construct a prediction nomogram, followed by internal validation. During the study, a total of 10,007 patients underwent heart surgery, and 164 pairs of patients were successfully matched using propensity score matching. Gram-negative bacteria were the most common pathogens (64.1%), followed by Fungi (18.2%) and Gram-positive bacteria (17.6%). Among Enterobacterales, 33.8% were carbapenem-resistant, with carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) accounting for 63.6% of K. pneumoniae isolates. Meanwhile, 85.0% (17/20) of A. baumannii isolates were multidrug-resistant A. baumannii (MDRAB). The 90-day mortality rate in the BSI group was 39.0%, significantly higher than that in the non-BSI group (4.9%, P < 0.001). Multivariate logistic regression identified impaired cardiac function (New York Heart Association II-IV, NYHA II-IV) (OR=5.583, 95% CI:2.681-11.627), pulmonary infection (OR =4.053, 95% CI:1.692-9.710), emergency surgery (OR=9.629, 95% CI:2.962-31.301), coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) (OR=2.796, 95% CI:1.096-7.134), continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT Postoperative ICU stay ≥ 14 d) (OR=4.758, 95% CI:1.854-12.211) and postoperative ICU stay ≥14 d (OR=14.616, 95% CI:6.765-31.577) as independent risk factors for postoperative BSI. The nomogram showed good discrimination and calibration after internal validation, with an optimism-corrected C-index of 0.913 and a mean absolute calibration error of 0.026. Postoperative BSI in cardiac surgery patients is associated with high mortality. A nomogram based on impaired cardiac function (NYHA II-IV), pulmonary infection, emergency surgery, CABG, CRRT and postoperative ICU stay ≥14 d displayed high accuracy and consistency in predicting the risk of postoperative BSI. These results facilitate early risk stratification and guide preventive strategies in high-risk cardiac surgical patients.

42993902.title: Beyond Prophylaxis: Antimicrobial Stewardship for Bacterial Infections in Cirrhosis.

42992670.title: Genomic Features and Risk Factors of Carbapenem-Resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa Bloodstream Infections.
42992670.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (CRPA) bloodstream infection is associated with high mortality and limited treatment options. This retrospective cohort study was conducted at a single Chinese hospital from January 2020 to January 2026 and included adult patients with P. aeruginosa bloodstream infection. Clinical data were extracted from the hospital information system, and whole-genome sequencing was performed on 48 CRPA isolates to determine multilocus sequence types, carbapenemase genes, and capsular serotypes. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression were used to identify factors associated with CRPA acquisition. Among 110 patients, 48 (43.6%) had CRPA bloodstream infection. Prior ICU stay within 1 month (adjusted OR = 5.67, 95% CI: 2.81-11.45, p < 0.001) and prior carbapenem exposure within 30 days (adjusted OR = 3.89, 95% CI: 1.92-7.88, p < 0.001) were independent risk factors for CRPA acquisition. ST-3757 was the predominant sequence type (39/48, 81.3%), KPC-2 was the predominant carbapenemase gene (32/48, 66.7%), and O11 was the most frequent serotype (12/48, 25.0%). All ST-3757 isolates shared pairwise average nucleotide identity above 98.5%, and phylogenetic analysis placed them in a single well-supported clade. These findings indicate that prior healthcare exposure and carbapenem use drive CRPA bloodstream infection in this setting and that an ST-3757-O11-KPC-2 lineage is locally epidemic, supporting targeted antimicrobial stewardship and genomic surveillance.

42993995.title: How to read a systematic review and meta-analysis critically: Lessons from the lactate-to-albumin ratio in sepsis.

42996535.title: Clinical characteristics of ICU patients with gastrointestinal colonisation by Candida auris.
42996535.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
42996535.abstract: This study aimed to analyse the detection of Candida auris in faecal cultures of intensive care unit (ICU) patients and its impact on clinical outcomes, whilst constructing a predictive model for the risk of intestinal carriage of this fungus to inform clinical screening and infection control strategies. A retrospective study design was employed, enrolling 970 eligible patients admitted to the ICU of Guangdong Provincial Second Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine between January 2024 and December 2025. Participants were categorised into a C.auris-positive group (n=13) and a negative group (n=957) based on stool culture results. Data were collected on patients' underlying medical conditions, antibiotic use and invasive procedures prior to stool culture, treatment-related data and clinical outcome measures. Univariate analysis compared clinical characteristics between groups. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)regression screened potential predictors, establishing a multivariate logistic regression model visualised as a nomogram. Model performance was assessed via area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration curves, and decision curves. Among 970 patients, the detection rate of C.auris in stool cultures was 1.34% (13/970). Univariate analysis revealed that the prevalence of anaemia and a history of antifungal drug exposure, as well as the duration of broad-spectrum antibiotic use, were all significantly higher in the positive group than in the negative group. Furthermore, the duration of antimicrobial use and length of hospital stay were both longer in the positive group. Anaemia and a history of exposure to antifungal drugs were independent predictors of intestinal C.auris carriage. After incorporating these two factors into the predictive model, the AUC value was 0.828. Calibration curves demonstrated good agreement between predicted and actual detection rates, whilst decision curves indicated clinical net benefit within the 0-15% risk threshold. The presence of C.auris in the faeces of patients in ICU is associated with anaemia, a history of exposure to antifungal drugs. The predictive model developed in this study demonstrates good discriminatory performance, offering a practical means of implementing targeted screening and infection control measures in clinical practice.

42995620.title: Structural imbalances in open-access critical care research: a bibliometric analysis of abstracts from ICU database studies, 2018-2025.
42995620.abstract: Open access intensive care unit (ICU) databases, including MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD), AmsterdamUMCdb, HiRID-high time resolution ICU data set, and the Salzburg Intensive Care Database (SICdb), have fundamentally transformed critical care research over the past decade. Despite their widespread use, no comprehensive bibliometric analysis has systematically mapped the scientific output generated by studies relying on these resources. A structured search was conducted in PubMed and Web of Science covering 2018 to 2025, retrieving original articles citing at least one of six defined open access ICU databases in title or abstract. Database selection followed the methodology of two prior systematic reviews of publicly available adult ICU datasets. Structured fields covering database used, machine learning (ML) methods, study design, clinical outcomes, AUROC values and patient counts were extracted via a semi-automated AI pipeline (DeepSeek API, multi-label JSON schema). The extraction pipeline was validated against a manually coded reference sample of 110 publications. Bibliometric analyses used R (bibliometrix v4.0.1) and Python. Citation counts, open-access status and SCImago journal quartile were retrieved via OpenAlex and SCImago to characterise the visibility and venue quality of the corpus. Four network analyses were performed: database-to-ML-method co-occurrence, country-to-database, international collaboration, and clinical topic co-occurrence networks. A total of 4,648 publications were included. Annual publication counts increased 45-fold from 42 (2018) to 1,907 (2025), accelerating markedly after 2021 following the release of MIMIC-IV. MIMIC-IV dominated database attributions (54.6%), followed by MIMIC-III (30.0%) and eICU-CRD (13.5%); European databases (AmsterdamUMCdb, HiRID, SICdb) collectively accounted for only 1.9%. China contributed 65.6% of publications (n = 3,048) and the USA 10.6%. Median citations per paper were 5.0 (1.50 per year). 76.4% of publications were open access and 49.3% appeared in a Q1 SCImago-ranked journal. AUROC showed no meaningful correlation with citation impact (p = 0.10). Logistic regression was the most frequent ML method (38.5%), followed by neural networks (15.6%) and gradient boosting (13.8%). Retrospective observational designs dominated (67.9%), with mortality prediction in sepsis as the primary research focus. Median AUROC among 1,263 publications with extractable values was 0.798. Open access database-based critical care research is growing almost exponentially, driven primarily by Chinese groups using MIMIC-IV for retrospective mortality studies. European databases remain underutilized. The field exhibits methodological homogeneity and a heavy bias toward US-American clinical practice patterns, with cross-dataset external validation rarely foregrounded in study abstracts. Greater use of European databases, systematic external validation and topical diversification are key priorities.

42995612.title: Fluid-intolerance signals as bedside safety limits during early septic shock resuscitation: a multicenter randomized trial.
42995612.abstract: Fluid resuscitation in early septic shock has a narrow therapeutic index. Signals of fluid intolerance are frequently present during early resuscitation, yet current resuscitation strategies do not incorporate them to guide when to limit fluid administration. We evaluated whether integrating fluid-intolerance signals as safety limits could reduce fluid-induced harm without compromising hypoperfusion resolution. In this multicenter, open-label randomized trial in three Chilean ICUs, mechanically ventilated adults with septic shock, persistent hypoperfusion, fluid responsiveness, and at least one high-risk criterion for fluid-induced harm were randomized 1:1 to a fluid-intolerance-limited resuscitation strategy or standard care during a 6-hour protocol window. In the intervention arm, before each bolus, fluid-intolerance signals (lung ultrasound score, VExUS, E/lateral e', and central venous pressure) were graded as traffic-light: green received a 500-mL bolus, yellow 250 mL, and red no further fluid. Standard care delivered 500-mL boluses while hypoperfusion and fluid responsiveness persisted. The primary outcome was the change in PaO2:FiO2 from baseline to 6 h (ΔPaO2:FiO2). Recruitment was discontinued before the planned sample size was reached because continued enrollment was no longer feasible. Among 113 screened patients, 36 of a planned 62 were randomized, and 35 were analyzed (18 standard care, 17 intervention). The intervention group received a lower protocol bolus volume during the 6-hour intervention window than the standard-care group (250 [125-500] vs. 650 [500-1500] mL; between-group difference, - 500 mL [95% CI, - 750 to - 250]). Cumulative fluid exposure from pre-randomization through the end of the protocol window was similar between groups (3375 [2375-3875] vs. 3750 [1875-4851] mL; between-group difference, - 150 mL [95% CI, - 1470 to 1250]). The primary outcome favored the intervention: median ΔPaO2:FiO2 was 40.5 [24.0-58.5] versus - 37.9 [-69.2 to -12.5]; p < 0.001 (between-group median difference + 78.3 points; 95% CI 50.5 to 110.0), and 0-6-hour changes in lactate and capillary refill time did not differ. Because the trial was stopped early, the effect of a fluid-intolerance-limited resuscitation strategy on oxygenation remains uncertain. A larger trial would be needed to determine whether this strategy improves oxygenation. Such a trial appears feasible. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier NCT06568744, registered August 21, 2024.

42997605.title: Comparison of costs and health outcomes of mPOCT NEAR technology to PCR and LFD for influenza detection in the United Arab Emirates.
42997605.abstract: Influenza shares many symptoms with other respiratory diseases, making clinical diagnosis challenging. This study evaluated the clinical and economic outcomes of influenza testing using a rapid molecular point-of-care platform based on isothermal nicking enzyme amplification reaction (mPOCT NEAR), compared with laboratory-based polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and lateral flow diagnostic (LFD) antigen testing, from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) private healthcare payer perspective. A 1-year health economic model was developed. Two high-risk populations were assessed: older adults and children under 5 years. Outcomes included antimicrobial use, otitis media cases, intensive care unit admissions, mechanical ventilation, and prevention of secondary transmissions. Direct medical and complication costs were included. Two antimicrobial scenarios were modeled: antimicrobial use-derived from literature (scenario 1), and antiviral-only treatment for test-positive patients (scenario 2). Across both scenarios, mPOCT NEAR reduced total healthcare costs and improved clinical outcomes compared with PCR-lower antibiotic use, fewer otitis media cases and intensive care unit admissions, and reduced mechanical ventilation and secondary transmissions.Compared with LFD testing, mPOCT NEAR reduced secondary transmissions by 57% in scenario 1 and demonstrated broader clinical benefits in scenario 2. Overall cost savings were observed versus comparators. mPOCT NEAR is cost-saving and clinically advantageous, supporting efficient resource allocation in UAE private healthcare settings.

42997403.title: Evolving Epidemiology of Invasive Candidiasis in Southwest China: A Four-year Analysis of Species Distribution, Antifungal Resistance Profiles, and Mortality Risk Factors.
42997403.abstract: The purpose of this study was to explore the strain distribution, clinical characteristics, antifungal sensitivity and risk factors of 30-day mortality of invasive Candida infection of hospitalized patients. We conducted a four-year retrospective study at a tertiary teaching hospital in Southwest China, enrolling non-duplicate strains isolated from invasive candidiasis samples obtained from hospitalized patients. Of the 345 non-duplicate invasive candidiasis cases, 145 (42%) were candidemia cases. Candida albicans (44.3%) was the most identified species, followed by C. glabrata (18.2%), C. tropicalis (14.5%), and C. parapsilosis (12.5%). Amphotericin B and echinocandins demonstrated potent in vitro activity, whereas Candida species exhibited high resistance rates to azole antifungals, particularly C. tropicalis, whose resistance rate approaches 30%. Compared to patients in general wards, ICU patients exhibited more severe clinical symptoms, higher rates of invasive medical procedures and antibiotic exposure. Multivariate analysis identified hepatobiliary disease, surgical interventions within 6 months, tracheal intubation, ICU admission, and use of aminoglycosides and tetracyclines as independent risk factors for 30-day mortality. Additionally, the study revealed that elevated levels of BDG, and IL-6, as well as reduced PLT, were associated with increased 30-day mortality. A better understanding of the specific risk factors associated with ICU stays could facilitate earlier identification of high-risk candidates for antifungal therapy initiation, thereby improving clinical outcomes for critically ill patients with invasive candidiasis.

42997367.title: Clinical Profile of Patients With Pseudomonas aeruginosa Infection and Antimicrobial Susceptibility Patterns of Pseudomonas aeruginosa: A Cross-sectional Prospective Study From a Tertiary Care Hospital in Central India.
42997367.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an important healthcare-associated opportunistic pathogen in healthcare settings, particularly among critically ill and hospitalized patients. Multidrug resistance, particularly carbapenem resistance, is a major problem that restricts treatment options and increases morbidity rates for patients admitted to intensive care. This study aimed to evaluate the clinical profile of patients with P. aeruginosa infection and determine the antimicrobial susceptibility pattern of the isolates in a tertiary care hospital in Central India. A hospital-based, cross-sectional prospective study was conducted in the Department of Microbiology, Index Medical College, Hospital and Research Centre, Indore, from January 2023 to December 2025. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee (ref. no.: MU/Research/EC/Ph.D/2023/028). A total of 171 non-duplicate clinical isolates of P. aeruginosa obtained from patients of all age groups were included. Isolates were identified using standard phenotypic methods, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed by the Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion method according to CLSI 2023 guidelines. Clinical and laboratory data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics, version 27.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, USA), with the chi-square test used to assess associations. From a total of 171 P. aeruginosa isolates, 72 (42.1%) were recovered from respiratory specimens, followed by pus/wound swabs (24.0%), urine (16.4%), and blood (10.5 %). Most isolates were obtained from ICU patients (69.6%), and male patients constituted 65.5% of cases. Hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated pneumonia was the commonest clinical presentation (35.7%). The highest antimicrobial resistance was observed with ceftriaxone (69.0%), ceftazidime (60.2%), and cefepime (57.9%), followed by aztreonam (55.6%), piperacillin-tazobactam (53.8%), and levofloxacin (49.7%). Resistance to imipenem and meropenem was 44.4% and 40.4%, respectively, whereas polymyxin B showed the lowest resistance (2.3%). Significant associations were observed between antimicrobial resistance and ICU stay, prior antibiotic exposure, mechanical ventilation, urinary catheterization, central line/IV catheter use, diabetes mellitus, COPD, chronic kidney disease, and immunocompromised status (p<0.05). P. aeruginosa showed a substantial antimicrobial resistance burden, particularly among ICU patients. Regular local antibiogram surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, and stringent infection prevention and control measures are essential for optimizing therapy and limiting the emergence of resistant strains.

42996715.title: Deep learning-based CT lesion analysis and radiological burden stratification in clinically diagnosed ventilator-associated pneumonia.
42996715.abstract: Ventilator associated pneumonia (VAP) is a major complication in the intensive care unit (ICU) and requires objective computed tomography (CT) evaluation. Therefore, this article conducted a retrospective research analysis and developed a multimodal deep learning framework. Firstly, this retrospective study included 512 patients clinically diagnosed with VAP, and then utilized a developed multimodal deep learning framework for voxel-level lesion segmentation, multi-label radiological discovery classification, and radiological burden grading. This framework integrates the anatomical priors of TotalSegmenter, a three-dimensional (3D) Swin UNETR multitasking network, and cross attention fusion of CT features and ventilation parameters. Ultimately, the study showed that the Dice score for internal validation was 0.847, the macroscopic mean area (AUC) under the subject's working characteristic curve was 0.919, and the weighted kappa was 0.826. External validation showed a Dice score of 0.821, with no significant difference between scanner manufacturers. After adjusting for clinical covariates, including acute physiology and chronic health assessment II (APACHE II) scores, there was still a significant correlation between radiation load level and 28 day mortality (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.34, P < 0.001), supporting its potential prognostic relevance.

42997017.title: Sepsis-associated atrial fibrillation: Current insights and research priorities for standardized care.
42997017.abstract: Sepsis-associated atrial fibrillation (SAAF) is a common but serious complication in critically ill patients that is characterized by new-onset atrial fibrillation (AF) during sepsis. This secondary type of arrhythmia typically resolves with sepsis treatment but is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, including prolonged hospital stays, high recurrence rates of AF, and increased risks of heart failure, stroke, and short-term and long-term mortality. In contrast to primary AF, no standardized guidelines have been established for SAAF. To support the development of evidence-based protocols, we conducted a comprehensive review to synthesize the current knowledge of SAAF. Here, we highlight the definition, incidence, and risk factors of SAAF and distinguish it from primary AF and other types of secondary AF, including postoperative and post-myocardial infarction AF. We also describe the multifactorial pathophysiologic mechanisms of SAAF involving systemic inflammation, cytokine release, autonomic dysfunction, myocardial injury, and hemodynamic stress. Key outcomes of patients with SAAF and other types of secondary AF are compared, including in-hospital mortality, long-term AF recurrence, and stroke risk. Furthermore, we discuss various management strategies for SAAF, including methods of rhythm control and rate control in patients with SAAF. Anticoagulation recommendations and challenges for patients with SAAF are highlighted, particularly with respect to thrombotic risk, bleeding risk, and anticoagulation use. We propose a process for anticoagulation decisions in SAAF, which are challenging due to the dynamic interplay between sepsis-induced coagulopathy and thromboembolic risk. Finally, we provide a summary of future research priorities to support large-scale, multicenter trials to define evidence-based protocols that are critical for improving outcomes in this high-risk population.

42996723.title: Time-dependent associations of documented low-dose aspirin administration with 28-day mortality and early safety outcomes in adults with sepsis: a MIMIC-IV cohort study.
42996723.abstract: Associations between aspirin use and sepsis outcomes may reflect treatment timing and clinical selection. This retrospective Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) study included 31,888 adults with Sepsis-3. T0 was defined as the later of intensive care unit (ICU) admission or suspected infection; sepsis ascertainment could occur subsequently. Piecewise time-dependent Cox models evaluated actual enteral aspirin administration of 75-100 mg and 28-day restricted in-hospital and ICU mortality. Baseline sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) measurements were restricted to T0 or earlier. Sensitivity analyses examined exposure history, eligibility timing, and a 24-h matched landmark cohort. A continuous-time marginal structural model (MSM) incorporated lagged clinical information. Modified Poisson models evaluated laboratory and transfusion outcomes. Eligible aspirin administration was recorded at or after T0 for 4,771 patients, including 3,646 within 24 h. Adjusted in-hospital mortality hazard ratios (HRs) were 0.48 (95% CI 0.31-0.75) during 0-24 h and 0.63 (0.51-0.78) during 24-72 h, without clear associations thereafter. ICU estimates were similar. Qualifying SOFA scores occurred after T0 in 24,916 patients; restriction to the 6,972 patients with qualifying SOFA scores by T0 yielded HRs of 0.54 (0.28-1.03) and 0.62 (0.44-0.88) in the first two intervals. The MSM had residual imbalance and truncation-sensitive early estimates. After multiple imputation, the first two in-hospital HRs were 0.50 (0.32-0.79) and 0.66 (0.53-0.82), close to the primary estimates.
