A hemoglobin decline of ≥2 g/dL during 0-72 h was associated with early aspirin administration [adjusted risk ratio (RR) 1.10, 1.03-1.17], but 606 early recipients had a qualifying decline recorded before their first dose. The temporality-restricted 24-72-h analysis showed no clear association (RR 1.05, 0.91-1.21). Documented aspirin administration was associated with lower early restricted mortality. Retrospective eligibility, residual confounding, and uncertain prior exposure prevent causal interpretation; these findings do not justify initiating aspirin solely for sepsis.

42996144.title: Artificial intelligence simulation study of Therapeutic Plasma Exchange (TPE) using an 8- State Markov State-Transition Model integrated within a Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo Framework.
42996144.abstract: Introduction Sepsis-induced organ dysfunction remains a leading cause of mortality in critical care. While recent evidence suggests that Therapeutic Plasma Exchange (TPE) may improve outcomes, significant heterogeneity among septic patient populations in prior trials might have contributed to mixed responses and thus fueled clinical skepticism. To address this challenge and to model TPE effectiveness across varying levels of sepsis severity, we utilized a time-dependent, 8-state transition Markov model integrated with a Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) framework. Methods An AI-generated "digital twin" cohort (N = 10,000) was randomized 1:1 to standard care (SC) or adjuvant TPE groups. Transition probabilities were parameterized using a pooled relative risk (RR) of 0.58, derived from five recent meta-analyses. The model incorporated specific hazard multipliers for acute kidney injury (AKI; 1.5x), thrombocytopenia (1.3x), and high-dose vasopressor requirements (1.25x). Patient flow was simulated through eight clinically defined health states over a 28-day horizon. Outcomes included 28-day survival, absolute risk reduction (ARR), and number needed to treat (NNT) stratified by Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score quartiles (8, 12, 16, and 20). Bayesian methods were employed to determine survival probabilities and hazard ratios (HR) with 95% credible intervals (CrI). Results Across the modelled full 10,000-patient cohort, TPE increased 28 day survival compared to standard care (67.3% vs. 44.7%). The survival benefit was modest in the group with the lowest degree of organ failure (SOFA 8) (TPE 87.6% vs. SC 78.4%; ARR 9.2%; NNT 11). However, this benefit was more pronounced in cases of higher burden of organ failure, particularly within the SOFA 20 cohort (TPE 48.8% vs. SC 12.8%; ARR 36%; NNT 3) and in cases with AKI + thrombocytopenia + higher doses of vasopressors (ARR 36%; NNT 3). For SOFA 20 patients, TPE was associated with a 38% reduction in the hazard of death (HR 0.62; 95% CrI 0.54-0.71). Conclusion These simulation results suggests that the efficacy of TPE might be dependent on baseline illness severity. While the clinical impact is more limited in moderate sepsis (SOFA 8), TPE appears to offer a profound survival advantage and high therapeutic yield for patients with multi-organ failure.

42995744.title: Tetraspanin changes in septic blood are organized by cell type, with monocyte CD82 induction and leukocyte CD37 loss associated with mortality.
42995744.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
42995744.abstract: Tetraspanins organize membrane domains that regulate inflammation. The antagonistic pair CD82 (pro-inflammatory, pro-vascular leakage) and CD151 (anti-inflammatory, anti-vascular leakage) coordinate endothelial activation and dysfunction in severe and systemic inflammation such as sepsis. Whether blood-cell tetraspanin networks are reorganized and regulated in cell-type-specific and -coordinated fashions in human sepsis and relate to mortality is unknown. We integrated bulk meta-analysis (8 ICU-sampled cohorts, 241 controls, 550 sepsis patients), 28-day survival analysis (GSE65682, n=468), single-cell RNA-sequencing (3 datasets, 1.6 million PBMCs from 184 donors), co-expression networks (WGCNA), immune deconvolution with composition-adjusted survival, and mortality prediction models judged against matched random-gene controls. Mendelian randomization tested whether inherited variation in tetraspanin expression alters sepsis susceptibility. Single-cell RNA-sequencing of LPS-challenged mouse lung provided an orthogonal test. Thirteen of 33 tetraspanins changed significantly in septic blood (up: CD63, CD82, CD151, ROM1, TSPAN9, UPK1A; down: CD81, TSPAN3, TSPAN13, TSPAN32, TSPAN18, TSPAN4, TSPAN31), and the direction of change followed myeloid versus lymphoid lineage bias, reflecting the leukocyte composition shift of sepsis. WGCNA placed CD82 and CD151 in distinct modules. The CD82:CD151 ratio did not predict 28-day mortality (HR=1.09, p=0.37). In the discovery cohort, CD37 was the strongest survival-associated tetraspanin (HR=0.72 per SD, FDR=0.002), even after adjusting for leukocyte composition (HR=0.70, p=0.007). Single-cell analysis of three datasets of sepsis patients resolved two cell-type-specific programs, monocyte CD82 up-regulation and pan-leukocyte CD37 loss. CD37 expression was directionally protective in all three independent ICU cohorts, significantly so only in the largest. Mendelian randomization found no evidence that genetically proxied baseline tetraspanin expression affects sepsis susceptibility (0 of 24 genes). In mouse lung, we found macrophage CD82 increased and endothelial CD151 decreased after LPS. Blood-cell tetraspanin networks are reorganized cell-type-specifically in sepsis. Much of the bulk signal reflects leukocyte composition rather than a coordinated membrane program. The CD82/CD151 antagonism, established in endothelium, is not captured by whole-blood ratios, in which the two genes reflect different cell types.

42997308.title: Genomic epidemiology unravels simultaneous clusters of linezolid-resistant Staphylococcus epidermidis isolated in Austria, 2023-2025.
42997308.abstract: Staphylococcus epidermidis is an opportunistic pathogen causing bloodstream and device-associated infections. Due to the use of linezolid (LZD) against infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-positive bacteria, the emergence of LZD-resistant S. epidermidis (LRSE) is an increasing concern. This study aimed to characterize genomic clusters, resistance mechanisms, and epidemiological links among LRSE isolates collected during a suspected outbreak in two Austrian hospitals. A confirmed case was defined as a patient with LRSE (MIC > 4 mg/L) isolated from clinical or screening samples in Hospital A or Hospital B between March 2023 and April 2025. All isolates underwent whole-genome sequencing (WGS) for typing and identification of resistance determinants. Epidemiological data, including the hospital and ward of detection as well as inter-hospital transfers, were analyzed to explore potential epidemiological links between cases. A total of 53 LRSE cases were identified, including 22 in Hospital A and 31 in Hospital B. A LZD-resistant Staphylococcus hominis isolate originating from a patient admitted to Hospital B after traveling abroad and no epidemiological link with the LRSE cases was also recovered. Epidemiological and genomic data identified five clusters belonging to three sequence types (ST2, ST5, ST22). Most Cluster 1 cases were detected in Hospital B, especially in the surgical ICU, while Clusters 2-4 were exclusively identified in Hospital A. However, the available epidemiological information was insufficient to determine transmission direction or identify the origin of the clusters. Forty-five of 53 LRSE isolates displayed high-level LZD resistance (MIC ≥48 mg/L). Distinct resistance-associated mutations were identified in each ST, including G2576U in ST2 isolates, C2534U and U2504A in ST22 isolates, and characteristic alterations in ribosomal proteins L3 and L4. Genomic analysis identified five distinct LRSE clusters belonging to three STs and revealed ST-specific resistance mutations, suggesting multiple independent evolutionary pathways to LZD resistance. However, limited epidemiological information, including incomplete data on LZD administration and patient movements, prevented definitive assessment of transmission dynamics. Our findings demonstrate the utility of WGS for the detection and characterization of LRSE clusters and highlight the importance of comprehensive epidemiological data for interpreting genomic links.

42995194.title: A Shock to the System: Vasopressors for Sepsis in Africa and Beyond.

42999837.title: Population Pharmacokinetics and Model-Informed Precision Dosing of Colistin Sulfate in Critically Ill Patients with Carbapenem-Resistant Gram-Negative Infections: A Prospective Pharmacokinetic-Pharmacodynamic Study.
42999837.abstract: Independently evaluated population pharmacokinetic models and clinically derived pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic targets for colistin sulfate remain limited. We aimed to develop and evaluate a model, explore an efficacy threshold, and construct a research model-informed precision dosing calculator. This prospective study included 55 critically ill patients with microbiologically confirmed infection caused by carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacteria (CR-GNB) for model development and 15 with suspected CR-GNB infection without microbiological confirmation for independent evaluation of concentration predictions. Plasma concentrations were measured by validated ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Modeling used nonlinear mixed-effects modeling software (NONMEM). Logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis assessed efficacy predictors and the exploratory threshold. Monte Carlo simulations evaluated probability of target attainment (PTA). A two-compartment model with creatinine clearance (CrCL) as a covariate on clearance (CL) best described the data (typical CL = 6.67 × (CrCL/76.9)0.648 L/h). Independent evaluation yielded a relative root mean square error of 37.4%, with 53.7% of predictions within ±30% of observations. Clinical efficacy was achieved in 24/55 patients. The ratio of 24-hour steady-state area under the concentration-time curve (AUCss,24h) to minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II) score were independently associated with efficacy (odds ratios per one-unit increase, 1.04 and 0.81, respectively). The exploratory AUCss,24h/MIC cut-off was 40.53 (area under the ROC curve, 0.712). At MIC ≥ 1 mg/L, no evaluated monotherapy regimen achieved PTA ≥ 90% in patients with normal or augmented renal function. This study provides a pharmacokinetic model with preliminary independent predictive evaluation, an exploratory exposure threshold, and an open-access research dosing calculator. Prospective multicenter validation is required before clinical implementation.

42999829.title: Boerhaave Syndrome: Case Report on a Rare Complication of Semaglutide Use.
42999829.abstract: Esophageal perforation is a rare but life-threatening condition with high morbidity and mortality, particularly when diagnosis is delayed. Boerhaave syndrome, a spontaneous esophageal rupture often triggered by forceful emesis, can present variably and is frequently difficult to recognize early. We report the case of a 62-year-old female patient who developed Boerhaave syndrome two days after initiating semaglutide therapy for weight loss. She presented with intractable nausea, vomiting, and acute chest pain. The chest CT was concerning for esophageal perforation. She rapidly deteriorated into hypoxemic respiratory failure and septic shock. She underwent emergent thoracotomy with primary repair of the perforation. She continued to be treated for septic shock in the ICU, but ultimately she recovered and was discharged on hospital day 17. As GLP-1 use continues to expand, clinicians should maintain awareness of rare but life-threatening complications such as Boerhaave syndrome, as early recognition, prompt imaging, and timely surgical intervention are critical to improving outcomes.

42999903.title: Recurrent Unexplained Fever and Suspected Promazine Toxicity: Why Probable Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome Was Left Undiagnosed in a Healthcare Worker.
42999903.abstract: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a potentially fatal adverse reaction to dopamine-antagonist medication that can resemble sepsis. A 51-year-old woman working in healthcare experienced recurrent episodes of fever, confusion and muscle rigidity, with six hospital presentations over approximately 10 months. Her prescribed medicines included promazine and amitriptyline. During an earlier severe admission, she developed hyperthermia, agitation, shock, and a creatine kinase concentration of 7272 U/L, requiring intensive care. Investigations did not identify a unifying diagnosis. During the most recent admission, review of previous records and a non-judgemental discussion elicited possible use of additional medication for sleep and neuropathic pain, although the preparation and quantity remained unclear. Six months' supply of promazine had been approved and dispensed within the preceding three months, supporting increased access without establishing the amount ingested. The clinical pattern supported a working diagnosis of probable promazine-associated NMS, with possible concomitant amitriptyline toxicity. Promazine was discontinued three days after admission. At follow-up approximately six months later, the patient remained off promazine and reported sustained symptom resolution and no further hospital attendances. This case highlights the importance of considering NMS in unexplained fever during antipsychotic treatment, conducting repeated medication reviews, and asking sensitive questions, regardless of a patient's professional healthcare background.

42999537.title: Acute Kidney Injury in East Africa in an Era of Converging Renal Stressors: A Multiple-Hit Narrative Review.
42999537.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) remains an important cause of morbidity and mortality in East Africa, where infectious disease, volume depletion, hemodynamic instability, and nephrotoxic exposure frequently occur in resource-constrained clinical settings. This review aimed to synthesize regional evidence through a multiple-hit framework focused on three modifiable renal stressor domains. A structured narrative review of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus was conducted for peer-reviewed human studies published from January 2012 to 18 August 2026 across the 18 Eastern African countries defined by the United Nations M49 framework. Eligible studies examined AKI in relation to volume depletion or hemodynamic compromise, infection or inflammatory illness, and/or nephrotoxic exposure. Of 902 records identified, 420 duplicates were removed, 482 records were screened, 66 full-text reports were assessed, and 45 studies were included. Evidence originated from only six countries: Ethiopia, Uganda, Tanzania, Kenya, Somalia/Somaliland, and Rwanda. Across adult, pediatric, neonatal, obstetric, infectious-disease, emergency, cardiac, and critical-care populations, AKI was associated with dehydration, hemorrhage, hypotension, shock, malaria, sepsis and other infections, nephrotoxic medications, iodinated contrast, and traditional or herbal medicines. The most consistently documented pattern was cohort-level clustering of more than one renal stressor domain within the same clinical populations. Individual-level coexistence was documented in selected studies, whereas detailed temporal sequencing was uncommon. Most studies assessed exposures separately and rarely examined cumulative effects, exposure timing, or statistical interaction. The currently available evidence from East Africa supports a multiple-hit perspective as a clinical organizing framework rather than a proven biological or prognostic model. Because the evidence is geographically concentrated, particularly in Ethiopia, Uganda, and Tanzania, these findings should not be interpreted as representative of all East African settings. Recurrent cohort-level clustering of infectious or inflammatory, hemodynamic, and nephrotoxic stressors was well documented, but patient-level coexistence and temporal sequence remain incompletely characterized. Prospective multicountry studies with patient-level temporal data are needed to determine whether the timing, overlap, duration, or combination of these stressors influences AKI severity, recovery, and longer-term outcomes.

42999535.title: Preliminary experience with controlled hypothermic storage of donor heart in combined heart transplantation.
42999535.abstract: While studies have demonstrated improved clinical outcomes with the use of controlled hypothermic storage (CHS) devices in isolated heart transplantation, it has not been evaluated in combined heart transplantation. In this small retrospective study (n=17), we evaluate clinical outcomes after combined heart-liver and heart-kidney transplantation in recipients of donor hearts preserved with conventional ice cold storage (ICS, n=10) versus CHS (n=7). The study found severe early graft dysfunction (EGD) occurred more frequently in the ICS cohort when compared to the CHS cohort (70% vs 0%, respectively). In addition, the CHS cohort had shorter median intensive care unit length of stay (7 days compared to 15.5 days, respectively) as well as fewer post-transplant complications, including sepsis (60% in ICS and 28.6% in CHS), pneumonia (40% in ICS and 14.3% in CHS), stroke (30% in ICS and 0% in CHS), and acute kidney injury requiring dialysis (60% in ICS and 28.6% in CHS). These preliminary findings suggest CHS may improve outcomes in combined heart transplantation.

43000297.title: Impact of rapid pathogen detection in ICU patients with suspected pneumonia on antimicrobial therapy: randomized, controlled open-label feasibility trial (IRISPAT-1).
43000297.abstract: Evidence that multiplex polymerase chain reaction (mPCR) improves antimicrobial therapy and clinical outcomes in the critical care setting is limited. We assessed the impact of rapid mPCR on antibiotic therapy in mechanically ventilated critically ill patients with suspected pneumonia. IRISPAT-1 was a single center, randomized, controlled open-label trial designed to determine the feasibility, safety, and potential impact of rapid respiratory pathogen detection on antibiotic therapy in mechanically ventilated critically ill patients with suspected pneumonia. Mechanically ventilated adults with suspected pneumonia and treated with new antibiotics within 24 h were randomized to standard care or mPCR using BioFire® FilmArray® Pneumonia Panel in addition to standard care (FA Pneumonia Panel group). Primary outcome was time interval (hours) to appropriate antimicrobial therapy. Forty mechanically ventilated patients with suspected pneumonia were randomized (20 = standard care, 20 = FA Pneumonia Panel) between July 7, 2024 and October 4, 2025. Median (IQR) time to appropriate antibiotic therapy was shorter in the FA Pneumonia Panel group compared to the standard care group (7 [5-16] vs. 72 [41-140] hours, HR 3.3; 95%CI [1.6, 6.6], p = 0.001). Adherence to treatment algorithm was observed in 90% (18/20) of patients in the FA Pneumonia Panel group. There were no differences in use of broad-spectrum antibiotics, duration of antibiotics, ventilator free days or vasopressor free days and 28-day mortality between treatment groups. Rapid mPCR with high adherence to antibiotic algorithms shortened time to appropriate antibiotics compared to standard care in mechanically ventilated patients with suspected pneumonia. Registered at clinicaltrials.gov (NCT06478953) on June 23, 2024.

43000261.title: High 28-day mortality in resistant gram-negative bloodstream infections in the ICU: retrospective cohort study.
43000261.abstract: Hospital-acquired bloodstream infections (BSI) caused by carbapenem-resistant and difficult-to-treat resistant (DTR) Gram-negative bacteria are a global threat associated with high mortality in (ICUs). The aim of this study was to evaluate 28-day mortality, independent risk factors, and the effect of empirical treatment on survival in ICU patients who developed BSI due to carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, and DTR Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This retrospective observational study was conducted in the anesthesia ICUs of a 700-bed tertiary-care hospital between January 2020 and August 2025. Adult patients with hospital-acquired bloodstream infections caused by carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae, carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii, or DTR P. aeruginosa were included. The primary outcome was 28-day all-cause mortality. Demographic, clinical, microbiological, and treatment-related factors associated with mortality were evaluated. Of the patients included in the study, 87.4% (n = 585) died within the 28-day follow-up period. The most frequently isolated pathogen was A. baumannii (58.3%), with 80.9% of isolates identified as extensively drug-resistant (XDR) and 13.1% as pandrug-resistant (PDR). In multivariate logistic regression analysis, advanced age (OR 1.03, p = 0.009), higher SOFA score on the day of bacteremia (OR 1.13, p = 0.009), presence of COVID-19 co-infection (OR 3.96, p = 0.034), and aminoglycoside resistance (OR 3.68, p = 0.014) were identified as independent predictors of 28-day mortality. Initiation of appropriate empirical antimicrobial therapy within the first 24 h did not show an independent effect on survival in multivariate analysis (OR 1.24, p = 0.576). Carbapenem-resistant and DTR Gram-negative BSI developing in ICUs located in endemic regions are associated with a high mortality rate. The main determinants of mortality are the clinical severity at the time of infection (high SOFA score), COVID-19 co-infection, and accompanying antibiotic resistance. In this critically ill patient population, the effect of early appropriate empirical therapy on survival may have been influenced by factors such as disease severity and organ dysfunction. Not applicable.

43002827.title: Direct ICU admission versus floor-to-ICU upgrade in geriatric patients with multiple rib fractures and flail chest: A national analysis.
43002827.journal: The American journal of emergency medicine
43002827.abstract: It remains unclear whether direct ICU admission benefits geriatric patients compared with delayed floor-to-ICU upgrade. The study evaluated the association of direct ICU admission versus floor-to-ICU upgrade with clinical outcomes in geriatric trauma patients with flail chest and thoracic injury, stratified by oxygenation compromise, frailty, and rib fracture burden. This retrospective cohort study used the 2017-2024 ACS-TQIP-PUF to identify patients aged 65 years or older with blunt trauma, flail chest, at least three rib fractures, an Injury Severity Score of 9 or greater, and thoracic injury. Patients were classified as floor admission without ICU upgrade, direct ICU admission, or floor-to-ICU upgrade. The primary adjusted analysis compared direct ICU admission with floor-to-ICU upgrade, using floor-to-ICU upgrade as the reference group. A total of 6743 patients were included. Mortality did not differ significantly between direct ICU admission and floor-to-ICU upgrade in the primary adjusted analysis (aOR 0.732, 95% CI 0.467-1.148, p = 0.174). Direct ICU admission was associated with lower odds of unplanned intubation (aOR 0.355, 95% CI 0.251-0.502, p < 0.001), ARDS (aOR 0.412, 95% CI 0.172-0.987, p = 0.047), sepsis (aOR 0.352, 95% CI 0.171-0.725, p = 0.005), and DVT (aOR 0.444, 95% CI 0.209-0.942, p = 0.034). Mortality was lower with direct ICU admission among patients with 3-5 documented rib fractures (aOR 0.535, 95% CI 0.296-0.969, p = 0.039), and the association with fewer unplanned intubations persisted across all subgroups. In the secondary analysis, both direct ICU admission and floor-to-ICU upgrade were associated with higher mortality, lower odds of discharge home, and fewer ventilator-free days than floor admission without ICU upgrade. Direct ICU admission was associated with lower odds of unplanned intubation, ARDS, sepsis, and DVT compared with floor-to-ICU upgrade. These findings support identifying at-risk geriatric rib fracture patients for direct ICU admission before deterioration occurs.

43001781.title: Draft genome sequences of two Stenotrophomonas muris isolates, CBAS 1154 and CBAS 1234, recovered from patients with ICU-acquired ventilator-associated sepsis.
authors: Ribeiro Gomes de Queiroz Crespo I
43001781.abstract: We report the high-quality draft genome sequences of two clinical Stenotrophomonas muris isolates recovered from the lower respiratory tract of intensive care unit patients with ventilator-associated sepsis in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Based on our review of the available literature, we found no previous records of this species from Brazil.

43001150.title: Development and Validation of a Machine Learning‑based Prediction Model for ICU‑Acquired Weakness in Critically Ill Patients: A Prospective Multicenter Cohort Study.
43001150.abstract: ICU-acquired weakness (ICU-AW) is a common and devastating complication of critical illness associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation and increased mortality, whereas externally validated tools for early risk stratification remain insufficient. This study aimed to construct and validate machine learning models to predict ICU-AW risk in critically ill patients. A total of 535 patients from three medical centers were divided into a training set (n = 276), an internal validation set (n = 119) and an external validation cohort (n = 140). Candidate predictors were restricted to variables available within the first 48 hours of ICU admission. Five algorithms including logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), classification and regression tree (CART) and XGBoost were trained with 10-fold cross-validated grid search and compared using DeLong tests. Six predictors were retained: age, Glasgow Coma Scale score, SOFA score, sepsis, renal failure and hypoalbuminemia. All five models displayed favorable predictive capacity in the internal validation set (AUROC 0.906-0.939). In external validation, SVM (0.853, 95% CI 0.779-0.915) and LR (0.841, 0.765-0.906) outperformed RF (0.802), XGBoost (0.790) and CART (0.685), and the difference between SVM and LR was not statistically significant (DeLong P = 0.085). Tree-based algorithms presented near-perfect apparent performance that attenuated markedly in the external cohort, indicating overfitting. The LR model, which offered statistically comparable discrimination with full transparency, was converted into a nomogram (external AUROC 0.841) with positive net clinical benefit across threshold probabilities of 1-81%. A six-predictor logistic model based on variables available within 48 hours of ICU admission predicted ICU-AW comparably to tuned machine learning classifiers and showed stable cross-center performance. The nomogram may assist early risk stratification, and prospective studies are warranted to confirm whether model-guided care improves patient outcomes.

43003685.title: Cold septic shock: recognising the low-output phenotype.
43003685.abstract: Septic shock is commonly taught as a warm, vasodilated state, but the cold, low-output phenotype, in which the underlying process is still sepsis but cardiac output is low and vascular resistance high, is under-recognised. Escalating vasopressors alone in these patients support the blood pressure while leaving the low output untreated. I describe how I separate low from high cardiac output shock at the bedside using peripheries, pulse pressure and central venous oxygen saturation and where cold septic shock and its mechanisms sit within this framework. The phenotype is recognised at the bedside, whereas identifying the underlying mechanism usually requires echocardiography. The central principle is to treat the haemodynamic phenotype, not the label.

43002258.title: Predictors of postoperative infections in a tertiary neurosurgical center.
43002258.abstract: Postoperative infections are common neurosurgical complications with considerable morbidity. We assessed the incidence, type and outcomes of postoperative infections in a pragmatic cohort of non-ICU neurosurgical patients. Demographics, medical history, operative details, perioperative interventions and hospitalization metrics were prospectively collected. Patients requiring intensive care unit hospitalization were excluded. 137 postoperative infection events were recorded in 126 patients. Of 137 infections, pneumonia accounted for 70.1%, urinary tract infection for 10.2%, central-line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) for 3.6%, bacteremia of undetermined source for 5.1%, surgical site infection (SSI) for 9.5% and meningitis for 1.5%. The hospitalization was extended due to postoperative infection in 10.5% of operations, while 0.8% of the patients died. Independent factors associated with postoperative infection after multivariable analysis were age (adjusted OR 1.017, 95% CI 1.002-1.033), immobilization > 24 h (aOR 2.91, 95% CI 1.62-5.24), indwelling foley catheter > 48 h (aOR 4, 95% CI 2.01-7.99), central venous catheter (CVC) > 48 h (aOR 3.99, 95% CI 1.64-9.74), foreign material insertion (aOR 5.15, 95% CI 2.61-10.15) and spinal compared to cranial surgery (aOR 4.90, 95% CI 2.63-9.15). Independent factors associated with postoperative infection included older age, immobilization beyond 24 h, retention of urinary and central venous catheters beyond 48 h and foreign-material insertion; prolonged operative time was associated specifically with postoperative pneumonia. Aggressive preoperative and postoperative measures utilizing ERAS-like protocols may reduce infection burden and optimize outcomes. These findings validate infection risk factors specifically within the ward-level neurosurgical population and should not be extrapolated to patients requiring ICU management.

43002070.title: Association Between the Neutrophil:Lymphocyte Ratio After Hospitalization for Sepsis and Long-Term Outcomes: A Population-Based Cohort Study.
43002070.abstract: Long-term outcomes after sepsis survival remain poor. No clinical laboratory tests are in use for stratifying long-term risk after sepsis, limiting the development of secondary prevention. The peripheral blood neutrophil:lymphocyte ratio (NLR) reflects innate and adaptive immune cell balance, and may reflect an immune milieu which is associated with long-term risk after sepsis. Accordingly, we evaluated the association between the NLR in the weeks after sepsis hospitalization discharge-a time when patients are routinely seen in post-ICU clinics-and long-term outcomes. Population-based cohort study. Ontario, Canada, 2010-2020. Adults discharged alive from a sepsis hospitalization. None. The exposure was the first outpatient NLR-derived from the complete blood count-measured 15-90 days after sepsis discharge. Among 37,250 survivors with available NLR, the median (interquartile range [IQR]) time-to-measurement was 34 days (22-54 d), and the median NLR was 2.7 (1.8-4.2). Within 1 year, 17,732 patients (47.6%) were rehospitalized or died (median [IQR] time-to-event, 82 d [27-185 d]). The frequency of rehospitalization or death increased across increasing NLR quartiles: 34.2%, 41.5%, 50.3%, and 64.4% (ptrend < 0.001). Compared with the lowest quartile, adjusted hazard ratios (95% CI) were 1.24 (1.18-1.29), 1.54 (1.48-1.62), and 2.25 (2.15-2.35) across higher quartiles. For most patients, NLR after sepsis returned to its patient-specific presepsis ambient level, which was itself prognostic. Among sepsis survivors, outpatient NLR measured 15-90 days after discharge is strongly associated with 1-year risk of rehospitalization or death. As a simple, widely available biomarker, the NLR may support early postsepsis risk stratification and inform development of secondary prevention strategies.

43003286.title: Clinicobacteriological profile, Mortality Predictors and Antimicrobial Resistance in Necrotising Soft Tissue Infections: A prospective study.
43003286.abstract: Necrotising soft tissue infections (NSTIs) are rapidly progressive infections requiring prompt diagnosis and management. This study assessed predictors of mortality, microbiological spectrum, antimicrobial resistance patterns, and differences between polymicrobial and monomicrobial NSTIs in a prospective manner. This study enrolled patients aged 15 years or older with clinically suspected NSTIs who presented between March 2022 and February 2023. Clinical, laboratory, surgical, and outcome data were collected. Tissue and pus samples were processed for aerobic and anaerobic cultures. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed according to CLSI guidelines. Mortality-associated factors were analysed using univariate analysis, binary logistic regression, and survival analysis. Eighty-seven patients were included, predominantly male (87.3%), with a median age of 47.5 years. Extremities were most commonly affected. The mortality rate of this cohort was 25.3%. Polymicrobial infections predominated (49.4%), while monomicrobial NSTIs were associated with higher mortality (p = 0.022). Gram-negative organisms, particularly Acinetobacter baumannii and Escherichia coli, were the most frequent pathogens. Obligate anaerobes were significantly associated with polymicrobial infections. Chronic liver disease (p = 0.003) and systemic toxicity (p = 0.018) independently predicted mortality, whereas higher haemoglobin levels were protective. High antimicrobial resistance was observed, including carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii and Enterobacterales. Among the anaerobes, resistance to clindamycin and cefoxitin, along with reduced susceptibility to metronidazole, was reported. NSTIs remain associated with substantial mortality, especially in monomicrobial infections due to multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. Early recognition, prompt surgery, and region-specific empirical antimicrobial therapy are crucial for improving outcomes.

43002075.title: The Post-Sepsis Neutrophil: Lymphocyte Ratio: A Population Signal in Search of Individual Meaning.

42985168.title: The efficacy of taurolidine lock solution in preventing catheter-related bloodstream infections in pediatrics: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42985168.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety of taurolidine lock solutions in preventing catheter-related bloodstream infections in pediatric patients with central venous access devices. This meta-analysis systematically searched four electronic databases to identify studies comparing taurolidine with standard lock solutions for catheter lock in pediatric patients. The primary outcome measure was the incidence density of catheter-related bloodstream infections. Secondary outcomes included the incidence density of central line-associated bloodstream infection, cumulative incidence of catheter-related bloodstream infections, catheter removal due to infection, central venous access device (CVAD)-related thrombosis, and adverse events. Random-effects models were used to pool incidence rate ratios (IRRs) for incidence-density outcomes and risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes, with corresponding 95% confidence intervals. In the primary analysis of five studies, taurolidine-containing catheter lock solutions were associated with a significantly lower incidence rate of catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBSI) compared with control solutions (IRR = 0.23, 95% CI: 0.15-0.36; I2 = 0%; P < 0.00001). The separate secondary analysis of three studies also showed a lower incidence density of central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI), although substantial heterogeneity was observed (IRR = 0.25, 95% CI: 0.08-0.85; I2 = 90%; P = 0.03). The cumulative incidence of catheter-related bloodstream infections was lower in the taurolidine group (RR = 0.37, 95% CI: 0.23-0.61; I2 = 54%; P = 0.0001). No statistically significant differences were detected in catheter removal due to infection (RR = 1.25, 95% CI: 0.60-2.62; I2 = 12%; P = 0.56), CVAD-related thrombosis (RR = 0.88, 95% CI: 0.29-2.64; I2 = 0%; P = 0.82), or adverse events (RR = 3.93, 95% CI: 0.82-18.80; I2 = 64%; P = 0.09). Taurolidine-containing lock solutions may reduce the incidence density and cumulative incidence of CRBSI in pediatric patients requiring central venous access. However, the available evidence is insufficient to establish their comparative safety. Given the substantial heterogeneity, mixed study designs, variability in infection definitions, and limited safety data, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Further large-scale, multicenter randomized controlled trials with adequate safety monitoring are needed before broad routine implementation can be recommended. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?ID=CRD420251162414 identifier, CRD420251162414.

43004255.title: The association of ICU admission time with mortality in patients with severe pneumonia requiring invasive mechanical ventilation: a retrospective, single-center, multicampus cohort study.
43004255.abstract: Nighttime admission to the intensive care unit (ICU) has been associated with worse outcomes in some critically ill populations. However, evidence specific to patients with severe pneumonia is limited. We evaluated the association between ICU admission time and 30-day mortality among patients with severe pneumonia requiring invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV). We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with ICD-coded severe pneumonia who received IMV in four campuses at a tertiary medical center between 2020 and 2024. Patients were categorized according to their ICU admission time and our institutional staffing schedule: daytime admission (08:00-15:59) and nighttime admission (16:00-07:59 the following day). The primary outcome was 30-day mortality after ICU admission. Survival analysis and multivariable Cox regression were used to test the association between admission time and 30-day mortality. A total of 9,611 patients were included in the analysis. Among them, 6,058 patients were admitted at night, and 3,553 during the daytime. After 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM), 3,476 patients remained in each group. There was no statistically significant difference in 30-day mortality following ICU admission between the two groups (hazard ratio [HR], 1.00; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.92-1.09; P = 0.914). After adjustment for age, sex, relative weight, lactate, patient source, type of admission, and septic shock, multivariable Cox regression showed that daytime ICU admission was not an independent protective factor for 30-day mortality (adjusted HR, 1.01; 95% CI, 0.93-1.10; P = 0.794). In this cohort of patients with severe pneumonia requiring IMV, ICU admission timing was not significantly associated with 30-day mortality. The findings should be interpreted in light of residual confounding and the institution-specific staffing model.

43006428.title: Association of medication burden and potential drug-drug interactions with acute kidney injury among critically ill patients receiving anticancer therapy at a tertiary care centre.
43006428.journal: Journal of oncology pharmacy practice : official publication of the International Society of Oncology Pharmacy Practitioners
43006428.abstract: BackgroundCritically ill patients with cancer are exposed to many drugs, including anticancer agents, antimicrobials and supportive medications, which increases the risk of nephrotoxicity and potential drug-drug interactions (pDDIs). The contribution of medication burden and pDDIs to acute kidney injury (AKI) in this population is not well characterised.ObjectiveTo assess the association of medication burden and pDDIs with AKI among critically ill patients receiving anticancer therapy.MethodsThis retrospective observational study was conducted in the intensive care units (ICUs) of a tertiary care centre from August 2025 to September 2026. Adults with malignancy who received anticancer therapy within 30 days before or during ICU stay were included. AKI was defined and staged by KDIGO criteria. Medication burden (total drugs and nephrotoxic drugs) and pDDIs (screened using a standard interaction database) were recorded. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of AKI.ResultsOf 210 patients, 86 (41.0%) developed AKI. Patients with AKI had a higher median number of drugs (11 vs 8, p < 0.001) and pDDIs (6 vs 3, p < 0.001). Independent predictors of AKI were ≥10 distinct drugs (aOR 2.62; 95% CI 1.32-5.18), at least one nephrotoxicity-related pDDI (aOR 2.87; 95% CI 1.43-5.76), APACHE II score (aOR 1.09 per point), pre-existing CKD, sepsis, and cisplatin exposure. In-hospital mortality was higher with AKI (39.5% vs 21.8%, p = 0.007).ConclusionHigh medication burden and nephrotoxicity-related pDDIs were independently associated with AKI in critically ill cancer patients. Routine pharmacist-led medication review and renal-focused interaction screening may help reduce preventable kidney injury.

43005602.title: Development and Temporal Validation of an Interpretable Machine Learning Model for Classifying Linezolid Trough Concentrations in Critically Ill Patients.
43005602.abstract: Linezolid exposure is highly variable in critically ill patients, increasing the risk of subtherapeutic or supratherapeutic concentrations. This study aimed to develop an interpretable machine learning model for classifying steady-state linezolid trough concentrations as subtherapeutic (<2 mg/L), target (2-8 mg/L), or supratherapeutic (>8 mg/L), and to assess model performance in a temporally separated test cohort. This single-center retrospective study included 299 adult intensive care unit patients who received linezolid and underwent therapeutic drug monitoring between June 2023 and March 2026. Missing data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations, and Elastic Net was used for feature selection. Multinomial logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, and multilayer perceptron models were compared using five-fold cross-validation across five imputed datasets. The best-performing model was interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations. The six models were additionally evaluated in a temporal test cohort. Among the 299 patients, 37 (12.4%) had subtherapeutic, 186 (62.2%) target, and 76 (25.4%) supratherapeutic trough concentrations. Fifteen predictors were retained. CatBoost showed the best internal multiclass discrimination (AUROC 0.742, 95% CI 0.732-0.752; AUPRC 0.551, 95% CI 0.531-0.572). In the temporal test cohort, CatBoost achieved an AUROC of 0.754 (95% CI 0.684-0.826) and an AUPRC of 0.620 (95% CI 0.529-0.727). Estimated glomerular filtration rate was the most influential predictor, with additional contributions from inflammatory and hematologic indices, dosing variables, age, body mass index, and pathogen-related context. Routinely available clinical variables provided moderate discrimination among clinically distinct linezolid exposure categories, and performance was retained in a temporal test cohort. Because eGFR was the dominant predictor, the model may be most useful for flagging patients with altered renal function for earlier or more intensive TDM. Given its moderate discrimination and imperfect calibration, it should be regarded as a risk-stratification tool and should not be used for empirical dose modification without measured concentrations. Multicenter external and prospective validation is required before routine clinical implementation.

43004400.title: Multidisciplinary management of disseminated tuberculosis with tuberculous meningitis and active hepatitis B in a critically ill pregnant woman in the third trimester: a case report.
43004400.abstract: Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) in pregnancy is rare but life-threatening, with substantial maternal and fetal risks. Third-trimester disseminated tuberculosis involving the central nervous system with concurrent active hepatitis B infection has scarcely been reported, particularly among remote pastoral populations with limited healthcare access. This report highlights the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges of this triple comorbidity and underscores the value of multidisciplinary team (MDT) management in such complex scenarios. A 24-year-old pastoralist at 30 weeks of gestation presented with headache, vomiting, fever, and nuchal rigidity. Cerebrospinal fluidanalysis confirmed TBM, and chest computed tomography revealed diffuse miliary nodules suggestive of hematogenous disseminated tuberculosis. Serology was positive for hepatitis B surface antigen, e-antigen, and core antibody, indicating active viral replication. Given life-threatening intracranial hypertension [intracranial pressure (ICP) > 330 mmH2O] in late pregnancy, osmotic agents were withheld for fetal safety, and lumbar cisternal drainage was performed. An MDT comprising respiratory medicine, obstetrics, hepatology, pharmacy, and critical care nursing specialties was assembled. Anti-tuberculosis therapy was intensified to isoniazid, rifampicin, linezolid, and moxifloxacin; ethambutol was discontinued due to fetal optic neuritis, and tenofovir was added for hepatitis B management. Following stabilization, the patient was transferred to a higher-level facility at 35 weeks of gestation and underwent cesarean section at 36 weeks, delivering a live preterm female infant (2320 g, 1-min Apgar score of 8). Both mother and neonate were discharged without complications on December 1, 2025. This case demonstrates that early recognition, individualized anti-tuberculosis regimens, and coordinated multidisciplinary collaboration are critical for achieving favorable outcomes in pregnant patients with disseminated tuberculosis complicated by TBM and concurrent hepatitis B infection. The successful management relied on integrated critical care and a multidisciplinary approach, which proved effective even in resource-limited pastoral settings.

43009022.title: Sepsis in Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-Cell Therapy: A Six-Year Nationwide Analysis of Clinical Outcomes and Healthcare Resource Utilization in Hospitalizations for Hematologic Malignancies.
43009022.abstract: Patients receiving chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy are at increased risk for infection and sepsis due to malignancy-related immune dysfunction, lymphodepleting chemotherapy, and immunosuppression used to treat CAR T-cell toxicities; however, nationally representative estimates of sepsis burden and economic impact remain limited. This study uses nationally representative U.S. data to evaluate patient characteristics, clinical outcomes, and healthcare utilization associated with sepsis among hospitalizations involving CAR T-cell therapy. Adult hospitalizations for acute lymphoblastic leukemia, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, or multiple myeloma in which CAR T-cell therapy was administered between 2017 and 2022 were identified from the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) and stratified by sepsis status. After excluding records with missing covariates, survey-weighted analyses were performed to generate nationally representative estimates. Multivariable regression models were used to evaluate differences in mortality and secondary outcomes, with statistical significance defined as a two-sided p value < 0.05. Among 10,450 weighted CAR T-cell therapy hospitalizations, 645 (6.2%) were complicated by sepsis. In-hospital mortality was significantly higher in hospitalizations with sepsis (28.7% vs 1.1%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 33.96; 95% confidence interval [CI] 18.67-61.75). Sepsis was independently associated with higher odds of acute kidney injury (aOR 4.31), respiratory failure (aOR 11.85), acute hepatic failure (aOR 44.42), and septic shock (aOR 411.05), along with greater use of renal replacement therapy, mechanical ventilation, and vasopressors. Thrombohemorrhagic events were more frequent among hospitalizations with sepsis, including disseminated intravascular coagulation (aOR 9.30), acute venous thromboembolism (aOR 2.95), acute coronary syndrome (aOR 27.63), acute ischemic stroke (aOR 7.53), gastrointestinal hemorrhage (aOR 6.47), and intracranial hemorrhage (aOR 4.84), as well as increased need for cryoprecipitate and fresh frozen plasma transfusion (aOR 2.70). Sepsis was also associated with longer hospital stay (adjusted incidence rate ratio [aIRR] 1.96) and higher hospitalization charges (adjusted charge ratio [aCR] 1.22). Sepsis was documented in approximately 6% of CAR T-cell hospitalizations and was associated with higher in-hospital mortality, organ dysfunction, critical-care utilization, longer hospitalization, and higher hospitalization charges. These findings highlight the substantial clinical and healthcare burden associated with sepsis in this population.

43007959.title: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococci: Local epidemiology and clinical outcomes.
43007959.abstract: Aim: To study local epidemiology, antimicrobial susceptibility patterns, and clinical outcomes of VRE infections among inpatients. Materials and Methods: A retrospective observational study was carried out on all patients admitted with culture-confirmed Vancomycin-resistant enterococci infections between July 2025 and January 2026 in Najaf, Iraq. Data on demographic characteristics, clinical information, antimicrobial exposure, microbiological findings, and outcomes were obtained from medical records. Results: A total of 84 patients with Vancomycin-resistant enterococci infection were included. The mean age was 56 ± 18 years, and 57.1% were male. Prior antibiotic exposure was seen in 75.0% of the patients, while 33.3% had previously received Vancomycin therapy. Enterococcus faecium was the predominant species 73.8%, followed by Enterococcus faecalis 21.4%. All isolates were resistant to Vancomycin, while resistance rates against ampicillin, ciprofloxacin, and high-level gentamicin were 70.2%, 63.1%, and 52.4% respectively. Susceptibility to linezolid and daptomycin was still high (97.6% and 98.8% respectively). Urine was the most common specimen source 40.5%, followed by blood cultures 26.2%. In terms of clinical outcomes, 36.9% were admitted to the ICU, 26.2% had a bloodstream infection, 21.4% needed mechanical ventilation, 14.3% had septic shock, and there was an overall mortality rate of 23.8%. Conclusions: infections due to Vancomycin-resistant enterococci impose a huge healthcare burden in our setting; E. faecium is the leading species and is multidrug resistant. It was, however, associated with significant mortality despite preserved susceptibility to linezolid and daptomycin. Therefore, continuous surveillance coupled with antimicrobial stewardship and strict infection control practices is needed to contain the spread and impact of VRE infections.

43005159.title: Global trends and emerging frontiers in neutrophil extracellular trap-related sepsis research: a bibliometric analysis.
43005159.abstract: Sepsis remains a major challenge in critical care medicine, and NETs have emerged as important regulators linking inflammation, immunity, coagulation, and tissue injury. However, the global development trajectory and research frontiers of NET-related sepsis studies remain unclear. Publications related to NET-related sepsis research from 2004 to September 19, 2026, were independently retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus databases. After database-specific screening, 263 WoSCC records and 499 Scopus records were retained for separate analyses using VOSviewer and CiteSpace to evaluate publication trends, collaboration networks, knowledge structures, thematic evolution, and emerging research attention. The WoSCC and Scopus analytical datasets contained 263 and 499 records, respectively. WoSCC analysis showed that China had the highest publication output, whereas the United States had the highest citation impact and collaboration strength among the listed countries. Cleaned author-keyword analysis highlighted sepsis, neutrophil extracellular traps, NETosis, inflammation, neutrophil, platelet, acute lung injury, and septic shock. Cross-database comparison showed a high correlation in complete-year publication trends (Spearman's ρ = 0.986) and partial overlap in high-frequency author keywords. Independent database analyses indicate sustained growth and a progressively interconnected knowledge structure in NET-related sepsis research. The results describe publication, collaboration, citation, and thematic attention patterns; they do not establish biomarker performance or therapeutic efficacy. Future studies may benefit from standardized NET measurement and reporting, multicenter validation of NET-related biomarkers and predictive models, and appropriately designed clinical investigations.

43008776.title: Fibrinolytic Response to Protein C Zymogen and Plasma in Sepsis-Associated Purpura Fulminans: A Case Series of Nine Consecutive Patients.
43008776.journal: Clinical and applied thrombosis/hemostasis : official journal of the International Academy of Clinical and Applied Thrombosis/Hemostasis
43008776.abstract: Purpura fulminans (PF) is a rare and life-threatening manifestation of disseminated intravascular coagulation, leading to multiorgan failure. Protein C (PC) zymogen supplementation has a strong pathophysiological rationale, but its effects on the viscoelastic fibrinolytic profile have not been described. We retrospectively analyzed nine patients (six adults, three children) admitted to our intensive care units between 2017 and 2025 with PF associated with septic shock, treated with PC zymogen concentrate and fresh frozen plasma (FFP). In the six adults, PC and fibrinolysis were measured before and a median of 13 hours after the PC loading dose, fibrinolysis with modified viscoelastic hemostatic assays (urokinase-modified thromboelastography [UK-TEG] in three, tissue plasminogen activator test [TPA-test, ClotPro] in three). Median (interquartile range) PC rose from 23 (10-31)% to 102 (63-137)% and Lysis, the percentage of clot lysis at the modified assays, from 15 (0-47)% to 78 (60-100)%. All six patients had fibrinolysis resistance before treatment. Lysis increased in five and returned within the reference interval in one; in the three TPA-test patients, lysis time became measurable after treatment but remained above 300 s. Three patients died and four required surgery for necrotic skin or soft tissue lesions. PC and FFP administration was followed by a partial recovery of the fibrinolytic response, which cannot be attributed to PC alone, since plasma was given at the same time. Modified viscoelastic assays may help monitor the response to PC and plasma therapy.

43007330.title: Elevated Neutrophil-to-Lymphocyte Ratio Predicts Early Aggravation of Organ Dysfunction in Septic Patients in the Emergency Department.
43007330.abstract: To investigate whether neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), a simple marker of immune dysregulation, is associated with early organ dysfunction progression in emergency department (ED) patients with sepsis. Exploratory secondary analysis of observational clustering cohort. Single-center ED. Among 999 patients with adjudicated infection, 364 fulfilled Sepsis-3 criteria for sepsis or septic shock and had available Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) scores at admission and 24 hours. None. Organ dysfunction trajectory was defined according to the evolution in SOFA score during the first 24 hours (ΔSOFA) and categorized as improving (ΔSOFA ≤ -2), stable (ΔSOFA -1 to +1), or worsening (ΔSOFA ≥ +2). Of the 364 patients, 135 (37%) were classified as improving, 187 (51%) as stable, and 42 (12%) as worsening. NLR differed significantly across trajectory groups, with median values of 12 (7-21), 12 (7-22), and 23 (10-37), respectively (p = 0.015). In multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, lactate concentration, and baseline SOFA score, NLR remained independently associated with worsening organ dysfunction trajectory (odds ratio [OR] 5.55, 95% CI, 1.86-18.18; p = 0.003). Patients with worsening trajectories more frequently required ICU admission (26% vs. 5% vs. 4%; p < 0.001) and experienced higher 28-day mortality (36% vs 17% vs 17%; p = 0.013). NLR was independently associated with early worsening of organ dysfunction in ED patients with sepsis. Beyond its prognostic value, NLR may provide complementary information to conventional severity assessment by reflecting immune dysregulation.

43005943.title: Apigenin Attenuates Lipopolysaccharide-Induced Endothelial Activation and Injury-Associated Phenotypes in Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells.
43005943.abstract: Sepsis represents a severe challenge in critical‑care medicine. Protecting endothelial function and alleviating microvascular inflammation and oxidative stress help reduce sepsis‑associated mortality. Apigenin, a natural flavonoid, exerts anti‑inflammatory and anti‑oxidant effects; its mechanisms against endothelial injury relevant to sepsis remain unclear. This study combined computational biology and in‑vitro assays to explore potential targets of apigenin against lipopolysaccharide‑triggered endothelial dysfunction. Network pharmacology was performed for target screening followed by GO and KEGG enrichment. Transcriptomic profiles were analyzed. Molecular docking and 100‑ns molecular dynamics simulations predicted apigenin‑protein interactions. An LPS‑stimulated HUVECs injury model was established. qRT-PCR, ELISA, flow cytometry and fluorescent probes were used to evaluate inflammation, apoptosis, reactive oxygen species and monocyte adhesion. A total of 104 intersecting targets were identified. AKT1, HSP90AA1, EGFR, ESR1 and HIF1A were potential core candidates, with PI3K‑Akt, TNF and HIF‑1 signaling possibly involved. Simulations predicted relatively stable apigenin‑protein complexes. At 40 μM, apigenin mitigated LPS‑provoked inflammatory response, oxidative stress, apoptosis and monocyte adhesion in HUVECs. Apigenin protects HUVECs from LPS‑induced endothelial injury possibly via multi‑target and multi‑pathway patterns. This study provides preliminary computational and in vitro evidence for further investigation of apigenin against LPS-triggered endothelial injury, with potential implications for sepsis-associated vascular damage that requires further in vivo validation.

43005929.title: Hemorrhagic Cardiac Tamponade in an End-Stage Renal Disease Patient on Apixaban.
43005929.abstract: Direct oral anticoagulants are used for stroke prevention in selected patients with atrial fibrillation who receive hemodialysis. Randomized trial data remain limited in this population, and the anticoagulant effect of a given dose may vary considerably between patients. We report a 56-year-old man receiving hemodialysis three times weekly who was taking apixaban 5 mg twice daily and developed persistent hypotension and abdominal pain during dialysis. The early findings suggested dialysis-associated hypotension or sepsis. Emergency department point-of-care cardiac ultrasound showed a large circumferential pericardial effusion, leading to urgent cardiology evaluation for obstructive shock. Computed tomography obtained during the same evaluation described the effusion as large and possibly hemorrhagic. Pericardiocentesis was unsuccessful because most of the fluid was posterior. Shortly after transfer to the intensive care unit, the patient developed pulseless electrical activity arrest and underwent an emergent subxiphoid pericardial window. Approximately 450 mL of bloody fluid was drained, followed by hemodynamic improvement. Cytology showed no malignant cells, and fluid cultures were negative. This case also highlights the uncertainty surrounding the use of full-dose apixaban in patients receiving hemodialysis, particularly after a major bleeding event.

43005796.title: Gut microbiota-host co-metabolism in sepsis and critical illness: source, compartment, immune state, and host defense.
43005796.abstract: Critical illness can profoundly disturb the intestinal microbiota-metabolite-host immune axis through the combined effects of shock, hypoxia, altered nutritional intake, antimicrobial exposure, organ dysfunction, and impaired epithelial barrier integrity. These changes can reshape microbial metabolic capacity, host co-metabolism, and systemic metabolite exposure, while the host may simultaneously exhibit overlapping features of hyperinflammation, immune tolerance, lymphocyte dysfunction, impaired antimicrobial defense, and tissue repair. Metabolites generated through microbial metabolism or shared microbial-host pathways may therefore contribute to immune reprogramming, although their effects are highly context dependent and cannot be regarded as uniformly beneficial or detrimental. This narrative review examines short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan-derived indoles, secondary bile acids, succinate, lactate, trimethylamine N-oxide, polyamines, and aromatic metabolites, with particular attention to source attribution, anatomical compartment, host co-metabolism, receptor signaling, and their potential influence on antimicrobial immunity. These metabolites may act through G-protein-coupled receptors, AhR, PXR, FXR, TGR5, VDR, HIF-1α, inflammasome pathways, mitochondrial signaling, and epigenetic mechanisms to modulate macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells, innate lymphoid cells, T lymphocytes, epithelial barriers, and endothelial responses. The direction and magnitude of these effects are likely to vary according to timing, concentration, anatomical compartment, immune-cell state, pathogen burden, and renal or hepatic clearance. Within this framework, attenuation of inflammatory signaling may help limit early collateral tissue injury, yet the same response could become disadvantageous when antimicrobial competence is already impaired. Similarly, succinate and lactate may reflect or contribute to distinct inflammatory, regulatory, or reparative programs depending on whether they arise from microbial or host metabolism and whether they act within intracellular or extracellular compartments. Human studies in critically ill populations have linked dysbiosis and metabolomic alterations with secondary infection, prolonged organ support, and mortality; however, most have not been able to resolve microbial source attribution or establish causal mediation. Future work would therefore benefit from integrating longitudinal microbiome, metabolome, immune-function, and organ-clearance measurements with source-resolved approaches, including isotope tracing, as well as state-specific and trajectory-informed clinical endpoints. Microbiome-directed interventions may be most appropriately investigated as context-dependent modulators of host defense rather than as broadly anti-inflammatory strategies.

43005361.title: Biomarkers for differential diagnosis of myocarditis, acute coronary syndrome, and sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy.
43005361.abstract: Diagnosing acute myocardial injury remains a significant challenge in contemporary cardiovascular and critical care medicine. Myocarditis, acute coronary syndrome (ACS), and sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy (SICM) frequently present with overlapping features, chest pain, elevated cardiac biomarkers, and electrocardiographic abnormalities, yet require divergent management, making rapid and accurate etiological diagnosis essential for optimal patient outcomes. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the pathophysiology and biomarker signatures of myocarditis, ACS, and SICM, and examines how these signatures can be integrated into a practical diagnostic approach for the emergency department and intensive care unit. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) remains the central biomarker of acute myocardial injury, but its kinetics differ across the three conditions. A steep rise and fall in ACS, a sustained moderate elevation in myocarditis, and a gradual, severity-parallel course in sepsis. Among complementary biomarkers, C-reactive protein lacks specificity, whereas procalcitonin supports the recognition of bacterial sepsis in SICM, and natriuretic peptides reflect myocardial wall stress, disproportionately elevated relative to troponin in SICM. Emerging molecular biomarkers, circulating microRNAs (like miR-4763-3p and miR-155) and extracellular matrix remodeling markers, show promise for distinguishing inflammatory from ischemic myocardial injury, but remain investigational owing to the lack of standardized assays and practical constraints on acute bedside use. Therefore diagnosis rests on an integrated, multimodal assessment. The differential diagnosis of acute myocardial injury requires a systematic, biomarker-centered multimodal approach. Future research should prioritize the prospective validation of multi-biomarker panels and the development of rapid non-invasive tools to reduce reliance on emergency coronary angiography.

43005274.title: Comparative effectiveness of enoxaparin versus unfractionated heparin for 30- and 90-day mortality in sepsis patients without severe renal dysfunction: a retrospective cohort study.
43005274.abstract: Although enoxaparin is known to be superior to UFH for thromboprophylaxis, the comparative effect of enoxaparin versus UFH on mortality in sepsis remains unknown. To address this gap, we compared the two agents in sepsis patients without severe renal impairment, thereby minimizing confounding due to differential drug clearance. In this retrospective cohort study, we analyzed data from the eICU Collaborative Research Database. We included adult patients with sepsis and no severe renal impairment (eGFR ≥ 30 mL/min/1.73 m2) who received prophylactic anticoagulation with either enoxaparin or UFH. The primary outcomes were 30-day ICU mortality and 90-day in-hospital mortality. Survival analyses were performed using Kaplan-Meier estimates and Cox proportional hazards models. Sensitivity analyses were conducted using inverse probability of treatment weighting. A total of 2,341 patients were enrolled (1,260 in the enoxaparin group and 1,081 in the UFH group). After adjusting for confounders, multivariate Cox regression showed that the hazard ratio (HR) for enoxaparin versus UFH was 0.94 (95% CI: 0.67-1.32, P = 0.726) for 30-day ICU mortality and 0.86 (95% CI: 0.66-1.12, P = 0.271) for 90-day in-hospital mortality. Subgroup analyses showed no significant heterogeneity across predefined strata of age, sex, or BMI (all P for interaction >0.05). These findings were supported by inverse probability of treatment weighting analysis. In this cohort of sepsis patients without severe renal impairment, enoxaparin was associated with numerically lower but not statistically significant hazard ratios for both 30-day ICU and 90-day in-hospital mortality compared with UFH. These findings do not establish the superiority of either agent. Larger, prospective studies are warranted to confirm the observed associations.

43003797.title: Relationship between selected microRNAs, pentraxin 3 and uromodulin in pathophysiology of septic acute kidney injury.
43003797.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common complication of sepsis and is associated with increased morbidity and mortality in critically ill patients. Combined assessment of serum pentraxin 3 (PTX3), uromodulin (UMOD), and circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) may improve understanding of the pathophysiology of septic AKI. In this study, 81 critically ill adults with sepsis were stratified into AKI and non-AKI groups, and 90 healthy volunteers served as controls. Blood samples were collected on days 1 and 4 after the diagnosis of sepsis. PTX3 and UMOD concentrations were measured by ELISA, and miRNA expression was assessed by RT-qPCR. Seven miRNAs were validated, and their target genes associations were analyzed using TargetScanHuman8.0. PTX3 and UMOD distinguished healthy controls from septic patients, whereas only PTX3 differentiated patients with AKI from non-AKI. Baseline PTX3 and procalcitonin were independently associated with AKI on days 1 and 4. In AKI group, four analyzed miRNAs showed significant intercorrelations on day 1; however, these weakened by day 4 with changes in renal function and sepsis. Selected miRNAs were interpreted in the context of predicted target genes and pathways related to NF-κB signaling, renal cell apoptosis, and autophagy/mitophagy, rather than as direct causal regulators demonstrated in this study. PTX3, UMOD, and selected miRNAs provide complementary information on septic AKI and support a multifactorial concept of its pathophysiology.The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (ID: NCT06498336) on May 2, 2024 to March 31, 2026.

43004942.title: Real-world experience with cefepime/zidebactam under compassionate use.
43004942.abstract: Cefepime/zidebactam is a β-lactam/β-lactam enhancer combination with activity against carbapenem-resistant (CR) Gram-negative pathogens, including metallo-β-lactamase (MBL)-producing organisms. Before regulatory approval, cefepime/zidebactam was available through a compassionate-use programme for patients with CR Gram-negative infections who had limited available treatment options. We conducted a retrospective, multi-country analysis of patients who received cefepime/zidebactam through compassionate use between 2022 and 2025. Data included demographics, comorbidities, acute complications, prior antibiotic exposure, infection characteristics, microbiology, treatment details, and investigator-assessed outcomes. Eighty-five patients were included (median age 48 years; 57.6% in an intensive care unit at initiation). Primary infections included pneumonia/respiratory infection (30.6%), bone and joint infection (24.7%), and complicated urinary tract infection/pyelonephritis (14.1%). Pseudomonas aeruginosa was the predominant pathogen (77.6%), followed by Klebsiella pneumoniae (14.1%) and Acinetobacter baumannii (11.8%); infections involving at least two Gram-negative pathogens occurred in 10.6%. Among isolates with available genotypic data, MBLs were common and predominantly NDM. The cefepime/zidebactam minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC)50 and MIC90 were 8 and 32 mg/L, respectively. Investigator-assessed clinical success at the end of therapy was achieved in 88.2% of patients (95% CI, 79.7-93.5), and microbiological eradication in 89.4% (95% CI, 81.1-94.3); on-therapy mortality was 10.6% (95% CI, 5.7-18.9). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in five patients (5.9%, 95% CI, 2.5-13.0), with one discontinuation. In this uncontrolled compassionate-use case series, cefepime/zidebactam treatment was accompanied by high investigator-assessed clinical success and microbiological eradication in patients with severe infections caused by CR Gram-negative pathogens. These observations require confirmation in prospective controlled studies.

42490008.title: Regional Citrate Anticoagulation Versus No Anticoagulation During Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy in Critically Ill Patients at High Risk of Bleeding: A Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
42490008.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) in critically ill patients often requires anticoagulation to maintain circuit patency, but systemic anticoagulation may increase bleeding risk. Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) has been proposed as an alternative. This meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy and safety of RCA versus no anticoagulation (NA) during CRRT in critically ill patients at high risk of bleeding. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, Wanfang, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure were searched for randomized controlled trials comparing RCA with NA during CRRT in adult critically ill patients with high bleeding risk. Mean differences (MDs) or risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models accounting for potential heterogeneity. RESULTS: Seventeen RCTs involving 893 patients were included. Compared with NA, RCA significantly prolonged filter lifespan (MD: 13.82 h; 95% CI 10.83-16.81) and reduced the incidence of circuit clotting (RR: 0.20; 95% CI 0.12-0.35). RCA was associated with higher risks of citrate accumulation (RR: 4.67; 95% CI 1.30-16.77) and hypocalcemia (RR: 1.78; 95% CI 1.12-2.83), while acid-base disturbances were not significantly different between groups (RR: 1.34; 95% CI 0.60-3.03). In addition, RCA significantly reduced major bleeding (RR: 0.37; 95% CI 0.16-0.87), but did not significantly affect the in-hospital mortality (RR: 0.82; 95% CI 0.65-1.04). CONCLUSIONS: RCA improves circuit patency during CRRT in critically ill patients with a high risk of bleeding, although it increases the risk of certain metabolic complications but does not affect mortality. While RCA was associated with fewer reported major bleeding events than no anticoagulation, the certainty of evidence for this outcome was low and the finding should be interpreted with caution.

42477630.title: Explainable machine learning model for early prediction of ICU death in chronic heart failure with pulmonary infection.
42477630.journal: BMC medical informatics and decision making
42477630.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To develop and validate a machine learning model for predicting ICU mortality in CHF patients with pulmonary infection. METHODS: Clinical data were extracted from the MIMIC-IV database, and ICU mortality within 15 days was defined as the primary endpoint. Patients were stratified into HFrEF, HFmrEF, and HFpEF based on left ventricular ejection fraction. Six models were constructed-logistic regression, random forest, light gradient boosting machine, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), multilayer perceptron, and k-nearest neighbor-and optimized using cross-validated grid search. Predictive performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC, Brier score, Youden index, and calibration slope. Model interpretability was assessed using SHAP and LIME. External validation was conducted using the eICU-CRD database. RESULTS: A total of 1308 patients were included, with an ICU mortality of 15.98%. Among all models, XGBoost achieved the best balance of discrimination and calibration (AUC 0.968; calibration slope 1.070), and retained useful but attenuated discrimination in external testing (AUC 0.718). SHAP analysis identified lactic acid, white blood cell count, prior diagnosis of hypertension, serum potassium, and pre-existing diabetes mellitus as the five most influential predictors of the outcome. Subgroup analyses further demonstrated distinct pathophysiological trajectories associated with mortality: HFrEF predominantly exhibited hemodynamic instability, impaired tissue perfusion, and electrolyte disturbances; in contrast, HFpEF were more frequently associated with chronic metabolic-inflammatory dysregulation and coagulopathy. CONCLUSION: The XGBoost-based model provides interpretable prediction of ICU mortality in CHF patients with pulmonary infection. Phenotype-specific interpretability analysis further suggested that mortality risk mechanisms differ between heart failure subtypes, supporting more individualized risk assessment and management in critically ill CHF patients.

42471569.title: Prognostic impact of sepsis-induced coagulopathy on mortality and clinical outcomes in ICU patients.
42471569.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to assess the prognostic impact of sepsis-induced coagulopathy (SIC) on mortality and clinical outcomes in patients with sepsis admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included 1,305 adult patients with sepsis admitted to a tertiary pulmonary ICU between January 2016 and May 2025. SIC was defined using the International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis (ISTH) criteria, based on platelet (PLT) count, prothrombin time/international normalized ratio (PT/INR), and total Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score components. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality, and secondary outcomes included vasopressor requirement, escalation to second-line vasopressor therapy, invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). Multivariable logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were conducted to assess the prognostic value of SIC. RESULTS: The prevalence of SIC was 19.2%. Patients with SIC had significantly higher in-hospital mortality than those without SIC (79.3% vs. 60.6%, p < 0.001). Vasopressor use and escalation to second-line vasopressor therapy were more frequent in the SIC-positive group (98.0% vs. 92.5%, p = 0.001; 45.8% vs. 31.3%, p < 0.001, respectively). In multivariable analyses, both SIC positivity (OR: 2.172, 95% CI: 1.528-3.087, p < 0.001) and the SIC score (OR: 1.324, 95% CI: 1.175-1.492, p < 0.001) were independently associated with mortality. ROC analysis showed that the SIC score had moderate discriminative performance for predicting mortality (AUC: 0.619, 95% CI: 0.588-0.649, p < 0.001), with an SIC score ≥ 4 identified as the clinically interpreted threshold. CONCLUSION: SIC was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality and greater need for vasopressor support in critically ill patients with sepsis. These findings suggest that SIC may provide complementary prognostic information when interpreted alongside established severity assessment tools; however, prospective studies are needed to clarify its clinical relevance and potential role in patient management.

42469406.title: A distributional reinforcement learning model for temporal coagulation balance evaluation and state‑guided supportive suggestions.
42469406.abstract: Bleeding and thrombosis represent a dynamic continuum in critically ill patients, where overlapping etiologies and heterogeneous pathophysiological mechanisms give rise to mixed-pattern coagulopathy. Conventional risk models usually focus on static, single-timepoint predictions and fail to adapt to rapidly evolving clinical states. Here, we retrospectively analyzed 2537 unique patients with 10,851 longitudinal records, constructing cycles based on clinical practice and engineering pharmacokinetic features. We then developed Adaptive Coagulopathy RL with BiLSTM-Attention (ACRLA), a distributional offline reinforcement learning framework designed to guide dynamic, individualized management of coagulopathy under laboratory-guided monitoring. Model performance was validated against clinician-adjudicated phenotypes, and sensitivity analyses to ensure robustness. The model showed stable convergence, achieving a positive per-patient test reward (0.077 ± 0.1651, 95% CI: 0.046-0.107) with a mean cumulative reward of 1.317. Model-derived tendencies aligned with clinical phenotypes, and feature importance identified D-dimer and platelet count as dominant drivers. The model's therapeutic preference hierarchy mirrored clinical guidelines. These findings indicate that ACRLA effectively captures dynamic coagulopathy trajectories in a clinically interpretable state space and provides a data-driven tool for personalized, adaptive management of coagulopathy in critically ill patients.
