Although earlier research has focused mainly on quantifying thirst severity and its clinical correlates, less is known about the subjective experiences of patients, including their emotional responses, sense of helplessness, help-seeking actions, and the challenges they face in obtaining relief within the ICU. Therefore, this study aimed to examine how post-extubation ICU patients experience thirst and the strategies they use to manage or alleviate it. Between January and August 2024, this qualitative research was carried out in Tehran, Iran, using conventional content analysis. Participants were recruited through purposive sampling, and data were collected via semi-structured interviews conducted in Persian with 20 patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) following extubation. Interviews proceeded until data saturation occurred, and even though they were held after extubation, the thirst experiences participants reported mostly pertained to the time of mechanical ventilation and intubation. The Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) guideline was followed in this study. Three main categories were identified in this study: 'Unrelieved Thirst' (Hope despite Disappointment and Cognitive and Emotional Burden of Thirst), 'Seeking Relief' (Spiritual Coping and Endurance and Non-Verbal Pleading for Water), and 'Emotional Collapse and Withdrawal' (Resigned Withdrawal and Emotional Isolation and Perceived Neglect). Participants experienced persistent thoughts about water, employed spiritual coping strategies, used gestures without words to express thirst, and eventually emotionally withdrew when their needs were persistently ignored. The study revealed that post-extubation thirst is experienced as a deeply upsetting phenomenon affecting physical, psychological, and existential levels, where patients face physical discomfort, emotional distress, challenges in communication, and a sense of being overlooked in the ICU. The findings highlight the urgent necessity for systematic thirst assessment, improved non-verbal communication techniques, and compassionate, patient-focused nursing care to reduce thirst-related distress. Healthcare providers must be trained to identify both verbal and non-verbal thirst signals and to incorporate patients' cultural and spiritual resources into supportive care. The research delivers a comprehensive understanding of the multifaceted nature of thirst in ICU patients, demonstrating that unresolved thirst may result in emotional collapse and withdrawal. It highlights the significance of managing thirst as an essential human requirement in critical care. The study followed the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) guideline. No patient or public contribution.

42847304.title: Pressure ulcer prevention in mechanically ventilated patients in intensive care units: a quality improvement project.
42847304.abstract: Despite ongoing attempts to prevent hospital-acquired pressure ulcers (HAPUs), they remain a common occurrence in hospitalised patients. Improving policies and processes to provide a standardised approach to assessments, documentation and equipment is linked to decreasing HAPUs. Among hospitalised patients, those in intensive care units (ICUs) and who are mechanically ventilated are at the highest risk of developing a pressure ulcer (PU). A quality improvement (QI) project was created to provide a foundation of basic nursing care to be delivered to the patient for the prevention of HAPUs. The primary objective of the QI project was to decrease the incidence of HAPUs at the author's facility, Mercy Hospital, Arkansas, US. The year prior to the implementation of the QI project, the HAPU incidence was n=17 in the ICU at this facility. This article highlights the importance of education, training and the use of a preventive dressing upon admission to the ICU. It can be used as an approach to improve current policies. The overall length of the QI project including education, implementation and monitoring was 12 weeks. The framework used in the QI project was that of Failure Modes and Effects Analysis. The outcome of this QI project resulted in a reduction of HAPUs. Within the 12-week timeframe, one HAPU developed. An effective prevention tool was the use of a preventive dressing at pressure points (coccyx/sacral) upon arrival to the ICU before an injury occurred. Providing continuous structured education on interventions for the prevention of HAPUs was found to be a successful component of prevention during this QI project. Although many of the risk factors, such as poor perfusion and lack of mobility, for HAPUs are not able to be prevented, the incorporation of evidence-based research into practice in the clinical setting can facilitate a reduction in the prevalence of HAPUs.

42847302.title: Pressure injuries in an intensive care unit exclusively dedicated to treating patients with COVID-19: a prospective cohort study.
42847302.abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, and as growing numbers of critically ill patients were treated in prone position in COVID-19-dedicated intensive care units (ICUs), the incidence of pressure injuries (PIs) remained relevant. Limited data are available on this topic; this study is intended to add to the literature on these injuries in proned patients who are ventilated during intensive care to contribute to prevention of PIs and better management of these patients. All patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome treated via invasive mechanical ventilation (endotracheal tube or tracheostomy) in an ICU exclusively dedicated to patients with COVID-19 in Porto Alegre, Brazil from 15 March-10 September 2020 were recruited prospectively following admission to the ICU, including patients who received extracorporeal membrane oxygenation therapy. Patients treated with non-invasive ventilation were excluded. The following variables were analysed: body mass index, immobility time (assessed via duration of mechanical ventilation), nutritional status (assessed by albumin level), age, smoking status, and history of previous PI. During the study period, 267 patients were admitted to the ICU for COVID-19 support. The median patient age was 61 years, and most were male (58.8%). Most patients (235, 88.0%) had associated comorbidities-186 (69.7%) had multiple comorbidities, and hypertension and diabetes were most common. PIs were present in 150 (56.2%) patients. In 132 patients, the ulcers were examined and ranked according to the Shea classification-65.16% were classified as grade 2. Duration of mechanical ventilation and age were associated with higher ulcer grades. For each additional day on mechanical ventilation, the risk of PIs rose by approximately 7%. The incidence of PIs in patients on invasive mechanical ventilation in an ICU exclusively dedicated to treating patients with COVID-19 was high. The risk of developing a PI in these conditions rose significantly for each day on mechanical ventilation. Ventilation in the prone position was associated with development of PIs in less common areas.

42844803.title: The First 48 Hours: Incidence, Timing and Predictors of Adverse Events After ICU-To-Ward Transfer: A Prospective Cohort Study.
42844803.abstract: The transition from the intensive care unit (ICU) to a general ward is a period of heightened vulnerability, yet the precise timing and modifiable predictors of adverse events remain poorly defined. To determine the incidence, timing and types of adverse events following ICU-to-ward transfer, evaluate the predictive accuracy of four early-warning scores and identify independent risk factors. A prospective cohort study of 207 adult patients transferred from ICUs to general wards at a tertiary university hospital over 20 months (March 2024-October 2025) was enrolled. Four early warning scores (PACS, MEWS, SWIFT, LACE) were calculated daily for 5 days post-transfer. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent risk factors. The total number Adverse events occurred in 52 patients (25.1%), most commonly ICU readmission (n = 46, 22.2%) and healthcare-associated infections (n = 29, 14.0%). Critically, 88% of events occurred within the first 48 h (day 1: 56.0%; day 2: 32.0%). SWIFT demonstrated the highest predictive accuracy at transfer (AUC 0.856). Mechanical ventilation was the strongest independent risk factor (OR 10.11), followed by prolonged ICU stay (OR 6.40), respiratory diagnosis (OR 4.99), > 3 invasive devices (OR 4.41) and comorbidities (OR 3.64). These five factors collectively explained 88.5% of adverse events. Adverse events affect one in four patients after ICU-to-ward transfer, with the vast majority occurring within the first 48 h. A simple set of readily identifiable risk factors can guide nursing surveillance and targeted interventions during this critical window. Bedside nurses should prioritize enhanced monitoring for patients with a history of mechanical ventilation, prolonged ICU stay, multiple invasive devices and significant comorbidities during the first 48 h post-transfer. Daily use of early-warning scores can inform monitoring frequency and rapid response activation.

42842833.title: Determinants of Adoption of a Mechanical Ventilation Dashboard in Intensive Care: Measurement Instrument for Determinants of Innovations-Based, Single-Center, Cross-Sectional Evaluation.
42842833.abstract: Lung-protective ventilation (LPV) reduces complications of mechanical ventilation, yet adherence in intensive care units (ICUs) remains inconsistent. Digital dashboards may support LPV by improving situational awareness and supporting protocol adherence. However, adoption of such tools in high-acuity clinical environments depends on a range of cognitive, professional, and contextual determinants. The Measurement Instrument for Determinants of Innovations (MIDI) provides a validated framework to systematically assess these factors. This study aims to identify determinants influencing the adoption of a newly piloted mechanical ventilation dashboard in the ICU using the MIDI framework. We conducted a single-center, cross-sectional evaluation among ICU health care professionals during a dedicated survey period within a pilot introduction of a mechanical ventilation dashboard at Amsterdam University Medical Center. Participants completed a structured questionnaire consisting of 24 MIDI items adapted to the ICU context rated on a 5-point Likert scale ("completely disagree" to "completely agree"), supplemented by open-ended questions on perceived barriers and facilitators to its use. Determinants were classified as facilitators when ≥80% of respondents selected "agree" or "completely agree" and as barriers when ≥20% selected "disagree" or "completely disagree." Open-ended responses were analyzed using a general inductive thematic approach. A total of 71 completed questionnaires were analyzed, including responses from nurses, physicians, intensivists, ventilation specialists, and researchers in mechanical ventilation. Six determinants met the criteria for facilitators: outcome expectations, self-efficacy, procedural clarity, low complexity, correctness, and observability. Two determinants met the criteria for barriers: relevance for client and professional obligation. Analysis of open-ended responses highlighted perceived barriers such as additional workload, the need for an extra device, overlap with existing systems, and limited role-specific relevance. Facilitators included improved situational overview, educational value, easier trend monitoring, and increased efficiency. This evaluation identified key determinants influencing the adoption of a mechanical ventilation dashboard in the ICU. While the dashboard was generally perceived as useful and easy to understand, adoption was shaped by determinants related to workflow integration, role-specific relevance, and professional responsibility. These findings suggest that successful introduction of digital clinical support tools in intensive care requires attention not only to technical design, but also to how such tools align with users' roles, daily work processes, and shared clinical responsibilities. Systematic assessment of determinants provides actionable insights into the adoption of digital decision-support tools in high-acuity care settings.

42842548.title: Association between red blood cell distribution width-to-albumin ratio and ICU/hospital mortality in patients receiving mechanical ventilation within 24 hours of ICU admission: A multicenter retrospective study.
42842548.abstract: ObjectiveTo assess the association of early red blood cell distribution width-to-albumin ratio (RAR) with mortality in mechanically ventilated ICU patients and its value alongside routine clinical assessment.MethodsThis retrospective cohort study used MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD data. Adults receiving invasive mechanical ventilation within 24 hours of ICU admission who remained in the ICU at 24 hours were included. RAR was calculated from first-day laboratory measurements. Multivariable Cox regression assessed its association with subsequent in-hospital and ICU mortality. Additional analyses examined whether RAR improved prediction beyond its components and established severity scores.ResultsThe study included 3,534 MIMIC-IV patients and 1,929 eICU-CRD patients. Compared with the lowest RAR quartile, the highest quartile was associated with greater in-hospital mortality in both databases (adjusted HR 1.855, 95% CI 1.474-2.335, and HR 1.698, 95% CI 1.231-2.341, respectively). The corresponding ICU mortality association was significant in MIMIC-IV but not in eICU-CRD. Adding RAR to clinical models improved discrimination and reclassification for in-hospital mortality, with performance similar to including RDW and albumin separately. Improvements beyond severity scores varied by outcome and measure.ConclusionsHigher first-day RAR was associated with subsequent in-hospital mortality among mechanically ventilated adults in two ICU databases. RAR may provide supplementary prognostic information, although its role in clinical decisions requires prospective evaluation.

42842343.title: Perme Mobility Scale Is Associated With Morbidity and Mortality in Patients Undergoing Lung Transplant: 1-Year Follow-Up.
42842343.journal: Physiotherapy research international : the journal for researchers and clinicians in physical therapy
42842343.abstract: Lung transplantation (LTx) is an effective treatment for patients with advanced chronic lung disease who are unresponsive to other therapies. Functional capacity is increasingly recognized as an important prognostic indicator in transplant candidates and recipients. To assess functional status using the Perme Mobility Scale in patients undergoing LTx, and to examine its association with mechanical ventilation (MV) duration, ICU and hospital length of stay, and mortality over a 1-year follow-up. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of patients admitted to the ICU at Dom Vicente Scherer Hospital, Porto Alegre, following lung transplantation between January 2018 and December 2019. Perme Mobility Scale scores were recorded at ICU admission and hospital discharge. Data on MV duration, ICU and hospital length of stay, readmissions, and mortality were collected from medical records and follow-up calls. Sixty-seven patients were included (median age 57 years; 52.2% female). Higher Perme scores were significantly associated with shorter MV duration, shorter ICU and shorter hospital stay. Specifically, the total Perme score at hospital discharge was negatively correlated with mechanical ventilation duration (r = -0.408; p = 0.001) and ICU length of stay (r = -0.314; p = 0.01). Additionally, mechanical ventilation duration categories were significantly associated with 1-year mortality (p = 0.005), with the highest mortality observed in patients requiring mechanical ventilation for > 48 hours. Improved functional status as measured by the Perme Mobility Scale was associated with better clinical outcomes in lung transplant recipients. The Perme Mobility Scale represents a potentially useful prognostic marker that warrants further validation in prospective multicenter studies before being established as a tool for prognostic risk stratification.

42841896.title: Management of renal failure in earthquake-related crush syndrome: Multicenter intensive care outcomes.
42841896.journal: Ulusal travma ve acil cerrahi dergisi = Turkish journal of trauma & emergency surgery : TJTES
42841896.abstract: Crush syndrome (CS) is a clinical condition associated with multisystem organ dysfunction that develops after traumatic rhabdomyolysis and primarily affects the kidneys. The aim of this study was to characterize the incidence, risk factors, and treatment patterns of acute kidney injury (AKI) in earthquake victims with CS, with a particular focus on renal replacement therapy (RRT) use and clinical outcomes. In this retrospective multicenter study, 247 adult patients with earthquake-related CS who were admitted to intensive care units (ICUs) in 22 hospitals after the Kahramanmaraş 2023 earthquakes were analyzed. Demographic data, injury patterns, laboratory parameters, treatment protocols, and outcomes were evaluated during the first 15 days following ICU admission. AKI developed in 78.5% (n=194) of patients, and RRT was required in 62.4% (n=121) of those with AKI. Multiple logistic regression analysis demonstrated that myoglobin and creatinine levels were associated with an elevated risk of developing AKI (odds ratio [OR]: 1.001; 95% confidence interval CI: 1.000-1.001 and OR: 1.735; 95% CI: 1.151-2.615, respectively). Similarly, creatinine level and reasons for ICU admission were identified as factors influencing RRT administration. (OR: 1.7; 95% CI: 1.28-2.15 and OR: 2.9; 95% CI: 1.26-6.90, respectively). The 30-day mortality rate was higher in patients with AKI than in those without AKI. Mortality rates were similar between patients with AKI who received RRT and those who did not. This study demonstrates the high incidence of AKI in earthquake-related CS, underscores the need for improved disaster preparedness with adequate dialysis capacity and early risk stratification using serum myoglobin and creatinine levels for optimal management.

42841893.title: Clinical burden and predictors of hospitalization in extremity gunshot wounds: A single-center retrospective study.
42841893.journal: Ulusal travma ve acil cerrahi dergisi = Turkish journal of trauma & emergency surgery : TJTES
42841893.abstract: This study aimed to retrospectively evaluate the clinical characteristics, temporal admission patterns, and clinical outcomes of patients with extremity gunshot wounds (GSW) presenting to a tertiary care teaching and research hospital. A total of 123 patients presenting with GSWs affecting at least one extremity between January 2024 and December 2025 were retrospectively analyzed. Injury characteristics, interventions, and clinical outcomes were evaluated. Factors independently associated with hospital length of stay (LOS) and intensive care unit (ICU) admission were identified using negative binomial regression and multivariate logistic regression analyses, respectively. Of the patients, 116 (94.3%) were male, with a mean age of 29.9±11.9 years. The lower extremity was the most frequently affected region (69.1%), and 42 of 43 fractures (97.7%) were open fractures. The ICU admission rate was 26.0% (n=32), and in-hospital mortality was 4.1% (n=5). A total of 43.1% of admissions occurred between 18: 00 and 23: 59. In negative binomial regression, concomitant injury (incidence rate ratio [IRR]=6.93; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 3.82-12.57; p<0.001), fracture (IRR=5.02; 95% CI: 2.82-8.93; p<0.001), and reoperation (IRR=2.73; 95% CI: 1.44-5.16; p=0.002) were independently associated with length of hospital stay. In logistic regression, neurovascular injury (odds ratio [OR]=28.12; 95% CI: 7.60-104.09; p<0.001) and concomitant injury (OR=20.36; 95% CI: 5.62-73.81; p<0.001) independently predicted ICU admission. Extremity GSWs predominantly affect young males and cluster during evening hours. Concomitant injury and fracture were independently associated with length of hospital stay, whereas reoperation was associated with prolonged hospitalization during the clinical course, while neurovascular injury and concomitant injury independently predict ICU admission.

42841720.title: Pulmonary Herpes Simplex Virus Reactivation in Invasively Mechanically Ventilated Patients With COVID-19 in Intensive Care Unit.
42841720.abstract: Patients in intensive care units (ICU) under mechanical ventilation, particularly those with SARS-CoV-2 infection, are highly susceptible to Herpes simplex virus (HSV) reactivation. Given the lack of data on the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron and Delta variants, this study aimed to assess the prevalence of pulmonary HSV reactivation in mechanically ventilated patients with SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia. The impact of HSV replication on SARS-CoV-2 replication, and conversely, was investigated, along with the susceptibility of HSV strains to antiviral therapies. This retrospective study included 381 mechanically ventilated ICU patients in Lyon. Overall, 103 patients (27.0%) experienced HSV reactivation, with a trend toward a higher prevalence among SARS-CoV-2-positive patients (32.8%) compared to SARS-CoV-2-negative (24.1%; p value = 0.058). HSV reactivation was significantly higher with the Delta variant (46.2%) compared to Omicron (27.1%; p value = 0.045); the Delta variant was associated with a 2.38-fold increased risk of HSV reactivation. HSV-positive patients exhibited a 1-log lower SARS-CoV-2 viral load compared to HSV-negative patients, a finding indicative of the natural course of SARS-CoV-2 infection followed by HSV reactivation, rather than viral interference. Unexpectedly, acyclovir resistance mutations appeared in the UL23 gene in at least 13.6% of HSV-1 strains in patients with an HSV load above 105 copies/mL. Complementary phenotypic and genotypic approaches allowed to identify three novel substitutions in UL30: Q217R, D741A, and E756K, classified as polymorphisms. Further optimization is needed in the management of mechanically ventilated ICU patients with pulmonary HSV reactivation, especially regarding antiviral resistance testing.

42841276.title: Hospital Workforce Staffing and Work-Pace Safety Perceptions During the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Cross-Sectional Analysis.
42841276.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic placed unprecedented strain on US hospitals, creating conditions of high patient acuity, elevated mortality, and staffing shortages. These pressures threatened care quality and shaped how workers perceived their ability to provide safe care. This study examined national trends in hospital workers' staffing and work-pace safety perceptions (SWSP) during the pandemic and evaluated whether changes in hospital mortality rates were associated with worsening perceptions. We further assessed whether intensive care unit (ICU) staff experienced sharper declines in SWSP compared with non-ICU counterparts. We conducted a quantitative analysis using de-identified responses from the Hospital Survey on Patient Safety Culture, linked with mortality data from the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project State Inpatient Databases. A total of 258 987 responses from more than 400 hospitals were included from the pandemic period (April 2020-July 2022). Staffing and work-pace safety perception was measured using a composite of 2 Hospital Survey on Patient Safety Culture items on staffing adequacy and work pace, dichotomized into negative/neutral versus positive perceptions. Logistic regression models assessed associations between monthly mortality rates and SWSP, adjusting for individual- and hospital-level covariates. Stratified analyses compared ICU and non-ICU settings. Nationwide, SWSP declined steadily, decreasing by an average of 3.5 percentage points per year. Periods of heightened mortality, including the Delta and Omicron waves, coincided with sharper deterioration. A doubling of overall mortality was associated with a 38% increase in odds of negative/neutral SWSP (odds ratio [OR] = 1.38, standard error [SE] = 0.02, P < .01). Stratified analyses showed differences by setting: for non-ICU patients, a mortality doubling was linked to a 14% increase (OR = 1.14, SE = 0.02, P < .01), while for ICU patients, odds rose by 40% (OR = 1.40, SE = 0.12, P < .01). During the pandemic, healthcare workers' perceptions of staffing adequacy and work pace deteriorated, varying by position group and showing greater sensitivity to mortality surges among ICU staff than non-ICU peers. These findings indicate that SWSP represents an important dimension of safety culture that responds dynamically to systemic strain. For health system leaders, this underscores the value of complementing external performance measures with proactive monitoring of workforce perceptions. Attention to SWSP may provide early warning of stress, inform resource allocation, and support interventions to mitigate burnout, improve retention, and strengthen resilience in times of crisis.

42839543.title: The Role of Emotional Intelligence in Intensive Care Nursing: A Scoping Review.
42839543.abstract: Emotional intelligence (EI) is critical in intensive care unit (ICU) nursing, where nurses face high stress, clinical instability and emotionally demanding situations. EI helps nurses manage emotions, improve communication and support clinical performance. It has also been linked to lower burnout and more adaptive coping among ICU nurses. This scoping review aimed to map the available evidence on emotional intelligence among nurses working in ICUs, including its key dimensions, associated professional outcomes and current knowledge gaps. A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and reported following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. A structured search was conducted in MEDLINE, CINAHL, PubMed and Scopus for studies published in the past 10 years in Portuguese, English or Spanish. In total, this review included nine studies. The evidence highlights the crucial role of EI in emotional regulation, communication and clinical performance among ICU nurses. Key dimensions of emotional intelligence, including empathy, emotional clarity and self-regulation, were consistently identified as important. Training programmes demonstrated significant improvements in EI and reduced burnout symptoms, and EI was also associated with more adaptive coping strategies and improved professional performance. Emotional intelligence is an important competency in ICU nursing and has been linked to improved communication, clinical decision-making and lower burnout among nurses. Despite these benefits, research still shows gaps, particularly in standardising EI assessment tools and in the need for longitudinal studies. Targeted emotional intelligence training programmes may strengthen ICU nurses' emotional resilience and enhance care quality. Integrating EI development into ICU nursing education and institutional policies can help reduce burnout, improve communication with patients and families, and enhance overall clinical performance, thereby supporting a healthier work environment and strengthening nurses' communication and professional performance in intensive care settings.

42834811.title: Postoperative Delirium in Intensive Care Units: A Bibliometric Analysis of Nursing Studies.
42834811.abstract: Delirium is a common and serious postoperative complication in intensive care units, associated with increased morbidity, mortality and long-term cognitive impairment, and despite the pivotal role of nurses in its assessment and management, variations in prevalence and gaps in intervention-focused nursing research persist, underscoring the need for a bibliometric evaluation of the literature. The aim of the study was to quantitatively analyse and visually map trends, citations, key terms and country contributions in nursing research on postoperative delirium in intensive care as well as to characterize the overall structure of the literature. This study was conducted as a retrospective and descriptive research using the bibliometric analysis method on December 1, 2025. No time restrictions were imposed on the literature. Data analysis was performed using R Studio software. The earliest study on postoperative delirium in intensive care units within the field of nursing was published in 2001, and the analysed publications covered the period from 2001 to December 2025. In addition, 55.96% of all publications have been released in the past 7 years. The journal with the highest number of publications is Nursing in Critical Care, while the United States stands out as the country with the highest research output. It can be suggested that topics such as 'cardiac surgery', 'nursing care', 'postoperative delirium', 'postoperative care' and the 'Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit' represent areas that warrant further investigation and development in future research. The analysis showed a marked increase in publications on postoperative delirium in intensive care nursing in recent years. The United States and the Journal Nursing in Critical Care were identified as the leading contributors to the literature. Thematic mapping indicated that the literature primarily focused on delirium assessment and intensive care nursing, with several interconnected research areas. The findings emphasize the critical role of nurses in delirium screening and management in intensive care units. While assessment tools are well represented in the literature, further research is needed to develop and evaluate nurse-led interventions aimed at delirium prevention and care. Enhancing nursing education and institutional support may contribute to improved patient outcomes and quality of postoperative intensive care.

42830038.title: IMPACT OF THE COVID-19 PANDEMIC ON THE SEVERITY AND OUTCOMES OF GUNSHOT INJURIES.
42830038.abstract: To evaluate the impact of COVID-19 infection on injury severity, clinical course, complications, and hospital outcomes in patients with gunshot injuries. This retrospective descriptive-analytical study was conducted at the Central Clinical Military Hospital of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Armenia. The study included 80 male patients with gunshot injuries who were hospitalized during 2020. Of these, 55 (68.8%) patients were COVID-19-positive and 25 (31.2%) were COVID-19-negative. Injury severity was assessed using the Injury Severity Score (ISS) and the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). The rates of intensive care unit (ICU) admission, requirement for mechanical ventilation, length of hospital stay, complications, and in-hospital mortality were analyzed. The mean ISS was significantly higher in COVID-19-positive patients than in COVID-19-negative patients (22.8±7.4 vs. 15.2±5.8, p<0.01). Conversely, the mean GCS score was significantly lower in the COVID-19-positive group (12.9±2.5 vs. 14.6±1.8, p<0.05). ICU admission was required in 43.6% of COVID-19-positive patients compared with 16.0% of COVID-19-negative patients. Mechanical ventilation was required in 21.8% and 8.0% of patients, respectively. The incidence of complications was 29.1% in the COVID-19-positive group and 12.0% in the COVID-19-negative group. In-hospital mortality was 10.9% and 4.0%, respectively. Correlation analysis demonstrated a significant positive association between ISS and length of hospital stay (r=0.61, p<0.001), as well as between ISS and mortality (r=0.58, p<0.001). COVID-19 infection in patients with gunshot injuries is associated with greater injury severity, an increased need for intensive care, a higher incidence of complications and mortality, and prolonged hospitalization. The coexistence of COVID-19 infection and gunshot trauma may be regarded as a mutually aggravating clinical condition that requires early diagnosis, intensive monitoring, and a multidisciplinary treatment approach.

42827460.title: Early prediction of in-hospital acute brain injury following cardiac arrest using machine learning: development and external validation.
42827460.abstract: Neurological injury is common after cardiac arrest (CA), but early and accurate assessment remains challenging. Existing evaluation methods often lack sensitivity and specificity. This study aims to develop and validate an interpretable machine learning model for early and reliable assessment of brain injury and its prognostic relevance in ICU patients. In this study, we analyzed 1,419 CA patients from the MIMIC-IV database, randomly split into training and validation cohorts. Six machine learning (ML) algorithms-logistic regression (LR), XGBoost, artificial neural network (ANN), random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), and k-nearest neighbors (KNN) were developed and evaluated. The top-performing model was interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), identifying eight key predictors of brain injury. Finally, clinical data from cardiac arrest patients at our hospital were collected for external validation to assess the model's generalizability and practical utility in an ICU setting. Among the six machine learning models, the Random Forest model achieved the highest numerical performance in both the internal test and external validation cohorts. In the internal test cohort, Random Forest achieved an ACC of 88.7%, sensitivity of 80.0%, specificity of 90.6%, F1 score of 0.714, NPV of 95.5%, PPV of 64.5%, and AUC of 0.901. In the external validation cohort, Random Forest achieved an ACC of 88.8%, sensitivity of 77.8%, specificity of 90.8%, F1 score of 0.677, NPV of 95.8%, PPV of 60.0%, and AUC of 0.889. SHAP analysis identified eight influential predictors: age, hemoglobin, OASIS, temperature, blood urea nitrogen, white blood cell count, non-invasive diastolic pressure, and non-invasive systolic pressure. Machine learning offers strong potential for early prediction of acute brain injury in in-hospital cardiac arrest patients. Our interpretable model addresses the "black box" concern by providing transparent insights into key predictive features.

42823746.title: A specialist-led interprofessional weaning program to prevent weaning failure in high-risk patients: the PRiVENT study.
42823746.abstract: Effective strategies to prevent weaning failure and prolonged invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in patients at high risk of weaning failure are limited. We evaluated a structured, specialist-led interprofessional weaning program. In this prospective, multicenter, non-randomized interventional study, mechanically ventilated patients were screened 96 h to 11 days after intubation. Patients meeting predefined high-risk criteria received a specialist-led interprofessional weaning program, while a parallel control group was derived from health insurance claims data. The primary outcome was successful weaning at ICU discharge. The primary analysis included 349 intervention patients and 1,768 controls. Successful weaning occurred in 58.3% of intervention patients and 51.7% of controls. In the adjusted primary analysis, the odds ratio for successful weaning was 1.46 (95% CI, 0.99-2.17; P = 0.057), and the difference did not reach statistical significance. In prespecified propensity score-matched analysis, successful weaning occurred in 58.3% of intervention patients and 46.4% of matched controls (OR, 2.90; 95% CI, 1.61-5.24; P < 0.001). An exploratory analysis restricted to ICU survivors also showed higher odds of successful weaning in the intervention group (OR, 2.10; 95% CI, 1.09-4.04; P = 0.026). Overall, 16.3% of intervention patients were transferred to a specialized weaning center. These patients had longer ventilation durations, contributing to a longer overall duration of IMV in the intervention group. The PRiVENT intervention was feasible and successful weaning was numerically more frequent in the intervention group, although the prespecified adjusted primary analysis did not reach statistical significance. These findings suggest a potential benefit of structured, multidisciplinary weaning support. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05260853, registered on March 2, 2022.

42954350.title: Effect of Progressive Muscle Relaxation and Nature Sounds on Alarm Fatigue in Intensive Care Unit Nurses: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
42954350.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) nurses are exposed to numerous alarms, many of which are unnecessary and lead to alarm fatigue. This phenomenon, caused by desensitization to alarm sounds, reduces nurses' responsiveness to critical alerts and threatens both their well-being and patient safety. Alarm fatigue has been linked to elevated stress, burnout and errors in patient care, underscoring the need for effective interventions. Progressive muscle relaxation involves the gradual and systematic contraction and relaxation of different muscle groups throughout the body and nature sounds use for decrease stress and alarm fatigue. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) and exposure to nature sounds in reducing alarm fatigue among ICU nurses. A three-arm, parallel, single-blinded randomized controlled trial was conducted. Ninety-six ICU nurses from three hospitals in southern Iran, were randomly assigned to one of three groups: PMR (n = 32), nature sounds (n = 32) or control (n = 32). Alarm fatigue was assessed using a validated alarm fatigue scale at baseline, immediately after the intervention and 2 months post-intervention. Both PMR and nature sound interventions significantly reduced alarm fatigue among ICU nurses (p < 0.001). Between-group comparisons showed significant differences between the PMR and control groups (p < 0.001) and between the nature sound and control groups (p < 0.001). No significant difference was observed between the PMR and nature sound groups (p = 0.650). PMR and exposure to nature sounds significantly reduced alarm fatigue among ICU nurses, as reflected in lower fatigue scores. These interventions improved nurses' capacity to manage stress and fatigue, thereby supporting better job performance and enhanced patient safety. Given their simplicity and accessibility, both approaches represent promising strategies for addressing alarm fatigue in critical care settings. Progressive muscle relaxation and nature sounds may offer practical, non-pharmacological approaches to managing alarm fatigue among intensive care unit nurses. These interventions could be incorporated into nurses' work routines, although further research is needed to confirm their effectiveness and long-term benefits.

42952228.title: The Impact of 12-Hour Versus 8-Hour Shifts on Intensive Care Unit Nurses' Physical and Mental Well-Being and Job Satisfaction: A Systematic Review.
42952228.abstract: Twelve-hour shifts have been widely implemented in intensive care units (ICUs), where nurses work in high-acuity environments requiring sustained clinical attention. However, evidence regarding the impact of shift length on ICU nurses' physical health, mental well-being, job satisfaction and patient-care outcomes remains limited and inconsistent. To investigate the impact of 12-h compared with 8-h shifts on ICU nurses' physical health, well-being and job satisfaction. This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251021178). A systematic search of CINAHL, Ovid MEDLINE and Embase was conducted in February 2025 and updated in June 2026. Additional searches of Scopus and Web of Science were undertaken in June 2026. Eligible studies included ICU nurses and compared 12-h with 8-h shifts. Risk of bias and methodological quality were assessed using design-specific Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal tools and the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach. Findings were synthesised narratively due to the heterogeneity of the included studies. Of 815 records identified, five studies met the inclusion criteria. Findings on fatigue, sleep and burnout were inconclusive across studies. Twelve-hour shifts were generally associated with greater roster satisfaction, flexibility and work-life balance, while evidence for sick leave was limited or mixed. Evidence did not consistently favour either 12- or 8-h shifts for ICU nurses, with low to very low certainty of evidence. Shift duration should therefore be considered alongside overall roster design, staffing needs and nurses' well-being when planning ICU schedules. Nurse managers should avoid a one-size-fits-all approach to shift duration, as evidence does not clearly favour 12- or 8-h shifts. Shift-length decisions should consider roster design, staffing needs, workload, recovery time and nurses' preferences. Managers should also monitor staff well-being, satisfaction, absenteeism, retention and patient-care outcomes when reviewing shift patterns. Given the low certainty of evidence, ongoing local evaluation is essential to ensure rosters support workforce sustainability and safe, high-quality care.

42952074.title: Incidence of Intensive Care Unit Delirium After Heart Surgery: A Feasibility Study of a Forest Environment Intervention.
42952074.abstract: Postoperative delirium is a serious complication in intensive care units (ICUs), particularly following cardiac surgery. It is associated with circadian rhythm disruption, sleep disturbances and adverse outcomes. ICU environments often lack natural time cues, which may exacerbate circadian misalignment and increase delirium risk. The primary aim of the study was the evaluation of the implementation of two chronotherapeutic ICU interventions regarding recruitment, implementability and safety. Its secondary aim was to descriptively assess postoperative delirium across intervention groups. This randomized feasibility study was conducted in a tertiary cardiac surgery ICU in Austria. Adult patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery were allocated to one of three groups: (1) forest environment, (2) light exposure or (3) standard ICU care. Interventions were applied for 12 h daily. Delirium was assessed at three postoperative time points using the confusion assessment method for the ICU (CAM-ICU) and intensive care delirium screening checklist (ICDSC). This study was conducted between March 2020 and 2025. Seventy-seven patients were enrolled, and 64 remained in the final analytical cohort. Interventions were delivered within routine care. Patients and ICU staff did not report intervention-related concerns. Implementation challenges included ICU restructuring, patient transfers due to COVID-19 and deviations from randomized allocation because of operational constraints. No intervention-related adverse events occurred. Delirium assessments were limited at several time points because of sedation, early ICU discharge or transfer. Across all groups, postoperative delirium was detected in 5 of 130 CAM-ICU completed assessments (3.8%) and 8 of 115 ICDSC completed assessments (6.9%), precluding inferential group comparisons. Chronotherapeutic environmental interventions were feasible and safe in ICU care. Feasibility results highlighted challenges related to ICU logistics, sedation-related assessment limitations and pandemic-related disruptions. The unexpectedly low delirium incidence limited conclusions regarding intervention efficacy. Future trials should include larger high-risk populations and prospectively defined feasibility outcomes. Optimized ICU environments, including noise reduction and light management, may support delirium prevention. Chronotherapeutic environmental interventions are feasible additions to routine ICU care.

42952050.title: Psychological Detachment Among Intensive Care Unit Nurses: A Cross-Sectional Study.
42952050.abstract: Intensive care unit nurses face sustained workload, vigilance and emotionally demanding care. Psychological detachment during non-work time is an important recovery experience, but evidence in this population remains limited. To describe psychological detachment among intensive care unit nurses and identify demographic, departmental psychological support resources availability, social support and burnout dimensions associated with it. A single-centre cross-sectional survey. Registered intensive care unit nurses from a tertiary grade A general hospital in eastern China were recruited by convenience sampling between June and July 2025. Participants completed demographic, psychological detachment, burnout and social support questionnaires. Descriptive analyses, univariate comparisons, correlation analyses and multivariable linear regression were performed. The study was reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology checklist. Of 220 questionnaires submitted, 199 valid responses were analysed (90.45%). The mean psychological detachment score was 11.68 ± 3.85. Mean emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation and personal accomplishment scores were 37.75 ± 8.15, 16.93 ± 4.87 and 25.91 ± 6.25, respectively. Psychological detachment correlated negatively with emotional exhaustion (r = -0.230, p = 0.001) and positively with subjective support (r = 0.175, p = 0.013). Departmental psychological support resources availability (B = 1.674, β = 0.216, p = 0.001), head-nurse position (B = -4.776, β = -0.195, p = 0.004) and emotional exhaustion (B = -0.115, β = -0.243, p < 0.001) were independently associated with psychological detachment. In this single-centre sample of intensive care unit nurses, the reported availability of departmental psychological support resources was associated with higher psychological detachment, whereas head-nurse position and emotional exhaustion were associated with lower psychological detachment. These findings suggest that critical care nursing managers may consider departmental psychological support resources availability, nursing position and emotional exhaustion when assessing recovery needs among intensive care unit nurses.

42942363.title: Evaluation of Prognostic Factors for Prolonged Intensive Care Unit Hospitalization After Trauma: Roles of Hemorrhagic Burden and Admission Laboratory Abnormalities.
42942363.abstract: Background and Objectives: Prolonged intensive care unit (ICU) hospitalization after trauma reflects sustained critical-care needs, but early prognostic assessment remains challenging. The primary objective was to identify factors associated with prolonged ICU hospitalization (≥7 days) using admission characteristics and treatment information available during the first 24 h. The secondary objective was to explore whether these associations differed according to a composite score of admission laboratory abnormalities (CE score). Materials and Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 2638 patients admitted between 1 January 2006 and 31 December 2021 from a prospectively maintained Level I trauma registry. Prolonged ICU hospitalization was defined as ICU length of stay (LOS) ≥7 days. Multivariable regression evaluated independent associations between early clinical factors and prolonged ICU hospitalization. Exploratory interaction analyses evaluated effect modification by the CE score, a composite of admission laboratory abnormalities. In-hospital deaths were retained in the primary cohort. The potential influence of in-hospital death on ICU LOS was evaluated in an additional survivor-restricted sensitivity analysis. Sensitivity analyses used ICU LOS ≥ 10 days and log-transformed ICU LOS. Results: Overall, 757/2638 patients (28.7%) had an ICU LOS ≥ 7 days. Older age (adjusted OR [aOR] 1.01 per year, 95% CI 1.01-1.02; p < 0.001), higher Injury Severity Score (aOR 1.06 per point, 95% CI 1.05-1.08; p < 0.001), massive transfusion (aOR 1.52, 95% CI 1.09-2.12; p = 0.013), and damage control surgery (aOR 2.35, 95% CI 1.60-3.46; p < 0.001) were independently associated with prolonged ICU hospitalization, whereas admission lactate, systolic blood pressure, and angioembolization were not. CE interactions were observed for lactate, SBP, and massive transfusion (likelihood-ratio p < 0.001, p = 0.006, and p = 0.037, respectively). Using the ≥10-day threshold, associations persisted for massive transfusion (aOR 1.56, 95% CI 1.10-2.22; p = 0.012) and DCS (aOR 1.88, 95% CI 1.27-2.79; p = 0.002). Among 688 hospital survivors in the additional analysis, none of the three CE interactions was statistically significant (p = 0.208, p = 0.572, and p = 0.574, respectively). Conclusions: Older age, greater injury severity, massive transfusion, and DCS were associated with prolonged ICU hospitalization after trauma. Exploratory CE interactions were not statistically significant in the survivor-restricted analysis and require further investigation. These findings do not establish the clinical utility of the CE score.

42934558.title: Albumin-corrected anion gap-chloride index for Mortality risk in ICU-managed Gastrointestinal bleeding: a multicentre cohort analysis.
42934558.abstract: Gastrointestinal bleeding is frequent in the ICU and is associated with poor outcomes. Acid-base and electrolyte abnormalities may indicate early physiological instability; however, the prognostic relevance of the albumin-corrected anion gap-to-chloride ratio (ACAG/Cl) has not been well defined. We examined the relationship between ACAG/Cl and short-term mortality in this population. Adult ICU patients with gastrointestinal bleeding were identified from two public critical care databases for derivation and external validation. ACAG/Cl was calculated from laboratory data collected within 24 h of ICU admission. The primary endpoint was 28-day all-cause mortality. Cox regression, Kaplan-Meier (K-M) analysis, restricted cubic splines (RCS), subgroup analyses, ROC curves, and external validation were used. A total of 1740 patients were included in the MIMIC-IV cohort, of whom 302 died within 28 days. Higher ACAG/Cl was independently associated with increased 28-day mortality after full adjustment (HR 1.06, 95% CI 1.03-1.08). Patients with ACAG/Cl ≥ 0.16 had a significantly higher risk of 28-day mortality than those with ACAG/Cl < 0.16 (HR 1.68, 95% CI 1.28-2.22). K-M and RCS analyses supported a significant and approximately linear association. ACAG/Cl provided a modest capacity to identify patients at higher risk of short-term death, with an area under the curve of 0.689. The result was confirmed in the eICU-CRD cohort, where patients with ACAG/Cl values of 0.16 or above had a persistently higher risk of short-term mortality after adjustment for confounders (HR 2.16, 95% CI 1.74-2.70). ACAG/Cl was independently associated with 28-day mortality in critically ill patients with gastrointestinal bleeding and showed external reproducibility in the eICU-CRD cohort. As a simple laboratory-derived marker, ACAG/Cl may help support early short-term risk stratification in this high-risk population. Not applicable.

42909495.title: Health economic evaluation of polytrauma treatment in the current aG-DRG system - Results of a Level I Trauma Center.
42909495.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
42909495.abstract: Resource-intensive polytrauma care is associated with high treatment and readiness costs and poses a financial challenge for hospitals. The aim of this retrospective single-center study of the years 2020 to 2022 was to analyze polytrauma reimbursements and costs. Based on billing and clinical data of 201 polytrauma cases from a German University Hospital and Level I Trauma Center, revenues and costs of the eleven MDC 21 A polytrauma DRGs were analyzed. Ratios of the revenue in relation to LOS, ventilation hours, OR time and implant costs as well as personnel costs were calculated. Contribution margins were determined as an upper-bound estimate. DRG reimbursement was highest for the most severely injured patients (50,852 €, DRG W36Z). It was lowest for patients who died within five days (2,214 €, DRG W60Z) or without surgeries (4,056 €, DRG W61B). The contribution margin was also highest for the most severely injured patients (52,775 €, DRG W36Z). Revenues in relation to ICU LOS (3,455 €/day, DRG W36Z) and ventilation time (238 €/hour, DRG W01B) were lowest for the most severe polytraumas. Regarding OR time and implant costs, reimbursement was lowest for injuries of the spine, pelvis and extremities with 62 €/min (DRG W02B) and 5 €/€ (DRG W02A). Treatment of polytrauma patients with long ICU stay, extended mechanical ventilation and multiple injuries of the extremities, pelvis and spine is not adequately reflected by the current per-case reimbursement in relation to the resources used (ICU days, ventilation hours, OR time and implant costs).

42966650.title: Efficacy and Safety of Low-Dose Versus Standard-Dose Alteplase to Treat High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism.
42966650.journal: American journal of critical care : an official publication, American Association of Critical-Care Nurses
42966650.abstract: The optimal dosing of alteplase in patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism is widely debated. To evaluate outcomes in patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism who received alteplase at a low dose or a standard dose. This was a retrospective cohort analysis of 65 patients who received alteplase for high-risk pulmonary embolism at a large academic medical center between June 1, 2011, and August 31, 2022. Patients were placed in 2 cohorts according to initial dose: low-dose alteplase (50 mg) and standard-dose alteplase (100 mg). The primary outcome was sustained hemodynamic stability within 24 hours of the start of alteplase infusion. Secondary outcomes included in-hospital mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, hospital and intensive care unit length of stay, and major bleeding. The primary outcome of sustained hemodynamic stability within 24 hours did not differ significantly between the 2 cohorts (achieved in 32% of patients in the low-dose group and 38% in the standard-dose group; P = .65). In-hospital mortality did not differ significantly between groups (48% in the low-dose group vs 45% in the standard-dose group; P = .81). Patients in the low-dose group had fewer days of mechanical ventilation than patients in the standard-dose group (1.5 vs 6 days; P = .03) and a smaller percentage had major bleeding (12% vs 25%; P = .34). In patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism, sustained hemodynamic stability within 24 hours did not differ significantly between low-dose and standard-dose alteplase treatment strategies. Low-dose alteplase may be an appropriate alternative dosing strategy for patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism.

42876490.title: Prognostic value of platelet-to-white blood cell ratio in critically ill patients with non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage: a machine learning-driven study of the public database and the hospital information system.
42876490.abstract: Assessment of prognosis is crucial for managing non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage (NSAH) patients. The study aimed to explore the association between platelet-to-white blood cell ratio (PWR) and all-cause mortality in this high-risk population and to develop machine learning models to improve prognostic accuracy. Using data from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-IV). The observational endpoints were 30-day and 365-day mortality. Patients were categorized into four groups based on the quartiles of PWR. Kaplan-Meier curves, multivariate Cox regression analyses, restricted cubic splines (RCS), and subgroup analyses were applied. We also developed machine learning models that include PWR and clinical features selected with the Boruta and LASSO algorithms to predict 30-day mortality. Model performance was evaluated by the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and the area under the curve (AUC). Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method was utilized to provide model interpretability. External validations in the eICU-Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD) and the Hospital Information System (HIS) of the First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University were used to assess generalizability. A total of 1,176 patients with critically ill NSAH were enrolled from MIMIC-IV, predominantly male (58.8%), with a median age of 62 years. In multivariable Cox models, higher PWR quartiles were independently associated with lower risk of 30-day (HR = 0.55, 95% CI 0.35, 0.86, p = 0.009) and 365-day (HR = 0.53, 95% CI 0.37, 0.77, p = 0.001) mortality after fully adjusting. RCS suggested a linear association. No significant interaction was observed by subgroup analysis across all subgroups. The top-performing machine learning model attained an AUC of 0.868 during internal validation (MIMIC-IV). External validations yielded AUC values of 0.874 (eICU-CRD) and 0.763 (HIS). SHAP analysis revealed a correlation between decreased PWR and an elevated predicted risk of mortality. PWR is an independent predictor of short- and long-term mortality in ICU patients with NSAH. Machine learning models incorporating PWR significantly improve risk stratification, thereby providing precious support for the early identification and personalized management of patients in the ICU.

42875250.title: [Heat stroke: a critical care perspective].
42875250.journal: Zhonghua wei zhong bing ji jiu yi xue
42875250.abstract: Heat stroke is a life-threatening clinical syndrome caused by an imbalance between heat production and heat dissipation resulting from exposure to a hot environment and (or) strenuous physical activity. It is characterized by a core body temperature>40 centigrade and central nervous system abnormalities (such as altered mental status, seizures, or coma), accompanied by multiple organ injury. Against the backdrop of global warming and the marked increase in extreme heat events, the incidence of heat-related illnesses has risen significantly. As the most severe form of heat-related illness, heat stroke has an abrupt onset and a critical clinical course, with high rates of severe illness and mortality, posing a serious threat to human health. The progression from mild heat-related illness to the most severe form, heat stroke, represents a continuum of progressively worsening conditions. Clinically, heat stroke presents as an acute syndrome involving complex pathophysiological processes that lead to multiple organ dysfunction. Critical illness represents a state dysregulated host response to disease or injury, ultimately resulting in multiple organ dysfunction and progression toward death. Therefore, how do heat-related illnesses evolve into the life-threatening critical state of heat stroke? This article analyzes the pathogenesis of heat stroke from a critical care perspective, aiming to deepen the understanding of heat stroke and enhance critical care-oriented clinical decision-making.

42864767.title: Critical Care Nurses' Encounters With Multicultural Patients and Families in Saudi Arabia: A Qualitative Study.
42864767.abstract: To examine the perceptions and experiences of local and expatriate critical care nurses when interacting with multicultural patients and their families in Saudi healthcare settings. A descriptive qualitative exploratory design was employed to gain an in-depth understanding using purposive sampling. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, conducted in English, with 18 nurses from intensive care, cardiac care, burn and emergency units. We operationally defined multicultural patients and families as those whose nationality, language, religion, or cultural background differed from that of the treating nurse (see Section 1 for the full definition). Interviews explored nurses' perceptions and encounters with multicultural patients and families. Transcribed data were analysed using thematic analysis. Four major themes emerged. Communication barriers, particularly language differences, were the most frequently reported and, according to participants, the most immediately consequential challenge, since language determined whether basic clinical information could be exchanged at all; cultural and religious beliefs, limited health literacy and organisational constraints shaped how well that information was received and acted upon. Nurses employed adaptive strategies, including teamwork, translation technologies and institutional support (e.g., embassies, social workers), largely in the absence of formal interpreter services. Nurses described a strong personal and professional commitment to diversity, equity and inclusion; however, most reported little or no structured training in cultural competence, relying instead on informal, experience-based learning and identified specific system-level gaps in interpreter provision and culturally adapted policy. Critical care nurses face substantial challenges in caring for multicultural patients. Enhancing cultural competence requires tailored training, adequate resources and system-level support. These findings underscore the importance of organisational policies and infrastructure that promote culturally sensitive, patient-centred care. Structured cultural competence training and access to system-level resources, including professional interpreters and culturally adapted policies, are essential. These measures enable nurses to communicate effectively, respect patients' cultural and religious practices, and deliver equitable, patient-centred care. The study highlights key communication barriers and effective strategies for culturally competent care in post-Vision 2030 Saudi healthcare settings. Findings may inform education, policy and practice and support efforts to strengthen patient-family-nurse interactions and culturally responsive care. We adhered to the relevant EQUATOR Network reporting guidance using the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ); the completed COREQ checklist is provided in Table S1. No patient or public contribution.

42859736.title: Effect of Virtual Reality Relaxation on Alarm Fatigue and Professional Quality of Life Among Nurses in Intensive Care Units.
42859736.abstract: Intensive care unit nurses are faced with a large number of equipment alarms daily, which can increase the likelihood of errors and threaten their professional quality of life. Today, the use of virtual reality to create relaxing experiences in stressful environments has received attention. This study aimed to determine the effect of virtual reality relaxation on alarm fatigue and the professional quality of life among ICU nurses. This is an intervention study with a pretest-posttest design with a control group. ICU nurses who met the inclusion criteria were selected conveniently and were randomly assigned to two intervention and control groups (30 people in each group). The intervention was implemented as three 20-min virtual reality relaxation sessions over a week. The data collection tools included the Alarm Fatigue Scale (AFS) and the Professional Quality of Life (ProQOL) questionnaire. The questionnaires were completed before and immediately after the intervention. The results showed that the mean AFS score improved significantly after the intervention (p < 0.001), and there was a significant difference between the intervention and control groups (p = 0.014). The mean dimensions of ProQOL also improved significantly in all three dimensions of compassion satisfaction, burnout, and secondary trauma stress after the intervention (p < 0.001). There was a significant difference between two groups in all dimensions after the intervention (p < 0.001). The significant improvement in AFS and ProQOL scores indicates that the use of new technologies, such as virtual reality can be considered as a complementary tool in promoting the mental and professional health of nurses in stressful environments.

42858643.title: Nursing management of postoperative hemorrhagic shock: A case study in intensive care.
42858643.abstract: Postoperative hemorrhagic shock is a time-critical complication associated with high morbidity and mortality, particularly in older surgical patients, requiring rapid, coordinated management in the intensive care unit (ICU). This case report describes specialized nursing management guided by the International Classification for Nursing Practice (ICNP®/CIPE®) and Benner's Clinical Wisdom Theory. An 89-year-old woman underwent emergency gastrojejunostomy for intestinal obstruction and subsequently developed hemorrhagic shock with profound anemia (hemoglobin nadir 5.8 g/dL), severe hyperlactatemia (12 mmol/L), hypothermia (33.6 °C), peripheral hypoperfusion, and hypotension (mean arterial pressure <65 mmHg). She required orotracheal intubation, invasive mechanical ventilation, and deep sedation. Diagnostic reassessment included serial hemoglobin and arterial blood gas analyses, lactate trending, invasive hemodynamic monitoring, and surgical re-exploration with intraoperative upper endoscopy, which suggested an upper gastrointestinal source (suspected Mallory-Weiss type lesion) treated endoscopically. Nursing priorities, structured using ICNP®, focused on perfusion restoration and correction of the lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy), multimodal analgesia, continuous monitoring, prevention bundles (infection and pressure injury prevention), and structured family communication. The patient progressively stabilized, with hemoglobin increasing to 9.6 g/dL, lactate decreasing to <1 mmol/L, normothermia recovery, discontinuation of vasopressors, and no documented ICU-acquired complications during the ICU stay. This case highlights how standardized nursing language (ICNP®/CIPE®), combined with advanced clinical reasoning and evidence-based ICU bundles, can improve the structure, traceability, and continuity of nursing care in postoperative hemorrhagic shock.

42956896.title: Dysnatremia in critically ill burn patients: incidence, timing and association with kidney outcomes.
42956896.abstract: Dysnatremia is common in critically ill patients and has been linked to poor outcomes and renal prognosis. Burn patients are particularly vulnerable, but the prognostic significance of dysnatremia in this population remains unclear. We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of 1,758 burn patients admitted to a French burn center between 2011 and 2023. Dysnatremia was defined as at least one episode of hyponatremia (<135 mmol/L) or hypernatremia (>145 mmol/L) during intensive care unit (ICU) stay. The primary endpoint was the incidence of dysnatremia; secondary endpoints included major adverse kidney events (MAKE) at ICU discharge and acute kidney injury (AKI) occurrence and severity. Dysnatremia occurred in 56.3% of patients (n = 990), with hyponatremia in 50.5% (n = 888) and hypernatremia in 23.8% (n = 418). MAKE at ICU discharge did not differ between hyponatremic and normonatremic patients (12.6% vs. 10.9%, p = 0.304) but was sixfold higher with hypernatremia (32.3% vs. 5.4%, p < 0.001). After adjustment for age and burned total body surface area, hypernatremia was independently associated with MAKE at ICU discharge (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 4.03; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.92-5.56; p < 0.001), whereas hyponatremia was not (aHR 1.15; 95% CI: 0.85-1.55; p = 0.377). Clustering analysis identified three phenotypes: Cluster B (severe burns, worst outcomes), Cluster A (older patients, mostly hyponatremic, intermediate outcomes), and Cluster C (younger patients, mild burns, best outcomes). Dysnatremia affects over half of burn patients. Sodium disturbances should be viewed as markers of systemic severity, warranting close monitoring and preventive strategies.

42952867.title: Comparative analysis of the hemodynamic and metabolic effects of alternative fluid resuscitation strategies in critically ill patients with combined chest trauma and hemorrhagic shock: impact on oxygen delivery-consumption balance and coagulation homeostasis.
42952867.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the effects of different fluid resuscitation strategies on clinical efficacy, oxygen metabolism, coagulation function, and inflammatory response in critically ill patients with chest trauma complicated by hemorrhagic shock, so as to provide evidence for optimizing emergency treatment strategies. A total of 107 patients with severe chest trauma and hemorrhagic shock who were admitted to our hospital between June 2023 and April 2025 were retrospectively enrolled. According to the type of treatment received, patients were divided into two groups. The control group (n = 55) received conventional fluid resuscitation, while the observation group (n = 52) received restrictive fluid resuscitation. The two groups were compared in terms of fluid resuscitation parameters, oxygen metabolism indicators [mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2), oxygen consumption (VO2), oxygen delivery (DO2)], coagulation indicators [activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), prothrombin time (PT), hematocrit (HCT)], inflammatory indicators [interleukin-6 (IL-6), interleukin-10 (IL-10), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)], as well as mortality and complication rates during resuscitation. Compared with the control group, the observation group had significantly lower fluid input volume (P < 0.05); there were no significant differences in early resuscitation time or colloid use between the two groups (P > 0.05). After resuscitation, SvO2, VO2, DO2, and HCT levels were all significantly increased compared with before resuscitation, while APTT, PT, IL-6, IL-10, and TNF-α levels were significantly decreased in both groups. The magnitude of changes in the observation group was significantly greater than in the control group (P < 0.05). During the resuscitation period, the survival rate of the observation group was significantly higher than that of the control group, while the incidence of ARDS, DIC, and MODS was significantly lower (P < 0.05). Compared with conventional fluid resuscitation, restrictive fluid resuscitation shows more significant clinical advantages. Its application in patients with severe chest trauma complicated by hemorrhagic shock can reduce unnecessary fluid overload, more effectively improve oxygen metabolism, correct coagulation dysfunction, suppress inflammatory responses, thereby increasing survival rates and reducing the risk of complications.

42946875.title: Environmental scan of Indigenous resources and culturally specific tools across intensive care units in Alberta, Canada.
42946875.journal: Canadian journal of anaesthesia = Journal canadien d'anesthesie
42946875.abstract: Indigenous Peoples in Canada are disproportionately burdened with a spectrum of health issues and consistently report lower satisfaction with their health care; nevertheless, little is known about their experiences with critical care and the support received during critical illness. We aimed to describe the current scope of critical-care-specific resources available to Indigenous patients and their families across Alberta to identify gaps and opportunities to implement actionable change to realize more equitable and culturally safe care. We conducted a two-phase environmental scan. Phase 1 entailed searching websites for information to support Indigenous patients, their families, and health care workers. Phase 2 facilitated 21 interviews with intensive care unit (ICU) stakeholders from across Alberta to further describe site-specific resources, services, tools, or initiatives to support Indigenous Peoples. Indigenous partners were engaged through all aspects of the project. Our environmental scan identified a paucity of ICU-specific resources, programs, or policies to support Indigenous patients and families' navigation with critical care. We identified two national resources aimed at clinicians, rather than patients or families. Interviews with ICU stakeholders confirmed the paucity of Indigenous-specific resources. Stakeholders cited numerous barriers, including inadequate culture training, staff time constraints and burnout, physical space limits, and insufficient personnel, such as Indigenous liaisons and social workers. Multiple gaps exist in the availability of critical-care-focused resources and supports for Indigenous Peoples experiencing critical illness in Alberta, Canada. Addressing these care gaps may improve health equity, access, and the experience for Indigenous patients and families during critical illness and further build trust and strengthen relationships with health care workers.

42938474.title: The Interface Between Parental and Occupational Burnout in Critical Care Unit Staff: A Multicentre Cross-Sectional Study.
42938474.abstract: Occupational burnout among Critical Care Unit (CCU) staff is a pressing issue, yet the relationship between parental burnout and this high-demand professional domain remains underexplored. Thus, this study aimed to analyze the association between parental and occupational burnout in critical care healthcare professionals. A multicentre cross-sectional study was conducted across three CCUs in hospitals within the Vigo Health Area (northern Spain). The sample included 106 CCU staff members with dependent children. Data were collected using the Burnout Screening Inventory, Parental Burnout Assessment, and Oslo Social Support Scale. Although the overall prevalence of occupational burnout was low in this sample, total parental burnout emerged as a statistically significant positive predictor of occupational burnout (β = 0.303, p = 0.003). Among its dimensions, parental emotional distancing acted as the most salient predictor (β = 0.409, p = 0.006). Parental burnout is significantly associated with higher levels of occupational burnout among CCU professionals, with parental emotional distancing being the most relevant dimension in this relationship, with perceived social support as an inverted association. These findings highlight the co-occurrence of both phenomena and the need to acknowledge the intersection of family demands and high-intensity work environments when addressing occupational wellbeing in critical care settings.

42926795.title: Impact of direct transfer to critical care on mortality for patients who undergo emergency colorectal cancer resection: a national population-based cohort study in England.
42926795.abstract: It is recommended that patients receiving emergency surgery and with 'high-risk' of morbidity and mortality should be transferred directly from theatre to critical care. Using a national, population-based cohort study, we estimated the effect of direct transfer to critical care on 90-day mortality after emergency colorectal cancer resection, and the variation amongst English NHS hospitals. Patients who underwent emergency colorectal cancer resection between December 2016 and November 2019 according to Hospital Episodes Statistics, National Bowel Cancer Audit or National Emergency Laparotomy Audit were included. Patients were identified as having a direct transfer to critical care through linkage with the Intensive Care National Audit and Research Centre Case Mix Programme. Multivariable logistic regression and propensity score methods were used to measure the effect of direct transfer to critical care on 90-day mortality. In total, 10,441 patients underwent an emergency colorectal cancer resection. Unadjusted 90-day mortality was higher in the direct transfer to critical care cohort (10.9%) than in patients without direct transfer to critical care (3.7%) (odds ratio [OR]: 3.16, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.65-3.77). There was no evidence of an association after risk adjustment (adjusted OR: 1.16, 95% CI: 0.94-1.43) or after propensity score analysis (weighted OR: 0.94, 95% CI: 0.69-1.27). For patients at high risk with a predicted mortality ≥5%, the proportion of patients with a direct transfer to critical care varied widely amongst hospitals (interquartile range 68%-92%; median 83%). Our findings suggest that apparent higher postoperative mortality in patients having direct transfer to critical care can be mostly explained by characteristics of patients, tumours, physiology and surgery. However, the extent to which direct transfer to critical care is used varies widely amongst hospitals. Further work to understand this variation has the potential to improve patient outcomes after emergency colorectal cancer resection.

42907890.title: The effect of sleep quality and depressive symptoms on the relationship between burnout and health-related productivity loss in nurses working in intensive care: a cross-sectional study from the Chinese nurses' health cohort study (TARGET).
42907890.abstract: Burnout is highly prevalent among ICU nurses and compromises physical and psychological well-being, leading to productivity loss. However, limited evidence exists regarding the pathways through which burnout influences productivity, particularly the role of sleep disturbance and depression. Few studies have examined the mechanisms through which burnout affects health-related productivity in intensive care unit (ICU) nurses. This study addresses this gap by investigating the sequential mediating role of sleep quality and depressive symptoms in the relationship between burnout and health-related productivity loss. A cross-sectional study. Baseline data from the Chinese Nurses' Health Cohort Study, collected between December 2020 and February 2024, included 3,491 ICU nurses. Burnout, health-related productivity loss, sleep quality and depressive symptoms were assessed using the Maslach Burnout Inventory-Human Services Survey, Stanford Presenteeism Scale, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and Patient Health Questionnaire-9. Chain mediation analysis was conducted using the SPSS PROCESS macro, and subgroup analyses were performed. Data from 3,491 ICU nurses were analyzed. Subgroup analyses showed female nurses aged 18-30 years, with a master's degree or above, senior titles, contract positions, clinical roles, and 6-10 years of experience reported higher productivity loss. Productivity loss correlated with burnout, poor sleep quality, and depressive symptoms. Mediation analysis using Bootstrap resampling (5,000 iterations) revealed that burnout had a significant total effect on productivity loss (β = 0.1019, 95% CI [0.0963, 0.1076]). The direct effect remained significant after accounting for mediators (β = 0.0587, 95% CI [0.0527, 0.0647]). The sequential indirect effect through sleep quality and depressive symptoms was significant (β = 0.0422, 95% CI [0.0395, 0.0469]), indicating that burnout impaired sleep quality, which increased depressive symptoms and ultimately contributed to greater productivity loss. The relationship between burnout and health-related productivity is mediated by sleep quality and depressive symptoms. Interventions reducing burnout, improving sleep quality, and preventing depression may help mitigate productivity loss. The study protocol for TARGET was registered with the China Clinical Trial Registry (registration number: ChiCTR2100043202, February 8, 2021, https://trialsearch.who.int/Default.aspx ).
