Whilst patients with preserved muscle mass may have a survival advantage, the phenotypes characterised by ectopic visceral fat or sarcopenia are frequently complicated by multimorbidity and polypharmacy, likely increasing the risk of adverse effects such as suboptimal sedation, prolonged ventilation and immobilisation, malnutrition, and impaired recovery. Targeted respiratory interventions, including secretion-clearance techniques and appropriate patient positioning to prevent atelectasis, reduce the work of breathing. Optimisation of communication and swallowing function is an essential component for facilitating safe oral intake and promoting active patient participation in rehabilitation. Concurrently, targeted nutrition strategies combined with early, targeted, progressive mobilisation might mitigate ICU acquired weakness and support functional recovery. The availability of appropriate weight‑based equipment is fundamental to ensuring safe mobilisation for both patients and healthcare professionals. CONCLUSION: Interprofessional collaboration is central to optimising outcomes and should extend beyond the ICU to structured post-ICU follow-up to address persistent, worsening, or newly emerging health impairments. Early rehabilitation in critically ill patients with obesity should integrate physiological, logistical, and psychosocial considerations to support equitable and functional recovery.

42301229.title: Impact of Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System Therapy on Piperacillin Concentration in Critically Ill Patients: An Observational Cohort Study.
42301229.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To assess the impact of Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System (MARS) therapy on total plasma piperacillin concentrations in critically ill patients with acute liver failure or acute-on-chronic liver failure. DESIGN: Retrospective, single-center observational cohort study. SETTING: University ICU. PATIENTS: Consecutive adult patients treated with MARS therapy and piperacillin-tazobactam between March 2023 and June 2025. INTERVENTIONS: MARS therapy was delivered as 8-hour sessions for up to three consecutive days. Piperacillin-tazobactam was administered by continuous infusion following a loading dose. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Venous blood samples were collected immediately before and after each MARS session. Total piperacillin concentrations were quantified using ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography. The primary endpoint was the relative reduction in plasma piperacillin concentration induced by MARS therapy. Thirty patients (121 piperacillin measurements across 77 sessions) were analyzed. Seventy-three percent had cirrhosis (median Model for End-Stage Liver Disease Score 31 [23-38]). The mean relative reduction in piperacillin concentration per session was 34% (± 7.9%; p < 0.05). In univariable mixed-effects analysis, MARS session (β -47.49 mg/L; p < 0.001) and creatinine clearance (β -0.37 mg/L per mL/min; p < 0.001) were associated with lower concentrations. In multivariable modeling, higher creatinine clearance was independently associated with greater intra-session piperacillin loss ( p < 0.001), whereas higher bilirubin levels were associated with reduced drug loss ( p = 0.01). Overall, 31.6% of post-session concentrations were less than 80 mg/L, and 38% of patients had at least one concentration outside the predefined target range. CONCLUSIONS: MARS therapy was associated with a one-third reduction in total plasma piperacillin concentrations per session. These findings support systematic therapeutic drug monitoring and individualized antibiotic dose adjustment during MARS therapy.

42294965.title: Determinants of Delayed Recovery of Consciousness After Analgosedation Discontinuation in the ICU: Insights From Patients With COVID-19 Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure.
42294965.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Prolonged disorders of consciousness are common in critically ill patients receiving mechanical ventilation and are often attributed to prolonged sedative exposure in the setting of decreased drug clearance and/or reduced metabolism. Here, in a large sample of critically ill COVID patients obtained over a short period, we tested the assumption that prolonged unconsciousness following benzodiazepine and/or propofol sedation can be attributed to residual exposure. Further, we examine associations between clinical variables on time to recovery of consciousness (RoC) as a framework for the broader critically ill population. DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study. SETTING: Massachusetts General Hospital, Weill Cornell Medicine, Columbia University Irving Medical Center. PATIENTS: Seven hundred eighty-four patients with COVID-19 critical illness in Spring-Summer 2020. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We estimated the latest expected RoC (LERoC) using models of sedation exposure that account for sedative-specific pharmacokinetics and critical illness. Our primary exposure variable was a time-weighted dose of analgosedative agents at benzodiazepine and/or propofol cessation; our primary outcome was time to RoC. We estimated relative risks for late RoC (i.e., after LERoC) via multinomial logistic regression. Among individuals with late RoC, we fit a multivariate subdistribution hazard model for time to RoC. Seventy-three percent of patients had RoC before hospital discharge, yet 34% of patients achieving RoC did not do so within pharmacologically plausible sedative elimination times. Patients with late RoC were older and exhibited hypoxemia and acute kidney injury. Patients with dexmedetomidine as an adjunct sedative had a disproportionately larger incidence of early recovery. Patients with early vs. late RoC did not have significantly different discharge dispositions. CONCLUSIONS: In our cohort, the time to RoC was commonly prolonged beyond that expected from sedation exposures alone. These data may aid clinicians and families with expectations of RoC and warrant investigation of alternative determinants of delayed RoC in this population.

42210338.title: Early inhaled isoflurane sedation in neurocritical patients with invasive intracranial pressure monitoring: the NEURO-CONDA randomized pilot trial.
42210338.abstract: PURPOSE: Evidence on inhaled sedation in neurocritically ill patients remains limited, mainly due to concerns about potential increases in intracranial pressure (ICP). We aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of early isoflurane sedation compared with propofol in invasively monitored neurocritical patients without intracranial hypertension. METHODS: NEURO-CONDA is a phase IV, randomized, open-label, parallel-group pilot trial conducted in a tertiary ICU (May 2024-October 2025). Adult neurocritical patients requiring ICP monitoring and without intracranial hypertension were randomized to receive either propofol or isoflurane. The primary endpoints were efficacy (assessed with RASS and BIS™) and safety, defined as the occurrence of serious adverse drug reactions (ADRs), including sustained ICP elevation or cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) < 60 mmHg requiring increased vasopressor support. Nociception (NOL®) and other systemic parameters were recorded for up to 72 h. Analyses were performed according to the intention-to-treat principle. RESULTS: Thirty patients were included (15 per group), and baseline characteristics were comparable; 19 had traumatic brain injury. Sedation efficacy was 100% in both groups throughout the study period. No serious ADRs occurred. ICP and CPP remained stable throughout the study period without requiring higher doses of vasopressors in the isoflurane sedated group. CONCLUSIONS: In this randomized pilot trial, early sedation with isoflurane was feasible and achieved reliable deep sedation without compromising intracranial or cerebral perfusion parameters in invasively monitored neurocritical patients without intracranial hypertension. Larger randomized studies are warranted to confirm these findings and assess long-term neurological outcomes.

42152115.title: Impact of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation on antimicrobial exposure in critically ill patients: a prospective observational study.
42152115.abstract: BACKGROUND: Antimicrobial pharmacokinetics (PK) in patients receiving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) remains poorly defined. Drug sequestration within the ECMO circuit has been reported; however, existing evidence is primarily based on ex vivo studies and small clinical series, resulting in conflicting findings with limited clinical applicability. This study aimed to characterize antimicrobial sequestration within different ECMO circuit components and to describe the PK of meropenem, piperacillin/tazobactam, linezolid, and ceftaroline in critically ill patients receiving ECMO support. METHODS: We conducted a prospective, single-center observational study in critically ill patients receiving ECMO (veno-venous (VV) or veno-arterial (VA)) and treated with meropenem, piperacillin/tazobactam, linezolid, or ceftaroline. Serial blood samples were collected simultaneously from the patient's arterial line and from pre- and post-membrane oxygenator sampling sites. Non-compartmental analysis was used to derive PK measures, and concentration differences across sampling sites were analyzed to estimate circuit-related drug sequestration. Antimicrobial target attainment was assessed according to established PKPD targets. RESULTS: A total of 237 samples from 8 patients (4 VV, 4 VA) were analyzed. Limited, component-specific sequestration was observed in the membrane oxygenator for meropenem (9.28% ± 21.6%, p = 0.046) and ceftaroline (14.6% ± 17.5%, p = 0.010), for linezolid it was also identified (10.1% ± 12.3%, p = 0.005), but in tubing and connectors. Piperacillin/tazobactam showed negligible retention. However, when considering the ECMO circuit as a whole, no statistically significant reductions in systemic concentrations were observed for any antimicrobial. PK measures were generally consistent across sampling sites. In 20% of treatments, predefined PKPD efficacy targets were not achieved. CONCLUSIONS: Antimicrobial sequestration within the ECMO circuit is detectable and drug- and component-specific. However, overall impact on systemic antimicrobial exposure appears limited. Inadequate PKPD target attainment in a subset of antimicrobial treatments likely reflects the marked PK variability of critical illness rather than ECMO-related drug loss alone. These exploratory results support the use of therapeutic drug monitoring to individualize antimicrobial therapy in ECMO-supported patients and the need to conduct further population PK studies to better characterize determinants of antimicrobial exposure and to clarify the clinical relevance of circuit-related drug sequestration.

42129898.title: Intrapulmonary penetration of ceftolozane/tazobactam and ceftazidime/avibactam administered by continuous infusion in critically ill patients with nosocomial pneumonia: a randomized pharmacokinetic trial.
42129898.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ceftolozane/tazobactam (TOL/TAZ) and ceftazidime-avibactam (CAZ/AVI) are increasingly used to treat pneumonia caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacilli. However, data on intrapulmonary penetration to confirm dosing adequacy are limited. Therefore, the aim of this study was to compare epithelial lining fluid (ELF) penetration and pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) target attainment of TOL/TAZ versus CAZ/AVI administered by continuous infusion (CI) in critically ill patients with nosocomial pneumonia. METHODS: Single-center, open-label, randomized pharmacokinetic (PK) study. Thirty patients were randomized 1:1 to receive 6 g/3 g of TOL/TAZ or 6 g/1.5 g of CAZ/AVI administered by CI. A population PK model was constructed using plasma and ELF concentrations. Lung penetration was estimated based on the ratio AUC0-8ELF/AUC0-8plasma. Simulations were performed to estimate the probability of attaining predefined joint ELF PK/PD target defined as free concentration 100% fT> minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) for the β-lactam component and 100% fT> concentration threshold (CT) for the β-lactamase inhibitors, among relevant MIC scenarios. Three different dosing regimens (low, standard and high) were evaluated for each combination. RESULTS: A total of 298 plasma and 58 ELF samples were analyzed. The median [IQR] age, body mass index, and creatinine clearance were 77 [9.8] years, 26.48 [5.5] kg/m², and 76.0 [96.0] mL/min, respectively. Median intrapulmonary penetration was 0.66 [0.32] for ceftolozane, 0.41 [0.30] for ceftazidime 0.44 [0.05] for tazobactam and 0.44 [0.46] for avibactam. Under the prespecified ELF PK/PD target, standard dosing achieved adequate target attainment for both combinations. Simulations showed that all CAZ/AVI regimens achieved high ELF target attainment under conservative inhibitor threshold assumptions (assuming ceftazidime MIC = 8 mg/L and avibactam CT =1 mg/L), whereas for TOL/TAZ (assuming ceftolozane MIC = 4 mg/L and tazobactam CT 2 mg/L) at least the standard-dose regimen was required. More aggressive target scenarios reduced the probability of target attainment, particularly for inhibitor thresholds of 4 mg/L and for Enterobacterales-oriented joint targets. CONCLUSIONS: In critically ill adults with nosocomial pneumonia receiving TOL/TAZ or CAZ/AVI by CI, standard doses achieved ELF exposures consistent with dual PK/PD target attainment against all susceptible isolates. Interindividual variability and the risk of plasma overexposure support individualized dosing and consideration of therapeutic drug monitoring. TRIAL REGISTRATION: The trial was registered in the European Union Drug Regulating Authorities Clinical Trials Database (EudraCT No. 2021-006908-32). Registered 10 February 2022; https://www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ctr-search/trial/2021-006908-32/ES .

41998735.title: Lung protective characteristics of volatile anesthetic sedation.
41998735.abstract: This narrative review serves as an update to previous reviews on the topic after the results of recent randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses. It describes some of the latest evidence around the use of volatile sedation as an alternative to intravenous sedation in mechanically ventilated patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) and their possible lung-protective properties. Preclinical evidence supporting an anti-inflammatory protective effect of volatile anesthetics suggests that volatile sedation could be employed in patients with inflammatory lung injury, including acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Large randomized controlled non-inferiority trials of isoflurane for general ICU sedation have suggested that it is effective, with no differences between groups in safety outcomes; however, the results of a recent RCT in patients with ARDS have demonstrated significant harm with the use of sevoflurane sedation. Therefore, the utility and safety of volatile sedation in patients with inflammatory lung injury, including ARDS, is now in question.

41989178.title: Disparities in Finding Delirium in Critically Ill Latinos.
41989178.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Delirium is common in the ICU and is associated with devastating consequences. However, the accuracy of delirium detection tools has not been evaluated when patient-provider language discordance is present. This study aimed to assess the accuracy of delirium screening practices in Spanish-speaking ICU patients, evaluate whether caregiver-administered tools improve detection amid language barriers, and examine language-based differences in delirium care. DESIGN: Prospective observational cohort study. SETTING: Two MICUs at the University of California, San Diego. PATIENTS: 142 ICU patients and 100 caregivers were enrolled between August 2024 and January 2025. INTERVENTIONS: Usual-Care (Confusion Assessment Method [CAM]-ICU completed by bedside providers), Reference-standard (English or Spanish-language CAM-ICU performed by research staff), and FAM-CAM (English or Spanish-language Family-CAM administered by caregivers). MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Among 71 English-speakers, 34 female (47%), with a mean ( sd ) age of 62 years (16). Among 71 Spanish-speakers, 26 female (37%) and the mean age was 60 years (15). The prevalence of delirium was 39% overall, affecting 26 (37%) English-speakers and 32 (45%) Spanish-speakers. Agreement between Usual-Care and Reference-standard was higher in English-speakers than in Spanish-speakers (κ=0.71 vs. κ=0.11; z=-4.98, p < 0.01), with 72% of delirium missed in Spanish-speakers. Among Spanish-speakers, FAM-CAM showed higher agreement with Reference-standard than did Usual-Care (κ=0.68 vs. κ=0.11; z= -4.69, p < 0.05) and reduced the rate of missed delirium by 47%. Spanish-speakers were more deeply sedated (mean Richmond Agitation Sedation Scale -1.46 [ sd 1.38] vs. -0.77 [ sd 1.31]; mean difference 0.69; 95% CI, 0.24 to 1.14, p < 0.01) and had higher odds of restraint use (odds ratio 4.53; 95% CI 1.91 to 10.74; p < 0.01) than English-speakers. CONCLUSIONS: Usual-Care demonstrated poor accuracy in delirium detection among Spanish-speakers, who also experienced deeper sedation and more frequent restraint use than English-speakers. FAM-CAM improved delirium detection among Spanish-speakers and may help overcome language barriers to equitable delirium detection.

42206929.title: Reducing Physical Restraint in the ICU: Multicenter Phase II Randomized Trial of a Novel Device Versus Traditional Wrist Restraints.
42206929.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate a novel device, developed under a National Institutes of Health Small Business Technology Transfer program grant, designed as an alternative to traditional wrist restraints. DESIGN: Within-patient crossover phase II randomized trial. SETTING: Four U.S. academic medical centers. PATIENTS: ICU patients ( n = 54) who were verbally responsive with a provider order for wrist restraints and expected stay greater than or equal to 2 days. INTERVENTIONS: Alternating use of novel device vs. traditional restraint during 4-hour assessment periods over 2 days (four assessment periods), with randomization of initial allocation to novel device vs. restraint. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Upper extremity activity (measured via wrist actigraphy) was the primary outcome, with safety, sedation, delirium, satisfaction (via Quebec User Evaluation of Satisfaction with Assistive Technology [QUEST] survey), and qualitative analyses of survey data as secondary outcomes. Analysis of actigraphy data demonstrated similar mean activity counts per 4-hour session for the novel device vs. traditional restraints, with a range of mean activity across the four sessions of 2930-4395 vs. 3898-4910, respectively, with relative mean total activity count per session of 0.93 (95% CI, 0.76-1.13; p = 0.45). Across 98 sessions using the novel device, 2 (2%) potential safety events were reported. No statistically significant differences were observed in sedation/agitation, or delirium status and severity. Of the QUEST satisfaction surveys completed by patient/family ( n = 25) and clinicians ( n = 79), 58% and 51%, respectively, indicated high satisfaction with qualitative analyses demonstrating four positive and six constructive themes. CONCLUSIONS: No differences in upper extremity activity, delirium, sedation, or agitation were demonstrated between the novel device and traditional wrist restraints. The novel device had overall moderate patient/family and clinician satisfaction, and qualitative analyses provide important insights for advancing the development of novel restraint alternative devices.

42612901.title: Induction Agents for Tracheal Intubation of Critically Ill Patients: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
42612901.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tracheal intubation is a common yet high-risk procedure in critically ill patients, with as many as one-half experiencing peri-intubation adverse outcomes. RESEARCH QUESTION: What is the comparative effectiveness and safety of various sedative agents used for endotracheal intubation of critically ill patients in the emergency department (ED), ICU, operating room, and prehospital setting? STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: We conducted a network meta-analysis and systematic review of randomized controlled trials. We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, PubMed, Cochrane, and trial registries from inception through December 10, 2025, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing ≥ 2 sedative agents in critically ill adults or children undergoing endotracheal intubation. Outcomes of interest were hemodynamic instability during intubation, hypoxemia, cardiac arrest, mortality, ICU and hospital length of stay, vasopressor use, adrenal insufficiency, and first-pass success. Reviewers screened, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool independently and in duplicate. We performed frequentist random-effects model network meta-analysis and used the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach to rate certainty in estimates. RESULTS: We included 21 RCTs enrolling 6,031 patients across ICU, ED, operating room, and prehospital settings. Compared with etomidate, more hemodynamic instability exists during intubation with ketamine (relative risk [RR], 1.31; 95% CI, 1.15-1.48; moderate certainty). Ketamine-propofol may decrease hemodynamic instability during intubation compared with etomidate (RR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.27-0.72; low certainty) and ketamine (RR, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.21-0.56; low certainty). Compared with etomidate, ketamine may decrease the need for the initiation of postintubation continuous infusion vasopressors (RR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.50-1.28; low certainty). Etomidate caused increased adrenal suppression compared with other agents. INTERPRETATION: Our results show that when considering sedation agents for endotracheal intubation of critically ill patients, etomidate probably causes less hemodynamic instability during intubation when compared with ketamine. However, etomidate may increase the need for the initiation of postintubation continuous infusion vasopressors when compared with ketamine and increases adrenal suppression. The clinical importance of these competing effects remains uncertain. Ketamine-propofol may decrease hemodynamic instability during intubation when compared with etomidate and ketamine, although the available evidence is too limited and uncertain to support firm conclusions, and further randomized trials are needed. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews; No.: CRD42024600739; URL: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/.

41823503.title: Sex Disparities in the Clinical Management and Outcomes of Critically Ill Adults Undergoing Electroencephalography Monitoring.
41823503.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sex-related discrepancies concerning the treatment of patients in intensive care are increasingly described. However, information about management and outcome of critically ill patients undergoing electroencephalography is scarce. OBJECTIVES: This study explores sex-related disparities in management and clinical outcomes in critically ill patients needing electroencephalography for clinical purposes. DESIGN, SETTING, PATIENTS, AND INTERVENTIONS: In this post hoc analysis of the multicenter Continuous Electroencephalography Randomized Trial in Adults (CERTA), which included patients with impaired consciousness requiring electroencephalography, we explored correlations between sex and the timing of electroencephalography, detection of electroencephalography abnormalities, mechanical ventilation, sedation, antiseizure therapy, mortality, and favorable functional outcome (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 1-2) at 6 months, using univariable and multivariable analyses. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Among 364 patients (33.8% women), women showed a higher prevalence of intracranial hemorrhage (women 30.9%, men 19.5%; p = 0.015) and epileptiform electroencephalography discharges (women 27.6%, men 21.2%; p = 0.008), but use of sedation, antiseizure medication and mechanical ventilation was similar between sexes. Although mortality was similar (adjusted odds ratio [OR], 0.70; 95% CI, 0.39-1.28), women were less likely to reach CPC 1-2 (adjusted OR, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.28-0.90). CONCLUSIONS: Critically ill women and men requiring electroencephalography appear to receive similar clinical management and have comparable mortality, although long-term functional outcome in surviving women is worse. These findings warrant further investigation to identify modifiable factors contributing to sex-related outcome differences.

42593537.title: Decades of intensive care medicine trials: what randomised evidence has changed, corrected, and still questions to resolve.
42593537.abstract: BACKGROUND: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) have reshaped intensive care medicine (ICM), a discipline defined by acute, interacting organ failures, time-sensitive decisions, biological uncertainty, and heterogeneous recovery trajectories. Many interventions supported by strong physiological rationale failed to improve patient-centred outcomes, whereas durable advances often emerged from optimisation of supportive care, avoidance of iatrogenic harm, and reassessment of established practices. METHODS: We conducted an interpretive historical review of landmark multicentre RCTs in adult ICM from the early 1990s onwards. PubMed searches, reference lists from major trials and reviews, and international guidelines were used to identify trials with conceptual influence on practice, guidelines, physiological reasoning, therapeutic strategy, research priorities, de-implementation, or outcome framing. Evidence was organised into overlapping paradigms rather than rigid chronological periods. FINDINGS: Across haemodynamic support, mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, antimicrobial treatment, nutrition, glucose control, transfusion, and sedation, landmark RCTs describe more than therapeutic expansion. Early biological and haemodynamic trials exposed the limits of reductionist strategies in syndromic critical illness. Protocol-driven approaches improved timeliness and consistency, but later pragmatic trials showed that rigid targets and invasive algorithms often added little once high-quality usual care was established. More recent trials challenge the assumption that greater intervention intensity improves outcomes, emphasising timing, disease phase, baseline risk, heterogeneity, patient selection, and treatment-related harm. Modern ICM RCTs have clarified not only what works, but what can be reduced, delayed, avoided, or applied selectively. Future progress requires biologically informed, context-sensitive trials focussed on meaningful survival, recovery, and long-term function.

42455344.title: Antiseizure medication dosing and monitoring in the intensive care unit: a practical narrative review.
42455344.abstract: PURPOSE: Antiseizure medications (ASMs) are commonly used in the intensive care unit (ICU) and often exhibit pharmacokinetics that differ substantially from those in healthy volunteers or in the outpatient setting. Organ dysfunction, polypharmacy, exogenous devices, and greater severity of illness all influence ASM pharmacokinetics, dosing decisions, and monitoring parameters. It is essential for critical care clinicians to familiarize themselves with the pharmacokinetics, dosing considerations, effects of exogenous devices, and therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)-all covered in this narrative review-to incorporate in their approach to ASMs in the critical care setting. METHODS: We identified relevant literature from MEDLINE from inception to March 2026 related to ASMs in the ICU. Data on pharmacokinetics, dosing in the ICU, the effect of renal replacement therapy, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), and plasmapheresis (PLEX) on ASM exposure, and the role of TDM in the ICU were collected and summarized. RESULTS: Considerations for 15 ASMs (brivaracetam, cannabidiol, carbamazepine, cenobamate, clobazam, lacosamide, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, perampanel, phenobarbital, phenytoin, topiramate, valproate, and zonisamide) were included in the review. Dosing considerations for TDM, including indications and target reference ranges, and specific settings such as organ dysfunction, illness severity, renal replacement therapy, ECMO, and PLEX are discussed. CONCLUSION: The use of ASMs in the ICU require a distinct approach from outpatient settings. Severity of illness, organ dysfunction and replacement devices, and frequent drug-drug interactions warrant tailored agent selection, dosing, and monitoring.

42839269.title: Comparison of two automated pupillometry indices in patients with acute brain injury: the prospective multicentre LYNX cohort study.
42839269.abstract: BACKGROUND: Automated pupillometry quantifies the pupillary light reflex in acute brain injury. The neurological pupil index (NPi) is the established composite index and carries prognostic value. A second index from a different device, the quantitative pupil index (QPi), has recently become available, but whether it conveys equivalent information in non-anoxic acute brain injury is unknown. METHODS: LYNX was a prospective cohort study in three European intensive care units (September 2022-July 2024). Consecutive adults with traumatic brain injury, subarachnoid or intracerebral haemorrhage, or ischaemic stroke ventilated for more than 12 h were enrolled and followed for 6 months. Paired NPi (NPi-300) and QPi (NeuroLight) measurements were obtained at least every 6 h to day 7. Ancillary cohorts of healthy volunteers (dark vs. bright light) and surgical patients (before and after sufentanil and propofol) were also studied. The primary outcome was the correlation between the two indices; secondary outcomes were their association with intracranial hypertension and unfavourable 6-month outcome (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended ≤ 4). Values below 3 were considered abnormal, with QPi thresholds of 2 and 4 as sensitivity analyses; multivariable models were adjusted for age, sex, admission Glasgow Coma Scale score and focal deficit. RESULTS: Among 108 patients (median age 57 years [IQR 44-67], 60.2% male), 7089 paired measurements were obtained. The two indices were moderately to strongly correlated (r = 0.717, 95% CI 0.705-0.730). Each 10-percentage-point increase in abnormal values independently predicted unfavourable outcome (NPi: OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.09-2.04, p = 0.013; QPi: OR 1.76, 95% CI 1.31-2.37, p < 0.001). QPi was associated with intracranial hypertension (OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.04-1.82, p = 0.025), whereas NPi was not. Ambient lighting and contralateral eye opening had no meaningful effect in 75 volunteers. In 20 sedated non-brain-injured patients, propofol reduced QPi to a median of 1 (IQR 1-3) and NPi to 4.0 (IQR 3.6-4.3). CONCLUSIONS: NPi and QPi were correlated and both predicted 6-month outcome, but QPi was far more sensitive to anaesthetics, which probably confounds its association with intracranial hypertension. The indices are not interchangeable in sedated critically ill patients. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05567978. Registered 5 October 2022.

42904879.title: Music Therapy During Weaning From Invasive Mechanical Ventilation in the ICU: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
42904879.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The study examined the effect of daily music therapy on weaning from invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in the ICU, with a primary focus on weaning duration. Secondary agitation, sedation, and analgesia doses, pain, delirium, and perceived stress after 90 days were assessed. Additionally, total IMV and ICU stay durations and tracheostomy rates were studied. Physiologic parameters were assessed in the music therapy group (MG). The study also aimed to promote the humanization of critical care through a biopsychosocial and creative music therapy approach. DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups: control group receiving standard care during weaning and MG receiving music therapy additionally. SETTING AND PATIENTS: Adult critically ill patients (n = 100) admitted to a general ICU who received IMV for at least 48 hours. INTERVENTIONS: MG received daily, individualized music therapy sessions averaging 25 minutes, based on patient needs and musical preferences, which included music relaxation, music listening, and clinical improvisation. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: No significant difference in weaning duration was observed between groups (p = 0.97). Patients in the MG group showed significant improvements in agitation and sedation levels (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale) on days 1 and 3 (p = 0.048, 0.005, and 0.024) and a lower percentage required propofol (p = 0.028). No significant difference in perceived pain (Visual Analog Pain Scale). The MG obtained lower Perceived Stress Scale-14 scores (p = 0.24). Additionally, MG significantly reduced tracheostomy rates (14%; p = 0.025). Median total IMV and ICU stay duration were shorter in the MG group, but not significantly (p = 0.206 and 0.203). Heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygenation showed no significant difference before and after music therapy. CONCLUSIONS: Music therapy may serve as a nonpharmacological complementary adjunct during weaning by reducing agitation, sedation, and tracheostomy rate. It may potentially decrease perceived stress and IMV and ICU stay durations. Further research is warranted.

42911397.title: Principles of drug dosing for obese patients in the intensive care unit.
42911397.abstract: PURPOSE: The increasing prevalence of severe obesity in intensive care unit (ICU) patients has led to several challenges with medication dosing. Doses listed in product labels or tertiary references typically do not account for the pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic variability encountered with obesity, leading to the potential for treatment failure or an adverse effect. The purpose of this review is to provide guidance for ICU clinicians when crafting pharmacotherapy regimens in critically ill patients with extreme obesity. METHODS: A literature search was performed to identify relevant articles pertaining to the pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics of medications in obese patients. Articles describing both general treatment principles and medication specific assessments were retrieved. Bibliographies were searched for additional publications. RESULTS: Evidence guiding medication use in critically ill obese patients is limited by the small number of patients with more extreme forms of obesity, the lack of clinical outcome measurements, and the few studies that are specific to the ICU. Obesity-related alterations in pharmacokinetic parameters, such as apparent volume of distribution and drug clearance, may hinder attainment of pharmacodynamic targets. Individualized dosing strategies are essential to optimize therapeutic outcomes. This review provides dosing recommendations for selected ICU medications and proposes a practical framework to guide medication dosing decisions in this patient population. CONCLUSION: Drug dosing in critically ill obese patients should be individualized by assessing pharmacokinetic variability and whether pharmacodynamic goals can be achieved. Selecting the correct weight for weight-based calculations or dose for fixed regimens is paramount for achieving these goals. Consultation with a clinical pharmacist may be beneficial.

42878613.title: Developing Models for Complicated Outcomes in Acutely Intoxicated ICU Patients With and Without Toxicity Information.
authors: and the INTOXICATE Study Investigators Group
42878613.abstract: To assess the prognostic value of the mean Lethality Risk Score (LRS), reflecting the toxicity of substances involved in an exposure, and to develop prediction models for complicated outcomes in ICU patients with acute intoxication. Multicenter prospective cohort study. Seventy-eight ICUs in Europe, Australia, and the Eastern Mediterranean (2020-2023). A total of 2265 adult patients were admitted to the ICU with acute intoxication as the main reason for admission for at least 4 hours. None. The primary outcome was defined as ICU complications or death (22.5%). Clinical data were collected in an electronic capture system. We developed two prediction models: one incorporating laboratory variables ("Laboratory Model"), and one including the mean LRS ("Expo Model"). The mean LRS was calculated as the average of the individual LRS values assigned to the toxicants involved in the exposure. Key predictors were age, severity at presentation, systolic blood pressure, Glasgow Coma Scale score, and hospital type. The mean LRS remained significant only when laboratory variables were not considered. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC), calibration plots, likelihood ratio tests, and decision curve analysis. Internal validation demonstrated good performance for both models (AUROCs of 0.79 and 0.77; calibration slopes of 0.94 and 0.95; intercepts of -0.06 and -0.06), with minimal overfitting. Decision curve analysis revealed clinically relevant threshold probability ranges of 0-50% for the Laboratory Model and 0-40% for the Expo Model. The mean LRS had prognostic value only in the absence of laboratory test results. Both models may aid decision-making regarding the management of acutely intoxicated patients in the ICU.

42846739.title: Ethylene Glycol Poisoning Without Fomepizole in a Regional Australian Intensive Care Unit: The Lactate Gap as the Diagnostic Key and the Consequences of Nasogastric Ethanol Therapy.
42846739.abstract: A 62-year-old man presented comatose with pH 6.88 and no ingestion history. A point-of-care lactate above 31 mmol/L with a laboratory lactate of 0.8 mmol/L revealed a lactate gap, diagnosing ethylene glycol poisoning despite a near-normal osmolar gap. High-dose continuous renal replacement therapy corrected the acidosis; he survived.

42909414.title: A Case of Suspected Scombroid Poisoning in Intensive Care Staff: Is It Anaphylaxis?
42909414.abstract: Scombroid poisoning (histamine fish poisoning) is an uncommon foodborne illness that frequently mimics immunoglobulin E-mediated anaphylaxis. We report a case of a previously well 28-year-old intensive care nurse who developed abrupt facial flushing, wheeze, dizziness, and hypotension after consuming canned tuna. Initial observations demonstrated sinus tachycardia and hypotension. She was treated according to established anaphylaxis guidelines with two doses of intramuscular adrenaline, intravenous crystalloid resuscitation, and subsequent adrenaline infusion in intensive care. She recovered rapidly and was discharged the following day. Serial serum mast cell tryptase measurements at approximately one hour, six hours, and 24 hours after symptom onset were all within normal limits. In the absence of previous allergy history and given the temporal association with tuna ingestion, scombroid poisoning was considered as a possible diagnosis. This case highlights the difficulty of distinguishing severe histamine fish poisoning from anaphylaxis in the acute setting and reinforces that life-threatening presentations should initially be managed according to anaphylaxis protocols until an alternative diagnosis can be established.

42898047.title: The hidden severity of new psychoactive substances: clinical evidence from emergency and intensive care admissions in Taiwan.
42898047.abstract: New psychoactive substances (NPS) have emerged as a growing threat in Taiwan, yet their clinical severity compared with traditional illicit drugs (TID) remains uncertain. This study aimed to compare the clinical characteristics and critical outcomes between patients with NPS and TID poisoning confirmed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). We conducted a multicenter retrospective cohort study across 10 hospitals within six medical systems in Taiwan. Between March 2019 and January 2020, 1,378 patients with suspected drug intoxication underwent urine LC-MS/MS analysis at certified toxicology laboratories. A total of 362 patients (26.3%) tested positive, including 147 (40.6%) with NPSs, 130 (35.9%) with TIDs, and 85 (23.5%) with mixed substances.Demographic, clinical, and laboratory data were collected through a chart review. Synthetic cathinones and ketamine analogs were the most frequently detected NPSs, whereas methamphetamine/amphetamine and morphine were predominant among TID cases. Critical outcomes were defined as intensive care unit admission or death in the emergency department. The overall rate of critical outcomes was 18.3% (252/1,378). The odds of critical illness did not significantly differ between NPS and TID users (adjusted odds ratio, 0.94; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.51-1.74). Kaplan-Meier survival analysis revealed no significant difference in short-term survival among the NPS, TID, and mixed-drug groups (log-rank p = 0.665). No statistically significant difference in clinical severity or mortality risk was observed between NPS and TID poisoning. These findings highlight that NPS exposure has a similar potential for critical illness and should be managed with the same clinical vigilance as conventional drug poisoning.

42892178.title: Age and intensive care unit admissions following opioid overdose.
42892178.abstract: Older adults are increasingly impacted by the opioid crisis, yet age-related differences in overdose presentation, management, and outcomes leading to intensive care unit (ICU) admission remain poorly characterized. This study examined age-related variations in drug exposures, interventions provided, and hospital utilization among patients experiencing an opioid overdose. The Toxicology Investigators Consortium (ToxIC) Fentalog Study was conducted at 10 US medical centers and collected data on patients who presented to emergency departments with confirmed non-fatal opioid overdose, and available waste serum samples between 9/21/2020-4/14/2026 were included. Chart reviews captured presentations, treatments, and hospital utilization. Toxicologic analyses were performed at the Center for Forensic Science Research and Education. Nested multivariable logistic regressions assessed whether age improved predicted ICU admission, after accounting for sociodemographic characteristics and drug classes detected. Among 1930 patients, 15.3% were admitted to the ICU, 7.8% received cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and 5.8% were intubated. Length of hospital stay varied by age, with patients 65 + years old staying longest (median: 22.0h, IQR: 87.0, p < 0.001). Illicit opioids were less commonly detected in older adults (p < 0.001), while prescription opioids were more common (p < 0.001). Age cohort did not significantly predict ICU admission, although prescription benzodiazepine (AOR: 1.4, 95% CI: 1.1, 1.9) and opioid (AOR: 0.7, 95% CI: 0.5, 0.9) detection did. Older age was associated with longer hospital stays but did not predict ICU admission after adjustment for relevant covariates. Benzodiazepine and opioid exposures showed a modest association with ICU utilization. Further work should clarify how pharmacologic combinations influence clinical severity across age groups.

42885179.title: Harm reduction opportunities following ICU admission for prescription opioid overdose: An 8-year comparative audit at the Royal Melbourne Hospital.
42885179.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) admission following prescription opioid overdose represents an important opportunity for multidisciplinary intervention and harm reduction, yet Australian data describing inpatient management are limited. A retrospective audit was conducted of 70 adults admitted to the ICU at the Royal Melbourne Hospital with prescription opioid overdose between 2021 and 2024. The primary outcome was provision of take-home naloxone (THN) before discharge among patients meeting institutional eligibility criteria. Secondary outcomes included opioid education, multidisciplinary involvement and discharge opioid management, with comparison with the previous institutional audit where comparable data were available. Only five patients (7.5%, 95% confidence interval 3.2-16.3) were supplied with THN despite all meeting institutional eligibility criteria. Polypharmacy overdose was common (77%). Most patients received at least one specialist referral (83%), although 15% received no inpatient specialist referral. Opioid education was documented in 58 patients (87%) compared with 17% previously (P <0.001), although content and documentation were inconsistent. These findings demonstrate persistent gaps in THN provision, structured opioid education and coordinated discharge planning, highlighting ICU admission as an important opportunity for prescription opioid harm reduction. Strengthening guideline-based multidisciplinary interventions during admission may improve patient outcomes and inform harm reduction strategies nationally.

42862032.title: Association between leukocytosis and adverse clinical outcomes in thrombocytopenic patients with acute pesticide poisoning: a cross-sectional study from a referral poisoning center in Iran.
42862032.journal: International journal of environmental health research
42862032.abstract: This study evaluated the association between leukocytosis and adverse clinical outcomes in patients with pesticide poisoning who also had thrombocytopenia. This cross-sectional study used medical records of patients who presented between 2016 and 2021, including 241 adult patients with confirmed pesticide poisoning. We extracted demographic data, clinical signs, laboratory parameters, and outcomes. We categorized hospitalization duration as >72 hours, 24-72 hours, and <24 hours. Leukocytosis was present in 43.2% of patients (n = 104). The overall mortality rate was 25.3% (n = 61), with 49.8% requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission (n = 120) and 44.4% requiring intubation (n = 107). Patients with elevated WBC had higher odds of prolonged hospitalization than those with normal counts: OR = 3.36, p = 0.004 for 24-72 h; and OR = 4.63, p < 0.001 for hospitalizations longer than 72 h. Leukocytosis was also strongly associated with intubation (OR = 3.50, p < 0.001) and ICU admission (OR = 3.58, p < 0.001). After adjustment, only ICU admission and leukocytosis remained significantly associated (OR = 2.20, p = 0.024). Leukocytosis may be a valuable parameter in predicting ICU admission and hospitalization duration in thrombocytopenic patients with acute pesticide poisoning. Further prospective multicenter studies are needed.

42824012.title: Case Report: Massive sustained-release valproate overdose with prolonged gastric tablet retention and partial pharmacobezoar formation managed by endoscopic removal and delayed extracorporeal therapy.
42824012.abstract: Valproate poisoning is a potentially life-threatening condition that may result in central nervous system depression, hyperammonemia, metabolic disturbances, and multiorgan dysfunction. Management of massive sustained-release valproate overdose remains challenging because delayed gastrointestinal absorption may lead to prolonged toxicity despite conventional decontamination measures. A 23-year-old woman with a history of previous suicide attempts was admitted approximately 6 hours after ingesting ninety 500-mg sustained-release valproate tablets (total dose 45 g) with alcohol. Upon arrival, she exhibited severe agitation and delirium. Endotracheal intubation was performed for airway protection because she was unable to cooperate with treatment and was at risk of aspiration. Gastric lavage and cathartic therapy were subsequently administered. The initial serum valproate concentration was 1,093.66 μg/mL. Because incomplete decontamination was suspected, bedside upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed approximately 11.5 h after ingestion. Fourteen intact and markedly swollen tablets were removed; some were separate, whereas others were adherent and partially aggregated, supporting partial pharmacobezoar formation and prolonged gastric drug retention. During intensive care unit management, the patient developed severe hyperammonemia (peak ammonia 205 μmol/L), hyperlactatemia with mixed metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis, acute kidney injury, marked creatine kinase elevation, hypernatremia, and suspected transient central diabetes insipidus. Meropenem was administered empirically from May 31 to June 3 because impaired airway defenses after intubation raised concern for aspiration-related infection, although no definite infectious focus or causative pathogen was identified. Because of substantial financial hardship, extracorporeal treatment was initially deferred. It was initiated at 20:00 on June 1, approximately 62 h after ingestion and 56 h after hospital admission. Two consecutive 2-h sessions of hemoperfusion combined with CVVH were followed by CVVH alone until 08:30 on June 2. The serum valproate concentration decreased from 397.05 μg/mL before extracorporeal treatment to 12.72 μg/mL during ongoing CVVH and was 8.61 μg/mL approximately 70 h after treatment cessation. The patient was discharged on June 15 without evident neurological, cognitive, or motor impairment. Massive sustained-release valproate overdose may cause prolonged gastric retention of intact and partially aggregated tablets, thereby sustaining systemic toxicity. In selected patients, endoscopic tablet removal may provide toxicological source control, while extracorporeal treatment may remain beneficial even when its initiation is delayed. The respective contributions of endoscopy, meropenem exposure, spontaneous elimination, and extracorporeal treatment cannot be separated in this single case.

42953629.title: Severe and Prolonged Paroxetine Intoxication With Delayed Absorption and Extreme Serum Concentrations: A Case Report.
42953629.abstract: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are commonly prescribed antidepressants, known for their relatively safe pharmacological profile and mild symptoms in cases of overdose compared with other antidepressants. In this case report, we describe a near-fatal case of a 70-year-old woman who ingested multiple drugs with suicidal intent, including an unknown quantity of celecoxib 200 mg, clorazepate acid 5 mg, omeprazole 20 mg, and immediate-release paroxetine 30 mg tablets. The patient developed severe serotonin syndrome complicated by acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and required admission to the intensive care unit (ICU). Because of progressive respiratory deterioration, she required intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation. Serotonin syndrome persisted for an unusually long period, with serum paroxetine concentrations of 4805 µg/L at admission that continued to rise to a maximum of 7824 µg/L on day four, both well above the lethal threshold. Intensive therapeutic interventions aimed at lowering paroxetine concentrations and resolving serotonin syndrome included activated charcoal, whole-bowel irrigation lavage, and rifampicin. Paroxetine concentrations gradually declined and reached the therapeutic range after 16 days. Following further ICU treatment, including prone ventilation and corticosteroids, the ARDS resolved, and the patient was extubated 21 days after ingestion. This case highlights that paroxetine overdose may present more severely than commonly reported in the literature, with delayed and prolonged toxicity, including serotonin syndrome and ARDS. Paroxetine overdose may be life-threatening and underscores the need for close monitoring of serum paroxetine concentrations and timely consideration of activated charcoal and whole-bowel irrigation.

42898721.title: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome in a 28-Year-Old Male Subsequent to Inappropriate Naloxone Administration.
42898721.abstract: Tramadol, a centrally-acting analgesic, is widely used for the management of moderate to severe pain. It is preferred in clinical settings due to its superior effectiveness and safety profile compared to other opioids. However, recent research has indicated a potential risk of tramadol-induced seizures, especially when consumed in high dosages or in combination with other substances. We present a case of a 28-year-old male who was brought to the Emergency Department approximately 30 minutes after administering 0.4 mg of naloxone intravenously by Emergency Medical Services (EMS) personnel. The administration was necessitated by a decline in the patient's level of consciousness, the onset of lip cyanosis, and suspected tramadol poisoning. The patient was intubated on-site before being transported to the Emergency Department. Upon arrival, despite receiving 40% FiO2, his O2 saturation was at 88%. Bibasilar crackles were detected during chest auscultation. A CT scan of his chest revealed the presence of bilateral alveolar infiltrates, primarily in the lower lobes. As a result, the patient was diagnosed with acute respiratory distress syndrome and was transferred to the intensive care unit for further care.

42928247.title: High-dose regular insulin as a potential rescue therapy in severe aluminum phosphide poisoning: a case report.
42928247.abstract: Aluminum phosphide (rice tablet) can cause cardiocirculatory collapse and has negative cardiac inotropic effect. Positive inotropic effect of insulin on the cardiac myocytes is through calcium flux. Insulin increases the intramyocytes calcium concentration by increasing conductance of calcium through the L-type calcium channels and by increasing intramyocytes concentration of cyclic adenosine monophosphate. In addition to increasing the intramyocytes calcium level, insulin also enhances the responsiveness of the cardiac cells to calcium. High-dose insulin is a potential therapy for hypodynamic and hypotensive septic shock due to its positive inotropic qualities. In this paper, a critical aluminum phosphide poisoning patient (a 25-year-old Iranian young woman), presented with mixed severe metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis, tachypnea, tachycardia, and hypotension. In contrast to our previous experiences that ingestion of aluminum phosphide tablets associated with multiple organ failure and severe shock in approximately all critical poisoning patients, early initiation of high-dose intravenous regular insulin for this patient prevented multiorgan dysfunction and death. Treatment with high-dose intravenous insulin associated with IV fluids, sodium bicarbonate, hydrocortisone, potassium, dextrose therapy and supportive care resolved completely signs and symptoms of patient after 3 days in ICU. High-dose intravenous regular insulin may be act as a rescue therapy for aluminum phosphide poisoning patients. While this single case suggests a potential benefit, further studies are required to confirm these findings.

42871608.title: Fatal multiple organ dysfunction syndrome induced by colchicine poisoning in a patient with underlying alcoholic liver disease: a case report.
42871608.abstract: Colchicine is a drug used primarily to treat and prevent gout. Yet its narrow therapeutic index makes the lethal dose highly variable, influenced by patient-specific factors such as hepatic function and concomitant medications. In vulnerable patients, even doses substantially below the traditionally cited lethal threshold can result in fatal outcomes. We report a case of a 58-year-old male with a history of gout, alcoholic liver disease, and hyperlipidemia who presented with vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain that lasted three days after ingesting 15 mg of colchicine (0.22 mg/kg) for gout pain relief. Upon admission, laboratory findings revealed acute kidney injury, severe metabolic acidosis, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia. Despite aggressive supportive care in the intensive care unit (ICU), including broad-spectrum antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, steroids and recombinant human thrombopoietin (rhTPO), the patient developed progressive multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS), disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage. On the eighth day of admission, the family opted to discontinue further organ support, and the patient died shortly thereafter. This case shows that in patients with hepatic impairment, severe colchicine toxicity and fatal outcomes may occur even at doses below the traditionally cited threshold. The case also demonstrates that it is critical for physicians to be alert to the serious adverse effects of inadvertent colchicine overdose when prescribing the drug.

42912570.title: Serum ammonia improves early risk stratification beyond West Haven criteria in acute liver failure.
42912570.journal: Liver transplantation : official publication of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and the International Liver Transplantation Society
authors: US Acute Liver Failure Study Group
42912570.abstract: The prognosis of patients with acute liver failure (ALF) presenting with low grade hepatic encephalopathy (HE) defined by the West Haven criteria (WHC) is difficult to establish. We studied the association between HE severity, assessed by WHC and serum ammonia, with outcomes across different age groups. Retrospective analysis of the prospective multicentre United States ALF Study Group registry (2000-2016). Exposures were WHC and serum ammonia on day 1 post inclusion. Endpoints were transplant-free survival (TFS) and mortality due to cerebral events on day 21. Findings were validated in a different and more recent (2010-2023) European cohort. Among 1092 patients, median age was 39 years and 526 (48.2%) had acetaminophen toxicity. On day 1, 968 (88.6%) patients were in the intensive care unit and 669 (61.3%) were receiving any specific organ support (ventilation vasopressors, or renal replacement therapy). TFS and cerebral mortality on day 21 were 45.2% and 6.3%, respectively. Patients with hyperammonemia (≥50 µmol/L) on day 1 had lower TFS on day 21 than others, both for WHC grades 1-2 (53.0% vs. 65.2%) and 3-4 (31.8% vs. 60.9%). Higher ammonia on day 1 was independently associated with lower TFS on day 21, irrespective of WHC grade (odds ratio of 0.958 per each 10 µmol/L increment). Ammonia on day 1 of ≥100 µmol/L showed a significant threshold effect for TFS or cerebral mortality on day 21. Patients with <40 years had the highest probability of cerebral mortality on day 21. In ALF, serum ammonia may help to define HE and assess prognosis earlier, irrespective of WHC grade. Patients with early serum ammonia of ≥100 µmol/L require optimized monitoring and treatment.

42900939.title: Hemodynamic Effects of Interfacility Dexmedetomidine Infusions During Transport of Patients with Alpha-2-adrenergic Agonist Withdrawal.
42900939.journal: The western journal of emergency medicine
42900939.abstract: In the Philadelphia region, there has been an increase in the potency of illicit opioids as well as the addition of nonopioid adulterants. Currently, medetomidine, a veterinary anesthetic that acts as an alpha-2-adrenergic agonist, is a common adulterant in the illicit opioid supply, causing both unique overdose and withdrawal syndromes. Although opioid withdrawal alone is not deadly, with added adulterants, especially medetomidine, this is no longer the case. Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2-adrenergic agonist frequently used for sedation in the emergency department and intensive care unit. Dexmedetomidine is also used off-label to treat the life-threatening withdrawal from alpha-2-agonists. This study describes the dosing and hemodynamic effects associated with the interfacility administration of dexmedetomidine in patients with alpha-2 adrenergic agonist withdrawal. Secondarily, we describe the safety of dexmedetomidine in this patient population. We conducted a retrospective case review of patients receiving dexmedetomidine infusions in the interfacility setting for presumed alpha-2-adrenergic agonist withdrawal. Demographic data, dosing, and vital signs were analyzed descriptively. Over a six-month period, of 217 cases identified, 182 contained complete hemodynamic data. The average age was 39.5 years, and 67% were male. The average transport time was 15.7 minutes (range, 5-40 minutes). The mean dexmedetomidine infusion rate was 1.32 (0.31) mcg/kg/hr. The average mean arterial pressure decreased from 122.1 mm Hg (21.7) at the time of initial patient contact to 118.3 mm Hg (21.7) (mean difference, 3.80; 95% CI, 1.96-5.64) at final patient interaction. Heart rate also showed a minimal change from 104.9 (23.7) to 103.6 (21.8) beats/min (mean 1.3; 95% CI, -0.48 to 3.08). No cases of severe hypotension or clinically significant bradycardia requiring intervention were documented (one-sided 95% CI, 0-1.7%). In this case series of patients, prehospital dexmedetomidine infusions to treat alpha-2-agonist withdrawal were associated with stable hemodynamics without significant bradycardia or hypotension. These findings support the safety of dexmedetomidine infusions for interfacility transport and provide a rationale for examining whether advanced life support clinicians can safely transport patients receiving dexmedetomidine infusions for this indication.

42895303.title: Assessing Medication Confounders Before Determination of Brain Death/Death by Neurologic Criteria: A Primer, with Opioids as a Worked Example.
42895303.journal: American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists
42895303.abstract: To provide a primer on how clinicians, particularly pharmacists, can systematically assess whether a medication may confound determination of brain death/death by neurologic criteria (BD/DNC), using pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic principles that can be applied to any agent with the aid of tertiary references, and using opioids as a worked example. All major guidelines require exclusion of central nervous system (CNS) depressant effect before BD/DNC determination, yet none provides a general method for deciding when a given medication has cleared. Rather than cataloging every agent, this primer sets out the parameters that govern how long any drug can suppress the neurologic examination: lipophilicity and volume of distribution, elimination pathway and the effect of hepatic or renal dysfunction, active metabolites, and the context-sensitive half-life, which lengthens with the duration of an infusion and is not predicted by the elimination half-life. Special states, including obesity, hypothermia, extracorporeal support, and overdose, further prolong effect; in overdose, delayed absorption and saturable elimination can invalidate the customary five-half-life rule. Routine toxicology screens miss many relevant substances, including synthetic opioids. Opioids illustrate the framework across three common scenarios: exposure before arrival, continuous infusion, and overdose. No validated serum concentration threshold defines clearance for most CNS depressants, and the safest determination rests on structured pharmacokinetic reasoning, toxicology consultation, and institutional protocols that specify how confounders are screened for and excluded, rather than on any single number or fixed waiting period.

42833842.title: Fulminant multi-organ failure associated with cereulide-producing Bacillus cereus after consumption of improperly stored rice.
42833842.abstract: A male in his 20s with no medical history was found with generalised seizures and profound hypoglycaemia after consuming improperly stored, reheated rice.Initial laboratory tests showed acute liver failure with hyperammonaemia, acute kidney injury and lactic acidosis, which rapidly progressed to multi-organ failure requiring urgent liver transplantation evaluation.With maximal supportive therapy, including glucose, ammonia and glutamine scavengers, renal replacement therapy, haemodynamic and respiratory support, he gradually improved, avoiding transplantation and achieving full neurological recovery. Toxicological analysis of the rice and serum revealed high concentrations of cereulide, a toxin produced by Bacillus cereus This case illustrates that cereulide intoxication can be associated with potentially fatal multi-organ failure, particularly after ingestion of improperly stored starchy foods.Early recognition through targeted dietary history, focused laboratory evaluation and prompt supportive therapy are essential. Increasing awareness among healthcare professionals and safe food storage practices are key preventive measures.

42905412.title: Ex Vivo Assessment of Lamotrigine Clearance During Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy.
42905412.abstract: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) provides renal support for unstable ICU patients but significantly alters drug concentrations. For patients on long-term antiepileptics such as lamotrigine, CRRT may increase risk for breakthrough seizures due to subtherapeutic levels. Conversely, CRRT may aid in lamotrigine overdose. While partial clearance of lamotrigine by intermittent hemodialysis has been reported, CRRT clearance is not well studied. This study determined lamotrigine extraction by CRRT in an ex vivo system. Medication was administered at two concentrations: one therapeutic and one supratherapeutic to closed-loop, blood-primed, ex vivo CRRT circuits. Drug concentrations were measured in plasma, hemofiltrate (effluent), and matching control samples at specific time points. For each time point, percent recovery of lamotrigine was calculated, and differences between CRRT circuits and controls were analyzed using two-sample t-tests. Plasma lamotrigine concentrations decreased rapidly, with 10% (n = 3, SD = 4%) and 17% (n = 2, SD = 3%) recovery at four hours for therapeutic and supratherapeutic doses, respectively. Although lower starting concentrations trended toward greater clearance, differences were not statistically significant (P = .13). Control concentrations remained stable, with approximately 100% recovery. Lamotrigine concentrations were significantly affected by CRRT circuits. Patients receiving lamotrigine who require CRRT may need dosing adjustments to maintain clinical efficacy. Additionally, CRRT effectively clears lamotrigine, suggesting potential utility in overdose management.

42878277.title: Voluntary levamisole intoxication: a rare case of reversible neurological toxicity without cocaine co-ingestion.

42957340.title: [A case of rescue and nursing care of a patient with intestinal necrosis secondary to severe acute organophosphate pesticide poisoning].
42957340.journal: Zhonghua lao dong wei sheng zhi ye bing za zhi = Zhonghua laodong weisheng zhiyebing zazhi = Chinese journal of industrial hygiene and occupational diseases
42957340.abstract: This article reports the treatment and nursing care of a patient with intestinal necrosis secondary to acute severe organophosphate pesticide poisoning. After accidentally ingesting approximately 100 mL of an undiluted dichlorvos formulation, the patient rapidly developed toxic shock. In the early stage, the recognition of intestinal necrosis was difficult due to overlapping symptoms. Through continuous monitoring of abdominal signs, blood lactate levels, and tissue perfusion status, the medical and nursing team identified the disease progression in a timely manner and, relying on multidisciplinary collaboration, carried out aggressive detoxification, organ function support, and surgical intervention for intestinal necrosis, together with continuous perioperative nursing care and psychological support. After 25 days of aggressive treatment and nursing care, the patient recovered and was discharged. A follow-up visit one month after discharge showed that the patient was in stable condition, with activities of daily living basically restored.

42948727.title: Fatal Fruit: Unveiling the Risks and Responses to Ackee Poisoning in a South Florida Inpatient Unit.
42948727.abstract: The ackee fruit is a staple in many Afro-Caribbean diets. Yet, when consumed in its unripe form, it can induce Jamaican vomiting sickness, a potentially fatal condition caused by hypoglycin, a toxin that disrupts fatty acid oxidation and gluconeogenesis. Although cases are well-documented in endemic regions, reports outside the Caribbean remain rare. We report the case of a 33-year-old male with no comorbidities who presented in South Florida with acute metabolic encephalopathy, severe hypoglycemia, and profound electrolyte disturbances following the ingestion of unripe ackee fruit. Despite early recognition and aggressive interventions, including glucose administration, supportive therapy, and management coordinated by internal medicine, neurology, nephrology, toxicology, intensive care, and palliative care teams, the patient's clinical condition continued to deteriorate over 21 days post-exposure. This case is distinctive for its occurrence in a non-endemic region, the absence of comorbidities, and the refractory course despite multidisciplinary intervention. It highlights both the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges of ackee poisoning in unfamiliar clinical settings. Increased globalization and the availability of culturally specific foods in diverse regions may increase the likelihood of similar presentations outside endemic areas. Awareness among healthcare providers is therefore essential. Ackee poisoning should be considered in patients presenting with unexplained hypoglycemia and encephalopathy, particularly in communities with Afro-Caribbean dietary practices. Early recognition, timely intervention, and interdisciplinary collaboration remain critical to improving patient outcomes. This case underscores the importance of provider awareness regarding culturally specific dietary exposures and their potential for severe toxicological consequences.

42907148.title: Injury Epidemiology in Emergency Departments in Tbilisi, Republic of Georgia: A Multicenter Study.
42907148.abstract: Injuries are a major cause of mortality, disability, and economic loss worldwide, disproportionately affecting low- and middle-income countries. In the Republic of Georgia, limited emergency department-level data constrain evidence-based injury prevention and trauma care planning. This study aimed to describe the epidemiological profile of injuries presenting to hospital emergency departments. A retrospective observational study was conducted using data extracted from hospital electronic medical records and organized into a predefined injury registry dataset from selected tertiary, multi-profile hospitals in Tbilisi, Republic of Georgia. All patients presenting with acute physical injuries or acute poisoning/toxic exposure were included. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and multivariable binary logistic regression were applied. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. A total of 12,563 patients were analyzed; 67.0% were male, the mean age was 24.5 years (SD 15.3), and the median age was 21 years (IQR 16-29). Individuals aged 17-65 years accounted for 51% of cases. Falls were the leading injury mechanism (47%), followed by road traffic injuries (16%). Contusions (18%) and fractures (16.3%) were the most common injury types, with upper extremities (28%) and head injuries (24%) most frequently affected. Most injuries occurred at home (40%). Nearly 80% of patients were discharged within 24 hours, while 20.1% required hospitalization or intensive care. Road traffic injuries were independently associated with higher odds of hospital-level care. Overall, emergency department mortality was 0.6%. Injury-related emergency department presentations in tertiary hospitals in Tbilisi, Republic of Georgia, primarily affected young and working-age populations, placing substantial demands on emergency care. Targeted prevention, improved road and home safety, strengthened emergency medical services, and a national injury surveillance system are urgently needed.

42904314.title: Chlorine Gas Exposure: Clinical Course, Outcomes, and Lessons Learned Following a Mass-Exposure Incident in Oman.
42904314.journal: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness
42904314.abstract: To characterize the clinical manifestations of acute chlorine gas exposure and evaluate recovery outcomes at 48 hours and 14 days post-exposure. Retrospective observational case series of 31 patients exposed to chlorine gas during a mass incident in Sohar, Oman. Information regarding clinical presentation, treatment outcomes, and post-treatment complications was collected using a structured data collection tool to ensure consistency and accuracy during data extraction. Data analysis was performed using IBM SPSS v31. Thirty-one patients presented to the study site and were included in the analysis. All were male with a mean age of 32.3 ± 9.4 years. At presentation, 90.3% of patients were symptomatic, with respiratory manifestations being the most reported symptoms. Eight patients (25.8%) required admission, including 3 admitted to the intensive care unit. At 48-hour follow-up, 18 (58.1%) remained symptomatic. Nine of 29 patients who attended follow-up on day 14 reported persistent symptoms, most commonly cough. No fatalities occurred. This study reports on the clinical course of acute chlorine exposure, highlighting that recovery often exceeds 2 weeks. Findings underscore the need for standardized clinical management, public awareness, and more rigorous industrial safety oversight to mitigate future chemical surge impacts.

42965604.title: Methiodone (IC-26) a case series: an old, but novel, opioid substance causing severe toxicity.
42965604.abstract: Methiodone (IC-26; 4-ethylsulfonyl-N,N-dimethyl-4,4-diphenylbutan-2-amine) is a synthetic opioid derivative of methadone that has recently emerged on the designer drug market. Data on its clinical toxicity and pharmacokinetics remain limited. We describe four cases of severe methiodone intoxication requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission, taking place between July and November 2025. Clinical presentation, treatment, and outcomes were evaluated. In addition, systematic toxicological analysis was performed including Liquid Chromatography - High Resolution Mass Spectrometry (LC-HRMS) and targeted Liquid Chromatography - tandem Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). All patients presented with a classical opioid toxidrome, characterized by respiratory depression, miosis, and decreased consciousness. Naloxone administration resulted in clinical improvement in all cases. Methiodone plasma concentrations ranged from 0.20 to 0.64 mg/L. The elimination half-life in plasma was estimated at approximately 13 h based on one case. Metabolite analysis revealed N-dealkylation as an important metabolic pathway, with additional hydroxylation and limited glucuronidation. Methiodone was variably detected in routine immunoassays, depending on assay specificity. No electrocardiogram (ECG) clinically relevant abnormalities were observed, in contrast to observations in methadone intoxications. Methiodone is an emerging opioid capable of causing severe, but treatable, intoxication. Increased clinical and analytical awareness is essential, as further cases are likely to emerge with the ongoing evolution of the new psychoactive substance market.

42964945.title: Clinical Severity and Serotonin Toxicity in Antidepressant Self-Poisoning: Implications for Clinical Risk Assessment.
42964945.abstract: Background: Antidepressant self-poisoning is a common form of intentional self-harm, and comparisons across antidepressant groups are complicated by differences in ingested dose and coexposures. Methods: This retrospective cross-sectional study reviewed emergency department presentations coded with International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) X61/X64 between 01 January 2023 and 15 May 2025. Among 15,160 screened records, 168 patients with documented antidepressant ingestion with self-harm/suicidal intent were included. Antidepressant exposures were classified by group and standardized using defined daily dose (DDD). Clinical presentation, serotonin toxicity based on the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria, management, and short-term outcomes were evaluated. Multivariable logistic regression was used to adjust for log-transformed DDD. Results: The median age was 27.0 years, and 66.7% of patients were female. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) were the most frequently ingested antidepressants (79.8%). Symptomatic presentation occurred in 33.3% of patients and was more frequent in non-SSRI than in SSRI exposures (55.9% vs 27.6%; adjusted OR, 3.40; 95% CI, 1.55-7.43; P = .002). Serotonin toxicity was identified in 7.7% and was also more frequent in non-SSRI exposures (23.5% vs 3.7%; adjusted OR, 8.17; 95% CI, 2.45-27.26; P = .001). Serotonin toxicity was associated with intensive care unit (ICU) admission (53.8% vs 10.3%; P < .001). Conclusion: Non-SSRI antidepressant exposures were associated with greater short-term clinical severity than SSRI exposures. Because non-SSRI subgroups were small and heterogeneous, class-specific findings should be interpreted as exploratory. The early clinical pattern of toxicity may inform short-term risk assessment.

42879787.title: Immobilized Neuroglobin Scavenges Carbon Monoxide From Circulating Carboxyhemoglobin.
42879787.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
42879787.abstract: Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning is responsible for around 50,000 emergency department visits per year in the United States alone. Currently, there is no available antidote for CO poisoning. We have previously developed an antidotal therapy based on an engineered hemeprotein, human neuroglobin (Ngb-H64Q-CCC). Intravenous infusion of Ngb-H64Q-CCC removes CO from circulating red blood cells and improves survival in a lethal CO poisoning mouse model. However, the infusion of heme-containing proteins has inherent heme toxicity risks that may limit the dose that can be used safely without liver or kidney toxicity. To overcome these problems, we have investigated the development of immobilized Ngb in a solid matrix. This approach allows for the development of a CO removal system using an extracorporeal blood-circulating system coupled with a stationary matrix with immobilized Ngb-H64Q-CCC. Such a system avoids drug infusion and possible organ injury, allows for antidote recycling, and provides advantages for storage and handling of the antidote. Here we have developed Ngb-H64Q-CCC covalently bound to N-hydroxysuccinimide agarose. The immobilized protein shows preserved heme redox activity and retains its CO removal capacity after successive regeneration cycles. We expect that this novel approach will advance the development of new scavenger-based therapies for CO poisoning.

42872940.title: Integrated Use of Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation and Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System for Refractory Cardiotoxic Ingestion: A Single-Center Case Series.
42872940.abstract: Cardiotoxic ingestions of calcium-channel blockers and beta-adrenergic antagonists are highly lethal, often causing refractory vasoplegic shock and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.
