Given the sample size, all inferential analyses were regarded as exploratory. Twenty women (62.5%) were admitted to the ICU. They were older and had lower arterial pH and serum bicarbonate, whereas plasma glucose did not differ between groups. Thresholds examined were ≤ 18.5 mmol/L for bicarbonate (AUC 0.80, 95% CI 0.65-0.95) and ≤ 7.33 for pH (AUC 0.72, 95% CI 0.53-0.90). In a two-variable logistic regression model, lower bicarbonate (OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.37-0.91) and older age (OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.07-2.08) were associated with ICU admission. Women with DKA-related adverse outcomes had lower pH (7.20 versus 7.34; p = 0.004) and lower bicarbonate (8.0 versus 17.0 mmol/L; p = 0.014). In this small single-centre cohort, the depth of maternal acidosis rather than the degree of hyperglycaemia was associated with ICU admission and with adverse obstetric outcomes. These findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating; the thresholds reported here require validation in larger, multicentre cohorts before any clinical application.

42888842.title: Lived Experiences and Coping Strategies of Newly Recruited ICU Nurses in a Resource-Constrained Hospital in Ghana.
42888842.abstract: To explore the lived experiences and coping strategies of newly recruited intensive care unit (ICU) nurses in a resource-constrained setting in Accra, Ghana. An exploratory, descriptive qualitative study was conducted. We purposively recruited 12 newly recruited nurses from the ICUs of a teaching hospital in Accra. The participants were interviewed using a pilot-tested interview guide. The interviews were audio-taped, transcribed verbatim, and analysed using thematic analysis with the aid of Nvivo 11. The main themes identified were experiences and coping strategies of the newly recruited nurses. On the sub-themes under experiences, we identified the following: shift mismatches, unavailability of mentors and lack of supportive learning environment. On the coping strategies, the following sub-themes were identified: self-directed learning, the expectation of implementation of structured orientation programmes, regular evaluation and peer support networks. There is ineffective mentorship of newly recruited ICU nurses due to the absence of institutional mentorship protocols. Peer mentoring, periodic competence-based assessment, and protected mentorship time are useful strategies that can be harnessed to promote nursing skills transfer in newly recruited nurses. Nursing heads of hospitals should ensure structured mentorship protocols are put in place as well as protected mentor time to ensure effective nursing mentorship. Furthermore, heads of in-service training units of hospitals need to institute competence-based orientation programmes and periodic competence-based assessment to help newly recruited nurses' transition effectively into the work environment. This study explored gaps in mentorship and identified strategies to promote effective nursing skills transfer. The findings will help nurse managers in hospitals ensure effective mentorship of newly recruited nurses. We adhered to COREQ guidelines. Twelve newly recruited nurses actively participated in the study.

42888530.title: Impact of portal hypertension on clinical outcomes in critically Ill adult patients: A retrospective study: Outcomes in critically Ill patients with portal hypertension.
42888530.abstract: Liver dysfunction is a common complication in critically ill patients, and portal hypertension (PHT) represents a severe hepatic pathological condition closely associated with adverse patient outcomes. This study aims to investigate the impact of PHT on clinical outcomes in critically ill adult patients. Data were extracted from the Medical Information Market for Intensive Care IV database. All critically ill patients admitted to the hospital were included in this study. Logistic regression analysis was used to assess the correlation between PHT and hospital mortality, length of stay in the intensive care unit (LOS-ICU), and length of stay in hospital in critically ill patients, and multiple collinearity checks were performed. Propensity score matching was used to minimize group differences, and subgroup analyses were conducted. A total of 46,804 adult critically ill patients were included in this study. The hospital mortality rate for critically ill patients with PHT was 19%, significantly higher than the 8.8% mortality rate for patients without PHT (P < .05). Critically ill patients with PHT also had longer LOS-ICU and length of stay in hospital and higher total bilirubin levels (P < .05). Furthermore, multivariate logistic regression analysis showed that PHT was significantly associated with hospital mortality (OR: 2.716, 95% CI: 2.330-3.158, P < .001). After propensity score matching, the baseline differences between the 2 groups were significantly reduced, and the results showed that critically ill patients with PHT had worse clinical outcomes. However, the LOS-ICU was not significantly different after matching. PHT is a significant predictor of poor prognosis in critically ill adult patients, necessitating enhanced clinical monitoring and management to improve their clinical outcomes.

42888502.title: Bridging Critical Care and Mental Health: Jordanian ICU Nurses' Self-Reported Knowledge, Skills, Attitudes and Confidence in Caring for Patients With Mental Illness.
42888502.abstract: Intensive Care Unit (ICU) nurses frequently care for patients with mental illness, yet many report feeling insufficiently prepared to address mental health needs in critical care settings. Understanding nurses' knowledge, skills and attitudes toward mental health care is essential to improving the quality and safety of care. This study assessed Jordanian ICU nurses' self-reported knowledge, skills and attitudes regarding the care of patients with mental illness and examined factors associated with their perceived competence in managing mental health conditions in critical care settings. A cross-sectional descriptive design was used, involving 502 ICU nurses from 20 public, private and university hospitals in Jordan. The primary outcomes were nurses' self-reported perceived knowledge and preparedness, self-reported skills and attitudes toward caring for patients with mental illness. The questionnaire also assessed previous experience and receipt of formal training specifically related to mental health care for critically ill patients. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Kruskal-Wallis test, Pearson correlations and multiple regression. Instrument reliability was acceptable (Cronbach's α = 0.81-0.92). Nurses reported moderate self-reported perceived knowledge and beliefs (mean = 3.19 ± 0.70), self-reported skills (mean = 3.20 ± 0.51) and attitudes (mean = 3.28 ± 0.44). Important gaps were identified in knowledge of psychotropic medication use, clinical assessment tools and legal aspects of mental health care, as well as confidence in managing suicidal behaviour, psychotic symptoms and mental status assessment. Only 32% of nurses had received formal training specifically in mental health care for critically ill patients, whereas 79% reported that they could be better prepared to manage such situations with additional education. Perceived knowledge-and-beliefs scores, skills and attitudes were strongly and positively correlated (r = 0.606-0.790, p < 0.001). Higher educational qualification (β = 0.129, p = 0.011) and longer professional nursing experience (β = 0.229, p = 0.005) were associated with higher self-reported skills. More positive attitudes were associated with educational qualification (β = 0.174, p < 0.001), years as a qualified nurse (β = 0.362, p < 0.001) and ICU experience (β = 0.211, p < 0.001). Jordanian ICU nurses reported moderate perceived competence in mental health care, alongside important gaps in perceived knowledge, perceived preparedness, self-reported clinical assessment skills and confidence in managing complex mental health situations. Some responses also indicated potentially stigmatizing beliefs that require attention in future education. The strong associations among knowledge, skills and attitudes suggest that these domains should be addressed together through structured mental health education, practical skills training and organizational support. Objective assessment of clinical competence is warranted to complement self-reported preparedness.

42885876.title: Nurse-Led Interventions to Mitigate High-Alert Medication Errors in Critical Care: A Systematic Review of Effectiveness and Implementation Strategies.
42885876.abstract: Intensive care units (ICUs) are high-risk environments where nurses administer the majority of high-alert medications, making them the final checkpoint in the medication-use process. However, evidence on nurse-led interventions specifically targeting high-alert medication errors has not been systematically synthesized across all ICU populations. This systematic review evaluated the effectiveness of nurse-led interventions in reducing high-alert medication errors in neonatal, paediatric and adult intensive care units and examined implementation strategies that enhance patient safety. We followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. A comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus for studies published between January 2000 and June 2026. Inclusion criteria required nurse-led interventions, measurement of high-alert medication error rates and critical care settings. The risk of bias was assessed. A narrative synthesis was performed due to heterogeneity in study designs and outcome measures. Six studies met the inclusion criteria. Interventions included simulation-based training, staff education, smart pump integration, clinical decision support systems and standardization of medication orders and protocols. All studies reported improvements in medication safety outcomes, including reductions in medication error rates, improved compliance, enhanced accuracy and increased efficiency. Secondary outcomes included improved compliance with PRN orders (from 62.0% ± 9.2% to 77.7% ± 10.1%), reduced medication dispensing time (to < 1 min) and cost savings ($90 000-$130 000 per year). Risk of bias was moderate to low in five studies and high in one study. Nurse-led multicomponent interventions are associated with reductions in high-alert medication errors and improvements in safety outcomes in critical care settings. However, technology alone is insufficient without workflow integration and nursing education. Education and standardization require concurrent process redesign for sustained improvement. Nurses should advocate for multicomponent strategies combining training, technology and standardized protocols. Healthcare organizations must ensure workflow integration to maximize the benefits of smart pumps and clinical decision support systems. Future research should employ rigorous designs, include diverse ICU settings and low- to middle-income countries and evaluate long-term sustainability.

42885869.title: Nursing Mechanisms of Intravenous Medication Loss in Adult Intensive Care: A Mixed-Methods Systematic Review.
42885869.abstract: Adult ICU medication loss is reported using non-equivalent forms and denominators, limiting interpretation and intervention design. To examine loss measurement, nursing mechanisms, intervention evidence and balancing outcomes. Convergent segregated mixed-methods systematic review. Three databases were searched to 1 July 2026, with citation searching, metadata checks and an uncapped rerun of two capped PubMed arms. Quantitative results remained in native units; qualitative findings were synthesised separately and integrated. MMAT 2018 was applied by design category; two reviewers checked screening, extraction and appraisal. Of 768 screened records (576 primary; 192 rerun), 79 reports were assessed with retained sources. Four reports could not be retrieved. Twenty-five reports from 21 independent studies were included; the rerun added none. Categories were prepared-unused medication (11), post-order or post-event loss (7), partial-container residual (8), delivery-system residual (3) and material-flow loss (4); categories were nonexclusive. Denominators were explicit in 10 studies, partial in 5 and absent in 6. No studies met pooling criteria. Two qualitative studies generated six low-confidence CERQual findings. Intervention evidence was uncontrolled, modelled or proposal-based; balancing outcomes were uncommon. Adult ICU loss comprised non-equivalent quantities, not one waste prevalence, and no study related it to a patient outcome. Studies would need to specify loss form, numerator, denominator, observation window, workflow node, result origin and balancing outcomes alongside resource use. Order review before non-urgent preparation, reconstitution and checking, storage and return pathways, and syringe, pump and line handling are candidate targets; no controlled adult ICU study has shown reduced loss without affecting access, dose delivery, sterility, compatibility or workload.

42966648.title: Pilot Testing of the Teaching Engagement and Caregiving Help in the Intensive Care Unit (TEACH-ICU) Scale.
42966648.journal: American journal of critical care : an official publication, American Association of Critical-Care Nurses
42966648.abstract: Family members often assume caregiving responsibilities after a patient's discharge from the intensive care unit (ICU). Many family members are inadequately prepared due to limited training and support. Intensive care unit nurses can prepare family members to perform caregiving by proactively teaching family members in the ICU. However, no quantitative measure exists to examine nurses' willingness to teach caregiving skills to family members. To examine the Teaching Engagement and Caregiving Help in the ICU (TEACH-ICU) scale, adapted from the Family Willingness for Caregiving Scale. Refinements from cognitive interviews readied the TEACH-ICU scale for pilot testing to assess the broader survey process before examining the scale's validity and reliability in a larger-scale study. This was a descriptive, cross-sectional study of 30 adult ICU nurses recruited via convenience and snowball sampling through social media platforms and the American Association of Critical-Care Nurses Participate in Research website. Relationship testing was conducted between the TEACH-ICU scale, Hospital Ethical Climate Survey (HECS), and Marlowe-Crowne Social Desirability Scale-Short Form (MCSDS-Short Form). The TEACH-ICU scale showed high mean willingness scores across all items. The TEACH-ICU total scores significantly correlated with HECS total scores and 4 subscales: peers, managers, hospital, and physicians. No significant relationship was observed between TEACH-ICU scores and social desirability scores. The scale and survey process were modified based on this pilot study's results, in preparation for examining the validity and reliability of the TEACH-ICU scale.

42879586.title: From muscle dysfunction to functionality: challenges and pathways for rehabilitation in critically ill patients.

42878854.title: Reply to the letter to the editor: comment on "Usefulness of the phase angle for inflammation criteria of the global leadership initiative on malnutrition in critically ill patients".

42878611.title: Association of Tele-Critical Care Capability With Interhospital Transfers and Potentially Low-Value Transfers Among Critically Ill Medicare Beneficiaries.
42878611.abstract: Interhospital transfer is essential for accessing specialized critical care services, yet it poses clinical risk and substantial burden for patients and the healthcare system. Tele-critical care (TCC) programs extend expertise to resource-limited hospitals and may influence transfer decisions by identifying patients requiring escalation or supporting local management. We examined the association between TCC capability at index ICU hospitalizations, interhospital transfer, and post-transfer outcomes. Nationwide retrospective cohort study using 2021-2023 Medicare claims linked to the American Hospital Association Annual Survey Database (AHAASD). U.S. acute care hospitals. Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries with ICU hospitalizations between 2022 and 2023. None. TCC capability was identified by AHAASD reporting and/or the presence of five or more TCC claims annually. The primary outcome was interhospital ICU transfer. Exploratory post-transfer outcomes included receipt of specialty procedures, death or hospice discharge within 1 day of transfer, in-hospital and 30-day mortality, and discharge disposition. Hierarchical logistic regression adjusted for patient demographics, comorbidities, acute organ failures, and transferring/accepting hospital characteristics, with transferring hospitals as random intercepts. Among 2,140,919 ICU hospitalizations, 33.4% occurred at 1,066 TCC-capable hospitals. Absolute transfer rates were similar (2.5% vs. 3.0%), but TCC capability was associated with higher adjusted odds of transfer (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.08; 95% CI, 1.01-1.14). In exploratory post-transfer analyses, transferred patients from TCC hospitals had greater illness severity yet were less likely to die or be discharged to hospice within 1 day of transfer (4.6% vs. 6.6%; aOR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.76-0.97) and more likely to be discharged home within 2 days (4.7% vs. 3.7%; aOR, 1.17; 95% CI, 1.03-1.33). TCC capability was associated with modestly increased transfer rates, fewer potentially low-value transfers, and improved post-transfer outcomes, suggesting improved transfer selection.

42877248.title: Population Pharmacokinetics and Exposure-Response Analysis of Voriconazole in ICU and Non-ICU Hospitalized Adults.
42877248.abstract: Voriconazole has marked pharmacokinetic variability and a narrow therapeutic window, making individualized dosing difficult. Published population pharmacokinetic (PopPK) models most derive from ICU or general-ward patients, and exposure-response studies are limited. This retrospective study aimed to characterize voriconazole PopPK and exposure-response analysis in real‑world hospitalized patients containing both ICU and non-ICU patients. Adults receiving voriconazole with therapeutic drug monitoring were included. PopPK analysis used NONMEM. Demographic variables and lab biomarkers were screened. Monte Carlo simulations were used to show covariates' effect on drug exposure under standard dosing regimen. Model-derived voriconazole exposure was linked to treatment outcome and adverse drug reactions (ADR) using logistic regression. 292 patients with 473 voriconazole concentrations were included. A one-compartment model with first-order elimination adequately described the data, with estimated population clearance, volume of distribution and derived half-life of 3.3 L/h, 92 L and 19 h, respectively. Voriconazole clearance increased with body weight and albumin and decreased with age, CRP, total bilirubin, and serum creatinine. These covariates decrease clearance inter-individual variability from 44.5% to 32.6 %; all parameters fell within bootstrap 90% interval. With a standard regimen 300 mg every 12 h for first day then 200 mg every 12 h, simulations showed underexposure in younger patients without organ dysfunction and overexposure in elderly patients with elevated CRP, total bilirubin or serum creatinine. In multivariable logistic regression, excessively high average concentration (Cavg) derived by model was associated with treatment failure (adjusted odds ratio 1.45 per mg/L, 95% CI 1.07-2.03, p=0.019). Cavg was not significant, whereas older age was associated with higher ADR risk (adjusted odds ratio 1.05, 95% CI 1.01-1.10). Age, CRP, albumin, total bilirubin and creatinine explain clinically relevant variability in voriconazole exposure and indicate that a fixed regimen may not benefit all patients. The association between higher Cavg and treatment failure is observational and needs further prospective studies and external validations.

42875972.title: Female Representation and Quality Indicators in Anesthesiology and Critical Care Podcasts.
42875972.abstract: Podcasts have emerged as prominent tools for asynchronous medical education, widely adopted across training levels and specialties. Diverse representation strengthens medical discourse, making an evaluation of speaker demographics essential for understanding equity and quality in digital knowledge dissemination. This study systematically evaluates female representation and quality assurance indicators in anesthesiology and critical care podcasts, including longitudinal publication trends. We systematically searched Apple Podcasts and Spotify using specialty-specific terms and manually reviewed the top twenty journals in the field for affiliated podcasts. Included were active, English-language, physician-hosted podcasts. Eighty-five podcasts (53.0% US-based) comprising 10,190 episodes were analyzed. Of 12,522 hosts, 31.5% (n = 3945) were female; of 10,822 guests, 35.9% (n = 3882) were female. Notably, among US-based podcasts, female guest representation exceeded the 26.5% female workforce proportion among US anesthesiologists. Episodes with exclusively male hosts had 2.13 times the odds of featuring only male guests (95% CI 1.88-2.41). A positive trend of increasing female participation was observed from 2010 to 2024. Content support was variable: using broad, inclusive definitions, 42.0% of episodes had show notes and 48.4% provided supplemental material. Analysis of quality-related structures showed that 40.0% (n = 34) of podcasts produced episodes linked to a publication, 50.6% featured some episodes with three or more speakers, 21.2% of podcasts were journal-affiliated, and 20.0% were university-affiliated. While a sex imbalance persists in anesthesiology and critical care podcasting, female participation among US-based podcasts exceeds local workforce demographic benchmarks, with a clear positive trend from 2010 to 2024. However, persistent sex similarity in speaker selection suggests ongoing biases. Quality assurance mechanisms remain highly variable, highlighting opportunities for incremental improvement. Future efforts could focus on structured guest selection and transparent quality indicators to accelerate progress toward equitable representation and educational quality in this influential medium. In modern times, many clinicians look for, and listen to, podcasts aimed at education in clinical specialties. This sampling of podcasts related to our specialty looked at how females and males contributed to podcast content generation and dissemination, as a marker for male versus female representation in speakership for continuing specialty education.

42875249.title: [Research progress on the role of geniohyoid muscle ultrasound in the assessment of swallowing function in critically ill elderly patients].
42875249.journal: Zhonghua wei zhong bing ji jiu yi xue
42875249.abstract: Swallowing dysfunction severely affects the quality of life in elderly individuals. In China, the prevalence of dysphagia among people aged 80 years or older is 41%, with even higher rates seen in critically ill elderly patients. Currently, available methods for assessing swallowing function are complex to perform and inconvenient for bedside evaluation. However, this functional disorder, which is common and has a significant impact on prognosis in critically ill elderly patients, has not received widespread attention from intensivists. With the increasing use of ultrasound in critical care, identifying a convenient and reliable ultrasound method for evaluating swallowing function will offer more tools for precise monitoring, scientific intervention, therapeutic assessment, and prognostic evaluation of swallowing function in critically ill patients. Atrophy of the geniohyoid muscle is an important factor in reduced swallowing safety and aspiration in the elderly. Using ultrasound to measure the cross-sectional area, movement, and muscle quality changes of the geniohyoid muscle in the sagittal plane to evaluate swallowing function has demonstrated good accuracy and operability. This article summarizes the pathogenesis of swallowing dysfunction, the role of the geniohyoid muscle in swallowing, the progress of research on ultrasound detection of the geniohyoid muscle, and the methods of ultrasound measurement of the geniohyoid muscle. The aim is to provide a reference for research and application of ultrasound evaluation of swallowing function in critically ill elderly patients.

42875155.title: [The dignity of older people put to the test in critical care].
42875155.abstract: End-of-life care is often approached from the perspective of dignity and respect for autonomy, which enable individuals to choose how to spend their final moments. However, in a critical care setting, where older people may be incapable of making decisions or may become temporarily so due to an altered level of consciousness, the burden of decision-making falls on their loved ones and the medical team. How is dignity preserved when treatment choices clash with socio-cultural issues and the sometimes conflicting interests of those involved? Through short accounts drawn from a qualitative study conducted amongst nurses, we explore the concept of dignity in the context of futile medical treatment.

42874532.title: In response to "Indications for intensive care unit transfer during delivery hospitalizations": the potential role of echocardiography in obstetric critical care escalation.

42872943.title: Tools Measuring Health Literacy in Critically Ill Patients and Their Caregivers: A Scoping Review.
42872943.abstract: Health literacy, the ability to understand and use health information, is important for critically ill patients and their caregivers in the neonatal ICU (NICU), PICU, and adult ICU to make informed decisions and navigate complex care. This review aimed to identify and summarize tools used to assess health literacy in critically ill patients or their caregivers. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and PsycINFO through July 24, 2025. Included articles reported on tools to assess health literacy in critically ill patients or their caregivers. Two reviewers independently performed screening and data extraction. Two independent reviewers extracted data in Covidence. Data items included study characteristics (country in which the study was conducted, study funding, study setting) and health literacy tool characteristics (tool user, types of questions in the tool, method of tool administration, if the tool was created by the study team, and if a full version was available in the publication). We included 92 articles describing 84 health literacy tools. Tools measured: 1) topic-specific clinical knowledge (e.g., organ donation, cardiopulmonary resuscitation; n = 24/84, 29%; NICU: n = 9; PICU: n = 1; ICU: n = 14); 2) ICU prognosis, diagnosis, and treatment (n = 23/84, 27%; NICU: 6; PICU: 3; ICU: n = 15); 3) neonatal and parenting (n = 13/84, 15%; all NICU); 4) general health literacy abilities (n = 11/84, 13%; NICU: n = 6; PICU: n = 2; ICU: n = 7); 5) information needs (n = 4/84, 5%; NICU: n = 1; PICU: n = 0; ICU: n = 3); 6) readiness for discharge (n = 3/84, 4%; all NICU); 7) decision-making (n = 3/84, 4%; all NICU); 8) health-related behaviors (n = 2/84, 2%; NICU: n = 1; ICU: n = 1); and 9) research participation (n = 1/84, 1%; NICU). Although several health literacy tools exist, they often focus on individual knowledge of specific aspects of ICU care, with less attention to how understanding is produced within the clinical context through interactions among patients, caregivers, and healthcare providers. This may limit their ability to reflect how health literacy functions in critical illness. Assessment of health literacy requires pairing the appropriate tools with interaction-focused approaches to guide communication and support informed decision-making in ICU settings.

42871362.title: AI-augmented cardiopulmonary point-of-care ultrasound: a narrative review for pulmonary and critical care clinicians.
42871362.abstract: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is an increasingly utilised tool in pulmonary and critical care medicine, yet its effectiveness remains limited by operator dependency and the required cognitive demands of real-time image acquisition and interpretation. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising approach to augment POCUS by supporting image acquisition, interpretation and quantitative analysis. Given the rapid evolution of this field, clinicians must understand both the capabilities and limitations of AI-enabled POCUS. However, prior reviews have largely catalogued applications without focusing on how these tools integrate into bedside workflows. This narrative review examines AI in cardiopulmonary POCUS through a workflow-based lens relevant to pulmonologists and intensivists. We discuss the role of AI as a bedside coach, interpreter and quantifier, highlighting applications in lung and focused cardiac ultrasound, including pneumothorax detection, B-line analysis, left ventricular function assessment, and identification of other cardiopulmonary pathologies. Across domains, AI demonstrates strong performance in controlled settings, although variability persists in real-world environments due to differences in image quality, patient factors and dataset limitations. Future directions include interactive, clinician-in-the-loop systems, protocol-driven integration, and multimodal data synthesis. A clear understanding of these developments will be essential for clinicians as AI becomes increasingly embedded within bedside patient care.

42869723.title: Reply - Letter to the editor: Interpreting the effects of protocolized nutrition in critically ill adults.

42869652.title: Leadership in the intensive care unit: an international perspective.

42869290.title: Yearly relative variations of bacteraemia and pneumonia incidence acquired in intensive care units at Lyon University Hospitals (2004-2024): a scatterplot visualization.
42869290.journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases

42866585.title: Early piperacillin exposure during continuous infusion in critically ill patients: the impact of renal and liver dysfunctions.
42866585.abstract: To assess early piperacillin exposure in critically ill patients receiving continuous infusion piperacillin-tazobactam, identify clinical determinants of underexposure and overexposure, and evaluate piperacillin concentrations across organ dysfunction phenotypes. Retrospective, single-center observational study. A 20-bed medical-surgical intensive care unit of a university hospital. All consecutive adult critically ill patients receiving continuous-infusion piperacillin-tazobactam with at least one total plasma piperacillin concentration measurement. None. Observed plasma piperacillin concentrations were measured at predefined time points (day 1, day 3 and day 7). Target attainment was defined as total plasma concentrations of 80-160 mg/L, corresponding to 4-8 times the minimum inhibitory concentration of Pseudomonas aeruginosa.A total of 350 patients were included, contributing 775 piperacillin measurements. At first sampling (day 1), 30% of patients were underexposed, 35% achieved the target range, and 35% were overexposed. In multivariable analyses, underexposure was less frequent in older patients and in those with renal dysfunction or shock, while male sex was independently associated with a higher risk of underexposure. Overexposure was strongly associated with renal dysfunction, higher bilirubin concentrations, and higher daily piperacillin dose. Piperacillin concentrations were highest in patients with combined hepato-renal dysfunction. Only one-third of critically ill patients achieved target piperacillin exposure at initial therapeutic drug monitoring during continuous infusion. Early deviations from target concentrations were frequent and primarily determined by renal dysfunction despite routine dose adjustment. These findings support early individualized dosing strategies integrating organ function assessment and therapeutic drug monitoring to optimize piperacillin exposure.

42865074.title: Explainable Machine Learning Model for Personalized Assessment of the Need for Intensive Care in Patients with Myasthenia Gravis Based on Phenotype and Inflammatory Markers.
42865074.journal: QJM : monthly journal of the Association of Physicians
42865074.abstract: Early identification of myasthenia gravis (MG) severe exacerbations that require intensive care unit (ICU) admission remains challenging due disease highly heterogeneous. Existing models seldom incorporate phenotype stratification, limiting interpretability and clinical utility. This study aimed to develop an explainable machine learning (ML) model to assess phenotype-specific risk factors and predict ICU admission for patients with MG. This retrospective study included 319 hospitalized patients with MG. We utilized clinical variables and systemic inflammation markers for ML modeling. Subgroups were prespecified by thymoma status and age at onset. Primary outcome was need for intensive care during the hospitalization. Model performance was assessed. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was employed for interpretation of global and individual features. Of 319 admissions, 33 (10.3%) required ICU care. Four ML models were trained with nested 3-fold validation. eXtreme Gradient Boosting performed best (AUC: 0.94). SHAP ranked MGFA clinical classification, infection during admission, body mass index, and inflammatory indices as principal predictors. Subgroup analyses revealed phenotype-specific patterns, including opposite SHAP directions for inflammatory markers between thymoma and non-thymoma groups and distinct rankings between different age of onset groups. SHAP-based personalized explanations revealed patient-specific variations in risk ranking and directionality of predictive features. A web-based calculator was developed to support real-time clinical implementation of the model, potentially allowing for risk stratification. An explainable machine learning framework that integrates clinical features with systemic inflammation indices reliably predicts ICU admission in MG and reveals phenotype-specific risk patterns, enabling personalized risk stratification in MG management.

42864724.title: Electronic Intensive Care Unit Diaries: A Scoping Review of Applications, Implementation, and Evaluation.
42864724.abstract: To map evidence on the applications, implementation, and evaluation of electronic intensive care unit diaries in critical care. Scoping review. Joanna Briggs Institute methodology guided eligibility, independent screening and data extraction, and descriptive and framework-guided narrative synthesis. Methodological quality was not appraised because the review aimed to map evidence. Twelve databases and two registries were searched from inception to 17 September 2026. Fifteen sources of evidence published between 2012 and 2026 represented eight distinct programmes; sources were from the Netherlands, China, the United States, Italy and the United Kingdom. Five broad platform or delivery modes were identified: web-based platforms, mobile or tablet applications, an online document platform, an electronic clinical record-integrated diary module and digital scrapbooking. Framework-guided synthesis identified multilevel implementation determinants, while reported strategies varied by implementation stage. Evaluations covered platform- and user-related, implementation and patient- and family-related outcomes, but evidence on sustained implementation and benefits was limited. Electronic intensive care unit diaries are implemented through diverse digital platforms and participation models, but implementation and evaluation remain heterogeneous, and evidence on sustained use and benefits is limited. Nurses and organisations should clarify writing roles and content boundaries, integrate diary work into workflows, provide training and support, protect privacy and monitor sustained use. The review identifies nursing-relevant requirements for workflow integration, role clarity, training, organisational support and privacy. Findings can inform nurses, nurse leaders, critical care teams and healthcare organisations implementing digital diary programmes. Reporting followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews.

42863164.title: Assessing the feasibility of reusing oral nutritional supplements in a quaternary intensive care unit.
42863164.abstract: Healthcare generates substantial carbon emissions and waste, and sustainability initiatives increasingly aim to reduce environmental impact without compromising care. In our Intensive Care Unit (ICU), unused oral nutritional supplements (ONS) are routinely discarded, contributing to financial and carbon waste. Reuse may offer benefits but must be balanced against infection prevention requirements. This study assessed microbiological contamination of ONS to inform feasibility of a safe reuse program. In our ICU, three ONS products were sampled using standardised surface-swabbing. Twenty "ingoing" products entering patient rooms and twenty cleaned, unconsumed "outgoing" products leaving patient rooms were cultured for both total organisms and Enterobacterales. Values were calculated as colony forming units (CFU) per centimetre-squared (CFU/cm2) and compared with food-surface contamination thresholds. Group differences were analysed using non-parametric statistical tests. Forty ONS items were sampled (20 ingoing, 20 outgoing). Outgoing products had significantly lower overall bacterial counts than ingoing products (median 0.27 CFU/cm2 versus 0.00 CFU/cm2; p < 0.001). Enterobacterales were uncommon at baseline - only detected on four (20%) products - and absent on all outgoing samples. There was no significant difference observed between the three different product types. Cleaning unopened ONS after ICU room exposure resulted in significantly reduced bacterial burden, with no Enterobacterales detected, supporting the feasibility of safe reuse. These findings suggest that reusing unopened ONS could deliver meaningful financial and carbon savings while upholding infection prevention measures essential for patient safety.

42863091.title: Predicting ICU Seizures Using 1 hour of cEEG.
42863091.journal: Journal of clinical neurophysiology : official publication of the American Electroencephalographic Society
42863091.abstract: Continuous electroencephalography (cEEG) is the gold standard for detecting electrographic seizures in the intensive care unit (ICU), but limited resources limit prolonged monitoring for all patients. We developed an automated, interpretable pipeline that uses a single hour of cEEG to estimate near-term seizure risk across multiple prediction windows. We retrospectively studied 50 adults who underwent ICU cEEG monitoring at a single tertiary center. From a 1-hour segment, we computed automated interictal-ictal continuum (IIC) burden probabilities for lateralized periodic discharges (LPDs), generalized periodic discharges (GPDs), and lateralized rhythmic delta activity (LRDA), along with quantitative background EEG features reflecting signal organization and hemispheric asymmetry. Segments were labeled by seizure occurrence within the subsequent 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, or 24 hours. Support vector machine (SVM) and bagged-tree classifiers were trained using clinical-only, background-only, and combined feature sets with a 70/30 patient-level train-test split and cross-validation within the training set. For the 4-hour horizon, the combined-feature SVM achieved 76% accuracy and the lowest Brier score (0.25), outperforming clinical-only (72%) and background-only (70%) models. Across horizons, SVM accuracy declined from 94% (1 hour) to 79% (24 hours) with increasing Brier scores, indicating reduced calibration at longer intervals. AUC-receiver operating characteristic increased with wider prediction windows, consistent with higher seizure prevalence at longer lead times. Integrating automated IIC probabilities with quantitative background EEG features enables moderate, interpretable near-term seizure prediction from a single hour of ICU cEEG. Initial external validation on an independent multicenter ICU cohort supports generalizability, although broader prospective and multicenter evaluation are needed before clinical deployment.

42862745.title: Association of 24-Hour Anion Gap Difference with Short-Term Mortality in Critically Ill Patients with Heart Failure and Infection.
42862745.abstract: Introduction High anion gap (AG) indicates poor prognosis in critical illness. However, the prognostic significance of dynamic early AG changes in patients with concurrent heart failure and infection remains unclear. We aimed to evaluate the association between the 24-hour AG difference and short-term mortality in this population. Methods This retrospective cohort study utilized the Zigong Fourth People's Hospital database. Patients with HF and infection admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) were included. A 24-hour landmark analysis was applied. The AG difference was categorized based on the change (ΔAG) from admission to 24 hours: Decreasing (ΔAG < -2 mmol/L), Stable (-2 to 2 mmol/L), and Increasing (ΔAG > 2 mmol/L). The primary outcome was 7-day all-cause mortality. Results A total of 299 patients were included. The 7-day mortality was 24.1%. In multivariable Cox analysis adjusted for confounders including baseline lactate and renal function, the Stable difference was significantly associated with increased 7-day mortality compared to the Decreasing group (HR 2.43, 95% CI 1.27-4.63, p=0.007). The Increasing group showed a trend toward higher risk (HR 1.74, p=0.126). Subgroup analyses revealed significant interactions, where the risk of an increasing difference was amplified in patients with hyperlactatemia (>2.0 mmol/L, HR 2.65), or renal dysfunction (eGFR <60, HR 6.27). Albumin-corrected AG sensitivity analysis confirmed these findings. Conclusion Failure to decrease the anion gap within the first 24 hours of ICU admission is associated with a higher risk of short-term mortality in patients with HF and infection. The prognostic value of AG difference is particularly pronounced in high-risk subgroups with hemodynamic or metabolic instability.

42862327.title: Association of 24-hours net positive fluid balance with log-transformed vancomycin trough concentrations in the early phase of therapy among critically ill patients.
42862327.abstract: Early vancomycin troughs are frequently low in critical illness and fluid accumulation may contribute through distribution effects. This study estimated the association between net positive fluid balance and early vancomycin troughs as a hypothesis-generating analysis and explored variation across early-therapy windows and by hypoalbuminemia. A retrospective cohort study used ICU electronic health record data from MIMIC-IV. ICU stays with a timing-validated trough were included. The primary cohort N = 255 required at least 80% EMAR dose capture in the prior 24 h and delta serum creatinine at or below 0.2 mg/dL across the 48 h before trough and trough within 72 h of first IV dose. Net fluid balance in the prior 24 h was modeled per + 5 L. Outcome was log trough. Models adjusted for serum creatinine and administered dose and administration count in the prior 24 h. Sensitivity windows were within 48 h (N = 162) and within 96 h (N = 289). Hypoalbuminemia below 3 g/dL was explored in the measured subset. Median trough was 14.00 mg/L (IQR 10.15 to 18.15) and 62 of 255 were below 10 mg/L (24.3%). The point estimate suggested an 11.7% lower trough concentration per + 5 L net positive balance (β =  - 0.1247; SE = 0.079; p = 0.115), but the 95% CI (- 24.4% to + 3.1%) included no association. Serum creatinine had a positive coefficient (β = 0.2995; p = 0.061). Point estimates were similar across early-therapy windows with all confidence intervals including no association. The exploratory albumin interaction was imprecise and limited by substantial missingness and small subgroup sizes. The point estimate suggested lower early vancomycin troughs with higher net positive fluid balance, but the confidence interval included no association. These hypothesis-generating findings require prospective validation to clarify whether fluid balance is associated with early trough concentrations and area under the curve exposure.

42861714.title: Deconstructing the Modified Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (mSOFA) Score: A Decision Tree Analysis Reveals the Pathophysiological Hierarchy of Organ Dysfunction Predictors in Prehospital Critical Care.
42861714.journal: QJM : monthly journal of the Association of Physicians
42861714.abstract: Early recognition of multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) in the prehospital setting remains challenging and is critical for reducing mortality among critically ill patients. The modified Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (mSOFA) score was developed for prehospital use with point-of-care testing; however, the internal decision architecture of this score remains unexplored. A prospective, multicentre, observational study was conducted across three emergency medical systems (EMS) in Spain, included adults (n = 12,212) with acute illness transferred to emergency departments with high priority. A decision tree (DT) model was developed using the five components of the mSOFA score, lactate, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), oxygen saturation-to-fraction of inspired oxygen ratio (SaFi), mean blood pressure (MBP), and creatinine, to predict in-hospital mortality at 2 days. The study followed the STROBE and TRIPOD+AI guidelines. Cohort mortality was 5.0% (n = 609). Lactate emerged as the primary decision variable, with a threshold of 3.8 mmol/L, followed by SaFi, GCS, and creatinine in patients with hyperlactataemia, and by GCS and creatinine when lactate was below the threshold. The DT deconstructs the mSOFA from a static score into a dynamic, interpretable clinical decision framework. By revealing the pathophysiological hierarchy underlying the score, with lactate as the central stratification axis, this approach enables EMS clinicians to identify distinct clinical phenotypes and anticipate deterioration based on the sequential evaluation of organ dysfunction rather than a single numerical threshold.

42861692.title: Characterization of 24-Hour Rhythms in Vital Signs in Intensive Care Populations: A Scoping Review.
42861692.abstract: Circadian rhythms in intensive care unit (ICU) patients are vulnerable to disruption, which may contribute to adverse clinical outcomes. Continuously monitored vital signs offer a unique opportunity to assess 24-hour rhythms in real-world ICU settings. The aim of this scoping review is to systematically map methodological approaches used to characterize 24-hour rhythms in vital signs in ICU populations and to summarize reported associations with patient characteristics, clinical outcomes, or interventions. A systematic literature search was conducted to identify studies that assessed 24-hour rhythms in routinely collected vital signs in adult, pediatric and neonatal ICU patients published between January 2015 and December 2025. Thirty-five studies comprising nearly 288 000 patients were included, with most studies conducted in adult ICUs (n = 32), 3 in neonatal ICUs, and none in pediatric ICUs. Substantial heterogeneity existed in preprocessing strategies, assessment windows, analytical methods, and derived rhythmicity metrics that were used to determine 24-hour variation, as well as in the level of detail with which these were reported. Cosinor analysis was the most frequently used method to characterize rhythmicity, followed by day-night comparisons, and max-min approaches. Across studies, rhythmicity analyses revealed that 24-hour rhythms in vital signs were detectable in ICU patients, although methodological heterogeneity and lack of detail on analytical decisions limit evidence synthesis. In addition, the direction and magnitude of associations between rhythmic properties (such as amplitude or acrophase) and mortality and other clinically relevant outcomes varied considerably among studies. While most, though not all, studies reported that higher amplitudes were associated with mortality, it remains unclear whether this reflects circadian physiology rather than clinical instability. Harmonization of reporting practices and the development of a core outcome set on circadian parameters derived from vital signs in critical care contexts will help to guide future research in this burgeoning field.

42861654.title: Direct measurement of eravacycline effluent concentrations during continuous venovenous haemodiafiltration: negligible clearance in a critically ill patient.

42860123.title: Applied nutritional investigation determinants of lower quadriceps skeletal muscle measured by ultrasound at ICU admission: a cross-sectional analysis.
42860123.abstract: Low skeletal muscle (SM) is common at ICU admission and is associated with worse prognosis. Early identification of at-risk patients is essential, but determinants of low SM in critically ill patients remains unclear. To identify sociodemographic, nutritional, and clinical characteristics associated with low SM at ICU admission. This cross-sectional analysis included critically ill patients ≥18 years admitted within 24 hours. Sociodemographic and nutritional data were obtained through anamnesis, while clinical data were extracted from records. Quadriceps muscle layer thickness (QMLT) was measured using a B-mode US. Lower QMLT was defined as values below the sex-specific 25th percentile of the sample. Binary logistic regression was performed. 399 patients were included (age 61.4 ± 14.9 years; 56.6% male). Older age (OR = 1.02; CI 95% 1.0-1.04), previous unintentional weight loss (OR = 1.64; CI 95% 1.03-2.61), reduced food intake before admission (OR = 2.32; CI 95% 1.44-3.74), and pressure injuries (OR = 1.83; CI 95% 1.05-3.20) were associated with low QMLT. However, in multivariate analysis, only older age (OR = 1.02; CI 95% 1.00-1.04) and reduced food intake (OR = 2.26; CI 95% 1.22-4.18) remained independent determinants. Older age and reduced food intake were independently associated with lower QMLT at ICU admission. These findings highlight the need for early screening and targeted strategies to mitigate muscle loss and improve outcomes in critically ill patients.

42859799.title: Peripartum Cardiomyopathy in the Obstetric Intensive Care Unit: Seasonal Associations and the Impact of Winter in the Kashmir Valley.
42859799.abstract: Background Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a form of idiopathic systolic heart failure that presents in late pregnancy or the early postpartum period in the absence of an identifiable etiology. Because its symptoms overlap with those of normal pregnancy, the diagnosis is frequently delayed or missed. Seasonal peaks in cardiovascular morbidity and mortality are well described in older, non-obstetric populations, but no previous study has examined this phenomenon in obstetric patients with PPCM. We aimed to determine whether the proportion of obstetric intensive care unit (ICU) admissions attributable to PPCM and its associated mortality are higher during winter than during the remaining seasons. Materials and methods This retrospective observational study included all obstetric patients admitted to the ICU of a tertiary-care referral center in the Kashmir Valley, North India, between January 1, 2018 and April 1, 2024. Medical records were reviewed to identify cases of new-onset PPCM; women with pre-existing cardiac disease were excluded. Admissions were stratified by season (spring: February 15 to May 15; summer: May 15 to August 15; autumn: August 15 to November 15; winter: November 15 to February 15). Groups were compared using the chi-square test, with odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered significant. Results Of 1,899 obstetric ICU admissions, 166 (8.74%) received a new diagnosis of PPCM. Winter accounted for 88 of the 166 PPCM admissions (53.01%), compared with 78 (46.99%) for the other three seasons combined, whereas only 365 of 1,733 non-PPCM admissions (21.06%) occurred in winter. The odds that an obstetric ICU admission was attributable to PPCM were therefore more than four times higher in winter (OR 4.22, 95% CI 3.05-5.85; χ² = 85.14; p < 0.001). Fifteen patients with PPCM died in hospital, of whom 11 (73.33%) died during winter; the case fatality rate among patients with PPCM was 12.50% in winter compared with 5.13% in the other seasons. Hypertensive disorder of pregnancy was the commonest comorbidity (52.41%), and 43.98% of patients presented in New York Heart Association functional class IV. Conclusions A clinically and statistically significant seasonal association was observed regarding the proportion of PPCM admissions among obstetric ICU patients in the Kashmir Valley, with the greatest burden concentrated in winter; however, these findings may be confounded by delayed presentation due to winter transport difficulties.  Heightened surveillance, intensified antenatal follow-up, and a low threshold for echocardiography during the cold season are recommended, particularly for women referred from peripheral facilities.

42859707.title: Self-inflicted thoracoabdominal nail-gun injury presenting as STEMI: diagnostic challenges in a time-critical care pathway.
42859707.abstract: A 60-year-old male with a history of depression and a prior nail-gun thoracic injury was found in shock at home, with inferior ST-segment elevation on the paramedic electrocardiogram prompting pre-hospital ST-elevation myocardial infarction pathway activation. Initial high-sensitivity troponin was elevated, consistent with the presumed diagnosis. Normal coronary angiography and preserved ventricular function were discordant with the patient's ongoing haemodynamic instability. Four small anterior chest puncture wounds and radiopaque foreign bodies demonstrated on chest radiograph and angiographic imaging did not initially prompt consideration of penetrating injury. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography, performed to exclude pulmonary embolism, identified four nail-gun projectiles penetrating the heart and stomach. The patient underwent sternotomy and laparotomy with repair of cardiac, diaphragmatic, and gastric injuries. The case illustrates the challenges of situation awareness and diagnostic reassessment within time-critical, protocol-driven care.

42859621.title: Guidelines for the prevention and treatment of stress ulcers in critically ill patients (2026).
authors: Guideline Working Group of the Chinese Society of Critical Care Medicine
42859621.abstract: Stress ulcers is a common complication in critically ill patients, associated with increased mortality risk and prolonged intensive care unit stay. In recent years, several large-scale clinical studies on risk factors, prevention, and treatment of stress ulcers have provided new evidence for guideline development. Moreover, the lack of standardized protocols for the prevention and treatment of stress ulcers in clinical practice underscores the urgent need for authoritative guidelines to address inconsistent in management strategies. Accordingly, the Chinese Society of Critical Care Medicine established a multidisciplinary expert panel to develop the "Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Stress Ulcers in Critically Ill Patients(2026)". Following the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology, the guideline formulation process involved proposing clinical questions, literature retrieval and screening, meta-analysis and evidence synthesis, initial formation of recommendation items, panel reviews, three rounds of remote meetings, four rounds of face-to-face meetings, manuscript revisions, and final approval by the Standing Committee of the Society. The guidelines were finalized in the form of 23 evidence-based recommendations. These guidelines cover key aspects of stress ulcer management, including risk factors, prevention, treatment, and adverse effects of acid-suppressive drugs. The aim is to provide evidence-based guidance for healthcare professionals and promote standardized clinical management of stress ulcers in adults.

42858894.title: Re: 'Pharmacokinetics, target attainment, and outcomes of piperacillin/tazobactam in critically ill patients receiving continuous infusion with therapeutic drug monitoring: a retrospective analysis' by Chiriac et al.
42858894.journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases

42858614.title: Guidelines for Decisions to Withhold or Withdraw Life-Sustaining Treatments (LST) in Adult ICU.
42858614.abstract: The French Society of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care Medicine (Société française d'anesthésie et de réanimation, SFAR) and the French Society of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (Société Française de Médecine Physique et de Réadaptation (SOFMER)) aimed at providing guidelines for decisions to withhold or withdraw life-sustaining treatments (LST) in adult ICU. A consensus committee of 20 experts from the SFAR and the SOFMER was convened. A formal conﬂict-of-interest (COI) policy was developed at the beginning of the process and enforced throughout. The entire guideline construction process was conducted independently of any industrial funding (i.e., pharmaceutical, medical devices). The authors were required to follow the rules of the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) system to guide the assessment of the quality of evidence. The potential drawbacks of making strong recommendations in the presence of low-quality evidence were emphasized. 3 fields were defined: (1) modalities of the LST decision-making process; (2) modalities for implementing an LST decision; (3) Relationships with family members, communication, disagreements, and conflicts. For each field, the objective of the recommendations was to answer a number of questions formulated according to the PICO model (population, intervention, comparison, and outcomes). Based on these questions, an extensive bibliographic search was carried out using predefined keywords according to PRISMA guidelines and analyzed using the GRADE® methodology. The recommendations were formulated according to the GRADE® methodology and then voted on by all the experts according to the GRADE® grid method. The experts' work on synthesis and application of the GRADE® method resulted in 9 recommendations. Among the formalized recommendations, 1 was found to have a high level of evidence (GRADE 1), and 2 had low levels of evidence (GRADE 2). For 6 recommendations, the GRADE® methodology could not be fully applied, resulting in an expert's opinion. 2 questions could not be answered due to a lack of literature. After 1 round of rating, strong agreement was reached for all the recommendations. There was strong agreement among experts to provide recommendations to improve practices for decisions to withhold or withdraw LST in the adult ICU.

42858369.title: Analysis of pharmacist authorship in leading critical care journals.
42858369.journal: American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists
42858369.abstract: To evaluate first and last (senior) pharmacist authorship in high-impact critical care journals with a focus on the representation and evolution of pharmacist contributions over time. This literature-focused review analyzed pharmacist authorship across 6 high-impact critical care journals: Intensive Care Medicine, American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine, Critical Care, Critical Care Medicine, CHEST, and Annals of Intensive Care. First and last authors were assessed for pharmacy-related degrees using article data and supplemental searches, with articles with unconfirmed pharmacist authorship excluded. Included study designs encompassed a variety of research and review article types, including, but not limited to, retrospective cohort studies, case-control studies, systematic reviews, case reports, surveys, narrative reviews, literature reviews, animal studies, clinical studies, evaluation studies, methods studies, and observational studies; nonresearch publications were excluded. A total of 83,608 articles published between 1973 and 2024 were identified, of which 24,257 met the inclusion criteria. Pharmacist authorship was identified in 272 articles (1.12%), with an overall upward trend observed over time. The highest annual representation occurred in 1988 (12 articles; 3.67%). CHEST, evaluated from 2020 to 2024, had the highest proportion of articles with pharmacist authorship (11 articles; 4.47%). Pharmacist-authored studies were commonly classified as "other study designs," including narrative reviews, literature reviews, experimental studies, and survey studies. Pharmacist authorship generally increased over the study period, although interpretation of temporal trends is limited by differences in journal inclusion across years; however, pharmacists remain underrepresented as first and last authors.

42856993.title: Nutritional Therapy for Acute Heart Failure Patients Admitted to the Cardiovascular Intensive Care Unit and Its Impact on the Nutritional Status at Discharge.
42856993.abstract: Nutritional status at discharge is a prognostic factor in acute heart failure (AHF) patients, but its relationship with early-phase nutritional therapy in the cardiovascular intensive care unit (CICU) remains unclear, so we evaluated the effects of HF severity, respiratory management, and nutritional dosage on nutritional status in AHF patients. We retrospectively analyzed 141 of 160 AHF patients admitted to the CICU in 2021, excluding those with acute coronary syndrome, who had died, or had been discharged early. Patients were divided into 3 groups by respiratory support: invasive ventilation (IPPV, n=21), non-invasive ventilation (NPPV, n=36), and other forms of oxygen supplementation (O2S, n=84). The mean age of the patients was 72±15 years. On day 3, the IPPV group received less nutrition than the O2S group, but by day 7 there was no significant difference among the groups in the nutritional doses administered. No significant differences in the Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index (GNRI) at discharge were observed among the groups. Multiple regression analysis identified the energy (standardized β=0.210, P=0.029) and protein (standardized β=0.248, P=0.007) doses on day 3 as being correlated with the GNRI at discharge, independent of HF severity or respiratory management. The nutritional dose on day 3, rather than HF severity, respiratory management or the day 7 nutritional dose, may be associated with the GNRI at discharge.

42856746.title: Critical care and the law: Pertinent cases from 2025.
42856746.journal: Journal of the Intensive Care Society
42856746.abstract: This review by the Legal and Ethical Advisory Group (LEAG) follows the 2024 summary, reviewing the important legal cases and Prevention of Future Deaths reports (PFDs) ruled or issued in 2025 that are pertinent to Intensive Care Medicine. The legal cases include Human Rights cases, Clinical Negligence cases, and rulings of the Court of Protection. Not all of the cases relate to events which have occurred in Intensive Care, however the rulings will have a bearing on Intensive Care practice.

42854967.title: Comment on "Impact of evidence-based feeding protocols on clinical outcomes and nutritional delivery in critically ill adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis".

42854823.title: Escalation of Care: Association of Weekend and Nighttime Postoperative ICU Admission with Poor Outcomes After Gastrointestinal Cancer Surgery.
42854823.journal: Journal of gastrointestinal surgery : official journal of the Society for Surgery of the Alimentary Tract
42854823.abstract: Postoperative intensive care unit (ICU) admission represents an important escalation of care after surgery. We evaluated the association between ICU admission timing and outcomes after gastrointestinal (GI) cancer surgery. Adults undergoing GI cancer surgery with postoperative ICU care were identified in Epic Cosmos from 2016 to 2025 and classified as weekday, weekend-day, weeknight, or weekend-night admission. Outcomes included complications during the index hospitalization and within 30 days, 30-day mortality, readmission, discharge home, and prolonged length of stay (LOS ≥75th percentile of the cohort). Multivariable logistic regression evaluated associations between ICU timing and outcomes. Among 77,054 patients, 36.4% were classified as weekday, 15.4% weekend-day, 25.0% weeknight, and 23.2% weekend-night. Weekend-night classification was associated with the highest adjusted odds of 30-day mortality (aOR 1.52, 95% CI 1.42-1.63), any 30-day complication (aOR 1.76, 95% CI 1.69-1.84), and prolonged LOS (aOR 2.32, 95% CI 2.21-2.44), as well as lower odds of discharge home (aOR 0.70, 95% CI 0.67-0.73). Weeknight classification was also associated with higher odds of mortality (aOR 1.28, 95% CI 1.20-1.37), complications (aOR 1.42, 95% CI 1.36-1.48), and prolonged LOS (aOR 1.55, 95% CI 1.47-1.64). Nighttime ICU classification, particularly weekend-night classification, identified patients at elevated postoperative risk after GI cancer surgery and may help inform surveillance and escalation strategies during off-hours.

42854465.title: Assessing the consistency of a prognostic transition to persistent critical illness across two U.S. ICU databases: a daily risk-set analysis.
42854465.abstract: To test whether an apparent prognostic transition to persistent critical illness persists after daily clinical-state updating. Retrospective daily risk-set analysis using multicenter eICU discovery, single-health-system MIMIC-IV concept replication, cluster-resampled simultaneous inference, and post-primary explanatory updated-state analyses. Two deidentified U.S. critical care databases: eICU Collaborative Research Database v2.0 and MIMIC-IV v3.1. Adults alive and hospitalized within the prespecified continuous ICU episode at completed ICU days 3-14. None. Predisposition (P) was compared with clinical state from episode hours 0-24, then fixed (I), or from the 24 h before each daily risk set (S). ΔP-X = L_X - L_P was the state-only minus P-only out-of-fold log-loss difference; negative values favor state. The outcome was in-hospital death within 14 days after risk-set time and before live discharge. Paired comparisons used hospital-cluster inference in eICU and patient-cluster inference in MIMIC-IV. Day-3 risk sets included 46,182 eICU episodes from 203 hospitals and 24,185 MIMIC-IV episodes. At day 10, ΔP-I was 0.0060 (simultaneous 95 % CI, -0.0010 to 0.0130) and 0.0126 (0.0033 to 0.0220), respectively; ΔP-S was -0.0360 (-0.0471 to -0.0249) and -0.0387 (-0.0543 to -0.0230). Every ΔP-S interval was below zero through day 14. eICU nominated no fixed-state transition; MIMIC-IV had an aggregate run from day 5, but care settings and predictor definitions disagreed. Post-result analyses retained negative ΔP-S after removing Glasgow Coma Scale and/or missingness indicators, using gradient boosting, and excluding documented entry treatment limitation. In these U.S. data, crossover occurred only against an aging admission snapshot. With the studied predictor blocks through ICU day 14, no consistent transition was identified; transitions in other health systems or later ICU periods remain possible.

42854328.title: Feasibility and acceptability of a toolkit to guide patient and family participation in intensive care unit rounds.
42854328.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
42854328.abstract: Engaging families in multidisciplinary bedside patient care rounds in the intensive care unit (ICU) can improve communication, shared decision-making, and family satisfaction, yet few interventions support structured family involvement. We evaluated the feasibility and acceptability of an ICU rounds toolkit designed to promote family participation in rounds. We conducted a pilot prospective study using a before-and-after quasi-experimental design combined with structured rounds observations in a 12-bed general systems ICU in Calgary, Alberta. The intervention consisted of printed materials and a brief educational video outlining six toolkit elements: invitation, orientation, active engagement, summary, question-asking, and structured communication. Surveys assessed perceptions of rounds, and observations documented family participation and toolkit use. Quantitative data were summarised descriptively; qualitative responses underwent content analysis. Consistent with the pilot objectives, analyses were descriptive and intended to assess feasibility and acceptability. We enrolled 17 families and 22 healthcare providers before education and 15 family members and 16 healthcare providers post education (total of 70 participants) and observed 46 rounds before education and 37 rounds post education. Most family members reported reviewing the printed toolkit (13/15, 87%), and 73% (11/15) reported that the toolkit increased their confidence participating in ICU rounds. Families reported that the toolkit improved their understanding of the rounds process and helped them prepare questions. Healthcare providers familiar with the toolkit viewed it positively and described it as practical and consistent with family-centred care practices. Median rounding time per patient remained similar between study periods (pre-education: 14 min [interquartile range: 10-19]; post-education: 15 min [interquartile range: 13-19]). Staff awareness and engagement with toolkit materials varied. This pilot study demonstrated that a structured ICU rounds toolkit was feasible to introduce and acceptable to participating family members and healthcare providers who engaged with the materials. However, healthcare provider awareness and uptake were variable. Future studies should evaluate strategies to improve uptake and sustainability, alongside the toolkit's impact on family engagement, communication, and patient- and family-centred outcomes.

42853832.title: Enhancing Culturally Sensitive Care for Critically Ill Native American Patients and Families: An Educational Initiative and Resource Guide for Nursing and Medical Teams.
42853832.journal: The American journal of hospice & palliative care
42853832.abstract: BackgroundNative American (NA) patients experience persistent inequities in advance care planning (ACP) and often present to tertiary centers with critical illness; culturally respectful serious-illness communication is therefore essential in emergency and intensive care settings.InterventionWe developed and implemented a nursing-led, multidisciplinary educational initiative at a large academic medical center serving patients from >50 tribal nations. Informed by a literature review, local practice needs, and expert input from a Native American Patient Experience Ambassador, we created (1) an "Honoring Your Choices" (HYC) communication card with culturally sensitive prompts for serious illness conversations and (2) a quick reference guide (QRG) outlining key cultural considerations and unit-specific resources. Tools were disseminated to seven intensive care units and the emergency department through nurse leader engagement, unit rounding, and staff education, and the initiative was presented at departmental Grand Rounds/didactics with pre/post surveys to assess impact.ResultsTwenty-seven pre-session and twenty-four post-session surveys were collected from clinicians and trainees. Prior to the session, >80% of respondents reported being not or only slightly confident discussing end-of-life issues with NA patients/families; post-session surveys demonstrated increased self-reported confidence in recognizing when cultural beliefs may influence care and in conducting end-of-life discussions.ConclusionsThis initiative demonstrates how culturally congruent approaches to serious illness conversations may support more meaningful engagement with NA patients and families. Our experience suggests that developing and evaluating a brief, point-of-care communication tool like Honoring Your Choices may be accomplished with existing interdisciplinary partnerships, offering a practical model that other institutions can readily mirror.

42852438.title: Pharmacist Consults in a Canadian Post-Intensive Care Clinic: A 5-Year Quantitative Analysis.
42852438.journal: The Canadian journal of hospital pharmacy
42852438.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) survivors face significant drug-related challenges. Pharmacists can play a crucial role in addressing these issues in critical care recovery clinics. To describe the nature and number of pharmacy interventions per patient within a post-ICU clinic, while also exploring the patient characteristics that might predict those who would benefit from a pharmacist's intervention. A retrospective cohort study, which included all patients with a pharmacist consult record from a post-ICU clinic between March 2019 and July 2024, was conducted at the McGill University Health Centre, Montréal, Quebec. The pharmacists' interventions were categorized as follows: medication changes, such as medication cessation, medication initiation, medication substitution, or dosage adjustment; review of adverse drug events; review of drug interactions; laboratory monitoring; patient education; coordination of care; vaccination; and others. The relationship between patient characteristics and benefits derived from a pharmacist intervention was analyzed using stepwise logistic regression. Across the 129 patients who met the inclusion criteria, a mean of 3 interventions (range 0-10) were recorded. The most frequent interventions were patient education (provided to 72 patients, 55.8%), coordination of care (68 patients, 52.7%), medication cessation (42 patients, 32.6%), and dosage adjustment (21 patients, 16.3%). The stepwise logistic regression identified the number of medications being taken when the patient was seen at the post-ICU clinic as the only significant factor determining the likelihood of benefit from a pharmacist intervention (odds ratio 1.182, 95% confidence interval 1.085-1.289, p < 0.001). Pharmacists working in multidisciplinary post-ICU clinics provided a range of patient-centred interventions, with the number of medications at the time of attending the post-ICU clinic identified as the primary factor influencing which patients would benefit from a pharmacist encounter.

42851644.title: Ultrasonographic evaluation of quadriceps femoris muscle mass in critically ill patients aged 60 years and older: a prospective observational study.
42851644.abstract: Muscle wasting is a common complication in critically ill older adults admitted to intensive care units (ICU), with significant implications for morbidity and mortality. Ultrasound represents a promising bedside tool for assessing muscle mass changes. This study aimed to evaluate changes in quadriceps femoris muscle mass using ultrasonography at ICU admission and after 7 days of stay in patients aged 60 years and older. A prospective cohort study with repeated measurements was conducted between December 2024 and May 2025. Patients aged ≥60 years admitted to the ICU were included. Ultrasonographic measurements included rectus femoris cross-sectional area (RFCSA), bilateral quadriceps muscle thickness, and rectus femoris pennation angle at admission and day 7. Clinical characteristics, severity scores (APACHE II, SOFA), and functional status (Barthel index) were recorded. Statistical analysis included Wilcoxon signed-rank test and robust statistics. Fifty patients were analyzed (60% male, median age 72.5 years). Significant muscle mass reductions were observed: RFCSA decreased by 16.2% (2.525-2.115 cm2, p < 0.001), right quadriceps thickness by 14.6% (2.012-1.719 cm, p < 0.001), left quadriceps thickness by 20.2% (2.049-1.635 cm, p < 0.001), and pennation angle by 18.2% (7.664°-6.270°, p < 0.001). ICU mortality was 30%. Multivariate analysis identified advanced age, female sex, hypoglycemic agent use, higher SOFA scores, and lower premorbid Barthel index as factors associated with greater muscle loss. Critically ill older adults experience significant quadriceps muscle mass loss within the first week of ICU stay, as measured by bedside ultrasonography. These findings support the implementation of early muscle assessment and targeted interventions in this vulnerable population.

42850921.title: Management of postoperative hypothermia in the cardiovascular surgery intensive care unit: A qualitative study based on insights from nurses.
42850921.abstract: Monitoring and managing postoperative hypothermia in patients undergoing cardiac surgery is essential. Nevertheless, little is known about nurses' experiences in assessing and managing postoperative hypothermia after cardiac surgery, highlighting the need for studies to explore their clinical experiences and perspectives. This study aimed to explore the experiences of cardiovascular surgery intensive care unit nurses in managing postoperative hypothermia after cardiovascular surgery. This interpretative/constructivist phenomenological study was conducted with 12 nurses working in a cardiovascular surgery intensive care unit. Data were collected through in-depth online interviews using a semi-structured questionnaire and analysed using content analysis. Participants were selected purposively to obtain diverse perspectives on postoperative hypothermia management. Data analysis identified five themes and 35 sub-themes: clinical challenges associated with postoperative hypothermia, strategies for managing postoperative hypothermia, barriers to effective postoperative hypothermia management, strategies for achieving standardised practices and suggestions for improving postoperative hypothermia management. Nurses emphasised early recognition, continuous temperature monitoring and timely interventions to prevent postoperative hypothermia-related complications. To our knowledge, this is the first qualitative study focusing on postoperative hypothermia management in a cardiovascular surgery intensive care unit. Findings highlight the need for advanced warming technologies, ongoing staff education and standardised protocols. Enhancing healthcare professionals' knowledge and developing evidence-based protocols and care bundles are essential for optimising perioperative hypothermia management.Reporting:COREQ (the consolidated criteria for reporting qualitative research).
