42850296.title: Do structural ICU requirements reflect critical care demand in elective metabolic and bariatric surgery? A retrospective cohort study.
42850296.abstract: Metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) is increasingly delivered in lower-acuity settings, yet on-site intensive care unit (ICU) capability remains a structural requirement for the highest center-designation tier. Direct data on critical-care utilization after elective MBS without an on-site ICU are limited. We describe 30-day outcomes at such a center, using contemporaneous elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) in the same environment as a reference. Retrospective cohort study of consecutive adults undergoing elective MBS (sleeve gastrectomy or Roux-en-Y gastric bypass) or LC (2022-2025) at a single center without an on-site ICU but with a pre-defined escalation and transfer protocol. The primary outcome was the 30-day complication rate (Clavien-Dindo); ICU utilization was grade ≥IV. Outcomes are reported descriptively with 95% confidence intervals (CIs); regression and propensity-score-matched analyses are exploratory (Supplementary Material). Of 1,065 patients (MBS n=351, LC n=714), 30-day complication rates were 4.27% (95% CI 2.39-6.94%) versus 3.64% (95% CI 2.37-5.27%). No MBS patient was admitted to intensive care (0/351), compatible with a true rate up to 1.05% (upper 95% CI); two LC patients required ICU admission (0.28%), both for retained-stone acute pancreatitis. All five MBS reoperations were for postoperative hemorrhage; none developed organ dysfunction or met ICU-transfer criteria, and none died. Because events were rare, this study cannot exclude clinically meaningful ICU demand, and absence of a detected difference does not establish equivalence. In this single-center experience, elective MBS without an on-site ICU under a structured escalation protocol showed no observed ICU admissions over 30 days, though the confidence interval remains compatible with infrequent critical-care need. These hypothesis-generating findings demonstrate feasibility in one environment and should not be generalized to accreditation policy; prospective multicenter data are required. Research Registry (UIN: researchregistry11829); retrospectively registered; https://www.researchregistry.com.

42849345.title: Effect of virtual reality during cycle ergometer session in the intensive care unit: A pilot randomised cross-over trial.
42849345.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
42849345.abstract: Early mobilisation, including a cycle ergometer, is a cornerstone of best practices in the intensive care unit (ICU). Virtual reality (VR) has increasingly been integrated into healthcare, showing benefits in reducing depressive symptoms, improving mobility, and managing pain. However, the combined use of VR and cycle ergometry to enhance physical performance in the ICU has not been investigated. The primary objective of this study was to assess whether a single session of VR-based cycle ergometry increases active cycling distance (ACD) compared with a conventional session. Secondary objectives were to examine its effects on motivation, immersion, and perceived exertion and to monitor the occurrence of adverse events. This single-centre, randomised, open-label, two-period crossover trial compared two 30-min cycle ergometer sessions, one with VR and one without, delivered in a randomised order. Eligible participants were adults (aged ≥18 years) admitted to a surgical ICU for more than 48 h, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15 and the ability to sit in a chair. The primary outcome was ACD (km) per session. Secondary outcomes included adverse events and self-reported perceived effort, sense of immersion, and motivation, assessed using 11-point visual analogue scale (0-10). Estimated mean difference in ACD between VR and no-VR sessions was 0.25 km (95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.50 to 1.00; p = 0.50). No period effect was observed (p = 0.15). No serious adverse events occurred. VR did not significantly affect perceived effort (mean difference: 0.53; 95% CI: -1.29 to 0.23; p = 0.163). VR significantly increased sense of immersion (mean difference: 4.08; 95% CI: 2.80 to 5.36; p < 0.0001) and motivational state (mean difference: 1.15; 95% CI: 0.16 to 2.14; p = 0.024). VR did not significantly increase ACD, it substantially enhanced subjective immersion and motivation. These findings support further investigation of immersive technologies as adjuncts to early rehabilitation strategies in the ICU.

42849344.title: To report or not? A qualitative study of critical care nurses' experiences of incident reporting.
42849344.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
42849344.abstract: Critical care nurses have a key role in identifying and reporting incidents. These reports are used to improve patient safety and to deliver high-quality care, particularly within intensive care settings where patients are highly vulnerable. However, critical care nurses reporting behaviours are influenced by various organisational and individual factors. The aim of this study was to explore the experiences of critical care nurses in Australia with incident reporting and the perceived barriers and facilitators that influence reporting behaviours in critical care settings. Using a qualitative descriptive method, semistructured interviews with eight nurses from intensive care units across Australia were conducted. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Three overarching themes were found: Facilitators of effective incident reporting, Barriers to incident reporting, and To report or not. Findings showed that organisational culture played a substantial role in shaping intensive care nurses' willingness to report incidents. Intensive care nurses were more likely to engage in reporting when a supportive, nonpunitive culture was present and when incident reports led to constructive feedback and educational opportunities. A lack of support from management, complicated reporting systems, insufficient education, and using reporting as a weapon were identified as barriers preventing incident reporting. Due to heavy workloads and the perception that some incidents seemed minor, nurses occasionally preferred to report problems informally, which could limit efforts to improve safety. This study highlights the impact organisational and supportive culture play a major role in critical care nurses' willingness to report incidents. These findings explore the experiences of incident reporting among critical care nurses in Australia, which organisations may use to address the barriers and emphasise the facilitators to encourage effective reporting.

42849057.title: A Structured Framework for Translation of the ACNS Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology Into Spanish.
42849057.journal: Journal of clinical neurophysiology : official publication of the American Electroencephalographic Society
42849057.abstract: The American Clinical Neurophysiology Society (ACNS) Critical Care EEG Terminology provides standardized language for describing electroencephalographic (EEG) patterns in critically ill patients but has not been formally translated into Spanish. We aimed to develop a consensus-based Spanish translation of the ACNS Critical Care EEG Terminology using a multi-phase methodology involving physicians from Spanish-speaking countries. This qualitative study aimed to establish a standardized Spanish ACNS Critical Care EEG terminology through a three-phase process: Phase 1: Initial iterative translation by 14 Spanish-speaking physicians working in subgroups. Discrepancies were documented for further discussion. Phase 2: Focus groups with specialists practicing in Spanish-speaking countries, guided by qualitative research experts. Sessions explored terminology preferences, implementation challenges, and regional variations. Phase 3: Qualitative analysis and final consensus using a modified Delphi methodology. Ranked choice voting analysis to achieve ≥75% consensus was used and when needed, a two-option runoff determined the final selected term. Forty-five physicians from all Spanish-speaking countries except Nicaragua participated in 10 focus groups to review 25 terms. Seven terms generated two possible Spanish translations, four generated three, five generated four, and nine generated five. A consensus-based Spanish terminology was established, prioritizing semantic fidelity to the ACNS terminology while also accounting for terms already in wide regional use. Examples of final consensus terms included: Generalized Periodic Discharges → Descargas Periódicas Generalizadas (98%, Round 1); Lateralized Rhythmic Delta Activity → Actividad Delta Rítmica Lateralizada (100%, round 1); and Sharp Wave → Onda Aguda (82%, round 1). The outdated term periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges remained widely used because of familiarity among intensivists. This effort provides the first structured Spanish adaptation of the ACNS Critical Care EEG terminology. The resulting lexicon reflects linguistic diversity across regions and supports consistent communication, training, research, and broader adoption of evidence-based continuous EEG practices.

42847267.title: Needs of Families of Critically Ill Patients in Latin America: A Multicenter Study.
42847267.abstract: Care in ICUs is often focused on critically ill patients, leaving the needs of their families overlooked. In Latin America, it is necessary to gain insight into these needs for future standardised protocols focused on family-centred care. To determine the needs of family members of patients hospitalised in intensive care units (ICUs) in five Latin American countries: Colombia, Argentina, Mexico, Ecuador, and Peru. Multicentre cross-sectional descriptive observational study. The short version of the CCFNI scale (Critical Care Family Needs Inventory) was applied to identify the needs of families of critically ill patients. A total of 1843 family members were included. The statistical software Jamovi 2.3.28.0 was used for data analysis. Descriptive and inferential statistics were used to present the results. The STROBE checklist for cross-sectional studies was used in this study. Total of 1843 participants from five Latin American countries were analysed; 63.05% were women, and the median age was 44 years (IQR: 34-55). The overall median family-needs score was 21 (IQR: 17-24). The greatest perceived needs were identified in the 'Information and family satisfaction' and 'Perceived improvements' dimensions, whereas lower levels of need were reported in 'Proximity and safety' and 'Care provided by healthcare staff.' Scores differed significantly by ICU type (p < 0.001), being higher in surgical ICUs and lower in maternal ICUs. Participants who travelled less than 10 min to the hospital reported lower needs than those with longer travel times (p = 0.005). Families of critically ill patients in five Latin American countries reported prominent needs related to information and family satisfaction, as well as perceived improvements in care, with family-needs scores varying according to ICU type and travel time to the hospital.

42845963.title: The relationship between thanatophobia and perceptions of spirituality and spiritual care among intensive care nurses.
42845963.abstract: This study aims to determine the relationship between thanatophobia and perceptions of spirituality and spiritual care among intensive care nurses. The research was conducted using a descriptive and correlational design. This study included 198 nurses working in the intensive care units of state and university hospitals in a province in western Turkey between January 2025 and April 2025. Data were collected using three different instruments: a sociodemographic information form, the Thanatophobia Scale (TS), and the Spirituality and Spiritual Care Rating Scale (SSCRS). The mean TS score of the nurses participating in the study was 26.52 ± 9.02 (high). The mean SSCRS score was 52.79 ± 9.22 (high). A significant positive correlation was found between TS and SSCRS (r = 0.28; p < 0.001). The effect of TS on SSCRS was positive and significant (β = 0.28, p < 0.001). The coefficient of determination of the model (R2 = 0.07) indicates that TS explains 7% (medium) of the variation in SSCRS. This study found that as the fear of death increased among intensive care nurses, their perception of spirituality and spiritual care also increased moderately. Since intensive care nurses frequently encounter death, it is recommended that they receive institutional support to cope with their fear of death. Furthermore, it is suggested that interdisciplinary training programs be organized and provided to enable intensive care nurses to provide spiritual care.

42845943.title: Unraveling the pathways from alexithymia to work engagement among critical care nurses: the mediating effects of social support and organizational trust.
42845943.abstract: Critical-care nurses (CCNs) are exposed to intense emotional demands that may impair work engagement, particularly in the presence of alexithymia. However, the mechanisms that link alexithymia to work engagement remain unclear. This study aimed to determine how organizational trust and social support mediate the relationship between alexithymia and work engagement among CCNs in Hail, Northwest Saudi Arabia. This cross-sectional correlational study involved 308 CCNs in Hail from August to November 2025. Data were collected using the Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS-20), Oslo Social Support Scale (OSSS-3), Organizational Trust Scale, and Utrecht Work Engagement Scale (UWES). Data were analyzed using AMOS 24. More than half of the CCNs (52.3%) exhibited a high level of alexithymia, followed by moderate (36%) and low (11.7%) levels. Higher alexithymia levels were significantly associated with lower levels of social support (β = -0.229, p = 0.001), organizational trust (β = -0.286, p = 0.001), and work engagement (β = -0.287, p = 0.001). By contrast, work engagement was positively impacted by social support (β = 0.185, p = 0.002) and organizational trust (β = 0.236, p = 0.001). Alexithymia negatively impacted work engagement via social support (indirect effect = -0.044, 95% CI: -0.140 to -0.011, p = 0.014) and organizational trust (indirect effect = -0.070, 95% CI: -0.158 to -0.028, p = 0.001). Overall, alexithymia significantly decreased work engagement (β = -0.401, p = 0.001). Enhancing organizational trust and strengthening social support may buffer the negative effects of alexithymia on work engagement. Interventions such as leadership development, peer support programs, and emotional skills training may help promote psychological well-being and sustained engagement among CCNs. Alexithymia is a significant psychological barrier to work engagement among CCNs. Organizational trust and social support can effectively mitigate this impact.

42844898.title: Comparison of Success of Long-axis versus Short-axis Ultrasound-guided Right Internal Jugular Vein Cannulation in Adult Intensive Care Unit Patients: A Prospective Comparative Observational Study.
42844898.abstract: Ultrasound-guided internal jugular vein (IJV) cannulation is recommended to improve the success and safety of central venous catheterization. Both long-axis and short-axis ultrasound approaches are widely practiced; however, evidence regarding their comparative performance remains inconclusive. To compare the success and safety of long-axis and short-axis ultrasound-guided right IJV cannulation in adult intensive care unit patients. This prospective comparative observational study was conducted in the Department of Anaesthesiology and Critical Care Medicine, JSS Medical College and Hospital, Mysuru, over 18 months. A total of 106 adult patients requiring right IJV cannulation were enrolled and allocated into the long-axis group (n = 53) and the short-axis group (n = 53). The primary outcome was first-pass cannulation success. Secondary outcomes included needle redirections, skin punctures, guidewire and catheter insertion times, hemodynamic changes, electrocardiographic findings, and procedure-related complications. Baseline characteristics were comparable between the groups. First-pass success was achieved in 90.6% of the long-axis group and 96.2% of the short-axis group (P = 0.240). Needle redirection was significantly less frequent with the short-axis approach (15.1% vs. 32.1%; P = 0.039). The number of skin punctures, guidewire insertion time, catheter insertion time, total procedural time, and overall complication rates were comparable. No carotid artery puncture, pneumothorax, hemothorax, or catheter malposition occurred in either group. Both long-axis and short-axis ultrasound-guided techniques provide high success rates and excellent safety for right IJV cannulation. Although the short-axis approach required fewer needle redirections, both techniques demonstrated comparable procedural efficiency and complication rates. The choice of approach should therefore be guided by operator experience and patient anatomy.

42844291.title: Narsoplimab in critically ill patients with high-risk transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy requiring intensive care.

42844232.title: Top Ten Tips Palliative Care Clinicians Should Know About Caring for People Receiving Critical Care for Cardiovascular Disease.
42844232.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of death worldwide and is a major driver of critical illness, resulting in admission to cardiac intensive care units (CICUs). Patients with acute, life-threatening CVD often experience episodes of acute decompensation characterized by high symptom burden that may portend progressive loss of function, significantly impair quality of life (QOL), and involve high-intensity, technologically advanced therapies to sustain life. Despite these advances, up to 30% of patients die during CICU hospitalizations, and those who survive may subsequently face persistent functional impairment and psychosocial distress. During critical CVD (CCVD), patients often endure prognostic uncertainty and face complex decisions regarding life-sustaining therapies alongside refractory symptoms. Thus, care that focuses exclusively on disease-directed or life-prolonging therapies is often insufficient to address the full spectrum of patient and caregiver needs. When integrated alongside intensive cardiovascular care, palliative care (PC) offers a complementary and essential approach to the management of CCVD to inform therapeutic decisions, improve QOL, and address psychosocial and spiritual well-being. In this article, a multidisciplinary team featuring PC clinicians (physicians, nurse practitioners, social worker, psychologist, and chaplain), cardiologists, cardiac surgeons, cardiothoracic anesthesiologists, and intensivists present evidence-based guidance in a "Top Ten Tips" format to support PC clinicians caring for CICU patients and their caregivers.

42843127.title: ICU onboarding, boot camp, and procedural readiness curricula as entry-phase competency development for residents and fellows entering adult critical care: A scoping review.
42843127.abstract: Entry into an adult intensive care unit (ICU) requires adaptation to unstable physiology, invasive support, local workflows, team roles, and supervision practices. We mapped onboarding, orientation, boot camp, and procedural-readiness curricula for residents and fellows entering adult critical care. We conducted a prospectively registered scoping review (OSF DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/H2SN4). PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, CINAHL Plus with Full Text, and ERIC were searched on April 25, 2026 and updated through September 10, 2026. Embase was searched on September 10, 2026 to address its omission from the initial search. Supplementary citation and gray-literature searches were conducted. Records were independently screened by two reviewers, with third-reviewer adjudication when required. Intervention and landscape/needs studies were synthesized separately. Following database updates, the corrective Embase search, and eligibility re-adjudication, 31 reports representing 26 independent studies and five linked reports were included. Twenty-three studies evaluated interventions and three were landscape/needs studies; 20 interventions were entry-window and three were entry-anchored longitudinal. Non-mutually exclusive outcome mapping identified Level 1 outcomes in 14 studies, Level 2a in 15, Level 2b in 14, Level 3 in 2, Level 4a in 1, and Level 4b in 1. Twelve independent studies were conference-abstract-only. Adult critical care entry curricula were heterogeneous and predominantly US-based. Technical and respiratory readiness were the largest evidence clusters, although nonprocedural transition domains were also represented. No superior curriculum model was identified; workplace-transfer evidence was uncommon, and patient-level evidence was limited to one uncontrolled airway-program evaluation.

42843123.title: Improving fairness of large language model-based ICU mortality prediction via case-based prompting.
42843123.abstract: Accurately predicting mortality risk in intensive care unit (ICU) patients is critical for clinical decision-making. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for clinical prediction using structured medical data, but their outputs may exhibit demographic disparities. Mitigating such disparities without degrading predictive performance remains challenging. We systematically investigate demographic bias in LLM-based ICU mortality prediction and propose Case-Based Prompting (CAP), a training-free framework designed to improve the empirical balance between predictive performance and subgroup fairness. CAP retrieves clinically similar historical misprediction and demographic-sensitive cases with known outcomes and incorporates them as case-level contextual evidence. We further evaluate model discrimination, subgroup fairness, and feature-dependence consistency. On MIMIC-IV, CAP improved AUROC from 0.806 to 0.873 and AUPRC from 0.497 to 0.694 compared with the Baseline Prompt. CAP also reduced several subgroup disparities, particularly for sex and White-Black comparisons, although age-related disparities remained non-negligible. Controlled demographic-information ablations showed that removing demographic information did not uniformly improve both predictive performance and subgroup fairness, indicating distinct performance-fairness patterns rather than a uniform benefit from demographic suppression. Feature-dependence analysis showed generally consistent expressed clinical factor patterns across demographic subgroups. These findings suggest that CAP is a promising inference-time strategy for LLM-based clinical prediction under the evaluated retrospective setting. Further validation across additional LLMs, external datasets, and prospective clinical scenarios is required before deployment.

42842996.title: Vancomycin dosing and monitoring in the intensive care unit: Guideline adherence and efficacy.
42842996.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
42842996.abstract: Vancomycin has a narrow therapeutic window requiring careful drug dosing and monitoring to ensure efficacy while avoiding toxicity. Although protocolised prescribing and monitoring are recommended in antibiotic guidelines, adherence in clinical practice is infrequently reported. We sought to describe compliance with a new vancomycin dosing guideline in the intensive care unit (ICU) and to describe its efficacy in reaching serum levels within the therapeutic range. In this single-centre retrospective observational study, we assessed compliance with, and efficacy of a newly implemented vancomycin prescribing protocol. All ICU patients prescribed intravenous vancomycin between May and July 2024 were screened for inclusion. Collected data included indication, weight, age, creatinine, urine output, loading dose, maintenance dose, plasma vancomycin concentration, and timing of monitoring. Augmented renal clearance (ARC) was defined as a creatinine level below the reference range and/or an urine output >3 L in 24 h. A total of 148 patients were included. Protocol compliance was 82% for the loading dose (101/123), 49% for maintenance dosing (49/101), and 51% for timing of monitoring (46/91). Compliance across all protocol domains occurred in 27% of instances (17/64). Therapeutic drug levels were achieved in only 20% of prescribing episodes. Central nervous system (CNS) infection vs non-CNS infection (odds ratio [OR]: 9.5, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.7-41.3; P < 0.01) and ARC vs no ARC (OR: 15.1, 95% CI: 4.0-80.4; P < 0.01) were independently associated with subtherapeutic levels, while impaired renal function (glomerular filtration rate: <60 mL/min) vs normal renal function (glomerular filtration rate ≥60 mL/min) was associated with supratherapeutic levels (OR: 3.6, 95% CI: 1.1-13.2; P < 0.05). Protocol compliance was not associated with therapeutic levels. Vancomycin protocol adherence in a mixed medical-surgical ICU was low; however, adherence was not associated with therapeutic levels. Patients with CNS infection, ARC, or renal impairment are at risk of nontherapeutic levels.

42842995.title: Healthcare professionals' perspectives on the use of virtual reality for intensive care patients: A cross-sectional survey.
42842995.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
42842995.abstract: Despite improvements in hardware and software availability, and a growing body of research on the use of virtual reality (VR) in intensive care settings, significant barriers to its widespread adoption remain. The aim of this study was to explore intensive care unit healthcare providers' perceptions of the risks, concerns, and opportunities associated with the use of VR in the intensive care setting. An online survey (QualtricsXM) focused on perceived relative and absolute contraindications to VR use, as well as perceived risks, safety and privacy concerns, their impact on implementation, and suggested research priorities was undertaken between February and December 2025. Within a cohort of 108 respondents, significant dispersion was observed between responses relating to relative and absolute contraindications. Professional differences were observed relating to the suitability of the use of VR for patients with a history of epilepsy. Similarly, significant dispersion was observed relating to perceived benefits of VR with relaxation, rehabilitation, patient education, and patient cognitive stimulation being perceived as extremely or very useful by more than 50% of respondents. This survey highlights that intensive care unit healthcare professionals, with little VR experience, lack a cohesive perspective on the risks associated with VR use in this setting. Moving forward, the development of robust implementation strategies should be incorporated into VR research which address healthcare provider concerns and assist in the development of interprofessional clarity on the use of VR between healthcare providers.

42842994.title: Safety issues and harms of communication vulnerability for adult patients in critical care: A qualitative descriptive study.
42842994.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
42842994.abstract: Patients, family members, and healthcare providers value and prioritise patient safety in critical care settings. Communication difficulties experienced by patients during critical illness increases their vulnerability to harms and preventable adverse events. Despite their importance, safety issues and harms related to communication vulnerability in adult critical care settings have not yet been described or systematically characterised. The objective of this study was to identify, describe, and understand safety issues and harms related to communication vulnerability as experienced or observed by patients, family members, and healthcare providers in adult ICU settings. We used a qualitative descriptive methodology including semistructured interviews which were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Paired content analysis was conducted using an inductive approach. Between January and April 2024, 22 participants were interviewed including 11 professionally diverse healthcare providers, seven family members, and four patients from a community academic hospital in Toronto, Canada. Participants identified and described actual and potential physical, psychological, social, and self-determination harms related to their understanding of communication vulnerability during critical illness. Physical harms included respiratory distress and failure, unmet care (e.g., treatment of pain), falls, equipment failures, medication errors, and pressure injuries. Psychological harms included emotional distress (e.g., frustration and anxiety). Social harms included isolation and disrespect (e.g., being mislabelled as "difficult"). Self-determination harms were loss of agency and care without consent. Communication difficulties experienced during critical illness contribute to safety issues and harms across multiple physical, psychological, and social domains. Findings contribute to a growing body of evidence characterising the experiences and perceptions of patient safety in the adult intensive care unit. Findings have multiprofessional clinical implications in critical care settings particularly in relation to patient communication assessment and treatment and the creation of communication accessible and safe critical care settings.

42842537.title: Experience of Families Facing Emergent Donation Procedures: A Qualitative Analysis of Donor Relatives' Perceptions of "Intensive Care to Facilitate Organ Donation".
42842537.abstract: Intensive care to facilitate organ donation (ICOD) is a recently developed procedure involving life support for donation purposes. It has been scarcely studied, especially from the perspective of family members. This study thus investigated the views of families who have experienced donation through ICOD, aiming to identify and characterize the conditions influencing this process. Data were collected by interviewing 29 donor families recruited through seven Spanish hospitals. The systematic constant comparative method was employed for data analysis. Two routes to donation were found. The primary, and simple, route involves cases of high coherence between the patient's positive will (expressed or inferred) about donation and decision-makers' attitudes; it is more likely for expected loss. The secondary, more complex, route applies to cases in which unexpected loss or patient health trajectories predominate and several influential factors converge, such as expressions of doubt about the potential donor's will, weaker family attitudes toward donation, slow and difficult deliberation, and a need for more support. The study enriches understanding of families' decision-making process on donation and could inform psychosocial strategies to support their grieving process.

42842263.title: Multiplexed Aptamer-Based Proteomic Data Normalization (Adaptive Normalization by Maximum Likelihood) Significantly Influences Results in Critically Ill Patients.
42842263.journal: The journal of applied laboratory medicine
42842263.abstract: Blood-based proteomics are employed in cohorts of patients with critical illness to provide biologic insights and improve diagnosis and risk stratification. Somalogic developed a multiplex aptamer-based platform (Somascan) with thousands of proteins assayed in a single plasma sample. Results are reported in 2 forms: (a) adaptive normalization by maximum likelihood (ANML), which normalizes measurements to a healthy US population and (b) a non-ANML-normalized form. It is unknown how ANML-normalization influences measurements and associations with outcomes. We correlated ANML and non-ANML protein quantification with 9 immunoassay biomarkers measured in the same patients' blood samples from the COVID-19 Host Response and Clinical Outcomes (CHROME) cohort. We compared the association of log2 relative fluorescent units (RFUs) with hospital mortality with and without ANML-normalization using adjusted (age, sex, body mass index [BMI]) logistic regression. Results report the odds ratio per doubling of each protein's RFU and declared significance at a false discovery rate (FDR) <0.05. Among 197 patients the average age was 54 years (±16), 51% had COVID-19, 65% were male and hospital mortality was 26%. All biomarkers had equal or higher Pearson correlation between non-ANML-normalization and immunoassay data compared to ANML-normalization. Thousands of proteins changed directionality and significance for risk of mortality based on whether data was ANML-normalized, with 108 of the associations being significant in both, but opposite directionality. The paired Cohen D agreement between beta estimates was moderate (D = 0.61; 95% CI, 0.58-0.64). In this cohort of critically ill patients, ANML-normalization attenuated correlations with immunoassays and largely changed the distribution and direction of significant mortality-associated proteins compared with non-ANML-normalization.

42841946.title: Training for humanization in intensive care: a competency-based educational continuum for patient- and family-centred practice.

42841674.title: Tricuspid Regurgitation Severity and 1-Year Mortality in Echocardiography-Selected Adult Intensive Care Unit Patients: A Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV-Echocardiogram Cohort Study.
42841674.abstract: To evaluate the association between tricuspid regurgitation (TR) severity measured near intensive care unit (ICU) admission and 365-day all-cause mortality in echocardiography-selected adult ICU patients. This secondary analysis linked Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV (MIMIC-IV) version 3.1 with MIMIC-IV-echocardiogram. Adults with transthoracic echocardiography from 24 hours before to 72 hours after ICU admission and documented TR severity were included. None/trivial and mild TR were combined as the low-grade reference group; moderate and severe TR were compared with this group. Multiple Cox regression analyses evaluated 28-, 90-, and 365-day mortality. Sodium-adjusted and biomarker-availability analyses evaluated additional laboratory information. The cohort included 16 991 patients: 12 417 (73.1%) had low-grade, 3467 (20.4%) moderate, and 1107 (6.5%) severe TR. Crude mortality increased across TR severity at 28 days (15.1%, 24.5%, and 32.7%), 90 days (20.3%, 32.5%, and 42.7%), and 365 days (27.2%, 42.9%, and 53.4%). Compared with low-grade TR, 365-day multiple-adjusted estimates were hazard ratio (HR) = 1.32, P < .001, 95% CI: 1.24-1.41 for moderate TR and HR = 1.67, P < .001, 95% CI: 1.52-1.83 for severe TR; 28- and 90-day estimates were directionally consistent, and sodium-adjusted estimates were similar. Moderate and severe TR on early echocardiography were associated with higher 1-year mortality in echocardiography-selected adult ICU patients. This observational association remained consistent after sodium adjustment but should not be interpreted as a treatment effect.

42840738.title: The incremental prognostic effect of red blood cell distribution width in 28-day mortality among critically ill patients with HFpEF.
42840738.journal: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice
42840738.abstract: The prognostic impact of red blood cell distribution width (RDW) on adverse outcomes in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) has been established. However, its non-linear relationship and incremental prognostic value in critically ill HFpEF patients remain insufficiently explored. A retrospective cohort study was conducted involving 3802 HFpEF patients from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV, v3.1) database. Multivariable Cox regression and restricted cubic spline (RCS) analyses were performed to evaluate the association between RDW and 28-day mortality, adjusting for potential confounders. A prediction model was constructed by the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (Lasso)-Cox regression, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was utilized to assessed the incremental prognostic effect of RDW on 28-day mortality prediction. Within the final cohort of 1962 HFpEF patients, the incidence of 28-day mortality showed a significant increase across RDW tertiles (T1 9.4% vs T2 13.1% vs T3 22.9%, P < 0.001). The Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated significantly higher all-cause mortality risk among patients with higher RDW levels (log-rank P < 0.001). Multivariable Cox regression analysis revealed that RDW levels were independently correlated with all-cause mortality after adjusting for multiple variables for both continuous (HR 1.13, 95% CI: 1.07-1.19; P < 0.001) and categorical comparisons (T3 vs T1: HR 1.66, 95% CI: 1.20-2.29; P = 0.002). RCS analysis indicated a significant linear relationship between RDW levels and the risk of mortality (P < 0.001 for overall association; P = 0.222 for non-linearity). When RDW was incorporated into the basic prediction model constructed by Lasso-Cox regression (AUC = 0.814), it slightly improved the predictive ability for 28-day mortality (AUC = 0.819), as evidenced by an IDI of 0.017 (95% CI: 0.006-0.036) and an NRI of 0.140 (95% CI: 0.041-0.203). This study established a significant linear association between RDW at admission and poor prognosis in critically ill patients with HFpEF. Higher RDW levels were associated with increased 28-day mortality risk, suggesting that it may be a relevant biomarker for mortality risk stratification in HFpEF patients.

42840046.title: Estimated pulse wave velocity and risk of new-onset heart failure in ICU patients with acute myocardial infarction: a multicenter cohort study.
42840046.abstract: To investigate the association between estimated pulse wave velocity (ePWV) and new-onset heart failure (HF) in ICU patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI), and to evaluate its incremental predictive value. ICU patients with AMI were identified from the eICU-CRD cohort, and an independent real-world ICU cohort was used for external validation. New-onset HF was the primary outcome. Multivariable regression models were used to assess the association between ePWV and new-onset HF across different time periods. Restricted cubic spline analysis was performed to evaluate the dose-response relationship, and incremental value analysis was conducted to determine the added predictive value of ePWV beyond traditional risk models. In the eICU-CRD cohort, the incidence of new-onset HF was 10.2%. After full adjustment, each 1-unit increase in ePWV was associated with a 13% higher risk of in-hospital heart failure (HR = 1.13, 95% CI: 1.09-1.18, P < 0.001), and the high-ePWV group had a significantly increased risk (HR = 1.84, 95% CI: 1.50-2.24, P < 0.001). In the validation cohort, the incidence of heart failure was 12.9%; each 1-unit increase in ePWV was associated with a 16% higher risk (OR = 1.16, 95% CI: 1.01-1.35, P = 0.046), and the high-ePWV group also showed increased risk (OR = 2.21, 95% CI: 1.02-4.78, P = 0.044). ePWV showed a nonlinear positive association with heart failure risk, and significantly improved model discrimination. Higher ePWV was independently and nonlinearly associated with in-hospital new-onset HF among ICU patients with AMI and improved risk discrimination beyond conventional clinical models. Its association with 1-year post-discharge HF in this high-risk population showed a consistent direction but requires further validation in larger prospective cohorts.

42839240.title: Direct, real-time visualization-assisted nasoenteral tube placement in critically ill patients: a multicenter experience.

42838357.title: The association between early core body temperature in ICU and mortality in spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage: a binational registry study.
authors: Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Centre for Outcome and Resource Evaluation
42838357.abstract: Fever and hypothermia are important risk factors for mortality in critically ill patients. We examined the association between day-one (D1) core body temperature and in-hospital mortality in ICU patients with spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH). We performed a multicentre retrospective cohort study using the Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Adult Patient Database. Adults (≥18 years) with SAH admitted to ICU between January 2018 and June 2024 were included (n = 7,567). Primary exposures were core temperature used for the Australian and New Zealand Risk of Death (ANZROD) score (TANZ), and the highest (THI) and lowest (TLO) core temperatures recorded during the first 24 ICU hours. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Associations were modelled using generalised linear models with natural cubic splines and covariate adjustment. Mean TANZ was 36.0 °C (SD 0.97), mean THI 37.3 °C (SD 0.68), and mean TLO 36.0 °C (SD 0.96). Overall in-hospital mortality was 17% (n = 1,304). TANZ, THI and TLO showed non-linear U-shaped associations with mortality. Lowest observed mortality occurred at TANZ 35.8-38.2 °C, THI 36.8-38.2 °C and TLO 36.1-37.8 °C. Mortality increased below these ranges for TANZ (OR:1.55, 95% CI:1.34-1.79), THI (OR:1.42, 95% CI:1.20-1.69) and TLO (OR:1.38, 95% CI:1.19-1.60), and above the optimal range of THI (OR: 1.47, 95% CI:1.19-1.80). In critically ill SAH patients, D1 core temperature had a U-shaped association with in-hospital mortality. Further research should determine whether temperature variation is a modifiable risk factor in this population.

42837902.title: Complications associated with the insertion site of arterial catheters in intensive care: A propensity score-matching analysis.
42837902.abstract: To identify complications associated with insertion, use, and removal of radial and brachial arterial catheter in two adult ICUs in Bogotá, Colombia, using a comparative cohort design with propensity score matching. A retrospective cohort study was conducted in two adult ICUs. Adult patients who underwent ultrasound-guided arterial catheter insertion between January and December 2024 were included. The exposure was catheter insertion site, classified as radial or brachial. The primary outcome was the occurrence of at least one device-related complication during insertion, maintenance, or removal. Secondary outcomes included complications, procedural variables, and ICU length of stay. To reduce confounding, 1:1 propensity score matching was applied; covariate balance was assessed using standardized mean differences. Post-matching binary outcomes were analyzed using generalized estimating equations (GEE) with robust standard errors and matched-pair clustering. A total of 995 patients were included: 496 in the radial group and 499 in the brachial group. After matching, 842 patients were analyzed, with 421 patients in each group and covariate balance (SMD < 0.1). Brachial catheterization was associated with lower odds of at least one catheter-related complication (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.44-0.86; p = 0.005). Post-insertion hematoma was associated with brachial access after multivariable GEE adjustment (aOR 4.11, 95% CI 1.49-11.31; p = 0.006), whereas brachial access was associated with lower odds of vasospasm (aOR 0.35, 95% CI 0.22-0.55; p < 0.001). No significant differences were observed in other complications or ICU length of stay. In critically ill adults, brachial arterial catheter insertion was associated with fewer complications, although it showed a higher risk of post-insertion hematoma. Radial insertion was associated with increased vasospasm. These findings support individualized selection of arterial catheter insertion site according to clinical profile and complication risk.

42836558.title: Sodium Administration and the Contribution of Fluid Creep to the Sodium Burden of Hospitalized Dogs in the ICU.
42836558.journal: Journal of veterinary emergency and critical care (San Antonio, Tex. : 2001)
42836558.abstract: To assess the fluid volume and quantity of sodium administered each day to a population of hospitalized dogs and evaluate the major sources of administered fluid volume and sodium. Prospective, observational study. University teaching hospital. Twenty-nine dogs expected to require ICU hospitalization for at least 24 h. All sources, types, and volumes of fluid administered were recorded. The volume and sodium content of each fluid source administered daily were calculated. Fluid creep was defined as fluid given as drugs, diluents, and intravenous flush. The mean (SD) daily fluid volume (mL/kg/day) and mean (SD) sodium administered (mEq/kg/day) for all dogs were 64.6 (±36.9) mL/kg/day and 8 (±4.6) mEq/kg/day (Day 1), 48.6 (±36.3) mL/kg/day and 6.2 (±4.5) mEq/kg/day (Day 2), and 43.1 (±32.1) mL/kg/day and 5.7 (± 4.2) mEq/kg/day (Day 3), respectively. Total fluid volume and sodium administration significantly decreased during hospitalization (p = 0.002 and p = 0.002, respectively). Fluid creep accounted for a median volume of 5.6, 4.6, and 2.7 mL/kg/day, and a median sodium content of 0.35, 0.28, and 0.22 mEq/kg/day on Days 1, 2, and 3, respectively. Daily total fluid creep volume decreased during hospitalization (p = 0.016), while daily fluid creep sodium content did not change (p = 0.06). There was no difference in proportional contribution of fluid creep to volume or sodium burden from Day 1 to 3 (p = 0.8, p = 0.6). Critically ill dogs have a clinically important sodium burden during hospitalization. Fluid creep accounts for a small but constant source of sodium administration despite significantly reduced fluid volumes over the course of hospitalization.

42835996.title: Public versus private trauma intensive care unit outcomes: A retrospective cohort study.
42835996.journal: Journal of the colleges of medicine of South Africa
42835996.abstract: Trauma remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), with South Africa experiencing a high burden of intentional and high-energy injuries. Disparities in critical care resources between the public and private healthcare sectors have been reported, but comparative trauma intensive care unit (ICU) outcomes remain incompletely described. This retrospective cohort study compared adult trauma patients admitted to public and private healthcare sector ICUs in Johannesburg between July 2022 and June 2023. The primary outcome was 30-day in-hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included injury characteristics, severity of illness and factors associated with mortality. Descriptive statistics and multivariate logistic regression were used for data analysis. A total of 453 trauma patients were included (private ICU n = 209; public ICU n = 244), with male predominance in both cohorts. Private ICU patients were older, more frequently sustained blunt trauma, and had longer ICU stays. Public ICU patients were younger and more likely to sustain penetrating trauma (68.4% vs 14.4%; p < 0.001). Thirty-day mortality did not differ significantly (private 8.6% vs public 11.9%; p = 0.255), despite greater illness and injury severity among private ICU patients. Greater severity of illness and injury independently predicted mortality, while public ICU admission was associated with increased adjusted odds of mortality. Despite differences in injury profiles, patient mortality was similar in both healthcare sectors. Illness severity remains the prevailing determinant of outcome, underscoring the importance of severity scoring systems and potential system-level factors in LMICs' trauma care. Level of evidence: Level III; prognostic and epidemiological study. This study provides comparative trauma ICU outcomes data from the public and private healthcare sectors in Johannesburg, highlighting the role of illness severity and healthcare sector infrastructure on patient mortality and informing trauma critical care in LMICs.

42835766.title: Artificial Intelligence Prognostic Models for Healthcare-Associated Infection Prediction in Adult Intensive Care Units: A Systematic Review Protocol.
42835766.abstract: Despite widespread Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) measures, Healthcare-Associated Infections (HAIs) remain a major concern in Intensive Care Units (ICUs), leading to increased mortality, prolonged hospital stays, and additional healthcare costs. Prognostic prediction models support identification of patients at high infection risk, and Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence (ML/AI) methods offer the potential to improve such predictions. However, no systematic review has specifically examined ML/AI-based prognostic models for HAI prediction in adult ICU populations. This review aims to identify ML/AI-based prognostic models for estimating the HAI risk in adult ICU-patients, investigate their methodological characteristics, risk of bias and reporting quality. A systematic search will be conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science to identify studies developing and/or validating ML/AI-based prognostic models of HAI prediction in adult ICU-admitted patients. Any study developing or evaluating supervised ML/AI-based models for the prediction of any HAI occurring after ICU admission will be included. Three reviewers will independently screen articles, extract data, and assess risk of bias using the Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool for prediction models using Artificial Intelligence (PROBAST + AI). Extracted information will include study characteristics, patients and setting, predictors, sample size, missing data, analysis methods, performance, and model presentation and interpretation. A narrative synthesis will be conducted for all included studies. Finally, the SPIN-Prediction Models (SPIN-PM) framework will be used to assess quality of reporting. This systematic review protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework (osf. io/bzqfp). This systematic review's findings on methodological aspects, risk of bias, and applicability of ML/AI-based prognostic models for HAI prediction in adult ICU patients will help inform researchers, clinicians, and IPC decision-makers about these models' reliability and readiness for clinical use.

42835343.title: Evaluating a large language model (ChatGPT-5) for detecting potential drug-drug interactions in intensive care: a cross-sectional comparative study with a clinical decision support system.
42835343.abstract: Polypharmacy in intensive care units (ICUs) substantially increases the risk of potential drug-drug interactions (pDDIs), which may lead to adverse drug events and worsen clinical outcomes. Conventional rule-based clinical decision support systems (CDSSs), although widely used, are limited by static logic and restricted contextual reasoning. Recently, large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have emerged as potential adjunctive tools capable of generating clinically interpretable outputs; however, their diagnostic reliability in safety-critical settings remains unclear. This cross-sectional study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of ChatGPT-5 in detecting clinically significant pDDIs in ICU patients, using the UpToDate Drug Interaction Checker as the reference comparator. Data were collected from 101 adult ICU patients on a predefined index date. The model referred to as "ChatGPT-5" corresponds to the version available via the OpenAI API in September 2025. A standardized prompt was applied for each patient to ensure consistency. Diagnostic performance metrics, including sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), overall accuracy, and Cohen's κ coefficient, were calculated. ChatGPT-5 identified a higher number of pDDIs per patient compared with UpToDate (median [IQR]: 6 vs. 0 [0-2]). The mean number of pDDIs per patient was also higher for ChatGPT-5 (7.2 ± 4.1) compared with UpToDate (1.1 ± 1.8). The diagnostic performance analysis was conducted at the patient level. Of the 101 included patients, 17 without a category D or X interaction in the UpToDate reference assessment were excluded from this analysis, leaving 84 patients. Sensitivity, specificity, and overall accuracy were 69.8%, 52.4%, and 65.5%, respectively, with a positive predictive value of 81.5% and negative predictive value of 36.7%. In a conservative full-cohort scenario analysis, treating the 17 excluded patients as discordant cases reduced overall exact agreement from 65.5% (55/84) to 54.5% (55/101). Agreement between the two systems was poor (κ = 0.19), indicating considerable variability in classification. Although ChatGPT-5 demonstrated limited diagnostic performance and the ability to generate clinically interpretable explanations, its low specificity and limited agreement with a rule-based system highlight important safety concerns. These findings suggest that LLMs may serve as complementary tools rather than standalone solutions in ICU pharmacovigilance. Further multicenter validation studies are required before clinical integration.

42833979.title: Dedicated speech and language therapist in the ICU: a one-year experience in a tertiary hospital in Italy.

42833603.title: Implementation of beta-lactam Therapeutic Drug Monitoring in clinical practice: A prospective, comparative, interventional study in intensive care unit patients.
42833603.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate whether implementation of TDM of beta-lactams in clinical practice improved the achievement of PK/PD targets and clinical outcomes in a population of ICU patients receiving high doses by continuous infusion. It was a prospective, comparative, non-randomised, and interventional study conducted in two ICUs (11/2018 to 01/2021), in which TDM of beta-lactams was sequentially implemented. Eligible patients were aged 18 years or older, treated with one of the following five beta-lactams administered in continuous infusion: cefepime, ceftazidime, cefotaxime, piperacillin/tazobactam, and meropenem. The primary endpoint was the PK/PD target attainment at D4 and D7. In the non-TDM group (n = 60), 54%, 46%, and 25% of patients reached the targets at D1, D4, and D7 vs. 51%, 57%, and 57% in the TDM group (n = 112), respectively. Target achievement at D4 or D7 was not correlated with TDM implementation (p = 0.89), unlike reaching the target concentrations at D1 (p < 0.001) and a documented infection (p = 0.008). There was no significant difference in electroencephalogram (EEG) neurotoxicity at D4 between the TDM and the non-TDM groups (10% vs. 18%, p = 0.34). A concentration at D1 and/or D4 above the toxicity threshold was reported in patients with acute kidney dysfunction (OR: 8.5 [2.1; 35.4], p = 0.002) and associated with neurotoxicity (OR: 6.0 [1.7; 21.7], p = 0.005). In this study, the implementation of TDM did not significantly impact PK/PD target attainment, which underscores the importance of integrating a protocolised dose adaptation algorithm. Neurological adverse events were associated with drug overexposure and kidney function impairment. ClinicalTrials.gov, under I.D. NCT03339869.

42833420.title: The impact of blood gas sample waiting time on laboratory parameters in intensive care patients.
42833420.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the impact of blood gas sample waiting time on laboratory parameters in intensive care patients, focusing on pH-related changes. This prospective longitudinal observational study was conducted in the pulmonary diseases intensive care unit of a training and research hospital in Turkey between July 1 and November 30, 2023. A total of 81 patients were included in the study. Blood gas samples were categorized into three groups based on initial pH levels: acidosis, normal, and alkalosis. The samples were stored at 22 °C and analyzed at 0, 30, and 60 min after collection. Statistical analyses were conducted using ANOVA and the Friedman test, and effect sizes were evaluated with Eta squared and Kendall's W. Significant time-dependent changes were observed in PaO2 and SaO2 levels in the acidosis group. In the normal pH group, significant changes occurred in pH, PaCO2, PaO2, SaO2, glucose, and lactate levels. Similarly, in the alkalosis group, significant changes were detected in pH, PaCO2, SaO2, HCO3, glucose, and lactate levels. These findings suggested that slower metabolic activity in acidosis samples led to limited changes, whereas earlier changes were observed in normal and alkalosis samples. To ensure accuracy in laboratory parameters, blood gas samples should be analyzed immediately after collection. Future studies with larger sample sizes and diverse methodologies are required to validate these findings and address the study's limitations, if unavoidable, aim for ≤30 min and document delay for interpretation.

42831954.title: Hourly Blood Urea Nitrogen Trajectories and ICU Mortality Risk in Critically Ill Patients with Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Multicenter Retrospective Cohort Study.
42831954.abstract: Elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN) is associated with adverse outcomes in gastrointestinal bleeding (GIB), but isolated measurements may not capture early temporal patterns. A multicenter retrospective cohort study included 5847 adult patients with GIB from four databases (2008-2022). Serial BUN measurements during the first 24 h after ICU admission were mapped to hourly intervals, with at least 12 observed values required. Generalized additive models assessed concentration-duration patterns, adjusted logistic regression evaluated 15 BUN ranges, and restricted cubic splines examined time-weighted BUN. Meta-analysis, measurement-density sensitivity analyses, and static-dynamic model comparisons were performed. Male and female patients comprised 56.5-58.7% and 41.3-43.5% of each cohort,, respectively. ICU mortality ranged from 18.0% to 19.7%. BUN < 30 mg/dL sustained for > 12 h lowered mortality odds (OR: 0.40-0.62), while BUN ≥ 50 mg/dL for >18 h markedly increased them (OR: 1.55-3.39). Prolonged time within 5-30 mg/dL was associated with lower mortality odds, while greater exposure to 40-70 mg/dL increased risk, with no detectable between-database heterogeneity. Associations were nonlinear and remained broadly consistent in denser-measurement subsets. Dynamic models improved AUC from 0.678-0.701 to 0.718-0.748 (all DeLong P ≤ 0.05), with improved reclassification and lower Brier scores. Early dynamic BUN trajectories were associated with ICU mortality and provided incremental prognostic information beyond admission BUN alone. Incorporating both the magnitude and persistence of BUN abnormalities may support early risk stratification in critically ill patients with GIB.

42831026.title: The role of timely assessment of appropriate care in reducing greenhouse gas emissions in intensive care medicine.
42831026.abstract: Our era is characterized by the significant impact of anthropogenic activity, resulting in the paradox of short-term benefits, such as improved health, alongside potentially devastating long-term consequences for our species and the living world. Critical care, by attempting to preserve human lives through the massive mobilization of human, energy, and material resources, is a quintessential example of this paradox. It is therefore an ideal setting to explore the necessary compromise between care provided for the benefit of patients and the requirement to protect future ecological viability. The objective of our study was twofold: first, to evaluate whether conducting ethical reflections that lead to the early limitations, withdrawal, or non-initiation of certain invasive treatments to avoid disproportionate care would result in a reduction of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions associated with critical care stays; and second, to quantify such a reduction. We conducted a retrospective study analyzing both the medical activity and GHG emissions of a French critical care department throughout the year 2023. Our analysis found that one day of hospitalization required an average atmospheric emission of 194 kg CO2 equivalent (CO2eq) in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) and 160 kg CO2eq in the Intermediate Care Unit (IMCU). Procurement (medications, medical devices, medical equipment) and transport (employees and patients) represented the primary sources of GHG emissions. The analysis of medical activity covered 828 patient stays, corresponding to 2913 patient-days in the ICU and 1225 in the IMCU. The overall mortality rate in critical care was 17% (31% in ICU, 5% in IMCU). In the subgroup for which a total or partial limitation of invasive care was decided within 48 h of admission (240 stays or 29%), each stay required an average atmospheric emission of 586 kg CO2eq, compared to 1055 kg CO2eq for the remainder of the cohort (p = 0.004). An ethical approach consisting of a timely assessment of the appropriate level of care for each patient, with the goal of avoiding disproportionate care, appears to significantly reduce GHG emissions per stay. This approach could constitute a vital component of sustainability within critical care services.

42830886.title: Hypertensive crisis in the critically ill.
42830886.abstract: Hypertensive crises encompass a spectrum of clinical presentations ranging from severe asymptomatic blood pressure (BP) elevation to life-threatening hypertensive emergencies and represent a frequent and challenging situation in the critically ill. While hypertensive urgency, defined as a marked elevation in blood pressure without acute organ damage, can generally be managed in the outpatient setting, hypertensive emergencies require immediate in-hospital management. Hypertensive emergencies are defined by a BP ≥180/110 mmHg associated with acute target-organ damage. Malignant hypertension represents a distinct and severe subset, further characterized by microvascular complications including hypertensive retinopathy and fibrinoid necrosis affecting multiple organs. Initial evaluation is critical to decipher between hypertensive urgency and emergency, with a systematic screening for end-organ damage: cardiovascular system (heart, aorta, and large vessels), central nervous system, retina, and kidneys. The acuity of BP rise, rather than its absolute level alone, largely determines the risk of organ injury, underscoring the importance of a thorough clinical and paraclinical assessment. Once a hypertensive emergency is identified, prompt initiation of intravenous antihypertensive therapy is mandatory. Drug selection, target BP, and the rate of BP reduction must be individualized according to the specific type of end-organ damage. In this narrative review, we summarize current definitions and epidemiology of hypertensive emergencies, detail the clinical approach to initial assessment, and provide an etiology-based overview of management strategies with a focus on intravenous antihypertensive agents and BP targets. Finally, we emphasize the importance of structured long-term follow-up after the acute phase, including etiological workup and optimization of antihypertensive therapy, to prevent recurrence and target-organ failure.

42830603.title: Intensive care unit utilization following the elimination of intermediate care.
42830603.abstract: Many hospitals have established intermediate care units (IMCU) to improve intensive care unit (ICU) utilization. There is little data on how eliminating an existing IMCU affects ICU utilization and the characteristics of ICU patients. Effect of IMCU elimination on ICU utilization and characteristics of patients admitted to the ICU. Retrospective observational before-after study. ICU utilization and characteristics of patients admitted to the ICU were evaluated. Following IMCU elimination ICU utilization significantly increased. ICU admissions increased from 14.2% to 20.5% of hospital admissions, p < .001, monthly ICU admissions increased 42% while total ICU and hospital days increased 32% and 30%, respectively. Pre-elimination IMCU to ICU transfers comprised 6.7% of ICU admissions. Post elimination emergency department (ED) to ICU admissions increased (31.0% vs. 23.6%) as did ward to ICU admissions (41.3% vs. 37.6%). Low-risk monitoring ICU admissions increased 23% to 33%. There was no increase in ICU readmissions or time from ED to ICU or hospital admission. For ICU patients, propensity-adjusted odds ratio (OR) indicated lower ICU and hospital mortality following IMCU elimination, OR 0.82 (0.71, 0.96) and OR 0.83 (0.73, 0.95), respectively. Interrupted Time Series analysis demonstrated that IMCU elimination did not significantly affect secular trends in ICU or hospital mortality. Eliminating IMCU increased ICU utilization and affected the characteristics of ICU admissions. Despite increased utilization, the outcomes of patients admitted to the ICU did not worsen. Further study is warranted on the clinical outcomes of patients previously admitted to IMCU and hospital outcomes following IMCU elimination.

42830294.title: Multi-valvular burden score and one-year mortality in ICU patients undergoing echocardiography: an exploratory cohort study.
42830294.abstract: Multiple regurgitant lesions coexist in critically ill patients, yet cohort-level analyses typically represent each valve separately. We evaluated whether a Multi-Valvular Burden (MVB) score could summarize regurgitant involvement and whether its prognostic information differed from models retaining individual valve grades. This retrospective cohort used MIMIC-IV v3.1 linked with MIMIC-IV-ECHO. Adults with an ICU admission and complete ordinal grading of tricuspid, mitral, and aortic regurgitation on an index echocardiogram within 72 h of ICU admission were included. MVB was the arithmetic sum of TR, MR, and AR grades (0-12). Cox models assessed 1-year all-cause mortality. Additional analyses compared MVB with separate valve-grade models, tested a high-burden definition requiring MVB > = 4 and at least two involved valves, used missing-aware AS/MS evidence proxies, and examined LVEF with structured RV-function classification. The cohort included 5,362 patients; 1,979 (36.9%) died within 1 year. Mortality increased from 24.6% at MVB 0 to 47.4% at MVB > = 4. After clinical adjustment, continuous MVB remained associated with mortality (HR 1.07 per point, 95% CI 1.05-1.09; P < 0.001), and MVB > = 4 was associated with higher mortality (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.22-1.48; P < 0.001). The high-burden category predominantly reflected multivalve involvement: 2,206 of 2,257 patients with MVB > = 4 had at least two affected valves. A model with separate TR, MR, and AR grades showed similar discrimination to the MVB model (C-index 0.7585 vs. 0.7582). Incremental discrimination over the clinical model was small (C-index 0.7543 to 0.7582; delta 0.0039), although likelihood-ratio improvement was statistically significant (chi-square 50.61; P < 0.001). MVB remained associated with mortality in the missing-aware AS/MS sensitivity model (HR 1.07, 95% CI 1.05-1.09) and the LVEF/structured RV-function subset (HR 1.05, 95% CI 1.03-1.08). MVB is an exploratory summary marker rather than an outcome-derived or mechanistic weighting system. Its near-identical discrimination to a model retaining individual valve grades and very modest incremental discrimination suggest that it is best viewed as a compact descriptive marker of broader cardiovascular burden within systemic critical illness, not as a stand-alone clinical decision tool or evidence of a causal pathway to mortality. Not applicable. Not applicable.

42829754.title: Developing a model for conflict management in intensive care units: A grounded theory study.
42829754.journal: Journal of education and health promotion
42829754.abstract: Conflict is a very common phenomenon in the intensive care unit (ICU). Nonetheless, the aim of conflict-related strategies is not to eliminate conflicts but to effectively manage them. The aim of this study was to develop a model for conflict management (CM) in the ICU. This qualitative study was conducted in 2024 by using Corbin and Strauss's grounded theory design. Data were collected via 32 semi-structured interviews with 18 ICU nurses, observational notes, field notes, and memo writing. Participants were purposefully selected from hospitals affiliated to Zanjan University of Medical Sciences, Zanjan, Iran. Corbin and Strauss's method was used to analyze the data. Then, Walker and Avant's method was used to develop a prescriptive CM model. Participants' main concern was a vicious relational cycle, and their strategy for its management was striving to build CM-based relational bridges. The outcome of this strategy was doubtfulness over compromise or silence. The compromise-based relationship model for CM was developed with three main components, namely the management of the situation, awareness of CM strategies, and development of communication skills. The CM process depends on the sociocultural characteristics of nurses and healthcare organizations. The establishment of appropriate relationships is the key prerequisite to CM and depends on the development of nurses' professional skills and strong organizational support. Therefore, health policymakers should consider developing communication and CM skills in nurses.

42829278.title: Early prognostic assessment of upper gastrointestinal bleeding requiring intensive care: comparison of SOFA and bleeding-specific risk scores.
42829278.journal: Digestive and liver disease : official journal of the Italian Society of Gastroenterology and the Italian Association for the Study of the Liver
42829278.abstract: Bleeding-specific risk scores are widely used in upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) but were primarily developed in non-critically ill populations. We compared the prognostic performance of the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score with bleeding-specific scores in patients with UGIB requiring intensive care. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using MIMIC-III, including adults presenting with UGIB and requiring direct ICU admission. The primary outcome was 30-day mortality. Discrimination of SOFA, Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS), AIMS65, pre- and post-endoscopic Rockall scores, serum lactate, and blood urea nitrogen-to-creatinine ratio was assessed using areas under the receiver operating characteristic curves. Among 979 patients, 73 (7.5%) died within 30 days. SOFA showed the highest discrimination (AUC 0.818), followed by lactate (0.774), GBS and AIMS65 (0.767 each), pre-endoscopic Rockall (0.649), post-endoscopic Rockall (0.632), and blood urea nitrogen-to-creatinine ratio (0.604). A SOFA threshold of 5.5 provided 67.1% sensitivity and 84.0% specificity. Higher SOFA was associated with significantly lower 30-day survival (P < 0.0001). In critically ill patients with UGIB, SOFA showed better discrimination for 30-day mortality than bleeding-specific scores, supporting the prognostic relevance of early organ dysfunction assessment.

42829230.title: Comment on "Data-driven phenotypes across the full AKI severity spectrum in patients admitted to the ICU".

42829219.title: Validity and Reliability of the Turkish IPREA-18: A Psychometric Study in Intensive Care Unit Patients.
42829219.abstract: Background and Purpose: Assessing patient-reported discomfort in intensive care units (ICUs) is essential for individualized nursing care. This study aimed to translate and evaluate the psychometric properties of the Incomfort of Patient Reanimation-18 (IPREA-18) scale in Turkish ICU patients. Methods: Following forward-backward translation and expert content validation, psychometric testing was conducted with 250 adult ICU patients hospitalized for at least 48 hours. Construct validity was examined using exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. Internal consistency and convergent validity were assessed. Results: A three-factor structure explained 50.90% of the variance, while bifactor analyses supported a dominant general factor. Confirmatory factor analysis showed mixed model fit (root mean square error of approximation = .099, comparative fit index = .966). Internal consistency was good (α = .836), and convergent validity was supported by a strong correlation with the Intensive Care Unit Environmental Stressor Scale (r = .764, p < .001). Conclusions: The Turkish IPREA-18 demonstrated satisfactory validity and reliability for assessing patient-reported discomfort in ICU settings.

42823695.title: Evaluating plasma ferritin and suPAR as treatable traits for critically ill patients with COVID-19 treated with anakinra: an exploratory analysis of the immune modulation domain of the REMAP-CAP randomised clinical trial.
42823695.abstract: Identifying treatable traits in critically ill patients offers potential to enable a precision medicine approach to treatment. The aim of this exploratory analysis of the REMAP-CAP immune modulation domain was to evaluate whether plasma ferritin or soluble urokinase plasminogen activator receptor (suPAR) represent treatable traits for anakinra in critically ill patients with coronavirus disease (COVID-19). An exploratory analysis of patients randomised within the COVID-19 immune modulation domain of the REMAP-CAP trial was conducted. Adults within 24 h of receiving respiratory or cardiovascular organ support in an ICU with suspected or microbiologically confirmed COVID-19 were included. Plasma ferritin was measured at study sites, and plasma suPAR measured in stored plasma samples. The primary outcome was organ support-free days (OSFD) until day 21. Analyses were performed using a Bayesian cumulative logistic regression model, and results are presented as the posterior median odds ratio (OR), along with 95% credible intervals (CrI), for anakinra being superior to control. In ferritin analyses, 1243 patients were included. Patients with increasing ferritin levels had numerically fewer OSFDs. The posterior probabilities of anakinra having benefit (OR > 1) were 64%, 71%, and 21% across increasing ferritin terciles, compared to 53% in analyses that did not adjust for ferritin levels. 145 patients were included in the suPAR analyses. Patients with high baseline plasma suPAR (≥ 6 ng/ml; n = 85) had numerically fewer OSFDs than patients with low plasma suPAR (-1.0 (-1.0, 9.0) vs. 13.0 (-1.0, 17.0)). The posterior probabilities of anakinra having benefit (OR > 1) were 94.8% (OR 2.28 [0.85-6.06]) in patients with low baseline suPAR, and 38.6% (OR 0.88 [0.39-2.00]) in patients with high baseline suPAR. Plasma ferritin does not identify patients with COVID-19 who benefit from treatment with anakinra, whilst anakinra may be beneficial in patients with low, rather than high, baseline plasma suPAR. These hypothesis-generating findings contrast with the results of clinical trials in non-critically ill patients with COVID-19. NCT02735707. Date of trial registration: 06/04/2016.

42821592.title: STREAM: A data-driven framework for physiological state monitoring in ICU patients.
42821592.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) monitoring systems face a critical gap: translating continuous physiological data into interpretable patterns that support clinical assessment. Existing approaches rely on static thresholds or severity scores that fail to capture dynamic disease progression patterns and provide limited insight into why patients change over time. We developed STREAM (State Trajectory Representation and Evolution-Aware Monitoring), which models each patient as a point in a multidimensional physiological space and applies geometric analysis of routine ICU data to track physiological instability. STREAM analyzes 26 routinely collected clinical measurements using optimal transport theory to discover data-derived physiological states without predefined categories and maps each patient to their nearest state. We evaluated STREAM using the multicenter eICU Collaborative Research Database (N = 158,294) for development and MIMIC-IV (N = 84,517) for external validation. STREAM identified five reproducible data-derived physiological states with distinct clinical signatures. Patients who spent less than 10% of their ICU stay within their expected state (state outliers) had ICU mortality of 37.6%, 16-fold higher than those who remained within their assigned states (2.3%). Mortality prediction achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.863 at 8 hours and 0.903 at 72 hours, with excellent calibration (expected calibration error of 0.002). External validation on MIMIC-IV maintained robust performance (0.798 and 0.857, respectively), with state outliers exhibiting 10-fold higher mortality (33.5% vs. 3.2%). Feature importance analysis identified which laboratory values and vital signs are associated with movement toward higher-risk states, providing interpretable clinical explanations. STREAM provides transparent monitoring across data-derived physiological states, linking state dynamics with outcome prediction. Strong discrimination, calibration, and reproducibility across multicenter datasets support the method's potential for prospective evaluation.
