42955534.title: Candidozyma auris in intensive care units: A point prevalence study and six-month colonization-infection surveillance.
42955534.journal: International microbiology : the official journal of the Spanish Society for Microbiology
42955534.abstract: Candidozyma auris has emerged as a globally significant nosocomial pathogen due to its multidrug antifungal resistance, environmental persistence, and high mortality rates. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of C. auris colonization through a point prevalence screening in the intensive care units (ICUs) of our hospital and to evaluate colonization and infection outcomes during a subsequent six-month follow-up period. The present study aimed to evaluate C. auris colonization rates through point prevalence screening in the ICUs of our hospital, to assess colonization and infection outcomes during a subsequent six-month follow-up period, and to establish a diagnostic algorithm for C. auris identification in our laboratory. Following the detection of an index C. auris case in our hospital in February 2025, a point prevalence study was conducted in all ICUs. Composite swab samples (bilateral axilla and groin) were obtained from hospitalized patients on the same day. In addition, urine and wound cultures were collected from eligible patients. Isolates were identified using chromogenic media, conventional microbiological methods, and MALDI-TOF MS. After the point prevalence study, surveillance for colonization and bloodstream infection was performed over a six-month period. C. auris colonization was detected in 7 of 70 ICU patients (10%) based on composite swab samples. During the six-month follow-up, colonization was identified in 15 patients, and C. auris fungemia developed in nine patients. All patients with positive blood cultures died. The most frequently identified risk factors were broad-spectrum antibiotic use, prolonged ICU stay, and the presence of urinary catheters. Our findings demonstrate that C. auris colonization can be detected at a high rate in ICUs and that severe invasive infections may develop following colonization. Early diagnosis, active screening strategies, and effective infection control measures are critical for reducing C. auris-associated morbidity and mortality.

42955319.title: What do the findings of compartmentalised sub-phenotypes in lungs of patients with pneumonia mean for critical care?

42954706.title: Critical Care Cardiology: Key Tenets of Clinical Management.

42954287.title: The Future of AI in Critical Care: An Exploration in Ten Parables.
42954287.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
42954287.abstract: We cannot know how artificial intelligence (AI) will ultimately change critical care, only that it is driving substantial change quickly. Through ten parables, we describe plausible benefits, harms, and trade-offs involving prognosis, monitoring, liability, research, clinical work, data governance, education, and triage. These parables are not predictions. They are intended to help clinicians, institutions, and regulators envision a range of potential scenarios and think broadly about which applications to pursue, which risks to consider, and which rules to establish before AI systems become entrenched. Each parable reveals how the outlook for AI in critical care is characterized by uncertainty. This includes uncertainty about what a single prediction means for the patient in front of us, how an application built and tested in one setting performs in another, accountability frameworks, professional practice and learning, patient privacy and autonomy, and more. Within each parable we try to keep visible what current evidence already supports and what remains speculative. We close with a set of questions designed to focus that speculation among the interested parties who will shape the future of AI in critical care.

42952536.title: The impact of hospital ethical climate on ICU nurses' ethical behavior: mediated by moral courage.
42952536.abstract: This study purpose to explore the influence of hospital ethical climate on moral courage and ethical behavior of ICU nurses and to examine the mediating role of moral courage. Nurses were selected from the intensive care units (ICUs) of three Grade-A tertiary hospitals in Henan Province by convenience sampling and data collated from General Information Questionnaire, Hospital Ethical Climate Scale, Nurses' Moral Courage Scale and Ethical Behavior Scale for Nurses-Revised. Pearson correlation analysis was used to evaluate associations among the three variables and structural equation modeling to test the influence of hospital ethical climate and ICU nurses' moral courage on ethical behavior. A total of 243 questionnaires were distributed, and 222 valid responses were returned, yielding an effective response rate of 91.4%. Correlation analysis revealed significant positive pairwise correlations among hospital ethical climate, ICU nurses' moral courage, and ethical behavior (r = 0.740 ~ 0.814, p < 0.01). Further mediation analysis indicated than there was a positive association between hospital ethical climate and ICU nurses' ethical behavior (t = 17.032, p < 0.01), moral courage was also positively associated with ethical behavior (t = 3.877, p < 0.01). Moreover, moral courage partially mediated the relationship between hospital ethical climate and ethical behavior, with the mediating effect accounting for 32.1% of the total effect. Moral courage plays a mediating role between perceived hospital ethical climate and ethical behavior in ICU nurses. Accordingly, nursing managers are advised to implement multiple strategies to promote a supportive ethical climate and nurture moral courage, so as to improve ethical conduct among ICU nurses, guarantee patient safety and care quality, and maintain their professional competency and psychological well-being.

42952284.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence in Creating Educational Material for Critical Care Clinicians: A Survey.
42952284.abstract: One Minute Wonders (OMWs) are workplace-based microlearning resources that support continuing professional development in healthcare. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to create educational materials, but little is known about its application in OMWs development. To examine the use, experiences, opportunities and challenges related to AI-assisted generation of OMWs as perceived among healthcare professionals participating in the German-speaking OMW Network. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among members of the German-speaking OMW Network in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. A study-specific questionnaire assessed AI use, quality assurance practices, perceived benefits and risks and educational support needs. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively, and free-text responses underwent qualitative content analysis. A total of 136 healthcare professionals were included, predominantly nurses (n = 128, 94.1%). Overall, n = 63 (46.3%) reported using AI to create OMW. Among AI users, AI was most used for generating figures (n = 41, 65.1%), graphics (n = 35, 55.6%) and design elements (n = 33, 52.4%), with ChatGPT being the most frequently used tool (n = 60, 95.2%). Most AI users critically reviewed AI-generated content (n = 50, 79.4%). Inaccuracies requiring revision were reported by all AI users, most commonly ambiguous wording (n = 32, 50.8%), inappropriate images (n = 32, 50.8%) and incorrect content (n = 29, 46.0%). The content analysis identified a main theme for opportunities: AI as a facilitator of educational resource development and knowledge translation and a main theme for risks: AI as a potential threat to the trustworthiness and professional integrity of educational resources. The use of AI for developing educational materials such as OMWs seems to be established practice among participants of this study. AI offers benefits for efficiency and content creation but requires careful human oversight because inaccuracies and fabricated information are common. AI can support the rapid development of workplace-based educational resources. However, critical review and quality assurance are essential to ensure accuracy and safety.

42951813.title: Assessment of healthcare professionals' perceptions regarding the implementation of a musical intervention in an intensive care unit.

42950897.title: Lactate-to-albumin ratio and 28-day mortality in older postoperative ICU patients: A prospective cohort study with MIMIC-IV replication.
42950897.abstract: Older postoperative intensive care patients have heterogeneous mortality risk related to acute illness severity, frailty, and reduced physiological reserve. The lactate-to-albumin ratio (LAR) integrates routinely available markers of perioperative physiological stress, but its prognostic value remains uncertain. Patients aged ≥65 years admitted to a postoperative intensive care unit were prospectively enrolled. LAR was measured at ICU admission, whereas APACHE II used the worst values during the first 24 h. The primary outcome was 28-day all-cause mortality. LAR was compared with lactate, albumin, blood urea nitrogen-to-albumin ratio, systemic immune-inflammation index, Prognostic Nutritional Index, and Hemoglobin-Albumin-Lymphocyte-Platelet index. Multivariable logistic regression was adjusted for age, APACHE II score, Clinical Frailty Scale score, surgical urgency, and comorbidity burden. A harmonized replication analysis was conducted in the MIMIC-IV surgical ICU cohort. Internal validation using 1000 bootstrap resamples provided optimism-corrected estimates of discrimination, calibration, and overall model performance. Among 647 patients, 79 (12.2%) died within 28 days. LAR showed the highest discrimination (AUC, 0.803; 95% CI, 0.753-0.851) and was independently associated with mortality (adjusted OR per SD, 3.40; 95% CI, 2.33-4.96). LAR slightly outperformed lactate as a single marker (ΔAUC, 0.029; p = 0.002). Clinical models with LAR or lactate showed similar discrimination (optimism-corrected AUC, 0.885 vs 0.883; ΔAUC, 0.0014; 95% CI, -0.0071 to 0.0099; p = 0.750). In MIMIC-IV, LAR remained independently associated with 28-day mortality (OR, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.28-1.94; AUC, 0.704). LAR was independently associated with 28-day mortality and performed similarly to lactate when added to the 24-h clinical model, supporting its role as a complementary biomarker. The association was reproduced in MIMIC-IV with attenuation.

42948454.title: Association of triglyceride-glucose index and triglyceride-glucose-body mass index with all-cause mortality in critically ill patients with aortic disease: A retrospective cohort study.
42948454.abstract: Aortic diseases represent a group of life-threatening vascular disorders that impose a substantial socioeconomic burden. This study aimed to investigate the association between insulin resistance indices and all-cause mortality in with aortic diseases who are critically ill. Patients diagnosed with aortic diseases were identified, and relevant data were extracted from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database. The outcomes of interest were in-hospital, 30-day, 360-day, and 5-year all-cause mortality. Kaplan-Meier survival curves and multivariable Cox regression models were constructed to evaluate the associations of the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index and triglyceride-glucose-body mass index (TyG-BMI) with mortality. Subgroup analyses were performed to assess the robustness of the associations. Receiver operating characteristic curves were used to compare the predictive performance of the 2 indices. A total of 1726 patients were included in the final analysis. Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression revealed that elevated TyG and TyG-BMI indices were significantly associated with mortality of aortic diseases. The robust association between the TyG index and mortality was consistent across most subgroups and remained significant even in patients without diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, or stroke. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis indicated that only the model incorporating the TyG index yielded a significant improvement in predictive performance for 360-day and 5-year mortality. Both the TyG and TyG-BMI indexes were significantly associated with mortality risk in critically ill population with aortic diseases. The TyG index served as a potential prognostic index of all-cause mortality in critically ill population with aortic diseases.

42948022.title: Continuous vs. intermittent vancomycin infusion in critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42948022.abstract: Vancomycin is a first-line antibiotic for severe gram-positive infections in critically ill patients; however, its narrow therapeutic window and marked interindividual pharmacokinetic variability pose challenges in achieving optimal exposure. This meta-analysis aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of continuous vs. intermittent vancomycin infusion in critically ill patients. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Web of Science. Randomized controlled trials and observational studies were included. Statistical analyses were performed using Stata 19.0, and pooled risk ratios (RR) or mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using random-effects models. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool for RCTs and the ROBINS-I tool for observational studies; publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger's test. Sensitivity analyses were performed using the leave-one-out method to assess the robustness of the findings. The certainty of evidence was graded using the GRADE approach. Twenty-two studies (2,140 patients) were included. Continuous infusion significantly improved serum concentration attainment (RR = 2.23, 95% CI: 1.77-2.80, P < 0.001; I 2 = 50.8%) and AUC/MIC attainment (RR = 2.17, 95% CI: 1.60-2.95, P < 0.001; I 2 = 39.7%), and significantly reduced the risk of nephrotoxicity (RR = 0.57, 95% CI: 0.46-0.71, P < 0.001; I 2 = 0.0%). No significant difference in mortality was observed between the two groups (RR = 1.05, 95% CI: 0.85-1.30, P = 0.629; I 2 = 0.0%). Continuous infusion was associated with significantly higher steady-state concentrations (MD = 6.81 mg/L, 95% CI: 3.09-10.54, P < 0.001; I 2 = 90.4%) and shorter time to target attainment (MD = -21.64 h, 95% CI: -35.99 to -7.29, P = 0.003; I 2 = 84.1%), but no significant difference in AUC/MIC ratio was found (MD = 66.74, 95% CI: -56.20 to 189.67, P = 0.287; I 2 = 89.8%). Publication bias was detected for serum concentration attainment (Egger P = 0.001); however, the effect estimate remained significant after trim-and-fill correction (adjusted RR = 1.89, 95% CI: 1.38-2.58). The certainty of evidence was moderate for the primary outcomes and low for the secondary outcomes. Compared with intermittent infusion, continuous vancomycin infusion significantly improves target concentration attainment and reduces nephrotoxicity without increasing mortality. These findings should be interpreted in the context of potential publication bias and between-study heterogeneity.Systematic Review Registration: (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261431488), identifier CRD420261431488.

42947291.title: Assessment of tools for the diagnosis of malnutrition and ICU outcomes in critically ill adults: A comparison study.
42947291.journal: JPEN. Journal of parenteral and enteral nutrition
42947291.abstract: To evaluate the concurrent and predictive validity of the Academy of Nutrition & Dietetics/ASPEN Indicators for Malnutrition (AAIM) in critically ill patients compared with the SGA, considering disease etiology and fluid accumulation. This was a comparison study. Malnutrition was assessed within 24 h of ICU admission using the Subjective Global Assessment (SGA) and the AAIM consensus. The AAIM approach was applied assuming all patients had acute disease (AAIM I) or differentiating acute versus chronic disease-related malnutrition (AAIM II). Two variations were tested based on fluid accumulation: including (AAIM a) or excluding (AAIM b) this component. Concurrent validity was evaluated against SGA using diagnostic accuracy metrics, and predictive validity was assessed using hospital and ICU length of stay and mortality. Among 450 critically ill patients [median age 64 (54-71) years; 53.1% male; APACHE II score 18 (11-23)], 46.3% were malnourished by SGA, whereas AAIM prevalence ranged from 70.9% to 75.5%. AAIM showed moderate sensitivity (75.1%-78.9%) but low specificity (28.6%-32.4%) and poor agreement with SGA (κ = 0.066-0.073). AAIM-defined malnutrition was not associated with outcomes, while SGA-defined malnutrition predicted prolonged hospital stay (OR 1.48; 95% CI 1.00-2.20) and ICU mortality (HR 2.26; 95% CI 1.42-3.49). In critically ill patients, AAIM overestimated malnutrition prevalence and lacked concurrent and predictive validity, whereas SGA showed prognostic value.

42946841.title: Temocillin versus piperacillin-tazobactam for ICU pneumonia caused by Enterobacterales: a Belgian single-centre retrospective study.
42946841.journal: European journal of clinical microbiology & infectious diseases : official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology
42946841.abstract: The aim of this study was to explore the clinical outcomes of ICU patients with Enterobacterales pneumonia treated with temocillin or piperacillin-tazobactam. This retrospective, single-centre study included ICU patients with culture-confirmed Enterobacterales pneumonia over 5 years. Only isolates susceptible to both study antibiotics were included. Patients were excluded if they received the study antibiotic for less than 48 h, had more than 72 h of prior empirical therapy, or required escalation to broad-spectrum antibiotics for a new infection. Primary outcomes were 28-day mortality and clinical failure, and secondary outcomes included ICU and hospital length of stay. Multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to assess the association between treatment group and the primary outcomes. 167 ICU patients (66 temocillin, 101 piperacillin-tazobactam) were included. Baseline characteristics, comorbidities, and severity markers were largely comparable, although in the temocillin group pneumonia more often developed later during ICU stay and treatment was less frequently initiated empirically. 28-day mortality occurred in 23% and 29% of patients in the temocillin and piperacillin-tazobactam groups, respectively (p = 0.39), while clinical failure occurred in 47% and 46%, respectively (p = 0.86). In multivariable analysis, the adjusted OR for temocillin versus piperacillin-tazobactam was 0.931 (95% CI, 0.380-2.276; p = 0.87) for 28-day mortality and 1.224 (95% CI, 0.591-2.536; p = 0.59) for clinical failure. Although the study was not designed to establish non-inferiority of temocillin and the sample size was limited, our findings raise the possibility that temocillin may be a viable treatment option for Enterobacterales-associated pneumonia. Prospective studies are needed to clarify its role.

42946515.title: Enhancing High-Fidelity Simulation Flight-Based Training for Critical Care Paramedics in EMS Aviation: A Systematic Review.
42946515.abstract: High-fidelity simulation (HFS) is used with critical care paramedics (CCPs) to enhance preparedness in high-stake scenarios. This systematic review aims to assess the evidence on the role and effectiveness of HFS flight-based training, evaluating its application in education for CCPs operating within emergency medical services aviation settings. A systematic literature search was performed using a set of inclusion and exclusion criteria, resulting in 7 articles which were appraised using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme tool. HFS training equips learners with skills relevant to their practice. CCPs register improved expertise, engagement and motivation, responsiveness, and general mood. There was insufficient evidence on whether this modality enhances self-awareness. HFS learning is feasible in training CCPs in emergency medical services aviation. However, there is limited evidence on the performance of CCPs trained using HFS learning in the prehospital setting. The findings suggest that standardizing training and assessment methods is recommended to optimize skill acquisition, improve team performance, and enhance patient safety in high-acuity emergencies.

42946511.title: Peer Support for a Specialty Critical Care Transport Team.
42946511.abstract: First responders experience higher rates of psychological distress than the general population, driven by repeated exposure to traumatic events and limited recovery time. Members of neonatal and pediatric critical care transport teams face additional cumulative stressors related to high-acuity patients and emotionally challenging transports. This study describes the development, implementation, and utilization of a peer-led support program within a hospital-based neonatal and pediatric critical care transport service. Following a 2019 internal survey that identified a preference for peer-based emotional support, the Children's Mercy Critical Care Transport Team implemented a structured peer support program. Peer Support Persons (PSPs) were selected from a multidisciplinary transport team and completed standardized initial and ongoing training. Peer support was accessed through self-referral, leadership referral, and a confidential QR code (Quick Response Code) request system. Minimal, non-identifiable encounter data were tracked in a secure database. Descriptive analysis was used to evaluate program utilization from March 2023 to August 2025. During the study period, 209 peer support encounters were documented, including 11 formal debriefings and 199 informal interactions. Encounters involved registered nurses, respiratory therapists, emergency medical technicians, communication specialists, and other team members, most of which were related to difficult transports, patient deaths, and emotional distress. Program utilization increased over time, demonstrating the integration of peer support into routine team culture. Staff feedback was consistently positive, highlighting the value of timely, confidential, peer-led support. A structured, confidential, peer-led support program is feasible and sustainable in a neonatal and pediatric critical care transport setting. This model promotes resilience, reduces stigma, and may serve as a framework for similar first-responder programs.

42946258.title: Depressive and Anxiety symptoms associated with ICU admission in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy: a prospective cohort study.
42946258.journal: Journal of the Academy of Consultation-Liaison Psychiatry
42946258.abstract: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) are a leading cause of maternal morbidity and mortality, particularly in Latin America. Depression and anxiety are frequent during pregnancy and may influence HDP severity, yet their impact on clinical outcomes remains unclear. To determine whether depressive and anxiety symptoms are associated with obstetric intensive care unit (ICU) admission and hospital length of stay among women with HDP. A prospective cohort study was conducted at a Colombian tertiary-care referral hospital (July 2024-January 2025). Women aged ≥16 years in their third trimester hospitalized for HDP completed the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7). Multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression and Cox regression models assessed associations with ICU admission and length of stay RESULTS: Among 234 participants (median age 25 years), 61.1% required ICU care; only 14 of the 143 ICU patients (9.8%) were assessed before ICU transfer. An EPDS score ≥10 or a positive response to item 10 was independently associated with ICU admission (OR 4.83 , 95% CI 1.56 -14.94, p=0.006) and longer hospitalization (HR 0.69 , 95% CI 0.48 -1.00, p=0.048). In an exploratory finding, a GAD-7 score ≥10 showed an inverse association with ICU admission (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.09-0.88, p=0.029). Hemoglobin <11 g/dL and a post hoc mean arterial pressure threshold ≥102.5 mmHg were also significantly associated with ICU admission. Depressive symptoms were associated with obstetric ICU admission and prolonged hospitalization in patients admitted for HDP, whereas anxiety appeared protective, which seems counterintuitive and requires future research to confirm its association; however, because most assessments took place after ICU transfer, causality could not be established. Integrating mental health screening into HDP management may improve maternal outcomes.

42946250.title: Associations between Global Immune-Nutrition-Inflammation Index and Risk of Mortality in Intensive Care Unit Patients.
42946250.journal: The American journal of the medical sciences
42946250.abstract: This retrospective study aimed to evaluate the association between the newly developed Global Immune-Nutrition-Inflammation (GINI) index and the risk of all-cause mortality among patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). Data were extracted from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV version 3.0 (MIMIC-IV-3.0) database. Associations between the GINI index and all-cause mortality were assessed using Kaplan-Meier survival curves and multivariate weighted Cox regression models. Additionally, restricted cubic spline (RCS) analyses were performed to explore potential non-linear relationships between the GINI index and hazard ratios (HRs). Subgroup analyses were conducted to evaluate possible interactions between the GINI index and selected clinical features. A total of 970 patients were included, of whom 11.75% (N = 114) experienced all-cause mortality. A significant association was observed between a higher GINI index and increased risk of all-cause mortality. This association remained consistent when the GINI index was treated as a continuous variable (HR = 1.12; P = 0.03) and when categorized into groups (Group 2 vs. Group 1: HR = 1.97; P = 0.02; Group 3 vs. Group 1: HR = 2.17; P = 0.01). The RCS analysis supported a linear, rather than a non-linear, relationship between the GINI index and all-cause mortality (P > 0.05 for non-linearity). The GINI index is associated with elevated all-cause mortality risk among ICU patients and may serve as a promising candidate for mortality risk stratification, which highlights the potential benefit of timely targeted intervention.

42942287.title: Alactic Base Excess as a Predictor of Mortality in Trauma ICU Patients: Retrospective Study and Evaluation of Integration into Trauma Scoring Systems.
42942287.abstract: Risk stratification in severe trauma remains a major clinical challenge: standard trauma scores (Injury Severity Score, ISS; Trauma and Injury Severity Score, TRISS) rely on anatomical and physiological data but lack metabolic components, potentially underestimating risk in haemodynamically compensated patients with underlying derangements. Alactic base excess (ABE) isolates the non-lactic fraction of metabolic acidosis by correcting base excess for lactate. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the MIMIC-IV v3.1 database, including adult trauma patients with an ISS ≥ 16 and an arterial blood gas measurement within two hours of admission (n = 134), to assess ABE's independent and incremental prognostic value for in-hospital and 30-day mortality, handling missing covariates by multiple imputation (m = 20). ABE was independently associated with in-hospital mortality after adjustment for age, New ISS (NISS), and mechanism of injury (odds ratio 0.84; 95% CI 0.745-0.946; p = 0.004; AUC 0.643), but its prognostic content overlapped substantially with lactate, and its incremental value beyond a clinical base model and beyond TRISS was small and statistically fragile; decision curve analysis showed no consistent net benefit from adding ABE to TRISS. The findings were consistent for 30-day mortality and stronger in a 60 min sensitivity cohort (n = 54; AUC 0.803), though this small subgroup may reflect selection effects. ABE should not be regarded as evidence of a novel physiological pathway in this trauma cohort; its practical contribution, if any, lies in immediate availability from a routine blood gas before ISS or TRISS can typically be computed. These findings are hypothesis-generating, given the single-centre design and absence of external validation, and require prospective, multicentre confirmation before clinical application.

42941315.title: Association of Body Mass Index with Early Inflammatory and Coagulation Biomarker Patterns and Intensive Care Unit Mortality in Critically Ill Patients with COVID-19: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
42941315.abstract: Background/Objectives: The association of body mass index (BMI) with outcomes after intensive care unit (ICU) admission remains uncertain. We examined ICU mortality and early biomarker patterns in adults with COVID-19. Methods: This single-center retrospective secondary analysis included 201 patients. BMI was analyzed per 5 kg/m2 using logistic regression for mortality and generalized estimating equations for biomarkers, adjusted for age, sex, and calendar time. Six inflammatory and coagulation biomarkers were averaged within four consecutive 24 h intervals covering the first 96 h after ICU admission. False-discovery-rate correction and missingness sensitivity analyses were performed. Results: Eighty patients died (39.8%). The adjusted mortality odds ratio was 1.02 (95% CI 0.82-1.26). Joint tests of interval-specific BMI associations were significant for interleukin-6 (IL-6) and white blood cell count, but not the other four biomarkers under the primary specification. Only IL-6 at 24-48 h remained significant after correction across 24 contrasts (-35.9% per 5 kg/m2 higher BMI; 95% CI -49.4 to -18.8; q = 0.006), based on 40/201 patients. Conclusions: Within this selected ICU cohort, BMI showed no clear adjusted mortality association and biomarker findings were heterogeneous. The isolated inverse IL-6 association remains exploratory because of sparse measurements and potentially informative missingness and requires independent confirmation with standardized sampling.

42940517.title: Development and Psychometric Validation of the Geriatric Patient Safety Culture Questionnaire for Intensive Care Nurses.
42940517.abstract: Background: Critically ill geriatric patients represent a unique group with specific care needs due to the physiological and pathological changes associated with aging, which make them susceptible to adverse events and complications during their stay in the Intensive Care Units. This study aimed to develop and psychometrically validate the Geriatric Patient Safety Culture Questionnaire (GPSC-Q), which assesses ICU nurses' knowledge, attitudes, self-reported practices, and perceptions of the work environment related to the safety of critically ill geriatric patients. Method: A methodological study was conducted among 330 ICU nurses to develop and evaluate the psychometric properties of the multidimensional GPSC-Q. The psychometric evaluation included content validity, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, internal consistency, and convergent and discriminant validity assessments. Results: The final questionnaire comprised 43 items: 15 Knowledge, 7 Attitude, 12 Practice, and 9 Work Environment items. Exploratory factor analysis identified four, one, four, and three factors, respectively. Internal consistency coefficients were 0.902, 0.936, 0.749, and 0.721, respectively. Knowledge and Practice showed satisfactory primary CFA fit, whereas Attitude showed mixed fit, including an elevated RMSEA of 0.083. Work Environment showed weaker fit (CFI = 0.907, TLI = 0.855, RMSEA = 0.089) and lower reliability and convergent validity in two domains. The second-order CFA showed mixed fit (CFI = 0.936, TLI = 0.930, RMSEA = 0.048, SRMR = 0.070), with CFI and TLI below the prespecified criteria. Conclusions: The GPSC-Q provides preliminary psychometric support for assessing ICU nurses' knowledge, attitudes, self-reported practices, and perceptions of the work environment related to geriatric patient safety. However, support varied across subscales, with weaker findings for Work Environment. Further refinement and validation in independent samples are needed before recommending broad application. Implications for Practice: The GPSC-Q provides a structured approach to assessing nursing and work environment dimensions relevant to geriatric patient safety in intensive care. Further validation may support its use in identifying educational priorities and informing organizational safety initiatives.

42940488.title: Infection Control Knowledge, Job Stress, and Self-Efficacy in Relation to Infection Control Performance Among Intensive Care Unit Registered Nurses: A Descriptive Cross-Sectional Study.
42940488.abstract: Healthcare-associated infections remain a critical patient-safety concern in intensive care units (ICUs), where invasive procedures and immunocompromised patients elevate infection risk. Infection control knowledge, job stress, and self-efficacy have each been linked to infection control performance, but few studies have examined these factors simultaneously among ICU registered nurses (RNs). This study aimed to investigate ICU RNs' infection control knowledge, infection control job stress, self-efficacy, and infection control performance, and to identify factors associated with infection control performance. This descriptive cross-sectional study surveyed 191 ICU RNs (of 219 recruited) with ≥6 months of ICU experience at two tertiary hospitals in the Republic of Korea (December 2024-January 2025) using structured, validated questionnaires. Data were analyzed with descriptive statistics, independent t-tests, one-way ANOVA (Scheffé/Games-Howell post hoc), Pearson correlation, and hierarchical multiple regression (SPSS 22.0). Mean scores were 19.16 ± 1.07 (of 20) for infection control knowledge, 3.23 ± 0.67 (of 5) for infection control job stress, 3.62 ± 0.53 (of 5) for self-efficacy, and 4.82 ± 0.26 (of 5) for infection control performance. Infection control performance was positively correlated with knowledge (r = 0.151, p = 0.037), job stress (r = 0.161, p = 0.026), and self-efficacy (r = 0.178, p = 0.014). Hierarchical regression showed that current ICU department (surgical, cardiac, emergency, trauma, and general ICU vs. internal medicine ICU as reference), infection control job stress (β = 0.188, p = 0.008), and self-efficacy (β = 0.157, p = 0.022) significantly predicted infection control performance, together explaining 17.4% of the variance (F = 5.995, p < 0.001); infection control knowledge was a nominally significant predictor in this model (β = 0.164, p = 0.016), but this association was not robust to sensitivity analyses (Spearman ρ = 0.034, p = 0.636; heteroscedasticity-robust regression p = 0.095) or to a covariate-adjusted robustness check (p = 0.091), and should be interpreted with caution. Infection control job stress, self-efficacy, and current department were robustly associated with infection control performance among ICU RNs across all sensitivity analyses; infection control knowledge showed a comparatively weaker, fragile association that did not survive rank-based, heteroscedasticity-robust, or covariate-adjusted sensitivity checks. Effect sizes were small to moderate overall, and the final model explained only 17.4% of variance. Department-tailored education and organizational support strategies-channeling job stress constructively and strengthening self-efficacy through hands-on training and mentoring-may help sustain and improve infection control performance; recommendations regarding knowledge-related training should be treated as preliminary given the fragility of this association.

42937563.title: Wearable Sweat Biosystem with Dual Diffusion-Limiting Interface for Dynamic Hyperlactatemia Management in Critical Care.
42937563.abstract: Hyperlactatemia is a critical indicator of tissue hypoperfusion, metabolic dysfunction, and an adverse prognosis in critically ill patients. Yet conventional monitoring depends entirely on intermittent, invasive blood sampling, which cannot capture the dynamic metabolic fluctuations required to guide timely clinical interventions. Herein, we report a wearable sweat-sensing device built on a dual-diffusion-limiting architecture for the continuous and accurate assessment of clinical hyperlactatemia. This system synergistically modulates lactate diffusion in sweat through a silane-network-encapsulated lactate oxidase layer coupled to a polyvinyl chloride layer. This design effectively delays enzyme saturation, extending the linear detection range for sweat lactate to 0-60 mM and thereby fulfilling the stringent requirements of critical care monitoring. The device also integrates real-time pH and temperature calibration to safeguard measurement accuracy in complex physiological environments. Moreover, linear mixed-effects analysis of 82 paired samples from 33 critically ill patients demonstrated a strong association between sweat and blood lactate levels, with a marginal R2 of 0.840. Sweat lactate effectively identified hyperlactatemia and predicted in-hospital mortality, yielding areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve values of 0.943 and 0.785, respectively. The integrated iontophoresis-microfluidics module further ensures high consistency with bedside arterial blood gas analysis, as validated by a marginal R2 of 0.811. Together, these results establish sweat biosensors as a promising platform for continuous metabolic monitoring, resuscitation assessment, and objective prognostic stratification in critical care settings.

42936284.title: Fungal Versus Gram-Negative Bloodstream Infection and 30-Day Mortality in Critically Ill Patients: A Propensity Score-Matched MIMIC-IV Analysis with an Allo-HSCT Comparison Cohort.
42936284.abstract: Fungal bloodstream infections (BSIs) are linked to substantial morbidity and mortality among critically ill patients; however, comparative analyses with Gram-negative BSIs remain scarce. In this retrospective MIMIC-IV v3.1 study, adults were included if their first bloodstream infection (BSI) occurred during an ICU stay. The primary propensity score model included age, sex, Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score within 24 hours of ICU admission (SOFA_24hours), Simplified Acute Physiology Score II (SAPS II), Charlson comorbidity index, and immunosuppressive therapy within 30 days before the index culture. Patients were matched 1:1 using a 0.2-SD logit caliper. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), doubly robust, extended-window, and SOFA_24hours ≥2 analyses were performed. The primary endpoint was 30-day all-cause mortality. An independent allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) comparison cohort was also analyzed. The ICU-stay BSI cohort included 363 patients (129 fungal and 234 Gram-negative; 123 deaths). Unadjusted analysis showed higher 30-day mortality with fungal BSI (hazard ratio [HR], 2.89; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.02-4.13). In the primary expanded matched cohort (119 pairs; n = 238), fungal BSI remained associated with higher mortality (HR, 1.96; 95% CI, 1.35-2.86). Results were consistent in expanded IPTW (HR, 1.86; 95% CI, 1.27-2.74), doubly robust (HR, 1.99; 95% CI, 1.38-2.87), and sensitivity analyses. In the external allo-HSCT comparison cohort (n = 186; 14 fungal cases), mortality was 42.9% versus 7.6% (adjusted HR, 7.58; 95% CI, 2.74-20.99); precision was limited. Among patients with BSI during an ICU stay, fungal BSI was associated with higher 30-day mortality than Gram-negative BSI. These hypothesis-generating findings require confirmation; causality and treatment benefit were not assessed.

42935361.title: K-MIMIC and the next stage of multimodal critical care data.

42935026.title: From Professional Commitment to Continuity: How Resilience and Empowerment Reduce Turnover Intention Among Critical Care Nurses.
42935026.abstract: To examine the mediating effects of resilience and psychological empowerment on the relationship between professional commitment and intention to leave among critical care nurses (CCNs). The intention of CCNs to leave their jobs is considered a primary problem faced by hospitals and healthcare executives worldwide. There is a need to analyze its relationship with professional commitment, resilience, and psychological empowerment. A cross-sectional study. This study was conducted among 430 CCNs from October 2024 to January 2025. Data were collected using a sociodemographic sheet, Psychological Empowerment Scale (PES), Intention to Leave Scale, Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale, and Nursing Professional Commitment Scale (NPCS). A path analysis was performed using AMOS 24.0 software. Professional commitment demonstrated a significant total negative effect on intention to leave (β = -0.420, p = 0.005). Both resilience and psychological empowerment significantly mediated this relationship. The indirect effect through resilience was stronger (β = -0.071, p = 0.011) than that through psychological empowerment (β = -0.041, p = 0.004). Professional commitment was positively associated with both resilience (β = 0.208, p = 0.009) and psychological empowerment (β = 0.462, p = 0.009), while each mediator was negatively related to intention to leave (β = -0.343 and β = -0.091, respectively). The direct effect of professional commitment on intention to leave remained significant (β = -0.306, p = 0.005), indicating partial mediation. This study indicates that professional commitment, through fostering resilience and psychological empowerment, directly and indirectly lowers turnover intentions. These findings highlight the importance of enhancing nurses' commitment, empowerment, and resilience in order to support workforce retention. Practical and administrative policy efforts that promote professional development, autonomy, and psychological support for nurses may help to reduce turnover rates in critical care settings. Hospital administrators and nursing leaders should give top priority to initiatives that strengthen professional commitment, psychological empowerment, and resilience among CCNs, as these factors were found to directly and indirectly reduce intention to leave. Supportive leadership techniques, resilience-building seminars, structured mentorship programs, and participatory decision-making models may all help to reinforce nurses' commitment to the profession. By incorporating these strategies into organizational policy, critical care settings can promote a stable nursing workforce, increase employee retention, decrease the desire to leave, and ultimately enhance the quality of patient care. Enhancing the psychological empowerment, resilience, and professional commitment of CCNs may successfully reduce their intention to leave and improve workforce stability and patient care quality. These results can be used by nursing administrators to create retention-focused interventions, such as resilience training, empowerment initiatives, and mentorship, that promote nurses' mental health and job happiness. The STROBE checklist was used as a guideline. No patient or public contribution.

42934992.title: From catheter to infection: Risk factors for central venous catheter-related infections in the intensive care unit.
42934992.journal: The International journal of artificial organs
42934992.abstract: A substantial proportion of critically ill patients require central venous catheterization, with infection being the most significant complication. Catheter-related infections may increase ICU length of stay, morbidity, and mortality. This study aimed to identify factors contributing to these infections. This retrospective observational study included 1985 central venous and hemodialysis catheters meeting predefined inclusion criteria. Catheters were classified by insertion site as femoral, internal jugular, or subclavian. Catheter-related infections were assessed as percentages and as incidence per 1000 catheter-days. Infection risks were compared using relative risk (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Catheter-related infection occurred in 309 catheters (15.6%). Infection rates did not differ significantly by insertion site when analyzed as percentages (femoral 16.7%, internal jugular 15.3%, subclavian 13.6%; p = 0.474). However, incidence analysis accounting for dwell time showed a higher infection incidence in femoral catheters (13.9 per 1000 catheter-days). Compared with subclavian catheters, femoral catheters had a significantly increased infection risk (RR 1.56; 95% CI 1.07-2.28). Central venous catheter-related infections are more frequent in femoral sites in a time-dependent manner. Early replacement of femoral catheters is important to reduce infection risk. In clinical practice, prevention strategies should consider not only the insertion site but also expected duration of use, frequency of access, catheter type, patient characteristics, and infection control measures.

42934619.title: Development of an educational intervention to enhance critical care nurses' mentoring competence - a qualitative study.
42934619.abstract: The global shortage of nurses places additional pressure on healthcare systems and nursing education. Effective mentoring is crucial for students, and various interventions have been developed to enhance the mentoring competences of nurses working with undergraduate nursing students. However, research on mentoring competences in the context of post-registration critical care nursing remains limited. This study aimed to develop an educational intervention to enhance the critical care nurses' mentoring competence. We employed a qualitative design, guided by the UK Medical Research Council's framework for complex interventions and the European guideline on clinical nurse mentor's mentoring competence development. We conducted three focus group interviews with 11 critical care nurses from university and local hospitals in Northern Norway and used reflexive thematic analysis to analyse the data. We identified four themes essential for the intervention: mentoring as its own skillset, mentoring as an act of power, mentoring as a collaborative effort, and organisational support for mentoring. Participants emphasised the need for practical tools to address challenges such as diverse student learning needs, fostering reflection, and managing power dynamics. They also highlighted the importance of shared understanding of mentoring practices within the units and robust organisational support, including time allocation for both daily mentoring and competence development, and leadership commitment. The findings informed the development of a blended learning educational intervention combining online learning with in-person simulated discussions. The intervention focuses on practical tools, simulations, and fostering a supportive mentoring environment tailored for critical care nursing context.

42933957.title: Irritant Contact Dermatitis Related to Fecal and Urinary Incontinence in the Critical Care Population.
42933957.journal: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
42933957.abstract: Irritant contact dermatitis due to fecal, urinary, or dual incontinence is a common but often under recognized complication in critically ill patients that contributes to pain, skin breakdown, infection, and pressure injury risk. Despite advances in understanding its prevention and management, practice remains variable. This article contrasts traditional and evidence-based approaches, reviewing terminology, risk factors, pathophysiology, diagnosis, and interventions. A practical critical care application of the Manage→Clean→Protect→Restore care bundle, adapted from the 2026 Wounds International Best Practice Update, is presented to support standardized, proactive incontinence skin care, and improve patient outcomes.

42933863.title: Timeliness versus diagnostic accuracy in ICU pneumonia sampling: is ND-BAL ready for broader adoption?

42931898.title: Restoring patients' voice in intensive care: augmentative and alternative communication for human-centred care.

42930918.title: Association of the Vasoactive-Inotropic Score with Postoperative Intensive Care Unit Stay Following Arterial Switch Operation.
42930918.journal: Journal of cardiovascular development and disease
42930918.abstract: Transposition of the great arteries (TGA) is one of the most common cyanotic congenital heart diseases in the neonatal period, and arterial switch operation (ASO) is the standard surgical treatment. Postoperative low cardiac output syndrome remains an important cause of morbidity. This study evaluated the association between serial vasoactive-inotropic score (VIS) measurements and postoperative intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay in neonates with TGA undergoing ASO. This retrospective study included neonates with TGA who underwent ASO and were followed in a tertiary Pediatric Cardiac Intensive Care Unit between 1 August 2020, and 1 August 2022. ICU length of stay was analyzed as a continuous primary outcome. Prolonged ICU stay, defined as the upper quartile of ICU length of stay in the study cohort (≥9 days), was evaluated as a secondary exploratory outcome. VIS values were recorded at ICU admission and at 24, 48, and 72 h after surgery. Associations between VIS parameters and continuous ICU length of stay were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation. ROC analysis and logistic regression were performed for prolonged ICU stay. A total of 60 neonates were included, and 15 patients (25%) had a prolonged ICU stay. Admission VIS values were similar between groups. However, VIS values at 24 and 48 h were significantly higher in the prolonged ICU stay group (p = 0.005 and p = 0.001, respectively), whereas no significant difference was observed at 72 h. VIS at 48 h showed the strongest correlation with ICU length of stay (Spearman's r = 0.52, p < 0.001), followed by ΔVIS48 (r = 0.48, p = 0.001) and VIS at 24 h (r = 0.44, p = 0.002). In secondary exploratory analyses, VIS at 48 h demonstrated a numerically higher AUC than VIS at 24 h (0.82 vs. 0.74). ΔVIS48 was associated with prolonged ICU stay in multivariable logistic regression (OR, 1.18 per unit increase; 95% CI, 1.05-1.33; p = 0.006). Firth's penalized logistic regression yielded a similar estimate (OR, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.03-1.30; p = 0.012). In neonates with TGA undergoing ASO, higher VIS during the first 24-48 postoperative hours, particularly an increase from admission to 48 h, was associated with longer ICU stay. These findings support serial VIS assessment as a marker of early postoperative clinical trajectory. Cohort-derived VIS thresholds should be considered exploratory and require external multicenter validation before clinical application.

42930778.title: From Protocols to Phenotypes: The Evolution of Precision Medicine in Critical Care and Its Alignment with "Choosing Wisely".
42930778.abstract: Over the last decade, the scientific literature has witnessed a conceptual shift from "personalized medicine" to "precision medicine" [...].

42930193.title: Baseline AI Economic Literacy and Enacted Adoption of Artificial Intelligence Tools by Oncology and Critical Care Professionals.
42930193.abstract: We examined whether baseline artificial intelligence (AI) economic literacy was associated with sustained use of oncology AI tools. This prospective cohort included 96 oncology and critical care professionals at two centres in Timișoara, Romania, followed for 12 months after institutional roll-out. Participants were classified by AI Economic Literacy Index (AIELI) scores as high (≥14) or low (<14). Sustained use required log-verified activity in at least two of the final three months. Analyses included regression, inverse probability of treatment weighting and exploratory indirect-association analysis through return-on-investment (ROI) confidence. Among 91 completers, sustained use occurred in 29/53 high-literacy participants (54.7%) and 7/38 low-literacy participants (18.4%; risk ratio 2.97, 95% confidence interval 1.46-6.06). The weighted risk ratio was 2.24 (1.15-4.34), and the profession-stratified risk ratio was 2.80 (1.36-5.76). Median time to first use was 5.8 months in the high-literacy group and was not reached in the low-literacy group. Nine participants (eight high-literacy, one low-literacy) had recorded use before the baseline assessment; in a delayed-entry analysis restricted to the 87 participants unused at assessment, the crude hazard ratio for subsequent first use was 2.98 (1.62-5.48) and the crude risk ratio for sustained use after excluding prior users was 3.01 (1.36-6.64); the corresponding covariate-adjusted estimates were less precise (hazard ratio 1.81, 0.89-3.69; risk ratio 2.19, 0.99-4.86) and their confidence intervals included the null. Roll-out-based time-to-first-use comparisons are descriptive because they include events preceding measurement. Sustained use increased across literacy bands. An indirect association through ROI confidence was observed but was not interpretable as causal mediation. Higher baseline economic literacy was associated with earlier and more sustained recorded AI-tool use, although opportunity for use differed by profession, and the adjusted timing-corrected estimates leave the independent contribution of literacy uncertain. Larger multicentre studies should evaluate whether literacy training improves adoption and whether adoption translates into clinical or economic benefit.

42928942.title: Sequential Organ Failure Assessment Score as a Predictor of Intensive Care Unit Mortality in Patients With Maxillofacial Trauma: A Prospective Observational Study.
42928942.abstract: Maxillofacial trauma that requires intensive care may be complicated by systemic organ dysfunction and mortality. The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score provides an objective measure of physiological deterioration, whereas serial assessments may offer greater prognostic information than a single measurement. This study evaluated the prognostic performance of the admission SOFA score, 48-hour SOFA score, and ΔSOFA score (ΔSOFA) for predicting intensive care unit (ICU) mortality. This prospective observational study included 130 consecutive patients with maxillofacial trauma admitted to the ICU over a one-year period from June 2018 to May 2019. SOFA scores were recorded at admission to the ICU (SOFA-0) and at 48 hours (SOFA-48). ΔSOFA was calculated as SOFA-48 minus SOFA-0. The patients were categorized according to their ICU survival status. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the discriminatory ability of each SOFA score. Of 130 patients, 105 survived, and 25 died during ICU admission. Non-survivors had higher SOFA-0 scores than survivors (11.0 ± 3.5 vs. 6.5 ± 3.0; p < 0.001) and higher SOFA-48 scores (13.8 ± 4.2 vs. 5.2 ± 3.0; p < 0.001). ΔSOFA demonstrated worsening organ dysfunction among non-survivors compared with improvement among survivors (2.8 ± 3.6 vs. -1.3 ± 2.5; p < 0.001). ROC analysis showed an area under the curve (AUCs) of 0.79 for SOFA-0, 0.91 for SOFA-48, and 0.93 for ΔSOFA. A ΔSOFA cut-off of >+1.5 demonstrated 92.0% sensitivity and 81.0% specificity. Serial SOFA assessment, particularly ΔSOFA, demonstrated strong prognostic utility for ICU mortality in patients with maxillofacial trauma. Early worsening of organ dysfunction may help identify patients at increased risk of poor outcomes.

42927388.title: Combined Case-Based and Problem-Based Learning in a Cardiothoracic ICU: A Retrospective Nonrandomized Comparative Educational Study.
42927388.journal: Advances in medical education and practice
42927388.abstract: To compare immediate knowledge improvement, simulation performance, and participant satisfaction between combined case-based learning and problem-based learning (CBL-PBL) and traditional lecture-based training among cardiothoracic intensive care unit (ICU) professionals in a single-center retrospective nonrandomized comparative study. This single-center retrospective nonrandomized comparative study reviewed training records for 46 healthcare professionals at Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, China, from January to December 2024. Training-group membership was preference-based, with 23 participants per group. Outcomes included pre-to-post knowledge change, simulation performance, and satisfaction. Additional unadjusted comparisons used the Welch method. Exploratory logistic regression examined membership in a median-defined higher post-training score category, adjusting for age, sex, professional experience, and baseline knowledge. Clinical indicators were reported descriptively. The between-group difference in knowledge improvement favored CBL-PBL by 7.60 points (approximate 95% CI 1.01-14.19; P = 0.025). Simulation-score differences favored CBL-PBL across three scenarios, ranging from 1.60 to 1.90 points (all P ≤ 0.001). Satisfaction was higher by 2.80 points (95% CI 1.91-3.69; P < 0.001). CBL-PBL was associated with higher odds of membership in the higher-score category (adjusted OR 8.961; 95% CI 1.861-43.156; P = 0.006), although the estimate was imprecise. Structured case discussion and collaborative problem-solving warrant further evaluation as components of cardiothoracic ICU training. Prospective studies with validated assessments and delayed follow-up are needed before recommending routine adoption or claiming sustained learning or patient benefit.

42926330.title: Predicting for severity in DRESS: When to speak to ICU.
42926330.journal: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV

42925663.title: Pressure injury prevention in critical care: A reflexive thematic analysis of clinicians' perspectives on complexity and clinical judgement.
42925663.abstract: Pressure injury prevention in critical care remains a persistent global challenge. Despite established guidelines, implementation is often constrained by physiological instability, device burden, and competing clinical priorities. Emerging digital and artificial intelligence approaches offer potential support, yet their role within the complexity of critical care practice remains unclear. To explore clinicians' perspectives on pressure injury prevention in critical care, with particular attention to complexity, clinical decision-making and the potential role of emerging technologies. Qualitative study using reflexive thematic analysis. We analysed 12 brief written reflections from clinicians working in critical care and related roles, predominantly in the United Kingdom. We purposively invited contributors through professional networks, who responded to shared prompts on prevention challenges, practice tensions, and potential roles for artificial intelligence. The first author led iterative semantic and latent coding within a contextualist-constructionist reflexive thematic analysis, supported by reflexive discussion among the author team. Five interconnected themes emerged: negotiating physiological stability and guideline adherence; device-centred care as a source of iatrogenic harm; organisational constraints, incomplete prevention, and the illusion of compliance; diagnostic and conceptual uncertainty; and technology as supportive, not substitutive. Pressure injury prevention was constructed as a context-dependent process in which clinicians continually negotiated preventive actions against physiological instability, device dependence, organisational capacity and competing treatment priorities. Clinicians viewed technology as potentially supportive of risk recognition and clinical decision-making, but not as a substitute for clinical judgement. The findings suggest that guideline-driven pressure injury prevention may not fully accommodate the physiological instability, device dependence and organisational constraints encountered in critical care. They highlight the need for prevention approaches that support context-sensitive clinical judgement while recognising the limits of standardised protocols and emerging technologies. Pressure injury prevention in critical care involves context-sensitive clinical decision-making rather than protocol adherence alone. Emerging technologies may have a supportive role, but their clinical value and safety require development and prospective evaluation. This study provides qualitative insights into how clinicians negotiate pressure injury prevention in complex critical care environments and identifies considerations for future development and evaluation of decision-support technologies. Not registered.

42924603.title: The Relationship Between Moral Distress and Quiet Quitting in Intensive Care Nurses: The Mediating Role of Moral Injury.
42924603.abstract: Intensive care nurses encounter numerous ethical problems in clinical practice. When these morally challenging situations remain unresolved, they may lead to moral distress and moral injury among nurses and may ultimately result in quiet quitting behaviours. Studies examining the relationships among moral distress, moral injury and quiet quitting among intensive care nurses within a comprehensive model are limited. This study aimed to examine the relationships among moral distress, quiet quitting and moral injury among intensive care nurses. The study employed a cross-sectional correlational design. It was conducted between 1 April and 31 October 2025 among intensive care nurses working in a university hospital in Türkiye. The data were collected using the Nurse Introductory Information Form, the Moral Distress-Appraisal Scale, the Moral Injury Symptom Scale-Healthcare Professional, and the Quiet Quitting Scale. The relationships among moral distress, moral injury, and quiet quitting were examined using the Pearson correlation coefficient. The statistical significance of the mediating effects was evaluated using 95% confidence intervals from 5000 bootstrap samples. The study included 138 intensive care nurses. A moderate positive relationship was found between moral distress and moral injury among intensive care nurses (r = 0.524, p < 0.001). In addition, a low but statistically significant positive relationship was identified between quiet quitting and both moral injury (r = 0.258, p < 0.001) and moral distress (r = 0.201, p < 0.001). The mediation analysis revealed that moral injury played a full mediating role in the relationship between moral distress and quiet quitting (B = 0.083; 95% CI [0.003, 0.170]). This study demonstrates that the relationship between moral distress and quiet quitting among intensive care nurses operates through moral injury. The findings indicate that moral injury constitutes a key mechanism that negatively affects nurses' professional engagement and organisational commitment. In this context, quiet quitting may be seen as an outcome arising from unresolved ethical problems. Strengthening ethical support mechanisms to prevent moral injury is therefore important for the professional sustainability of nurses. These findings highlight the clinical importance of recognising and addressing moral distress and moral injury among intensive care nurses, as early interventions targeting these ethical challenges may help reduce quiet quitting tendencies and support sustained professional engagement. Accordingly, strengthening ethical support mechanisms and improving working conditions may foster a more supportive clinical environment and help sustain nurses' engagement in intensive care practice.

42923659.title: Frailty in anaesthesia and intensive care.

42923000.title: Head-to-head comparison of glucose-to-albumin ratio against five albumin-derived indices for predicting 28-day ICU mortality in critically ill patients with spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage: a multicenter retrospective study.
42923000.abstract: Spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) carries a 30-day mortality exceeding 40%. The glucose-to-albumin ratio (GAR) reflects metabolic stress and nutritional status. Although previous studies have demonstrated its prognostic value in ICH, its utility specifically in ICU-admitted patients and its comparative performance against other albumin-derived indices remain incompletely characterized. We included 1,625 ICU ICH patients from MIMIC-IV (derivation) and 861 from two Chinese centers (external validation). Log-transformed GAR (LogGAR) was the exposure; 28-day ICU mortality was the primary outcome. Cox regression, restricted cubic splines, Kaplan-Meier, and Fine-Gray competing-risk models assessed LogGAR's independent prognostic value, compared head-to-head with five albumin-derived indices. Lasso-selected features informed a multilayer perceptron (MLP), benchmarked against severity scores and a penalized logistic regression on identical features. LogGAR was independently associated with 28-day ICU mortality (derivation: HR = 1.81, 95% CI 1.33-2.47, p < 0.001; external: HR = 3.48, 95% CI 2.54-4.78, p < 0.001), with linear dose-response (RCS P-nonlinear = 0.315). Fine-Gray competing-risk analysis confirmed robustness (subdistribution HR = 2.01, 95% CI 1.58-2.57, p < 0.001). Adding LogGAR to six severity scores improved discrimination (external ΔAUC = 0.085-0.107, all p < 0.001). Among six indices, LogGAR was comparable to logLDAR in the derivation cohort (0.679 vs. 0.681, p = 0.78) and highest in the external cohort (0.691). Subgroup analyses identified significant effect modification only for AKI (FDR = 0.029). The Lasso-MLP (8 features) and penalized logistic regression achieved comparable performance (validation AUC 0.718 for both; external AUC 0.759 vs. 0.783), indicating no added value from nonlinearity. Calibration slopes were 0.66 (validation) and 0.91 (external). SHAP identified LogGAR as the top predictor. LogGAR is independently associated with 28-day ICU mortality in critically ill patients with ICH and shows discriminative performance comparable to logLDAR and superior to the remaining four indices. A penalized logistic regression on Lasso-selected features matched the MLP, suggesting the predictive signal lies in features rather than model complexity-a pragmatic consideration for clinical implementation. As a readily available biomarker, LogGAR may support early ICU risk stratification.

42921049.title: Inflammatory Biomarkers as Predictors of In-Hospital Mortality in Critically Ill COVID-19 Patients: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
42921049.abstract: Inflammatory biomarkers have been proposed as prognostic indicators in COVID-19; however, their prognostic associations within critically ill ICU-admitted patients remain of interest. This study aimed to evaluate the associations of selected inflammatory biomarkers with in-hospital mortality and their discriminatory performance among critically ill COVID-19 patients. In this retrospective cohort study, 244 adult patients with confirmed COVID-19 pneumonia admitted to the ICU between August 2020 and June 2021 were analyzed. Disease severity was assessed using the ISARIC 4 C Mortality Score. Associations between inflammatory biomarkers and mortality were evaluated using univariable and multivariable logistic regression, and discriminatory performance was assessed using ROC curve analysis. The in-hospital mortality rate was 90.6%. ESR and LDH levels were significantly higher in non-survivors. In a biomarker-restricted multivariable logistic regression model, ESR (OR 1.023 per 1 mm/h increase; 95% CI 1.004-1.042; p = 0.016) and LDH (OR 1.002 per 1 U/L increase; 95% CI 1.000-1.003; p = 0.009) remained significantly associated with in-hospital mortality after mutual adjustment for the other prespecified inflammatory biomarkers. LDH demonstrated good discriminatory performance (AUC 0.725; 95% CI 0.645-0.805). ESR showed modest discriminatory performance (AUC 0.646; 95% CI 0.559-0.732). ESR and LDH remained significantly associated with in-hospital mortality after adjustment for the other prespecified inflammatory biomarkers. These findings suggest that ESR and LDH may provide adjunctive prognostic information in critically ill ICU patients; however, they should be interpreted in the context of the biomarker-restricted model and the limited adjustment set. Confirmation in larger prospective studies incorporating established clinical prognostic factors is warranted.

42920918.title: Restrictive Potassium Supplementation Strategy in a General Intensive Care Unit: A Before-and-After Quality Improvement Audit in a Mixed Critical Care Population.
42920918.abstract: Potassium supplementation thresholds in intensive care vary widely and have historically lacked strong supporting evidence. The TIGHT K trial demonstrated non-inferiority of a restrictive potassium threshold in cardiac surgical patients; applicability to general intensive care populations is unclear. Retrospective before-and-after quality improvement audit in a mixed adult intensive care unit (ICU), comparing two one-week periods before (May 2025) and after (September 2025) reducing the intravenous potassium supplementation threshold from <4.5 to <3.6 mmol/L. Forty-eight patients were included (22 pre-, 26 post-guideline) with comparable baseline characteristics. Mean intravenous potassium administrations per patient fell by 17.4% (from 9.41 to 7.77 administrations per patient), and the proportion of supplementation episodes initiated at K⁺ ≥4.0 mmol/L fell from 32.9% to 11.4% (a 21.5 percentage-point absolute reduction, equivalent to a 65.2% relative reduction). Pre-supplementation potassium was lower post guideline (3.44 vs 3.83 mmol/L; p <0.001), but potassium correction (ΔK) was unchanged (p = 0.51), and arrhythmia burden did not increase. A restrictive potassium supplementation threshold reduced potassium use without evidence of harm in a general intensive care population, supporting wider applicability beyond cardiac surgery, although larger prospective studies are needed.

42920808.title: HQML-ICU: hybrid quantum-classical machine learning for ICU mortality prediction using MIMIC-IV electronic health records.
42920808.abstract: Accurate prediction of mortality in the intensive care unit (ICU) is crucial for informing clinical decision-making and optimizing resource allocation. Although machine learning methodologies have enhanced traditional severity-of-illness scoring systems, they encounter intrinsic limitations in modeling complex feature interactions within electronic health record (EHR) data. In this study, we introduced a hybrid quantum-classical machine learning (HQML) framework for predicting ICU mortality, evaluated using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV, version 2.2) database. Our methodology incorporates a classical autoencoder for dimensionality reduction (from 87 features to 16 latent dimensions), a 4-qubit parameterized quantum circuit (PQC) utilizing ZZFeatureMap encoding and RealAmplitudes variational ansatz (L = 3 layers, 48 trainable parameters), and a classical post-processing layer. In a retrospective cohort of 38,624 ICU admissions (12.8% mortality rate), the HQML model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.871 (95% CI: 0.859-0.883), outperforming XGBoost (0.858; 95% CI: 0.844-0.872), deep neural network (0.847), random forest (0.838), logistic regression (0.813), and SAPS-II (0.771). The improvement over XGBoost was statistically significant (DeLong p = 0.012) and corroborated by 5-fold cross-validation. The model demonstrated superior calibration (Brier score 0.089 vs. 0.095) and enhanced data efficiency. Comprehensive ablation experiments have elucidated the effects of circuit depth, quantum feature map selection, autoencoder latent dimensionality, class imbalance management, and quantum noise. Noise analysis suggests that gate error rates below 10-3 are necessary to maintain this advantage. These findings substantiate that hybrid quantum-classical architectures can yield incremental but statistically significant improvements in clinical prediction tasks under idealized simulation conditions. As the study is limited to a single-center dataset (MIMIC-IV), external validation on independent cohorts is required before clinical generalizability can be established.

42920655.title: Educational outcomes of CDIO-guided progressive case-based learning and gamification in undergraduate critical care nursing: an exploratory two-class quasi-experimental study.
42920655.abstract: This study compared educational outcomes between nursing students receiving a CDIO-guided case-based and gamified teaching program and those receiving conventional teaching. This two-class quasi-experimental study included 140 nursing students from two classes between March and June 2025. Classes were assigned by lottery to the intervention (n = 65) or control (n = 75) group. The intervention integrated progressive cases, microlectures, teamwork, board games, and escape-room simulation, whereas the control received traditional lectures and Small Private Online Course self-study. Self-directed learning, critical thinking, and learning engagement were assessed before and after the course. Post-course outcomes included theoretical performance, cardiopulmonary resuscitation performance, course performance, and teaching evaluation. Analysis of covariance, Welch's t tests, and Holm correction were applied. The intervention class had higher adjusted post-course scores for self-directed learning (mean difference, 7.68; 95% CI, 3.29-12.07), critical thinking (15.27; 95% CI, 11.53-19.00), and learning engagement (7.06; 95% CI, 1.82-12.30). It also achieved higher theoretical, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, course, and teaching-evaluation scores. Students generally found the activities engaging, although some reported nervousness. The program was associated with improved educational outcomes, but intervention and class effects could not be separated. Multicenter studies with multiple classes per arm are required.

42919298.title: Much of the excess mortality in immunocompromised patients with viral severe acute respiratory infection occurs after ICU discharge.

42918577.title: Risk Factors for Admission to the Intensive Care Unit and Mortality in Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplant Recipients with Acute Myeloid Leukemia.
42918577.abstract: Adults with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are at risk of requiring intensive care unit (ICU)-level care following allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT). Risk factors for admission to the ICU and outcomes are, however, poorly defined. To assess risk factors associated with ICU admission in such patients, identify variables associated with ICU mortality, and analyze the outcome of ICU survivors in comparison to HCT recipients not admitted to the ICU. Here, we retrospectively analyzed a cohort of 1,265 adults with MDS/AML or AML who received an allograft while in first or second remission between 2006 and 2023. The cumulative incidence of ICU admission was 9.2% on day +100 after HCT. HCT-comorbidity index (hazard ratio [HR]=1.15, P=0.005), treatment-related mortality (TRM) score (HR=1.07, P=0.004), and graft from an HLA-mismatched donor (HR=2.19, P=0.018) were independently associated with ICU admission. Within 100 days of ICU admission, 50 patients (43%) died; poor performance status (odds ratio [OR]=5.45, P=0.005), higher TRM score (OR per one unit increase=1.14, P=0.035), and secondary AML (OR=2.71 P=0.035) were associated with increased day +100 mortality after ICU admission. In a landmark analysis, patients admitted to the ICU during the first 100 days after HCT and alive at day +150 had significantly higher NRM (HR=2.36, P<0.001) after multivariable adjustment. Together, these results highlight that ICU admission is common after allografting in adults with AML and is associated with high mortality. Identification of patients at increased risk may, ultimately, help develop possible preventive strategies and allow testing in particularly vulnerable individuals.

42915004.title: Biomarker tests for invasive Candida infection in critically ill patients in the UK (A-Stop): a multicentre diagnostic test accuracy study.
42915004.abstract: The current practice of empirical antifungal treatment for suspected invasive Candida infection in the intensive care unit (ICU) leads to overtreatment. Biomarkers might better target treatment; however, their diagnostic accuracy in this patient group is uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate whether a biomarker or a combination of biomarkers has sufficiently high negative predictive value (NPV) to enable early cessation of empirical antifungal treatment in patients in ICUs. In this prospective, multicentre, diagnostic test accuracy study, we recruited patients who had been started on empirical antifungal treatment for suspected candidiasis and had blood cultures drawn within 24 h of starting treatment from 43 UK ICUs. We tested a research blood sample, collected within 24 h of the standard-of-care care blood culture (ie, within 48 h of starting empirical antifungal treatment), with three DNA detection tests (Fungiplex, T2Candida, and CandID) and one (1,3)-β-D-glucan test (Fungitell). We assessed the accuracy of these tests against an international consensus definition of proven invasive Candida infection and a constructed reference standard for proven or probable infection. The primary outcome was NPV for exclusion of proven Candida infection; we also reported sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios. Among 4005 patients screened, 1251 were enrolled. A total of 1225 participants, recruited between April, 2018 and Feb, 2023, were evaluable, among whom 54 (4·4%) had proven invasive Candida infection. The median duration of antifungal treatment was 9 days (IQR 5-15), and survival at 28 days was 76·8%. The index tests had similar NPVs: 96·6% (95·3-97·6) for Fungiplex, 97·1% (94·7-98·6) for T2Candida, 96·7% (95·4-97·8) for CandID, and 97·2% (95·5-98·4) for Fungitell; however, sensitivity varied widely among the tests, from 27·5% to 68·6%. The optimal test combination was Fungitell and CandID, which had an NPV of 97·5% (95·7-98·7) and a sensitivity of 75·0%. Combining these biomarkers with standard-of-care blood culture testing further increased the NPV to 98·6% (97·0-99·4), with a sensitivity of 85·1%. No single biomarker had sufficiently high sensitivity to justify stopping empirical antifungal treatment. Combining Fungitell and CandID with standard-of-care blood culture testing could provide a sufficiently high NPV to allow early cessation of empirical antifungal treatment in this patient group, thereby reducing overtreatment, although this gain in sensitivity is accompanied by a reduction in specificity. Randomised trials are needed to confirm the clinical and cost-effectiveness of this diagnostic strategy before it is adopted in practice. UK National Institute for Health and Care Research Health Technology Assessment Programme and the Research Charitable Trust Fund of the Belfast Health & Social Care Trust.

42914716.title: Knowledge and attitudes toward advance directives among ICU nurses.
