42914716.abstract: End-of-life decision-making in Intensive Care Units (ICUs) may be hindered not only by the absence of advance directives (ADs), but also by limited knowledge among ICU nurses. The aim of this study was to analyse knowledge and attitudes regarding advance directives among ICU nurses. An observational, descriptive, cross-sectional and multicentre study was conducted among ICU nurses working in public hospitals in Las Palmas (Spain). An anonymous electronic questionnaire was used. Statistical analysis was performed using R Core Team 2024. A total of 229 responses were obtained from a population of 260 professionals, yielding a response rate of 88.1%. Most participants were women (75.6%) and had a median of 6 years of ICU experience (interquartile range: 3-14). Overall, 87.7% reported not having received specific training on advance directives (ADs). Although attitudes toward ADs were highly favorable (scores above 9/10), the level of knowledge was limited, particularly regarding legal aspects, procedures, documentation, and content. A discrepancy exists between nurses' favorable attitudes toward ADs and their limited practical knowledge. The implementation of targeted training programs, along with the development of institutional protocols, could enhance the integration of ADs into ICU clinical practice.

42911398.title: What's new in trauma critical care?
authors: ESICM Trauma and Emergency Medicine Section

42911397.title: Principles of drug dosing for obese patients in the intensive care unit.
42911397.abstract: The increasing prevalence of severe obesity in intensive care unit (ICU) patients has led to several challenges with medication dosing. Doses listed in product labels or tertiary references typically do not account for the pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic variability encountered with obesity, leading to the potential for treatment failure or an adverse effect. The purpose of this review is to provide guidance for ICU clinicians when crafting pharmacotherapy regimens in critically ill patients with extreme obesity. A literature search was performed to identify relevant articles pertaining to the pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics of medications in obese patients. Articles describing both general treatment principles and medication specific assessments were retrieved. Bibliographies were searched for additional publications. Evidence guiding medication use in critically ill obese patients is limited by the small number of patients with more extreme forms of obesity, the lack of clinical outcome measurements, and the few studies that are specific to the ICU. Obesity-related alterations in pharmacokinetic parameters, such as apparent volume of distribution and drug clearance, may hinder attainment of pharmacodynamic targets. Individualized dosing strategies are essential to optimize therapeutic outcomes. This review provides dosing recommendations for selected ICU medications and proposes a practical framework to guide medication dosing decisions in this patient population. Drug dosing in critically ill obese patients should be individualized by assessing pharmacokinetic variability and whether pharmacodynamic goals can be achieved. Selecting the correct weight for weight-based calculations or dose for fixed regimens is paramount for achieving these goals. Consultation with a clinical pharmacist may be beneficial.

42910767.title: Comment on "Phenobarbital Versus Benzodiazepine-Based Pathways for Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome in Critically Ill Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis".

42910748.title: Response to Comment on "Phenobarbital Versus Benzodiazepine-Based Pathways for Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome in Critically Ill Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis".

42909172.title: Bacterial contamination of mobile phones used by healthcare workers in intensive care units in Sudan: A cross-sectional study.
42909172.abstract: To determine the prevalence and bacterial profile of contamination on mobile phones used by healthcare workers (HCWs) in intensive care units (ICUs) and to evaluate mobile phone disinfection practices in hospitals in Khartoum State, Sudan. A descriptive cross-sectional laboratory-based study was conducted among 44 HCWs from ICUs in four hospitals in Khartoum State, Sudan. Mobile phone swabs were cultured on Blood and MacConkey agar, and bacterial isolates were identified using conventional methods. Factors associated with bacterial contamination were assessed. Bacterial growth was detected in 31 (70.5%) mobile phones. Staphylococcus epidermidis was the predominant isolate (61.3%), followed by Staphylococcus aureus (12.9%), Micrococcus spp. (9.7%), Bacillus cereus (9.7%), and Klebsiella pneumoniae (6.5%). No significant associations were found between bacterial contamination and gender, healthcare worker category, duration of phone use, or phone use inside the ICU (p > 0.05). Regular phone disinfection was significantly associated with lower bacterial contamination (33.3% vs 80.0%, p = 0.012). Mobile phone contamination among HCWs in ICUs was common. Regular phone disinfection significantly reduced bacterial contamination, emphasizing the importance of routine mobile phone decontamination as part of infection prevention and control practices.

42909125.title: Factors associated with probable sarcopenic dysphagia and development of a clinical classification model in older ICU patients: a cross-sectional study.
42909125.abstract: To analyze factors associated with probable sarcopenic dysphagia in older ICU patients, develop a clinical classification model, and provide evidence for early bedside identification and targeted intervention. A cross-sectional study was conducted with 160 older patients admitted to a tertiary ICU from January to December 2025 via convenience sampling. Patients were grouped using the Ishii sarcopenia screening score and the Modified Water Swallowing Test (MWST). Data collected included general patient characteristics, ultrasound measurements of swallowing-related muscles, gastric motility ultrasound parameters, functional status indicators, and nutritional risk screening results. Univariate analysis and binary logistic regression were applied to identify factors associated with the outcome. A classification model was constructed and visualized as a nomogram using R software. The prevalence of probable sarcopenic dysphagia among older ICU patients was 65.62%. Multivariable logistic regression showed that NRS 2002 score ≥ 3, severe genioglossus muscle thinning, presence of comorbidities, abnormal vocalization, and voluntary cough ability score ≤ 2 were independently associated with higher odds of probable sarcopenic dysphagia. The apparent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.837 (95% CI: 0.775-0.900), and the bias-corrected AUC after bootstrap internal validation was 0.812. Probable sarcopenic dysphagia is highly prevalent in older ICU patients and is associated with nutritional status, swallowing muscle morphology, comorbidity burden, vocal function, and airway protective capacity. The classification model demonstrates good discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility, and may serve as a bedside tool for risk stratification. Multicenter external validation is required before clinical implementation.

42908821.title: Specialty-associated differences in intensive care unit rotation exit examination performance: a single-center retrospective cross-sectional study.
42908821.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) rotations bring together residents from multiple specialties. Comparisons of exit performance may be distorted when departments differ in postgraduate-year (PGY) composition and when non-equivalent examination forms are used across PGY levels. We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of ICU exit examination records from 412 residents at a tertiary teaching hospital in China between November 2025 and April 2026. Three 100-item, 60-min examinations containing four question types were administered according to PGY. Departmental differences were evaluated using four complementary strategies: a same-examination subgroup of 227 PGY-2 residents, within-examination standardization, analysis of covariance adjusting for the combined PGY/form grouping, and hierarchical regression. Item characteristics, version-specific reliability, and exploratory differential item functioning were assessed retrospectively. In the same-examination subgroup, the total-score effect size was η 2 = 0.098 (p < 0.001), with surgery having the lowest mean score (75.9; SD 9.1; n = 77; 95% CI 73.9-78.0). Department explained an additional 7.6% of total-score variance after adjustment for PGY/form. The descriptive attenuation ratio was 21.3% for total scores, ranging from 7.3% for case-series items to 80.2% for basic-knowledge items. These ratios do not identify separate training-year or examination-version effects. The largest negative case-analysis gaps occurred in surgery and anesthesiology. Specialty-associated differences in examination performance were observed within this single-center educational setting and using this assessment instrument. The absence of baseline scores and incomplete evidence of cross-form comparability preclude causal or inherent-specialty interpretations; prospective baseline-controlled studies are needed before specialty-tailored interventions are adopted.

42908810.title: VoiceLove for patient-family communication in the ICU: a usability study of a novel voice messaging app.
42908810.abstract: Family engagement has been associated with improved outcomes following critical illness, but communication barriers challenge family engagement. Traditional video or phone call strategies to navigate communication barriers are time-, resource-, and labor-intensive for hospital staff, often limiting their use. VoiceLove is a Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)-compliant mobile phone app that enables family members to send real-time voice messages to intensive care unit (ICU) patients without relying on the clinical team to coordinate calls. We conducted iterative usability testing of VoiceLove to optimize use for patients, families, and their clinical teams in the adult ICU. We completed 2 rounds of usability testing of the VoiceLove app in a simulated environment. Usability was assessed through System Usability Scale (SUS) scores and task success rates. Semi-structured interviews were used to identify themes, concerns, and design priorities. Mean SUS scores for rounds 1 and 2 of testing were 77.5 (SD 11.1) and 75.9 (SD 26.8), respectively. The app concept was overall viewed favorably as a tool with the potential to provide comfort and streamline communication. Key usability issues included navigation, clarity of labels, and accessibility, which were addressed through iterative app improvements. Implementation concerns included nursing workload, family cognitive burden, and interplay with complex family dynamics. A diverse group of ICU stakeholders found the VoiceLove app demonstratedpotential to improve communication with critically ill patients inherently disadvantaged in their ability to communicate. Further testing in a real-world setting is needed to assess the impact of VoiceLove implementation on clinical team work load and family dynamics.

42908208.title: Methodological considerations in prognostic assessment of critically ill patients with cirrhosis.

42907407.title: Current Status and Future Directions of Cardiovascular Intensive Care in Japan: Workforce, Structure, Education, and Regional Disparities - Report of the Japan Critical Care Cardiology Committee (J4CS).
42907407.journal: Circulation journal : official journal of the Japanese Circulation Society
authors: Japanese Circulation Society Emergency and Critical Care Committee
42907407.abstract: Rapid population aging has increased the number of patients with severe acute cardiovascular diseases requiring intensive care. Contemporary cardiovascular intensive care has evolved beyond traditional management of acute coronary syndromes to encompass hemodynamic instability, multiple organ dysfunction, and advanced life-support technologies. Accordingly, cardiovascular intensive care units (CICUs) must provide comprehensive, tailored critical care for increasingly complex clinical conditions. In Japan, cardiovascular intensive care remains heterogeneous, with critically ill patients managed in various critical care settings. Structured care systems and specialist training remain underdeveloped. To clarify the current status, we reviewed nationwide survey data from the JROAD-DPC database. Substantial variability in institutional care systems, limited availability of dedicated cardiac care units/CICUs, and marked regional disparities in infrastructure and human resources were identified. Intensive care unit admission was associated with lower in-hospital mortality in cardiovascular emergencies, although these observational findings should be interpreted with caution because of potential residual confounding, differences in patient characteristics, and end-of-life care pathways. These findings support the need for appropriate triage and resource allocation according to patient acuity and institutional capability, rather than the uniform establishment of dedicated CICUs. Addressing these challenges will require optimized resource allocation, strengthened regional coordination, and structured training programs to establish sustainable cardiovascular intensive care systems in Japan.

42906290.title: Exploring and strengthening day-to-day teamwork in critical care: a qualitative study.
42906290.abstract: To examine how teamwork is enacted, constrained, and strengthened in the day-to-day practice of critical care units, and to identify participant suggested approaches to strengthen teamwork. This qualitative study used interpretive description to explore clinicians' experiences of teamwork in critical care. Thirty-five healthcare professionals from six Canadian provinces participated in semi-structured interviews. Participants represented diverse roles, including nurses, physicians, respiratory therapists, pharmacists, and allied health professionals. Interviews were analyzed using an inductive and interpretive process involving open coding, constant comparison, and iterative theme development. Reflexivity was integrated throughout data collection and analysis to support credibility and interpretive coherence. Teamwork in critical care was described as a multidimensional social process shaped by four interconnected themes: (1) relational practice built through familiarity, trust, and shared experience; (2) leadership, hierarchy, and unit culture, including the ways relational power shaped psychological safety and collaboration; (3) communication and coordination challenges; and (4) structural barriers to integration, learning, and stability. Across these four themes, participants frequently described nurses as central coordinators of relational and informational work, in part because of their continuous presence at the bedside. Participants' experiences suggested that teamwork in critical care is a social process shaped by the dynamic interplay of relational practice, relational power, communication structures, and structural stability. Together, these conditions influenced participants' experiences of how clinicians connect, coordinate, and make decisions in the critical care context. Participants identified relational stability, psychologically safe leadership, communication structures that support shared understanding, and staffing and orientation practices that promote continuity as potential points for strengthening teamwork. These participants suggested approaches warrant organizational consideration and prospective evaluation to determine their effects on teamwork in critical care settings.

42906288.title: Death and dying in the ICU in the age of social media.

42906255.title: Alarm fatigue levels and associated factors among intensive care unit nurses: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
42906255.abstract: To estimate the pooled mean alarm fatigue score among intensive care unit nurses and to synthesise evidence on factors associated with alarm fatigue. Eight Chinese and international databases were systematically searched to identify original observational studies of alarm fatigue among ICU nurses published between January 2017 and February 2026. Two reviewers independently screened the records, appraised the methodological quality of the included studies, and extracted the data. A random-effects meta-analysis was conducted using Stata version 14 to pool mean alarm fatigue scores and their 95% confidence intervals. Sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the robustness of the findings, and potential publication bias was evaluated using Begg's and Egger's tests. Sixteen studies were included in the systematic review, of which 15 provided data suitable for meta-analysis, comprising 4084 intensive care unit nurses. The meta-analysis revealed a pooled mean alarm fatigue score of 25.93 (95% CI, 24.38-27.48). Subgroup analysis indicated that higher levels of alarm fatigue were observed in female nurses (25.89, 95% CI: 22.72-29.06), those aged ≤25 years (26.80, 95% CI: 23.26-30.34), unmarried individuals(24.56, 95% CI: 22.70-26.43), junior-level nurses (27.42, 95% CI: 23.60-31.24), and those with a master's degree (27.15, 95% CI: 24.32-29.99). Elevated alarm fatigue was also observed among nurses without a critical care specialty (24.09, 95% CI: 22.75-25.44), those engaged in rotating night shifts (24.07, 95% CI, 21.98-26.16), nurses without alarm management training (31.52, 95% CI, 25.97-37.07), and those working in general ICUs (26.80, 95% CI, 22.27-31.34). The pooled mean alarm fatigue score among ICU nurses fell within the moderate range. Hospitals and nursing managers should strengthen standardised alarm management procedures and provide alarm management training for all ICU nurses. These measures may help mitigate alarm fatigue, improve the quality of nursing care, and promote patient safety.

42906251.title: Nurse-led continuity-oriented family support across the adult ICU trajectory: a systematic review and meta-analysis of PICS-F-related outcomes.
42906251.abstract: Family members of adult ICU patients are at risk of post-intensive care syndrome-family (PICS-F), but the psychological effects and optimal timing of nurse-led support remain uncertain. To evaluate nurse-led, continuity-oriented family support for PICS-F-related psychological outcomes and explore differences by intervention phase and nurse type. PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, PsycINFO, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to May 2026. Randomized and quasi-experimental studies were eligible if they evaluated nurse-led family support in adult ICUs and assessed at least one family-level PICS-F psychological outcome. Short-term outcomes assessed from 2 weeks to 3 months after ICU discharge formed the primary analyses. Random-effects meta-analyses used Hedges' g standardized mean differences (SMDs). Subgroup analyses were conducted by primary intervention phase and nurse type. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using validated tools and GRADE. Seventeen reports representing 16 independent studies and 3,887 family participants were included. Nurse-led support was not associated with short-term anxiety (SMD = -0.05, 95% CI -0.24 to 0.14; very low certainty), depression (SMD = -0.01, 95% CI -0.23 to 0.21; very low certainty), or post-traumatic stress disorder-related symptoms (SMD = 0.02, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.15; moderate certainty). In-ICU support was associated with lower depression scores (SMD = -0.40, 95% CI -0.67 to -0.12), although phase comparisons included few studies. No ICU transition study contributed an eligible short-term primary outcome. Nurse-type analyses showed no consistent differences. Nurse-led, continuity-oriented family support was not associated with improvements in short-term PICS-F-related psychological outcomes. Current evidence does not identify an optimal intervention phase or nurse type. Intervention timing should be considered, although the optimal phase remains uncertain. Nurse-led support may strengthen family-centred care, but persistent distress may require tailored psychological support and referral.

42904944.title: Cluster Versus Individual Randomization in Prehospital, Emergency and Critical Care Trials: A Meta-Epidemiological Study.
42904944.abstract: Cluster-randomized clinical trials (cRCTs) are pooled with individually randomized clinical trials (iRCTs) in meta-analyses. However, cRCTs are associated with methodological characteristics potentially inducing systematic differences compared with iRCTs. In acute settings, trial inclusion is time-sensitive, exacerbating inclusion-based biases. We conducted a meta-epidemiological study to assess deviations in effect estimates between cRCTs and iRCTs in these settings. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed and Embase. We screened and identified all meta-analyses in prehospital, emergency, or critical care within the last decade that included at least one cRCT and one iRCT. Data were extracted in duplicate from the meta-analyses. If overlapping trials were identified, results were pooled. The primary outcome was mortality; the secondary outcome comprised length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes. Using absolute ln(odds ratio [OR]) for mortality and absolute Hedges' g for the secondary outcome, mean differences (MDs) in effect estimates between cRCTs and iRCTs were analyzed using mixed regression models, presented with 95% CIs. We identified 94 eligible meta-analyses; 44.7% reported on randomization type (cRCT or iRCT). We included 65 meta-analyses in quantitative analyses, encompassing 212 randomized clinical trials (39 cRCTs and 173 iRCTs) and 315,276 patients. No statistically significant difference in absolute ln(OR) for mortality between cRCTs and iRCTs was found (MD, -0.110; 95% CI, -0.093 to 0.313). For length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes, a significant difference in absolute Hedges' g was found (MD, -0.202; 95% CI, -0.392 to -0.012). A systematic difference between cRCTs and iRCTs in length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes, but not mortality, was identified, with cRCTs reporting smaller effect size magnitudes than iRCTs. With under half of identified meta-analyses reporting on randomization modality, these results highlight the need for improved transparency and statistical consideration of randomization type in future meta-analyses in prehospital, emergency, and critical care.

42904749.title: A Bridge to Comfort: Nurses Driving Early Palliative Consults in the Intensive Care Unit.
42904749.journal: Journal of hospice and palliative nursing : JHPN : the official journal of the Hospice and Palliative Nurses Association
42904749.abstract: This project established a protocol that enabled all intensive care unit (ICU) patients to receive a palliative care (PC) screening. Those who met criteria received timely access to PC in the ICU setting. Delayed access to PC can result in untreated symptoms, lack of understanding of care preferences, unwanted invasive procedures, and underutilization of hospice care. A Plan-Do-Study-Act framework was utilized to establish this protocol. The multidisciplinary team sought to increase PC consults in the ICU by 30% using a nurse-driven standardized screening tool. The PC Referral Criteria established by the Center to Advance Palliative Care were used as a framework to establish the workflow/protocol. The outcome measures were the number of patients screened for PC on admission to the ICU, the number of PCs placed in the ICU, the number of code blues, and ICU staff satisfaction. PC consults increased by 163% (471) in 2024 and 143% (435) in 2025 as compared with 2023 (179). In 2023, there were 33 code blues in the ICU, and these decreased by 21% (26) in 2024 and 12% (29) in 2025. ICU staff (87%) felt that the PC screening process had a positive impact on staff and their practice.

42903440.title: Early sitting within 72 hours in the intensive care unit and post-intensive care outcomes: a multicenter cohort study.
42903440.abstract: Early mobilization is recommended in the intensive care unit (ICU), yet clinically meaningful early milestones remain unclear. We investigated whether achievement of sitting within 72 h of ICU admission was associated with post-intensive care outcomes among ICU survivors who underwent rehabilitation. In this multicenter observational cohort study, we included mechanically ventilated adult ICU survivors who underwent rehabilitation. Early sitting was defined as achievement of sitting at the bedside within 72 h after ICU admission. The primary outcome was death or functional decline at 3 months after hospital discharge, assessed using the Kihon Checklist. Prespecified secondary and exploratory outcomes included domain-specific impairments (physical, cognitive, and depressive), hospital readmission, and a composite of readmission or death within 3 months. Overlap propensity score weighting was used to balance baseline covariates. Multiple prespecified sensitivity analyses (48-h alternative definition, landmark analysis, exclusion of never-sitters, adjustment for Day-3 clinical status and rehabilitation dose) and Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) multiplicity adjustment were performed. Among 423 patients, 173 achieved early sitting (≤72 h) and 250 did not. After overlap weighting, baseline characteristics were balanced. Early sitting was not associated with the primary outcome (adjusted risk ratio [aRR] 0.94, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.80-1.09; p = 0.401). In exploratory analyses, early sitting was associated with a lower risk of cognitive domain impairment or death (aRR 0.80, 95% CI 0.67-0.97; p = 0.024; BH-adjusted p = 0.096) and of readmission or death (aRR 0.53, 95% CI 0.32-0.88; p = 0.014; BH-adjusted p = 0.027). No individual KCL item showed a clear association after weighting, and the cognitive association was not observed under a stricter definition. Associations with readmission-related outcomes were attenuated after adjustment for Day-3 clinical status. Achieving sitting within 72 h of ICU admission was not associated with death or functional decline at 3 months. The exploratory associations with cognitive-functional impairment and readmission-related outcomes may reflect the selection of clinically stable patients for early sitting rather than an effect of sitting itself. These findings support the feasibility of early sitting in clinically stable patients but do not establish early sitting as a therapeutic target; randomized trials are needed.

42901379.title: 'Pharmacokinetics, target attainment and outcomes of piperacillin/tazobactam in critically ill patients receiving continuous infusion with therapeutic drug monitoring: a retrospective analysis' - Author's reply.
42901379.journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases

42901372.title: Temporal Trends in Invasive Pulmonary Aspergillosis Among Critically Ill Patients: Serum Galactomannan Testing Intensity and Host Risk Status.
42901372.journal: International journal of infectious diseases : IJID : official publication of the International Society for Infectious Diseases
42901372.abstract: We evaluated temporal trends in invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) incidence in relation to serum galactomannan (GM) testing intensity and compared outcomes by classical host-risk status. Adults with ICU stays ≥72 hours during 2017-2024 were retrospectively screened for proven/probable IPA. Consensus EORTC/MSGERC and FUNDICU definitions defined the primary cohort. Modified criteria were exploratory. Negative binomial and Cox regression assessed incidence and 30-day mortality. Among 11,707 ICU stays, 135 patients met consensus definitions; 55 (40.7%) lacked classical host risk factors, rising to 48.9% under modified criteria. IPA incidence increased over time (IRR/year 1.40; 95% CI 1.06-1.85). After adjustment for serum GM testing intensity, the calendar-year IRR was 0.73 (95% CI 0.54-0.98), whereas testing intensity was strongly associated with measured incidence (IRR 6.15; 95% CI 2.81-13.43). Patients without classical host risk factors received antifungal therapy less often (12.7% vs 67.5%) and had higher crude 30-day mortality (58.2% vs 36.2%). The adjusted host-status association was attenuated (aHR 1.48; 95% CI 0.82-2.66). The temporal rise in measured IPA incidence was associated with serum GM testing intensity, underscoring diagnostic ascertainment. Patients without classical host risk factors were treated less often and had higher mortality, although the adjusted association was attenuated.

42900976.title: Structured communication interventions for families of patients in the intensive care unit: A scoping review.
42900976.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
42900976.abstract: The aim of this study was to map structured communication interventions for families or surrogate decision-makers of adult intensive care unit (ICU) patients, describe their main characteristics and reported outcomes, and organise reported intervention components into a descriptive communication-domain map. A scoping review using descriptive evidence mapping and a combined deductive-inductive synthesis of communication domains. Sources of evidence included PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and reference list screening. Eligibility criteria included primary studies reporting structured communication protocols, frameworks, checklists, bundles, tools, or reproductible interventions implemented by ICU clinical teams to support communication with families or surrogate decision-makers of adult ICU patients. Two reviewers independently extracted study and intervention characteristics, outcomes, measurement approaches, and quantitative findings, and reported limitations using a standardised form. Reported intervention components were charted and organised into descriptive communication domains through a combined deductive-inductive synthesis process; disagreements were resolved by consensus. Nine studies (2010-2022) were included and grouped into structured communication frameworks, educational/training interventions, and multicomponent bundles. Reported communication components were unevenly represented across included sources. Empathy/emotional support, knowledge transmission, summarisation, and value elicitation were among the most frequently described components, whereas ethical considerations, cultural adaptation, time management, nonverbal communication, and supportive aids were less frequently reported in published intervention descriptions. Outcomes were predominantly perceptual and process related. Structured ICU family communication interventions are heterogeneous in design, delivery, and outcome assessment. This review provides an evidence map of intervention types and a descriptive-domain map of reported communication components. These findings may support the development and reporting of more comprehensive, context-sensitive ICU family communication interventions.

42900434.title: Development, implementation and evaluation of a sustainable medication-use process in the intensive care unit: a lean-based quality improvement study.
42900434.abstract: In the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), substantial quantities of medication are wasted, negatively affecting ecological and economic sustainability. This study aimed to develop, implement, and evaluate an ecologically and economically sustainable medication-use process to reduce medication waste in the ICU of a Dutch academic hospital. This lean-based quality improvement study comprised three phases: (I) Three-week baseline medication waste assessment in terms of quantity (i.e., disposed medication units) and economic value per 100 ICU beds per day. (II) Development and implementation of a sustainable medication-use process using lean principles. Causes of medication waste were identified among hospital staff using qualitative methods, and targeted interventions were identified and implemented accordingly. (III) Post-implementation effect evaluation of the sustainable medication-use process on medication waste. At baseline, a mean total of 113 units, worth €1037, were wasted daily per 100 ICU beds. Causes for medication waste were: insufficient knowledge among hospital staff about quantities and impacts of medication waste; suboptimal medication ordering, supplying and preparing, resulting in unnecessary medication waste; and patient's therapy changes/discontinuation. Interventions implemented were: awareness campaigns on medication waste; adjustment of protocols and work processes to prevent excess order, supply and preparation of medication; and dispensing individually labelled medication to the patient following transfer or discharge. Implementing these interventions reduced medication waste by 31.8% to 77 units per 100 ICU beds per day, and economic losses decreased by 18.4% to €846. Implementation of a sustainable medication-use process targeting staff's knowledge and work processes, reduced the extent of wasted medications in the ICU and associated costs.

42899396.title: An Attending-Directed Intervention to Enhance Interprofessional Teaching on ICU Rounds.
42899396.abstract: Interprofessional teaching (IPT) during rounds may enhance teamwork and collaborative patient care, but previous studies have shown low rates of IPT during intensive care unit (ICU) rounds. We designed a study to explore contributions by interprofessional providers (IPPs) during ICU rounds and an attending-targeted intervention to promote IPT. Using a novel observation tool, we collected details regarding contributions made by IPPs during rounds in two ICUs at an academic medical center. A study team member conducted observations for six weeks before and after implementation of an attending-directed intervention. Comparisons were made between pre- and post-intervention data. Before the intervention, six attendings were observed for 59 patient-rounds with 309 contributions recorded, and after, eleven attendings were observed for 94 patient-rounds with 512 contributions recorded. The majority of contributions from IPPs were classified as "reporting" (pre/post: 42.7% vs. 43.6%) and "observing" (pre/post: 29.1% vs. 29.7%). "Teaching" contributions were rare, but increased from 3.9% (12/309) to 4.7% (24/512) of all contributions (p > 0.05). The mean number of contributions per patient did not change after the intervention (5.24 vs. 5.45), and the types of contributions were similar across different attendings. When an IPP spontaneously provided a recommendation (pre: 33, post: 55), the contribution often changed the care plan (pre/post: 97.0% (32/33), 83.6% (46/55)). IPPs predominantly contribute to rounds by reporting data and providing observations. An intervention to improve attending facilitation of IPT did not affect rates of teaching. However, recommendations made by IPPs consistently impacted the patient care plan.

42899389.title: Geo-economic variations in structure and organization of intensive care units: the ISOREA survey.
42899389.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
42899389.abstract: Little is known on critical care services globally. This study aimed to describe ICU resources and organization across countries and assess variability by income group, between countries, and within countries. Participating centers provided structured data on hospital and ICU characteristics via electronic case report form (January 2018 to July 2020). Questionnaire included 237 items covering general characteristics (2 topics) and ICU resources and organization (18 topics). We computed standardized functional domain scores (ISOREA score), classified ICUs using Marshall criteria, and readiness for essential emergency and critical care using a modified Schell score. A total of 1,426 ICUs from five continents were recruited, and 1,225 were analyzed, from high-income countries (HICs, 58%), upper-middle-income (20%), and low/lower-middle-income countries (LLMICs, 22%). Most ICUs were in referral centers (90%) and large urban areas (80%). Most variables (93%) were significantly associated with income group, Most variables (93%) were significantly associated with income group, with 88% showing higher levels in HICs and lower levels in LLMICs. Six domains showed major disparities: extracorporeal support, respiratory support, emergency access to interventional radiology and surgery, neurology and trauma care, patient file and general monitoring, and cardiovascular and hemodynamic monitoring. According to the Marshall classification, 79% of ICUs in HICs were classified as level III, whereas 55% of ICUs in LLMICs were classified as level I. Domains with higher ISOREA scores varied primarily between countries, whereas lower-performing domains exhibited greater variability across ICUs within the same country. Adjustment for income group reduced, but did not eliminate, country-level clustering. Substantial disparities exist in ICU resources and organization across income groups, countries, and ICUs. ICU capacities appeared multidimensional, extending beyond resource limitations.

42899253.title: Family Engagement in the ICU: Not Just Information Sharing and Decision-Making.
42899253.abstract: Patient and family engagement (PFE) in the ICU is proposed to encompass 5 domains: information sharing, respect and dignity, collaboration, activation and participation, and decision-making. However, less is known about how PFE in the ICU is achieved and experienced by clinicians and families. How do clinicians and families experience PFE in the ICU? We conducted a secondary analysis of a qualitative study (conducted 2016-2019) exploring PFE in the ICU that included 35 hours of observation, 15 shadowing experiences, and 22 interviews with ICU clinicians and family members at 2 medical ICUs. Using these data, we performed a framework analysis, a method for applying an existing analytical framework to the data. In this thematic analysis, subcodes were developed and categorized according to the 5 domains of PFE in the ICU. Data and subcodes that did not fit within the existing domains were flagged for further thematic analysis. The research team reviewed the data and subcodes that aligned with and diverged from the PFE in the ICU domains, generating additional themes about processes that enable family engagement. Our data support the 5 domains of PFE in the ICU (information sharing, respect and dignity, collaboration, activation and participation, and decision-making). We found that PFE in the ICU is enabled through relationships between families and clinicians that (1) are built on trust, honesty, and rapport and (2) are dependent on effective communication and repair. Our results show that family and clinician experiences are consistent with the 5 previously conceptualized domains of PFE in the ICU. Family and clinicians in the ICU experience dynamic relationships built through ongoing interactions. PFE in the ICU is not a unidirectional product delivered to patients and families, but instead is a relational experience dependent on trust and effective communication between family members and ICU clinicians.

42898562.title: New Delhi Metallo-β-Lactamase Plasmidomes of Intensive Care Unit Clinical and Environmental Enterobacterales Isolates.
42898562.abstract: There are limited data on the molecular epidemiology of New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM)-producing carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) in Latin America, despite the high burden of NDM-CRE in the region. This study characterized bla NDM-harboring plasmids from CRE from patients and the environment of an Argentine hospital. We performed whole-genome sequencing of 40 environmental isolates (Klebsiella complex, n = 11; Enterobacter cloacae, complex n = 16; Citrobacter freundii, n = 10; Serratia marcescens, n = 3) and 4 clinical isolates (Klebsiella pneumoniae, n = 4) recovered from the environment and rectal surveillance samples of patients in the same intensive care units (ICUs) at a tertiary care center in Argentina, July 2023-February 2024, respectively. Representative genomic groups underwent Oxford Nanopore sequencing and hybrid genome assembly for complete plasmid characterization. Resolved bla NDM-harboring plasmids were compared across species and publicly available reference sequences to characterize plasmid relatedness and dissemination patterns. Ten representative genomic groups were identified across species, including 7 defined sequence types and 3 assigned in this study. bla NDM-1 and bla NDM-5 were present in 72.5% (29/40) and 27.5% (11/40) of environmental isolates, respectively (all 4 clinical isolates were bla NDM-5). Hybrid assembly of the representative genomic groups revealed bla NDM-1 was located on highly conserved plasmids belonging to the IncC incompatibility group across multiple CRE species. bla NDM-5 was restricted to Klebsiella spp. and was associated with structurally diverse plasmids including IncF- and IncHI1B/IncFIB-type backbones in both environmental and patient isolates. These findings highlight the ICU environment as a reservoir for bla NDM plasmids.

42898230.title: Association between early intravenous magnesium sulfate administration and mortality according to systemic immune-inflammation index in critically ill patients with acute heart failure: A retrospective cohort study.
42898230.journal: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice
42898230.abstract: Magnesium sulfate is commonly administered in acute heart failure (AHF). We investigated the association between early intravenous magnesium sulfate and mortality across baseline systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) strata in critically ill patients with AHF. We conducted a retrospective study using the MIMIC-IV database of critically ill patients with AHF. Early intravenous magnesium sulfate was defined as treatment initiated from 6 h before to 24 h after intensive care unit admission. SII was categorized into quartiles. The primary and secondary outcomes were 30-day and 90-day all-cause mortality. Multivariable Cox regression, restricted cubic spline, and sensitivity analyses were performed. Among 4293 patients, 1561 (36.4%) received intravenous magnesium sulfate. Magnesium sulfate administration was associated with lower 30-day (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 0.68, 95% CI 0.56-0.82) and 90-day mortality (aHR 0.74, 95% CI 0.63-0.86). For 30-day mortality, multivariable Cox regression demonstrated significant associations in the lowest (aHR 0.64, 95% CI 0.43-0.95) and highest (aHR 0.52, 95% CI 0.36-0.75) SII quartiles, whereas no significant associations were identified in the intermediate quartiles. Comparable patterns were observed for 90-day mortality. Restricted cubic spline analyses showed visual separation between treatment groups at the extremes of the SII distribution, although formal interaction testing was not significant. Sensitivity analyses consistently reproduced the association in the highest SII quartile. Stratified analyses suggested that the association between early magnesium sulfate administration and lower mortality was most evident in the highest SII quartile and less consistent in the lowest quartile. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation. Not applicable.

42897821.title: Navigating the translational chasm: a scoping review of large language models and hybrid architectures in intensive care.
42897821.abstract: Foundation models, particularly large language models, can process the unstructured data central to the intensive care record, yet their clinical readiness remains poorly defined. This study aimed to map foundation-model and large language model applications in adult intensive care, characterise their architectural paradigms, and chart their validation and deployment features. Empirical studies applying a large language model or other foundation model to adult intensive care tasks were eligible for inclusion. Traditional machine-learning-only, non-intensive care, and paediatric studies were excluded. PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched (January 2022-February 2026). A supplementary preprint and conference search through mid-2026 was analysed separately. Data were extracted in duplicate using an operationalised taxonomy (generative large language models, clinical language models, retrieval-augmented generation, and hybrid pipelines). Evidence-maturity mapping was performed without formal risk-of-bias appraisal. Sixty-four studies addressed decision support (51.6%), clinical NLP (23.4%), predictive analytics (20.3%), and ICU operations (4.7%). Standalone configurations predominated (79.7%); retrieval-augmented generation (6.3%) and hybrid (14.1%) architectures concentrated in higher-stakes tasks. Maturity was limited: 46.9% relied solely on retrospective MIMIC data, 6.3% reported external validation, 90.6% remained internally retrospective, and only 3.1% achieved prospective evaluation. Hybrid and retrieval-augmented architectures appear better aligned with high-risk ICU tasks, though no comparative synthesis was performed. Prospective validation and a risk-stratified 'clinical co-pilot' framework are needed.

42897760.title: Emotional experiences of workplace violence in the intensive care unit.
42897760.abstract: BackgroundWorkplace violence is common in intensive care units and is often regarded as an inevitable aspect of the job. This normalisation may obscure the emotional impact of violence on healthcare professionals and the ethical tensions that arise when altruistic caregiving values conflict with personal safety. Therefore, this study was conducted to explore healthcare professionals' emotional experiences of workplace violence within the context of intensive care.Research designThis study constitutes a secondary, inductive analysis of data originally collected in 37 semi-structured interviews. The interviews were conducted between November 2024 and March 2025 in intensive care units across five hospitals in Sweden. Data were interpreted using Reflexive thematic analysis.Ethical considerationsEthical aspects were carefully considered throughout the study in line with established ethical principles. Participation was voluntary, and informed consent was obtained from all individuals before the interview. Data confidentiality was ensured, and all direct quotes were anonymised.FindingsParticipants' descriptions of their emotional experiences generated three themes. A conflict between professional obligation and human vulnerability captured how participants experienced a tension between the expectation to remain composed in their professional roles and their human vulnerability. Balancing core values of caregiving with safety illustrated the professional and moral dilemmas that emerged when violence or escalating aggression forced healthcare professionals to reconcile their commitment to compassionate care. Organisational conditions influencing emotional responses reflected the conditions that either support or undermine ICU healthcare professionals' emotional resilience when they encounter violence.ConclusionsWorkplace violence in intensive care was experienced as more than a threat to personal safety; participants described how it challenged their professional identity and caring values. Organisational conditions influenced how healthcare professionals experienced and managed these challenges.

42896810.title: A Carbapenem-Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii Outbreak in an Intensive Care Unit: Detection Before Recognition and Persistence After Containment.
42896810.abstract: We analyzed a carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) outbreak in an intensive care unit (ICU) to improve insight into how this pathogen spreads within health care facilities and to inform the development of targeted control procedures. A CRAB outbreak in a tertiary referral center was investigated over a 5-month window with clinical data, molecular typing (AP-PCR, PFGE), and one month of environmental sampling. All ICU patients (n=31) were compared-epidemic-clone-positive (n=7) versus -negative (n=24)-using Mann-Whitney/Fisher tests and Firth penalized logistic regression. Although the outbreak spanned 6 days clinically, index patients had been colonized up to 41 days earlier. CRAB was recovered from high-touch surfaces; 6/7 patients developed pneumonia/VAP and 6/7 died (4 CRAB-attributable). Prior A. baumannii isolation (57% vs 0%) was the only independent risk factor (Firth odds ratio 34.7; P=.004). Despite treatment, infected patients redeveloped epidemic-clone infection up to 3.5 months later. In CRAB outbreaks, spread may begin weeks before clinical recognition, and-even months after the outbreak is contained-the epidemic clone can cause reinfection in previously treated patients; only high-resolution analyses spanning an extended period can document this. Multidisciplinary and administrative collaboration, extended and effective environmental disinfection, and effective isolation of positive patients are important for containing CRAB outbreaks.

42895539.title: Promoting equity, diversity and inclusion in intensive Care: a position paper of the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine.

42895528.title: Job-related stress, workplace incivility and quality of nursing care among Jordanian critical care nurses.
42895528.abstract: BackgroundQuality of nursing care is one of the most important patient outcomes. The goal of Health care professionals is to provide patients and clients with safe assessment and treatment.ObjectiveThis study was conducted to explore the relationship between Job-related Stress, Workplace Incivility and Quality of Nursing Care among Jordanian Critical Care Nurses.MethodsA cross-sectional design was used. One hundred and eighty-five nurses from different hospitals participated in the study and completed the study's questionnaires including Nurses' Occupational Stress Scale (NOSS), Nursing workplace incivility (NIS) and Quality of nursing care (QONC).ResultsThe results showed that patients'/visitors' incivility (M = 41.11, SD = 7.03) was the major type of incivility in workplace among critical nurses. Critical care nurses reported high levels of job-related stress (M = 64.17, SD = 6.74). The results showed that insufficient support from coworkers was the highest among many of the participants (M = 9.45, SD = 1.51). The results from the current study show that nurses' responsibility for decision-making and delegation was highest among the participants (M = 20.11, SD = 3.27) in contrast to nursing care organization being the lowest (M = 7.14, SD = 1.13). A positive relationship between job-related stress and quality of nursing care (r = 0.551, p = 0.001, respectively) and a negative relationship between workplace incivility and quality of nursing care (r = -0.625, p = .002) were found.Conclusionsthese results might help administrators develop strategies and educational programs to improve the quality of nursing care in hospitals.

42895439.title: Infections Acquired in the ICU Among Cancer and Other Immunosuppressed Patients: A Nationwide Cohort Study.
42895439.abstract: To compare the cumulative incidence of ICU-acquired infections (ICU-AIs) across distinct immunosuppression diagnostic categories (solid cancer, hematological cancer, other immunosuppression) and nonimmunosuppressed patients, accounting for competing risks of death and discharge. Retrospective cohort study using prospectively collected data. A total of 50 participating ICUs in Brazil. A total of 38,126 adult patients admitted between October 2019 and December 2021 with an ICU stay exceeding 48 hours and no infections diagnosed within the first 48 hours. None. The primary outcome was the incidence of the first ICU-AI during the ICU stay, evaluated using Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard ratios (sHR). In the multivariable competing-risk analysis, patients with hematological malignancies (sHR, 1.64; 95% CI, 1.01-2.65) and other immunosuppressive conditions (sHR, 1.61; 95% CI, 1.02-2.54) were associated with an increased cumulative incidence of ICU-AI, while solid malignancy was not significantly different from non-immunosuppressed patients (sHR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.68-1.14). Patients with hematological malignancies and other immunosuppressive conditions face a significantly higher risk of ICU-AIs.

42895438.title: Critical Care Diaries: A Promising Intervention to Mitigate the Consequences of Secondary Trauma From a PICU Stay?
42895438.journal: Pediatric critical care medicine : a journal of the Society of Critical Care Medicine and the World Federation of Pediatric Intensive and Critical Care Societies

42894761.title: The effect of time-varying left ventricular ejection fraction on clinical outcome in critically ill COVID-19 patients.
42894761.abstract: Although right ventricular (RV) dysfunction and acute cor pulmonale are associated with adverse outcomes in critically ill patients with COVID-19, the prognostic significance of left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction remains insufficiently characterized. In particular, dynamic changes in cardiac function during intensive care has seldom been studied. We therefore investigated the association between time-varying LV systolic function, assessed by LV ejection fraction (LVEF) and intensive care unit (ICU) mortality in patients with COVID-19, taking into account right ventricular function and forward flow. This retrospective observational cohort study combined three ICU data repositories comprising 808 patients with 1614 echocardiographic examinations. Time-varying LV systolic function (LVEF ≤ 50%, 51-70%, >70%) was the primary exposure, and ICU mortality was the outcome. Multivariable Cox models with time-varying covariates, including, acute cor pulmonale, left ventricular outflow tract velocity time integral and key clinical characteristics were used to assess associations between LV systolic function phenotypes and outcome. At baseline, 27% of patients had abnormal LV systolic function (LVEF ≤ 50%) and 17% had hyperdynamic LV function (LVEF > 70%). The proportion of patients with normal LV systolic function increased over time. Abnormal LV systolic function was most prevalent at the first echocardiographic examination (27%) and least prevalent at the fifth examination (17%), whereas hyperdynamic LV function became more frequent during ICU stay, peaking at the 4th echocardiographic examination. Abnormal (aHR; 1.174, 95% CI: 0.901-1.531) or hyperdynamic (aHR: 1.041, 95% CI: 0.785-1.379) LV systolic dysfunction was not independently associated with ICU mortality. In critically ill patients with COVID-19, LV systolic dysfunction, including both abnormal and hyperdynamic LV phenotypes, were common and dynamic during ICU stay. LV systolic dysfunction was not independently associated with ICU mortality when modelled longitudinally and adjusted for RV dysfunction, forward flow and other clinical covariates. These findings suggest that the prognostic value LVEF phenotypes in severe COVID-19 may be limited. Further studies incorporating more sensitive measures of LV function and biomarkers of myocardial injury may be required to delineate subtle changes not captured by LVEF.

42892752.title: Early dietitian-led nutrition intervention and unplanned intensive care unit transfer in hospitalized adults with nutritional risk: A retrospective cohort study.
42892752.journal: JPEN. Journal of parenteral and enteral nutrition
42892752.abstract: Malnutrition and nutritional risk are common among inpatients and are associated with adverse outcomes. Although dietitian-led individualized nutrition intervention is recommended, evidence from routine practice among non-critically ill inpatients remains limited. We aimed to evaluate the association between early dietitian-led nutrition intervention and deterioration-related outcomes among adults at nutritional risk. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using electronic medical records from a Chinese tertiary hospital (2016-2023). Adults aged 18-90 years with Nutritional Risk Screening 2002 scores ≥3 were included; patients directly admitted to intensive care unit were excluded. Patients receiving early dietitian-led nutrition intervention within 72 h after hospital admission were propensity score matched 1:1 to comparators. Outcomes were unplanned intensive care unit transfer, major gastrointestinal events after admission, and predefined clinically meaningful changes in laboratory indicators. Associations were estimated using logistic regression and reported as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Among 96,532 eligible patients, 16,661 (17.3%) received early dietitian-led nutrition intervention. After matching, 16,419 pairs were analyzed. Early dietitian-led nutrition intervention was associated with lower odds of intensive care unit transfer (3.0% vs. 3.4%; OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77-0.99), major gastrointestinal events (4.0% vs. 4.4%; OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.80-0.99), and higher odds of clinically meaningful reduction in C-reactive protein (12.6% vs. 10.9%; OR 1.18, 95% CI 1.11-1.27). Early dietitian-led nutrition intervention was associated with lower odds of deterioration-related outcomes among hospitalized adults at nutritional risk. Limited early dietitian involvement despite routine nutritional risk screening suggests an implementation gap and warrants further prospective evaluation.

42892108.title: Mobility in ICU survivors: A concept analysis.
42892108.abstract: Mobility limitations are common and clinically important among ICU survivors, yet the concept of mobility remains inconsistently defined and is often conflated with physical capacity, functional status, and activities of daily living. This study aimed to clarify the concept of mobility in ICU survivors using Walker and Avant's concept analysis methodology. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, CINAHL, and Web of Science from database inception to August 15, 2026. Walker and Avant's eight-step framework guided the identification and synthesis of uses, related concepts, defining attributes, antecedents, consequences, and empirical referents. Thirty-eight studies were included. One defining attribute of mobility was identified: purposeful transition in body position or spatial location. Antecedents comprised predisposing factors, critical illness-related factors, physical prerequisites and limiting conditions, and contextual and modifying factors. Consequences spanned functional and daily-life, psychosocial and participation, and care and service domains. Mobility-focused task measures were the most conceptually aligned empirical referents, whereas measures of muscle strength, exercise capacity, activities of daily living, disability, participation, and quality of life assessed related but distinct constructs. Mobility in ICU survivors is defined as patient-generated or patient-controlled movement that produces a purposeful transition in body position or spatial location following critical illness. Such transitions may be performed independently or with assistance. This definition distinguishes mobility from enabling physical capacities, passive repositioning, contextual influences, and broader functional and social outcomes. This concept analysis may help nurses and rehabilitation professionals distinguish mobility from physical capacity and broader functional outcomes, supporting more consistent mobility assessment, individualized rehabilitation planning, and the development of nursing-sensitive mobility outcomes.

42891265.title: The 23(rd) AMN Congress | Integrated Pathway Management in Neurotrauma: From ER and ICU to Rehabilitation and Mental Health.

42890873.title: Are Gallbladder Abnormalities in Critically Ill Patients Clinically Relevant? Insights from the Medical Intensive Care Unit of a Medical Center.
42890873.abstract: Gallbladder (GB) abnormalities are frequently observed in critically ill patients, but their clinical relevance remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the prevalence of GB abnormalities and their association with clinical outcomes in patients admitted to a medical intensive care unit (ICU). We conducted a retrospective study of adult patients admitted to the medical ICU of Changhua Christian Hospital from February to September 2023 who underwent abdominal ultrasound. Patients with prior cholecystectomy or diagnosed acute cholecystitis were excluded. Clinical variables, ultrasound findings, and 30-day outcomes were analyzed. A total of 59 patients were included (mean age 68.9 ± 14.7 years; 69.5% male). GB abnormalities were identified in 33 patients (55.9%), with wall thickening (35.6%) and pericholecystic fluid (30.5%) being most common. GB abnormalities were significantly associated with lower serum albumin (2.8 ± 0.5 vs. 3.3 ± 0.8 g/dL, P = 0.018) and prolonged nil per os status (P = 0.002), but not with age, sex, acute physiology and chronic health evaluation II score, or 30-day mortality (P = 0.980). Sludge was more frequent in patients with ICU stays ≥48 h (30.0% vs. 5.1%, P = 0.008). GB abnormalities are common among medical ICU patients and are associated with hypoalbuminemia and prolonged fasting, but not with increased short-term mortality. These findings may help guide clinical management and avoid unnecessary interventions.

42889455.title: CT-derived radiological markers for predicting severity and ICU admission in acute pulmonary embolism.
42889455.abstract: Acute pulmonary embolism (APE) is a potentially life-threatening condition requiring rapid risk stratification. Although computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiography is the diagnostic gold standard, the prognostic value of CT-derived radiological markers remains incompletely defined. This retrospective study included 91 patients with APE. CT-derived radiological parameters - including the Qanadli obstruction index (QI), Mastora score, right ventricle/left ventricle (RV/LV) ratio, and RV wall thickness - were evaluated together with clinical severity scores (Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index [PESI], and its simplified version [sPESI]) and laboratory markers. Associations with disease severity and intensive care unit (ICU) admission were assessed using correlation and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses. Among the patients, 52.7% were female and 27.5% required ICU admission. PESI, sPESI, QI, Mastora score, and RV/LV ratio were significantly higher in ICU-admitted patients (all p < 0.01). QI correlated significantly with PESI (r = 0.433), disease severity (r = 0.565), D-dimer (r = 0.510), and troponin levels (r = 0.536) (all p < 0.001). The Mastora score showed similar significant associations with clinical severity indices, RV/LV ratio, and laboratory markers. ROC analysis demonstrated that PESI had the highest predictive accuracy for ICU admission (area under the curve, AUC = 0.849), followed by RV/LV ratio (AUC = 0.838), sPESI (AUC = 0.791), and both QI and Mastora score (AUC = 0.782). Platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, systemic immune-inflammation index, and RV wall thickness were not significant predictors. CT-derived obstruction indices and RV/LV ratio provide clinically meaningful prognostic information for ICU requirement in APE, particularly when integrated with established clinical severity scores.

42887689.title: Assessing the ecotoxicological impact of drugs used in anesthesia and intensive care: do we have enough data and tools?

42887225.title: Cognitive types of research learning barriers among ICU clinical nurse specialist trainees: A Q methodology study.
42887225.abstract: This study used Q methodology to identify cognitive types of research learning barriers among intensive care unit (ICU) clinical nurse specialist (CNS) trainees and to uncover the attributional structure underlying these perceptions, thereby informing type-specific training. The research capacity of clinical nurse specialists is a core marker of their professional development. Existing studies have mainly used conventional questionnaires to assess the severity of barriers, without revealing how different trainees perceive the same barriers, which limits the ability to target training interventions. A Q methodology study. A 40-statement Q sample was developed and 84 trainees completed valid Q sorts on a nine-point forced distribution from -4 to + 4. Factors were extracted by principal component analysis with varimax rotation and post-sort interviews were conducted to aid interpretation. Four cognitive types were identified: Skill-Anxious (42.9%), Double-Jeopardy (19.0%), Growth-Oriented (17.9%) and Time-Constrained (8.3%). A "same score, different meaning" pattern emerged, with the same barrier attributed in systematically different ways across types. Among trainees with research experience, 52.9% belonged to the Growth-Oriented type. The factor solution was robust despite the P-set exceeding the Q-set (composite reliabilities 0.97-0.99; 88.1% clean single-factor assignment). The perceptions of research barriers among ICU CNS trainees fall into four distinct cognitive types. Training should shift from standardised delivery to type-specific targeted intervention, with particular emphasis on institutional research support for Double-Jeopardy trainees after they return to their clinical posts. The single-site, single-cohort sample limits the generalisability of these findings.

42887176.title: Patient and family engagement in patient safety in resource-limited intensive care units: A qualitative exploratory study.
42887176.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
42887176.abstract: Patient and family engagement (PFE) in the intensive care unit (ICU) enhances patient safety through detection and reporting of safety incidents that may be missed by healthcare professionals, providing an important and additional safeguard against harm. However, empirical evidence to inform policy and practice in resource-limited critical care settings remains scarce. The aim of this study was to explore the perspectives and experiences of patients, families, and healthcare professionals on PFE in patient safety in Ethiopian ICUs. A pragmatic, exploratory qualitative descriptive study was conducted using in-depth interviews guided by a semistructured interview protocol. Participants were purposively selected and included patients, families, and healthcare professionals. Participants were recruited from four ICUs, including both adult and paediatric/neonatal ICUs in a major university hospital in Eastern Ethiopia. Reflexive thematic analysis with inductive orientation guided by Braun and Clarke's six-phase approach was employed. Convergence and divergence of perspectives across participant groups were identified and reported. Criteria for rigour and trustworthiness including credibility, dependability, transferability, confirmability, and integrity guided the research process. The consolidated criteria for reporting qualitative research were followed to ensure the transparency and consistency of reporting. Fifty-nine in-depth interviews were conducted, including patients (5; 9%), families (15; 25%), and healthcare professionals (39; 66%). Three overarching themes were identified: First, contested safety roles reflected the competing views on engagement, which were endorsed rhetorically but constrained in practice due to structural and hierarchical power dynamics. Second, sociocultural logics of engagement underscored inequities between rural and urban patients/families shaped by sociocultural attributes and faith-based sense-making. Third, tensions inpatient safetyincident disclosure highlighted the discordance between the expectation of transparency and hesitancy to involve patients and families in incident disclosure due to fear of reprisals. PFE in patient safety in Ethiopian ICUs was endorsed in principle yet remained constrained by sociocultural contexts, hierarchical power dynamics, and limited institutional support mechanisms. Clearly defining patient safety roles, implementing family-activated escalation pathways, and strengthening formal patient safety incident reporting and disclosure systems are essential to promote inclusive, equitable, and sustainable PFE in patient safety across Ethiopian ICUs and beyond.

42887164.title: Beyond information delivery: Candidate competencies for ICU nurses navigating prognostic uncertainty with patients and families.
42887164.abstract: Prognostic uncertainty is intrinsic to critical illness, yet communication education often treats the clinician's task as accurate information transfer. This Discussion Paper presents and critically examines author-derived candidate competencies for intensive care unit (ICU) nurses supporting adult patients and families when prognosis remains uncertain. A four-step, author-led narrative synthesis integrated uncertainty theory, adult patient and family evidence, ICU communication literature, and nursing role constraints. Recurrent nursing functions were compared, grouped, and cross-checked against reported needs, harms, and role boundaries. The resulting domains are: align roles and messages; map patient participation, uncertainty, and preferences; name what is known, unknown, and next; respond to emotion and verify understanding; and revisit uncertainty across time and transitions. Their enactment depends on trust, interdisciplinary coherence, staffing, continuity, interpreter access, family-centred policies, and a suitable communication environment. The process was interpretive rather than systematic and did not include independent coding or patient and family partners. The domains are a transparent conceptual proposal for education and debate, not a disclosure protocol or validated standard. Patient and family co-design, content validation, context-sensitive behavioral assessment, and testing of learner, relational, and system outcomes are required before implementation.

42885993.title: A Quality Improvement Initiative to Achieve Provincial Implementation of a Web-Based Family Satisfaction in ICU (FS-ICU) Survey to Inform Patient-Centered Care.
42885993.abstract: To review the web-based Family Satisfaction in ICU (FS-ICU) survey across all adult level 3 Ontario ICUs to capture patient and family experiences with critical care, and to evaluate feasibility, participation, and satisfaction scores. A province-wide, multisite quality improvement study using an electronic, key-based FS-ICU survey with prospectively collected anonymous data linked to encounters through a centralized database. All 83 adult level 3 ICUs (52 community, 31 academic) in ON, Canada, from July 1, 2019, to May 31, 2024. The population comprised adult ICU patients, family members, or substitute decision-makers, with one survey per ICU encounter regardless of length of stay or number of family members. ICUs implemented a web-based FS-ICU using a unique seven-digit key in three formats (Staff-Provided, Quick Response-Driven, Website-Code), supported by training, resources, and tablets, with no clinical care interventions beyond routine practice. Feasibility metrics included onboarding (keys generated per ICU admission), opening, participation, and completion rates, calculated for different centers using provincial data. Over the study period, 24,679 unique keys were generated for 353,400 ICU admissions (onboarding rate, 7.0%), 13,596 keys were opened (opening rate, 55.1%), and 7,542 surveys met the greater than or equal to 70% completion threshold (completion rate, 57.6% among opened surveys; reflection rate, 2.1% of ICU encounters). Survey initiation was highest with the Staff-Provided format (88.4% of keys initiated), and overall satisfaction was high, with mean FS with Care, 87.8; FS with Decision-Making, 84.4; and FS-TOTAL 86.5 on a 0-100 scale, with nursing care rated highest and adequacy of time for questions rated lowest. A provincial, web-based FS-ICU was implemented across all adult level 3 Ontario ICUs, producing a large dataset with high satisfaction scores. A small proportion completed the survey, highlighting feasibility and workflow barriers. Future efforts should improve activation and completion rates and integrate FS-ICU data into routine quality improvement to enhance patient- and family-centered care.

42885980.title: ICU Physical Environments Used for Family Conferences: A Multimodal Qualitative Evaluation with ICU Team Members.
42885980.abstract: Family-clinician communication is central to high-quality care for critically ill patients. Although previous work has focused on improving how and what is communicated, little is known about where this high-stakes communication takes place and how it is shaped by the physical environment. Our objectives were to characterize ICU spaces typically used for family conferences and identify modifiable environmental features that influence communication. We conducted a multimodal qualitative study of 17 spaces typically used for family conferences across four adult ICUs in a U.S. academic medical center. Healthcare design and architecture experts independently assessed architectural plans and photographs to characterize spatial features. Then, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 23 ICU team members (nurses, social workers, case managers) to elicit perspectives on and experiences within these spaces. We conducted qualitative content analysis using a combined inductive and deductive approach. A total of 17 family conference spaces across four adult ICUs in a U.S. academic medical center. A total of 23 ICU team members. None. The 17 analyzed spaces included designated family-communication rooms (n = 2), multipurpose rooms (n = 6), visitor lounges (n = 4), and public areas (n = 5; lobbies/hallways). Study participants preferred designated spaces, as they provide privacy, prevent interruption, and facilitate emotional support. Conversely, multipurpose and public areas are prone to distractions and interruptions from conflicting uses. We identified key environmental features that support communication: proximity to patients, flexible furniture layout, and nonclinical ambiance. Family conferences occur in a variety of physical environments in and around adult ICUs, ranging from intentionally designed rooms to elevator lobbies. ICU team members perceive that physical environments have an important influence on communication quality, and we identified pragmatic opportunities to improve existing spaces.

42882903.title: Intensive Care in Patients with Solid Tumours: A Practical Framework for Integrated Onco-Critical Care.
42882903.abstract: The number of patients with solid tumours requiring intensive care is increasing as cancer survival improves and oncological treatments become more complex. Intensive care unit (ICU) admission decisions should not be based on cancer diagnosis, metastatic status or palliative treatment intent alone. This narrative review presents a practical, multidisciplinary framework for assessing critically ill patients with solid tumours. It integrates acute illness severity and reversibility, organ failure, baseline performance status and frailty, cancer trajectory, remaining treatment options, expected functional recovery and patient preferences. We discuss contemporary anticancer treatment toxicities, cancer-associated thromboembolic disease, older adults, palliative care, communication and ethical decision-making. We also propose an algorithm ranging from full ICU support to a time-limited ICU trial with predefined reassessment or comfort-focused care. Early joint assessment by oncology and intensive care teams, followed by dynamic reassessment, may reduce both inappropriate escalation and premature exclusion from potentially beneficial organ support. Future research should prioritize structured pathways, improved prognostic tools and outcomes beyond survival, including functional recovery, quality of life and the ability to resume meaningful cancer treatment.

42882308.title: On-Device ECG and Vital-Sign Prediction of 24-Hour Mortality and Unplanned ICU Admission in Emergency Department Patients: A Retrospective Evaluation of MEDI-AI.
42882308.abstract: Background/Objectives: Smartphone-based analysis of electrocardiograms (ECGs) and vital signs may support risk assessment without an integrated electronic health record feed. We evaluated MEDI-AI for 24 h mortality and unplanned intensive care unit (ICU) admission, with secondary diagnostic and triage assessments. Methods: This single-center retrospective evaluation included 2000 encounters from 2025 after supplementary development on 3000 encounters from 2024, with patient-level separation. Stored probabilities were assessed for area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUROC), calibration, and threshold performance. Post hoc exploratory NEWS2 and paired comparisons were performed; accepted inputs were also analyzed separately. Results: There were 189 deaths and 378 ICU admissions. Fusion AUROCs were 0.9994 and 0.9982; NEWS2 AUROCs were 0.8801 and 0.8131. Fusion-minus-vital-only AUROC differences were -0.000039 (95% CI, -0.000450 to 0.000366) and 0.002114 (0.000632 to 0.003920). Fusion calibration slopes were 5.62 and 6.09. STEMI and ACS sensitivities were 90.9% (58.7-99.8%) and 92.3% (74.9-99.1%). Triage critical-class recall was 24.9%. Input rejection occurred in 48 encounters; median recorded latency was 1235 ms. These stored-score estimates do not measure end-to-end deployable performance. Conclusions: Near-ceiling stored-score discrimination did not establish reliable absolute risks or a clinically usable workflow. Incomplete predictor-timing and model-development records limit reproducibility and assessment of bias. The evaluated triage configuration is unsuitable for clinical deployment, and the diagnostic analyses do not validate rule-out use. Independent external and prospective validation are required.

42882214.title: Serial TAPSE and Subsequent 60-Day Mortality Among Critically Ill Adults with Reduced Baseline TAPSE: A MIMIC-IV-ECHO Cohort Study.
42882214.abstract: Background/Objectives: Tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) is routinely available in critical-care echocardiography, but the prognostic relevance of serial change is uncertain. We examined serial TAPSE and subsequent mortality among critically ill adults with reduced baseline TAPSE. Methods: This retrospective MIMIC-IV-ECHO cohort included adults with at least two TAPSE measurements and baseline TAPSE < 1.7 cm. Serial TAPSE status was classified as improved (increase >0.2 cm) or non-improved (change ≤0.2 cm). Cox regression evaluated 60-day mortality from the follow-up echocardiogram. Results: Among 227 patients, 101 (44.5%) were improved and 126 (55.5%) non-improved over a median interval of 10 days. Non-improved status was associated with higher subsequent mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 1.72, 95% confidence interval 1.06-2.80; p = 0.028).
