After adjustment for follow-up TAPSE, neither binary status nor continuous change was significantly associated with mortality. Conclusions: In this exploratory study, non-improved serial TAPSE was associated with higher 60-day mortality. Added prognostic value beyond follow-up TAPSE was not demonstrated.

42881801.title: Narrative Review of the Bacterial Profile Involved in Severe COPD Exacerbations Complicated by Pneumonia in Patients Admitted to the Intensive Care Unit.
42881801.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a chronic progressive respiratory disease characterized by respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation and is one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide. The evolution of the disease is associated with episodes of acute exacerbations (AECOPD), characterized by worsening symptoms and accelerated deterioration of lung function. Acute exacerbations of COPD have different severity, being mild, moderate or severe depending on how aggravated the patients' symptoms are, but they also depend on pulmonary functional and biological changes. Around 70% of AECOPD cases are infectious in nature, through upper or lower respiratory tract infections. Often, exacerbations associated with lower respiratory tract infections are more severe and have a higher risk of unfavorable outcome compared to AECOPD associated with upper respiratory tract infections. Severe exacerbations require hospital management, with most of them being treated in the intensive care unit (ICU). In this narrative review, we evaluated the frequency of different bacterial pathogens involved in severe COPD exacerbations associated with lower respiratory tract infections and the need for treatment in the ICU. Identifying patients with exacerbated COPD at high risk of respiratory infections, especially with Gram-negative bacilli, is extremely important to choose the optimal treatment, thus reducing the risk of death.

42881745.title: Digital-Use/Efficiency Phenotypes Versus Professional Role in Explaining Perceived Digital Benefit in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care.
42881745.abstract: Background and Objectives: We compared professional role with digital-use/efficiency phenotype as explanations of perceived digital benefit in anaesthesia and intensive care. Materials and Methods: Cross-sectional survey data from 161 professionals were analysed. Latent class analysis used 12 indicators of technology/educational-resource use and perceived operational efficiency; four benefit items remained external outcomes. Although BIC favoured two classes, a three-class exploratory solution was retained using aBIC, entropy, bootstrap testing, class size and interpretability. Nested logistic models with seniority retained in every model, likelihood-ratio tests and Shapley partitioning of McFadden's pseudo-R2 compared role and phenotype; pre-planned sensitivity analyses re-estimated the comparison under two- and four-class solutions, with classification-error (BCH) correction and with use-only indicators, and discrimination was internally validated by bootstrap. Descriptive decomposition and Rasch/DIF analyses were exploratory. Results: The three phenotypes (n = 83, 44 and 34; entropy of 0.815) crossed professional boundaries (Cramér's V = 0.439). Phenotype did not improve seniority-and-role models for broad benefit (likelihood ratio 2.4, p = 0.301) or high uncertainty (2.8, p = 0.248), whereas adding role to seniority-and-phenotype models improved fit (23.6 and 26.2; both p < 0.001); this pattern was unchanged across all sensitivity specifications. Role received 68.3% and 62.3% of the Shapley-partitioned pseudo-R2, versus 11.9% and 11.4% for phenotype. Exploratory decompositions provided little evidence of an indirect association through adoption breadth or phenotype. Rasch analysis suggested patient safety was easiest and managerial benefit hardest to endorse; person separation reliability was 0.07, and DIF contrasts were descriptive. Conclusions: In this sample, professional role carried more explanatory information about perceived benefit than the exploratory phenotype, and this ranking was robust to class enumeration and classification-error correction. The phenotype findings remain exploratory, and cross-sectional associations do not establish causation.

42881740.title: Intensive Care Unit Nurses' Views on Recognizing and Caring for Inpatients' Anxiety Levels: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.
42881740.abstract: Background/Objectives: Anxiety in intensive care patients is a significant concern, yet limited evidence exists regarding nurses' perspectives on its assessment and management. This study aimed to explore intensive care nurses' views and experiences regarding the recognition, assessment, and management of anxiety among hospitalized intensive care patients. Methods: A qualitative descriptive design was employed, and the study sample consisted of 21 nurses selected from 50 nurses working in the intensive care unit of the hospital. The data were collected through in-depth interviews conducted in person between July and September 2021. The data were analyzed manually using an inductive thematic analysis approach. Results: A thorough analysis of the interviews yielded four overarching themes: the nurses' initial assessment priorities, the nurses' recognition of and responses to patient anxiety, approaches to reducing anxiety, and factors affecting anxiety assessment. Four main themes and ten sub-themes emerged from the interviews. The theme "Nurses' Initial Assessment Priorities" comprised the sub-themes "Prioritizing the Emergency" and "Getting to Know the Patient." The theme "Nurses' Recognition of and Responses to Patient Anxiety" included "Under-recognition of Anxiety," "Compliance with Care and Treatment," and "Recognizing Psychological Needs." The theme "Approaches to Reducing Anxiety" comprised "Providing Information" and "Therapeutic Communication and Emotional Support." Finally, the theme "Factors Affecting Anxiety Assessment" included "Workload," "Organizational and Work-Related Factors," and "Training Needs." Conclusions: It is recommended that in-service training programmes covering psychosocial care, anxiety assessment and management be organised for intensive care nurses and that more emphasis be placed on psychosocial care and patient anxiety in intensive care in nursing undergraduate and graduate education programmes.

42881637.title: Trigger-Based Referral and Needs Assessment in the Intensive Care Unit: A Narrative Review and Conceptual Synthesis.
42881637.abstract: Background/Objectives: Trigger-based referral systems are widely used to identify intensive care unit (ICU) patients who may benefit from palliative care, but the extent to which trigger status corresponds to multidimensional patient and family need remains uncertain. This narrative review examines trigger-based referral, needs assessment, and integrated approaches to ICU palliative care. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and reference lists were searched, and a purposive thematic synthesis was conducted. The original identification-stage record counts were unavailable; selection was reconstructed from an archived full-text library, and screening was primarily performed by one author. Results: Trigger-based systems improved recognition of clinically vulnerable patients and several care processes. Direct evidence comparing trigger status with measured need is limited, however, and derives principally from one multicenter study using a family-member-reported NEST score. The literature supports distinguishing clinical risk from measured need but does not establish the superiority of trigger-based, needs-based, or integrated models. Conclusions: Current evidence supports comparative testing rather than adoption of any integrated configuration. Candidate components, timing, thresholds, feasibility, and applicability across healthcare systems require prospective evaluation.

42966643.title: Eco-Conscious Nursing in Critical Care: Nurses' Perspectives and Practices Related to Environmental Sustainability.
42966643.journal: American journal of critical care : an official publication, American Association of Critical-Care Nurses

42966199.title: The hidden work of vigilance: a phenomenological study of how intensive care nurses recognise deterioration in older adult patients.
42966199.abstract: Older adults represent a growing proportion of intensive care unit (ICU) admissions, yet deterioration in this population is often subtle and atypical, requiring heightened nursing vigilance. This study explored how ICU nurses recognise early deterioration in older adult patients and how experiential knowledge shapes clinical judgement. An interpretive phenomenological study was conducted in tertiary hospitals in Al-Ahsa, Saudi Arabia. Fourteen ICU nurses participated in semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed using hermeneutic thematic analysis, and reporting followed COREQ guidelines. Three themes emerged: seeing beyond the monitor, describing recognition of subtle physiological and behavioural changes; embodied and experiential knowing, reflecting intuitive concern grounded in clinical experience; and legitimising intuitive concern, highlighting nurses' efforts to translate tacit knowledge into actionable clinical communication. Nursing vigilance is essential for detecting deterioration in older ICU patients. Clinical systems should support nurses in articulating early concern alongside physiological data and should strengthen geriatric-sensitive assessment and escalation practices.

42965388.title: Defining best practice for very old patients following unplanned intensive care admission: protocol of the Delphi consensus study.
42965388.abstract: Very old patients (≥80 years) represent a rapidly increasing proportion of intensive care unit (ICU) admissions across Australia and New Zealand. Care of this population is characterised by substantial prognostic uncertainty and variability in ICU triage, treatment limitation and post-ICU pathways. In particular, the role and implementation of time-limited ICU trials remain inconsistent. To establish multidisciplinary consensus on best-practice management of very old patients following unplanned ICU admission in Australia and New Zealand, including the role, structure and implementation of time-limited ICU trials. We will conduct a modified, multiround Delphi consensus study. A multidisciplinary, multispecialty panel of expert clinicians (intensive care, geriatrics, emergency medicine), doctors in training, nurses, allied health professionals, ethicists and health service leaders across Australia and New Zealand will be recruited through purposive and snowball sampling. Participants will rate statements using the Likert scale across multiple rounds. Anonymised aggregated feedback will be provided to participants between rounds to facilitate convergence of opinion. Consensus will be defined a priori using predefined thresholds and median scores. Quantitative analyses will include descriptive statistics and exploratory subgroup comparisons, while free-text responses will undergo thematic analysis. The primary outcome is to establish multidisciplinary consensus on best-practice management of very old patients following unplanned ICU admission, including the role and implementation of time-limited ICU trials. Secondary outcomes include identifying areas of agreement and variation across groups and convergence across Delphi rounds. A tertiary outcome is to explore barriers and facilitators to implementation to inform a structured decision-making framework. This study will generate consensus-based recommendations and a structured framework for the use of time-limited ICU trials in Australia and New Zealand ICUs. By addressing current practice variability, it aims to support transparent, patient-centred decision-making and inform future research and policy in the care of very old critically ill patients.

42965191.title: Discriminatory power of organ-specific Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) scores: Predictors of maternal mortality in obstetric intensive care units (ICU).
42965191.journal: Journal of family medicine and primary care
42965191.abstract: Critically ill obstetric patients in intensive care units (ICUs) present unique challenges, and maternal mortality remains a major concern, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, though widely used in general ICUs, has not been adequately studied for its organ-specific discriminatory power in predicting maternal mortality. This study aimed to evaluate the prognostic accuracy of individual organ SOFA sub-scores to improve risk stratification in obstetric critical care. This prospective observational study was conducted over one year in the obstetric ICU of a tertiary center in Northern India. A total of 125 obstetric patients (pregnant or within 42 days postpartum) were enrolled. SOFA sub-scores for respiratory, cardiovascular, hepatic, renal, coagulation, and neurological systems were calculated on admission and throughout ICU stay. Patients were classified into survivors and non-survivors. Associations between individual organ dysfunction and maternal mortality were assessed. Discriminatory accuracy of organ-specific SOFA scores was determined using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Mortality increased proportionally with the number of dysfunctional organs (χ² =39.693; P < 0.001). Escalating organ-specific SOFA scores were significantly associated with maternal mortality. ROC analysis revealed that cardiovascular dysfunction had the highest predictive accuracy (area under the curve [AUC] =0.875), followed by hepatic (AUC = 0.808), respiratory (AUC = 0.804), hematological (AUC = 0.763), and renal (AUC = 0.757) dysfunction. Cardiovascular, hepatic, and respiratory SOFA sub-scores provide strong discriminatory power for predicting maternal mortality in Obstetric ICU patients. Incorporating organ-specific SOFA assessments may enhance early risk stratification and guide life-saving interventions in resource-limited settings.

42964988.title: From Gaps in Maternity Care to Maternal Rescue: An Interprofessional Implementation Agenda for Anesthesia and Maternal Critical Care in Somalia.
42964988.abstract: Somalia's maternal health system faces a dual challenge: limited access to skilled maternity care and insufficient capacity to rescue women who deteriorate during or after obstetric emergencies. Hemorrhage, hypertensive emergencies including eclampsia, sepsis, obstructed labor, and urgent cesarean delivery require coordinated maternity, anesthesia, nursing, resuscitation, postoperative surveillance, and critical-care functions. This evidence-informed commentary shifts the discussion from documenting gaps to an interprofessional implementation agenda. We propose five linked priorities: a regulated and supported maternity and obstetric-anesthesia workforce; an evidence-based cesarean safety bundle; step-up maternal high-care capacity; early-warning, crisis resource management, escalation, and referral pathways; and routine measurement through maternal and perioperative quality systems. The approach emphasizes actions that referral maternity hospitals can introduce progressively, with named local accountability, team training, minimum resource requirements, and measurable indicators, while avoiding unsupported assumptions about national critical-care capacity. Somalia does not need to wait for a fully developed intensive-care system before improving maternal rescue. The immediate opportunity is to connect five functions that are too often fragmented: competent anesthesia provision, reliable cesarean safety processes, early recognition of deterioration, monitored maternal high care, and accountable review of outcomes. Strengthening these functions as one interprofessional maternal-rescue pathway offers a practical route to reducing preventable severe maternal morbidity and mortality in Somalia.

42963893.title: Maternal Intensive Care Admission, Unplanned Peripartum Hysterectomy, and Breast Milk Feeding by Hospital Discharge: A Population Based Repeated Cross-Sectional Study.
42963893.journal: BJOG : an international journal of obstetrics and gynaecology
42963893.abstract: Characterize trends and factors associated with breast milk feeding among patients undergoing maternal ICU admission or peripartum unplanned hysterectomy. Population-level repeated cross-sectional study. United States National Vital Statistics System data between 2016 and 2023. Liveborn singleton, non-anomalous deliveries from 34 + 0 to 42 + 6 weeks. Temporal trends were assessed using Joinpoint regression reported as annual average percentage change (AAPC). Multivariable logistic regression models were fit to assess the association between morbidity and breast milk feeding by hospital discharge. Temporal trends in severe morbidity defined as maternal ICU admission and/or unplanned hysterectomy and associated breast milk feeding by hospital discharge. Of the 23 589 073 births included, 33 121 (0.14%) were complicated by severe morbidity. Any severe morbidity increased from 102 to 157 per 100 000 (AAPC 4.1%, 95% CI: 1.3% to 7.2%) with increased hysterectomy only from 15 to 24 per 100 000 (AAPC 4.2%, 95% CI: 0.7% to 8.2%), ICU admission only from 75 to 117 per 100 000 (AAPC 4.5%, 95% CI: 1.5% to 7.8%), and no change in concurrent hysterectomy and ICU admission. Patients with any severe morbidity had lower breast milk feeding by hospital discharge (65.2% vs. 84.1%, adjusted OR 0.46, 95% CI 0.45-0.47). Despite temporal increases in breast milk feeding by hospital discharge for patients without severe morbidity, the same was not seen for those with severe morbidity. These findings identify a population in whom additional support and services would help individuals who wish to breastfeed or provide expressed breast milk, when clinically appropriate.

42963775.title: Nocturnal intravenous gamma-hydroxybutyrate and sleep architecture in non-sedated intensive care unit patients: a polysomnographic experience.

42963296.title: Prognostic value of the sPESI score in critically ill patients with severe pulmonary embolism admitted to the intensive care unit.
42963296.abstract: Intermediate-high- and high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE) is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. However, uncertainty remains regarding the usefulness of prognostic scores for identifying patients at risk of progression to more severe forms of PE. This study aimed to describe the clinical characteristics and outcomes of patients with intermediate-high- and high-risk PE admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) and to explore the association between baseline simplified Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (sPESI) and subsequent progression to high-risk PE among patients initially classified as intermediate-high risk. We conducted a retrospective, single-center observational study including patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) of the University Hospital of Salamanca between 2021 and 2022 with a diagnosis of intermediate-high or high-risk PE. Clinical variables, prognostic scores, biomarkers, treatment strategies, and mortality were analyzed. A total of 64 patients were included; 57 (89.1%) were initially classified as intermediate-high risk and 7 (10.9%) as high risk. Among the 57 patients initially classified as intermediate-high risk, 4 (7.0%) subsequently progressed to high-risk PE. Patients who progressed had higher baseline sPESI scores than those who remained haemodynamically stable (3.5 [IQR: 2.5-4.2] vs 2.0 [IQR: 1.0-2.0]; P=.029). In exploratory Firth penalised logistic regression, a higher baseline sPESI score was associated with progression to high-risk PE (OR per 1-point increase: 2.75; 95%CI: 1.23-8.44; P=.012). In-hospital mortality was 7.8%. Among patients with PE initially classified as intermediate-high risk, a higher baseline sPESI score was associated with subsequent progression to high-risk PE.

42962613.title: Association of Neutrophil-to-Prognostic Nutritional Index Ratio With Prognosis in Critically Ill Patients Undergoing Gastric Procedures.
42962613.abstract: Inflammation and malnutrition frequently coexist in critically ill patients, yet single inflammatory or nutritional indices capture only part of this state. We examined how the preoperative neutrophil-to-prognostic nutritional index ratio (NPNI), a composite of both, relates to mortality across follow-up in patients undergoing gastric procedures. We studied 1821 adults in the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV database who underwent a gastric procedure. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality; secondary outcomes included 15-d, 30-d, 60-d, 90-d, 1-y, 3-y, and 5-y mortality. Logistic regression, time-window Cox models, and landmark analysis were used to assess the association between NPNI and mortality. Receiver operating characteristic curves were generated to calculate the area under the curve. The signal source of NPNI was explored through interaction analysis between the inflammatory axis (neutrophils) and the nutritional axis (Onodera Prognostic Nutritional Index). Higher NPNI was associated with greater odds of death at every horizon (per 1 standard deviation, odds ratio (OR)in-hospital = 1.24, 95% confidence interval: 1.10-1.40; OR5-y = 1.28, 95% confidence interval: 1.15-1.42). NPNI demonstrated "cross-temporal stability," maintaining significant associations in both the early mortality (0-30 d) and late mortality (30 d-5 y) windows. Time-window analysis revealed that the nutritional axis was associated with early mortality (heart rate = 0.81, P = 0.032), while the inflammatory axis was associated with late mortality (heart rate = 1.13, P < 0.001). The interaction between the two axes was subadditive (relative excess risk due to interaction = -0.32). NPNI showed modest discriminative ability (area under the curve: 0.568), inferior to Simplified Acute Physiology Score II (0.647) and Oxford Acute Severity of Illness Score (0.625). Elevated NPNI is an independent risk factor for mortality in critically ill patients undergoing gastric procedures. Its value lies in cross-temporal risk integration rather than discriminative ability.

42961661.title: [Tiered emergency care structures in 2026 : Recent developments for emergency departments and intensive care medicine].
authors: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internistische Intensivmedizin und Notfallmedizin (DGIIN)

42959899.title: Feature-token clinical transformer for 24-h landmark mortality risk stratification in critically ill patients with heart failure: development and multicenter external validation.
42959899.abstract: The first 24 h after ICU admission in critically ill patients with heart failure yield heterogeneous EHR evidence across vital signs, laboratory tests, treatments, organ support, and nurse-charted monitoring. Conventional scores and flat-vector ML models may not preserve individual variable identity or context. We developed FTCT, encoding each predictor recorded during the first 24 h after ICU admission as a clinically tagged token (value, missingness, identity, group). MIMIC-IV (2008-2019) served for development, validation, and internal testing; eICU-CRD (2014-2015) served for external validation. Included were adults with heart failure, a complete 24-h ICU observation window, and known discharge status. The endpoint was in-hospital all-cause death. MIMIC-IV included 11,156 stays and 1,484 deaths, partitioned into training (n = 7,809), validation (n = 1,673), and internal test (n = 1,674) sets. eICU-CRD included 9,837 stays and 1,319 deaths. FTCT achieved an AUROC of 0.849 (95% CI, 0.835-0.863) internally and 0.804 (0.788-0.820) externally. Patient-paired AUROC differences vs. XGBoost were 0.027 (0.011-0.043) internally and 0.032 (0.014-0.050) externally. A matched FT-Transformer-style baseline achieved an external AUROC of 0.781 (0.760-0.801). In eICU-CRD, FTCT achieved an AUPRC of 0.296 (0.278-0.314), Brier score of 0.091 (0.085-0.097), and expected calibration error of 0.036 (0.030-0.042). In a post hoc cohort-specific descriptive operating analysis targeting approximately 85% specificity, external sensitivity was 0.662 (0.636-0.687), positive predictive value 0.406 (0.385-0.427), negative predictive value 0.942 (0.937-0.947), and F1 score 0.503. Removing feature-token encoding produced the largest ablation loss in external AUROC (-0.031). FTCT combines established feature-token Transformer modeling with clinical-group embeddings, explicit missingness representation, and group-aware pooling for 24-h landmark mortality risk stratification from structured EHR data recorded during the first 24 h after ICU admission. Its external validation and ablation results support prospective investigation, but do not yet demonstrate clinical utility, workflow integration, admission-time applicability, or autonomous use.

42959645.title: Association between triglyceride high-density cholesterol-glucose body index and 28-day mortality in critically ill patients: a multicenter observational study in China.
42959645.abstract: The triglyceride high-density lipoprotein cholesterol-glucose body mass index (TyHGB) is a novel composite indicator integrating triglyceride, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, fasting glucose and body mass index and may provide a more comprehensive assessment of systemic metabolic status than current indices. This multicenter landmark cohort study aimed to determine the association between TyHGB measured at the landmark time and 28-day mortality in patients present in the intensive care units (ICUs) at that time and to evaluate its potential utility as a prognostic marker. This multicenter observational cohort study included 1649 patients from 113 ICUs in China. The association between TyHGB and 28-day mortality was evaluated using three sequentially adjusted logistic regression models with restricted cubic splines: Model 1 adjusted for demographics; Model 2 further adjusted for disease severity and organ dysfunction; Model 3 additionally adjusted for therapeutic interventions. Subgroup analyses with interaction tests were conducted. Model performance was assessed by discrimination (AUC), calibration (Brier score and calibration slope) and internal validation via bootstrap resamples. Restricted cubic spline analysis demonstrated a positive association between TyHGB and 28-day mortality across fully adjusted models (P < 0.05). Subgroup analyses identified a statistically significant interaction with diabetes (P for interaction = 0.011). In the overall cohort, adding TyHGB to the base model improved AUC from 0.731 to 0.745 (ΔAUC = +0.014, P = 0.043), with significant improvements in reclassification (NRI = 0.328, P < 0.001; IDI = 0.012, P = 0.009) and model fit (LRT P < 0.001). Among diabetic patients (N = 401), TyHGB significantly improved AUC from 0.673 to 0.723 (ΔAUC = +0.050, P = 0.049; NRI = 0.515, P < 0.001; IDI = 0.041, P = 0.022). In contrast, no significant improvement was observed in non-diabetic patients (ΔAUC = +0.009, P = 0.152). Among patients present in participating ICUs at the landmark time, higher TyHGB was associated with subsequent 28-day mortality. However, adding TyHGB to the baseline risk prediction model led to only small improvements in overall predictive performance. Findings in diabetic patients are exploratory and require further validation.

42959540.title: Bedside pharmacist interventions for managing intravenous drug incompatibilities in critically ill patients.
42959540.journal: Exploratory research in clinical and social pharmacy
42959540.abstract: Patients admitted to intensive care units are at increased risk of intravenous drug incompatibilities, owing to polypharmacy and the limited number of available venous access devices. To evaluate bedside pharmacist interventions for managing drug incompatibilities identified during intravenous administration in intensive care unit patients. A cross-sectional study with prospective data collection was conducted between June and December 2025 in five intensive care units of a university hospital. Two pharmacists assessed medication administration at the bedside and checked compatibility using the Micromedex and American Society of Health-System Pharmacists (ASHP) Injectable Drug Information databases. The type and number of central venous access devices, infusion modality, proposed interventions, and the healthcare team's response were recorded. Data were described using absolute and relative frequencies. A total of 887 infusions were analyzed in 88 patients, of which 159 corresponded to occurrences of incompatibility or lack of compatibility data (73 distinct drug combinations). Of these 159 occurrences, 135 (84.9%) were incompatible, and 24 (15.1%) lacked compatibility studies. Most of the pharmacist interventions performed were accepted by the healthcare team (130/159; 81.8%). The high frequency of incompatibilities observed is related to the large number of intravenous medications and the complexity of therapeutic regimens used in intensive care. Bedside pharmacist involvement proved feasible and contributed to safer medication administration practices in these units.

42959277.title: Autonomic nervous system dysfunction in critically ill cancer patients: Hemodynamic consequences and multimodal assessment strategies.
42959277.abstract: In critically ill cancer patients, autonomic nervous system (ANS) dysfunction may contribute to hemodynamic instability and organ dysfunction and may be exacerbated by malignancy-related injury and anticancer treatment. This narrative review summarizes conventional methods for assessing ANS function, including heart rate variability (HRV), blood pressure variability (BPV), baroreflex sensitivity (BRS), and cardiovascular autonomic reflex testing, together with emerging approaches such as high-resolution multimodal monitoring (MMM) and artificial intelligence (AI). Host-organ unregulated response (HOUR) framework is used to integrate interactions among autonomic, neuroendocrine, inflammatory, immune, coagulation, metabolic, bioenergetic, and microcirculatory dysregulation. Collectively, these approaches may facilitate real-time assessment of autonomic function and tissue perfusion, thereby supporting risk stratification and individualized management in critically ill cancer patients.

42958588.title: ICU-led remote vital sign trends monitoring of selected non-ICU-patients: a first year experience.

42958500.title: Association between platelet-to-white blood cell ratio trajectories and all-cause mortality in critically ill patients with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a retrospective cohort study.
42958500.abstract: AECOPD is a leading cause of ICU admission and death in patients with COPD, yet readily accessible biomarkers for dynamic risk stratification remain scarce. The platelet-to-white blood cell ratio (PWR) is a promising inflammatory marker reflecting inflammatory burden and regenerative capacity. However, no studies have investigated PWR in AECOPD, and single-time-point measurements in critical illness are inherently limited by rapid physiological fluctuations. Whether longitudinal PWR trajectories outperform static measurements or conventional severity scores in AECOPD remains unknown. Accordingly, we investigated the association between dynamic PWR trajectories and all-cause mortality in this critically ill population. Data were extracted from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC)-IV database. This retrospective cohort study enrolled critically ill patients with acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD). Group-based trajectory modeling (GBTM) was used to identify distinct platelet-to-white blood cell ratio (PWR) trajectories; model selection was based on the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), average posterior probability (AvePP), odds of correct classification (OCC), and clinical interpretability. The primary outcome was 28-day all-cause mortality, with secondary outcomes including in-ICU, in-hospital, 90-day, and 365-day mortality. Multivariable Cox and logistic regression models were constructed to evaluate independent associations. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves with the DeLong test were used to compare predictive performance. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses were performed to assess robustness, and restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis was conducted to evaluate nonlinearity. Among 1,056 AECOPD patients, five distinct PWR trajectories were identified: Traj 1 (persistently low, n = 210), Traj 2 (low-to-moderate increasing, n = 333), Traj 3 (moderate-to-high increasing, n = 269), Traj 4 (moderate-to-low decreasing, n = 98), and Traj 5 (persistently high, n = 146). The primary findings demonstrated that compared with Trajectory 1, Trajectories 2, 3, and 5 were associated with significantly reduced risks of 28-day all-cause mortality, with adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) of 0.35 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.23-0.53), 0.45 (95% CI: 0.29-0.70), and 0.23 (95% CI: 0.12-0.46), respectively. In contrast, Trajectory 4 exhibited a comparable risk of 28-day mortality relative to Trajectory 1 (HR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.43-1.20). Consistent patterns were observed for secondary outcomes, including the risks of in-hospital mortality, ICU mortality, 90-day mortality, and 365-day mortality. The PWR trajectory model (AUC = 0.661) outperformed single PWR (AUC = 0.596, P = 0.007) and was comparable to SOFA (AUC = 0.607, P = 0.051); their combination yielded the highest AUC (0.674, P = 0.002 vs. SOFA). In critically ill patients with AECOPD, PWR trajectories are independently associated with short- and long-term mortality. PWR trajectories offer superior prognostic performance to single PWR, comparable performance to SOFA, and significant incremental value when combined.

42857028.title: Comparison of Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA), Quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA), Obstetrically Modified SOFA, and Obstetrically Modified qSOFA Scores for Predicting Maternal Outcomes in High-Risk Obstetric Patients.
42857028.abstract: Introduction Maternal morbidity and mortality remain significant challenges in obstetric critical care. Early identification of organ dysfunction is essential for timely intervention and improved outcomes. This study compared the prognostic performance of the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA), quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA), obstetrically modified SOFA (omSOFA), and obstetrically modified qSOFA (omqSOFA) scores in predicting maternal outcomes among high-risk obstetric patients. Methods A prospective observational study was conducted among 200 high-risk obstetric patients admitted to a tertiary care center. Twelve patients who left against medical advice were excluded from outcome-based analyses, leaving 188 patients for final evaluation. SOFA, qSOFA, omSOFA, and omqSOFA scores were calculated at admission. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to determine the predictive performance of each scoring system for maternal mortality. Area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and optimal cutoff values were calculated. Results Among the 188 patients included in the final analysis, 15 maternal deaths occurred. SOFA demonstrated the highest discriminatory ability for predicting maternal mortality, with an AUC of 0.97 (95% CI: 0.94-0.99) at a cutoff value of ≥10, followed by omSOFA with an AUC of 0.93 (95% CI: 0.89-0.97) at a cutoff value of ≥9. qSOFA and omqSOFA showed AUCs of 0.76 (95% CI: 0.68-0.84) and 0.79 (95% CI: 0.71-0.87), respectively. qSOFA and omqSOFA demonstrated 100% sensitivity and negative predictive value at a cutoff score of ≥2, while SOFA and omSOFA provided superior specificity and overall discriminatory performance. Conclusions Among high-risk obstetric patients, SOFA demonstrated the highest discriminatory ability for predicting maternal mortality, followed by omSOFA. While qSOFA and omqSOFA showed lower specificity, they demonstrated excellent sensitivity and negative predictive value, making them useful bedside screening tools for early risk identification. Incorporation of these scoring systems into obstetric critical care practice may facilitate timely risk stratification and early intervention. Further multicentre studies are required to validate these findings in larger and more diverse obstetric populations.

42936862.title: Obstetric Shock Beyond Hemorrhage: Microcirculatory Shunting, Endothelial Glycocalyx Injury, and Mitochondrial Failure in Pregnancy-A Narrative Review.
42936862.abstract: Obstetric shock has traditionally been conceptualized within the framework of hemorrhage and macrocirculatory collapse. However, clinical deterioration may occur despite preserved blood pressure and cardiac output, indicating that disturbances in tissue perfusion and cellular metabolism can precede overt hemodynamic instability. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence examining the contributions of microcirculatory dysfunction, endothelial glycocalyx injury, mitochondrial impairment, immune-metabolic dysregulation, and placental signaling to the development and progression of obstetric shock beyond conventional hemodynamic paradigms. A literature review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE and PubMed Central, focusing on studies in obstetrics, critical care, endothelial biology, microcirculatory physiology, and mitochondrial function, with articles selected for their mechanistic, translational, and clinical relevance. Available evidence suggests that disruption of the microcirculation, endothelial injury, and impaired cellular energy metabolism may interact to produce tissue hypoperfusion despite preserved systemic hemodynamics, a phenomenon described as hemodynamic incoherence. These mechanisms may contribute to diverse clinical phenotypes, including normotensive hypoperfusion, endothelial dysfunction-associated shock, microthrombotic states, and impaired cellular oxygen utilization. Although much of the supporting evidence derives from studies of preeclampsia, sepsis, and non-obstetric critical illness rather than obstetric shock itself, these findings provide biologically plausible mechanistic insights that may improve understanding of unexplained maternal deterioration. Emerging physiologic monitoring techniques may facilitate earlier recognition of occult tissue hypoperfusion, although their validation and routine clinical application in obstetric practice remain limited. Overall, obstetric shock should be considered a heterogeneous syndrome that extends beyond hemorrhage alone, and an integrated framework incorporating microvascular, endothelial, metabolic, and placental processes may improve understanding of its pathophysiology while informing future diagnostic and therapeutic research. Further obstetric-specific studies are required to validate these concepts and define their clinical implications.

42934571.title: Risk factors associated with maternal near miss in tertiary hospitals in Eskişehir, Türkiye: a case-control study.
42934571.abstract: Maternal near miss (MNM) cases provide valuable insight into the quality and performance of maternal health services. Understanding the factors associated with MNM is crucial for developing effective public health interventions. This study aimed primarily to identify factors associated with MNM and secondarily to report the MNM ratio in tertiary hospitals in Eskişehir, Türkiye. This retrospective, multicenter, case-control study was conducted at two tertiary hospitals in Eskişehir, Türkiye. The medical records of 10,360 women who gave birth between January 1, 2022, and December 31, 2023, were reviewed. A total of 53 MNM cases were identified based on the World Health Organization criteria defined by organ dysfunction and life-threatening conditions. For each case, three controls without serious complications were selected, resulting in 159 controls (1:3 ratio). Descriptive statistics, univariate analysis, and multivariate logistic regression were used to identify factors associated with MNM. The incidence of MNM was calculated as 5.18 per 1,000 live births. The most common maternal complications were severe postpartum hemorrhage (45.2%), uterine rupture (34.0%), and severe preeclampsia (17.0%). The most commonly performed critical interventions were blood transfusion (73.6%), laparotomy (45.3%), and intensive care unit admission (30.2%). Coagulation/hematological dysfunction (58.5%) and uterine dysfunction (47.2%) were the most frequently observed MNM criteria. Multivariate analysis identified anemia (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 16.57; 95% CI: 7.19-38.19), previous cesarean delivery (aOR = 6.22; 95% CI: 2.18-17.77), short interpregnancy interval of two years or less (aOR = 3.68; 95% CI: 1.63-8.32), absence of antenatal care (aOR = 4.69; 95% CI: 1.44-15.21), and presence of chronic disease (aOR = 4.83; 95% CI: 2.11-11.04) as independent risk factors, while preterm birth (aOR = 12.86; 95% CI: 5.95-27.78) emerged as a strong clinical indicator associated with MNM. The results of this study underscore the importance of early identification and management of modifiable risk factors for MNM. Strengthening antenatal care services, improving anemia screening and treatment, promoting evidence-based cesarean delivery practices, and ensuring postpartum family planning support may help improve maternal outcomes and reduce preventable maternal morbidity.

42872265.title: A single center cross-sectional study examining the prevalence of inpatient postpartum anxiety and post-traumatic stress symptoms using the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist for DSM-5.
42872265.abstract: Mental health conditions are now the leading cause of maternal mortality in the United States, prompting calls for universal postpartum anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder screening. However, standardized guidelines for screening implementation remain deficient. This cross-sectional study evaluated the prevalence of inpatient postpartum anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder while exploring associated risk factors. Over a three-week period, we prospectively assessed adult postpartum patients following all delivery modes (vaginal and cesarean, live and stillbirth) at a single academic institution in the US. Screening was performed within 36 hours of delivery using the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (score cut off ≥80) and post-traumatic stress disorder checklist for DSM-5 (score cut off ≥28). Data collection included demographic, medical, anesthesia, obstetric and neonatal variables, with assessments conducted in-person or via telephone for any spoken language. Cross-sectional study. Among 275 eligible patients, 263 (95.6%) completed the screening measures. The prevalence of positive postpartum anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder screening was 12.5% and 4.9% respectively, with 3.8% of patients screening positive for both conditions. Worse State-Trait Anxiety Inventory scores were associated with ASA ≥3, pre-term birth and neonatal Apgar scores at 5 minutes <7. Worse post-traumatic stress disorder scores were associated with ASA ≥3, primiparity, spontaneous vaginal delivery, pre-eclampsia, pre-term birth, blood transfusion, Apgar score <7 and neonatal intensive care unit admission. Factors after adjustment associated with positive anxiety screening were a psychiatric history or medication use. No factors after adjustment were associated with positive PTSD screening. Positive screening for inpatient postpartum anxiety was two and a half times more prevalent than for post-traumatic stress disorder. Positive anxiety screening was independently associated with psychiatric history or medication use. Targeted screening for post-traumatic stress disorder may be more appropriate, particularly among patients with pre-existing psychiatric conditions, complicated pregnancies or neonatal morbidity. Future research should focus on determining optimal screening parameters and timing, and intervention guidelines to better support high-risk obstetric populations.

42853129.title: BUN/Albumin Ratio in Preeclampsia: A Comparative Study of Seven Biomarker Ratios.
42853129.journal: The journal of obstetrics and gynaecology research
42853129.abstract: To evaluate whether the admission blood urea nitrogen to albumin ratio (BAR) predicts adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes in preeclampsia, and to compare its performance against six other laboratory-derived ratios. Records of 252 preeclamptic pregnancies were reviewed and dichotomised at a BAR cut-off of 3.0: low (< 3.0, n = 135) and high (≥ 3.0, n = 117). Composite adverse maternal outcomes included severe complication, intensive-care admission, or transfusion; composite adverse perinatal outcomes included growth restriction, stillbirth, neonatal death, neonatal-unit admission, or 5-min Apgar below 7. BAR was benchmarked against six other ratios: uric acid/albumin ratio (UAR), lactate dehydrogenase/albumin ratio (LAR), C-reactive protein/albumin ratio (CAR), fibrinogen/CRP ratio, fibrinogen/albumin ratio (FAR), and aspartate aminotransferase/alanine aminotransferase (AST/ALT) ratio (De Ritis) by ROC analysis. Independent predictors were sought through multivariable logistic regression. Patients in the high-BAR stratum showed substantially higher rates of composite adverse obstetric outcome (78.6% vs. 54.1%; p < 0.001), composite adverse maternal outcome (28.2% vs. 6.7%; p < 0.001), maternal intensive-care admission (16.2% vs. 3.7%; p = 0.001), and transfusion (12.0% vs. 2.2%; p = 0.002). BAR yielded the most balanced discrimination across endpoints, with AUCs of 0.68 (95% CI: 0.61-0.75) for the obstetric composite, 0.74 (95% CI: 0.65-0.83) for the maternal composite, and 0.66 (95% CI: 0.59-0.73) for the perinatal composite (all p < 0.01); fibrinogen/albumin and AST/ALT ratios were not predictive. BAR did not differ significantly from UAR or LAR by DeLong test (all p > 0.05) and retained independent association with adverse perinatal outcome after adjustment (adjusted OR 1.32; 95% CI: 1.03-1.70; p = 0.03). Sensitivity analyses showed that UAR retained independent significance for all three composite endpoints, positioning BAR and UAR as complementary bedside markers. An elevated admission BAR identifies preeclamptic women at higher risk of severe maternal and perinatal events, with performance comparable to that of UAR. Both BAR and UAR may serve as simple complementary bedside adjuncts to existing risk stratification tools in preeclampsia.

42948504.title: Refractory Obstetric Hemorrhage As the Initial Presentation of Acquired Hemophilia: A Case Report on the Diagnostic Limitations of Viscoelastic Testing.
42948504.abstract: Acquired hemophilia A is a rare autoimmune bleeding disorder caused by the development of autoantibodies against coagulation factor VIII. It is frequently associated with the postpartum period and may present as severe and persistent bleeding in patients without a prior history of coagulopathy, often leading to diagnostic delay. We report the case of a 26-year-old woman in the postpartum period following cesarean section for severe preeclampsia, who developed refractory hemorrhage despite multiple surgical interventions, including exploratory laparotomies, hematoma drainage, and abdominal packing. Laboratory evaluation revealed an isolated prolongation of activated partial thromboplastin time. Mixing studies showed incomplete correction, raising suspicion of a circulating inhibitor. Further testing confirmed severely reduced factor VIII activity and the presence of a factor VIII inhibitor. Serial thromboelastography demonstrated profound hypocoagulability with impaired thrombin generation and episodes of hyperfibrinolysis. The patient was treated with bypassing agents and combined immunosuppressive therapy, resulting in progressive reduction of inhibitor levels and recovery of factor VIII activity, ultimately achieving complete hematologic remission. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of acquired hemophilia A in the postpartum setting and emphasizes the importance of early recognition of isolated coagulation abnormalities. Prompt diagnosis and a coordinated multidisciplinary approach are essential for effective bleeding control and inhibitor eradication in critically ill patients.

42927239.title: Antenatal diagnosis and classification for placenta accreta (adherence) spectrum: Clinical practice guideline and recommendations by the World Association of Perinatal Medicine and the Perinatal Medicine Foundation.
42927239.abstract: This practical guidance was developed by the World Association of Perinatal Medicine in collaboration with the Perinatal Medicine Foundation to support antenatal diagnosis and clinical management in pregnancies at risk for placenta accreta spectrum (PAS). It provides an evidence-informed approach to screening, diagnosis, referral, and peripartum planning across healthcare settings with different resources. PAS is increasingly encountered alongside rising cesarean delivery rates, use of in vitro fertilization, and a history of uterine surgery. It remains associated with severe maternal morbidity, including massive hemorrhage, large-volume transfusion, uterine rupture, peripartum hysterectomy, pelvic organ injury, intensive care admission, and maternal death. Early recognition and multidisciplinary care are therefore central to management. Cesarean scar pregnancy (CSP) is considered a potential precursor of PAS. Women with a low implantation site and a previous cesarean delivery are at increased risk. Early transvaginal ultrasound is advised in women with a previous cesarean delivery to establish the implantation site, identify CSP, and support counseling and timely consideration of uterine-preserving treatment. In the second and third trimesters, combined transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound assesses placental location, myometrial thickness and contour, and the uterovesical interface. Sonographic markers include placental lacunae, placental bulge, uterovesical hypervascularity, and bridging vessels, which may occur individually or in combination. Two-dimensional grayscale ultrasound is the mainstay of antenatal assessment, supported by color Doppler; three-dimensional imaging may provide additional information in selected specialist settings. Magnetic resonance imaging has a complementary role when ultrasound is inconclusive, placental location is non-anterior or non-previa, or technical factors limit visualization. Suspected CSP or PAS should prompt referral to a perinatal center with multidisciplinary expertise, blood product support, adult and neonatal intensive care, and access to complex pelvic surgery. Delivery timing and surgical preparation should be individualized.

42923921.title: Successful vaginal birth after two or more cesareans versus failed trial of labor: A systematic review and meta-analysis of maternal and fetal outcomes.
42923921.journal: Revista brasileira de ginecologia e obstetricia : revista da Federacao Brasileira das Sociedades de Ginecologia e Obstetricia
42923921.abstract: To assess maternal and neonatal outcomes associated with a failed versus successful (VBAC-2). A systematic search across Pubmed, Embase and Cochrane was conducted up to October 2025, supplemented by backward snowballing. Studies with pregnant women with a two or more previous cesarean deliveries undergoing a trial of labor were included. No restrictions were applied. Data on maternal and neonatal outcomes and risk and protective factors were extracted. The DerSimonian and Laird random effects model was applied, reporting Odds Ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals. Heterogeneity was evaluated using I2 statistics and the Cochran Q test. Methodological quality was appraised using the Cochrane Risk-of-bias tool for non-randomized trials (ROBINS-I). Out of 4065 studies screened, 12 studies (n= 3429) were included. We observed higher odds of postpartum hemorrhage (OR 1.98), maternal transfusion (OR 3.29), uterine rupture (OR 6.47), and neonatal intensive care unit admission (OR 6.44) in the VBAC-2 failure group. Epidural anesthesia (OR 0.56) and a history of previous vaginal birth (OR 0.27) were identified as protective factors, while a higher Body Mass Index was a risk factor for VBAC- 2 failure. These findings highlight the critical need for comprehensive patient counseling, risk assessment, and heightened clinical vigilance to optimize care strategies in this high-risk population.

42858282.title: Papaverine administration during labor induction in nulliparous patients: a retrospective cohort study.
42858282.abstract: To evaluate the association between papaverine administration during labor induction and maternal and neonatal outcomes among nulliparous patients, with particular emphasis on cesarean delivery, labor duration, and timing of administration relative to rupture of membranes. Retrospective cohort study. Participants/Materials: The study included 1,889 nulliparous patients with singleton pregnancies who underwent medically indicated labor induction with intravenous oxytocin between January 2020 and December 2024. Patients were categorized according to papaverine exposure: no papaverine (n=1,185), one 80-mg intramuscular dose (n=618), or two 80-mg intramuscular doses (n=86). A tertiary university-affiliated medical center in northern Israel. Maternal, intrapartum, postpartum, and neonatal data were extracted from electronic medical records. The primary outcome was mode of delivery. Secondary outcomes included cesarean delivery due to non-progressive labor, delivery within 24 hours, postpartum hemorrhage, puerperal endometritis, 5-minute Apgar score <7, umbilical cord pH <7.2 and <7.1, and neonatal intensive care unit admission. Pairwise comparisons were performed between each papaverine group and the no-papaverine group using the independent-samples t test, Mann-Whitney U test, Pearson's chi-square test, or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. A multivariable logistic regression model was used to evaluate factors associated with cesarean delivery. Mode of delivery was also evaluated according to the timing of papaverine administration relative to rupture of membranes. Compared with no papaverine, one-dose papaverine administration was associated with a lower cesarean delivery rate (24.4% vs. 33.9%; RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.61-0.85; P<0.001), whereas the cesarean delivery rate did not differ significantly between the two-dose and no-papaverine groups (30.2% vs. 33.9%; P=0.484). Cesarean delivery due to non-progressive labor was less frequent with one dose compared with no papaverine (11.5% vs. 17.1%; RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.52-0.86; P=0.002), whereas no significant difference was observed between the two-dose and no-papaverine groups (20.9% vs. 17.1%; P=0.369). Delivery within 24 hours was more frequent with one dose than with no papaverine (65.0% vs. 53.9%; RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.12-1.30; P<0.001) and less frequent with two doses than with no papaverine (37.2% vs. 53.9%; RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.52-0.91; P=0.003). Vaginal delivery rates were highest when papaverine was administered before rupture of membranes (77.0%), followed by administration after rupture of membranes (73.0%) and no papaverine exposure (66.1%; P<0.001). In multivariable analysis, papaverine administration was independently associated with lower odds of cesarean delivery (adjusted OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.50-0.81; P<0.001). Maternal postpartum complications and neonatal outcomes were generally similar between groups. The retrospective, single-center design may introduce selection bias and residual confounding. Papaverine administration was based on clinician discretion, and the relatively small two-dose group limited evaluation of dose-dependent effects. Long-term maternal and neonatal outcomes were not assessed. Papaverine administration during labor induction, particularly as a single dose, was associated with a lower cesarean delivery rate and a greater likelihood of delivery within 24 hours, without an observed increase in adverse maternal or neonatal outcomes. Vaginal delivery was most frequent among patients who received papaverine before rupture of membranes; however, this exploratory finding requires prospective confirmation.

42835655.title: Prevalence, types, maternal and perinatal outcomes of cardiac disease in pregnancy at a tertiary Hospital in the Eastern Cape, South Africa.
42835655.journal: Journal of the colleges of medicine of South Africa
42835655.abstract: Cardiac disease is a leading non-obstetric cause of maternal morbidity and mortality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Retrospective cross-sectional review of all deliveries from 01 January 2020 to 31 December 2022. Echocardiography-confirmed cardiac disease cases were identified. Data included demographics, lesion type and/or severity (New York Heart Association [NYHA]), timing of diagnosis, delivery characteristics and outcomes. Associations were examined using χ2 and t-tests (p < 0.05). Among 11 728 deliveries, 182 had cardiac disease (prevalence 1.6%, 95% CI: 1.34-1.80). Median age was 26 years (IQR 22-31); 50.6% presented with NYHA III-IV. Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) predominated (61.5%), mainly mitral stenosis (43.8%) and mitral regurgitation (38.3%). Cardiomyopathy accounted for 31.3%; peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) comprised 78.9% of cardiomyopathies, most diagnosed postpartum (64.9%) and frequently with Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction (LVEF) < 45%. Preterm birth occurred in 46.9% of pregnancies, particularly with RHD-MS (mean gestational age (GA) 33.0 ± 6.0 weeks; p = 0.005). Caesarean delivery occurred in 72.0% (131/182), mainly for obstetric (41.8%) rather than cardiac indications. Maternal complications were common (67.6%), including pulmonary oedema (28.6%, 95% CI: 22.1-35.7), pulmonary hypertension (13.2%, 95% CI: 8.6-19.0) and ICU admission (12.1%, 95% CI: 7.8-17.6). Maternal case fatality was 4.9% (9/182; 95% CI: 2.3-9.2). Most neonates had favourable short-term outcomes (5-min Apgar ≥ 7 in 83.5%) and were discharged (87.7%). Rheumatic heart disease and PPCM were the dominant lesions and major drivers of severe morbidity and mortality. The high burden of late presentation and severe functional limitation underscores the need for earlier detection, systematised cardio-obstetric care and strengthened primary prevention of RHD.

42954428.title: Maternity versus non-maternity healthcare settings for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy.
42954428.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
42954428.abstract: Substantial uncertainty exists regarding how healthcare system factors, especially care setting types, affect the uptake and implementation of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy screening in practice. Evidence suggests that the care environment may influence diagnostic processes. To assess the effectiveness of maternity and non-maternity healthcare settings for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus or diabetes in pregnancy. We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL) for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) up to April 2026, and for controlled non-randomised studies of interventions (NRSIs) up to December 2025. We also searched CENTRAL to identify ongoing trials. We included RCTs and planned to include cluster-RCTs and NRSIs, but we did not find any. Eligible participants were pregnant women being screened for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) or diabetes in pregnancy. We defined maternity healthcare settings as those specialising in care for pregnant, birthing, and postpartum individuals, with appropriate screening protocols, and non-maternity healthcare settings as general medical environments lacking a focus on pregnancy and women's care. We considered any screening format (e.g. risk-factor-based screening) and any diagnostic test (e.g. one- and two-step oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTT)). Critical health service outcomes were compliance with screening and follow-up guidelines, diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy, maternal emergency department visits during pregnancy, maternal antenatal hospitalisation, length of maternal hospitalisation, length of neonatal hospitalisation, and care accessibility. Critical maternal outcomes included hypertensive disorders, maternal death, intensive care admissions, hyperglycaemia requiring pharmacological treatment, infections, and postpartum glucose intolerance, including progression to diabetes, within 15 years after birth. Critical child-related outcomes encompassed perinatal death, neonatal intensive care admissions, preterm birth, neonatal hypoglycaemia, large-for-gestational-age, shoulder dystocia, and birth trauma. Further critical and important outcomes not included in the summary of findings tables can be found in the full text. We used the Cochrane RoB 2 tool to assess bias in the RCTs. We had planned to use ROBINS-I version 2 to assess bias in the NRSIs if we had identified any. We used standard Cochrane methodology. We planned to synthesise results for each outcome using meta-analysis where possible (inverse-variance or Mantel-Haenszel approaches; fixed-effect model). We used GRADE to assess the certainty of the evidence for each outcome. We included one RCT with 781 participants: 390 were randomised to screening in a maternity healthcare setting and 391 were randomised to screening in a non-maternity healthcare setting. Except for screening compliance, trialists evaluated all outcomes using a per-protocol analysis instead of by original randomised groups. This approach created substantial disparities in sample sizes between settings and largely nullified the methodological protections typically provided by a randomised design. The trial evaluated screening for GDM only. We did not identify any ongoing studies or studies awaiting classification. Health service outcomes Screening in a maternity healthcare setting may increase compliance with screening and follow-up guidelines (risk ratio (RR) 1.69, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.53 to 1.87; 781 participants) and may improve care accessibility, assessed as time to access antenatal diabetes care, measured in days (mean difference (MD) -4.70, 95% CI -6.03 to -3.37; 690 participants), both with low-certainty evidence. We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on diagnosis of gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.60 to 2.01; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and length of neonatal hospitalisation (MD 0.04, 95% CI -0.57 to 0.65; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No direct evidence was available on screening for diabetes in pregnancy as distinct from GDM. No data were reported on maternal emergency department visits, maternal antenatal hospitalisation, length of maternal hospitalisations, and costs. Maternal outcomes We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on pre-eclampsia (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.56 to 2.75; 690 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The following outcomes were not reported: eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, maternal death, admission to intensive care, hyperglycaemia requiring pharmacological treatment, infections, and postpartum glucose intolerance. Child-related outcomes We are very uncertain about the effect of screening in a maternity healthcare setting versus a non-maternity healthcare setting on: stillbirth or foetal death (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.08 to 9.93), admission to neonatal intensive care (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.71), preterm birth (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.41 to 2.71), neonatal hypoglycaemia (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.23 to 3.59), large-for-gestational-age (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.04), shoulder dystocia (RR 0.15, 95% CI 0.01 to 3.70), and birth trauma (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.08 to 9.93), all with 690 participants each and very low-certainty evidence. An effect estimate for neonatal death was not estimable (maternity setting: 0/475; non-maternity setting: 0/215). There is insufficient evidence to determine whether screening for gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy in maternity healthcare settings compared with non-maternity healthcare settings improves health service, maternal, or child-related outcomes. Low-certainty evidence from a single study indicates that screening in maternity healthcare settings may result in a reduction in time to access antenatal diabetes care and may increase compliance. The effects on other outcomes remain unknown. Conducting studies using intention-to-treat analyses could bridge existing research gaps, enhancing effect estimates and certainty. This Cochrane review was funded by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the UNDP-UNFPA-UNICEF-WHO-World Bank Special Programme of Research, Development and Research Training in Human Reproduction (HRP). Protocol available via PROSPERO: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251108692.

42953781.title: High-Grade Glioma Mimicking Eclampsia in Pregnancy: A Case Report.
42953781.abstract: Eclampsia is the most common cause of new-onset seizures after 20 weeks of gestation and requires immediate treatment. However, not all seizures in pregnancy are caused by hypertensive disorders, and structural intracranial lesions may present with similar clinical features. A 39-year-old primigravida at 25+6 weeks' gestation presented to Prashanth Super Speciality Hospital with severe hypertension (200/100 mmHg), proteinuria, altered sensorium, and recurrent generalized tonic-clonic seizures. She was initially managed as eclampsia with suspected posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). Owing to maternal instability, an emergency lower-segment caesarean section was performed. Persistent neurological impairment after delivery prompted neuroimaging. Computed tomography demonstrated a left frontal intracerebral haemorrhage, while magnetic resonance imaging revealed a haemorrhagic left frontal mass with surrounding oedema, midline shift, and PRES-like imaging features. Following urgent neurosurgical intervention, the patient underwent left frontal craniotomy and complete tumour excision. Histopathological examination confirmed a high-grade glioma. The patient recovered well postoperatively and was referred to the neuro-oncology team and subsequently underwent adjuvant radiotherapy and chemotherapy. The neonate was delivered at 25+6 weeks' gestation and died on day 2 of life despite neonatal intensive care. This case demonstrates that structural brain tumours may closely mimic eclampsia, even in the presence of severe hypertension and proteinuria. Persistent neurological abnormalities following standard treatment for eclampsia should prompt urgent neuroimaging to exclude underlying intracranial pathology. Early multidisciplinary collaboration between obstetricians, critical care specialists, radiologists, neurologists, neurosurgeons, neonatologists, and oncologists is essential to optimise maternal outcomes.

42927117.title: Perioperative Management of Decompensated Peripartum Cardiomyopathy With Severe Left Ventricular Dysfunction: A Case Report.
42927117.abstract: Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a potentially life-threatening cause of heart failure that may be difficult to distinguish from the physiological symptoms of pregnancy. We report the case of a 42-year-old woman at 34 weeks of gestation who presented with progressive dyspnea and was found to have severe global left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of approximately 20%. Despite initial improvement with diuresis, she developed recurrent acute decompensated heart failure requiring intensive care unit readmission. Point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) demonstrated pulmonary congestion and reduced forward flow, with a left ventricular outflow tract velocity-time integral (LVOT VTI) of 10 cm. Following hemodynamic optimization with diuresis and inotropic support, cesarean delivery was performed under general anesthesia with invasive monitoring and titrated vasoactive support. Postoperatively, LVOT VTI increased to 15 cm with corresponding clinical improvement. This case highlights the value of serial hemodynamic assessment, including POCUS, and multidisciplinary perioperative management in severe PPCM with recurrent decompensation.

42923278.title: Development and internal validation of explainable machine learning models for predicting failure of first ambulation within 12 h after cesarean delivery: A retrospective cohort study.
42923278.abstract: Early ambulation is a notable component of postoperative recovery after cesarean delivery, but some women fail to complete first ambulation within the early postoperative period because of pain, dizziness, orthostatic discomfort, residual lower limb numbness, nausea or vomiting, hypotension or poor activity tolerance. Early identification of women at high risk of ambulation failure may support timely and individualized nursing interventions. The present study aimed to develop and internally validate explainable machine learning models for predicting failure of first ambulation within 12 h after cesarean delivery using routinely collected obstetric perioperative nursing assessment data. The present single-center retrospective cohort study included relatively stable women who underwent cesarean delivery between January 2022 and December 2025 and were considered clinically eligible for early mobilization. The primary outcome was failure of first ambulation within 12 h after surgery, defined as no documented successful ambulation within 12 h or discontinuation of an ambulation attempt because of nursing-documented intolerance. Candidate predictors included demographic, obstetric, pregnancy-related, laboratory, anesthetic, surgical and early postoperative nursing assessment variables. Postoperative symptoms and vital signs were assessed within predefined early postoperative intervals, whereas first turning time was treated as a dynamically updated indicator that became available when the first spontaneous or assisted turning event was documented. The model was therefore interpreted as a dynamic early postoperative risk-assessment approach rather than a prediction model applied exclusively at a fixed 4-h time point. The final analytic dataset contained no item-level missing values; therefore, no imputation was performed. The cohort was randomly divided into training and internal validation cohorts at a ratio of 7:3. Logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and LightGBM models were developed and compared. Model performance was assessed using discrimination, classification metrics, calibration, Brier score and decision curve analysis. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was used to interpret the final model. A total of 1,486 women were included, and 326 women experienced failure of first ambulation within 12 h, with an incidence of 21.9%. The training and validation cohorts included 1,040 and 446 women, respectively. In the validation cohort, LightGBM achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.809 and a Brier score of 0.132, whereas XGBoost achieved an AUC of 0.805 and a Brier score of 0.134. The paired DeLong test showed no statistically significant difference between the validation AUCs of the two models (P=0.647). XGBoost achieved higher sensitivity, negative predictive value and F1 score than LightGBM (0.714 vs. 0.653, 0.906 vs. 0.892 and 0.567 vs. 0.561, respectively). Because these metrics were particularly relevant to identifying high-risk women and minimizing missed high-risk cases, XGBoost was selected as the final model. Calibration curves showed acceptable agreement between predicted and observed risks, and decision curve analysis demonstrated net benefit across relevant threshold probabilities. The 10 highest-ranked predictors according to mean absolute SHAP value were postoperative pain NRS score at 2 h, emergency cesarean delivery, time to first documented turning, lower limb numbness within 0-4 h, systolic blood pressure at 2 h, body mass index, preoperative hemoglobin, age, intraoperative fluid volume and dizziness or orthostatic discomfort within 0-4 h. In conclusion, in the present single-center retrospective cohort of relatively stable women considered clinically eligible for early mobilization, the explainable XGBoost model showed promising internal performance for predicting failure of first ambulation within 12 h after cesarean delivery. The model should not be extrapolated to women transferred to intensive care, women with severe postpartum hemorrhage, women with explicit medical restrictions on ambulation or women with severe postoperative complications. These findings support further evaluation but do not establish clinical utility, transportability or readiness for implementation. Temporal and external validation, followed by prospective assessment of workflow feasibility and clinical impact, is required before clinical use can be considered.

42909174.title: Cost-Utility and Clinical Impact of a Multicomponent Maternal Safety and High-Dependency Care Model in Three Colombian Caribbean Hospitals: A Before-and-After Study.
42909174.abstract: Background: Obstetric high-dependency units may improve rescue care when embedded within broader maternal safety strategies. Objective: To evaluate a multi-component maternal safety and technological strengthening model, including obstetric high-dependency capacity, across three Colombian Caribbean institutions with different governance models. Methods: We conducted a multisite before-and-after implementation evaluation within a Ministry-funded maternal safety project. The model was implemented in one private clinic and two public hospitals in La Guajira and Bolívar, Colombia, with staggered implementation and varying data maturity. Data sources included billing records, administrative databases, and monthly quality indicators. Costs, severe maternal morbidity indicators, and longitudinal quality metrics were analysed by institutional implementation window. Pandemic-period variation from 2018 to 2023 was treated descriptively. Interrupted time series analyses were performed where post-implementation data allowed. Findings: Implementation was associated with heterogeneous but generally favourable patterns. At Clínica CEDES, costs increased after implementation, while intensive care utilisation and several severe maternal morbidity indicators declined. At ESE Hospital San José de Maicao, mature post-implementation economic and conventional pre/post-clinical comparisons were unavailable; however, interrupted time series analyses showed favourable changes in longitudinal quality indicators, including reductions in weighted adverse outcome score (WAOS) level (β = -8.30, P = 0.0016) and slope (β = -1.20, P = 0.0064), adverse outcome index (AOI) level (β = -1.13, P = 0.0032), and severity index (SI) slope (β = -0.27, P = 0.030). ESE Hospital La Divina Misericordia showed mixed early clinical signals and descriptive quality improvement, but follow-up was limited. Conclusions: A multi-component maternal safety model including obstetric high-dependency capacity may improve maternal care in high-risk settings, although effects vary by institutional context. High-dependency units appear most effective as part of an integrated rescue system rather than isolated infrastructure.

42900860.title: Progesterone Receptor Antagonists for Labor Induction: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
42900860.abstract: To evaluate mifepristone, a progesterone receptor antagonist, for labor induction and cesarean delivery and related measures of maternal and neonatal safety. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials was conducted in accordance with PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses) 2020 guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251236886). MEDLINE, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Scopus were searched through October 2025. Eligible studies included randomized trials evaluating mifepristone for labor induction in singleton pregnancies at 37 weeks or more of gestation. Studies involving pregnancy termination, intrauterine fetal death, preterm induction, or concomitant cervical ripening interventions in which the effects of mifepristone could not be isolated were excluded. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. The primary outcome was cesarean delivery. Secondary outcomes included induction-to-delivery interval, time to labor onset, Bishop score, need for prostaglandin or oxytocin, postpartum hemorrhage, neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission, and 5-minute Apgar score less than 7. Data were pooled with a random-effects model. The primary analysis included all 15 eligible randomized controlled trials across mifepristone dosing regimens (n=1,063) and control conditions (n=811). Mifepristone was associated with 33% reduced odds of cesarean delivery (33.1% vs 41.9%, odds ratio 0.67, 95% CI, 0.54-0.82) compared with the control method of induction. Mifepristone was associated with higher Bishop scores at 24 hours, shorter induction-to-delivery intervals, and less prostaglandin and oxytocin use compared with control methods. Findings were similar in sensitivity analysis limited to placebo-controlled and high-quality trials (cesarean delivery odds ratio 0.58, 95% CI, 0.40-0.83). No differences were observed in postpartum hemorrhage, NICU admission, or low Apgar score, although most studies did not report these outcomes. Use of mifepristone for labor induction was associated with reduced odds of cesarean delivery, as well as improved cervical ripening and labor induction efficiency. No evidence of short-term maternal or neonatal risk was found, although robust data were limited. Findings support the role of progesterone antagonists for labor induction. PROSPERO, CRD420251236886.

42962864.title: Implementation and Impacts of Maternal and Perinatal Quality Collaboratives across U.S. States: A Scoping Review.
42962864.abstract: Maternal and Perinatal Quality Care Collaboratives (M/PQCs) are voluntary state-based initiatives that leverage shared data systems, evidence-based toolkits, and quality improvement science to reduce preventable maternal and infant harm. A scoping review of academic and grey literature was conducted following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, and registered in Open Science Framework. Seven databases were searched for U.S.-based M/PQC studies published between January 2000 - November 2024, analyzed in 2025. Two independent reviewers screened 456 deduplicated records; 31 met eligibility criteria. Quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Findings were synthesized narratively, organized by implementation theme and intervention topic. Thirty-one studies spanning 16 states and one national analysis were included. Five themes were identified across two domains.
