42960828.title: The secretory life of pets: bites from western hognose snakes reported to the California Poison Control System.
42960828.abstract: The western hognose snake (Heterodon nasicus) is a popular pet reptile. While sometimes classified as nonvenomous, it produces mildly toxic saliva from a low-pressure secretory organ in the temporal region (Duvernoy's gland), causing local reactions following snakebites. We aim to review cases from a statewide poison control system to characterize clinical effects and outcomes. This is a 10-year retrospective review of calls about western hognose snakebite to the California Poison Control System, using product-substance codes and a free-text keyword search. Demographic, clinical, and bite-circumstance data were summarized and analyzed. There were 35 cases from January 2016 to March 2026, ranging from 11 to 82 years (median 22; IQR 18-29 years), of whom 69% were female and 46% were aged 21 years or younger. A large majority (89%) were bitten by their own pets; one bite occurred at a reptile exposition. All bites affected the hands, typically during feeding, handling, or enclosure cleaning. Local swelling occurred in 91% of cases, with extension to the wrist or forearm in 43%. Skin changes (ecchymosis, erythema or blistering) were noted in 26%, and 6% developed nausea and vomiting. Vital signs and labs, checked in 23% and 11% of cases respectively, were unremarkable. Management typically included wound care, tetanus vaccination update, and anticipatory guidance for infectious complications. Two patients required hospitalization for two or more days for treatment of presumed cellulitis. In one case with extensive edema, rattlesnake antivenom was administered due to doubts about the reported bite history; in the second case, antivenom was recommended for similar reasons, but withheld after photographic identification confirmed the pet snake. The western hognose snakebite can cause cytotoxic edema, and prolonged bites may pose a higher risk of severe injury. Clinical care should focus on pain control, wound care, and anticipatory guidance for post-bite infection and hypersensitivity reactions due to the components of snake saliva, which may require specific treatment with antibiotics or anti-inflammatory medications. Rattlesnake antivenom has no role in managing this type of snakebite. Western hognose envenomation can lead to mild to moderate soft tissue injuries, which require supportive and symptomatic care and, rarely, hospital admission. Many bites occurred in pet owner adolescents, who may benefit from preventive safety education.

42958645.title: Clinician-guided digital CBT-I improves sleep quality and apnea severity in patients with co-morbid insomnia and OSA: A Double-Blind, Randomized Clinical Trial.
42958645.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
42958645.abstract: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the accepted first-line treatment for insomnia, but its scalability and safety in patients with co-morbid insomnia and obstructive sleep apnea (COMISA) remain unclear. Clinician-guided digital CBT-I (D-CBT-I) is a potential treatment option that may address these limitations in COMISA. To evaluate the effectiveness of clinician-guided D-CBT-I versus sleep hygiene education (SHE) in patients with COMISA. This randomized trial (n = 88) compared clinician-guided D-CBT-I (6 weekly online sessions: sleep restriction, sleep hygiene, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, relapse prevention) with SHE alone. Blinded outcome assessments were conducted at baseline, posttreatment (6 weeks), and 3-month follow-up. Primary outcomes were Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores at posttreatment and 3-month follow-up. Secondary outcomes included daytime sleepiness, sleep parameters, OSA severity, neurocognitive function, and adverse events. At 3-month follow-up, intention-to-treat analysis showed significantly greater improvements with D-CBT-I versus SHE on ISI (-9.5 vs. -4.0 points; d = -1.18, P = 0.001) and PSQI (-4.9 vs. -1.8 points; d = -0.87, P = 0.001); D-CBT-I also reduced subjective sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale; -3.4 vs. -1.0 points; d = -0.68, P < 0.001). At posttreatment, D-CBT-I reduced the apnea-hypopnea index (attended in-laboratory polysomnography; -6.0 vs. +2.0 events/h; d = -0.64, P = 0.019). Although transient increases in ESS occurred at weeks 2-4, no functional impairment or sleepiness-related adverse events were reported. Additional benefits were observed in metacognition and executive function. Clinician-guided D-CBT-I improved insomnia and OSA severity, and enhanced cognitive function in COMISA patients. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry; NO.: ChiCTR2500099854; URL: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=267457.

42957871.title: Adjustment for Early Care and the Estimated Effect of Initial Treatment at a Neurosurgery-Capable Facility.

42957870.title: Response to "Adjustment for Early Care and the Estimated Effect of Initial Treatment at a Neurosurgery-Capable Facility".

42823013.title: When No ICU Bed is Available: Critical Care Services in the Emergency Department.
42823013.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
42823013.abstract: This review article, focused on the care of the critically ill adult when no intensive care unit (ICU) bed is available, describes current models addressing critical care services in the emergency department (ED), reviews available evidence on the impact of different approaches, and explores best practices in implementation of ED-ICU models. Based on these findings, the article explores potential benefits of leveraging the ED-ICU concept in the regional organization of critical care services.

42819316.title: Emergency Critical Care as a Continuum: The All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) Three-Tiered Framework for the Assessment and Management of Critically Ill Patients in the Emergency Department.
42819316.abstract: Emergency critical care (ECC) is increasingly recognized as an indispensable component of the critical care continuum, beginning at the point of first medical contact in the emergency department (ED). As critically ill patients spend longer periods in the ED and emergency physicians assume an expanding role in providing ongoing critical care, existing assessment frameworks may not fully address the evolving cognitive demands of ECC. This article describes a conceptual three-tier framework intended to provide a pragmatic strategy for the assessment and management of critically ill patients throughout their ED course. The framework was conceived and implemented at All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Rishikesh. The framework aligns patient assessment and management with three complementary clinical priorities. Tier 1 emphasizes physiological rescue through simultaneous assessment and stabilization using an expanded ABCDEF approach, with a focus on identifying and managing immediately life-threatening and time-sensitive conditions. Following initial stabilization, Tier 2 focuses on diagnostic reasoning, integrating clinical evaluation to establish an ED working diagnosis and guide subsequent management. Tier 3 addresses longitudinal ECC through structured reassessment, optimization of organ support, diagnostic refinement, and prevention of secondary complications while patients remain under ED care. Although presented as three sequential tiers for conceptual clarity, the framework is intended to be dynamic and iterative, allowing movement between tiers according to the patient's evolving clinical status. By integrating principles of emergency medicine and critical care, this conceptual framework provides a cognitive scaffold for clinicians managing critically ill patients in the ED and may support continuity of care, education, and quality improvement. As the framework is currently conceptual, further studies are required to evaluate its feasibility and potential impact on patient outcomes.

42823129.title: A historical irony-quantitative measurement in critically ill patients is not a panacea.

42823123.title: Interpreting EVERDAC: Deferring arterial cannulation in critically ill patients with shock.
42823123.abstract: Patients admitted to the intensive care unit with shock do not automatically need to have an arterial catheter inserted immediately. This is the main take-away point from the Early Versus Deferred Arterial Catheterization in Critically Ill Patients With Acute Circulatory Failure (EVERDAC) trial, which found that slightly fewer patients died in a group randomly assigned to not have an arterial catheter inserted unless it was truly needed, compared with putting one in immediately. This result easily met the trial's predefined criterion for noninferiority of deferring arterial catheterization, and it challenges our standard practice.

42819136.title: Clinical outcomes and their relationship with tigecycline exposure in critically ill patients with drug resistant infections.
42819136.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
42819136.abstract: Dosing tigecycline, an important last resort for carbapenem-resistant organisms, should be under the guidance of pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) theory. However, tigecycline has shown large interindividual variability in PK among different patients, and its PK/PD target has limited data support. This study aimed to evaluate the clinical outcome and the relationship with exposure in critically ill patients with drug-resistant infections. A single center, prospective observational, single-arm cohort study was performed to assess the outcome and its relationship with exposure in critically ill patients with drug-resistant pathogen infections. Patients were enrolled according to the inclusion and exclusion criteria. The clinical outcomes, including clinical response rate, 28-day mortality rate, and major adverse events (AEs), were followed up. Plasma concentrations in steady status were intensively collected and determined for tigecycline concentration, and the 24-hour area-under-curves (AUCs) were calculated. The exposure-clinical outcome relationship was analyzed, and multivariate logistic regressions were performed to identify risk factors that associated with outcome. A total of 130 patients were included. The most common infection type was low respiratory tract infection (76/130), and carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii was the most common pathogen (64/130). The median tigecycline treatment length was 12 days. The median AUC was 14.0 mg h/L. The overall response rate and 28-day mortality rate were 50.0% and 36.2%, respectively. A lower fibrinogen level was the most common AE (51/130). ALB, PLT and combined use of cefoperazone-sulbactam were independent factors associated with clinical response, but AUC was negatively associated with clinical response. The clinical outcome of tigecycline in critically ill patients with resistant pathogen infection was satisfactory, but negative relationship between tigecycline exposure and outcome was found and the PK/PD profile in these patients should be revisited.

42823015.title: Managing the Critically Ill Postpartum Patient in the Emergency Department.
42823015.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
42823015.abstract: This review article prepares emergency physicians to recognize and manage critical illness in postpartum patients, a population at heightened risk of preventable morbidity and mortality in North America amid persistent racial/geographic disparities and shrinking obstetric access. It highlights key physiologic changes after delivery that complicate patient management. The article focuses on 3 immediate postpartum emergencies (postpartum hemorrhage, postpartum preeclampsia, and amniotic fluid embolism) and 3 subacute (pulmonary embolism, peripartum cardiomyopathy, and spontaneous coronary artery dissection). It concludes with system-level strategies to improve safety and outcomes.

42823006.title: Modern Approach to Vascular Access in the Critically Ill Patient.
42823006.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
42823006.abstract: Vascular access is a key intervention in the management of critically ill emergency department patients. This can include peripheral or central venous access and intraosseous access. In combination with arterial catheterization, central venous access can provide key information to guide volume and vasoactive medication titration in isolation as well as in combination with dynamic measures of fluid responsiveness. This article will review the indications and contraindications as well as decision-making for the use of these modalities in light of the current evidence.

42823007.title: Safely Transferring the Critically Ill Patient out of Your Emergency Department.
42823007.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America
42823007.abstract: Regionalized systems of care increasingly rely on critical care transport (CCT) to move high-acuity patients to centers with specialized resources. This article outlines the complex clinical, operational, and ethical considerations that shape interfacility transport, emphasizing the need for deliberate risk-benefit assessment, patient optimization, and clear communication among sending clinicians, transport teams, and receiving facilities. Variability in CCT team training, capabilities, and staffing models requires clinicians to understand regional resources. By applying systems-based thinking and the "right patient, right time, right team, right place" framework, clinicians can ensure safe, equitable, high-quality transport within regionalized care networks.

42820512.title: Limited prognostic value of the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio compared with severity scores for mortality prediction in elderly critically ill patients.

42823304.title: Continuous vs intermittent meropenem administration in critically ill patients and renal function. A secondary post-hoc analysis of the MERCY trial.
42823304.abstract: In septic patients renal function changes are common, potentially affecting antibiotic therapies. Time-dependent antibiotics, administered as continuous infusion, can improve the time above the minimal inhibitory concentration, but the relationship between meropenem administration strategy and renal function remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate such relationship for a composite primary outcome of 28-day mortality and emergence of pandrug (PDR) or extensively drug-resistant (XDR) pathogens. Secondary aims were to investigate the impact of renal function on clinical and microbiological outcomes, regardless of meropenem administration strategy. Secondary analysis of the MERCY randomized controlled trial (Continuous Infusion versus Intermittent Administration of MERopenem in CriticallY Ill Patients). Thirty-one ICUs in 4 countries. MERCY patients with available estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Meropenem administration as continuous infusion or intermittent boluses. eGFR, mortality, PDR/XDR pathogens. Among MERCY patients, eGFR was available at randomization for 586 patients: 311 had an eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73m2, 181 between 60-129 ml/min/1.73m2, and 94 patients ≥130 ml/min/1.73m2. Meropenem administration strategy did not affect the primary outcome across eGFR categories (p for interaction = 0.60). Considering renal subgroups regardless of randomization arm, patients with eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73m2 had a lower incidence of new XDR/PDR pathogens compared with the normal renal function group (adjusted RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.95, p = 0.026). Among the MERCY population, there was no benefit from meropenem continuous infusion or intermittent boluses in any renal function subgroup. Having a lower eGFR was associated with a reduced emergence of PDR/XDR pathogens.

42823018.title: Critical Care in the Emergency Department.
42823018.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

42820551.title: Beyond survival: the imperative, innovation, and implementation of long-term intensive care unit follow-up.

42819626.title: Organizational and Musculoskeletal Factors of Job Satisfaction and Work Ability Among Critical Care Nurses: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study.
42819626.abstract: Nursing shortage is a global challenge driven by the imbalance between the number of nurses entering and leaving the profession, with job satisfaction (JS) and work ability (WA) as key retention factors influenced by organizational and health conditions, including musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs). Although critical care nurses experience high MSDs, low JS, and reduced WA, their interrelationships remain underexplored. This multicenter cross-sectional study investigated individual, organizational, and musculoskeletal factors associated with JS and WA among intensive care unit (ICU) and emergency department (ED) nurses. Data were collected using a researcher-developed questionnaire assessing individual, organizational, and MSD-related variables, together with validated instruments assessing upper-limb disability and symptoms (DASH), Work Ability Index (WAI), and JS (COPSOQ II). Multivariable regression was performed. Participants reported moderate JS (3.4 ± 0.9) and good WA (41.3 ± 5.4). Lower JS was associated with ICU employment (β = -0.38, p = 0.005) and long shifts (β = -0.32, p = 0.003). Reduced WA was associated with chronic conditions (β = -3.14, p = 0.001), work adjustments (β = -2.58, p = 0.001), ICU employment (β = -1.38, p = 0.031), unit or role changes due to MSDs (β = -1.60, p = 0.015), and hip (β = -1.69, p = 0.009) or upper-limb MSDs (β = -1.41, p = 0.006). JS and WA were also significantly associated (β = 0.08 for WAI in the JS model; β = 2.22 for JS in the WAI model). A multidisciplinary, multilevel, and multicomponent approach may support JS and WA and inform strategies to reduce MSD-related burden and promote nurse retention.

42821861.title: A Relational Coordination Training Intervention to Improve Communication Among Health Care Professionals in the Intensive Care Unit: A Pilot Study.
42821861.journal: Dimensions of critical care nursing : DCCN
42821861.abstract: High-quality communication among interdisciplinary team members in the intensive care unit (ICU) is potentially a team's greatest asset or gravest shortcoming. Relational coordination (RC) is a framework to improve communication and the quality of care among health care professionals in various settings. Additional research is needed to determine whether an RC training intervention improves communication among health care professionals in the ICU. To explore whether a virtual RC training intervention improves communication among health care professionals in the ICU. We conducted a 2-group pilot study using a randomized controlled trial design in 4 ICUs. Participants in the intervention group participated in a single 1-hour virtual RC training intervention and completed surveys at baseline, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks after the RC training intervention. Only participants in the control group completed the surveys. We used a difference-in-difference model to investigate changes in RC scores. A total of 22 participants in the intervention group participated in the RC training intervention. Survey completion rates varied across data collection time points for both the intervention and control groups. The RC training intervention did not improve RC scores. Participants with associate degrees and African American/Black participants reported lower RC. A single RC training intervention may not be enough to influence communication or relationships within teams. Developing and testing educational interventions to enhance interprofessional communication and function through RC is key to improving communication and quality of care. Future investigators can glean lessons learned from our pilot study to design a more comprehensive study.

42819383.title: Dynamic changes in quadriceps and diaphragm thickness for early diagnosis of ICU-acquired weakness in elderly ICU patients: a prospective bedside ultrasound study.
42819383.abstract: To investigate the value of bedside ultrasound in dynamically monitoring quadriceps and diaphragm thickness for early diagnosis of ICU-acquired weakness (ICU-AW) in elderly critically ill patients. This prospective observational study enrolled elderly patients (aged ≥60 years) with an expected ICU stay of ≥7 days. Bedside ultrasound was performed on days 1 (D1), 3, 5, and 7 after ICU admission to measure rectus femoris cross-sectional area (RF-CSA), rectus femoris muscle layer thickness (RF-MLT), vastus intermedius muscle layer thickness (VI-MLT), end-inspiratory diaphragm thickness (DTei), and end-expiratory diaphragm thickness (DTee). Muscle strength was assessed using the Medical Research Council (MRC) sum score. The rates of change of each parameter were compared between the ICU-AW group (MRC ≤ 48) and non-ICU-AW group. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were used to evaluate predictive performance. Of 74 enrolled patients, 52 (70.3%) developed ICU-AW. No significant differences in baseline ultrasound parameters were found between groups. The rate of change of RF-MLT on D5 and D7 and the rate of change of DTee on D7 were significantly different between groups (P = 0.049, 0.021, and 0.009, respectively). The rate of change of DTee on D7 showed the strongest negative correlation with MRC score (r = -0.413, P < 0.001). ROC analysis showed that the D7 relative change in DTee had the numerically highest AUC (0.693, 95% CI: 0.556-0.830), with an optimal cutoff value of a decrease ≥6.07% (sensitivity 73.1%, specificity 59.1%), while RF-MLT yielded an AUC of 0.672 with a cutoff value of a decrease ≥3.45% (sensitivity 50.0%, specificity 86.4%). However, the difference between the two AUCs was small (0.021) and not formally tested, and the low specificity (59.1%) limits its clinical utility. Progressive quadriceps and diaphragm atrophy occurs early in elderly ICU patients. The D7 relative change in DTee showed the numerically highest AUC among the evaluated parameters, suggesting modest discriminatory ability for ICU-AW and warranting further validation. Dynamic muscle ultrasound monitoring is feasible and reproducible at the bedside.

42823019.title: Critical Care in the Emergency Department: A Dynamic Practice with Many Pivots Along the Way.
42823019.journal: Emergency medicine clinics of North America

42821098.title: [Interdisciplinary training concept for evacuation of intensive care patients in fire events : Development, implementation and first experiences from a simulation exercise].
42821098.abstract: Fires in intensive care units (ICU) are rare but pose unique challenges due to patients' limited mobility, dependence on life-sustaining treatment, complex medical equipment and oxygen-enriched environments. Conventional evacuation strategies are often inadequate for critically ill patients requiring intensive care. Development and evaluation of an interdisciplinary training concept for the evacuation of critically ill ICU patients during fire emergencies involving both fire service personnel and hospital staff. In this single-center exploratory simulation study, a 6-module training program was developed following a structured hazard analysis. The contents included critical care medical principles, medical devices, crew resource management, hospital layout and evacuation planning, medical equipment management and simulation-based training. Subsequently, a realistic evacuation exercise involving firefighters, intensive care nursing personnel and physicians was conducted using two complex ICU patient scenarios. The primary endpoint was the successful evacuation of all patients. Both simulated patients were successfully evacuated in all simulation runs. The mean evacuation time to reach the next safe fire compartment was 4 min 5 s, while an additional firefighting water supply was established after a mean of 3 min 15 s. Only one minor technical error was observed; no relevant disconnection of life support devices or interruptions of patient care occurred. The interdisciplinary training concept enabled the safe and feasible evacuation of critically ill ICU patients under realistic fire conditions. Regular joint simulation training involving fire service personnel and hospital staff, together with standardized evacuation protocols, could substantially improve patient safety and emergency preparedness in intensive care units.

42820521.title: General intermediate care units: can they effectively support intensive care units and ensure patient safety?

42902627.title: Temperature Effects on Large Language Model-Generated Clinical Reports in Critical Care: A Pilot Post Hoc Study.
42902627.abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) can generate case-specific clinical guidance informed by SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-driven intensive care unit (ICU) mortality risk. Temperature is a key adjustable setting that influences output variability and determinism. We evaluated whether adjusting temperature affects the quality and interpretability of GPT-4o clinical reports, and whether similar effects appear in the smaller GPT-4o-mini. Methods: Thirty ICU cases were selected from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV, version 3.1) database, equally distributed across low, moderate, and high mortality risk groups. SHAP values and predicted risks were provided to GPT-4o using three prompting strategies (P1, P2, and P3) at three temperature settings (0.2, 0.6, and 1.0). We evaluated report quality using the IMPACT (Integration, Mastery, Precision, Applicability, Comprehensiveness, and Timeliness) framework and noted differences across report sections. We also tested GPT-4o-mini under the same conditions for comparison. Results: Only the multi-turn prompting strategy (P3) exhibited improved report quality at higher temperatures, with especially noticeable gains in sections such as Interpretation of Risk Factors. No significant temperature-related changes were observed under P1 or P2 in GPT-4o. In GPT-4o-mini, report quality remained consistent across all temperature settings, demonstrating that the beneficial effects of temperature modulation are evident only in higher-capacity models with sufficient reasoning capability. Conclusion: Temperature tuning in high-capacity LLMs like GPT-4o enhances the richness and precision of clinical reports without sacrificing clarity, offering a pragmatic means to improve support for critical care documentation.

42944085.title: Efficacy and Safety of Adoptive BK Polyomavirus-Reactive T-Cell Therapy for Active Infection or Disease in Transplant Recipients: A Systematic Review.
42944085.abstract: BK polyomavirus (BKPyV) causes haemorrhagic cystitis (HC) after allogeneic haematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) and nephropathy (BKPyVAN) after kidney transplantation, with no antiviral of established efficacy. We evaluated the clinical activity and treatment-emergent safety of adoptively administered BKPyV-reactive T cells. PubMed, Europe PMC and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched to 1 September 2026 with citation checking; full-length reports of therapeutic infusion were eligible and prophylaxis-only reports excluded, following PRISMA 2020 and SWiM. Twenty-two reports (about eighteen analytic datasets) were included, and overlapping publications linked and not summed. Fifteen independent cohorts contributed 241 evaluable recipients, of whom 178 (73.9%) responded by their own definitions (pooled proportion 87%, 95% CI 73 to 97; I2 = 70%). Response did not follow the expected phenotype gradient (69.1% HC, 70.0% DNAemia, 75.0% BKPyVAN, overlapping intervals), and organ-level outcomes diverged: haematuria or cystitis resolved in 19 of 25 (76.0%), whereas no cohort documented consistent renal recovery once nephropathy was established. In the only placebo-controlled trial, more kidney recipients achieved a week-24 viral load decline with biweekly posoleucel than placebo, but three placebo-controlled posoleucel trials after HCT, including a phase III HC trial of 97 participants, were discontinued in December 2023 for futility without safety concerns. Acute graft-versus-host disease ranged from 0% to 25% (4.0% BKPyV-restricted, 12.2% whole-cohort denominators), rejection occurred in 4 of 69 (5.8%) exposed kidney recipients versus 0 of 19 on placebo, and one fatal cytokine-release syndrome was reported. BKPyV-reactive T cells show reproducible virological activity and acceptable short-term tolerability, but overlapping, mostly uncontrolled evidence does not establish comparative clinical efficacy or graft benefit. Development should target persistent DNAemia after failed reduction in immunosuppression and before irreversible fibrosis.

42883713.title: Fibroblast Growth Factors and Their Receptors in Major Depressive Disorder: A Scoping Review of Translational Research.
42883713.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a complex psychiatric condition whose pathophysiology extends beyond the classic monoamine hypothesis, involving impaired neuroplasticity, neuroinflammation, HPA axis dysregulation, and altered neurotrophic signaling. The fibroblast growth factor (FGF) system, comprising ligands and their receptors (FGFRs), has emerged as a key candidate regulator of these processes. This scoping review qualitatively synthesizes current clinical, postmortem, and preclinical evidence on the role of the FGF system in MDD and antidepressant response. A structured literature search according to PRISMA-ScR was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus without date restrictions. Eligible studies included human (clinical, postmortem), preclinical, and translational data investigating FGF/FGFR expression, signaling, manipulation, or peripheral biomarker associations in the context of depression or antidepressant action. Of 287 unique records screened, 68 met the inclusion criteria; together with 11 studies identified through backward citation searching, 79 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. This synthesis outlines a bidirectional role for the fibroblast growth factor (FGF) system in major depressive disorder (MDD). Rather than acting as a uniform pathway, different FGF ligands exert opposing regulatory effects on mood, neuroplasticity, and stress responses. FGF-2 exerts protective and neurotrophic effects, while factors like FGF-9 act as endogenous prodepressants. Although circulating biomarkers show heterogeneity, central FGF/FGFR signaling represents a promising target for novel therapeutic strategies and personalized treatment approaches in MDD.

42818950.title: Placental Pathology in preeclampsia and gestational hypertension; A comparative study.
42818950.abstract: To evaluate placental histopathological lesions in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and their association with maternal and fetal outcomes. This cross-sectional study was conducted in the Departments of Pathology and Gynecology & Obstetrics, Dow Hospital, Dow University of Health Sciences, from January-December 2021. Seventy-six pregnant women were included: preeclampsia (n=29), gestational hypertension (n=24), and normotensive controls (n=23). Placentae were examined microscopically, and lesions were classified according to the Amsterdam criteria into maternal vascular malperfusion (MVM), fetal vascular malperfusion (FVM), and inflammatory lesions. Association with clinical group was assessed by Poisson regression analysis, expressed as incidence rate ratio (IRR). Placental lesion categories were significantly different across the clinical groups (p=0.018). MVM lesions, including accelerated villous maturation, distal villous hypoplasia, villous infarction, decidual arteriopathy, and low fetal-to-placental weight ratio, were increased in preeclampsia (IRR=4.4, p<0.001) and gestational hypertension (IRR=2.5, p=0.005). FVM showed no association. Inflammatory lesions demonstrated a borderline association with preeclampsia (IRR=3.2, p=0.039). Adverse maternal outcomes (eclampsia, ICU admission) and fetal outcomes (low birthweight, NICU admission, stillbirth) were significantly frequent in preeclampsia (p=0.002). Maternal vascular lesions were significantly increased, with a 4.4-fold increase in preeclampsia and a 2.5-fold increase in gestational hypertension, compared with normotensive pregnancies. These findings highlight the central role of maternal vascular pathology in the pathogenesis of hypertensive disorders and adverse maternal and fetal outcomes. We recommend high-quality antenatal care for early detection of hypertensive disorders and placental histopathology as a valuable diagnostic tool.

42967869.title: The Mediating Role of Self-Efficacy in the Relationship Between Knowledge and Palliative Care Practices Among ICU Nurses in Timor-Leste: A Cross-Sectional Study.
42967869.abstract: Access to palliative care remains limited in low- and middle-income countries, including Timor-Leste, where healthcare systems face structural and resource constraints. In intensive care units (ICUs), nurses play a critical role in delivering PC. However, the translation of knowledge into clinical practice remains inconsistent. Self-efficacy has been proposed as a key psychological mechanism that may bridge this gap. This study aimed to examine the mediating role of self-efficacy in the relationship between knowledge and palliative care practices among ICU nurses in Timor-Leste. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 107 ICU nurses. Data were collected using convenience sampling with validated instruments: the Palliative Care Knowledge Test (PCKT), the Self-Efficacy in Palliative Care Scale (PCSE-S), and the Palliative Care Self-Reported Practices Scale (PCPS). Rasch analysis was applied to transform ordinal data into interval-level measures. Pearson correlation and regression-based mediation analyses were performed using Jamovi. A total of 107 ICU nurses participated in this study. The mean Rasch person measures were 0.515 (SD = 0.985) for palliative care practice, 0.136 (SD = 1.210) for self-efficacy, and -2.623 (SD = 0.973) for knowledge. Knowledge was significantly associated with self-efficacy (β = 0.316, p < 0.001), while self-efficacy was significantly associated with palliative care practice (β = 0.514, p < 0.001). In contrast, knowledge was not directly associated with palliative care practice (β = 0.0002, p = 0.998). Mediation analysis using bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals demonstrated a significant indirect effect of knowledge on palliative care practice through self-efficacy (β = 0.163, p = 0.003, 95% BC CI [0.0548, 0.365]), indicating that self-efficacy significantly mediated the relationship between knowledge and palliative care practice. Self-efficacy may represent an important pathway linking palliative care knowledge with practice among ICU nurses. Interventions may consider strengthening both palliative care knowledge and self-efficacy, particularly in resource-limited ICU settings. Nursing education and clinical practice should incorporate strategies that strengthen nurses' self-efficacy alongside palliative care knowledge. Practice-based training, simulation, clinical mentoring, and supportive supervision may help nurses apply their knowledge more confidently in palliative care delivery, particularly in resource-limited ICU settings.

42966647.title: Effects of Skin Pigmentation on Pulse Oximetry: A Pilot Study.
42966647.journal: American journal of critical care : an official publication, American Association of Critical-Care Nurses
42966647.abstract: Pulse oximetry is an essential, noninvasive tool in critical care, yet mounting evidence indicates that readings may be inaccurate in patients with darker skin pigmentation. These discrepancies can delay recognition of hypoxemia and contribute to racial disparities in clinical outcomes. To quantify the difference between oxygen saturation as measured by pulse oximetry and arterial blood gas measurements across a spectrum of skin pigmentation using objective measures of melanin and skin tone. A prospective observational study was conducted in an adult critical care unit. Skin pigmentation was measured using reflectance spectrophotometry. Simultaneous pulse oximetry and arterial blood gas readings were collected during routine arterial blood gas sampling. Bias (pulse oximetry value - arterial blood gas value) was calculated for each measurement pair. Multivariate linear regression models were used to assess the association between skin pigmentation and measurement bias, adjusting for potential confounders such as age, sex, and perfusion index. Forty-two measurement pairs were analyzed. A weak and nonsignificant relationship was found between the individual typology angle and melanin index and the difference between pulse oximetry and arterial blood gas measures. Individual typology angle and melanin index are not strong predictors of the difference in oxygen readings between pulse oximeters and arterial blood gas measurements, even in critically ill patients. The weak fit of all models and the lack of statistical significance indicate that other unmeasured factors may play a more substantial role in explaining the variability.

42968274.title: Beyond casemix: identifying an unpriced ICU cost driver in Victorian public hospitals.
42968274.journal: Australian health review : a publication of the Australian Hospital Association
42968274.abstract: Australia's National Pricing Model (NPM) adjusts public hospital funding for type, size, location, and patient complexity, but whether these adjustments adequately address structural cost variation at the jurisdictional level remains unknown. This study aimed to identify exogenous structural attributes associated with case-mix adjusted cost variation in Victorian public hospitals, and assess the adequacy of their compensation under activity-based funding. A cross-sectional analysis of 1,934,946 inpatient episodes across 55 Victorian public hospital campuses (2024-25) was undertaken using linked administrative and cost data. Associations between 20 structural variables and cost per National Weighted Activity Unit (NWAU) were examined using Pearson/Spearman correlation, principal component analysis, and multivariable regression with HC3 heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors. After adjustment for multiple comparisons, four variables were significantly associated with cost variation: weekend admissions (r = -0.524), after-hours admissions (r = -0.422), hospital remoteness (ρ = 0.328), and medical officer ratio (r = -0.305). In multivariable modelling, ICU non-Level 3 hours was the only consistent independent predictor of higher costs (P = 0.020). ICU non-Level 3 episodes cost $13,187 per NWAU - a $4063 gap above the National Efficient Price (62.8%) and a $73.0 million annual shortfall - with no current NPM adjustment. This contrasts with the more complex Level 3 ICU episodes, which have a NPM adjustment and no shortfall. Structural cost variation in Victorian hospitals follows a two-tiered pattern. First, after-hours, weekend, and teaching-intensity variables appear consistent with current NWAU pricing, despite being individually associated with cost variation. Second, ICU non-Level 3 hours represent a potentially unpriced structural cost driver warranting further investigation.

42970370.title: Residency Features Linked to Family Medicine Graduates' Inpatient and Critical Care Practice: An Outcomes Project Study.
42970370.abstract: Family medicine residency programs equip graduates for diverse practice environments, including inpatient and critical care medicine. Understanding how residency program characteristics correlate with graduates' hospital-based practice is crucial for workforce development. Our objective was to evaluate the correlation between residency program structures and curriculum with graduates caring for adult patients in hospital and critical care settings. We conducted a prospective cohort study of family medicine graduates using the 2018 Council of Academic Family Medicine Educational Research Alliance program director survey to measure program characteristics and curricular elements and the 2021 Family Medicine National Graduate Survey of residents who graduated in 2018 to measure the primary outcomes-practicing adult inpatient medicine and critical care medicine. Of 752 respondents, 37.5% reported practicing inpatient medicine and 19.1% providing critical care. Multivariate analysis revealed metropolitan practice location (OR 0.53; 95% CI 0.33-0.85) and presence of an internal medicine program (OR 0.41; 95% CI 0.26-0.66) were associated with lower odds of practicing inpatient medicine. Nine or more months of inpatient medicine during residency was associated with higher odds of both inpatient (OR 1.59; 95% CI 1.10-2.29) and critical care practice (OR 1.92; 95% CI 1.23-3.02). For critical care practice, metropolitan location and having only family medicine attendings were associated with lower odds, while being from a single residency institution showed higher odds. Duration of inpatient medicine exposure and training environment are significantly associated with graduates practicing inpatient and critical care medicine. These findings can guide residency program design to meet workforce needs.

42968769.title: Junior Doctors' Perceptions of Critical Care Education in Medical School and the Association with Confidence in Core Clinical Skills: A Survey of Graduates in Queensland, Australia.
42968769.abstract: Confidence in critical care skills is essential for junior doctors. However, exposure to anaesthetics and critical care during medical school remains limited. This study evaluates how perceptions of undergraduate critical care teaching influence junior doctors' confidence in core clinical skills. A cross-sectional survey was distributed to junior doctors across Queensland, Australia. Quantitative data captured exposure to anaesthetics, perceived quality of teaching, and confidence in skills such as bag-mask ventilation (BMV) and pre-anaesthetic assessment. Qualitative data explored factors influencing career interest in critical care. Quantitative analysis was performed using chi-square testing, and qualitative responses underwent thematic analysis. Sixty junior doctors completed the survey. Most reported 0-2 weeks of anaesthetic placement, and 48.3% rated their teaching as "intermediate." Despite limited exposure, 61.7% reported confidence performing BMV, and 50% in pre-anaesthetic assessments. Higher perceived quality of teaching was significantly associated with greater confidence in BMV (p = 0.009) and pre-anaesthetic assessment (p = 0.008). Placement duration alone did not correlate with BMV confidence but did correlate with pre-anaesthetic assessment confidence (p = 0.004). Qualitative analysis identified themes relating to lifestyle, shift work, speciality exposure and competing interests in other specialties. l Perceived quality of undergraduate critical care education was associated with increased confidence in core skills. Placement duration alone may not improve confidence in high-risk procedures such as BMV. Implementing standardised learning objectives, structured placements, and earlier clinical exposure may improve preparedness, support safer clinical practice, and better inform career choices among junior doctors.

42968391.title: Lung Allograft Function After Primary Graft Dysfunction in the Lung Transplant Outcomes Group Cohort.
42968391.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
42968391.abstract: Primary graft dysfunction (PGD) after lung transplant is associated with increased mortality. Whether PGD increases mortality via long-term effects on allograft function is poorly understood. Evaluate the association of PGD with potential lung function and chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD). We included lung transplant recipients enrolled in an 8-center prospective cohort study from 2007-2018. PGD was defined by ISHLT criteria. Linear mixed effects and logistic regression models evaluated the association between PGD and maximum potential forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and whether Global Lung Function Initiative defined (GLI) predicted FEV1 was attained, respectively. Flexible parametric survival models evaluated the association between PGD and CLAD, accounting for confounding and mortality as a competing risk. Among 2419 recipients, 510 had PGD. Recipients with PGD had lower maximum potential FEV1 (-311 ml, 95% CI -245 to -377 ml) and were less likely to achieve GLI-predicted FEV1 (probability difference -12.5%, 95% CI -17 to -8%). 930 recipients developed CLAD (405 obstructive, 525 restrictive) over median (IQR) 5.9 (3.0-8.0 years). The 5-year cumulative incidence of CLAD did not differ by PGD (cumulative difference: -2.2%, 95% CI - 6.4% to 1.9%). This association was not modified by age, sex, BMI, pretransplant diagnosis, or transplant type. PGD was not associated with a difference in cumulative incidence of obstructive or restrictive CLAD (cumulative difference -1.2% and -0.8%, respectively). PGD is associated with reduced lung function and lower likelihood of achieving GLI-predicted maximum potential lung function but not CLAD.

42968390.title: Dupilumab is associated with improved lung functions in patients with COPD and type 2 inflammation: a post hoc analysis of the BOREAS and NOTUS trials.
42968390.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
42968390.abstract: Type 2 inflammation is present in 20%-40% of patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). To perform in-depth analyses of the efficacy of dupilumab on lung function parameters in patients with COPD and type 2 inflammation. In BOREAS (NCT03930732) and NOTUS (NCT04456673), patients with COPD and type 2 inflammation were randomized to dupilumab 300 mg (n = 938) or placebo (n = 936) subcutaneously every 2 weeks for 52 weeks. Dupilumab versus placebo improved pre-bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1; least squares mean difference: 83 [95% confidence interval (CI): 53-112] mL; P < .0001), post-bronchodilator FEV1 (71 [41-101] mL; P < .0001), pre-bronchodilator forced vital capacity (FVC; 64 [26-102] mL; P = .0009), post-bronchodilator FVC (41 [3-79] mL; P = .0341), post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC (0.016 [0.010-0.022]; P < .0001), and forced expiratory flow 25%-75% of FVC (78 [45-111] mL/s; P < .0001) at week 12 and sustained to week 52. Improvements in pre-bronchodilator FEV1 were observed regardless of smoking status or the presence of co-existing emphysema; greater improvements were observed in patients with higher baseline eosinophil counts or fractional exhaled nitric oxide. Dupilumab versus placebo achieved >100 mL improvements in pre-bronchodilator FEV1 at week 12 (42.2% vs 31.1%) and week 52 (36.9% vs 31.2%), with a similar proportion for post-bronchodilator FEV1 at weeks 12 and 52. Dupilumab treatment resulted in early and sustained improvements across multiple spirometric lung function parameters in patients with COPD and type 2 inflammation.

42968156.title: Accelerating tracheostomy decannulation with intermittent oro-esophageal feeding in neurogenic dysphagia: a multicenter randomized controlled trial.
42968156.abstract: Neurogenic dysphagia frequently constitutes a major barrier to decannulation for tracheostomized patients. Conventional nasogastric tube (NGT) feeding may promote disuse atrophy of swallowing musculature and persistent aspiration risk. Intermittent oro-esophageal tube (IOE) feeding, a physiologically oriented modality mimicking natural swallowing, may accelerate decannulation, yet high-quality evidence is lacking. In this multicenter randomized controlled trial conducted at three tertiary academic centers in China, tracheostomized adults with neurogenic dysphagia were randomly assigned 1:1 to IOE or NGT. All participants received standardized pharmacological treatment, pulmonary rehabilitation, and structured swallowing training, and entered an institutional decannulation protocol with predefined readiness criteria. The primary outcome was time from protocol entry to actual decannulation. Secondary outcomes included the 30-day successful decannulation rate, nutritional indices, swallowing function, and swallowing-related quality of life. Outcome assessors and statisticians were blinded to allocation. Analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle. A total of 140 patients were randomized to IOE (n = 70) or NGT (n = 70). Time to decannulation was shorter with IOE (22.16 ± 1.86 vs. 26.33 ± 1.30 days; between-group difference, 4.17 days; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.90-6.44; p < 0.001; log-rank p = 0.005). The 30-day successful decannulation rate was higher with IOE (65.71% vs. 47.14%; absolute difference, 18.57% points; 95% CI, 2.43-34.71; p = 0.028). At 1 month, the IOE group demonstrated greater improvements in body mass index, serum albumin, serum prealbumin, swallowing function, and swallowing-related quality of life (all p < 0.001). Pharyngeal discomfort was less frequent with IOE (14.06% vs. 34.21%; p = 0.006); no Grade Ⅲ or higher adverse events occurred. Intermittent oro-esophageal tube feeding shortens time to decannulation and improves nutritional, swallowing, and quality-of-life outcomes compared with nasogastric tube feeding in tracheostomized patients with neurogenic dysphagia. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06791590, registration date January 19, 2025.

42968112.title: Understanding cerebral autoregulation and cerebrovascular reactivity: mechanistic perspectives and clinical insights from TBI.
42968112.abstract: Cerebrovascular reactivity and cerebral blood flow autoregulation are critical determinants of brain homeostasis but are often conflated in clinical practice. Although these constructs are closely related and arise from vascular responses to vasoactive stimuli, they reflect distinct physiological responses and measurement approaches: autoregulation is assessed through changes in cerebral blood flow, and pressure reactivity through changes in cerebral blood volume. A fundamental clinical challenge is that the full autoregulatory curve is rarely observable in an individual patient at a single point in time; consequently, isolated measurements from classical assessments or continuous indices such as the pressure reactivity index (PRx), mean flow index (Mx), and arterial mean flow index (Mxa) are each associated with different components of cerebrovascular physiology, providing only partial views of cerebrovascular function and frequently yielding apparently conflicting results. This Review addresses a central clinical question: can multimodal neuromonitoring help determine where a patient is operating on the autoregulatory curve? We synthesise current understanding of the physiological relationships among cerebral perfusion pressure, cerebral blood flow, and cerebral blood volume, and examine the mechanisms underlying divergent autoregulatory index behaviour. By integrating mechanistic physiological schematics and representative clinical cases, we propose an objective educational framework that links classical cerebrovascular physiology with contemporary bedside monitoring. Within this framework, six conceptual physiological zones are delineated. These zones demonstrate how variations in vascular tone, intracranial compliance, and critical closing pressure shape autoregulatory responses generate differing patterns in PRx, Mx, and Mxa. Fully defining a patient's complex cerebrovascular state requires looking beyond any single parameter. Together, PRx, Mx, and Mxa provide complementary information, where discordant findings may represent distinct physiological mechanisms rather than measurement error. Interpreting these indices together within a mechanistic framework may improve identification of a patient's position along the autoregulatory curve, support more consistent bedside interpretation, and ultimately facilitate personalised cerebral perfusion pressure management.

42976192.title: Higher Daily Hospitalization Costs and Intensive Care Utilization Among Decedents With Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Bioethical Analysis of End-of-Life Care.
42976192.journal: Journal of evaluation in clinical practice
42976192.abstract: End-of-life care creates financial burdens. This study examines medical procedures/interventions and costs for inpatients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA), comparing those who died during hospitalization to those who survived, analyzing the findings through a bioethical perspective. This observational 1:1 case-control study was conducted at a tertiary care center. Patients with SLE and RA (ICD-10-CM diagnostic codes) who were hospitalized for at least 24 h during two distinct periods-January-June 2019 and January-June 2023-were included. Patients were designated as cases if they died during hospitalization and as controls if they were discharged alive. Data were abstracted from electronic medical records using standardized formats. Microcosting data for each hospitalization were obtained from the accounting department. We identified 29 matched pairs of cases and controls, primarily comprising middle-aged females, with SLE. Cases and controls had similar sociodemographic and disease-related characteristics. However, cases spent a greater proportion of their hospitalization time in the intensive care unit (100% [33.9-100] vs. 27.5% [13.4-45], p ≤ 0.001) and had higher incidence of complications (75.9% vs. 34.5%, p = 0.003). Daily hospitalization costs were significantly higher for cases (USD 3348 vs. 2707.4, p = < 0.001). More cases utilized blood bank services, while fewer engaged in clinical nutrition-related procedures. Decedents with SLE/RA had higher daily hospitalization costs than matched survivors, in the context of greater ICU utilization, complications, and blood bank use. End-of-life scenarios are complex; clinical decisions should be examined through bioethical lens.

42975515.title: Laboratory Investigation in Critical Care Medicine: Why It Matters.

42974384.title: Community perspectives on Exception from Informed Consent (EFIC) in the intensive care unit (ICU) setting: a mixed methods study.
42974384.abstract: The U.S. Exception from Informed Consent (EFIC) regulatory pathway enables clinical research in life-threatening situations where delays may preclude trial participation or reduce treatment efficacy. The use of EFIC in the intensive care unit (ICU) setting remains limited. In preparation for a prospective, multi-centre, ICU-based randomised controlled interventional trial, community consultations and public disclosures were conducted at three quaternary paediatric centres to assess the acceptability of an EFIC framework among community members and clinical staff. Session content was standardised, meetings were recorded and transcribed, and surveys with seven-point Likert scales (0-6) were distributed, with scores ≥5 considered affirmative. We conducted 18 clinician meetings (cumulative attendance n=313) and 26 community meetings (cumulative attendance n=43). Survey responses (n=128) demonstrated strong EFIC support: 100% (24/24) community participants viewed the trial as important; 88% (49/56) of clinicians viewed reperfusion injury as clinically important. Also, 100% (24/24) community members and 93% (97/104) clinicians reported willingness to enrol a relative or patient. In the qualitative analysis, significant concerns about the feasibility, utility, and messaging of the pre-enrolment opportunities to object (OTO) led to it being left to enrolling clinicians' discretion. The post-enrolment OTO to ongoing participation process was considered appropriate. In this mixed methods study, community members and clinicians across three centres expressed support for use of EFIC in this ICU-based trial. These findings highlight the importance of structured and multi-perspective community engagement in EFIC trials and support its future use in the ICU setting.

42974028.title: Associations between psychiatric comorbidity and intensive care unit length of stay, hospital length of stay, and in-hospital mortality: A retrospective observational study.
42974028.journal: PCN reports : psychiatry and clinical neurosciences
42974028.abstract: Psychiatric comorbidities are common among patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU), but findings regarding their impact on clinical outcomes remain inconsistent. Additionally, existing studies have often included patients admitted for suicide attempts or self-harm, leaving insufficient evidence about the independent effects of psychiatric comorbidity on clinical outcomes. To address this gap, this study investigated the independent association of psychiatric comorbidity with ICU length of stay, hospital length of stay, and in-hospital mortality among patients admitted to the ICU, excluding those admitted for suicide attempts or self-harm. Of the 2599 patients admitted to the ICU of a university hospital, 2192 were included in the analysis. After adjusting for age, sex, body mass index, admission category, and severity score, generalized linear models were used to evaluate ICU and hospital length of stay, and logistic regression analysis was used to assess in-hospital mortality. Among the 2192 patients included in the analysis, 75 had psychiatric comorbidity. In adjusted analyses, psychiatric comorbidity was not significantly associated with ICU length of stay, hospital length of stay, or in-hospital mortality. No participants were admitted to the ICU for suicide attempts or self-harm, and psychiatric comorbidity was not an independent predictor of ICU length of stay, hospital length of stay, or in-hospital mortality. Thus, in this ICU population, no statistically significant association was detected between psychiatric comorbidity and short-term clinical outcomes. Therefore, caution is needed when estimating ICU outcomes based solely on the presence of psychiatric comorbidity.

42973127.title: Heterogeneity in Procedural Training, Self-Assessed Competence and Supervising Skills Among New Pulmonary and Critical Care Fellows.
42973127.abstract: Performing procedures relevant to a future career path is a core component of Internal Medicine training (e.g. central line, arterial line, thoracentesis, paracentesis, and lumbar puncture). Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, Pulmonary Disease, and Critical Care Medicine (P/CCM) fellows must demonstrate procedural proficiency and competency and are often tasked with supervising procedures performed by resident trainees. To (1) determine the perceived level of procedural competence among P/CCM trainees at the start of their fellowship and (2) describe how P/CCM trainees are integrated into procedure workflows at their respective institutions, including supervision practices. PCCM fellows received the annual Association of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine (APCCMPD) Fellow's survey between January - March 2025. Of the 2240 eligible fellows, 592 responded (26.4%). Several indicated they would have been comfortable at the start of fellowship performing central line (81%), arterial line (81%), paracentesis (74%), thoracentesis (40%) or lumbar puncture (42%) independently, or with a supervisor available if needed. The distribution of prior procedural experience was similar, with more than 5 procedures performed by 92% of respondents for central line, 86% for arterial line, 76% for paracentesis, 49% for thoracentesis, and 37% for lumbar puncture. Most respondents (90%) indicated they - as the primary fellow - are frequently tasked with supervising central line placement. Yet, at the start of fellowship, not all fellows were comfortable supervising procedures (58% comfortable supervising central line, 66% arterial line, 61% paracentesis, 29% thoracentesis, 30% lumbar puncture). Only 56% indicated a formal central line procedural competency assessment in their fellowship. Our survey highlights that pre-fellowship procedure training is heterogenous. P/CCM fellows identified variable comfort with performing and supervising common procedures. Fellowship programs must evaluate their own local practices to ensure fellows demonstrate procedural competence prior to asking them to supervise.

42972576.title: Concomitant assessment of immunosuppression and Herpesvirus reactivation in blood at Day 7 after ICU admission in a mixed population.

42972573.title: The guardians of personhood: a qualitative study of nurses' perspective on person-centred care in the intensive care unit.
42972573.abstract: The intensive care unit (ICU) is a place where standardized procedures and advanced technology intersect with profound human vulnerability. Here, a person-centred approach to care becomes not only desirable but crucial, as it proposes an approach to safeguard personhood amidst life-saving routines. This study forms part of a broader investigation of Person-centred Practice in the ICU, drawing on McCance and McCormack's framework and Levinas's philosophy of the radical Other. This qualitative study explored how ICU nurses understand and enact person-centred care. Data were collected from 16 nurses working in adult ICUs across three hospitals in Austria through focus groups, individual interviews, and accounts of person-centred moments in practice. The analysis process was informed by the philosophy of radical alterity and, derived from this, focused on uncovering two strategies that nurses use to shape the care environment; i) 'creating the context' (grounding values and beliefs to allow personhood to emerge) and ii) 'breaking up the frames' (how nurses respond to disruptions through the radical Other to ensure personhood can be valued and sustained). Findings address these two interrelated strategies. Nurses 'create a context' by adhering to inner credos - guiding values like recognising the person, taking responsibility and acting ethically - applied in shaping relationships and navigating the patient's journey, balancing personal, clinical, and technological demands. They understand themselves as guardians of patients' personhood. Person-centred moments emerged from challenging situations. Here, nurses were able to 'break up the frames' - routines, standard procedures, and even personal expectations - by opening to the situation and embracing the strangeness and disruption they faced. By going the extra mile, they created moments in which person-centred care could unfold, generating positive care experiences for patients, families, and nurses alike. Person-centred care in the ICU means caring for the person behind tubes, wires, and machines. It cannot be reduced to checklists or protocols but depends on nurses' ability to pause, notice, and respond, supported by organizational cultures that enable such care. In this way, 'breaking up the frames' is not about dismantling clinical care but expanding it to include the person. Not registered. As part of a dissertation thesis the protocol for the study was approved by the Faculty board of Social Sciences of the University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria.

42972511.title: Fungal pneumonia in non-neutropenic critically ill patients: a Delphi consensus from the Fungal Infection Study Forum, India, with implications for resource-limited settings.
42972511.abstract: To develop consensus-based, pragmatic recommendations for the diagnosis and management of fungal pneumonia in non-neutropenic critically ill adults in India and Asia, where the dual burden of mucormycosis and resource-limited healthcare settings creates distinct challenges. Using a modified Delphi process, 20 multidisciplinary experts participated in the first round, and 19 completed the second and third rounds of anonymous voting on risk factors, diagnostic strategies, and management of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA), pulmonary mucormycosis (PM), and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP). Consensus was defined as ≥ 70% agreement or disagreement; statements with 60-69% agreement were categorized as "suggest," while the remaining were classified as "no consensus." Key risk factors included severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, influenza, COVID-19, diabetes mellitus, and chronic liver or kidney disease. A multimodal diagnostic strategy combining contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT), early bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), microscopy, culture, and galactomannan (BAL threshold ≥ 1.0) was recommended, with molecular methods used where available. Liposomal amphotericin B was the preferred empiric agent in regions with high mucormycosis prevalence; voriconazole, posaconazole, or isavuconazole are first-line for proven IPA. Therapeutic drug monitoring is essential for azole antifungals, with a minimum treatment duration of 6-12 weeks. For PCP, empiric trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is recommended in immunosuppressed patients with diffuse ground-glass opacities on CT after exclusion of competing diagnoses. Adjunctive corticosteroids are recommended for PCP with severe hypoxemia (PaO₂ <70 mmHg) despite limited evidence in non-HIV patients. We provide practical, resource-adapted guidance for managing fungal pneumonia in non-neutropenic ICU patients, while highlighting research priorities. The proposed diagnostic criteria for IPA and PM are provisional consensus-based frameworks intended to support clinical decision-making and require prospective multicentre validation. Not applicable.

42972371.title: Developing a screening tool for in-hospital deep venous thrombosis risk in severe pneumonia patients admitted to respiratory intensive care unit.
42972371.abstract: The incidence of deep venous thrombosis (DVT) is higher for severe pneumonia patients hospitalized in respiratory intensive care unit (RICU). Currently, no validated risk assessment tool specifically exists for evaluating DVT risk in this population. This study aimed to develop a screening tool to estimate the risk of in-hospital DVT in patients with severe pneumonia admitted to the RICU. In this retrospective cohort study, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used to identify candidate predictors of in-hospital DVT. We then developed two prediction models, a support vector machine (SVM) algorithm and a nomogram model, to predict DVT risk in patients with severe pneumonia in the RICU. We included 368 patients with severe pneumonia admitted to the RICU. DVT occurred in 124 patients (33.7%) during hospitalization. The area under the Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC) of Padua scores, SVM algorithm and nomogram model to predict the risk of DVT were 0.504 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.442-0.566], 0.526 (95%CI: 0.466-0.587) and 0.754 (95%CI: 0.703-0.805) respectively. The radar chart also indicated that nomogram model had better performance in multiple metrics. For nomogram model, the calibration plot displayed good concordance between predicted and actual outcomes. Clinical utility was assessed using decision curve analysis (DCA). With a range of threshold probability values between 0.1 and 0.8, the nomogram model provided greater net clinical benefit to predict the risk of DVT than Padua scores and SVM algorithm. We developed a nomogram to predict the risk of in-hospital DVT in severe pneumonia patients admitted to RICU. The nomogram showed moderate discriminatory performance and may help identify patients who warrant intensified surveillance or confirmatory ultrasonographic assessment.

42974962.title: Advances in HIV-associated pulmonary diseases: an official American Thoracic Society workshop report.
42974962.journal: Annals of the American Thoracic Society
authors: American Thoracic Society Assembly on Pulmonary Infections and Tuberculosis
42974962.abstract: People with HIV (PWH) are at increased risk of a broad range of infectious and non-infectious pulmonary diseases. Since the last ATS Workshop on HIV-associated pulmonary disease, large national and international cohorts have demonstrated ongoing gaps in our understanding of lung disease in this vulnerable population that range from underappreciation of disease incidence and prevalence to lack of targeted treatments. Translational work on the underlying mechanisms of disease has demonstrated novel, HIV-specific mechanisms that may lend themselves to tailored therapies. Twenty-four experts in HIV-associated lung disease from across the translational spectrum were invited to participate in this ATS-sponsored Workshop utilizing a modified Delphi method that included a series of pre- and post-workshop electronic surveys and a two-day virtual workshop. Lung disease among PWH is driven by complex and interrelated mechanisms including persistent immune dysregulation, oxidative stress, accelerated aging, and microbiome alterations. Despite these advances in our understanding, important gaps persist between mechanistic insights and clinical care that include limited HIV-specific trials, underrepresentation of PWH in studies of lung disease, and the absence of tailored care strategies. These gaps are further accentuated by substantial variation in the availability of data from the most affected populations, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and among children and adolescents. Overcoming these challenges will require coordinated, globally representative research efforts that leverage large cohorts, integrate multi-omics and longitudinal phenotyping, use mechanistic insights to inform clinical trials, and consider implementation science approaches with the ultimate goal of developing tailored prevention and treatment strategies for HIV-associated pulmonary diseases.

42974958.title: As-needed inhaled corticosteroids in asthma: an Official American Thoracic Society clinical practice guideline.
42974958.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
authors: American Thoracic Society Assembly on Allergy, Immunology and Inflammation
42974958.abstract: Inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-containing reliever therapy has demonstrated efficacy in improving asthma outcomes when compared to short-acting beta2-agonists (SABA) alone but remains underutilized. The purpose of this guideline is to provide recommendations surrounding the use of combination ICS-formoterol or ICS+SABA (in combination or separate inhalers) as reliever therapy across the asthma severity spectrum in adolescents and adults. The American Thoracic Society clinical practice guideline panel evaluated six research questions in the PICO format addressing the use of ICS-containing reliever therapy across National Asthma Education and Prevention Program (NAEPP) asthma treatment steps 1-5. The methodology team conducted systematic literature reviews and GRADE assessments, which the panel utilized to inform the recommendations for each specific PICO and overall. In patients at NAEPP steps 1 and 2, the panel made strong recommendations for the use of as-needed-only ICS-SABA or ICS-formoterol over SABA-only therapy, and conditional recommendations over scheduled ICS + as-needed SABA. In patients at NAEPP steps 3-5, the taskforce made a strong recommendation for the use of maintenance-and-reliever therapy (MART) with ICS-formoterol over scheduled ICS-LABA plus as-needed SABA. In patients at NAEPP steps 3-5 who are using scheduled maintenance ICS-LABA, the panel made a conditional recommendation for use of ICS+SABA reliever over SABA reliever. In considering these recommendations, the panel valued the importance of preventing severe exacerbations and considered the risk of SABA-only treatment, as well as ICS and systemic corticosteroid (SCS) exposure. This clinical practice guideline, informed by systematic reviews and GRADE-based appraisals of PICO-framed evidence, makes these evidence-based recommendations for the safe and effective use of ICS-containing reliever therapy in asthma.
