42996370.title: Nurse-led non-ICU early rehabilitation after liver transplantation: a quasi-experimental historical-control study.
42996370.abstract: Early rehabilitation after liver transplantation is increasingly encouraged, but most programs are implemented after intensive care unit (ICU) stabilization. We evaluated a nurse-led pathway in which selected liver transplant recipients were transferred directly to the general ward after surgery. Because the intervention was introduced sequentially over time, the study was analyzed as a non-randomized historical-control quasi-experiment. Recovery-timing, device-duration, length-of-stay, and hospitalization-charge analyses were conducted in the 102 recipients who survived to complete postoperative outcome ascertainment (57 intervention and 45 control) and are therefore survivor-conditional. Continuous outcomes were assessed for distributional assumptions and compared using two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests when non-normal. Sparse binary outcomes were analyzed using Fisher's exact test. Multivariable linear regression with HC3 heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, preoperative diagnosis, surgery duration, and log-transformed intraoperative blood loss. Log1p-transformed models were used as sensitivity analyses for skewed outcomes. Compared with historical controls, recipients treated during the intervention period had earlier initiation of oral intake (median 13.0 vs. 48.0 h, P < 0.001), respiratory training (13.0 vs. 48.0 h, P < 0.001), and first out-of-bed activity (39.0 vs. 72.0 h, P < 0.001), as well as shorter urinary and central venous catheter retention (both P < 0.001). In adjusted models, intervention-period status was associated with earlier initiation of oral intake (adjusted difference -51.76 h, 95% CI -70.71 to -32.82), earlier respiratory training (-56.58 h, 95% CI -83.66 to -29.50), earlier ambulation (-60.48 h, 95% CI -103.24 to -17.72), shorter urinary catheter retention (-85.93 h, 95% CI -114.11 to -57.75), shorter central venous catheter retention (-66.17 h, 95% CI -89.70 to -42.63), and shorter length of stay (-4.48 days, 95% CI -8.23 to -0.73). Multidrug-resistant bacterial infection was numerically lower (3.5% vs. 13.3%) but not statistically significant (RR 0.26, 95% CI 0.06-1.24; Fisher's exact P = 0.134). Total hospitalization charges were lower in the unadjusted comparison but showed no statistically significant adjusted association with the pathway (P = 0.467). In this historical-control quasi-experimental study, implementation of the nurse-led non-ICU transition pathway was associated with earlier achievement of several postoperative rehabilitation milestones and shorter hospital stay after adjustment for measured covariates. Because intervention status was inseparable from calendar period and unmeasured temporal confounding could not be excluded, these findings should be interpreted strictly as associations rather than evidence of direct intervention effects. Prospective multicenter studies with contemporaneous controls and predefined safety criteria are needed before broader implementation.

42995583.title: Explainable machine learning for predicting 28-day mortality in ICU patients with stroke complicated by chronic kidney disease.
42995583.journal: BMC medical informatics and decision making
42995583.abstract: Patients with stroke complicated by chronic kidney disease (CKD) face high mortality in the intensive care unit (ICU) due to complex "brain-kidney crosstalk." We aimed to develop and externally validate an explainable machine learning (ML) model based on routine bedside indicators to predict 28-day all-cause mortality, in strict adherence to the TRIPOD-AI reporting guidelines. Clinical data were extracted from the MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-III (external validation) databases. To prevent data leakage, the internal cohort was partitioned into training (70%) and testing (30%) sets before any preprocessing. Class imbalance was addressed using the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) exclusively within the training set. Core predictors were identified using a dual dimensionality-reduction strategy that combined LASSO regression and the Boruta algorithm. Thirteen ML algorithms were evaluated, and the optimal model's discriminative performance was formally compared to traditional severity scores. The Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) framework was utilized for clinical interpretability. A total of 1,550 eligible patients were included. The feature selection pipeline identified 14 primary physiological and biochemical baseline indicators. The Random Forest (RF) model demonstrated stable generalizability, yielding an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.654 in the internal testing set and 0.672 in the external validation cohort. SMOTE application substantially improved the sensitivity for identifying non-survivors (66.7% and 55.6% in the respective cohorts), albeit with an expected trade-off in specificity. DeLong's test confirmed that the RF model performed comparably to complex clinical scores (e.g., SOFA, SAPS II) with no statistically significant difference (all P > 0.05). SHAP analysis identified creatinine, white blood cell count, anion gap, heart rate, and respiratory rate as the top five drivers of mortality, elucidating critical non-linear pathological thresholds. By relying solely on 14 easily accessible routine clinical indicators, the proposed RF model offers a streamlined and transparent alternative to complex traditional scoring systems. It offers data-driven, non-linear insights for early high-risk screening and individualized clinical decision-making in critically ill stroke patients.

42998056.title: Development and Feasibility of In Situ Simulation for Pressure Injury Prevention in Intensive Care.
42998056.abstract: To develop, validate and test in situ simulation scenarios aimed at pressure injury (PI) prevention for nursing professionals working in an intensive care unit (ICU). A multi-method study is planned across four phases. Conducted at a high-complexity Brazilian university hospital, this four-phase study: (1) development of simulation scenarios and checklists; (2) content validation by 11 experts (CVI/MKC); (3) pilot testing with 12 nursing professionals; and (4) ICU-based educational intervention. Scenarios were grounded in international guidelines and the NLN/Jeffries Simulation Theory. Feasibility was assessed via metrics of acceptability, appropriateness, adoption and fidelity. Two evidence-based simulation scenarios and checklists were developed for registered nurses and nursing technicians, achieving high content validity among 11 experts. The in situ intervention reached 83% of the unit's nursing staff, demonstrating strong operational feasibility and acceptability. Beyond education, the scenarios served as a diagnostic tool, successfully identifying critical practice gaps, notably in Braden Scale utilization, pressure redistribution and the execution of standardized preventive measures. The scenarios demonstrated satisfactory content validity and proved feasible for use in ICUs. In situ simulation showed potential to support continuing education actions, promote critical reflection on clinical practice and identify gaps in care processes related to PI prevention. In situ simulation can contribute to strengthening continuing health education, support the review of care practices and favour the implementation of evidence-based preventive measures for PI prevention in intensive care. No patient or public involvement in the development of this study. https://ensaiosclinicos.gov.br/rg/RBR-4xc2sk8.

42997026.title: Sex differences in limitations of life-sustaining treatment in the intensive care unit: A nationwide cohort study.
42997026.abstract: Previous research suggests that limitations of life-sustaining treatment (LST) may be more common in women than men, but few studies have included data on clinical reasoning or limitation type. This study aimed to investigate sex differences in LST-limitations in the ICU and in their documented characteristics. All adult (≥18 years) ICU patients registered in the Swedish Intensive Care Register between 2019 and 2024 were included. A multivariable logistic regression model, adjusted for SAPS3 and age, analysed the association between sex and LST-limitations. Limitation characteristics were compared using Chi-square test (categorical variables) and Wilcoxon rank-sum test (numeric variables). The cohort included 111,354 patients; 41.7% women. LST-limitations occurred in 24.4% of patients and were more frequent in women than in men (25.3% vs. 23.8%, p < 0.0001). In adjusted analyses women had higher odds of receiving an LST-limitation than men, both in the full cohort (OR 1.21, 95% CI 1.17-1.25) and among 30-day non-survivors (OR 1.24, 95% CI 1.18-1.32). Women received LST-limitations earlier than men (2.8 h after admission vs 4.5 h, p < 0.0001). Acute disease and therapy failure were more often documented reasons in men than in women (78.8% vs 74.3%, p < 0.0001; 21.2% vs. 18.6%, p = 0.0001), whereas autonomy and chronic disease were more frequent in women (7.8% vs 5.9%, p < 0.0001; 63.2% vs. 60.7%, p = 0.0021). Women were more often involved in decision-making (13.3% vs 11.8%, p = 0.0074). Women were more likely to receive LST-limitations and received them earlier. Men who died within 30 days were less likely to have had an LST-limitation than women. Documented reasons for LST-limitations differed by sex, and women had higher rates of documented patient involvement.

42996841.title: Association between white blood cell-to-hemoglobin ratio and in-hospital mortality among critically ill patients with pancreatic cancer: a retrospective cohort study based on MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD.
42996841.abstract: Critically ill patients with pancreatic cancer represent a high-risk population in whom systemic inflammation, anemia, organ dysfunction, and acute physiological derangement may jointly contribute to poor short-term outcomes. The white blood cell-to-hemoglobin ratio (WHR) is an easily obtainable hematologic index that may reflect both inflammatory burden and reduced oxygen-carrying reserve. Whether WHR adds prognostic information beyond routine clinical assessment in this population remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the association between WHR and in-hospital mortality among critically ill patients with pancreatic cancer. This retrospective cohort study used Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) version 3.1 (2008-2022) and electronic ICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD) version 2.0 (2014-2015). Adults aged ≥18 years with International Classification of Diseases (ICD)-9-CM/ICD-10-CM-coded pancreatic cancer and a first qualifying intensive care unit (ICU) stay of ≥24 hours were included, patients without white blood cell count or hemoglobin data were excluded. WHR was calculated from the earliest available white blood cell count and hemoglobin measurements within the first 24 hours after hospital admission. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Multivariable logistic regression was used for the binary outcome analysis, and 24-hour landmark cause-specific Cox and Fine-Gray competing-risk models were added as key time-to-event sensitivity analyses. Predictive performance and the incremental value of WHR beyond clinical variables and its individual components were also assessed. A total of 638 patients were included (MIMIC-IV, n=253, eICU-CRD, n=385); mean age was 67.5±11.3 years, 347 (54.4%) were male, and 53 (8.3%) died during hospitalization. Patients with WHR ≥1.7 were older and had higher white blood cell counts, lower hemoglobin concentrations, and higher SOFA scores. In the fully adjusted Model IV, WHR ≥1.7 remained associated with in-hospital mortality [odds ratio (OR) =2.75, 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.39-5.42, P=0.004]. Time-to-event analyses were consistent: the cause-specific hazard ratio was 2.34 (95% CI, 1.30-4.21, P=0.004), and the Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard ratio was 2.38 (95% CI, 1.34-4.24, P=0.003). WHR alone showed modest discrimination [area under the curve (AUC) =0.662], adding WHR to the clinical model increased the AUC from 0.786 to 0.796, but the bootstrap AUC difference was not statistically significant (P=0.49). Elevated WHR was associated with increased in-hospital mortality among critically ill patients with pancreatic cancer. WHR may serve as a simple adjunctive risk marker, although its incremental discrimination beyond clinical variables was modest. Further prospective studies are warranted to validate its added prognostic value and clarify its potential role in clinical risk assessment.

42997979.title: Systemic Inflammation in Bronchiectasis: Data from the EMBARC-BRIDGE Study.
42997979.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
42997979.abstract: Neutrophilic inflammation in the airways is associated with exacerbation risk in patients with bronchiectasis. Systemic inflammation and neutrophil function are less characterised. The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between systemic inflammation and neutrophil function with severity of disease and clinical outcomes. Observational international multi-centre study of adults with bronchiectasis (EMBARC-BRIDGE). Serum inflammatory profiling was performed in 487 patients using Olink® proteomics, and associations with key clinical and patient reported outcomes, including severe exacerbations during follow-up, were analysed. In a sub-study, peripheral blood neutrophils from bronchiectasis patients and controls were analysed for surface activation and functional markers, and functional responses including degranulation and neutrophil extracellular trap formation. Systemic inflammatory profiling revealed a dominant neutrophil-endothelial signature. Several proteins including PR3, AZU1, MPO, the soluble IL-33 receptor ST2, and the cellular stress marker GDF-15 were associated with increased disease severity using the bronchiectasis severity index, lower lung function, increased symptoms and for many markers, higher rates of severe exacerbations during follow-up. Neutrophils from bronchiectasis patients exhibited reduced surface CD11b and increased CXCR2, with lower CD11b correlating with lower lung function. Basal degranulation was reduced in bronchiectasis, whereas responsiveness to LPS stimulation was preserved. Bronchiectasis is associated with a systemic neutrophil and endothelial inflammatory signature linked to disease severity and risk of severe exacerbations, alongside altered but functionally-responsive circulating neutrophils.

42997975.title: Fear of Falling After Critical Illness: The Missing Role of Muscle Assessment.
42997975.journal: Annals of the American Thoracic Society

42995585.title: Controlling time-related biases in ECPR observational studies.

43000120.title: Streamlining the Evidence-to-Practice Pathway With Computerised Decision Support in Anaesthesiology and Critical Care: A Qualitative Study of Clinician and System-Level Interest Holder Perspectives Across Five Scandinavian Countries.
43000120.abstract: Implementing evidence-based recommendations in anaesthesiology and critical care remains challenging due to guideline, workflow and contextual barriers. Guideline-based computerised clinical decision support systems (CDSS), embedded in structured pathways linking international guidelines to Scandinavian-endorsed recommendations and delivered via electronic health records, may help strengthen the evidence-to-practice pathway. This study aimed to explore perceived barriers and facilitators to their use. This qualitative study interviewed 10 clinicians (anaesthesiologists and intensivists; specialists and non-specialists; < 40 and ≥ 40 years; male and female) and nine system-level stakeholders (hospital and health authority representatives) from Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. We integrated endorsed international guidelines into a CDSS providing patient-specific reminders linked to recommendations, as well as shared decision-making tools and decision-analytic components. Using a simulation application, participants explored the CDSS in a demo electronic health record. Through a framework analysis based on the GUIDES checklist, we categorised perspectives as barriers, facilitators or suggestions. Clinicians and system-level interest holders expressed broad interest in this multifunctional CDSS to support evidence-based, patient-centred care and appreciated the collaborative international pathway facilitated by digital tools. Key themes included the challenges hospitals face in translating international guidelines into up-to-date, locally adapted guidance. Artificial intelligence (AI) was perceived as having the potential to both enhance and challenge traditional CDSS. Opportunities were identified to strengthen shared decision-making for major decisions through the proposed system. Finally, participants highlighted the potential value of using a decision-analytic tool to prioritise reminders, although the tool was considered conceptually challenging in its current form and would require clearer presentation before being applied in CDSS. This prototype study indicates support for a multifunctional CDSS. Building on the barriers and facilitators identified in this study, interviewees advocated for real-world evaluation with particular attention to sustainable implementation. This study aimed to describe how ICU clinicians experience interaction in a simulated electronic health record where there were chosen elements of decision support based on international treatment guidelines incorporated into the simulation. Participants were interviewed for their perceptions of what types of decision support might be most helpful to support their clinical work in future patient information and management systems.

42999498.title: Teaching LLMs How ICU Physicians Approach Clinical Reasoning Through OMOP-Aligned Retrieval Improves Reasoning Across Clinical Domains.
42999498.abstract: Clinical decision-making relies on identifying relevant patient information to guide diagnosis and treatment, a challenge that is especially difficult in the data-dense and rapidly changing intensive care unit (ICU). Large language models (LLMs) could support this task. However, existing applications and datasets mostly emphasize surface-level retrieval or factual recall rather than the inductive and deductive reasoning clinicians practice to select and reason over decision-relevant evidence. We hypothesized that training LLMs on expert ICU reasoning could yield clinical reasoning skills that generalize beyond critical care. Here we introduce ICU-REACT, a reasoning dataset developed with 19 clinicians through a clinician-in-the-loop framework to teach LLMs to perform information retrieval and context-aware clinical reasoning in the ICU. Using ICU-REACT, we fine-tuned Clin-REACT models spanning 8B-70B parameters and three model families. Across five clinical reasoning benchmarks, Clin-REACT consistently outperformed its backbone models and open-source general-purpose and medical LLMs. Gains extended to different tasks including script concordance tests, and downstream diagnosis and treatment tasks. These findings suggest that expert reasoning supervision in critical care can improve broader clinical reasoning, although prospective evaluation is needed before real-world clinical use.

43003546.title: Prediction, Prescription, and Proactive Medication Management in the Intensive Care Unit.
43003546.abstract: This narrative review examines the evolving role of prediction analytics in comprehensive medication management for critically ill patients. Intensive care unit pharmacotherapy is challenged by medication complexity, physiologic instability, heterogeneous treatment response, and continuous data streams. Predictive systems may support proactive medication management by identifying medication-related harm, therapeutic failure, optimization opportunities, and pharmacist workload earlier in the patient trajectory. The review discusses medication-informed prediction models, prescriptive analytics, workload-aware critical care pharmacist allocation, and potential future applications. Implementation requires actionable predictions, workflow integration, clinician oversight, and attention to equity, safety, and model credibility.

43003543.title: Redesigning Intensive Care Unit Workflows: A Learning Health System Approach to Improving Care Delivery.
43003543.abstract: Critical care leaders are increasingly asked to improve outcomes, reduce burden, and implement evidence-based care in complex, highly interdependent clinical environments. Meeting this challenge requires redesigning the workflows through which care is delivered, not simply measuring outcomes or adding new tools. This article presents a learning health system model that integrates sociotechnical systems thinking, quality improvement, health services research, and informatics to support workflow redesign. Multidimensional workflow signals inform the Diagnose, Redesign, Implement, Verify, Evolve (DRIVE) cycle to make care delivery more reliable, less burdensome, and better aligned with outcomes that matter to patients.

43003542.title: Intensive Care Unit Staffing Ratios: Evidence, Experience, Economics, and Execution.
43003542.abstract: The clinician-to-patient ratio is a simple construct which can be useful in strategizing for intensive care unit (ICU) staffing. Evidence is limited and inconsistent, but overall suggests such ratios may impact patient outcomes, clinician experiences, and health system economics. Importantly, however, ICU clinicians function as part of an interprofessional team, and no single staffing metric can be considered in isolation. As such, no one-size-fits-all approach to clinician-to-patient ratios exists. Yet, typical ranges are now known and decisions to operate outside of these ranges should be done with care, at least until new evidence can better guide practice.

43003541.title: Optimizing Team Integration of Critical Care Pharmacists: Where We Go Next.
43003541.abstract: Critical care pharmacists (CCPs) are essential members of the intensive care unit team who provide comprehensive medication management to improve patient outcomes, safety, and cost efficiency. This article highlights barriers to optimal integration of CCPs within multidisciplinary teams as well as opportunities to address them. Persistent barriers include financial, workforce, data, interprofessional, and regulatory. Strategies to address these gaps may involve standardized metrics, innovative staffing models, and research to strengthen evidence-based implementation. Metrics should include all members of the Stakeholder Triad and should include a mix of workload metrics, safety and efficacy metrics, and work-design metrics.

43003540.title: Optimizing Team Integration of Critical Care Pharmacists: A History of Critical Care Pharmacy Practice and Evolving Definition of "Optimal Practice".
43003540.abstract: Critical Care Pharmacists (CCPs) are essential members of the intensive care unit (ICU) team who provide comprehensive medication management to improve patient outcomes, safety, and cost efficiency. This article highlights best practices for optimal CCP integration, including optimal patient-to-pharmacist ratios, participation in interprofessional rounds, team-based practice models, and expanded coverage across all shifts. The Triple Domain framework is useful to evaluate CCP value across patients, health care teams, and institutions. Best practices include an ICU patient-to-CCP ratio of less than or equal to 15:1 and inclusion of CCPs on daily interprofessional rounds.

43003539.title: The COVID-19 Pandemic as a Stress Test of the Intensive Care Unit Workforce.
43003539.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic monumentally strained the intensive care unit (ICU) workforce and revealed both the strengths and vulnerabilities in contemporary critical care delivery. In this review, we briefly describe the composition of the US ICU workforce and the organizational features most relevant to staffing. Next, we examine how the pandemic disrupted critical care delivery, specifically health care workers. Finally, we discuss the lasting psychological toll and workforce attrition; highlight adaptations that emerged, such as tele-ICU expansion, virtual family engagement, tiered staffing models, rapid-onboarding curricula, and peer support programs; and outline priorities for policy, practice, and research to strengthen workforce resilience.

43003537.title: The Intensive Care Unit Team: Roles, Scope, and Interprofessional Interdependence in the Intensive Care Unit.
43003537.abstract: A hallmark feature of an intensive care unit (ICU) is the presence of a structured team-based interprofessional model. Although composition of the ICU team varies by organization and patient population, it typically includes critical care nurses, intensivists, respiratory therapists, and clinical pharmacists. Interprofessional teams in ICUs are associated with increased collaboration and improved patient outcomes. However, the ICU team faces challenges in workforce shortages, staffing gaps, and ineffective information sharing, which can inhibit effective team function. Proven strategies to support collaboration among the ICU team include structured interprofessional rounds, strong leadership of the team, care protocols, and quality bundles.

43003548.title: The Intensive Care Unit Workforce-Masters of Complexity.

43003545.title: Intensive Monitoring, Big Data, and Artificial Intelligence in Critical Care.
43003545.abstract: Intensive care is defined by providing a higher level of patient monitoring, but only a fraction of the data created through continuous hemodynamic monitoring are captured in the electronic health record. The monitoring data that is captured misses clinically important deterioration events and is not adequate to represent critical illness physiology for care at the bedside or for research. This article describes the current state of patient monitoring in intensive care, advanced monitors in development, metadata and its role in creating rich intensive care data sources, and machine learning and its current and future applications in intensive care medicine.

43003432.title: Advances in the hospital management of hyperglycemia and type 2 diabetes in non-critical care settings.

43002908.title: Cognitive load of healthcare professionals in the intensive care unit: A bibliometric analysis from 2016 to 2025.
43002908.abstract: To identify research hotspots, major contributors, and developmental trends in studies on cognitive load among ICU healthcare professionals. A bibliometric analysis was conducted on data retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection, covering scholarly publications from January 1, 2016, to December 31, 2025. CiteSpace software was used to visualize and analyze countries, institutions, cited journals, and keywords. A total of 169 articles were included. The annual publication output showed a steady upward trend over the decade, rising from 7 publications in 2016 to 34 in 2025. Notably, 82 articles (48.5% of the total) were published between 2023 and 2025. The United States ranked first in contributions (63 publications, 37.28%). Capital Medical University in China was the most productive institution (6 publications, 3.55%). The most frequently cited journal was Critical Care Medicine (75 citations). Research hotspots centered on three thematic directions: workload and mental demand among ICU nursing staff, psychological outcomes and occupational well-being, and clinical assessment and patient-centered management. Emerging trends included psychological well-being promotion and risk prevention related to cognitive load. Research on cognitive load in ICU healthcare professionals has grown substantially, with increasing attention to nursing workload, mental health, and patient safety.

43002905.title: Health-related quality of life after intensive care: a longitudinal cohort study using item-level network analysis.
43002905.abstract: To examine relationships between individual SF-36 items at 3 and 12 months after intensive care unit (ICU) discharge using network analysis with conventional health-related quality of life (HRQoL) scores as complementary context. This single-center longitudinal cohort study included adult ICU survivors admitted between March 2011 and December 2021 who completed the 36-item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36) at 3 and 12 months. Item-level Gaussian graphical models were estimated and compared using a paired-sample Network Comparison Test. Conventional SF-36 scores were described over time and compared with French population reference values. Overall, 479 ICU survivors completed both assessments. Bodily Pain item 2 (BP2), assessing pain interference with normal work, ranked among the three items with the highest node strength at both assessments and was associated with the Social Functioning item 1 (SF1). Network structure (M = 0.178, p = 0.14) and global strength (S = 0.032, p = 0.90) did not differ significantly between 3 and 12 months. Seven of the 319 descriptively retained edges had unadjusted p values below 0.005. HRQoL remained below French reference values at 12 months particularly in physical and role-related domains, despite partial improvement. Item-level network analysis provided a complementary perspective on SF-36 responses by describing relationships between individual HRQoL items alongside the extent of impairment captured by conventional scores. Its implications for follow-up and rehabilitation remain hypothesis-generating. Conventional HRQoL scores alone may not fully capture how symptoms and functional dimensions are interconnected. Combining score-based assessment with network information may support a more comprehensive evaluation of recovery after critical illness.

43002853.title: Critical Care Nurses' acceptance of health information system based on technology acceptance model 3.
43002853.abstract: This study aimed to assess critical care nurses' acceptance of HISs using the Technology Acceptance Model 3 (TAM3). A cross-sectional study was conducted with 240 critical care nurses from six conveniently selected governmental hospitals in Jordan, using a self-administered questionnaire based on the TAM3. Correlations and linear multiple regression were utilized to analyze the data. The sample consisted of 56% female nurses, with a mean age of 34.4 years (SD = 7.18), ranging from 24 to 55 years. The nurses exhibited a positive perception of the usefulness and ease of use of HISs, which significantly influenced their behavioral intention to use technology and, subsequently, their acceptance of it. The explored perceived usefulness explained 61.6% of its variance. Perceived ease of use (B = 0.45, p < 0.001), job relevance, and output quality significantly influenced perceived usefulness. Predictors of perceived ease of use explained 66.3% of its variance. Collectively, computer playfulness (B = 0.39, p < 0.001), perceptions of external control, computer self-efficacy, training in using HISs, and education degree significantly contributed to nurses' perceptions of ease of use. This study reveals significant relationships among the variables in the TAM 3 model. The findings confirm that TAM 3 serves as an effective assessment instrument for understanding nurses' acceptance of health information technology, aiding healthcare administrators in enhancing its adoption in nursing practice. Additionally, this study contributes to the growing body of knowledge in health informatics by providing insights into the factors influencing nurses' acceptance of HISs.

43001749.title: Turning Points: Reducing Hospital-Acquired Pressure Injuries in Critical Care.
43001749.journal: Journal of wound, ostomy, and continence nursing : official publication of The Wound, Ostomy and Continence Nurses Society
43001749.abstract: The purpose of this quality improvement initiative was to evaluate the effectiveness of education and the implementation of a turning and repositioning system in critical care for unstable patients in reducing hospital-acquired pressure injuries (HAPIs). Fourteen patients met inclusion criteria. This project was conducted in 2 intensive care units of a large academic teaching hospital in Central Texas of the United States. The project used a pre-post quasi-experimental design. The wound nurse, Intensive Care Unit leadership, and nursing staff collaborated to address the practice gap. The wound care nurse recommended educating nurses on critical care-specific prevention strategies and trialing a turning and repositioning system. A risk assessment algorithm and a repositioning checklist were created. Daily rounds on participating patients validated staff nurse's knowledge, skills, and the proper use of the system. Evaluation forms were collected for feedback. Positive feedback was received, demonstrating the effectiveness of the education provided and the usability of the turning and repositioning system in preventing pressure injury in critically ill patients. Hospital-acquired pressure injury rates decreased to zero at the end of the QI project. Post-trial rates remained zero for 2 months, with 1 HAPI identified in the third month, yielding a rate of 0.4 per 1000 patient days. Providing education and implementing the turning and repositioning reduced the incidence of HAPIs by more than 90%. Adding the turning and repositioning system to pressure injury prevention interventions reduced the number of HAPIs in the critical care population.

43001670.title: Delivering optimal renal care in critically ill patients.

43003345.title: From Rescue to Donation: Embedding Ethics into the ECPR Outcomes Framework.

43000652.title: Learning to Live With a Ventricular Assist Device: Patient, Caregiver, and Clinician Concerns Following Implantation and Hospital Discharge.
43000652.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
43000652.abstract: Patients undergoing ventricular assist device (VAD) implantation and their caregivers must attain knowledge and skills to perform VAD self-care safely. Little is known about the similarities and differences among patients, caregivers, and VAD clinicians related to VAD self-care training and management. This study explored the perspectives of 15 VAD patients, 12 VAD caregivers, and 18 VAD clinicians through individual semi-structured interviews focused on understanding barriers related to VAD self-care training and concerns about VAD self-care post-discharge. We identified four major themes (training related, care transitions, fear and uncertainty, clinical consequences). All participant groups discussed concerns related to daily VAD self-care and the transition home after implantation. Caregivers and clinicians discussed the steep VAD self-care learning curve. Caregivers and patients discussed fears in general (eg, constant fear) and specific terms (eg, VAD malfunction), whereas clinicians who discussed fear/uncertainty identified strategies for dealing with emergent situations. Concerns regarding adverse events and non-adherence arose primarily from clinicians. Although some alignment was found, concerns varied among stakeholders. A common understanding of these nuanced concerns may improve VAD self-care training and the preparation of patients and caregivers.

42996949.title: Ethical considerations in the management of complications after lung resection: a narrative review.
42996949.abstract: Complications following lung resection present complex clinical, ethical and interpersonal challenges that extend beyond technical management. Although substantial literature addresses the prevention and treatment of complications after lung resection, there is limited guidance regarding the ethical principles that should shape clinical decision-making as complications evolve. This review proposes a practical ethical framework for the management of complications following lung resection. Recommendations were developed based on clinical expertise and relevant published sources. A narrative literature search was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase, supplemented by targeted searches of relevant clinical resources and reference lists. English-language literature published within the last fifteen years was considered, with more recent evidence prioritized alongside foundational literature. Where lung resection-specific evidence was limited, related thoracic surgery, critical care, perioperative medicine, and surgical ethics literature was incorporated. The developed framework is focused on six foundational ethical principles spanning patient-centered and provider-/systems-centered domains. Patient-centered principles include autonomy, shared decision-making and proportionate goal-concordant care, which help define patient values and integrate those values with clinical expertise to align treatment strategies with meaningful outcomes. Provider-/systems-centered principles include beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, transparency and accountability, all of which guide professional responsibility, equitable care, honest communication and collaboration throughout recovery. The application of these principles is examined across the preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative phases of care. This framework emphasizes aligning treatment decisions with patient-defined goals, while balancing the potential benefits and burdens of intervention. Overall, these six ethical principles provide a structured and durable framework for navigating complications following lung resection.

42996806.title: Whey proteins revisited: from an amino acid source to therapeutic potential-a narrative review.
42996806.abstract: Whey proteins are well-established sources of indispensable amino acids, but their relevance to clinical nutrition may also depend on rapid digestion, leucine availability, sulfur-containing amino acids, and bioactive fractions. Previous reviews have commonly focused on sports nutrition, muscle protein synthesis, individual metabolic outcomes, or food-derived peptides, with less emphasis on how these characteristics may inform the formulation of Foods for Special Medical Purposes (FSMPs). This narrative review integrates clinical, preclinical, and mechanistic literature identified in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, with emphasis on muscle metabolism, glycemic regulation, antioxidant and immunomodulatory pathways, wound healing, gut microbiota, and experimental protein-lipid complexes. The most consistent human evidence supports rapid postprandial aminoacidemia, stimulation of muscle protein synthesis, and acute modulation of postprandial glycemia. Evidence for improvements in muscle-related outcomes is also available for selected older or malnourished populations, although whey protein has frequently been administered as part of a multinutrient formulation. Antioxidant, immunomodulatory, wound-healing, microbiota-related, and anticancer-related effects remain supported mainly by mechanistic, in vitro, animal, or limited clinical evidence. Whey proteins should be considered high-quality protein sources with potentially relevant biofunctional properties rather than established therapeutic agents. Their use in FSMPs should be tailored to the target population, required protein and leucine delivery, tolerance, processing characteristics, and overall formulation. Comparative randomized trials are needed to define formulation-specific effects, dose-response relationships, long-term efficacy, and safety.

43008221.title: Association Between Interprofessional Collaborative Competencies and the Quality of Tracheostomy Care Among Intensive Care Unit Nurses: A Cross-Sectional Study.
43008221.abstract: To determine the association between Interprofessional Collaborative Competencies (IPCC) and the Quality of Tracheostomy Care (QTC) among intensive care nurses (ICNs). A cross-sectional correlational study was conducted with 103 ICNs who were selected via stratified random sampling from teaching hospitals in Iran between August 2024 and February 2025. Data were collected using a demographic and occupational questionnaire, the Chiba Interprofessional Competency Scale and the Quality of Tracheostomy Care Checklist. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and nonparametric inferential tests. Among IPCC dimensions, Attitudes and behaviours that improve team cohesion received the highest score, while Providing care that respects patients received the lowest. QTC scores were highest for Tracheostomy insertion and lowest for Feeding and communication care. The overall IPCC score was not significantly associated with the overall QTC score. However, significant associations were observed between the overall IPCC score (r = 0.23), Attitudes and beliefs as a professional (r = 0.31) and Team management skills (r = 0.21) with Tracheostomy insertion care (p < 0.05). Furthermore, Fulfilling one's role as a professional was significantly associated with Feeding and communication care (r = 0.22; p < 0.05). Although no significant association was observed between total IPCC and QTC scores, significant associations between several IPCC dimensions and specific aspects of QTC among nurses highlight the need to further investigate the role of these competencies across different ICU settings. These findings underscore the potential importance of Attitudes and beliefs as a professional, Team management skills and Fulfilling one's role as a professional in supporting high-quality care in Tracheostomy insertion and Feeding and communication care. The findings may inform targeted interprofessional education focusing on professional attitudes, team management and professional roles in tracheostomy care. Identifying these areas may support team-based efforts to improve patient-centered tracheostomy care in ICU settings. No Patient or Public Contribution.

43008189.title: Participatory Development of a Digital Self-Management Intervention for Intensive Care Recovery: Multimethod Study.
43008189.abstract: Despite promising developments in eHealth, a critical gap remains in understanding how to design and implement digital self-management interventions that effectively align with users' needs and the complex context of recovery after treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU). This study aimed to develop and iteratively refine a digital self-management intervention for post-intensive care recovery and to explore related user experiences and usability among individuals with lived ICU experience. A multimethod participatory development process was used including individuals with lived ICU experience (both survivors and family members) and health care professionals involved in ICU recovery. Between April 2022 and July 2026, guided by the Center for eHealth Research and Disease Management Roadmap consisting of 5 phases, data were collected through inspiration sessions and feedback rounds, individual interviews, usability testing, and pilot use, with qualitative data analyzed thematically and quantitative data analyzed descriptively. Findings from each phase informed the subsequent development steps and were revisited when necessary. The study focused on the specification and iterative refinement of the intervention's core components based on identified values and contextual requirements, complemented by preliminary indicators of usability and descriptive usage metrics. Through stakeholder engagement, key functionalities were defined, including structured recovery information, easy 24-7 access, and guidance in navigating care. Two digital self-management modules, the ICU-RecoveryPointer for ICU survivors and the ICU-FamilyCoach for family members, were developed comprising (1) structured information aligned with the different phases of ICU recovery, (2) concise information tiles with layered content for more in-depth background information, (3) patient-reported e-monitoring features, (4) tailored suggestions addressing recovery challenges and emotional processing, (5) an e-diary with a timeline summary function, and (6) a comprehensive content library. During the pilot phase, the ICU-RecoveryPointer reached 33 linked accounts, with 27 users logging in at least once, whereas the ICU-FamilyCoach reached 66 accounts, with 90 monthly unique-user observations. Usage was primarily concentrated on the information tiles, suggesting that users mainly accessed the informational content within the modules. Two digital self-management modules were designed through a participatory and iterative development process, supporting individuals with lived ICU experience during the recovery trajectory. Preliminary user experiences and usage data provided initial insights into usability and engagement, while also highlighting the need for further evaluation before broader implementation.

43007949.title: Prevalence of thyroid dysfunction in patients with acute atrial fibrillation attending coronary care unit at Al-Sadder Teaching Hospital.
43007949.abstract: Aim: Assessment of prevalence of thyroid dysfunction in patients with acute atrial fibrillation. Materials and Methods: A total of 110 patients participated in this cross-sectional study, admitted to the coronary care unit with AF not more than 48 hours from symptom onset and investigated by TSH, T3, and T4 to show how prevalent thyroid dysfunction in patients with acute AF, a study done at Al-Sadr Medical City - Najaf Al-Ashraf city, Iraq. Results: This study showed Prevalence of thyroid dysfunction was 21.7% which represents 24 patients that include (one patient with subclinical hypothyroidism 0.9%, 4 patients with subclinical hyperthyroidism 3.6%, 5 patients with hypothyroidism 4.5%, 14 patients with hyperthyroidism 12.7% and patients with euthyroid represent (N=86, 78.3%) of patients. Conclusions: For patients who admitted to the coronary care unit with acute atrial fibrillation both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism were frequent with the latest exceeding the prevalence in the general population necessitating screening for hidden thyroid dysfunction for early diagnosis and management to reduce morbidity and mortality.

43004939.title: Developing Personas Based on the Identified Characteristics and Needs of ICU Patients: A Mixed-Methods Study.
43004939.abstract: The high demand for critical care, limited medical resources and patient variability among Intensive Care Units (ICUs) suggest that standardized resource allocation may not fully address individual ICU patient needs. Patient persona, a representative profile synthesized from individuals with similar characteristics and needs, is gaining traction in the healthcare field but remains underexplored in ICUs. To develop patient personas of ICU patients to support stratified resource management. We employed an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. Quantitatively, we analysed 48 709 ICU patients from the MIMIC-IV database using K-prototypes clustering to identify subgroups. Qualitatively, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 ICU nurses from three ICUs in China between May and July 2025 and analysed using conventional content analysis. Quantitative and qualitative findings were integrated to comprehensively characterize ICU patients. Three distinct personas were identified. (1) Critical & Complex Support: elderly, highest disease severity, most life-support interventions, complete loss of disease management capacity, psychosocial disruption, longest hospitalization, highest mortality and need comprehensive support. (2) Severe & Intensive Support: significantly older, Medicare coverage, high disease severity and comorbidity burden, many life-support interventions, partial disease management capacity, dysfunctional psychosocial adaptation, short hospital stays then discharged to nursing facilities and need intensive support. (3) Sub-intensive & Basic Support: middle-aged, considerable disease severity but few life-support interventions, collaborate with healthcare providers yet show psychosocial maladaptation, shortest hospital stays, discharged home and need self-management support. The three patient personas developed in this study may provide a reference for delivering precise care and optimizing ICU resource allocation. Further research is needed to evaluate the generalizability of these personas across different clinical settings. Based on these personas, ICU managers can dynamically allocate resources (beds, staff, equipment) by subgroup characteristics and needs, while ICU nurses can prioritize and individualize bedside care.

43004237.title: Risk model prediction of ICU mortality in aortic dissection patients based on MIMIC-IV.
43004237.abstract: This study aimed to explore risk factors derived from clinical characteristics that are associated with intensive care unit (ICU) outcomes in patients with aortic dissection (AD). Total 478 patients' data including demographic characteristics, vital signs, hematological parameters, and other laboratory tests, were extracted from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC‑IV) database. Five different machine-learning methods were used to construct the prediction models. Patients with Stanford type B dissection exhibited significantly lower heart rate (P = 0.022), neutrophil count (P = 0.015), chloride level (P = 0.018), and SOFA score (P = 0.008), but higher red blood cell count (P = 0.003), white blood cell count (P = 0.02), monocyte count (P < 0.001), basophil count (P = 0.019), platelet count (P < 0.001), glucose (P = 0.003), sodium (P = 0.03), and total calcium (P < 0.001) compared with type A patients. Non‑survivors in the ICU had significantly higher body mass index (P = 0.042), anion gap (P = 0.004), urea nitrogen (P = 0.041), creatinine (P = 0.011), alanine aminotransferase (ALT, P < 0.001), aspartate aminotransferase (AST, P < 0.001), and SOFA score (P = 0.024), along with lower levels of SaO₂ (P = 0.005), SvO₂ (P = 0.002), red blood cell count (P = 0.006), mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (P = 0.001), white blood cell count (P = 0.029), eosinophils (P = 0.03), platelets (P = 0.004), and urine output (P = 0.02) compared with survivors. In predictive modelling, the random‑forest‑based approach achieved a higher area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.825, versus 0.678 for logistic regression and 0.553 for the neural network. We developed and internally validated predictive models of ICU mortality in AD patients. Risk factors for ICU mortality in AD patients include SvO₂, anion gap, and AST, among which SvO₂ appears to be a reliable predictor of clinical outcome.

43006874.title: A novel interprofessional experience caring for post-intensive care and long COVID patients: the optimal clinic experience.
43006874.abstract: This short report describes the development of an interprofessional ambulatory care clinic with an interprofessional education program at an academic medical center providing comprehensive care to patients previously hospitalized in the intensive care unit (ICU) or with COVID-19 from May 2020 to May 2026. The OPTIMAL Clinic (lOng COVID/PosT-Icu MultidisciplinAry cLinic) was created during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, with limited staff and temporary funding. Our team consisted of clinical pharmacy and physician trainees, nurse practitioners, occupational therapists, physical therapists, pharmacists, physicians, and social workers, who collaborated strategically and synergistically to optimize patient care. Across repeated evaluations, the clinic model was associated with increased preventive care and financial sustainability, and decreased emergency department visits and unplanned hospitalizations. Our interprofessional education program achieved high ratings from trainees in preceptor support, onboarding, clinical activities, and interprofessional education. Our OPTIMAL clinic exemplifies a model for interprofessional care and education for the support of complex patients after ICU or COVID-19 hospitalizations.

43006042.title: Dietary intervention to attenuate inflammation in patients with hyperphenylalaninemia in ICU: a preliminary study.
43006042.journal: Journal of clinical biochemistry and nutrition
43006042.abstract: Inflammation severity predicts mortality risk in intensive care unit (ICU) patients. Hyperphenylalaninemia (HPA) is associated with inflammation. We investigated whether a phenylalanine (PHE)-free diet (PFD) reduces PHE, downstream metabolite, and proinflammatory cytokine levels in patients with HPA. This study enrolled ICU patients with PHE levels of ≥95 ‍μM. They were divided into PFD and usual diet (UD) groups. Changes in PHE, downstream metabolite, and proinflammatory cytokine levels were assessed over a 5-day period. We included 66 propensity score-matched patients (PFD: 33; UD: 33). Reductions in PHE levels were greater in the PFD group (from 136 ± 44.7 to 97.0 ± 41.7 ‍μM) than in the UD group (from 125 ± 24.5 to 108 ± 30.9 ‍μM; p = 0.008). PFD group exhibited greater reductions in phenylpyruvate, hydroxyl-phenyllactate, interleukin-6, interleukin-10, tumor necrosis factor-α, and macrophage inflammatory protein-1β levels and a smaller increase in interferon-inducible T-cell α chemoattractant level than did the UD group (all p<0.05). Lower PHE intake was associated with lower cytokine levels. PFD intake was associated with a trend of lowering 15-day mortality (p = 0.072). Our findings suggest that PFD intake reduces the levels of PHE and proinflammatory cytokines in ICU patients with HPA. Randomized placebo-controlled trials are required to elucidate the benefits of PFDs.

43005942.title: Mapping Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Other Prospective Risk Analysis Approaches in Intrahospital Transport Involving Critically Ill Patients: A Scoping Review.
43005942.abstract: Intrahospital transport exposes critically ill patients and their care teams to clinical and organizational vulnerabilities, and proactive risk analysis can inform preventive interventions. This scoping review mapped the use of failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA), its variants, and complementary prospective risk analysis approaches in intrahospital transport pathways involving critically ill patients or critical care transitions. Studies of multi-area transfers, imaging pathways, and mixed adult and pediatric populations were included for their organizational relevance, not because all participants were critically ill. The review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and was reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed, the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched on October 3, 2026, for studies published from 2002 to 2026. Three reviewers independently screened all records and full-text reports. All included studies were appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) 2018, and the six studies with quantitative comparisons were also appraised with the JBI checklist for quasi-experimental studies. Of the 789 records identified, 689 were screened after the removal of 100 duplicates. Fourteen studies, reported in 15 publications, were included. Seven studies used FMEA, five used healthcare failure mode and effects analysis (HFMEA), and one used failure modes, effects and criticality analysis (FMECA); the remaining study used the bow-tie model. Recurring vulnerabilities involved communication and handoff, patient identification, medication management, equipment readiness, device security, and monitoring. Four studies reported fewer adverse events after implementation, one reported improved perceived preparedness, and one reported a lower risk priority number (RPN). Designs and outcomes were heterogeneous. The mapping can inform local risk analysis and the design of interventions, but the reported associations do not establish causal effectiveness. Controlled multicenter evaluations with measures of fidelity, sustainability, and cost are needed. The vulnerabilities and preventive strategies identified are particularly relevant to nursing practice, given the central role of nurses in patient preparation, monitoring, device protection, medication continuity, and interprofessional handoff. No dedicated studies have addressed transport from the intensive care unit or emergency department to the operating room or between intensive care units, and research is needed in underrepresented regions, such as the Middle East, Southeast Asia, Latin America, and most of Europe.

43005895.title: Competency Based Education in Anesthesia and Intensive Care Medicine: Educational Innovations, Implementation Challenges, and Future Directions.
43005895.journal: Advances in medical education and practice
43005895.abstract: Anesthesia and intensive care medicine require clinicians to integrate technical expertise with rapid decision making, communication, teamwork, leadership, and patient-safety behaviors. Competency based medical education (CBME) seeks to make these capabilities explicit and link progression to demonstrated performance, yet implementation across anesthesia and intensive care training remains uneven. This structured narrative review used a targeted PubMed/MEDLINE search updated through 13 September 2026, supplemented by citation chaining and authoritative professional and curriculum sources. Sources were considered when they addressed postgraduate anesthesia or intensive care education and predefined themes including competency frameworks, assessment, simulation, non-technical skills, faculty development, technology, equity, and implementation; purely clinical, undergraduate only, duplicate, or thematically irrelevant sources were excluded. A prospective screening log was not maintained; 45 sources were included in the final narrative synthesis. Evidence supports CBME as a coherent architecture for outcomes and longitudinal assessment, but anesthesia specific evidence for superior patient outcomes remains limited. Simulation has the most mature evidence for procedural mastery, crisis management, and team performance, whereas entrustment, digital learning, extended reality, and artificial intelligence show promise but remain constrained by variable implementation and heterogeneous outcomes. Resource constrained settings further highlight the importance of locally adapted curricula, low cost simulation, and faculty capacity. We propose a five domain framework that integrates competency-defined curricula, multimodal learning, longitudinal assessment and feedback, faculty and institutional capacity, and equitable patient safety implementation. Unlike generic CBME models, the framework is designed as a practical implementation bridge for anesthesia and intensive care programs across diverse resource settings.

43005663.title: Drug-Induced Linear IgA Bullous Dermatosis in a Critically Ill Patient Exposed to Polypharmacy.
43005663.abstract: Drug-induced linear IgA bullous dermatosis (DILABD) is typically associated with single-agent triggers, such as vancomycin, but its occurrence in the setting of polypharmacy is poorly understood. We report a 36-year-old female who developed DILABD during intensive care admission following exposure to multiple recognised triggering medications across different drug classes, with histological and immunofluorescence findings confirming the diagnosis. To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of DILABD arising in the context of such extensive polypharmacy, highlighting the diagnostic challenges in critically ill patients and raising the hypothesis that cumulative or synergistic drug effects may contribute to disease onset. However, this proposed interaction remains theoretical and cannot be established as a causal mechanism from a single case.

43005099.title: Preoperative frailty risk in older patients with colorectal cancer admitted to the ICU after surgery: prevalence, associated factors, and association with in-hospital outcomes.
43005099.abstract: Frailty is recognized as an important predictor of adverse outcomes in older surgical patients. However, evidence regarding preoperative frailty among older patients with colorectal cancer (CRC) admitted to the ICU after surgery remains limited. This study aimed to investigate the prevalence, associated factors, and impact of preoperative frailty risk on in-hospital outcomes in this high-risk population. This single-center retrospective cohort study included 308 older CRC patients who underwent radical surgery and were admitted to the ICU postoperatively between June 2023 and March 2026. Preoperative frailty risk was assessed using the five-item modified Frailty Index (mFI-5). Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with frailty risk and evaluate the association between preoperative frailty risk and postoperative complications. Generalized linear models were applied to assess the associations of frailty risk with total hospital stay, ICU stay, and hospitalization costs. The prevalence of preoperative frailty risk was 55.52% in this study. Higher albumin levels were a protective factor, whereas higher blood glucose levels, elevated NLR, BMI ≥ 26.9 kg/m², polypharmacy, pain, and high fall risk were significantly associated with increased frailty risk. After adjustment for confounders, frailty risk remained an independent predictor of overall complications and severe complications and was significantly associated with prolonged total hospital stay, longer ICU stay, and increased hospitalization costs. Preoperative frailty risk is highly prevalent among older CRC patients admitted to the ICU after surgery and is independently associated with adverse in-hospital outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating frailty assessment into perioperative management. The mFI-5 is a simple and feasible tool for preoperative risk stratification in this high-risk population and may help guide prehabilitation strategies to ultimately optimize postoperative recovery.

43004421.title: ICU communication experiences and needs among patients, family members, and healthcare professionals: a qualitative meta-synthesis.
43004421.abstract: In the ICU, communication is fundamental to high-quality critical care and depends on the involvement of patients, family members, and healthcare professionals. While existing research has mainly examined the perspectives of individual groups or focused on dyadic interactions, the ways in which the experiences and needs of these three groups intersect within ICU communication have received comparatively little attention. This review aimed to synthesise qualitative evidence on the communication experiences and needs of patients, family members, and healthcare professionals in ICU settings, and to develop an interpretive framework explaining how these experiences and needs shape ICU communication. A systematic search was performed in eight electronic databases from their inception to 1 February 2026. Reference lists of included studies were also screened manually. Eligible studies were identified according to predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The quality of the included studies was evaluated with the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme checklist and the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Findings were synthesized using thematico synthesis, and an interpretive framework was developed based on the integrated findings. The synthesis included 35 studies and developed four analytical themes: (1) information imbalance as a structural driver of instability in ICU communication; (2) multi-level structural barriers constraining communication; (3) emotional experiences as both outcomes of communication and regulatory mechanisms; and (4) adaptive strategies sustaining communication under constrained conditions. Information imbalance arose from mismatches between information complexity and recipients' interpretive capacity, selective information disclosure, and fragmented communication delivery. Communication was further constrained by physiological and environmental conditions, interactional limitations, individual differences, and institutional factors. Communication experiences could generate both positive and negative emotions, which may subsequently influence how patients, family members, and healthcare professionals communicate. Cognitive adjustment, emotional support, and behavioral compensation partially maintained communication under constrained conditions. ICU communication is a dynamic process shaped by information imbalance, structural barriers, and emotional feedback mechanisms. Although constrained by multiple factors, communication can be maintained through adaptive strategies, highlighting its resilience even under challenging ICU conditions. Improving ICU communication therefore requires coordinated interventions targeting information delivery, structural support, emotional responsiveness, and multi-party collaboration.

43009181.title: Patient choice and uptake of Home-based rehabilitation with Health coaching versus Center-based pulmonary rehabilitation after a COPD-related hospitalization.
43009181.journal: Annals of the American Thoracic Society
43009181.abstract: Adherence to center-based pulmonary rehabilitation after a COPD-related hospitalization-which improves all outcomes, including survival-is only 3%. Home-based programs have been proposed as a more feasible option, but they are not systematically offered, and patient preference is unknown. This pragmatic randomized trial involving patients with COPD recently hospitalized for a COPD exacerbation, originally aimed to investigate the comparative effect two arms: The choice of a facilitated referral to a center-based outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation program or a home-based program versus a home-based program on adherence to post-hospitalization rehabilitation and disease-specific QoL measured by the Chronic Respiratory Questionnaire. The trial aimed to investigate the patient's preference of home vs center-based rehabilitation in individuals randomized to the choice arm. Daily steps were measured by Actigraph ®.The asynchronous home-based program included weekly health coaching and daily monitoring of daily steps, symptoms, and a 20-minute daily flexibility-balance exercise routine. Of 1,906 patients approached, 294 (15%) were randomized and agreed to the rehabilitation options offered by the study arms (uptake); of those, 56% completed the 12-week intervention (adherence). Of the 145 randomized to the choice arm, only one patient chose center-based PR; therefore, both groups received the same intervention, and results are presented as a one-group (before-after) analysis. Compared with baseline, the home intervention significantly improved (p < 0.01) physical and emotional QoL (Chronic Respiratory Questionnaire) and increased daily steps beyond the minimal clinically important difference. Trajectory models adjusted for age, FEV1%, and mMRC (breathlessness) confirmed sustained improvements in QoL at 6 and 12 months from baseline. When offered a choice of rehabilitation setting after a COPD-related hospital admission for an exacerbation, home-based rehabilitation is patients' preferred option. Sustained quality-of-life improvements in 1 year may represent an opportunity to regain well-being and/or deliver primary palliative care. Our results may have important implications for clinical practice.

43008755.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea: an overlooked challenge in the current NHS Strategy.
43008755.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is common, frequently symptomatic, and closely associated with conditions already prioritised by the UK National Health Service (NHS), including obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation, cardiovascular disease, and stroke. Previous estimates suggest that approximately 8 million UK adults aged 30-69 years could have OSA, although the proportion remaining undiagnosed is uncertain. Evidence supports treatment benefits for daytime sleepiness, symptom burden, quality of life, driving safety, and blood pressure in some patients, but not a consistent reduction in major cardiovascular events. UK data indicate long diagnostic waits, regional variation, and gaps in follow-up. A proportionate NHS response should prioritise targeted case-finding within existing chronic-disease pathways, access to validated home-based diagnostics, specialist capacity for complex disease, and sustained treatment support. Implementation should be phased and evaluated prospectively for clinical outcomes, equity, workforce requirements, affordability, and budget impact.

43006841.title: Development and Validation of EPIC-US: A Reference Model for COPD Policy Evaluation in the United States.
43006841.journal: Annals of the American Thoracic Society
43006841.abstract: The large and growing burden of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) requires evidence-based policies to improve patient outcomes and reduce healthcare costs. We developed the Evaluation Platform in COPD in the U.S. (EPIC-US), a whole-disease model of COPD capable of evaluating interventions across all stages of disease progression within a single policy platform. The objectives were to develop EPIC-US by adapting a model version developed for Canada (EPIC) and internally and externally validate EPIC-US to an independent clinical cohort. EPIC-US is a stochastic discrete-event simulation model of COPD for U.S. individuals aged ≥40 years. It simulates COPD progression based on individualized trajectories of lung function decline and exacerbations. We matched population size to U.S. census projections for 2015-2060. All-cause mortality was taken from U.S. life tables. Historical and projected trends in tobacco smoking prevalence were aligned with 2018 and 2023 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) results, while COPD prevalence was informed by National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) data. We used clinical trials, meta-analyses and U.S. administrative data to inform the rate and severity of exacerbations. We externally validated moderate exacerbations and severe exacerbations using the U.S. sub-sample of the NOVEL observational longiTudinal studY (NOVELTY). EPIC-US simulated outputs closely matched module-specific internal validation targets. The predicted population size of ≥ 40-year-olds was within 1-2% of U.S. Census projections. Predicted mean COPD prevalence (8.1% for ages 40-59 years; 14.4% for ages 60-79 years), and smoking prevalence in 2018 (12.9%) and 2023 (10.1%) were within 0.1-0.4% of NHIS and NHANES estimates. In 2016, EPIC-US predicted 560 hospitalizations for COPD per 100,000 person-years, consistent with the observed rate of 510 hospitalizations. In external validation, severe exacerbations rates in EPIC-US (0.039; 95% CI 0.035-0.043 per patient-year) were comparable to NOVELTY (0.022 per patient-year, 95% CI 0.008-0.065). EPIC-US replicated differences in exacerbation rate across classes of inhaled therapies. However, EPIC-US overpredicted the rate of moderate exacerbations relative to NOVELTY. EPIC-US is the first multi-purpose, whole-disease model of COPD in the U.S., providing a policy-ready platform for simulating both the clinical and economic burden of the disease.

43009368.title: Patient-reported disability has insufficient clinical accuracy for predicting physical function in survivors of critical illness: a secondary analysis of a cluster-randomised trial.
43009368.abstract: Post-ICU care often misses patients unable to attend in-person clinic visits. Remote assessments of physical function might increase access to ICU aftercare. We investigated whether patient-reported disability predicts handgrip strength (HGS) and the 2-Minute Walk Test (2MWT) distance with sufficient clinical accuracy. This secondary analysis of the stepped-wedge cluster-randomised Enhanced Recovery after Intensive Care trial included patients from 10 German ICU clusters who completed the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS) 2.0 plus either HGS, the 2MWT, or both, 6 months after ICU discharge. Relationships between WHODAS 2.0, HGS, and 2MWT were analysed using scatter plots, correlation coefficients, linear regressions, and Bland-Altman plots. Predictions of HGS and the 2MWT were compared with the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for both measures. Of 1463 enrolled patients, 620 were analysed. The median WHODAS 2.0 sum score was 11 (Q1, Q3: 3, 22). The median HGS, expressed as a percentage of the expected value (%exp), was 70.6%exp (Q1, Q3: 54.4, 85.6), and the median 2MWT distance was 73.7%exp (Q1, Q3: 61.5, 85.8). The 2MWT was not completed by 59% of patients. Higher disability was moderately correlated with lower HGS (Spearman %exp: -0.41) and shorter 2MWT distance (Spearman %exp: -0.47). In multivariable regression models, the WHODAS 2.0 sum score predicted HGS in kg (β: -0.27 [95% CI: -0.33 to -0.22]; P<0.001) and 2MWT distance in m (β: -1.94 [95% CI: -2.37 to -1.51]; P<0.001), but the limits of agreement exceeded the MCIDs. With increasing disability, HGS and 2MWT performance declined, although correlations were moderate and uncertainty of predictions exceeded MCIDs of both instruments. Remote WHODAS 2.0 assessments cannot replace in-person physical function testing. NCT03671447.

42246225.title: Central venous cannulation in critically ill patients: guidelines of the Polish Society of Anaesthesiology and Intensive Therapy.
42246225.abstract: These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for central venous cannulation in critically ill patients in the intensive care unit. The document was developed by the Working Group of the Polish Society of Anaesthesiology and Intensive Therapy (Polskie Towarzystwo Anestezjologii i Intensywnej Terapii - PTAiIT) based on the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) methodology, which encompasses systematic reviews of the literature, meta-analyses, and - in the absence of sufficient data - expert consensus. These guidelines aim to standardise the approach to central venous cannulation, increase the effectiveness of procedures, and minimise the risk of complications. The guidelines address pre-procedural ultrasound assessment, selection of the optimal vascular access site, comparison of ultrasound-guided versus landmark cannulation at different access sites, confirmation of catheter position after cannulation, and the role of positional manoeuvres.

42087034.title: Guidelines for Seizure Prophylaxis in Patients Undergoing Supratentorial Neurosurgery: A Statement for Healthcare Professionals from the Neurocritical Care Society.
42087034.abstract: BACKGROUND: There is significant heterogeneity related to the use of prophylactic antiseizure medications (ASM) following supratentorial craniotomy. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis assessing ASM primary prophylaxis in adults hospitalized following supratentorial neurosurgery with no prior seizure history. The following population, intervention, comparator, and outcome (PICO) questions were assessed: (1) Should ASM versus no ASM be used as seizure prophylaxis in adult patients undergoing supratentorial neurosurgery? (2) If an ASM is used, should levetiracetam (LEV) or phenytoin/fosphenytoin (PHT) be preferentially used? and (3) Should a long (> 7 days) versus short (≤ 7 days) duration of prophylaxis be used? The main outcomes were early seizure (≤ 14 days), late seizures (> 14 days), adverse events, mortality, and functional and cognitive outcomes. We utilized Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology to generate recommendations. RESULTS: The initial literature search yielded 1988 articles, and 16 formed the basis of the recommendations. PICO 1: while meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) demonstrated a significant benefit for early seizure prevention, meta-analyses including all study designs was nonsignificant. Further, there were no differences in late seizure or mortality rates, and there was a trend toward higher adverse event rates with ASM. PICO 2: LEV was associated with significantly lower early seizure rates than PHT, and there were trends toward fewer late seizures and adverse events with LEV. PICO 3: only three studies examined the duration of ASM treatment, and there was no significant difference in seizure events between subjects treated for a short versus long duration. CONCLUSIONS: We suggest that either prophylactic ASM or no ASM be used for seizure prophylaxis in patients undergoing supratentorial neurosurgery (conditional recommendation, low quality of evidence). If an ASM is used, we suggest LEV over PHT (conditional recommendation, very low quality of evidence) for a short duration (conditional recommendation, very low quality of evidence).

41942818.title: Guidelines for Neuroprognostication in Critically ill Adults with Acute Ischemic Stroke.
41942818.abstract: BACKGROUND: Patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS) may require intensive care unit admission for several reasons, including post-procedural care, management of large hemispheric infarction, and cardiopulmonary instability. The objective of this document is to provide recommendations on the reliability of select individual predictors of outcome, and multivariate prediction models, in the context of counseling critically ill patients with AIS and their surrogates. In addition, broad principles of neuroprognostication in this population were identified. METHODS: A narrative systematic review was completed using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology. Candidate predictors, including clinical variables and prediction models, were selected on the basis of clinical relevance and the presence of an appropriate body of evidence. The Population/Intervention/Comparator/Outcome/Timing/Setting (PICOTS) question was framed as follows: "When counseling critically ill adults with AIS or their surrogates, should <predictor> be considered a reliable predictor of poor functional outcome at 3 months or later?" Recommendations were based on quality of evidence, balance of desirable and undesirable consequences, values and preferences, and resource use. Recommendations that met GRADE criteria for good practice statements addressed broad principles of neuroprognostication. RESULTS: A total of 518 articles met eligibility criteria to guide recommendations. Good practice recommendations include avoiding premature neuroprognostication, avoiding confounders, the use of multimodal assessment, predicting recovery of swallow function, predicting tracheostomy decannulation, and counseling of patients with large hemispheric infarction and their surrogates prior to neurological decline. Early neurological improvement within 24 h of revascularization was identified as a moderately reliable predictor of good functional outcome. No other individual predictor was considered reliable for the prediction of mortality or functional outcome.
