Evidence is promising but limited by small study numbers, heterogeneous interventions and sparse nurse-reported outcomes. Critical care implementation should prioritise nurse-centred design, alert burden, equity, safety monitoring and rigorous evaluation before scale-up. RELEVANCE TO CLINICAL PRACTICE: Nurse-used AI-CDSS show potential to improve patient outcomes and care processes, but evidence remains limited and context dependent.

42316052.title: Timing of renal-replacement therapy in patients with acute kidney injury and sepsis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
42316052.abstract: BACKGROUND: The optimal timing for initiating renal replacement therapy (RRT) in sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (AKI) patients remains controversial. Early RRT initiation offers benefits by preventing metabolic complications and fluid overload, while delayed initiation avoids unnecessary procedures and conserves resources. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to compare early versus delayed RRT strategies in adult patients with sepsis-associated AKI. METHODS: We conducted a comprehensive search on PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane CENTRAL from inception to February 2026. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational cohorts comparing early versus delayed RRT initiation in patients with sepsis-associated AKI. Outcomes included 28-day and 90-day mortality, multi-organ dysfunction score (MODS), and intensive care unit (ICU) and hospital length of stay. Data were pooled using random-effects models. RESULTS: Fifteen studies (4 RCTs, 11 retrospective cohorts) comprising 6,289 patients were included. Early RRT was associated with significant reduction in 28-day mortality compared to delayed RRT (RR 0.81, 95% CI: 0.68-0.95, p = 0.01; I²=31.38%). However, trim-and-fill analysis suggested potential publication bias, with adjusted estimates showing non-significance (RR 0.88, 95% CI: 0.75-1.04). No significant differences were observed for 90-day mortality (RR 0.85, 95% CI: 0.69-1.04, p = 0.12), MODS (MD 0.24, 95% CI: -0.94-1.42, p = 0.69), ICU length of stay (MD -1.76, 95% CI: -4.18-0.66, p = 0.15), or hospital length of stay (MD 0.34, 95% CI: -3.24-3.92, p = 0.85). CONCLUSION: Early RRT initiation in sepsis-associated AKI was associated with reduction in 28-day mortality rates but did not result in any differences of 90-days mortality rates, and was not associated with improvements in MODS, suggesting that timing alone may not substantially alter long-term outcomes in this high-risk population. These findings are driven from mixed study designs with heterogeneity among the included patients, underscoring the need for more individualized approaches to RRT initiation in the future trials. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable.

42690848.title: Acinetobacter baumannii resistance trends in an ICU from Saudi Arabia over 12 years.
42690848.journal: The Indian journal of medical research
42690848.abstract: Background and objectives Acinetobacter baumannii is a major intensive care unit (ICU)-associated pathogen due to associated extensive drug resistance. Regional data from southern Saudi Arabia remain limited. This study aimed to describe overall and temporal resistance patterns of ICU-associated A. baumannii. Methods We conducted a 12-y retrospective study (August 2012- August 2024) at Aseer Central Hospital, Saudi Arabia, analysing Acinetobacter spp. clinical isolates from ICU and non-ICU settings. Species identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) were performed using the VITEK® 2 system, with susceptibility interpreted per CLSI M100 guidelines. Carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB) and difficult-to-treat resistance phenotypes were defined. Temporal trends were assessed via logistic regression. Results Of 3,935 isolates, 96.6% were A. baumannii. ICU-derived isolates (48.5%) showed significantly higher resistance rates across nearly all antibiotic classes compared to non-ICU isolates (P<0.001). Carbapenem resistance rates remained above 90% throughout the study period, while difficult to treat resistance ranged between 65.2 to 96.1%. Logistic regression revealed significant temporal declines in resistance to cefepime, ceftazidime, aminoglycosides, and fluoroquinolones (P<0.001). Interpretation and conclusions Acinetobacter baumannii isolates from ICU settings in southern Saudi Arabia exhibit persistently high resistance, including carbapenem resistance and difficult-to-treat resistance. We observed significant temporal declines in resistance to selected agents, particularly cefepime, aminoglycosides, and fluoroquinolones. These findings highlight the critical role of ICU-focused antimicrobial stewardship, enhanced infection control strategies, and regional molecular surveillance to limit further spread.

42693541.title: Wearable Sleep and Circadian Monitoring in Intensive Care Nursing: A Scoping Review.
42693541.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sleep and circadian disruption are common in critical illness, yet bedside assessment remains difficult. Wearables are unobtrusive and extend observation across 24 h, but their measurement performance in critical illness requires appraisal. AIMS: To map wearable sleep and circadian monitoring during intensive care, its measurement performance, clinical applications and nursing implications. STUDY DESIGN: A scoping review followed JBI and PRISMA-ScR guidance. PubMed, Europe PMC and OpenAlex were searched from inception to 22 July 2026, with citation searching. Eligible primary reports used a body-worn sensor during intensive care to estimate sleep or circadian/rest-activity outcomes at any age. Conventional polysomnography/electroencephalography without an eligible wearable, non-contact systems, staff studies and post-ICU-only monitoring were excluded. No risk-of-bias appraisal was undertaken. RESULTS: Sixty-one reports (43 adult; 18 paediatric/neonatal; 1996-2026) were included. Actigraphy dominated; commercial trackers, smartwatches and one respiratory-belt/heart-rate-variability system were less common. Monitoring was feasible, but performance varied by device, patient state and age group: wake specificity was often poor in ventilated, sedated or immobile patients and agreement with patient or nurse reports was weak to modest. Records showed fragmented and daytime sleep, weak day-night consolidation and attenuated circadian rhythmicity. Nursing bundles, massage, positioning, light and chronotype-informed care changed selected outcomes, but effects were heterogeneous. CONCLUSIONS: Wearables usefully describe rest-activity patterns and support nursing assessment, but agreement with physiological sleep varied by device, patient state and age; movement-derived estimates need clinical context and are not a stand-alone sleep measure. RELEVANCE TO CLINICAL PRACTICE: Nurses should combine wearable trends with patient report, sedation and mobility, delirium screening and care-interaction records; escalation thresholds require prospective validation.

42707926.title: Beyond the Diagnosis: A Comprehensive Case Report on Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy.
42707926.abstract: BACKGROUND: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive genetic disorder characterized by the absence of dystrophin, leading to progressive muscle degeneration and generalized weakness. It primarily affects males in early childhood and progresses to loss of ambulation and cardiac and respiratory complications. CASE REPORT: This case report describes a 26-year-old male with terminal-stage DMD who was admitted to the surgical intensive care unit (SICU) in a critically ill state with multiple-organ failure. He was ventilator-dependent via tracheostomy, hypotensive, anemic, and required cardiovascular support. He also had multiple pressure ulcers, including a Stage IV ulcer with associated edema, acute renal failure managed with continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), and sepsis due to mixed bacterial and fungal infections. Broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy and intensive wound care were provided. This case highlights that advanced-stage DMD is a severe multisystem condition requiring intensive, specialized, and multidisciplinary care. CONCLUSION: This case underscores the critical importance of a multidisciplinary approach in managing complex patient conditions, emphasizing the prevention of secondary complications such as pressure ulcers and pulmonary infections. Adherence to evidence-based guidelines, coupled with psychosocial and ethical considerations related to quality of life, remains essential. Establishing standardized care protocols, enhancing healthcare team training on the specific needs of these patients, and promoting home-based and palliative care services are strongly recommended to ensure comprehensive, coordinated, and patient-centered management.

42712088.title: Immersive Virtual Reality for Procedural Pain and Anxiety During Postoperative Wound Dressing in Cardiac Surgery ICU Patients: A Quasi-Experimental Study.
42712088.abstract: BACKGROUND: Postoperative wound dressing procedures are a common source of pain and anxiety among intensive care unit (ICU) patients following cardiac surgery. Virtual Reality Distraction Therapy (VRDT) has emerged as a promising non-pharmacological intervention for symptom management; however, evidence regarding its use during postoperative wound care in critically ill cardiac surgery patients remains limited. AIM: To evaluate the effect of Virtual Reality Distraction Therapy on physiological parameters, pain intensity, anxiety levels and patient satisfaction during wound dressing procedures among ICU patients following cardiac surgery. STUDY DESIGN: A one-group pretest-posttest quasi-experimental study was conducted among 50 adult patients admitted to the Cardiothoracic Intensive Care Unit at Tanta University Hospital. Participants received routine postoperative care in addition to VRDT during three consecutive wound dressing sessions. Physiological parameters, pain intensity and anxiety levels were assessed before the intervention, immediately after dressing and 15 min post-dressing. Patient satisfaction with the VR experience was evaluated on the final dressing day. Data were analysed using repeated-measures analysis of variance, paired-samples t-tests, Friedman tests and Pearson correlation coefficients, with a significance level of p < 0.05. RESULTS: Among the 50 enrolled participants who completed the study, VRDT significantly reduced pain intensity (mean difference = -2.44, 95% CI -2.72 to -2.16) and anxiety scores (mean difference = -17.76, 95% CI -18.84 to -16.68) during dressing procedures. Improvements were also observed in selected physiological parameters, particularly respiratory rate and oxygen saturation, while cardiovascular parameters remained stable throughout the intervention period. Most participants reported high levels of satisfaction with the VR experience and expressed willingness to reuse and recommend the intervention. Significant positive correlations were identified between pain intensity and anxiety levels across assessment periods. CONCLUSION: The findings suggest that VRDT may be a feasible and acceptable non-pharmacological adjunct for reducing pain and anxiety during postoperative wound dressing procedures among ICU patients following cardiac surgery. The intervention demonstrated potential benefits in enhancing patient comfort and procedural experiences. Further randomized controlled trials with larger multicentre samples are recommended to confirm these findings and establish the effectiveness of VRDT in critical care practice. RELEVANCE TO CLINICAL PRACTICE: Virtual Reality Distraction Therapy (VRDT) may provide a feasible and acceptable non-pharmacological adjunct to routine postoperative wound care for cardiac surgery patients in intensive care units. Integrating VRDT into nursing practice has the potential to reduce procedural pain and anxiety, improve patient comfort and satisfaction and support more patient-centred care during painful dressing procedures.

42790254.title: Cerebrospinal fluid-venous fistula in hospitalized and critically ill patients.
42790254.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cerebrospinal fluid-venous fistulas are a treatable cause of spontaneous intracranial hypotension, but severe inpatient presentations remain poorly characterized. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed adults hospitalized from 2022 to 2025 with myelography-confirmed cerebrospinal fluid-venous fistula related spontaneous intracranial hypotension at a quaternary referral centre. RESULTS: Fifteen patients were included. Subdural hematomas were present in 13 patients, and 4 required level-1 intensive care admission with depressed consciousness. Brain MRI showed features of spontaneous intracranial hypotension in 13 patients. Fistulas were localised by decubitus CT myelography in 13 patients and digital subtraction myelography in 2. Definitive treatment was achieved by transvenous embolization in 14 patients and high-volume multilevel epidural blood patching in 1. At 3 months, all patients improved, with complete symptom resolution in 13. No procedural complications occurred. CONCLUSION: Cerebrospinal fluid-venous fistula related spontaneous intracranial hypotension can cause severe inpatient morbidity. Early recognition and timely fistula closure are the most important aspects of treatment. Adjunct surgical treatment is necessary for timely recovery in selected cases.

42788067.title: Evidence-Based Guidelines versus Enteral Nutrition Practices in Intensive Care Units: A Descriptive Cross-Sectional Study.
42788067.abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite established guidelines, enteral nutrition (EN) practices among critical care nurses (CCNs) often vary, leading to suboptimal nutritional delivery. Evidence regarding EN practices in Saudi Arabian intensive care units (ICUs) is limited. This study aimed to assess CCNs' EN practices in Al-Madinah and evaluate their alignment with current evidence-based guidelines. METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among CCNs working in adult ICUs of governmental hospitals in Al-Madinah Al-Munawarah, Saudi Arabia, using a census sampling approach. Data were collected using a 61-item self-administered questionnaire comprising three sections: ICU and nurse characteristics (11 items), EN practices (34 items), and assessment and management of EN intolerance and complications (16 items). An online survey was distributed via social media platforms between November 2023 and January 2024. RESULTS: Of 500 eligible nurses, 178 completed the questionnaire (35.6% response rate) and were included in the final analysis. Most reported the availability of EN guidelines (62.4%), performing nutritional assessments (66.9%), initiating EN early within 48 hours or less (87.2%), and using gastric access (98.31%). However, significant inconsistencies were observed in tube placement verification, monitoring and management of gastric residual volume (GRV) and feeding intolerance. Outdated methods for confirming tube placement, such as auscultation, remained common (67.4%). GRV was frequently measured more often than recommended (78.7%), and EN was often withheld at GRV thresholds below recommended (72.5%). Management of diarrhea involved non-recommended practices, although adherence to recommended tube-flushing procedures was high. CONCLUSION: The self-reported EN practices among CCNs showed partial adherence to guidelines, with notable gaps in tube placement verification, GRV and feeding intolerance monitoring and management. These findings underscore the need for standardized protocols, targeted training, and quality improvement initiatives to optimize EN delivery and prevent underfeeding in critically ill patients.

42796337.title: Mortality Associated with Intensive Care Unit Admission and Mechanical Ventilation in Adults with Acute Chest Syndrome: A Systematic Review.
42796337.abstract: Background and Objectives: Acute chest syndrome (ACS) is the leading cause of sickle cell disease (SCD)-related mortality (~25% of deaths). A subset of patients develops severe respiratory compromise requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission or mechanical ventilation (MV), a high-risk group with widely variable reported mortality. This review aimed to determine the mortality rates, ICU/hospital length of stay, and reported complications among adult SCD patients with ACS admitted to the ICU or placed on MV. Materials and Methods: This PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review was prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261295111). Cochrane Library, PubMed, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, EBSCOhost, and Scopus were searched without date restriction. Due to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, the pre-specified meta-analysis was replaced by a narrative synthesis. Methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Results: Eight studies were included (one multicenter prospective cohort, two national database studies, three single-center cohorts, and one before-after antimicrobial stewardship study). In-hospital mortality ranged from 0.95% to 3.8%; overall mortality including follow-up reached 12.9% in a dedicated ICU cohort, a distinct endpoint from in-hospital death. Mechanical ventilation was the strongest indicator of mortality, with odds ratios of 67.53 (MV < 96 h) and 8.73 (MV ≥ 96 h) in the largest national cohort. Tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity ≥3 m/second was associated with cor pulmonale, invasive ventilation, and all immediate hospital deaths in one severe cohort. Documented bacterial infection was uncommon (10-20% of episodes), despite frequent antibiotic use, and procalcitonin-guided discontinuation safely reduced antibiotic exposure. All eight included studies were rated high quality on the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (score ≥ 7/9). Conclusions: Mechanical ventilation, pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale, and comorbidity burden are the most consistent markers of poor outcome in ACS. The findings support early recognition, severity-based respiratory support, and antimicrobial stewardship, but should be interpreted cautiously given the substitution of narrative synthesis for meta-analysis, heterogeneous populations, and the geographic concentration of the included studies.

42753314.title: Professional self-efficacy as a mediator and moderator between workaholism and work-related quality of life in intensive care unit nurses: A multicentre cross-sectional study.
42753314.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
42753314.abstract: BACKGROUND: Workaholism, professional self-efficacy (PSE), and work-related quality of life (WRQoL) are well studied individually, yet their inter-relationships remain underexplored in intensive care unit (ICU) nurses. OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to examine the mediating and moderating roles of PSE between workaholism and WRQoL among ICU nurses. METHODS: A cross-sectional, correlational study was conducted among ICU nurses (n = 319) across five hospitals in the three provinces of Saudi Arabia. Participants were recruited via consecutive and snowball sampling. Three self-report scales were used to collect data between February and July 2025. Structural equation modelling was conducted to test the study hypotheses and display the inter-relationships of the study variables. RESULTS: Workaholism was found to be negatively associated with WRQoL (βD = -0.33, 95% confidence interval [CI] = -0.62 to -0.10, p = 0.004) and PSE (βD = -0.68, 95% CI = -0.85 to -0.51, p = 0.008). PSE positively correlated with WRQoL (βD = 0.45, 95% CI = 0.14 to 0.67, p = 0.008). Additionally, workaholism predicted 46.50% of the total variance of PSE, while both workaholism and PSE explained 50.20% of the total variance of WRQoL. PSE partially mediated the association between workaholism and WRQoL (βI = -0.30, 95% CI = -0.49 to -0.10, p = 0.008). The PSE, as moderator, had a statistically significant association with WRQoL (βD = 0.15, 95% CI = 0.04 to 0.242, p = 0.006). CONCLUSIONS: Workaholism was associated with lower PSE and poorer WRQoL among ICU nurses. PSE partially mediated and moderated the relationship between workaholism and WRQoL, suggesting that it may be an important psychological factor in this association.

42855915.title: Exploring Nurses' Experiences of Autonomy in Intensive Care Units: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.
42855915.abstract: BACKGROUND: Nursing autonomy is essential in intensive care units (ICUs). However, there is limited understanding of how nurses perceive autonomy within their practice. AIM: To explore nurses' perception and experience of autonomy in ICUs. DESIGN: A qualitative descriptive study. METHODS: The study was conducted with 14 ICU nurses through interviews from May to August 2025. Nurses' characteristics were described, and interviews were transcribed verbatim and analyzed using a primarily inductive, semantic codebook thematic analysis informed by Braun and Clarke's six-phase framework. RESULTS: Seven main themes and 25 subthemes emerged from the interviews, revealing personal and organizational factors that influence nursing autonomy in ICUs. The themes were as follows: nursing autonomy's definition and perception, clinical practices, facilitators, barriers, perceived influence on patient care, perceived influence on nurse personal and professional development, and future advancements. CONCLUSION: The findings provide insight into ICU nurses' experiences and perceptions of autonomy. Nurses reported that autonomy was influenced by clinical competence, organizational support, and clear guidelines. Nurses perceived that independent nursing care and timely actions undertaken under approved protocols could support patient care, professional confidence, and job satisfaction. Limited decision-making authority, inadequate staffing, and unclear institutional support were reported as barriers. Nursing autonomy could strengthen nurses' confidence and job satisfaction, which nurses perceived as contributing to better patient care. IMPLICATIONS FOR NURSING MANAGEMENT: The findings can guide nurse managers in implementing structured competency-based education, reinforcing clearly defined scopes of practice that are consistent with institutional policies, and adopting supportive leadership practices to promote nursing autonomy. Hospital administrators and national policymakers can further use the findings to advance nursing practice through developing organizational and regulatory frameworks required to authorize and safely support expanded autonomous practice.

42860727.title: Nurses' Experiences With Artificial Intelligence and the Association Between Clinical Decision-Making and Missed Nursing Care: A Convergent Mixed-Methods Study.
42860727.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being incorporated into clinical nursing practice, but evidence remains limited on how nurses experience AI-supported systems and how decision-making orientation relates to missed nursing care (MNC). AIM: To explore nurses' experiences with AI-supported clinical decision support (CDS) and examine associations among clinical decision-making orientation, professional characteristics, and MNC. DESIGN: A convergent parallel mixed-methods study. METHODS: The study was conducted in six hospitals in Beni Suef Governorate, Egypt. The quantitative sample included 210 intensive care unit (ICU) nurses who completed the Nursing Decision-Making Instrument-Revised 2014 (NDMI-R) and the Missed Intensive Nursing Care Scale (MINCS). Fourteen nurses completed semistructured interviews, and all transcripts were included in the thematic analysis. RESULTS: NDMI-R scores showed a small negative bivariate correlation with MNC (r = -0.178, p < 0.01), but the adjusted association was not statistically significant (β = -0.124, p = 0.063). The regression model explained 16.9% of the variance in MNC (adjusted R2 = 14.5%). Years of experience (β = 0.198, p = 0.004) and bachelor's degree or above compared with a technical nursing diploma (β = -0.255, p < 0.001) were significant predictors. The other education contrast, AI training/support and MISSCARE Reasons were not statistically significant. In interviews, nurses described AI-related tools as potentially helpful for alerts, information review, workflow, and communication while also raising concerns about trust, overreliance, empathy, and training. CONCLUSION: Nurses perceived potential benefits from AI-supported tools, but the quantitative findings did not establish an independent effect of AI or a statistically significant adjusted association between decision-making orientation and MNC. These findings support cautious, nurse-centered implementation and further longitudinal evaluation. IMPLICATIONS FOR NURSING MANAGEMENT: Managers should pair any AI-supported CDS implementation with role-specific training, clear accountability, usability monitoring, and safeguards that preserve clinical judgment and humanistic care.

42862327.title: Association of 24-hours net positive fluid balance with log-transformed vancomycin trough concentrations in the early phase of therapy among critically ill patients.
42862327.abstract: Early vancomycin troughs are frequently low in critical illness and fluid accumulation may contribute through distribution effects. This study estimated the association between net positive fluid balance and early vancomycin troughs as a hypothesis-generating analysis and explored variation across early-therapy windows and by hypoalbuminemia. A retrospective cohort study used ICU electronic health record data from MIMIC-IV. ICU stays with a timing-validated trough were included. The primary cohort N = 255 required at least 80% EMAR dose capture in the prior 24 h and delta serum creatinine at or below 0.2 mg/dL across the 48 h before trough and trough within 72 h of first IV dose. Net fluid balance in the prior 24 h was modeled per + 5 L. Outcome was log trough. Models adjusted for serum creatinine and administered dose and administration count in the prior 24 h. Sensitivity windows were within 48 h (N = 162) and within 96 h (N = 289). Hypoalbuminemia below 3 g/dL was explored in the measured subset. Median trough was 14.00 mg/L (IQR 10.15 to 18.15) and 62 of 255 were below 10 mg/L (24.3%). The point estimate suggested an 11.7% lower trough concentration per + 5 L net positive balance (β =  - 0.1247; SE = 0.079; p = 0.115), but the 95% CI (- 24.4% to + 3.1%) included no association. Serum creatinine had a positive coefficient (β = 0.2995; p = 0.061). Point estimates were similar across early-therapy windows with all confidence intervals including no association. The exploratory albumin interaction was imprecise and limited by substantial missingness and small subgroup sizes. The point estimate suggested lower early vancomycin troughs with higher net positive fluid balance, but the confidence interval included no association. These hypothesis-generating findings require prospective validation to clarify whether fluid balance is associated with early trough concentrations and area under the curve exposure.

42866101.title: Response to "Fragility of Observed Associations in Selection of Empirical Antifungal Therapy for Critically Ill Non-Neutropenic Patients" [Response to Letter].

42903563.title: Feeding practices during high-flow nasal cannula: current evidence and clinical implications for respiratory care.
42903563.abstract: High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy is increasingly used as a noninvasive respiratory support modality across acute and critical care settings. Although nutritional management is integral to the care of patients with respiratory failure, established guidelines for feeding patients receiving HFNC are lacking, and clinical decisions vary widely, reflecting persistent uncertainty about HFNC's effects on swallowing function, airway protection, and aspiration risk. This narrative review found that HFNC may alter swallowing biomechanics, particularly at flow rates >40 L/min, potentially increasing the risk of choking and aspiration. Evidence on aspiration risk is heterogeneous, deriving largely from healthy volunteers and pediatric bronchiolitis cohorts. Adult evidence is limited to retrospective studies; the largest found no increase in respiratory deterioration with enteral feeding. Most institutions lack formal feeding protocols, and practice is driven by individual clinician judgment. Areas of consensus include the safety of early enteral feeding in hemodynamically stable patients and the avoidance of routine prolonged withholding of nutrition based solely on HFNC use. Disagreement persists regarding routine swallowing assessment, optimal flow thresholds during feeding, and the prioritization of oral versus tube feeding. Safe feeding in patients receiving HFNC requires a multidisciplinary, individualized approach that balances respiratory support against nutritional adequacy. Prospective multicenter studies are needed to define safe flow thresholds, validate bedside assessment tools, and establish standardized feeding guidelines, particularly in adult and critically ill populations.

42903103.title: Clinical evaluation of AI Chatbots' performance and safety for total parenteral nutrition planning in critically ill patients: a simulation-based benchmarking study.
42903103.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) is essential for critically ill adults unable to meet their nutritional needs via the gastrointestinal tract. Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have sparked interest in their potential to support healthcare providers in complex clinical decisions. Nonetheless, no prior research has systematically compared publicly accessible chatbots to pharmacist-developed reference TPN plans across a diverse patient cohort, using a predefined, guideline-based rubric assessing accuracy, completeness, safety, error types, and numerical precision. This study presents a simulation-based benchmarking to evaluate (i) the accuracy and comprehensiveness of chatbot-generated TPN plans, (ii) their safety, acceptability, and error profiles, and (iii) the numerical agreement and concordance with expert pharmacist references. METHODS: This benchmarking study, based on simulations and cross-sectional analysis, evaluated the performance of four publicly accessible AI chatbots-ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, and Perplexity-in formulating TPN plans for critically ill adults. Copilot declined to generate patient-specific TPN plans; this refusal was retained as a performance outcome, while Copilot was excluded from analyses requiring an analyzable TPN prescription. Each chatbot produced one plan for each of 10 standardized clinical cases, resulting in a total of 30 TPN plans. Friedman tests, Kendall's W, and Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used for comparative analyses. RESULTS: ChatGPT produced comprehensive plans for all 10 cases, compared to 6 plans from Gemini and 4 from Perplexity. The median accuracy was 57.7% for ChatGPT, 43.9% for Gemini, and 38.5% for Perplexity, with no statistically significant overall difference (p = 0.124). However, ChatGPT performed better than Perplexity in pairwise comparison (adjusted p = 0.035). There was a significant difference in completeness among the chatbots (p = 0.003; Kendall's W = 0.57), with median scores of 64.6, 41.9, and 32.3%, respectively. All 30 plans had at least one major or critical safety issue, 7 (23.3%) contained a critical concern, and 19 (63.3%) were rejected. The most common errors were related to electrolytes (90.0%), micronutrients (70.0%), and monitoring (66.7%). Recommendations from chatbots often exceeded pharmacist-derived values, with median relative differences of +47% for energy, +120% for lipids, and +100% for potassium. Bland-Altman analysis revealed considerable variability in the agreement. CONCLUSION: ChatGPT produced the most comprehensive TPN plans among chatbots. However, none showed enough accuracy, safety, or concordance for independent use. All plans had critical issues, especially with electrolytes, micronutrients, monitoring, and refeeding precautions. AI chatbots can support education or planning but require review by a well-trained clinician before clinical use.

42855082.title: Barriers to early rehabilitation and mobilization in adult ICUs: A multicenter survey in the Eastern region of Saudi Arabia.
42855082.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Prolonged Intensive Care Unit (ICU) immobilization leads to complications such as ICU Acquired Weakness (ICU-AW). While Early Rehabilitation and Mobilization (ERM) is proven to improve functional independence and reduce mechanical ventilation (MV) duration, its implementation remains inconsistent. This study aimed to identify barriers to ERM as perceived by adult ICU healthcare practitioners in the Eastern region of Saudi Arabia. METHODS: A multicenter, cross-sectional survey using a 21-question adapted self-administered questionnaire was conducted between January and April 2023 through QuestionPro platform. The survey was distributed to critical care practitioners including physicians, nurses, respiratory therapists, physiotherapists, and other allied health staff. Respondents represented three hospital categories in the Eastern region: private, Eastern Health Cluster, and other governmental sector hospitals. Barriers were assessed a priori at three levels: patient, provider, and institutional. Internal consistency of the patient-level barrier scale was assessed using Cronbach's alpha. Chi-square and Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact tests compared ERM protocol availability between hospital sectors and knowledge, practice, and resource variables across professional groups. RESULTS: Of 137 practitioners who accessed the survey, 121of 137 who accessed the link completed the questionnaire (88%completion rate). Although 66 (55%) rated ERM as very important, only 48 (40%) reported always participating in or observing it in practice. The most frequently endorsed ideal initiation time was within 24 h of admission (38, 31%), whereas the most commonly reported actual initiation point was when patients were conscious and able to cooperate (28, 23%); only 10 (8%) reported initiation within 24 h. Patient-level barriers were mainly sedation and physiological instability. Provider-level barriers included safety concerns, limited staffing, and inadequate training. At the institutional level, only 57 (47%) respondents reported the presence of a formal ERM protocol, with a significant difference between private hospitals (36/54, 67%) and government hospitals (21/67, 31%) (χ2 = 13.59 df = 1, p < 0.001; OR 4.38, 95% CI 2.04-9.42). Protocol availability, ERM participation, and physiotherapy access also differed significantly across professional groups, with respiratory therapists consistently reporting the lowest access p = 0.013; p < 0.001; p = 0.038; p < 0.001. CONCLUSION: Despite high awareness of its benefits, ERM implementation across adult ICUs in the Eastern region remains suboptimal relative to the 72-h initiation window recommended by current consensus guidance and is delivered reactively rather than proactively. Barriers operate at patient, provider, and institutional levels, and both formal ERM protocol availability and profession-based access to ERM structures differ significantly, with respiratory therapists the most excluded despite managing the highest-risk patients. These findings identify protocol availability and interdisciplinary delivery structures as the principal targets for regional implementation efforts.

42947165.title: The effect of high-fidelity simulation with live actors on nursing students' communication self-efficacy: a pre-post intervention study.
42947165.abstract: BACKGROUND: Effective communication is essential for safe and patient-centered care, particularly in intensive care units (ICUs), where interactions with critically ill patients and their families are emotionally demanding. Nursing students often lack confidence in such high-stakes communication, and culturally tailored educational strategies are limited in Saudi Arabia. This study evaluated the effectiveness of High-Fidelity Simulation (HFS) with live actors on nursing students' communication self-efficacy in ICU settings. METHODS: A one-group pre-post repeated-measures study was conducted with 50 fourth-year nursing students at a public university in Saudi Arabia, with assessments at four time points. Participants completed two HFS sessions with live actors portraying patients' families, followed by ICU clinical placements. Self-efficacy was measured using the 10-point SE-12 scale at four time points: T0 (pre-simulation), T1 (post 1st HFS-LA), T2 (post 2nd HFS-LA), and T3 (post-ICU placement). Repeated-measures ANOVA with Greenhouse-Geisser correction analyzed changes over time. RESULTS: Mean self-efficacy scores increased from T0 = 7.33 (SD 1.81) to T1 = 7.91 (SD 1.76), T2 = 8.39 (SD 1.57), and T3 = 8.02 (SD 1.58). Repeated-measures ANOVA indicated a significant time effect (F = 9.25, p < .001, partial η² = 0.16). Clinical significance analysis showed small but meaningful improvement (Δ = 0.69; effect size d = 0.41). CONCLUSION: High-fidelity simulation with live actors improves nursing students' perceived communication competence in ICU settings. Beyond statistical significance, this improvement has clinical and educational significance as well, since being more confident about communicating may help students to be better equipped to deal with critically ill patients and their family members in actual clinical settings. Repeated, culturally relevant simulation experiences foster confidence in engaging with patients and families, aligning with Saudi cultural norms of family involvement in care. These findings support the integration of multiple actor-based HFS scenarios into undergraduate curricula to enhance communication skills in critical care. CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

42952294.title: Updated Management of Sodium Disorders During Continuous Venovenous Hemofiltration.
42952294.abstract: Severe hyponatremia or hypernatremia in critically ill patients requiring continuous venovenous hemofiltration (CVVH) presents a therapeutic challenge. Adjusting replacement-fluid sodium concentrations may help control correction and reduce the risk of neurologic complications. This practical narrative review summarizes approaches to customizing standard 5-L CVVH replacement-fluid bags, drawing on physiologic principles, published case reports, small case series, and protocol-based experiences. Calculations, correction targets, compounding precautions, and biochemical monitoring are described. For hypernatremia, calculated volumes of 3% NaCl can replace equal volumes of baseline fluid to increase sodium concentration while maintaining a final bag volume of 5.0 L. For hyponatremia, sterile-water dilution lowers replacement-fluid sodium but also reduces all other solute concentrations, requiring product-specific calculations and co-electrolyte monitoring. In chronic hyponatremia, correction is generally limited to ≤ 8 mmol/L per 24 h, with a more conservative 4-6 mmol/L target in patients at very high risk for osmotic demyelination. Individualized prescriptions should account for final fluid volume, effluent dose, and concurrent sodium and water inputs. Serum sodium should initially be measured every 4-6 h. Customized CVVH replacement fluid provides a practical approach to gradual sodium correction when implemented through a validated local compounding protocol with pharmacy or ICU oversight and frequent biochemical monitoring. Evidence remains largely case-based and protocol-derived, and comparative efficacy and safety are not established.

42952228.title: The Impact of 12-Hour Versus 8-Hour Shifts on Intensive Care Unit Nurses' Physical and Mental Well-Being and Job Satisfaction: A Systematic Review.
42952228.abstract: BACKGROUND: Twelve-hour shifts have been widely implemented in intensive care units (ICUs), where nurses work in high-acuity environments requiring sustained clinical attention. However, evidence regarding the impact of shift length on ICU nurses' physical health, mental well-being, job satisfaction and patient-care outcomes remains limited and inconsistent. OBJECTIVE: To investigate the impact of 12-h compared with 8-h shifts on ICU nurses' physical health, well-being and job satisfaction. DESIGN: This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251021178). METHODS: A systematic search of CINAHL, Ovid MEDLINE and Embase was conducted in February 2025 and updated in June 2026. Additional searches of Scopus and Web of Science were undertaken in June 2026. Eligible studies included ICU nurses and compared 12-h with 8-h shifts. Risk of bias and methodological quality were assessed using design-specific Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal tools and the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach. Findings were synthesised narratively due to the heterogeneity of the included studies. RESULT: Of 815 records identified, five studies met the inclusion criteria. Findings on fatigue, sleep and burnout were inconclusive across studies. Twelve-hour shifts were generally associated with greater roster satisfaction, flexibility and work-life balance, while evidence for sick leave was limited or mixed. CONCLUSION: Evidence did not consistently favour either 12- or 8-h shifts for ICU nurses, with low to very low certainty of evidence. Shift duration should therefore be considered alongside overall roster design, staffing needs and nurses' well-being when planning ICU schedules. IMPLICATIONS FOR NURSING MANAGEMENT: Nurse managers should avoid a one-size-fits-all approach to shift duration, as evidence does not clearly favour 12- or 8-h shifts. Shift-length decisions should consider roster design, staffing needs, workload, recovery time and nurses' preferences. Managers should also monitor staff well-being, satisfaction, absenteeism, retention and patient-care outcomes when reviewing shift patterns. Given the low certainty of evidence, ongoing local evaluation is essential to ensure rosters support workforce sustainability and safe, high-quality care.

42952127.title: QUIET Care: A Nursing-Led Conceptual Analysis of Alarm-Related Acoustic Burden in Adult Critical Care.
42952127.abstract: BACKGROUND: Adult intensive care units (ICUs) generate a persistent acoustic burden from alarms, care activity, equipment and communication. This burden can undermine patient rest and contribute to alarm fatigue, cognitive workload and distress among nurses. AIM: To present a nursing-led conceptual framework for addressing alarm-related acoustic burden in adult critical care. STUDY DESIGN: Literature-informed conceptual analysis. A structured purposive evidence map was audited using two PubMed searches run on 9 September 2026 (3377 unique records after PMID deduplication) and citation checking. Twenty-nine selected sources were charted against the five domains. This was not a systematic review; no original data, formal consensus or framework validation was undertaken. RESULTS: QUIET Care proposes five connected practice domains: quantify and qualify the sound environment; use patient-specific monitoring and alarms; integrate quiet into workflow; engage people and culture; and track, test and learn. It treats the domains as locally adaptable hypotheses and requires explicit safety balancing measures. CONCLUSIONS: QUIET Care is a pragmatic proposal for local co-design and evaluation, not a validated intervention or universal sound target. RELEVANCE TO CLINICAL PRACTICE: The framework may help critical care nurses and leaders organise source mapping, alarm customisation, workflow redesign, team ownership and small safety-monitored tests of change while preserving the audibility of urgent alerts.

42922243.title: Effectiveness of Quality Improvement Strategies in Preventing Healthcare-Associated Infections Among Neurosurgical Patients Admitted to Intensive Care Units: A Systematic Review.
42922243.abstract: BACKGROUND: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) remain a major and largely preventable cause of morbidity, excess mortality, prolonged hospitalization, and escalating healthcare costs in intensive care units (ICUs) worldwide. Neurosurgical patients are particularly vulnerable because of frequent exposure to invasive devices such as external ventricular drains (EVDs), central venous catheters, urinary catheters, and mechanical ventilation, combined with impaired neurological status and prolonged ICU stays. Although quality improvement (QI) strategies have been widely implemented across critical care settings, evidence specific to neurosurgical and neurocritical care populations remains fragmented. OBJECTIVES: To systematically evaluate the effectiveness of QI interventions in reducing HAI incidence among neurosurgical and neurological ICU patients and to assess their impact on secondary outcomes including ICU length of stay, device utilization, and bundle compliance. METHODS: A comprehensive search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science from January 2010 to May 2026, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Eligible studies for the primary evidence synthesis included randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies, and observational cohort studies evaluating structured QI interventions for HAI prevention in neurosurgical or neurological ICU populations, or mixed ICU settings with extractable neurocritical care data. Systematic reviews identified during screening were retained for contextual interpretation and reference screening but were excluded from the primary evidence synthesis to avoid duplication of overlapping primary data. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I, Cochrane RoB 2, and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale according to study design. RESULTS: Seventeen primary studies from 14 countries met eligibility criteria and were included in the primary narrative synthesis. Three systematic reviews were retained for contextual interpretation. Structured QI interventions consistently reduced device-associated infection rates across studies. The strongest evidence was observed for EVD-specific care bundles, with EVD-related infection rates decreasing from 14.35 to 3.21 per 1,000 catheter-days following bundle implementation, and one study reporting 20 consecutive infection-free months after interprofessional bundle adoption. Device-associated infection prevention bundles also demonstrated clinically meaningful reductions, including VAP rates decreasing from 68.2 to 47.4 per 1,000 ventilator-days and CAUTI rates from 24.9 to 13.4 per 1,000 catheter-days following structured educational interventions. CLABSI rates declined substantially following standardized central venous catheter bundle implementation, reaching zero in one study with sustained monitoring. Risk of bias was predominantly low to moderate across included primary studies. CONCLUSIONS: Structured QI interventions, particularly EVD-specific care bundles, device-associated infection prevention protocols, and staff education programs with compliance monitoring, consistently reduce HAI incidence in neurosurgical and neurological ICU settings. Although the evidence base is predominantly non-randomized, findings are directionally consistent across diverse healthcare systems and institutional contexts. Universal adoption of evidence-based infection prevention frameworks in neurocritical care is strongly supported.

42786791.title: Family Caregivers' Goals-of-Care Decisions for Critically Ill Older Adults: A Reflexive Thematic Analysis.
42786791.abstract: BACKGROUND: Family caregivers often act as surrogate decision-makers for critically ill older adults, but little is known about how goals-of-care decisions are experienced in Saudi intensive care units, where family hierarchy, Islamic values, restricted visiting and physician-led communication shape care. AIM: To explore family caregivers' experiences of goals-of-care decision-making for critically ill older adults admitted to intensive care units in Al-Ahsa, Saudi Arabia. STUDY DESIGN: A qualitative study using reflexive thematic analysis. Semi-structured face-to-face interviews were conducted in Arabic with 18 purposively sampled family caregivers across three adult intensive care units in two government hospitals. Data were analysed inductively using Braun and Clarke's six-phase approach, supported by reflexive journaling and peer debriefing. FINDINGS: Four themes were developed: Navigating the Unknown; The Weight of an Impossible Responsibility; Faith as a Compass, Community as a Gaze; and Present but Unheard. Together, they describe compounding vulnerability created by informational opacity, moral responsibility, family hierarchy, diverse Islamic ethical interpretations, and inconsistent professional support. CONCLUSIONS: Goals-of-care decision-making in the participating Saudi intensive care units was emotionally demanding, culturally embedded and relationally mediated. Nurses were trusted relational anchors, but their supportive potential was constrained by workload and unclear formal roles. RELEVANCE TO CLINICAL PRACTICE: ICU nurses can support values-aligned decision-making through plain-language communication, inclusive engagement of both the family spokesperson and primary caregiver, culturally sensitive opportunities for marginalised caregivers to contribute and coordination of spiritual and psychosocial support.

42786711.title: Nurse-Administered and Nurse-Feasible Post-Extubation Dysphagia Screening in Adult Intensive Care Units: A Scoping Review of Test Performance, Implementation and Patient Outcomes.
42786711.abstract: BACKGROUND: Post-extubation dysphagia (PED) is common after invasive mechanical ventilation. Nurses can provide timely bedside risk screening, but instrument validity, performance in nurses' hands and implementation effectiveness are distinct questions. AIM: To map direct nurse-administered evidence, transferability of nurse-feasible tools, nursing implementation context, and reported patient outcomes in adult intensive care units (ICUs). METHODS: Literature searches were conducted in six databases, with the search updated in August 2026. Evidence was stratified according to the actual screening administrator and reference-standard assessment. Criterion-level MMAT and QUADAS-2 assessments were applied without summary scores. RESULTS: The source-verified map comprised 34 reports representing 31 study families. Instrumental-reference evidence with nurse or nursing-assistant administration included two complete-verification cohorts: modified Volume-Viscosity Swallow Test versus FEES in 44 extubated patients (sensitivity 89.5%, specificity 72%) and GUSS-IVA versus FEES in 51 of 56 enrolled patients (81.0%, 88.9%). A third nurse screen had optional FEES in 38 of 123 patients (86%, 21%). Other nurse-administered studies used clinical or proxy comparators or positive-only verification. SLP-administered FEES studies informed transferability, not nurse-administered accuracy. Implementation fidelity varied, and outcome studies were non-randomised. CONCLUSIONS: Nursing involvement in structured PED screening is feasible, but direct accuracy and patient-outcome evidence remain heterogeneous and at risk of selection, verification and confounding bias. ICUs may pilot governed pathways with competency assessment, documentation, specialist escalation and outcome audit; no single screen is established as standard care. RELEVANCE TO CLINICAL PRACTICE: Bedside screening is risk stratification rather than diagnosis. Failed, discordant or high-risk screens require prompt specialist assessment and, where indicated, FEES or VFSS.

42967515.title: Multidrug-Resistant Stenotrophomonas maltophilia Infections in Critically Ill and Immunocompromised Patients: Clinical Characteristics and Therapeutic Outcomes.
42967515.journal: International journal of infectious diseases : IJID : official publication of the International Society for Infectious Diseases
42967515.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is an emerging multidrug-resistant opportunistic pathogen associated with high morbidity and mortality, particularly among critically ill and immunocompromised patients. Data on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)-resistant isolates remain limited globally and in Saudi Arabia. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study at a tertiary care center including adult patients with TMP-SMX-resistant S. maltophilia isolated from blood or respiratory specimens between May 2016 and April 2025. Demographic, microbiological, treatment, and outcome data were analyzed. RESULTS: Among 949 blood or respiratory S. maltophilia isolates screened, 79 TMP-SMX-resistant cases were identified (8.3%). Respiratory specimens accounted for 89.9% of resistant isolates, while blood culture isolates represented 10.1%. True infections accounted for 36 cases (45.6%), while the remaining 43 cases (54.4%) were classified as colonization. TMP-SMX resistance increased from 3.4% of isolates in 2017 to approximately 10% in 2024, with a marked rise after 2020. Patients were predominantly older adults (median age 66 years), with frequent ICU exposure (84.8%) and significant comorbidities. Overall 30-day and 180-day mortality rates were 34.2% and 49.4%, respectively. Minocycline demonstrated the highest susceptibility (75%), whereas levofloxacin susceptibility was limited (33.3%). Combination therapy was associated with numerically higher survival compared with monotherapy at both 30 and 180 days, although these differences were not statistically significant. CONCLUSIONS: TMP-SMX-resistant S. maltophilia isolates are increasingly identified during the study periord, particularly among critically ill patients, and are associated with substantial mortality. Combination therapy was associated with numerically higher survival, but differences were not statistically significant. Larger comparative studies are needed to determine whether combination therapy improves clinical outcomes.
